conn: Polar/exponential form links to the algebraic factorisation: a root found by inspection (e.g. \(-j\)) gives \(w_1\), and multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) generates the others, which must match the quadratic's roots.
Modulus and argument (Argand diagram) link to de Moivre's theorem: taking an nth root divides the argument by \(n\) and takes the nth root of the modulus, with \(2k\pi\) added to give all branches.
Converting between polar and rectangular form (\(\cos\pi/6=\sqrt3/2\), \(\sin\pi/6=1/2\)) is needed to give exact answers.
Solving \(w^n=z\) is a polynomial-root problem, so the complex quadratic formula and the fact that a degree-\(n\) polynomial has \(n\) roots both apply.
exq: Find all cube roots of \(j\) in both polar and rectangular form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Show that \(w=-j\) is a root of \(w^3-j=0\), factorise the cubic as \((w+j)(w^2-jw-1)\), and solve the quadratic to find the other two roots.
Find all fourth roots of \(-16\) in the form \(a+jb\), and state their moduli and principal arguments.
Find the cube roots of \(-8j\) and show that their sum is zero.
Explain why the cube roots of \(j\) are the cube roots of unity rotated by \(\pi/6\), and use this to write down the cube roots of \(j\) from \(1,\ e^{j2\pi/3},\ e^{j4\pi/3}\).

notes.t: Calculating nth roots of complex numbers (heuristic approach)
pts: The nth root w of z satisfies \(w^{n}\) = z, so solve the polynomial equation \(w^{n}\) − z = 0 to find all roots.
Factor the polynomial by spotting a known root; here w = −j is a root because (w + j) is a factor of w³ − j.
The remaining roots come from the quadratic factor, solved with the quadratic formula, giving complex solutions involving ±√3/2 and j/2.
Using the quadratic formula with complex coefficients requires computing (−j)² = −1, so the discriminant becomes −1 + 4 = 3.
defs: nth root of z
A complex number w such that wⁿ = z; there are n such roots for any nonzero complex z, found by solving wⁿ − z = 0.
eqs: Cube roots of j via factorisation of w³ − j
w = complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
Quadratic formula for the remaining roots
w = complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget that j² = −1 when simplifying the discriminant; writing (−j)² as +1 or −1 incorrectly changes the roots.
An nth root equation has n solutions in the complex plane, so finding only one root (like w = −j) is incomplete.
rq: Why is w = −j a root of w³ − j = 0 even before using the quadratic formula?
Substituting gives (−j)³ = −j³ = −(−j) = j, so w³ = j holds; hence (w + j) is a factor.
Why does the quadratic formula still work when the coefficients are complex?
The formula is algebraic and holds over the complex numbers, provided square roots are taken as complex square roots.

notes.t: Cube roots of j (geometrical interpretation)
pts: The three cube roots of j all lie on the unit circle, so each has modulus 1 and they are equally spaced by 2π/3 in argument.
Writing j = \(e^{jπ/2}\), the roots are found by adding 2π/3 to the argument each time, giving arguments -π/2, π/6 and 5π/6.
Geometrically, w1 points straight down, while w2 and w3 sit symmetrically in the upper half-plane at angles π/6 and 5π/6 from the positive real axis.
Rectangular form of each root gives the exact coordinates: w2 = √3/2 + j/2 and w3 = -√3/2 + j/2.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = x + jy, |z| = √(x²+y²); the distance of z from the origin in the Argand diagram.
Argument of a complex number
The angle arg(z) that the vector from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise.
eqs: Cube roots of j via polar form
\(w_{k}\) = k-th cube root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; k = integer index 0,1,2
tips: Adding 2π/3 to an argument must be done before reducing; arguments such as 5π/6 are valid principal values, but arg(w) should be quoted in (-π, π] for consistency.
Do not confuse the cube roots of j with the cube roots of 1; the roots of j are rotated by π/6 from those of unity.
rq: Why do all three cube roots of j have modulus 1, and what does that imply geometrically?
Because |j|=1 and taking a cube root gives |w|³ = |j| = 1, so |w| = 1; all roots lie on the unit circle.
Why is the angle between successive cube roots 2π/3 rather than π/3?
Multiplying by \(e^{j2π/3}\) adds 2π/3 to the argument; the three roots must be spaced by 2π/3 to form an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle.

units.name: 3.7 Preview of Lecture 4
units.ov: The notes are only a short preview of Lecture 4. It covers De Moivre's theorem (the second part of section 3.3.1), then how to express powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles (section 3.3.2). The two connect because De Moivre's theorem, \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\), links powers of complex numbers to multiple angles. That link gives identities for \(\cos^n\theta\), \(\sin^n\theta\), \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\). The notes give no worked detail, so the points below rely on standard results for these topics and should be checked against the full lecture notes.
must: De Moivre's theorem: \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\), and the equivalent form \((e^{i\theta})^n = e^{in\theta}\)
Polar form: \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = re^{i\theta}\), so \(z^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)\)

Multiple-angle formulae: expand \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\) with the binomial theorem and equate real and imaginary parts to get \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\) as polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\)
Define \(z = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\). Then \(z^n + z^{-n} = 2\cos n\theta\) and \(z^n - z^{-n} = 2i\sin n\theta\)

Powers of trig functions: write \((2\cos\theta)^n = (z + z^{-1})^n\) or \((2i\sin\theta)^n = (z - z^{-1})^n\), expand, and pair terms \(z^k\) with \(z^{-k}\) to get sums of \(\cos k\theta\) or \(\sin k\theta\)
Know the binomial coefficients (Pascal's triangle) and apply them accurately, including the signs and powers of \(i\)
Use \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) to convert between forms, for example writing \(\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\)
Roots of complex numbers: \(z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n} + i\sin\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n}\right]\) for \(k = 0,\dots,n-1\)
The reduction identities are useful for integrating powers of trig functions, e.g. \(\cos^2\theta = \tfrac12(1 + \cos 2\theta)\)
conn: De Moivre's theorem and the binomial expansion: expanding \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\) and equating real and imaginary parts gives the multiple-angle formulae
\(z^n \pm z^{-n}\) and the exponential form: these give the expressions for \(\cos^n\theta\) and \(\sin^n\theta\) as sums of multiple angles, which is the reverse of the multiple-angle expansion
Powers-to-multiple-angles identities and integration: reducing \(\cos^n\theta\) to a sum of \(\cos k\theta\) makes \(\int\cos^n\theta\,d\theta\) straightforward
De Moivre's theorem and roots of unity: solving \(z^n = w\) uses the polar form, and the roots lie at equal angles on a circle in the Argand diagram
exq: Use De Moivre's theorem to show that \(\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\) and find a similar expression for \(\sin 3\theta\).
Express \(\cos^4\theta\) in terms of \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\cos 4\theta\), then use the result to evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta\,d\theta\).
Express \(\sin^5\theta\) as a combination of \(\sin\theta\), \(\sin 3\theta\) and \(\sin 5\theta\).
Evaluate \((1 + i\sqrt3)^8\) in the form \(a + ib\) using polar form and De Moivre's theorem.
Find all cube roots of \(-8\) and plot them on an Argand diagram. Then express \(\cos 5\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) only.

notes.t: Preview of Lecture 4: De Moivre's theorem and powers of trigonometric functions
pts: Lecture 4 continues with De Moivre's theorem, the second part of section 3.3.1.
Lecture 4 then covers expressing powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles, section 3.3.2.

units.name: 4.1 Recap of complex numbers and circular/hyperbolic links
units.ov: This material recaps complex numbers in Cartesian, polar and exponential form (modulus, argument, Euler's formula), then extends them to powers (De Moivre), complex logarithms and the links between circular and hyperbolic functions. All of it rests on Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), which turns multiplication, powers and logs into operations on modulus and argument, and which gives the circular-hyperbolic relationships.
must: Euler's formula: \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), so \(z=re^{j\theta}=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\)
Modulus \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); argument \(\theta=\arg(x+jy)\) must be chosen by quadrant (add \(\pi\) if \(x<0,y\ge0\); subtract \(\pi\) if \(x<0,y<0\); \(\pm\pi/2\) if \(x=0\))
Polar multiplication: \(z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)]\): multiply moduli, add arguments
Polar division: \(z_1/z_2=(r_1/r_2)[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)]\): divide moduli, subtract arguments (never subtract moduli)
De Moivre: \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)\) for integer \(n\); \(r\) must be positive and \(\theta\) in radians
Complex log: \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j(\theta\pm2n\pi)\); the principal value takes \(\theta\) in the principal range (\(n=0\))
Circular of imaginary argument: \(\cos jx=\cosh x\), \(\sin jx=j\sinh x\)
Hyperbolic of imaginary argument: \(\cosh jx=\cos x\), \(\sinh jx=j\sin x\); the factor \(j\) appears only on the sine/sinh relations
Always sketch the Argand diagram to check the quadrant and sanity-check the argument
conn: Euler's formula underlies polar multiplication/division, De Moivre and the complex log: all reduce to manipulating \(r\) and \(\theta\) in \(re^{j\theta}\)
Writing \(\cos\theta=(e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta})/2\) and comparing with \(\cosh x=(e^x+e^{-x})/2\) gives the circular-hyperbolic relations (\(\cos jx=\cosh x\), etc.)

The quadrant-dependent argument feeds directly into De Moivre (roots/powers) and \(\ln z\), where an error in \(\theta\) gives a wrong answer; the \(2n\pi\) ambiguity explains multiple logarithm values and the \(n\) distinct \(n\)th roots
exq: Express \(z_1=-1-j\sqrt3\) and \(z_2=2+2j\) in polar form (state the quadrant for each argument), then find \(z_1z_2\) and \(z_1/z_2\) in polar and Cartesian form.
Use De Moivre's theorem to evaluate \((1+j)^{8}\) and to find all cube roots of \(-8\), showing them on an Argand diagram.
Find the principal value and the general value of \(\ln(-3+3j)\), and of \(\ln(-j)\).
Show that \(\cos(jx)=\cosh x\) and \(\sin(jx)=j\sinh x\) from the exponential definitions, and hence write \(\cos(2+3j)\) in the form \(a+jb\) using \(\cos(A+B)\) and these results.
Using Euler's formula, derive \(\cos3\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) by expanding \((\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^3\) and equating real parts.

notes.t: Recap: modulus, argument, polar form, multiplication/division, Euler's formula
pts: The modulus of a complex number is the distance from the origin in the Argand diagram.
The argument is the angle measured from the positive real axis, and its value depends on the quadrant of x + jy.
A complex number can be written in polar form using its modulus r and argument θ.
In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments; dividing divides moduli and subtracts arguments.
Euler's formula links the exponential with cosine and sine, giving the compact exponential form of a complex number.
defs: Modulus of z
For z = x + jy, the modulus |z| = r is the distance from the origin, r = √(x² + y²).
Argument of z
The angle θ = arg(x + jy) measured from the positive real axis, with the value chosen according to the quadrant of z.
eqs: z = complex number; x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless)
Argument of a complex number (piecewise by quadrant)

\theta = \arg(x + jy) = \begin{cases} \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) & x > 0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + \pi & x < 0,\ y \ge 0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) - \pi & x < 0,\ y < 0 \\ +\frac{\pi}{2} & x = 0,\ y > 0 \\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & x = 0,\ y < 0 \\ \text{undefined} & x = 0,\ y = 0 \end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x = real part; y = imaginary part
Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
Product of two complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
Quotient of two complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
tips: For arg(x + jy), always check the quadrant; arctan(y/x) alone gives the wrong angle when x < 0.
When dividing in polar form, subtract the arguments and divide the moduli; do not subtract the moduli.
rq: Why must the argument be found using the quadrant rules rather than arctan(y/x) alone?
arctan(y/x) returns angles only in (−π/2, π/2), so the quadrant of (x, y) must be checked and π added or subtracted to get the correct θ.
Why does dividing in polar form subtract the arguments?
Because dividing by z₂ is multiplying by 1/z₂, whose argument is −θ₂, so θ₁ + (−θ₂) = θ₁ − θ₂.
What does Euler's formula imply about |\(e^{jθ}\)| for real θ?
Since cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, |\(e^{jθ}\)| = 1, so it lies on the unit circle.

notes.t: Relationships between circular and hyperbolic functions; logarithm of a complex number; De
pts: Circular functions of an imaginary argument equal hyperbolic functions of the real argument, and vice versa, with a factor j on the sine.
The natural log of a complex number has infinitely many values: the modulus gives the real part and the argument is defined only up to multiples of 2π.
For a complex number written in polar form, raising it to the power n multiplies the modulus by n-th power and the argument by n.
defs: Principal logarithm of a complex number
The value of ln z obtained by taking the argument θ in the principal range, giving ln z = ln|z| + j θ, with other branches differing by j2nπ.
De Moivre's theorem
For z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), the n-th power satisfies zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + j sin nθ) for integer n.
eqs: Hyperbolic cosine and sine in terms of circular functions (imaginary argument)
x = real number (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
Circular functions in terms of hyperbolic functions
x = real number (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer branch index (dimensionless)
De Moivre's theorem: power of a complex number
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse cos jx = cosh x with cosh jx = cos x; the j factor appears on the sine relation, e.g. sin jx = j sinh x.
The argument θ in ln z and De Moivre's theorem must be in radians when applying the formulas, and the modulus r must be positive before raising to the power n.
rq: Why does the argument in the logarithm of a complex number need a ±2nπ term?
The argument of a complex number is only defined up to multiples of 2π, since adding 2π returns the same point; each choice of n gives a different but valid value of ln z.
Why must n be an integer in De Moivre's theorem for it to give the correct result?
For integer n, the powers of z are unambiguous; for non-integer n, the expression depends on the chosen argument and gives multiple values, so the simple formula is only guaranteed for integers.

units.name: 4.2 De Moivre for rational powers and heuristic root finding
units.ov: This material defines rational powers of complex numbers as \(z^{m/n}=\sqrt[n]{z^m}\), which gives n distinct values rather than one. It introduces a heuristic way to find n-th roots by solving \(w^n=z\) through factorisation, using the example of the cube roots of j. This sets up the polar-form and De Moivre method, and later work on powers of trig functions and multiple angles.
must: Definition: \(z^{m/n}=\sqrt[n]{z^m}\), with m an integer and n a positive integer
A non-zero z has exactly n distinct n-th roots, so always list all n values
An n-th root w of z satisfies \(w^n=z\), i.e. \(w^n-z=0\)
Heuristic method: spot one root, factor out \((w-\text{root})\), then solve the remaining quadratic with the quadratic formula
Cube roots of j: \(w^3-j=(w+j)(w^2-jw-1)=0\), giving \(w=-j\) and \(w=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\)
Apply \(j^2=-1\) carefully in the discriminant: \((-j)^2-4(-1)=-1+4=3\)
Do not use only the principal value of \(z^{1/n}\), because it misses the other roots
Evaluate \(z^{m/n}\) by forming \(z^m\) first (polar form and De Moivre make this efficient) and then taking all n-th roots
Check answers by cubing (or raising to the n-th power) each root to confirm it returns z
conn: Polar form and De Moivre: the heuristic factorisation only works for easy cases, and the general method gives roots as \(r^{1/n}\,\text{cis}\big(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\big)\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\)
Roots on the Argand diagram: the n roots are equally spaced on a circle, so the factorised answers can be checked geometrically (the cube roots of j are 120° apart)
Polynomial factorisation and the quadratic formula: finding roots of \(w^n-z\) combines the factor theorem, polynomial division and complex discriminants
Rational powers lead to multiple-angle and trig-power identities, which come from expanding \((\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^n\)
exq: Find all cube roots of j by factorising \(w^3-j\), and show the three roots on an Argand diagram.
Evaluate \(z^{2/3}\) for \(z=-8\), stating all distinct values in both polar and Cartesian form.
Solve \(w^3=-j\) by spotting one root and factorising. Verify each root by cubing it.
Explain why \(z^{m/n}\) is not the same as taking the principal value of \((z^m)^{1/n}\). Give an example with n = 4 and list all four values of \(z^{1/4}\) for \(z=16\).
Use the quadratic formula to solve \(w^2-jw-1=0\), simplifying the discriminant with \(j^2=-1\). Then give the modulus and argument of each root.

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem (2): powers with rational exponents
pts: For a rational exponent m/n, the power \(z^{m/n}\) is defined as the n-th root of \(z^{m.}\)
The lecture poses the question of how to evaluate \(z^{m/n}\) once it is written as an n-th root of \(z^{m}\), which is the starting point for using polar form and De Moivre's theorem.
The page lists the next topic, powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles, which follows from De Moivre's theorem.
eqs: Rational power of a complex number written as an n-th root
z = complex number (dimensionless); m = integer exponent (dimensionless); n = positive integer root index (dimensionless)
tips: Remember that \(z^{m/n}\) generally has n distinct values, not a single value, so state all roots when asked to evaluate it.
Do not treat \sqrt[n]{\(z^{m}\)} as \(z^m\) to the power \(1/n\) without checking the branch: the principal root may not give all the values.
rq: Why can \(z^{m/n}\) be written as the n-th root of \(z^{m}\), and why does this make the answer multi-valued?
Because the rational exponent m/n is defined through the n-th root of \(z^{m}\); an n-th root of a non-zero complex number has n distinct values, so \(z^{m/n}\) has n values.

notes.t: Finding complex roots of z (heuristic approach via factorisation)
pts: The n-th root of z is found by solving \(w^{n}\) = z, i.e. \(w^{n}\) − z = 0, and factorising the polynomial.
Once a root is spotted, factor out (w − root) to reduce the degree, then solve the remaining quadratic with the quadratic formula.
Complex roots of a quadratic use the discriminant; j² = −1 must be applied when simplifying (−j)² − 4(−1).
The cube root of j gives three roots in total, so all solutions must be listed, not just the principal one.
defs: n-th root of a complex number z
A complex number w satisfying \(w^{n}\) = z; for z ≠ 0 there are n distinct such w.
eqs: Roots of the cube root of j: factorisation of w³ − j
w = unknown complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
Quadratic formula for the remaining roots
w = complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Remember that an n-th root of a non-zero complex number has n solutions, so check you have listed all three cube roots.
Do not forget j² = −1 when evaluating the discriminant; (−j)² is −1, not +1.
rq: Why is w = −j a root of w³ = j even though we started by asking for a cube root?
Substituting gives (−j)³ = −j³ = −(−j) = j, so it satisfies w³ = j; it is found by setting the factor (w + j) = 0.
Why does the quadratic w² − jw − 1 = 0 contain the imaginary unit in its coefficient, and how does this change the discriminant?
Because j is a complex coefficient, the discriminant (−j)² − 4(−1) = −1 + 4 = 3 is real, so the roots are ±√3/2 + j/2.
What if you forgot the factor (w + j) and only used the quadratic?
You would miss the root w = −j, so you would find only two of the three cube roots of j.

units.name: 4.3 Cube roots of j: geometry and De Moivre method
units.ov: This material finds the three cube roots of \(j\) by writing \(j=e^{j\pi/2}\) in polar form and applying De Moivre's theorem. The roots all lie on the unit circle, spaced \(2\pi/3\) apart on the Argand diagram, at arguments \(-\pi/2,\ \pi/6,\ 5\pi/6\). Geometry (equal spacing) and algebra (equating modulus and argument) give the same result.
must: The cube roots of \(j\) are \(w_k=e^{j(\pi/2+2k\pi)/3}\), \(k=0,1,2\), with arguments \(\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6,\ 3\pi/2\equiv-\pi/2\)
Explicit values: \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac{j}{2}\), \(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac{j}{2}\), \(-j\)
De Moivre's theorem: \((r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta))^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)\) for integer \(n\)
Method: set \(w=|w|(\cos\phi+j\sin\phi)\), form \(w^3\), and equate with \(j=\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}+j\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Modulus condition \(|w|^3=1\) with \(|w|\ge0\) gives \(|w|=1\) (all roots on the unit circle)
Argument condition \(3\phi=\pi/2+2\pi k\), so \(\phi=\pi/6+2\pi k/3\); you must include the \(2\pi k\) before dividing by 3
Only three distinct roots exist; \(k=3\) repeats \(k=0\) since angles are taken modulo \(2\pi\)
Geometry: the \(n\) roots of a number are equally spaced by \(2\pi/n\) (here \(120^\circ\)), forming an equilateral triangle on the unit circle

Definitions: \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); \(\arg z\) is measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis; state the argument range (principal value \(-\pi<\arg\le\pi\)), so \(3\pi/2\) is reported as \(-\pi/2\)
Check: cubing each root must return \(j\)
conn: Polar/exponential form \(e^{j\theta}\) links to De Moivre: powers multiply the angle, roots divide it and add \(2\pi k/n\)
Equating real and imaginary parts (\(\cos3\phi=0,\ \sin3\phi=1\)) links trigonometry to solving complex equations such as \(w^3=j\) or \(z^n=a+jb\)
Roots on the Argand diagram link algebra to geometry: equal angular spacing lets you find the remaining roots by rotating by \(120^\circ\)
Conversion between polar and Cartesian form (modulus and argument) is needed to give final answers as \(x+jy\)
exq: Find all cube roots of \(j\) using De Moivre's theorem, giving the answers in both polar and Cartesian form, and plot them on an Argand diagram.
Solve \(z^3=-8j\), giving the roots in the form \(x+jy\) and stating their moduli and principal arguments.
Show that the three cube roots of \(j\) sum to zero and that their product equals \(j\).
Explain why \(\phi=\pi/6\) alone is not the complete solution of \(w^3=j\), and find the other two roots geometrically by rotating through \(2\pi/3\).
Using De Moivre's theorem, find the fourth roots of \(j\) and state the angular separation between them.

notes.t: Geometrical interpretation of the cube roots of j
pts: The cube roots of j are three complex numbers w1, w2, w3, each lying on the unit circle, so each has modulus 1.
Writing j in polar form as \(e^{jπ/2}\), the three roots are obtained by dividing the argument by 3 and adding multiples of 2π/3.
Successive cube roots are separated by equal angles of 2π/3 (120°) around the circle.
The arguments of the roots are −π/2, π/6 and 5π/6, which are the points plotted on the Argand diagram.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = x + jy, |z| = √(x² + y²), the distance of z from the origin in the Argand plane.
Argument of a complex number
The angle arg(z) that the vector representing z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise.
eqs: Polar (exponential) form of the cube roots of j
\(w_{k}\) = k-th cube root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; k = integer index 0,1,2
tips: Use the principal argument π/2 for j, but remember that adding 2kπ to the argument before dividing by 3 gives all three distinct roots; forgetting the 2kπ/3 terms gives only one root.
Arguments must be reported in the correct range; for w3 the argument is 5π/6, not −7π/6 unless the principal-value convention is specified.
rq: Why do all three cube roots of j lie on the same circle, and why are they spaced 120° apart?
Taking cube roots divides the modulus by 3 and |j| = 1 gives modulus 1; the argument is divided by 3 and the three roots come from adding 2π/3 steps, which equals 120° spacing.
What would change if you wrote j = \(e^{j5π/2}\) instead of \(e^{jπ/2}\) when finding the cube roots?
The same three roots result, because 5π/2 differs from π/2 by 2π; the extra full turn is absorbed by the 2kπ/3 terms, showing the answer is independent of the chosen argument.

notes.t: Using De Moivre's theorem to find cube roots of j
pts: Write w in polar form with modulus |w| and argument φ, then raise to the power 3 using De Moivre's theorem.
Equate modulus and argument of w³ with those of j = cos(π/2) + j sin(π/2); the modulus equation gives |w| = 1 since cos² + sin² = 1.
Equating the trigonometric parts gives cos 3φ = 0 and sin 3φ = 1, so 3φ = π/2 + 2πk.
Dividing by 3 gives all distinct roots; only three distinct values arise, at angles π/6, 5π/6 and 3π/2 (i.e. −π/2).
Taking angles modulo 2π, the cube roots of j lie on the unit circle at equal 120° spacing.
defs: De Moivre's theorem
For any real modulus r and angle θ with integer n, (r(cos θ + j sin θ))ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + j sin nθ).
Polar form
A complex number written as w = |w|(cos φ + j sin φ), where |w| is the modulus and φ the argument.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for powers of a complex number
w = complex number (dimensionless); |w| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
Modulus condition for cube root of j
|w| = modulus of w (dimensionless); φ = argument of w (rad)
Argument of the cube roots of j
φ = argument of w (rad); k = integer index (dimensionless)
tips: Equating moduli gives |w|³ = 1, and since |w| ≥ 0 this gives |w| = 1; do not forget to take the positive real root.
Remember to divide the general angle by n (here 3) and check that only distinct roots are listed, since adding 2π to an argument gives the same point.
rq: Why does the modulus equation force |w| = 1 rather than some other value?
Because |w|⁶ multiplies cos²3φ + sin²3φ = 1, so |w|⁶ = 1 and |w| = 1 (taking the positive real root).
Why do we get only three distinct roots even though k can be any natural number?
Angles differing by 2π give the same point, and φ increases by 2π/3 per step, so k = 0, 1, 2 repeat cyclically.

units.name: 4.4 General nth roots via polar and exponential form
units.ov: This material shows how to find all n distinct nth roots of a complex number by writing it in polar or exponential form \( z=re^{j\theta} \), taking \( r^{1/n} \) for the modulus and dividing \( \theta+2\pi k \) by n for the arguments. The roots lie equally spaced on a circle and form a regular n-gon. They can be generated by repeated rotation through \( 2\pi/n \). The worked example is \( w^3=j \).
must: Formula for all n roots: \( z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}e^{j(\theta+2\pi k)/n},\ k=0,\dots,n-1 \)
Derive it from \( w^n=z \): equate moduli \( R^n=r \) and arguments \( n\phi=\theta+2\pi k \)
Always include the \( 2\pi k \) term; omitting it gives one root instead of n
Use only k = 0 to n−1; larger k repeats earlier roots (k = n repeats k = 0)
All roots share modulus \( r^{1/n} \) and are spaced by \( 2\pi/n \) in argument, forming a regular n-gon on a circle centred at the origin
Successive roots follow \( w_{k+1}=w_k e^{j2\pi/n} \), so find one root and rotate
Convert z to polar or exponential form first, with θ in radians and on the principal branch \( (-\pi,\pi] \)
Example: for \( w^3=j \) (r = 1, \( \theta=\pi/2 \)), \( \phi=\pi/6+2\pi k/3 \) gives \( \pi/6,\ 5\pi/6,\ -\pi/2 \)
Convert arguments consistently, e.g. \( 3\pi/2\to-\pi/2 \), before reading off Re and Im
conn: Roots link to De Moivre's theorem: \( w^n=R^n(\cos n\phi+j\sin n\phi) \) is the forward step, and root-finding is its inverse
Polar and Cartesian conversion feeds into root finding: compute r and θ correctly (check the quadrant), then convert the roots back to \( a+jb \)
Root geometry connects to solving polynomial equations \( w^n=z \): the roots are the vertices of a regular polygon and sum to zero
Rotation by \( e^{j2\pi/n} \) links roots to phasors and rotating vectors in engineering
exq: Find all cube roots of \( j \). Give them in exponential and Cartesian form and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Solve \( w^4 = -16 \). Give the roots in the form \( a+jb \) and state the polygon they form.
Find the fifth roots of \( 1+j\sqrt{3} \) in polar form, giving the modulus and arguments in radians.
Given that one cube root of z is \( 2e^{j\pi/9} \), find the other two roots and z itself.
Explain why only k = 0,…,n−1 are needed. Show that the n roots of unity sum to zero for n = 3.

notes.t: Roots of unity via the polar form: finding the nth roots of a complex number of modulus 1
pts: Every root w of the equation has modulus 1, so all roots lie on the unit circle.
The argument of each root is φ = (1/3)(π/2) + 2πk/3, and the roots are equally spaced around the circle by angle 2π/3 (here n = 3 roots are shown).
Taking k = 0, 1, 2 gives the three distinct roots at φ = π/6, 5π/6 and 3π/2 (= −π/2).
Only k = 0, …, |n|−1 are needed: larger k repeats the same points on the circle.
defs: Modulus of a complex number w
The distance of w from the origin in the Argand plane, |w| = √(Re(w)² + Im(w)²); for the roots here |w| = 1.
eqs: φ_k = argument of the k-th root (rad); k = integer index (dimensionless); n = integer exponent setting the number of roots (dimensionless)
tips: Keep arguments within a single period: convert φ = 3π/2 to −π/2 consistently when reading off Re w and Im w.
Use only k = 0 to |n|−1; listing extra values of k gives duplicate roots, not new ones.
rq: Why does the list of roots stop at k = |n| − 1 rather than continuing forever?
Adding |n| to k adds 2π|n|/|n|... more precisely, larger k changes φ by multiples of 2π, returning to angles already listed, so only |n| distinct roots exist.
Why are the three roots spaced exactly 2π/3 apart?
Consecutive k values change φ by 2π/3, so the roots are equally spaced around the unit circle, forming an equilateral triangle.

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem for roots: \(z^{1/n}\)
pts: To find the n-th root w of z, write w = \(z^{1/n}\) and equate moduli and arguments of \(w^{n}\) and z.
Write w in polar form with |w| = R and arg w = φ; then \(w^{n}\) = \(R^{n}\)(cos nφ + j sin nφ).
Matching real and imaginary parts of \(w^{n}\) and z gives \(R^{n}\) = r and nφ = θ (up to multiples of 2π).
The example \(w^{3}\) = j is solved by rewriting it as w = \(j^{1/3}\), i.e. taking the cube root of j.
defs: Argument of a complex number
The angle θ that z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) makes with the positive real axis, measured in radians.
Modulus of a complex number
The distance r = |z| of z from the origin in the Argand diagram.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for n-th roots (modulus and argument of w)
R = |w| (dimensionless); φ = arg w (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
r = |z| (dimensionless); θ = arg z (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Remember that nφ = θ holds only up to multiples of 2π, so all n roots must be listed by adding 2kπ to θ before dividing by n.
Use radians for arguments in the exponent formulas; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong roots.
rq: Why do we equate both the modulus and the argument when solving \(w^{n}\) = z, rather than just one of them?
A complex number is fixed by both its modulus and argument; equating only one would not determine w uniquely, so \(R^{n}\) = r and nφ = θ must both hold.
Why does the argument of the root come out as θ/n plus multiples of 2π/n rather than just θ/n?
Angles differing by 2π represent the same complex number, so nφ = θ + 2kπ, giving n distinct roots for k = 0,…,n−1.

notes.t: Roots of complex numbers via De Moivre-type polar form (\(z^{1/n}\))
pts: Taking the n-th root of a complex number: write z = r(cos θ + j sin θ); the modulus of the root is the n-th root of r, so the nth root is R = \(r^{1/n}\).
Equating real and imaginary parts of \(w^{n}\) = z and squaring-and-adding gives cos θ = cos nφ and sin θ = sin nφ, so nφ = θ + 2πk.
Because of 2π periodicity there are infinitely many angle solutions, but only n distinct roots arise, indexed by k = 0, 1, …, n−1.
All n roots lie on a circle of radius |w| = |z|^{1/n} and are equally spaced in angle by 2π/n.
The square-and-add step uses sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to separate the modulus equation from the angle equations.
defs: n-th root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that wⁿ = z; for z ≠ 0 there are exactly n distinct such w.
Principal argument / 2π periodicity
Angles differing by an integer multiple of 2π represent the same complex number, which produces the infinite family of angle solutions θ + 2πk.
eqs: Polar form of the n-th roots of z
z = complex number; r = |z| (dimensionless); θ = arg z (rad); n = positive integer root order; k = integer index (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
R = modulus of the root (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); n = root order
φ = argument of the root (rad); θ = argument of z (rad); n = root order; k = integer
tips: Use the principal argument θ (usually in (−π, π]) consistently; forgetting the 2πk terms gives only one root instead of n.
Angles must be in radians when substituted into \(e^{jθ}\); mixing degrees and radians is a common unit error.
rq: Why does the root equation give infinitely many angle solutions, yet only n distinct roots?
Adding 2πk to the angle returns the same point for every integer k, so angles repeat with period 2π; the roots φ = θ/n + 2πk/n repeat once k reaches n, leaving n distinct values k = 0,…,n−1.
What happens to the spacing of the roots if n increases?
The roots remain on a circle of radius \(r^{1/n}\) but the angular separation 2π/n shrinks, so there are more, more closely spaced roots.
Why is the modulus of the root \(r^{1/n}\) and not r/n?
Taking the modulus is multiplicative: |wⁿ| = |w|ⁿ = r, so |w| = \(r^{1/n}\).

notes.t: Roots of complex numbers (de Moivre's theorem for \(z^{1/n}\))
pts: The nth roots of z are found from the modulus-argument form with k = 0, 1, …, n−1, giving exactly n distinct roots.
Values of k beyond n−1 repeat earlier roots: k = n gives the same root as k = 0, k = n+1 as k = 1, and so on.
The n roots lie equally spaced on a circle of radius \(r^{1/n}\) centred at the origin of the Argand diagram.
Arguments of successive roots increase in arithmetic progression, so joining the roots gives a regular polygon inscribed in the circle.
defs: nth root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that wⁿ = z; for z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) there are exactly n such roots.
eqs: nth roots of a complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ)
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = positive integer; k = integer 0, 1, …, n−1; j = imaginary unit
tips: Only use k = 0 to n−1; larger k values repeat roots, so listing more gives duplicates.
Make sure θ is the correct argument (in radians, within the chosen branch) before dividing by n, otherwise the root arguments are wrong.
rq: Why does taking k = n give the same root as k = 0?
Adding 2πn to the argument (2πk/n with k = n adds 2π) rotates the point back to the same position, since cos and sin are periodic with period 2π.
Why must the roots of \(z^{1/n}\) all have the same modulus?
Each root has modulus \(r^{1/n}\), because taking the nth root of the modulus r of z gives the modulus of every root.

notes.t: Roots of complex numbers: exponential form and geometry
pts: The n-th roots of z are equally spaced in argument, so their tips form a regular n-gon inscribed in a circle of radius \( \sqrt[n]{|z|} \).
Successive roots are obtained by multiplying the previous root by \( e^{j2\pi/n} \), rotating by angle \( 2\pi/n \).
Equation (3.17) can equivalently be written in exponential form, listing all n roots from a single starting root w1.
defs: n-th root set of z
The set of n distinct complex numbers w1,…,wn whose n-th power equals z; written as \( z^{1/n} \).
eqs: Generating all n-th roots of z by successive rotation
\(w_{k}\) = k-th root of z (dimensionless complex number); n = number of roots (integer); j = imaginary unit
tips: Remember all n roots share the modulus \( \sqrt[n]{|z|} \); only the argument changes between them.
The angle step is \( 2\pi/n \) in radians, not degrees, when using \( e^{j2\pi/n} \).
rq: Why do the roots lie on a circle and form a regular polygon rather than a random pattern?
All roots have the same modulus \( \sqrt[n]{|z|} \), so they lie on one circle; their arguments differ by equal steps \( 2\pi/n \), so the points are equally spaced around it.
What happens to the n roots if you multiply the starting root by \( e^{j2\pi/n} \) one more time after wn?
You return to w1, because \( e^{j2\pi}=1 \); the sequence cycles and no new roots appear.

notes.t: Roots of complex numbers: the n-th roots z^(1/n)
pts: The n-th root of a complex number z has exactly n distinct values, obtained by rotating each successive root by the angle 2π/n.
Write z in exponential form z = r \(e^{jθ}\); the roots share modulus \(r^{1/n}\) and have arguments (θ + 2πk)/n.
Every root is found from the previous one by multiplying by the same factor \(e^{j2π/n}\), so the roots lie equally spaced on a circle.
For z = 1 (r = 1, θ = 0) the roots of \(z^{1/3}\) are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\).
The index k runs from 0 to n−1, giving exactly n roots; k = n would repeat the first root.
defs: n-th root of a complex number
A complex number w such that \(w^{n}\) = z; a nonzero z has exactly n distinct n-th roots.
Exponential (polar) form
Expression of a complex number as z = r \(e^{jθ}\), with modulus r and argument θ.
eqs: Recurrence generating the n roots from the first root
\(w_{k}\) = k-th root (dimensionless); n = root order (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
All n-th roots of z in exponential form
r = modulus of z (same unit as z); θ = argument of z (rad); n = root order; k = root index (integer)
tips: Write z in exponential form (r, θ) before taking roots; using the Cartesian form directly makes the angles hard to find.
Use θ + 2πk, not just θ, inside the root; forgetting the 2πk term gives only one root instead of n.
rq: Why does the n-th root of a complex number have exactly n values, not one?
Because the argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π, and dividing by n gives n distinct angles (k = 0,…,n−1) before the roots start repeating.
What would happen if you used k = 3 for n = 3 when finding cube roots of 1?
\(e^{j2π}\) = 1 gives \(w_{1}\) again, so it produces no new root; the roots cycle after n steps.

units.name: 4.5 Roots of unity and cube roots of unity
units.ov: These notes cover the three cube roots of unity, the solutions of \(w^3=1\), which sit on the unit circle at 0, \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\). They are written in exponential, polar and Cartesian forms, and each is obtained from the previous one by multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\), a 120° anticlockwise rotation on the Argand diagram. The geometric picture (equal spacing, rotation) links directly to the algebraic forms and to the conjugate pair \(-\tfrac12 \pm j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
must: Definition: \(w^3=1\) has exactly three solutions \(1,\ e^{j2\pi/3},\ e^{j4\pi/3}\)
All three roots lie on the unit circle (modulus 1) at angles \(0,\ 2\pi/3,\ 4\pi/3\), equally spaced by 120°
Cartesian forms: \(w_2=-\tfrac12+j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(w_3=-\tfrac12-j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
Successive roots: \(w_{n+1}=w_n e^{j2\pi/3}\); multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) rotates anticlockwise by 120°
\(w_2\) and \(w_3\) are complex conjugates, so \(w_3=\overline{w_2}=e^{-j2\pi/3}\) (equivalent to \(e^{j4\pi/3}\))
Going round three times returns to the start: \(w_3 e^{j2\pi/3}=1\), i.e. \((e^{j2\pi/3})^3=e^{j2\pi}=1\)
Polar form: \(w_k=\cos\theta_k+j\sin\theta_k\) with \(\theta_k=0,\,2\pi/3,\,4\pi/3\); this is how to derive the Cartesian forms
Use radians in exponential form (\(2\pi/3\), not 120); watch the sign of the imaginary part of \(w_3\)
Using \(e^{-j2\pi/3}\) as the multiplier rotates clockwise and gives the same set of roots in the opposite order
conn: Exponential \(\leftrightarrow\) polar \(\leftrightarrow\) Cartesian conversion: Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) gives \(\cos(2\pi/3)=-\tfrac12\) and \(\sin(2\pi/3)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
Geometry and algebra: rotation by multiplication on the Argand diagram explains both the successive-root formula and why the cube of each root is 1
Conjugate pairs: \(w_2,w_3\) are conjugates, so their sum is real (\(-1\)) and their product is 1, linking to the factorisation \(w^3-1=(w-1)(w^2+w+1)\)
General n-th roots (de Moivre): the same method of equal spacing \(2\pi/n\) extends to solving \(z^n=a\) for any complex \(a\)
exq: Solve \(w^3=1\) and give all roots in exponential, polar and Cartesian form, then sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Show that \(1+w_2+w_3=0\) using the Cartesian forms, and verify that \(w_2^2=w_3\).
Starting from \(w_1=1\), use \(w_{n+1}=w_n e^{j2\pi/3}\) to generate the roots, and state the rotation angle in degrees and radians at each step.
Factorise \(z^3-1\) into a linear and a quadratic factor and solve the quadratic to recover the two non-real cube roots of unity.
Find the cube roots of 8 by multiplying \(2\) by the cube roots of unity, and give each in Cartesian form.

notes.t: Cube roots of unity (Argand diagram)
pts: The three cube roots of unity are equally spaced on the unit circle, each 2π/3 apart.
Successive roots are obtained by multiplying the previous one by \(e^{j2π/3}\).
Multiplying by \(e^{j2π/3}\) rotates a point anticlockwise by 120° on the Argand diagram.
Going round the circle three times returns to the start, so w3 · \(e^{j2π/3}\) = 1.
defs: Cube root of unity
A complex number w satisfying w³ = 1; the three solutions are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\).
eqs: \(w_{n}\) = nth root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Exponential form of the second root
tips: Watch the sign: \(e^{j2π/3}\) rotates anticlockwise; using \(e^{-j2π/3}\) gives the other pair of roots.
Angles must be in radians in the exponential form (2π/3, not 120) unless working purely in degrees.
rq: Why do the three cube roots of unity lie at 120° intervals on the unit circle?
Because they satisfy w³ = 1, so their modulus is 1 and their arguments are 0, 2π/3 and 4π/3; these are spaced 2π/3 apart.
What happens if you multiply w3 = \(e^{j4π/3}\) by \(e^{j2π/3}\) again?
You get \(e^{j2π}\) = 1 = w1, so the sequence cycles back to the start.

notes.t: Cube roots of unity: exponential, polar and Cartesian forms
pts: The three cube roots of unity are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\); they lie on the unit circle at angles 0, 2π/3 and 4π/3.
The same three roots can be written in polar form using cosine and sine of the angles 2π/3 and 4π/3.
In Cartesian form the non-real roots are −1/2 ± j√3/2, so w₂ and w₃ are complex conjugates of each other.
eqs: Exponential form of the second cube root of unity
w₂ = second cube root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; π = pi (dimensionless)
Exponential form of the third cube root of unity
w₃ = third cube root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; π = pi (dimensionless)
Cartesian form of the second cube root of unity
w₂ = second cube root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Cartesian form of the third cube root of unity
w₃ = third cube root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Keep the angle in radians: 2π/3 and 4π/3, not 120° or 240° unless converting explicitly.
Watch the sign of the imaginary part: w₃ has −j√3/2, not +j√3/2.
rq: Why does w₃ equal the complex conjugate of w₂, and how can you confirm it from the polar form?
Their angles 2π/3 and 4π/3 are symmetric about π, so their cosines are equal and their sines are opposite in sign, giving w₃ = w₂*.
What happens if you cube each of 1, w₂ and w₃? What does this tell you about them?
Each gives 1, since \(e^{j2π}\)=1 and \(e^{j4π}\)=1, so all three are roots of z³ = 1.

units.name: 4.6 Powers and roots z^(m/n) and square roots in quadratics
units.ov: This material extends De Moivre's theorem to roots and rational powers of complex numbers. Writing z in polar form gives n distinct values for \(z^{1/n}\) and, for \(z^{m/n}\), n distinct values when m/n is in lowest terms. The same machinery supplies the complex square root needed to solve quadratics with complex coefficients, and the roots appear as equally spaced points on a circle in the Argand diagram.
must: Convert to polar form before any power or root: \( r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), \( \theta=\arg z \) in radians, taking care with the quadrant.

nth roots: \( z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}\left[\cos\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}+j\sin\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right] \), \( k=0,\dots,n-1 \). This gives n distinct roots, and the modulus becomes \( r^{1/n} \), not r/n.

Rational powers: \( z^{m/n}=r^{p}\left[\cos(p\theta+2\pi kp)+j\sin(p\theta+2\pi kp)\right] \), \( p=m/n \). Apply the power to the modulus as well as the argument (e.g. \( (\sqrt{41})^{-2/3}\approx0.29 \)).
Non-integer powers are multi-valued: take k=0,…,n−1 only (with m/n in lowest terms). Larger k just repeats values.
All branches share one modulus and are equally spaced by \( 2\pi/n \) in angle around a circle, which gives a quick check on your answers.
Square root of a complex number: \( \sqrt{z}=\pm\sqrt r\,[\cos(\theta/2)+j\sin(\theta/2)] \). The two roots differ only by sign, and the principal root has positive real part.

Quadratic formula with complex coefficients is unchanged: \( z=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} \). Here \( z=-\tfrac12(5+j4)\pm\tfrac12\sqrt{37+j12} \), giving \( z_1=-5.58-j2.49 \) and \( z_2=0.58-j1.51 \).
Use radians throughout (never mix degrees with 2π), keep j²=−1 in mind, and carry the ± through, applying the 2a denominator to both terms.
Convert each branch back to a+jb by evaluating cos and sin of the reduced angle, and check with |a+jb| and the sum or product of the roots.
conn: Polar form and Argand diagram: the argument must be in the correct quadrant before dividing by n, since a wrong θ shifts every root by the same angle.

De Moivre roots and the quadratic formula: the complex square root is just the n=2 case of the nth-root formula, so the ± in the root and the ± in the quadratic formula are linked but not the same sign choice.
Rational powers and multi-valuedness: \( z^{m/n} \) combines taking the nth root (k branches) with raising to the mth power, which requires reducing m/n first and then counting distinct values.
Checking roots by Vieta: for a quadratic, the sum of the roots is \( -b/a \) (here \( -(5+j4) \)), which tests the numerical answers \( z_1,z_2 \).
exq: Find all values of \( (-8)^{1/3} \) in polar and rectangular form, state which is the principal root, and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Evaluate all distinct values of \( (4+j5)^{-2/3} \) (modulus \( \sqrt{41} \)) giving the modulus and argument of each in radians to 2 d.p., and convert them to the form a+jb.

Express \( 37+j12 \) in polar form and hence find \( \sqrt{37+j12} \). Use the result to solve \( z^2+(5+j4)z+c=0 \) for the c that gives discriminant \( 37+j12 \) (c = −7+j7), and verify that the roots sum to \( -(5+j4) \).
Solve \( z^4=-16 \), give the four roots in the form a+jb, and explain why they lie on a circle of radius 2 spaced by \( \pi/2 \).
Explain why \( z^{3/2} \) has only two distinct values, and find them for \( z=1+j\sqrt3 \).

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem and roots/powers z^(m/n)
pts: Taking the nth root of z=r(cos θ + j sin θ) gives n distinct roots, obtained by adding 2πk/n to the argument for k = 0,1,…,(n−1).
A rational power \(z^{p}\) with p = m/n is found by first taking the nth root and then raising to the mth power.
Raising to the mth power multiplies the modulus exponent and the argument, giving the general form for z^(m/n).
The result for \(z^{p}\) carries the same family of values indexed by k, so non-integer powers are multi-valued.
defs: Modulus and argument form
A complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) is written with modulus r = |z| and argument θ.
eqs: nth root of a complex number (principal family over k)
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = positive integer root index; k = 0,1,…,(n−1); j = imaginary unit
p = m/n (dimensionless); m, n = integers; r = modulus; θ = argument (rad); k = 0,1,…,(n−1)
tips: Remember k runs only from 0 to (n−1); using k up to m or beyond double-counts roots.
Use the same argument convention (e.g. θ in radians) throughout; mixing degrees with 2π gives wrong roots.
rq: Why does z^(m/n) produce n different values rather than one?
Because the argument of z is defined only up to multiples of 2π, and dividing by n yields n distinct arguments 2πk/n shifts for k = 0,…,(n−1).
What happens if p = m/n is written as an integer multiple, e.g. m = n?
Then the factor 2πkp = 2πk·m/n becomes a multiple of 2π, so all n values collapse to the single value \(z^{m}\), consistent with ordinary De Moivre's theorem.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers via polar form (De Moivre's theorem for non-integer powers, mult
pts: Write the complex number in polar form, z = |z|(cos θ + j sin θ), before raising it to any power.
For a fractional power, the modulus is raised to that power and the argument is multiplied by it, with 2πk added inside the bracket to generate all branches.
A non-integer power of a complex number gives several distinct values, one for each integer k; here k = 0, 1, 2 gives three values.
The different values all lie on a circle of the same radius, spaced equally in angle around the origin.
Evaluate each branch by computing the modulus value and the cosine and sine of the reduced angle, then converting to rectangular form a + jb.
defs: Polar form
Representation of a complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), where r = |z| is the modulus and θ is the argument.
Argument of z
The angle θ of a complex number measured from the positive real axis; it is used with 2πk added when finding all powers or roots.
eqs: Power of a complex number in polar form (all k branches)
z = complex number (dimensionless); n = power (dimensionless); |z| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); k = branch index (integer); j = imaginary unit
a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
tips: Use the reduced angle consistently (in radians) when evaluating cos and sin; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong branch values.
Remember to apply the power to the modulus as well as the argument; forgetting the modulus gives the wrong magnitude (here 0.29 = (√41)^{-2/3}).
rq: Why do we add 2πk to the argument before multiplying by the fractional power?
Because the argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π; adding 2πk gives all equivalent angles, and a non-integer power then produces distinct values for each k.
What happens to the number of distinct values if the power were an integer such as 2?
Only one distinct value results, since the angles for different k differ by multiples of 2π and repeat around the circle.

notes.t: Powers and roots of complex numbers (De Moivre's theorem for roots)
pts: Quadratic roots with complex coefficients are found using the same formula as real quadratics, but the square root must be evaluated as a complex number.
Write the complex number under the root in polar form (modulus r, argument θ) before taking the root.
The n-th root of a complex number has n distinct values, found by varying k over 0, 1, …, n−1 in the angle term.
Taking the root divides the modulus by the root power and the angle by the root power, adding 2πk/n for each distinct root.
defs: Principal square root of a complex number
The two square roots of z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) are ±√r [cos(θ/2) + j sin(θ/2)], which differ by a sign.
eqs: z = unknown complex root (dimensionless); a, b, c = complex coefficients (dimensionless)
n-th roots of a complex number (de Moivre)
z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{\theta}{n} + \dfrac{2\pi k}{n}\right) + j\sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{n} + \dfrac{2\pi k}{n}\right)\right], \quad k = 0,1,\dots,n-1
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = root order (integer); k = root index (integer)
tips: Do not forget the ± sign in the quadratic formula; both roots must be found and the 2a denominator applies to both terms.
Angles from the polar form must be in radians consistently (here 0.31 rad), and dividing the angle by 2 for the square root is a common error.
rq: Why does the square root of a complex number give two answers, and how do you find both?
Because (−w)² = w² as well, so ±w are both roots; in polar form, adding 2πk/n to the angle with k = 0, 1 gives both values.
Why must the angle θ be divided by n but 2πk/n is added rather than divided?
The angle θ is the single argument being rooted, while 2πk/n represents the extra full turns that produce the other distinct roots, so it is added after division.
What happens if you use θ = 0.31 directly without dividing by 2 when finding √(37 + j12)?
You get the wrong angle; the square root halves the argument, so the angle must be 0.31/2.

notes.t: Square roots of complex numbers and solving quadratic equations with complex roots
pts: The square root of a complex number has two values that differ only by sign; the principal root is the one with positive real part.
Taking the square root of (37+j12) gives ±(6.16+j0.97), so the two roots of the quadratic differ by the sign of this root.
The quadratic formula with complex coefficients uses the complex square root; the two roots z1 and z2 are found by taking both signs.
Evaluating both signs gives z1 = -5.58 - j2.49 and z2 = 0.58 - j1.51, which are plotted in the complex plane.
defs: Square root of a complex number
A complex number w such that w² = z; every non-zero complex number has two square roots, equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
eqs: Quadratic formula with complex coefficients (roots z)
z = unknown complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; 5+j4 = coefficient term (dimensionless)
37+j12 = complex number (dimensionless); ±(6.16+j0.97) = its two square roots (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the two roots of the square root with the two roots of z: the ± in the square root and the ± in the quadratic formula both must be carried through.
Remember that j² = −1 when squaring or simplifying; errors in signs of the imaginary part are common when adding or subtracting the −½(5+j4) term.
rq: Why does the square root of a complex number give two values, and how do they relate to each other?
Because (−w)² = w² as well, so if w is a root, −w is also a root; the two roots are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
Why must both signs of the square root be used when solving for z?
The ± in the quadratic formula produces the two distinct roots z1 and z2; using only one sign gives only one solution.

units.name: 4.7 Powers of trig functions and multiple angles
units.ov: This topic uses Euler/de Moivre with a unit-modulus z = \(e^{jθ}\) to turn powers of sin θ and cos θ into sums of multiple-angle terms. The key identities are \(z^{n}\) + \(z^{-n}\) = 2cos nθ and \(z^{n}\) − \(z^{-n}\) = 2j sin nθ. Raising these to a power and expanding the binomial gives power-reduction formulas such as cos²3θ = (1+cos6θ)/2. These are useful for integration and for simplifying oscillatory signals.
must: For \(z=e^{j\theta}\) with \(|z|=1\): \(z^n=\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta\) (de Moivre).
Negative powers flip the sine sign: \(z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-j\sin n\theta\).
\(z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta\), so \(\cos n\theta=\tfrac12(z^n+z^{-n})\).
\(z^n-z^{-n}=2j\sin n\theta\), so \(\sin n\theta=\tfrac{1}{2j}(z^n-z^{-n})\).
Method: write \((2\cos\theta)^m=(z+z^{-1})^m\), expand with the binomial theorem, pair terms \(z^k+z^{-k}\) and convert each to \(2\cos k\theta\).
Squaring gives \((z^3+z^{-3})^2=z^6+z^{-6}+2\); the cross term is the constant +2, which is easy to forget.
\(4\cos^2 3\theta=2\cos6\theta+2\), so \(\cos^2 3\theta=\tfrac{1+\cos6\theta}{2}\). Divide by 4 in total, not by 2 only.
For sine powers, \((2j\sin\theta)^m=(z-z^{-1})^m\). Track the factor \(j^m\) and the alternating signs (\(j^2=-1\), \(j^4=1\)).
The same method gives \(\sin^2 n\theta=\tfrac{1-\cos2n\theta}{2}\). Use the result to check your answer, for example by substituting \(\theta=0\).
Polar and exponential forms are \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=re^{j\theta}=r\angle\theta\). The angle must be in radians.
conn: Power-reduction formulas feed directly into integration: \(\int\cos^2 3\theta\,d\theta\) and \(\int\sin^4\theta\,d\theta\) become sums of simple cosines.
The binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle supply the coefficients when expanding \((z\pm z^{-1})^m\).
Mean-square and RMS values of AC signals in mechanical and electrical vibration use \(\cos^2\) reduction. The average of cos 2ωt over a period is zero, leaving 1/2.
De Moivre's theorem is also used for roots of complex numbers and for deriving multiple-angle identities such as cos 3θ in terms of cos θ.
exq: Let \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\). Show that \(z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta\) and \(z^n-z^{-n}=2j\sin n\theta\).
Expand \((z^3+z^{-3})^2\) and hence show that \(\cos^2 3\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos6\theta)\).
Express \(\cos^4\theta\) in the form \(a\cos4\theta+b\cos2\theta+c\), and hence evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta\,d\theta\).
Use \((z-z^{-1})^5\) to express \(\sin^5\theta\) in terms of \(\sin\theta\), \(\sin3\theta\) and \(\sin5\theta\).
A displacement is \(x=A\cos^2(3\omega t)\). Rewrite it using multiple angles and find its mean value and the amplitude and frequency of its oscillating part.

notes.t: Powers of Trigonometric Functions and Multiple Angles
pts: Euler's form writes a complex number as a modulus times cos plus j sin of its angle, so powers of z follow directly from de Moivre's result.
Raising z to the power n multiplies the angle by n, giving cos nθ + j sin nθ.
Negative powers give the conjugate-angle result, since z^(-n) reverses the sign of the sine term.
Adding and subtracting \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) isolates cos nθ and sin nθ, which is the basis for expressing powers of sin θ and cos θ in terms of multiple angles.
defs: Euler's formula (polar form)
For a complex number z with modulus r and argument θ, z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) = re^(jθ) = r∠θ.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for powers of z
z = unit-modulus complex number (dimensionless); θ = angle (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Sum of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) giving cosine of multiple angle
z = unit complex number; θ = angle (rad); n = integer (dimensionless)
Difference of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) giving sine of multiple angle
z = unit complex number; θ = angle (rad); n = integer (dimensionless)
tips: Check the sign of the sine term: z^(-n) = cos nθ − j sin nθ, not + j sin nθ; dropping the minus sign flips the result.
Remember the factor of 2 when isolating cos nθ or sin nθ: \(z^{n}\) + z^(-n) = 2cos nθ, so divide by 2 (and by 2j for sine).
rq: Why does z^(-n) have the sine term with a negative sign, and what does this tell you about z^(-n) compared with \(z^{n}\)?

Because z^(-n) = 1/\(z^{n}\), which corresponds to the angle −nθ; cos is even and sin is odd, so the sine term changes sign while the cosine term stays the same. Thus z^(-n) is the complex conjugate of \(z^{n}\) when |z| = 1.
How would you use \(z^{n}\) + z^(-n) = 2cos nθ to express cos³θ in terms of cosines of multiple angles?
Write cos θ = (z + z^(-1))/2, cube it to get (z³ + 3z + 3z^(-1) + z^(-3))/8 = (2cos 3θ + 6cos θ)/8, so cos³θ = (cos 3θ + 3cos θ)/4.
What if you needed sin²θ instead of cos²θ — which combination of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) would you use?
Use sin θ = (z − z^(-1))/(2j), square it, and apply the result that z² + z^(-2) = 2cos 2θ, giving sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2.

notes.t: Powers of z and expanding cos² of multiple angles
pts: Using \(z^{n}\) + \(z^{-n}\) = 2cos nθ, squaring gives (\(z^{n}\) + \(z^{-n}\))² = 4cos² nθ, which lets cos² nθ be rewritten in terms of a single cosine of a double angle.
Expanding (z³ + \(z^{-3}\))² produces z⁶ + \(z^{-6}\) + 2, and the z⁶ + \(z^{-6}\) term is recognised again as 2cos 6θ.
Equating 2cos 6θ + 2 with 4cos² 3θ and dividing by 2 gives the power-reduction result cos² 3θ = (1 + cos 6θ)/2.
defs: Multiple-angle expansion
Writing a power of a trigonometric function (e.g. cos² 3θ) as a sum of sines and cosines of multiples of the angle, obtained via z = \(e^{iθ}\) and \(z^{n}\) + \(z^{-n}\) = 2cos nθ.
eqs: Exponential identity for cosine of multiple angles
z = \(e^{i\theta}\) (dimensionless complex number); n = integer (dimensionless); θ = angle (rad)
θ = angle (rad); cos²3θ and cos6θ are dimensionless
tips: Do not forget the constant +2 that arises from the cross term 2·\(z^{n}\)·\(z^{-n}\) = 2 when expanding the square.
Remember the factor 2² = 4 on the right-hand side; dividing by 2 (not 4) is needed to isolate cos²3θ after the cos 6θ term is identified.
rq: Why does squaring (\(z^{n}\) + \(z^{-n}\)) produce a constant term of 2 that eventually becomes a constant in the final answer?
Because (\(z^{n}\))(\(z^{-n}\)) = 1, so the cross terms give 2·1 = 2; this constant survives and combines with 2cos 6θ, yielding 2cos 6θ + 2 = 4cos²3θ.
What would change if we had used n = 2 instead of n = 3 to find cos²2θ?
Squaring (z² + \(z^{-2}\)) gives z⁴ + \(z^{-4}\) + 2 = 2cos4θ + 2, so cos²2θ = (1 + cos4θ)/2; the doubled index doubles the angle in the cosine term.

units.name: 5.1 De Moivre's theorem: powers and roots
units.ov: De Moivre's theorem expresses powers of a complex number in polar form: the modulus is raised to the power n and the argument is multiplied by n. Extending it with the 2πk shift in the argument gives all n distinct nth roots, which sit equally spaced on a circle and form a regular n-gon. Rational powers \(z^{m/n}\) combine both ideas: take the nth root, then raise to the mth power.
must: De Moivre: \( z^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + j\sin n\theta) \) for \( z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta) \), with \( r=|z| \) and \( \theta=\arg z \) in radians
nth roots: \( z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right)+j\sin\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right)\right],\ k=0,\dots,n-1 \)
Exponential form: \( z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}e^{j(\theta+2\pi k)/n} \), which is quicker to write and manipulate
Always include the \( 2\pi k \) term, because \( \theta \) is defined only modulo \( 2\pi \); omitting it gives one root instead of n
The n roots all have modulus \( r^{1/n} \) and are spaced \( 2\pi/n \) apart on a circle, forming a regular n-gon (e.g. 60° apart for n = 6)
Convert to polar form first: find \( r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \) and \( \theta \) in the correct quadrant (check the sign of x and y)
Rational powers: \( z^{m/n}=(z^{1/n})^m \), so take the nth root (n branches via k = 0..n−1) and then raise to the mth power, keeping the \( 2\pi k \) terms
Sanity checks: the roots sum to zero for n ≥ 2, and each root raised to the nth power returns z
Give the final answers in the requested form (polar, exponential or Cartesian), with the argument usually in \( (-\pi,\pi] \) for principal values
conn: Cartesian to polar conversion (modulus and argument, quadrant) is the first step of every power or root question, and an error in \( \theta \) carries through to all the answers
Roots of unity and solving \( z^n = w \) link De Moivre's theorem to polynomial equations, with the roots found geometrically on an Argand diagram
Expanding \( (\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^n \) binomially and equating real and imaginary parts gives multiple-angle identities such as \( \cos 3\theta \) and \( \sin 3\theta \)
The exponential form \( re^{j\theta} \) links to Euler's formula and to phasors and rotating vectors in vibrations and AC analysis
exq: Express \( z=-1+j\sqrt{3} \) in polar form and use De Moivre's theorem to find \( z^{8} \) in the form \( a+jb \)
Find all the cube roots of \( 8(\cos 90^\circ + j\sin 90^\circ) \), give them in polar and Cartesian form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram
Solve \( z^6 = 1 \), plot the roots and state the geometric shape they form; then solve \( z^4=-16 \)
Find all values of \( (1+j)^{3/4} \) in exponential form, taking the 4th root first and then cubing
Use De Moivre's theorem with the binomial expansion to derive an expression for \( \cos 4\theta \) in terms of \( \cos\theta \)

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem: powers and roots of complex numbers
pts: De Moivre's theorem gives the nth power of a complex number directly from its modulus and argument, with the modulus raised to the power n and the argument multiplied by n.
The nth roots of a complex number are found by taking the nth root of the modulus and dividing the argument by n, with the k-shift producing n distinct roots.
The n distinct nth roots lie equally spaced on a circle of radius the nth root of the modulus, forming a regular n-gon (shown for n = 6).
Raising a number to a rational power m/n is done by first taking the nth root and then raising the result to the mth power.
defs: Modulus and argument form
A complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) is written in polar form, with r = |z| its modulus and θ its argument.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for integer powers
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless)
nth roots of a complex number (trigonometric form)
\(r^{1/n}\) = modulus of each root (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); k = 0, 1, …, n−1 (integer); n = root index (dimensionless)
nth roots of a complex number (exponential form)
\(r^{1/n}\) = modulus of each root (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); k = integer index 0 to n−1; n = root index
p = m/n (dimensionless); r = modulus of z; θ = argument of z (rad); k = integer 0 to n−1; m, n = integers
tips: Argument θ is only defined modulo 2π; forgetting the 2πk term when finding roots gives only one root instead of n.
For \(z^{m/n}\), take the nth root first (giving n branches via k) and then raise to the mth power; do not treat the exponent as simply multiplying the argument without including the 2πk terms.
rq: Why does taking the nth root of a complex number produce n answers, while a real number's nth root in ordinary arithmetic is usually one?

Because the argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π, so adding 2πk to θ before dividing by n gives n different angles (k = 0, …, n−1) that all satisfy the equation, spaced 2π/n apart around the circle.
What happens to the roots' positions if n = 6 and the modulus of z is increased?
All six roots remain at equal angular spacing of 60° (2π/6) but move onto a larger circle, since the radius is the nth root of |z|.

units.name: 5.2 Loci as straight lines (Re, arg, Im conditions)
units.ov: This topic describes straight-line loci in the Argand diagram, using conditions on Re(z), Im of a rotated z, arg(z − z₀) and the equidistance condition |z − z₁| = |z − z₂|. Each one reduces to a linear relation in x and y after writing z = x + jy. Re and Im conditions give vertical or horizontal lines, an arg condition gives a ray, and equal moduli give a perpendicular bisector.
must: Write \(z=x+jy\) and convert every locus condition into a Cartesian relation in \(x,y\) before interpreting it.
\(\operatorname{Re}(z)=c\) is the vertical line \(x=c\), the whole line with y unrestricted. For example \(\operatorname{Re}(z)=-\sqrt2\) is the line \(x=-\sqrt2\), to the left of the imaginary axis.
\(\operatorname{Im}[-jz]=-x\), because \(-j(x+jy)=y-jx\). So \(\operatorname{Im}[-jz]=\sqrt2\) gives \(x=-\sqrt2\). Watch the sign and use \(j^2=-1\).

\(\arg(z-z_0)=\theta\) is a half-line (ray) from \(z_0\) at angle \(\theta\) to the positive real axis. In parametric form \(z=z_0+r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta),\ r\ge0\), with the start point \(z_0\) itself technically excluded.
For the ray from \(1+j\) with \(\theta=-\pi/3\), the direction is down and to the right. Arguments are measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis, in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
\(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). Square both sides and expand the brackets carefully.
Check a bisector by confirming it passes through the midpoint (here \((1.5,\,0.5)\)) and is perpendicular to the segment (segment gradient −1, line gradient 1).
\(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) is the distance from the origin, so \(|z-z_0|\) is the distance from \(z_0\). The polar form \(1+j=\sqrt2(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+j\sin\frac{\pi}{4})\) helps locate points.
Describe each locus completely: a line, a ray with \(r\ge0\), or a bisector, never a single point.
conn: Modulus–argument form links to the arg-locus: \(z-z_0=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\) gives the ray, and converting to Cartesian form gives the line's gradient \(\tan\theta\), restricted to one side of \(z_0\).
Equidistance loci combine the modulus definition with algebraic expansion and coordinate geometry (midpoint, gradient, perpendicular).
Multiplying by \(-j\) is a rotation by \(-\pi/2\), which links Im and Re conditions: \(\operatorname{Im}[-jz]=\operatorname{Re}(z)\) up to sign, so the locus changes from horizontal to vertical.

Questions often ask for the intersection of two loci (a ray with a bisector, or a ray with a vertical line), which means solving simultaneous linear equations and then checking the point lies on the ray.
exq: Sketch the locus \(\operatorname{Re}(z)=-\sqrt2\) and the locus \(\operatorname{Im}[-jz]=\sqrt2\). Show that they are the same line.
Sketch \(\arg(z-(1+j))=-\pi/3\). Give its parametric form and state where it meets the real axis.
Find the Cartesian equation of the locus \(|z-(1+j)|=|z-2|\), and verify that it is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points.
Find the point where the ray \(\arg(z-(1+j))=-\pi/3\) meets the line \(y=x-1\), if it does. Decide whether the intersection lies on the ray.
Find the locus of \(|z-3|=|z+j|\) as a line \(y=mx+c\), then find the locus of \(\operatorname{Im}[-jz]=-2\).

notes.t: Loci of complex numbers: straight lines
pts: Writing z = x + jy, the real part Re(z) equals x, so a condition on Re(z) is a condition on x alone.
Fixing Re(z) = -√2 gives a vertical line in the Argand diagram, since x is constant while y can be any real value.
The locus is the entire vertical line through x = -√2, extending infinitely in both directions (up and down).
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane (Argand diagram) that satisfy a given condition on z.
Real part
For z = x + jy, Re(z) = x is the real component of z, the horizontal coordinate in the Argand diagram.
eqs: Locus of points with fixed real part (vertical line)
x = real part of z (dimensionless); z = complex number; y = imaginary part of z, any real value (dimensionless)
tips: Do not describe Re(z) = -√2 as a single point; it is a whole line because y is unrestricted.
Be careful with the sign: the line lies at x = -√2 (left of the imaginary axis), not at x = √2.
rq: Why does the condition Re(z) = -√2 produce a vertical line rather than a point?
Because only x is constrained; y = Im(z) is free to take any real value, so every point (-√2, y) with y ∈ ℝ satisfies the condition.
How would the locus change if the condition were Im(z) = -√2 instead?
It would be a horizontal line y = -√2 in the Argand diagram, since the imaginary part is fixed and the real part is free.

notes.t: Straight lines as loci of complex numbers (arg form)
pts: A locus of the form arg(z − z₀) = θ is a half-line starting at z₀ and making angle θ with the positive real axis.
Write z − z₀ = r(cos θ + j sin θ) with r ≥ 0; fixing θ gives the ray, and r ranges over non-negative reals.
The starting point z₀ = 1 + j is the point (1, 1) in the Argand diagram; the ray extends from it in the direction of angle −π/3 (pointing down and to the right).
Converting the point 1 + j to modulus–argument form helps interpret its position: its modulus is √2 and its argument is π/4.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the Argand diagram satisfying a given condition on z.
Argument of a complex number
The angle arg(w) that the vector representing w makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise, taken in (−π, π].
eqs: Parametric form of the ray arg(z − z₀) = θ
z = complex point (dimensionless); z₀ = fixed starting point (dimensionless); r = distance from z₀ (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
z = complex point (dimensionless); r = non-negative real parameter (dimensionless); angle in rad
tips: Do not describe arg(z − z₀) = θ as a full line; it is a ray starting at z₀, so include the restriction r ≥ 0.
Check the sign of the argument: −π/3 points below the positive real direction, and the argument must be measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis.
rq: Why does the locus arg(z − 1 − j) = −π/3 form only a half-line rather than a full straight line?
Because the argument fixes only the direction of z − (1+j); r = |z − (1+j)| must be ≥ 0, so only one side of the point 1+j is included. The full line would require arg = −π/3 or 2π/3.
What would change if the condition were arg(z − 1 − j) = 2π/3?
The ray would start at 1 + j but point in the opposite direction (up and to the left), since angle 2π/3 = −π/3 + π.
Why must we note that r ≥ 0 rather than r ∈ ℝ?
A negative r would reverse direction by π, giving argument θ + π, which is a different argument; so r ≥ 0 keeps the argument exactly θ.

notes.t: Loci of complex numbers: straight lines (perpendicular bisector)
pts: Write z = x + jy and substitute into the locus condition, then convert the modulus equation into Cartesian form.
A condition of equal distances from two points defines a locus; here |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| means points equidistant from z₁ and z₂.
Squaring both sides removes the square roots, leaving a linear equation in x and y, which is a straight line.
The line obtained is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two given points z₁ = 1 + j and z₂ = 2.
Rearranging the linear equation gives the slope-intercept form y = x − 1, a line of gradient 1 crossing the real axis at x = 1.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane whose coordinates satisfy a given condition, typically describing a curve or line.
Modulus of a complex number
For z = x + jy, |z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance of the point z from the origin in the Argand diagram.
eqs: Equidistance condition for a straight-line locus
z = complex variable (dimensionless); z₁, z₂ = fixed complex points (dimensionless); |·| = modulus (dimensionless)
Cartesian form of the locus for z₁ = 1 + j, z₂ = 2
x, y = real and imaginary parts of z (dimensionless)
x, y = coordinates of z in the Argand plane (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget to expand the squared brackets fully; sign errors in (x − 1)² and (x − 2)² are common and change the line.
Check your final line against the Argand diagram: the line should pass through the midpoint of z₁ and z₂ and be perpendicular to the segment joining them.
rq: Why does squaring both sides of |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| produce a straight line rather than a circle?
The x² and y² terms are identical on both sides, so they cancel when expanded, leaving only linear terms in x and y.
Why is the locus a perpendicular bisector rather than just any line through the midpoint?
Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, by the geometric definition of equal distance.

notes.t: Locus of points: straight lines (Im[-jz] = constant)
pts: Write z = x + jy and multiply by -j; since j² = -1, the imaginary part of -jz is -x, so the condition becomes a vertical line.
Taking the imaginary part of -jz picks out the real coordinate x, so the locus depends only on x.
Setting the imaginary part equal to √2 gives -x = √2, so the locus is the vertical line x = -√2 in the Argand diagram.
eqs: Imaginary part of -jz for z = x + jy (gives the locus condition)
x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless); z = complex number (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the sign: Im[-jz] = -x, not +x, so the line is x = -√2, which lies in the left half-plane.
Use j² = -1 when expanding (x + jy)(-j); a missed sign turns y - jx into the wrong expression.
rq: Why does the locus depend only on x and not on y?
Multiplying by -j rotates z by -90°, so the imaginary part of -jz equals -x; y appears only in the real part, which is discarded by Im[ ].
What would change if the condition were Re[-jz] = √2 instead?
Re[-jz] = y, so the locus would be the horizontal line y = √2.

units.name: 5.3 Loci as circles and perpendicular bisectors
units.ov: This material shows how modulus conditions on complex numbers define loci in the Argand diagram. \(|z-z_1|=R\) is a circle, \(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is a perpendicular bisector (a line), and \(|z-z_1|=k|z-z_2|\) with \(k\neq1\) is an Apollonius circle. All three come from the same idea, that \(|z-z_1|\) is the distance between two points. They are solved by the same method: set \(z=x+jy\), square both sides, then simplify or complete the square.
must: \(|z-z_1|\) is the distance from z to \(z_1\), so \(|z-z_1|=R\) is a circle with centre \(z_1\) and radius R.
Cartesian form: \((x-x_1)^2+(y-y_1)^2=R^2\), with centre \((x_1,y_1)\). The signs in the brackets are reversed relative to the centre, and R is squared.
Parametric form: \(z=z_1+Re^{jt}\), \(-\pi<t\le\pi\), which traces the whole circle.
\(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). It is a straight line, not a circle.
\(|z-z_1|=k|z-z_2|\) with \(k\neq1\) is an Apollonius circle, and \(k=1\) gives the line. Check k first.
Standard method: write \(z=x+jy\), form the real and imaginary parts of each difference, square both sides to remove the roots, expand fully, then simplify.
For circles, collect terms and complete the square in x and y to read off the centre and radius.
Worked example: \(|z-1-j|=|z-2|\) gives \(y=x-1\), the bisector of (1,1) and (2,0).
Worked example: \(|z-1-j|=\sqrt2|z-2|\) gives \((x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=4\), so centre \((3,-1)\) and \(R=2\).
Write each point correctly as a coordinate pair, e.g. \(z_2=2=2+j0\) is (2,0). Sign slips in \(z_1\) give the wrong line or centre.
conn: The perpendicular bisector is the \(k=1\) case of the Apollonius locus. The \(x^2+y^2\) terms cancel only when \(k=1\), which leaves a linear equation.
Modulus as distance links the algebra (squaring, completing the square) to the geometry of circles and bisectors. Sketching the answer checks the algebra.
The parametric form \(z_1+Re^{jt}\) and the Cartesian form describe the same circle. Questions may ask you to convert between them or find the point at a given angle t.
A circle locus and a line locus can be combined, so you solve simultaneously for intersection points. An example is \(|z-z_1|=R\) with \(|z-z_2|=|z-z_3|\).
