exq: Sketch the locus \(|z-(2-3j)|=4\), give its Cartesian equation, and write down a parametric form for z.
Find the Cartesian equation of the locus \(|z-1-j|=|z-2|\) and show it is the perpendicular bisector of the points (1,1) and (2,0).
Show that \(|z-1-j|=\sqrt2|z-2|\) is a circle. Find its centre and radius by completing the square.
Describe the locus \(|z+2|=2|z-1|\). Find its centre and radius, and say what happens if the 2 is replaced by 1.
Find where the line \(y=x-1\) meets the circle \((x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=4\), and give the intersection points as complex numbers.

notes.t: Loci: Circles in the Argand Diagram
pts: The locus |z − z₁| = R, with R constant, is a circle of radius R centred at z₁ = a + jb.
Writing z − z₁ = R \(e^{jt}\) with −π < t ≤ π traces every point of the circle as t varies, giving a parametric form.
Substituting z = x + jy and z₁ = x₁ + jy₁ converts the modulus condition into the Cartesian equation of a circle.
Squaring the modulus equation removes the square root and gives the standard form (x − x₁)² + (y − y₁)² = R².
defs: Locus
The set of all points z in the complex plane that satisfy a given condition; here the condition is a fixed distance from a fixed point.
Centre and radius of a circle in the Argand diagram
For |z − z₁| = R, the centre is the point z₁ and the radius is the constant R, the distance from z₁ to any point z on the circle.
eqs: z = complex variable point (dimensionless); z₁ = centre of circle (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless, same units as the plane)
z = point on circle; z₁ = centre; R = radius; t = angle from the positive real direction (rad)
x, y = coordinates of point z; x₁, y₁ = coordinates of centre z₁; R = radius (m or unitless in plane)
tips: Do not confuse the centre z₁ = a + jb with the origin; the Cartesian form uses (x₁, y₁), not (x, y).
Remember to square both sides when converting |z − z₁| = R to Cartesian form, so R becomes R².
rq: Why does the equation |z − z₁| = R describe a circle rather than a line or other curve?
|z − z₁| is the distance between z and z₁; keeping this distance constant means every point is the same distance R from the fixed centre z₁, which is the definition of a circle.
What happens to the circle if you change t's range to 0 ≤ t < 2π instead of −π < t ≤ π?
Nothing changes geometrically: both ranges cover one full revolution once, so the same circle is traced exactly once.

notes.t: Locus of a circle in the complex plane: |z − z₁| = R
pts: Write z = x + iy and the centre z₁ = x₁ + iy₁; subtracting gives the real and imaginary parts of z − z₁.
The modulus |z − z₁| is the distance between the points z and z₁ in the Argand plane, so |z − z₁| = R describes all points a fixed distance R from the centre.
Applying the modulus formula to (x − x₁) + i(y − y₁) gives a square root of a sum of squares, which is then squared to remove the root.
The result is the Cartesian equation of a circle with centre (x₁, y₁) and radius R.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = a + ib, |z| = √(a² + b²), the distance of the point from the origin in the Argand plane.
eqs: Locus of points at constant distance R from centre z₁ (circle in Argand plane)
z = complex variable (dimensionless); z₁ = centre (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless, same units as the plane)
x, y = coordinates of z (dimensionless); x₁, y₁ = centre coordinates (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse |z − z₁| with z − z₁ itself; the modulus must be taken before squaring.
Remember the centre is (x₁, y₁) with signs reversed in the bracket: (x − x₁), not (x + x₁).
rq: Why does squaring both sides of √((x−x₁)²+(y−y₁)²) = R not introduce extra solutions here?
Because R is a non-negative distance, so both sides are non-negative and squaring is reversible; the result is equivalent to the original.
What does the locus |z − z₁| = R become if R = 0?
Only the single point z = z₁ satisfies it, a degenerate circle of zero radius.

notes.t: Locus of points equidistant from two complex numbers (perpendicular bisector)
pts: The equation |z − 1 − j| = |z − 2| is rewritten as |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| with z₁ = 1 + j and z₂ = 2, so the locus is the set of points equidistant from z₁ and z₂.
Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
For this case the locus is the straight line y = x − 1, which is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from (1,1) to (2,0).
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane that satisfy a given equation or condition.
eqs: Locus of points equidistant from two complex numbers z₁ and z₂
z = complex variable (dimensionless); z₁, z₂ = fixed complex numbers (dimensionless)
Cartesian locus found for z₁ = 1 + j, z₂ = 2
x, y = real and imaginary parts of z (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| (a line) with |z − z₁| = r (a circle of radius r).
Write z₂ = 2 + j0 as the complex number 2 with imaginary part zero; sign errors in z₁ = 1 + j (point (1,1)) lead to the wrong line.
rq: Why does the condition |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| describe a line rather than a circle?

Because it compares two distances from the same point z to two fixed points; equal distances define the perpendicular bisector of the segment z₁z₂, a straight line. A circle arises when a single distance equals a constant.
How could you check that y = x − 1 is correct for this locus?
Take a point on the line, e.g. z = 0 − j·1 = −j... more simply z = 1 (x=1,y=0 is not on it); test z = 2 + j: |z−1−j| = |1| = 1 and |z−2| = |j| = 1, which are equal, and (2,1) satisfies y = x − 1.
What if z₂ were moved to 2 + j0 with z₁ unchanged — would the locus change?
Only if the two points change; the locus is always the perpendicular bisector of z₁z₂, so it changes with the position of either point.

notes.t: Loci of complex numbers: Apollonius circle |z−z₁| = k|z−z₂|
pts: The locus |z − z₁| = k|z − z₂| with k ≠ 1 is a circle (Apollonius circle), found by converting to Cartesian form z = x + jy.
Write |z − z₁| as a distance: the modulus of a complex difference is the distance between two points in the Argand plane.
Squaring both sides removes the square roots and gives a quadratic equation in x and y.
Completing the square turns the quadratic into the standard circle form, from which the centre and radius are read off.
For this example the centre is (3, −1) and the radius is R = 2, so the locus is a circle, not a line.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane whose coordinates satisfy a given condition on z.
Apollonius circle
The locus of points z such that the ratio of distances to two fixed points is a constant k ≠ 1; it is a circle.
eqs: Locus condition for a circle with distance ratio k
z = complex variable (dimensionless); z₁, z₂ = fixed complex points (dimensionless); k = constant ratio (dimensionless)
Standard Cartesian equation of a circle
x, y = coordinates in the Argand plane (dimensionless); \(x_{c}\), \(y_{c}\) = centre coordinates (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless)
Resulting circle for z₁ = 1 + j, z₂ = 2, k = √2
tips: Do not forget that the modulus is a square root: square both sides carefully, expanding (x−1)² and (y−1)² fully, or the centre will be wrong.
Check the value of k: only when k ≠ 1 is the locus a circle; when k = 1 it is a straight line (perpendicular bisector).
rq: Why is squaring both sides of |z − z₁| = √2|z − z₂| a valid step, and what would you lose if k were 1 instead?

Both sides are non-negative real moduli, so squaring preserves equality and introduces no extraneous solutions. If k = 1 the quadratic terms cancel, leaving a linear equation: the locus is the perpendicular bisector (a straight line), not a circle.
How can you read the centre and radius of a circle from its expanded equation without completing the square by hand?
Expand to x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0; the centre is (−D/2, −E/2) and R² = (D² + E²)/4 − F.
Why does the point z₂ = 2 lie inside the circle here, and what does that imply about the ratio k?

The circle (x−3)²+(y+1)²=4 has radius 2 centred at (3,−1); the point (2,0) is at distance √2 < 2 from the centre, so it is inside. Points near the nearer point z₂ have small |z−z₂|, so k > 1 forces the circle to encircle z₂ and the other point is outside.

units.name: 5.4 General loci: mapped unit circle and ellipse
units.ov: This material finds loci in the Argand plane in two ways. First, it maps the unit circle \(z=e^{j\theta}\) through \(w=(z+1)^2\) to get a parametric image curve. Second, it converts a sum-of-distances condition \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\) into a Cartesian conic and classifies it as an ellipse. Both rely on reading complex expressions as geometry (modulus is distance, argument is angle) and on exact algebra with \(j^2=-1\) and squaring.
must: Parametrise \(|z|=r\) as \(z=re^{j\theta}\), \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). One full period traces the curve exactly once.
The locus of a mapping \(w=f(z)\) is the set of image points as \(z\) traverses a given curve. Substitute the parametrisation to get \(w(\theta)\).
\(w=(e^{j\theta}+1)^2=e^{2j\theta}+2e^{j\theta}+1\), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,w=1+2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,w=2\sin\theta+\sin2\theta=2(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta\).

Shortcut: \(e^{j\theta}+1=2\cos(\theta/2)\,e^{j\theta/2}\), so \(w=2(1+\cos\theta)e^{j\theta}\), i.e. \(r=2(1+\cos\theta)\). This is a cardioid with a cusp at \(w=0\) (at \(\theta=\pi\)) and \(w=4\) at \(\theta=0\). The notes call it a limaçon with an inner loop, but a cardioid has no inner loop.
Use \(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=\cos2\theta\) and \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\) when expanding. Keep \(j^2=-1\); forgetting it gives the wrong imaginary part.
\(|z-a|\) is the distance from \(z\) to \(a\). A locus \(|z-a|+|z-b|=k\) with \(k>|a-b|\) is an ellipse with foci \(a\) and \(b\).
For \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\), write \(z=x+jy\) and isolate one root before squaring. This gives \(2\sqrt{(x-1)^2+y^2}=2-x+y\), and squaring again gives \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\).
Classify a conic \(ax^2+bxy+cy^2+\dots=0\) by \(b^2-4ac\). Here \(4-36=-32<0\), so it is an ellipse. The \(xy\) term means the axes are rotated (here by 45°).
Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions. Check the sign condition \(2-x+y\ge0\) and test a point, e.g. the origin satisfies the distance sum \(1+1=2\).
Ellipse features here: centre \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\), \(a=1\), \(c=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(b=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), major axis along \(y=x\).
conn: Parametrisation with \(e^{j\theta}\) links to trig identities (double angle) and to polar form. A Cartesian curve can be recovered from the parametric equations by eliminating \(\theta\), or by converting to polar form as in the cardioid shortcut.
Modulus as distance links loci to Cartesian conics. Squaring is the bridge, and the discriminant test and extraneous-root check are the follow-up steps.

Mappings of loci: the image of a circle under \(w=f(z)\) can be a different curve (a cardioid here). Compare with the Möbius-type maps seen earlier, where circles map to circles, and with the shifts and scalings in \(z+1\) and the squaring.
Foci and focal sums connect to the standard ellipse \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1\) via \(b^2=a^2-c^2\). A rotation or translation of axes is needed to reach the standard form.
exq: Show that the image of \(|z|=1\) under \(w=(z+1)^2\) has \(u=1+2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\) and \(v=2\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\). Then show that \(|w|=2(1+\cos\theta)\) and \(\arg w=\theta\), and sketch the curve, marking the points for \(\theta=0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\).
Find \(w\) at \(\theta=0,\pi/2,\pi\) for \(w=(e^{j\theta}+1)^2\) and identify the cusp. State the range of \(\theta\) needed to trace the curve once.
Sketch and derive the Cartesian equation of the locus \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\). Show it reduces to \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\) and use \(b^2-4ac\) to confirm it is an ellipse.
For the ellipse \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\), find the centre, the semi-axes and the direction of the major axis. Verify that \(z=0\) and \(z=1+j\) lie on it.
Find the locus \(|z-2|+|z+2|=6\) in Cartesian form. Explain why \(|z-2|+|z+2|=3\) has no locus.

notes.t: More general loci: mapping the unit circle under w = (z+1)^2
pts: Parametrise the unit circle |z| = 1 as z = \(e^{jθ}\), with θ running over one full turn.
Substitute into the mapping to obtain w as a function of θ alone, giving a parametric curve in the complex plane.
Expanding in real and imaginary parts gives the Cartesian-form parametric equations of the image curve.
The image of the unit circle under this mapping is a limaçon, which has a small inner loop-like cusp at the origin.
Plotting by varying θ from 0 to 2π traces the whole image curve exactly once.
defs: Locus (of a mapping)
The set of image points w obtained when the input z traverses a given curve in the z-plane under the mapping w = f(z).
Parametric representation of a circle |z| = r
z = \(re^{jθ}\) with 0 ≤ θ < 2π, where θ is the argument (angle) of z.
eqs: z = complex variable (dimensionless); θ = angle parameter (rad)
Image of the unit circle under w = (z+1)^2
w = image point (dimensionless in pure mathematics); θ = angle parameter (rad)
Real and imaginary parts of the image curve
Re(w) = real part of image; Im(w) = imaginary part; θ = angle parameter (rad)
tips: Expand (\(e^{jθ}\)+1)^2 using cos²θ − sin²θ = cos 2θ, not by treating j as a real number; forgetting j² = −1 gives the wrong imaginary part.
The range of θ must cover exactly one period, 0 ≤ θ < 2π; using a different range or omitting the endpoint changes what is plotted.
rq: Why does choosing z = \(e^{jθ}\) turn a 2D condition |z| = 1 into a single-variable problem?
The modulus condition fixes r = 1, leaving only the angle θ free, so the whole circle is described by one real parameter.
What if θ were allowed to range over 0 to 4π instead of 0 to 2π?
Since \(e^{jθ}\) is periodic with period 2π, the curve would be traced twice; the image would not gain new points.

notes.t: Loci in the Argand plane: ellipse defined by sum of distances to two foci
pts: Write z = x + jy and interpret |z − w| as the distance from the point z to the point w in the Argand plane.
A locus where the sum of distances from z to two fixed points equals a constant (greater than the distance between the points) is an ellipse with those points as foci.
Convert the modulus equation to Cartesian form using the modulus of x + jy, then square to remove the square roots, leaving a general conic equation.
The resulting general conic is classified as an ellipse by the discriminant test.
defs: Locus
The set of all points z in the Argand plane satisfying a given condition, usually represented by a curve or region.
eqs: Locus equation for sum of distances to foci j and 1 equal to 2 (ellipse)
x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless)
Squared form after removing the first square root
General second-degree conic and ellipse test
a, b, c, d, f, g = constant coefficients (dimensionless); x, y as above
tips: Squaring both sides of an equation with two square roots can introduce extraneous solutions; the need to square twice must be handled carefully and the result checked.
Be sure to expand the squared terms fully, including the cross term 2xy, when converting to the general conic form.
rq: Why does the locus |z − j| + |z − 1| = 2 give an ellipse rather than a circle?

Because it is a sum of distances to two distinct fixed points (foci j and 1) equal to a constant greater than the distance between them, which defines an ellipse; a circle requires a fixed distance from a single centre.
Why must the constant 2 be checked against the distance between the foci before concluding it is an ellipse?

The distance between the foci is |j − 1| = √2 ≈ 1.414; since 2 > √2, the locus is a non-degenerate ellipse. If the constant equalled √2 it would be the line segment between the foci, and if smaller it would be empty.
What is the role of the discriminant b² − 4ac in the conic?
It classifies the conic: b² − 4ac < 0 gives an ellipse (or circle), = 0 a parabola, and > 0 a hyperbola.

units.name: 5.5 Complex functions and transformations (w = z³ on a strip)
units.ov: This material covers mapping regions of the complex z-plane to the w-plane through a function w = f(z), using the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 under w = z³ as the worked example. The method is to write z = x + jy, expand to get u(x,y) and v(x,y), then apply this to the boundary lines and trace the image curves. The region's image is bounded by the images of its boundaries. Note that the page 14 expansion contains an error: the imaginary part should be 3x²y − y³, and the notes give the correct real part x³ − 3xy².
must: A complex function maps \(z=x+jy\) to \(w=u+jv=f(z)\); both \(u\) and \(v\) generally depend on both \(x\) and \(y\).
To find the image of a region, map its boundary curves from the z-plane into the w-plane, then decide which side is filled.
\(u = x^3 - 3xy^2\) and \(v = 3x^2y - y^3\) are the real and imaginary parts of \(z^3\).
The strip is \(1\le x\le 2\) with \(y\) unrestricted, so the boundaries are the lines \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), each parameterised by \(y\).
Image of \(x=1\): \(u=1-3y^2\), \(v=3y-y^3\). Image of \(x=2\): \(u=8-6y^2\), \(v=12y-y^3\). Each is a curve in the w-plane parameterised by \(y\).

Check the images of boundaries with key points: e.g. \(y=0\) gives \(w=1\) and \(w=8\) on the real axis; the symmetry \(y\to -y\) gives \(u\) even and \(v\) odd, so the images are symmetric about the real axis.
Alternative polar check: \(z=re^{j\theta}\) gives \(w=r^3e^{3j\theta}\), so moduli are cubed and angles tripled.
State the answer with the strip condition kept explicit, and do not treat \(f(z)\) as real-valued. Sketch the curves on the \(u\)-\(v\) axes (Re w, Im w).
conn: Complex arithmetic and the binomial expansion combine with \(j^2=-1\); sign errors there carry into the whole image curve.
Cartesian parametrisation versus polar form: \(z^3\) is easier to understand geometrically in polar form (angle tripling), but boundary lines \(x=\) const are easier in Cartesian form.
Parametric curves and elimination of the parameter: the images are curves in \((u,v)\), which can be sketched from a table of \(y\) values or by eliminating \(y\).
Mapping boundaries to regions links to conformal mapping ideas, where angles between curves are preserved (except at \(z=0\) for \(z^3\)).
exq: Write \(z=x+jy\) and find \(u\) and \(v\) for \(w=z^3\). Hence find the image of the line \(x=1\), giving the parametric equations in terms of \(y\).
Find the image of the strip \(1\le x\le 2\) under \(w=z^3\). Give the parametric equations of both boundary images and sketch them, marking the points \(w=1\) and \(w=8\).
Find the images of the points \(z=1+j\), \(2+j\) and \(1-j\) under \(w=z^3\), and mark them on your sketch of the w-plane.
Show that the image of \(x=1\) is \(v^2 = (3-y^2)^2y^2\) with \(y^2=(1-u)/3\), and hence eliminate \(y\) to obtain a Cartesian equation relating \(u\) and \(v\).
Find the image of the line \(y=1\) (or \(y = x\)) under \(w=z^3\) and compare with the polar-form method \(w=r^3e^{3j\theta}\).

notes.t: Functions of a complex variable
pts: A complex function maps a complex independent variable z = x + jy to a dependent variable w = u + jv, so both real and imaginary parts of the output generally change.
By convention the dependent variable is written w, with real part u and imaginary part v.
Finding the image of a region means applying w = f(z) to the boundary lines of the region in the z-plane and tracing the resulting curves in the w-plane.
defs: Function of a complex variable
A rule that assigns to each complex number z = x + jy in a set a unique complex number w = f(z); the output w = u + jv is generally complex even when the input is complex.
eqs: w = u + jv = f(z), \quad z = x + jy
z = complex independent variable (dimensionless); w = complex dependent variable (dimensionless); x, y = real parts of z; u, v = real and imaginary parts of w
tips: Do not assume a real-valued function output: f(z) is generally complex, so keep both u and v when converting w = f(z).
Remember the strip is between two vertical lines x = 1 and x = 2 in the z-plane; the boundary images, not individual points, define the answer.
rq: Why must the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 be mapped by considering its two boundary lines x = 1 and x = 2 rather than by testing single points?
The strip is an infinite region; its image is bounded by the images of its edges, so mapping the boundary lines x = 1 and x = 2 (and checking the interior) determines the image region.

notes.t: Complex Transformation w = z³ on a Vertical Strip
pts: Parameterize the z-plane strip by letting z = x + jy with x fixed in [1,2] and y free to vary along the imaginary direction.
Substitute z = x + jy into w = z³ and expand the cube, separating the result into real part u and imaginary part v.
The real part u = x³ − 3xy² and imaginary part v = 3x²y − y³ are obtained by collecting real and imaginary terms of (x + jy)³.
Expanding (x + jy)³ uses j² = −1, so the term 3x(jy)² contributes −3xy² to the real part.
defs: Strip in the z-plane
A region bounded by two vertical lines, here x = 1 and x = 2, with y unrestricted, whose image under the mapping is found by eliminating the parameters.
eqs: Real part of the image of z³
u = real part of w (dimensionless); x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless)
Imaginary part of the image of z³
v = imaginary part of w (dimensionless); x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless)
Cube of a complex number in parametric form
x = real part of z; y = imaginary part of z; j = imaginary unit
tips: Forgetting that j² = −1 when expanding (x + jy)³ leads to a wrong sign on the xy² term in u.
Do not confuse the parameter x (fixed strip boundary) with the free variable y when stating the image; keep the strip condition 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 explicit in the answer.
rq: Why does the term 3xy² appear with a negative sign in the real part u, even though all terms in the binomial expansion look positive?
Because (jy)² = j²y² = −y², so the term 3x(jy)² = −3xy² contributes negatively to the real part.
If x were fixed at 1 and y varied, what kind of curve would the image of the line in the z-plane trace in the w-plane?
The curve given by u = 1 − 3y² and v = 3y − y³, a parametric curve in the w-plane traced as y varies.

units.name: 5.6 Engineering Maths Challenge: NAVIGATE
units.ov: This challenge applies complex-number multiplication to a navigation problem. A transmitter location \(z = X + Yj\) is transformed by a complex factor \((\beta + \alpha j)\), and a real navigation key is extracted from the real and imaginary parts of the result. It tests accurate algebra with \(j^2=-1\), separating real and imaginary parts, and giving the answer in exact form.
must: Signal transformation: \(w = (\beta + \alpha j)z\) with \(z = X + Yj\), so \(w\) comes from complex multiplication
\(j^2 = -1\): this is the step where sign errors most often occur
Expansion: \((\beta+\alpha j)(X+Yj) = (\beta X - \alpha Y) + (\alpha X + \beta Y)j\)
Read off \(\operatorname{Re}(w) = a = \beta X - \alpha Y\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(w) = b = \alpha X + \beta Y\); the \(j\) is not part of the imaginary part
Navigation key: \(K = \operatorname{Im}(w) - \operatorname{Re}(w) = b - a\), a real number
Substituting gives \(K = (\alpha X + \beta Y) - (\beta X - \alpha Y) = (\alpha-\beta)X + (\alpha+\beta)Y\)
Give the answer exactly, as fractions and surds with no decimals, and simplify surds and rationalise denominators where needed
Order matters in the subtraction: imaginary minus real, so check the sign of \(K\)
Quantities are dimensionless, except that \(z\) carries the units of metres from the coordinates; state this if asked
Check the result by substituting simple values or recomputing the product a second way
conn: Complex multiplication links to rotation and scaling in the Argand plane: \(\beta+\alpha j\) has modulus \(\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\) and argument \(\arctan(\alpha/\beta)\), so \(w\) is a rotated and scaled copy of \(z\)
Exact surds arise when \(\alpha,\beta\) or \(X,Y\) are given in polar form or contain roots, which links to exact trigonometric values such as \(\cos 30^\circ=\sqrt3/2\)
Finding \(z\) from a given \(w\) requires complex division and conjugates: \(z = w/(\beta+\alpha j)\)
Equating real and imaginary parts connects this to solving simultaneous equations for unknown \(X, Y\) or \(\alpha, \beta\)
exq: Given \(z = 3 + 2j\) and factor \((1+2j)\), find \(w\) and the key \(K = \operatorname{Im}(w)-\operatorname{Re}(w)\).
Show that for general \(X, Y, \alpha, \beta\), \(K = (\alpha-\beta)X + (\alpha+\beta)Y\).
Take \(\beta = \sqrt3\), \(\alpha = 1\), \(z = 2 + \sqrt3 j\). Find \(K\) exactly, with no decimals.
If \(w = 5 - j\) and the factor is \((2+j)\), find the transmitter location \(z\) and then \(K\).
For \(\alpha=\beta\), find \(K\) in terms of \(X, Y, \alpha\). Interpret the result and find the condition on \(X, Y\) for \(K=0\).

notes.t: Challenge 3: NAVIGATE — transforming a complex signal
pts: The transmitter location is written as a complex number z = X + Yj, with X and Y as its coordinates.
The navigation system multiplies z by the complex factor (β + αj), so w is found by complex multiplication.
Once w is expanded as a + bj, the key is the difference of its imaginary and real parts.
The answer must be exact: keep fractions and surds rather than rounding to decimals.
defs: Navigation key K
For w = a + bj, K = Im(w) − Re(w) = b − a, a real number obtained from the transformed complex signal.
eqs: w = transformed signal (dimensionless); β, α = real transformation constants (dimensionless); z = X + Yj = transmitter location as a complex number (m)
K = navigation key (dimensionless); Im(w) = imaginary part of w; Re(w) = real part of w
tips: Expanding (β + αj)(X + Yj) requires j² = −1; forgetting this sign error changes Re(w).
Give K in exact form (no decimals), as the question explicitly forbids decimal approximations.
rq: Why must w be written in the form a + bj before the key can be found?
Because the key is defined using the separate real part a and imaginary part b, so they must be identified explicitly.
What happens to K if you multiply out (β + αj)z and accidentally swap the real and imaginary parts?
The sign of K reverses, since K = b − a becomes a − b, giving the wrong answer.

units.name: 6.1 AC through R, C, L: phase relationships
units.ov: This material covers how a sinusoidal current i = i₀ sin ωt produces voltages across a resistor, capacitor and inductor, with the amplitude and phase of each. It begins with the time-domain laws (v = Ri, i = C dv/dt, v = L di/dt) and the sin/cos shift identities. It then represents the results as phasors, where reactance (1/ωC or ωL) plays the role of resistance and the ±π/2 shifts become rotations of the voltage phasor relative to the current phasor.
must: Resistor: \(v_R = R i_0 \sin\omega t\), in phase with current, amplitude \(R i_0\)
Capacitor: \(v_C = \frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t - \pi/2) = -\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\cos\omega t\); voltage lags current by \(\pi/2\), so current leads voltage
Inductor: \(v_L = \omega L i_0 \sin(\omega t + \pi/2) = \omega L i_0\cos\omega t\); voltage leads current by \(\pi/2\), so current lags voltage
Reactances: \(X_C = 1/(\omega C)\) (falls with frequency), \(X_L = \omega L\) (rises with frequency), both in ohms
Derivation: for the capacitor integrate \(i = C\,dv/dt\) to get \(v = \frac{1}{C}\int i\,dt\); for the inductor differentiate \(i\) in \(v = L\,di/dt\)

Phasor: a complex number whose modulus is the amplitude and whose argument is the phase; the diagram has \(v_L\) at \(+\pi/2\), \(v_C\) at \(-\pi/2\) and \(v_R\) along the current phasor at angle \(\omega t\)

Identities: \(\sin(\omega t \pm \pi/2)\) gives \(\pm\cos\omega t\) and \(\sin(\omega t - \pi/2) = -\cos\omega t\); use \(\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta\) to convert between forms
Keep signs consistent: dropping the minus in \(v_C\) flips the phase; the phase is a property of the voltage relative to the current, so state which one leads
Use \(\omega = 2\pi f\) in rad/s and angles in radians; the capacitor amplitude divides by \(\omega\) and the inductor amplitude multiplies by \(\omega\)
conn: Differential laws to phasors: \(i = C\,dv/dt\) and \(v = L\,di/dt\) give the \(\mp\pi/2\) shifts because differentiating or integrating a sinusoid shifts its phase by \(\pi/2\) and scales it by \(\omega\) or \(1/\omega\)

Frequency dependence and reactance: \(X_L\) and \(X_C\) vary oppositely with \(\omega\), so questions ask which element dominates at low or high frequency, and their opposite phasors (+π/2 versus −π/2) partly cancel in series
Time-domain graphs and phasor diagrams: the same lead/lag result can be read from the peaks of sin/cos waveforms or from the rotation angle, and questions often ask you to move between the two
Series circuits: a common current is the reference phasor, and the voltages across R, L and C combine as phasors at 0, +π/2 and −π/2 (a step towards impedance and resonance)
exq: A current \(i = 2\sin(1000t)\) A flows through a 10 µF capacitor. Find the amplitude and phase of the capacitor voltage, write \(v_C(t)\), and state which quantity leads.
A 50 mH inductor carries \(i = 0.5\sin(2\pi\cdot 50\,t)\) A. Calculate \(X_L\), write \(v_L(t)\) as a cosine and as a phase-shifted sine, and sketch both waveforms showing the quarter-cycle shift.

Starting from \(i = C\,dv/dt\) with \(i = i_0\sin\omega t\), derive \(v_C\) and show that \(-\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\cos\omega t = \frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)\) using the sine addition identity.

Draw the phasor diagram at \(\omega t = 30^\circ\) for a current through R, L and C in series with \(R=20\,\Omega\), \(X_L=30\,\Omega\), \(X_C=10\,\Omega\) and \(i_0=1\) A. Label each voltage phasor's magnitude and angle.
At what frequency are the capacitor and inductor reactances equal for \(L=10\) mH and \(C=1\) µF? Explain what this implies for the relative phase of \(v_L\) and \(v_C\).

notes.t: Alternating currents in electrical networks (resistor, capacitor, inductor)
pts: A sinusoidal current through a resistor gives a voltage in phase with the current.
For a capacitor, the voltage lags the current by a quarter cycle (π/2), since the voltage is a sine shifted by −π/2.
For an inductor, the voltage leads the current by a quarter cycle (π/2), since the voltage is a sine shifted by +π/2.
The sine and cosine identities for shifts of π/2 convert between sin and cos, showing the phase relationships explicitly.
Voltage–current relations: resistor v = Ri, capacitor i = C dv/dt, inductor v = L di/dt.
defs: Current generator
An ideal source supplying a sinusoidal current i = i0 sin ωt, where i0 is the peak current and ω the angular frequency.
Resistor law
The voltage across a resistor is proportional to the current through it, v = Ri, with no phase difference.
eqs: Voltage across a resistor driven by sinusoidal current
\(v_{R}\) = resistor voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
Voltage across a capacitor driven by sinusoidal current
\(v_{C}\) = capacitor voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s)
Voltage across an inductor driven by sinusoidal current
v_L = \omega L i_0 \cos \omega t = \omega L i_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
\(v_{L}\) = inductor voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
i = current (A); C = capacitance (F); v = voltage (V); t = time (s)
tips: Check the sign: \(v_{C}\) = −(i0/ωC)cos ωt and sin(ωt − π/2) = −cos ωt must be kept consistent; dropping the minus sign flips the phase.
Angles must be in radians: ω is in rad/s and π/2 is a phase in radians, not degrees.
rq: Why does the capacitor voltage lag the current by π/2 while the inductor voltage leads it by π/2?
Because \(v_{C}\) ∝ ∫i dt (integration shifts phase by −π/2), whereas \(v_{L}\) ∝ di/dt (differentiation shifts phase by +π/2).
What happens to the capacitor voltage amplitude if the frequency ω is doubled, for the same peak current?
It halves, since the amplitude i0/(ωC) is inversely proportional to ω.
Why is the resistor voltage in phase with the current while the reactive elements are not?
Ohm's law v = Ri is instantaneous and has no time derivative or integral, so no phase shift arises.

notes.t: Alternating currents in electrical networks (phasors)
pts: For a sinusoidal current through a resistor, voltage is in phase with current, with amplitude R i₀.
Across a capacitor the voltage lags the current by π/2; its amplitude is i₀/(ωC), so capacitive reactance is 1/(ωC).
Across an inductor the voltage leads the current by π/2; its amplitude is ωL i₀, so inductive reactance is ωL.
A phasor is a rotating vector whose length gives amplitude and whose angle gives phase; freezing the rotation at one instant gives a time-invariant representation for steady-state analysis.
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal function: its modulus is the amplitude and its argument is the phase, used to analyse AC circuits in steady state.
eqs: i = instantaneous current (A); \(i_{0}\) = peak current amplitude (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
\(v_{R}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
Voltage across a capacitor (lags current by π/2)
\(v_{C}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s)
Voltage across an inductor (leads current by π/2)
\(v_{L}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
tips: Check the sign of the phase shift: capacitor lags (−π/2), inductor leads (+π/2); mixing these up reverses the circuit's behaviour.
Reactances are amplitude ratios, not phase shifts: ωL and 1/(ωC) carry units of ohms, so ensure ω is in rad/s, not Hz.
rq: Why does the capacitor voltage lag the current by π/2 while the inductor voltage leads it by π/2?

Capacitor voltage is the integral of current (charge builds up after current flows), giving a lag; inductor voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current (L di/dt), and the derivative of sin ωt is cos ωt, which leads by π/2.
What happens to the capacitor's voltage amplitude as frequency increases, and why?
It decreases, since the amplitude i₀/(ωC) is inversely proportional to ω: a higher frequency lets the capacitor charge and discharge more readily, so it opposes current less.
Why does the phasor diagram use a rotating vector instead of just the sine function?
Rotating vectors turn phase differences into angles between arrows, so voltages and currents can be added geometrically or as complex numbers without solving differential equations at each instant.

notes.t: Phase relationships of voltage and current in R, C and L
pts: In a resistor the voltage and current are in phase, so they peak together.
For a capacitor the voltage lags the current by a quarter cycle, so the current leads the voltage by π/2.
For an inductor the voltage leads the current by a quarter cycle, so the current lags the voltage by π/2.
The phasor diagram shows \(v_{L}\) rotated +π/2 and \(v_{C}\) rotated −π/2 relative to the current phasor at angle ωt.
defs: Phase difference
The angular difference between a voltage and a current sinusoid of the same frequency, expressed in radians or degrees, indicating which quantity reaches its peak first.
eqs: \(v_{R}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
\(v_{C}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s)
\(v_{L}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
tips: Watch the sign: the capacitor voltage has −π/2 and the inductor has +π/2; mixing these up reverses the lead/lag answer.
Amplitudes use ω: the capacitor term is \(i_{0}\)/(ωC) (divide by ω) while the inductor term is ωL \(i_{0}\) (multiply by ω).
rq: Why does the capacitor's voltage amplitude fall as frequency rises, while the inductor's rises?
Capacitor amplitude is \(i_{0}\)/(ωC), inversely proportional to ω; inductor amplitude is ωL·\(i_{0}\), proportional to ω.
If the current is known, how can you tell from the phasor diagram which element has the voltage leading the current?
The inductor: \(v_{L}\) is rotated +π/2 (counterclockwise) from i, so its voltage leads the current.

units.name: 6.2 Phasors and complex exponential representation
units.ov: This module shows how sinusoidal currents can be written as the imaginary part of a rotating complex exponential \(i_0e^{j\omega t}\), so that the phase shifts of R, L and C become simple multiplications by complex factors. These factors are the complex impedances, which extend Ohm's law to AC as \(V=ZI\). Euler's formula and the idea that \(j\) is a +90° rotation link the algebra to the physical lead/lag behaviour.
must: Sinusoidal current as the imaginary part of a complex exponential: \(i=i_0\sin\omega t=\operatorname{Im}[i_0e^{j\omega t}]\), with \(I=i_0e^{j\omega t}\) as the complex current
Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), and \(j=e^{j\pi/2}\) so \(j^2=-1\)
Multiplying by \(j\) rotates by +π/2 in the complex plane; multiplying by \(-j\) rotates by −π/2
Generalised Ohm's law: \(V=ZI\), where \(Z\) is the complex impedance (in Ω)
Resistor: \(Z_R=R\), purely real, so voltage is in phase with current
Inductor: \(Z_L=j\omega L\), so voltage leads current by 90° and the amplitude is \(\omega L\,i_0\)
Capacitor: \(Z_C=-j/(\omega C)\), so voltage lags current by 90° and the amplitude is \(i_0/(\omega C)\)
Memory aid for the signs: the inductor has +j (leads) and the capacitor has −j (lags); dropping the minus sign reverses the phase
Use \(\omega=2\pi f\) in rad/s; \(\omega L\) and \(1/(\omega C)\) are reactances in Ω, and they become voltages only after multiplying by the current
The physical voltage is recovered by taking the imaginary part: \(v=\operatorname{Im}[ZI]\), e.g. \(v_L=\operatorname{Im}[j\omega L\,i_0e^{j\omega t}]\)
conn: Euler's formula with the \(j\) rotation: \(j e^{j\omega t}=e^{j(\omega t+\pi/2)}\) turns \(\operatorname{Im}\) into \(\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)=\cos\omega t\), which links the complex factor to the real lead/lag
Impedance and Ohm's law: \(Z\) combines resistance and reactance, so series elements add as \(Z=R+j\omega L-j/(\omega C)\), and its modulus and argument give the amplitude ratio and phase

Reactance depends on frequency: \(\omega L\) grows with ω and \(1/(\omega C)\) falls with ω, so the inductor and capacitor behave opposite ways at low and high frequency, which leads to resonance when \(\omega L=1/(\omega C)\)
Differential equations: the phasor results match \(v_L=L\,di/dt\) and \(v_C=\frac1C\int i\,dt\), since differentiating gives a factor \(j\omega\) and integrating gives \(1/(j\omega)\)
exq: A current \(i=2\sin(100\pi t)\) A flows through a 50 mH inductor. Find \(\omega\), \(Z_L\), the voltage amplitude and the phase relative to the current, and write \(v_L(t)\) as an imaginary part.
A 10 µF capacitor carries \(i=0.5\sin(2\pi\cdot 500\,t)\) A. Calculate the reactance, the peak voltage and the phase shift, and state whether voltage leads or lags.
Show using Euler's formula that multiplying \(i_0e^{j\omega t}\) by \(j\) shifts the phase by +π/2. Hence explain the lead/lag of the voltage for L and C.

A resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C are in series, with \(R=20\,\Omega\), \(L=0.1\) H, \(C=50\,\mu\)F and \(\omega=400\) rad/s. Find the total complex impedance, its magnitude and phase, and the peak voltage for \(i_0=1\) A.
Explain why 1/(ωC) and ωL are impedances rather than voltages, and find the frequency at which their magnitudes are equal for given L and C.

notes.t: Alternating currents and phasor representation of R, C, L using complex exponentials
pts: An alternating current can be written as the imaginary part of a rotating complex exponential, so sinusoidal quantities become simple complex multiplications.
A resistor's voltage is in phase with the current: multiplying by R leaves the phase unchanged.
A capacitor's voltage lags the current by π/2; this appears as multiplication by −j, with amplitude i0/(ωC).
An inductor's voltage leads the current by π/2; this appears as multiplication by +j, with amplitude ωL i0.
Multiplication by j is a rotation by +π/2 in the complex plane, and −j is a rotation by −π/2; this is why the phase shifts of ±π/2 correspond to factors of ±j.
defs: Imaginary unit j
j is defined by j = \(e^{jπ/2}\) = cos(π/2) + j sin(π/2), so j² = −1; it represents a 90° phase rotation in electrical analysis.
Euler's formula
\(e^{jθ}\) = cos θ + j sin θ, relating complex exponentials to sine and cosine.
eqs: Sinusoidal current as imaginary part of complex exponential
i = instantaneous current (A); \(i_{0}\) = peak current amplitude (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); j = imaginary unit
\(v_{C}\) = instantaneous capacitor voltage (V); C = capacitance (F); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A)
\(v_{L}\) = instantaneous inductor voltage (V); L = inductance (H); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A)
\(v_{R}\) = instantaneous resistor voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A)
tips: Do not confuse the sign of the phase shift: capacitor voltage lags (−j, −π/2) while inductor voltage leads (+j, +π/2).
Units trap: ωL is in ohms (Ω) and 1/(ωC) is in ohms (Ω), so the terms are impedances, not voltages, until multiplied by the current amplitude.
rq: Why does multiplying by −j give a capacitor's voltage a lag of π/2 rather than a lead?
Since −j = \(e^{−jπ/2}\), multiplying by it shifts the phase by −π/2, meaning the voltage lags the current by 90°.
What would happen to the capacitor's voltage amplitude if the frequency doubled, and why?
The amplitude i0/(ωC) halves, because capacitive impedance is inversely proportional to ω; the same current produces less voltage at higher frequency.

notes.t: Complex impedances for alternating currents (exponential form)
pts: In exponential form, current is written as a complex quantity I = i₀\(e^{jωt}\), with capital letters used for these complex quantities.
For each element, the voltage equals a complex impedance Z multiplied by the current I, so Ohm's law extends to AC circuits.
A resistor's impedance is purely real and equal to R, so voltage and current are in phase.
An inductor's impedance is jωL, which is imaginary and positive, so the voltage leads the current by 90°.
A capacitor's impedance is −j/(ωC), which is imaginary and negative, so the voltage lags the current by 90°.
defs: Complex impedance (Z)
The ratio of complex voltage to complex current for a circuit element in AC analysis, V = ZI; it generalises resistance to include reactance.
eqs: I = complex current amplitude-phasor expression (A); i₀ = peak current amplitude (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); j = imaginary unit
\(Z_{L}\) = impedance of inductor (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); j = imaginary unit
\(Z_{C}\) = impedance of capacitor (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
tips: Watch the sign: the capacitor impedance is −j/(ωC), not +j/(ωC); dropping the minus sign reverses the phase.
Make sure ω is in rad/s (ω = 2πf); using frequency in Hz gives wrong reactance values.
rq: Why is the resistor impedance purely real, while the inductor and capacitor impedances are purely imaginary?
A resistor dissipates energy in phase with current, so no phase shift occurs; inductors and capacitors store and release energy, producing a 90° phase difference represented by the j factor.
What happens to the capacitor impedance as frequency increases, and why does this make sense physically?
|\(Z_{C}\)| = 1/(ωC) decreases as ω increases, because a capacitor passes high-frequency current more easily since it charges and discharges faster.

units.name: 6.3 Impedance and voltage amplitude of a series circuit
units.ov: This material treats a series RLC circuit driven by a sinusoidal current using complex phasors. Each element has a complex impedance, and these add in series to give Z = R + j(ωL − 1/ωC). Its magnitude gives the voltage amplitude and its argument gives the phase shift, and the physical voltage is recovered as the imaginary part of V = ZI.
must: Series impedance: \(Z = R + j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)\), with real part R and imaginary part the net reactance (inductive minus capacitive)
Impedances add in series because voltages add (KVL): \(V=(Z_L+Z_C+Z_R)I\)
Magnitude: \(|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L-1/\omega C)^2}\), which is Pythagoras on the impedance triangle and equals the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude
Phase angle: \(\tan\phi=\frac{\omega L-1/\omega C}{R}\); φ is the argument of Z, so use arg(Z) and check the quadrant (tan alone is ambiguous, especially if R ≤ 0)
Polar form: \(Z=|Z|e^{j\phi}\); with \(I=i_0e^{j\omega t}\), \(V=|Z|i_0e^{j(\omega t+\phi)}\)
Physical voltage is the imaginary part: \(v=\operatorname{Im}[V]=|Z|i_0\sin(\omega t+\phi)\), which follows from Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\)
Voltage amplitude is \(V_0=i_0|Z|\); keep |Z| (amplitude scaling) separate from φ (phase offset in the sine argument)
Sign of φ: positive when ωL > 1/ωC (inductive, voltage leads current); negative when capacitive (current leads voltage)
Units: \(\omega=2\pi f\) in rad/s, and angles in radians when using \(e^{j\phi}\) and \(\sin(\omega t+\phi)\)
A phasor is a complex number whose magnitude is the amplitude and whose argument is the phase, and \(e^{j\omega t}\) rotates anticlockwise at ω
conn: Phasors and Euler's formula: the rotating exponential \(e^{j(\omega t+\phi)}\) turns into a sine waveform by taking Im, linking complex algebra to the time-domain voltage
Reactance balance and resonance: when \(\omega L = 1/\omega C\), the imaginary part vanishes, so |Z| = R (minimum), φ = 0, and the current amplitude is maximum for a given voltage
Complex arithmetic and the quadrant check: converting Z between Cartesian and polar form needs arg(Z) rather than a bare arctan
Analogy with mechanical systems: mass-spring-damper (L ↔ mass, 1/C ↔ spring stiffness, R ↔ damper) gives the same impedance and phase relations in forced vibration
exq: A series circuit has R = 50 Ω, L = 0.2 H and C = 20 µF driven at f = 50 Hz. Calculate ω, the net reactance, |Z| and φ, and state whether current leads or lags the voltage.
For the circuit in the previous question with i₀ = 0.5 A, write the instantaneous voltage v(t) = |Z| i₀ sin(ωt + φ) and find the peak voltage.
Derive Z = R + j(ωL − 1/ωC) from V = (\(Z_{L}\) + \(Z_{C}\) + \(Z_{R}\))I, and show how V = ZI gives |Z|i₀ \(e^{j(ωt+φ)}\). Explain why the physical voltage is Im[V].
Find the angular frequency at which φ = 0 for R = 10 Ω, L = 5 mH, C = 2 µF. What is |Z| there, and how does it compare with |Z| at ω twice that value?
A student computes φ = arctan(X/R) and gets an answer in the wrong quadrant for a complex impedance with negative real part. Explain the error and the correct method, using Z = −3 + j4 as an example.

notes.t: Impedance of a series RLC circuit driven by an alternating current
pts: The total voltage across a series circuit is the sum of the voltages across each element, so impedances add in the same way.
The impedance of a series RLC circuit is a complex number: the resistance gives the real part and the net reactance (inductive minus capacitive) gives the imaginary part.
The impedance can be written in polar form, with magnitude |Z| and phase angle φ, which describes how the current lags or leads the applied voltage.
The magnitude of impedance combines resistance and reactance as a right-angled triangle (Pythagoras).
The phase angle is found from the ratio of reactance to resistance, and the quadrant must be checked when R is not positive.
defs: Impedance Z
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, Z = V/I, with real part equal to resistance and imaginary part equal to reactance.
Phase angle φ
The argument of the complex impedance, arg(Z) = φ, giving the phase difference between the voltage and current.
eqs: Impedance of a series RLC circuit (complex form)
Z = impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); j = imaginary unit; ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
|Z| = magnitude of impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
φ = phase angle (rad or °); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
Kirchhoff voltage sum in terms of impedances
V = total voltage phasor (V); \(Z_{L}\), \(Z_{C}\), \(Z_{R}\) = impedances of inductor, capacitor, resistor (Ω); I = current phasor (A)
Z = impedance (Ω); |Z| = magnitude (Ω); φ = phase angle (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Phase from tan φ alone is ambiguous: when R ≤ 0 use arg(z) and check the quadrant.
Keep ω in rad/s (ω = 2πf); using frequency in Hz directly in ωL or 1/ωC gives wrong impedance values.
rq: Why does the capacitive term appear with a minus sign and 1/ωC rather than ωC?
Capacitive reactance is \(X_{C}\) = 1/(ωC) and opposes current, so it enters the imaginary part with a negative sign; the inductive reactance ωL enters with a positive sign.
What happens to the imaginary part of Z when ωL = 1/(ωC), and what does this mean for the phase angle?
The imaginary part becomes zero, so Z = R is purely real, φ = 0, and voltage and current are in phase (resonance).
Why can't you simply use arctan(X/R) to get the phase angle when R is negative or zero?
tan φ does not identify the quadrant; with R ≤ 0 the correct angle must be determined from the signs of R and the reactance, using arg(z) rather than the principal arctan.

notes.t: Alternating currents as complex phasors: impedance and voltage amplitude
pts: Voltage is found by multiplying the complex impedance by the complex current phasor; the magnitude of the impedance scales the current amplitude and the argument gives the phase shift.
The real-valued physical voltage is the imaginary part of the complex voltage, so the sinusoidal waveform is recovered by taking Im[V].
Multiplying by \(e^{jωt}\) represents a phasor rotating anticlockwise at angular frequency ω; the phase φ sets its offset from the reference direction.
Euler's formula links the exponential form to sine and cosine, which is why the imaginary part yields the sine waveform.
For a series RLC circuit, the impedance magnitude combines resistance and the net reactance (inductive minus capacitive), giving the voltage amplitude.
defs: Phasor
A complex number whose magnitude is the amplitude and whose argument is the phase of a sinusoidal quantity, used to represent it at a fixed angular frequency ω.
Impedance Z
The complex ratio V/I in an AC circuit, generalising resistance; its magnitude |Z| is the ratio of voltage to current amplitudes and its argument φ is the phase angle between them.
eqs: Complex voltage from impedance and current phasor

V = complex voltage phasor (V); Z = complex impedance (Ω); I = complex current phasor (A); |Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); φ = phase angle (rad); \(i_{0}\) = peak current amplitude (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); j = imaginary unit
v = instantaneous voltage (V); |Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); φ = phase angle (rad)
Voltage amplitude for series RLC circuit
v = instantaneous voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); φ = phase angle (rad)
tips: Do not confuse |Z| with Z: the amplitude relation uses the magnitude, while the phase φ must be kept separately in the sine argument.
Keep angles in radians when using \(e^{jφ}\) and sin(ωt+φ); mixing degrees with ω (rad/s) is a common unit error.
rq: Why is the sine waveform obtained by taking the imaginary part of V rather than the real part?

Because the physical current is taken as i = \(i_{0}\) \(e^{jωt}\) with the real-valued signal being its imaginary part (sine convention); consistency requires voltage to be extracted the same way so the phase relationship between v and i is preserved.
What happens to the impedance magnitude at the frequency where ωL = 1/(ωC)?
The reactance term vanishes, so |Z| = R is at its minimum, the current amplitude is maximised, and the voltage and current are in phase (φ = 0).

units.name: 6.4 Complex impedance of series R–L and RLC circuits
units.ov: This material treats AC circuit elements as complex impedances: R is real, an inductor is \(j\omega L\) and a capacitor is \(1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)\). In series, impedances add (Kirchhoff's voltage law applied to phasors), giving \(Z=R+jX\). The magnitude and phase of Z, read from a phasor diagram, give the current amplitude and the voltage-current phase shift.
must: Impedance is the phasor ratio \(Z=V/I\), a complex number \(R+jX\): the real part is resistance and the imaginary part is reactance (Ω).
Element impedances: \(Z_R=R\), \(Z_L=j\omega L\), \(Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)\).
Series impedances add: \(Z=Z_R+Z_L+Z_C\), because \(V=V_R+V_L+V_C=(Z_R+Z_L+Z_C)I\).
Series R–L: \(Z=R+j\omega L\), \(|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L)^2}\), \(\phi=\tan^{-1}(\omega L/R)\).
Series RLC: \(Z=R+j(\omega L-1/\omega C)\), \(|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L-1/\omega C)^2}\), \(\tan\phi=(\omega L-1/\omega C)/R\).
Phase angle φ is the angle by which voltage leads current. φ>0 means inductive, φ<0 means capacitive, and φ=0 means resistive (resonance when \(\omega L=1/\omega C\)).
Always use \(\omega=2\pi f\) (not f) and convert units (mH→H, μF→F) before computing reactances.
Inductor voltage leads current by \(\pi/2\): \(v_L=\omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\). Capacitor voltage lags by \(\pi/2\).
Polar form \(Z=|Z|e^{j\phi}\) is convenient for \(I=V/Z\): \(|I|=|V|/|Z|\), and the current phase is the voltage phase minus φ.
Keep the sign of the capacitive term (\(-j/\omega C\)), and check the quadrant of φ when using \(\tan^{-1}\), since it is only automatically correct for R>0.
conn: Phasor diagram and algebra: the vector sum of \(Z_R\) (real axis) and \(Z_L\), \(Z_C\) (imaginary axis) gives the same \(|Z|\) and φ as the rectangular-form calculation. Use one to check the other.
Impedance and Ohm's law: \(I=V/Z\) links |Z| to the current amplitude and φ to the phase shift, and from there to the time-domain \(v(t)\), \(i(t)\) and the individual element voltages.

Frequency dependence and resonance: ω enters through \(\omega L\) and \(1/\omega C\), so the circuit changes from capacitive to inductive as frequency rises, passing φ=0 and minimum |Z|=R at \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\).

Kirchhoff's voltage law in complex form: the element voltages add as phasors, not as magnitudes, so \(V\neq V_R+V_L+V_C\) in magnitude. In an RLC circuit, \(V_L\) and \(V_C\) can individually exceed the supply voltage.
exq: A coil of L = 41.3 mH is in series with R = 20 Ω on a 50 Hz supply. Find Z in rectangular and polar form, |Z| and φ, and state whether the current lags or leads the voltage.

A series RLC circuit has R = 50 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 20 μF and is driven at 100 Hz with a 10 V rms supply. Calculate the total impedance, the rms current, the phase angle, and the voltage across each element.
For the same RLC circuit, find the frequency at which the impedance is purely real, and the current and phase angle there. Comment on the voltages across L and C.

A series R–L circuit with \(i=i_0\sin\omega t\) is considered. Derive expressions for \(v_R\), \(v_L\) and the supply voltage v in the time domain, and show that the supply leads the current by \(\tan^{-1}(\omega L/R)\).

Sketch the phasor (impedance) diagram for a series RLC circuit when (a) \(\omega L>1/\omega C\) and (b) \(\omega L<1/\omega C\). Explain how the sign of φ differs and why it matters for the phase between V and I.

notes.t: Complex impedance of series R–L elements in AC circuits
pts: Impedance of an inductor is j\omega L, purely imaginary, so it shifts voltage phase relative to current.
Series impedances add: total voltage is the sum of element voltages, so the impedances sum.
The magnitude |Z| and phase φ of the total impedance are found from the real (R) and imaginary (ωL) parts, shown as a phasor diagram.
In the phasor diagram, \(Z_{R}\) lies on the real axis and \(Z_{L}\) on the imaginary axis; Z is their vector sum at angle φ.
defs: Complex impedance Z
The ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current in an AC circuit, Z = V/I, written as a complex number with real part (resistance) and imaginary part (reactance).
Phase angle φ of impedance
The angle of Z in the complex plane, φ = tan⁻¹(Im Z / Re Z), giving the phase difference between voltage and current.
eqs: \(Z_{L}\) = impedance of inductor (Ω); \(Z_{R}\) = impedance of resistor (Ω); Z = total impedance (Ω)
Impedance of a series R–L element
Z = complex impedance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H); R = resistance (Ω); j = imaginary unit
|Z| = magnitude of impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H)
φ = phase angle (rad); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H); R = resistance (Ω)
\(v_{L}\) = inductor voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
tips: Watch units: convert mH to H (41.3 mH = 41.3 × 10⁻³ H) and ensure ω = 2πf, not f, before computing ωL.
The phase angle from tan⁻¹ gives the correct quadrant only when R > 0 and ωL > 0; check the sign for other element combinations.
rq: Why does the inductor's impedance have a j in front of it while the resistor's does not?

The inductor voltage leads the current by 90°, and multiplying by j represents a 90° phase rotation in the complex plane, whereas the resistor voltage is in phase with current so its impedance is real.
If the frequency doubled, what would happen to |Z| and φ for this element?
The inductive reactance ωL doubles, so |Z| increases and φ increases (moves closer to 90°), since φ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R).
Why must impedances be added as complex numbers rather than as magnitudes?
Because the real and imaginary parts represent different phase relationships; adding magnitudes ignores phase, so the correct sum of complex impedances gives the true total magnitude and phase.

notes.t: Complex impedance of series RLC circuits
pts: In a series circuit the total impedance is the sum of the resistor, inductor and capacitor impedances, which adds voltages phasor-wise.
Inductive reactance is positive on the imaginary axis (ωL) while capacitive reactance is negative (−1/ωC), so they partly cancel.
Impedance can be written in rectangular form R + jX or polar form |Z|\(e^{jφ}\); the magnitude and phase follow from the real and imaginary parts.
Angular frequency ω = 2πf links the frequency of the supply to the reactances of L and C.
defs: Impedance Z
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, Z = R + jX, measured in ohms; its real part is resistance and its imaginary part is reactance.
Angular frequency ω
ω = 2πf, where f is the supply frequency in hertz; it is measured in rad/s.
eqs: Total impedance of a series RLC circuit (rectangular form)
Z = total impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
|Z| = magnitude of impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
φ = phase angle (rad or °); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); R = resistance (Ω)
|Z| = magnitude (Ω); φ = phase angle (rad); j = imaginary unit
Kirchhoff voltage sum in complex form
V = V_L + V_C + V_R = (Z_L + Z_C + Z_R)\,I
V = supply voltage phasor (V); \(V_{L}\), \(V_{C}\), \(V_{R}\) = voltage phasors across L, C, R (V); \(Z_{L}\), \(Z_{C}\), \(Z_{R}\) = impedances (Ω); I = current phasor (A)
tips: Use ω = 2πf, not f, in every reactance calculation; using f gives a wrong answer by a factor of 2π.
Keep the sign of the capacitive term: 1/(jωC) becomes −j/(ωC), and forgetting the minus sign changes the phase angle.
rq: Why does the capacitor's impedance carry a negative imaginary sign while the inductor's is positive?
Inductor voltage leads current by 90°, giving +jωL; capacitor current leads voltage by 90°, so 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC).
What happens to the net reactance ωL − 1/(ωC) when the supply frequency is at the value where ωL = 1/(ωC)?
The reactance is zero, so Z = R is purely real and the current is in phase with the supply (resonance).
Why can't you simply add the magnitudes |\(Z_{R}\)| + |\(Z_{L}\)| + |\(Z_{C}\)| to get the total impedance?
The components are out of phase; impedances must be added as complex numbers, then the magnitude taken with Pythagoras.

units.name: 6.5 Series and parallel impedance combinations
units.ov: This material covers how to combine complex impedances in AC networks: add them for series, add reciprocals for parallel, and reduce mixed networks stepwise to a single impedance \( a + jb \). Everything rests on complex arithmetic, especially rationalising reciprocals with the complex conjugate. The same rules as for resistors apply, but with phasor-valued \( Z = R + jX \).
must: Series: \( Z = Z_1 + Z_2 \); add real and imaginary parts separately
Parallel: \( \frac{1}{Z} = \frac{1}{Z_1} + \frac{1}{Z_2} \), so \( Z = \left(\frac{1}{Z_1}+\frac{1}{Z_2}\right)^{-1} \); never add parallel impedances directly
Complex impedance is \( Z = R + jX \) in \( \Omega \), with R the resistance and X the reactance
Reduce a mixed network stepwise: combine the parallel pair first, then add the series element (e.g. \( Z = Z_1 + (1/Z_2 + 1/Z_3)^{-1} \))
Rationalise by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator: \( \frac{1}{a+jb} = \frac{a-jb}{a^2+b^2} \)
Never invert the real and imaginary parts separately: \( 1/(a+jb) \ne 1/a + 1/(jb) \)
Track the sign of j carefully, using \( j^2=-1 \) and the conjugate sign flip
Identify the configuration (series or parallel) before combining; the two rules are not interchangeable
Give the final answer in rectangular form \( a+jb \) with units of \( \Omega \); reciprocals (admittance) are in S
conn: Rationalising with the conjugate links complex arithmetic to the parallel formula: each \( 1/Z \) must be converted to rectangular form before the reciprocals can be summed
Reactances of R, L and C (\( R,\ j\omega L,\ 1/(j\omega C) = -j/\omega C \)) supply the \( Z_i \) values that are then combined in series or parallel
The total impedance converts to magnitude and phase \( |Z|,\ \phi=\tan^{-1}(b/a) \), which then gives current via \( I = V/Z \) and power factor
Stepwise network reduction (parallel then series) is the same structure as in resistor networks and prepares for voltage/current division and Thevenin-type analysis
exq: Two impedances \( Z_1 = 1 + j \) \( \Omega \) and \( Z_2 = 1 - j \) \( \Omega \) are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent impedance in the form \( a+jb \).

In a network, \( Z_2 \) and \( Z_3 \) are in parallel and this pair is in series with \( Z_1 \). Given \( Z_1 = 2 + j1 \), \( Z_2 = 5 - j5 \), \( Z_3 = 5 + j5 \) (all \( \Omega \)), find the total impedance \( Z \).
Rationalise and evaluate \( (0.3 - j0.3)^{-1} \), showing the conjugate multiplication, and state its units if it is interpreted as an admittance.

A 10 \( \Omega \) resistor is in series with the parallel combination of an inductor (\( j10\ \Omega \)) and a capacitor (\( -j5\ \Omega \)) at a given frequency. Find the total impedance, its magnitude and its phase angle.

Explain the error in computing the parallel combination of \( Z_1 \) and \( Z_2 \) as \( Z_1 + Z_2 \) or as \( 1/Z_1 + 1/Z_2 \), and show the correct numerical result for \( Z_1 = 3 + j4 \), \( Z_2 = 3 - j4 \).

notes.t: Complex impedance of series and parallel networks
pts: Impedances in series add directly: the total impedance is the sum of the individual complex impedances.
Impedances in parallel combine through their reciprocals: the reciprocal of the total impedance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual impedances.
Complex impedances are handled with complex-number arithmetic, so rationalising by the complex conjugate is used to divide complex numbers into real and imaginary parts.
A combined network is reduced stepwise: first the series pair, then the parallel combination, giving the final impedance in rectangular form a + jb.
defs: Series impedance
For elements connected in series, the equivalent impedance is the sum of the individual complex impedances, Z = Z₁ + Z₂.
Parallel impedance
For elements connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the equivalent impedance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual impedances.
eqs: Equivalent impedance of two elements in series
Z = equivalent impedance (Ω); Z₁, Z₂ = individual complex impedances (Ω)
Equivalent impedance of two elements in parallel
Z = equivalent impedance (Ω); Z₁, Z₂ = individual complex impedances (Ω)
j = imaginary unit (dimensionless); result in S (siemens)
tips: Do not add impedances in parallel directly; always invert each impedance, add, then invert the result, otherwise the answer is wrong.
When rationalising a complex reciprocal, multiply by the complex conjugate of the denominator, and keep track of the j sign (for example (5 − j5)(5 + j5) = 50).
rq: Why can the series and parallel rules not be swapped, i.e. why do we add reciprocals for parallel but not for series?
Series elements share the same current, so their voltage drops add and impedances add. Parallel elements share the same voltage, so their currents add, and admittances (reciprocals of impedance) add.
Why is the equivalent impedance of Z₁ and Z₂ in parallel less than either impedance alone when both are of similar size?
Parallel connection provides an additional path for current, so the combined impedance is smaller than each individual branch impedance, as the reciprocal sum is larger.
What is the first step to convert 1/(5 − j5) into real and imaginary parts, and why does it work?
Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate (5 + j5); the denominator becomes the real number 50, so the result separates into real and imaginary parts.

notes.t: Series and parallel impedance combination in AC networks
pts: Impedances of elements in series add directly, giving the total impedance of the branch.
Impedances of elements in parallel combine via the sum of reciprocals; the total is the reciprocal of that sum.
Complex impedances are handled with complex arithmetic: reciprocals of complex numbers are computed first, then the result is inverted.
For the network in Figure 3.23, Z2 and Z3 are in parallel and that combination is in series with Z1.
defs: Complex impedance
The opposition to alternating current in a circuit element, written as a complex number \( Z = R + jX \) in ohms, where R is resistance and X is reactance.
eqs: \( Z \) = total impedance (\( \Omega \)); \( Z_1, Z_2 \) = individual impedances (\( \Omega \))
\( Z \) = total impedance (\( \Omega \)); \( Z_1, Z_2 \) = individual impedances (\( \Omega \))
\( Z \) = total impedance (\( \Omega \)); \( Z_1, Z_2, Z_3 \) = element impedances (\( \Omega \))
tips: Do not add reciprocals of impedances in series or add impedances in parallel; check which configuration you have before combining.
Keep complex arithmetic careful: for \( (0.3 - j0.3)^{-1} \), multiply by the conjugate to get \( 1.67 + j1.67 \) rather than inverting the real and imaginary parts separately.
rq: Why can't you simply add Z2 and Z3 when they are in parallel?
Parallel elements share the same voltage, so admittances (reciprocals of impedance) add, not impedances; the total is the reciprocal of the summed reciprocals.
Why is Z1 added directly to the parallel combination rather than combined with it by reciprocals?
Z1 is in series with the parallel pair, so it carries the same current and its impedance adds directly to the parallel group's impedance.

units.name: 6.6 Parallel LC circuit and resonance
units.ov: This material derives the equivalent impedance of an ideal parallel LC circuit by adding the capacitor and inductor admittances. It shows that the reactances cancel at \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\), where the impedance magnitude diverges. Normalising frequency as \(x=\omega/\omega_0\) gives a compact, dimensionless form that makes the resonance peak at \(x=1\) easy to see. The notes also mention that resonators of this type are used in quantum-computing qubit readout.
must: Parallel elements combine by adding admittances: \(\frac{1}{Z_1}=\frac{1}{Z_C}+\frac{1}{Z_L}\). Adding impedances directly is a common error.
Element impedances: \(Z_C=\frac{1}{j\omega C}\) and \(Z_L=j\omega L\), so the admittances are \(j\omega C\) and \(\frac{1}{j\omega L}\).
Equivalent impedance: \(Z_1=j\frac{\omega L}{1-\omega^2 LC}\).
Resonant angular frequency: \(\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), in rad/s. Convert with \(f_0=\omega_0/2\pi\) when Hz is required.
At \(\omega_0\) the inductive and capacitive susceptances cancel, so the admittance is zero and the impedance diverges (an open circuit for an ideal LC).
Normalised form: \(Z_1(x)=\frac{j\omega_0 L\,x}{1-x^2}\) with \(x=\omega/\omega_0\). Use \(\omega_0^2LC=1\) to derive it.
Behaviour either side of resonance: for \(x<1\), \(Z_1\) is positive imaginary (inductive); for \(x>1\), it is negative imaginary (capacitive). The sign flips through the pole at \(x=1\).
Limits: as \(x\to0\), \(Z_1\to0\) (the inductor shorts the circuit); as \(x\to\infty\), \(Z_1\to0\) (the capacitor shorts it).
Always use \(\omega\) in rad/s when forming \(x=\omega/\omega_0\). Mixing Hz and rad/s is a common slip.
Parallel LC is the opposite of series LC: parallel gives maximum impedance at resonance, series gives minimum (zero).
conn: Complex impedance and admittance: \(Z_L=j\omega L\) and \(Z_C=1/(j\omega C)\) feed into the parallel rule, so the algebra (common denominators, \(1/j=-j\)) must be fluent.
Resonance and normalisation: \(\omega_0\) links component values to the peak position, and \(x\) turns any \(L\), \(C\) combination into one universal curve scaled by \(\omega_0 L\).

Impedance to circuit response: with a source of fixed amplitude, large \(|Z_1|\) near resonance means small supply current and large voltage. This links to filters (band-stop or tank circuits) and to phase (the inductive-to-capacitive sign change).
Parallel LC and series LC compared: questions often contrast the two, or place them in a larger network, which requires choosing between admittance and impedance addition.
exq: Derive \(Z_1=j\omega L/(1-\omega^2LC)\) for a parallel LC circuit by adding admittances, then show that it can be written as \(Z_1(x)=j\omega_0 L\,x/(1-x^2)\).
A parallel LC circuit has \(L=10\,\mu\)H and \(C=100\) pF. Calculate \(\omega_0\) and \(f_0\), then find \(Z_1\) at \(x=0.5\) and \(x=2\), stating whether each is inductive or capacitive.
Sketch \(|Z_1|\) and the phase of \(Z_1\) against \(x\) from 0 to 3. Explain the behaviour at \(x\to0\), \(x=1\) and \(x\to\infty\) in physical terms.
Explain why adding impedances directly for parallel elements gives the wrong result. Show that doing so for L and C would give a resonance that does not match the correct \(\omega_0\).
At what frequency (in Hz) does a parallel LC circuit with \(L=2\) mH block a signal if the capacitor is 0.5 µF? Describe what happens to the supply current at that frequency.

notes.t: Parallel LC circuit impedance and resonance
pts: The equivalent impedance of a parallel LC circuit is found by adding admittances of the capacitor and inductor.
Parallel LC impedance becomes very large at the resonant frequency, where the reactances cancel.
Normalising frequency by ω₀ gives a compact form for the impedance and shows a sharp peak at x = 1.
This simple LC circuit underpins today's quantum computers, since resonators of this type are used in qubit readout and control.
defs: Resonant frequency ω₀
The angular frequency at which the parallel LC circuit's reactances cancel, giving a maximum impedance; ω₀ = 1/√(LC).
Normalised angular frequency x
The ratio of the operating angular frequency to the resonant frequency, x = ω/ω₀, used to write impedance in dimensionless form.
eqs: Equivalent impedance of parallel LC circuit
Z₁ = equivalent impedance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
Z₁ = equivalent impedance (Ω); \(Z_{C}\) = capacitor impedance (Ω); \(Z_{L}\) = inductor impedance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); L = inductance (H)
ω₀ = resonant angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
Z₁(x) = impedance as function of x (Ω); ω₀ = resonant angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); x = ω/ω₀ (dimensionless)
tips: Combine parallel elements using admittances (1/Z), not impedances directly; adding impedances in parallel is a common error.
Remember that ω₀ = 1/√(LC) uses angular frequency in rad/s, not frequency in Hz, when normalising x = ω/ω₀.
rq: Why does the impedance peak sharply at x = 1, and what happens to the current drawn from the source there?
At ω₀ the capacitor and inductor admittances cancel (jωC and 1/(jωL) sum to zero), so the denominator 1 − x² goes to zero and |Z₁| is maximal; the circuit draws almost no current from the source.
Why is the impedance written as a purely imaginary quantity?
Both ideal capacitor and inductor are reactive elements with no resistance, so the impedance has only a j (imaginary) component and no real part, meaning no power is dissipated.

units.name: 7.1 3D coordinates, position vector length and direction cosines
units.ov: This module covers locating a point in 3D with Cartesian coordinates, the position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) from the origin, its length from Pythagoras extended to 3D, and direction cosines giving its orientation relative to the axes. The ideas connect because the components \(x,y,z\) give both the length and, divided by the length, the direction cosines. These then obey the unit-length identity and feed into right-triangle problems such as theodolite sightings.
must: Length of a position vector: \(r=|OP|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\), always non-negative, with units (m).
Direction cosines: \(l=\cos\alpha=x/r,\ m=\cos\beta=y/r,\ n=\cos\gamma=z/r\), with angles measured from the positive x, y, z axes.
Unit-length identity: \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\); use it as a check, and to find a missing direction cosine from two known ones.
Always divide by the length \(r\) (after taking the square root), not by \(r^2\) or a coordinate.
Angles come from inverse cosine: \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}(l)\), etc.; check the calculator is in degree or radian mode as required.
Position vector components are the coordinates of P: \(\mathbf{r}=x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}+z\mathbf{k}\), and the vector is the space diagonal of the box with sides \(x,y,z\).
Right-handed axis convention (x, y, z; also written \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) in indexed notation).
Theodolite or height problems: \(\gamma\) is measured from the z-axis, so the elevation above horizontal is \(\pi/2-\gamma\), and \(|TP|=|OT|\tan(\pi/2-\gamma)\).
Keep units consistent and give exact forms where they arise (e.g. \(|TP|=50\sqrt3\) m).
conn: Length and direction cosines: \(r\) is the denominator in each of \(l,m,n\), so an error in \(r\) carries into all three angles and breaks the \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\) check.
Unit-vector link: \((l,m,n)\) are the components of \(\mathbf{r}/r\), so \(\mathbf{r}=r(l\mathbf{i}+m\mathbf{j}+n\mathbf{k})\), connecting to vector resolution and force components.
Direction cosine angles and trigonometry: the angle from the z-axis, \(\gamma\), converts to an elevation angle \(\pi/2-\gamma\) for right-triangle height or distance problems.
The identity lets you find a missing angle from two known angles, but note the sign ambiguity of the third cosine, which is fixed by the quadrant or octant of the point.
exq: Point P has coordinates (3, 4, 12) m. Find \(|OP|\), the direction cosines \(l,m,n\), the angles \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\), and verify \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\).
A vector makes angles \(\alpha=60^\circ\) and \(\beta=45^\circ\) with the x and y axes. Find the possible values of \(\gamma\) and the direction cosine n, explaining why there are two solutions.
A position vector has length 10 m with direction cosines \(l=0.5\), \(m=0.5\) and n positive. Find n and the coordinates of P.

A theodolite at O sights a point P with \(\gamma=30^\circ\) from the vertical axis and the horizontal distance \(|OT|\) is known. Using \(|TP|=|OT|\tan(\pi/2-\gamma)\), find the height of P, and discuss the effect of using \(\gamma\) directly.
Show that for any point P(x, y, z) the direction cosines satisfy \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\), and use this to state the unit vector along OP.

notes.t: Cartesian coordinates and position vector magnitude
pts: A point P in 3D space is located by its coordinates along three mutually perpendicular axes (x, y, z) measured from the origin O.
The position vector r runs from the origin O to the point P, and its length equals the straight-line distance from O to P.
Right-angled construction: projecting P onto each axis gives the components x, y, z, which form the sides of a rectangular box whose space diagonal is r.
The same geometry applies with generic axis labels x1, x2, x3, so coordinates may be written with subscripts for indexed notation.
The right-hand figure shows a screw-like rotation about the x axis, indicating the handedness (right-handed) convention of the axis system.
defs: Cartesian coordinates
An ordered set of perpendicular distances (x, y, z) from the origin to a point, measured along three mutually perpendicular axes that meet at the origin O.
Position vector
The vector r from the origin O to a point P, whose components are the Cartesian coordinates of P.
eqs: Magnitude (length) of the position vector r from origin to P(x,y,z)
r = distance from origin O to P (m); x = coordinate along x axis (m); y = coordinate along y axis (m); z = coordinate along z axis (m)
tips: Squaring removes signs, so r is always non-negative; do not drop the square root when stating the magnitude.
Keep consistent units (e.g. metres) across x, y, z before computing r, and state the unit in the answer.
rq: Why does the formula for r come from Pythagoras applied twice rather than once?
First, the diagonal in the xy-plane gives \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); then this diagonal and z form a right-angled triangle, so \(r=\sqrt{(x^2+y^2)+z^2}\).
What would happen to r if one coordinate were negative, e.g. P(3, -4, 0)?
Nothing changes in magnitude because the coordinates are squared, so \(r=\sqrt{9+16}=5\); the sign only indicates the side of the axis.
Why must the axes be mutually perpendicular for the simple formula to hold?
Right angles make the projections form rectangular sides, allowing Pythagoras to apply; non-perpendicular axes would require a different distance formula.

notes.t: Vectors: length of a position vector and direction cosines (Cartesian)
pts: The length (magnitude) of OP is found from the Pythagorean extension of the coordinates: r² = x² + y² + z².
Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles the position vector makes with the x, y and z axes; each is the component divided by the length r.
The three direction cosines of a vector satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1, which provides a check on the working.
