Because a·b is a scalar, and the dot product requires two vectors, so there is no valid second dot product with c; associativity needs three objects of the same type that can be grouped.
If a·b = b·a, why can't we say the same about the order in a·b·c?
Commutativity concerns swapping two vectors in one dot product; grouping in a·b·c is not meaningful at all, so the question of order of grouping does not arise.

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product: distributive laws
pts: Multiplying a dot product by a scalar λ can be applied to either vector or to the product itself; all give the same result.
The dot product distributes over vector addition, so a·(b+c) can be expanded term by term.
The proof works componentwise: expand each aᵢ(bᵢ+cᵢ) and regroup the sums.
The dot product can be computed from components or from magnitudes and the angle between vectors.
defs: Scalar product (dot product)
For vectors a and b, the scalar a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between them; the result is a number, not a vector.
eqs: λ = scalar (dimensionless); a, b = vectors (units of their quantity)
aᵢ, bᵢ = components of a and b (same units as each vector)
tips: Do not confuse the dot product (scalar result) with the cross product (vector result).
Ensure the angle θ in |a||b|cos θ is measured between the vectors tail-to-tail.
rq: Why does the dot product of two vectors give a scalar rather than a vector?
Each term aᵢbᵢ is a number, and the three numbers are summed; equivalently |a||b|cos θ is a scalar, so no direction remains.
If a·b = 0 for nonzero vectors, what can you conclude about their geometry?
cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°: the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).

notes.t: Powers of a vector: dot product of a vector with itself
pts: The dot product of a vector with itself equals the sum of the squares of its components.
Because the angle between a vector and itself is zero, a·a equals the squared magnitude of the vector.
The unit vectors i, j, k each square to 1 under the dot product.
eqs: Square of a vector's magnitude via the dot product
a = vector; a₁, a₂, a₃ = components of a (dimensionless or same unit as a); |a| = magnitude of a (same unit as a)
Unit vector squares under dot product
i, j, k = unit basis vectors (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse a·a = |a|² with a·a = |a|; the dot product gives the squared magnitude.
Remember cos 0 = 1 when simplifying a·a, otherwise the result is wrong by a factor.
rq: Why does a·a give the magnitude squared rather than just the magnitude?
The dot product of a vector with itself is |a||a|cos 0 = |a|²; it returns the squared length, so a square root is needed to recover |a|.
Why is the angle term cos 0 in a·a?
A vector makes zero angle with itself, and cos 0 = 1, so the product reduces to |a|².

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product and the law of cosines for vectors
pts: The squared magnitude of a sum of two vectors expands using the cosine of the angle between them.
The squared magnitude of a difference is found by dotting the difference with itself and expanding.
The dot product of two vectors equals the product of their magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them, so the cross terms carry the angle information.
Since a·b = |a||b|cos θ, the sign of the cross term depends on whether θ is acute or obtuse, which changes whether |a+b| or |a−b| is larger.
defs: Scalar (dot) product
For vectors a and b with angle θ between them, a·b = |a||b|cos θ; it is a scalar obtained by multiplying the magnitudes by the cosine of the included angle.
eqs: Squared magnitude of the sum of two vectors
|\mathbf{a}|, |\mathbf{b}| = magnitudes of the vectors (m or any consistent unit); \theta = angle between a and b (rad or degrees)
Squared magnitude of the difference of two vectors
|\mathbf{a}|, |\mathbf{b}| = magnitudes of the vectors (m or any consistent unit); \theta = angle between a and b (rad or degrees)
Dot product expansion used in the derivation
\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} = vectors; \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = scalar product (units of the product of the vector units)
tips: Do not confuse the dot product a·b (a scalar) with the cross product a×b (a vector); only the dot product appears in these expansions.
Check the angle convention: θ must be the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail, and |a−b| uses the same θ as the triangle with sides a, b, and a−b.
rq: Why does the cross term change sign between |a+b|² and |a−b|²?
Because the expansion of (a−b)·(a−b) contains −2a·b while (a+b)·(a+b) contains +2a·b, and the dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ carries the sign.
What happens to |a+b|² when θ = 90°?
cos 90° = 0, so |a+b|² = |a|² + |b|², which is Pythagoras' theorem for perpendicular vectors.
What if θ is obtuse (e.g. 120°)? Which squared magnitude is larger?
cos θ < 0 makes the cross term negative, so |a−b|² > |a+b|².

units.name: 8.5 Magnitudes and angles using the dot product
units.ov: This material uses the scalar (dot) product to find vector magnitudes and angles between vectors. The key link is \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}=|\mathbf{v}|^2\), together with \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\). Expanding combined vectors such as \(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\) or \(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}\) lets you compute magnitudes and then the angle between the combined vectors. The notes are fragmentary and the specific values for a and b are not given, so the numbers below come only from the worked-example hints.
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), so \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}\)
Magnitude from the dot product: \(|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\)
Magnitude of a difference (law of cosines): \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{|3\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2-2|3\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta}\)
Scaling: \(|k\mathbf{a}|=|k||\mathbf{a}|\), so \(|3\mathbf{a}|=3|\mathbf{a}|\) (the notes' example gives 9, not 3)
Sign of the cross term: subtraction gives \(-2|3\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\). Dropping the minus gives \(\sqrt{81+4+30}=\sqrt{115}\), which is wrong
Angle between combined vectors: \(\cos\phi=\dfrac{(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b})\cdot(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})}{|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}||3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|}\)

Expand first: use the distributive property of the dot product, \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2\), to get the numerator and the magnitudes of the combined vectors
Find the magnitudes of the combined vectors, not of a and b separately, before dividing
Simplify surds: \(\sqrt5\cdot\sqrt55=\sqrt{275}=5\sqrt{11}\); watch the coefficient 3 when expanding
Angle units: state whether the answer is in degrees or radians and check the calculator mode
conn: The law of cosines and the dot product expansion \(|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2=|\mathbf{u}|^2+|\mathbf{v}|^2-2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) are the same result, so you can use either route to check an answer
The angle formula needs the dot product (numerator) and the magnitudes (denominator), and both come from the same expansion of the combined vectors
Scaling and sign errors (\(|3\mathbf{a}|\), the minus cross term) feed into the angle calculation, so one slip in the magnitude ruins the angle
Physical uses: work done \(W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}\) and resolving a force along a direction use the same cosine relation
exq: Given \(|\mathbf{a}|=3\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=2\) and the angle between them, find \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\). Show the law of cosines step and the effect of the sign of the cross term.

Given \(|\mathbf{a}|\), \(|\mathbf{b}|\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\), find the angle between \(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}\) and \(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\). Give the exact cosine, simplifying the surds, then the angle in degrees.

Show that \(|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2=|\mathbf{u}|^2+|\mathbf{v}|^2-2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) from \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}=|\mathbf{v}|^2\), and use it to find \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) for given vectors in component form.

For given component vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), find \(|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}|\), \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) and the angle between them, and check that the vectors are not perpendicular.
A force \(\mathbf{F}\) moves an object through displacement \(\mathbf{d}\), both given in components. Find the angle between them and the work done.

notes.t: Scalar product: finding the magnitude of 3a − b
pts: The magnitude of a difference of vectors follows from the law of cosines using the angle between them.
Scaling a vector by k multiplies its magnitude by |k|, so |3a| = 3|a|.
The cross term uses the angle θ between a and b; its cosine is taken from the scalar product value.
eqs: Magnitude of the difference of two vectors (law of cosines form)
|3a − b| = magnitude of resultant vector (m or same unit as a, b); |3a| = magnitude of 3a (same unit as a); |b| = magnitude of b (same unit as b); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °)
tips: Do not write |3a| = 3 — the scalar multiplies the magnitude, giving 9 here.
Check the sign of the cross term: the subtraction gives −2|3a||b| cos θ; forgetting the minus sign gives the wrong answer (√(81+4+30)=√115).
rq: Why does |3a| equal 9 rather than 3 when |a| = 3?
Multiplying a vector by the scalar 3 multiplies its length by 3, so |3a| = 3 × |a| = 3 × 3 = 9.
What would change in the final result if the angle θ were 90° instead of the value used here?
cos 90° = 0, so the cross term −2·9·2·cos θ vanishes and the magnitude becomes √(81 + 4) = √85.

notes.t: Angle between two vectors using the scalar product
pts: The angle between two vectors follows from the scalar product divided by the product of their magnitudes.
Magnitudes of combined vectors must be found first, using the square root of the dot product with itself.
Square roots of products can be combined under a single root, which simplifies the denominator.
eqs: Cosine of the angle between two vectors via scalar product
φ = angle between the vectors (rad or °); a, b = vectors; · = scalar product; |v| = magnitude of v (same units as the vector components)
tips: Do not forget to expand the vectors (e.g. 3a − b) before taking the magnitude; magnitudes are of the combined vectors, not of a and b separately.
Check the denominator simplification: √5·√55 = √275 is valid, but leaving the answer unsimplified or mis-multiplying the coefficient 3 is a common slip.
rq: Why must the scalar product be divided by both magnitudes rather than just one?
The scalar product equals |u||v|cos φ, so dividing by both magnitudes isolates cos φ and makes the result independent of vector lengths.
What would the value of cos φ tell you if it came out greater than 1?
It signals an arithmetic error, since cosine of any real angle lies between −1 and 1.

units.name: 8.6 Unit vectors i, j, k and dot products
units.ov: This material introduces the orthonormal unit vectors \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) along the x, y, z axes and uses them to write any 3D vector in component form. Because the unit vectors are mutually perpendicular with magnitude 1, expanding a dot product collapses to a sum of matching-component products, giving a scalar result. The notes do not cover the geometric form \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), but the component formula is the computational route to it.
must: Unit vectors \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) have magnitude 1 and point along the +x, +y, +z axes; any vector is \(\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}\)
Component formula: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\)
The dot product is a scalar (a number), not a vector; do not confuse it with the cross product
Orthonormality: \(\mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}=1\)
Orthogonality: \(\mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{i}=0\)
Derivation: expand the 9 terms of \((a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k})\cdot(b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k})\); the 6 cross terms vanish, leaving 3
Match components by position (x with x, y with y, z with z) and keep signs for negative components
Dot with itself gives the squared magnitude: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2\)
Zero dot product between nonzero vectors means they are perpendicular (use this to find unknown components)
A unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\) is \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}|\)
conn: Dot product with \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) gives the angle between vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}\)
Work done \(W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}\) and resolved components (projection of a force onto a direction using a unit vector) in mechanics
Perpendicularity tests (\(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\)) combine with solving for unknown constants, and with the cross product to build orthogonal sets or normals to planes
Magnitude and normalisation link unit vectors and dot products: \(|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}}\), then \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}|\)
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=4\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k}\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and state whether the vectors are perpendicular.
Find the value of \(p\) such that \(\mathbf{u}=3\mathbf{i}+p\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k}\).

Show by expanding that \((a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k})\cdot(b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k})=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\, ,\) stating which unit-vector products equal 0 and which equal 1.

A force \(\mathbf{F}=(3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k})\) N moves a particle through displacement \(\mathbf{d}=(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k})\) m. Calculate the work done and the angle between \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(\mathbf{d}\).
Find the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\) and the component of \(\mathbf{b}=3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) along it.

notes.t: Unit vectors i, j, k and the scalar (dot) product
pts: The unit vectors i, j and k are mutually perpendicular, so each pair has zero dot product.
Each unit vector dotted with itself gives 1, while dot products between different unit vectors give 0.
Expanding the product of two component-form vectors and using the orthogonality rules reduces the scalar product to the sum of products of matching components.
defs: Unit vector
A vector of magnitude 1 used to indicate a direction; i, j and k are the unit vectors along the x, y and z axes.
Scalar (dot) product
For vectors a and b, the scalar product is the sum of products of corresponding components, giving a scalar result.
eqs: Scalar product of two vectors in component form
a₁, a₂, a₃ = components of vector a (dimensionless or same unit as a); b₁, b₂, b₃ = components of vector b (same unit as b)
tips: Do not confuse the scalar product (result is a number) with the vector/cross product (result is a vector).
Ensure the components are matched in the same position (x with x, y with y, z with z) before summing.
rq: Why does the dot product of i with j vanish, and what does this tell us geometrically?
i and j are mutually perpendicular, and a·b = |a||b|cos θ with θ = 90°, so cos 90° = 0.
Why do only the terms a₁b₁, a₂b₂ and a₃b₃ survive in the expansion?
Every cross term such as a₁b₂ i·j contains a dot product of two different unit vectors, which is zero, while i·i = j·j = k·k = 1.

units.name: 9.1 Dot product and orthocenter proof
units.ov: This material covers the scalar (dot) product in component and geometric forms, its use to test perpendicularity, and to find the magnitude of a vector difference (leading to the law of cosines). These ideas are then applied to prove that the three altitudes of a triangle meet at the orthocenter, by placing the origin at the intersection of two altitudes and turning perpendicularity into dot-product equations.
must: Component form: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3 \); the result is a scalar, not a vector.
Geometric form: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \), so \( \cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} \) gives the angle between vectors.
Perpendicularity test: for non-zero vectors, \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \iff \mathbf{a}\perp\mathbf{b} \).
Magnitude: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2 \), so \( |\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}} \).
Vector difference: \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})} \); expand with the distributive law and do not forget the square root.

Law of cosines: \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2-2|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \), which follows from the expansion since \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \).
Orthocenter set-up: put the origin O at the intersection of two altitudes, with position vectors a, b, c for A, B, C.
Altitude conditions: from C, \( (\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0 \); from A, \( (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \).
Expand both and add: \( \mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=0 \), so OC is perpendicular to AB and the third altitude also passes through O.
Avoid sign errors in expansion, and do not confuse the dot product (scalar) with the cross product (vector).
conn: Dot product with the law of cosines: expanding \( (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}) \) links the algebraic and geometric definitions and yields triangle side lengths and angles.
Perpendicularity with geometric proof: each altitude is a statement \( \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}=0 \), so concurrency proofs reduce to adding or subtracting dot-product equations.
Angle between vectors with magnitude: finding an angle needs both \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} \) and the magnitudes from \( \sqrt{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}} \), often within a triangle problem.
Engineering application: the dot product gives the component of a force along a direction, and zero dot product means no work done (force perpendicular to displacement).
exq: Given \( \mathbf{a}=(2,-1,3) \) and \( \mathbf{b}=(1,4,-2) \), compute \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} \), the angle between them, and \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}| \).
Find the value of \( t \) for which \( (t,2,-1) \) is perpendicular to \( (3,t,4) \).

Expand \( (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}) \) and use it to derive the law of cosines for a triangle with sides \( |\mathbf{a}| \), \( |\mathbf{b}| \) and \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}| \).
Prove that the three altitudes of a triangle ABC are concurrent, taking the origin at the intersection of the altitudes from A and C and stating each dot-product condition.
Triangle with vertices A(1,0,2), B(3,1,0), C(0,2,1): verify whether the angle at A is a right angle and find the length of BC.

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product and magnitude of a vector difference
pts: The scalar product of two vectors is found by multiplying matching components and adding the results.
If the dot product of two non-zero vectors is zero, the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).
The dot product of a vector with itself equals the square of its magnitude.
The magnitude of a - b can be found from the dot product (a - b)·(a - b), expanded using the distributive law.
Using the law of cosines form, |a - b|² = |a|² + |b|² - 2|a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between a and b.
defs: Scalar (dot) product
For vectors a and b, a·b = |a||b|cos θ, a scalar obtained by summing products of corresponding components; it is zero when the vectors are perpendicular.
Magnitude of a vector
The length of a vector, given by the square root of its dot product with itself: |a| = √(a·a).
eqs: \(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = components of a and b (dimensionless or units of a and b); a·b = scalar product (units of a × units of b)
Magnitude of a difference of vectors
|a - b| = length of the difference vector (same unit as a and b)
θ = angle between a and b (degrees or radians); |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same unit as a and b)
tips: The scalar product is a scalar, not a vector: do not write a unit vector or direction for the result of a·b.
Do not forget the square root when finding |a - b|; (a - b)·(a - b) gives the squared magnitude only.
rq: Why does a·b = 0 in the example imply that the magnitude |a - b|² reduces to |a|² + |b|²?
Because the cross terms -a·b - b·a are both zero, leaving only a·a + b·b = |a|² + |b|², which is the case θ = 90° (cos θ = 0) in the law of cosines.
If you computed |a - b| but forgot to square the components of b before summing, what would go wrong?
The dot product (a - b)·(a - b) would be incorrect, so the magnitude would be wrong; each component of a - b must be squared and summed.
How can you tell from the sign of a·b whether the angle between two vectors is acute or obtuse?
a·b > 0 means θ < 90° (acute), a·b < 0 means θ > 90° (obtuse), and a·b = 0 means θ = 90° (perpendicular).

notes.t: Orthocenter proof using the scalar (dot) product
pts: Place the origin at the intersection O of two altitudes, so the position vectors of A, B, C are a, b, c.
Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero, which turns each altitude condition into an equation in a, b, c.
The altitude from C is perpendicular to AB, giving (b − c)·a = 0; the altitude from A is perpendicular to BC, giving (c − a)·b = 0.
Adding the two expanded equations gives c·(b − a) = 0, meaning the third altitude from C is perpendicular to AB, so all three altitudes pass through O.
defs: Orthocenter
The point where the three altitudes of a triangle (perpendiculars from each vertex to the opposite side) intersect.
Scalar (dot) product
For vectors u and v, u·v = |u||v|cos θ, a scalar that is zero when u and v are perpendicular.
eqs: Perpendicularity condition for the altitude from C
a = position vector of A (m); b = position vector of B (m); c = position vector of C (m)
Perpendicularity condition for the altitude from A
a = position vector of A (m); b = position vector of B (m); c = position vector of C (m)
Third altitude condition obtained by addition
a, b, c = position vectors of A, B, C (m)
tips: Do not confuse the dot product (a scalar, zero for perpendicular vectors) with the vector product (a vector); using the wrong product gives meaningless results.
Remember the side vector is b − a, not a − b; the direction of the vector does not matter for perpendicularity but sign errors in expansion do.
rq: Why does choosing O as the origin simplify the proof?
Because the position vectors a, b, c then measure directly from O, so the altitude conditions reduce to dot-product equations with no extra offset terms.
What does it mean geometrically if c·(b − a) = 0?
The vector c (from O to C) is perpendicular to b − a, which is the side AB, so the line from C through O is an altitude.

units.name: 9.2 Cross product definition, magnitude and right-hand rule
units.ov: This material defines the vector (cross) product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), which produces a vector perpendicular to both inputs. Its magnitude depends on the sine of the angle between the vectors, and its direction comes from the right-hand rule. Together these explain why the product is anti-commutative, and they contrast it with the scalar (dot) product, which gives a scalar and uses \(\cos\theta\).
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), and the result is a vector, not a scalar
Magnitude: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\), with \(0\le\theta\le\pi\) the angle between the vectors
Direction: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), so the result is perpendicular to the plane containing them
Right-hand rule: fingers point along the first vector and curl towards the second, and the thumb gives the direction of the product
Right-handed set: \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) taken in that order form a right-handed triad (thumb, index and middle fingers)
Anti-commutativity: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\). The magnitude is unchanged and the direction flips, so order matters
Special cases: the product is zero for parallel or anti-parallel vectors (\(\theta=0,\pi\)) and has its maximum magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\) when they are perpendicular
Do not confuse it with the dot product: the cross product is a vector and uses \(\sin\theta\), while the dot product is a scalar and uses \(\cos\theta\)
Units: the result has the product of the units of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\theta\) can be in degrees or radians as long as the calculator mode matches
conn: Cross product and dot product: both use the angle between two vectors, with \(\sin\theta\) giving a perpendicular vector and \(\cos\theta\) giving a scalar projection. Questions often ask for both, or ask you to find \(\theta\) from them.
Right-hand rule and anti-commutativity: swapping the order flips the thumb direction, so sign and direction errors in any cross product come from the ordering.
Magnitude and parallel vectors: \(\sin\theta=0\) means the product vanishes, which gives a test for parallel vectors. The magnitude also equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors.

Cross product and mechanics: moment and torque (\(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\)) are cross products, so their magnitude depends on the perpendicular component of force and their direction follows the right-hand rule.
exq: Vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) have magnitudes 4 and 6 and the angle between them is \(30^\circ\). Find \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) and \(|\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}|\), and state how the directions of the two products compare.

Using the right-hand rule, state the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) when \(\mathbf{a}\) points along +x and \(\mathbf{b}\) points along +y. Then give the direction of \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\) and explain the difference.

Explain why \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}\) for non-zero vectors implies they are parallel. For what angle \(\theta\) is \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) a maximum, and what is its value if \(|\mathbf{a}|=3\) and \(|\mathbf{b}|=5\)?
A force of 50 N acts at \(60^\circ\) to a 0.4 m spanner. Calculate the magnitude of the moment \(|\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}|\) and state its direction using the right-hand rule.
Two vectors in a plane have \(|\mathbf{a}|=2\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=5\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=6\). Find \(\theta\) and then \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\).

notes.t: Vector (Cross) Product
pts: The cross product of two vectors a and b is a vector, not a scalar.
Its magnitude is |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between a and b, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.
Its direction is along the unit vector n̂, perpendicular to both a and b, such that a, b, n̂ form a right-handed set.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the direction of n̂, so the cross product is not commutative.
defs: Vector (cross) product
The product a × b of two vectors, equal to |a||b| sin θ n̂, which is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
Unit vector n̂
A vector of length 1 perpendicular to both a and b, defining the direction of the cross product.
eqs: Magnitude and direction of the vector (cross) product of a and b

a, b = vectors; |a|, |b| = magnitudes (dimensionless if a, b are unitless, otherwise their units); θ = angle between a and b (rad), 0 ≤ θ ≤ π; n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the cross product with the scalar (dot) product; the cross product result is a vector, while the dot product is a scalar.
Order matters: b × a = −(a × b), so reversing the vectors flips the direction of n̂.
rq: Why does the cross product give a vector perpendicular to both a and b rather than a scalar?
Because it is defined to point along n̂, which is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b; its magnitude |a||b| sin θ is the area of the parallelogram they span.
What happens to a × b if a and b are parallel?
θ = 0 or π gives sin θ = 0, so a × b = 0 (the zero vector).

notes.t: Vector product (cross product) and the right-handed set
pts: The cross product of two vectors gives a third vector perpendicular to both.
The magnitude of the cross product equals the product of the magnitudes times the sine of the angle between them.
The direction of the result is given by the unit vector n, found using the right-hand rule.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the direction of the result, so the cross product is not commutative.
Using the right hand: fingers point along the first vector and curl towards the second; the thumb gives the direction of the product.
defs: Vector (cross) product

The vector product of a and b is a vector c = a × b whose magnitude is |a||b|sin θ, where θ is the angle between a and b, and whose direction is perpendicular to both a and b, given by the right-hand rule.
Right-handed set
A convention for ordering three vectors (e.g. A, B, C = A × B) so that the thumb, index and middle fingers of the right hand point along them respectively.
Unit vector n̂
A vector of length one that specifies the direction of the cross product, perpendicular to the plane containing a and b.
eqs: c = resultant vector (unitless here, product of units of a and b); a, b = input vectors; |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same units as a, b); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless)
|c| = magnitude of the cross product (SI units of a × b); |a|, |b| = magnitudes of vectors (SI units of a, b); θ = angle between the vectors (rad or °)
tips: Do not confuse the cross product (vector, uses sin θ) with the scalar product (scalar, uses cos θ).
Order matters: a × b ≠ b × a; always check the sign/direction when swapping vectors.
rq: Why is the cross product zero when the two vectors are parallel?
Because θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0 and the magnitude |c| = 0.
What would happen to the direction of the result if you swapped a and b?
It would reverse (B × A = −A × B), since the right-hand rule gives the opposite direction.
Why does the cross product produce a vector perpendicular to both inputs?
By definition its direction is set by n̂, which is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b, as shown by the right-hand rule.

units.name: 9.3 Algebraic properties: anti-commutativity, non-associativity, distributivity
units.ov: This material covers the algebraic rules of the vector (cross) product: it is anti-commutative, non-associative, and distributes over addition, with scalars factoring out. All rules follow from the definition \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) and its perpendicularity to both inputs, which also determines where triple products lie geometrically.
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), with \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) (right-hand rule); the result is a vector.
Anti-commutativity: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=-(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a})\); swapping order flips direction but not magnitude.
Non-associativity: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\neq(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) in general, so brackets always matter.
Never write \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) without brackets; it is ambiguous.

Geometry of triple products: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) lies in the plane of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\); \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) lies in the plane of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\).
Scalar law: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\lambda\mathbf{b})=\lambda(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})=(\lambda\mathbf{a})\times\mathbf{b}\).
Distributive law: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c}\); expand term by term, keeping the order of the factors.
Calculator angle mode (degrees vs radians) must match when evaluating \(\sin\theta\).
Keep \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) (or the vector components) in the final answer; do not give a scalar for a cross product.
conn: Anti-commutativity combined with distributivity: expanding \((\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\times(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\) gives \(\mathbf{0}\) since the cross terms cancel (\(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}\)).
The perpendicularity of \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) links the definition to the plane arguments for triple products, showing why the two bracketings differ in direction.

Distributivity and the scalar law allow the component (\(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\)) expansion of a cross product, which uses anti-commutativity for \(\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{i}=-\mathbf{k}\), etc.
In mechanics (moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\)), the order of the factors sets the moment's sign, and distributivity lets you sum moments from several forces.
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\), \(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}\), \(\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k}\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) and \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\), and show they differ.

State and justify, using the definition, whether \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\). Find \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\) for \(|\mathbf{a}|=3\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=4\), \(\theta=30^\circ\).
Expand and simplify \((\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\times(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\) using distributivity and anti-commutativity.
Explain why \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) lies in the plane of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\), and why \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) is not a valid expression.
Show that \(\mathbf{a}\times(\lambda\mathbf{b}+\mu\mathbf{c})=\lambda(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})+\mu(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})\), and evaluate it for given numeric vectors and scalars.

notes.t: Vector/Dot Product Properties: Anti-commutativity and Non-associativity of the Vector Prod
pts: The vector (cross) product is anti-commutative: swapping the order reverses the sign of the result.
The vector product is non-associative: bracketing changes the result in general.
b×c is perpendicular to both b and c, so a×(b×c) is perpendicular to a and (b×c), meaning it lies in the plane of b and c.
a×b is perpendicular to both a and b, so (a×b)×c lies in the plane of a and b.
Because of non-associativity, a triple product written without brackets is ambiguous and must never be written.
eqs: a, b = vectors (dimensionless as symbols; magnitude in their own units)
Non-associativity of the vector product (general case)
Magnitude and direction of the vector product
|a|, |b| = magnitudes (same units as a, b); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless)
tips: Unit trap: the cross product magnitude uses sin θ, so θ must be in the correct angle mode (radians vs degrees) on your calculator.
Do not assume a×b×c can be evaluated left-to-right like ordinary multiplication; always insert brackets first.
rq: Why must the brackets be included in a×(b×c) when you compute a triple vector product?
Because the vector product is non-associative, so a×(b×c) and (a×b)×c generally give different vectors; without brackets the expression is ambiguous.
If a×(b×c) always lies in the plane of b and c, what does this imply when b and c are parallel?
b×c = 0, so a×(b×c) = 0; the result is the zero vector, consistent with lying in a 'plane' of parallel vectors.
What happens to a×b if you swap a and b, and why?
It changes sign: b×a = −(a×b), because the unit normal n̂ reverses direction by the right-hand rule while the magnitude is unchanged.

notes.t: Distributive laws of the vector product
pts: The vector product a × b has magnitude |a||b| sin θ and direction n̂ perpendicular to both vectors.
A scalar can be pulled out of a vector product, so scalar multiplication commutes with the cross product.
The vector product distributes over vector addition, so the second vector can be expanded term by term.
eqs: Magnitude and direction of the vector product
a, b = vectors; θ = angle between a and b (rad or°); n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless); |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same units as a, b)
Scalar multiplication law for the vector product
tips: Do not treat the cross product as commutative; a × b = −(b × a).
The result of a × b is a vector, not a scalar; keep the unit vector n̂ in your final answer.
rq: Why does the cross product give a vector perpendicular to both a and b, and what happens if a and b are parallel?
n̂ is defined perpendicular to both a and b; if they are parallel, θ = 0 or π so sin θ = 0 and a × b = 0.
Why is the order of the vectors important for the cross product?
Reversing the order flips the direction of n̂ (right-hand rule), so b × a = −(a × b); the product is not commutative.

units.name: 9.4 Computing cross products with determinants
units.ov: This material covers computing the vector (cross) product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) of 3D vectors using a 3×3 determinant with \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) in the first row (or the equivalent diagonal mnemonic). It links the algebra to the geometry: the result is perpendicular to both vectors, has magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) (the parallelogram area), and follows the right-hand rule. Anticommutativity (\(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\)) ties the row order in the determinant to the direction of the result.
must: Determinant form: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\end{vmatrix}\), with row order i,j,k then a then b.
Expanded form: \((a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\mathbf{i}-(a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\mathbf{j}+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\mathbf{k}\). The signs alternate +, −, + along the first row.
The j-component carries a minus sign. Forgetting it is the most common error.
Anticommutativity: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\). Swapping the rows flips every component's sign, and \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}\).
Magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) is the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b. The triangle area is half of this.
Direction: perpendicular to both a and b, given by the right-hand rule. Check with \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0\) and \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\).
Worked example: \(\mathbf{a}=(3,2,1)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1)\) gives \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(-1,2,-1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=(1,-2,1)\).
Graphic (mnemonic) method: write the a and b components in two rows and take cross-diagonal products, with the sign set by the crossing direction. It gives the same result as the determinant.
The cross product is defined only in 3D. For 2D vectors, set the third component to 0, so the result lies along \(\mathbf{k}\).
Units: the components of the product have units of a times units of b (e.g. N·m for \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\)), not dimensionless.
conn: Cross product and the dot product: a zero dot product of the result with a or b verifies the calculation, and \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|^2+(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2|\mathbf{b}|^2\) links the two for finding the angle.
Cross product and geometry: a×b gives the normal to a plane (for the equation of a plane) and the area of a parallelogram or triangle from position vectors.

Cross product and mechanics: moment \(\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\), angular momentum and \(\mathbf{v}=\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{r}\). Here the order of r and F fixes the sign and direction.

Determinants and cross product: a zero cross product means the vectors are parallel (\(\sin\theta=0\)), the same as linear dependence, and the scalar triple product is a 3×3 determinant giving volume.
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(1,4,-2)\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) by the determinant method, verify it is perpendicular to both vectors, and state \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\).
Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1,0,2), B(3,1,1), C(2,4,0), using \(\tfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|\).

Find a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}=(3,2,1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1)\), and hence the angle between them from \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\).

A force \(\mathbf{F}=(10,-5,2)\) N acts at position \(\mathbf{r}=(0.3,0.4,0)\) m. Calculate the moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) about the origin, with its magnitude and units, and explain what happens to its sign if the order is reversed.
Show that \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,4,6)\) are parallel using the cross product, and find the value of \(k\) for which \((1,k,2)\times(2,4,4)=\mathbf{0}\).

notes.t: Vector product: determinant method and graphic (mnemonic) method
pts: The vector product a × b is computed by expanding a 3×3 determinant whose first row is the unit vectors i, j, k.
Each component of a × b is a 2×2 minor, with signs alternating +, −, + along the first row.
The graphic method lists a1 a2 a3 and b1 b2 b3 in rows; the diagonal products give the i, j, k components, with red (+ve) and blue (−ve) crossing lines.
defs: Vector (cross) product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span and whose direction follows the right-hand rule.
eqs: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a (dimensionless or units of a); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b (units of b); i, j, k = unit basis vectors (dimensionless)
Expanded component form of the vector product
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a; \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b; i, j, k = unit basis vectors
tips: Remember the middle (j) term is subtracted; forgetting this flips the j-component's sign.
Keep the row order a then b in the determinant; reversing rows changes the sign of the result.
rq: Why does the j-term carry a minus sign while the i and k terms are positive?
Cofactor expansion along the first row alternates signs (+, −, +), so the j-component's minor is subtracted.
What happens to a × b if you swap a and b?
The sign reverses: b × a = −(a × b), because the determinant changes sign when two rows are swapped.

notes.t: Vector (cross) product: definition and worked example
pts: The cross product a × b is computed as a determinant with unit vectors in the first row, components of a in the second, and components of b in the third.
Expanding the 3×3 determinant along the first row gives the components of the resulting vector.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the sign of the cross product, so b × a = −(a × b).
Worked example: for a = (3, 2, 1) and b = (−1, −1, −1), the cross product a × b evaluates to (−1, 2, −1).
defs: Cross (vector) product

The vector a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b, computed as the determinant of the unit-vector matrix with rows i, j, k, a and b.
eqs: Cross product of two 3D vectors as a determinant

\(\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\) = first vector (dimensionless components in the same unit as the vector); \(\mathbf{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)\) = second vector; \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) = unit vectors along x, y, z
Expanded component form of the cross product
tips: Watch the signs in the cofactor expansion: the j-term carries a minus sign, and forgetting it is a common error.
The cross product is only defined for 3D vectors; do not apply the determinant method to 2D vectors without a zero third component.
rq: Why does swapping the order of the vectors change the sign of the result, and what does this imply for the direction of a × b?
Swapping two rows of a determinant changes its sign, so b × a = −(a × b); the result points in the opposite direction, following the right-hand rule reversed.
If you computed a × b and got the zero vector, what would that tell you about a and b?
The vectors are parallel (or one is zero), since the parallelogram they span has zero area.

notes.t: Vector product: worked example and anticommutativity
pts: The vector product is anticommutative: swapping the order of the two vectors reverses the sign of the result.
Given a = (3, 2, 1) and b = (−1, −1, −1), the vector product a × b equals (−1, 2, −1), so b × a = (1, −2, 1).
The result of a vector product is a vector perpendicular to both input vectors, so the direction of b × a is opposite to that of a × b.
defs: Vector (cross) product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector whose magnitude is |a||b|sin θ, directed perpendicular to both a and b following the right-hand rule.
Anticommutativity
The property of the vector product that b × a = −(a × b), i.e. interchanging the operands reverses the sign of the product.
eqs: a, b = position/direction vectors (dimensionless or units of the vectors used)
Vector product of a = (3, 2, 1) and b = (−1, −1, −1) written in unit vectors
î, ĵ, k̂ = unit vectors along x, y, z (dimensionless)
tips: Do not assume a × b = b × a; swapping the order changes the sign of every component.
Keep track of the sign of each component when subtracting the components of the cross product, as a sign error is the most common mistake.
rq: Why does the figure show a × b and b × a pointing in opposite directions?
Because the vector product is anticommutative, b × a = −(a × b), so the two results have equal magnitude but opposite sign and hence opposite direction.
If you know a × b, how can you find b × a without recomputing the determinant?
Simply reverse the sign of every component of a × b, since b × a = −(a × b).

units.name: 9.5 Cross product and unit normal to a plane
units.ov: The cross product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) of two 3D vectors is a new vector perpendicular to both, so it is normal to the plane they span. Its magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) is the area of the parallelogram on \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and dividing by that magnitude gives the unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\). The worked example is \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,1)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(2,2,1)\).
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), with direction given by the right-hand rule
Compute it as a 3×3 determinant with \(\hat\imath,\hat\jmath,\hat k\) in the top row, then \(\mathbf{a}\), then \(\mathbf{b}\)
Worked example: \((2,0,1)\times(2,2,1)=-2\hat\imath+4\hat k\)
Unit normal: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|}\). Divide by the magnitude of the cross product, not by \(|\mathbf{a}|\) or \(|\mathbf{b}|\)
Example result: \(|-2\hat\imath+4\hat k|=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\), so \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}=(-1/\sqrt5,\,0,\,2/\sqrt5)\)
Area: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) is the parallelogram area, and half of it is the triangle area. Here the parallelogram area is \(2\sqrt5\approx4.47\)
Order matters: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), so swapping rows reverses \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\)
The cross product is a vector and the scalar (dot) product is a scalar. Do not confuse them
Check the determinant signs carefully: the \(\hat\jmath\) component carries a minus sign in the cofactor expansion (here it is \(0\))
A unit vector has length 1 and gives direction only. Check your answer: \(|\hat{\mathbf{n}}|=1\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{a}=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\)
conn: Cross product with dot product: use \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{a}=0\) to verify perpendicularity, and use \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) with \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) to find \(\theta\) via \(\tan\theta\)

Normal vector with the equation of a plane: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) gives \((A,B,C)\) in \(Ax+By+Cz=D\), and a point on the plane fixes \(D\). The plane can be defined by three points using two edge vectors
Cross product with area and moments: triangle area \(=\tfrac12|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\), and the same determinant method gives moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) in mechanics
Unit normal with projection: the component of a vector or force normal to a surface is \(\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), which needs a correctly oriented \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\)
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,2,1)\), find \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), its magnitude, and the unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) to the plane containing them.
Find the area of the triangle with vertices \(P(1,0,0)\), \(Q(3,0,1)\), \(R(3,2,1)\), and a unit vector perpendicular to its plane.

notes.t: Vector (cross) product and unit normal to a plane
pts: The cross product of two vectors produces a new vector perpendicular to both original vectors, i.e. normal to the plane they span.
The magnitude of a × b equals |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors, and its direction is given by the unit normal n̂.
The cross product is evaluated as a 3×3 determinant with unit vectors i, j, k in the first row and the vector components in the next two rows.
Dividing the resulting perpendicular vector by its magnitude gives the unit normal vector n̂.
defs: Vector (cross) product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector whose magnitude is |a||b| sin θ and whose direction is perpendicular to both a and b, given by the right-hand rule.
Unit vector
A vector of length 1 that indicates direction only; obtained by dividing a vector by its magnitude.
eqs: a, b = vectors; θ = angle between a and b (rad); n̂ = unit normal vector (dimensionless)
Cross product as determinant (for a=(2,0,1), b=(2,2,1))
î, ĵ, k̂ = unit basis vectors (dimensionless)
tips: Remember the unit normal requires dividing by the magnitude: n̂ = (a × b)/|a × b|, here |−2i+4k| = √20 = 2√5, so n̂ = (−1/√5, 0, 2/√5).
Keep the row order of a and b fixed in the determinant; swapping them reverses the sign of the normal.
rq: Why does the cross product give a vector perpendicular to both a and b, and how can you check the result?
By definition the cross product is orthogonal to both factors; check by showing the dot product of a × b with a and with b is zero (here (−2,0,4)·(2,0,1)=0 and (−2,0,4)·(2,2,1)=0).
What would happen to a × b if a and b were parallel?
sin θ = 0, so a × b is the zero vector, meaning no unique plane normal exists.

notes.t: Vector (cross) product and unit normal to a plane
pts: The cross product a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, so it gives a normal to the plane they span.
Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by a and b, using the sine of the angle between them.
To make a unit normal, divide the cross product by its own magnitude.
defs: Cross (vector) product
The vector a × b whose magnitude is |a||b|sin θ and whose direction is perpendicular to both a and b, given by the right-hand rule.
Unit vector
A vector of magnitude 1 that indicates direction only, found by dividing a vector by its magnitude.
eqs: Magnitude of the cross product (area of parallelogram)
|a|, |b| = magnitudes of the vectors (dimensionless if unitless components); θ = angle between a and b (rad)
Unit normal to the plane of a and b
n̂ = unit normal vector (dimensionless); a × b = cross product; |a × b| = its magnitude
tips: Do not confuse the cross product (a vector) with the scalar product; the cross product requires a vector result and a unit normal must be divided by |a × b|, not by |a| or |b|.
Watch signs when computing the determinant for components, e.g. a × b = −2i + 4k here; sign errors flip the direction of n̂.
rq: Why does dividing a × b by its magnitude give a unit normal rather than just any normal?
A normal vector only fixes direction; dividing by its magnitude scales it to length 1 while keeping the same direction, so it is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane.
If you swapped a and b, how would the unit normal change?
Since b × a = −(a × b), the unit normal would reverse direction, giving the opposite unit normal (still perpendicular to the plane).

rep.ov: The module has so far covered two strands. The AC strand starts from waveforms, radians and phasors, then moves through complex numbers and the impedances of R, L and C, and ends with first-order RC/LR filters, decibels and the series LCR band-pass, with speaker crossovers as the running application. The DC strand starts from voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's law and power, then adds Kirchhoff's laws and series/parallel reduction, followed by Thévenin/Norton, maximum power, superposition, star-delta and mesh-current analysis. Each topic builds on the one before it: Ohm's law becomes V = IZ, voltage dividers become filter transfer functions, and the DC network theorems rest on KVL, KCL and resistor reduction.
must: Impedances: \( Z_R=R,\; Z_L=j\omega L,\; Z_C=\frac{1}{j\omega C}=\frac{-j}{\omega C} \), with \( \omega=2\pi f \) (rad/s, not Hz), and the generalised Ohm's law \( V=IZ \)
Complex number skills: rectangular and polar forms, \( j^2=-1 \), \( |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), phase \( \arctan(b/a) \), conjugate multiplication to rationalise denominators
Capacitor and inductor behaviour: \( I=C\,dV/dt \) (current leads voltage by 90°) and \( V=L\,dI/dt \) (current lags voltage by 90°); \( Q=CV \)

First-order RC/LR filters as voltage dividers: low-pass (output across C, or across R in the LR case) and high-pass (output across R in the RC case), \( \omega_0=1/RC \) or \( R/L \), \( f_0=\omega_0/2\pi \), \( |V_o/V_{in}|=1/\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_0)^2} \) for the low-pass
Decibels: \( 20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in}) \) for voltage and \( 10\log_{10} \) for power; the cut-off is at \( 1/\sqrt2 \), which is −3 dB (half power); reading Bode magnitude plots
Series LCR band-pass: the output across R is a divider \( \frac{R}{R+j\omega L+1/(j\omega C)} \), with peak gain at \( \omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC} \) and an \( \omega^2 \) term showing it is second order
Series and parallel combination rules: R and L add in series, C adds in parallel; parallel R and L and series C combine by reciprocals; two parallel resistors give \( R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2) \)
Phasors and phase: amplitude is the arrow length, phase difference is the angle, and the phasors only make sense for a common \( \omega \); convert phase to time delay using the frequency
Ohm's law and power: \( V=IR \), \( P=VI=I^2R=V^2/R \), \( R=\rho l/A \), with consistent SI units
KCL and KVL, voltage and current dividers, and sign conventions for sources and polarity

Thévenin/Norton: \( V_T=V_{oc} \), \( R_T \) found by zeroing sources (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened), \( I_N=V_T/R_T \), \( R_N=R_T \); maximum power when \( R_L=R_T \), giving \( P_{max}=V_T^2/4R_T \)

Multi-source and non-series/parallel methods: superposition (voltages and currents only, never powers), delta-star conversion \( R_A=\frac{R_3R_1}{R_1+R_2+R_3} \), and mesh-current analysis with matrix or Cramer's rule, including meshes that contain current sources
conn: Complex impedance + voltage divider + decibels: a filter question gives R, C (or L) and asks for \( V_o/V_{in} \), its magnitude and phase at a given f, the −3 dB frequency, and the gain in dB.
Capacitor/inductor \( dV/dt \) and \( dI/dt \) laws lead to \( Z_C \) and \( Z_L \) and to the ±90° phase shifts, which show up as the phasor diagram or Argand plot of a series RC or RL impedance.

Thévenin/Norton + maximum power: reduce the network to \( V_T,R_T \), set \( R_L=R_T \) and compute \( P_{max} \). \(R_{T}\) is often found with star-delta or series/parallel reduction after zeroing sources.

Superposition vs mesh analysis vs Thévenin: the same multi-source circuit can be solved by any of the three. Questions ask you to pick one and then check the answer with another, or to use mesh currents to find \( V_{oc} \).
DC rules (KVL, dividers, series/parallel) carry over to AC by replacing R with Z, so the LCR band-pass and the filters are just divider problems with complex numbers.
exq: A series RC low-pass filter has R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find the cut-off frequency in Hz, then the gain magnitude, gain in dB and phase of \( V_o/V_{in} \) at 2 kHz.

Show that the series LCR band-pass transfer function is \( \frac{R}{R+j(\omega L-1/\omega C)} \). Find \( \omega_0 \) and the gain and phase at \( \omega_0 \) for L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF, R = 50 Ω. Sketch the Bode magnitude plot.
A 10 µF capacitor is driven by \( V=5\sin(2\pi\cdot 50\,t) \) V. Find \( |Z_C| \), write \( I(t) \), state the phase relationship and sketch the phasor diagram.
Express \( Z=R+\frac{1}{j\omega C} \) for R = 100 Ω, C = 1 µF at 1 kHz in rectangular and polar form, giving the magnitude and phase; show the working by rationalising any complex denominator.

Find the Thévenin and Norton equivalents seen from terminals A–B of a network containing two sources and four resistors. Give the load resistance for maximum power and the power delivered, and confirm \( I_N=V_T/R_T \).

Use mesh-current analysis on a two-mesh circuit (e.g. R₁ = 470 Ω, R₂ = 820 Ω, R₃ = 220 Ω, \(V_{A}\) = 10 V, \(V_{B}\) = 5 V). Write the matrix equation, solve by Cramer's rule, find the current in R₃, and repeat one source's contribution by superposition.
weak: Choosing where to take the filter output and deriving the phase and magnitude. Students swap low-pass and high-pass, forget the \( -j \) in \( Z_C \), or fail to rationalise the complex denominator, so phase signs come out wrong. Practise limits (ω→0 and ω→∞) as a sanity check.

Sign conventions in mesh and KVL equations, including shared-resistor terms, source polarity and meshes containing current sources. The equations are easy to write but a single sign slip gives wrong currents, and current sources do not have zero voltage across them.

Deactivating sources and choosing the right theorem (Thévenin, Norton, superposition, star-delta). Short vs open is easily confused, powers cannot be superposed, and bridge circuits need star-delta before any series/parallel reduction.

units.name: 1.1 Voltage and current basics
units.ov: This material introduces the two basic electrical quantities, voltage and current, as the foundation for analogue electronics and AC waveforms. Voltage is energy per unit charge, and current is the rate of flow of charge. Ohm's law links them through resistance, and conventional current direction is the sign convention used when analysing circuits.
must: Voltage (potential difference) is energy transferred per unit charge: \( V = E/q \), with 1 V = 1 J/C
Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor cross-section: \( I = \Delta q/\Delta t \), with 1 A = 1 C/s
Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), with V in volts, I in amps and R in ohms
Ohm's law only holds for ohmic components at constant temperature, so it is not a universal law for every device
Conventional current points from + to −, opposite to the direction electrons actually drift in a metal
Charge carriers in copper are free electrons (negative). Current is set by the drift of carriers, which is slow even though the signal propagates quickly
Voltage is always measured between two points. The source drives charge round a loop and the voltage drop across a resistor is \( IR \)
Distinguish voltage (J/C) from current (C/s) and use consistent SI units, converting mA, kΩ etc. before calculating
Rearrangements: \( I = V/R \), \( R = V/I \), and energy \( E = qV \) for a charge moved through a potential difference
conn: Energy, charge and voltage: \( E = qV \) links to the mechanical energy/work ideas, and with \( q = It \) gives \( E = VIt \) and power \( P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R \)
Current and Ohm's law: a given current through a resistor produces a voltage drop \( IR \), the basis of Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws and of potential dividers
Conventional current versus electron flow: sign and direction conventions affect the polarity of voltage drops and later the phase and direction of AC waveforms
Constant (DC) voltage and current lead into time-varying waveforms, where \( v(t) \) and \( i(t) \) are related instantaneously by \( v(t) = i(t)R \) for a resistor
exq: A charge of 12 C moves through a potential difference of 9 V. Calculate the energy transferred, and state how this changes if the charge is doubled at the same voltage.
A 330 Ω resistor has a current of 15 mA through it. Calculate the voltage across it, and the charge passing a point in 2 minutes.
Define voltage and current, giving SI units in terms of base ratios (J/C and C/s). Explain why they are different quantities.
Explain why conventional current flows in the opposite direction to electron motion in a copper wire. State which direction you would mark on a circuit diagram and why.
A component gives these readings: 1 V, 2 mA; 2 V, 4 mA; 4 V, 10 mA. Decide whether it obeys Ohm's law, justify your answer with calculations, and suggest a physical reason for any deviation.

notes.t: Voltage: energy per unit charge and Ohm's law
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge moving between two points in a circuit.
Voltage is measured in volts (V), where 1 V equals 1 joule per coulomb.
In a circuit, charges (electrons) are pushed around a loop by the source, and the voltage drop across a resistor is related to the current through it by Ohm's law.
defs: Voltage (potential difference)
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts, where 1 V = 1 J/C.
eqs: Voltage as energy per unit charge
V = voltage (V); E = energy transferred (J); q = charge (C)
Ohm's law: voltage across a resistor
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not confuse voltage (energy per unit charge, V = E/q) with current (charge per unit time); the units are J/C versus C/s.
Ohm's law V = IR applies to ohmic components at constant temperature; use consistent SI units (volts, amps, ohms).
rq: Why does a higher voltage not automatically mean more charge flows, and what else must you know?
Current depends on both voltage and resistance (I = V/R); the same voltage across a larger resistance gives less current.
If the charge q doubles while the energy E stays the same, what happens to V?
V = E/q halves, since voltage is inversely proportional to the charge moved for a fixed energy.

notes.t: Electric current as flow of charge carriers in a conductor
pts: Current in a copper wire is the drift of negatively charged electrons (carriers) along the conductor.
The arrow shows the direction of conventional current, which is opposite to the direction electrons actually move.
Free electrons are shown moving through the lattice of a copper wire, so charge flows when a voltage drives them along the wire.
defs: Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor cross-section, measured in amperes.
Conventional current direction
The direction in which positive charge would flow, taken as opposite to the motion of electrons.
tips: Do not confuse electron drift direction with conventional current direction; always state which convention you use.
Current is the rate of charge flow (A = C/s), not the charge itself; the carriers themselves do not travel quickly along the wire.
rq: Why does the arrow point right while the negative charges in the wire are drawn moving the opposite way?
Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would flow, which is opposite to electron motion.
What would change in the picture if the current were alternating?
The carriers would periodically reverse direction, oscillating back and forth rather than drifting steadily one way.

units.name: 1.2 Course intro, HiFi systems and loudspeaker waveforms
units.ov: This introductory material frames AC circuits through HiFi audio. A system has three blocks: a source producing a small signal, an amplifier boosting its power, and a loudspeaker converting the AC electrical signal into sound. The loudspeaker example motivates AC waveforms: a time-varying current in a voice coil sitting in a permanent magnet's field makes the cone oscillate and produce pressure waves.
must: HiFi chain: source (small signal, mV) \(\rightarrow\) amplifier (raises power, measured in W) \(\rightarrow\) loudspeaker (transducer to sound)
Source (e.g. turntable cartridge, CD player) converts physical or stored information into a small time-varying electrical signal
Amplifier increases voltage, current and/or power without changing the waveform shape, so it can drive a load
Speaker is a transducer: alternating electrical signal \(\rightarrow\) acoustic pressure waves via cone/diaphragm motion
Loudspeaker mechanism: voice coil carrying current in a constant permanent-magnet field experiences a force (\(F = BIL\)), which moves the cone
Current reversal reverses the force, so the cone moves back and forth; DC gives only a steady displacement and no sustained sound
The magnet supplies a constant field; the varying current drives the motion
Waveform shape (e.g. sinusoidal) is distinct from frequency; frequency sets the perceived pitch
Distinguish the small source output from the large amplifier output delivered to the speaker
conn: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (\(F = BIL\)) links the loudspeaker to electromagnetism, and the same principle works in reverse in microphones and guitar pickups
Amplifier gain links signal levels (mV at the source) to power (W) at the speaker, which leads to power calculations with AC voltage and current
Frequency and waveform of the current determine the cone's oscillation and hence the pitch of the sound, linking electrical waveforms to acoustics
The block-diagram view (source, processing, transducer) carries over to the other applications, such as radar and heart rate monitors
exq: Draw a block diagram of a HiFi system, naming the three main blocks and stating the type and approximate magnitude of the signal at each stage.
Explain, with a labelled sketch, how an alternating current in a voice coil produces sound. Why would a steady DC current not produce sustained sound?

A voice coil of length 5 m in a field of 1 T carries a current of 2 A. Calculate the force on the coil, and describe how this force varies if the current is sinusoidal at 440 Hz. What is the cone's oscillation frequency?
Distinguish between the waveform shape and the frequency of a signal. Which determines the pitch heard, and what does the amplifier change and not change?
Define source, amplifier and speaker, and give an example of each. Explain why the amplifier is needed between a turntable cartridge and a loudspeaker.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits – course introduction
pts: The course covers the basics of electronics and how they relate to several types of technology.
Application examples used to illustrate the course include HiFi audio systems, guitar pickups and microphones, radar systems, and heart rate monitors.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - HiFi Systems
pts: A HiFi system is built from three main blocks: a source that produces a small signal, an amplifier that boosts it, and a speaker that converts the electrical signal into sound.
The source (e.g. a turntable with a cartridge) converts the physical groove modulations of a record into a small, time-varying electrical signal.
The amplifier increases the power of the signal from the source so it can drive the speakers; its power level meters show output in watts.
The speaker converts the amplified alternating electrical signal back into sound waves by moving its cone/diaphragm.
defs: Source
The part of a HiFi system that produces the original low-level electrical signal representing the music, such as a turntable or CD player.
Amplifier
A circuit that increases the amplitude (voltage, current and/or power) of an input signal without changing its waveform, so it can drive a load such as a loudspeaker.
Speaker
A transducer that converts an alternating electrical signal into acoustic (sound) pressure waves.
tips: Do not confuse the source's output (a small signal, often millivolts) with the amplifier's output (large power delivered to the speaker).
Remember that the signal is alternating: the speaker responds to the varying AC waveform, not a steady DC level.
rq: Why is an amplifier needed between the source and the speaker rather than connecting the source directly to the speaker?
The source signal is far too small in power to move the speaker cone audibly; the amplifier increases the signal's power so the speaker can produce loud sound.
What would happen to the sound quality if the amplifier changed the shape of the waveform rather than only its size?
The sound would be distorted, because the speaker would reproduce a different waveform from the original signal; a good amplifier preserves the waveform while increasing its amplitude.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms
pts: This slide is an introduction to AC waveforms, motivated by how loudspeakers reproduce music, which is an alternating signal.
tips: Do not confuse the waveform's shape (e.g. sinusoidal) with its frequency, which determines the perceived pitch of the sound.
rq: Why does a loudspeaker need an alternating (rather than steady) current to produce sound?

A steady current gives a constant cone position, producing no pressure variation; sound requires the cone to oscillate back and forth, so the current must alternate in direction and amplitude, following the waveform of the music.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms (loudspeaker example)
pts: An alternating current supply drives the loudspeaker's voice coil, which sits in the field of a permanent magnet.
The alternating current reverses direction periodically, so the force on the coil reverses and the cone moves back and forth.
Moving the cone pushes and pulls the air, producing pressure waves that we hear as sound.
The magnet provides a constant magnetic field; the varying current is what makes the coil and cone oscillate.
tips: Do not confuse the permanent magnet (constant field) with the time-varying current that actually drives the motion.
Remember that the cone moves in both directions only because the current reverses; a DC supply gives no sustained sound.
rq: Why does a loudspeaker need an alternating rather than a steady (DC) current to produce sound?
A steady current gives a constant force, so the cone would just sit displaced; only a current that reverses direction makes the cone oscillate and push air back and forth to create sound waves.
What would happen to the sound if the frequency of the alternating current were doubled?
The cone would oscillate twice as fast, so the sound would have double the frequency (higher pitch), while the wave shape determines the tone quality.

units.name: 1.3 Period, frequency and combining waves
units.ov: This material introduces periodic AC waveforms and the reciprocal link between period and frequency, \(f = 1/T\). It then shows how waves of different frequency combine by superposition (adding instantaneous values), which explains how chords and music arise from many frequencies. Amplitude, frequency and phase are the three descriptors that must be kept distinct.
must: Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\) and \(f = \frac{1}{T}\)
Period \(T\) is the time of one complete cycle (in seconds), read from the horizontal time axis, not from the voltage axis
Frequency \(f\) is cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz); higher frequency means shorter period and more tightly packed cycles
UK mains is about 50 Hz, so \(T = \frac{1}{50} = 20\ \text{ms} = 0.02\ \text{s}\)
Convert units before calculating: ms to s (and kHz to Hz) so that \(f\) is in Hz and \(T\) in s
Amplitude (peak value, e.g. ±1.0 V) is independent of frequency; changing \(f\) does not change peak height
Superposition: when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements, \(y = y_1 + y_2\); interference is the same process
Add instantaneous values at each time point, never peak amplitudes of waves with different frequencies; same-sign values reinforce, opposite-sign values reduce
Phase difference is the horizontal offset between waves, not a difference in peak height; in phase reinforces, out of phase cancels
Musical pitch is set by frequency (e.g. 440 Hz sounds higher than 240 Hz), and chords and music come from combinations of different frequencies
conn: Period and frequency conversion is often combined with unit handling: a period read from a graph in ms must be converted to s before finding \(f\) in Hz
Superposition depends on both frequency and phase: waves of different frequency drift in and out of phase, so the combined waveform is not a simple sinusoid and its shape changes over time
Amplitude, frequency and phase are separate properties; questions often ask which one changes when a graph is altered (e.g. tighter cycles means higher \(f\), same amplitude)
The mains example links the abstract \(T = 1/f\) to real engineering AC: 50 Hz gives 50 cycles per second and a 20 ms period, which sets the time scale on an oscilloscope trace
exq: A waveform on an oscilloscope has successive peaks 4 ms apart. Calculate its period and frequency, stating the units, and explain why the 1.0 V peak value is not the period.
UK mains is 50 Hz. Calculate the period in ms, and state how many complete cycles occur in 0.5 s. A US supply has a period of 16.7 ms; find its frequency.
Three sinusoids of equal amplitude have frequencies 240 Hz, 340 Hz and 440 Hz. Find each period, state which is highest in pitch, and explain why their peak heights are identical.

Two sinusoidal waves, each between +1.0 and −1.0, have different frequencies. Explain using superposition how to sketch the combined waveform, and state the possible range of the resultant at an instant when one wave is +0.6 and the other is −0.8.

Explain the difference between amplitude, frequency and phase difference when two waves are superimposed, and describe how the combined amplitude differs when they are in phase and when they are out of phase.

notes.t: AC Waveforms and the Period
pts: A periodic waveform repeats its shape at regular intervals; the time for one full repetition is the period T.
The period is measured between two identical points on consecutive cycles, such as successive peaks.
The plotted waveform is a voltage (V) varying with time, oscillating between +1.0 V and −1.0 V about zero.
defs: Period (T)
The time taken for a waveform to repeat itself exactly; the duration of one complete cycle, measured in seconds.
tips: Read the period from the time axis in the correct time units; the period is a time, not a voltage, so do not use the 1.0 V peak value as T.
Do not confuse the period with the amplitude: the amplitude here is 1.0 V, while T is the horizontal duration of one cycle.
rq: Why is the distance between two successive peaks, rather than between a peak and a zero crossing, used to define the period?

Successive peaks are identical points on consecutive cycles, so the interval between them is exactly one full repetition. A peak and a zero crossing are not equivalent points (one is a maximum, the other is rising or falling), so they do not define a full period.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Frequency and Period
pts: Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz, and is the inverse of the period.
One period is the time taken for one complete repetition of the waveform, shown as the distance between successive peaks.
UK mains supply is AC at approximately 50 Hz, so the waveform repeats 50 times per second.
Substituting f = 50 Hz into T = 1/f gives a period of 20 ms for mains voltage.
defs: Frequency (f)
The number of complete cycles of a periodic waveform per second, measured in hertz (Hz); the reciprocal of the period.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform, measured in seconds.
eqs: Period of mains voltage at 50 Hz
tips: Convert units before calculating: a period given in ms must be converted to seconds (20 ms = 0.02 s) when used with f in Hz.
Do not confuse the period with the frequency: the period is the time for one cycle, while frequency counts cycles per second.
rq: Why does doubling the frequency of an AC supply halve the period, and what would this do to the number of cycles in one second?
Since T = 1/f, doubling f halves T; the waveform then completes twice as many cycles per second, e.g. 100 Hz gives T = 10 ms.
If the time axis of the graph were read in milliseconds, how would you find the period from the peak-to-peak distance?
Measure the time between two successive peaks on the time axis; that interval is T, and f = 1/T gives the frequency.

notes.t: AC Waveforms and Frequency
pts: An AC signal is a sinusoidal waveform that repeatedly reverses direction, oscillating between positive and negative peaks.
Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz; higher frequency means more cycles in the same time.
The three waveforms have the same amplitude (peaks at ±1.0) but different frequencies, so they look different only in how tightly the cycles are packed.
In audio terms, frequency determines perceived pitch: the 440 Hz signal has the most cycles and sounds highest, while 240 Hz sounds lowest.
defs: Frequency (f)
The number of complete cycles of a periodic waveform per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a waveform; it is the reciprocal of frequency.
tips: Do not confuse frequency (Hz) with amplitude (peak value); changing frequency does not change the peak height of the waveform.
Remember that period and frequency are reciprocals; using T = f instead of T = 1/f is a common error.
rq: Why does the 440 Hz waveform look 'compressed' compared with the 240 Hz waveform if both have the same peak amplitude?
Because it completes more cycles per second, so each cycle occupies a shorter time interval; amplitude is unchanged, only the period is shorter.
What would happen to the perceived tone if the frequency of a signal doubled, and why?
The tone would be perceived an octave higher, since pitch increases with frequency.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms (Superposition and Interference)
pts: Music heard is a combination of many different waves, not a single wave.
Each guitar string vibrates at its own frequency; the waves combine as they travel through air to produce the sound of a chord.
When waves overlap, their displacements add together; this combining process is superposition, also called interference.
defs: Superposition
The principle that when two or more waves overlap in the same medium, the resulting displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual wave displacements.
Interference
The effect produced when overlapping waves combine, reinforcing or cancelling each other depending on their relative phase; another name for superposition.
tips: Superposition adds displacements algebraically (with sign), not magnitudes; waves in phase reinforce and out of phase cancel.
Superposition and interference are the same process here; do not treat interference as a separate phenomenon.
rq: Why does a single guitar chord sound different from a single string played alone, even though each string is a wave?
