For a sinusoidal voltage, the current is also sinusoidal at the same frequency, but its peak is set by the steepest slope of the voltage waveform.
Current peaks occur where the voltage curve is steepest (crossing zero), not where the voltage peaks.
eqs: Current through a capacitor as a function of the rate of change of voltage
I = current (A); C = capacitance (F); V = voltage (V); t = time (s); dV/dt = rate of change of voltage (V/s)
tips: Current is governed by dV/dt, so current peaks where the voltage waveform is steepest (zero crossings), not at voltage peaks.
Do not confuse frequency with amplitude: changing frequency alters the current amplitude even when the voltage amplitude is fixed.
rq: Why does doubling the frequency of the supply double the peak current, even though the voltage amplitude is unchanged?
Peak current is proportional to the maximum rate of change of voltage, dV/dt. For a sinusoid this is ωV₀, so doubling frequency (ω) doubles the peak current while V₀ stays the same.
What current flows through a capacitor connected to a constant DC voltage in steady state, and why?
Zero, because dV/dt = 0 when the voltage is constant, so I = C·dV/dt = 0.

notes.t: Capacitor impedance in AC circuits
pts: A capacitor produces a phase difference between voltage and current, so its impedance has an imaginary (reactive) component.
Impedance of a capacitor falls as frequency (angular frequency) rises, because more current flows.
Current through a capacitor is proportional to capacitance, so a larger capacitance gives a lower impedance.
eqs: Z = impedance (\Omega); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless); \omega = angular frequency (rad \(s^{-1}\)); C = capacitance (F)
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (\Omega)
tips: Do not confuse angular frequency \( \omega \) with frequency \( f \); use \( \omega = 2\pi f \) in the impedance formula.
The factor \( j \) in \( \frac{1}{j\omega C} = \frac{-j}{\omega C} \) represents a phase shift, so keep it when combining impedances rather than treating Z as a real resistance.
rq: Why does the capacitor impedance become smaller as frequency increases?

Higher frequency means the capacitor charges and discharges more rapidly, so more current flows for a given voltage; since \( Z = \frac{1}{\omega C} \) in magnitude, larger \( \omega \) gives smaller \( |Z| \).
What would happen to the impedance if you doubled the capacitance at a fixed frequency?
The impedance magnitude would halve, since \( |Z| = \frac{1}{\omega C} \) is inversely proportional to \( C \).

units.name: 3.3 Phasors and complex impedance
units.ov: This module covers phasor analysis of AC circuits: sinusoids are represented as complex numbers (magnitude and phase), and complex impedance generalises resistance through V = IZ. It builds from the capacitor's impedance to series RC circuits, then to transfer functions Vout/Vin and Bode magnitude plots, which show attenuation against frequency in dB on a log axis.
must: Phasor: complex number encoding amplitude and phase of a sinusoid, so circuit analysis uses algebra rather than differential equations
AC Ohm's law: \( V = IZ \), with Z complex so both magnitude \( |Z| \) and phase \( \arg Z \) matter
Capacitor impedance \( Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C} = -\frac{j}{\omega C} \): phase \(-90^\circ\), so voltage lags current by 90°, and |Z| falls as frequency rises
Series RC: \( Z_t = R + \frac{1}{j\omega C} \); add real and imaginary parts separately; \( |Z_t| = \sqrt{R^2 + 1/(\omega C)^2} \), phase \( = -\tan^{-1}\!\big(1/(\omega RC)\big) \)
Use \( \omega = 2\pi f \) in rad/s, never f in Hz, when computing reactance
Convert phasor to time domain: \( v(t) = V_0\cos(\omega t + \theta) \) using peak amplitude \( V_0 \) (not RMS) and the correct angle; the notes' example has i at +45° and v at −45°
Rectangular form \( I = a + jb \): magnitude \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), angle \( \tan^{-1}(b/a) \) (check quadrant); V = IZ multiplies magnitudes and adds angles
Transfer function \( H = V_{out}/V_{in} \); its magnitude \( |V_{out}/V_{in}| \) is the attenuation at each frequency
Bode magnitude plot: \( 20\log_{10}|V_{out}/V_{in}| \) in dB against log frequency; always check whether a question wants a linear ratio or dB
Phase relationships: capacitor voltage lags current (−90°), inductor leads (+90°); sign of the imaginary part tells lead or lag
conn: Capacitor impedance \( 1/(j\omega C) \) feeds into a potential divider to give the RC transfer function \( H = \frac{1}{1+j\omega RC} \), whose magnitude gives the Bode plot
Complex-number skills (rectangular and polar forms) link impedance arithmetic to phase angles and to time-domain expressions \( v(t), i(t) \)
Frequency dependence of |\(Z_{C}\)| explains Bode behaviour: low-pass shape, with attenuation increasing with frequency beyond the corner \( \omega = 1/RC \)
Phase lead/lag from the phasor diagram links to the sign of the imaginary part of Z and to the time-domain phase shift
exq: A series circuit has R = 100 Ω and C = 10 µF at f = 200 Hz. Find \( Z_t \) in rectangular and polar form, and the phase of the voltage relative to the current.
A current phasor is I = 2 + j2 A through a capacitor of reactance 5 Ω. Find the voltage phasor V = IZ, write i(t) and v(t) in cos form, and state the phase lag.
Derive the transfer function \( V_{out}/V_{in} \) for an RC circuit with output across the capacitor, give its magnitude and phase, and find the attenuation in dB at \( \omega = 1/RC \).
Sketch the Bode magnitude plot for an RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ, C = 100 nF. Find the corner frequency and the attenuation at 10 times that frequency.
Explain why using the impedance of a capacitor as a real number gives wrong answers, and show with a numerical example how the voltage lags the current by 90°.

notes.t: Phasors, complex impedance and Bode magnitude plots
pts: On this course, AC circuits are analysed either with phasors (magnitude and phase of voltages and currents) using complex impedances, or via transfer functions.
A phasor voltage equals the phasor current times the complex impedance, so impedance acts like a generalised resistance.
In the phasor diagram shown, the voltage and current are 90° out of phase, so the voltage leads or lags the current by a quarter cycle.
A transfer function is the ratio Vout/Vin; its magnitude gives the attenuation of the circuit at each frequency.
A Bode magnitude plot shows the magnitude of the transfer function against frequency, with magnitude usually in decibels and frequency usually on a log scale.
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal quantity by its amplitude and phase, allowing AC circuit analysis using algebra instead of differential equations.
Transfer function
The ratio of output to input of a circuit, expressed as a function of frequency, Vout/Vin, which describes how the circuit modifies a signal.
Bode magnitude plot
A graph of the magnitude of a transfer function (often in decibels) against frequency, usually plotted on a logarithmic frequency axis.
eqs: V = phasor voltage (V); I = phasor current (A); Z = complex impedance (Ω)
\(V_{out}\) = output voltage phasor (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage phasor (V); the ratio is dimensionless
tips: Remember that Z is complex: its magnitude and phase both matter, so do not treat it as a simple resistance when voltage and current are out of phase.
Magnitudes on Bode plots are usually given in decibels (20 log10 of the ratio), so check whether a question wants a linear ratio or dB before answering.
rq: Why is a phasor relation V = IZ useful when the current and voltage are sinusoidal but out of phase?
Because the complex impedance Z carries both the magnitude ratio and the phase shift, so V and I can be combined with ordinary complex algebra rather than solving differential equations.
Why are Bode plots drawn with a logarithmic frequency axis?
Because circuit behaviour changes over many decades of frequency, and a log scale shows these wide ranges compactly and makes asymptotic straight-line approximations possible.
What does a transfer function magnitude of 1 at low frequency and 0 at high frequency tell you about the circuit?
The circuit passes low-frequency signals unchanged and blocks high-frequency signals, so it behaves as a low-pass filter.

notes.t: Phasors, impedance and AC voltage-current relationships
pts: A current phasor is written in rectangular form as a + jb, and its angle on the complex plane gives the phase of the sinusoid.
The impedance of a capacitor is a purely imaginary complex number, so it shifts the phase by -90° relative to the current.
The voltage phasor is found by multiplying the current phasor by the impedance, V = IZ, which is the complex form of Ohm's law for AC circuits.
In a capacitor the voltage lags the current by 90°, shown by the voltage phasor sitting at -45° while the current is at +45°, a relative phase difference of 90°.
Time-domain expressions of a sinusoid are obtained from the phasor angle: the current is I₀cos(ωt + 45°) and the voltage is V₀cos(ωt − 45°).
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal quantity by its magnitude and phase angle, allowing AC circuit analysis using algebra instead of differential equations.
Impedance
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, generalising resistance to include reactive (capacitive or inductive) effects.
eqs: Z = impedance (Ω); j = imaginary unit; ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F)
Voltage phasor from current phasor and impedance
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
I = phasor (A); a = real part (A); b = imaginary part (A); j = imaginary unit
i(t) = instantaneous current (A); I₀ = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
v(t) = instantaneous voltage (V); V₀ = peak voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
tips: Watch the sign: for a capacitor Z = 1/(jωC) has phase -90°, so the voltage lags the current; do not write +90° as with an inductor.
Phasor angles are not the same as time-domain phase shifts when converting; always write v(t) with cos(ωt + θ) using the correct angle and peak amplitude V₀, not the RMS value.
rq: Why does the capacitor impedance have an angle of -90° rather than a magnitude alone?
Because 1/(jωC) = -j/(ωC), a purely imaginary number whose negative imaginary sign corresponds to a phase angle of -90°, so the voltage lags the current by 90°.
What would happen to the impedance magnitude if the frequency doubled?
|Z| = 1/(ωC) would halve, so a capacitor passes more current (lower reactance) at higher frequency, while the phase angle stays at -90°.
Why does the voltage phasor in the diagram appear at -45° while the current is at +45°?
The phase difference is 90°, so with the current at +45° the voltage sits 90° behind at -45°, consistent with V = IZ and Z at -90°.

notes.t: Phasors, impedance and phase relationships in AC circuits
pts: Current, voltage and impedance can each be represented as complex numbers / phasors on an Argand diagram, with the real and imaginary axes.
Voltage phasor is found from the current phasor multiplied by impedance, so its magnitude and angle follow from both.
For an RC series circuit the impedance is R plus the capacitive reactance term 1/(jωC), which points in the negative-imaginary direction.
In this example the phase angle between current and voltage phasors is 45°, shown on the phasor diagram.
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal quantity by its magnitude and phase angle, allowing AC circuit analysis using algebra.
Impedance
The complex opposition to AC current flow, combining resistance (real part) and reactance (imaginary part).
eqs: Ohm's law for AC phasors (voltage from current and impedance)
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
Total impedance of resistor in series with capacitor
\(Z_{t}\) = total impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
I = current phasor (A); a = real part (A); b = imaginary part (A); j = imaginary unit
tips: Don't confuse phasor (complex) quantities with instantaneous time-domain values; always use complex algebra for magnitude and angle.
Ensure ω is angular frequency in rad/s (ω = 2πf), not frequency in Hz, when calculating reactance.
rq: Why does the capacitive term 1/(jωC) appear with a negative imaginary direction on the impedance diagram, and what does that imply about the voltage relative to current?
Dividing by j gives -j/(ωC), a negative imaginary term, so the voltage lags the current in a capacitive circuit.
What happens to the capacitive part of impedance as frequency increases, and why?
It decreases, because ω appears in the denominator, so the capacitor opposes current less at high frequency.

notes.t: Phasors, impedance and voltage in AC circuits
pts: Current and voltage in an AC circuit can be represented as phasors, which are complex numbers rotating at the supply frequency.
The voltage phasor is found by multiplying the current phasor by the complex impedance, so V = IZ.
Impedance combines resistance with the reactance of a capacitor; for a series RC circuit the reactance term is 1/(jωC), which contributes a negative imaginary part.
In a series RC circuit the voltage phasor lags the current phasor, as shown by the voltage phasor sitting at a smaller angle than the current phasor.
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal quantity by its amplitude and phase angle, allowing AC circuit analysis using algebra.
Impedance
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, combining resistance (real part) and reactance (imaginary part).
eqs: Ohm's law for AC circuits (voltage phasor from current phasor and impedance)
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
Total impedance of a series resistor and capacitor
\(Z_{t}\) = total impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
Complex form of a current phasor
I = current phasor (A); a = real part (A); b = imaginary part (A); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not treat the impedance as a simple real number; the capacitor term is imaginary, so always add real and imaginary parts separately.
Remember that phasor angles describe phase lead or lag, and the voltage across a capacitor lags the current, so check the sign of the imaginary part.
rq: Why does the capacitor term 1/(jωC) have a negative imaginary part, and what does this mean for the voltage relative to the current?
Since 1/j = −j, the term becomes −j/(ωC), a negative imaginary contribution; this makes the voltage lag the current, so the voltage phasor is rotated clockwise relative to the current phasor.
What happens to the magnitude of the capacitive impedance if the frequency doubles?
The reactance 1/(ωC) halves, because it is inversely proportional to ω, so the capacitor opposes the current less at higher frequency.

units.name: 3.4 RC low-pass filter and frequency response
units.ov: This material introduces the RC low-pass filter, in which the output is the voltage across the capacitor and the resistor is in series with the input. Capacitor impedance falls with frequency, so low frequencies pass and high frequencies are shunted to ground. This behaviour is captured by the complex transfer function \(H(\omega)=1/(1+j\omega/\omega_0)\), its magnitude, and the characteristic frequency \(\omega_0=1/RC\) that marks the cut-off on a Bode plot.
must: Circuit topology: R in series with the input, C from the output node to ground, and \(V_o\) is the voltage across C only, referenced to the same ground as \(V_{in}\)
Transfer function: \(H(\omega)=\frac{V_o}{V_{in}}=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}=\frac{1}{1+j\omega/\omega_0}\)
Characteristic (cut-off) angular frequency: \(\omega_0=\frac{1}{RC}\) in rad/s, and \(f_0=\frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}=\frac{1}{2\pi RC}\) in Hz; always use \(\omega=2\pi f\)
Gain magnitude: \(|H|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_0)^2}}\), the modulus of the complex denominator by Pythagoras (not \(1/(1+\omega RC)\))
At \(\omega=\omega_0\): \(|H|=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707\) (−3 dB), so the output is still about 70.7% of the input at cut-off
Limiting behaviour: for \(\omega\ll\omega_0\), \(|H|\to1\) (C acts as an open circuit); for \(\omega\gg\omega_0\), \(|H|\to0\) (C acts as a short circuit, so all of \(V_{in}\) drops across R)
Bode plot: a flat passband at gain 1 (0 dB), then a roll-off beyond \(\omega_0\), plotted against log frequency
\(H(\omega)\) is complex (gain and phase) while \(|H(\omega)|\) is real (gain only, phase lost); the phase is \(-\tan^{-1}(\omega/\omega_0)\)
Definitions: a low-pass filter passes frequencies below cut-off and attenuates those above; \(\omega_0\) is where gain falls to \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of the passband value
conn: Capacitor impedance \(1/(j\omega C)\) together with the potential divider rule gives the transfer function, which then yields \(\omega_0=1/RC\) and the cut-off frequency
Complex numbers and the Argand diagram: the modulus gives the gain \(|H|\) and the argument gives the phase shift, so a question may ask for both at a given frequency
Converting between rad/s and Hz, and between gain ratio and dB (\(20\log_{10}|H|\)), links \(\omega_0\) to the Bode plot features such as the −3 dB point
Output amplitude calculations: \(V_{o,\text{amp}}=|H|V_{in,\text{amp}}\) for a sinusoidal input at a given frequency, using component values to find \(\omega_0\) first
exq: A low-pass RC filter has R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Calculate \(\omega_0\) and the cut-off frequency in Hz, and state the gain magnitude at that frequency.
Derive the transfer function \(V_o/V_{in}=1/(1+j\omega RC)\) for the RC filter with output across the capacitor, then find its magnitude and explain why the circuit is a low-pass filter.
For the filter in the previous question, a 5 V amplitude sinusoid at 2 kHz is applied. Calculate \(|H|\), the output amplitude, and the phase shift of the output relative to the input.
Sketch the Bode plot (magnitude in dB against log frequency) for an RC low-pass filter, marking \(\omega_0\), the −3 dB point, and the gain at \(\omega_0/10\) and \(10\omega_0\).

Explain physically, using capacitor behaviour, why the output tends to \(V_{in}\) at low frequency and to zero at high frequency. Then determine the frequency at which the output amplitude is half the input.

notes.t: RC Lowpass Filter – output taken across capacitor
pts: In an RC lowpass filter, the output voltage is taken as the voltage across the capacitor only, not the total input voltage across both components.
The resistor R is in series with the input, and the capacitor C is connected from the output node to ground, so the capacitor voltage is \(V_{o}\).
A filter circuit passes or attenuates signals depending on their frequency; here \(V_{\text{in}}\) is the input and \(V_{o}\) is the output.
defs: Output voltage (\(V_{o}\)) in this circuit
The voltage measured across the capacitor, taken with respect to ground.
tips: Do not confuse \(V_{o}\) with \(V_{\text{in}}\): \(V_{o}\) is only the voltage across C, not the total across R and C.
Make sure the output is referenced to the same ground as the input.
rq: Why does taking the output across the capacitor rather than across both components make the circuit a filter?

The capacitor's impedance falls with frequency, so high-frequency signals are shunted to ground and attenuated, while low-frequency signals appear at \(V_{o}\); this frequency-dependent division is what makes it a lowpass filter.

notes.t: RC Low-Pass Filter – High-Frequency Behaviour
pts: At very high frequencies the capacitor behaves as a short circuit, shunting the signal to ground.
High-frequency components are therefore not passed to the output; only low frequencies appear at Vo, which is why this is a low-pass filter.
With the capacitor shorted, Vo is effectively connected to ground, so almost no voltage appears across the output terminals.
Essentially all of the input voltage drops across the series resistor R at high frequency.
defs: Low-pass filter
A circuit that passes signals below a cut-off frequency to the output while attenuating signals at higher frequencies.
tips: Do not confuse the capacitor's behaviour: it is an open circuit at DC/low frequency but a short circuit at high frequency.
The output is taken across the capacitor (shunt) branch, so Vo small at high frequency means the filter attenuates highs; check which component the output is measured across.
rq: Why does the output voltage fall to almost zero at high frequencies in the RC circuit?
At high frequency the capacitor's reactance becomes very small, so it acts as a short circuit across the output; the input voltage then drops almost entirely across R and Vo is negligible.
What would happen to Vo if the capacitor were replaced by an open circuit at high frequency?
Vo would equal Vin, since no current would flow through R and no voltage would drop across it, so high frequencies would pass unattenuated.

notes.t: Low-pass RC filter frequency response (Bode plot)
pts: At low frequency the capacitor is effectively open circuit, so the output equals the input and the gain is 1.
As frequency rises, the capacitor's impedance falls, shunting the signal to ground, so the gain decreases toward 0 at high frequency.
The Bode plot of |Vout/Vin| against frequency shows a flat passband followed by a roll-off, characteristic of a low-pass filter.
defs: Bode plot
A graph of the magnitude (often in dB) or phase of a transfer function plotted against frequency, usually on a logarithmic frequency axis, used to characterise a circuit's frequency response.
Filter (low-pass)
A circuit that passes signals below a cut-off frequency with little attenuation while attenuating signals at higher frequencies.
eqs: Transfer function of the RC low-pass filter (output/input voltage ratio)
\(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
tips: Use ω = 2πf when substituting into the transfer function; using f directly in ωRC gives the wrong cut-off frequency.
The magnitude is |Vout/Vin| = 1/√(1+(ωRC)²), not 1/(1+ωRC); the j term must be treated as a complex quantity.
rq: Why does the output magnitude tend to 1 at low frequency and 0 at high frequency?
At low frequency the capacitor impedance 1/(jωC) is very large, so little current flows and Vout ≈ Vin; at high frequency the impedance is very small, shorting the output to ground so Vout ≈ 0.
What happens to the gain magnitude when ωRC = 1, and why does this define the cut-off?
|Vout/Vin| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB), the point where the output power is halved; this is the cut-off frequency \(f_{c}\) = 1/(2πRC).

notes.t: RC filter analysis: transfer function and characteristic frequency
pts: The transfer function of the RC filter depends on frequency through the product ωRC, so the output-to-input ratio is a function of ω/ω₀.
The characteristic frequency ω₀ is set by the component values as the reciprocal of RC, so RC and ω₀ are interchangeable ways of describing the same circuit.
Well below ω₀ the output equals the input (gain tends to 1), so the signal passes through unattenuated.
Well above ω₀ the output tends to zero, so high frequencies are blocked: this is the low-pass behaviour.
At exactly ω = ω₀ the magnitude of the gain is 1/√2, about 0.707, which is the −3 dB point.
defs: Characteristic frequency (ω₀)
The frequency ω₀ = 1/(RC) at which the magnitude of the filter's transfer function falls to 1/√2 of its passband value; it marks the boundary between passed and attenuated frequencies.
eqs: Transfer function of the RC filter (magnitude and phase in normalised form)
\(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = characteristic angular frequency (rad/s); j = imaginary unit
Characteristic angular frequency of the RC circuit
ω₀ = characteristic angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
Gain magnitude at the characteristic frequency
tips: Check units: ω₀ = 1/(RC) is in rad/s, so convert to Hz (f = ω/2π) if the question asks for a frequency in hertz.
Do not confuse the gain of 1/√2 at ω₀ with zero output: the output is still about 70.7% of the input at cutoff.
rq: Why does the output tend to zero when ω >> ω₀ even though the input is still present?

With ωRC large, the term jω/ω₀ dominates the denominator, making |\(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\)| ≈ ω₀/ω → 0, so the capacitor's reactance becomes very small and shunts the high-frequency signal away from the output.
What would happen to ω₀ if you doubled R while keeping C fixed, and what does that do to the cutoff?
ω₀ = 1/(RC) halves, so the cutoff (−3 dB point) moves to a lower frequency; the filter passes fewer frequencies.
Why is the magnitude 1/√2 rather than 1/2 at ω = ω₀?
|1 + j·1| = √(1² + 1²) = √2, so the magnitude is 1/√2; the √2 arises from adding the real and imaginary parts in quadrature.

notes.t: Transfer function vs magnitude of transfer function
pts: The transfer function H(ω) is a complex quantity; its denominator 1 + j(ω/ω₀) is a complex number whose real part is 1 and imaginary part is ω/ω₀.
The magnitude of H(ω) is found by taking the modulus of the complex denominator, which is the length of the phasor on the Argand diagram, found using Pythagoras' theorem.
The magnitude of the denominator is the square root of the sum of the squared real and imaginary parts, so |H(ω)| decreases as ω increases.
defs: Transfer function H(ω)
The ratio of output voltage to input voltage as a function of angular frequency, written as a complex quantity H(ω) = Vo/Vin.
Magnitude of transfer function |H(ω)|
The modulus of the complex transfer function, giving the ratio of output to input voltage amplitudes at a given frequency, independent of phase.
eqs: Transfer function of the RC low-pass filter
H(ω) = transfer function (dimensionless); Vo = output voltage (V); Vin = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); j = imaginary unit
|H(ω)| = magnitude of transfer function (dimensionless); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
tips: The magnitude of a complex denominator is the square root of the sum of squares of real and imaginary parts, not the sum itself: √(1 + (ω/ω₀)²), not 1 + (ω/ω₀)².
Do not confuse H(ω) (complex, includes phase) with |H(ω)| (real, gain only); phase information is lost when taking the magnitude.
rq: Why does taking the magnitude remove the j from the denominator, and what does the result tell you about the circuit's gain as ω increases?
The modulus of 1 + j(ω/ω₀) is √(1 + (ω/ω₀)²), so |H(ω)| is real and falls as ω rises: the filter attenuates high frequencies.
What happens to |H(ω)| when ω = ω₀, and why is this value important?
|H| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB), the half-power point defining the cut-off frequency.

units.name: 3.5 Decibels and power/voltage attenuation
units.ov: This material introduces the decibel as a logarithmic measure of power or voltage ratios, used for gain and attenuation in filters. It starts from P = V²/R, which shows that a voltage ratio must be squared to give a power ratio. That is why power ratios use 10 log₁₀ and voltage ratios use 20 log₁₀, and why a filter output that is 1/√2 of the input voltage has half the power (about −3 dB).
must: Power dB: \( \mathrm{dB}=10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1) \), with output over input
Voltage dB: \( \mathrm{dB}=20\log_{10}(V_2/V_1) \), valid only when the resistance is the same at both points
Filter result: \( V_{out}=V_{in}/\sqrt{2} \) gives \( P_{out}=P_{in}/2 \), which is \( 10\log_{10}0.5\approx-3\) dB (the half-power point)

Anchor values: a ratio of 1 is 0 dB. Each ×10 change in power is ±10 dB, and each ×10 change in voltage is ±20 dB. Power ratios of 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 give −10, −20 and −30 dB, and voltage ratios of 0.01 and 0.001 give −40 and −60 dB
A negative dB value means attenuation (output smaller than input), not negative power or voltage
Power depends on V², so square the voltage ratio. Power does not fall by the same factor as voltage
Using 10 log₁₀ on voltage ratios gives half the correct answer, and 20 log₁₀ on power ratios doubles it
dB is dimensionless and relative. Absolute levels need a stated reference such as dBV or dBm
The log scale compresses a huge range of ratios, for example sound from 0 dB (weakest audible) through about 60 dB (conversation) to 140 dB (threshold of pain)
conn: Resistor power \( P=V^2/R \) links to the voltage dB formula: the square turns the factor 10 into 20, provided R is constant
The filter's \( 1/\sqrt{2} \) voltage reduction links to a power ratio of 1/2 and to −3 dB. Both the 20 log₁₀ and 10 log₁₀ routes must give the same answer
Converting dB back to a ratio (\( 10^{dB/10} \) for power, \( 10^{dB/20} \) for voltage) links to cascaded stages, where dB values add while ratios multiply
The logarithmic dB scale links to real-world quantities such as sound level, where a large change in ratio becomes a manageable number
exq: A filter reduces the output voltage by a factor of √2 relative to the input. Show that the output power is half the input power for a fixed resistance R, and calculate the attenuation in dB using both the power and voltage formulae.
An amplifier raises a signal from 2 mW to 50 mW. Calculate the gain in dB. Then calculate the dB change if the voltage across the same resistor rises from 0.1 V to 0.5 V.
A signal is attenuated by −40 dB. Find the output/input ratio for (a) voltage and (b) power. If the input is 5 V across 50 Ω, find the output voltage and output power.
Explain why voltage ratios use 20 log₁₀ and power ratios use 10 log₁₀. State the assumption that must hold, and give the error made by using 10 log₁₀ on a voltage ratio of 0.01.
Two filter stages have gains of −3 dB and −17 dB. Find the total attenuation in dB and the overall power ratio and voltage ratio.

notes.t: Voltage vs power attenuation
pts: Power dissipated in a resistor depends on the square of the voltage, so reducing voltage has a larger effect on power.
Filtering reduces the output voltage by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\) compared with the input voltage.
Because power scales with V², a voltage reduced by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives a power reduced by a factor of 2 (half the input power).
eqs: Input power dissipated in resistor R
Output voltage after filtering (RMS-type reduction by √2)
Output power dissipated in resistor R
\(P_{out}\) = output power (W); \(V_{out}\) = output voltage (V); \(R\) = resistance (Ω); \(P_{in}\) = input power (W)
tips: Do not assume power falls by the same factor as voltage; power depends on V², so a voltage ratio must be squared.
Keep R constant when comparing input and output power, otherwise the ratio \(P_{\text{out}}\)/\(P_{\text{in}}\) is not valid.
rq: Why does a √2 reduction in voltage halve the power rather than reduce it by √2?
Power is proportional to V², so \((V_{in}/\sqrt{2})^2 = V_{in}^2/2\); the square cancels the √2, giving a factor of 2.
If the output voltage were reduced to one-third of the input voltage, what fraction of the input power would remain?
Power would be \((1/3)^2 = 1/9\) of the input power, since power scales with the square of voltage.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: introduction to the decibel (dB)
pts: In engineering, gain and attenuation are usually expressed in decibels (dB) rather than as plain ratios.
The decibel scale is a logarithmic scale, so very large or very small ratios are compressed into manageable numbers.
The decibel chart shows typical sound levels: 0 dB is the weakest audible sound, about 60 dB is conversation, and 140 dB is the threshold of pain.
defs: Decibel (dB)
A logarithmic unit expressing the ratio of two power or voltage quantities; a dimensionless measure of relative level.
tips: Do not confuse dB with a linear ratio: 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power but only about 3.16 in voltage (since dB = 20 log10 for voltage ratios).
dB is dimensionless; a reference level (e.g. dBV, dBm) must be stated when expressing absolute levels.
rq: Why do engineers prefer a logarithmic unit like dB when describing filter gain?
Filter gains can span many orders of magnitude, and multiplying gains becomes simple addition of dB values, which is convenient for cascaded stages and Bode plots.
Why does a sound at 80 dB not sound twice as loud as one at 40 dB?
The decibel scale is logarithmic, so equal dB steps correspond to multiplicative changes in intensity, not linear changes in perceived loudness.

notes.t: Decibels (dB) – expressing power ratios on a logarithmic scale
pts: Engineers use decibels rather than raw power ratios because the dB scale compresses very large or very small ratios into manageable numbers.
A power ratio of 1 corresponds to 0 dB, meaning no change in power between the two points.
Each factor of 10 reduction in the power ratio subtracts 10 dB, so a ratio of 0.1 gives −10 dB, 0.01 gives −20 dB and 0.001 gives −30 dB.
A negative dB value indicates that the output power P2 is smaller than the reference power P1 (a loss or attenuation).
defs: Decibel (dB)
A logarithmic unit of the ratio between two powers, equal to ten times the base-10 logarithm of the power ratio.
eqs: dB = power ratio in decibels (dB); \(P_{2}\) = output or measured power (W); \(P_{1}\) = reference input power (W)
tips: The dB formula uses a factor of 10 for power ratios; voltage or current ratios use 20log₁₀ instead, so do not mix them up.
Check the sign: a ratio below 1 gives a negative dB value, which means a loss, not a negative power.
rq: Why does a power ratio of 0.1 give −10 dB rather than +10 dB?
Because the logarithm of a number less than 1 is negative, so 10·log₁₀(0.1) = 10·(−1) = −10 dB; the output power is smaller than the reference.
If a signal's power is doubled, what is the change in dB, and why is the dB scale convenient for cascaded stages?
10·log₁₀(2) ≈ +3 dB; because logarithms turn multiplication of gains into addition, so the dB gains of cascaded stages simply add.

notes.t: Calculating decibels (dB) using voltage ratios
pts: The decibel is defined in terms of a power ratio, so voltage ratios must be converted using the power–voltage relationship.
Substituting P = V²/R into the power definition gives the voltage form; the squared terms bring the factor 10 up to 20 (assuming equal resistances at both points).
Power is proportional to the square of voltage, so the voltage-ratio formula uses 20 log₁₀ rather than 10 log₁₀.
defs: Decibel (dB)
A logarithmic unit expressing the ratio of two power levels: dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁).
eqs: dB = decibel gain (dB); P₂ = output power (W); P₁ = input power (W)
P = power (W); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω)
dB = voltage gain (dB); V₂ = output voltage (V); V₁ = input voltage (V)
tips: Use 20 log₁₀ only for voltage ratios with equal resistances; using 10 log₁₀ with voltages gives an answer half the correct size.
Keep the ratio order consistent: output over input (V₂/V₁) gives a positive dB value for gain.
rq: Why does the voltage-ratio formula use 20 log₁₀ instead of 10 log₁₀?
Because power is proportional to V², and log(V²) = 2 log V, so the factor 10 × 2 = 20 appears.
What assumption must hold to go from 10 log₁₀(V₂²/V₁²) to 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁)?
The resistance must be the same at both points (R₁ = R₂), so it cancels in the power ratio.

notes.t: Using decibels (dB) for voltage ratios
pts: The decibel expresses a voltage ratio on a logarithmic scale, with a factor of 20 for voltage quantities.
A voltage ratio of 1 corresponds to 0 dB, meaning no change in voltage.
Each tenfold reduction in the voltage ratio subtracts 20 dB, so ratios below 1 give negative dB values.
Ratios of 0.01 and 0.001 give −40 dB and −60 dB, showing the logarithmic pattern continues.
defs: Decibel (dB) for voltage
A logarithmic unit of voltage ratio, defined as 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of two voltages.
eqs: dB = decibel value (dB); \(V_{2}\) = output or second voltage (V); \(V_{1}\) = input or reference voltage (V)
tips: Use a factor of 20 for voltage ratios and a factor of 10 for power ratios; mixing them up doubles or halves the answer.
A negative dB value means the output is smaller than the reference (attenuation), not that the voltage is negative.
rq: Why does a voltage ratio of 0.1 give −20 dB rather than −10 dB?
Voltage decibels use a factor of 20, so 20·log10(0.1) = 20·(−1) = −20 dB; the factor 10 is used only for power ratios.
What does a result of 0 dB tell you about V2 and V1?
V2 equals V1 (the ratio is 1), so there is no gain or attenuation.

units.name: 3.6 -3 dB point, Bode plots and low-pass design examples
units.ov: This material defines decibel gain, shows that the -3 dB point of a first-order filter is where |Vout/Vin| = 1/√2, and uses it to draw asymptotic Bode plots with a -20 dB/decade roll-off. It then applies these ideas to design an RC low-pass filter (choosing C for a given cut-off) and to estimate attenuation at higher frequencies. The chain is: dB definition → cut-off at -3 dB → corner frequency and slope on a Bode plot → component design and attenuation estimate.
must: Voltage gain in dB: \( R = 20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in}) \); use 10 log10 for power ratios, not 20
At cut-off \( |V_{out}/V_{in}| = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707 \), giving \( 20\log_{10}(1/\sqrt{2}) \approx -3\) dB, which is the half-power point
First-order RC low-pass transfer function: \( V_{out}/V_{in} = 1/(1 + j\omega/\omega_0) \), with magnitude \( 1/\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_0)^2} \)
Cut-off: \( \omega_0 = 1/RC \) and \( f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC) \); convert with \( \omega = 2\pi f \), since forgetting this gives a factor 2π error
Design: \( C = 1/(2\pi R f_0) \); for R = 1 kΩ and f0 = 1 kHz, C ≈ 0.159 µF (use base units: 1000 Ω, farads)
Bode asymptotes: flat (0 dB) below \( f_0 \), then -20 dB/decade above it. The true curve is 3 dB below the corner intersection at \( f_0 \)
Decades between frequencies: \( d = \log_{10}(f_2/f_1) \), a ratio and not a difference. Attenuation ≈ d × (-20 dB)
Example: 100 kHz with f0 = 1 kHz is 2 decades, so about -40 dB. The exact value is |H| ≈ 0.00999, or -40.0004 dB, i.e. a voltage ratio of about 1/100
The -20 dB/decade estimate is valid only well above \( f_0 \); near \( f_0 \) use the exact magnitude formula
dB scales are logarithmic, compressing a wide range and making high attenuation easy to read, and equal dB steps are not equal linear voltage steps
conn: The 1/√2 magnitude at \( \omega=\omega_0 \) comes from substituting ω/ω0 = 1 into the transfer function magnitude, and this gives the -3 dB value via the dB definition
The design formula \( C = 1/(2\pi R f_0) \) sets the corner frequency of the Bode plot, which then fixes the attenuation at any higher frequency via the decades × slope rule
The asymptotic estimate (-40 dB) can be checked against the exact |H(ω)| and dB formulas, and the two agree when ω ≫ ω0 but differ by 3 dB at ω0
Voltage (20 log) versus power (10 log) ratios link the -3 dB point to half power, since a power ratio of 1/2 corresponds to a voltage ratio of 1/√2
exq: Show that a voltage ratio of 1/√2 corresponds to approximately -3 dB, and state what power ratio this represents.
Design a first-order RC low-pass filter with a -3 dB frequency of 1 kHz using R = 1 kΩ. Calculate C and state ω0 in rad/s.
Sketch the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot for the filter with f0 = 1 kHz from 10 Hz to 1 MHz, marking the corner frequency, the slope, and the actual gain at f0.
Estimate the attenuation in dB at 100 kHz for the 1 kHz filter using the roll-off slope, then calculate the exact value from |H(ω)| and comment on the difference.
A first-order low-pass filter has f0 = 2 kHz. Find the gain in dB and the voltage ratio at 5 kHz using the exact expression, and explain why the -20 dB/decade approximation is poor there.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Decibel Gain at the Cut-off Frequency
pts: Gain in decibels is defined as 20 times the log10 of the voltage ratio Vout/Vin.
At the cut-off frequency ω_o, the output voltage is 1/√2 of the input voltage.
Substituting Vout/Vin = 1/√2 into the decibel formula gives approximately -3 dB, the standard half-power point.
defs: Decibel gain R
A logarithmic measure of voltage gain, R = 20 log10(Vout/Vin), expressed in dB.
Cut-off frequency ω_o
The angular frequency at which the output voltage falls to 1/√2 (about 0.707) of the input voltage, corresponding to -3 dB.
eqs: R = gain (dB); \(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V)
\(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) = dimensionless voltage ratio; ω_o = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
tips: Use 20log10 for voltage ratios and 10log10 for power ratios; mixing these up gives the wrong dB value.
The value -3 dB applies only at the cut-off frequency ω_o where Vout/Vin = 1/√2; do not apply it at other frequencies.
rq: Why is the cut-off point defined at 1/√2 rather than 1/2 of the input voltage?
Because power is proportional to V², so V = 1/√2 gives half the power, which is the -3 dB half-power point.
What happens to the dB value if Vout/Vin falls to 0.1 instead of 0.707?
R = 20 log10(0.1) = -20 dB, so the attenuation is much greater than -3 dB.

notes.t: Why we use decibels (dB) and the -3 dB point of a first-order filter
pts: dB are defined using logarithms, so gain is expressed on a logarithmic scale.
The logarithmic scale compresses the plotted range, letting very large and very small gains fit on one graph.
On a dB plot, high attenuation is easier to read than on a linear voltage-ratio plot, where the curve flattens near zero.
At the cut-off frequency of a first-order filter, the voltage ratio is 1/√2 which corresponds to -3 dB.
defs: Decibel (dB)
A logarithmic unit used to express a ratio of voltages, currents or powers; for voltage gain, gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(Vout/Vin).
eqs: \(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); dB = gain (dB, dimensionless)
Voltage ratio at the cut-off frequency of a first-order filter
tips: Do not confuse the voltage-ratio formula 20 log₁₀ with the power formula 10 log₁₀; -3 dB corresponds to a power ratio of 1/2 but a voltage ratio of 1/√2.
Remember the dB scale is logarithmic, so equal dB steps do not mean equal linear changes in voltage.
rq: Why does a voltage ratio of 1/√2 correspond to exactly -3 dB?
Using dB = 20 log₁₀(1/√2) = 20 × (−0.1505) ≈ −3.01 dB, i.e. approximately −3 dB.
Why is a logarithmic frequency axis useful for filter plots?
It compresses a wide range of frequencies (10 Hz to 100 kHz) into a readable plot and makes the roll-off appear as a straight line.

notes.t: Bode plots: asymptotic approximation of gain
pts: A Bode plot shows gain in dB against frequency on a logarithmic axis.
At the characteristic frequency \(f_{o}\) the gain is down by 3 dB relative to the passband.
Knowing \(f_{o}\) and the slope lets you estimate attenuation at frequencies away from \(f_{o}\).
The asymptotic fit is flat below \(f_{o}\) and falls at a constant slope above it, giving -20 dB per decade for a first-order low-pass filter.
Each decade of frequency above \(f_{o}\) produces an additional attenuation of 20 dB.
defs: Characteristic (corner) frequency \(f_{o}\)
The frequency at which the asymptotes meet and the actual gain is 3 dB below its passband value.
Decade
A tenfold change in frequency, the unit used to express slope on a logarithmic frequency axis.
Asymptotic fit
A piecewise straight-line approximation of the true gain curve, accurate well away from the corner frequency.
eqs: Number of decades between two frequencies
d = number of decades (dimensionless); \(f_{1}\) = lower frequency (Hz); \(f_{2}\) = higher frequency (Hz)
tips: The -3 dB point is only exact at \(f_{o}\); the asymptotic fit is off by about 3 dB there, so do not read \(f_{o}\) gain from the straight lines.
Slope is quoted per decade (factor of 10 in frequency), not per octave or per Hz.
rq: Why does the true curve sit 3 dB below the asymptotic fit at \(f_{o}\) rather than on it?
Because the two straight asymptotes intersect at \(f_{o}\), but the real response is smooth there; the actual gain at the corner is 1/√2 of the passband amplitude, which is -3 dB.
If a filter falls at -20 dB/decade, what is the attenuation at 10 \(f_{o}\) compared with the passband?
Approximately -20 dB, since one decade above \(f_{o}\) gives an extra 20 dB of attenuation.

notes.t: Designing an RC low-pass filter with a -3 dB cut-off at 1 kHz
pts: For a first-order RC low-pass filter, the -3 dB point occurs at the characteristic (cut-off) frequency, where ω/ω₀ = 1.
The cut-off angular frequency is set by the product RC, so for a given resistor the capacitor is found by rearranging f₀ = 1/(2πRC).
With R = 1 kΩ and f₀ = 1 kHz, the required capacitance is about 0.159 µF.
defs: -3 dB cut-off frequency

The frequency at which the output power falls to half of the passband value, i.e. the gain magnitude drops to 1/√2 (≈0.707) of its low-frequency value; for a first-order RC low-pass filter this is ω₀ = 1/RC.
eqs: Transfer function of a first-order RC low-pass filter
\(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency of input (rad/s); ω₀ = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
Cut-off angular frequency of an RC filter
ω₀ = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
Relation between angular and cyclic frequency
Capacitance required for a given cut-off frequency
C = capacitance (F); R = resistance (Ω); f₀ = cut-off frequency (Hz)
tips: Convert frequency to angular frequency (ω = 2πf) before using ω₀ = 1/RC; using f directly gives the wrong capacitance by a factor of 2π.
Keep units consistent: use Ω and F (not kΩ or µF) in the formula, so 1 kΩ must be entered as 1000 Ω.
rq: Why does the -3 dB point occur exactly where ω = ω₀ in the transfer function?
At ω = ω₀ the denominator becomes 1 + j, with magnitude √2, so |\(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\)| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, which is a drop of 3 dB.
What would happen to the cut-off frequency if you doubled the capacitance while keeping R fixed?
The cut-off frequency halves, since f₀ = 1/(2πRC) is inversely proportional to C.

notes.t: Estimating attenuation of a first-order RC low-pass filter at 100 kHz
pts: Above the characteristic frequency, a first-order RC low-pass filter rolls off at about -20 dB per decade.
The roll-off approximation is valid only well above the cut-off frequency ω₀, so the estimate is accurate far from ω₀.
Number of decades between two frequencies is the log of their ratio; here 100 kHz / 1 kHz = 100 gives 2 decades.
Estimated attenuation = number of decades × roll-off slope, giving about -40 dB at 100 kHz.
The exact magnitude from the transfer function confirms the estimate: |Vo/Vin| ≈ 0.00999, i.e. -40.0004 dB.
defs: Decade
A factor of 10 in frequency; the number of decades between f₁ and f₂ is d = log₁₀(f₂/f₁).
eqs: Magnitude of transfer function of first-order RC low-pass filter
|H(ω)| = gain magnitude (dimensionless); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = characteristic (cut-off) angular frequency (rad/s); Vo = output voltage (V); Vin = input voltage (V)
Number of decades between two frequencies
d = number of decades (dimensionless); f₁, f₂ = frequencies (Hz)
tips: Decades are a ratio of frequencies (log base 10), not a difference; 100 kHz / 1 kHz = 100, so use log₁₀(100) = 2 decades.
The -20 dB/decade slope is only valid well above the characteristic frequency; do not apply it near ω₀ where the gain is about -3 dB.
rq: Why does the -20 dB/decade estimate only work well far above ω₀, and what does the exact formula show at ω₀?
Far above ω₀ the term (ω/ω₀)² dominates the denominator, so |H| ≈ ω₀/ω, falling 20 dB per decade. At ω = ω₀ the gain is 1/√2 ≈ -3 dB, so the approximation is poor near cut-off.
If the frequency range were 1 kHz to 10 kHz instead of 1 kHz to 100 kHz, how much attenuation would you estimate and why?
One decade, so about -20 dB, since d = log₁₀(10) = 1 and attenuation = 1 × -20 dB/decade.

units.name: 3.7 RC high-pass filter
units.ov: This material covers the first-order RC high-pass filter: a capacitor in series with the input and the output taken across R. Its behaviour follows from comparing the capacitor impedance \(1/(\omega C)\) with R. This gives the transfer function \(V_{out}/V_{in}=1/(1+\omega_0/(j\omega))\), the cut-off \(\omega_0=1/(RC)\), and the Bode magnitude plot with its -3 dB point and 20 dB/decade roll-off.
must: Topology: C in series with the input, output across R. Output across C would be a low-pass filter, so do not swap them.
Capacitor impedance \(Z_c=-j/(\omega C)\), with magnitude \(1/(\omega C)\). The filter behaves as a potential divider, so \(V_{out}/V_{in}=R/(R+Z_c)\).
Transfer function \(\dfrac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=\dfrac{1}{1+\omega_0/(j\omega)}\), which is equivalent to \(\dfrac{j\omega RC}{1+j\omega RC}\).
Cut-off \(\omega_0=1/(RC)\) rad/s and \(f_0=\omega_0/2\pi=1/(2\pi RC)\). Always check whether a question gives angular or ordinary frequency.
Low-frequency limit (\(\omega\ll\omega_0\)): \(|Z_c|\gg R\), so \(V_{out}\to0\) and the capacitor blocks the signal (it acts as an open circuit).
High-frequency limit (\(\omega\gg\omega_0\)): \(|Z_c|\ll R\), so \(V_{out}\approx V_{in}\) and the capacitor acts as a short circuit.
At the cut-off the gain magnitude is \(1/\sqrt2\approx0.707\), which is -3 dB and half the output power. It is not zero output.
Gain in dB is \(20\log_{10}|V_{out}/V_{in}|\). Below cut-off the Bode plot rises at +20 dB/decade, i.e. the gain falls at 20 dB/decade as frequency decreases. It flattens to 0 dB well above cut-off.
Use magnitudes when comparing impedances: the \(-j\) only gives phase. The Bode frequency axis is logarithmic, so equal spacing means equal ratios.

Magnitude is \(|V_{out}/V_{in}|=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega_0/\omega)^2}}\). Phase leads by 45° at cut-off, approaching 90° at low frequency and 0° at high frequency (derived from the transfer function).
conn: Complex impedance and the potential divider give the transfer function, which gives the limiting behaviours and the cut-off frequency.
Transfer function magnitude, dB conversion and the Bode plot: -3 dB at \(\omega_0\) and the 20 dB/decade slope both follow from \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+(\omega_0/\omega)^2}\).
Component choice and frequency: R and C set \(\omega_0=1/(RC)\), so designing a filter for a given \(f_c\) requires converting between \(f\) and \(\omega\).
High-pass versus low-pass: the same RC divider with the output taken across the other component, so the limits and Bode shape are mirrored.
exq: Derive the transfer function \(V_{out}/V_{in}\) of an RC high-pass filter using impedances, and show it can be written as \(1/(1+\omega_0/(j\omega))\) with \(\omega_0=1/(RC)\).
A high-pass filter has R = 160 Ω and C = 1 µF. Calculate \(\omega_0\) and \(f_c\), then find the gain in dB and the output amplitude for a 1 V input at \(f_c/10\), \(f_c\) and \(10f_c\).

Sketch the Bode magnitude plot for a high-pass filter with cut-off 1 kHz, labelling the -3 dB point, the slope in dB/decade, and the high-frequency asymptote. Explain physically, using capacitor impedance, why each region behaves as it does.
Choose R for C = 100 nF so that a high-pass filter attenuates 50 Hz mains hum by at least 20 dB. State the resulting cut-off frequency and the gain at 5 kHz.
Explain why the -3 dB point corresponds to a voltage ratio of 0.707 and to half the power, and distinguish the high-pass arrangement from the low-pass one.

notes.t: High-pass RC filter introduction
pts: The circuit is a high-pass filter: the capacitor C is in series with the input, and the output \(V_{o}\) is taken across the resistor R.
The output is taken across R, so low-frequency signals are blocked by the capacitor while high-frequency signals pass through to the output.
defs: High-pass filter
A filter circuit that passes signals above a cut-off frequency with little attenuation and attenuates signals below it.
tips: Do not confuse the high-pass arrangement (output across R) with the low-pass arrangement (output across C), which swaps the components' roles.
rq: Why does the output of this circuit appear across R rather than across C?

Because the output is taken across R; with C in series, low-frequency signals are blocked by C's high reactance, so the voltage across R is small at low frequency and approaches \(V_{\text{in}}\) at high frequency.

notes.t: RC Filter Circuits: Low-Frequency and High-Frequency Limits
pts: For a RC filter, the cutoff angular frequency is ω₀ = 1/(RC); it sets the boundary between low- and high-frequency behaviour.
When ω << ω₀, the term ω₀/(jω) becomes very large, so the gain Vout/Vin tends to zero: low frequencies are blocked, characteristic of a high-pass response.
When ω >> ω₀, the term ω₀/(jω) tends to zero, so Vout/Vin tends to 1: high frequencies pass unattenuated.
defs: Cutoff angular frequency ω₀
The frequency ω₀ = 1/(RC) at which the RC filter transition between passing and blocking signals occurs.
eqs: Transfer function of the RC filter in terms of ω₀
Vout = output voltage (V); Vin = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = cutoff angular frequency (rad/s); j = imaginary unit
Cutoff angular frequency of RC filter
ω₀ = cutoff angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Don't confuse ω₀ = 1/(RC) with the frequency f₀; ω₀ is angular (rad/s), so f₀ = ω₀/2π.
Remember the limits: 1/0 → ∞ and 1/∞ → 0; check which term dominates before concluding the gain.
rq: Why does the gain go to zero at low frequency, even though the expression contains only 1 and a fraction?
Because at ω << ω₀ the term ω₀/(jω) becomes very large (dividing by a tiny ω), so the denominator tends to infinity and the ratio tends to 0.
What happens to the output if the input frequency is much higher than ω₀, and why?
Vout ≈ Vin, since ω₀/(jω) → 0 as ω → ∞, so the denominator tends to 1 and the signal passes unattenuated.

notes.t: High-Pass RC Filter: Low and High Frequency Behaviour
pts: In the high-pass filter the capacitor is in series with the input and the resistor is across the output, so the output is taken across R.
At low frequencies the capacitor impedance is large compared with R, so almost all the input voltage is dropped across the capacitor and the output is near zero.
At high frequencies the capacitor impedance is small compared with R, so the capacitor acts like a short circuit and the output follows the input.
defs: High-pass filter
A filter circuit that passes signals above a cut-off frequency with little attenuation while strongly attenuating signals below it.
eqs: \(Z_c\) = capacitor impedance (\(\Omega\)); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(C\) = capacitance (F); \(j\) = imaginary unit
Low-frequency output condition of high-pass filter
\(|Z_c|\) = magnitude of capacitor impedance (\(\Omega\)); \(|Z_R|\) = magnitude of resistor impedance (\(\Omega\)); \(V_{out}\) = output voltage (V)
High-frequency output condition of high-pass filter
\(|Z_c|\) = magnitude of capacitor impedance (\(\Omega\)); \(|Z_R|\) = magnitude of resistor impedance (\(\Omega\)); \(V_{out}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V)
tips: Do not confuse the two limits: at low frequency the output is near zero, while at high frequency \(V_{out} \approx V_{in}\).
Impedance comparisons use magnitudes \(|Z|\); the \(-j\) term only indicates phase, so compare \(1/(\omega C)\) with \(R\) in ohms.
rq: Why does the capacitor's impedance fall as frequency rises, and how does this make the circuit pass high frequencies?
Since \(|Z_c| = 1/(\omega C)\), increasing \(\omega\) reduces \(|Z_c|\). A small capacitor impedance means little voltage is dropped across it, so nearly all the input appears across R.
What would happen to the output if R were made much smaller?
A smaller R means \(|Z_R|\) is smaller, so the output across R falls relative to the input for a given frequency; the cut-off frequency moves to higher frequencies and less signal passes.

notes.t: Bode magnitude plot of an RC high-pass filter
pts: Low-frequency gain falls off at about 20 dB per decade, so the filter blocks low frequencies.
At the cut-off frequency the output is about 3 dB below the passband (≈ 0.707 of the input amplitude).
At high frequencies the magnitude flattens to 0 dB, so signals pass with essentially no attenuation.
For this filter the cut-off frequency is 1 kHz, marked by the dashed vertical line on the log-frequency axis.
defs: Cut-off frequency (\(f_{c}\))
The frequency at which the magnitude of the filter gain is 1/√2 of its passband value, i.e. −3 dB; for an RC high-pass filter it is where the output power is half the input power.
Decibel (dB) gain
A logarithmic measure of voltage gain, 20 log10 |Vout/Vin|, so a ratio of 1 corresponds to 0 dB and 1/√2 corresponds to about −3 dB.
eqs: Magnitude gain in dB of the RC high-pass filter
tips: Do not read the −3 dB point as zero output; it corresponds to a ratio of 1/√2 (≈0.707) in voltage.
The frequency axis is logarithmic, so equal distances represent equal ratios (decades), not equal frequency differences.
rq: Why does the curve approach 0 dB at high frequency rather than continuing to rise?
Above \(f_{c}\) the capacitor's reactance becomes negligible, so the output essentially equals the input, giving a gain of 1 (0 dB).
Why is the −3 dB point marked rather than a point where the output is zero?
The output never reaches zero at finite frequency; −3 dB (half power) is the conventional defined bandwidth edge where the response has dropped to 1/√2.

units.name: 3.8 Band-pass filters, speaker crossovers and summary
units.ov: This material covers how passive RC/LC filters (low-pass, high-pass and their combination, the band-pass) are used in loudspeaker crossovers to split audio between drivers, and how Bode plots describe them. The key ideas are the -3 dB cut-off point, the 20 dB/decade first-order roll-off, and the fact that a band-pass response needs a high-pass and a low-pass section together, which is why the mid-range driver is the hardest to filter.
must: At the characteristic (cut-off) frequency of a first-order RC filter, \( V_{out}/V_{in}=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707 \), which is -3 dB.
Power ratio at cut-off is \( P_{out}/P_{in}=1/2 \); use \( 10\log_{10} \) for power and \( 20\log_{10} \) for voltage, giving -3 dB either way.
First-order roll-off is 20 dB per decade; state the sign explicitly (negative slope for low-pass, positive for high-pass below cut-off).
Cut-off frequency is set by choosing R and C: \( \omega_c = 1/RC \), so \( f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) \) (design R and C for a target \( f_c \)).
Capacitors pass high frequencies and block low; inductors pass low frequencies and block high.
A band-pass filter passes a band around the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and attenuates above and below; the Bode magnitude plot peaks at \( \omega_0 \) and rolls off on both sides.
A band-pass response needs a high-pass and a low-pass section combined; no single component can achieve it.
A crossover is a passive network (R, L, C) that divides the signal into bands and routes each to the right driver; the mid-range driver needs a band-pass, so is hardest to filter.
Read the actual peak gain from the Bode plot: 0 dB means unity gain, and the band-pass peak is at 0 dB only in the ideal case.
conn: The -3 dB point links the transfer function, the Bode plot and the power-halving idea. The cut-off frequency defines the band edges of both the high-pass and the low-pass sections of a band-pass filter.

Cascading a high-pass RC (sets lower cut-off) with a low-pass RC (sets upper cut-off) gives the band-pass; the 20 dB/decade slope applies on each side, and component choices set both corner frequencies.

Crossover design combines the capacitor/inductor frequency behaviour with the chosen \( f_c \) for each driver (woofer low-pass, tweeter high-pass, mid-range band-pass), and dB conversions are used to check the attenuation at given frequencies.
exq: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Calculate its cut-off frequency, the output/input voltage ratio and the gain in dB at that frequency, and the attenuation one decade above.
Explain why power ratio ½ and voltage ratio 1/√2 both correspond to -3 dB, showing the calculations with 10log10 and 20log10.
Design a first-order RC high-pass filter for a tweeter with a cut-off of 3 kHz given C = 10 nF. Find R and sketch the Bode magnitude plot, labelling the slope in dB/decade.
Describe how a band-pass filter for a mid-range driver is built from high-pass and low-pass sections. For band edges of 400 Hz and 4 kHz, sketch the Bode plot and state the roll-off on each side.
State which of a capacitor and an inductor passes high frequencies and which blocks them, and use this to explain how a simple two-way crossover routes signals to a woofer and a tweeter.

notes.t: Filter circuits in speaker crossovers
pts: Mid-range drivers need a bandpass filter so they only reproduce a limited band of frequencies.
A crossover uses passive components (resistors, capacitors, inductors) to split the audio signal between drivers by frequency.
Mid-range is the hardest driver to filter because it needs both a high-pass and a low-pass action at once.
defs: Bandpass filter
A circuit that passes signals within a defined frequency range and attenuates frequencies above and below that range.
Crossover
A filter network that divides an audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate loudspeaker driver.
tips: Do not confuse which element passes which frequencies: capacitors pass highs and block lows, inductors pass lows and block highs.
Bandpass behaviour needs a combination of high-pass and low-pass sections; a single component cannot achieve it.
rq: Why can a single capacitor or inductor not produce the mid-range band on its own?
A single reactive element gives only one cutoff, a high-pass or low-pass slope; a mid-range driver needs both a lower and an upper cutoff, so high-pass and low-pass sections must be combined.
Why do inductors (coils) block high frequencies while capacitors block low frequencies?
An inductor's reactance increases with frequency, so it impedes highs; a capacitor's reactance decreases with frequency, so it impedes lows.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Bandpass Filter Bode Plot
pts: A bandpass filter passes signals near a central frequency and attenuates signals on both sides of the peak.
The Bode magnitude plot peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \), where the gain is at its maximum (0 dB reference).
Bandpass filters are widely used across many engineering disciplines and will be revisited for different applications.
defs: Bandpass filter
A filter whose Bode magnitude plot curves down on both sides of a central frequency, passing a band of frequencies near \( \omega_0 \) while attenuating frequencies above and below it.
tips: Do not confuse the plot's dB axis: 0 dB means unity gain, and the bandpass peak is at 0 dB only in an ideal case; read the actual peak value from the plot.
A bandpass filter must roll off on both sides; a plot that falls off on only one side describes a low-pass or high-pass filter instead.
rq: Why does a bandpass filter's gain fall off on both sides of \( \omega_0 \) rather than just one side?

It must reject both low frequencies (below the band) and high frequencies (above the band), so it combines a high-pass-like roll-off at low frequency with a low-pass-like roll-off at high frequency, giving a peak in between.
What does the value 0 on the vertical axis of the plot represent for \( V_{out}/V_{in} \) in dB?
A gain of 0 dB, meaning \( V_{out} = V_{in} \); the peak of a bandpass filter reaches this level so signals at \( \omega_0 \) pass unattenuated.

notes.t: Summary of first-order RC filters: -3 dB point, roll-off, design, high-pass and band-pass
pts: At the characteristic frequency a first-order RC filter gives Vout/Vin = 1/√2, i.e. power ratio Pout/Pin = ½, which is -3 dB.
The roll-off of a first-order filter is 20 dB per decade; the slope is negative for a low-pass filter.
An RC filter can be designed for a chosen cut-off (characteristic) frequency by selecting R and C appropriately.
An RC high-pass filter was demonstrated, and a band-pass filter passes only a selected band of frequencies.
defs: -3 dB attenuation
The point where output voltage falls to 1/√2 (≈0.707) of input voltage, or output power is half the input power.
Roll-off
The rate at which the gain of a filter falls (or rises) beyond the cut-off frequency; for a first-order filter it is 20 dB per decade.
Band-pass filter
A filter that passes frequencies within a selected band and attenuates frequencies outside it.
eqs: Voltage gain at the characteristic frequency of a first-order RC filter
Power ratio at the characteristic frequency
tips: Do not mix up the 3 dB power and voltage rules: power ratio ½ uses 10 log10, voltage ratio 1/√2 uses 20 log10.
A low-pass filter has a negative slope in the roll-off; state the sign explicitly in answers.
rq: Why does a power ratio of ½ correspond to -3 dB rather than -6 dB?

Decibels for power use 10 log10(\(P_{\text{out}}\)/\(P_{\text{in}}\)) = 10 log10(0.5) ≈ -3 dB, whereas voltage ratios use 20 log10, which would give -6 dB for a voltage ratio of ½; here the voltage ratio is 1/√2, so 20 log10(1/√2) ≈ -3 dB.
Why is the roll-off of a first-order filter 20 dB per decade?
A first-order RC filter has one reactive element, so its gain falls as 1/f beyond the cut-off; 20 log10 of a tenfold frequency change gives 20 dB per decade.
How does a band-pass filter differ from a low-pass filter in its frequency response?
A low-pass filter passes frequencies below cut-off and attenuates above it, while a band-pass filter passes frequencies within a selected band and attenuates both below and above that band.

units.name: 4.1 Bandpass filters and speaker crossovers (recap)
units.ov: This recap covers passive loudspeaker crossovers built from resistors, capacitors and inductors, focusing on the bandpass filter needed for mid-range drivers. A bandpass response is made by combining high-pass and low-pass action, and it is read from a Bode plot of gain in dB against angular frequency, with a peak at \( \omega_0 \) and roll-off on both sides. The links to understand are component frequency behaviour, cascaded filter sections, cut-off frequencies and the Bode plot shape.
must: A bandpass filter passes a band of frequencies and attenuates those both below and above it; its Bode plot peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \).
A mid-range driver needs a bandpass filter because it must be bounded at both ends of the band, unlike a woofer (low-pass) or tweeter (high-pass).
A bandpass can be built by cascading a high-pass section (sets the lower cut-off) and a low-pass section (sets the upper cut-off); both cut-offs must be defined.
Capacitors pass high frequencies and block low ones, since \( X_C = 1/(\omega C) \) falls as \( \omega \) rises.
Inductors pass low frequencies and block high ones, since \( X_L = \omega L \) rises with \( \omega \).
A crossover is a filter network that splits the audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate driver.
Bode plot: gain \( 20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in}) \) in dB against \( \omega \) (log scale); the peak is near 0 dB and attenuation appears as negative dB.
Distinguish the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) (the peak) from the cut-off frequencies on either side, where gain is down 3 dB (\( 1/\sqrt{2} \) of the peak voltage gain).
Passive crossovers use only R, L and C, with no power gain, so the output can never exceed the input.
conn: Impedance of C and L vs frequency determines whether each section acts as high-pass or low-pass, which sets the overall bandpass shape.
Cascading high-pass and low-pass sections links the cut-off frequencies \( \omega_{c1} \) and \( \omega_{c2} \) to the bandwidth and the position of \( \omega_0 \) on the Bode plot.
Potential-divider analysis of the RC or RL circuits gives \( V_{out}/V_{in} \), which is converted to dB for the Bode plot.
The crossover design links to the driver layout: woofer low-pass, mid-range bandpass and tweeter high-pass must overlap sensibly around their cut-offs.
exq: Explain why a mid-range driver requires a bandpass filter and sketch a block diagram of a three-way crossover showing the filter type for each driver.

Design a passive bandpass filter for a mid-range driver passing about 500 Hz to 5 kHz using a high-pass RC and a low-pass RC section; calculate the component values given \( R = 8\,\Omega \) using \( f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) \).
Sketch the Bode plot (gain in dB vs \( \omega \)) of a bandpass filter, label \( \omega_0 \), the cut-off frequencies and the -3 dB points, and state the gain in dB at the cut-offs.

State and justify which of a capacitor and an inductor blocks low frequencies, using reactance expressions, and calculate their reactances at 100 Hz and 10 kHz for \( C = 10\,\mu F \) and \( L = 1\,mH \).
A bandpass filter has a voltage gain of 0.5 at a given frequency relative to a peak gain of 1; express this in dB and say whether this frequency is inside or outside the passband.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Passive Speaker Crossovers
pts: Mid-range drivers need a bandpass filter so they only receive a limited band of frequencies, rejecting both very low and very high signals.
A passive crossover in a loudspeaker is built from resistors, capacitors and inductors (coils), each shaping which frequencies reach each driver.
Mid-range speakers are the trickiest to filter because they must be bounded at both ends of the band, requiring combined high-pass and low-pass action.
defs: Bandpass filter
A circuit that passes signals within a specific range of frequencies while attenuating frequencies outside that range.
Crossover
A filter network that divides an audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate loudspeaker driver.
tips: Do not confuse which component blocks which band: capacitors pass high frequencies and block low, inductors do the opposite.
A mid-range bandpass is usually formed by cascading high-pass and low-pass sections; check that both cut-off frequencies are defined.
rq: Why can't a single capacitor or single inductor alone isolate the mid-range driver's band?

A single reactive element only cuts off on one side (high-pass with a capacitor in series, low-pass with an inductor in series); a band needs both a high-pass and a low-pass section to bound the frequencies at both ends.
Why do capacitors block low frequencies while inductors block high frequencies?
A capacitor's reactance 1/(2πfC) falls as frequency rises, so it passes highs; an inductor's reactance 2πfL rises with frequency, so it passes lows.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Bandpass Filter Bode Plot
pts: A bandpass filter passes a band of frequencies around a central frequency and attenuates signals on either side of the peak.
On the Bode plot, the gain curve peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and falls off on both sides.
The output-to-input voltage ratio is plotted in decibels against angular frequency \( \omega \).
Bandpass filters are widely used across many engineering disciplines.
defs: Bandpass filter
A filter circuit whose Bode plot has a peak at a central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and attenuates frequencies both above and below that band.
tips: Gain is plotted in dB, so the peak is at 0 dB reference and attenuation appears as negative dB values below it.
Do not confuse the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) (the peak) with the cut-off frequencies on either side of the band.
rq: Why does a bandpass filter's Bode plot fall off on both sides of \( \omega_0 \) rather than only on one side?

A bandpass filter must reject both low-frequency and high-frequency signals, so it combines a high-pass response (attenuating low frequencies) with a low-pass response (attenuating high frequencies), producing a peak between them.

units.name: 4.2 Faraday's law, magnetic fields and Lenz's law
units.ov: This material covers how a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces a voltage (Faraday's law), how the direction of the induced current is fixed by Lenz's law, and how currents in wires and coils create magnetic fields. These ideas link together in generators: mechanical work moves a magnet or coil, the flux changes, a voltage and current are induced, and the induced field opposes the motion, so mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy.
must: Faraday's law: induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, \( \varepsilon = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \), where N is the number of turns
Induction needs changing flux, not just the presence of a field; a steady field or a static magnet in a coil induces no voltage
Lenz's law: the induced current creates a field that opposes the change in flux that caused it; this is the origin of the minus sign
Magnetic flux: \( \Phi = BA\cos\theta \), the field passing through a surface; flux can change through B, A or θ
Energy conservation: work done against the opposing force on the magnet becomes electrical energy; it is not created from nothing
Right-hand rule: the field around a straight wire forms concentric loops following the current direction; do not confuse current direction with field direction
A solenoid's loop fields add inside the coil, giving a strong, nearly uniform axial field; the coil acts as a magnet with N and S poles
Method for Lenz's law: (1) state whether flux increases or decreases, (2) state the opposing field direction, (3) use the right-hand rule to find the current direction
Closed loop is needed for a current; an open coil still has an induced emf but no current flows
conn: Faraday and Lenz together: the magnitude of the emf comes from \( d\Phi/dt \) and the direction from the opposing field, which is found with the right-hand rule for coils
Solenoid fields and induction: the induced current in a coil makes its own solenoid field, whose poles oppose the approaching or retreating magnet
Lenz's law and energy conservation: the opposing force explains why mechanical work is needed and why generators convert mechanical power to electrical power
Generators: the speed of the moving magnet or rotating coil sets \( d\Phi/dt \), so it sets the emf amplitude and frequency
exq: A bar magnet is pushed north pole first into a coil. State the direction of the induced current, as seen from the magnet side, and the polarity of the coil end facing the magnet. Justify using Lenz's law.

A coil of 200 turns and area \(5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2\) lies perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.8 T to 0.2 T in 0.1 s. Calculate the induced emf and say which way the induced field points relative to the original.
Explain why a stationary magnet inside a coil produces no electrical energy, and why pushing a magnet into a closed coil requires more force than into an open one.
Sketch the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire and a solenoid. Mark the directions with the right-hand rule and identify the poles of the solenoid.
A flat coil rotates at constant angular speed in a uniform field. Sketch the flux and induced emf against time, and explain how doubling the speed changes the peak emf.

notes.t: Generators and Faraday's law of induction
pts: A changing magnetic flux through a coil induces a voltage in the coil.
If the coil forms a closed loop, the induced voltage drives a current, which creates its own magnetic field opposing the change (Lenz's law).
Power generation works because a moving magnet inside a coil induces a voltage; the flux must change, since a static magnet in a coil produces no energy.
defs: Magnetic flux
A measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area.
tips: Induction depends on changing flux, not on the presence of a magnetic field; a steady field gives no induced voltage.
Lenz's law sign: the induced current opposes the change, so the induced voltage is a sign reversal of the rate of change of flux.
rq: Why can't a stationary magnet sitting inside a coil generate energy?
Induction requires a changing magnetic flux; with a stationary magnet the flux is constant, so no voltage is induced.
Why does the induced current create a field that opposes the change rather than reinforcing it?
Lenz's law: opposing the change is required by conservation of energy; reinforcing it would create energy from nothing and runaway growth.

notes.t: Magnetic field around current-carrying wires and coils
pts: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field that circles the wire.
Field lines around a straight wire form concentric loops whose direction follows the current (right-hand rule).
Coiling a current-carrying wire makes the field from each loop add in the same direction inside the coil.
A current-carrying coil therefore behaves like a magnet, with a north and south pole at its ends.
defs: Magnetic field B
A vector field describing the magnetic force influence around a current-carrying conductor or magnet; its field lines form closed loops.
Solenoid (coil)
A helical winding of wire carrying current whose individual loop fields reinforce inside the coil, producing a strong, nearly uniform axial magnetic field.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of current with the direction of the field; use the right-hand rule to determine the field direction around a wire.
The field lines in the coil diagram are drawn as closed loops; the field inside a coil is strongest and most uniform along its axis.
rq: Why does the field inside a coil add up, while the field outside the coil largely cancels?

Inside the coil the loop fields all point along the axis in the same direction, so they add; outside, the return paths of the field run in opposite directions and tend to cancel, weakening the external field.
If the current in a coil is reversed, what happens to the magnet's poles?
The magnetic field direction reverses, so the north and south poles swap positions.

notes.t: Changing magnetic flux and induced current (Lenz's law)
pts: A moving magnet changes the magnetic flux through the coil, which induces a current in the coil.
The induced current produces a field that opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused it.
Work must be done against this opposing field to push the magnet into the coil; this work is converted into electrical energy.
tips: Energy conservation: the electrical energy output comes from the mechanical work done, not from nowhere; the opposing force is what makes the work necessary.
The induced effect acts to oppose the change in flux, so do not state that it reinforces or assists the motion.
rq: Why does pulling the magnet out of the coil require work just as pushing it in does?

Withdrawing the magnet also changes the flux, so the induced current opposes the change in both directions; the opposing force must be overcome either way, so mechanical work is needed to keep the magnet moving.
What would happen to the induced current if the magnet were held stationary inside the coil?
The flux would not change, so no current would be induced and no opposing field would be produced.

units.name: 4.3 Self-inductance and inductors
units.ov: This module introduces self-inductance: a changing current in a coil changes its own magnetic flux, which induces a voltage that opposes the change (Lenz's law). An inductor is a coil, often on an iron core, that exploits this effect and stores energy in its magnetic field. The notes give only the qualitative picture and definitions, so the standard quantitative relations (\(v=L\,di/dt\), \(E=\tfrac12 LI^2\), \(L=N\Phi/I\)) should be learned alongside them.
