Random motion versus drift: thermal random motion gives zero net current, and an applied field superimposes a net drift, so current is the net flow.
Electron flow versus conventional current: questions on circuit direction often need both to be stated consistently.
exq: Copper has \( \sigma \approx 10^{7} \) S/m. Calculate its resistivity and state the units. Then compare it with fused quartz (\( 10^{-14} \) S/m) as a ratio of conductivities.
Explain, using the atomic structure of copper (29 protons and 29 electrons), why copper is a good conductor.
Describe the motion of free electrons in a copper wire (a) with no voltage applied and (b) when connected to a battery. Why is there a current in only one case?
State the direction of conventional current and of electron flow in a simple circuit with a battery and a lamp, and explain why they differ.
Define electrical conductivity and resistivity, give their units, and explain why a material with a very large \( \sigma \) is not one with a large \( \rho \).

notes.t: Electron flow through a material: copper and conductivity
pts: Copper has 29 protons and 29 electrons, arranged in shells around the nucleus; its outermost electron is loosely bound and can move freely.
Copper has very high electrical conductivity (about \(10^{7}\) S/m), meaning electrons flow through it very easily.
Copper has very low resistivity (about \(10^{-7}\) Ω·m), the reciprocal of its conductivity, so it offers little opposition to current.
Materials span a huge range of conductivity: copper sits at the top, while fused quartz (about \(10^{-14}\) S/m) is a near-perfect insulator.
defs: Electrical conductivity (σ)
A measure of how easily a material allows electric current to flow; the reciprocal of resistivity, measured in siemens per metre (S/m).
Resistivity (ρ)
A material property describing how strongly it opposes current flow, measured in ohm-metres (Ω·m); the reciprocal of conductivity.
tips: Conductivity and resistivity are inversely related: do not confuse a large conductivity value with a large resistivity value.
Check units: conductivity is in S/m and resistivity in Ω·m; the table gives orders of magnitude, so compare powers of ten rather than exact values.
rq: Why does copper, with its loosely bound outer electrons, conduct so much better than fused quartz?
Copper's outer electrons are weakly bound and free to drift under an applied field, whereas in fused quartz electrons are tightly bound in covalent bonds with no free charge carriers.
If a material's conductivity is \(10^{-7}\) S/m, what is its resistivity and how does it compare to copper?
Resistivity is 1/\(10^{-7}\) = \(10^{7}\) Ω·m, which is about \(10^{14}\) times larger than copper's \(10^{-7}\) Ω·m, so it is a far poorer conductor.

notes.t: Electron flow through a material
pts: Free electrons in a material move randomly when no voltage is applied, so there is no net flow of charge.
When a battery is connected, electrons drift from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal, giving a net flow of charge.
The moving electrons transfer energy between circuit elements, and this organised movement constitutes an electric current.
defs: Current flow
The organised (net) movement of charge carriers, such as free electrons, through a conductor caused by a potential difference; it is the rate of charge flow.
tips: Conventional current is taken to flow from positive to negative, opposite to the direction of electron flow; state the convention clearly in exam answers.
Random electron motion does not constitute current; only the net drift of electrons does.
rq: Why does the random motion of free electrons produce no current, while a battery makes them produce one?
Random motions in all directions cancel out, giving zero net charge transfer; the battery's potential difference biases the motion so electrons drift in one direction, giving a net flow.

units.name: 1.4 Resistance, conductance and resistivity
units.ov: This section defines resistance (Ω) and its reciprocal, conductance (S), then links resistance to a conductor's physical properties through resistivity using \( R = \rho l / A \). Most of the marks come from careful unit handling (kΩ to Ω, mm² to m²) and from knowing how R and G scale with length, area and temperature.
must: Resistance of a uniform conductor: \( R = \frac{\rho l}{A} \), with R in Ω, ρ in Ω·m, l in m and A in m²
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: \( G = 1/R \), unit siemens (S). It is undefined at R = 0 (a zero-resistance path has infinite conductance)
Unit conversion: \( 1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2 \) and \( 1\,\text{k}\Omega = 1000\,\Omega \). Leaving area in mm² gives an answer 10⁶ times too small
Proportionality: \( R \propto l \) and \( R \propto 1/A \). Doubling the length doubles R, and doubling the area halves R. Since \( A = \pi d^2/4 \), halving the diameter multiplies R by 4
Resistivity ρ is a material property: the resistance of unit length and unit cross-section. It is constant only at a fixed temperature, so state the temperature
Worked example: a 40 kΩ resistor has \( G = 1/40\,000 = 25\,\mu\text{S} \). Lower R gives higher G
Worked example: a 100 m copper wire of 2.5 mm² has \( R \approx 0.688\,\Omega \), which implies \( \rho_{Cu} \approx 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m} \). Check the power of ten on the calculator
Distinguish resistance (a property, in Ω) from a resistor (the component). Resistors limit current and divide voltage, and their heating is usually unwanted
Parallel resistors each have the full battery voltage across them and the current splits between branches. Identify series or parallel before applying equivalent-resistance formulas
Check units by dimensional analysis: \( \Omega\text{m} \times \text{m} / \text{m}^2 = \Omega \)
conn: Resistivity, length and area give R, and G = 1/R then gives conductance. Questions often ask for both from the wire dimensions
Unit conversions (mm² to m², kΩ to Ω, µS prefixes) run through every calculation, so a single slip carries into all later parts
Parallel circuits link to conductance: in parallel, conductances add, \( G_{total} = G_1 + G_2 + \dots \). Two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel give 500 Ω, or 2 mS
Temperature changes ρ and therefore R, so a wire's resistance at a different temperature differs from the value calculated from a tabulated ρ
exq: Calculate the resistance of a 100 m length of copper wire with cross-sectional area 2.5 mm², given \( \rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m} \). Then find its conductance in siemens.
A 40 kΩ resistor is replaced by one with twice the conductance. State the new resistance and the conductance in µS.
A wire has resistance R. It is drawn out to twice its length at constant volume, so its area halves. Find the new resistance in terms of R and justify your answer using \( R = \rho l/A \).

Two 1 kΩ resistors are connected in parallel across a battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the equivalent conductance. Explain how the current splits and what the voltage is across each resistor.
A wire of diameter 1.8 mm and length 50 m has resistance 0.34 Ω. Determine the resistivity of the material and suggest which metal it is. Comment on the temperature condition on your answer.

notes.t: Resistance and Resistors
pts: Resistance is the property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons.
Resistance is measured in ohms, symbolised by the Greek letter omega.
A resistor is a component deliberately designed to have a specific resistance.
Resistors are used to limit current, divide voltage, and sometimes generate heat or light.
defs: Resistance (R)
The property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons; measured in ohms (Ω).
Resistor
A component specifically designed to have a certain amount of resistance.
tips: Do not confuse resistance (a property of a material or component, measured in Ω) with resistor (the physical component designed to have that resistance).
Resistors can limit current and divide voltage, but their heating effect is usually unwanted; only in certain cases is heat or light the intended purpose.
rq: Why would a circuit designer deliberately insert a resistor rather than rely on the resistance of the wires?
Wire resistance is very small and unplanned; a resistor provides a known, controlled resistance to limit current or set voltage levels.
Why does a resistor used to divide voltage need to be placed in series with other resistors?
Voltage divides across series components in proportion to their resistances, so series placement is what creates the split.

notes.t: Resistance and Conductance
pts: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance and measures how easily current flows.
Conductance is symbolised by G and its SI unit is the siemens (S).
Resistance is analogous to the restriction water experiences flowing through a pipe.
defs: Conductance
The reciprocal of resistance, G = 1/R, measuring the ease with which a component allows current to pass; its SI unit is the siemens (S).
eqs: G = conductance (siemens, S); R = resistance (ohm, Ω)
tips: Do not confuse conductance (siemens, S) with resistance (ohms, Ω); the unit of G is S, not Ω.
Remember G = 1/R only holds for R ≠ 0; a zero-resistance path has infinite conductance.
rq: Why does a larger resistance give a smaller conductance?
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance (G = 1/R), so as R increases, 1/R decreases; a more opposed path conducts less readily.
If a resistor has R = 4 Ω, what is its conductance and in what unit is it expressed?
G = 1/4 = 0.25 S (siemens).

notes.t: Resistance and Resistor
pts: A resistor opposes the flow of current; the simulated circuit shows two 1 kΩ resistors connected in parallel across the battery.
In a parallel arrangement, each resistor has the same voltage across it as the battery, while the total current splits between the branches.
defs: Resistance
The opposition a component or material offers to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω).
Resistor
A circuit component designed to provide a specific resistance, used to limit current or divide voltage.
tips: Watch units: 1k means 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω, not 1 Ω; convert before calculating.
Check whether resistors are in series or parallel before applying resistance formulas, since the circuit topology determines the equivalent resistance.
rq: Why do both 1 kΩ resistors have the same voltage across them even though the current through each may differ?
They are connected in parallel directly across the same two nodes of the battery, so they share the battery's voltage.

notes.t: Conductance of a resistor
pts: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so a lower resistance gives a higher conductance.
Substitute the resistance in ohms (40 kΩ = 40 000 Ω) and the result is in siemens.
A 40 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 25 µS.
defs: Conductance
The measure of how easily current flows through a component; it is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemens (S).
eqs: G = conductance (siemens, S); R = resistance (ohms, Ω)
G = conductance (siemens, S); R = 40 kΩ = 40 000 Ω
tips: Unit trap: 40 kΩ must be treated as 40 000 Ω, giving 25 µS, not 25 S or 0.025 S.
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so do not divide R by 1 or confuse G = 1/R with G = R.
rq: Why must the resistance be converted to ohms before calculating conductance?
Because the SI unit of conductance, the siemens, is defined from ohms; using kΩ directly gives a result in kS (or µS after conversion), which is only correct if units are handled consistently.

notes.t: Resistance and Resistor
pts: Resistance of a wire depends on the material, its length and its cross-sectional area.
Resistance is directly proportional to the length of the wire: longer wire, greater resistance.
Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area: thicker wire, lower resistance.
Resistivity is a material property that stays constant only at a given temperature.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length of a unit cross-sectional area of that material; it is constant at a fixed temperature.
Cross-sectional area (A)
The area of a slice taken perpendicular to the length of the conductor through which the current flows.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity of material (Ω·m); l = length of wire (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert area to m² (e.g. mm² × 10⁻⁶) before using R = ρl/A with ρ in Ω·m.
Resistivity ρ is only constant at a fixed temperature; resistance changes if temperature changes, so state the temperature condition.
rq: Why does doubling the wire's diameter reduce its resistance to one quarter?
Area A = πd²/4 scales with d², so doubling d multiplies A by 4; since R ∝ 1/A, R becomes one quarter of its original value.
What happens to resistance if the length is doubled and the area is also doubled?
R = ρl/A: length doubles (×2) and area doubles (÷2), so R stays the same.

notes.t: Resistance of a conductor from resistivity, length and cross-sectional area
pts: Resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the material constant.
Resistivity is a material property, so the same formula applies to any conductor once ρ, l and A are known.
Area must be converted from mm² to m² before substituting, since resistivity is in Ω·m.
Checking units (Ω·m × m / m² = Ω) confirms the formula gives resistance in ohms.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-sectional area of that material; measured in Ω·m.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Unit trap: leaving area in mm² gives a result that is 10⁶ times too small; always convert to m².
The answer for the 100 m copper wire is about 0.688 Ω; check the powers of ten when entering 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ on a calculator.
rq: Why must the area be converted from mm² to m² before calculating?
Because resistivity is given in Ω·m, so every quantity must be in SI base units for the result to be in ohms; 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m².
What would happen to the resistance if the wire were doubled in length and its diameter doubled?
Length doubling doubles R, but doubling diameter quadruples area so R is divided by 4; net effect R → R/2.

units.name: 1.5 Resistor types and colour codes
units.ov: This material classifies resistors as linear (ohmic) or nonlinear, and as fixed or variable, then shows how to read a four-band colour code to get nominal resistance and tolerance. The link is that colour codes apply to fixed linear resistors, where Ohm's law \(V=IR\) holds with constant \(R\). Nonlinear devices (thermistors, LDRs) and variable ones (potentiometers, rheostats) change R, so the circuit analysis differs.
must: Colour code formula: \(R=(10d_1+d_2)\times10^{n}\ \Omega\), where band 3 gives \(n\), the number of zeros
Digit chart: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9
Tolerance band: gold = ±5%, silver = ±10%; it is never a digit and is read last, so start from the end opposite it
Band 3 is a power of ten, not a multiplying value: brown-black-red = \(10\times10^2=1\,\text{k}\Omega\), not \(10\times2\)
Tolerance range: actual \(R\) lies in \(R_{nom}(1\pm t)\), giving minimum and maximum values
Linear (ohmic) resistors have constant R, so V and I are directly proportional; \(V=IR\) applies only to these
Nonlinear resistors change R with a physical condition: a thermistor with temperature, an LDR with light (LDR resistance falls as intensity rises)
Potentiometer = 3 terminals, voltage divider; rheostat = 2 terminals (one fixed, one sliding contact), current control
Fixed linear types: carbon film, thick film, thin film
Convert prefixes carefully: 27,000 Ω = 27 kΩ; 5,600,000 Ω = 5.6 MΩ
conn: Colour code reading feeds directly into tolerance calculations, which give the range of current or voltage in an Ohm's law problem
Linear versus nonlinear decides whether Ohm's law can be used with a constant R or whether an I–V graph or a value at given conditions is needed
Potentiometer (voltage divider) with an LDR or thermistor gives a light- or temperature-sensing circuit whose output voltage changes with the condition
Rheostat current control combines with \(V=IR\): changing R changes I for a fixed supply
exq: A resistor has bands yellow, violet, orange, gold. Find its nominal resistance in kΩ and its minimum and maximum possible values.
A resistor is coded green-blue-green-silver. Give its resistance in MΩ with tolerance, and the current range when 10 V is applied.
Explain with I–V sketches why a thermistor is nonlinear whereas a carbon film resistor is linear, and state whether \(V=IR\) applies to each.
Distinguish a rheostat from a potentiometer by terminals and function, and say which you would use to vary the current in a series circuit and which to provide an adjustable output voltage.
A student reads a resistor from the gold end as brown-black-red and gets 1 kΩ. Explain why this is wrong, give the correct reading procedure, and describe how an LDR's resistance changes with light.

notes.t: Resistors: classification by type
pts: Resistors split into linear (ohmic) and nonlinear types; linear resistors have constant resistance across voltage changes.
Fixed linear resistors are made as carbon film, thick film or thin film types, each with a fixed value.
Variable linear resistors include the potentiometer (voltage divider use) and the rheostat (current control use), with adjustable resistance.
Nonlinear resistors change resistance with a physical condition: thermistors respond to temperature and LDRs respond to light.
defs: Linear resistor
A resistor whose resistance stays constant as the voltage across it (or current through it) changes, so V and I are directly proportional.
Nonlinear resistor
A resistor whose resistance changes with a physical quantity such as temperature or light intensity, so V and I are not directly proportional.
Potentiometer
A variable resistor with three terminals used as a adjustable voltage divider.
Rheostat
A variable resistor with two terminals (one fixed, one sliding contact) used to control current in a circuit.
Thermistor
A nonlinear resistor whose resistance changes significantly with temperature.
LDR (light-dependent resistor)
A nonlinear resistor whose resistance decreases as the intensity of incident light increases.
tips: Do not confuse a rheostat (two terminals, current control) with a potentiometer (three terminals, voltage division).
Ohm's law V = IR only applies to linear resistors; nonlinear resistors such as thermistors and LDRs do not have constant R.
rq: Why is a thermistor classed as a nonlinear resistor while a carbon film resistor is linear?
A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, so V and I are not proportional; a carbon film resistor keeps a constant resistance over the operating range, so it obeys Ohm's law.
How does a rheostat differ from a potentiometer in a circuit?
A rheostat uses two terminals to vary resistance and control current; a potentiometer uses three terminals to act as a variable voltage divider.

notes.t: Resistor Colour Coding
pts: The first band (nearest one end) gives the first digit of the resistance; never start from a gold or silver band.
The second band gives the second digit of the resistance value.
The third band is the multiplier: the number of zeros following the second digit.
The fourth band gives the percent tolerance and is usually gold (±5%) or silver (±10%).
defs: Percent tolerance
The permitted percentage deviation of a resistor's actual value from its stated (coded) value, shown by the fourth band: gold = ±5%, silver = ±10%.
Multiplier
The power of ten (number of zeros) appended to the two significant digits of a resistor's colour code, given by the third band.
eqs: Resistance from colour bands (first two digits and multiplier)
R = resistance (\Omega); \(d_{1}\) = first digit (band 1); \(d_{2}\) = second digit (band 2); n = number of zeros (band 3 multiplier)
tips: Read the bands from the end nearest the first band, not the tolerance band; reading from the gold/silver end gives the wrong value.
The multiplier band gives a number of zeros (a power of ten), not the multiplier value itself; e.g. brown-black-red = 10 × 10² = 1 kΩ, not 10 × 2.
rq: Why must you never start reading the colour code from a gold or silver band?
Gold and silver are not digit colours; they are used only for tolerance, which sits at the end, so starting from them would misread the value.
A resistor has bands yellow, violet, orange, gold. What is its value and tolerance?
Digits 4 and 7, multiplier ×10³: 47 kΩ (47 000 Ω) with ±5% tolerance.

notes.t: Reading resistor colour codes: resistance value and tolerance
pts: The first two bands give the two significant digits of the resistance.
The third band gives the power-of-ten multiplier as the number of zeros appended.
The fourth band gives the tolerance; gold means ±5% and silver means ±10%.
The colour chart maps each colour to a digit: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9.
Read the bands from the end without the wider gap or gold/silver tolerance band, then combine digits and zeros into the resistance.
defs: Tolerance
The maximum allowed percentage deviation of a resistor's actual value from its marked nominal value.
Colour code
A system of coloured bands on a resistor body that encodes its nominal resistance in ohms and its tolerance.
eqs: Resistance from colour bands (band 1 and 2 digits, band 3 multiplier)
\(d_{1}\) = first digit (band 1); \(d_{2}\) = second digit (band 2); m = number of zeros (band 3) (dimensionless); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Watch units: 5,600,000 Ω is 5.6 MΩ, and 27,000 Ω is 27 kΩ; convert prefixes carefully.
Do not read the tolerance band as a digit; the gold or silver band is always the tolerance.
rq: Why does the 4th band of 27,000 Ω ± 10% mean the true value could be 24,300 Ω to 29,700 Ω?
Tolerance is a percentage of the nominal value: 10% of 27,000 Ω is 2,700 Ω, so R lies in 27,000 ± 2,700 Ω.
What if the 3rd band of the green-blue-green resistor were brown instead of green?
The multiplier would be \(10^{1}\) instead of \(10^{5}\), giving 56 Ω instead of 5,600,000 Ω.

units.name: 1.6 Electric current: definition and notation
units.ov: This material defines electric current as the time rate of flow of charge (1 A = 1 C/s) and shows how current is described as a function of time (DC, AC, other waveforms). It also covers reference-direction notation, which fixes the sign of a current, and the current source symbol. The ideas connect because \(I=Q/t\) is the constant-current special case of \(i=dq/dt\), and the sign of any current only has meaning relative to its reference arrow.
must: Current is the rate of flow of charge: \(i(t)=\frac{dq}{dt}\); unit ampere, 1 A = 1 C/s
For constant current only, \(I=Q/t\); for time-varying current use \(i=dq/dt\) or \(Q=\int i\,dt\)
Charge (C) is not current (A): current is charge per unit time
Reference direction is an assumed positive direction shown by an arrow; a negative value means flow opposite to the arrow, not zero current
Reversing the reference direction negates the current: \(i_{ab}=-i_{ba}\)
DC is constant in magnitude and direction, e.g. \(i_a(t)=2\) A
AC varies sinusoidally and periodically reverses, e.g. \(i_b(t)=2\cos(2\pi t)\) A: amplitude 2 A, \(\omega=2\pi\) rad/s, \(f=1\) Hz, \(T=1\) s
Other time-varying waveforms (triangular, square) are also valid currents; read their values and signs from the graph

Current source symbol: circle with an arrow giving the direction of the current; reversing the arrow flips the sign. Parallel sources in the same direction are equivalent to one source with the same current as stated in the notes
One coulomb is about \(6\times10^{18}\) electrons, each with charge \(-1.6\times10^{-19}\) C; use consistent units (C, s) and radians in cos
conn: Charge–current calculus: differentiate \(q(t)\) to get \(i(t)\), and integrate a waveform (area under an \(i\)-\(t\) graph) to get the charge transferred, which is common for square or triangular waveforms
Reference direction with waveform sign: for AC, the sign of \(i(t)\) at an instant tells you whether actual flow is with or against the arrow, linking notation to \(\cos\) phase and period
Electron charge with the coulomb: converting between number of electrons, charge Q and current via \(I=Q/t\), remembering that electron flow is opposite to conventional current direction
Current source direction with KCL-style circuit analysis: the arrow and sign convention determine what current enters or leaves a node
exq: A charge of 20 C passes a point in a wire in 5 s at constant current. Find the current, and the number of electrons passing per second.
The charge through a device is \(q(t)=3t^2-2t\) C. Find \(i(t)\) and the current at \(t=2\) s, stating the units.
A current is \(i(t)=2\cos(2\pi t)\) A. State the amplitude, frequency and period, evaluate \(i\) at \(t=0.25\) s and \(t=0.5\) s, and find the charge passed from \(t=0\) to \(t=0.25\) s.
A square-wave current is +3 A for 2 s then -3 A for 2 s. Sketch it and find the net charge passed over one period and over the first 3 s.
Given \(i_{ab}=-4\) A, find \(i_{ba}\) and explain in words the actual direction of flow. How does this change if the reference arrow of a current source is reversed?

notes.t: Electrical Current Forms & Notations
pts: DC current has constant value over time; here a constant 2 A.
AC current varies sinusoidally with time, here a cosine with 1 Hz frequency (period 1 s).
Triangular and square currents are examples of time-varying current waveforms.
Current direction notation: reversing the reference direction changes the sign of the current.
defs: Direct current (DC)
Current whose magnitude and direction remain constant with time.
Alternating current (AC)
Current that periodically reverses direction, typically varying sinusoidally with time.
Time-varying current
Current whose value changes with time, such as triangular or square waveforms.
Reference direction
The assumed positive direction of current flow, marked by an arrow; reversing it negates the current value.
eqs: \(i_{a}\)(t) = current in branch a at time t (A); constant value 2 A
\(i_{b}\)(t) = current at time t (A); t = time (s); amplitude 2 A; angular frequency 2π rad/s
\(i_{ab}\) = current from a to b (A); \(i_{ba}\) = current from b to a (A)
tips: Mind the reference direction: a negative value means current flows opposite to the arrow, not that it is absent.
Check units: the amplitude is in amperes (A), and the argument of cos must be in radians, so t is in seconds with 2π rad.
rq: Why does the AC current \(i_{b}\)(t) = 2 cos 2πt A have a period of 1 s even though the amplitude is 2 A?
The period is set by the angular frequency: cos(2πt) repeats every t = 1 s, since T = 2π/(2π) = 1 s; amplitude only sets peak height.
If the arrow for branch ab is reversed, what happens to the numerical value of the measured current, and why?
Its sign flips: \(i_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(i_{\text{ba}}\), because the current flows the opposite way relative to the reference direction.
What distinguishes a DC current from an AC current in terms of how it changes with time?
DC is constant in magnitude and direction; AC periodically changes direction and magnitude (sinusoidally here).

notes.t: Electrical Current Form & Notations
pts: A current source is drawn as a circle with an arrow showing the direction of current flow through it
The symbol labelled I with an arrow indicates the source supplies current I in the arrow's direction
Two current sources in parallel with the same direction are equivalent to a single source with the same current
tips: Always check the arrow direction on a current source, since reversing it flips the sign of the current.
rq: Why does the arrow direction matter when drawing a current source?
The arrow sets the reference direction of the current I; reversing it changes the sign of the current.

notes.t: Electrical Current: Definition, Units and Notation
pts: Electrical current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a conductor or circuit element.
The SI unit of current is the ampere, equal to one coulomb per second.
A constant current of 1 A means 1 C of charge passes a cross-section each second.
Current is the derivative of charge with respect to time, so it generalises to time-varying current.
One coulomb corresponds to roughly 6 × \(10^{18}\) electrons, each carrying charge −1.6 × 10^−19 C.
defs: Electrical current (I)
The time rate of flow of electrical charge through a conductor or circuit element.
Ampere (A)
The SI unit of electrical current, equal to one coulomb of charge passing a point per second.
eqs: I = current (A); Q = charge transferred (C); t = time interval (s)
I = current (A); q(t) = charge as a function of time (C); t = time (s)
tips: Do not confuse charge (coulombs) with current (amperes): current is charge per unit time, so 1 A = 1 C/s.
Use Q/t only for constant current; for time-varying current you must integrate or use I = dq/dt.
rq: Why does the instantaneous form dq/dt reduce to Q/t when the current is constant?
For constant current the charge rises linearly with time, so the derivative equals the total charge divided by the elapsed time: I = Q/t.
If 0.5 A flows for 10 s, how much charge has passed, and how many electrons is that?

notes.t: Electric current as rate of charge flow
pts: Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a wire.
Current is found by dividing charge transferred by the time taken.
Worked example: 20 C in 5 s gives a current of 4 A.
defs: Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor; the charge passing a given point per unit time.
eqs: Electric current from charge and time
I = current (A); Q = charge transferred (C); t = time taken (s)
tips: Ensure charge is in coulombs and time in seconds before dividing; ampere = coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
Current is a rate, so do not confuse it with total charge Q; the answer is the quotient, not the charge itself.
rq: Why does the same 20 C of charge produce a larger current if it flows in 2 s instead of 5 s?
Current is charge divided by time, so a shorter time for the same charge means a larger rate of flow: I = 20/2 = 10 A.

units.name: 1.7 Voltage and current/voltage sources
units.ov: This material introduces voltage as energy transferred per unit charge between two points, and shows how it is measured across elements and labelled with polarity. It then applies the idea to ideal voltage sources and to real bench supplies that set a voltage and a current limit. The ideas connect through V = W/Q, sign conventions, and the contrast between voltage across an element and current through it.
must: Voltage is energy per unit charge: \(V = W/Q\), with \(1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}\)
Rearrangements: \(W = QV\) and \(Q = W/V\). Worked example: 80 J moving 20 C gives 4 V
Voltage is measured across an element's two ends; current flows through it. Never mix them up
Uniform-field relation: \(V = El\), so \(W = QEl\), with E in V/m and l in m
Reference reversal: \(v_{ab} = -v_{ba}\). Voltage is always relative to a chosen reference point
Source polarity: the + terminal is at higher potential, and V is the potential of + relative to −. Reversing the markings flips the sign of V
Circle and battery symbols both denote an ideal voltage source. Use the +/− markings for polarity, not the plate lengths
An ideal voltage source holds a specified V regardless of the current drawn
On a bench supply, the set current limit is a maximum. The load determines the actual current, up to that limit
Check units and convert prefixes (mC, kJ) before substituting. Voltage is not energy (J), current (charge per time) or power (energy per time)
conn: \(V = W/Q\) combines with current (\(I = Q/t\)) to give power \(P = VI\), so energy questions chain voltage, charge, current and time
Polarity and \(v_{ab} = -v_{ba}\) underpin sign conventions in later circuit analysis (KVL, passive sign convention)
\(V = El\) links circuit voltage to electric field and work done on a charge, so field problems can be converted into energy problems
The ideal voltage source (fixed V, any current) contrasts with a real bench supply with a current limit, so questions ask what the load actually draws
exq: A source transfers 150 J of energy to move 30 C of charge between two terminals. Find the voltage, and the energy needed to move 0.5 C across the same terminals.
A charge of 5 mC moves through a 12 V potential difference. Calculate the energy transferred in joules, taking care with units.
A uniform electric field of 200 V/m acts over a 5 cm length. Find the voltage across it and the work done moving 2 µC along it.
If \(v_{ab} = 6\,\text{V}\), state \(v_{ba}\). A 9 V source is redrawn with its +/− labels swapped. What is its voltage relative to the original reference, and why?
A bench supply is set to 5 V with a 1 A current limit and connected to a 10 Ω resistor. What current flows? What happens if the load is changed to 2 Ω? Explain the role of the limit.

notes.t: Voltage
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge as charge moves between two points in a circuit.
Voltage is measured across the two ends of a circuit element, whereas current measures charge flowing through the element.
In a battery-driven headlight, stored chemical energy is converted by the headlight into heat and light.
Voltage across an element reverses sign when the reference direction is reversed: \(v_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(v_{\text{ba}}\).
defs: Voltage (V)
The energy transferred per unit of charge when charge moves from one point in an electrical circuit to a second point; measured in volts (V = J/C).
eqs: Voltage as energy per unit charge
V = voltage (V); W = energy (J); Q = charge (C)
Voltage as electric field times length
V = voltage (V); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
W = energy (J); Q = charge (C); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
\(v_{\text{ab}}\) = voltage at a relative to b (V); \(v_{\text{ba}}\) = voltage at b relative to a (V)
tips: Units trap: voltage is in volts (J/C), not joules; do not confuse energy W with voltage V.
Do not confuse voltage (measured across an element) with current (measured through an element); mixing these up loses marks.
rq: Why does reversing the reference polarity of a voltage change only its sign rather than its magnitude?
Voltage is a potential difference between two points, so swapping which point is the reference gives the same magnitude with opposite sign: \(v_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(v_{\text{ba}}\).
If a charge of 2 C gains 10 J of energy passing through a headlight, what is the voltage across it, and what would happen if the charge was doubled while the energy stayed the same?
V = W/Q = 10/2 = 5 V; doubling the charge to 4 C with the same energy would halve the voltage to 2.5 V.
Why is voltage not the same thing as current, even though both relate to a circuit element?
Voltage is energy per unit charge across the element's ends, while current is the rate of charge flow through the element; they measure different quantities.

notes.t: Electrical Voltage Form & Notations
pts: A voltage source is drawn as a circle (or battery symbol) with a + and − terminal marking its polarity.
Circle symbol and battery symbol represent the same ideal voltage source V; the + terminal is the higher-potential end.
Voltage V is labelled beside the source and its polarity is given by the +/− signs.
defs: Voltage source
An element that maintains a specified voltage V between its two terminals, independent of the current drawn through it.
Polarity (+/−)
The marking on a source terminals showing which end is at higher electric potential; V is the potential of the + terminal relative to the − terminal.
tips: Watch the polarity: reversing the + and − signs changes the sign of V, a common source of sign errors in circuit analysis.
Do not confuse the battery symbol's long/short plates with polarity; always use the + and − markings to determine direction.
rq: Why can the circle symbol and the battery symbol be used interchangeably for the same source?
Both represent an ideal voltage source with the same V and polarity; the battery symbol is just a traditional graphic for the same element.
What would change if the + and − markings were swapped on the source?
The voltage would have the opposite sign relative to the chosen reference direction, reversing the direction of potential difference and current flow.

notes.t: Voltage as energy per unit charge
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge moved between two points in a circuit.
Worked example: 80 J to move 20 C gives a voltage of 4 V, i.e. 4 J of energy per coulomb.
defs: Voltage (potential difference)
The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge moved between two points: V = W/Q, measured in volts (1 V = 1 J/C).
eqs: Voltage from work done and charge moved
V = voltage (V); W = energy/work done (J); Q = charge moved (C)
tips: Keep units consistent: energy in joules and charge in coulombs give volts directly; watch for mC or kJ inputs needing conversion.
Do not confuse voltage (energy per charge, V = W/Q) with current (charge per time) or power (energy per time).
rq: Why does the calculation divide energy by charge rather than multiply?
Voltage is energy per unit charge, so the energy supplied is shared across each coulomb; more charge for the same energy means a lower voltage.
What would the voltage be if the same 80 J moved 40 C of charge?
V = 80/40 = 2 V, half the original voltage, since the energy is spread over twice the charge.

notes.t: Current and Voltage Sources
pts: Bench power supplies act as voltage sources or current sources, and can be set to a required output voltage and current limit.
The example bench supply displays set voltage (V) and current (A), with output terminals and controls for setting values.
A programmable DC supply lets the user set the output voltage and current limit before connecting to a circuit.
tips: Do not confuse the displayed current limit with the current the circuit actually draws; the load determines the actual current, up to the set limit.
rq: Why does a DC power supply have both a voltage setting and a current setting?
The voltage setting determines the output potential difference, while the current setting limits the maximum current the supply can deliver, protecting the circuit and supply from overload.

units.name: 1.8 Ohm's Law and its history
units.ov: This module covers Ohm's law in both its circuit form (V = IR) and its material or field form (J = σE), and shows how resistance follows from geometry and resistivity. It also introduces conductance and the conditions under which the law holds: constant temperature and a linear resistor. The same relationship appears at three levels: macroscopic V–I, geometric R = ρl/A, and microscopic J–E. A short historical note on Georg Ohm closes the section.
must: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, \( V = IR \), so V ∝ I for a fixed linear resistance, and the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin
Resistance from geometry: \( R = \rho l / A \), so R grows with length and resistivity and falls with cross-sectional area
Field form: \( J = \sigma E \), equivalently \( E = \rho J \), is the material-level statement of Ohm's law
Definitions and links: \( E = V/l \) (V/m), \( J = I/A \) (A/m²), and \( \sigma = 1/\rho \) (S/m)
Derive the field form from the circuit form: substitute \( V = El \), \( I = JA \) and \( R = \rho l/A \) into \( V = IR \) to get \( E = \rho J \)
Conductance \( G = 1/R \) (siemens), giving \( V = I/G \) as an equivalent form
At constant V, \( I = V/R \) gives a decreasing hyperbola on an I–R graph
Validity limits: the law fails for non-linear or heating components, and real resistors give curved V–I graphs because R changes with temperature and material effects
Units: ρ is in Ω·m, σ in S/m, J in A/m², E in V/m; convert length to m and area to m² (e.g. mm² × 10⁻⁶) before using \( R = \rho l/A \)
Do not confuse I (total current, A) with J (current density, A/m²), or ρ (Ω·m) with R (Ω)
conn: Geometry and material: \( R = \rho l/A \) joins the circuit form \( V = IR \) to the field form \( J = \sigma E \), so questions often ask you to move between them
Temperature and linearity: heating changes ρ, so R changes and the V–I line curves, which limits where Ohm's law applies
Resistivity and conductivity: \( \rho = 1/\sigma \) and \( R = 1/G \), so a problem may be set in S or S/m and need converting to Ω or Ω·m
Wire reshaping: stretching or drawing a wire changes l and A together (constant volume), so R changes by the square of the length ratio
exq: A copper wire has length 50 m and cross-sectional area 2.5 mm², with \( \rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m} \). Find its resistance, the voltage needed for 10 A, and the electric field and current density in the wire.
Starting from \( V = IR \) and \( R = \rho l/A \), derive \( J = \sigma E \), defining each quantity and giving its units.
A resistor has conductance 0.04 S. Find its resistance and the current at 12 V. Then find the new current if the voltage is doubled, assuming the resistor is ideal.
A wire is drawn out to twice its original length at constant volume and constant resistivity. By what factor does its resistance change, and what happens to J for the same current?
Sketch the V–I graph for an ideal resistor and for a real one that heats up. Explain why Ohm's law fails for the real resistor, and sketch I against R at constant V.

notes.t: Ohm's Law
pts: At constant temperature, current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the voltage across it, so V ∝ I.
Resistance is the constant of proportionality between V and I; the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin for an ideal resistor.
Real resistors deviate from the ideal straight line, shown by the practical curves, because temperature and material effects change resistance.
Conductance G is the reciprocal of resistance, so V = I/G is an equivalent form of Ohm's law.
At constant voltage, current is inversely related to resistance, so the I–R graph is a decreasing hyperbola.
defs: Ohm's Law
At constant temperature, the current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the voltage across it.
eqs: V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); \rho = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length of conductor (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); G = conductance (S)
tips: Ohm's law only holds at constant temperature and for a linear (fixed) resistance; a non-linear or heating component will give a curved V–I graph.
Keep units consistent: length in metres and area in m² when using \( R = \rho l / A \), otherwise the resistance will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
rq: Why does the ideal V–I graph pass through the origin, and what does a curved 'practical' line tell you about the resistor?
Zero voltage gives zero current, since V = IR with R constant; a curved line means R is not constant, typically because the resistor heats up and its resistance changes.
If the resistance R doubles while the voltage stays constant, what happens to the current, and why?
The current halves, because I = V/R, so I is inversely proportional to R at constant V.

notes.t: Ohm's Law
pts: Ohm's Law is presented as a cartoon: Volt pushes Amp through a resistance controlled by Ohm, showing the relationship between voltage, current and resistance.
tips: Ohm's Law itself is not shown explicitly on this page; the relation V = IR and its units (V, A, Ω) must be recalled from the surrounding notes rather than from this image.
rq: Why does the cartoon show Ohm as the one holding back the flow between Volt and Amp?
Resistance (Ohm) opposes the flow of current driven by voltage, so for a given voltage a larger resistance gives a smaller current.

notes.t: Ohm's Law in Field Form (Resistivity, Conductivity, E and J)
pts: Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its length and resistivity, and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Voltage across a conductor equals electric field times length, so E is voltage per unit length.
Resistivity is the reciprocal of conductivity, linking the two material properties.
Current density is current per unit area, and in the field form the current density is proportional to the electric field.
The field-form Ohm's law J = σE is the material-level statement of Ohm's law.
defs: Electric field E
The voltage drop per unit length along a conductor, measured in V/m.
Current density J
Current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of a conductor, measured in A/m².
Conductivity σ
A material's ability to conduct current, the reciprocal of resistivity, measured in S/m.
Resistivity ρ
A material property giving resistance per unit length and area, measured in Ω·m.
eqs: Resistance of a conductor from resistivity
R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
Electric field from voltage and length
E = electric field (V/m); V = voltage (V); l = length (m)
J = current density (A/m²); σ = conductivity (S/m); E = electric field (V/m)
Resistivity from electric field and current density
E = electric field (V/m); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); J = current density (A/m²)
J = current density (A/m²); I = current (A); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Check units: ρ is in Ω·m (not Ω), and σ is in S/m; mixing these with R (Ω) gives wrong results unless length and area are included.
Do not confuse J (current density, A/m², per area) with I (total current, A); divide by area A when converting between them.
rq: Why does doubling the wire's length double its resistance, but doubling its cross-sectional area halve it?
R = ρl/A: resistance is directly proportional to length (more material to push current through) and inversely proportional to area (a wider path offers less opposition).
If two materials carry the same electric field, how does their current density compare when one has twice the conductivity?
From J = σE, the current density is doubled, since J is directly proportional to σ at fixed E.

units.name: 1.9 Power, energy and lecture summary
units.ov: This material covers the basic DC circuit quantities (charge, voltage, current, resistance, conductance, energy and power) and how Ohm's law links V, I and R. Combining Ohm's law with P = VI gives the three power formulae, so any two known quantities fix the other two. It closes Lecture 1 and leads into Kirchhoff's laws.
must: Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), \( I = V/R \), \( R = V/I \)
Three power forms: \( P = VI = I^{2}R = V^{2}/R \); each follows from substituting Ohm's law into \( P = VI \)
Choose the power formula by the known pair: \( I^{2}R \) for current and resistance, \( V^{2}/R \) for voltage and resistance, \( VI \) for voltage and current
Any two of V, I, R, P determine the other two, so solve by selecting the equation that contains the two knowns
Units and symbols: V (volt), I (ampere), R (ohm, Ω), P (watt), Q (coulomb), W (joule)
Conductance \( G = 1/R \) is measured in siemens (S)
Convert prefixes before substituting: mA to A (\(\times10^{-3}\)) and kΩ to Ω (\(\times10^{3}\))
Definitions: power is the rate of energy transfer (\( P = dW/dt \), so energy in joules = power × time); voltage is energy per unit charge; current is the rate of flow of charge
Symbol and unit clashes: W is the symbol for energy but also the unit abbreviation for watts, and A is the unit for amps. Quantity symbols are italic and units upright
conn: Ohm's law with the power equations: eliminate V or I to get \( I^{2}R \) or \( V^{2}/R \), which is used in resistor power rating and heating questions
Power with energy: \( W = Pt \), so a power calculation is often followed by energy used or cost over a time period
Resistance with conductance: \( G = 1/R \) is used later for parallel combinations, where conductances add
Lecture 1 quantities with Kirchhoff's laws: Ohm's law supplies the voltage-current relation for each element, and KCL and KVL give the circuit equations
exq: A 330 Ω resistor carries 25 mA. Find the voltage across it and the power dissipated, and state which power formula you used and why.
A 12 V supply is connected across a 470 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the power. How does the power change if the voltage doubles?
A 0.25 W resistor of 1 kΩ is used in a circuit. Find the maximum voltage and maximum current it can take without exceeding its rating.
A heater rated at 2 kW operates at 230 V. Find its current and resistance, and the energy in joules and kWh used in 3 hours.
Convert a 200 Ω resistance to conductance. A component has G = 5 mS and carries 2 mA. Find the voltage across it and the power dissipated.

notes.t: Power and Energy: Ohm's Law Relationships
pts: Power, voltage, current and resistance are linked so any two known quantities determine the other two.
Voltage is measured in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms and power in watts.
Power can be found from voltage and current, or from current and resistance, or from voltage and resistance.
defs: Power (P)
The rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted, measured in watts (W).
Voltage (V)
The electric potential difference driving charge around a circuit, measured in volts (V).
Current (I)
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A).
Resistance (R)
The opposition to current flow in a component, measured in ohms (Ω).
eqs: P = power (W); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
P = power (W); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
P = power (W); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω)
Voltage from current and resistance (Ohm's law)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
Current from voltage and resistance (Ohm's law)
I = current (A); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω)
Resistance from voltage and current (Ohm's law)
R = resistance (Ω); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert mA to A and kΩ to Ω before substituting into the power and Ohm's law equations.
Do not confuse the power formulas: P = I²R applies to current and resistance, while P = V²/R applies to voltage and resistance.
rq: Why can the power equation P = V²/R be used instead of P = V × I when only voltage and resistance are known?
Because substituting I = V/R (Ohm's law) into P = V × I gives P = V²/R, so current need not be measured.
What happens to the power dissipated in a fixed resistor if the voltage doubles?
Power quadruples, since P = V²/R and doubling V multiplies V² by four.

notes.t: Summary of DC circuit terms and quantities
pts: Circuit notation and element depiction give the basic language for drawing DC circuits.
Resistance, current and voltage are the core quantities introduced in this lecture.
Each quantity has a standard symbol, SI unit and unit abbreviation that must be used consistently.
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance and is measured in siemens.
Power and energy are linked to electrical quantities and measured in watts and joules.
defs: Resistance
Opposition to current flow in a circuit element, measured in ohms (Ω) with symbol R.
Conductance
The reciprocal of resistance, a measure of how easily current flows, measured in siemens (S) with symbol G.
Electric charge
A fundamental property of matter measured in coulombs (C) with symbol Q.
Electric potential
Electric potential energy per unit charge, measured in volts (V) with symbol V.
Energy
The capacity to do work, measured in joules (J) with symbol W.
Power
The rate at which energy is transferred or converted, measured in watts (W) with symbol P.
tips: Do not confuse the quantity symbol A (current) with the unit abbreviation A (amp); keep quantity symbols italic and units upright.
Watts (W) and ohms (Ω) use different symbols; do not mix up the power symbol P with the unit abbreviation W for watt, or the energy symbol W with watts.
rq: Why is the symbol for current A while the unit abbreviation is also A, and how could this cause confusion?

Current uses the symbol A in the table, which is also the abbreviation for amp; context must show whether a letter denotes the quantity or its unit, so write quantities in italics and units in roman type.
Why are conductance and resistance both needed if they describe the same property?
They are reciprocals; conductance is more convenient for parallel elements where conductances add, while resistance is more convenient for series elements where resistances add.

notes.t: DC Circuits Lecture 1 Summary
pts: Lecture 1 covered circuit notation, element depiction, and the core quantities resistance, current and voltage.
A formulae sheet is provided for each lecture to support revision.
A Moodle test quiz is available to practise before real quizzes begin after the next lecture.
The next lecture moves on to Kirchhoff's laws.
tips: Practise on the Moodle test quiz before the real quizzes start, since those will count toward assessment.
rq: Why is the next topic, Kirchhoff's laws, a natural follow-on from resistance, current and voltage?
Kirchhoff's laws describe how current and voltage behave across connected elements in a circuit, so they build directly on the three quantities introduced in Lecture 1.

units.name: Formula sheet DC lecture 1
units.ov: This sheet covers the basic DC circuit quantities (resistance, current, voltage and power) and the relationships linking them. Resistance comes from material geometry (\(R=\rho l/A\)). Ohm's law relates voltage to current through R, and power \(P=IV\) follows from energy per charge times charge per time. Together these form the toolkit for all later circuit analysis.
must: Ohm's law: \(V = IR\), valid only for a fixed linear resistance at constant temperature
Resistance of a conductor: \(R = \rho l / A\) (ρ in Ω·m, l in m, A in m²)
Power: \(P = IV\), and by substituting Ohm's law \(P = I^2R = V^2/R\)
Current is charge per unit time: \(I = Q/t\), with 1 A = 1 C/s
Voltage is energy per unit charge: \(V = W/Q\), and \(V = El\) for a uniform field (E in V/m)
Voltage is measured across an element; current is measured through it
Conductance: \(G = 1/R\) in siemens (S)
Slope of an I vs V graph gives \(1/R\) (conductance), not R; a straight line indicates ohmic behaviour
Unit hygiene: convert mA, cm² and mm² to SI before calculating; 1 W = 1 J/s
Combined form: \(V = I\rho l/A\), so doubling length doubles R and doubling area halves R
conn: Resistivity formula plus Ohm's law: geometry changes (stretching or changing wire diameter) alter R, which changes the current for a given V
Ohm's law plus power: substitute to get \(P=I^2R\) or \(V^2/R\) when only two of V, I, R are known (heating, fuse and rating problems)
Charge-time and current relations: \(Q = It\) combined with \(W = QV = Pt\) gives energy delivered over a time period
Electric field and voltage: \(V = El\) links field strength across a conductor to its potential difference and thus to current via \(R=\rho l/A\)
exq: A copper wire of length 50 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² has resistivity \(1.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}\). Calculate its resistance and the current when 12 V is applied.
A 230 V heater draws 10 A. Find its resistance, power, and the energy used in 3 hours in joules and kWh.
A charge of 120 C passes through a resistor in 40 s while the voltage across it is 9 V. Find the current, resistance, and power dissipated.
A wire is drawn to twice its length with constant volume and resistivity. By what factor does its resistance change, and what happens to the current at fixed voltage?
An I vs V graph for a component is a straight line through the origin with I = 0.25 A at V = 5 V. Find R and G, and explain why Ohm's law might fail if the component heats up.

notes.t: DC circuits: resistance, current, voltage, Ohm's law and power
pts: Resistance is the property of a material that restricts electron flow; it is measured in ohms and depends on resistivity, length and cross-sectional area.
Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor or circuit element, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).
Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points and is measured across a circuit element, whereas current is measured through it.
At constant temperature, current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the applied voltage; the slope of an I vs. V graph gives R.
Power is the rate of electrical energy transfer, measured in watts, where one watt is one joule per second.
defs: Resistance
The property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons; measured in ohms (Ω).
Current (I)
The time rate of flow of electrical charge through a conductor or circuit element; measured in amperes (A), where 1 A = 1 C/s.
Voltage (V)
The energy transferred per unit charge when a charge moves from one point in an electrical circuit to a second point; measured in volts.
Power
The rate of electrical energy transferred within a circuit; measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
Resistor
A component with a value of resistance.
eqs: resistivity = material resistivity (Ω·m); length = conductor length (m); area = cross-sectional area (m²)
Conductance = reciprocal of resistance (siemens, S); Resistance = (Ω)
I = current (A); Q = charge (C); t = time (s)
V = voltage (V); W = energy (J); Q = charge (C); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = area (m²)
P = power (W); I = current (A); V = voltage (V)
tips: Ohm's law (V = IR) requires constant temperature and a fixed linear resistance; do not apply it blindly to temperature-dependent components.
Keep units consistent: resistivity in Ω·m with length in m and area in m² gives resistance in Ω; watch for mA or cm² conversions.
rq: Why does the I vs. V graph of a fixed linear resistor have a steeper slope when the resistance is lower?
Since I = V/R, slope = 1/R; lower resistance gives a larger slope, so the line is steeper.
If a resistor's temperature rises, what happens to the proportionality between I and V, and why does the formula's condition matter?
Ohm's law only holds at constant temperature because resistance changes with temperature, so the proportionality breaks down.
Why is voltage measured across a component while current is measured through it?
Voltage is an energy-per-charge difference between two points, so it needs two connection points; current is charge flow, so it must pass through the element.

units.name: Mentimeter Questions Lecture1
units.ov: This is a short set of lecture-1 Mentimeter notes covering course logistics (formula sheet, quiz weighting, no need to memorise the resistor colour code) and one core technical idea: the resistance of a uniform conductor, R = ρl/A. The technical content is mostly about using SI units correctly, especially converting mm² to m², and checking dimensional consistency. The notes contain very little technical content, so a top-grade student should master this formula and its unit handling thoroughly.
must: Resistance of a uniform conductor: \( R = \frac{\rho l}{A} \), with R in Ω, ρ in Ω·m, l in m and A in m²
R is proportional to resistivity and length, and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (doubling l doubles R; doubling A halves R)
Resistivity ρ is a material property: the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-section of the material, in Ω·m
Copper resistivity is given as \( 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m} \)
Area conversion: \( 1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2 \), because the length factor \( 10^{3} \) is squared to give \( 10^{6} \)
Convert everything to SI base units (m, m²) before substituting, otherwise the answer can be off by orders of magnitude
Dimensional check: \( \Omega\,\text{m}\times\text{m}/\text{m}^2=\Omega \), which confirms the formula is consistent
Different resistor symbols (zigzag or rectangle) represent the same component; read the label R and its value

Admin: the formula sheet is on Moodle and the resistor colour code need not be memorised; the Moodle quizzes allow unlimited attempts, the highest grade counts, and together they are worth 5% of the module
conn: Resistivity and geometry link to Ohm's law: calculate R = ρl/A first, then use V = IR to find the current or voltage drop across a wire

Unit conversion and the resistance formula appear together: a wire diameter or area given in mm² must be converted to m² before use, and a diameter must first be turned into area with \( A=\pi d^2/4 \)
Dimensional analysis can be used to check any rearrangement of R = ρl/A, for example making ρ or l the subject
Wire resistance feeds into circuit analysis: a wire's R can be treated as a resistor in series or parallel with other components, with the symbol having no effect on the analysis
exq: A copper wire (ρ = 1.72×10⁻⁸ Ω·m) is 50 m long with cross-sectional area 2.5 mm². Calculate its resistance, stating the unit conversion used.
A copper conductor of length 100 m must have a resistance no greater than 0.5 Ω. Find the minimum cross-sectional area in mm².
A wire has resistance R. It is replaced by a wire of the same material with twice the length and twice the diameter. Find the new resistance in terms of R.
Show by dimensional analysis that \( R=\rho l/A \) gives units of ohms, and explain why using A in mm² without conversion gives an error of a factor of 10⁶.
A 20 m copper cable of diameter 1.8 mm carries 10 A. Calculate its resistance and the voltage drop along it.

notes.t: Grading of end-of-lecture Moodle quizzes

Repeated attempts reinforce recall and reveal misunderstandings; the 5% weight is small, but the feedback helps prepare for the exam-weighted assessment.

notes.t: Resistor circuit symbols
pts: Two different resistor symbols are shown, and either can be used in a circuit diagram.
The zigzag and rectangular symbols both represent a resistor with resistance R; the answer to whether it matters is no.
tips: Do not treat different circuit symbols for the same component as different components; check the label (R) and value instead.
rq: Why does it not matter which resistor symbol is used, even though the drawings look different?
Both symbols represent the same component, a resistor with resistance R; the symbol is only a convention, and the circuit behaviour depends on the resistance value, not the drawing style.

notes.t: Unit conversion of area (mm² to m²) and resistance of a wire
pts: Converting mm² to m² requires a factor of a million, because each metre is 1000 mm and area is squared.
Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its resistivity and length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Resistivity of copper is given as 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so all lengths and areas must be in metres and metres squared before substitution.
The unit of resistance works out as Ω·m × m / m² = Ω, confirming the formula is dimensionally consistent.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-sectional area of the material; measured in ohm-metres (Ω·m).
eqs: Resistance of a conductor of uniform cross-section
R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Unit trap: a factor of 10³ is used for length conversions (mm to m) but the area conversion must be squared, giving 10⁶.
Always convert all quantities to SI base units (m, m²) before substituting into R = ρl/A to avoid an answer off by orders of magnitude.
rq: Why does converting 2.5 mm² to m² give 10⁻⁶ rather than 10⁻³?
Because 1 m = 1000 mm, so 1 m² = (1000)² mm² = 10⁶ mm²; the area is squared, so the factor is a million, not a thousand.
What happens to the resistance if the wire's cross-sectional area is doubled, with length and material unchanged?
The resistance halves, since R = ρl/A is inversely proportional to area.

units.name: Mentimeter Questions Lecture1 2025
units.ov: This first lecture is mostly administrative: assessment (Moodle quizzes worth 5%), two labs (PSpice simulation and oscilloscope filter measurement), and social events. The technical content is circuit symbols and the resistance of a wire, \(R=\rho l/A\), with careful unit conversion. The notes contain little else, so the key skill is applying the resistance formula accurately with consistent SI units.
must: Resistance of a uniform conductor: \(R=\frac{\rho l}{A}\), with R in Ω, ρ in Ω·m, l in m, A in m²
Convert area by squaring the linear factor: \(1\,\text{mm}^2=10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), not \(10^{-3}\)
Always convert A to m² before substituting, otherwise the answer is wrong by a power of 10
Resistivity ρ is a material property (units Ω·m); for copper \(\rho=1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)
R is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area: doubling l doubles R, doubling A halves R
Dimensional check: \(\Omega\,\text{m}\times\text{m}/\text{m}^2=\Omega\)
The zigzag and rectangular resistor symbols are the same component; label each with R
Moodle quizzes allow unlimited attempts and together count 5%, so aim for full marks
Two labs: PSpice circuit simulation and measuring a filter with an oscilloscope (details on Moodle)
conn: Wire resistance from geometry (\(R=\rho l/A\)) feeds into later circuit analysis, where the calculated R is used in Ohm's law and series/parallel combinations
Unit conversion errors (mm² vs m²) combine with the resistance formula, so a wrong power of 10 in A gives a wrong R and wrong voltages and currents downstream
The PSpice lab connects to the theory: simulated circuits use the same resistor values and symbols, and the results can be checked against hand calculations
The oscilloscope filter lab uses circuit components whose values must be correctly identified and labelled, as with the resistor symbols
exq: A copper wire (\(\rho=1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)) is 50 m long with cross-section 1.5 mm². Calculate its resistance, stating the area in m².
A wire's length is doubled and its diameter is halved. By what factor does its resistance change? Justify using \(R=\rho l/A\).
Show by dimensional analysis that \(R=\rho l/A\) gives units of ohms.
Convert 2.5 mm² to m² and explain why the factor is \(10^{-6}\) rather than \(10^{-3}\).
A 100 m copper cable must have resistance no greater than 0.5 Ω. Find the minimum cross-sectional area in mm².

notes.t: Resistor circuit symbols
pts: Two different symbols are used for a resistor, and either is acceptable.
The zigzag and rectangular symbols represent the same component, so the choice does not change the circuit.
tips: Do not treat the zigzag and rectangular resistor symbols as different components; label each with its resistance R regardless of which symbol is drawn.
rq: Why does the choice of resistor symbol not change how the circuit behaves?
Both symbols represent the same ideal resistive component with the same resistance R, so the circuit's electrical behaviour is identical.

notes.t: Unit conversion of area (mm² to m²) and resistance of a wire
pts: Area conversion from mm² to m² uses the square of the length factor, not the length factor itself, because 1 mm = 10⁻³ m gives 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².
Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Resistivity ρ is a material property; for copper it is 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so the result depends on geometry only through l and A.
Check units: Ω·m × m ÷ m² reduces to Ω, confirming the resistance formula is dimensionally consistent.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit-length, unit-area sample of the material; units Ω·m.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Do not convert mm² to m² by multiplying by 10⁻³; square the linear conversion factor to get 10⁻⁶.
Make sure area is in m² before substituting into R = ρl/A, otherwise the answer will be wrong by a power of 10.
rq: Why does converting 2.5 mm² to m² give a factor of 10⁻⁶ rather than 10⁻³?
Area is two-dimensional: (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², so the linear factor must be squared.
If the wire's cross-sectional area doubled, what would happen to its resistance, and why?
It would halve, since R is inversely proportional to A (R = ρl/A).

units.name: 2.1 Lecture intro, recap and learning outcomes
units.ov: This material recaps circuit notation and Ohm's law (V = IR) and sets out Lecture 2's outcomes: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, series and parallel resistor networks with voltage and current dividers, and power in these circuits. Ohm's law applies to single components, and Kirchhoff's laws link components together, so together they form the basis of all later circuit analysis.
must: Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), with the rearrangements \( I = V/R \) and \( R = V/I \); use the triangle as a memory aid
Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the sum of currents into a node is zero, which expresses conservation of charge
Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero, which expresses conservation of energy
Do not confuse KCL (node, charge) with KVL (loop, energy); name the correct law and apply it to the correct node or loop
Ohm's law applies to one component and the voltage across that component; do not mix up voltages across different branches
Convert units before calculating: mA to A, k\(\Omega\) to \(\Omega\)
Series and parallel resistor combinations are analysed with voltage dividers (series) and current dividers (parallel)
Power in series and parallel circuits, using \( P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R \) (standard relations, not in these notes), is the third learning outcome
Know the circuit symbols: voltage source (battery), switch, conductor (wire), resistance (load such as a headlamp)
conn: Ohm's law with KVL: write the loop equation, substitute \( V = IR \) for each resistor, and solve for the current
Ohm's law with KCL: at a parallel junction the branch currents (each \( V/R \)) sum to the supply current, which leads to the current divider
KVL in a series circuit gives the voltage divider, because the source voltage splits in proportion to resistance
Power calculations need the voltages and currents found by Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws, and the total power supplied equals the total power dissipated
exq: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 k\(\Omega\) resistor. Find the current in mA and the power dissipated, converting units correctly.

Three resistors of 100 \(\Omega\), 220 \(\Omega\) and 330 \(\Omega\) are in series with a 9 V source. Use KVL to find the current and the voltage across each resistor, and check that the voltages sum to 9 V.
At a node, currents of 3 A and 2 A flow in and one current of 1.2 A flows out. Use KCL to find the remaining current and its direction.

Two resistors of 6 \(\Omega\) and 12 \(\Omega\) are in parallel across a 24 V supply. Use a current divider to find each branch current and the total power, then compare with the power in the equivalent single resistor.
Explain the physical principle behind KCL and KVL, and describe a common mistake made when applying Ohm's law to a multi-branch circuit.

notes.t: Previous Lecture: Circuit Notation, Voltage, Current, Resistance and Ohm's Law
pts: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: a voltage source represents the battery, a switch controls the circuit, conductors represent wires, and resistances represent loads such as headlamps.
Voltage, current and resistance are the three linked quantities of a circuit, and Ohm's law relates them.
The triangle diagram is a memory aid for Ohm's law: cover the quantity you want to find and the remaining positions give its formula.
eqs: Ohm's law: voltage across a resistor from current and resistance
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (\Omega)
Current from voltage and resistance (rearranged Ohm's law)
I = current (A); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (\Omega)
Resistance from voltage and current (rearranged Ohm's law)
R = resistance (\Omega); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert milliamps to amps and kilo-ohms to ohms before applying \( V = IR \).
Ohm's law applies to the resistance of a single component across which the voltage is measured; do not mix up the voltage across different branches of a circuit.
rq: Why does the triangle diagram show V on top with I and R underneath?

V is the product of I and R, so it sits above; I and R are the quantities that are multiplied together, while the single line shows division, so covering V leaves I × R and covering I or R leaves V ÷ the other quantity.
What happens to the current in the circuit if the resistance of a headlamp doubles while the 12 V supply stays the same?
By I = V/R, the current halves, since the voltage is fixed and the resistance is doubled.

notes.t: Learning Outcomes: Kirchhoff's Laws, Series-Parallel Circuits
pts: This lecture covers Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws as the foundation of circuit analysis.
Resistors in series and parallel are analysed using voltage dividers and current dividers.
Power in series and parallel circuits is the third learning outcome.
tips: Do not confuse Kirchhoff's current law (node/charge conservation) with the voltage law (loop/energy conservation).
rq: Why are Kirchhoff's laws listed before resistor divider rules?
Divider rules are derived from Kirchhoff's laws applied to series (voltage) and parallel (current) connections, so the laws come first.

units.name: 2.2 Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
units.ov: This module introduces Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL), which says charge is conserved at any node, so the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. It is applied first to general nodes with a sign convention, then to parallel circuits where \(I_{T}\) = \(I_{1}\) + \(I_{2}\) + \(I_{3}\), and finally to a ladder-style circuit where unknown currents are found by working node by node (X then Y). Together these give a systematic method for finding unknown branch currents.
must: KCL statement: \(\sum I_{IN} = \sum I_{OUT}\), equivalent to the algebraic sum of currents at a node being zero; this expresses conservation of charge
A node is any point where two or more circuit elements join, so identify nodes before writing equations
Sign convention: currents entering are positive and leaving are negative (or the reverse), applied consistently in every node equation, e.g. \(i_1 + i_2 - i_3 = 0\)
Parallel circuits: \(I_T = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\), because the source current splits across the branches
Finding an unknown branch current: \(I_2 = I_T - I_1 - I_3\)
Convert all currents to the same units (mA or A) before adding or subtracting, e.g. 100 − 30 − 20 = 50 mA
Parallel branches share the same voltage but divide the current, whereas KCL concerns currents at a node and KVL concerns voltages around a loop; do not mix them up
A negative result for a current means its true direction is opposite to the one assumed; it is not an error
conn: KCL with Ohm's law: branch currents in parallel are \(I = V/R\) at a common voltage, so \(I_T = V(1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3)\), which gives the equivalent resistance and the current divider
KCL with KVL: nodal and loop equations together solve circuits with several unknowns, and the sign convention must be consistent across both
Sequential nodes (X then Y): the output current from one node becomes the input to the next, so errors propagate down the chain
KCL with ammeter readings: ammeters in series read branch current, so questions give some readings and ask for the others by applying KCL
exq: A node has currents \(i_1 = 4\) A and \(i_2 = 3\) A entering and \(i_3\) leaving. Write the KCL equation with a stated sign convention and find \(i_3\). Then find the current in a further branch if \(i_3\) splits into 2 A and an unknown.
A source supplies \(I_T = 100\) mA to three parallel resistors. \(I_1 = 30\) mA and \(I_3 = 20\) mA. Find \(I_2\). If the supply is 10 V, calculate \(R_1\), \(R_2\) and \(R_3\).
In the ammeter circuit, A1 reads 5 mA and A2 reads 1.5 mA at node X, and A4 reads 1 mA at node Y. Find the readings of A3 and A5, showing the KCL equation at each node.
A node has three branch currents with directions marked: \(i_5 + i_6 + i_7 = 0\). Given \(i_5 = 2\) A and \(i_6 = -5\) A, find \(i_7\) and state its actual direction relative to the node.
Explain the difference between KCL and KVL. State which one you would use at a junction and which around a loop, and explain why parallel branches share a voltage but not a current.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
pts: At any node, the total current flowing in equals the total current flowing out, so charge is conserved.
A node is any point where two or more circuit elements are joined together.
Currents entering a node are taken as positive and leaving as negative when writing the node equation as a sum equal to zero.
In a parallel branch arrangement, the total current from the source splits across the branches so the total equals the sum of the branch currents.
defs: Node
A point in an electrical circuit at which two or more circuit elements are joined together.
Kirchhoff's Current Law
The sum of the currents entering a node equals the sum of the currents leaving that node.
eqs: KCL in summation form: total current entering a node equals total current leaving it
\(I_{IN}\) = current entering the node (A); \(I_{OUT}\) = current leaving the node (A)
KCL at node a: net current into the node is zero
\(i_1\), \(i_2\) = currents entering node a (A); \(i_3\) = current leaving node a (A)
KCL at node b: net current into the node is zero
\(i_5\), \(i_6\), \(i_7\) = branch currents at node b with signs set by direction (A)
Total source current split across parallel branches
\(I_T\) = total current from source (A); \(I_1, I_2, I_3\) = branch currents (A)
tips: Be consistent with sign convention: currents entering are positive and leaving negative (or vice versa) in every node equation; mixing conventions gives wrong results.
Do not confuse KCL (currents at a node) with Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (voltages around a loop).
rq: Why does KCL follow from conservation of charge?
Charge cannot accumulate at a node, so the charge arriving per unit time must equal the charge leaving per unit time; hence incoming and outgoing currents balance.
If a node has three currents, two entering at 2 A and 3 A, what is the leaving current?
Leaving current = 2 A + 3 A = 5 A, since entering current equals leaving current.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Current Law in a Parallel Circuit
pts: In a parallel circuit the total current entering a junction equals the sum of the branch currents leaving it.
An unknown branch current can be found by subtracting the known branch currents from the total current.
Branch currents divide the total current; each branch with its own resistor carries its own share of \(I_{T}\).
defs: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
The algebraic sum of currents entering a node equals the sum of currents leaving it; in a parallel circuit, the total current equals the sum of the branch currents.
eqs: Total current in a parallel circuit (KCL)
\(I_{T}\) = total source current (A); \(I_{1}\), \(I_{2}\), \(I_{3}\) = branch currents through \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) (A)
\(I_{2}\) = current through \(R_{2}\) (A); \(I_{T}\) = total current (A); \(I_{1}\) = current through \(R_{1}\) (A); \(I_{3}\) = current through \(R_{3}\) (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: 100 mA - 30 mA - 20 mA must all be in mA before subtracting (or convert to A).
