tips: Do not confuse the source type: Thévenin uses a voltage source in series, Norton uses a current source in parallel; mixing these up gives wrong load currents.
Both forms must describe the same terminal behaviour, so the resistance is the same in each; do not change it when converting.
rq: Why is the Thévenin or Norton equivalent useful when analysing a load connected to a complex network?
The whole network is replaced by one source and one resistance, so the load current or voltage can be found quickly by treating the load as connected to a simple two-element circuit.
What would the Norton equivalent of a Thévenin circuit with a series resistance look like, and why must the resistances match?

It is an ideal current source in parallel with the same resistance. The resistance must be equal in both forms because it is the network's internal resistance seen from the load terminals, which does not change with the choice of source model.

units.name: 3.2 Resistor networks: series, parallel and current/voltage dividers
units.ov: This topic covers reducing resistor networks with the series rule (resistances add, same current) and the parallel rule (reciprocals add, same voltage). It then uses voltage and current dividers to find voltages and currents without solving the whole circuit. Worked examples combine staged reduction, Ohm's law and KCL to get from source values to every branch quantity.
must: Series resistors carry the same current and their resistances add: \(R_T=R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n\)
Parallel resistors share the same voltage and their reciprocals add: \(1/R_T=1/R_1+1/R_2+\cdots\). The total is always smaller than the smallest branch.
Two parallel resistors: \(R_T=\dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}\) (product over sum). Check for equal resistors, e.g. two 20 Ω in parallel give 10 Ω.
Voltage divider: \(V_{R2}=\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V_B\). The larger resistor takes the larger share of voltage, and R2 is in the numerator for its own voltage.
Current divider (two branches only): \(I_{R2}=I_{tot}\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}\). The numerator is the OTHER resistor, and the smaller resistance takes the larger current.

Reduce networks in stages: identify what truly shares both end nodes, combine series and parallel groups, and redraw after each step. Example: R3+R4 = 20 Ω, in parallel with R2 = 20 Ω gives 10 Ω, then in series with R1 = 10 Ω gives 20 Ω.

Standard solving route: find \(R_{eq}\), then source current \(i=v_s/R_{eq}\) using the TOTAL resistance (e.g. 90/30 = 3 A), then the parallel-section voltage \(v_2=R_{eq1}i\) (20×3 = 60 V), then branch currents \(i=v_2/R\).
Never apply the full source voltage to a parallel branch that sits after a series resistor. Use the voltage across the parallel pair, which is smaller because of the drop across R1.
KCL at a node: \(i_1=i_2+i_3\) (e.g. 3 = 2 + 1 A). Use it as a check on every answer.
Check units and sanity: Ω, V and A; the parallel total must be less than the smallest resistor; and the divider shares must sum to the total (voltages to \(V_B\), currents to \(I_{tot}\)).
conn: Equivalent-resistance reduction gives the total current, and Ohm's law then gives the voltage across the parallel section. Branch currents follow from that voltage, and the current divider is a shortcut for the last step.
KCL verifies the current divider and Ohm's-law branch currents (\(i_1=i_2+i_3\)). Series voltage drops likewise sum to the source voltage (KVL).

A current divider with three or more branches, or with a branch that is itself a series/parallel group, first needs reduction to two branches. Then the divider formula applies with \(R_{eq}\) as the 'other' resistance.

Voltage and current dividers use opposite numerator conventions, so exam questions often mix them. Check each answer against the rule that the larger R takes more voltage and the smaller R takes more current.
exq: Find the equivalent resistance seen by the source for a network where R3 = 5 Ω and R4 = 15 Ω are in series, that combination is in parallel with R2 = 20 Ω, and the result is in series with R1 = 10 Ω.

A 15 A source current feeds R1 = 10 Ω in parallel with a branch made of R2 = 30 Ω and R3 = 60 Ω in parallel. Use current division to find the current in R1 and in the R2/R3 branch, and confirm with KCL. Note the notes' working shows '10+30' in the denominator, but it should be 10+20.
A 90 V source drives R1 = 10 Ω in series with R2 = 30 Ω parallel R3 = 60 Ω. Find the source current, the voltage across the parallel pair, and the currents in R2 and R3. Verify that i1 = i2 + i3.
A two-resistor voltage divider has \(V_{B}\) = 12 V, R1 = 4 kΩ and R2 = 8 kΩ. Find \(V_{R1}\) and \(V_{R2}\), and explain how the result changes if a load is connected across R2.

Two resistors, 12 Ω and 24 Ω, are in parallel with a 6 A total input current. Find the equivalent resistance, the current in each branch and the voltage across them, and explain why the smaller resistor carries more current.

notes.t: Resistor Networks: Voltage and Current Dividers, Series and Parallel Resistance
pts: In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor, and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
A voltage divider splits the source voltage across series resistors in proportion to their resistances; the larger resistor takes the larger share of voltage.
In a parallel circuit the voltage across each branch is the same, and the reciprocals of the resistances add to give the reciprocal of the total resistance.
A current divider splits the total current between parallel branches in inverse proportion to their resistances; the smaller resistance takes the larger current.
For exactly two parallel resistors the total resistance is the product over the sum, a shortcut worth memorising.
defs: Voltage divider
A series arrangement of resistors across a source so that each resistor receives a fraction of the source voltage proportional to its resistance.
Current divider
A parallel arrangement of resistors in which the total current splits between branches inversely proportional to their resistances.
Series resistors
Resistors connected end to end so that they carry the same current; their resistances add.
Parallel resistors
Resistors connected across the same two nodes so that they share the same voltage; their reciprocal resistances add.
eqs: Voltage across R2 in a two-resistor voltage divider
\(V_{R2}\) = voltage across R2 (V); \(R_{2}\) = resistance of R2 (\Omega); \(R_{1}\) = resistance of R1 (\Omega); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage (V)
Voltage across R1 in a two-resistor voltage divider
\(V_{R1}\) = voltage across R1 (V); \(R_{1}\) = resistance of R1 (\Omega); \(R_{2}\) = resistance of R2 (\Omega); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage (V)
Current through R2 in a two-resistor current divider
\(I_{R2}\) = current through R2 (A); \(I_{tot}\) = total input current (A); \(R_{1}\) = resistance of R1 (\Omega); \(R_{2}\) = resistance of R2 (\Omega)
Total resistance of two parallel resistors
tips: Do not confuse the formulas: in the voltage divider the voltage across R2 has R2 in the numerator, while in the current divider the current through R2 has R1 in the numerator (the opposite branch).
Check units: resistances in \(\Omega\), voltages in V, currents in A, and ensure \(1/R_T\) is inverted to give \(R_T\) in parallel calculations.
rq: Why does the larger resistor in a voltage divider get the larger voltage, and what would happen to the ratio V1/V2 if R1 doubled?
Series resistors carry the same current, so V = IR makes voltage proportional to resistance; V1/V2 = R1/R2, so doubling R1 doubles V1/V2.
Why does a current divider send more current into the branch with the smaller resistance?
Parallel branches share the same voltage, so I = V/R is larger when R is smaller; the current divides inversely to resistance.
Why is the total resistance of parallel resistors always smaller than the smallest individual resistance?
Each added parallel branch provides an extra path for current, so the sum of conductances (1/R) increases and \(R_{T}\) decreases.

notes.t: Current division with parallel resistances (Example 1)
pts: Current division applies to exactly two resistances in parallel, so combine R2 and R3 first into one equivalent resistance.
Parallel pair equivalent: product over sum, \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = R2R3/(R2+R3) = 20 Ω here.
Once reduced to two branches, the source current splits so the branch current i1 is the source current times \(R_{\text{eq}}\) divided by the total of R1 and \(R_{\text{eq}}\).
The source current \(i_{s}\) = 15 A divides between R1 = 10 Ω and \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = 20 Ω; the branch with the smaller resistance carries more current, so i1 = 10 A is the larger share.
defs: Current division principle
For two resistances in parallel carrying a total current \(i_{s}\), the current in one branch equals \(i_{s}\) times the other resistance divided by the sum of the two resistances.
Equivalent resistance of two parallel resistors
\(R_{\text{eq}}\) = \(R_{a}\) \(R_{b}\) /(\(R_{a}\) + \(R_{b}\)), the product divided by the sum of the two resistances.
eqs: Equivalent resistance of R2 and R3 in parallel
Current division for branch current i1
\(i_{1}\) = branch current through R1 (A); \(i_{s}\) = source current = 15 A; \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = 20 Ω; \(R_{1}\) = 10 Ω
tips: Use \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = \(R_{a}\) \(R_{b}\)/(\(R_{a}\)+\(R_{b}\)) for parallel pairs, not \(R_{a}\) + \(R_{b}\); adding gives 90 Ω instead of 20 Ω.
In the current-division formula the ratio uses the OTHER parallel resistance: i1 = \(i_{s}\)·\(R_{\text{eq}}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{\text{eq}}\)), not \(i_{s}\)·\(R_{1}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{\text{eq}}\)).
rq: Why must R2 and R3 be combined before applying the current-division formula rather than applied directly to all three resistors?
The current-division formula is derived for exactly two parallel branches; with three branches you must first reduce two of them to a single equivalent resistance.
What would happen to i1 if R3 were removed (open circuit)?
\(R_{\text{eq}}\) would become R2 = 30 Ω, so i1 = 15 × 30/(10+30) = 11.25 A, showing that i1 rises as the parallel branch resistance increases.

notes.t: Solving for equivalent resistance (series and parallel reduction)
pts: Resistors in series (R3 and R4 here, shown as a single block) are combined by adding their resistances, so R3 + R4 = 5 Ω + 15 Ω = 20 Ω, giving Req1.
Resistors in parallel (R2 and Req1, both 20 Ω) combine as reciprocal sums; two equal 20 Ω resistors in parallel give 10 Ω, which is Req2.
Once the network is reduced to a single chain, the remaining series resistors (R1 and Req2) are added to give the final equivalent resistance of 20 Ω.
defs: Equivalent resistance
The single resistance that could replace a network of resistors between two terminals without changing the current-voltage relationship seen from those terminals.
tips: Do not add resistors that are in parallel; use the reciprocal rule (or the product-over-sum formula for two resistors) instead.
Always reduce the network in stages and redraw after each combination, checking which resistors truly share both end nodes.
rq: Why can R3 and R4 be combined by simple addition, while R2 and Req1 cannot?

R3 and R4 are in series: the same current flows through both, so their resistances add. R2 and Req1 share the same two nodes (are in parallel), so the same voltage appears across both and they must be combined by the reciprocal rule.
What would the final equivalent resistance be if R2 were 40 Ω instead of 20 Ω?
Req1 would still be 20 Ω; R2 ∥ Req1 = (40×20)/(40+20) ≈ 13.3 Ω, then adding R1 gives 10 + 13.3 ≈ 23.3 Ω.

notes.t: Current division and equivalent resistance in a parallel branch circuit
pts: Parallel resistors R2 and R3 combine into one equivalent resistance, which is then in series with R1.
The total current from the source flows through R1 and the equivalent parallel resistance; the voltage across the parallel pair is found from it.
Once the parallel voltage v2 is known, Ohm's law gives the current in each parallel branch separately.
defs: Equivalent resistance of parallel resistors
Two resistors in parallel combine to a single resistance equal to their product divided by their sum; this replaces them in the circuit for analysis.
eqs: Equivalent resistance of two parallel resistors R2 and R3
Source current through the total resistance
\(v_{s}\) = 90 V (source voltage); \(R_{eq}\) = 30 Ω (total equivalent resistance, \(R_{1}\) + \(R_{eq1}\)); \(i_{1}\) = 3 A (source current)
\(R_{eq1}\) = 20 Ω; \(i_{1}\) = 3 A; \(v_{2}\) = 60 V (voltage across R2 and R3)
tips: Use the total resistance (R1 + Req1 = 30 Ω) when finding the source current, not just the parallel part (20 Ω).
Check units: resistance in ohms, voltage in volts, current in amperes; a 10 Ω resistor with 3 A gives 30 V, not 3 V.
rq: Why can the 20 Ω equivalent be used in series with R1 to find the source current?
Because R2 and R3 are in parallel, they can be replaced by Req1 = 20 Ω, which is in series with R1 = 10 Ω, giving a total of 30 Ω across the 90 V source.
Why is the current through R2 (2 A) larger than through R3 (1 A)?
The parallel branches share the same voltage, so current is inversely proportional to resistance: the lower-resistance branch (30 Ω) carries more current.
Why is v1 = 30 V and not 90 V?
The source voltage divides between R1 and the parallel pair; v1 = R1·i1 = 10 × 3 = 30 V, and the remaining 60 V appears across the parallel branches.

notes.t: Finding branch currents in a parallel circuit using equivalent resistance, Ohm's law and K
pts: Reduce the circuit to an equivalent resistance seen by the source, then find the total source current.
The voltage across the parallel branches (V₂) is found from the reduced circuit (Figure b), where the source current flows through R₁ and \(R_{eq1}\).
Once V₂ is known, each parallel branch current follows from Ohm's law, since each branch is directly across V₂.
KCL at Node A: the source current splits into the branch currents, so the total current equals the sum of the branch currents.
defs: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
The algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero; equivalently, the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it.
eqs: Branch current from Ohm's law across the parallel branches
i₂, i₃ = branch currents (A); V₂ = voltage across the parallel branches (V); R₂ = 30 Ω; R₃ = 60 Ω
i₁ = source (total) current (A); i₂, i₃ = branch currents (A)
tips: Do not apply Ohm's law to R₂ or R₃ using the full 90 V source; use the voltage V₂ across the parallel branches, which is smaller because of the drop across R₁.
Use the correct sign convention for currents entering and leaving a node when applying KCL.
rq: Why can we replace R₂ and R₃ with a single equivalent resistance when finding the source current?
R₂ and R₃ are in parallel, so \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = (R₂·R₃)/(R₂+R₃) = 20 Ω, which gives the total resistance seen by the source (R₁ + \(R_{eq1}\) = 30 Ω) and the total current i₁ = 90/30 = 3 A.
Why must V₂ be found before i₂ and i₃, rather than using the source voltage directly?
Because R₁ drops part of the 90 V source voltage (v₁ = i₁R₁ = 30 V), so the voltage across the parallel branches is V₂ = 90 − 30 = 60 V, which is the voltage Ohm's law must use for each branch.

units.name: 3.3 Thévenin's theorem: statement and equivalent circuit
units.ov: Thévenin's theorem lets any linear two-terminal network be replaced, as seen from the load terminals, by one voltage source \(V_T\) in series with one resistance \(R_T\). \(V_T\) comes from the open-circuit voltage and \(R_T\) from the dead network (sources zeroed). The payoff is quick load analysis when the load changes, using only Ohm's law and a voltage divider once the equivalent is found. The equivalence holds at the terminals only, not inside the network.
must: Thévenin equivalent = ideal voltage source \(V_T\) in series with resistance \(R_T\), giving identical terminal voltage and current to the original network for any load.
\(V_T = V_{AB,\text{open}}\): remove the load and find the open-circuit voltage across A and B using KVL, KCL, nodal analysis or a divider.
\(R_T\): remove the load, replace independent voltage sources with short circuits and independent current sources with open circuits, then find the resistance looking into A and B.
Never reverse the rule: shorting current sources or opening voltage sources gives wrong \(R_T\).
Load current in the equivalent circuit: \(I_L = V_T/(R_T+R_L)\) and \(V_L = V_T R_L/(R_T+R_L)\).
The theorem only applies to linear networks. Dependent sources must be kept, so \(R_T\) needs a test source or \(R_T = V_{oc}/I_{sc}\).
Equivalence is only at the output terminals; internal currents, voltages and power dissipation of the original circuit are not reproduced.

Worked example: load \(R_2 = 2\,\Omega\), source branches 28 V with \(R_1 = 4\,\Omega\) and 7 V with \(R_3 = 1\,\Omega\). Remove \(R_2\), find \(V_T\) and \(R_T = R_1\parallel R_3\) (the two source branches in parallel with the sources shorted), then reconnect \(R_2\).
Check that the load is connected across the same terminals A and B in both circuits, and keep units consistent (V, Ω, A).
conn: Thévenin builds on KVL/KCL and nodal analysis: these find \(V_{oc}\), while series/parallel reduction finds \(R_T\).
Superposition and source zeroing: the rule for finding \(R_T\) is the same as for superposition (voltage sources become shorts, current sources become opens).
Voltage divider and Ohm's law: once the equivalent is found, the load voltage and current follow directly, and repeating this for several \(R_L\) values shows the method's benefit.
Short-circuit current link: \(R_T = V_{oc}/I_{sc}\) ties Thévenin to Norton and is the route for networks with dependent sources.
exq: For the circuit with B₁ = 28 V, R₁ = 4 Ω, B₂ = 7 V, R₃ = 1 Ω and load R₂ = 2 Ω, remove R₂ and find \(V_T\) and \(R_T\) at the terminals. Then draw the Thévenin equivalent and calculate the current through and voltage across R₂.

Using the equivalent from the previous question, find the load current when \(R_L\) is changed to 1 Ω, 5 Ω and 10 Ω. Explain why Thévenin's method is quicker than re-solving the original network each time.

State Thévenin's theorem and describe step by step how to find \(V_T\) and \(R_T\) for a network containing both voltage and current sources. State what happens to each type of source when finding \(R_T\).
A network containing a dependent source has \(V_{oc} = 12\) V and \(I_{sc} = 3\) A. Find \(R_T\), and the power in a 6 Ω load. Explain why simply zeroing the sources is not valid here.
True or false, with justification: the power dissipated inside the original network equals the power dissipated in the Thévenin equivalent's \(R_T\).

notes.t: Thévenin's Theorem
pts: Complex circuit analysis with KVL, KCL, nodal analysis and Ohm's law is time-consuming, especially when the load value changes.
Thévenin's theorem replaces the rest of a network, seen from the load terminals, with a single equivalent circuit containing only the load resistance of interest.
The method was developed by Léon Charles Thévenin to make complex circuit analysis easier.
In the example, the load is R₂ = 2 Ω, and the source network consists of B₁ = 28 V with R₁ = 4 Ω, B₂ = 7 V with R₃ = 1 Ω.
defs: Thévenin equivalent circuit
A simplified circuit consisting of a single voltage source in series with a single resistance, which behaves identically to the original network at the load terminals.
tips: Remember that the simplified circuit only holds for the load terminals; internal values are not preserved.
Take care with units: resistances in ohms and voltages in volts must be consistent throughout the calculation.
rq: Why is Thévenin's theorem especially useful when the load resistance changes?
The equivalent source (\(V_{\text{Th}}\) and \(R_{\text{Th}}\)) is computed once, so each new load value only needs a simple series calculation instead of re-analysing the whole network.
Why must the load be removed before finding the Thévenin equivalent?

The equivalent represents the network seen from the load terminals; with the load removed, the open-circuit voltage and the resistance looking back into the network can be found without the load's influence.

notes.t: Thévenin's Theorem
pts: Any linear two-terminal (two-port) network can be replaced, as seen by an external load, by a single voltage source in series with a single resistance.
The Thévenin voltage is the open-circuit voltage measured across terminals A and B.
The Thévenin resistance is found by setting all independent voltage sources to short circuits and all independent current sources to open circuits, then measuring the resistance across A and B.
The equivalent circuit reproduces the terminal behaviour of the original network for any external load connected between A and B.
defs: Thévenin voltage (\(V_T\))
The open-circuit voltage across the terminals A and B of a network.
Thévenin resistance (\(R_T\))
The resistance measured across terminals A and B with all independent voltage sources shorted and all independent current sources opened.
eqs: \(V_T\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(V_{AB,\text{open}}\) = open-circuit voltage across A and B (V)
tips: Do not short current sources or open voltage sources when finding \(R_T\); this reverses the rule and gives wrong answers.
Thévenin's theorem applies to linear networks only; dependent sources must be kept when finding \(R_T\) (use a test source or short-circuit current method).
rq: Why must voltage sources be shorted and current sources opened when finding \(R_T\), but not when finding \(V_T\)?

Finding \(V_T\) uses the network's actual sources to produce the open-circuit voltage. Finding \(R_T\) isolates the passive resistance of the network, so the sources are removed (shorted or opened) and only the internal resistance remains.
What happens to the load's current if the load resistance equals \(R_T\)?
Maximum power is transferred to the load when the load resistance equals \(R_T\), giving a load current of \(V_T/(2R_T)\).

notes.t: Thévenin's equivalent circuit: equivalent behaviour at output terminals
pts: A complex linear network seen from its output terminals can be replaced by an equivalent circuit that gives identical load current and voltage.
The load \(R_{L}\) sees the same \(I_{L}\) and \(V_{L}\) readings whether connected to the original circuit or to the Thévenin equivalent.
The equivalence applies only to what happens at the output terminals; internal behaviour of the original circuit is not represented.
defs: Thévenin's equivalent circuit
A network consisting of a single voltage source in series with a single resistance that, connected to any load, produces the same terminal voltage and current as the original network.
Output terminals
The pair of terminals across which the load is connected; equivalence is judged only at these terminals.
tips: Equivalence is only guaranteed at the output terminals; do not claim the internal currents or voltages of the original circuit are reproduced.
Remember the load \(R_{L}\) must be connected across the same output terminals in both circuits when comparing readings.
rq: Why must the load readings \(I_{L}\) and \(V_{L}\) be identical for the two circuits to count as equivalent?
Because equivalence is defined by matching the behaviour seen by any load at the output terminals; if the readings differ for some load, the replacement is not valid.
What if we changed \(R_{L}\) to a different value – would the Thévenin equivalent still give the same readings as the original?
Yes; Thévenin's equivalence holds for any load connected to the output terminals, so the readings should still match for every \(R_{L}\).

units.name: 3.4 Ideal and practical sources with internal resistance
units.ov: This material contrasts ideal voltage and current sources with practical sources, which have internal resistance, and uses that model to introduce Thévenin's Theorem. A practical generator is an ideal voltage source in series with \(R_{o}\). Kirchhoff's voltage law then gives the terminal voltage, and the same series-source model generalises to any linear two-terminal network as a Thévenin equivalent (\(V_{t}\), \(R_{t}\)).
must: Ideal voltage source: fixed V across its terminals whatever the current. Ideal current source: fixed I through its branch whatever the voltage.
Practical source model: ideal voltage source \(V_o\) in series with internal resistance \(R_o\).
KVL for the generator loop: \(V_o = I R_o + I R_L\), so \(I = \frac{V_o}{R_o+R_L}\).
Terminal voltage: \(V_L = I R_L = V_o - I R_o\). It falls as load current rises, and equals \(V_o\) only at \(I=0\) (open circuit).
Thévenin equivalent: a linear two-terminal network is replaced by an independent source \(V_t\) in series with \(R_t\), with identical terminal behaviour.
Open-circuit voltage: no current flows through \(R_t\), so \(V_t = v_{oc}\).

Thévenin resistance: \(R_t = \frac{v_{oc}}{I_{sc}}\), using the short-circuit current at the same terminals A–B. This is valid for linear networks with independent sources only; dependent sources need a different method.
Power: \(R_o\) dissipates heat inside the source, and only the load power \(I^2R_L\) is useful output.
Keep units consistent (V, A, Ω), and do not treat a real source as ideal: always include \(R_o\) when finding load voltage or current.
Short-circuit current of a practical source is \(I_{sc}=V_o/R_o\), which is why \(R_t\) can be extracted from \(v_{oc}/I_{sc}\).
conn: The practical generator model is a special case of a Thévenin equivalent: \(V_o \leftrightarrow V_t\) and \(R_o \leftrightarrow R_t\). So a load-voltage calculation reduces to a voltage divider: \(V_L = V_t \frac{R_L}{R_t+R_L}\).
The open-circuit and short-circuit tests combine in one question: measure \(v_{oc}\) and \(I_{sc}\), get \(R_t\), then predict the current and voltage for a given load.
KVL, Ohm's law and power are used together: terminal voltage drop, losses in \(R_o\), and power delivered to the load (and hence efficiency \(R_L/(R_o+R_L)\)).
Ideal versus practical sources: a real source's behaviour (voltage sag under load) is the bridge to source transformation and to maximum power transfer when \(R_L=R_t\).
exq: A battery has open-circuit voltage 12 V and measured terminal voltage 11.4 V when supplying 3 A. Find its internal resistance, the load resistance, and the power lost inside the battery.

A generator with \(V_o = 24\) V and \(R_o = 0.5\,\Omega\) supplies loads of 1 Ω, 5 Ω and 50 Ω. Calculate the current and terminal voltage for each, and comment on how close it is to an ideal voltage source.
A network's terminals A–B give \(v_{oc}=10\) V and \(I_{sc}=2\) A. Determine the Thévenin equivalent, then the current and power when a 3 Ω resistor is connected across A–B.
Starting from KVL, derive \(V_L = V_o - I R_o\) for a practical source and sketch \(V_L\) against \(I\), labelling the intercepts and the slope.
Explain why \(R_t = v_{oc}/I_{sc}\) cannot be applied naively to a network containing dependent sources, and state how you would find \(R_t\) instead.

notes.t: Ideal voltage and current sources (Thévenin's Theorem intro)
pts: An ideal voltage source maintains a constant potential difference across its terminals regardless of the current drawn through it.
An ideal current source drives a constant current through its branch regardless of the voltage across its terminals.

Thévenin's Theorem is practically useful because circuits are usually energised by one of these ideal source types, which allows a complex network to be simplified to an equivalent source plus resistance.
defs: Ideal voltage source
A two-terminal element that keeps a fixed voltage V between its terminals, whatever current flows through it.
Ideal current source
A two-terminal element that delivers a fixed current I through its branch, whatever voltage appears across its terminals.
tips: Do not confuse ideal source behaviour with real sources: a real source has internal resistance that changes its terminal voltage under load.
Units: voltage source is in volts (V) and current source in amperes (A); keep these distinct when converting between source types.
rq: Why does an ideal voltage source with zero internal resistance behave differently from an ideal current source when the external load resistance becomes very large?

The voltage source still holds V across the terminals, so the current falls to V/R; the current source still forces I through the load, so the voltage rises to IR, becoming very large (open-circuit limit).
What would happen to a circuit if you tried to connect two ideal voltage sources of different values directly in parallel?
The circuit is inconsistent: the two terminal voltages must be equal, so it is impossible, and the currents would be undefined/infinite in the ideal case.

notes.t: Thévenin's Theorem – practical generators and internal resistance
pts: Practical generators cannot hold voltage and current constant for every load because they have internal resistance.
A real generator can be modelled as an ideal voltage source in series with a resistor (the internal resistance).
Internal resistance dissipates power as heat inside the generator, so less power reaches the external load.
defs: Internal resistance
The resistance inside a practical source (e.g. a battery's electrolyte and electrodes) that causes the terminal voltage to fall as load current increases.
tips: Do not treat a real source as an ideal constant-voltage source: always include the series internal resistance when calculating load voltage or current.
Heat in the diagram occurs in both the source's internal resistance and the load; only the load power is useful output.
rq: Why does the terminal voltage of a real battery drop when a large load current is drawn?
Current flowing through the internal resistance produces a voltage drop \(IR_{\text{int}}\) inside the source, so the terminal voltage is \(V = E - IR_{\text{int}}\).
What would happen to the terminal voltage if the internal resistance were zero?
It would equal the ideal EMF \(E\) for every load, since there is no internal voltage drop – which is why real sources deviate from this ideal.

notes.t: Thévenin's Theorem: practical generators with internal resistance
pts: Practical generators cannot hold voltage and current constant for every load because they have internal resistance.
A real generator can be modelled as an ideal voltage source in series with a resistor.
Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop, the ideal source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops across the internal and load resistances.
The terminal voltage falls as load current rises, because more voltage is dropped across the internal resistance.
The measurable terminal voltage is the ideal source voltage minus the internal resistance drop.
defs: Internal resistance
The resistance inside a practical generator, modelled as a resistor in series with an ideal voltage source, that causes the terminal voltage to drop when current is drawn.
eqs: Kirchhoff's voltage law for the generator loop
\(V_{o}\) = ideal generator voltage (V); I = load current (A); \(R_{o}\) = internal resistance (Ω); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
Terminal (load) voltage of a practical generator
V_L = I R_L = V_o - I R_o
\(V_{L}\) = terminal voltage across the load (V); \(V_{o}\) = ideal source voltage (V); I = load current (A); \(R_{o}\) = internal resistance (Ω); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not treat the terminal voltage as the ideal source voltage \(V_{o}\); always subtract the drop I \(R_{o}\) caused by the load current.
Keep units consistent: \(R_{o}\) and \(R_{L}\) in ohms (Ω), I in amperes (A), so I \(R_{o}\) gives volts (V).
rq: Why does the terminal voltage drop as you connect a heavier load (smaller \(R_{L}\))?
A smaller \(R_{L}\) draws more current I; the drop I \(R_{o}\) across the internal resistance grows, so \(V_{L}\) = \(V_{o}\) − I \(R_{o}\) falls.
What would happen to the terminal voltage if \(R_{o}\) were zero?
The drop I \(R_{o}\) would vanish, so \(V_{L}\) = \(V_{o}\) for any load: an ideal generator that holds its voltage regardless of load.

notes.t: Thévenin Equivalent Circuit
pts: A Thévenin equivalent is an independent voltage source in series with a resistance.
With an open circuit no current flows, so no current flows through \(R_{t}\) and the open-circuit voltage equals \(V_{t}\).
Applying KVL to the open-circuit case gives \(V_{t}\) equal to the open-circuit voltage.
The short-circuit current is the same in the original network and in the Thévenin equivalent, so \(R_{t}\) can be found from it.
defs: Thévenin equivalent
A linear two-terminal network replaced by an independent voltage source \(V_{t}\) in series with a resistance \(R_{t}\) that gives identical terminal behaviour.
eqs: Thévenin resistance from open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current
\(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω); \(v_{oc}\) = open-circuit voltage across terminals A–B (V); \(I_{sc}\) = short-circuit current through terminals A–B (A)
tips: Do not confuse the short-circuit current \(I_{\text{sc}}\) (capital I, used in \(R_{t}\)) with the lowercase \(i_{\text{sc}}\) in the figure; both refer to the same current in the same circuit.
\(R_{t}\) is the ratio of open-circuit voltage to short-circuit current only for a linear network with independent sources; dependent sources must be handled differently.
rq: Why does no current flow through \(R_{t}\) when the terminals are open, and what does that imply for the voltage?
An open circuit carries no current, so the drop across \(R_{t}\) is zero and the terminal voltage equals \(V_{t}\), i.e. \(V_{t}\) = \(v_{\text{oc}}\).
Why can \(R_{t}\) be found by dividing the open-circuit voltage by the short-circuit current?
Shorting the terminals makes the voltage across \(R_{t}\) equal to \(V_{t}\), so \(I_{\text{sc}}\) = \(V_{t}\)/\(R_{t}\), giving \(R_{t}\) = \(v_{\text{oc}}\)/\(I_{\text{sc}}\).

units.name: 3.5 Thévenin example: open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current
units.ov: This material finds the Thévenin equivalent of a resistive network (\(v_{s}\) = 15 V, R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 50 Ω) by measuring the open-circuit voltage and the short-circuit current at the output terminals. The ratio of the two gives \(R_{t}\). The equivalent is then used to find the load current for a load \(R_{L}\) and checked against direct series-parallel analysis of the original circuit.
must: Thévenin's theorem: any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a voltage source \(V_t\) in series with a resistance \(R_t\), giving the same terminal behaviour for any load.

Open-circuit voltage: remove the load so that no current leaves the terminals. Then \(i_1 = \frac{v_s}{R_1+R_2} = \frac{15}{150} = 0.1\,\text{A}\), and \(V_{oc} = R_2 i_1 = 50\times0.1 = 5\,\text{V} = V_t\).

Short-circuit current: a wire across the terminals shorts out R₂, so \(I_{sc} = \frac{v_s}{R_1} = \frac{15}{100} = 0.15\,\text{A}\). This uses R₁ alone, unlike the open-circuit case, which uses R₁+R₂.
Thévenin resistance: \(R_t = \frac{V_{oc}}{I_{sc}} = \frac{5}{0.15} = 33.3\,\Omega\). This equals R₁ ∥ R₂ with the source replaced by a short circuit, which is a useful cross-check.

Load current from the equivalent: \(i_{RL} = \frac{V_t}{R_t+R_L}\) and \(V_{RL} = \frac{V_t R_L}{R_L+R_t}\). With \(R_L = 10\,\Omega\), \(i_{RL} = 5/43.3 \approx 0.115\,\text{A}\). The notes imply \(R_{L}\) = 10 Ω from the 8.333 Ω parallel value, so confirm this against the original figure.

Direct check without Thévenin: \(R_{eq1} = \frac{R_2R_L}{R_2+R_L} = 8.333\,\Omega\), \(R_{eq2} = R_1 + R_{eq1} = 108.3\,\Omega\), \(i_1 = v_s/R_{eq2} \approx 0.138\,\text{A}\), and \(V_{RL} = i_1R_{eq1} \approx 1.15\,\text{V}\). The load current is then about 0.115 A, which matches the Thévenin result.
Parallel resistors combine as product over sum, never by direct addition (8.333 Ω, not 60 Ω).
Do not include \(R_{L}\) when finding \(V_{\text{oc}}\), and keep the polarity of \(V_{\text{oc}}\) consistent with the marked + and − terminals.
Keep units straight: V/A gives Ω, and 50 Ω × 0.1 A is 5 V. Do not confuse the open-circuit loop current (0.1 A) with the short-circuit current (0.15 A).
conn: Series and parallel resistance reduction with the voltage divider: \(V_{\text{oc}}\) comes from a divider, \(R_{t}\) is a parallel combination, and the direct check uses all three.
Ohm's law and KVL/mesh analysis: i₁ from the mesh, \(V_{\text{oc}}\) = R₂i₁, and \(I_{\text{sc}}\) from the shorted mesh all feed the Thévenin parameters.
Thévenin as a shortcut for variable loads: once \(V_{t}\) and \(R_{t}\) are known, the current and voltage for any \(R_{L}\) follow, which leads to maximum power transfer at \(R_{L}\) = \(R_{t}\).
Equivalence checking: two routes to the same load current (the original circuit versus the Thévenin circuit) are often asked for together as verification.
exq: For the circuit with \(v_{s}\) = 15 V, R₁ = 100 Ω and R₂ = 50 Ω, find \(V_{\text{oc}}\) and \(I_{\text{sc}}\) at the output terminals, then calculate \(R_{t}\) and draw the Thévenin equivalent.

Using the Thévenin equivalent, calculate the current and voltage for a 10 Ω load connected across the terminals. Verify your answer by analysing the original circuit using R₂ ∥ \(R_{L}\) in series with R₁.
Show that \(R_{t}\) = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) by deactivating the source, and confirm it agrees with \(V_{\text{oc}}\)/\(I_{\text{sc}}\) = 33.3 Ω.
If R₁ is changed to 200 Ω, recalculate \(V_{t}\), \(R_{t}\) and the load current for \(R_{L}\) = 10 Ω. State which of these quantities change.

Explain why the load must be removed when finding \(V_{\text{oc}}\) and why the terminals are shorted when finding \(I_{\text{sc}}\). What would go wrong if R₁ were omitted from the open-circuit current calculation?

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent: open-circuit voltage analysis
pts: With the output terminals open, no current flows through the load, so the mesh current i₁ is set by the source and the series resistors R₁ and R₂ alone.
The open-circuit voltage \(V_{\text{oc}}\) is the voltage across the open terminals, which equals the voltage across R₂ because no current leaves through the terminals.
defs: Open-circuit voltage (\(V_{\text{oc}}\))
The voltage measured across the two terminals of a network when no load is connected (zero current through the terminals); it is the Thévenin voltage of the equivalent circuit.
eqs: Mesh current with terminals open (voltage divider through series resistors)
i₁ = mesh current (A); \(v_{s}\) = source voltage (V); R₁ = 100 Ω; R₂ = 50 Ω
\(V_{\text{oc}}\) = open-circuit voltage (V); R₂ = 50 Ω; i₁ = 0.1 A
tips: Keep the polarity of \(V_{\text{oc}}\) consistent with the marked + and − terminals when writing the answer.
Use the series resistance R₁ + R₂ in the current calculation; forgetting R₁ gives the wrong i₁ and \(V_{\text{oc}}\).
rq: Why does the open-circuit voltage equal the voltage across R₂ rather than across the source?
Because R₁ and R₂ are in series with the source, and with the terminals open the only current path is through R₁ and R₂; the voltage across R₂ is the output voltage at the open terminals.
What would \(V_{\text{oc}}\) become if R₂ were doubled to 100 Ω, with the source and R₁ unchanged?
i₁ = 15/(100+100) = 0.075 A, so \(V_{\text{oc}}\) = 100 × 0.075 = 7.5 V; the output voltage rises because R₂ takes a larger share of the source voltage.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent via open-circuit and short-circuit analysis
pts: Open-circuit voltage is found with the load removed; here it equals the voltage across R2 since no current flows out of the terminals.
Short-circuit current is found by shorting the output terminals; with R2 = 0 Ω, all source current flows through R1 alone.
Open-circuit loop current divides the source across R1 and R2 in series, so i1 = vs/(R1+R2).
Thévenin resistance is then found from the ratio of open-circuit voltage to short-circuit current.
Short-circuit current with R2 shorted gives isc = vs/R1 = 0.15 A.
defs: Open-circuit voltage (Voc)
The voltage measured across the two terminals when no load is connected, i.e. no current flows out of the terminals.
Short-circuit current (Isc)
The current flowing between the two terminals when they are joined directly by a wire (zero resistance).
eqs: \(i_{1}\) = loop current (A); \(v_{s}\) = source voltage (V); \(R_{1}\) = series resistor (Ω); \(R_{2}\) = resistor in series with the loop (Ω)
tips: Do not confuse the loop current i1 (open-circuit case) with the short-circuit current; they use different resistances (R1+R2 versus R1 alone).
Keep units consistent: 100 Ω and 50 Ω must be added before dividing 15 V; \(V_{\text{oc}}\) = 50 × 0.1 gives 5 V in volts, not mA.
rq: Why does the short-circuit current depend only on R1 and not on R2 here?
Because R2 = 0 Ω is shorted across the terminals, so it carries no current and the source current flows only through R1: Isc = vs/R1.
Why is Voc equal to R2·i1 even though the terminals are open?
With the terminals open, the current i1 must flow through R2 (the only remaining path), so the voltage across the open terminals is the drop across R2.
How would the Thévenin resistance be obtained once Voc and Isc are known?
RTh = Voc / Isc, which here gives 5 / 0.15 ≈ 33.3 Ω.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent via open-circuit and short-circuit analysis
pts: Thévenin resistance is found as open-circuit voltage divided by short-circuit current.
Open-circuit voltage is the voltage across the load terminals with no load connected; here it equals R2 times the loop current i1.
Short-circuit current is the current flowing when the terminals are shorted, found from vs divided by R1 alone.
defs: Thévenin equivalent
A circuit consisting of a single voltage source in series with a single resistance that gives the same terminal voltage-current behaviour as the original network.
Open-circuit voltage
The voltage measured across the two terminals when no external load is connected (zero current drawn).
Short-circuit current
The current that flows between the two terminals when they are directly connected by a zero-resistance path.
eqs: \(i_{1}\) = loop current (A); \(v_{s}\) = source voltage (V); \(R_{1}\) = series resistance (Ω); \(R_{2}\) = resistance across the terminals (Ω)
\(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω); \(v_{oc}\) = open-circuit voltage (V); \(i_{sc}\) = short-circuit current (A)
tips: Do not include the load resistance when computing voc: the terminals must be open so that no current flows through R2 in the external branch being removed.
Keep units consistent: 50 Ω × 0.1 A gives 5 V, and dividing volts by amps gives ohms (33.3 Ω), so check every result carries the correct unit.
rq: Why is R2 = 0 Ω the correct value to use when finding the short-circuit current, and what would change if R2 were nonzero?

With R2 = 0 Ω the terminals are shorted, so all current flows through R1 only and isc = vs/R1; a nonzero R2 would be in parallel with the output path and would no longer give the short-circuit condition.
Why does the Thévenin resistance come out as 33.3 Ω rather than R1 = 100 Ω?
Because the Thévenin resistance is the ratio voc/isc, which depends on how the source and resistors combine as seen from the terminals, not simply on the single resistor R1.
What is the effect on Rt if the source voltage vs doubles but the resistors stay the same?
Rt is unchanged: both voc and isc are proportional to vs, so their ratio stays the same.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent circuit: resistor combination, source voltage and load current
pts: Parallel resistors R2 and RL combine as a product over sum, giving the equivalent resistance seen by the source (Req1).
The total series resistance is R1 plus the parallel combination, so the source current is the source voltage divided by that total.
The voltage across the parallel branch is the source current times Req1; this voltage is then used to find the load current by Ohm's law.
The Thévenin equivalent replaces the network seen by RL with a single voltage source Vt in series with a single resistance Rt.
The load current in the Thévenin equivalent is Vt divided by the sum of Rt and RL.
defs: Thévenin equivalent circuit

A network of linear elements seen from two terminals can be replaced by a single voltage source Vt in series with a single resistance Rt, giving identical terminal voltage and current behaviour for any load.
eqs: Equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel
\(R_{eq1}\) = parallel equivalent resistance (Ω); \(R_{2}\) = resistance (Ω); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
Source current through the series resistance
\(i_{1}\) = source current (A); \(v_{s}\) = source voltage (V); \(R_{eq2}\) = total series resistance (Ω)
Voltage across the load branch (voltage divider form)
\(V_{\text{RL}}\) = voltage across RL (V); \(V_{t}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω); \(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω)
Load current in the Thévenin equivalent
\(i_{\text{RL}}\) = load current (A); \(V_{t}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not add resistors in parallel directly; use the product-over-sum formula, which gives 8.333 Ω rather than 60 Ω.
Keep units consistent: convert all resistances to ohms and voltages to volts before dividing, and note currents are in amperes.
rq: Why is the current through R2 and RL not simply found from the source voltage divided by R1 alone?
Because R2 and RL are in parallel, so they combine into Req1 which is in series with R1; the total resistance is Req2 = R1 + Req1.
Why does the Thévenin equivalent give the same load current as the original circuit?
Because it reproduces the same open-circuit voltage and the same equivalent resistance seen at the load terminals, so the load sees identical behaviour.

units.name: 3.6 Thévenin resistance by zeroing sources
units.ov: This module shows how to find the Thévenin resistance \(R_t\) of a linear circuit by zeroing its independent sources (voltage sources become shorts, current sources become opens) and reducing the resistance seen at the terminals. It then combines \(R_t\) with the short-circuit current \(i_{sc}\) to get the open-circuit voltage, giving the full Thévenin equivalent. The result depends on which terminal pair is chosen.
must: Zeroing independent sources: voltage source \(\rightarrow\) short circuit, current source \(\rightarrow\) open circuit (never reversed)
\(R_t\) is the resistance seen looking into the chosen two terminals with all independent sources zeroed
Only independent sources are zeroed; this method fails if dependent sources are present (they stay in the circuit and need a different method)
Parallel combination: \(R_t = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} = \frac{5\times20}{5+20} = 4\,\Omega\), not the series sum of 25 Ω
Thévenin equivalent = voltage source \(v_{oc}\) in series with \(R_t\), with the same terminal behaviour as the original network
Open-circuit voltage from short-circuit current: \(v_{oc} = i_{sc}R_t\) (e.g. \(6\,\text{A}\times4\,\Omega = 24\,\text{V}\))
Finding \(i_{sc}\): put a short across the terminals and apply KCL at the node, e.g. \(i_{sc} = i_1 + 2\,\text{A}\) when \(i_2 = 0\), with \(i_1 = v_s/R_1 = 20/5 = 4\,\text{A}\)
Keep KCL current directions and signs consistent, since mixed directions give the wrong \(i_{sc}\)
The equivalent depends on the terminal pair (A–B, B–C, A–C): recalculate \(R_t\) and \(v_{oc}\) for each pair and identify which resistors lie between the terminals
Keep units consistent (Ω, A, V) and check the final answer against \(v_{oc}/i_{sc}=R_t\)
conn: Zeroing sources gives \(R_t\), and the short-circuit current gives \(v_{oc}\) through \(v_{oc}=i_{sc}R_t\), so the two methods are combined to build the complete Thévenin equivalent
Series/parallel resistor reduction is the working step in finding \(R_t\), so errors in parallel-combination arithmetic carry into \(v_{oc}\)
KCL at the shorted node links circuit-law analysis to the equivalent: \(i_{sc}\) must be found correctly before \(v_{oc}\)
Changing the terminal pair changes which resistors are in series or parallel and which sources matter, so \(R_t\) and \(v_{oc}\) must be recomputed for a different load connection
exq: A circuit has a 20 V source with \(R_1 = 5\,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 20\,\Omega\) and a 2 A current source. Zero the sources and find \(R_t\) at the output terminals, then explain how each source is replaced.
For the same circuit, apply KCL with the terminals shorted to find \(i_{sc}\), then calculate \(v_{oc}\) and draw the Thévenin equivalent with a load connected.
A three-resistor network with a source has terminals A, B and C. Find the Thévenin resistance seen between A–B, B–C and A–C, and explain why the three differ.
A student finds \(R_t = 25\,\Omega\) for 5 Ω and 20 Ω resistors after zeroing the sources, and shorts the current source. Identify both errors and give the correct \(R_t\).
Explain why zeroing sources cannot be used directly when the circuit contains a dependent source, and state what must be done to find \(R_t\) instead.

notes.t: Thévenin Resistance by zeroing sources
pts: Thévenin resistance can be found directly by zeroing all independent sources, provided there are no dependent sources.
A zeroed voltage source is replaced by a short circuit, so its voltage is set to zero.
A zeroed current source is replaced by an open circuit, so its current is set to zero.
Thévenin resistance equals the resistance seen between the two terminals of the deactivated circuit.
defs: Thévenin resistance (\(R_{t}\))
The equivalent resistance seen looking into the terminals of a circuit with all independent sources turned off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened).
tips: Only zero independent sources; dependent sources must not be zeroed with this method.
Confusing the two replacements: voltage source → short circuit, current source → open circuit (the reverse is a common error).
rq: Why can a voltage source be replaced by a short circuit when finding \(R_{t}\)?
Because an ideal voltage source has zero voltage when turned off, which behaves as a short circuit (zero resistance path).
Why must dependent sources be handled differently when finding \(R_{t}\)?
Dependent sources are controlled by circuit variables and cannot simply be zeroed; the direct zeroing method only works without them, so a test source is needed instead.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent resistance by zeroing sources
pts: To find Thévenin resistance, set independent voltage sources to short circuits and current sources to open circuits, then find the resistance seen at the terminals.
With the voltage source shorted and the current source opened, R₁ and R₂ are in parallel as seen from the output terminals.
For two resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance is the product over the sum, giving \(R_{t}\) = 4 Ω here.
defs: Thévenin resistance (\(R_{t}\))
The equivalent resistance seen between two terminals of a circuit after all independent voltage sources are replaced by short circuits and all independent current sources by open circuits.
eqs: Thévenin resistance of two parallel resistors with sources zeroed
tips: Do not short current sources or open voltage sources when zeroing; reversing these gives a wrong \(R_{t}\).
Parallel resistance is not the simple sum: 5 + 20 = 25 Ω is wrong; use the product-over-sum formula to get 4 Ω.
rq: Why is the 2 A current source replaced by an open circuit when finding \(R_{t}\), but the 20 V source by a short?
A voltage source has zero internal resistance so it is shorted; a current source has infinite internal resistance so it is opened, leaving no contribution to \(R_{t}\).
Why does \(R_{1}\) appear in parallel with \(R_{2}\) at the terminals once the voltage source is shorted?
Shorting the source connects the left end of \(R_{1}\) to the bottom wire, so \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) both span the same two nodes between the terminals.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent: short-circuit current and equivalent resistance
pts: Thévenin resistance is found by zeroing independent sources (voltage source becomes short, current source becomes open) and finding the resistance seen at the terminals.
With R1 and R2 in parallel seen from the terminals, Rt is their parallel combination.
The short-circuit current is found by applying KCL at the node joining R1, R2 and the short; the short carries \(i_{\text{sc}}\).
Since i2 = 0 A here, the short-circuit current equals i1 plus the 2 A source current.
The open-circuit voltage is obtained from the short-circuit current and Rt.
defs: Thévenin equivalent
A linear network replaced by a single voltage source \(v_{\text{oc}}\) in series with a single resistance \(R_{t}\) that gives the same terminal behaviour.
Short-circuit current (\(i_{\text{sc}}\))
The current flowing between the output terminals when they are connected together directly.
eqs: Thévenin resistance of two resistors in parallel
\(v_{\text{oc}}\) = open-circuit voltage (V); \(I_{\text{sc}}\) = short-circuit current (A); \(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω)
\(i_{1}\) = current through \(R_{1}\) (A); \(i_{2}\) = current through \(R_{2}\) (A); \(i_{3}\) = current in the short-circuit branch (A)
tips: Zero independent sources correctly: voltage sources become short circuits and current sources become open circuits when finding \(R_{t}\).
Check the sign convention of currents in KCL; mixing directions of \(i_{1}\), \(i_{2}\) and \(i_{3}\) gives wrong \(i_{\text{sc}}\).
rq: Why must the voltage source be replaced by a short circuit, but the current source by an open circuit, when finding \(R_{t}\)?
Setting an independent voltage source to zero makes it a short (zero voltage drop); setting an independent current source to zero makes it an open (zero current).
Why is \(i_{2}\) = 0 A in this circuit even though \(R_{2}\) is connected?
The node voltage at the top of \(R_{2}\) is forced by the short, so the voltage across \(R_{2}\) is zero and no current flows through it.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent via short-circuit current and equivalent resistance
pts: Zero the independent sources (voltage source becomes a short, current source becomes open) to find the equivalent resistance \(R_{t}\) seen from the terminals.
\(R_{t}\) is the parallel combination of \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) when the 2 A current source is opened and the voltage source is shorted.
Find the short-circuit current \(i_{\text{sc}}\) at the output terminals; it is used with \(R_{t}\) to give the open-circuit voltage.
The Thévenin voltage equals the open-circuit voltage, obtained as the short-circuit current times the Thévenin resistance.
The Thévenin equivalent is the voltage source \(V_{t}\) in series with \(R_{t}\), with the load connected across the output terminals.
defs: Thévenin resistance \(R_{t}\)
The equivalent resistance seen looking into the terminals of a network with all independent sources set to zero (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened).
Short-circuit current \(i_{\text{sc}}\)
The current flowing through a short placed across the output terminals of a network.
Thévenin equivalent
A simplified circuit consisting of a single voltage source \(V_{t}\) in series with a single resistor \(R_{t}\) that behaves identically at the terminals.
eqs: Thévenin resistance of two parallel resistors
\(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω); \(R_{1}\) = 5 Ω resistor (Ω); \(R_{2}\) = 20 Ω resistor (Ω)
\(v_{\text{oc}}\) = open-circuit voltage (V); \(I_{\text{sc}}\) = short-circuit current (A); \(R_{t}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not confuse zeroing sources: a voltage source is shorted, while a current source is opened when finding \(R_{t}\).
Keep units consistent: \(R_{t}\) in ohms, \(I_{\text{sc}}\) in amperes, giving \(v_{\text{oc}}\) in volts (e.g. 6 A × 4 Ω = 24 V).
rq: Why must the 2 A current source be opened, not shorted, when finding \(R_{t}\)?
An ideal current source has infinite internal resistance, so setting it to zero means replacing it with an open circuit; a voltage source is set to zero by shorting it.
Why does \(R_{t}\) = 4 Ω appear in series with \(V_{t}\) rather than parallel with the load?
The Thévenin equivalent is a series combination of \(V_{t}\) and \(R_{t}\), so the load sees \(R_{t}\) in series with the source, which reproduces the original terminal behaviour.
What if the short-circuit current were found without the 2 A source included?
The result would be wrong, because the current source contributes to \(i_{\text{sc}}\) at the terminals and must be included in the short-circuit analysis.

notes.t: Thévenin's circuit between different terminals
pts: The Thévenin equivalent depends on which pair of terminals is used, so each pair (A–B, B–C, A–C) must be treated as its own two-terminal network.
Looking into terminals A and B, the resistors R2 and R3 appear in series with R1 on the source side, so R2 is the element between A and the common node B.
Looking into terminals B and C, only R3 lies between the two terminals, so the equivalent is seen through R3 alone.
Looking into terminals A and C, the full network (R1, R2 and R3 with the source) is seen, so the Thévenin resistance is found from this pair.
tips: Do not reuse a Thévenin voltage or resistance from one terminal pair for another pair; recalculate for each pair of terminals.
Be careful to identify which resistors lie between the chosen terminals, since the source-side resistance changes with the pair.
rq: Why does the Thévenin equivalent change when you move the load from terminals A–B to terminals B–C?

Because the two-terminal network seen from each pair is different: the path between those terminals contains different resistors (R2 for A–B, R3 for B–C), so the source voltage and resistance seen differ.

units.name: 3.7 Norton's theorem and Thévenin-Norton equivalence
units.ov: This material covers Norton's theorem: any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a current source \(I_N\) in parallel with a resistance \(R_N\). It is equivalent to the Thévenin form (a voltage source \(V_T\) in series with \(R_T\)) at the terminals, so the two are linked by source transformation. The three quantities \(V_{oc}\), \(I_{sc}\) and \(R_T\) are tied together by \(V_T = R_T I_N\), so any two of them give the third.
must: Norton equivalent: ideal current source \(I_N\) in parallel with \(R_N\) across terminals A–B; it is valid for any linear two-terminal network.
Source transformation: \(R_N = R_T\) and \(I_N = V_T/R_T\) (equivalently \(V_T = R_T I_N\)).
\(V_T\) equals the open-circuit voltage at A–B (no load, infinite resistance).
\(I_N\) equals the short-circuit current between A and B when the terminals are shorted together.
Only two of the three quantities \(V_{oc}\), \(I_{sc}\), \(R_T\) need to be found directly; the third follows, e.g. \(R_T = V_{oc}/I_{sc}\).
To find \(R_T\), zero the independent sources only (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened); keep dependent sources active.
If dependent sources are present, \(R_T\) cannot be found by simple series/parallel reduction alone. Use \(V_{oc}/I_{sc}\), or apply a test source.
The equivalence holds only for external behaviour at A–B. Internal currents, voltages and power dissipation differ from the original network.
Check the direction of \(I_N\) (it must point so that it drives current out of the terminal that is positive in the Thévenin form) and the units (V/Ω = A, not V·Ω).
conn: Thévenin and Norton are interchangeable by source transformation. Choose whichever is easier to compute, then convert to the form the question asks for.
\(V_{oc}\) and \(I_{sc}\) together give \(R_T = V_{oc}/I_{sc}\), which is especially useful when dependent sources prevent direct resistance reduction.
Load analysis: once the equivalent is found, connecting \(R_L\) gives \(I_L = I_N R_N/(R_N+R_L)\) (current divider) or \(V_L = V_T R_L/(R_T+R_L)\). Maximum power transfer occurs at \(R_L = R_T\).

Superposition and nodal/mesh analysis are used to find \(V_{oc}\) or \(I_{sc}\) in multi-source circuits, and zeroing sources for \(R_T\) follows the same rules as in superposition (but with dependent sources kept).
exq: A network has a 12 V source and resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in a given arrangement between terminals A–B. Find \(I_N\) and \(R_N\), draw the Norton equivalent, and calculate the current through a 3 Ω load.
A Thévenin equivalent has \(V_T = 24\) V and \(R_T = 8\ \Omega\). Convert it to a Norton equivalent, then find the power delivered to a 4 Ω load using both forms to show they agree.

Measurements on a black-box network give an open-circuit voltage of 10 V and a short-circuit current of 2 A. Find \(R_T\), give both equivalent circuits, and find the load resistance for maximum power and that power.
A circuit contains an independent source and a dependent source. Explain how to find \(R_T\), and compute \(V_{oc}\), \(I_{sc}\) and \(R_T\), justifying why the dependent source is not zeroed.
Explain why the power dissipated inside the original network differs from that in its Norton equivalent even though the load behaviour is identical. Illustrate with an open-circuit example.

notes.t: Norton's Theorem
pts: Any two-terminal linear network can be replaced, for external loads, by a Norton current source \(I_{N}\) in parallel with a Norton resistance \(R_{N}\).
Norton's theorem is not fundamentally different from Thévenin's theorem; the two equivalents are interchangeable.
The Norton equivalent and Thévenin equivalent describe the same terminal behaviour A–B, so one can be converted into the other.
defs: Norton equivalent circuit
A two-terminal network viewed externally as an ideal current source \(I_{N}\) in parallel with a resistor \(R_{N}\) across terminals A and B.
eqs: Relation between Norton and Thévenin equivalents (source transformation)
\(R_{N}\) = Norton resistance (\(\Omega\)); \(R_{T}\) = Thévenin resistance (\(\Omega\)); \(I_{N}\) = Norton current (A); \(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V)
tips: Only the external behaviour at terminals A and B is preserved; internal components are not equivalent.
Check the direction of \(I_{N}\) and convert with \(I_{N}\) = \(V_{T}\)/\(R_{T}\), not \(V_{T}\)·\(R_{T}\), to avoid unit errors (A vs V).
rq: Why does Norton's theorem add no new information compared with Thévenin's theorem?
Both describe the same external V–I behaviour at terminals A–B, so one equivalent can be converted into the other via a source transformation with \(R_{N}\) = \(R_{T}\).
If a network has a Thévenin equivalent of \(V_{T}\) = 12 V and \(R_{T}\) = 4 Ω, what is the Norton equivalent?

notes.t: Thévenin and Norton Equivalent Circuits
pts: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by an equivalent voltage source in series with a resistance (Thévenin) or a current source in parallel with a resistance (Norton).
Only two of the three quantities (open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current, Thévenin resistance) need to be found directly; the third follows from \(V_{T}\) = \(R_{T}\) \(I_{N}\).
To find \(R_{T}\), zero the independent sources only; dependent sources must be kept active.
Thévenin equivalent: voltage source \(V_{T}\) in series with \(R_{T}\).
Norton equivalent: current source \(I_{N}\) in parallel with \(R_{T}\).
defs: Open-circuit voltage
The voltage across the two terminals when no load is connected (infinite resistance), equal to \(V_{T}\).
Short-circuit current
The current flowing between the two terminals when they are shorted together, equal to \(I_{N}\).
Thévenin resistance \(R_{T}\)
The equivalent resistance seen looking back into the terminals with all independent sources set to zero (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) and dependent sources left in place.
eqs: Relationship between Thévenin voltage, Norton current and resistance
\(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_{T}\) = Thévenin resistance (\Omega); \(I_{N}\) = Norton current (A)
tips: Do not zero dependent sources when computing \(R_{T}\); doing so gives a wrong resistance.
Ensure units are consistent: \(V_{T}\) in volts, \(I_{N}\) in amperes, so \(R_{T}\) must be in ohms.
rq: Why must dependent sources be left active when finding \(R_{T}\), while independent sources are zeroed?

Dependent sources are controlled by circuit variables and represent the circuit's behaviour, so zeroing them would change the network; independent sources are fixed inputs that are removed (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) to isolate the resistance seen at the terminals.
If you find \(V_{T}\) and \(R_{T}\), how do you obtain the Norton equivalent without further analysis?
Compute \(I_{N}\) = \(V_{T}\) / \(R_{T}\) and place it in parallel with \(R_{T}\).

units.name: 3.8 Thévenin/Norton worked example
units.ov: This worked example finds the Thévenin and Norton equivalents of a resistive network with a 100 V source, a 10 Ω series resistor, a 40 Ω shunt resistor and a 16 Ω + 8 Ω branch, with terminals A–B across the 8 Ω resistor. The method is to find \(V_{T}\) from the open-circuit voltage using successive voltage dividers, find \(R_{T}\) with the source shorted, and then get the Norton current as \(I_{N}\) = \(V_{T}\)/\(R_{T}\). Note: the source notes are inconsistent. They label 15 Ω (40 ∥ 24) as the Thévenin resistance, but it is only the intermediate load the source sees. Reworking the circuit gives \(R_{T}\) = 6 Ω, as the p31 equation implies, and \(I_{N}\) ≈ 3.33 A.
must: Thévenin equivalent = \(V_T\) in series with \(R_T\); Norton equivalent = \(I_N\) in parallel with \(R_N=R_T\). They match each other only at the terminals.
\(V_T\) is the open-circuit voltage across A–B, found with the source ACTIVE and the load removed.
\(R_T\) is found with independent voltage sources SHORTED (current sources opened), looking into A–B. Shorting the 100 V source puts the 10 Ω in parallel with the 40 Ω.
Series/parallel combination for \(R_T\): \(10\parallel40=8\,\Omega\), so \(16+8=24\,\Omega\), and \(R_T=\frac{8\times24}{8+24}=6\,\Omega\).
Step 1 of \(V_T\): the 40 Ω is in parallel with the 24 Ω branch, giving \(R_{eq1}=\frac{40\times24}{64}=15\,\Omega\). Then \(V_{R15}=\frac{15}{10+15}\times100=60\) V is the node voltage.
Step 2 of \(V_T\): with A–B open, no current flows in the 16 Ω, so \(V_T=\frac{8}{16+8}\times60=20\) V.
Norton current: \(I_N=V_T/R_T=20/6\approx3.33\) A. It equals the short-circuit current, so check it by shorting A–B (the 8 Ω is bypassed).
Voltage divider rule: \(V_R=\frac{R}{R_{total}}V_s\), with the resistor of interest on top and the total series resistance below.
Do not confuse the intermediate \(R_{eq1}=15\,\Omega\) (the load seen by the source) with \(R_T\) (seen from A–B with the source shorted).
Load current from the equivalent: \(I_L=V_T/(R_T+R_L)\). Maximum power transfer occurs at \(R_L=R_T\).
conn: Series/parallel reduction is used twice: once with the source active to get the divider input (15 Ω), and once with the source shorted to get \(R_T\). Using the wrong network for either is the most common error.
Voltage dividers give \(V_T\), and Thévenin–Norton conversion (\(I_N=V_T/R_T\)) lets you check the answer through a short-circuit calculation.
The Thévenin equivalent feeds load analysis: connect \(R_L\) to get the load current, voltage and power, and use maximum power transfer at \(R_L=R_T\).
Source transformation is the same equivalence as the Norton–Thévenin conversion, so it can be used to simplify a network before the divider steps.
exq: For the circuit with a 100 V source, 10 Ω series resistor, 40 Ω shunt resistor, and 16 Ω + 8 Ω branch with A–B across the 8 Ω, find \(V_T\), \(R_T\) and \(I_N\). Show the intermediate 15 Ω and 60 V steps.
Verify \(I_N\) for the circuit above by directly calculating the short-circuit current between A and B, and compare it with \(V_T/R_T\).
A load \(R_L=10\,\Omega\) is connected across A–B. Using the Thévenin equivalent, find the load current, voltage and power. What value of \(R_L\) would receive maximum power, and what is that power?
Explain why the voltage source is shorted when finding \(R_T\) but kept active when finding \(V_T\). What changes if the source were opened instead of shorted?
Explain why the Thévenin and Norton equivalents dissipate different internal power even though they are identical at the terminals. Give an example using an open-circuit condition.

notes.t: Thévenin / Norton equivalent: open-circuit analysis of resistive network
pts: Thévenin resistance is found by looking into the terminals A-B with all independent sources deactivated (voltage source replaced by a short circuit).
In the open-circuit analysis, the 16 Ω and 8 Ω branches to terminal A-B are in series, and that series combination is in parallel with the 40 Ω resistor.
The equivalent resistance is the parallel combination of 40 Ω and (16 + 8) Ω, giving 15 Ω.
The 10 Ω resistor in series with the source is not part of the Thévenin resistance when the source is shorted, as it is then not in the path seen from A-B.
defs: Thévenin equivalent resistance
The resistance seen between two terminals of a network with all independent voltage sources shorted and current sources opened.
eqs: Thévenin equivalent resistance by parallel combination of 40 Ω with series 16 Ω + 8 Ω
\(R_{eq1}\) = equivalent resistance seen at terminals A-B (Ω); 40 = resistance in parallel (Ω); 16 = series resistance (Ω); 8 = series resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not forget to short the voltage source (not open it) when computing the Thévenin resistance; opening it is a common error.
Keep units consistent: all resistances must be in ohms before using the parallel formula, and the result is 15 Ω.
rq: Why is the 100 V source replaced by a short circuit when finding \(R_{\text{eq}}\)?
Thévenin resistance is a property of the passive network; independent voltage sources are set to zero (shorted) so only the resistances determine the impedance seen at A-B.
Why are the 16 Ω and 8 Ω resistors added before being placed in parallel with 40 Ω?
They form a series path from the 40 Ω node to terminal A, so their resistances add to give a single branch resistance of 24 Ω that is then combined in parallel with 40 Ω.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent via open-circuit analysis
pts: With terminals A and B open, no current flows through the 10 Ω resistor, so the 15 Ω resistor carries the full source voltage through a voltage divider.
The open-circuit voltage across terminals A–B is the voltage across the 15 Ω resistor, found by the voltage divider rule.
The Thévenin resistance is found by looking into the terminals with sources deactivated; here the 10 Ω and 15 Ω resistors appear in parallel with the 100 V source shorted.
The Norton equivalent uses the same resistance in parallel with a current source equal to the short-circuit current, which is \(V_{\text{th}}\) / \(R_{\text{th}}\).
defs: Thévenin equivalent
A circuit seen from two terminals replaced by a single voltage source \(V_{\text{th}}\) in series with a resistance \(R_{\text{th}}\).
Open-circuit voltage
The voltage measured across two terminals when no load is connected, equal to \(V_{\text{th}}\).
eqs: Voltage divider for open-circuit voltage across the 15 Ω resistor
\(V_{R15}\) = voltage across the 15 Ω resistor (V); 15 = resistance (Ω); 10 = series resistance (Ω); 100 = source voltage (V)
tips: Do not confuse the voltage divider ratio: the 15 Ω resistor is in the numerator, and the total series resistance (10+15) is in the denominator.
Remember to deactivate the voltage source (short it) when finding \(R_{\text{th}}\), not when finding \(V_{\text{th}}\).
rq: Why is there no voltage drop across the 10 Ω resistor when terminals A and B are open?
With the terminals open there is no return path for current through the 10 Ω resistor, so it carries zero current and drops no voltage.
How would the open-circuit voltage change if the 15 Ω resistor were replaced by a 30 Ω resistor?
The divider ratio becomes 30/(10+30) × 100 = 75 V, so the open-circuit voltage rises because a larger share of the source voltage appears across the load branch.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent by open-circuit analysis (voltage division)
pts: Thévenin resistance is found by looking into the terminals A–B with sources set to zero; the parallel/series combination of the 40 Ω branch with the 16 Ω + 8 Ω branch gives Rₑq₁.
The 100 V source is first reduced by voltage division across the 10 Ω and 15 Ω (40 Ω ∥ 24 Ω) combination to find the node voltage before the 16 Ω resistor.
With the terminals open, no current flows through the 16 Ω resistor, so the open-circuit voltage at A–B is the voltage across the 8 Ω resistor, found by a second voltage divider.
defs: Thévenin voltage (Vₜ)
The open-circuit voltage measured across the two terminals of a network.
Thévenin resistance (Rₜₕ)
The equivalent resistance seen looking into the terminals with all independent voltage sources replaced by short circuits.
Voltage division
In a series string, the voltage across one resistor equals the source voltage multiplied by that resistor divided by the total series resistance.
eqs: Equivalent resistance seen at the terminals (parallel 40 Ω with 16 Ω + 8 Ω)
Voltage across the 15 Ω equivalent (voltage divider with 10 Ω)
\(V_{R15}\) = voltage across 15 Ω (V); 10, 15 = resistances (Ω); 100 = source voltage (V)
Thévenin (open-circuit) voltage across the 8 Ω resistor
\(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); 8, 16 = resistances (Ω); 60 = voltage across the divider input (V)
tips: Do not include the 16 Ω resistor in the Thévenin resistance when the terminals are open-circuited for \(V_{T}\); it carries no current, so no voltage drops across it.
Remember to set the voltage source to zero (short circuit) for \(R_{eq1}\) but keep it active for \(V_{T}\); mixing these up gives wrong answers.
rq: Why is the voltage across the 16 Ω resistor zero when A–B is open, so that \(V_{T}\) equals the voltage across 8 Ω alone?
With terminals open there is no return path for current through the 16 Ω resistor, so no current flows and no voltage drop occurs across it; the full node voltage appears across the 8 Ω branch.
Why do we set the 100 V source to zero when finding \(R_{eq1}\)?
Setting the source to zero (short circuit) removes its contribution so that only the passive resistance seen from A–B is measured; the source's effect is captured separately in \(V_{T}\).
What would happen to \(V_{T}\) if the 8 Ω resistor were replaced by a 24 Ω resistor?
The second divider would become 24/(16+24) × 60 = 36 V, since the voltage across the terminals rises with a larger share of the series resistance.

notes.t: Thévenin and Norton equivalent of a resistive network
pts: Thévenin voltage is the open-circuit voltage across terminals A and B; find it by voltage division across the 8 Ω resistor.
Thévenin resistance is found by zeroing independent sources (voltage sources become short circuits) and finding the resistance seen from A–B.
Combine resistances in parallel or series step by step, starting from the far end (the 16 Ω + 8 Ω branch) and working back to the terminals.
Voltage division: the voltage across a resistor in a series divider equals the total voltage times its resistance divided by the total series resistance.
Norton equivalent uses the same resistance as Thévenin, with Norton current equal to \(V_T / R_T\).
defs: Thévenin equivalent
A single voltage source \(V_T\) in series with a single resistance \(R_T\) that reproduces the terminal behaviour of a linear network.
Norton equivalent
A single current source \(I_N\) in parallel with a single resistance \(R_N\) that reproduces the terminal behaviour of a linear network.
eqs: Equivalent of two resistors in parallel
Voltage divider across a series resistor
\(V_R\) = voltage across resistor (V); \(R\) = resistance of interest (\(\Omega\)); \(R_{total}\) = total series resistance (\(\Omega\)); \(V_s\) = source voltage (V)
\(I_N\) = Norton current (A); \(V_T\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_T\) = Thévenin resistance (\(\Omega\))
tips: Do not confuse the open-circuit voltage with the source voltage: \(V_T\) is found after dividing the 100 V source down the network, here giving 20 V.
Always check units and series/parallel order: combine series resistances (16 Ω + 8 Ω) before taking parallel combinations, and keep all resistances in \(\Omega\).
rq: Why must independent voltage sources be replaced by short circuits, not open circuits, when finding \(R_T\)?

A voltage source has zero internal resistance when ideal, so zeroing it means setting its voltage to 0, which is a short circuit. Open-circuiting it would wrongly remove its effect on the resistance network.
Why is \(V_T\) found with the terminals open rather than shorted?
With A–B open, no current flows through the external load, so the voltage measured across A–B is the open-circuit voltage, which defines \(V_T\).
What if you added the 16 Ω and 8 Ω resistors directly in parallel with the 40 Ω?
That would be wrong: 16 Ω and 8 Ω are in series along the top path, so they must be added first to give 24 Ω before any parallel combination with the 40 Ω.

notes.t: Thévenin and Norton equivalent circuits
pts: A general linear network can be replaced, as seen from external terminals, by a Thévenin voltage source in series with a resistance, or by a Norton current source in parallel with that resistance.
The Norton resistance equals the Thévenin resistance, so the Norton current is the Thévenin voltage divided by that resistance.
The Norton current is the short-circuit current, the current that flows between terminals A and B when they are shorted.
The two equivalents are equivalent only at the external terminals; their internal behaviour differs.
defs: Thévenin equivalent circuit
A voltage source \(V_{T}\) in series with a resistance \(R_{T}\) that reproduces the terminal behaviour of a linear network at its output terminals.
Norton equivalent circuit
A current source \(I_{\text{sc}}\) in parallel with a resistance \(R_{T}\) that reproduces the terminal behaviour of a linear network at its output terminals.
eqs: Norton current (short-circuit current) from Thévenin voltage and resistance
\(I_{sc}\) = Norton (short-circuit) current (A); \(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_{T}\) = Thévenin/Norton resistance (Ω)
tips: Units trap: the Norton current is in amperes, so use \(V_{T}\) in volts and \(R_{T}\) in ohms; do not mix mA and Ω.
Equivalence holds only as seen from the terminals A and B; internal power dissipation can differ between the two equivalents.
rq: Why must the Norton resistance be the same as the Thévenin resistance?
Both equivalents must give the same voltage-current relationship at terminals A and B; the source-free resistance seen from the terminals is the same in both, so \(R_{N}\) = \(R_{T}\).
Why is the Norton current 3.33 A here, and what would it be if the Thévenin voltage doubled?
\(I_{\text{sc}}\) = \(V_{T}\) / \(R_{T}\) = 20 V / 6 Ω ≈ 3.33 A; doubling \(V_{T}\) to 40 V with \(R_{T}\) unchanged gives \(I_{\text{sc}}\) ≈ 6.67 A.

units.name: 3.9 Summary and next lecture
units.ov: This material summarises Thévenin and Norton theorems, which reduce any linear circuit to a simple equivalent seen by a load: a voltage source in series with a resistance, or a current source in parallel with the same resistance. The two forms are interchangeable through the relation \(V_{\text{th}}\) = \(I_{N}\) \(R_{\text{th}}\). The next lecture (superposition, maximum power transfer, star-delta) builds on these reduction techniques.
must: Thévenin equivalent: a voltage source \(V_{th}\) in series with \(R_{th}\), replacing a linear circuit as seen from the load terminals
Norton equivalent: a current source \(I_N\) in parallel with \(R_N\), where \(R_N=R_{th}\)
Source transformation and equivalence: \(V_{th}=I_N R_{th}\), so \(R_{th}=V_{oc}/I_{sc}\)
\(V_{th}\) is the open-circuit voltage at the load terminals (load removed, no current flows)
