units.name: 5.2 When to use mesh-current analysis and loop-current setup
units.ov: This material introduces mesh-current analysis for planar circuits where source voltages and resistances are known and currents are the unknowns. Each open area (mesh) gets a fictitious clockwise loop current, and one independent KVL equation is written per mesh. Shared branches carry a combination of adjacent mesh currents, so careful sign handling links the setup to the solution.
must: Use mesh-current analysis when source voltages and resistances are known and currents are the unknowns; it solves for mesh currents rather than node voltages
Mesh (open area) = a loop in a planar network containing no other loop; mesh currents are assigned to each one
The number of independent KVL equations equals the number of meshes (e.g. 2 meshes give 2 equations); the outer enclosing loop adds none
Mesh currents are fictitious mathematical quantities, not necessarily the physical current in any single branch
Assign all mesh currents clockwise as a consistent convention; direction is arbitrary but consistency keeps shared-element signs uniform
A negative solved current just means the true flow is opposite to the assumed direction; it is a valid answer
A branch shared by two meshes carries the difference of the mesh currents (e.g. \(i_1-i_2\) through \(R_3\)), or the sum if the currents are defined in opposing directions
Method applies only to circuits drawable as planar meshes; define current directions before writing equations
Example circuit: mesh 1 contains \(v_A\), \(R_1\), \(R_3\); mesh 2 contains \(R_3\), \(R_2\), \(v_B\), with \(R_3\) shared
conn: Mesh counting links to KVL: number of independent KVL equations = number of meshes, so choosing meshes correctly fixes the system size
Clockwise convention links to sign rules: shared resistors give opposite-direction mesh currents, producing \((i_1-i_2)R_3\) terms
Mesh currents link to branch currents: after solving, branch currents and then voltages (Ohm's law) and power are recovered from combinations of mesh currents
Mesh-current vs node-voltage choice: mesh suits known voltage sources with unknown currents, while node analysis suits the dual case
exq: For a two-mesh circuit with \(v_A\), \(R_1\), \(R_3\), \(R_2\), \(v_B\), assign clockwise mesh currents \(i_1\), \(i_2\), write both KVL equations, and solve for \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) given numerical values.
A planar circuit has three open areas and an outer loop. How many independent KVL equations are needed, and why does the outer loop not add one?
After solving, you find \(i_2=-0.5\) A. Explain what this means physically, and find the actual current and its direction in the shared resistor \(R_3\) in terms of \(i_1\) and \(i_2\).
Explain when mesh-current analysis is preferable to node-voltage analysis, and state why mesh currents are described as fictitious.
Given \(v_A=12\) V, \(v_B=6\) V, \(R_1=2\ \Omega\), \(R_2=4\ \Omega\), \(R_3=6\ \Omega\), find the power dissipated in \(R_3\) using mesh currents.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: when to use it
pts: Mesh-current analysis is suited to problems where source voltages and resistances are known and the currents are the unknowns to be solved for.
The method solves a circuit for its mesh (loop) currents, such as \(i_1\), \(i_2\) and \(i_3\) in the circuit shown, rather than node voltages.
tips: Mesh-current analysis applies to circuits that can be drawn as planar meshes; the chosen mesh current directions (here \(i_1\), \(i_2\), \(i_3\)) must be consistently defined before writing equations.
rq: Why would you choose mesh-current analysis rather than node-voltage analysis for this circuit?
Because the known quantities are source voltages and resistances and the unknowns required are currents; mesh analysis works directly with loop currents, which suits this problem.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: loop currents and independent KVL equations
pts: Loop (mesh) currents are mathematical quantities used to simplify circuit analysis, not actual physical currents.
The number of independent KVL equations equals the number of open areas (meshes) defined by the network layout.
The example circuit has two open areas, so two independent KVL equations can be written: one for the loop with \(v_A\), \(R_1\), \(R_3\) and one for the loop with \(R_3\), \(R_2\), \(v_B\).
defs: Loop current (mesh current)
A mathematical current assigned to each open area (mesh) of a circuit, used as the unknown in mesh-current analysis; it is not necessarily a physical current in any single branch.
Open area (mesh)
A loop in a planar network layout that contains no other loop within it; the number of such areas gives the number of independent KVL equations.
tips: Do not treat loop currents as physical currents; a branch shared by two meshes carries the difference (or sum) of the two loop currents.
Count open areas (meshes) rather than all possible loops; an outer loop that encloses other meshes does not add an independent equation.
rq: Why is it useful to use loop currents rather than branch currents directly?
Loop currents automatically satisfy KCL at every node, so only KVL equations (one per mesh) are needed, reducing the number of unknowns and equations.
How can you tell how many independent KVL equations a planar circuit needs?
Count the open areas (meshes) in the layout; each open area gives one independent KVL equation.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: Step 1 - assigning loop currents
pts: Loop current direction is arbitrary; a consistent pattern reduces errors.
Mesh currents are conventionally chosen to flow clockwise around each open area (mesh) of the circuit.
A negative result later simply means the true current flows opposite to the assumed direction.
In this circuit, i1 and i2 are assigned clockwise in the two meshes, with R3 shared between them.
defs: Mesh
An open loop in a planar circuit diagram that contains no other loops inside it; mesh currents are assigned to each mesh.
Mesh current
A fictitious loop current assigned to a mesh, flowing around its periphery, used as the unknown variable in mesh-current analysis.
tips: Do not assume the assigned clockwise direction is the physical current; a negative answer later is valid and just means reversed flow.
Keep the same clockwise convention for every mesh so that the KVL sign of shared elements (such as R3) is handled consistently.
rq: Why does it not matter if you assign a loop current in the wrong direction?
Because the circuit equations are solved for the assumed direction; a wrong guess yields a negative value for that mesh current, which correctly indicates the opposite actual direction.
Why is a consistent pattern such as clockwise flow useful even though direction is arbitrary?
It standardises the sign conventions when writing KVL equations for each mesh, so sign mistakes and errors are reduced.

units.name: 5.3 Writing KVL mesh equations and standard form
units.ov: This module shows how to analyse a planar resistive circuit with mesh currents. You assign one clockwise current to each mesh, write KVL around each mesh, and rearrange the equations into standard form: self-resistance on the diagonal, shared resistance coupling the meshes with a negative sign. Solving the linear system gives the mesh currents. Branch currents and voltages then follow from them and from Ohm's law.
must: A mesh is a loop containing no other loop; assign one clockwise mesh current to each mesh, giving one KVL equation per mesh.

Sign convention for sources: add \(V\) if the + terminal is met first when travelling round the mesh, otherwise subtract it. Resistor voltages are always added (\(+Ri\)) in the direction of the mesh current.
A resistor shared by two meshes carries \(i_1 - i_2\), so the branch current is \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\) (with both meshes clockwise). Never use only its own mesh current.
Mesh 1 in standard form: \((R_1+R_3)i_1 - R_3 i_2 = V_A\).
Mesh 2 in standard form: \(-R_3 i_1 + (R_2+R_3)i_2 = -V_B\). The \(-V_B\) comes from the source polarity relative to the clockwise direction.
Concise rule: (sum of all resistances in the mesh)\(\times\) own current \(-\) (shared resistance)\(\times\) neighbouring current \(=\) net source voltage driving that mesh.

Standard form puts the \(i_1\) term first and the \(i_2\) term second. The coefficient matrix is symmetric, with positive diagonal and negative off-diagonal terms when all meshes are clockwise. Use this as a check on your algebra.

Branch currents come from combining the mesh currents through that branch: a branch in one mesh only carries that mesh current, and a shared branch carries the difference. Branch voltages then follow from \(V=iR\).
Check your work: every term must have units of volts (\(\Omega\cdot\)A). Flipping the loop direction changes the source signs. A negative solved current means it flows anticlockwise.
conn: KVL and Ohm's law: mesh equations are KVL with each resistor voltage written as \(Ri\), so sign errors in the source polarity propagate into every current found.

Mesh analysis and linear algebra: the standard form is a matrix equation \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{v}\), solved by substitution, elimination or Cramer's rule. Exam questions often add a numerical solve.
Mesh currents and branch currents: the shared-branch current \(i_3=i_1-i_2\) links to KCL at the junction, which gives a check on the answer, and then to power \(i^2R\) in each resistor.
Source polarity and loop direction: reversing a battery or a loop direction flips the sign on the right-hand side, which changes the direction (sign) of the resulting currents.
exq: For a two-mesh circuit with \(R_1=2\,\Omega\), \(R_2=4\,\Omega\), \(R_3=6\,\Omega\), \(V_A=12\) V and \(V_B=6\) V, write the clockwise KVL equation for each mesh, put them in standard form and solve for \(i_1\) and \(i_2\).
Using your solution, find the current \(i_3\) through the shared resistor \(R_3\) (magnitude and direction), the voltage across it, and the power dissipated in it.

A circuit has a source whose polarity is reversed relative to the clockwise direction of mesh 2. Explain how the right-hand side of the mesh 2 equation changes, and state the effect on the sign of \(i_2\).
Derive the general standard-form equations \((R_1+R_3)i_1-R_3 i_2=V_A\) and \(-R_3 i_1+(R_2+R_3)i_2=-V_B\) from KVL, explaining the sign of each term, including the shared-resistor terms.
Check your mesh-current results from the previous question by applying KCL at a junction, and verify KVL around the outer loop of the circuit.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: applying KVL around each loop
pts: Write one KVL equation per mesh, traversing each mesh clockwise, to obtain a system of equations in the mesh currents.
Take the first end of each resistor encountered as its positive reference, so resistor voltages are always added.
A source voltage is added if its positive terminal is met first when travelling around the mesh; otherwise it is subtracted.
A resistor shared by two meshes contributes its voltage to both mesh equations, with the mesh-current terms of the neighbouring mesh appearing with a negative sign.
defs: Mesh
A loop in a planar circuit that contains no other loop inside it; mesh-current analysis assigns one current to each mesh.
tips: Mind the sign of shared-resistor terms: the same resistor enters two mesh equations with opposite signs when mesh currents oppose each other through it.
Check the polarity of each source relative to the direction of travel before assigning +V or -V on the right-hand side.
rq: Why does the shared resistor \(R_{3}\) appear with a negative sign in the mesh 2 equation but a positive sign in the mesh 1 equation?

The mesh-2 traversal direction through \(R_{3}\) is opposite to the mesh-1 direction (both are clockwise), so the current \(i_{3}\) flows against the clockwise direction of mesh 2 and the voltage drop is subtracted.
What would change in the mesh 2 equation if \(V_{B}\) were installed with its polarity reversed?
The sign of the right-hand side would flip, giving -\(R_{3}\) \(i_{3}\) + \(R_{2}\) \(i_{2}\) = +\(V_{B}\), since the source would then be encountered negative-first in the clockwise traversal.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: applying KVL around each loop
pts: Write a KVL equation for each mesh, going around the meshes clockwise.
Take the first end of each resistor encountered as its positive reference, so resistor voltages are always added.
Add a source voltage if its positive reference is met first when traversing the mesh; subtract it if the negative reference is met first.
The branch shared by two meshes carries the difference of the mesh currents, i₃ = i₁ − i₂.
defs: Mesh
A loop in a circuit that contains no other loop inside it; mesh-current analysis assigns one loop current to each mesh.
tips: Keep track of the direction of each source: a source is added if its + terminal is met first while traversing the mesh, subtracted otherwise.
Shared resistors contribute (\(i_{\text{mesh}}\) − \(i_{\text{neighbour}}\)) with the sign set by the traversal direction; forgetting the neighbouring current is a common error.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R₃ appear as (i₁ − i₂) in both mesh equations, but with opposite signs?
Both loop currents flow through R₃ in opposite directions, so the net current is i₁ − i₂ in mesh 1 and, seen from mesh 2 traversed clockwise, the voltage drop has the opposite sign.
What would happen to the mesh equations if you traversed mesh 2 counterclockwise instead?
All voltage terms for mesh 2 would change sign, so the right-hand side becomes +\(V_{B}\) and the signs of the R₂ and R₃ terms flip, but the solution for the currents is unchanged.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: KVL equations and shared elements
pts: A resistor shared by two meshes carries the algebraic sum (difference, depending on direction) of the two mesh currents.
Each resistor contributes a term equal to its resistance times the mesh current minus the adjacent mesh current (if any).
Writing KVL around each mesh gives one equation per mesh, forming a linear system solved for the mesh currents.
defs: Mesh current
A fictitious current circulating around the perimeter of a mesh (window) of a planar circuit; the branch current of an element belonging to one mesh only equals that mesh current.
eqs: \(R_1, R_3\) = resistances (\(\Omega\)); \(i_1, i_2\) = mesh currents (A); \(V_A\) = source voltage (V)
\(R_2, R_3\) = resistances (\(\Omega\)); \(i_1, i_2\) = mesh currents (A); \(V_B\) = source voltage (V)
tips: Be careful with signs: shared-element terms take opposite signs in the two mesh equations when mesh currents are both clockwise.
Source voltage signs in KVL depend on the polarity relative to the mesh current direction (here \(V_B\) appears as \(-V_B\)).
rq: Why does the shared resistor \(R_3\) appear with a minus sign in the mesh 2 equation but a plus sign in the mesh 1 equation?
Because the mesh currents flow in opposite directions through \(R_3\); relative to each mesh's reference direction, mesh 1 sees \(i_1 - i_2\) and mesh 2 sees \(i_2 - i_1\), giving opposite signs.
What would change in the equations if both mesh currents were chosen to flow clockwise?
The sign pattern through the shared resistor would change so each mesh sees a term consistent with the common direction; the solution values would reflect the new reference directions.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: developing loop equations in standard form
pts: Each mesh equation is rearranged so the i₁ term comes first and the i₂ term second, giving a consistent standard form.
The self-resistance of a mesh (total resistance in that loop) multiplies its own loop current.
The resistance shared by two meshes multiplies the other loop current and is subtracted, because the loop currents flow in opposite directions through it.
The same pattern appears in the mesh 2 equation, with the terms simply rearranged.
defs: Mesh current
A fictitious current assumed to circulate around a closed loop (mesh) of a circuit; actual branch currents are found by combining mesh currents.
Standard form (of loop equations)
Writing every mesh equation with the same ordering of terms (i₁ first, i₂ second) so that the system can be solved conveniently.
eqs: Mesh 1 loop equation in standard form
R₁ = resistance of the left branch (Ω); R₃ = shared resistance (Ω); i₁ = mesh 1 current (A); i₂ = mesh 2 current (A); \(V_{A}\) = source voltage in mesh 1 (V)
Mesh 2 loop equation in standard form
R₂ = resistance of the right branch (Ω); R₃ = shared resistance (Ω); i₁ = mesh 1 current (A); i₂ = mesh 2 current (A); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage in mesh 2 (V)
tips: When writing the mesh 2 equation, keep the sign of the shared resistance term negative in the i₁ position; forgetting this reverses the coupling.
Ensure the source voltage sign matches the chosen loop direction (here −\(V_{B}\) in mesh 2), since flipping the loop direction changes the sign of the source term.
rq: Why does the shared resistance R₃ appear with a negative sign in both mesh equations?
The two mesh currents flow in opposite directions through R₃, so the voltage drop from one mesh current opposes the other; this is expressed as subtraction of R₃ times the other loop current.
What would happen to the mesh equations if R₃ were removed from the circuit?
The coupling terms would vanish, so each equation would contain only its own loop current and the system would decouple into two independent single-mesh equations.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: applying the concise rule
pts: For each loop, the sum of resistors in the loop times the loop current, minus each shared resistor times the adjacent loop current, equals the source voltage in that loop.
Shared resistors contribute with a negative sign in the adjacent loop's equation because the loop currents flow in opposite directions through them.
Solving the loop-current equations gives the mesh currents; all branch currents then follow from them.
Once branch currents are known, branch voltages are found from Ohm's law.
defs: Mesh (loop) current
A fictitious current assumed to circulate around each independent loop of a planar circuit; actual branch currents are found by combining the mesh currents that pass through each branch.
eqs: \(R_{1}\), \(R_{3}\) = resistances (\(\Omega\)); \(i_{1}\), \(i_{2}\) = loop currents (A); \(V_{A}\) = source voltage in loop 1 (V)
\(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) = resistances (\(\Omega\)); \(i_{1}\), \(i_{2}\) = loop currents (A); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage in loop 2 (V)
tips: Keep all loop currents in a consistent direction, otherwise the shared-resistor sign flips incorrectly.
Check that each equation's units are volts: resistance in \(\Omega\) times current in A gives V.
rq: Why does the shared resistor appear with a negative sign in the other loop's equation?
The two loop currents flow in opposite directions through the shared branch, so the current relative to the adjacent loop subtracts from the voltage drop.
Why are source voltages on the right-hand side with the signs set by loop direction?
The right-hand side collects the source voltages met when traversing each loop in its assumed direction; a source opposed to the loop direction enters with a minus sign, as \(V_{B}\) does in loop 2.

units.name: 5.4 Solving simultaneous equations: elimination and Cramer's rule
units.ov: This material turns KVL mesh equations into a linear system, \([R][I]=[V]\), and solves it by elimination or by Cramer's rule (determinants). The worked circuit (R₁=470 Ω, R₂=820 Ω, R₃=220 Ω, \(V_{A}\)=10 V, \(V_{B}\)=5 V) gives \(690i_1-220i_2=10\) and \(-220i_1+1040i_2=-5\). Both methods give the same currents, so each can be used to check the other.
must: Write mesh equations in the standard form \((R_1+R_3)i_1-R_3i_2=V_A\) and \(-R_3i_1+(R_2+R_3)i_2=-V_B\). The diagonal terms are the sum of the resistances in that mesh, the off-diagonal terms are minus the shared resistance, and the source sign depends on whether it aids or opposes the mesh direction.
2×2 determinant: \(\begin{vmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc\). Subtract the cross-diagonal product from the main-diagonal product, and keep the column order \(I_1\) then \(I_2\).
Cramer's rule: \(I_i=\det(R_i)/\det(R)\). \(\det(R_i)\) is \(\det(R)\) with only column \(i\) replaced by the voltage vector, and \(\det(R)\) itself is never altered.

Full solution of the circuit: \(\det R=690\cdot1040-220^2=669200\). Then \(i_1=9300/669200\approx13.9\) mA and \(i_2=-1250/669200\approx-1.87\) mA. The negative \(i_2\) means the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction.
Elimination: multiply equation (2) by \(69/22\) and add it to equation (1). This gives \(3041.82\,i_2=-5.682\), so \(i_2=-1.87\) mA. Back-substitute to get \(i_1=13.9\) mA.
Units: the ratio \(-5.682/3041.82=-0.00187\) is in A, which is \(-1.87\) mA. The notes label it mA without showing the conversion, so state it explicitly in an exam.
The shared branch R₃ carries \(i_1-i_2\) (here ≈15.8 mA). Branch currents come from mesh currents, and the mesh currents themselves are not physical.
Always check by substituting both values into both original equations. Keep mesh directions consistent, because reversing one flips the sign of the shared-resistor terms.
Second-order determinants handle 2 unknowns only. A three-mesh circuit needs a 3×3 determinant.
conn: KVL gives the mesh equations, and linear algebra solves them. A sign error in the loop equation (the source polarity or the \(-R_3\) cross term) carries through both elimination and Cramer's rule.
Elimination and Cramer's rule must agree. The pivot \(3041.82=\det R/220\) is the determinant divided by the multiplier, so one method can check the other.
Mesh currents lead to branch currents, voltage drops and power. For example, \(I_{R3}=i_1-i_2\), \(V_{R3}=R_3(i_1-i_2)\) and \(P=I^2R\). The sign of a mesh current decides the true direction.
Matrix form \([R][I]=[V]\) links to the units: \(\det R\) is in Ω², \(\det R_i\) is in V·Ω, and the ratio is in A. This extends to 3×3 systems for three-mesh circuits.
exq: Write the KVL mesh equations for a two-mesh circuit with R₁=470 Ω, R₂=820 Ω, R₃=220 Ω (shared), \(V_{A}\)=10 V and \(V_{B}\)=5 V opposing the mesh direction. Solve for \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) by elimination, then find the current in R₃ and its direction.
Solve \(690i_1-220i_2=10\) and \(-220i_1+1040i_2=-5\) using Cramer's rule. Show \(\det R\), both modified determinants and the currents in mA.

For \(\begin{bmatrix}10&5\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I_1\\I_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}15\\8\end{bmatrix}\), find \(\det R\), \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) (expected 30, 0.667 A, 1.67 A). Verify by substitution.

Explain why \(i_2\) comes out negative in the worked circuit. Then redo the problem with mesh 2 reversed and show how the signs of the \(R_3\) terms and the source term change, and that the physical branch currents are unchanged.
Find the power dissipated in R₃ and the power delivered by each source in the two-mesh circuit, using the mesh currents found.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: solving loop equations (numerical example)
pts: Once the KVL loop equations are written, they form a linear system whose unknowns are the mesh currents, solved by substitution or determinants.
Mesh current i₁ flows around loop 1 and i₂ around loop 2; the shared branch R₃ carries i₁ − i₂ (the difference of the two mesh currents).
Substituting the component values (R₁ = 470 Ω, R₂ = 820 Ω, R₃ = 220 Ω, \(V_{A}\) = 10 V, \(V_{B}\) = 5 V) turns each loop equation into a numerical equation with two unknowns.
Loop 1 is written with a positive voltage source \(V_{A}\), while loop 2 has −\(V_{B}\) because the source polarity opposes the chosen mesh direction.
defs: Mesh current
A fictitious current circulating around a single mesh (window) of a planar circuit; the actual branch currents are found from the mesh currents.
Loop equation
A Kirchhoff Voltage Law equation written around one mesh, summing voltage drops across resistors and source voltages equal to zero.
tips: Keep consistent mesh current directions; reversing one mesh current flips the sign of the shared-resistor terms and the source term.
Check units: resistances in Ω and voltages in V give currents in A; forgetting to combine R₂ + R₃ (220 + 820 = 1040) is a common arithmetic slip.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R₃ appear with a minus sign in one loop equation and a plus sign in the other?

Because R₃ is shared, the current through it is i₁ − i₂ in loop 1 (giving +R₃i₁ − R₃i₂) and in loop 2 the opposite direction gives −R₃i₁ + R₃i₂ when both meshes are traversed clockwise, so the cross-term is negative in both equations.
What if the two mesh currents were both chosen clockwise — would the off-diagonal terms change sign?
Yes, the off-diagonal terms are negative (−R₃) when mesh currents are chosen in the same direction through the shared branch; the answer's sign depends on the chosen directions.

notes.t: Solving simultaneous equations by elimination
pts: Simultaneous equations can be solved by substitution, elimination, or matrix methods such as Gaussian elimination and determinants.
Elimination removes one unknown by multiplying one equation by a suitable factor and adding it to the other, leaving a single equation in one unknown.
Once one unknown is found, substitute its value back into either original equation to find the other unknown.
Here the elimination step multiplies equation (2) by \( \frac{69}{22} \) and adds it to equation (1), giving \( 3041.82\,i_2 = -5.682 \).
tips: Keep track of signs when multiplying by a negative or fractional factor; a sign slip changes the whole solution.
Check the answer by substituting both values back into both original equations.
rq: Why does multiplying equation (2) by \( \frac{69}{22} \) make the \(i_1\) term disappear when added to equation (1)?
Because \(-220 \times \frac{69}{22} = -690\), which exactly cancels the \(+690\,i_1\) term in equation (1).
What would you do if you had substituted \(i_2\) into an equation and got a different \(i_1\) from the other equation?
That signals an arithmetic error, since the solution must satisfy both original equations; recheck the elimination and substitution.

notes.t: Solving simultaneous equations by determinants (Cramer's rule)
pts: The determinant method is a cookbook approach from matrix algebra for solving simultaneous equations with two or three variables.
Second-order determinants solve two-variable systems; third-order determinants solve three-variable systems.
Equations must first be written in standard form before the determinant method can be applied.
In mesh analysis, the coefficient matrix holds resistances (ohms) and the constant vector holds voltages (volts).
Cramer's rule gives each unknown current as a ratio of determinants: the matrix with column i replaced by the voltage vector over the determinant of R.
defs: Matrix
An array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.
Determinant
A single specific scalar value obtained from a square matrix.
eqs: Matrix form of the mesh equations, [R][I] = [V]
[R] = resistance matrix (Ω); [I] = mesh current vector (A); [V] = voltage vector (V)
Cramer's rule for the i-th unknown current
\(I_{i}\) = mesh current i (A); det(R) = determinant of coefficient matrix (Ω²); det(\(R_{i}\)) = determinant of R with column i replaced by [V] (V·Ω)
tips: Units trap: the coefficient matrix contains resistances in ohms and the constant vector contains voltages in volts, so the resulting currents are in amperes.
Second-order determinants apply only to two variables; do not use them for three-mesh circuits.
rq: Why must the equations be in standard form before applying Cramer's rule?
Because the method reads coefficients by position; each variable's terms must align in columns with constants on the right, otherwise the matrix built from them is wrong.
What would happen to the method if det(R) = 0?
The division by det(R) is undefined, so the system has no unique solution (the matrix is singular).

notes.t: Solving mesh-current equations by determinants
pts: The characteristic determinant is formed from the matrix of coefficients of the unknown mesh currents, with column 1 holding the I₁ coefficients and column 2 holding the I₂ coefficients.
For the 2×2 characteristic determinant shown (rows 10, 5 and 2, 4), evaluation takes three steps: multiply down the main diagonal, multiply along the other diagonal, then subtract.
In the example, the main-diagonal product is 10 × 4 = 40 and the cross-diagonal product is 2 × 5 = 10, giving a determinant of 40 − 10 = 30.
defs: Characteristic determinant
The determinant formed from the matrix of coefficients of the unknown mesh currents, whose columns correspond to the coefficients of each unknown current (I₁, I₂, …).
eqs: a, b, c, d = matrix entries (dimensionless in this context); |A| = determinant of A
Characteristic determinant of the example mesh equations
entries = resistance coefficients (Ω) of the mesh-current equations
tips: Keep the column order consistent with the unknown currents (I₁ first, I₂ second) before evaluating; mixing the order gives a wrong sign.
Subtract the cross-diagonal product (bc) from the main-diagonal product (ad); reversing the subtraction gives the negative of the correct determinant.
rq: Why must the first column hold the I₁ coefficients and the second column the I₂ coefficients, and what would go wrong if they were swapped?

Each column must correspond to one unknown current consistently with the equation order; swapping columns changes the sign of the determinant, so the solved current for that column would be inconsistent with the mesh equations.
Why is the determinant of the 2×2 matrix computed as ad − bc rather than ad + bc?
The cross-diagonal product bc is subtracted because the determinant measures the signed area/scaling of the matrix, and the second diagonal enters with a negative sign.

notes.t: Solving mesh currents by determinants (Cramer's rule)
pts: Form the characteristic determinant from the coefficients of the mesh-current equations.
To find I1, replace the first column of the characteristic determinant with the constants from the right-hand sides of the equations.
Evaluate the new determinant for I1 by the 2×2 rule: product of leading diagonal minus product of off-diagonal.
Each mesh current is the ratio of its determinant to the characteristic determinant.
defs: Characteristic determinant
The determinant formed from the coefficients of the unknown mesh currents in the mesh equations; it is the common denominator for every mesh current.
eqs: \(I_{i}\) = mesh current i (A); \det(R) = characteristic determinant; \det(\(R_{i}\)) = determinant with column i replaced by the constants from the right-hand sides (same units as the constants, e.g. V)
entries are resistances (Ω) and constants (V); result in the same combined units
tips: Only the column for the mesh being solved is replaced; the characteristic determinant itself is not changed.
Check the sign and order of the 2×2 subtraction (ad − bc) and keep consistent units when dividing determinants.
rq: Why does the same characteristic determinant appear in the denominator for every mesh current?
Because the denominator depends only on the coefficient matrix (the resistances), which is the same for all meshes; only the replaced column (the source voltages) changes.
What happens to I1 if the characteristic determinant is zero?
The division is undefined, so the mesh equations have no unique solution (the system is singular, e.g. the mesh equations are dependent).

notes.t: Solving mesh currents by determinants (Cramer's rule)
pts: To find a mesh current, form a new determinant by replacing the coefficients of that current with the constants from the right-hand side of the equations.
The characteristic determinant is the matrix of resistance coefficients; the required mesh current is the ratio of the modified determinant to the characteristic determinant.
In the worked example the second column is replaced by the constants 15 and 8, and the result is divided by the characteristic determinant value 30 to give I₂ = 1.67 A.
defs: Characteristic determinant
The determinant formed from the coefficients of the mesh currents in the mesh equations; its value is the common denominator when solving for any mesh current.
eqs: Mesh current I₂ by determinants (Cramer's rule)
I₂ = mesh current 2 (A); 10, 2, 15, 8 = coefficients and constants from the mesh equations (Ω or V as appropriate); 30 = value of the characteristic determinant (Ω²)
tips: Only the column of the required current is replaced; leaving the other column unchanged is a common error.
Keep units consistent: the denominator determinant carries the units of resistance squared, so check the final current in amperes.
rq: Why does only the second column change when finding I₂?
Because the second column holds the coefficients of I₂ in the characteristic determinant; replacing it with the right-hand constants isolates I₂ while the denominator stays the same.
What would happen to I₂ if the denominator determinant were zero?
The system would have no unique solution, so the mesh currents cannot be found by this method.

units.name: 5.5 Solving loop equations: worked methods and simplification
units.ov: This material covers mesh-current analysis of a two-loop resistive circuit. KVL is written around each mesh, the equations are collected into the matrix form \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{V}\), and the loop currents are solved by substitution or Cramer's rule. Branch currents are then recovered from the mesh currents, and a shared resistor carries the difference of the two. The worked example has diagonal terms 690 Ω and 1040 Ω, off-diagonal terms −220 Ω, and sources of 10 V and −5 V.
must: Mesh equations in matrix form: the diagonal entry is the sum of the resistances in that mesh, the off-diagonal entry is minus the shared resistance, and the right-hand side is the net source EMF around each mesh. Example: \(\begin{bmatrix}690&-220\\-220&1040\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I_1\\I_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\-5\end{bmatrix}\)
Deriving the simplified equations from KVL: \(R_1 i_1+R_3(i_1-i_2)=V_A\) becomes \((R_1+R_3)i_1-R_3 i_2=V_A\), and \(-R_3(i_1-i_2)+R_2 i_2=-V_B\) becomes \(-R_3 i_1+(R_2+R_3)i_2=-V_B\)
Cramer's rule: \(I_1=\Delta_1/\Delta\), where \(\Delta_1\) is the determinant with column 1 replaced by the voltage column. Here \(\Delta=690\cdot1040-220^2=669200\ \Omega^2\)
The notes print the \(I_1\) numerator as 102900, which is a typo. The correct value is \(10400-1100=9300\), and only 9300 gives 13.9 mA. Always recompute the determinants yourself.
Branch currents from mesh currents: a non-shared resistor carries its own mesh current, and the shared R3 carries \(I_1-I_2\approx 15.8\) mA, which is 13.9 mA plus 1.87 mA
A negative mesh current (such as \(I_2\)) only means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed one. It is not an error.
Sign discipline: with all meshes taken in the same direction, off-diagonal terms are negative. A source opposing the mesh direction enters the right-hand side with a negative sign (\(-V_B\)).
Sanity checks: the matrix is symmetric for resistor-only circuits, units are Ω, V and A (convert to mA at the end), and the answers should satisfy both original equations when substituted back.
conn: Mesh analysis and Kirchhoff's laws: the mesh method applies KVL automatically, so KCL is built in. Questions often ask for branch currents, voltages and power after solving for the mesh currents.
Matrix and determinant methods from maths: Cramer's rule or matrix inversion solves the system, and a non-zero determinant guarantees a unique solution. Expect to be marked on the arithmetic.

Mesh versus nodal analysis: mesh analysis uses KVL with current unknowns, while nodal analysis uses KCL with voltage unknowns. Questions may ask which needs fewer equations, or ask for the same circuit solved both ways as a check.
Power and voltage drops: once you have \(I_1-I_2\) through R3, you can calculate \(V_{R3}=R_3(I_1-I_2)\) and \(P=I^2R\). You can also check that the sources' power equals the total power dissipated.
exq: Write the mesh equations for a two-mesh circuit with R1 = 470 Ω, R2 = 820 Ω, shared R3 = 220 Ω, \(V_{A}\) = 10 V and \(V_{B}\) = 5 V (opposing). Put them in matrix form and solve for \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) using Cramer's rule.
For the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}690&-220\\-220&1040\end{bmatrix}\), calculate the determinant. Then find \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) and explain the physical meaning of the negative sign on \(I_2\).
Using \(I_1=13.9\) mA and \(I_2=-1.87\) mA, find the current through R3, the voltage across it and the power it dissipates. State the direction of the current.
A student gets \(I_1=0.154\) A from \(102900/669200\). Find the error, give the correct numerator and result, and explain how a quick substitution check would have caught it.

Derive the simplified mesh equations \((R_1+R_3)i_1-R_3i_2=V_A\) and \(-R_3i_1+(R_2+R_3)i_2=-V_B\) starting from KVL with the shared-resistor term \(R_3(i_1-i_2)\). Explain why \(V_B\) appears with a negative sign.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: solving loop equations
pts: Once mesh (loop) KVL equations are written, they form a linear system in the unknown loop currents, which can be solved by substitution or determinants.

Writing the loop equations in matrix form R·I = V puts the coefficients of the loop currents into a square matrix; the diagonal holds the sum of resistances in each loop and the off-diagonal holds the shared resistance with a negative sign.
For this circuit, the shared resistor R3 contributes −220 to both off-diagonal entries, while the diagonal terms 690 and 1040 are the total resistances around loops 1 and 2.
Loop currents i1 and i2 are the unknowns; the right-hand side holds the net source voltages around each loop (10 V and −5 V).
defs: Loop (mesh) current
A fictitious current circulating around a closed loop/mesh of a circuit; the actual branch current is found by combining the loop currents that flow through that branch.
eqs: Matrix form of mesh equations for the two-loop circuit
\(I_{1}\) = loop 1 current (A); \(I_{2}\) = loop 2 current (A); coefficients in Ω; right-hand side in V
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: off-diagonal terms are negative when all loop currents are defined in the same direction.
Check units: resistances in ohms, voltages in volts, so the loop currents come out in amperes.
rq: Why does the off-diagonal entry equal the negative of the shared resistance?
Because the shared branch carries the two loop currents in opposite directions relative to each other when both are defined clockwise, so their voltage drops subtract in each loop's KVL equation.
How would you solve this 2×2 system using determinants?

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: solving loop currents with determinants
pts: Mesh-current equations are written in matrix form R·I = V, where the diagonal terms are the sums of resistances in each loop and off-diagonal terms are the shared resistances, with a negative sign.
Cramer's rule gives each loop current as the determinant with the voltage column replacing the relevant column, divided by the determinant of the resistance matrix.
A negative loop current means the assigned direction is opposite to the actual current direction.
A branch shared by two meshes carries the difference of the two loop currents when they flow in opposite directions through it.
Branch currents in non-shared resistors equal the loop current flowing through them.
defs: Mesh (loop) current
A fictitious current assumed to circulate around each independent loop of a circuit; used as the unknown in mesh-current analysis.
Branch current
The actual current flowing through a single circuit element, obtained from the loop currents that pass through it.
eqs: Loop current I1 by Cramer's rule
\(I_{1}\) = mesh current in loop 1 (A); numerator and denominator are determinants of the mesh resistance matrix and voltage column
Loop current I2 by Cramer's rule
\(I_{2}\) = mesh current in loop 2 (A); determinant of matrix with second column replaced by voltages
tips: Watch the sign when a voltage source value is negative or the loop is drawn against the source polarity; keep the matrix signs consistent.

Units trap: the determinant results are in ohms and volts, so the final loop currents must be quoted in mA only after dividing correctly (e.g. 102900/669200 gives 0.1538 A... check the unit scaling used in the slide).
rq: Why does I2 come out negative, and does that mean the solution is wrong?
No. A negative value means the current actually flows opposite to the direction assumed when the loop was drawn; the magnitude is still correct.
Why is the current through R3 the difference I1 − I2 rather than the sum?
Because the two loop currents pass through R3 in opposite directions, so their effects subtract; the net current is the difference of the two loop currents.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: simplifying loop equations
pts: Mesh-current analysis writes one KVL equation per loop, using loop currents as unknowns instead of branch currents.
A resistor shared by two meshes contributes its resistance times the difference of the two loop currents, so shared resistors appear with opposite signs in each loop equation.
Collecting terms gives a system where each loop's own resistances multiply its own current, and shared resistances form the off-diagonal (mutual) terms.
The two loop equations form a linear system that can be solved for i1 and i2 simultaneously, after which any branch current is the difference of the mesh currents passing through it.
defs: Mesh current
A current assumed to circulate around a single mesh (window) of a planar circuit; it is the unknown used in mesh-current analysis.
tips: Watch the sign of the shared-resistor term: it appears as −R3 in one loop equation and −R3 in the other after expansion, so check the direction of each mesh current before writing KVL.
Keep the source-voltage sign consistent with the loop direction; the right-hand side of loop 2 is −VB here, not +VB.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R3 appear as (i1 − i2) rather than i1 alone in the loop equations?
Because R3 lies between the two meshes, the current through it is the net of the two loop currents flowing in opposite directions, so the voltage across it is R3(i1 − i2).
What happens to the sign of the R3 term between the two loop equations, and why?
It is negative in loop 1 and negative in loop 2 when expanded, giving a symmetric −R3 off-diagonal term, because the shared branch carries opposite reference directions for the two meshes.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis writes KVL around each mesh using mesh currents, which reduces the number of unknowns compared with nodal analysis of every element.
A resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of the two mesh currents, so its voltage drop is R(i₁ − i₂) in the direction of the loop being written.
Writing the same shared-resistor term with consistent sign for each loop gives a symmetric system: the diagonal entries are the sum of resistances in each mesh and the off-diagonal entries are −R₃.
The two forms on the slide differ only in the direction chosen for the shared-resistor term; both give the same final equations once the sign is handled correctly.
defs: Mesh
A loop in a planar circuit that contains no other loop inside it; mesh currents are assigned to each such loop.
Mesh current
A fictitious loop current assumed to circulate around a single mesh; the branch current in a shared element is the algebraic sum of the mesh currents flowing through it.
eqs: R₁, R₃ = resistances (Ω); i₁, i₂ = mesh currents (A); \(V_{A}\) = source voltage (V)
R₂, R₃ = resistances (Ω); i₁, i₂ = mesh currents (A); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage (V)
R₁, R₃ = resistances (Ω); i₁, i₂ = mesh currents (A); \(V_{A}\) = source voltage (V)
R₂, R₃ = resistances (Ω); i₁, i₂ = mesh currents (A); \(V_{B}\) = source voltage (V)
tips: Keep the loop direction consistent: when writing the shared-resistor drop, check whether the mesh current direction agrees or opposes the loop you are summing around.
Sources must be written with the correct polarity relative to the mesh direction; a sign error on \(V_{B}\) is a common mistake.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R₃ appear in both loop equations but with opposite signs on the off-diagonal terms?
Because the current through R₃ is i₁ − i₂ in one direction for loop 1 and the opposite direction for loop 2, so the shared term enters with a sign that reverses between the two KVL equations.
What happens to the system if R₃ is removed (open circuit)?
The meshes decouple: the off-diagonal terms become zero, and each loop reduces to a single-mesh equation R₁i₁ = \(V_{A}\) and R₂i₂ = −\(V_{B}\).

units.name: 5.6 Advantages and multi-loop circuits
units.ov: This material covers mesh-current analysis as a more efficient alternative to the branch-current method: one clockwise circulating current per independent mesh, KVL equations written for each mesh, then branch currents recovered from the mesh currents. It links KCL/KVL (the branch method) to a reduced system of simultaneous equations that can be written in matrix form. Accurate sign handling for shared resistors and source polarity is the main source of marks and errors.
must: Mesh analysis uses one unknown per independent mesh (window), giving fewer simultaneous equations than branch-current analysis, which needs one unknown per branch.
Mesh current is a fictitious circulating current; real branch currents are found from mesh currents afterwards.

Standard rule for mesh \(k\): \(\sum R_{\text{in loop}}\, i_k - \sum R_{\text{shared}}\, i_{\text{adjacent}} = \sum V_{\text{sources}}\), with all mesh currents in the same direction (e.g. clockwise).
Shared resistors appear with a minus sign in the neighbouring mesh equation because the adjacent mesh currents oppose each other through it, e.g. \(R_2(i_1-i_2)\).
Source sign: a source is positive when the loop current leaves its + terminal (traversed - to +). A source opposing the loop direction gives a negative term, e.g. \(-V_B\).
Branch current in a shared resistor: \(I_R = i_k - i_m\). In an outer branch belonging to one mesh: \(I_R = i_k\). Never add mesh currents on a shared branch.

A negative branch current means the true direction is opposite to the assumed reference. In the notes' example \(i_2 - i_3 = -1\) A for \(R_3\), and the page lists 2 A, so check the sign/reference and the notes' consistency.
Branch-current method: KCL at nodes (e.g. \(I_1 - I_2 - I_3 = 0\)) plus KVL around loops, with the number of equations equal to the number of unknowns.
Example mesh values: \(i_1=4\) A, \(i_2=1\) A, \(i_3=2\) A give \(R_1\) (20 Ω) carrying \(i_1-i_3=2\) A and \(R_2\) (10 Ω) carrying \(i_1-i_2=3\) A.
Mesh analysis requires a planar circuit and counts only independent meshes, not all possible closed paths. For three meshes, write three equations in matrix form and solve.
conn: KCL and KVL underpin both methods: mesh currents automatically satisfy KCL, so only KVL equations are needed, whereas the branch method needs both.
Mesh currents to branch currents to power/voltage: after solving, use \(I_R = i_k - i_m\), then \(V = IR\) and \(P = I^2R\) for resistor voltages and dissipation.
Sign conventions link equation setup and interpretation: source polarity and shared-resistor minus signs in the equations determine whether the final branch currents come out positive or negative.
Matrix methods: the mesh equations form a symmetric resistance matrix equation \([R][i]=[V]\), solved by Cramer's rule or elimination.
exq: For a three-mesh circuit with clockwise currents, write the KVL equations in terms of \(i_1, i_2, i_3\), given \(R_1=20\ \Omega\), \(R_2=10\ \Omega\), \(R_3=12\ \Omega\) and sources \(V_A\), \(V_B\), then put them in matrix form.
Given \(i_1=4\) A, \(i_2=1\) A, \(i_3=2\) A, find the current in each resistor (including direction) and the power dissipated in the 10 Ω resistor.
Explain why mesh-current analysis needs fewer simultaneous equations than the branch-current method for a two-battery, five-resistor circuit, and compare the number of unknowns in each method.
Write the branch-current KCL and KVL equations for a two-source, five-resistor circuit and convert them to mesh-current form: \(-V_{B1}+R_2(I_1-I_2)+I_1R_1=0\), etc.
A source in a mesh is reversed in polarity. Show how the equation and the resulting branch currents change, and state how you would interpret a negative result.

notes.t: Advantage of Mesh-Current Analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis can be applied systematically to circuits with any number of loops.
Compared with the branch current method, it needs fewer unknown values and fewer simultaneous equations, because each loop current is one unknown rather than each branch current.
tips: Mesh analysis is built on independent loops, not all loops: count meshes (windows) rather than every possible closed path.
Ensure the circuit is planar (no crossing wires) before applying standard mesh analysis.
rq: Why does mesh-current analysis usually need fewer simultaneous equations than branch current analysis for the same circuit?

Mesh analysis uses one unknown per independent loop (mesh), whereas branch current analysis uses one unknown per branch; a circuit normally has more branches than independent meshes, so fewer unknowns and equations are required.
In the circuit shown, how many mesh currents would you need to define, and why?
Three mesh currents: the circuit has three independent loops (left loop with B1, R1, R2; middle loop with R2, R3, R4; right loop with R4, R5, B2).

notes.t: Advantage of mesh-current analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis can be applied systematically to circuits with any number of loops.
Compared with branch-current analysis it needs fewer unknowns and fewer simultaneous equations, since the loop currents replace individual branch currents.
Node-current (KCL) equations at each node relate the branch currents of the circuit.
Loop (KVL) equations sum the voltage drops around each mesh and set them to zero.
defs: Mesh-current analysis

A circuit analysis method that assigns a circulating current to each mesh (loop with no internal loop) and solves KVL equations for these loop currents, giving fewer unknowns than branch-current analysis.
Branch-current method
A circuit analysis method in which every branch current is an unknown, solved using KCL at nodes and KVL around loops.
tips: Watch sign conventions: a voltage drop in the direction of the assumed current is positive, and a source is positive when traversed from - to +.
Check that the number of equations equals the number of unknowns before solving.
rq: Why does mesh-current analysis need fewer unknowns than branch-current analysis for this circuit?
Mesh currents are defined per loop, so each one can represent several branch currents at once; with 3 meshes only 3 loop equations are needed, instead of solving for all 5 branch currents.
What if a branch is shared by two meshes?
The current in that branch is the difference of the two mesh currents (with sign set by the chosen directions), so the shared element appears in both KVL equations.

notes.t: Advantage of Mesh-Current Analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis can be applied systematically to circuits with any number of loops.
Compared with branch-current analysis, it needs fewer unknowns and fewer simultaneous equations, one unknown per mesh.
In the example circuit with three meshes, three unknown mesh currents I₁, I₂, I₃ give three simultaneous equations.
defs: Mesh current

A fictitious current circulating around a closed loop (mesh) of a circuit with no branches inside it; actual branch currents are found by combining the mesh currents of the meshes sharing that branch.
eqs: KVL equation for mesh 1 of the example circuit
\(V_{B1}\) = source voltage of B₁ (V); \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\) = resistances (Ω); \(I_{1}\), \(I_{2}\) = mesh currents (A)
KVL equation for mesh 2 of the example circuit
KVL equation for mesh 3 of the example circuit
\(V_{B2}\) = source voltage of B₂ (V); \(R_{4}\), \(R_{5}\) = resistances (Ω); \(I_{2}\), \(I_{3}\) = mesh currents (A)
tips: Shared branches carry the difference of the two adjacent mesh currents (e.g. R₂ carries I₁ − I₂), so watch the sign when writing KVL.
Check that the mesh-current direction is applied consistently around every loop when setting up the equations.
rq: Why does mesh analysis need fewer equations than branch-current analysis?
Because each mesh current is one unknown, and there is one KVL equation per mesh, so the number of unknowns equals the number of meshes, whereas branch-current analysis uses one unknown per branch.
In a circuit with 3 meshes and 6 branches, how many unknowns and equations does each method need?
Mesh analysis: 3 unknowns and 3 equations. Branch-current analysis: 6 unknowns and 6 equations.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: writing loop equations for a multi-loop circuit
pts: Each loop (mesh) gets its own clockwise loop current; the equations are written by applying KVL around every loop.
Rule for each loop equation: sum of resistors in the loop times the loop current, minus shared resistors times adjacent loop currents, equals the source voltage in that loop.
A resistor shared by two loops appears with a minus sign in the neighbouring loop's equation, because the two loop currents flow in opposite directions through it.
A voltage source is placed on the right-hand side with a sign set by its polarity relative to the loop direction; a source opposed to the loop current gives a negative term.
Three meshes give three simultaneous equations, which can be written in matrix form and solved for i1, i2 and i3.
defs: Mesh (loop) current
A fictitious current circulating around a single mesh of a circuit; the actual branch current in a shared element is the algebraic sum of the mesh currents flowing through it.
eqs: KVL for loop 1 (mesh with R1, R2 and \(V_{A}\))
KVL for loop 2 (mesh with R2, R3 and \(V_{B}\))
KVL for loop 3 (outer mesh with R1, R3, R4)
tips: Keep track of source polarity: a voltage source whose polarity opposes the chosen loop direction contributes a negative term, and the sign of \(V_B\) in the equation above reflects this.
Use the same direction convention for all mesh currents; mixing clockwise and counter-clockwise loops produces sign errors in the coupling terms.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R2 carry a negative sign in loop 1's equation but a negative sign in loop 2's equation as well?
Because the two mesh currents i1 and i2 flow in opposite directions through R2, so the voltage drop due to the neighbouring loop current subtracts from the drop due to the loop's own current.
What would change if the loop 2 current were defined counter-clockwise instead of clockwise?

The signs of the coupling terms (e.g. -R2 i1 and -R3 i3) would flip to +, since the shared resistor would then carry currents in the same direction; the solution for the branch currents would be unchanged.
Why is the right-hand side of the outer loop equation zero?
Because the outer mesh contains no voltage source, so the sum of voltage drops around it must equal zero by KVL.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: resolving element currents from mesh currents
pts: Each element current is the algebraic sum of the mesh currents flowing through it; shared branches carry the difference of adjacent mesh currents.
Mesh currents are i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A and i₃ = 2 A, taken clockwise in each loop.
The 20 Ω resistor R₁ lies only in mesh 1 (plus mesh 3 on its top branch), so its current is i₁ − i₃ = 2 A.
The 10 Ω resistor R₂ is shared by meshes 1 and 2, so its current is i₁ − i₂ = 3 A.
The 12 Ω resistor R₃ carries i₂ − i₃ = 1 − 2 = −1 A relative to mesh 2; the page lists magnitude 2 A, so direction must be checked against the reference sign convention.
defs: Mesh current
A fictitious current circulating around a closed loop (mesh) of a planar circuit; it is used as the unknown in mesh-current analysis.
Branch current
The actual current in a single element, found by superposing the mesh currents of all meshes that share that element.
eqs: Current in a shared resistor between meshes k and m
\(I_{R}\) = element current (A); \(i_{k}\), \(i_{m}\) = mesh currents of adjacent meshes (A)
Current in an outer-branch resistor of a single mesh
\(I_{R}\) = element current (A); \(i_{k}\) = mesh current of the only mesh containing the element (A)
tips: Watch the sign: a branch current is the difference of mesh currents with respect to the chosen reference direction; a negative result means the true current flows opposite to the assumed direction.
Do not add mesh currents on a shared branch; only subtract them, and only use the single mesh current for outer branches.
rq: Why does the 10 Ω resistor current equal a difference of mesh currents rather than a single mesh current?
Because it is shared by meshes 1 and 2, which circulate in opposite senses through it, so the net current is i₁ − i₂.
If the mesh current directions were all reversed, how would the element currents change?
Every mesh current changes sign, so each element current changes sign too; the magnitudes stay the same.

units.name: 5.7 Mesh-current analysis with current sources
units.ov: This material covers mesh-current analysis when a circuit contains current sources. A current source fixes its branch current but not its voltage, so a mesh current through it is known, which reduces the unknowns, and KVL is written only for the remaining meshes. The ideas connect through consistent sign conventions, correct mutual-resistor terms and substitution of the known current into the remaining equation.
must: A current source fixes the current through its branch, but its terminal voltage is unknown and set by the rest of the circuit; never assume \(V=0\).
A current source on the outer edge of only one mesh sets that mesh current directly, e.g. \(i_1=\pm I_s\); no KVL is needed for that mesh.
Do not write KVL through a mesh with a current source on its own, because its voltage is an unknown; use the known current instead.
Sign of the constraint depends on the source arrow relative to the chosen (clockwise) mesh direction: opposing gives \(i_1=-5\) A, not +5 A.
The shared resistor gives a mutual term \(R(i_2-i_1)\), not \(Ri_2\) alone; dropping \(-i_1\) is the commonest error.
KVL form: sum of resistor drops = sum of source rises, with voltage-source signs matched to the mesh direction (e.g. \(10(i_2-i_1)+5i_2-100=0\)).
Expand and rearrange: \(15i_2-10i_1=100\), then substitute the known \(i_1\). With \(i_1=-5\): \(i_2=\frac{100-50}{15}=3.33\) A.
Check the algebra: \(15i_2=100+10i_1\), so with \(i_1=-5\) the right side is 50, so keep the sign of \(i_1\) when substituting.
A current source shared between two meshes needs a supermesh: combine the two meshes into one KVL loop that excludes the source, plus a constraint equation from the source current.
Unknown source voltage can be recovered afterwards by applying KVL to a mesh that contains it.
conn: Current-source constraint plus mutual-resistor KVL: the known \(i_1\) is substituted into the mesh 2 equation, so sign errors in the constraint propagate to the answer.
Supermesh analysis links mesh analysis to KCL: the shared source gives a constraint such as \(i_a-i_b=I_s\) alongside the single supermesh KVL.
Mesh analysis with current sources parallels nodal analysis with voltage sources (supernodes): each uses the source's known quantity as a constraint and avoids writing the unknown one.
After finding mesh currents, branch currents, resistor voltages and power (including power delivered or absorbed by the current source, using its found voltage) are asked for together.
exq: Meshes 1 and 2 share a 10 Ω resistor; mesh 2 has a 5 Ω resistor and a 100 V source, and mesh 1 contains a 5 A current source opposing the clockwise direction. Find \(i_1\), \(i_2\) and the voltage across the 10 Ω resistor.
Explain why the voltage across an ideal current source cannot be assumed to be zero, and show how it is found in a two-mesh circuit once \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) are known.
In a circuit with a 2 A current source on the outer branch of mesh 1 and a 10 V source in mesh 2 with 10 Ω shared and 5 Ω resistors, write the KVL for mesh 2 and solve for \(i_2\).
A 3 A current source lies in the branch shared by two meshes. Set up the supermesh equation and constraint equation, then solve for both mesh currents.
Calculate the power absorbed or supplied by the current source in a given two-mesh circuit, stating the sign convention used and checking that total power balances.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis with current sources
pts: A current source forces a specified current through its terminals, but the voltage across it is not fixed in advance.
The voltage across a current source is set by the rest of the circuit it is connected to, so it must be solved for.
Do not assume a current source has zero voltage across it; this is a common beginner error.

In mesh analysis, a mesh current is assigned to each loop, and a branch carrying a current source fixes the mesh current through it, so the source's voltage becomes an unknown to be found from the other mesh equations.
defs: Current source
An ideal element that forces a specified current to flow through its terminals, independent of the voltage across it; its terminal voltage is determined by the connected circuit.
tips: Do not set the voltage across a current source to zero; treat it as an unknown voltage and include it in the KVL equation of the mesh(es) it belongs to.
A current source on the outer edge of a mesh fixes that mesh current directly (e.g. i₁ = 2 A), but a current source shared between two meshes requires a supermesh-style treatment.
rq: Why can't we assume the voltage across a 2 A current source is zero when writing the mesh equations?
Because the voltage across a current source is determined by the circuit it is connected to, so it is an unknown that must be solved for, not zero.
In this circuit, what fixes the value of i₁ directly, and why does that simplify the mesh analysis?
The 2 A source lies on the outer branch of mesh 1, so i₁ is forced to 2 A, reducing the number of unknown mesh currents.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis with current sources
pts: Avoid writing KVL for meshes containing a current source; its voltage is unknown, so use the known current directly.
A current source fixes the mesh current directly, so i1 is known and only the remaining mesh needs a KVL equation.
Apply KVL to the mesh not containing the current source; the shared 10 Ω resistor gives a term proportional to (i2 − i1).
The presence of a current source simplifies the solution because it reduces the number of unknown mesh currents.
defs: Mesh current
A current assumed to circulate around the perimeter of an individual mesh (loop with no internal branches) in a planar circuit.
eqs: Known mesh current from the current source
\(i_{1}\) = mesh current through the current source (A)
\(i_{2}\) = mesh 2 current (A); \(i_{1}\) = mesh 1 current (A); 10 = resistance in the shared branch (Ω); 5 = resistance in mesh 2 (Ω); 10 = source voltage (V)
tips: The shared resistor term in KVL is multiplied by (i2 − i1), not i2 alone; forgetting the mesh 1 contribution is a common error.
Keep sign conventions consistent: the 10 V source sign must match the chosen clockwise direction of i2.
rq: Why can we write i1 = 2 A without any KVL equation?
Because the branch carrying mesh current i1 is a current source, which forces that current to be 2 A regardless of the rest of the circuit.
Why is it wise to avoid writing KVL around a loop containing a current source?
That loop's KVL would contain an unknown voltage across the current source, adding an extra unknown that must be solved for.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: writing KVL equations for mesh currents with a current source
pts: A mesh current that flows through an independent current source is fixed by that source, so it needs no KVL equation.
Mesh currents shared by a resistor are subtracted around that resistor, giving the mutual term in each loop equation.
Apply KVL around each mesh: the sum of voltage drops across resistors equals the sum of source voltage rises.
Rearranging the loop equation gives a linear equation in the unknown mesh current, which is then solved by substitution.
defs: Mesh current
A current assumed to circulate around a single independent loop (mesh) of a planar circuit, used as the unknown in mesh analysis.
eqs: \(i_2\) = mesh current in loop 2 (A); \(i_1\) = mesh current in loop 1 (A); 10 = resistance shared by the meshes (Ω); 5 = resistance in loop 2 (Ω); 100 = source voltage (V)
tips: Check the direction of each mesh current relative to the source arrow: a current source pointing against the mesh direction gives \(i_1 = -5\) A, not +5 A.
Keep the shared-resistor term with the correct sign (\(i_2 - i_1\)) when expanding; dropping the \(-i_1\) term is a common error.
rq: Why is no KVL equation written for loop I1 even though it is a mesh?
Because it contains a current source whose current fixes \(i_1\) directly, so \(i_1 = -5\) A is the constraint.
What is the sign of the shared-resistor term, and why?
It is \(10(i_2 - i_1)\): the current in the shared resistor is the difference of the two mesh currents, taking loop 2's direction as positive.

units.name: 5.8 Mesh-current method recap and summary
units.ov: This recap covers the mesh-current method, a systematic way to analyse arbitrary planar resistive circuits. Each mesh is given a mesh current, KVL is applied around each mesh with an unknown current, and Ohm's law expresses resistor voltages in terms of those currents. The result is a smaller linear system that is solved for the mesh currents, and sign conventions on shared branches are the main source of error.
must: A mesh is a loop with no other loops inside it; not every loop is a mesh.
Identify all meshes first, then assign one mesh current per mesh (use a consistent direction, e.g. all clockwise).
Apply KVL \( \sum V = 0 \) around each mesh whose current is unknown.
Write resistor voltages with Ohm's law, \( V = RI \), in terms of mesh currents.
On a shared branch the resistor current is the difference of the two mesh currents, e.g. \( R(I_1 - I_2) \) in mesh 1, with the sign reversed in mesh 2.
A current source on an outside branch of a mesh fixes that mesh current, so no KVL equation is needed for that mesh.
With n unknown mesh currents you need n independent equations, which are solved as a linear system (substitution, elimination, or matrix form \( \mathbf{R}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{V} \)).
Check the reference direction of each mesh current before writing KVL; sign errors are the most common mistake.
The method reduces the number of unknowns and simultaneous equations, and works on circuits that cannot be simplified into series/parallel combinations.
Finish by checking results: recompute a KVL loop, or check power supplied equals power dissipated.
conn: Mesh current method combines KVL with Ohm's law: KVL gives the loop equations, and Ohm's law turns resistor voltages into expressions in the mesh currents.
Series/parallel reduction versus mesh analysis: reduce first where possible, then use mesh currents on what remains.
Current sources and meshes: a source on an outer branch fixes a mesh current and removes an equation, which links to counting unknowns and independent equations.
Mesh results feed into branch currents, voltages and power calculations, e.g. a shared-resistor current is \( I_1 - I_2 \) and its power is \( R(I_1-I_2)^2 \).
exq: A two-mesh circuit has a 12 V source and resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω (shared) and 3 Ω. Assign clockwise mesh currents, write the KVL equations, solve for both currents, and find the current in the shared resistor.

A three-mesh circuit has a 2 A current source on the outer branch of the right-hand mesh. State which mesh current is known, how many KVL equations are needed, and solve for the remaining currents given the resistor values.
Explain the difference between a loop and a mesh, and identify the meshes in a given bridge-type circuit that cannot be reduced by series/parallel combinations.
Write the mesh equations in matrix form \( \mathbf{R}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{V} \) for a given three-mesh circuit and solve for the mesh currents. Then calculate the power dissipated in a chosen resistor.

A student's mesh solution gives an incorrect answer because a shared branch was written as \( R(I_1+I_2) \). Identify the error, correct the equations, and explain how the reference directions determine the sign.

notes.t: Mesh-current method
pts: Identify every individual mesh in the circuit before doing anything else.
Assign one mesh current per mesh; a mesh current is already known if a current source sits on an outside branch of that mesh.
Apply KVL around each mesh with unknown current to write a loop equation, then use Ohm's law to express resistor voltages in mesh currents.
With n unknown mesh currents you need n independent equations; solve the resulting linear system to find the mesh currents.
tips: Only meshes with unknown currents need a KVL loop equation; meshes fixed by a current source do not.
Write resistor voltages as R times the mesh current with correct sign for the direction you assigned, especially for shared branches.
rq: Why does a mesh whose outside branch contains a current source not need a KVL equation?
Its mesh current is fixed by the source, so it is no longer an unknown; only meshes with unknown currents need loop equations.
Why must the number of independent equations equal the number of unknown mesh currents?
A unique solution requires as many independent linear equations as unknowns; fewer gives no unique answer, and extra ones are redundant.

notes.t: Summary: Mesh-Current Analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis can solve arbitrary circuits, not just simple ones.
It works even when circuits cannot be easily reduced to series or parallel combinations.
Using mesh currents reduces the number of unknowns and simultaneous equations needed.
tips: Do not confuse a mesh with any loop: a mesh is a loop that contains no other loops inside it.
Always check the reference direction of each mesh current before writing KVL, since sign errors are a common source of wrong answers.
rq: Why does mesh-current analysis usually need fewer simultaneous equations than applying KVL and KCL to every branch current?
Because each mesh current is defined once and automatically satisfies KCL at every node, so only one KVL equation per independent mesh is needed, reducing the number of unknowns.
What type of circuit would make you choose mesh-current analysis over simple series/parallel reduction?
A circuit with multiple sources and interconnected loops that cannot be reduced to simple series or parallel combinations.

units.name: Formulae sheet lecture 5
units.ov: This material covers mesh (loop) current analysis of resistive DC circuits. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law is applied to each independent mesh to give a set of simultaneous linear equations, which are then solved with Cramer's rule (determinants). The ideas connect as a pipeline: identify meshes, write KVL in standard form, build the resistance matrix, solve, then recover branch currents.
must: Mesh currents are mathematical loop quantities, not necessarily physical currents; branch currents are found from them, e.g. \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\)
Number of independent KVL equations = number of meshes (open areas), giving as many equations as unknown loop currents
KVL: \(\sum V = 0\) around a closed loop; go clockwise in every mesh and take resistor voltages as positive (\(+iR\))
Standard-form loop 1: \((R_1+R_3)i_1 - R_3 i_2 = V_A\)
Standard-form loop 2: \(-R_3 i_1 + (R_2+R_3)i_2 = -V_B\) (sign of source depends on its polarity relative to the clockwise direction)
Quick rule: (sum of resistors in loop)×(loop current) − (shared resistor)×(adjacent loop current) = source voltage in loop
Shared-resistor terms are negative because adjacent clockwise loop currents oppose each other through that resistor
Cramer's rule: \(I_i = \det(R_i)/\det(R)\), where \(R_i\) has column i replaced by the source-voltage vector
2×2 determinant: \(|A| = ad - bc\)
Keep units consistent (Ω, V, A) and convert mA carefully, e.g. 13.9 mA = 0.0139 A; check results by substituting back
conn: KVL to matrix form: writing the mesh equations in standard form gives \([R][I]=[V]\), which is directly solvable by Cramer's rule
Mesh currents to branch currents: the current in a shared resistor is the difference of the two loop currents (\(i_1 - i_2\)), which then feeds into voltage drops \(V=IR\) and power \(I^2R\)
Source polarity and clockwise convention: sign of \(V_A\), \(V_B\) on the right-hand side determines sign of the answers; a negative current means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed one
Mesh analysis versus nodal/KCL methods: the substitution \(i_3=i_1-i_2\) is essentially KCL built into the loop definition
exq: A two-mesh circuit has \(R_1=10\,\Omega\), \(R_2=20\,\Omega\), shared \(R_3=30\,\Omega\), \(V_A=12\) V and \(V_B=6\) V opposing. Write the mesh equations in standard form and solve for \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) using Cramer's rule.
For the same circuit, find the current in the shared resistor \(R_3\), its direction, the voltage across it and the power dissipated.
Explain why the number of independent KVL equations equals the number of meshes and why loop currents need not be physical currents.
Evaluate \(\det(R)\) for \(\begin{bmatrix}40 & -30\\ -30 & 50\end{bmatrix}\) and use it to find both loop currents when the source vector is \([12, -6]^T\) V; give answers in mA.
Derive the standard-form loop equations for a two-battery, three-resistor network from KVL, showing how \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\) is used to eliminate a variable.

notes.t: Mesh Current Analysis and Solving Simultaneous Equations
pts: Loop currents are mathematical quantities used to simplify circuit analysis, not necessarily physical currents.
The number of independent KVL equations equals the number of open areas (meshes) in the network layout.
Write KVL for each mesh going clockwise, always taking resistor voltages as positive so resistor voltages are added.
Substitute branch current i3 as i1 − i2 so the unknowns match the number of equations.
A quick rule writes loop equations directly: (sum of loop resistors)×(loop current) − (shared resistor)×(adjacent loop current) = source voltage in loop.
defs: Loop (mesh) current
A mathematical circuit current assumed to circulate around one independent mesh, used to simplify nodal/mesh analysis; it is not necessarily a physical current.
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
The sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
Determinant method (Cramer's rule)
A matrix-algebra method for solving simultaneous linear equations where each unknown equals the ratio of two determinants.
eqs: \(I_{i}\) = unknown loop current (A); det(R) = determinant of the resistance (coefficient) matrix; det(\(R_{i}\)) = determinant with column i replaced by the source-voltage vector (V)
a, b, c, d = matrix entries (dimensionless for coefficient matrices); |A| = determinant
tips: Watch the sign of shared-resistor terms: they appear with a negative sign in the loop equations because the loop currents oppose each other through that resistor.
Keep units consistent: resistances in ohms and voltages in volts give currents in amps, so convert mA carefully when checking answers (e.g. 13.9 mA = 0.0139 A).
rq: Why do we treat resistor voltages as positive when going clockwise around each mesh, and what does that imply for the signs in the KVL equation?

It is a consistent convention: with clockwise loop current, each resistor voltage is taken as a drop in the direction of the loop, so all resistor terms are added; only source signs depend on their polarity relative to the loop.
Why does the shared resistor R3 appear with a negative sign in the equation for loop 1 but as a positive term in its own loop?
The shared resistor carries i1 and i2 in opposite directions relative to its own loop, so the current from the adjacent loop subtracts from the self-term.
What would go wrong if you substituted i3 = i1 + i2 instead of i1 − i2?
The sign convention for i3 would be inconsistent with the chosen loop directions, giving incorrect loop equations and wrong currents.

formulas.name: Weighting factor of a criterion
formulas.latex: \alpha = \frac{\text{criterion's positive decisions}}{\text{total positive decisions for all criteria}}
formulas.vars: \alpha = weighting factor (dimensionless); positive decisions = number of pairwise wins (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Pairwise comparison when ranking criteria in a decision matrix; weights sum to 1.
