formulas.latex: I=I_0\sin\omega t\Rightarrow V=\omega LI_0\cos\omega t,\ V_0=\omega LI_0
formulas.vars: \(V_{0}\) = peak voltage (V); \(I_{0}\) = peak current (A)
formulas.use: Voltage leads current by 90°.

formulas.name: Capacitors in series and parallel
formulas.vars: C = capacitance (F)
formulas.use: Series: reciprocal sum; parallel: sum.

formulas.name: Inductors in series and parallel
formulas.vars: L = inductance (H)
formulas.use: Series: sum; parallel: reciprocal sum.

formulas.name: Series RC impedance
formulas.vars: R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F); ω = angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.use: Total impedance of R in series with C.

formulas.name: Magnitude and phase of series RC impedance
formulas.vars: |Z| = magnitude (Ω); φ = phase of Z (rad or °)
formulas.use: Voltage lags current by |φ|; |V|=|I||Z|.

formulas.name: Low-pass transfer function
formulas.vars: ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω_0 = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); R (Ω); C (F)
formulas.use: Output across C of series RC.

formulas.name: Cut-off frequency of RC
formulas.use: Corner (−3 dB) frequency; design C=1/(2π\(Rf_{0}\)).

formulas.name: Low-pass gain magnitude
formulas.vars: |H| = gain (dimensionless)
formulas.use: At cut-off gain is 1/√2, power halves.

formulas.name: Low-pass phase
formulas.vars: φ = output phase relative to input
formulas.use: Phase 0° at low f, −45° at ω_0, −90° at high f.

formulas.name: Voltage gain in dB
formulas.vars: \(V_{\text{out}}\), \(V_{\text{in}}\) = voltages (V)
formulas.use: Gain of filters; 1/√2 gives ≈ −3 dB.

formulas.name: Power ratio in dB
formulas.vars: \(P_{2}\) = output power (W); \(P_{1}\) = input power (W)
formulas.use: Power gain; at cut-off \(P_{\text{out}}\)/\(P_{\text{in}}\)=1/2.

formulas.name: Number of decades
formulas.vars: d = decades; \(f_{1}\), \(f_{2}\) = frequencies (Hz)
formulas.use: Bode slope e.g. −20 dB/decade for first-order filter.

formulas.name: High-pass transfer function
formulas.vars: ω_0 = 1/RC = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.use: Output across R of series CR.

formulas.name: High-pass gain magnitude
formulas.vars: ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω_0 = cut-off (rad/s)
formulas.use: Gain 1/√2 at ω_0.

formulas.name: Limiting behaviour
formulas.vars: \(Z_{C}\) = capacitor impedance (Ω)
formulas.use: Qualitative low/high-frequency reasoning.

formulas.name: LR cut-off frequency
formulas.use: First-order LR filter corner frequency.

formulas.name: First-order filter forms
formulas.vars: ω_0 = characteristic angular frequency (rad/s)
formulas.use: Same normalised forms for RC and LR; LR high-pass has output across R.

formulas.name: Transfer function (output across R)
formulas.vars: R (Ω); L (H); C (F); ω (rad/s)
formulas.use: Series RLC band-pass.

formulas.name: Magnitude of gain
formulas.vars: as above
formulas.use: Gain is 1 at resonance and falls either side.

formulas.name: Resonant (centre) frequency
formulas.use: Where ωL=1/ωC, reactances cancel and Z=R.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.vars: V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Any resistor with linear V–I relation; basis of nearly all DC analysis

formulas.name: Current as charge flow
formulas.vars: I = current (A); Q = charge (C); t = time (s)
formulas.use: Average (Q/t) or instantaneous (dq/dt) current

formulas.name: Voltage as energy per charge
formulas.vars: V = voltage (V); W = energy (J); Q = charge (C); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
formulas.use: Definition of voltage; uniform field over length l

formulas.name: Resistance of a uniform conductor
formulas.vars: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
formulas.use: Resistance from geometry and material

formulas.name: Conductance and resistivity
formulas.vars: G = conductance (S); σ = conductivity (S/m); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m)
formulas.use: Reciprocal relations

formulas.name: Field form of Ohm's law
formulas.latex: J = \sigma E,\quad E=\rho J,\quad J=\frac{I}{A},\quad E=\frac{V}{l}
formulas.vars: J = current density (A/m²); E = electric field (V/m); σ = conductivity (S/m); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m)
formulas.use: Links microscopic and circuit forms; gives V = I\rho l/A

formulas.name: Resistor colour code
formulas.vars: \(d_{1}\), \(d_{2}\) = digits of bands 1, 2; n = multiplier band (number of zeros)
formulas.use: Reading 4-band resistor values

formulas.name: Reference direction reversal
formulas.vars: \(i_{ab}\) = current a to b (A); \(v_{ab}\) = voltage of a relative to b (V)
formulas.use: Sign conventions

formulas.name: Electrical power
formulas.vars: P = power (W); V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Power absorbed by a resistor; P=VI for any element

formulas.name: Total power as sum of element powers
formulas.vars: \(P_{T}\) = total power (W); \(P_{k}\) = power of element k (W)
formulas.use: Power delivered by sources equals power absorbed in circuit (power balance, Σp = 0 with signs)

formulas.name: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)
formulas.vars: \(I_{\text{IN}}\), \(I_{\text{OUT}}\) = currents into and out of a node (A)
formulas.use: Apply at any node; equivalently the algebraic sum of currents is zero

formulas.name: Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)
formulas.vars: \(v_{k}\) = voltage across k-th element in a closed loop (V)
formulas.use: Apply around any closed loop with consistent signs, e.g. \(V_{S}\) = Σ\(V_{\text{drops}}\)

formulas.name: Resistors in series
formulas.vars: \(R_{T}\) = equivalent resistance (Ω); \(R_{k}\) = individual resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Resistors carrying the same current

formulas.name: Voltage divider
formulas.vars: \(V_{k}\) = voltage across \(R_{k}\) (V); \(V_{\text{total}}\) = total applied voltage (V)
formulas.use: Series resistors; two-resistor case \(V_{1}\) = \(V_{B}\) \(R_{1}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\)); unloaded divider only

formulas.name: Series circuit current
formulas.vars: I = series current (A); \(V_{\text{total}}\) = source voltage (V); \(R_{T}\) = total resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Current in a single-loop circuit

formulas.name: Voltage sources in series
formulas.vars: \(V_{k}\) = source voltage (V); + aiding, − opposing polarity
formulas.use: Net voltage of series batteries

formulas.name: Voltage ratio in series
formulas.vars: V = voltage across resistor (V); R = resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Quick comparison of series drops

formulas.name: Resistors in parallel
formulas.vars: \(R_{T}\) = equivalent resistance (Ω); \(R_{k}\) = branch resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Resistors sharing the same voltage (conductances add)

formulas.name: Two resistors in parallel
formulas.vars: \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\) = resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Exactly two parallel resistors

formulas.name: Current divider
formulas.vars: \(I_{\text{tot}}\) = total current into the pair (A); \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\) = branch resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Two parallel branches; larger share through smaller resistance

formulas.name: Parallel branch currents (KCL)
formulas.vars: \(I_{T}\) = total current (A); \(V_{B}\) = common voltage (V)
formulas.use: Parallel circuit with common voltage

formulas.name: Series-parallel reduction
formulas.vars: \(R_{eq}\) = equivalent resistance (Ω); \(R_{1}\) in series with \(R_{2}\)∥\(R_{3}\)
formulas.use: Reduce step by step, then find source current and work back with Ohm's law/dividers

formulas.name: Thévenin equivalent
formulas.vars: \(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V); \(R_{T}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω); \(v_{\text{oc}}\) = open-circuit voltage (V); \(i_{\text{sc}}\) = short-circuit current (A)
formulas.use: Replace any linear two-terminal network; \(R_{T}\) also found by zeroing sources (voltage sources short, current sources open) and combining resistors

formulas.name: Load current/voltage with Thévenin source
formulas.vars: \(i_{L}\) = load current (A); \(V_{L}\) = load voltage (V); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: After replacing the circuit by its Thévenin equivalent

formulas.name: Norton equivalent / source transformation
formulas.latex: I_N = i_{sc} = \frac{V_T}{R_T},\quad R_N = R_T,\quad V_T = R_T I_N
formulas.vars: \(I_{N}\) = Norton current (A); \(R_{N}\) = Norton resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Convert between Thévenin and Norton forms

formulas.name: Practical source terminal voltage
formulas.latex: V_L = I R_L = V_o - I R_o
formulas.vars: \(V_{o}\) = ideal source voltage (V); \(R_{o}\) = internal resistance (Ω); I = load current (A)
formulas.use: Source with internal resistance; terminal voltage drops with load

formulas.name: Maximum power transfer condition
formulas.vars: \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω); \(R_{T}\) = Thévenin resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Load receives maximum power when equal to source resistance (from dP/\(dR_{L}\) = 0)

formulas.name: Load power
formulas.vars: \(P_{L}\) = load power (W); \(V_{T}\) = Thévenin voltage (V)
formulas.use: Power vs \(R_{L}\); at matching, \(P_{\text{max}}\) = \(V_{T}\)²/(4R_T)

formulas.name: Superposition
formulas.vars: \(r_{k}\) = response (V or A) due to source k alone; \(r_{T}\) = total response
formulas.use: Linear circuits; set other voltage sources to short, current sources to open; add signed responses

formulas.name: Delta to star
formulas.use: Each star arm = product of two adjacent delta resistors over the sum; for bridge networks

formulas.name: Star to delta
formulas.use: Delta resistor = sum of pairwise products over opposite star arm

formulas.name: Two-mesh equations (standard form)
formulas.vars: \(i_{1}\), \(i_{2}\) = clockwise mesh currents (A); \(R_{3}\) = shared resistor (Ω); \(V_{A}\), \(V_{B}\) = source voltages (V)
formulas.use: KVL per mesh: self-resistance × own current − shared resistance × neighbour current = source EMF

formulas.name: Cramer's rule
formulas.vars: det(R) = determinant of resistance matrix; det(\(R_{i}\)) = determinant with column i replaced by voltage vector
formulas.use: Solve [R][I] = [V]

formulas.name: 2×2 determinant
formulas.latex: \begin{vmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc
formulas.vars: a, b, c, d = matrix entries
formulas.use: Evaluate Cramer's rule determinants

formulas.name: Branch current from mesh currents
formulas.latex: I_R = i_k - i_m \ (\text{shared}),\quad I_R = i_k \ (\text{outer branch})
formulas.vars: \(I_{R}\) = current in resistor (A); \(i_{k}\), \(i_{m}\) = adjacent mesh currents (A)
formulas.use: After solving; sign shows direction

formulas.name: Mesh with a current source
formulas.vars: \(I_{S}\) = current source value (A)
formulas.use: Source in only one mesh fixes that mesh current; write KVL for remaining meshes

formulas.name: Three-mesh matrix form
formulas.vars: \(i_{k}\) = mesh currents (A); R = resistances (Ω); V = source voltages (V)
formulas.use: Example of three-mesh circuit; diagonal = sum of mesh resistances, off-diagonal = −shared

rep.ov: Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016) first covers basic fluid machines and thermal/transmission elements: valves (globe, gate, butterfly, relief), pumps (positive displacement and centrifugal) and pumps in systems, heat exchangers (plate and shell-and-tube), clutches (positive contact, friction, overrunning, fluid coupling), then mountings and gearboxes. Each topic follows the same pattern of purpose, principle, types, construction, materials and design considerations. Pump work builds on valves and system resistance through system curves, static/dynamic head and operating points. Clutch work builds on torque-power-speed relations. Concept selection (PDS and decision matrices) and engineering drawing and fluid-diagram standards support the Semester 2 project. Note that assessment is coursework only (30% set exercises, 70% design project), so the Moodle quizzes and in-class exercise test this content.
must: Pump classification: positive displacement (fluid enclosed once per cycle, flow set by speed, pressure set by system, blocks flow when stopped, needs a relief valve) versus centrifugal (impeller gives kinetic energy, volute converts it to pressure, flow set by system, no relief valve needed)
System curve: head required vs flow, \( H = H_{static} + kQ^2 \); starts at the origin if there is no static head and above zero if there is; best/worst cases as valves change
Operating point = intersection of pump curve and system curve; PD pump curve is near-vertical, centrifugal falls with flow; selecting a pump means matching it to the required duty
Static head \( H_{static} = H_{suction} + H_{discharge} \) (elevation only, in m of fluid, independent of density) versus dynamic head (friction, rises with flow squared) and TDH as their sum

Theoretical suction lift \( H = \frac{P}{\rho g} \approx 10\) m for water; practical lift is lower because of vapour pressure, friction, leakage and cavitation (NPSH); the specific gravity effect on lift
Piston pump flow \( \dot v = (AK - V)S \) with consistent SI units (rev/s not rpm); pulsating delivery and accumulators; gear, lobe, vane and screw pumps

Valve types and duty: globe (linear, throttling, S-shaped path), gate (on/off only, low loss when fully open), butterfly (quarter-turn disc), relief and non-return; the four functions of on/off, rate, pressure, direction; globe lift \( h = D/4 \) from \( \pi R^2 = 2\pi R h \); dynamic seals (packing, PTFE) vs static seals

Heat exchanger conduction \( Q/t = kA\Delta T/d \) and the design drivers (large area, thin wall, high k, no mixing, thermal expansion); \( Q = UA\,\mathrm{LMTD} \); counter-flow is more effective than parallel-flow

Plate vs shell-and-tube exchangers: construction (corrugated plates, gaskets; tubes, tube plates, headers, floating end with O-rings and tell-tale), materials (SS 304/316, titanium, Hastelloy; NBR/EPDM seals), pros and cons, cleaning, vents, drains and sacrificial anodes

Clutch classification by engagement (positive contact, friction, overrunning, magnetic, fluid coupling) and by actuation; operating principle and applications of each, including centrifugal drum, multi-plate wet/dry disc, ratchet/roller/sprag and fluid coupling

Clutch torque analysis: \( P = T\omega \) (rad/s), place the clutch on the high-speed, low-torque side, inertial torque \( T = mk^2\alpha \), heat generated during slip, steady-state vs accelerating conditions

Gearbox power transmission needs both lubrication to the highest-loaded parts and cooling; concept selection with a PDS-weighted decision matrix; drawing standards (BS 5070-3, BS 1553, SI units, cross-over methods)
conn: Valves and pump systems: opening or closing a globe or gate valve changes system resistance, shifting the system curve and hence the operating point
Static head, suction lift and the system curve: a suction-side limit of about 10 m plus friction and NPSH constrains the pump and the static head offset of the curve
Heat exchanger conduction equation with LMTD and flow configuration: sizing area from Q, U and LMTD, linked to material conductivity and wall thickness

Clutch torque, power and gearbox position: \( P = T\omega \) fixes torque on each side of a gearbox, which sets clutch torque capacity; engagement heat from inertial torque links to wet/dry and cooling choices; gearbox heat links to lubrication
Material and seal selection recurs everywhere (valves, plate exchangers, pumps); it ties to corrosion, temperature and fluid compatibility, and feeds the decision matrix in concept selection
exq: A pump lifts water 4 m on the suction side and 12 m on the discharge side, with friction head 6 m at 20 m³/h and friction proportional to Q². Calculate the static head, sketch the system curve, and find the head and flow where it meets a given pump curve.

A single-acting piston pump has piston diameter 50 mm, stroke 80 mm, runs at 300 rpm with leakage 2 cm³ per stroke. Calculate the volumetric flow rate in m³/s and explain why the discharge is pulsed and how an accumulator helps.
Derive the maximum theoretical suction lift of water at 101 kPa. State and explain why the practical lift is lower, and how it changes for diesel with SG 0.86.

A copper wall of area 2 m², thickness 3 mm and k = 390 W/m K separates fluids with ΔT = 40 K. Calculate the heat transfer rate, then compare the effect of a stainless steel wall; compare counter-flow and parallel-flow arrangements using given terminal temperatures and LMTD.

A motor delivers 10 kW at 1500 rpm through a 5:1 reduction gearbox. Calculate the torque on each side, say where the clutch should be placed, and find the inertial torque needed to accelerate a load of known mass and radius of gyration to speed in a given time.

Compare gate, globe and butterfly valves for a clean-water shut-off supply. State the choice of valve, materials and seals, and justify them; or explain how a sprag clutch, a centrifugal drum clutch and a fluid coupling each operate and where each is suited.
weak: Reading and constructing system and pump curves: students mix up which curve is which, forget that static head offsets the curve, and misplace the operating point when valves change
Clutch torque, power and speed: unit slips between rpm and rad/s, squared radius of gyration, and deciding which side of the gearbox carries the lower torque; combining steady and accelerating cases
Head vs pressure and suction lift: head in metres is independent of density while pressure is not; the limit of about 10 m, vapour pressure and NPSH versus theoretical lift are easy to muddle

units.name: 1.1 Welcome, lecturer and class conduct
units.ov: These notes are the Week 1 introduction to Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016). They cover the lecturer's profile (Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering, Adviser of Studies, Chartered Engineer) and the expected standards of class conduct. They contain no technical engineering content such as design methods, equations or calculations. The two pages connect through professionalism: knowing who to approach for guidance, and behaving as a professional engineer would.
must: The module is Mechanical Design 1, code ENG1016, in the James Watt School of Engineering at Glasgow.
The lecturer is a Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering and works in the Centre for Medical and Industrial Ultrasonics (C-MIU) and the Materials and Manufacturing Research Cluster (MMRC).
The lecturer is Adviser of Studies for Mechanical Engineering students, so is your first point of contact for academic guidance and welfare.
The lecturer's credentials are Chartered Engineer, Fellow of the IMechE and Senior Member of the IEEE. This shows the professional route open to Mechanical Engineering graduates.
The lecturer has industry experience, mainly in aerospace, and collaborates extensively with industry, so expect design content with industrial relevance.
Students are expected to engage actively with scheduled content and activities.
Class etiquette: keep a respectful and focused atmosphere, use devices only when necessary, and stay until the lecturer ends the class.
Contribute positively and professionally in all interactions.
Staff may ask a student to leave if their behaviour disrupts others' learning.
The notes contain no formulas or quantitative methods. Do not expect marks for this material beyond awareness. Spend revision time on later technical weeks.
conn: Adviser of Studies role and professional conduct: knowing when to seek guidance early, such as for difficulties with workload or attendance, supports good performance and professional development.
Lecturer's IMechE/Chartered Engineer status and class conduct: professional registration requires ethical, respectful behaviour, which classroom expectations mirror.
Aerospace and industry experience and the ultrasonics research: this links the design module to real applications in materials, manufacturing and medical or industrial ultrasonics.
Active engagement and exam preparation: attending, focusing and participating in scheduled activities is how technical design content is actually learned.
exq: Name the professional bodies of which the lecturer is a Chartered Engineer, Fellow or Senior Member, and explain what Chartered Engineer status represents for a mechanical engineer.
Describe the two research groups the lecturer belongs to and give one way their work could relate to mechanical design.
State four behaviour expectations for students in class and justify why each matters for a professional engineering environment.
Explain the role of an Adviser of Studies and describe a situation in which you would contact yours.
Reflect on how industrial experience, for example in aerospace, might shape the way mechanical design is taught. Give two examples.

notes.t: About me – lecturer profile
pts: The lecturer is a Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering in the James Watt School of Engineering.
The lecturer works within the Centre for Medical and Industrial Ultrasonics (C-MIU) and the Materials and Manufacturing Research Cluster (MMRC).
The lecturer is Adviser of Studies for Mechanical Engineering students, so is a point of contact for student guidance.
Professional credentials include Chartered Engineer and Fellow of the IMechE, and Senior Member of the IEEE.
The lecturer has industry experience, mainly in aerospace, and extensive collaborative research with industry.

notes.t: Respectful engagement in class
pts: Students should actively engage with scheduled class content and activities.
Maintaining a respectful and focused atmosphere is expected of everyone.
Devices should be used only when necessary, and students should stay until the lecturer ends class.
Students should contribute positively and professionally in all interactions.
Staff may ask individuals to leave if their behaviour disrupts others' learning.
rq: Why might a student who finds the guidelines challenging be encouraged to speak to staff rather than simply stop following them?
Staff such as the Adviser of Studies or course coordinator can help resolve concerns, so the student can keep engaging appropriately rather than being disruptive or leaving.

units.name: 1.2 Purpose, engineering skills and course aims
units.ov: This introductory material sets out why the course exists, which skills engineers need, and what the course will teach. It frames engineering as creative, systematic problem solving that combines technical and non-technical skills. The specific aims (design process, sustainability and ethics, basic fluid machines, engineering drawing, group project) show how lectures feed into the collaborative design project. The notes contain no equations or calculations, so questions will probably be descriptive or applied.
must: Engineering is more than maths and physics: it is creative problem solving applied to real needs.
Design follows a systematic, learnable process, and the course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within design, so iteration and refinement are part of the process.
Core engineering skills span technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills (teamwork, communication, leadership) are as essential as technical ones.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail underpin sound engineering judgement.
A capacity for lifelong learning lets engineers keep pace with evolving technology.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed, not optional add-ons.
Basic fluid machines are studied through their design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
Students must be able to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings; the group project applies lecture knowledge to a real design problem.
conn: The systematic design process links to the group project: the project is where the process is applied and where mistakes and iteration serve as learning.
Sustainability and ethics apply to every design decision, including the design and operation of fluid machines.
Sketches and engineering drawings are the means of communicating design ideas, which links technical skill to teamwork and communication in the project.
Fluid machines serve as the worked example in which design, construction, operation and drawing skills come together.
exq: Describe the stages of a systematic engineering design process and explain how iteration and learning from mistakes improve the final design.
Discuss why non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are as important as technical knowledge for a mechanical engineer. Give examples from a group design project.
Explain how sustainability and ethical considerations could influence the design of a basic fluid machine such as a pump. Give at least three specific design decisions affected.
Sketch a simple fluid machine (e.g. a centrifugal pump) and label its main components. State what information an engineering drawing must convey so that it can be built.
Compare the design, construction and operation of a basic fluid machine, and say which engineering skills are needed at each stage.

notes.t: Purpose of the course
pts: Engineering is broader than just maths and physics; it involves creative problem solving.
Students learn common engineering solutions to recurring problems.
Design follows a systematic process that can be learned and applied.
Imagination and personal ideas are encouraged, and students get hands-on design opportunities.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within the design process.
tips: This page states course aims rather than technical content, so exam questions are unlikely to ask for these points verbatim; focus on the technical topics that follow.
rq: Why does the course stress that engineering is more than maths and physics?
Because real engineering design also requires creativity, practical judgement, and the ability to choose sensible solutions, not just solve equations.
What might be the benefit of following a defined design process rather than designing ad hoc?
It structures the work into repeatable steps, making problems easier to define, solutions easier to evaluate, and errors easier to find and correct.

notes.t: What are engineering skills?
pts: Engineering requires a set of core skills spanning technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are equally essential for engineers.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail support sound engineering judgement.
A capacity to learn lets an engineer keep pace with evolving technology throughout a career.
rq: Why might a graduate with strong technical knowledge still struggle in an engineering job?
Because engineering work also depends on teamwork, communication, management and leadership, which technical knowledge alone does not provide.

notes.t: Specific course aims
pts: The course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed.
Basic fluid machines are studied in terms of their design, construction and operation.
Students learn to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings.
A collaborative project applies lecture knowledge to a real engineering design problem.
tips: Note that the course covers fluid machines as "basic machines" focused on design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
rq: Why does the course pair technical design processes with sustainability and ethics?
Engineering designs affect society and the environment, so sustainability and ethical considerations must be built into design decisions from the start, not added afterwards.

units.name: 1.3 Course structure and timetables
units.ov: This material describes how engineering design is organised in first-year Mechanical Engineering at Glasgow. Mechanical Design 1 (unique design elements, in two parts: fundamental machines/systems, and the design process leading to a real-world project) is paired with Design and Manufacture 1 (repetitive elements). The notes also cover the Semester 1 timetable and the Semester 2 Design Project timetable, but the extracted pages contain no technical formulae and no timetable detail.
must: Mechanical Design 1 covers the more unique elements of design; Design and Manufacture 1 covers the more repetitive elements. Do not swap them.
The two courses are deliberately designed as partners and should be treated as complementary, not separate.
Mechanical Design 1 has two parts: (1) design and functionality of fundamental machines and systems, and (2) the design process leading to a completed real-world design project.
Semester 1 is mainly the taught side: fundamental machines and systems, with the course schedule on the timetable page.
Semester 2 centres on the Design Project, which applies the design process; check the timetable for milestone dates.
Know your own timetable: deadlines, session types and locations. The extracted notes give no specifics, so take these from the original slides or Moodle.
This page has no formulae or definitions. Credit comes from understanding structure and how the parts fit together, not from calculation.
conn: Fundamental machines and systems (part 1) provide the technical knowledge applied in the part 2 design project.
Design process steps (unique, creative decisions) link to Design and Manufacture 1 (repeatable manufacturing and production considerations), because a real design must be manufacturable.
The Semester 1 schedule feeds the Semester 2 project timetable: skills learned early are assessed through project deliverables later.
exq: Explain the difference in scope between Mechanical Design 1 and Design and Manufacture 1, and why the two are designed to work as partners.
Describe the two parts of Mechanical Design 1 and say how the first supports the second.
Using the Semester 2 Design Project timetable, outline the key stages and deadlines and say what you would aim to complete at each.
Give an example of a design element that is unique to a project and one that is repetitive, and say which course covers each.

notes.t: Course structure
pts: Engineering design is taught across two complementary courses: Mechanical Design 1 covers the more unique elements of design, while Design and Manufacture 1 covers the more repetitive elements.
The two courses are deliberately designed to work together as partners.
Mechanical Design 1 is split into two parts: the design and functionality of fundamental machines and systems, and the process of design leading to a completed real-world design project.
tips: Do not confuse the two courses: Mechanical Design 1 covers unique design elements, while Design and Manufacture 1 covers repetitive ones.
The slide describes course structure only; do not expect technical formulae or definitions from this page.
rq: Why are Mechanical Design 1 and Design and Manufacture 1 taught as partner courses rather than as one course?
Mechanical Design 1 covers the unique, non-routine aspects of design, while Design and Manufacture 1 covers the repetitive, routine aspects; together they give a complete view of engineering design.
How does the second part of Mechanical Design 1 differ from the first part?

The first part teaches the design and functionality of fundamental machines and systems, whereas the second part focuses on the overall design process that leads to completing a real-world design project.

units.name: 1.4 Assessments, grading and feedback
units.ov: This material explains how the module is assessed (coursework only, no exams), how the marks are weighted between Set Exercises and the Design Project, and what feedback you get on each component. The ideas connect because each assessment type matches a kind of knowledge (recall, creation, use of sources), and each has its own feedback route that you should use to improve.
must: The course has no exams: all assessment is coursework, so check deadlines and submission details on Moodle
Set Exercises are worth 30% of the credit and the Design Project 70%, so \(30\%+70\%=100\%\)
Set Exercises consist of two Moodle quizzes and one hand-written in-class exercise
Design Project (70%) = 50% project report + 20% poster presentation, both group-marked
Group marks are adjusted per student by 20% peer weighting, so individual contribution affects your final mark
Knowledge a professional engineer must know without looking it up is assessed by timed online quizzes
Knowledge used to create something is assessed by output quality and the processes followed; use of key sources is assessed by proof of use
The engineering drawing exercise is formative: it carries no marks but gives feedback before the Semester 2 projects

Feedback routes: Set Exercise 1 gets detailed written comments; Moodle quizzes give only a mark per question; drawing feedback is written; Set Exercise 2 feedback comes at the oral assessment; tutorials give detailed comments on progressed design work
Good feedback highlights positives, comments constructively on major errors, and advises how to reach at least one grade higher
conn: Assessment type matches knowledge type: recall is tested by timed quizzes, creation by report and poster quality and process, and source use by proof of use
Peer weighting links the group-marked report and poster (70% of credit) to your individual contribution and so to your final mark
Formative drawing feedback feeds into the Semester 2 design projects, and tutorial feedback only helps if you bring progressed design work
Because quizzes give marks without comments, you must use the per-question marks to find weak topics and review them before later assessments
exq: Although the course has no exam, outline the full assessment structure and give the percentage weighting of each component, showing that they total 100%.
A student's group scores 70% on the project report and 20% peer weighting is applied. Explain how the weighting could change the student's individual mark and what that implies for group work.
Match each type of knowledge (recall, creation, use of key sources) to how it is assessed in this course, and give an example of each.
Describe the feedback you receive for Set Exercise 1, the Moodle quizzes, the drawing exercise, Set Exercise 2 and tutorials, and explain how you would use each to improve.
Why is the engineering drawing exercise not graded, and how should you use it before Semester 2 projects?

notes.t: Course assessments
pts: Some knowledge is expected of a professional engineer and must be known without looking it up; this is assessed by timed online quizzes.
Knowledge used to create something is assessed by the quality of the output and the processes followed.
Key sources must be familiar; use of them is assessed by proof that you have used them.
The course has no exams; assessment is coursework only.
Full submission details and deadlines are on Moodle.
tips: Do not assume this course has exams; all assessment is coursework, so check deadlines and submission requirements on Moodle rather than relying on memory alone.
rq: Why are some facts assessed by timed quizzes while others are assessed by the quality of what you create?

Expected professional knowledge must be recalled instantly without reference, so it is tested under time limits; knowledge applied to create something is better judged by the output and the process used to produce it.

notes.t: Course assessments
pts: Set Exercises make up 30% of the credit, split across two Moodle quizzes and one hand-written in-class exercise.
The Design Project makes up 70% of the credit: a 50% project report and a 20% poster presentation, both group-marked.
Group marks are adjusted per student by peer weighting of 20%, so individual contribution affects the final mark.
A formative engineering drawing exercise is not graded but gives practice and feedback before Semester 2 projects.
tips: Check the weighting breakdown: Set Exercises are 30% total and the Design Project is 70% total, so the components sum to 100%.
Do not confuse the formative drawing exercise with graded assessment; it carries no marks.
rq: Why might a group-marked component still be adjusted for individual students?
Peer weighting by 20% reflects each student's individual contribution within the shared group mark.
Why is the formative drawing exercise unmarked yet still useful?
It provides practice and feedback that prepare students for the graded Semester 2 project work.

notes.t: Feedback
pts: Feedback can be individual or group, and written or verbal.
Feedback aims to highlight positives, comment constructively on major errors, and advise how work could be one grade higher.
tips: Feedback advice should be specific enough to show how to reach at least one grade higher, not just general comments.
rq: Why should feedback highlight positive aspects as well as errors?
Recognising strengths reinforces effective practice and keeps the student motivated, while errors are then addressed constructively and targeted for improvement.

notes.t: Feedback arrangements in the course
pts: Set Exercise 1 gives detailed written comments on your work
Moodle quizzes give only a mark per question, with no comments
Engineering drawing feedback is written, from the lecturer and possibly technical staff
Set Exercise 2 feedback is delivered at the oral assessment
Tutorial sessions give detailed comments on progressed design work from lecturer and GTAs
tips: Do not expect written comments on quizzes; use the marks to identify topics needing review.
Tutorial feedback depends on having progressed design work; arriving without it limits the comments you receive.
rq: Why might the Moodle quiz feedback be less useful for improving your work than the written report comments?
Quizzes give only a mark per question, so you learn your score but not why an answer was wrong or how to fix the reasoning.
How can you get the most useful feedback from tutorial sessions?
Bring progressed design work, since comments are given on developed work from the lecturer and GTAs.

units.name: 1.5 Expectations, course materials and group project
units.ov: This material sets out how the module runs: the study load, attendance and engagement expectations, how course notes are provided in each section, the set and recommended texts, and the Semester 2 group design project. These pieces connect because the Semester 1 preparation habits (pre-reading, self-annotated notes, Childs exercises) build the skills used in the Semester 2 EWB-based team project.
must: Study load: about \(2\) hours of additional study per taught hour, on top of contact time, either before or after class
Attendance is mandatory for all timetabled classes, as stated in the student handbook
Engagement means taking notes, participating and asking questions in class
Pre-reading is required only for some lectures; it forms the basis of the next lecture, so check the course materials for which ones
Moodle notes are reduced and only a basic record; you must annotate them with your own notes

Notes differ by section: S1 first section (read Moodle notes before class, PowerPoint posted afterwards with sketches and photos); S1 second section (large discussion element, pre-reading, you take your own notes); S2 project (PowerPoint plus extra material, all on Moodle in advance)
Set textbook: Mechanical Design (2nd Edition) by Peter Childs, used across the course and degree; pre-reading and exercises come from it
Recommended reading: Manual of Engineering Drawing (4th Edition), based on the current British Standard for engineering drawings, available as a Library download
Semester 2 group design project is based on the EWB National Engineering Design competition; the top five Glasgow projects are entered nationally
Project aims: devise a solution to a real problem, practise taught material, gain first team-working experience (dynamics, planning) and consider cultures and environments unlike your own
conn: Pre-reading and Childs exercises in Semester 1 prepare you for discussion-heavy sessions, where you must take your own notes
Engineering drawing standards (Manual of Engineering Drawing) link to communicating the design solution in the Semester 2 project
Team dynamics and planning in the project depend on the engagement and time-management habits (the 2:1 study ratio, attendance) set out earlier
Cultural and environmental context in the EWB brief shapes design decisions, linking the textbook design process to a real-world problem
exq: Explain how many hours of additional study are expected for a module with 4 taught hours per week, and state how this relates to contact time.
Compare how notes are provided in Semester 1 first section, Semester 1 second section and the Semester 2 project, and state what the student must do in each.
Which textbook is set for the course, what is it used for, and which recommended text covers British Standard engineering drawing?
Describe the aims of the Semester 2 group design project and how it connects to the EWB National Engineering Design competition.
Discuss why engineering teams should consider cultures and environments different from their own, using the group project as an example.

notes.t: Course expectations: preparation, attendance and engagement
pts: Expect about two hours of additional study for every taught hour, either before or after class.
Some lectures have required pre-reading that forms the basis of the next lecture, so it must be completed in advance.
Attendance is mandatory for all timetabled classes, as stated in the student handbook.

Pre-reading is required only for some lectures, so check the course materials to know which sessions need preparation.
rq: Why is pre-reading for some lectures treated as essential rather than optional?
Because the pre-reading provides the foundation for the following lecture, so without it the next lecture's material is harder to follow.
How should the two additional hours per taught hour be used to support learning?
Preparing before class and reviewing or working through material afterwards both reinforce understanding of lecture content.

notes.t: Course material and how notes are provided
pts: Course notes are on Moodle but reduced, so you write your own notes into the document.
Provided notes are only a basic record of the lecture and need annotating with more information.
Semester 1 first section: read course notes on Moodle before class; PowerPoint used in lectures and posted afterwards with sketches and photos.
Semester 1 second section has a large discussion element, requires pre-reading, and notes must be taken yourself.
Semester 2 project section uses a mix of PowerPoint notes and extra material, all available in advance on Moodle.
tips: Do not assume the Moodle notes are complete; they are a basic record and must be annotated.
Check which section (Semester 1 first, Semester 1 second, or Semester 2 project) determines whether you need to take your own notes.
rq: Why is it important to annotate the provided lecture notes rather than rely on them alone?
They are only a basic record of the lecture, so adding your own explanations, working and detail is needed to understand and revise the material.
Why might pre-reading matter more in the second Semester 1 section than in the first?
That section has a large discussion element and no provided notes, so you must arrive prepared and take your own notes.

notes.t: Course material and recommended reading
pts: The set textbook is Mechanical Design (2nd Edition) by Peter Childs, used throughout the course and the wider degree.
Pre-reading and exercises for the course are set from the Childs textbook.
Manual of Engineering Drawing (4th Edition) is recommended reading and is based on the current British Standard for engineering drawings.
The Manual of Engineering Drawing is available as a download from the Library.
rq: Why is the Childs textbook worth having access to beyond this course?
It is referred to throughout the entire degree course, so it serves as a long-term reference.
Why is the Manual of Engineering Drawing useful for engineering drawing work?
It is based on the current British Standard for engineering drawings, so its conventions match the standard.

notes.t: Group design project (second semester)
pts: The second semester centres on a group design project based on the EWB National Engineering Design competition.
The project aims to let students create an engineering solution to a real problem and practise taught material.
It provides a first experience of working as an engineering team, handling team dynamics and planning.
It encourages consideration of cultures and environments very different from one's own.
The top five Glasgow projects are entered into the national EWB competition.
rq: Why might basing the design project on a real-world competition like EWB's be valuable compared with a textbook exercise?
A real problem has ill-defined requirements, constraints from cultures and environments, and cannot be solved by a single known method, so it develops practical engineering judgement.

units.name: 1.6 AI caution, ethics and expectations of engineers
units.ov: This material covers three linked themes: cautious and honest use of AI tools in coursework, the four ethical principles the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering set for engineers, and the wider skills and attitudes industry and academia expect of 21st-century engineers. The ideas connect through integrity and rigour. Verifying and declaring AI output is a small-scale example of the professional ethics that protect safety, public trust and reputation.
must: AI use is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as your own is misconduct and plagiarism, with severe penalties.
AI output may be inaccurate, so verify it against your own research and engineering judgement; never assume it is correct.
Cite and acknowledge any AI-generated content, following the guidance linked on the course page.
The UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering define four fundamental ethical principles; know all four by name.
Principle 1: honesty and integrity.
Principle 2: respect for life, law, the environment and public good; name all the components.
Principles 3 and 4: accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication.
Why ethics matters: safety and protection from harm, public trust, company reputation, sustainability, and quality and professional standards. It goes beyond legal compliance.
Core 21st-century expectations: technical knowledge, work ethic, teamwork, ethics, organisation and independence, beyond pure technical knowledge.
Industry seeks skilled, reliable and industrious people, so maintaining high standards is key.
conn: AI caution and ethical principles: undeclared AI use breaches honesty and integrity, and unverified AI output breaches accuracy and rigour.
Ethics and its benefits: Principle 2 (life, environment, public good) links directly to safety, sustainability and public trust.
Ethics and employer expectations: high standards, reliability and independence are what industry looks for, and they also protect professional reputation.
Verification and engineering judgement: independent checking links the AI caution to independence and accuracy as expected skills.
exq: List the four fundamental principles of ethical behaviour defined by the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering, and briefly explain each.
Principle 2 covers respect for several things. Name all of them and give an engineering example of each.
A student uses ChatGPT to draft part of a report and submits it without comment. Explain why this is misconduct even though AI use is not prohibited, and state what they should have done.
Explain at least four reasons why ethical behaviour matters in engineering, going beyond legal compliance.
Discuss the skills and attitudes beyond technical knowledge expected of engineers in the 21st century, and say how ethics and AI use relate to them.

notes.t: Notes of caution about AI
pts: AI tools like ChatGPT are increasingly used in universities
Use of AI is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as your own is misconduct and plagiarism
Penalties for academic misconduct are severe, so do not risk it
AI-generated information may be inaccurate, so you must verify it with your own research and engineering judgement
Cite information generated from software using the guidance linked on the page
tips: Do not assume AI-generated information is correct; always check it against your own research and engineering judgement.
Undeclared AI use counts as misconduct even if the AI use itself is not prohibited; always acknowledge and cite AI-generated content.
rq: Why is spellchecking considered a form of artificial intelligence in a strict sense?
Because it uses automated algorithms to process and correct text, which falls under the broad definition of AI.
What would make the use of an AI tool become academic misconduct, even though AI use itself is allowed?
Failing to acknowledge how the AI was used, or presenting AI-generated output as your own work.

notes.t: Ethical principles in engineering
pts: Ethical principles sit at the forefront of modern engineering practice.
The UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering define four fundamental principles of ethical behaviour.
Principle 1: honesty and integrity.
Principle 2: respect for life, law, the environment and public good.
Principles 3 and 4: accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication.
defs: Ethical principles (engineering)
Fundamental standards of ethical behaviour defined for the engineering profession by the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering, guiding professional conduct.
tips: Know all four principles by name; exam questions often ask you to list or briefly explain them.
Principle 2 bundles several concepts (life, law, environment, public good); name them all when describing it.
rq: Why might respect for the environment and public good be listed alongside respect for law as a single principle?
Engineering decisions affect society and the environment beyond the client, so professional duty extends to public welfare, not just legal compliance.
What could go wrong if an engineer had accurate calculations but poor communication?
Correct analysis could still be misunderstood or ignored, leading to unsafe decisions; leadership and communication ensure results are acted on properly.

notes.t: Ethical principles in engineering
pts: Ethics underpins safe engineering practice, protecting people from harm.
Ethical conduct sustains public trust in the engineering profession.
Ethical behaviour protects the reputation of companies and organisations.
Ethics encourages sustainable engineering practices and maintains quality and professional standards.
Adhering to ethics ensures high quality work and a high standard of professional engineer.
tips: Ethics is about more than legal compliance; it covers safety, sustainability, quality and public trust, so answers should cover several of these.
rq: Why might a company's reputation depend on the ethical conduct of its engineers?
Unethical or unsafe work can lead to failures, legal action and loss of client and public trust, damaging the organisation's commercial standing.
How does ethical practice relate to public confidence in engineering?
When engineers consistently act safely, honestly and responsibly, the public trusts that engineered products and infrastructure are reliable.

notes.t: Expectations of engineers in the 21st century
pts: Engineers are expected by both industry and academia to meet a range of skills and attitudes beyond pure technical knowledge.
The core expectations include technical knowledge, work ethic, teamwork, ethics, organisation and independence.
Industry actively seeks skilled, reliable and industrious people, so maintaining high standards is key.
rq: Why might communication and teamworking matter as much as technical accomplishment for an engineer's career?
Engineering projects are collaborative and engineers must explain and coordinate their work with others, so technical skill alone is rarely sufficient in industry.
What might happen to an engineering organisation if individuals lacked ethics, openness and honesty?
Trust, safety and reliability would be undermined, leading to errors being hidden, poor decisions and damage to reputation or public safety.

units.name: 1.7 Course introduction and contents (summary notes)
units.ov: This is the introduction to Basic Machine Elements. It outlines the course topics: valves and pumps, pumps in systems, heat exchangers, clutches, machinery mountings and gearboxes, plus basic fluid systems and engineering drawing. It also sets the conventions for communicating technical information (SI units, number formatting). The notes are only an outline, so the technical content below comes from what the contents pages list and from standard knowledge of these topics.
must: Use SI units throughout and convert every quantity before substituting into formulas; unit errors give answers wrong by orders of magnitude
Number format: decimal point is a full stop, and no commas as thousands separators (write 12500 or 12.5, not 12,500)
Pump-system matching: the operating point is where the pump curve intersects the system curve
System curve: \(H_{sys}=H_{static}+kQ^2\), so with static head it starts at a non-zero height on the head axis; check for static head first
Suction lift and static head both affect the pump duty and must be included in the system analysis
Heat exchanger types: plate and shell-and-tube, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials, so be ready to compare and justify a choice
Clutch types by purpose: dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, fluid coupling
Clutch analysis separates steady state (\(P=T\omega\), torque balance) from accelerating conditions (\(T-T_{load}=I\alpha\), which must include inertia)
Machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes: transmitting power loads the gearbox, so consider the effects of the transmitted torque and power
conn: Pump curve with system curve (static head plus friction) gives the operating point, and suction lift limits where the pump can be placed
Clutch torque, power and speed link to gearbox loading: \(P=T\omega\) sets the torque transmitted through the gearbox and onto its mountings
Accelerating clutch engagement needs inertia, \(T=I\alpha\), and the slipping energy dissipated is a heating problem, which links to thermal management
Unit consistency underlies all of these calculations (pressure to head, rpm to rad/s, kW to W)
exq: A pump delivers water through a pipe system with 15 m static head and friction losses \(kQ^2\). Given the pump curve data, plot both curves and find the operating flow rate and head.
Explain how suction lift affects pump selection and positioning, and state what changes in the system curve when static head is added.
Compare plate and shell-and-tube heat exchangers in terms of advantages, disadvantages and materials, and recommend one for a stated application.

A friction clutch connects a motor of known power and speed to a load of known inertia. Calculate the steady-state torque transmitted, then the torque needed to accelerate the load to speed in a given time.
Describe how a sprag clutch (overrunning) and a fluid coupling work and give one suitable application for each.

notes.t: Table of contents: Pumps in Systems, Heat Exchangers, Clutches, Machinery Mountings
pts: The notes cover pump-system matching, including system curves and pump curves, with static head and suction lift considered.
Heat exchangers are split into plate type and shell and tube type, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials.
Clutches are organised by purpose and type, including dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, and fluid couplings.
Torque, power and speed are treated separately for steady state and accelerating conditions in clutch analysis.
The final section covers machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, including the effects of transmitting power on a gearbox.
tips: Do not confuse the steady-state and accelerating torque conditions; accelerating analysis must include inertia effects.
Check whether a pump problem includes static head before drawing the system curve, as the curve starts at a different height.
rq: Why would a dog clutch be unsuitable for engaging while the shafts are rotating at different speeds?
Dog clutches have interlocking teeth that must align; with a speed difference the teeth would clash and cause shock loading and damage, so they are engaged at rest or near matched speed.
What is the key difference between steady-state and accelerating torque in a clutch?
Steady-state torque is what the clutch transmits at constant speed; accelerating torque additionally includes the torque needed to change the rotating inertia's speed.

notes.t: Communicating Technical Information in this Course
pts: Always use SI units, whatever is customary in your home country.
Write the decimal point as a full stop, not a comma.
Do not use commas to separate thousands in numbers, to avoid confusion with European decimal commas.
tips: Unit trap: convert all quantities to SI units before substituting into formulas, otherwise answers will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
Number formatting: write 12500 or 12.5 rather than 12,500 or 12,5 so markers read values unambiguously.
rq: Why does a comma used as a thousands separator cause problems in an international engineering context?
Because in many European countries the comma is the decimal point, so 1,500 could be read as 1.5 rather than 1500, risking a serious numerical error.

units.name: 2.1 Course intro and learning outcomes
units.ov: The material is only the intro and learning outcomes page for the Week 2 'Valves' topic of Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016). It sets out what must be learned: the engineering principles behind valve design, the types of valve, their key components, and the advantages and limitations of each type. The notes give no technical detail, so the lecture content is needed, especially for the Moodle quiz.

Be able to identify the different types of valve, by name and from a diagram

For each valve type, know its advantages and its limitations
Be able to compare valve types and choose the right one for a given application, justifying the choice
Use correct terminology and sketch labelled diagrams, as quiz questions are likely to test recognition

Design principles and application choice: selecting a valve means matching its strengths and limits to the operating requirements
Components and function: knowing what each part does lets you explain why a valve works and how it can fail or leak
Course notes and lecture content: the notes give the framework and the lectures give the detail the quiz tests

Compare two valve types, giving two advantages and two limitations of each.
Given a described application, select the most suitable valve type and justify your choice using the engineering principles of valve design.
Describe the function of each key component in a named valve and explain what happens if one fails.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes (valves)
pts: The course notes are a basic version of the lecture content, so additional lecture notes are needed for the Moodle quiz.
Students should understand the engineering principles used in valve design.
Students should be able to identify the different types of valve.
Students should be able to identify the key components of a valve.
Students should understand the advantages and limitations of each valve type.
tips: Do not rely only on the course notes; the lecture content is needed for the Moodle quiz.
rq: Why does the page say the course notes alone are not enough to score well on the Moodle quiz?
Because the notes are only a basic version of the lecture content, so the lecture adds detail that the quiz may test.
Why is knowing the advantages and limitations of a valve type more useful than just naming it?
Because engineers must choose the right valve for an application, which requires comparing the strengths and weaknesses of each type.

units.name: 2.2 Purposes of valves
units.ov: This module introduces the four basic purposes of valves in fluid systems: starting or stopping flow, regulating flow rate, setting or limiting pressure, and selecting flow direction or path. Valves appear across everyday and industrial settings, from taps and irrigation to oil and gas. The notes are purely qualitative, so top marks depend on naming the specific function precisely and linking it to a suitable example. The notes do not cover valve types, equations or numerical data.
must: The four functions of a valve: on/off, flow rate, pressure, direction. Exam answers often list these exactly.
On/off (isolation) function: a valve stops or starts the flow of fluid in a line.
Flow-rate function: a valve regulates how fast fluid moves through a system, usually by varying the opening, i.e. throttling.
Pressure function: a valve sets, regulates or limits pressure in a system, as in pressure-relief or pressure-regulating roles.
Direction function: a valve selects or changes the path the fluid takes, determining which way it flows.
Name the specific function in an answer. 'Controls flow' alone is too vague and loses marks.
The four roles are distinct. Do not conflate stopping/starting, rate, pressure and direction.
Applications span everyday and industrial use: taps, irrigation, and oil and gas.
Be able to link each function to a concrete example. Taps and irrigation suit on/off and flow rate; oil and gas suit pressure limiting and routing.
conn: Flow rate and pressure are linked: throttling a valve to change flow rate also changes the pressure drop across it, so the two functions often occur together.
On/off and flow-rate functions both act on the valve opening. Full open/closed gives isolation, while partial opening gives regulation.
Direction control (path selection) works with on/off, since diverting flow means closing one path and opening another.
Pressure limiting is a safety function that complements normal flow control in industrial systems such as oil and gas.
exq: List and briefly describe the four main purposes of valves in a fluid system. (4 marks)

For each of the following applications, state which valve function is primary and justify it: a kitchen tap, a garden irrigation system, an oil pipeline relief valve, a diverter in a pipework network.
Explain the difference between a valve that regulates flow rate and one that regulates pressure, giving an example of each.
Why is the statement 'a valve controls flow' an insufficient answer to 'state the purpose of a valve'? Rewrite it as a full-mark answer.
Describe how a single system, such as an industrial oil and gas line, might use all four valve functions, naming where each would be applied.

notes.t: Purposes of valves
pts: Valves can stop or start the flow of a fluid in a line.
Valves regulate how fast fluid moves through a system.
Valves set or limit the pressure within a system.
Valves select or change the path the fluid takes through a system.
tips: Remember the four functions as: on/off, flow rate, pressure, and direction; exam answers often list these exactly.
rq: Why would a system need a valve that controls flow rate rather than simply an on/off valve?
Some processes need a specific, adjustable amount of fluid delivered over time, so a throttling valve sets the rate continuously rather than only fully open or fully closed.

notes.t: What valves are used for
pts: Valves can stop or start the flow of a fluid.
Valves regulate how fast fluid flows through a system.
Valves set or regulate the pressure within a system.
Valves determine which direction the fluid flows.
Valves are found in many everyday and industrial applications, from taps and irrigation to oil and gas.
tips: Distinguish the four functions clearly: stopping/starting, rate, pressure and direction are different roles, and an exam answer should name the specific function rather than just 'controls flow'.
rq: Why would a system need a valve to control direction of flow rather than simply stopping flow?
A direction-control valve lets fluid be routed to different paths or reversed (e.g. to change the motion of an actuator) without the flow having to be shut off entirely.

units.name: 2.3 Design principles: fluid mechanics, materials and statics
units.ov: The module links three areas of design: fluid mechanics (pressure difference, resistance, turbulence and flow-rate in pipes), materials (corrosion and erosion resistance for valves and meters) and statics (strength to contain pressure, plus the machine elements that make a valve work). A valve or flow meter shows how they combine. The fluid sets the pressure and velocity, which sets the material and strength requirements, and the machine elements (stem, seals, fasteners, bearings) deliver the function. The ultrasonic flow meter is the worked example of measurement.
must: Flow-rate is set by the driving pressure difference and the total system resistance together: \(Q \propto \Delta p/R\) in the simple picture. A pump supplies the \(\Delta p\).

Pressure drop accumulates along the pipe, so for the same flow rate \(\Delta p \propto L\) and doubling length doubles the pressure needed. Check the units: 1 m of water head \(\approx 0.1\) bar (\(p=\rho g h\approx 9.81\) kPa).

Resistance rises with internal roughness (measured in microns), with bends, corners and fittings, and with turbulence. Deviation from a circular bore raises resistance through secondary flows. The design aim is minimum resistance when a valve is fully open.
Turbulence is irregular swirling mixing caused by corners, high velocity and drag. It increases drag, noise, resistance and erosion, but it can help heat transfer and mixing, so it is not always bad.

Corrosion is chemical or electrochemical attack, while erosion is mechanical wear by the moving fluid, often carrying particles. A material can resist one and not the other, so choose it to match the fluid and conditions as well as the strength needed.

Typical materials: stainless steel, aluminium, bronze, copper and galvanised steel for corrosion and erosion resistance. Valves are commonly made from brass, bronze, cast iron and steel alloys, balancing strength, cost and compatibility.
Statics requirement: the valve body must be strong enough to resist internal pressure (stress from pressure must stay below the material's strength, with a safety factor).

Ultrasonic transit-time flow meter: pulses cross the pipe at an angle (60° to the flow axis in the notes), and the transit-time difference gives the velocity component along the beam. Correct for the angle with the geometry, e.g. \(v=\dfrac{L}{2\cos\theta}\dfrac{t_{up}-t_{down}}{t_{up}t_{down}}\) with \(\theta\) measured from the flow axis. Calibration is judged against the ideal \(y=x\) line, which the notes show holding over 0–40 m/s.
A valve is an assembly of machine elements: stems or shafts transmit motion to the closure, and fasteners join parts (bolts and washers are non-permanent).

Seals and bearings: static seals sit between parts that do not move relative to each other, and dynamic seals between parts that do. Bearings either constrain motion or reduce friction, so state which in an answer.
conn: Turbulence, resistance and erosion: corners and high velocity cause turbulence, which raises \(\Delta p\) (so a bigger pump is needed) and erodes surfaces. This feeds directly into material choice and the geometry of valve and pipe interiors.
Pressure and strength: the system pressure from the pump and the head sets the load on the valve body, which links fluid mechanics to wall-thickness and material-strength checks in statics.

Valve function and machine elements: the stem passing through the body needs a dynamic seal and bearings, the body joints need static seals and bolts, and all of these must be compatible with the fluid (corrosion) and the pressure (strength).

Flow measurement and geometry: the meter's accuracy depends on beam angle and path length (geometry), on the flow profile (turbulence and pipe shape) and on a body material that resists corrosion and erosion so the calibration does not drift.
exq: A pump must deliver a given flow through a pipe run. Explain how the required pressure difference changes if the length is doubled, and convert a 15 m head of water into bar and kPa.
List four factors that increase flow resistance in a pipe system. Discuss two situations where turbulence is a disadvantage and one where it is an advantage.

Distinguish corrosion from erosion. For a valve handling water with suspended particles at high velocity, recommend and justify a body material from stainless steel, bronze, cast iron or galvanised steel.

An ultrasonic meter has path length \(L\), beam angle 60° to the flow axis and measured up- and downstream transit times. Derive or use the transit-time expression to find the flow velocity, and explain why the angle correction is needed.
Name the machine elements in a gate or globe valve. State the function of each and explain the difference between static and dynamic seals, with a location for each in the valve.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: fluid mechanics
pts: Flow resistance in a pipe increases when the cross-section deviates from circular, because secondary flows raise the pressure drop.
Water can only flow through a pipe system if a pressure difference exists, usually supplied by a circulation pump.
Flow-rate depends on two primary factors, which the slide asks students to identify (for example, the pressure difference driving the flow and the resistance of the pipe system).
tips: Do not assume pressure drop is independent of pipe shape; any deviation from a circular bore increases resistance.
Flow-rate is not set by pressure alone; always consider the resistance of the system as well.
rq: Why does a non-circular pipe cross-section increase the pressure drop for the same flow?
Non-circular sections create secondary flows and local velocity variations, adding energy losses so a larger pressure difference is needed to maintain the same flow-rate.
What would happen to water flow in a pipe system if the circulation pump were removed?
There would be no pressure difference to drive the flow, so the water would stop flowing (apart from gravity-driven flow if there is a height difference).

notes.t: Fluid mechanics: resistance, pressure difference and flow-rate in pipes
pts: Flow through a pipe system requires a pressure difference, usually supplied by a circulation pump.
Flow-rate depends on the pressure difference between two points and the total restriction of the pipe.
Pressure drop accumulates with every metre of pipe, so doubling the length doubles the pressure needed for the same flow rate.
Non-circular cross-sections cause secondary flows that increase the pressure drop (Venturi effect).
defs: Pressure head
The height of a fluid column that produces a given pressure; here 1 m of water corresponds to 0.1 bar.
tips: Keep track of units: 1 m of water head is about 0.1 bar, not 1 bar.
Flow rate depends on pressure difference and total restriction together, not on pressure alone.
rq: Why does doubling the length of a pipe double the pressure needed for the same flow rate?
Because every metre of pipe adds a pressure drop (friction/restriction), and these drops accumulate along the length, so the total pressure required scales with length.
What would happen to the flow rate if the pipe bore were non-circular but the pressure difference stayed the same?
The flow rate would fall, because secondary flows increase the pressure drop and so the total restriction rises.

notes.t: Fluid mechanics: flow resistance and turbulence in pipes
pts: Resistance to flow depends on the internal roughness of a pipe, measured in microns.
Resistance to flow increases with turbulence and when the fluid stream changes shape.
Turbulence is mixing of fluid through swirls, caused by corners, high velocities and drag.
Turbulence causes erosion on the internal surfaces of a pipe.
Design aim is to minimise flow resistance in an open condition.
defs: Turbulence
Irregular, swirling mixing of a fluid's flow, which increases flow resistance and can erode pipe surfaces.
Roughness (of a pipe)
The measure of internal surface smoothness of a pipe, typically expressed in microns, which governs resistance to flow.
tips: Roughness is measured in microns, a length unit; do not confuse it with flow velocity or pressure.
Turbulence is caused by geometry (corners), high velocity and drag, not by smoothness alone.
rq: Why does a sharp corner in a pipe increase flow resistance?
It changes the fluid stream's shape, creating swirling turbulence that mixes the flow and dissipates energy, raising resistance.
Why might a smoother pipe lower the energy needed to pump a fluid, even at the same flow rate?
Smoother internal surfaces reduce turbulence and friction at the wall, so less energy is lost to swirling and drag.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: fluid mechanics and turbulent flow
pts: Turbulent flow can be either advantageous or disadvantageous in a design.
Turbulence increases air resistance (drag) and noise, which are usually undesirable in products.
Turbulence can also speed up heat conduction and thermal mixing, which may be beneficial.
Designers must understand, handle and control turbulent flows to achieve successful product design.
tips: Do not state that turbulence is always bad; the page stresses it can be advantageous depending on the application.
rq: Why might a designer deliberately create turbulence in one product but try to eliminate it in another?

Turbulence raises drag and noise (undesirable where streamlined, quiet operation matters) but enhances heat transfer and mixing (desirable in heat exchangers or mixing systems), so the design goal determines whether it is wanted.

notes.t: Engineering design principles and ultrasonic flow measurement
pts: Good engineering design draws on fluid mechanics, materials (including corrosion and erosion behaviour) and statics, particularly strength.
An ultrasonic flow meter infers fluid velocity by sending sound pulses across the pipe at an angle and measuring their transit times; an array of paths improves the measurement.
The measured flow velocity from the ultrasonic array closely tracks the reference velocity across the full range of 0 to 40 m/s, showing good linearity.
A single transducer fires at 60° to the flow axis, so the path length and the velocity component along the flow must be accounted for in the calibration.
defs: Corrosion
Chemical or electrochemical degradation of a material by its environment, reducing its section and strength over time.
Erosion
Progressive material loss caused by the mechanical action of a moving fluid, often carrying particles, on a surface.
Strength
The ability of a material or component to resist failure under applied stress, a key concern of statics in design.
tips: Ultrasonic transit-time velocity uses only the component of flow along the beam; with the transducer at 60° the measured velocity must be corrected by the geometric factor.
Corrosion and erosion are different mechanisms: corrosion is chemical/electrochemical, erosion is mechanical wear by the fluid.
rq: Why does the ultrasonic meter use several measurement paths across the diametral plane rather than one?
Flow velocity is not uniform across the pipe cross-section, so multiple chordal paths sample the profile and give a more representative mean velocity.
Why must corrosion and erosion be considered alongside fluid mechanics when designing a flow meter body?
Fluid flow can wear or chemically attack the meter wall, changing its geometry and strength, which would alter the measured flow and the structural integrity.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: materials for valves and flow-meter bodies
pts: Materials chosen for corrosion and/or erosion resistance, e.g. stainless steel, aluminium, bronze, copper and galvanised steel, suit fluid-handling components.
Valves are commonly made from brass, bronze, cast iron and steel alloys, balancing strength, cost and fluid compatibility.

Ultrasonic flow measurement uses transducers that send ultrasound obliquely across the pipe; the flow velocity is inferred from the transit times, and the measurement is compared against a reference velocity to check accuracy.
defs: Corrosion resistance
The ability of a material to withstand chemical or electrochemical attack from the surrounding fluid or environment without significant loss of material or function.
Erosion resistance
The ability of a material to withstand progressive material loss caused by the mechanical action of a flowing fluid, often carrying particles or at high velocity.
tips: Distinguish corrosion (chemical attack) from erosion (mechanical wear by flow); materials may resist one but not the other.
Material choice must match the fluid and operating conditions, not just strength.
rq: Why might a valve be made of bronze rather than plain carbon steel in a water line?
Bronze resists corrosion in water and is easy to cast and machine, so it lasts longer in wet, possibly aggressive environments.
Why are the ultrasonic transducers mounted at an angle (60°) rather than straight across the pipe?
The angled path lets the ultrasound travel partly along the flow, so the difference in transit times upstream and downstream gives the flow velocity.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: mechanics (statics) and ultrasonic flow measurement
pts: Valve bodies must have enough strength to resist the internal pressure of the system.
Opening and closing mechanisms for valves need basic mechanical components to operate.
Ultrasonic flow meters infer flow velocity from ultrasound travelling diagonally across the meter body at an angle to the flow; the measured velocities track the reference flow velocity closely.
tips: Do not confuse the 'strength to resist pressure' requirement (statics) with the flow measurement principle; the page covers both in one slide.
The reference line on the flow calibration graph is the ideal y = x relation; measured values should lie close to it.
rq: Why must the meter body be designed in statics as well as for flow measurement?
Because it is a pressure-containing part, so its wall and structure must resist the system pressure without failing, independent of how well it measures flow.
Why is the ultrasonic beam angled (about 60°) to the flow rather than sent straight across the pipe?
An angled path has a component along the flow, so the transit time difference between upstream and downstream beams depends on flow velocity and can be used to measure it.

notes.t: Machine elements required for valves
pts: A valve is an assembly of smaller machine elements, not a single part.
Shafts (stems) transmit motion to the valve closure element.
Seals prevent leakage; static seals sit between non-moving parts, dynamic seals between moving parts.
Fasteners connect parts together; non-permanent fasteners such as bolts and washers allow disassembly.
Bearings either constrain motion or reduce friction between moving surfaces.
defs: Static seal
A seal that prevents leakage between two surfaces that do not move relative to each other.
Dynamic seal
A seal that prevents leakage between surfaces that move relative to each other, such as a rotating or sliding stem.
Non-permanent fastener
A fastener, such as a bolt with a washer, that connects parts and can be removed without damaging them.
tips: Do not confuse static and dynamic seals: the key distinction is whether the sealed surfaces move relative to each other.
Bearings serve two different purposes (constraining motion and reducing friction); state which purpose applies in an answer.
