\(\dot{v}\) = flow rate (m³/s); \(A\) = area of piston crown (m²); \(K\) = piston stroke (m); \(V\) = leakage volume per stroke (m³); \(S\) = speed, e.g. revolutions per second (s⁻¹)
tips: Keep units consistent: \(A\) in m², \(K\) in m and \(S\) in s⁻¹ give flow in m³/s; RPS must not be mixed with RPM.
Remember that \(V\) is subtracted, so leakage always reduces the theoretical flow.
rq: Why does moving the piston backwards cause the discharge valve to close and fluid to enter the cylinder?

Backward motion increases the cylinder volume, reducing pressure below the suction side pressure; the higher pressure above pushes the discharge valve shut and the lower pressure opens the suction valve, drawing fluid in.
What happens to the flow rate predicted by the equation if the pump leaks more badly?
V increases, so (AK − V) decreases and the actual flow rate falls, since leakage subtracts from the swept volume delivered per stroke.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: simple piston pump
pts: A piston pump uses a cylinder in a casing with a piston attached to a connecting rod; the high-pressure seal reciprocates with the piston.
Piston pumps can move liquids or compress gases, and high pressure can be reached without a strong drop in flow rate.
Down-strokes create pressure differentials that fill the pump chamber; up-strokes force the fluid out for use.
Suited to viscous media and fluids containing solid particles, and to systems needing high, consistent pressure such as water irrigation or delivery.
Because pressure varies widely over each cycle, a safety mechanism (e.g. a relief valve) is required.
defs: Positive displacement pump

A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a chamber and mechanically displacing it, so flow is set by the swept volume and cycle rate rather than by the discharge pressure.
tips: Positive displacement pumps are not restricted to liquids: piston pumps can also compress gases, so do not state that they only move liquids.
Always include a pressure safety/relief device when describing piston pumps, since pressure variations are large.
rq: Why does a piston pump keep its flow rate roughly constant when the discharge pressure rises?
Each stroke displaces a fixed swept volume, so the delivered volume per cycle is set by geometry, not by the resistance against it; only leakage (slip) reduces flow at high pressure.
What would happen to the pump if the outlet were blocked and the piston kept moving?
Pressure would rise sharply because the fixed volume cannot escape, so the pump, pipework and seals could fail; this is why a safety (relief) mechanism is required.

notes.t: Characteristics of piston pumps (positive displacement pumps)
pts: Piston pumps are positive displacement machines: a piston draws fluid into a cylinder and then pushes it out through valves, so each stroke delivers a fixed volume.
Inlet and outlet check valves control flow direction; if the pump is inverted, valves must be retained (e.g., by springs, retainers or housing geometry) so they do not fall out.
Leakage paths exist between the piston and cylinder bore, around valve seats and at joints, and these reduce volumetric efficiency.
Seals are needed where the moving piston or rod passes through the housing and at valve seats to prevent leakage and loss of pressure.
Space usage should be judged: the dead volume around the cylinder and valve passages reduces efficiency and compactness of the design.
tips: Do not confuse the valves' purpose: check valves allow one-way flow, and their retention in an inverted pump is a mechanical design issue, not a flow issue.
Leakage paths and dead (unswept) volume are distinct: leakage reduces delivered flow, while dead volume reduces compression and space efficiency.
rq: Why does inverting a piston pump put the valves at risk, and what would you do to retain them?
Gravity acts on the valve elements, so they can drop out of their seats or housing; retain them with springs, caps, or a captive housing design.
Why must leakage be minimised in a positive displacement pump even though it still moves fluid?
Leakage lets fluid slip back past the piston or valves, so the actual delivered flow falls below the swept-volume flow, lowering volumetric efficiency.

notes.t: Double acting piston pump
pts: A double acting piston pump has two sets of check valves, with fluid acting on both sides of the piston.
Moving the piston in both directions completes a full pumping cycle, so each stroke delivers fluid.
While one side of the piston is intaking fluid, the other side is exhausting fluid simultaneously.
Drawbacks are more parts, difficult maintenance, and a large physical footprint.
defs: Double acting piston pump
A positive displacement pump in which fluid is drawn in and discharged on both sides of the piston, using two sets of check valves, so every stroke pumps.
tips: Do not confuse double acting with double-headed or two-cylinder pumps; the defining feature is fluid on both sides of one piston with two sets of check valves.
rq: Why does a double acting pump deliver fluid on both strokes, while a single acting pump delivers only on one?
Because fluid acts on both faces of the piston, so the side that is moving away from the inlet is simultaneously exhausting while the other side intakes, giving a discharge on each stroke.
What is the trade-off in choosing a double acting pump over a simpler design?
It gives higher, smoother output per cycle but needs more parts, more valves, more maintenance and more space.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: double acting piston pump and accumulator
pts: Dynamic seals (piston rings) seal the moving piston against the cylinder wall, while static seals are where the piston rod passes through the body.
A cross-head converts the rotary motion of the crank into linear reciprocating motion of the piston rod.
A relief valve is mandatory on a positive displacement pump, because the pump delivers flow regardless of downstream resistance and would otherwise over-pressurise the system.
An accumulator absorbs pressure pulses caused by large pressure variations, acting like a capacitor smoothing voltage fluctuations.
An accumulator stores energy for later use during low demand, which allows a smaller pump to be used.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping and mechanically displacing it, so flow is largely independent of discharge pressure.
Accumulator
A pressure vessel containing a gas (air bladder) that absorbs hydraulic pressure pulses and stores energy for later use.
tips: Do not confuse dynamic seals (moving, e.g. piston rings) with static seals (stationary interfaces, e.g. where the rod passes through the body).
An accumulator stores energy but does not generate flow; it only smooths pulses and supplies stored energy during low demand.
rq: Why must a relief valve always be fitted to a positive displacement pump, even if the system has other protection?
Because the pump forces a fixed volume per stroke regardless of resistance, so with a blocked outlet pressure would rise until the pump or pipework fails; the relief valve limits this pressure.
What would happen to pressure in the discharge line if the accumulator were removed, and why does a smaller pump become possible with it fitted?
Pressure would fluctuate strongly with each piston stroke; the accumulator smooths these pulses and stores energy during low demand, so the pump only needs to meet average rather than peak demand.

units.name: 3.4 Pressure ripple, accumulators and PD pump characteristics
units.ov: This module covers why positive displacement (PD) pumps produce pulsating discharge pressure, how single- and double-acting piston pumps differ, and how an accumulator smooths the ripple. It also covers the PD pump pressure-flow characteristic. The ideas are linked by electrical analogies (rectifier and smoothing capacitor, mass-inertia, compliance), which let pulsation and smoothing be treated as circuit behaviour.
must: PD pump definition: it traps and displaces a fixed volume per cycle, so flow is set by speed and geometry rather than by pressure.
Single-acting piston pump: pressure is delivered only on the delivery half-cycle, giving positive humps separated by zero-pressure gaps (analogue of half-wave rectification).
Double-acting piston pump: it delivers on both strokes, so there are no gaps, and the pulse frequency is twice that of a single-acting pump (analogue of full-wave rectification).
Accumulator: it charges during delivery and discharges more slowly, lengthening the pressure-decay periods and reducing ripple (analogue of a smoothing capacitor).
The accumulator does not raise the peak pressure and does not remove pulses; it only reduces fluctuation about the mean.
Accumulator absorbs part of the pump flow, so the system outlet flow is not the full pump flow; real delivery is also reduced by volumetric and mechanical efficiency below 100%.
PD pump characteristic: the discharge pressure vs flow curve is steep and nearly vertical, unlike the rising head-flow curve of a centrifugal pump.
The curve leans backwards because internal leakage (slip) increases with discharge pressure; higher speed shifts the whole curve to higher flow.
Flow is proportional to the pressure differential across the system, not to pressure alone.

Mechanical-electrical analogies map by role: voltage to force/pump, current to flow/velocity, resistance to friction, capacitance to compliance (accumulator), inductance to mass/inertia, transformer to lever.
conn: The rectifier analogy (half-wave, full-wave, three-phase) links pump type to ripple frequency and shape, and the accumulator acts as the smoothing capacitor on that waveform.
Accumulator compliance (capacitance) together with line inertia (inductance) and friction (resistance) forms an RLC-type circuit that determines how much ripple is attenuated.
Slip and efficiency link the characteristic curve to real delivered flow: leakage rises with pressure, so delivered flow falls, and the accumulator then diverts some of it from the outlet.
Pump speed sets the flow (shifts the curve) and also sets the pulse frequency, which affects ripple.
exq: Sketch the discharge pressure waveform for a single-acting and a double-acting piston pump over two revolutions, and state the ripple frequency of each at a given speed, e.g. 1200 rpm.
Explain with an electrical analogy how an accumulator reduces pressure ripple. Why does it not change the peak pressure? Draw the waveform with and without it.
Draw the pressure-flow characteristic of a PD pump and compare it with a centrifugal pump. Explain the backward lean and show the effect of doubling the speed.
Draw the hydraulic-electrical analogy table (pump, turbine, diaphragm, pipe friction, lever) and use it to build an equivalent circuit for a pump-accumulator-pipe system.
A PD pump has a theoretical flow of 20 L/min and a volumetric efficiency of 92%. Estimate the actual delivered flow, and discuss how the accumulator affects the mean and instantaneous outlet flow.

notes.t: Mechanical-electrical analogies
pts: In a pipe system, electrical current corresponds to the flow of fluid.
An inductor can be modelled by a turbine, since both resist changes in flow through inertia.
A voltage source can be modelled by a pump that drives the fluid.
A capacitor can be modelled by a diaphragm inside the pipe that stores displaced fluid.
Voltage maps to force, current to velocity, resistance to friction, capacitance to compliance, inductance to mass and transformer to lever.
tips: Analogies map quantities by role, not by units: voltage (V) is not the same unit as force (N), so keep the correspondence conceptual.
Inductance maps to mass (inertia), not to friction; confusing resistance with inertia is a common error.
rq: Why does a turbine behave like an inductor in the fluid analogy?
Its rotating mass resists changes in flow rate, just as an inductor opposes changes in current, so inertia corresponds to inductance.
Why is a diaphragm a sensible analogue for a capacitor?
It stores fluid by deflecting and resists pressure build-up, just as a capacitor stores charge and voltage builds up across it.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: discharge pressure characteristics
pts: A single-piston pump delivers pressure only during one half of each revolution; the other half is intake (suction) with no output pressure.
The discharge pressure waveform of a piston pump is a series of positive hump pulses separated by zero-pressure gaps, one hump per piston stroke.
The pulsed output of a piston pump is analogous to a half-wave rectified electrical signal, which is why it is useful to model it with rectifier ideas.
To analyse the waveform, imagine the piston is at the middle of its stroke when considering the cycle.
defs: Positive displacement pump

A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it and mechanically displacing it, so discharge is driven by the moving boundary (e.g. a piston) rather than by continuous kinetic energy transfer.
tips: Do not assume the piston pump gives a continuous output pressure; the waveform is zero during intake, so average and peak pressures must be treated separately.
Remember the waveform is shown in arbitrary units for both pressure and time, so only the shape and relative behaviour are meaningful, not numerical values.
rq: Why does a single-piston pump's output pressure drop to zero for half of each revolution, and what does this imply for smoothing the flow?

During the intake half-cycle the piston draws fluid in and nothing is pushed out, so there is no discharge pressure. The pulsating output means a single piston gives a pulsed, non-continuous flow, so multi-piston arrangements or accumulators are needed to smooth it, just as a half-wave rectifier needs a smoothing capacitor.
How is the piston pump's output waveform analogous to a half-wave rectifier, and what does the 'missing' half represent in each system?

A half-wave rectifier passes only the positive half of an AC cycle and blocks the negative half. Similarly the pump only delivers pressure during the discharge half-stroke; the intake half produces no output, playing the role of the blocked half-cycle.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: discharge pressure of a double-acting piston pump
pts: A double-acting piston pump delivers fluid on both strokes, so the discharge pressure has no gaps between pulses.
The discharge pressure waveform is a series of repeated humps that drop to zero twice per cycle, assuming both sides run at the same speed.
The output pressure pattern is analogous to full-wave rectification of an AC signal, so the pulse frequency is double that of a single-acting pump.
tips: The waveform shows pulses dropping to zero only at the points where the strokes change over; do not assume a constant pressure output.
The analogy to rectification describes the pulse pattern only; the pressure values are arbitrary units on this page.
rq: Why does a double-acting piston pump produce a smoother discharge than a single-acting pump?
Because it pumps fluid on both the forward and return strokes, so there is a delivery pulse on every stroke and no interval of zero flow, giving twice as many pulses per revolution.
What would the output waveform look like if only one side of the piston delivered fluid?
It would resemble half-wave rectification: a series of humps separated by gaps at zero pressure, with half as many pulses per cycle.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: accumulator effect on output pressure ripple
pts: An accumulator smooths the pulsating output pressure of a positive displacement pump, analogous to voltage smoothing after rectification.
Without an accumulator the pressure pulses sharply; with one, it charges during each delivery stroke and then discharges more slowly, producing a ripple.
The accumulator does not change the peak pressure; it reduces the fluctuation between peaks by lengthening the decreasing-pressure periods.
The response resembles three-phase rectification, where output pulses overlap to give a smoother waveform than single-phase rectification.
Ripple arises from alternating charging (pressurisation) and longer discharging (pressure decrease) phases.
tips: Do not claim the accumulator increases peak pressure; the peak is the same with or without it, only the ripple changes.
Ripple is a time-varying pressure about a mean; state that the smoothing effect comes from longer discharge periods, not from removing the pulses entirely.
rq: Why does adding an accumulator not raise the peak output pressure of a positive displacement pump?

The peak is set by the pump's delivery and the load/relief conditions; the accumulator only stores fluid during the peak and releases it later, so it flattens the variation between peaks rather than increasing the maximum.
Why would a hydraulic system need smoother pressure, e.g. in a braking or control circuit?
Pressure ripple causes vibration, noise, inconsistent actuator motion and wear; a steadier pressure gives more precise, predictable control and safer braking.

notes.t: Positive displacement pump characteristics and accumulator effect
pts: Pump output pressure rises when flowrate is increased; the pressure profile is pulsating because of the piston strokes.
Flow is directly proportional to the pressure differential across the pump system.
The accumulator absorbs part of the pump delivery, so the system outlet never receives the full pump flowrate.
Real pumps deliver less than the theoretical flow because mechanical and volumetric efficiencies are below 100%.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it and forcing it out, e.g. a piston pump.
Accumulator
A pressure storage device that absorbs pressure peaks from the pump and releases stored fluid, smoothing the output pressure and flow.
tips: Do not assume the theoretical pump flow equals the system outlet flow; account for accumulator storage and volumetric/mechanical efficiency losses.
Flow is proportional to pressure differential, not to pressure alone; check which difference is being used in calculations.
rq: Why does the accumulator make the system flowrate lower than the pump's maximum flowrate, even though the pump is delivering fluid continuously?
Part of the pump output is diverted into the accumulator to charge it during pressure peaks, so less fluid reaches the system outlet at that moment.
Why does a real pump never deliver the theoretical flow?
Internal leakage (volumetric losses) and friction (mechanical losses) mean efficiencies are below 100%, so actual delivered flow is less than the calculated displacement flow.

notes.t: Positive displacement pump characteristics
pts: For a positive displacement pump, discharge pressure is plotted as a function of flow rate, giving a steep curve.
The curve is classic positive displacement: the flow is almost fixed by pump speed and geometry, so the curve is nearly vertical rather than rising with head like a centrifugal pump.
The curve leans backwards (flow falls slightly as pressure rises) because internal leakage (slip) increases with discharge pressure.
Turning the pump faster increases the displaced volume per unit time, shifting the whole curve to higher flow rate.
tips: Do not confuse the positive displacement curve (near-vertical, flow almost independent of pressure) with the rising head-flow curve of a centrifugal pump.
Do not assume the backwards lean is caused by friction alone; it is due to internal leakage (slip) increasing with discharge pressure.
rq: What happens to the pump curve if you turn the pump faster, and why?
The curve shifts to higher flow rate at each pressure, because more fluid is displaced per revolution per unit time, so volumetric flow scales with pump speed.
Why does a positive displacement pump's flow barely change as discharge pressure rises?
Each cycle traps and displaces a fixed volume; only internal leakage (slip) past clearances increases with pressure, so flow falls only slightly.

units.name: 3.5 Rotary PD pumps: gear, lobe, vane and screw
units.ov: This material covers rotary positive displacement (PD) pumps: gear (spur, helical, herringbone), lobe, sliding vane and screw. Each traps a fixed volume of fluid in chambers and carries it from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed and is largely independent of discharge pressure. The ideas connect through displacement per revolution, slip and leakage through small clearances, and axial thrust and its balancing.
must: Definition of a PD pump: traps a fixed volume and forces it from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed and is largely independent of discharge pressure, apart from leakage/slip

Ideal gear pump flow: \(\dot{v} = A\,l\,N\,S\), with \(A\) the area between two teeth and the casing (m²), \(l\) tooth length (m), \(N\) number of teeth and \(S\) speed (rev/s). Keep units consistent and state that real flow is lower

Gear pump operation: fluid is carried round the outside of the gears in the casing on the side where the teeth unmesh (suction), not squeezed through the mesh. Clearances are microns, so wear or contamination raises slip and cuts efficiency
Gear pump types and thrust: spur, helical, herringbone and planetary. Helical is smoother and quieter than spur but gives axial end-thrust. Herringbone cancels the thrust with opposed helix angles
Lobe pump: a gear-pump variant with non-contacting lobed rotors, usually driven through external timing gears. Suited to viscous or shear-sensitive fluids

Sliding vane pump: eccentric rotor in a stator, with vanes sliding radially in slots. The eccentric geometry, not the spinning alone, changes chamber volume. Vanes are held against the wall by springs, pressure or centrifugal force, and vane wear and leakage are key failure modes
Vane material is matched to the fluid: steel for hydraulic oil pumps, graphite for air compressors

Screw pump: fluid moves axially in cavities formed by meshing screws and is discharged at the outlet. Flow is low-pulsation, quiet and reliable, and suits lubricating fluids. This differs from the radial flow of a centrifugal pump

Screw pump thrust balancing: a single screw needs a thrust bearing, usually in the motor. Two opposite-hand screws with suction at both ends and central discharge cancel the axial thrust. Location bearings are still needed
Auxiliary components: the relief valve is a pressure-limiting safety device that returns fluid to suction, not a flow control. The mechanical or lip seal stops leakage along the shaft
conn: Slip and leakage link every pump type: small clearances (gear), vane-to-wall contact (vane), and screw cavity sealing all set the gap between ideal flow \(A l N S\) and real flow, and so volumetric efficiency and wear

Axial thrust recurs in helical gears and screw pumps. The cure is symmetry: opposed helix angles (herringbone) and opposite-hand screws with double-ended suction. Questions ask why a thrust bearing is or isn't needed
Because flow is fixed per revolution, blocking the outlet makes pressure rise without limit, so a relief valve is needed. This links the PD definition to safety and circuit design
Fluid properties drive pump choice: viscous fluids suit gear and lobe pumps, lubricating fluids suit screw pumps, and the fluid type sets the vane material
exq: A gear pump has tooth-space area 40 mm² between two teeth and the casing, tooth length 25 mm, 12 teeth and speed 1500 rpm. Calculate the ideal volumetric flow rate in m³/s and L/min. If the measured flow is 85% of ideal, find the volumetric efficiency and the slip flow.
Explain, with a sketch, how a gear pump draws in and delivers fluid. State on which side of the mesh the fluid is carried and why the clearances must be so small.
Compare spur, helical and herringbone gears in a gear pump in terms of noise, smoothness and axial thrust. Explain how herringbone gears cancel end-thrust.

Describe the operation of a sliding vane pump. Explain how the eccentric rotor produces pumping, how the vanes stay in contact with the wall, and why vane material differs between hydraulic oil pumps and air compressors.
Explain how a double-ended screw pump with opposite-hand threads avoids needing a thrust bearing. State what the bearings in the drawing do, and the role of the relief valve and mechanical seal.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: gear pump
pts: A gear pump uses meshing gears to move fluid; it is a positive displacement pump.
Gear pumps suit viscous fluids because the sealed gear chambers carry the fluid positively.
As gears separate at the intake, a void forms and generates suction.
Fluid is carried round the outside of the gears in the casing from intake to exit, not squeezed through the mesh.
Internal clearances are very small, around microns, which limits leakage and slip.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that traps a fixed volume of fluid in a chamber and forces it from the inlet to the outlet, giving a flow largely independent of discharge pressure.
tips: Determine suction from the direction of rotation: fluid is carried round the casing on the side where the teeth unmesh, not where they mesh.
Gear pump clearances are microns, so contamination or wear quickly increases slip and reduces efficiency.
rq: Why does a gear pump deliver fluid even when the outlet is blocked (a relief valve is needed)?
Because it is positive displacement: it traps a fixed volume per revolution and pushes it regardless of pressure, so pressure rises until a relief valve opens or the pump is damaged.
What would happen to suction if the gears turned in the opposite direction?
The inlet and outlet would swap roles: the side where the teeth separate becomes the suction side, so the flow reverses direction.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: gear pump
pts: A gear pump is a positive displacement pump: fluid trapped between gear teeth and the casing is carried from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed.
The drawing shows the driven gear and idler gear meshing inside a body, with a lip seal and seal cover on the shaft and white metal bushes supporting the gears.
Ideal volumetric flow rate is proportional to the trapped area, tooth length, number of teeth and shaft speed; real pumps deliver less because of leakage and slip.
The question asks what may be wrong with the drawing, so the student should check the gear meshing and the sealing/bearing arrangement against how a real gear pump works.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per revolution or cycle by trapping it in cavities and forcing it out, so output is largely independent of outlet pressure apart from leakage.
Idler gear
The gear that is not directly driven but meshes with the driven gear, transferring fluid in the gear pump and rotating in the opposite direction.
eqs: Ideal volumetric flow rate of a gear pump

\(\dot{v}\) = volumetric flow rate (m³/s); \(A\) = area enclosed between two gear teeth and the casing (m²); \(l\) = length of gear tooth (m); \(N\) = number of gear teeth (–); \(S\) = speed, e.g. rev/s (s⁻¹)
tips: Keep units consistent: with \(S\) in rev/s, \(\dot{v}\) comes out in m³/s only if \(A\) is in m² and \(l\) in m; mixing mm and m gives errors of 10⁹.
The equation gives the ideal flow; always state that real flow is lower due to slip/leakage.
rq: Why does doubling the shaft speed double the ideal flow rate, but not the pressure developed?
Flow is proportional to speed (\(\dot{v}=AlNS\)) because more fluid is trapped and moved per second; pressure depends on the load/outlet resistance, not on the geometry-set displacement.
What would make the actual flow lower than the ideal value given by \(\dot{v}=AlNS\)?
Internal leakage (slip) past the teeth and casing clearances, and fluid compressibility or cavitation, reduce delivered flow; higher outlet pressure increases leakage.

notes.t: Gear pumps: types of positive displacement gear pump
pts: Gear pumps are positive displacement pumps; the main types are spur, helical, double-helical (herringbone) and planetary.
Helical gears give smoother and quieter operation than spur gears, but they produce an axial end-thrust that must be carried by bearings.
Double-helical (herringbone) gears reduce noise and produce no resultant end-thrust, because the opposing helix angles cancel the axial forces.
defs: Gear pump
A positive displacement pump in which meshing gears trap fluid between teeth and casing and carry it from inlet to outlet, delivering a flow largely independent of outlet pressure.
Helical gear
A gear whose teeth are cut at an angle to the axis, giving smoother, quieter meshing than spur gears but producing axial (end) thrust.
Herringbone (double-helical) gear
A gear with two opposed sets of helical teeth on one hub, which cancels axial thrust and reduces noise.
tips: Do not state that helical gears have no end-thrust; it is herringbone gears that cancel it.
Planetary gear pumps are listed as a type but no detail is given on this page; avoid inventing operating details for them.
rq: Why do helical gears need thrust bearings while herringbone gears do not?
The angled teeth of a helical gear push the gear axially; a herringbone gear's two opposed helices produce equal and opposite axial forces that cancel, so no net end-thrust arises.
Why are helical gears preferred in cars despite the extra bearing requirement?
Their smoother, quieter meshing outweighs the added cost of bearings to support the end-thrust load.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: lobe pump
pts: A lobe pump is a positive displacement pump that works as a variation on the gear pump, with two rotating lobed rotors trapping and carrying fluid from inlet to outlet.
Lobe pumps are well suited to highly viscous fluids because the fluid is displaced mechanically rather than relying on pressure-driven flow.
defs: Lobe pump

A positive displacement pump in which two (or more) meshing, non-contacting lobed rotors rotate in a casing, transferring fixed volumes of fluid from the suction to the discharge side; suited to viscous or shear-sensitive media.
tips: Do not confuse a lobe pump with a gear pump: lobe rotors do not contact each other and typically use timing gears externally.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump like a lobe pump handle highly viscous fluids better than a centrifugal pump?

A positive displacement pump traps and mechanically pushes a fixed volume of fluid each revolution, so its output is largely independent of viscosity-driven losses, whereas a centrifugal pump relies on kinetic energy transfer that viscosity greatly reduces.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: rotary sliding vane pump
pts: A rotary sliding vane pump has a rotor mounted eccentrically inside a stator, so chamber volume changes as it turns.
Sliding vanes seal off each chamber; spring-loading them helps the vanes stay in contact at slower pump speeds.
The eccentricity of the rotor produces the changes in chamber volume that give the pumping action.
Vane material must be chosen according to the fluid being pumped.
Steel vanes are used for hydraulic oil pumps; graphite vanes are used for air compressors.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in chambers whose volume is cyclically changed, rather than relying on velocity head.
Eccentric rotor
A rotor whose axis is offset from the axis of the surrounding stator, so the gap between them varies around the circumference and creates chambers of changing volume.
Sliding vane
A blade that slides radially in slots in the rotor and seals the chambers between rotor and stator, maintaining contact with the stator wall as the rotor turns.
tips: Do not confuse the rotor's eccentricity with its rotation: it is the offset geometry, not the spinning, that changes chamber volume.
Vane material must be matched to the fluid; the page's examples (steel for hydraulic oil, graphite for air) are not interchangeable.
rq: Why does the pump need the rotor to be eccentric rather than concentric with the stator?

With a concentric rotor the gap between rotor and stator would be constant, so no chamber volume change would occur and no pumping action would result. Eccentricity makes the volume of each chamber expand (drawing fluid in) and then shrink (expelling fluid).
What would happen to the sealing of the chambers if the pump runs slowly and the vanes are not spring-loaded?

At low speed centrifugal force on the vanes is small, so they may not be pressed firmly against the stator, causing leakage between chambers and reduced efficiency; spring-loading keeps them in contact.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: rotary / sliding vane pumps
pts: A sliding vane pump has a rotor set eccentrically inside a casing; vanes slide radially in slots and trap fluid in chambers that change volume as the rotor turns, displacing fluid from inlet to outlet.
Vanes must stay in contact with the casing wall, so they are pushed outward (by springs or pressure/centrifugal force) and wear is a key failure mode over time.

The vanes do not jam at the ports because the rotor is eccentric and the ports sit where vanes are moving radially, with the casing shaped so vanes slide along the wall rather than catching on the port edges.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a chamber and forcing it from inlet to outlet, giving a flow largely independent of outlet pressure.
tips: Positive displacement pumps deliver a near-constant flow per revolution; leakage past vanes reduces the effective delivered flow, so wear matters.
Do not confuse a sliding vane pump (vanes slide radially) with a gear pump (teeth mesh); sealing relies on vane-to-wall contact.
rq: Why does the eccentric position of the rotor matter for a sliding vane pump?
Eccentricity makes the chamber volume between vanes grow on the inlet side and shrink on the outlet side, so fluid is drawn in and then expelled.
What would happen if the vanes were not pushed outward against the casing?
Chambers would leak between vanes and the casing, lowering volumetric efficiency and pumping capacity, especially at low speed or high pressure.
How could the vanes be extended by hand without springs?
Use a manually operated mechanism such as a lever or cam, or rotate the vanes/rotor by hand so that the vane is pushed out by hand against the casing wall.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: screw pump
pts: Fluid is drawn in at the inlet, carried axially along the meshing screws by the rotating central screw, and discharged at the outlet, so flow moves along the pump axis.
The central (yellow) screw is the driven element, normally turned by a motor via the shaft, while meshing screws/collars seal and carry the fluid in cavities.
Fluid enters a suction manifold and passes through the meshing screws to the discharge, trapped in cavities that advance together as the screws turn.
Screw pumps are quiet and reliable because the smooth, continuous meshing motion gives low pulsation and low noise.
Screw pumps suit lubricating fluids, which are transported well by the sealed screw cavities without damage to the fluid.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a cavity and forcing it through the outlet, giving a flow largely independent of discharge pressure.
Meshing collars
Intermeshing features on the screws that form sealed cavities between the screw flights and the casing, preventing backflow and carrying fluid axially.
Relief valve
A pressure-limiting safety device that opens to return fluid to the suction side when discharge pressure exceeds a set value, protecting the pump and circuit.
Mechanical seal
A rotating shaft seal that prevents fluid leakage along the drive shaft where it passes out of the pump casing.
tips: Do not confuse the flow direction: in a screw pump fluid moves axially (along the shaft), not radially as in a centrifugal pump.
Remember the relief valve is a safety device for pressure limiting, not a flow-control device.
rq: Why does a screw pump's flow stay nearly constant even if the discharge pressure rises?
Because it is a positive displacement pump: each revolution traps a fixed volume in the screw cavities, so pressure rise mainly increases leakage slightly, not the displaced volume.
What would happen to the pump if the outlet were blocked and no relief valve were fitted?
Pressure would rise rapidly since the fixed volume cannot escape, risking overload of the casing, seals and motor; the relief valve prevents this by bypassing fluid to suction.

notes.t: Screw pump: thrust balancing and bearings
pts: A single-screw arrangement produces an axial end thrust that must be absorbed by a thrust bearing, usually in the motor.
Using two screws with opposite-hand threads, suction at both ends and discharge in the centre, lets the axial forces cancel so no thrust bearing is needed.
In the double-ended design the suction is at both ends of the screws with a central discharge, so the pressure loads on each end oppose one another.
The drawing shows only location bearings, which fix the shaft radially and axially in position but do not carry a net thrust load.
tips: Only the thrust is balanced by opposite threads and symmetric suction; location bearings are still needed to position the shaft.
Remember the drawing is of the balanced double-screw type, so its absence of a thrust bearing is not an omission.
rq: Why does a single-screw pump need a thrust bearing but the double-ended, opposite-hand design does not?

In a single-screw pump the discharge pressure acts on the screw end creating a net axial force. In the double-ended design the two screws have opposite-hand threads and suction at each end, so the axial forces from the two halves are equal and opposite and cancel, leaving no net thrust.
What would happen to the balanced design if the two screws had threads of the same hand?
The axial forces would no longer be opposed in the correct sense, so the thrust would add rather than cancel, and a thrust bearing would again be required.

units.name: 3.6 Centrifugal pump operation, casings and impellers
units.ov: This module covers how a centrifugal pump works: the impeller adds velocity to the fluid and the casing (volute or diffuser) converts that velocity to pressure. It then compares impeller types (enclosed, open, semi-open, shrouded, double-entry) and casing types, and covers operating limits, seals, bearings and wear rings. The unifying idea is that each design choice trades efficiency, solids handling, suction performance, stability and leakage control against the others.
must: Energy path: the impeller imparts rotational energy and velocity, fluid enters at the eye and leaves through the vane tips, and the casing slows it to convert kinetic energy to pressure
Impeller = rotating, adds energy; casing = stationary, guides flow and converts velocity to pressure (do not mix these up)
Volute casing: spiral, offset impeller, area increasing toward discharge, no fixed vanes. Diffuser casing: stationary guide vanes, more stable and tolerates higher pressure, but prone to blockage

Impeller types by shrouding: enclosed/fully shrouded (two discs, most efficient, clean liquids), semi-open (back shroud only), open (no shroud or cover plate); open and semi-open suit solids and sludge because they resist clogging
Double-entry impeller: lower NPSH requirement (good for poor suction), about twice the flow at similar head, balanced axial thrust. It is a separate property from shrouding
Operating window: low flow causes overheating (brief operation tolerated); high flow causes vibration (never allowed)
Centrifugal pumps give high flow rates but only low to medium pressure; the pressure rise happens in the volute or diffuser
NPSH: absolute suction head above vapour pressure; insufficient NPSH leads to cavitation

Seals: dynamic seals (gland packing, mechanical face seal) act at the rotating shaft, and a face seal runs hot and needs cooling; static seals (gaskets, O-rings) act at fixed joints. A shaft sleeve protects the shaft under the packing

Impeller rings and wear rings are non-contacting partial seals that limit backflow and are replaceable sacrificial parts; vanes are swept backwards; a vertical pump needs one bush bearing lubricated by the pumped fluid
conn: Impeller type and application: solids in the fluid require an open or semi-open impeller, but this lowers efficiency compared with a fully shrouded impeller, so the choice is a trade-off
Double-entry impeller, NPSH and cavitation: poor suction conditions call for lower NPSH, which a double-entry impeller provides, and it also balances axial thrust and so reduces bearing loads
Casing choice, pressure and reliability: a diffuser gives stability and higher pressure but blocks easily, while a volute is simpler, which links to the solids-handling choice

Leak paths, seals, wear rings and bearings: leakage along the shaft and between impeller and casing is controlled by dynamic seals, static seals and wear rings, and the seal type (face seal cooling, gland sleeve) affects maintenance and bearing lubrication
exq: Explain, with a sketch, how a centrifugal pump converts shaft power into pressure, stating the roles of the impeller eye, vane tips and volute.
Compare volute and diffuser casings, covering stability, pressure capability and blockage risk, and recommend one for a given duty.
A pump must handle sludge containing solids. Select an impeller type, justify the choice, and state the efficiency penalty compared with a fully shrouded impeller.
State the allowable flow limits of a centrifugal pump, the failure mode at each, and which one may be tolerated briefly.

For a horizontal pump cross-section, identify where leakage can occur along the shaft, and name and locate the dynamic and static seals, the shaft sleeve, the impeller nut and the two bearings, giving the function of each.

notes.t: Centrifugal pumps: general characteristics
pts: A centrifugal pump moves fluid by transferring rotational energy from a spinning impeller to the fluid.
Fluid enters the rotating impeller and is flung outward by centrifugal force, exiting through the impeller vane tips.
Impeller design can be optimised to control fluid velocity and pressure, and the impeller directs the fluid to the outlet.
The pump casing constricts fluid from the inlet, directs it to the impeller, and slows the fluid before discharge so that kinetic energy is converted to pressure.
defs: Centrifugal pump
A pump that moves fluid by using a rotating impeller to transfer rotational energy to the fluid, which is accelerated outward by centrifugal force and discharged through the casing.
Impeller
The rotating component of a centrifugal pump, fitted with vanes, that imparts energy to the fluid and directs it outward to the outlet.
Pump casing
The stationary housing of a centrifugal pump that channels fluid from the inlet to the impeller and slows the flow before discharge.
tips: Do not confuse the impeller (rotating, adds energy) with the casing (stationary, guides flow and converts velocity to pressure).
Remember that fluid exits through the impeller vane tips, not at the impeller centre.
rq: Why does the pump casing slow the fluid before discharge?
Slowing the fluid converts kinetic energy (velocity) into pressure energy, so the discharge has higher pressure.
What would happen to the fluid's outward velocity if the impeller rotated faster?
Centrifugal force increases with rotational speed, so the fluid leaves the vane tips at higher velocity and gains more energy, raising the pressure developed.

notes.t: Centrifugal pumps: allowable operating flow range
pts: Operating below the minimum allowable flow causes overheating, though brief operation is tolerated.
Operating above the maximum allowable flow causes vibrations and must be avoided, even briefly.
The safe operating window lies between the minimum and maximum allowable flow rates.
Overheating at low flow and vibration at high flow are the two key failure modes to remember.
tips: Distinguish the two limits: low flow → overheating (short duration allowed); high flow → vibration (never allowed).
Do not state that short-duration operation above maximum flow is acceptable; the notes say it is not allowed.
rq: Why does running a centrifugal pump at very low flow make it overheat?
At low flow the pumped liquid carries away less heat, and the energy input is largely converted into heat in the fluid and casing, so temperature rises.
Why is a short excursion above maximum flow more dangerous than a short excursion below minimum flow?
High flow causes vibration from hydraulic instability and loading that can damage bearings and seals quickly, whereas low flow heating develops more slowly and is tolerated briefly.

notes.t: Centrifugal pumps: general characteristics and impeller types
pts: The impeller is made of a series of curved vanes that impart energy to the fluid as it rotates.
A normal (enclosed) impeller has its vanes sandwiched between two discs, giving a closed flow passage.
Fluids carrying entrained solids need an open or semi-open impeller, which resists clogging and passes solids more easily.
A semi-open impeller is backed by a single disc rather than two, leaving the front of the vanes exposed.
The rotation direction is shown by the spiral volute and the curvature of the vanes; the fluid is discharged tangentially from the outer edge.
defs: Enclosed impeller
A centrifugal pump impeller whose curved vanes are fixed between two discs (shrouds), giving a closed flow channel suited to clean liquids.
Semi-open impeller
A centrifugal pump impeller with vanes backed by a single disc, leaving the other side open; used for liquids containing solids.
tips: Do not confuse the enclosed (two discs) and semi-open (single disc) impeller types; the disc count is the key distinguishing feature.
Determining rotation direction from the diagram requires checking the vane curvature relative to the volute outlet, not just the picture orientation.
rq: Why is an open or semi-open impeller preferred for fluids with entrained solids?
Without a second disc, the wide open passages let solids pass through without clogging or jamming between the vanes and the casing.
Why are the vanes curved rather than straight?
Curved vanes guide the fluid smoothly outward and add energy to it as it leaves the impeller, increasing pressure and head efficiently.

notes.t: Centrifugal pumps: general characteristics
pts: Liquid enters the eye of the impeller and is flung radially outward between the vanes by the impeller's rotation, gaining velocity.
The kinetic energy gained from the impeller is converted to pressure in a volute or diffuser in the casing.
Centrifugal pumps can deliver very high flow rates but only low and medium pressures.
Because pressure output is limited, the pump is suited to low and medium pressure duties.
defs: Impeller eye
The central inlet of a centrifugal pump impeller through which liquid enters axially before being directed radially outward.
Volute
A spiral-shaped casing surrounding the impeller that collects liquid leaving the impeller and converts its velocity into pressure.
tips: Centrifugal pumps suit low and medium pressures only; do not describe them as high-pressure pumps.
Velocity is increased by the impeller, but pressure rise occurs in the volute or diffuser, not the impeller alone.
rq: Why does a centrifugal pump not need a relief valve, as the final bullet asks?

Its output pressure is limited by the impeller's rotational speed and design; the pump cannot generate the very high pressures that would over-pressurise the system, so the pump cannot be over-pressurised the way a positive displacement pump can (the pump delivers a flow that falls as the system pressure rises).
Why is a volute used rather than a plain casing?
It gradually expands the flow area so the high-velocity liquid leaving the impeller slows down, converting kinetic energy into pressure energy efficiently.

notes.t: Centrifugal pump casings and impeller features
pts: A volute casing has an offset impeller creating a funnel-shaped channel that converts kinetic energy into pressure.
A diffuser casing uses stationary vanes around the impeller; it is more stable and tolerates higher pressure but is prone to blockages.
The fluid enters the pump at the eye, at the centre of the impeller.
Impeller rings form a partial dynamic seal that stops liquid flowing backwards through the pump without touching.
Centrifugal pump vanes are swept backwards, relative to the direction of rotation.
defs: Volute casing
A spiral-shaped pump casing whose cross-sectional area increases towards the discharge, converting kinetic energy of the liquid into pressure energy.
Diffuser casing
A pump casing containing stationary vanes around the impeller that guide and slow the liquid, converting velocity into pressure with greater stability.
Eye of the impeller
The central inlet region of the impeller through which liquid enters the pump.
tips: Do not confuse the volute (spiral casing, no fixed vanes) with the diffuser (stationary guide vanes); the diffuser is more prone to blockages.
The impeller rings are only a partial seal since they do not touch the casing; stating they seal completely is a common error.
rq: Why does a volute casing increase pressure as the liquid leaves the impeller?
The expanding flow area slows the liquid, so its kinetic energy is converted into pressure (energy conversion kinetic to pressure).
What would happen if the impeller rings were in direct contact with the casing?
Friction and wear would occur, and the rings would no longer act as a clearance-based partial seal; the design deliberately leaves a small gap.

notes.t: Single stage vertical centrifugal pump: seals, bearings and wear rings
pts: A static gland seal or a dynamic face seal can be used; a face seal runs hot and needs cooling.
A vertical pump needs only one radial bearing because axial loads are not carried by it in the same way as a horizontal arrangement.
The bearing is a simple bush bearing lubricated by the pumped fluid itself, so no separate lubrication system is needed.
Wear rings sit at the impeller inlet and casing interface (upper and lower) and are the replaceable parts that wear, protecting the casing and impeller.
tips: Wear rings are sacrificial clearance rings: they are replaced when worn, rather than damaging the costly casing or impeller.
Do not confuse static gland seals (no cooling needed) with dynamic face seals (cooling required).
rq: Why can a simple bush bearing be lubricated by the fluid being pumped rather than by oil?

The fluid acts as a lubricant film between the spindle and bush, so no separate oil system is needed; this works because the bearing is only radial and the pumped liquid (typically water) provides adequate lubrication.
Why does a dynamic face seal need cooling but a static gland seal does not?
A face seal has relatively moving faces that generate friction heat, which must be removed by cooling; a static gland seal has no relative sliding of sealing faces so it produces little heat.

notes.t: Centrifugal pump impeller types: open and semi-open
pts: An open impeller has vanes extending radially from the hub with no back shroud or cover plate.
Open impellers suit small pumps handling solids such as sludge, because particles pass without clogging.
A semi-open (semi-shrouded) impeller has vanes projecting forward from a back shroud but no cover plate.
Semi-open impellers are used in similar applications to open impellers.
defs: Open impeller
An impeller whose vanes extend radially from the hub with neither a back shroud nor a cover plate, suited to liquids containing solid particles.
Semi-open impeller
An impeller in which the vanes project forward from a back shroud but have no front cover plate; also called semi-shrouded.
tips: Do not confuse 'semi-open' (back shroud present, no cover plate) with 'open' (neither shroud nor cover plate).
Explain the choice of open impeller in terms of solids handling and clogging, not efficiency alone.
rq: Why would an open impeller be chosen for sludge rather than a fully shrouded impeller?
With no cover plate, the open passages are less likely to block or trap solid particles, so the pump tolerates solids; a shrouded design would clog and wear faster.
What is the key structural difference between a semi-open and a closed (shrouded) impeller?
A semi-open impeller has a back shroud but no front cover plate, whereas a closed impeller has cover plates on both sides.

notes.t: Centrifugal pump impeller types
pts: A fully shrouded single-entry impeller has back shroud and front cover plate supporting the vanes, making it more efficient.
A double-entry impeller needs lower NPSH, so it suits poor suction conditions.
A double-entry impeller can deliver about twice the discharge flow for a similar head.
Double-entry design balances axial thrust on the impeller shaft because flow enters from both sides.
defs: NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head)
The absolute pressure head available at the pump suction above the liquid vapour pressure; a pump needs sufficient NPSH to avoid cavitation.
Fully shrouded impeller
An impeller with a full back shroud and front cover plate that enclose and support the vanes, giving higher efficiency.
Double-entry impeller
An impeller that draws liquid in from both sides of the eye, giving lower NPSH requirement, higher flow and balanced axial thrust.
tips: Do not confuse the NPSH requirement (lower for double entry) with flow rate; double entry increases discharge quantity, not head.
Shrouded and double-entry are different features: a double-entry impeller may or may not be fully shrouded, so state each property separately.
rq: Why does a double-entry impeller balance the axial thrust on the shaft?
Liquid enters symmetrically from both sides, so the axial pressure forces on each side are roughly equal and opposite and cancel out.
Why might you choose a double-entry impeller over a single-entry one in a pump supplied from a poor suction source?
Its lower NPSH requirement means it is less likely to cavitate when suction pressure is low.

notes.t: Horizontal centrifugal pump – construction and sealing (discussion questions)
pts: The page poses design questions about a horizontal centrifugal pump cross-section: how the impeller is fixed to the shaft, why the impeller nut and two bearings are used, where leakage can occur, and the locations of dynamic and static seals.
Leak paths and seals are central to pump design: students must identify where fluid can escape along the shaft and which seals (gland packing, dynamic and static) prevent it.
A sleeve or liner on the shaft under the gland packing protects the shaft surface from wear and abrasion by the packing.
Two bearings support the rotating shaft and keep the impeller correctly located against radial and axial loads.
defs: Dynamic seal
A seal between a stationary casing and a rotating shaft that must allow relative motion while limiting fluid leakage (e.g. gland packing or mechanical seal).
Static seal
A seal between two stationary mating surfaces (e.g. gasket or O-ring at a casing joint) that prevents leakage without relative motion.
tips: Do not confuse dynamic seals (moving relative parts, e.g. at the shaft) with static seals (gaskets at fixed joints).
Answers should refer to the labelled parts in the drawing (gland packing, protection ring, spacer, impeller nut) rather than generic descriptions.
rq: Why would a liner be placed on the shaft exactly under the gland packing rather than along the whole shaft?
The packing rubs and abrades the shaft only where it contacts it; a replaceable sleeve there protects the shaft from wear and can be renewed cheaply.
What would happen to the pump if one of the two bearings were omitted?
The shaft and impeller would lose radial and axial support, causing excessive deflection, misalignment, rubbing on the casing and premature failure.

units.name: 3.7 Pump characteristic curves and pump selection
units.ov: This material covers how pump performance is represented by characteristic curves (head, efficiency and NPSHR against flow) and how these curves are used to select a pump. Centrifugal pump curves are matched against a system curve to find the operating point, which should lie near the BEP and keep available NPSH above NPSHR. Positive displacement pumps contrast with centrifugal pumps in both mechanism and curve shape.
must: A pump curve plots differential head (m) against flow (m³/h); the pump can only operate on this line, and the operating point is its intersection with the system curve.
Operating point = intersection of pump curve and system curve; changing either the valve setting (system curve) or the pump (speed, impeller) moves it.
Best Efficiency Point (BEP): the flow at peak efficiency; select the pump so the duty lies close to it, within the allowable min–max flow range.
Cavitation criterion: it occurs when NPSHA < NPSHR; NPSHR is read from the pump curve and rises with flow, while NPSHA is set by the suction arrangement.
Each impeller diameter has its own head–flow curve (e.g. the 200 mm label is the impeller diameter, not pipe bore or head); read all values from the curve for the correct diameter.
Shut-off head is the head at zero flow and the maximum the pump can develop; the centrifugal curve is flat at low flow and falls more steeply at high flow.
Affinity laws for speed change: \(Q\propto N\), \(H\propto N^2\) (and power \(\propto N^3\)); the curve is not simply shifted vertically, and points move along parabolas \(H\propto Q^2\).

Positive displacement pumps trap a fixed volume and give a near-straight, nearly constant-flow curve of pressure vs flow, tilting due to leakage at higher pressure; centrifugal pumps convert kinetic energy to pressure and have a curved head–flow characteristic.
Differential head is the energy per unit weight added between suction and discharge, in metres of fluid; keep units (m³/h vs m³/s) consistent.
Performance curves are mostly obtained empirically, and the pump manufacturer's curve sets (head, efficiency, NPSHR) are the basis for selection.
conn: Pump curve and system curve (static head plus friction \(\propto Q^2\)) combine to give the operating point, which is then checked against the BEP and efficiency curves.

Operating point flow determines NPSHR from the curve, which must be compared with NPSHA from the suction pipework (atmospheric pressure, static lift, friction losses, vapour pressure) to check for cavitation.
Affinity laws link speed or impeller changes to a new pump curve, and hence a new operating point, efficiency and power requirement.
Pump type choice (positive displacement vs centrifugal) links to curve shape: PD pumps give nearly fixed flow regardless of pressure, whereas centrifugal flow varies strongly with system resistance.
exq: A centrifugal pump with a 200 mm impeller has a given head–flow curve. Using the system curve \(H = H_s + kQ^2\), find graphically the operating point flow and head, and state whether it lies within the allowable range around the BEP.

At the operating flow found from the curves, read NPSHR. Given the suction tank level, atmospheric pressure, vapour pressure and suction-line losses, calculate NPSHA and decide whether cavitation will occur.
A pump running at 1450 rpm delivers a head of 30 m at 60 m³/h. Use affinity laws to find the head, flow and power at 1750 rpm, and sketch the new curve relative to the old one.
Explain with sketches the differences in mechanism and in pressure–flow characteristic between a positive displacement pump and a centrifugal pump, including why the PD curve tilts at high pressure.
Define shut-off head and BEP, and explain how changing the impeller diameter changes the head–flow, efficiency and NPSHR curves used in pump selection.

notes.t: Centrifugal pump characteristic curves
pts: A centrifugal pump curve plots head against flow; only points on the line are achievable by the pump.
The pump curve can be matched against a system curve to find the operating point.
Head falls as flow rate increases, with a flat region at low flow and a steeper drop at high flow.
The 200 mm label identifies the impeller diameter, which determines the curve's position.
defs: Pump characteristic curve
A graph of head (m of fluid) against volumetric flow rate (m³/h) showing the performance a pump can deliver at a given speed and impeller size.
tips: Do not confuse the label 200 mm with a pipe bore or head value; it refers to the impeller diameter.
Changing speed affects the curve through the affinity laws (flow ∝ N, head ∝ N²), not by a simple vertical shift.
rq: Why can a pump only operate at points lying on its characteristic curve?
The curve represents the head the pump can generate at each flow for its fixed impeller diameter and speed; off-curve points are not achievable by that pump.
What would happen to the head-flow curve if the impeller diameter were increased?
The curve shifts upward and outward: higher head and flow are available, since head scales with the square of the impeller tip speed (roughly with D²).

notes.t: Centrifugal pump characteristics and performance curves
pts: Pumps are selected from a set of performance curves showing head, efficiency and NPSHR against flow; most of these curves are obtained empirically.
Changing the impeller diameter (energy given to the fluid) shifts the head–flow curve, producing a different curve for each diameter.
The Best Efficiency Point (BEP) is the operating point of peak pump efficiency; the allowable operating range lies between minimum and maximum allowable flow around it.
NPSHR (net positive suction head required) increases with flow, so higher flow demands a higher suction head to avoid cavitation.
Shut-off head is the differential head at zero flow, the highest head the pump can develop.
defs: Best Efficiency Point (BEP)
The operating point on a pump curve at which the pump efficiency is highest; the pump is normally selected to operate close to it.
NPSHR (Net Positive Suction Head Required)
The minimum suction head (above vapour pressure) a pump needs at its inlet to avoid cavitation at a given flow rate; it rises as flow increases.
Shut-off head
The differential head developed by a centrifugal pump when the discharge is closed (zero flow).
Differential head
The increase in fluid head (energy per unit weight) provided by the pump between suction and discharge, measured in metres.
tips: Do not confuse NPSHR (a pump requirement, read from the curve) with NPSH available (a system property set by the suction arrangement); cavitation occurs when available NPSH is less than NPSHR.
Each impeller diameter gives its own curve; always read head, efficiency and NPSHR from the curve matching the impeller and the operating flow, and keep flow units (m³/h) consistent.
rq: Why does NPSHR increase as the flow through the pump increases?

Higher flow means higher fluid velocities and greater frictional/inlet losses and local pressure drops at the impeller eye, so more suction head is needed to keep the pressure above vapour pressure and avoid cavitation.
What happens to the head–flow curve if a smaller impeller is fitted, and why?
The curve shifts downward (lower head at each flow) because a smaller impeller imparts less energy to the fluid, giving a different curve as shown by the min/rated/max impeller diameter lines.

notes.t: Pump types and performance curves
pts: Positive displacement pumps trap a fixed volume of liquid in an enclosed space and push it out through an outlet.
Centrifugal pumps spin the liquid at high speed so it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to pressure.
Positive displacement pump types include piston/reciprocating, lobe, gear, sliding vane and screw designs.
A positive displacement pump curve is a near-straight line of discharge pressure against flow rate, tilting towards the pressure axis because leakage rises with pressure.
A centrifugal pump curve depends on impeller size and system pressure, not simply on a fixed straight-line relationship.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that draws in a fixed volume of liquid into an enclosed space and forces it out through an outlet.
Centrifugal pump
A pump that spins liquid at high speed so that it gains kinetic energy, which is then converted to pressure.
tips: Do not assume a centrifugal pump curve is a straight line like a positive displacement pump curve; it depends on impeller size and system pressure.
Confusing the mechanism: positive displacement pumps trap a volume, while centrifugal pumps rely on kinetic energy.
rq: Why does the positive displacement pump curve slope slightly rather than being perfectly vertical?
Because leakage through clearances increases with pressure, so the actual delivered flow drops slightly as discharge pressure rises.
Why does a centrifugal pump's performance change if you fit a larger impeller?
A larger impeller imparts more kinetic energy to the liquid, so the head and flow it can deliver change with impeller size.

units.name: 3.8 Positive displacement pumps (summary notes)
units.ov: This material introduces positive displacement (PD) pumps, which trap a fixed volume of fluid and force it out, so flow is set by pump speed while discharge pressure is set by the system. It covers reciprocating pumps (pulsation damping, relief valves), the near-linear pump characteristic with leakage, and rotary types (gear, sliding vane, screw). The ideas connect through displacement per cycle or revolution, internal clearances and leakage, lubrication, end-thrust balance and protection against overpressure.
must: PD pump definition: it draws in a fixed volume, encloses it, and forces it out, so flow stops when the pump stops. Contrast with centrifugal pumps, which impart kinetic energy and never enclose the fluid.
Flow rate is set by pump speed (displacement per revolution or stroke \(\times\) speed), not by the system. Discharge pressure is set by the downstream system resistance, not by the pump.
Pump characteristic: at fixed speed, pressure vs flow is almost a straight line. Flow falls slightly as pressure rises because of leakage through internal clearances (slip).

Reciprocating pump operation: on the suction stroke the inlet valve opens and the discharge valve stays shut; on the discharge stroke the reverse happens. Both valves are non-return and spring-assisted. Variants are single or double acting, single or twin cylinder, vertical or horizontal.

Reciprocating pumps give pulsating flow and pressure. An air vessel (or nitrogen bladder) on the discharge side smooths the pressure by compressing and expanding a gas cushion. It does not change the mean flow rate.
A relief valve is always fitted on the discharge side to limit maximum pressure, for example if the pump starts against a closed discharge valve. It is not the same device as the air vessel.

Gear pump: driver and idler gears mesh in a body and carry fluid round the outside from inlet to outlet. Bushes are lubricated by the pumped fluid. Non-lubricating fluids need gears kept apart and driven through an external gearbox. Helical teeth must be opposite double (herringbone) to cancel axial thrust. Reversing rotation reverses flow direction.

Sliding vane pump: an eccentric rotor in a stator carries radially sliding vanes that seal chambers. The inlet is where chamber volume increases and the outlet is where it decreases. Vane material depends on the fluid: steel for hydraulic oil, graphite for air compressors.

Screw pump: fluid moves axially through meshing screws. It is quiet, reliable, suits lubricating liquids such as oil, and tolerates air. Opposite-hand threads balance end-thrust, with suction at both ends and a central discharge. Timing gears keep the screws from touching, and a thrust bearing takes the residual axial load.
Classification: PD types include reciprocating, lobe, gear, vane, screw, mono, water-ring and diaphragm. PD pumps suit low flow and medium to high pressure.
conn: Pump characteristic and system: the pump sets flow by speed, the system sets pressure, and leakage slopes the curve. A closed discharge valve therefore causes pressure to rise until the relief valve opens, which links to why relief valves are mandatory.

Reciprocating pulsation: the discharge pressure fluctuation from the piston cycle is smoothed by the air vessel through gas compression, so gas laws (\(pV=\text{const}\)) link to damping. Mean flow is unchanged.

Lubrication and construction: gear and screw pumps rely on the pumped fluid for lubrication. This determines fluid suitability, the need for external gearboxes or timing gears, and the risk of overheating and seizure from friction.
Axial thrust balancing: opposite-hand helical gears and opposite-hand screw threads both cancel end-thrust. This is distinct from radial loads, which are handled by bearings.
exq: Define a positive displacement pump and contrast it with a centrifugal pump. Explain why flow depends on speed rather than on the system, and sketch the pump characteristic at fixed speed, explaining why it slopes.

A reciprocating pump delivers into a pipeline. Describe the suction and discharge strokes with valve states, explain why discharge pressure pulsates, and explain how an air vessel reduces the pulsation. State what it does not change.

Explain why a relief valve is fitted to the discharge side of a gear pump. Describe what happens if the pump is started with the discharge valve closed, and how the pump's discharge pressure is determined.

With a labelled sketch of a sliding vane pump, identify the stator, rotor, vanes, inlet and outlet. Explain how the pumping action arises from the eccentricity, and give vane materials for hydraulic oil and for air compressors.
Compare gear and screw pumps in terms of fluid suitability, lubrication, end-thrust balancing (opposite-hand helical gears or threads), timing gears and the effect of reversing rotation.

notes.t: Positive Displacement Pumps
pts: Pumps move fluids and are classed as either positive displacement or centrifugal; the category depends on how the fluid is moved.
Positive displacement pumps draw in a fixed volume of fluid, enclose it, and force it out of the outlet, so flow stops when the pump stops.
Positive displacement pumps suit low flow-rates and medium to high pressures, and their flow-rate is set by pump speed rather than by the system.
Engineering principles used in pump design include static and suction head, dynamic head, gas laws for gases, and friction causing heat.
Common positive displacement pump types are piston/reciprocating, lobe and gear pumps.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that draws in a fixed volume of fluid, encloses it at one point in the cycle, and forces it out of the outlet; flow cannot pass through it when stopped.
Centrifugal pump
A pump that spins fluid at high speed to impart kinetic energy to it; the liquid is never enclosed and flow can continue through the pump when stopped.
Pump
A device that moves a fluid (usually a liquid, but possibly a gas or solid/liquid mixture) from one place to another.
tips: Do not confuse the two categories: only positive displacement pumps enclose the fluid, and only centrifugal pumps impart kinetic energy by spinning.
Remember that pump flow-rate depends on pump speed, not on the system it feeds.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump stop all flow when it is switched off, while a centrifugal pump may not?

A positive displacement pump encloses a fixed volume of fluid and pushes it out mechanically, so without motion nothing moves through it; a centrifugal pump only imparts kinetic energy to unenclosed fluid, so fluid can still flow through when it is stopped.
Why would a positive displacement pump be chosen for high-pressure, low-flow duties?
Its enclosed-volume action can generate medium to high pressures, while its flow-rate is limited to low values set by pump speed.

notes.t: Piston and Reciprocating Pumps: Design Points
pts: A reciprocating pump uses a piston moving back and forth in a cylinder, driven by a crank/connecting rod, to draw in and discharge fluid via inlet and outlet valves.
The diagram shows the piston drawing fluid through a non-return valve on the suction side and expelling it through a valve on the discharge side.
The page lists other positive-displacement pump types (mono, water-ring, sliding vane, screw, diaphragm) to contrast with reciprocating pumps.
defs: Reciprocating pump
A positive-displacement pump in which a piston or plunger moves back and forth within a cylinder, alternately drawing fluid in and forcing it out through valves.
tips: Do not confuse reciprocating (positive-displacement, pulsating flow) pumps with rotodynamic/centrifugal pumps, which give smooth continuous flow.
The page is only a section heading and diagram; design equations are not given here, so do not invent them in an exam answer.
rq: Why do reciprocating pumps need inlet and outlet valves?
Non-return valves ensure fluid flows only in one direction: the inlet valve opens on the suction stroke and the outlet valve opens on the discharge stroke.

notes.t: Reciprocating positive displacement pumps: operation, pressure pulsation damping and relie
pts: Reciprocating positive displacement pumps can be vertical or horizontal, single- or double-acting, and single- or twin-cylinder.
On the suction stroke, the piston creates a vacuum above it that draws liquid in; the discharge valve stays shut, held by a spring.
On the discharge stroke, the piston pushes liquid out below it while the suction valve stays closed under light spring force and discharge pressure.

A major disadvantage is large pressure variations during discharge, which are damped by an air vessel (balancing chamber) on the discharge pipework; the air compresses as pressure rises and expands as it falls.
Some pulsation dampers use a nitrogen-filled bladder inside the pressure vessel; a relief valve is always fitted on the discharge side for protection.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of liquid per cycle by the mechanical displacement of a piston or similar element, delivering flow largely independent of discharge pressure.
Air vessel (balancing chamber)
A pressure vessel fitted to pump discharge pipework that stores energy by compressing a gas cushion, smoothing pressure pulses from the reciprocating action.
Relief valve
A safety valve, fitted on the pump discharge side, that opens to bypass liquid when pressure exceeds a set limit, protecting the pump and pipework.
tips: Do not confuse the air vessel with a relief valve: the air vessel smooths pressure pulses, whereas the relief valve limits maximum pressure.
The air vessel damps pressure fluctuations; it does not increase or change the average flow rate delivered by the pump.
rq: Why must the discharge valve stay closed during the suction stroke?
If it opened, the vacuum above the piston would be lost and liquid would flow back/discharge rather than being drawn in, so no net suction would occur.
Why does an air vessel reduce pressure pulsation rather than the pump flow rate?
The compressible air absorbs excess liquid volume when pressure peaks and releases it when pressure falls, smoothing the pressure without changing the average delivered volume.

notes.t: Pump Curve and Gear Pump
pts: A fixed-speed positive displacement pump's characteristic (pressure vs flow) is almost a straight line.
Flow rate falls as discharge pressure rises because of increased leakage losses through internal clearances.
The discharge pressure of a positive displacement pump is set by the system it pumps into, not by the pump itself.
A gear pump uses two meshing gears (driven and idler) in a body to carry fluid from inlet to outlet.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per revolution, with flow largely independent of discharge pressure apart from internal leakage.
Pump characteristic (pump curve)
A plot of pump discharge pressure against average flow rate at fixed speed, showing how flow falls as pressure rises.
tips: Do not state that the pump sets the discharge pressure; it is the downstream system resistance that does.
The pump curve axes are in arbitrary units on this page; do not quote numerical values from it.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump's flow fall as pressure rises, even though the displacement per revolution is fixed?
Higher pressure drives more fluid back through the internal clearances (leakage), so the net delivered flow decreases.
If a pump is connected to a system with a blocked outlet, what pressure will the pump produce?
The pressure is set by the system, so it rises until the relief/limit (e.g. a relief valve or pump failure); the pump does not define it.

notes.t: Gear Pumps and Sliding Vane Pumps
pts: A gear pump uses two meshing gears (driver and idler) on shafts; bushes are lubricated by the pumped fluid, so fluid lubrication matters.
If the fluid is non-lubricating, the gears can be kept apart and driven through an external gearbox so they do not touch.
Helical or herringbone gear teeth must be 'opposite double' to cancel axial end-thrust.
A relief valve is always fitted to protect the pump if it is started with the discharge valve closed.
A sliding vane pump has an eccentric rotor in a stator; vane sealing and changing chamber volume produce the pumping action.
defs: Sliding vane pump
A positive displacement pump in which a rotor mounted eccentrically in a stator carries sliding vanes that seal chambers whose volume increases and decreases as the rotor turns, pumping fluid.
Opposite double helical gears
Herringbone-type gear arrangement with two opposite-hand helical rows whose axial thrusts cancel, reducing end-thrust on the shafts.
tips: Reversing gear rotation reverses the pump's flow direction, which is a common exam trap when asked about direction of delivery.
Vane material depends on the fluid: steel for hydraulic oil, graphite for air compressors; do not swap them.
rq: Why must helical gears in a gear pump be 'opposite double' rather than single helical?
Single helical gears produce axial end-thrust that loads the bearings; opposite double (herringbone) rows produce equal and opposite thrusts that cancel.
Why are spring-loaded vanes needed at low speed in a sliding vane pump?
At low speed centrifugal force is too weak to press vanes against the stator, so springs keep the vanes sealing each chamber.

notes.t: Sliding Vane Pump: Side View
pts: A sliding vane pump has a rotor mounted eccentrically inside a circular stator (casing), so the cavity between them changes volume as the rotor turns.
Vanes slide radially in slots in the rotor and are pressed against the stator wall, dividing the space into chambers.
Fluid enters at the inlet where the chamber volume is increasing, and is carried around the stator and discharged at the outlet where the volume decreases.
Rotation (arrow shown in the diagram) drives the vanes around the casing, transferring fluid from inlet to outlet.
defs: Stator
The fixed outer casing of the pump, which forms the circular working surface against which the vanes seal.
Rotor
The rotating, eccentrically mounted central element carrying the sliding vanes, which drives fluid around the stator.
Sliding vane
A blade free to slide radially in a rotor slot so that its tip stays in contact with the stator wall, creating sealed pumping chambers.
