rq: Why does reversing the rotation direction cause the ratchet and pawl to freewheel rather than transmit torque?
The angled face of the ratchet tooth lets the pawl slide over it (pushing the pawl aside against its spring) when rotation is in the non-engaging direction, so no locking torque is transmitted.
What would happen to a centrifugally loaded pawl if the shaft speed increased sharply?
The increased centrifugal force pushes the pawl more strongly toward the ratchet, increasing its engagement force, so the clutch engages more firmly at higher speed.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: ratchet and pawl
pts: A ratchet and pawl overrunning clutch engages automatically when the drive shaft rotates, transmitting torque in one direction only.
Failure in service can occur and the failure modes are clear, so the design can be checked for them.
The pawl arm is deliberately long so that the angle through which it moves under load is as small as possible.
The pin connecting the pawl will fail in shear if overloaded, so it is a designed weak point.
The transmission surface of the tooth (point or flat) affects contact stress and the likely crack location at the tooth root/tip.
defs: Overrunning clutch
A clutch that automatically engages to transmit torque when the driving shaft rotates in one direction and disengages (overruns) when the driven member turns faster than the drive.
Pawl
A pivoting catch that engages the teeth of a ratchet wheel to transmit torque in one direction while allowing free rotation in the other.
tips: Do not confuse the overrunning clutch's automatic engagement with a positively controlled clutch that needs an external actuator.
Check failure modes separately: the pin fails in shear, while the teeth are prone to cracking at the root.
rq: Why is the pawl arm made deliberately long rather than short?
A long arm means that under load the pawl rotates through only a very small angle, so the engagement point moves little and the load is transferred more reliably with less impact and wear.
Why is it useful for the pin to fail in shear before other components?
The pin is designed as a sacrificial, predictable failure point: if overloaded it shears first, protecting the more expensive ratchet teeth and shaft from damage.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: roller type
pts: A roller overrunning clutch allows rotation in one direction only.
Cylindrical rollers (or spheres) sit in wedge-shaped chambers between an inner and outer race.
Reversing the rotation direction wedges the rollers between the races, jamming them together so torque is transmitted.
Springs keep the rollers in constant contact with the races so engagement is immediate.
When disengaged, the rollers rubbing on the races generate unwanted heat.
defs: Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits torque in one direction of rotation only and freewheels (overruns) in the opposite direction.
Race
A ring (inner or outer) in a roller clutch against which the rollers bear and are wedged to transmit torque.
tips: Do not confuse the wedging direction: the clutch locks when the rotation is reversed relative to free motion, so state clearly which direction is driving and which is overrunning.
Remember the rollers are spring-loaded; without springs the engagement would be delayed.
rq: Why does the clutch lock in one direction but freewheel in the other?

Rotation in the driving direction drags the rollers into the narrow end of the wedge-shaped chambers, jamming them between the races; reversed rotation pulls them to the wide end where they are not wedged, so the races slip freely.
Why are springs needed in a roller clutch?
They keep the rollers pressed against both races, so the clutch engages instantly when the direction reverses rather than after a delay.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches – roller type
pts: An overrunning clutch allows rotation in one direction only, transmitting torque one way while freewheeling the other way.
The roller type is one of the listed overrunning clutch designs, shown here with a manufacturer example (Renold, superior freewheel technology).
defs: Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits drive when the driving member turns in one direction and automatically disengages (freewheels) when the driven member overruns it or the drive reverses.
tips: Do not confuse an overrunning clutch (one-way, automatic) with a friction clutch that is engaged and disengaged by an external actuator.
rq: Why does a roller overrunning clutch lock up in one direction but freewheel in the other?

Rollers wedge between the inner and outer races when the outer race turns relative to the inner in the locking direction, transmitting torque; in the opposite direction they move to the wide part of the ramp and release, so no torque is transmitted.

units.name: 6.6 Sprag clutches
units.ov: This material covers the sprag clutch, a type of overrunning (one-way, freewheel) clutch in which non-circular, cam-like sprags wedge between inner and outer races to transmit torque in one direction and freewheel in the other. The central ideas are the geometry (AA > BB), the tilting and wedging action, and the resulting torque capacity and heat behaviour. The source pages are inconsistent about which race and which direction locks, so work the direction out from the sprag tilt in each sketch.
must: Definition: a sprag clutch is an overrunning clutch whose asymmetric, non-cylindrical sprags wedge between inner and outer races. It transmits torque one way, freewheels the other way and prevents reverse operation.
Wedging geometry: the sprag dimension across \(AA\) is greater than the race gap dimension \(BB\), so \(AA > BB\). If this is reversed the sprag cannot wedge and no torque is transmitted.

Locking action: relative rotation in the drive direction produces a turning moment on the sprag. The moment tilts it into the wedged position so the races lock. Locking depends on geometry, not on load magnitude.
Freewheel (overrun) condition: in the opposite direction, or when the driven member overruns the driver, the sprags tilt back. They make only light rubbing contact and no torque is transmitted.
Either race can be the drive side. Find the engaged direction from the sprag tilt in the sketch, and state which race is driving and the direction of rotation.
Spring-loaded sprags are kept in light contact, so they lock as soon as drive is applied.
Torque capacity depends on the number of sprags, the clamping (wedge) angle and the rigidity of the surrounding structure. It does not depend on a friction coefficient alone.
Compared with roller clutches, sprag clutches have a higher torque capacity but generate unwanted heat when disengaged. This matters in high-speed freewheeling.
A sprag clutch is a wedging device, not a conventional two-way friction clutch. Friction only binds the wedged sprags.
Compare the types: an overrunning clutch is one-way and automatic, while a two-way friction clutch transmits torque in both directions when engaged.
conn: Geometry and locking: \(AA > BB\) gives the wedge, the wedge gives the self-locking moment, and the clamping angle then sets torque capacity.
Drive race and direction: the choice of inner or outer race as drive determines which way the sprags must tilt, and so which direction locks and which freewheels.
Torque capacity and heat: more sprags and a stiffer structure raise capacity compared with roller clutches, but the heat generated while disengaged limits use at high freewheeling speeds.
Overrunning versus friction clutches: questions often ask you to choose a sprag clutch or a roller clutch for an application, which combines capacity, heat, one-way action and backstopping.
exq: Describe with a labelled sketch how a sprag clutch locks and freewheels. Explain the role of \(AA > BB\) and of the turning moment on the sprag.
A sketch shows sprags tilted between an inner and an outer race. State which direction of rotation is the drive direction for the inner race as driver, and what happens if the outer race overruns.
Compare sprag and roller overrunning clutches in terms of torque capacity, heat generation when disengaged and suitability for high-speed freewheeling. Recommend one for a given application.
List the factors that determine the torque a sprag clutch can transmit, and explain why a friction coefficient alone is not sufficient.
Explain why a sprag clutch is not classed as a friction clutch, and state the function of the spring-loaded pivots.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: sprag type
pts: A sprag clutch has an inner and outer race with sprags as the rolling elements instead of rollers.
Either the inner or the outer race can act as the drive side.
It transmits drive in one direction only and prevents reverse operation.
Compared with a roller clutch, the sprag clutch generally has a higher torque capacity, but it generates unwanted heat when disengaged.
The sprags are tilted so they wedge between the races in the engaged direction and freewheel in the other direction.
defs: Sprag clutch
An overrunning clutch in which asymmetric, non-cylindrical sprags wedge between inner and outer races to transmit torque in one rotational direction and freewheel in the other.
tips: Sprag clutches generate unwanted heat when disengaged, so consider this in high-speed freewheeling applications.
Read the sprag tilt from the sketch carefully to identify the engaged direction; the answer depends on whether the inner or outer race is the drive.
rq: Why does a sprag clutch usually carry more torque than a roller clutch of similar size?
Sprags wedge over a larger contact area and engage more fully, giving a higher torque capacity than rollers.
If the centre (inner race) is the drive, which direction of rotation is engaged, and what happens when the drive reverses?
Check the sketch's sprag tilt: the engaged direction is the one that wedges the sprags between the races; reversing the drive freewheels the clutch.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches – sprag type
pts: An overrunning clutch allows rotation in one direction only, freely disengaging when the driven member overruns the driver.
The sprag clutch is the third type of overrunning clutch listed on this page.
Commercial sprag clutches (e.g. Renold 'Superior Freewheel Technology') are a standard manufactured freewheel product.
defs: Overrunning clutch

A mechanical clutch that transmits torque in one direction of rotation only and freewheels (disengages) when the driven shaft turns faster than the drive in that direction or rotates in the opposite direction.
tips: Do not confuse an overrunning (freewheel) clutch, which is one-way, with a two-way friction clutch that transmits torque in both directions when engaged.
rq: Why does an overrunning clutch let a shaft keep spinning freely when the driving member slows down?
Because the clutch only locks (transmits torque) in one rotation direction; when the driven member overruns the driver, the locking elements release and the drive disengages.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: sprag clutch
pts: A sprag is a cam-like element wedged between inner and outer races; it locks when the inner race rotates, transmitting torque.
The sprag's dimension across AA is always larger than BB, so it jams between the races when rotated in the drive direction.
When the outer race is stationary (no motion), the sprag rests with light rubbing contact at the races, allowing freewheeling in the overrun direction.
A turning moment acts on the sprag as the inner race rotates, tilting it into the locked (wedged) position.
defs: Sprag
A non-cylindrical wedge-shaped element in an overrunning clutch that tilts to lock the inner and outer races in one rotational direction and freewheels in the other.
Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits torque in one direction only, automatically disengaging when the driven member rotates faster than the driver.
tips: Do not confuse the locking and freewheeling orientations: lock occurs when the inner race rotates in the drive direction, freewheel in the opposite direction.
Remember the condition AA > BB; if reversed, the sprag cannot wedge and the clutch will not transmit torque.
rq: Why must dimension AA be larger than BB for the sprag to work?
Because the sprag must wedge between the races: its larger dimension AA spans the gap when tilted, locking it, while the smaller BB allows it to fit and release when freewheeling.
What happens if the inner race is rotated in the reverse (overrun) direction?
The sprag tilts the other way so its narrow dimension BB sits across the gap, giving only light rubbing contact and no torque transfer (freewheeling).

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: the sprag clutch
pts: A sprag clutch locks when the inner race rotates, because the sprag is wedged between inner and outer races and the surfaces lock together.
The sprag has two distances across it, AA and BB; AA is always bigger than BB, which is what allows the sprag to wedge and transmit torque.
When the outer race rotates, a turning moment acts on the sprag which tilts it so the surfaces lock together.
The sprag is a non-circular cam-like element; its geometry lets it release (overrun) in one direction and lock in the other.
defs: Sprag clutch
An overrunning clutch in which non-circular sprags are wedged between inner and outer races, locking to transmit torque in one rotation direction and freewheeling in the other.
Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits torque in one direction of rotation only, automatically disengaging when the driven member rotates faster than the driver.
tips: Do not confuse which race drives: the locking condition depends on the direction of rotation of the inner versus outer race.
Remember the key geometric condition AA > BB; stating the wrong inequality is a common error.
rq: Why must dimension AA be larger than BB for the sprag to lock?
Because the sprag must be able to tilt and wedge between the races; if AA were not larger than BB it could not jam between the inner and outer surfaces to transmit torque.
What would happen if the inner race rotated in the opposite direction?
The sprag would tilt the other way, the surfaces would not wedge, and the clutch would overrun (freewheel) instead of transmitting torque.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches – sprag clutch
pts: A sprag clutch locks when the inner race rotates and the outer race tries to rotate relative to it; the sprag tilts and its surfaces wedge between the races.
The sprag is non-circular, so its dimension AA across the flats is always greater than BB across the contact points; this difference lets it wedge when tilted.
Rotation of the outer race in the locking direction produces a turning moment on the sprag that rotates it into the wedged, locked position.
In the free (overrunning) direction the sprag is not wedged, so the outer race can rotate freely past the inner race.
defs: Sprag clutch
An overrunning clutch using non-circular rollers (sprags) that tilt and wedge between inner and outer races to transmit torque in one direction while freewheeling in the other.
tips: Do not confuse which direction locks: locking occurs when the outer race tends to rotate relative to the inner race, not when the inner race simply turns.
Remember the sprag geometry condition: AA > BB is required for wedging, a common exam point.
rq: Why must dimension AA be bigger than BB for the sprag to work?
Because the sprag must tilt so its wider dimension AA can jam between the two races; if AA were not larger than BB it could never wedge and would not transmit torque.
What happens if the inner race rotates faster than the outer race?
The sprag tilts to its free position and the races slip past each other, so no torque is transmitted and the clutch overruns.

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: sprag clutch action
pts: A sprag is a non-circular element wedged between inner and outer races; its distance across the wider dimension AA exceeds the gap BB, so it jams when the outer race rotates.
When the outer race rotates, the sprag is turned by a moment and wedges between the races, locking them together to transmit torque.
When the inner race tries to overrun the outer, the sprag is not wedged and only makes light rubbing contact, so the clutch freewheels.
In the disengaged (freewheel) condition the sprag shows no motion, so no torque is transmitted.
defs: Sprag
A non-circular wedging element in an overrunning clutch whose larger diameter AA exceeds the race gap BB, so it locks by wedging when turned in one direction and freewheels in the other.
tips: Do not confuse the locking and freewheeling directions: the sprag locks only when the outer race rotates in the driving direction.
Remember the wedging condition is geometric (AA > BB); it does not depend on the magnitude of the load.
rq: Why must dimension AA always be larger than BB for the sprag to work?
If AA were not larger than the gap BB, the sprag could not wedge between the races, so it would never lock and could not transmit torque.
What happens to the sprag if the inner race is driven faster than the outer race?
The sprag is not turned into the wedging position, only light rubbing contact occurs, and the clutch overruns (freewheels).

notes.t: Overrunning clutches: sprag clutch
pts: A sprag clutch allows rotation in one direction only; it is a wedging device, not a friction clutch.
In the free direction the sprags slip or free-wheel; reversing torque tilts them, wedging them between races so they bind by friction.
Spring-loaded pivots keep the sprags ready to lock as soon as drive is engaged.
Transferable torque depends on the sprags (number and clamping angle) and on the surrounding structure's rigidity.
defs: Sprag clutch

An overrunning clutch in which tilting, spring-loaded wedges (sprags) lock between inner and outer races by friction when torque is applied in the locking direction, and free-wheel in the other direction.
tips: Do not describe a sprag clutch as a friction clutch; its locking action is wedging, with friction only binding the sprags.
Torque capacity is set by sprag number, clamping angle and structural rigidity, not by a friction coefficient alone.
rq: Why does a sprag clutch need friction to transmit torque even though it is not a friction clutch?
Wedging the sprags between the races produces normal forces, and the friction at the contact points is what binds them and transmits the torque.
What would happen to the transferable torque if the surrounding structure were less rigid?
The races could deflect under load, reducing the effective wedging and so reducing the torque the sprags can transfer.

units.name: 6.7 Fluid coupling clutches
units.ov: This short module introduces the fluid coupling, a hydrodynamic clutch in which an input impeller drives oil around a toroidal vortex to turn an output runner, with no solid contact. Because torque passes through the oil, the output speed can differ from the input speed. This gives speed variation, smooth start-up and shock protection, and the cost is continuous slip that turns power into heat. The notes are qualitative, so the main task is to explain the behaviour and its consequences clearly.
must: Definition: a hydrodynamic device in which an impeller (input) and runner (output) share oil, and torque is transmitted by oil circulation rather than solid contact
Slip: output speed is always lower than input speed, so \(s=\frac{\omega_{in}-\omega_{out}}{\omega_{in}}>0\) and full-load slip cannot be zero
Slip power loss is converted to heat: \(P_{loss}=T(\omega_{in}-\omega_{out})=sP_{in}\), and this heat must be dissipated to avoid overheating
With no mechanical contact, torque builds gradually, so the coupling gives smooth, shock-free start-up
Speed control: a fixed-speed drive can drive a load at variable speed because the output speed is free to differ
Protection: the coupling isolates the drive and driven systems from shock loads and overload
Oil circulates in a toroidal path between impeller and runner, forming an oil vortex that carries the torque
Contrast with a friction clutch: a friction clutch relies on solid contact and can reach zero slip, but it gives shock engagement and wears
Torque is the same on the input and output sides (no reaction member), so efficiency \(\eta=\frac{T\omega_{out}}{T\omega_{in}}=1-s\)
conn: Slip, heat and efficiency: higher slip gives more heat (\(P_{loss}=sP_{in}\)) and lower efficiency (\(\eta=1-s\)), so cooling requirements follow from the operating slip
Smooth start-up and shock protection both come from torque transmitted through oil rather than contact, and they are the same advantage seen from the drive side and the load side
Speed control and heat: running the load slowly with a fixed-speed motor needs high slip, which is the case where heat generation is greatest
Fluid coupling versus friction clutch comparisons combine the contact mechanism, the slip behaviour and the shock behaviour
exq: Describe the construction and operation of a fluid coupling, naming the impeller, runner and oil vortex, and explain how torque is transmitted without contact.
A fluid coupling transmits 50 kW with input speed 1500 rpm and output speed 1425 rpm. Calculate the slip, the efficiency and the power converted to heat.
Explain why a fluid coupling can never achieve zero slip at full load, and discuss what happens to the lost power and how it is dealt with.
Compare a fluid coupling with a friction clutch in terms of start-up smoothness, overload protection, slip and wear, and suggest suitable applications for each.
Explain how a fluid coupling lets a fixed-speed motor drive a load at variable speed, and comment on the implications for efficiency and cooling.

notes.t: Fluid coupling clutches
pts: A fluid coupling transmits torque hydraulically between an impeller on the input and a runner on the output, so the output speed can vary while the input speed stays fixed.
Power lost in slip is converted to heat inside the coupling, which must be dissipated.
The coupling is described as allowing rotation in one direction only, with oil circulating in a toroidal path between impeller and runner forming an oil vortex.
defs: Fluid coupling
A hydrodynamic device with an impeller (input) and runner (output) sharing oil, transmitting torque through oil circulation so that output speed can differ from input speed.
tips: Do not confuse a fluid coupling with a friction clutch: the fluid coupling transmits torque through oil, not solid contact, so it cannot give zero slip at full load.
rq: Why does the heat generated in a fluid coupling increase as the output speed falls further below the input speed?
The slip between impeller and runner grows, so more of the input power is dissipated as heat in the oil rather than transmitted to the output.

notes.t: Fluid coupling clutches
pts: Fluid couplings transmit torque hydraulically, allowing speed control of the driven load with a fixed-speed drive.
Fluid couplings give smooth start-up because torque builds gradually rather than as a shock load.
The coupling isolates the driven or drive system from shock and overload, providing protection.
Slip in the coupling produces heat continuously, so the heat must be removed to avoid overheating.
tips: Remember that the output speed of a fluid coupling is always lower than the input speed; the slip is the source of heat, not a loss that can be ignored.
Do not confuse fluid couplings with mechanical clutches: fluid couplings give no direct mechanical contact and therefore allow smooth, shock-free start-up.
rq: Why must heat be dissipated in a fluid coupling even when it is running at steady speed?
Some slip between input and output is always present to transmit torque, and the slip power is converted to heat, which must be removed continuously.
If a fixed-speed motor drives a pump through a fluid coupling, how could the pump speed be reduced?
By reducing the amount of fluid in the coupling (or filling level), which increases slip and lowers the output speed while the motor speed stays fixed.

units.name: 6.8 Torque, power and speed in clutch engagement
units.ov: This module links the basic power relation P = Tω to how clutches and gearboxes behave. Gearbox speed changes trade torque against speed at constant power, which determines where a clutch should sit. Engagement then requires an inertial torque T = mk²α to bring the driven side up to the drive side's speed, and this sets the torque demand and the heat generated.
must: Power transmitted by a shaft: \( P = T\omega \), with P in W, T in N·m and \( \omega \) in rad/s
Convert rpm to rad/s with \( \omega = 2\pi N/60 \) before using P = Tω; using rpm directly is a classic error
Ideal gearbox (no losses): power in = power out, so a speed reduction raises torque by the same ratio, \( T_1\omega_1 = T_2\omega_2 \)
Real gearboxes have efficiency below 100%, so the inverse torque-speed trade-off holds exactly only when losses are neglected
Place the clutch on the high-speed side of the gearbox, because the torque there is lowest and the clutch can be smaller
Inertial torque to accelerate the driven side: \( T = mk^{2}\alpha \), where \( I = mk^{2} \)
The radius of gyration k is not the physical radius; it is the radius at which the mass could be concentrated to give the same I. Remember to square it
Use \( \alpha \) in rad/s² and SI units for m and k so T comes out in N·m
A larger speed difference between the drive and driven sides demands a higher torque for a given engagement time, because \( \alpha = \Delta\omega / t \)
Heat generated in engagement depends on the driven shaft's angular acceleration, and unloading the driven shaft before engagement reduces the braking load
Clutch classes: positive contact, overrunning (one direction only), friction, and fluid coupling
conn: Gearbox ratio and clutch location: P = Tω gives the torque on each side of the gearbox, which shows why the high-speed side is the best place for a clutch
Engagement torque and speed difference: \( \alpha = \Delta\omega/t \) links the speed difference and engagement time to \( T = mk^2\alpha \), and hence to the required clutch torque
Reflected inertia: gearing changes the effective inertia and torque seen by the clutch, so combine the gear ratio with T = Iα
Power, torque and heat: the torque during slip multiplied by the slip speed is the power dissipated as heat, so a higher α or a larger speed difference means more heating
exq: A motor delivers 15 kW at 1500 rpm to a gearbox with a 5:1 reduction and 95% efficiency. Find the input and output torques and the output speed in rad/s. Explain why the clutch should go on the input side.

A driven shaft has mass 40 kg and radius of gyration 0.25 m. It must be accelerated from rest to survive a 2 s engagement with a drive side at 1200 rpm. Calculate α, the inertial torque required, and the peak power at the end of engagement.
Explain why a clutch is best placed on the high-speed side of a gearbox. Give a quantitative example using constant power and a 4:1 speed reduction.
A student calculates inertial torque using the physical radius 0.4 m instead of k = 0.28 m. By what factor is the torque in error? Explain what k represents.
Discuss how unloading the driven shaft before engagement and the choice of engagement time affect the torque requirement and the heat generated in a friction clutch.

notes.t: Torque, power, and speed
pts: Power transmitted by a rotating shaft equals torque multiplied by angular velocity.
Neglecting losses, power in equals power out, so a speed reduction raises torque for constant power.
Reducing angular velocity with a gearbox increases the transmitted torque when power is constant.
A clutch should be placed where it carries the lowest torque, which is the high-speed side of the gearbox.
eqs: Power transmitted by a rotating shaft
P = power (W); T = torque (N·m); \omega = angular velocity (rad/s)
tips: Use angular velocity in rad/s, not rpm, when applying P = Tω in SI units.
Torque and speed trade off inversely only when losses are neglected; real gearboxes have efficiency below 100%.
rq: Why is the clutch placed on the high-speed side of a gearbox rather than the low-speed side?
On the high-speed side the angular velocity is higher, so for the same power the torque is lower; the clutch therefore carries less torque and can be smaller.
If a gearbox halves the speed of a shaft with no losses, what happens to the torque?
Torque doubles, because P = Tω is constant, so T ∝ 1/ω.

notes.t: Torque, power, and speed in clutch engagement
pts: Torque needed to accelerate the driven side is set by its inertia and angular acceleration
One side of the clutch must be accelerated until both sides run at the same speed
A larger speed difference between drive and driven sides demands a higher torque
Unloading the driven shaft before engagement reduces the braking load on it
Heat generated during engagement depends on the driven shaft's angular acceleration
eqs: Torque required to accelerate the driven side of a clutch (inertial torque)
T = torque (N·m); m = mass (kg); k = radius of gyration (m); \alpha = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
tips: Radius of gyration is squared in the torque formula; forgetting the square or using radius instead of radius of gyration gives wrong torque values.
Ensure angular acceleration is in rad/s² (not rpm/s) and mass and radius of gyration are in SI units so torque comes out in N·m.
rq: Why does a larger speed difference between the two clutch sides require more torque at engagement?
Because the driven side must be accelerated over the same interval to match the drive speed, so a bigger speed change means a bigger angular acceleration, and torque = m k² α rises in proportion.
What would you change to reduce the heat generated when a clutch engages, and why does it work?
Reduce the driven shaft's angular acceleration (e.g. by unloading it first or engaging more gently), since the heat generated depends on that acceleration, so less acceleration means less heat.

notes.t: Clutches: purpose, classification and power-torque relationship
pts: Clutches transmit torque between shafts, can temporarily connect them, and can permit motion in one direction only.
Main clutch classes are positive contact, overrunning, friction, and fluid coupling.
Power equals torque multiplied by angular velocity, so power depends directly on both quantities.
Torque needed to accelerate a rotating body depends on its mass, radius of gyration and angular acceleration.
defs: Clutch
A device that connects or disconnects the transmission of torque between two shafts, either temporarily or in one direction only.
Torque
The turning moment produced by a force acting at a radius about an axis of rotation.
eqs: Power transmitted by a rotating shaft
P = power (W); T = torque (N·m); \omega = angular velocity (rad/s)
Torque to accelerate a rotating body
T = torque (N·m); m = mass (kg); k = radius of gyration (m); \alpha = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
tips: Use radians per second for angular velocity in P = Tω; using rpm directly gives wrong power values unless converted.
Radius of gyration k is not the physical radius; it is the distance at which the mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia (I = mk²).
rq: Why does a one-way (overrunning) clutch allow a shaft to spin freely in one direction but not the other?
It locks through a ratchet or roller mechanism when the driving member turns one way, transmitting torque, and disengages when the other member overruns it.
If angular velocity doubles while torque stays constant, what happens to the transmitted power?
Power doubles, since P = Tω is directly proportional to ω.

units.name: 6.9 Clutches and torque transmission (summary notes)
units.ov: This module classifies clutches first by engagement method (positive contact, friction, overrunning, magnetic, fluid coupling) and then separately by actuation method. It then examines how each type transmits torque: dog clutch (interlocking), ratchet/pawl and sprag (one-way), drum clutch and disc brake (friction), and fluid couplings (hydrodynamic). The quantitative core is P = Tω and T = mk²α, which determine the torque a clutch must carry in steady running and during acceleration at engagement.
must: Classification: engagement method (positive contact, friction, overrunning, magnetic, fluid) is distinct from actuation method (mechanical, pneumatic/hydraulic, electrical, magnetic)
Steady-state power \(P = T\omega\), with \(\omega\) in rad/s (\(\omega = 2\pi N/60\) for N in rpm); with no losses, power in = power out
Torque is inversely proportional to speed through a gearbox, so a clutch placed on the high-speed side carries the lowest torque
Acceleration torque \(T = m k^{2}\alpha = I\alpha\); the radius of gyration is squared, and \(I = mk^2\)
At engagement the driven side must be accelerated to the driver speed; torque depends on the acceleration and on the speed difference; unloading the driven shaft first reduces the clutch load
Dog clutch is positive engagement with no slip; engage only at low or zero relative speed to avoid shock loading

Overrunning clutches (ratchet and pawl, sprag, roller, spring wound) drive in one direction only and freewheel in the other; ratchet/pawl is intermittent toothed engagement, while sprag/roller are continuous wedging friction types
Sprag clutch: asymmetric cam-shaped wedges tilt and lock between the inner and outer races in the driving direction and release when overrunning

Drum friction clutch: centrifugal flyweights pull outward against springs to press the linings on the drum, so it engages automatically above a threshold speed and disengages when speed falls; a disc brake uses an axially moved pressure plate to resist rotation
Fluid coupling: oil circulates between impeller (input) and runner (output) with no mechanical contact, so it is smooth and allows slip
conn: Gearbox ratio with clutch position: P = Tω fixes torque at each shaft, so the choice of clutch location sets the required torque capacity
Engagement dynamics: the speed difference and the inertia (mk²) of the driven side set the acceleration torque, which sets the clutch sizing and the slip during engagement
Engagement type with speed suitability: positive clutches (dog) need matched speeds, friction and fluid types tolerate slip, and overrunning types self-select by direction
Drum clutch speed actuation links centrifugal force, spring tension and friction torque to the engagement speed and motor start-up under light load
exq: A motor delivers 15 kW at 1450 rpm through a gearbox with a 4:1 speed reduction. Calculate the torque at the motor shaft and at the output shaft, and explain on which side the clutch should be placed and why.

A flywheel-type load of mass 50 kg and radius of gyration 0.3 m must be accelerated from rest to 1000 rpm in 5 s by a clutch. Calculate the angular acceleration, the acceleration torque, and the power at the end of the acceleration.
Classify clutches by engagement method and actuation method, giving two examples of each engagement class, and explain why engagement and actuation are separate classifications.

Describe with sketches how a sprag clutch and a ratchet and pawl each transmit torque in one direction and overrun in the other, and compare their suitability for continuous versus intermittent drive.

Explain how a centrifugal drum clutch lets a prime mover start with minimal load and then engage automatically, and state why it will not grip at low speed. Contrast its function with a disc friction brake.

notes.t: Clutches: Clutch Types and Classification
pts: Clutches are classified first by method of engagement, then by method of actuation (mechanical, pneumatic/hydraulic, electrical, magnetic).
By engagement method, clutches are grouped as positive contact, friction, overrunning, magnetic, or fluid coupling types.
Friction clutches transmit torque through frictional contact and come in disc, drum, and cone forms.
Overrunning clutches transmit torque in one direction only and include roller, sprag, and spring wound types.
Magnetic clutches use magnetic particle, hysteresis, or eddy current effects, while fluid couplings use dry fluid or hydraulic fluid.
defs: Positive contact clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through mechanical interlocking of jaws or teeth (square jaw, spiral jaw, toothed) with no slip.
Friction clutch
A clutch that transmits torque by frictional pressure between mating surfaces (disc, drum or cone), allowing controlled slip during engagement.
Overrunning clutch
A clutch that automatically transmits torque in one rotational direction and freewheels in the other.
Magnetic clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through magnetic forces, using magnetic particles, hysteresis or eddy currents.
Fluid coupling
A clutch that transmits torque hydrodynamically through a fluid (dry fluid or hydraulic) between input and output elements.
tips: Do not confuse the method of engagement (the type of clutch) with the method of actuation (how it is operated), which is a separate branch of the classification.
Positive contact clutches should only be engaged at low or zero relative speed, as engaging at speed causes shock loading.
rq: Why might a designer choose a friction clutch over a positive contact clutch?

Friction clutches can engage at speed and under load because slip allows smooth engagement, whereas positive contact clutches should engage only at low or zero relative speed to avoid shock and damage.
What distinguishes an overrunning clutch from other clutch types in how it operates?
It engages automatically based on the direction of rotation rather than being actuated, transmitting torque one way and freewheeling the other.

notes.t: Dog Clutch
pts: A dog clutch transmits torque between two shafts by interlocking projections (dogs) on the drive and driven members, so it is a positive-engagement device rather than a friction device.
In the disengaged position the drive gear and driven gear are separated, so no torque is transmitted and the driven member does not turn.
In the engaged position the sliding dog member locks into the driven gear, so the drive gear turns the driven gear without slip.
defs: Dog clutch
A positive-engagement clutch in which interlocking teeth or dogs on mating faces or sleeves couple two rotating members so they turn together with no slip.
tips: Do not treat a dog clutch like a friction clutch: it gives no slip and cannot be safely engaged at large speed differences.
Remember the drive and driven gears are labelled in the figure; torque flows from the drive gear only when the clutch is engaged.
rq: Why must a dog clutch normally be engaged only when the two members are at (or nearly at) the same speed?
Because the dogs are rigid, positive interlocks; engaging them while they rotate at different speeds causes impact, shock loading and damage to the dogs.

notes.t: Overrunning Clutches – Ratchet and Pawl
pts: A ratchet and pawl is an overrunning clutch: the ratchet wheel drives in one direction only, with the pawl engaging its teeth and slipping over them in the reverse direction.
The pawl is pivoted and pushed against the toothed ratchet by a spring or gravity so it re-engages automatically on each tooth.
This page introduces overrunning clutches and their methods of failure, which are covered in the sub-section that follows.
defs: Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits torque in one rotational direction only and freewheels (overruns) when the driven member turns faster than the driver or in the reverse direction.
Ratchet and pawl
An overrunning mechanism in which a spring-loaded pawl engages the teeth of a ratchet wheel to transmit torque in one direction, slipping over the teeth in the opposite direction.
tips: Do not confuse a ratchet and pawl (intermittent, positive engagement with teeth) with a friction overrunning clutch (roller or sprag type, continuous engagement).
rq: Why does the pawl slip over the ratchet teeth when the wheel turns the opposite way?
The pawl's tip is shaped so the teeth push it aside in reverse, so no load is transmitted and the wheel freewheels.
What would happen if the pawl spring were removed?
The pawl would not reliably re-engage the teeth, so it could skip or ride over them, causing loss of drive and noise.

notes.t: Sprag Clutch
pts: A sprag clutch is a one-way clutch that transmits torque in one rotation direction and freewheels in the other, using wedge-shaped sprags between inner and outer races.
The sprags are shown in four positions (top to bottom), illustrating how the sprag tilts and wedges between the races when the clutch engages versus when it overruns.
defs: Sprag
A non-cylindrical, cam-like wedge element that tilts to lock between the inner and outer races when rotated in the driving direction, transmitting torque one way only.
tips: Do not confuse a sprag clutch (non-symmetric wedge, one-way) with a ratchet/pawl or a roller clutch; the sprag's locking depends on its asymmetric profile and contact geometry.
Specify the driving direction clearly when describing engagement; the answer reverses if the rotation direction is reversed.
rq: Why does the sprag lock in one direction but freewheel in the other?
Its asymmetric profile means that rotation in one direction tilts it so its contact points (B) wedge between the races, while reverse rotation tilts it away, letting it slide freely.
What would happen if the sprag profile were symmetric (e.g. circular)?
It would not wedge in either direction, so it could not lock and would transmit no torque; the asymmetric shape is essential for the wedging action.

notes.t: Drum friction clutch and disc friction brake
pts: A drum friction clutch lets the prime mover start and reach operating speed with minimal load, then engages automatically once the drive shaft spins fast enough.
The clutch disengages automatically when the prime mover slows down, and can stop an electric motor being turned by the load.
In the drum clutch, flyweights carried on the hub are pulled outward by centrifugal force against tension springs, pressing the linings onto the clutch drum.
In the disc friction brake, a pressure plate is moved axially to clamp the clutch plate drive, which is splined or keyed to the driven end.
defs: Drum friction clutch
A clutch in which centrifugally actuated flyweights press friction linings against the inside of a rotating drum, transmitting torque by friction once speed is high enough.
Disc friction brake
A brake in which an axially moved pressure plate clamps friction surfaces together to resist rotation of a shaft.
tips: Do not confuse the drum clutch (speed-actuated, automatic) with the disc brake (applied to stop rotation); the clutch transmits torque while the brake resists it.
Engagement depends on rotational speed, so the clutch will not grip at low speed even if the springs are present.
rq: Why does the drum clutch allow the motor to run up to speed with minimal load?
Because the flyweights are not yet thrown outward against the springs, so the linings are not pressed against the drum and no torque is transmitted until the shaft spins fast enough.
What would happen if the tension springs in the drum clutch were made much stiffer?
The flyweights would need a higher speed to overcome the springs, so the clutch would engage at a higher speed (and later).

notes.t: Steady State and Accelerating Torque, Power, Speed; Fluid Couplings
pts: With losses neglected, power in equals power out, so reducing angular velocity (e.g. via a gearbox) increases transmitted torque.
A clutch should be placed on the high-speed side of a gearbox so it transmits the lowest torque.
When a clutch engages, the driven side must be accelerated until both sides have the same speed; the torque needed depends on the acceleration and on the speed difference.
Unloading the driven shaft before engagement reduces the braking load the clutch must overcome.
A fluid coupling transfers torque through oil circulating between an impeller (input) and a runner (output), with no mechanical contact.
defs: Steady state power
Power transmitted by a rotating shaft equals the torque multiplied by the angular velocity, assuming no losses.
Radius of gyration
The radial distance at which the whole mass of a rotating body could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia.
eqs: Steady state power transmitted by a shaft
Torque required to accelerate a rotating mass
\(T\) = torque (N·m); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(k\) = radius of gyration (m); \(\alpha\) = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
tips: Keep units consistent: angular velocity must be in rad/s (not rpm) when using \(P = T\omega\).
Radius of gyration is squared in the acceleration torque equation; forgetting the square is a common error.
rq: Why is the clutch placed on the high-speed side of a gearbox rather than the low-speed side?
Because torque is inversely proportional to angular velocity for constant power, so the high-speed side carries the lowest torque, making the clutch smaller and lower-loaded.
What happens to the torque needed to engage a clutch if the speed difference between its two sides doubles?
The required torque increases, since a larger speed difference requires greater angular acceleration to match speeds.

units.name: 7.1 Machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes (summary notes)
units.ov: This material introduces design considerations for machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, using a pump-motor set on a common rigid steel baseframe as the example. It then focuses on what power transmission does to a gearbox: meshing teeth generate heat and wear, so lubrication and cooling are both needed. The linking idea is that the enclosure and mounting must keep components aligned while supporting lubrication and heat removal. Note that the source pages are brief and give no formulas.
must: A pump, coupling/guard and electric motor are mounted together on a rigid steel baseplate (common baseframe) so that their shafts stay aligned
Meshing gear teeth generate large amounts of heat, and the gearbox must be designed to remove it
Without lubricant between the teeth, meshing teeth damage each other mechanically (wear, scuffing)
Lubrication and cooling are two separate requirements, and lubrication alone is not sufficient
The lubrication system must deliver lubricant to the highest-loaded parts, not just be present in the gearbox generally
The gearbox needs a system that removes all the generated heat, not just some of it
The coupling is guarded and sits between the driver (motor) and the driven machine (pump) on the baseframe
Mounting and enclosure choices are driven by function: alignment, support, protection, and lubricant and heat management
conn: Baseframe rigidity links to shaft alignment, which affects coupling and bearing loads and so gear tooth loading, heat generation and wear
Power transmitted links to heat generated, which sets the required cooling capacity and the lubricant system design
Lubricant has a dual role: it separates the teeth to prevent mechanical damage and carries heat away, so lubrication and cooling are designed together
The enclosure must contain the lubricant, protect the gears and allow heat to be rejected, so it ties together mounting, lubrication and cooling
exq: Explain why a pump, coupling and electric motor are mounted on a common rigid steel baseframe, and describe what could go wrong if the baseplate were flexible.
List the main effects of transmitting power on a gearbox and state the design provisions needed to deal with each.
Why is lubrication alone insufficient for a gearbox? Describe how the lubrication system should deal with the highest-loaded parts and how the generated heat is removed.
Describe what happens to meshing gear teeth when lubricant is absent, and discuss how this affects gearbox life.
Sketch a pump-motor set on a baseframe, labelling the pump, coupling guard, motor and baseplate, and comment on the function of each.

notes.t: Machinery Mountings, Enclosures, and Gearboxes – Design Points
pts: This section introduces design considerations for machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, illustrated by a pump-motor set on a common baseframe.
The pump, coupling/guard and electric motor are mounted together on a rigid steel baseplate so their shafts stay aligned.
tips: The page contains only a heading and a photo; do not invent specific design formulas or rules that are not shown on this page.
rq: Why does a pump-motor set need a rigid common baseplate rather than individual floor mountings?
A rigid common baseplate keeps the pump and motor shafts aligned and limits relative movement and vibration, which would otherwise cause coupling wear and bearing failure.

notes.t: Effects of Transmitting Power on a Gearbox
pts: Meshing gear teeth generate large amounts of heat, so the gearbox must remove this heat.
Without lubricant between the teeth, meshing teeth damage each other mechanically.
Gearboxes need lubrication systems that deliver lubricant to the highest-loaded parts.
Gearboxes need systems that remove all the generated heat, i.e. cooling as well as lubrication.
tips: Lubrication and cooling are both required; do not treat lubrication alone as sufficient.
Lubricant must reach the highest-loaded parts, not just be present in the gearbox generally.
rq: Why does lubricant serve a dual role (protection and heat removal) in a gearbox rather than just reducing friction?

Lubricant separates the meshing teeth to prevent metal-to-metal contact and damage, and it also carries away the heat generated by meshing, so it must be circulated to the highest-loaded contact points.
What would happen to a gearbox transmitting high power if its cooling system failed but lubrication continued?
Heat would build up faster than it could be removed, raising the oil and component temperature, thinning the lubricant film and risking tooth damage and failure.

units.name: 7.2 Fluid system diagrams and engineering drawing requirements (summary notes)
units.ov: This module covers the conventions that make fluid system diagrams and engineering drawings unambiguous: the British standards for symbols (BS 5070-3, BS 1553, BS ISO 1219-1, BS EN 61082-2), rules for line cross-overs and junctions, and flow diagram layout. It then moves to the drawing hierarchy (diagrams, general arrangement, detail, manufacturing, single-part and assembly drawings) governed by BS 8888, with dimensioning rules, abbreviations and orthographic views. The unifying idea is that each drawing type has a defined purpose and content, and standards ensure it is read consistently.
must: Match standard to symbol set: BS 5070-3 for fluid flow diagrams, BS 1553 for general engineering graphical symbols, BS ISO 1219-1 for pneumatics, BS EN 61082-2 for electrical symbols
BS 1553 parts: Part 1 piping systems and plant (including heating and ventilation), Part 2 power generating plant (steam and IC engines, turbines), Part 3 compressing plant

Cross-overs: drawn at right angles with no change of direction; use one of the three methods (1, 2 or 3) consistently across a diagram set; with the hump method (2) the jumper preferably sits on the horizontal line
Junctions: no more than two lines meet at a point, and the dot is the preferred marking

Flow diagram: shows all essential parts so physical characteristics can be analysed and calculated, independent of physical layout; cause-to-effect runs left to right, and vertical orientation is shown with arrow symbols

Diagrams show flow and linkage, not physical position; the two types are control systems and main flow; general arrangement drawings show overall views, dimensions, weights, services and a list of associated drawings, and are used to check access, transport and installation
Detail drawings are fully dimensioned and describe a part for manufacture; manufacturing/fabrication drawings are process-specific and annotated (weld codes, bolt torques, lubrication, stress relief)
BS 8888:2000 is current and replaced BS 308 (withdrawn 2000); number format uses spaces for thousands and a comma for the decimal
Single-part drawings need shape, dimensions, tolerances, material/heat treatment and surface finish; assembly drawings need a parts list and use hatching to distinguish parts

Dimensioning rules: dimension each feature once only, on one view, outside the outline, with enough dimensions to machine without calculation, and watch error build-up in series dimensions; know the abbreviations A/F, PCD, CSK, SFACE, NTS, UCUT; distinguish dashed hidden detail from chain centre lines and identify the view before deducing hole positions
conn: Standards and symbols link to diagram type: BS 5070-3 and BS 1553 symbols are used in flow diagrams, and consistent symbol and cross-over conventions make the diagram readable

General arrangement, detail, manufacturing and assembly drawings are cross-referenced; the GA gives the parts list and references, and the detail drawings supply the dimensions and tolerances for manufacture
Orthographic views, line types and dimensioning rules combine in reading a part drawing, for example locating holes by centre lines and PCD and deciding which view to dimension on
BS 8888 ties to drawing practice: the numeric format and the referenced standards apply to every drawing type
exq: State which British standard applies to each of: fluid flow diagrams, pneumatic circuits, electrical symbols and piping system symbols. Name the three BS 1553 parts and what each covers.
Sketch the three acceptable methods of showing a line cross-over and a junction. State the rules on right angles, number of lines at a junction, and mixing methods in a diagram set.
Define a flow diagram and explain how it differs from a general arrangement drawing. State what information a GA drawing must carry and its uses.

Distinguish between detail, manufacturing/fabrication, single-part and assembly drawings, listing the content required for each. Explain why BS 308 should not be cited and how BS 8888 writes the number 3213.8 mm.

A block drawing has a row of five holes of decreasing diameter on one centre line and a central through hole in the end view. Explain how you would dimension it (PCD, one-view, external, avoiding series error build-up), distinguish the line styles used, and explain what NTS means for reading dimensions.

notes.t: Basic Fluid Systems: diagram standards and line cross-overs/junctions
pts: Engineering fluid diagrams follow named British standards, with BS 5070-3 covering mechanical/fluid flow diagram drawing practice.
Pneumatic control circuits use BS ISO 1219-1 symbols, while electrical symbols follow BS EN 61082-2.
A cross-over without joining is drawn at right angles without change of direction; only one of three acceptable methods may be used per diagram set.
When method 2 (hump/bridge) is used, the jumper should preferably sit on the horizontal line.
No more than two connecting lines should meet at a point to form a junction, with a dot marking the preferred junction method.
defs: Line cross-over
Two lines crossing on a diagram without being connected; shown at right angles with no change of direction, using one consistent drawing method (method 1, 2 or 3) across the diagram set.
Line junction
A point where connecting pipe lines meet and are joined; recommended to involve no more than two connecting lines, shown with a dot as the preferred method.
tips: Do not mix cross-over methods 1, 2 and 3 within one diagram or set of diagrams.
Know which standard applies to which symbol set: BS 5070-3 for fluid flow diagrams, BS ISO 1219-1 for pneumatics, BS EN 61082-2 for electrical symbols.
rq: Why does the standard insist that only one cross-over method is used on any one diagram set?
So that the reader never has to guess whether a crossing is joined or not; mixing methods causes ambiguity in interpreting the drawing.
Why is a junction with more than two connecting lines discouraged?
Too many lines meeting at one point make it hard to tell which connections exist and how flow is routed, so the diagram becomes ambiguous.

notes.t: BS 1553 graphical symbols and fluid/flow diagram guidelines
pts: BS 1553 is a multi-part standard of graphical symbols for general engineering; the key parts here are Part 1 (piping systems and plant, including heating and ventilation), Part 2 (power generating plant) and Part 3 (compressing plant).
Part 2 covers steam and internal combustion engines, turbines and auxiliary plant.
A flow diagram depicts all essential parts of a process or equipment so that physical characteristics can be analysed and calculated, arranged to show operation clearly regardless of physical layout.
Flow diagrams should be drawn so that the sequence from cause to effect runs from left to right; vertical orientation depends on pressure facilities and sequences and is indicated by arrow symbols.
BS 1553-1:1977 graphically shows all symbols used in piping systems and is used to prepare system diagrams.
defs: Flow diagram

A diagram depicting all essential parts of a process or item of equipment, arranged to show operation clearly and to enable analysis and calculation of physical characteristics, independent of physical layout.
tips: Use symbols consistently throughout a diagram; mixing symbols for the same component is a common mistake.
Vertical orientation of a flow diagram is not the default: it depends on pressure facilities and sequences and must be indicated with arrow symbols.
rq: Why should a flow diagram ignore the physical layout of the equipment?
Because its purpose is to show the process operation and sequence clearly, so the logic of cause and effect is not obscured by the physical positions of items.
Why is it good practice to use the simplest symbol that gives all the detail needed?
Simple symbols keep the diagram clear and readable, while still conveying every piece of information the reader requires; unnecessary detail adds clutter.

notes.t: Requirements for Engineering Drawings, Diagrams, and Models
pts: Engineering information is conveyed graphically through sketches, diagrams, general arrangement drawings, detail drawings and models (real or 3D virtual).
Diagrams are their own class of engineering drawing that convey the flow of something and how items are linked, not their physical placement in space.
Diagrams come in two types: those showing control systems and those showing the main flow.
General arrangement drawings show overall views of equipment and are used to produce detail drawings and to check access, transportation and installation.

General arrangement drawings carry overall dimensions, installation details, overall weight/mass, subsystem weights, service supply details, a list of associated drawings, and labels or reference numbers for assemblies and parts.
defs: Schematic / block diagram
A diagram conveying how items are linked and the flow of something, where item placement on the page need not match physical placement.
General arrangement drawing
A drawing showing overall views of equipment (layout, assembly, exploded view) used to produce detail drawings and check access, transportation and installation.
Detail drawing
A fully dimensioned drawing specific to a manufacturing process such as casting, fabrication, welding or machining.
tips: Do not assume the position of items in a diagram reflects their physical position in space.
Detail drawings must be fully dimensioned and specific to the manufacturing process (casting, fabrication, welding, machining).
rq: Why can a diagram's layout be misleading if read as a physical layout?
Because diagrams show flow and links between items, so the placement of items on the page often has no practical link to their placement in space.
Why is a general arrangement drawing useful beyond producing detail drawings?
It also serves as a check for access, transportation and installation, since it shows overall views and dimensions of the whole equipment.

notes.t: Detail Drawings, Manufacturing Drawings and Drawing Standards (BS 8888)
pts: A detailed drawing fully describes a part so it can be manufactured; complex parts may need several linked drawings that reference each other.

Manufacturing (fabrication) drawings form part of the detail drawings and are often drawn for a specific process or step, annotated with process notes such as weld codes, bolt torques, lubrication and stress-relieving requirements.

The old standard BS 308 was withdrawn in 2000 but remains downloadable; the current standard is BS 8888:2000, a harmonised standard that is essentially a list of other standards covering individual areas of drawing detail.
BS 8888 introduced a harmonised change in number formatting: thousands are separated by spaces and decimals by commas.
defs: Detailed drawing
A drawing that contains all the information required to fully describe a part so that it can be manufactured; several may be needed for one part, cross-referenced to each other.
Manufacturing (fabrication) drawing
A drawing that forms part of the detail drawings, prepared for a specific manufacturing process or step and annotated with process-specific notes.
The current UK harmonised standard for Technical Product Documentation, specifying how products are defined, specified and graphically represented by referencing a set of supporting standards.
BS 308
The former UK Engineering Drawing Practice standard, withdrawn in 2000 and superseded by BS 8888.
tips: Do not use the old BS 308 standard in answers; the current standard is BS 8888:2000, even though BS 308 is still downloadable.
Remember the BS 8888 number format: spaces separate thousands and a comma marks the decimal, unlike the usual UK 3,213.8 mm notation.
rq: Why might one part need several drawings rather than a single one, and what must they do to work together?
Because the level of detail and the number of manufacturing steps can exceed what one sheet can show; the drawings must reference one another so the complete description of the part is traceable.
Why is BS 8888 described as a list of other standards rather than a complete standard in itself?
It acts as an umbrella that points to specific standards (e.g. BS ISO 10209-1, BS EN ISO 5456-2, BS EN ISO 128-20) covering individual areas of drawing detail.

notes.t: Drawing Abbreviations, Single Part and Assembly Drawings, Dimensioning Principles
pts: A single part drawing must contain all information needed to produce the part: shape, dimensions, tolerances, material/heat treatment and surface finish.
An assembly drawing shows a complete assembly or subassembly and must include a parts list.
Hatching is used on assembly drawings to distinguish different parts.
Enough dimensions must be given so the component can be machined without extra calculations.
Dimensions should appear on only one view, be placed external to the drawing, and build-up of errors must be considered for series dimensions.
defs: A/F
Across flats: the distance between opposite flat faces of a hexagon or square section.
PCD
Pitch circle diameter: the diameter of the circle on which the centres of a set of holes or bolts lie.
CSK
Countersunk: a conical recess machined so a screw head sits flush with the surface.
SFACE / SF
Spotface: a flat-bottomed circular machined recess providing a bearing surface for a bolt head or nut.
NTS
Not to scale: indicates the drawing is not dimensionally accurate and dimensions must be relied upon.
UCUT
Undercut: a groove cut at the end of a shoulder or thread to allow clearance for a tool or mating part.
tips: Do not repeat the same dimension on several views; each dimension should appear once only.
Remember that 'NTS' means the drawing is not to scale, so measured lengths must not be used.
rq: Why must dimensions appear on only one view rather than on every view?
Repeating dimensions adds clutter and creates risk of conflicting values if one is changed; one clear placement keeps the drawing readable and unambiguous.
Why does build-up of errors matter when dimensioning a series of features?
Chained tolerances accumulate, so the final feature's position can deviate far more than any single tolerance; this must be considered when choosing how to dimension in series.
Why is a parts list essential on an assembly drawing but not required on a single part drawing?
An assembly combines several components that must each be identified and quantified; a single part is one item, so its identity is given in the title block.

notes.t: Basic Machine Elements – orthographic drawing of a block with through holes
pts: The page shows three orthographic views (plan/elevation style) of a rectangular block, with hidden detail drawn as dashed lines and centre lines drawn as chain lines.
The front-view square outline contains a single central circular hole, located by crossing centre lines, indicating a through-hole along the axis of the block.
The long rectangular view carries a row of five circular holes of decreasing diameter, all sharing one horizontal centre line, showing a stepped series of hole sizes.
tips: Do not confuse hidden-detail dashed lines with centre lines; they use different line styles and meanings.
Check which view you are reading (plan, front, side) before deducing hole positions, since a circle in one view appears as a line in another.
rq: Why are centre lines drawn as chain lines, and why do the dashed lines in the top view indicate hidden features?
Chain (centre) lines mark axes of symmetry and hole centres; dashed lines represent edges or features behind the visible surface that cannot be seen directly in that view.
If the five holes in the long view are all the same depth through the block, what does the decreasing diameter tell you about the drilling sequence?

Each hole is a different size, so they would typically be produced by separate drilling/boring operations with progressively smaller tools (or the block is a stepped/counterbored form), not one tool pass.

units.name: 7.3 Lec 11 drawing fault files course ENG 1016
units.ov: This lecture covers how to read and interpret engineering drawings from a set of example parts (plug plate, ratchet, cannon head, flange, bar, park layout, vane pump, steering head assembly). It covers orthographic, section, detail and isometric views, how dimensions, units, scales and title-block notes define a part, and how assembly drawings use parts lists and balloons. The common thread is that the stated dimensions and notes, not the printed image, define the part, so units and scale must be checked before any value is used.
must: 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS': read stated dimensions only and never measure the printed image
Check units first: most drawings are mm, but the cannon head is in cm and the park layout is in m
Scale is drawing:real. A detail view has its own scale (e.g. 5:1, 2:5, 1:2), but stated dimensions are already real sizes and must not be rescaled
Orthographic projection uses several 2D views (plan, front, side) at right angles. Elevation views give heights and plan views give footprint
Section views (e.g. A-A, B-B, shown by a cutting-plane line) reveal internal geometry; detail views enlarge small features
Isometric view is pictorial with equal foreshortening of the three axes. It aids visualisation but is not used for dimensioning
Dimensioning notation: R = radius, Ø = diameter, and angles and tolerances are given for linear and angular dimensions. Do not confuse R27 with Ø50, or R25 with Ø25

The title block holds drawing number, material (e.g. SUS303, austenitic stainless), scale, tolerances, surface finish and sheet number. General notes include 'deburr and break sharp edges' to remove burrs and reduce stress concentrations
Assemblies use an exploded view with balloons plus a bill of materials (item, part number, description, quantity). Check quantities such as 16 off M6 bolts and 4 off vanes
Standard components are specified by designation, e.g. key ISO 2491 6x4-50 (6 wide, 4 high, 50 long), bolts ISO 4014 M6x40 and ISO 4762 M8x16, and pipe thread BS EN 10226-2
conn: Units and scale combine in a single question: cm vs mm on the cannon head, or the 1:250 park scale with real areas and heights in m
Detail view scale vs main scale: a 5:1 detail of the ratchet keyway (3 mm wide, 2.86 mm deep, R0.25) shows a feature 5 times larger on the page but still carries its real dimensions
Plan and elevation views must be combined to build the 3D shape and overall size (e.g. 15.5 x 14.0 m footprint, heights of 2.5 and 3.0 m), with the isometric view used to check it
Assembly drawing links the parts list, balloons and standard fastener designations to the quantity and material in the title block; keys and crank length also tie in with torque transmission
exq: The cannon head drawing gives a 30 cm diameter outline and a 22.91 cm inner circle. Convert both to mm, state the radial wall thickness, and explain why the printed drawing must not be measured.
A park plan is drawn at 1:250 and its footprint is 15.5 m by 14.0 m. Calculate the footprint area in m², and the length a 3.0 m high structure would have on the sheet in mm.

Explain what is shown by detail A of the ratchet (5:1, 3 mm wide keyway, 2.86 mm deep, R0.25). What real size is a feature that measures 15 mm on the printed detail, and why is the 5 mm thickness read from the side view?

For the flange (150 mm square, 5 mm thick, 10 mm corner radius, Ø50 tube, gussets to R27, height 40 mm, drawn at 1:2), state which values are real sizes and sketch the plan and front views with the key dimensions.
Describe the information in a bill of materials and title block for the steering head assembly, and decode the designations 'ISO 2491 6 x 4 - 50' and 'ISO 4762 M8 x 16'.

notes.t: Engineering drawing: dimensioning and reading a 3J CentreModulePlug technical drawing
pts: The drawing is a multi-view orthographic projection (plan, front/side section and an isometric view) of a square plug plate with a central boss below it.
Dimensions are given in millimetres unless otherwise specified, so all values read from the drawing are in mm.
The plate is 116 mm square with four corner holes of diameter 4 mm located at the corners of the plate.
The lower boss is 100 mm wide and sits offset 10 mm from the plate edge, with a total thickness of 20 mm including the 5 mm plate.
Sharp edges must be deburred and broken, and the drawing must not be scaled; dimensions alone define the part.
defs: Isometric view
A pictorial projection in which the three principal axes are foreshortened equally, giving a 3D impression of the part; used alongside orthographic views to aid visualisation.
Tolerance
The permissible variation in a dimension, specified in the title block for linear and angular dimensions, within which a part is acceptable.
Surface finish
The specified texture and quality of a machined surface, given in the title block as a requirement for the finished component.
tips: Do not measure dimensions from the drawing image; always read the stated values, since the drawing is not to scale.
Check the unit note in the title block (millimetres) before converting any value.
rq: Why must the drawing not be scaled, even though the views look proportional?
Printed drawings may be reproduced at a different scale, so measuring them gives unreliable sizes; only the stated dimensions are authoritative.
What does the 4 mm diameter callout tell a machinist about the corner features, and how would you confirm their position?
It defines four through-holes of 4 mm diameter at the corners; their position is set by dimensions from the plate edges shown in the plan view.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a stainless steel ratchet (drawing 4(c)): dimensions, details and t
pts: The drawing gives the main ratchet outline with radii R25 (outer) and R10 (hub/boss), plus a 6.50 mm dimension locating the tooth/feature at the top.
Detail A shows a keyway/slot on the central bore: 3 mm wide and 2.86 mm deep, with a corner radius R0.25, drawn at scale 5:1.
Detail B shows a small circular feature (pin/hole) with radius R0.50, also drawn at scale 5:1 to make small features legible.
The part is 5 mm thick, shown in the side view, and the material is SUS303 stainless steel.
The title block states the note 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS', so all sizes must be taken from the stated dimensions, not measured on the page.
defs: Detail view
An enlarged view of a small feature, drawn at a stated scale (here 5:1) so its dimensions can be shown clearly.
Radius (R)
Distance from the centre of a circle or arc to its edge, dimensioned with the prefix R on engineering drawings.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A general note instructing removal of burrs and rounding of sharp edges after machining, for safety and to avoid stress concentrations.
Do not scale drawings
A drawing note meaning dimensions must be read from the annotated values; measuring the printed drawing is not reliable.
tips: Use the stated dimensions, not measurements taken from the image, because the drawing says not to scale it.
Keep units consistent: all dimensions are in millimetres unless otherwise specified.
rq: Why does the drawing give a separate Detail A and Detail B at 5:1 instead of only the main view?
The features (keyway and small hole) are too small to dimension clearly at the main view scale, so an enlarged view shows them legibly.
Why must the note 'Do not scale drawings' be followed when making the part?
The printed drawing may be distorted by reproduction or scaling, so only the stated dimensions are reliable for manufacture.

notes.t: Engineering drawing dimensions and views of a perimeter cannon head
pts: All dimensions on this drawing are given in centimetres, not millimetres, so unit conversion must be considered when reading values.
The drawing includes a detail view at a stated scale, and the drawing itself must not be scaled, so the printed dimensions govern.
The head is shown in several orthographic views, including a front view with a 30 cm diameter circular outline and a 20 cm overall height, with a rectangular cut-out of 25 cm width and 10 cm offset.
A 15° angled feature and an R20 radius are dimensioned on the side view, showing how angles and radii are specified on a drawing.
The bottom view shows a 22.91 cm diameter inner circle inside a 30 cm outer circle, with notches at the edge, indicating how concentric features are dimensioned.
defs: Detail view
An enlarged view of a small region of a drawing, drawn at a different scale (here 2:5) and labelled with a letter to show where it applies.
Scale
The ratio between a dimension on the drawing and the real size of the object, written as drawing:real.
Orthographic projection
A method of representing a 3D object by several 2D views (front, side, top) projected at right angles to one another.
Tolerance
The permitted variation in a dimension, specified on the drawing for linear and angular measurements.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A finishing instruction to remove burrs and sharp corners from machined edges for safety and fit.
tips: Mixing units: dimensions here are in cm, while many engineering drawings use mm; always check the units note before calculating.
Do not measure the page to find sizes; the drawing states it must not be scaled, so use the written values.
rq: Why does the drawing state 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' when a scale is given?
Printed copies may be reproduced at a different size, so only the dimensions written on the drawing are reliable; measuring with a ruler can give wrong sizes.
If a student measures the 30 cm outer diameter and gets a different length on a printout, what should they do?
Use the printed dimension (30 cm) rather than the measured length, because the drawing is not to scale.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a flange (Water Chimes, drawing 2.2)
pts: The flange is a 150 mm square plate with 10 mm radius corners, 5 mm thick, carrying a central tube and four radial gussets.
The central tube has a 50 mm diameter, and the four gussets are 5 mm thick and project to a radius of 27 mm.
The gussets are inclined at 30° to the base, and the overall height of the component is 40 mm.
Dimensions are given in millimetres at a scale of 1:2, so the drawn sizes are half the real sizes.
tips: Dimensions on the drawing are in mm and represent real sizes even though the sheet is drawn at 1:2; do not convert them by the scale again.
Do not confuse the 27 mm radius (gusset extent) with the 50 mm diameter (central tube).
rq: Why is the scale 1:2 important when reading dimensions from this drawing?
Lengths drawn on paper are half the real size, so dimensions must be read from the printed values, not measured on the sheet, to get true sizes in mm.
What would change if the gusset angle were 45° instead of 30°?
The gussets would be steeper, reducing their base footprint and changing the sloped profile seen in the side view; the stated height and radius would constrain the new geometry.

notes.t: Engineering drawing conventions: reading dimensioned views and title block of a tubular be
pts: Orthographic views (front, side) plus sectional and detail views together fully define the geometry of a component.
Dimensions are given in millimetres unless otherwise specified, so all values on the sheet are read in mm.
A section view shows internal or cut geometry, here the row of holes in the bar, and is referenced by a cutting-plane line labelled B–B.
A detail view magnifies a small area at a different scale, indicated by a circled region and its own scale label.
The title block records material, drawing number, scale and sheet count, which must be checked before manufacture.
defs: Section view
A view formed by an imaginary cut through a part, shown with hatching or outline to reveal internal features such as holes or slots.
Detail view
An enlarged view of a small region of a drawing, drawn at a larger scale than the main view so that small features can be dimensioned clearly.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A general note instructing removal of burrs and rounding of sharp edges after machining for safety and handling.
tips: Watch the scale: the sheet is 1:5 unless otherwise stated, so a detail labelled 1:2 or 1:15 must be read with its own scale.
Do not measure from the printed drawing; use the dimension values given, as the note states DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS.
rq: Why is the note 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' included even though the sheet is drawn to a stated scale?
Printing and copying can change the physical size of the drawing, so measuring with a ruler may give wrong values; the stated dimensions must be used instead.
What would you need to check if a detail view showed a feature at a different scale from the main view?
Read the scale label under that view (e.g. 1:5 or 1:2) and use it to interpret any measurements taken from it, rather than the main sheet scale.

notes.t: Engineering drawing: reading a park layout (plan and elevation views)
pts: The drawing shows the park in an isometric view, a plan view and two elevation views, each with dimensions in metres.
Overall plan dimensions are 15.5 m by 14.0 m of the park footprint, with the site boundary drawn in the plan view.
The scale is 1:250, so drawn lengths must be multiplied by 250 to obtain real sizes.
The elevation views give a maximum overall width of 25.0 m, and the structures sit at heights including 2.5 m and 3.0 m above the ground line.
Units are metres (M), and the drawing is numbered 6.1 and dated 04/04/19.
defs: Plan view
A view looking directly down onto the object, showing horizontal positions and footprint dimensions.
Elevation view
A view looking horizontally at the side of an object, showing heights and vertical dimensions.
Isometric view
A pictorial 3D projection in which the three principal axes are equally foreshortened, giving an overall impression of the object.
