tips: Do not mix units: all dimensions are in metres, so convert consistently before calculating areas or heights.
Do not measure the printed drawing to get real sizes; always use the dimensioned values or apply the 1:250 scale factor.
rq: Why must dimensions be read in metres rather than from the drawn size on the page?
Because the drawing is at scale 1:250, so printed measurements are reduced; real dimensions are the stated values in metres, not measured drawing lengths.
Why are several views (plan and elevations) needed to fully define the park?
A single view cannot show both horizontal footprint and vertical heights; the plan gives layout and the elevations give heights and widths.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a rotary vane pump (dimensions, materials, fittings)
pts: The drawing gives a multi-view layout (front section A-A, side and isometric views) so that the pump's internal cavity, rotor and shaft can be understood alongside its external fittings.
Internal geometry is specified by radii: the cavity radius R48, rotor radius R44 and shaft radius R10 define the clearances the vanes run in.
The pump is driven by hand through a crank arm of length 152 mm acting on pedals, so the crank length sets the lever arm for the input torque.
The inlet/outlet connection is a 50 mm pipe thread to BS EN 10226 2, which is welded to a weld neck flange in service.
Drive is transmitted to the shaft through a parallel key to ISO 2491, 6 x 4 - 50, and the base is fixed with four M8 bolts at normal clearance.
defs: A standard parallel key 6 mm wide by 4 mm high, 50 mm long, fitted into keyways in shaft and hub to transmit torque.
Weld neck flange
A flange with a long tapered hub welded to the pipe or body, giving good stress transfer at the joint.
Austenitic stainless steel
A corrosion-resistant steel with a face-centred cubic austenite structure, used here for the pump body.
tips: Read dimensions as millimetres and do not scale the drawing, since the sheet states DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS.
Do not confuse the crank arm length (152) with the diameter Ø50 of the pipe connection.
rq: Why does the drawing specify both a cavity radius (R48) and a rotor radius (R44) rather than only one?
The difference (48 − 44 = 4 mm) sets the eccentric clearance space in which the vanes slide and trap fluid, so both radii are needed to define the working chamber.
What would happen to the required hand force if the crank arm were made shorter than 152 mm?
For the same input torque, a shorter lever arm requires a larger force at the pedal, so the operator works harder.

notes.t: Engineering drawing parts list and title block (Square Vane Rotary Steering Head assembly)
pts: The parts list (bill of materials) identifies every component by item number, part number, description and quantity, and links to the balloons on the exploded view.
The title block records drawing number, material, title, scale and sheet number, giving the identity and manufacturing information for the whole drawing.
The drawing is annotated 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS', so all dimensions must be taken from stated values, not measured from the image.
Two square housing halves (top and bottom case) enclose four square stator vanes and a carrier ring, sealed with rubber strip seals and an O-ring.
Fasteners are called up by standard designations (e.g. ISO 4014 M6 x 40, ISO 4762 M8 x 16), and the notes call for deburring and breaking sharp edges.
defs: Exploded view
A drawing in which the parts of an assembly are shown separated along their assembly axis, with leader lines and balloons identifying each item.
Bill of materials (parts list)
A table listing each component of an assembly with its item number, part number, description and quantity required.
Title block
The information panel on an engineering drawing giving drawing number, material, title, scale, tolerances, and approval signatures.
tips: Do not measure dimensions from the drawing image; use the dimensions stated on it, as the drawing says not to scale it.
Check the quantity column: several items appear in multiples (e.g. 16 off M6 bolts, 4 off vanes), and counts must match when describing the assembly.
rq: Why does the drawing say 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' even though it is a precise technical drawing?
The image may be distorted or reproduced at a changed size, so only the stated dimensions are reliable; measuring from the drawing can give wrong sizes.
If you needed to order replacement seals, which items on the parts list would you check and why?
Items 7 and 8 (strip rubber seals, single and triple flange, 4 each) plus item 12 (O-ring 250x5.3) and item 4 (lip seals), using their part numbers and quantities.

units.name: 7.4 Concept Selection Preparation Notes
units.ov: These notes cover a structured, repeatable approach to concept selection in design: choosing a limited set of high-level criteria tied to PDS statements, scoring concepts on a consistent scale, weighting criteria, and totalling a decision matrix. The ideas connect as a pipeline: PDS gives criteria, criteria are weighted (e.g. digital logic), concepts are scored, and the weighted totals are then reviewed with engineering judgement rather than accepted blindly.
must: Concept selection must be methodical and repeatable, not ad hoc: choose key elements, score concepts, find an initial winner, then analyse and redesign until a clear winner emerges.
Digital logic weighting: compare every criterion pairwise, award 1 to the more important and 0 to the less important, and count each criterion's positive decisions.
Weighting factor \( \alpha = \frac{\text{positive decisions of criterion}}{\text{total positive decisions of all criteria}} \); the factors must sum to 1 (use this as a check).
For n criteria there are \( \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \) pairwise comparisons, which equals the total positive decisions (useful for checking the denominator).
Weighted score = rating (1-5) × \( \alpha \); the total is the sum of weighted scores, not of raw scores.
Use one common scoring scale and method throughout a matrix (e.g. relative -2 to +2 against the existing system, with 0 meaning no better and no worse, or 1-5 ratings); never mix methods.
Ranking gives each concept a unique score, so it cannot show large differences between concepts, and its scale equals the number of concepts.
Use only a limited number of high-level criteria (matrix of about 5-10 concepts), each justified and linked to specific measurable PDS statements so that a high score is clearly defined.
A minimum criterion (disqualifying condition) removes a concept automatically, before any weighting or scoring; discard clearly weak concepts first.
The highest total is not automatically the final design: review and analyse the result with engineering judgement, and set weights through group discussion.
conn: PDS statements and importance levels feed into criteria selection, which then determines the weighting (digital logic) and how scores are defined in the matrix.
Pairwise digital logic scoring (1/0) is distinct from the 1-5 rating scale, yet both are combined in the weighted score calculation, so questions often test whether you keep them separate.
Minimum criteria act as a filter before the matrix, while the choice of scoring method (ranking vs relative vs 1-5) affects how well the matrix distinguishes concepts.
Matrix results lead to analysis and redesign, linking the quantitative totals back to the iterative selection process and engineering judgement.
exq: Four criteria (cost, safety, weight, usability) are compared pairwise using digital logic. Construct the comparison table from the given preferences, calculate each weighting factor \( \alpha \), and verify they sum to 1.
Given a decision matrix with five concepts, 1-5 ratings and your calculated weightings, compute the weighted scores and totals and identify the best concept. Then explain why you might not select it.
Explain why a student who sums raw scores instead of weighted scores gets a misleading result, and show with a numerical example how the ranking could change.
Compare ranking with a relative -2 to +2 scale for scoring concepts. State one advantage and one limitation of each, and explain why methods must not be mixed in one matrix.
Why should you not use every PDS item as a criterion? Describe how you would choose and justify high-level criteria, and where a minimum criterion would be applied in the process.

notes.t: Advice for Concept Selection: Overview and Choosing Design Criteria
pts: Concept selection must follow a methodical, repeatable process rather than an ad hoc choice of design.
A good matrix compares roughly 5 to 10 concepts; discard clearly weak or unwanted concepts first.
Selection proceeds by choosing key design elements, scoring each concept against them, finding an initial winner, then analysing and redesigning until a clear winner emerges.
Use only a limited number of high-level, important criteria, with documented reasons and an importance level for each PDS statement, so the matrix stays manageable and accurate.
Simple headings such as cost or usability are a starting point; criteria should be defined through the specific PDS statements they relate to, since a high score must be clearly defined.
defs: PDS (Product Design Specification)
A document listing the requirements and attributes a design must satisfy, each of which can be given an importance level and used as a selection criterion.
tips: Do not use every PDS item in the matrix; select a limited set of high-level criteria and justify the choice.
Simplified headings like 'cost' must be linked to specific measurable PDS statements to score consistently.
rq: Why can't all PDS items be used directly as selection criteria in the matrix?
Using every PDS item makes the selection process unwieldy and inaccurate, so only a limited set of high-level, important criteria should be chosen and documented.
Why is a simple criterion such as 'cost' insufficient on its own for scoring?
Because the statement does not define what a high score must achieve; criteria need to be made specific, e.g. energy usage per litre of water produced.

notes.t: Scoring Concepts and Criteria Weighting in Decision Matrices
pts: A decision matrix identifies the best-meeting solution, but results must still be reviewed with engineering judgement before selecting a final design.
A common scale must be used for all criteria, and the same scoring method must be applied to every criterion in one matrix.
A relative scale of −2 to +2 scores each solution against the existing system, with 0 meaning no better and no worse.
Ranking gives each concept a unique score, so big differences between solutions cannot be shown clearly and the scale equals the number of concepts.
Criteria weighting is not equal; weights should be set as a group activity through discussion, since discussion is the most valuable way to judge importance.
defs: Decision matrix
A tool used to decide which solution to a problem best meets the criteria set out by the design statement and PDS; its result is not automatically the final design.
Minimum criterion (disqualifying condition)
A requirement where a product that cannot achieve a certain value must be automatically removed from the selection process.
Ranking method
Scoring solutions by ordering them from best (highest score) to worst (score 1), with each score used once.
tips: Do not mix scoring methods within one matrix; every criterion must be rated using the same method.
Weightings from the percentage method must total 100%, and each criterion should be justified rather than simply assigned.
rq: Why might a rating scale let more than one solution share the same score, while a ranking scale cannot?
A rating scale scores each concept on absolute merit, so equally performing concepts can receive the same score; ranking forces each concept to occupy a distinct position, so no score can repeat.
What does a score of 0 mean on the −2 to +2 scale, and why is it useful?
It means the new solution is no better and no worse than the existing system for that criterion, providing a baseline for comparison with the current design.
Why is a weighting of 0 a problem in the digital logic method?
Every criterion must carry a non-zero weighting to be considered, so a zero result must be manually changed, meaning the method alone does not guarantee valid weights.

notes.t: Criteria Weighting by the Digital Logic Method and the Decision Matrix
pts: Each criterion is pairwise compared with every other; the more important scores 1, the less important scores 0.
A property's weighting factor is its positive decisions divided by the total positive decisions for all criteria.
Weighting factors across all criteria should sum to 1, as a check on the calculation.
Decision matrix multiplies each solution's score (1 to 5) by its weighting to give a weighted score; the weighted scores are summed for a total.
The highest total is not automatically the answer; results must be fully analysed before choosing a solution.
defs: Positive decisions
The count of pairwise comparisons in which a criterion was judged more important (scored 1), summed for each criterion.
Weighting factor (α)
A criterion's positive decisions divided by the total positive decisions across all criteria, giving its relative importance.
Weighted score
The rating of a solution on a criterion multiplied by that criterion's weighting factor.
eqs: \alpha = \frac{\text{property's positive decisions}}{\text{total positive decisions for all criteria}}
α = weighting factor (dimensionless); positive decisions = count of pairwise wins (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the 1/0 pairwise scoring with the 1–5 rating scale used in the decision matrix.
Weighted score = score × weighting; a common error is summing raw scores instead of weighted scores.
rq: Why must a justification accompany each pairwise decision in the table?
Without justification the decisions lack validity; the scoring is only credible if the reasoning for each choice is recorded.
If the total of weighting factors does not equal 1, what has gone wrong?
The positive decision counts or the totals were miscalculated, since weighting factors are shares of the total positive decisions.

formulas.name: Weighting factor of a criterion
formulas.latex: \alpha = \frac{\text{criterion's positive decisions}}{\text{total positive decisions for all criteria}}
formulas.vars: \alpha = weighting factor (dimensionless); positive decisions = number of pairwise wins (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Pairwise comparison of criteria in a decision matrix; weights sum to 1.

formulas.name: Pressure head from pressure
formulas.vars: H = pressure head (m); P = pressure (Pa); \rho = fluid density (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
formulas.use: Converting pressure to equivalent liquid column height.

formulas.name: Ideal Gas Law
formulas.vars: P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = universal gas constant (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); T = absolute temperature (K)
formulas.use: Ideal gas; T in kelvin. Gives the gas laws below as special cases.

formulas.name: Boyle's Law
formulas.vars: P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); subscripts 1, 2 = two states
formulas.use: Constant temperature and amount of gas.

formulas.name: Charles's Law
formulas.vars: V = volume (m³); T = absolute temperature (K); subscripts 1, 2 = two states
formulas.use: Constant pressure; T in kelvin.

formulas.name: Avogadro's Law
formulas.vars: V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); subscripts 1, 2 = two states
formulas.use: Constant T and P.

formulas.name: Volumetric flow rate of a simple piston pump
formulas.vars: \dot{v} = flow rate (m³/s); A = piston crown area (m²); K = piston stroke (m); V = leakage volume per stroke (m³); S = speed (rev/s)
formulas.use: Piston pump; set V = 0 for ideal flow. Double acting: count both strokes.

formulas.name: Ideal volumetric flow rate of a gear pump
formulas.vars: \dot{v} = flow rate (m³/s); A = area between two gear teeth and casing (m²); l = tooth length (m); N = number of teeth (–); S = speed (rev/s)
formulas.use: Ideal gear pump, no leakage.

formulas.name: Total dynamic head (general)
formulas.vars: TDH = total dynamic head (m); z = elevation (m); P = pressure (Pa); \rho = density (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); V = fluid velocity (m/s); \(h_{f}\) = friction head loss (m); 1 = inlet, 2 = outlet
formulas.use: Head the pump must supply; equals \(H_{\text{static}}\) + \(H_{\text{pressure}}\) + \(H_{\text{velocity}}\) + \(H_{\text{friction}}\).

formulas.name: Total static head
formulas.vars: \(H_{st}\) = total static head (m); \(z_{d}\) = discharge surface elevation (m); \(z_{s}\) = suction surface elevation (m); \(H_{SDH}\) = static discharge head (m); \(H_{SSH}\) = static suction head (m, negative if pump is below source surface)
formulas.use: Static part of the system curve (flow independent).

formulas.name: Maximum theoretical suction lift
formulas.vars: \(H_{max}\) = max lift (m); P = atmospheric pressure (Pa); \rho = liquid density (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); SG = specific gravity (–)
formulas.use: Ideal limit (≈10 m for water); practical lift is lower due to vapour pressure and losses.

formulas.name: Force balance on suction column
formulas.latex: F_g = A H \rho g,\quad F_p = P A
formulas.vars: \(F_{g}\) = weight of column (N); \(F_{p}\) = air pressure force (N); A = surface area (m²); H = column height (m); \rho = density (kg/m³); P = air pressure (Pa)
formulas.use: Equating \(F_{g}\) = \(F_{p}\) derives the maximum suction height.

formulas.vars: Q = heat transfer rate (W); U = overall heat transfer coefficient (W/m²K); A = heat transfer area (m²); LMTD = log mean temperature difference (K)
formulas.use: Sizing a heat exchanger; counter-flow gives a larger LMTD than parallel flow.

formulas.vars: \Delta \(T_{1}\), \Delta \(T_{2}\) = hot–cold temperature differences at each end (K)
formulas.use: Parallel or counter-flow exchangers.

formulas.vars: Q/t = heat rate (W); k = thermal conductivity (W/m K); A = area (m²); \Delta T = temperature difference (K); d = wall thickness (m)
formulas.use: Steady conduction through a plane wall; guides material selection.

formulas.use: Lift at which annular flow area equals port area.

formulas.vars: S.F. = safety factor (–); \(T_{CAP}\) = torque capacity (N·m); \(T_{APP}\) = applied torque (N·m)
formulas.use: Clutch sizing; must exceed 1.

formulas.name: Power transmitted by a shaft
formulas.vars: P = power (W); T = torque (N·m); \omega = angular velocity (rad/s)
formulas.use: Steady-state rotation.

formulas.name: Torque to accelerate a rotating mass
formulas.vars: T = torque (N·m); m = mass (kg); k = radius of gyration (m); \alpha = angular acceleration (rad/s²)
formulas.use: Torque to accelerate the driven side during engagement.

rep.ov: So far Statics 1 has set up the logistics and the idea of equilibrium, then built the toolkit in order: forces as vectors (components, resultants), moments, couples and equivalent force systems, free-body diagrams and support reactions, and the two equilibrium conditions \( \sum \vec F=0 \) and \( \sum M=0 \). It then adds dry friction, with limiting equilibrium on inclines and in guides. It ends with the start of truss analysis: triangulation, determinacy, struts and ties, and the solution procedure. Each block depends on the previous one, so vectors feed moments, moments feed equilibrium, and equilibrium feeds friction and trusses. Note that the notes for several lectures are truncated, so check the method of joints, the method of sections and beams against the full slides.
must: Draw a complete free-body diagram: isolate the body, include weight, applied loads and all support reactions (pin: Rx, Ry and no moment; roller: one normal force; fixed: Rx, Ry and a moment; cable: tension along the cable, away from the body).
Static equilibrium of a planar body: \( \sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0 \) about any point. Choose the moment point to eliminate unknowns.
Resolve forces into components: \( F_x=F\cos\theta,\ F_y=F\sin\theta \), checking which axis the angle is measured from. Keep signs by quadrant.

Resultant of concurrent forces: sum the components, then \( R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2} \) and \( \theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x) \) placed in the correct quadrant. The cosine and sine rules are the alternative method.

Moment of a force: \( M=Fd \) with d the perpendicular distance to the line of action. Use a consistent sign convention (anticlockwise positive). Varignon's principle lets you sum the moments of the components.
Couples: two equal, opposite, parallel forces give \( M=Fd \), the same about every point, with zero net force.
Equivalent force-couple systems: replace a system by a resultant force plus a moment about a chosen point. Both the net force and the moment about that point must match.

Dry friction: \( F\le\mu_s N \), with equality only at impending slip. Kinetic friction is \( \mu_k N \) opposing motion. The friction angle satisfies \( \tan\varphi_s=\mu_s \). Friction direction follows the tendency of motion.

Inclined-plane friction: \( N=mg\cos\theta \), and for impending motion up the slope \( T=mg\sin\theta+\mu_s mg\cos\theta \). Also be able to find the P needed to prevent slip in either direction (friction reverses).

Truss basics: members are pin-jointed and loaded at joints only, so they carry axial force. Ties are in tension and struts in compression. Triangulation gives stability. The determinacy check is \( m=2j-r \), which is necessary but not sufficient.

Truss solution procedure: find the reactions from the whole truss, then apply the method of joints (\( \sum F_x=\sum F_y=0 \), starting at a joint with at most two unknowns) or the method of sections.
Units and weight: \( W=mg \) with g = 9.81 m/s², mass in kg, lengths in m (convert mm), force in N or kN.
conn: Vectors and moments: resolving a force into components feeds Varignon's principle, where a component through the pivot gives zero moment, and then the moment equation of equilibrium.
Free-body diagram, then equilibrium: every beam, frame or ladder question starts with the FBD and the support types, which fix the number of unknowns against the three equations.
Equilibrium with friction: a ladder or block problem combines \( \sum F=0 \), \( \sum M=0 \) and \( F=\mu N \) at the limit. Check friction direction and whether slip or tipping happens first.

Trusses use the whole-body reactions: the support reactions come from the earlier equilibrium work, then the joint or section equilibrium gives member forces, and the \( m=2j-r \) check tells you whether statics suffices.
Cable tension components link to moments: a inclined cable gives T cosθ and T sinθ, and only the component perpendicular to the arm contributes to the moment about the pin.
exq: Three concurrent cable forces of given magnitudes at 15° below, 45° and 135° from +x act at a point. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant and state the quadrant.
A weightless beam is hinged at A and supported by a vertical wire at C, with loads at given distances in mm. Find the wire tension and the hinge reaction components and resultant.
A uniform 8 m beam weighing 200 N, with a 600 N man at 2 m from the wall, is held by a cable at 53° to the beam and a pin at the wall. Find the cable tension and the pin reaction.

A 300 kg block rests on a rough incline of angle θ with μs given. Find the winch tension needed to start it moving up the slope, and the minimum force to stop it sliding down. Also find the friction angle.
A box in guide rails is supported by a spring (force kx) with friction on two faces, \( F_f=2\mu N \). Find the range of load P for which the box stays in equilibrium.

A pin-jointed truss with 7 joints and 11 members has pin supports at both ends. Apply \( m=2j-r \) to decide determinacy, then explain what triangulation does. For a simpler truss, find the reactions and the member forces by the method of joints, stating tension or compression.
weak: Moment arms and sign conventions: students use the distance to the point of application instead of the perpendicular distance, or use the full cable tension instead of its perpendicular component. Consistent signs and unit conversion (mm to m) are also easily lost.

Friction direction and limiting cases: it is hard to decide which way friction acts and whether \( F=\mu N \) applies (only at impending slip). N is also not always mg, as on an incline or with an inclined applied force.

Free-body diagrams and support reactions: omitted reaction moments at fixed supports, friction at smooth surfaces and wrong roller directions all produce the wrong number of unknowns, and then everything downstream fails. In trusses, determinacy and tension versus compression add further sign confusion.

units.name: 0.2 Short description of the statics course
units.ov: This introductory material defines engineering statics as the study of rigid bodies in equilibrium, where net force and net moment are zero. It builds mathematical models from the core concepts of forces, moments, resultants and friction, then applies them to structures such as truss bridges and cantilever beams. The worked cantilever example shows the standard method: draw the free body, apply \(\sum F=0\) and \(\sum M=0\), solve for reactions, then find the maximum internal loads.
must: Equilibrium requires both \(\sum \mathbf{F}=0\) and \(\sum M=0\); forgetting the moment equation is the classic error
Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance, \(M=Fd\), in N·m, and it depends on the chosen point
A uniformly distributed load (UDL) is replaced by the equivalent point load \(qL\) acting at its centroid, a distance \(L/2\) from the end of its span
Fixed-support (cantilever) reactions: a vertical force and a moment; for the notes' example \(R_A=qL\) and \(M_A=qL^2/2\)
Maximum shear force and bending moment in a cantilever occur at the fixed support (\(qL\) and \(qL^2/2\) in the example)
Tension pulls and stretches a member; compression pushes and shortens it; label truss members correctly
Resultant: a single force (and possibly a couple) with the same external effect as a force system
Friction acts tangentially to oppose sliding or the tendency to slide
Statics applies only to bodies at rest or at constant velocity; accelerating bodies need dynamics
Be consistent with sign conventions: a wrongly chosen reaction direction changes the sign of the answer, not its magnitude
conn: Free-body diagram → equilibrium equations → reactions → internal shear force and bending moment: one chain used in every beam problem
Resultants and moments: replacing a UDL with a point load at its centroid gives the moment arm needed in the moment equilibrium equation
Truss analysis combines equilibrium with identifying tension or compression in each member, and friction can add tangential contact forces to the equilibrium equations
Reactions found from overall equilibrium are the starting values for the internal forces at the support, where the maxima occur
exq: A cantilever fixed at A carries a UDL \(q = 5\) kN/m over a length of 4 m. Draw the free-body diagram and find the vertical reaction and the fixed-end moment at A. State the maximum shear force and bending moment.
Explain why the moment of a UDL about a support is calculated with the load acting at the centroid. Derive \(M_A=qL^2/2\) for a UDL of length \(L\) starting at the fixed support.
A simple truss bridge is loaded at a joint. Use equilibrium to find the support reactions, then determine whether selected members are in tension or compression.
Define equilibrium, and state the two vector conditions that must be satisfied. Explain why a body moving with constant velocity can still be analysed by statics but an accelerating body cannot.
A block rests on a rough surface and is pulled by a force at an angle. Using equilibrium and friction, find the friction force and determine whether the block slides.

notes.t: Short description: introduction to engineering statics
pts: Statics is the study of solid bodies in equilibrium, applied to real engineering solid mechanics problems.
Analysis is done by constructing and solving mathematical models based on the principle of equilibrium.
Core concepts covered are forces, moments of forces, resultants and friction.
These concepts are applied to simple solid mechanics problems in mechanical and structural systems.
The course aims to give you the ability to tackle real engineering solid mechanics problems.
defs: Engineering statics
The branch of mechanics concerned with bodies at rest or in equilibrium under the action of forces and moments.
Equilibrium
A state in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are both zero, so the body has no acceleration.
Force
A push or pull on a body, with magnitude, direction and line of action, measured in newtons (N).
Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from that point.
Resultant
A single force (and possibly couple) that has the same external effect as a system of forces acting on a body.
Friction
A resisting force acting tangentially between contacting surfaces that opposes relative sliding or tendency to slide.
tips: Do not confuse a moment with a force: a moment is measured in N·m and depends on the point about which it is taken.
Equilibrium equations apply only to bodies at rest or moving with constant velocity; a body that is accelerating is not in static equilibrium.
rq: Why must both the net force and the net moment be zero for a body to be in equilibrium rather than just one of them?
A net force alone causes translation and a net moment alone causes rotation; both must vanish so the body neither translates nor rotates.
Why is a mathematical model needed before any calculation in statics?
A model idealises the real structure into forces, supports and geometry that can be written as equations of equilibrium, making the real problem solvable.

notes.t: Short description: introduction to engineering statics
pts: Engineering statics is the foundation for tackling real solid mechanics problems.
Statics models are built by constructing mathematical models and solving them using equilibrium.
Equilibrium is the core principle used to analyse structures such as bridges.
In a truss bridge, members carry either tension (pulling, red) or compression (pushing, green); a cantilever section is shown in the diagram.
defs: Engineering statics
The branch of solid mechanics that studies bodies at rest or in equilibrium under applied forces, using mathematical models built on the principle of equilibrium.
Equilibrium
The state in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are zero, so the body has no acceleration.
Tension
An internal axial force in a member that tends to stretch or pull it apart.
Compression
An internal axial force in a member that tends to shorten or push it together.
Cantilever
A beam or structure supported at only one end, resisting loads through bending and internal forces at the fixed support.
tips: Do not confuse tension (pulling, member stretched) with compression (pushing, member shortened) when labelling member forces on a diagram.
Statics equations apply only when the body is in equilibrium; if it accelerates, dynamics methods are needed.
rq: Why does a statics model start from the principle of equilibrium rather than from motion?
Statics deals with bodies at rest or with no acceleration, so net force and net moment must both be zero; this gives solvable equations for unknown support and member forces.
In the bridge diagram, why are the top chords in tension while the bottom chords are in compression?
The truss carries bending like a beam: the top chords are pulled apart as the span sags, and the bottom chords are pushed together, so the top is in tension and the bottom in compression.

notes.t: Short description: introduction to engineering statics
pts: The course introduces engineering statics, the study of bodies in equilibrium.
Statics skills let you tackle real engineering solid mechanics problems.
Problems are solved by building and solving mathematical models based on equilibrium.
defs: Engineering statics
The branch of mechanics concerned with analysing forces acting on bodies that are at rest or in equilibrium.
Equilibrium
The state in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are zero, so the body does not accelerate.
tips: Do not confuse statics (equilibrium, zero acceleration) with dynamics, where net forces produce acceleration.
rq: Why does the course rely on the principle of equilibrium rather than on motion equations?
Statics concerns bodies at rest or moving at constant velocity, so the net force and net moment are zero and equilibrium equations can be solved for unknown forces.

notes.t: Short description: Introduction to engineering statics
pts: Statics is an introduction to engineering statics, the foundation for solving real solid mechanics problems.
The course builds the ability to tackle real engineering solid mechanics problems.
Problems are solved by constructing and solving mathematical models based on the principle of equilibrium.
For a cantilever-type beam (fixed at A, uniformly distributed load q over length 2L), equilibrium gives the reactions: the moment reaction \(M_{A}\) = qL²/2 and vertical reaction \(R_{A}\) = qL.
Maximum shear force and bending moment both occur at the fixed support A, with magnitudes qL and qL²/2.
defs: Statics
The branch of mechanics concerned with bodies in equilibrium, where the net force and net moment on the body are zero.
Equilibrium
The state in which the sum of all forces and the sum of all moments acting on a body are zero, so it has no acceleration.
eqs: Moment equilibrium about support A (finds the fixed-end moment reaction)
\(M_{A}\) = reaction moment at A (N·m); q = uniform load intensity (N/m); L = length of each span (m)
Vertical force equilibrium (finds the vertical reaction at A)
\(R_{A}\) = vertical reaction at A (N); q = load intensity (N/m); L = length (m)
tips: Check the moment arm: a uniformly distributed load acts through its centroid, so use half the span (L/2) for its moment.
Keep track of sign conventions for reactions and moments; a reaction direction chosen wrongly changes the sign of the answer, not the magnitude.
rq: Why must the moment reaction at A be qL²/2 rather than qL²?
The resultant of the uniform load qL acts at the midpoint of its span, a distance L/2 from A, so the moment arm is L/2 and \(M_{A}\) = qL × L/2 = qL²/2.

notes.t: Short description: introduction to engineering statics
pts: Engineering statics is the foundation for solving real solid mechanics problems.
Statics problems are solved by building mathematical models based on equilibrium.
defs: Engineering statics
The branch of mechanics concerned with bodies at rest or in equilibrium under the action of forces and moments, used to determine unknown reactions and internal loads.
Equilibrium
The state in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are zero, so the body has no acceleration.
tips: Equilibrium means both the sum of forces and the sum of moments are zero; forgetting the moment equation is a common error.
rq: Why must a statics model be built from equilibrium before any internal forces can be found?

Equilibrium supplies the equations (sum of forces and moments equal zero) needed to solve for unknown reactions; without them the internal force distribution cannot be determined from the free body diagram.

units.name: 0.3 Course delivery, labs and assessment

They set out the lecture, tutorial and lab structure, the weighting of the quiz and exam, and the procedure for reporting missed labs. must: Assessment weighting: Week 11 assessed quiz \(30\%\) plus December exam \(70\%\) gives \(100\%\) of the mark; labs carry \(0\%\)
Both statics lab classes are compulsory to pass or complete the course, despite their \(0\%\) weighting
December exam format: answer 2 questions in 1 hour, so time per question is about 30 minutes
The assessed Week 11 quiz covers Weeks 1-8; the practice mid-semester quiz covers only Weeks 1-5 and does not count

conn: Practice quiz (Weeks 1-5) vs assessed quiz (Weeks 1-8): the practice quiz is feedback only, so keep revising Weeks 6-8 for the \(30\%\) quiz
Tutorial sheets feed both the quiz and the exam: attempting all 9 sheets is the main preparation for the 2-questions-in-1-hour exam
Compulsory labs link to absence reporting: a missed lab, if unreported on MyCampus, can block course completion even though the labs carry no marks
Recorded lectures on Moodle support the tutorials and exam revision, but they do not replace attending labs in person

A student scores well on the practice quiz and the exam but has not attended one of the two labs. Explain whether they can complete the course and what they should have done.

notes.t: Delivery of the Statics course

Three tutorial classes are timetabled, with one tutorial sheet per topic (9 in total) on Moodle.
All tutorial questions should be attempted, as they support exam preparation.

Lab workbooks are issued in class, so bring the workbook to each lab session rather than relying on a digital copy that may not be available.
rq: Why is attempting all tutorial questions, rather than only the ones that look easy, important for this course?

Each of the 9 topic sheets covers a specific topic, and attempting every question exposes gaps in understanding that the easier questions would hide; it also builds the problem-solving practice needed for exams.
If you miss a lecture, how could you still keep up with the content?

How should a student plan their revision time given that the 30% quiz covers Weeks 1-8 but the exam is 70%?

notes.t: Reporting absences for statics labs

Because the lab is a course requirement; reporting lets ESAS arrange an alternative date and time so you can still complete it and pass the course.

units.name: 0.4 Learning resources: Moodle, textbooks and tutorials

It contains no technical engineering content. The resources connect as a study loop: attend lectures, review on Moodle, do the tutorial, check numerical answers, consult the textbook, then use worked solutions at revision time.
must: Moodle is the University's VLE and hosts recorded lectures, slides, additional notes, tutorial questions, worked examples and exam questions
Main textbook: Meriam, Kraige & Bolton, \(\textit{Engineering Mechanics: Statics, SI Version}\) (Wiley)
Acceptable alternative textbook: Hibbeler, \(\textit{Engineering Mechanics: Statics}\) (Pearson)
Textbooks are available from the library as hard copy or e-book
There are nine tutorial sheets, one per topic, released after the corresponding lectures
Tutorials are for feedback and for evaluating your own understanding

Complete each tutorial as soon as possible after release to reinforce learning
Check your own answer against the numerical answer before seeking help, and do not ask for worked solutions before the revision period
Use Moodle worked examples, exam questions and recorded lectures for revision

notes.t: Moodle Virtual Learning Environment
pts: Moodle is the University's Virtual Learning Environment (VLE), a web environment supporting learning and teaching.
The course's Moodle site hosts recorded lectures and slides for revision.
Additional course notes, tutorial questions and other resources such as worked examples and exam questions are provided on Moodle.
rq: Why would worked examples and past exam questions on Moodle be more useful for Statics than lecture slides alone?
Statics is learned by applying equilibrium to problems; worked examples show the method step by step and exam questions show the expected standard and format, which slides alone do not practise.

notes.t: Textbooks

notes.t: Tutorial classes

Attempting questions soon after the lectures gives timely feedback on understanding, so gaps can be corrected while the material is still fresh and before later topics build on them.

units.name: 0.5 Course aims, learning outcomes and topic schedule
units.ov: This material sets out the aims and learning outcomes of a first-year statics course: identifying force systems, finding resultants, building equivalent force-couple systems, and applying equilibrium to structures and beams. The ideas form a chain. Forces and moments are combined into a resultant, which is then replaced by a simpler equivalent system. Equilibrium (\(\sum F=0,\ \sum M=0\)) then gives reactions and internal forces. Notes on p17 (topic and lecturer schedule) contain no technical content.
must: Equilibrium requires both \(\sum \mathbf{F}=0\) and \(\sum \mathbf{M}=0\); force balance alone still allows rotation
Moment of a force: \(M=Fd\), with \(d\) the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action (or \(\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\))
Resultant: a single force (possibly plus a couple) with the same external effect as the whole system; \(\mathbf{R}=\sum\mathbf{F}\)
Force-couple system: moving a force \(F\) to a new point \(B\) requires adding a couple \(M=Fd\) about \(B\) to keep the effect equivalent
Classify force systems: concurrent (lines meet at one point, so no moment about that point) vs non-concurrent (moments matter)
Draw a correct free-body diagram showing applied loads, reactions (supports) and friction forces before writing any equations
Reactions at supports are found from the equilibrium equations; in 2D there are 3 equations (\(\sum F_x,\sum F_y,\sum M\))
Internal forces (axial, shear force, bending moment) are found by cutting the structure and applying equilibrium to one part
Friction: \(F\le\mu_s N\), with \(F=\mu_k N\) when sliding; check for impending slip or tipping
Use consistent units (N, m, N·m) and state the sign convention for moments
conn: Resultant and force-couple replacement feed directly into equilibrium: distributed loads are replaced by an equivalent point force, which then gives support reactions
Support reactions from equilibrium of the whole body are needed before cutting a beam to find shear force and bending moment
Friction adds an inequality constraint to equilibrium problems (ladders, blocks on slopes), where you must check slipping and tipping together
Concurrent force systems reduce to force balance only, while non-concurrent systems also need moment balance, so choosing the moment point cleverly removes unknowns
exq: A beam of length 6 m is pinned at A and supported on a roller at B. It carries a 10 kN point load at 2 m and a UDL of 5 kN/m over the right 3 m. Draw the FBD and find the reactions at A and B.
Replace a system of three non-concurrent forces acting on a plate by an equivalent force-couple system at point O, then find the single resultant force and its line of action.
A 4 m ladder leans against a wall at 60° to the ground, with friction at the floor (\(\mu_s=0.3\)). Find the minimum safe angle or the maximum height a 80 kg person can climb before slipping.
Cut a simply supported frame at a section and determine the axial force, shear force and bending moment there. Explain why the three internal quantities arise.

Explain with an example why a body can satisfy \(\sum F=0\) and still not be in equilibrium. Find the couple needed to restore equilibrium for two equal and opposite forces of 50 N separated by 0.4 m.

notes.t: Course aim: statics, forces and equilibrium
pts: The course teaches students to study forces, including moments and friction.
Forces are applied to simple but realistic engineering problems such as structures and beams.
Problems are solved by constructing and solving mathematical models based on equilibrium.
defs: Equilibrium
The state of a body in which the net force and net moment acting on it are zero, so it has no acceleration.
tips: Forces and moments must be included together: a system can be in force equilibrium yet still rotate if the net moment is not zero.
rq: Why must a beam's reactions be found from equilibrium before drawing shear force and bending moment diagrams?
The internal shear force and bending moment depend on the support reactions, which are unknown until equilibrium equations (sum of forces and sum of moments equal zero) are solved.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes of the statics course
pts: Students should be able to identify different force systems, including concurrent, non-concurrent, moments, friction and reactions.
Forces are combined to find their resultant effect.
Equivalent force-couple systems are created to replace complex loadings.
The principle of equilibrium is applied to study forces and their effect on engineering systems and structures.
Mathematical models relate applied forces, reactions and internal forces.
defs: Resultant
A single force (and possibly a couple) that has the same external effect as a given system of forces.
Equilibrium
The state of a body in which the net force and net moment acting on it are zero, so it remains at rest or moves with constant velocity.
Force-couple system
An equivalent representation of a force acting at a point together with a couple moment, replacing a force applied at a different point.
Internal forces
Forces and moments transmitted within a structure between its parts, such as shear force and bending moment.
tips: Do not confuse the resultant force with the resultant effect; a resultant may need a couple moment as well as a force.
Check that forces are in consistent units (N) and moments are taken with the correct distance measured perpendicular to the line of action.
rq: Why must a force be replaced by a force-couple system when moved to a new point?
Moving a force to a new point without changing its external effect requires adding a couple equal to the force times the perpendicular distance moved, so the moment about the new point is preserved.
How do reactions connect applied forces to internal forces in a structure?
Equilibrium equations use the applied forces to determine the reactions; cutting the structure then reveals internal forces that balance the applied loads and reactions on each segment.

units.name: 0.6 Engineering design and engineering mechanics
units.ov: This material introduces engineering design as an iterative, decision-making process that depends on engineering mechanics, the study of forces and their effects. It then maps the structure of engineering mechanics: Solid Mechanics (Statics and Dynamics) and Fluid Mechanics. Statics 1 builds the mathematical models of forces on which later design analysis rests.
must: Design definition: a decision-making process, often iterative, applying basic sciences, mathematics and engineering sciences to convert resources optimally to meet a stated objective
Design is iterative, not a one-pass linear procedure; say so explicitly in answers
Design is not just drawing or manufacturing; it is a decision process grounded in theory
Engineering mechanics is the underlying theory that makes design possible, so design cannot proceed without it
Engineering Mechanics = the study of forces and their effects on bodies and structures
Hierarchy: Engineering Mechanics → Solid Mechanics and Fluid Mechanics; Solid Mechanics → Statics and Dynamics
Statics = bodies at rest or in equilibrium under forces; Dynamics = bodies in motion and the forces causing that motion
Fluid Mechanics is a separate branch (liquids and gases), not a sub-branch of Statics or Dynamics
Do not confuse Engineering Mechanics (the whole field) with Statics (only the equilibrium branch)
Engineering comprises four activities: planning, analysis, design and construction/manufacture; Statics 1 builds and solves mathematical models of the effect of forces
conn: Design and mechanics: design decisions (sizing, material choice, optimising resources) are only justified by force analysis from engineering mechanics, and results feed back into redesign iterations
Statics and Dynamics: both are branches of Solid Mechanics; equilibrium (statics) is the special case of zero acceleration in dynamics, and both start from modelling forces
Engineering activities: analysis (mechanics models) informs design, which leads to construction/manufacture, so questions often ask where mechanics sits in the whole process
exq: Define engineering design and explain why it is described as iterative. Give an example of an iteration loop in designing a loaded structure.
Draw a hierarchy diagram of Engineering Mechanics down to Statics and Dynamics, giving a one-line definition of each branch and where Fluid Mechanics fits.
Explain why engineering mechanics must be understood before design is possible, with reference to a specific component under load such as a crane hook or bridge member.
A student says 'Statics is the study of forces and their effects.' Identify the error and give the correct definitions of Statics and Engineering Mechanics.
Distinguish the roles of planning, analysis, design and construction/manufacture in an engineering project, and state which depend most directly on mechanics.

notes.t: Engineering design and the role of engineering mechanics
pts: Engineering comprises planning, analysis, design and construction/manufacture.
Design is an iterative decision-making process that applies science and mathematics to convert resources optimally toward a stated objective.
Design is only possible when the underlying theory, engineering mechanics, is understood.
defs: Design
A decision-making process, often iterative, in which basic sciences, mathematics and engineering sciences are applied to convert resources optimally to meet a stated objective.
Engineering mechanics
The underlying theory of engineering that must be understood for the design process to be possible.
tips: Design is not just drawing or manufacturing: it is a decision process that must be grounded in engineering mechanics theory.
Remember that design is described as often iterative, so do not present it as a one-pass linear procedure in answers.
rq: Why can't an engineer design a structure without understanding engineering mechanics?
Design requires predicting how resources and forces will behave to meet an objective; engineering mechanics provides the underlying theory for that prediction.
Why is design described as iterative rather than a single calculation?
Initial designs are tested against analysis and objectives, and then refined repeatedly until the solution is acceptable and optimal.

notes.t: Engineering Mechanics: definition and branches
pts: Engineering Mechanics is the study of forces and their effects.
Engineering Mechanics divides into Solid Mechanics and Fluid Mechanics.
Solid Mechanics splits into Statics (forces in equilibrium) and Dynamics (forces causing motion).
Statics 1 builds and solves mathematical models describing the effect of forces.
A deeper understanding of forces and their effects is essential in Engineering Design.
defs: Engineering Mechanics
The study of forces and their effects on bodies and structures.
Solid Mechanics
The branch of Engineering Mechanics dealing with the behaviour of solid bodies under forces; includes Statics and Dynamics.
Fluid Mechanics
The branch of Engineering Mechanics dealing with forces and motion in liquids and gases.
Statics
The branch of Solid Mechanics concerned with bodies at rest or in equilibrium under applied forces.
Dynamics
The branch of Solid Mechanics concerned with bodies in motion and the forces causing that motion.
tips: Do not confuse Engineering Mechanics (the whole field) with Statics (only the equilibrium branch of Solid Mechanics).
Fluid Mechanics is a separate branch, not a sub-branch of Statics or Dynamics.
rq: Why must an engineer study the effects of forces, not just the forces themselves?
Because design depends on how forces change a structure, such as deformation, stress or motion, so the engineer must predict and control those effects to ensure safety and function.
How does Statics differ from Dynamics in what it asks about a body?
Statics asks whether a body remains at rest under forces (equilibrium); Dynamics analyses how forces produce acceleration and motion.

units.name: 1.1 Mechanics, forces and vectors vs scalars
units.ov: This introductory Statics material defines mechanics and its split into statics (equilibrium, including constant velocity) and dynamics (changing motion). It classifies forces as contact or body, and concentrated or distributed. It then sets up the scalar/vector distinction, using distance versus displacement as the first example. These ideas underpin free-body diagrams and vector force addition in later work.
must: A force is the action of one body on another, so every force involves an interaction between two bodies and acts on an identifiable body
Statics covers bodies in equilibrium, meaning at rest or moving at constant velocity; dynamics covers bodies whose motion changes
Equilibrium does not mean 'no motion': constant velocity is still equilibrium, i.e. \( \sum \vec{F}=0 \)
Contact forces need physical contact; body forces such as gravity act at a distance
A force is concentrated if its contact area is small compared with the body's other dimensions; otherwise it is distributed over an area or volume
Gravity is a body force even though it is drawn as a single arrow at the centre of gravity
Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction
Vectors add by the parallelogram law or by components, never by simply summing magnitudes: \( |\vec{A}+\vec{B}|\neq A+B \) in general
Distance is a path-dependent scalar and is always \( \ge 0 \); displacement is a vector from start to end and depends only on the endpoints
Displacement can be zero for a closed path, and \( |\text{displacement}|\le \text{distance} \)
conn: Free-body diagrams combine the force definition, the contact/body classification and the concentrated/distributed idealisation: identify the body, then draw each force acting on it as a vector
The equilibrium definition links to vector addition: showing that a body is in equilibrium requires adding all force vectors by components and getting zero
Distributed forces are replaced by an equivalent concentrated resultant, so deciding when a force can be treated as concentrated affects how a loading problem is modelled
Distance/displacement leads to speed/velocity, which is the scalar/vector distinction that dynamics later builds on
exq: Define statics and dynamics. A car travels at a constant 20 m/s on a straight road. Which branch applies, and why?
Classify each as contact or body force and as concentrated or distributed: a book on a table, the weight of a beam, wind on a wall, a pin pushing on a plate. Justify each choice.
A runner completes one 400 m lap of a track and returns to the start. State the distance and the displacement, and explain the difference.
Two forces of 30 N and 40 N act at a point at 90° to each other. Use the parallelogram law to find the magnitude and direction of the resultant, and explain why it is not 70 N.
Explain why gravitational force is a body force even though it is drawn as a single arrow at the centre of gravity, and state what this arrow represents on a free-body diagram.

notes.t: Mechanics, Forces and the Division into Statics and Dynamics
pts: Mechanics is the oldest physical science and studies how forces affect objects.
A force is an action of one body on another, so forces always come from an interaction between bodies.
Statics studies bodies that are in equilibrium under the action of forces (at rest or moving with constant velocity).
Dynamics studies the motion of bodies under the action of forces, i.e. bodies whose motion changes.
defs: Mechanics
The oldest physical science, concerned with the effects of forces on objects.
Force
The action of one body on another.
Statics
The branch of mechanics dealing with the equilibrium of bodies under the action of forces.
Dynamics
The branch of mechanics dealing with the motion of bodies under the action of forces.
tips: Do not confuse equilibrium with 'no motion': a body moving at constant velocity is still in equilibrium and is treated in statics.
Forces are always an interaction between two bodies; always identify the body on which the force acts when drawing free-body diagrams.
rq: Why is a force defined as an action of one body on another rather than as a property of a single body?
Forces arise from interactions; an isolated body cannot experience a force without another body acting on it, so each force has a source and a receiver.
A block slides across a table at constant velocity. Does it belong to statics or dynamics, and why?
Statics, because constant velocity means zero acceleration and the net force is zero, i.e. the body is in equilibrium.

notes.t: Definition of a force
pts: Forces are classified by how they act: contact forces need direct physical contact, body forces act by remote action.
Body forces, such as gravitational force, act at a distance without touching the body.
Forces may be concentrated (acting at a point) or distributed (acting over an area or volume).
All contact forces are really applied over a finite area, so they are distributed unless that area is small compared with the body's other dimensions.
A contact force is treated as concentrated when its contact area is small relative to the other dimensions of the body.
defs: Contact force
A force produced by direct physical contact between two bodies.
Body force
A force applied by remote action, without physical contact; gravitational force is the main example considered.
Concentrated force
A force whose line of action is treated as acting at a single point, used when the contact area is small compared with the body's other dimensions.
Distributed force
A force spread over a finite area or volume of a body rather than acting at a single point.
tips: Do not call a force concentrated just because it looks small; compare the contact area with the body's other dimensions.
Gravitational force is a body force even though it is often drawn as an arrow at a single point (the centre of gravity) on diagrams.
rq: Why is a force applied by a pin on a beam often treated as concentrated even though it acts over a small finite area?
Because the contact area is small compared with the other dimensions of the beam, so the load can be idealised as acting at a point without significant error.
Is the weight of a bridge deck a contact or body force, and is it concentrated or distributed?
It is a body force (gravity acts remotely), and it is distributed because it acts throughout the volume of the deck.

notes.t: Vectors and Scalars
pts: Scalars have magnitude only, with no direction.
Vectors have both magnitude and direction.
Vector addition follows the parallelogram law, not simple arithmetic addition of magnitudes.
Mechanics deals with both scalar and vector quantities.
defs: Scalar quantity
A physical quantity fully described by a magnitude (a number with units) alone, with no associated direction.
Vector quantity
A physical quantity requiring both a magnitude and a direction for complete description.
tips: Do not add vectors by simply summing magnitudes; use the parallelogram law or components, accounting for direction.
Scalars such as distance and speed must not be given a direction; displacement and velocity must.
rq: Why can speed be a scalar while velocity is a vector, even though both describe motion?
Speed is only the magnitude of how fast something moves, whereas velocity also specifies the direction of motion.
Why can't two forces of 3 N and 4 N always be added to give 7 N?
Forces are vectors, so their resultant depends on the angle between them, found via the parallelogram law; 7 N only occurs when they act in the same direction.

notes.t: Distance and Displacement
pts: Distance is a scalar: it records the total ground covered along the path, so it is always positive and depends on the path taken.
Displacement is a vector: it is the change in position from start to end, with both magnitude and direction, and depends only on the endpoints.
For a path that loops back or curves, distance can be much larger than the magnitude of displacement, and displacement can even be zero.
Displacement is the straight-line arrow from start to finish, while distance follows the actual curved route.
defs: Distance
A scalar quantity giving the total length of path an object has covered during its motion, regardless of direction.
Displacement
A vector quantity giving the change in an object's position, measured as the straight-line vector from its initial to its final position.
Scalar
A quantity described by magnitude only.
Vector
A quantity described by both magnitude and direction.
tips: Do not treat distance and displacement as interchangeable: distance depends on the path, displacement only on start and end points.
Remember that displacement needs a direction (vector) and distance does not; a negative distance is meaningless.
rq: Why can an object have a non-zero distance but zero displacement?
If the object travels a closed loop and returns to its starting point, its change in position is zero (displacement = 0) while the total path length covered (distance) is greater than zero.
What happens to the magnitude of displacement compared with distance on a curved path, and why?
Displacement magnitude is always less than or equal to distance, because the straight line between two points is the shortest route; the curved path is longer.

units.name: 1.2 Newton's three laws of motion
units.ov: This material introduces Newton's three laws of motion for particles: equilibrium under zero net force, acceleration proportional to resultant force, and action-reaction pairs acting on different bodies. Together they underpin the free-body-diagram method: identify every force on a single body (weight, normal reaction, friction, tension), resolve into components, then apply \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\), with \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=0\) as the special case.
must: Newton's Second Law: \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\), using the vector resultant of all forces, with \(\boldsymbol{a}\) in the direction of the resultant
Particle equilibrium: \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=0\) as a vector sum, so resolve into components and set each to zero (a zero-magnitude check alone is not enough)
Equilibrium means zero acceleration, not zero velocity: rest or constant velocity in a straight line (First Law)
Newton's Third Law: \(\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{B on A}}=-\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{A on B}}\); equal, opposite, collinear, and acting on different bodies
Action-reaction pairs never cancel within one free-body diagram, because each force appears only on the body it acts upon
Weight \(\boldsymbol{W}=m\boldsymbol{g}\): weight is a force in N, mass is in kg; consistent units (kg gives N)
Contact and connection forces: tension (pulls along a rope on bodies at both ends), normal reaction (perpendicular to the surface), friction (tangential, opposes sliding or its tendency)
Free-body-diagram discipline: isolate one body, draw only forces acting on it, label the source of each (e.g. T on block), and use subscript order correctly
Resultant force is the single equivalent force that alone determines acceleration; use it, not one individual force, in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\)
conn: First Law and Second Law: equilibrium is the \(\boldsymbol{a}=0\) case of \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\), so the same free-body diagram and component resolution serve both static and dynamic problems

Third Law and free-body diagrams: the reaction to a force on body A appears on body B's diagram, so connected-body problems (block and man on a rope) need separate diagrams linked by equal and opposite tension and contact forces

Weight, normal reaction and friction: \(W=mg\) together with the normal reaction sets the perpendicular balance, which in turn determines the friction available along the surface and hence the acceleration
Component resolution links all three laws: choose axes, sum forces in each direction, and apply equilibrium or \(ma\) per component
exq: A block of mass 20 kg is pulled by a rope along rough horizontal ground by a man. Draw free-body diagrams for the block and the man, identify all action-reaction pairs, and state which forces act on each body.

A 50 kg crate is pulled by a rope at 30° above the horizontal with tension 200 N and accelerates along the ground with friction 60 N. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration, using \(g=9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\).

A particle is acted on by three coplanar forces and is in equilibrium. Given two forces in magnitude and direction, find the third by resolving into components, and explain why the particle may still be moving.

Two carts A and B are in contact and A pushes B with 40 N. State the force of B on A, explain why these do not cancel when finding the acceleration of A, and find each cart's acceleration if the masses are 5 kg and 3 kg and an external force drives the system.
Explain the difference between mass and weight, and calculate the weight in N of a 75 kg person and the resultant force when a 10 kg body has \(a=3\,\text{m/s}^2\).

notes.t: Newton's First Law and equilibrium
pts: A particle at rest stays at rest, or moves uniformly, when no unbalanced force acts on it.
Motion with no net force is a straight line at constant velocity, so acceleration is zero.
A body in equilibrium has zero net force; the vector sum of all forces on it vanishes.
defs: Newton's First Law
A particle remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line with constant velocity if there is no unbalanced force acting on it.
Equilibrium (particle)
The state of a body where the sum of all forces acting on it is zero, so it is at rest or moving with constant velocity.
eqs: Equilibrium condition for a particle: net force is zero
\(\sum \boldsymbol{F}\) = vector sum of all forces acting on the particle (N)
tips: Equilibrium means zero net force, not zero velocity; a body moving at constant velocity is still in equilibrium.
Equilibrium equations use the vector sum, so resolve forces into components before summing; a zero magnitude sum alone is not enough.
rq: Why does a body moving at constant velocity need no net force, even though it is moving?
Newton's First Law: force changes velocity (produces acceleration), so with zero net force the acceleration is zero and velocity stays constant; motion itself does not require a force.
What if a particle is moving and the net force on it suddenly becomes zero?
It keeps moving in the same straight line at the same constant speed and direction, without slowing or curving.

notes.t: Newton's Second Law
pts: Acceleration of a particle is proportional to the resultant force acting on it.
Acceleration points in the same direction as the resultant force.
Weight of a body is its mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration.
defs: Resultant force
The single force equal to the vector sum of all forces acting on a particle, which alone determines its acceleration.
eqs: Newton's Second Law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration
\(\sum \boldsymbol{F}\) = resultant force (N); \(m\) = mass of the particle (kg); \(\boldsymbol{a}\) = resulting acceleration (m/s²)
Weight of a body of mass m
tips: Use the vector sum of all forces (resultant) in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F} = m\boldsymbol{a}\), not a single force.
Keep units consistent: mass in kg gives force in N; do not confuse weight (N) with mass (kg).
rq: Why must the resultant force, not an individual force, be used in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F} = m\boldsymbol{a}\)?
Because acceleration depends on the net effect of all forces acting on the particle; individual forces alone do not determine the motion.
What happens to the acceleration if the same resultant force acts on a body with twice the mass?
The acceleration halves, since \(\boldsymbol{a} = \sum \boldsymbol{F}/m\) is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force.

notes.t: Newton's Third Law
pts: Forces between two interacting bodies form an action–reaction pair; they are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other out when analysing a single body.
The forces are collinear: they act along the same line of action, as shown by the two arrows between the carts.
defs: Newton's Third Law
When body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts a force of equal magnitude, opposite direction and along the same line on body A.
eqs: Action–reaction force relation between bodies A and B
\(\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{B on A}}\) = force exerted by B on A (N); \(\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{A on B}}\) = force exerted by A on B (N)
tips: Do not cancel action–reaction pairs in a free-body diagram; each force appears only on the body it acts upon.
Keep the subscript order clear: \(F_{B}\) on A is the force on A exerted by B, the reverse of \(F_{A}\) on B.
rq: Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel when you analyse the motion of body A alone?
Because each force acts on a different body; only forces acting on the same body are summed in a free-body diagram.
If the two carts have different masses, which one experiences the larger acceleration, and why?
The lighter cart, because the same force magnitude produces a larger acceleration when mass is smaller (F = ma).

notes.t: Forces as the action of one body on another
pts: A force is always an action of one body on another; forces come in pairs acting on different bodies.
The rope tension acts on the block and on the man, pulling each toward the other.
Weight of each body acts vertically downward from gravity on that body.
The ground exerts a normal reaction upward on each body, and a friction force horizontally on each body.
Each force on a body is paired with an equal and opposite reaction on the other body or surface.
defs: Tension
The pulling force transmitted along a rope or cable, acting on the bodies at each end of it.
Normal reaction
The perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on a body resting on or pressed against it.
Friction force
The tangential contact force between two surfaces that opposes relative sliding or tendency to slide.
eqs: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m \(s^{-2}\))
tips: Draw each force on the body it acts on only; do not put a force on a body from itself, and always label the source (e.g. T on block).
Mass m is in kg but weight is in newtons; do not confuse m g with m.
rq: Why does the rope tension appear twice in the diagram, once on the block and once on the man?
A rope transmits tension to both bodies at its ends; each end pulls its attached body toward the rope, so the tension acts on both, in opposite directions.
If the block is stationary, why are the forces on it balanced even though the man pulls it?
The friction force on the block from the ground balances the rope tension horizontally, and the normal reaction balances the weight vertically, giving zero net force.

units.name: 1.3 Newton (SI unit), weight and gravitation
units.ov: This material defines the newton from Newton's second law (\(F=ma\)), then uses it to define weight as the Earth's gravitational pull on a mass (\(W=mg\)). It then generalises to Newton's law of universal gravitation, \(F=Gm_1m_2/r^2\), and shows that \(g=GM/r_e^2\) at the Earth's surface, so weight is a special case of gravitation.
must: Newton's second law uses the resultant force: \(F=ma\), with \(F\) in N, \(m\) in kg and \(a\) in m/s²
Definition: \(1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m/s^2}\), the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²; it is a derived SI unit
Weight is a force (N), not a mass (kg): \(W=mg\) with \(g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\); a 1 kg mass weighs 9.81 N
Newton's law of gravitation: \(F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\), attractive and acting along the line joining the centres
Inverse-square dependence: doubling \(r\) divides \(F\) by 4, and doubling either mass doubles \(F\)
\(G=6.673\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) is universal and very small, so gravitational forces are noticeable only when at least one body is huge
The force pair is equal and opposite (mutual attraction), so each body pulls on the other with the same magnitude of force
\(r\) is the distance between centres, not surfaces; for a body above the Earth, \(r_e=6.371\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}+\text{altitude}\)
At the surface \(mg=\dfrac{GmM}{r_e^2}\), so \(g=\dfrac{GM}{r_e^2}\approx9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\), independent of \(m\)
Convert to SI units (kg, m, s) before substituting; benchmark weights: apple ≈ 1 N, 1-tonne car ≈ 10 kN (1 tonne = 1000 kg, not 1 kN)
conn: Weight and gravitation: equating \(W=mg\) with \(F=GmM/r_e^2\) gives \(g=GM/r_e^2\), which can be used to find \(M\) or to find \(g\) at altitude
Second law and weight: a freely falling body has resultant force \(mg\), so \(a=g\); with other forces present (e.g. tension, drag) you must use the resultant in \(F=ma\)
Inverse-square scaling and unit consistency: a question may change altitude (adding the Earth's radius) and give mass in tonnes, so \(r\) and \(m\) must be converted to SI
Newton's third law and gravity: the Earth pulls on a body with force \(W\), and the body pulls on the Earth with the same force, though the Earth's acceleration is negligible because of its huge mass
exq: A 1500 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 27 m/s in 9 s against a constant 400 N resistance. Find the resultant force and the driving force, and state the car's weight in kN.
Calculate the gravitational force between two 1000 kg spheres whose centres are 2 m apart, using \(G=6.673\times10^{-11}\). Compare it with the weight of a 1 kg mass and comment.

A satellite of mass 500 kg orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface (\(r_e=6.371\times10^6\) m, \(g_{surface}=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\)). Find the gravitational force on it and the local value of \(g\), and explain why the satellite is not weightless.
Using \(g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\) and \(r_e=6.371\times10^6\) m, derive the mass of the Earth from Newton's law of gravitation.
At what height above the Earth's surface is the weight of a body reduced to one quarter of its surface value? Justify your answer using the inverse-square law.

notes.t: SI unit of force (the Newton)
pts: Newton's second law relates resultant force to mass and acceleration, which is used to define the SI unit of force.
One newton is the force needed to give a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
The newton is a derived SI unit, equal to kg·m/s² in base units.
defs: Newton (N)
The SI unit of force: the force that gives a body of mass 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
eqs: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²)
N = newton (force unit); kg = kilogram (mass); m/s² = metre per second squared (acceleration)
tips: Use the resultant (net) force in F = ma, not just one of several forces acting on the body.
Convert mass to kilograms and acceleration to m/s² before calculating, otherwise the result in newtons will be wrong.
rq: Why is the newton called a 'derived' unit rather than a base SI unit?
Because it is defined from the base units kilogram, metre and second through F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
If a 2 kg body accelerates at 3 m/s², how many newtons of resultant force act on it, and why?
6 N, since F = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

notes.t: Weight and gravitational force
pts: Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body due to the Earth's pull.
Weight is found by multiplying mass by the acceleration due to gravity (g = 9.81 m/s²).
A 1 kg mass has a weight of 9.81 N on Earth.
Typical everyday weights: an apple ≈ 1 N, a bag of sugar ≈ 10 N, a bag of cement ≈ 500 N, a 1-tonne car ≈ 10 kN.
defs: Weight
The force exerted on a body by the gravitational pull of the Earth.
eqs: Weight of a body from its mass
\(W\) = weight (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = acceleration due to gravity (m/s²), taken as 9.81 m/s²
tips: Weight is a force measured in newtons (N), not a mass in kilograms; always multiply mass by g to convert.
Do not confuse 1 tonne (1000 kg) with 1 kN; a car of 1 tonne weighs about 10 kN, so keep units consistent when converting.
rq: Why is a 1 kg mass's weight 9.81 N rather than 1 N, and what would change if you took it to the Moon?
Weight is mass × g, so the 9.81 m/s² gravitational acceleration scales the force; on the Moon g is about 1.62 m/s², so the same 1 kg mass would weigh roughly 1.62 N while its mass stays 1 kg.
Why do the sugar and cement examples differ so much in weight even though both are everyday bags?
Their masses differ greatly (roughly 1 kg versus 50 kg), and since weight is proportional to mass, the cement bag weighs about 50 times more.

notes.t: Newton's law of gravitation
pts: Gravity is a mutual attraction: the two bodies pull on each other with equal and opposite forces.
The force magnitude is proportional to the product of the two masses and falls off with the square of their separation.
G is a universal constant, the same everywhere in the universe, with a very small value.
defs: Gravity
The mutual attractive force between two bodies, acting along the line joining their centres, whose magnitude depends on their masses and separation.
Universal gravitational constant (G)
A constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², the same for all pairs of bodies.
eqs: Magnitude of the gravitational force between two masses

\(F\) = gravitational force magnitude (N); \(G\) = universal gravitational constant, 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ (m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²); \(m_1, m_2\) = masses of the two bodies (kg); \(r\) = distance between the bodies' centres (m)
tips: Use SI units throughout: masses in kg and r in metres, so that G's units cancel to give newtons.
r is measured between the centres of the two bodies, not between their surfaces.
rq: Why does the force on m₁ point toward m₂ and the force on m₂ point toward m₁ with the same magnitude?
Gravity is a mutual interaction; by Newton's third law the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, both along the line joining the masses.
What happens to F if the separation r is doubled?
F becomes one quarter of its original value, because F is proportional to 1/r².

notes.t: Newton's law of gravitation
pts: Gravitational force between two masses is attractive and falls off with the square of the separation distance.
Near Earth's surface the gravitational force on a mass m equals its weight, which reduces to mg with g ≈ 9.81 m/s².
Distance \(r_{e}\) is measured from the centre of the Earth to the body, not from its surface.
defs: Gravitational constant G
Universal constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, G ≈ 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².
eqs: Newton's law of gravitation (force between masses m and M)
F = gravitational force (N); G = gravitational constant (m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²); m = mass of body (kg); M = mass of Earth (kg); \(r_{e}\) = distance between centres (m)
Weight of a body at Earth's surface
F = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration ≈ 9.81 (m/s²)
tips: Use \(r_{e}\) as the distance from the Earth's centre (6.371 × 10⁶ m), not the height above the surface; forgetting to add altitude is a common error.
Keep SI units throughout: convert radius to metres and mass to kg before substituting into F = GmM/\(r_{e}\)².
rq: Why can the weight formula be written as mg, with g = GM/\(r_{e}\)² treated as a constant?
Because M, G and \(r_{e}\) are fixed for the Earth and a body near its surface, so GM/\(r_{e}\)² is a constant ≈ 9.81 m/s²; only m varies.
What would happen to the force on a body if its distance from Earth's centre doubled?
The force would fall to one quarter of its original value, since F is proportional to 1/\(r_{e}\)².

units.name: 1.4 Vector addition of displacements
