The moment about A is the force times the perpendicular distance, giving a magnitude in N·m with the sense shown by the curved arrow.
defs: Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from a point (pivot) to the line of action of a force; it is the lever arm used to calculate the moment of the force about that point.
eqs: d = moment arm length (mm); 100 = vertical height from A to the reference line (mm); 45° = angle of F to horizontal
\(M_{A}\) = moment about point A (N·m); F = applied force (N); d = moment arm (m)
tips: Convert millimetres to metres before multiplying by force in newtons, otherwise the moment is wrongly scaled by 1000.
Check that the angle used is between the measured length and the perpendicular to the force, not simply the given angle to horizontal.
rq: Why is the 100 mm height multiplied by cos 45° rather than sin 45° to get the moment arm?

The 100 mm is measured along the vertical, and the perpendicular distance to the inclined line of action of F is obtained by projecting it with cos 45° (the angle between the vertical and the perpendicular direction).
Why must d be converted to metres before computing \(M_{A}\)?
The force is in newtons, so to obtain moment in N·m the arm must be in metres; using 70.71 mm directly would give an answer 1000 times too large.

notes.t: Moments via rectangular components (Method 2)
pts: Resolve the inclined force F at B into horizontal and vertical components, then take moments of each component about A.
Components of a 200 N force at 45° are equal, so each has magnitude F cos45° = F sin45°.
Moment about A is the sum of each component's moment; the sign depends on the direction of rotation about A.
defs: Moment of a force about a point
The product of the force component perpendicular to the lever arm and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force; positive when it tends to rotate anticlockwise.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); F = applied force (N); \theta = angle to horizontal (°)
\(F_{y}\) = vertical component (N); F = applied force (N); \theta = angle to horizontal (°)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = force components (N); \(d_{1}\) = vertical distance (m); \(d_{2}\) = horizontal distance (m)
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: a component's moment arm is the perpendicular distance, so use \(d_{1}\) for \(F_{x}\) and \(d_{2}\) for \(F_{y}\), not the other way round.
Convert distances to metres before multiplying (100 mm = 0.1 m, 200 mm = 0.2 m) to obtain the moment in N·m.
rq: Why can the moment of F about A be found by summing the moments of its components rather than the full force?
Moments are additive (Varignon's theorem): the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point, since the components together produce the same effect as F.
Why does \(F_{x}\) contribute a negative moment while \(F_{y}\) contributes a positive one here?

\(F_{x}\) acts at height \(d_{1}\) above A and tends to rotate the member clockwise, while \(F_{y}\) acts at horizontal distance \(d_{2}\) and tends to rotate it anticlockwise, so their signs are opposite.

notes.t: Moments: Method 3 – sliding a force along its line of action to eliminate a component's mo
pts: A force can be moved along its line of action without changing its moment about a point, so F can be slid to a convenient location.
Choose the point along the line of action where the moment due to the x-component is eliminated, so only the y-component produces a moment about A.
Resolve F into components; the y-component's moment about A is the product of its magnitude and the perpendicular distance d.
eqs: Vertical component of the force F at 45°
\(F_{y}\) = vertical component of force (N); 200 = magnitude of F (N); 45° = angle of line of action to horizontal
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{y}\) = vertical force component (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
tips: Ensure d is the perpendicular distance to the force's component, measured in metres (100 mm = 0.1 m) before multiplying by force in N to get N·m.
Only the component whose line of action does not pass through the reference point produces a moment; check the sign (direction) of the moment when combining with other moments.
rq: Why does sliding F along its line of action to a point directly above or in line with A remove the x-component's moment about A?
Because the x-component's line of action then passes through A (its perpendicular distance becomes zero), so its moment about A is zero; only \(F_{y}\) contributes a moment.
What would change if F were moved to a different point on its line of action without this choice?

The moment of F about A would be unchanged in total, but it would now be split between the components, making the calculation more complex; the moment of F itself is invariant along its line of action.

notes.t: Moments: Method 4 – sliding a force along its line of action to eliminate a component's mo
pts: A force can be moved along its line of action without changing its moment about any point, so the force can be slid to a convenient position to simplify the moment calculation.
Sliding F to the point where its y-component produces no moment leaves only the x-component contributing to the moment about A.
The moment about A is found from the perpendicular distance d of the remaining component's line of action from A.
eqs: Moment of the force about point A using the x-component at perpendicular distance d
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{x}\) = x-component of force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Horizontal component of a 200 N force at 45°
\(F_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); F = resultant force (N); 45° = angle to horizontal
tips: Convert d to metres before multiplying by a force in newtons so that the moment is in N·m (100 mm must become 0.1 m).
Only slide the force along its own line of action; moving it sideways changes the moment.
rq: Why does sliding F along its line of action leave the moment about A unchanged?
The moment is F multiplied by the perpendicular distance from A to the line of action, and sliding along the line keeps both the force and that perpendicular distance the same.
Why is the moment of \(F_{y}\) eliminated at the chosen point on the line of action?
The point is chosen so that the line of action of \(F_{y}\) passes through A, giving zero perpendicular distance and therefore zero moment.

notes.t: Moment of a force using the vector cross product (unit vectors)
pts: The moment about a point is the cross product of the position vector from that point to the force line of action with the force vector.
Express both the position vector and the force vector in terms of unit vectors i, j, k, then expand the cross product.
For vectors lying in the x–y plane, only the k component of the moment is non-zero, so the result is a scalar couple acting perpendicular to the plane.
defs: Position vector r
A vector from the reference point (here A) to any point on the line of action of the force.
Moment (vector form)
The moment of a force about a point equals the cross product of the position vector and the force vector, M = r × F.
eqs: Moment of force F about point A using the cross product
\underline{M}_A = moment about A (N·m); \underline{r} = position vector from A (m); \underline{F} = force vector (N)
Force vector components from magnitude and 45° angle
F = force magnitude (N); \theta = 45^\circ angle to horizontal
tips: Ensure the position vector r runs from the moment point (A) to the line of action of the force, not from the origin to the force.
Check the sign of the k component: subtract the j-term contribution from the i-term contribution correctly, since \( i \times j = k \) but \( j \times i = -k \).
rq: Why does the cross product only produce a component along k when both r and F lie in the x–y plane?
The cross product of two vectors is perpendicular to both; for vectors in the x–y plane, the result must point along the z-axis (k), so only the k component survives.
What would happen to the moment if the force acted along the line through A?
The position vector and force would be parallel, so their cross product is zero and the moment about A is zero.

units.name: 6.1 Equivalent force systems
units.ov: This material covers replacing a system of forces and couples with a simpler equivalent system, usually a single resultant force with a located line of action. The resultant's magnitude and direction come from summing components. Its position then comes from equating moments about a chosen point. The ideas connect because the force sum fixes R and the moment sum fixes where R acts.
must: Two systems are equivalent if they have the same resultant force AND the same resultant moment about any point (matching only the force gives the wrong location)
Resultant components: \(R_x=\sum F_x\), \(R_y=\sum F_y\), with signs set by direction and the chosen axes
Magnitude and direction: \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\), \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\), checking the quadrant from the signs of both components
Resolve inclined forces correctly: the 500 N at 60° gives \(500\cos60^\circ\) in x and \(500\sin60^\circ\) in y (don't swap them)
Locate the line of action with the moment equivalence \(\sum M_A = R\,d\), so \(d=M_A/R\) (for parallel forces \(d_R=M_A/F\))

Moment = force × perpendicular distance; for a horizontal beam only the vertical component of a force gives a moment about a point on the beam, but a horizontal force acting off the beam (the 100 N at 0.5 m height) also gives a moment and must be included
Use one consistent sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive) and the same reference point for every term; the point is arbitrary and any choice gives the same line of action
Equal and opposite forces at a point can be added or removed without changing the system (net force and moments both cancel)
Worked example: \(R_x=350\) N, \(R_y=-233\) N, \(R=420.5\) N, \(\theta=33.7^\circ\), line of action 0.9 m from A
Concurrent forces have the resultant through the common point; for non-concurrent forces the position must come from moments, not from an intersection point
conn: Component resolution feeds the moment calculation: the same \(R_x\), \(R_y\) give both the resultant magnitude and direction and the moment equation used to find \(d\)
Taking moments about a different point (A versus D) must give the same line of action, which serves as a check; resultant components at their own lever arms give \(\sum M_D=R_xd_y+R_yd_x\)
Equivalence of force systems leads into equilibrium: if \(R=0\) and the resultant moment is 0, the system is in balance, and a nonzero moment with \(R=0\) is a pure couple
Sign convention and unit consistency (N, m, N·m) affect both the resultant and its position, so one slip carries through the whole answer
exq: A beam carries a 500 N force at 60° to the beam at B (2 m from A), a 200 N vertical force at 3.5 m and a 100 N horizontal force 0.5 m above the beam. Find the resultant's magnitude and direction, and the distance from A at which its line of action crosses the beam.
Three parallel forces \(F_1\), \(F_2\), \(F_3\) act on a bar at known spacings. Replace them with a single resultant and find \(d_R=M_A/F\) from A. Then check by taking moments about a second point.
Explain why a pair of equal and opposite forces added at one point leaves a force system unchanged, and show that the moment about A of a three-force system equals \(F_1 d\).
Using the same beam loading, take moments about D rather than A to find the position of the resultant, and show that \(233\,d_x+350(0.5)\) equals the original system's moment about D.

Resolve a concurrent system with a 500 N force at 60°, a 100 N horizontal force and a 200 N vertical force. Find \(R\) and \(\theta\), and state the quadrant. Say what changes if one component's sign is wrong.

notes.t: Equivalent force systems
pts: Two force systems are equivalent if they produce the same total translational effect (net force) and the same rotational effect (moment about a point).

Adding a pair of equal and opposite forces at the same point does not change the system; here \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) are equal and opposite, so they cancel in net force, and their moments about A also cancel.
The moment about pivot A of the three-force system equals the moment of the single force \(F_{1}\) at distance d, so the single force can replace the whole system.
Moments are taken about the same point A in both systems, so the rotational comparison is valid only for that reference point.
defs: Equivalent force systems
Force systems that have the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any given point, so they produce identical translational and rotational effects on a body.
eqs: Net force of the system (translational effect)
Moment about pivot A of the single force (a)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{1}\) = force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Moment about pivot A of the three-force system (b)
M_A = (F_1 \times d) + (F_2 \times d) - (F_3 \times d) = F_1 \times d
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = forces (N); d = distance from A (m)
tips: Check moment directions (clockwise vs anticlockwise) carefully when summing moments; opposing forces on opposite sides of the pivot subtract.
Equivalence of moments holds only about the same reference point; always state which point the moments are taken about.
rq: Why does the pair \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) leave the system unchanged even though they add extra forces?

They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their net force is zero, and their moments about A (\(F_{2}\) d and \(F_{3}\) d acting in opposite senses) cancel, giving no change in translation or rotation.
What would happen to the equivalence if \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) were not equal in magnitude?
The net force would no longer equal \(F_{1}\) and the net moment about A would no longer equal \(F_{1}\) d, so the systems would not be equivalent.

notes.t: Equivalent systems of forces
pts: Any system of concurrent or non-concurrent forces on a body can be replaced by one equivalent resultant force.
For concurrent forces, the resultant acts where all lines of action intersect.
For non-concurrent forces, the resultant's location must be found by constructing an equivalent system.
An equivalent system must have the same resultant moment (rotational effect) as the original forces.
If the equivalent system is a single resultant force, the original system's moment about the point of application of that resultant must be zero, which locates its line of action.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that is statically equivalent to a system of forces, producing the same net force and the same resultant moment on a body.
Resultant moment
The net turning effect of a system of forces about a given point, equal to the sum of the moments of all forces about that point.
Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point.
Non-concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action do not all intersect at a single point.
tips: Do not place the resultant at the intersection point for non-concurrent forces; the line of action must be found from moment equivalence.
Ensure the equivalent system matches both the net force and the resultant moment; matching only force gives an incorrect location.
rq: Why must the resultant moment of the original forces about the resultant's point of application be zero when the system reduces to a single force?
A single force passing through a point produces no moment about that point, so the original system must produce none either to be equivalent; this condition locates the resultant's line of action.
Why can't you simply place the resultant at the centroid of the forces when they are non-concurrent?

Equivalence requires matching both force and moment; a non-concurrent system produces a moment that must be reproduced by offsetting the resultant's line of action, which the equivalent-system method determines.

notes.t: Equivalent systems: resultant force and moment about a point
pts: Equivalent force systems share the same resultant force and the same moment about any point; here the three parallel forces are replaced by one resultant F acting at distance \(d_{R}\) from A.
Take moments about any convenient point (here A) for the original system, with anticlockwise moments treated as positive according to the sign convention used.
The moment of the resultant about A must equal the total moment of the original forces about A, which fixes the line of action of the resultant.
The line of action of the resultant is found by dividing the moment by the resultant force: \(d_{R}\) = \(M_{A}\) / F.
defs: Resultant force
A single force equivalent to a system of forces, having the same net force (vector sum) and the same moment about any point as the original system.
Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from that point.
eqs: F = resultant force (N); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = individual forces (N), signed by direction
Moment of the original system about point A
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N m); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = forces (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Line of action of the resultant
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N m); F = resultant force (N); \(d_{R}\) = distance of resultant's line of action from A (m)
tips: Keep sign conventions consistent: forces and moments in one direction positive (here upwards forces and anticlockwise moments), and apply them the same way throughout the calculation.
Units trap: distances must be in metres (d = 0.5 m) so that moments come out in N m before dividing by force in N to get a distance in m.
rq: Why must the moment of the resultant about A equal the moment of the original forces about A?
Equivalent systems must have the same effect on the body; matching both net force and moment about a point ensures the resultant reproduces the original system's turning effect everywhere.
What would happen to \(d_{R}\) if \(F_{3}\) were 0 instead of 20 N, with \(F_{1}\) = \(F_{2}\) = 20 N and d = 0.5 m?
\(M_{A}\) = 20(0.5) + 20(0.5) = 20 N m and F = 20 - 20 = 0, so the resultant is a pure couple of 20 N m; no single resultant force exists and \(d_{R}\) is undefined.
Why does the choice of point A not change the final answer for the resultant force?
The resultant force F is the same regardless of point; only the moment changes with the reference point, and the line of action found from any point is the same once the moment is consistent.

notes.t: Equivalent systems: resultant of co-planar forces on a beam
pts: A resultant force R is found by summing the force components in x and y, and its line of action is located by summing moments about a chosen point.
The 500 N force acts at 60° to the beam, so it must be resolved into horizontal and vertical components before summing.
A couple/moment is created by the offset of the 100 N horizontal force 0.5 m above the beam at point D, which must be included in the moment sum.
The line of action of R is found where its moment about the reference point equals the sum of the moments of the original system.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same external effect as a system of forces acting on a body, found by vector summation of the forces.
Co-planar forces
Forces whose lines of action all lie in the same plane.
eqs: Horizontal component of the resultant (sum of x-components)
\(R_{x}\) = horizontal component of resultant (N); \(F_{x}\) = component of each force in x-direction (N)
Vertical component of the resultant (sum of y-components)
\(R_{y}\) = vertical component of resultant (N); \(F_{y}\) = component of each force in y-direction (N)
Location of line of action via moment equivalence
\bar{x} = distance along beam from O to line of action of R (m); \sum \(M_{O}\) = sum of moments about O (N·m); \(R_{y}\) = vertical resultant (N)
tips: Watch units and angles: the 500 N component must use cos 60° horizontally and sin 60° vertically, not the reverse.
Do not forget the moment of the horizontal 100 N force, which acts at a height of 0.5 m above the beam.
rq: Why must the 500 N force be resolved into components rather than added directly to the 100 N force?
Forces acting in different directions cannot be added as scalars; only their components along the same axes can be summed, giving \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).
Why does the 100 N force at D contribute to the moment even though it acts horizontally?
Because it acts 0.5 m above the beam, its perpendicular distance to the beam axis produces a moment about points on the beam.

notes.t: Equivalent force systems: resultant of concurrent forces by components
pts: Resolve each inclined force into rectangular x and y components before adding.
Components of the resultant are the algebraic sums of the components of all forces, with sign set by direction.
The magnitude of the resultant follows from the Pythagorean theorem applied to its components.
The direction is the angle the resultant makes with the x-axis, found from the arctangent of the component ratio.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect is equivalent to the combined effect of a system of forces acting on a body.
eqs: x-component of the 500 N force at B
y-component of the 500 N force at B
tips: Keep the sign of each component consistent with the chosen axes; a sign error changes both the magnitude and direction.
Use \( \tan^{-1} \) with the signs of both components to find the correct quadrant of θ, not just the magnitude of the ratio.
rq: Why must the 500 N force be resolved into components rather than added directly to the 100 N and 200 N forces?
Forces act in different directions, so only components along the same axis can be added algebraically; a vector sum requires component-wise addition.
Why is the y-component of the 500 N force negative while the 200 N load is taken as positive?
Signs follow the chosen axes: the 500 N force points downward (negative y), while the 200 N load at C points upward (positive y).
What happens to θ if \(R_{y}\) were positive rather than negative?
The resultant would point above the x-axis, so θ would be measured in the opposite sense; the quadrant must be checked from the signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).

notes.t: Location of the Resultant (Equivalent Systems)
pts: Once the resultant force magnitude is known, its line of action must be located so the system is fully equivalent.
The line of action is found by equating moments: the moment of the resultant about a point equals the moment of the original forces about that same point.
The choice of reference point is arbitrary; any point gives the same line of action, which can be checked by using two different points.
tips: Be consistent with the sign convention for moments (clockwise vs anticlockwise) when equating the two sides.
Use the same reference point for all forces when summing moments; mixing points gives an incorrect line of action.
rq: Why must the moment of the resultant about a point equal the moment of the original forces about that same point?
Equivalent systems must produce the same force and the same moment at every point; otherwise the beam would respond differently to the two systems.
If you choose a different moment point, why does the resultant's line of action stay the same?
Because the moment condition holds for every point, so the location of the resultant derived from any point must agree with the others.

notes.t: Equivalent moment – locating the line of action of a resultant
pts: Moments about point A of the resultant equal the sum of moments of the original forces; this locates the resultant along the beam.
The resultant's moment about A is its vertical component times the perpendicular distance \(d_{A}\) from A.
A positive force-couple sign convention must be applied consistently when summing moments.
The line of action of the resultant is 0.9 m along the beam from A, so the equivalent system is the resultant at that position.
defs: Equivalent system
A simpler set of forces and/or couples that has the same resultant force and resultant moment about a point as the original system.
Line of action
The straight line along which a force acts; for a resultant it is the position at which the single force reproduces the moment of the original system.
eqs: Moment of the resultant about A
\(R_y\) = vertical component of resultant (N); \(d_A\) = distance from A to line of action of resultant (m)
\(d_A\) = distance from A (m); forces in N, distances in m
tips: Only the vertical component of inclined forces contributes to moments about A along a horizontal beam; do not use the full force magnitude.
Keep units consistent: forces in N and distances in m give moments in N·m, and sign conventions for clockwise/anticlockwise must match throughout.
rq: Why is the moment of the 500 N inclined force computed using only its vertical component, \(500\sin 60^\circ\), about A?
Because the horizontal component \(500\cos 60^\circ\) acts along the beam line through A, so its moment arm about A is zero.
What would happen to \(d_A\) if the 100 N force at E were omitted from the moment sum?
The denominator would still be −233 only if the vertical forces are unchanged; omitting the 100 N moment term changes the numerator, so \(d_A\) would change accordingly.

notes.t: Equivalent moment – replacing a force system with a resultant and moment about point D
pts: Taking moments about a point gives the moment of the resultant equal to the sum of the moments of the original forces
A resultant force R acting at distance d from a point produces the same moment as its components Rx and Ry acting at their own lever arms
Solving the moment equation for the unknown lever arm dx locates the resultant along the beam, measured from point A
defs: Equivalent system
A set of forces and moments that has the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any point as the original loading.
Moment about a point
The product of a force and its perpendicular distance from the point, equal to F × d; positive or negative depending on rotation sense.
eqs: Moment balance about point D for the resultant components
\(\Sigma M_D\) = sum of moments about D (N·m); \(R_x\) = horizontal resultant component (N); \(R_y\) = vertical resultant component (N); \(d_x\), \(d_y\) = perpendicular lever arms (m)
Solved moment equation giving the lever arm \(d_{x}\)
\(d_x\) = lever arm of resultant (m); forces in N; distances in m
tips: Ensure the 60° angle is applied correctly: horizontal component uses cos 60° and vertical uses sin 60° depending on the chosen axes, and mixing them gives wrong moments.
Convert all distances to metres before summing moments, and remember to subtract from the total span when reporting the position measured from point A.
rq: Why can we choose any point, such as D, to take moments about when finding an equivalent system?
Because an equivalent system must give the same resultant moment about every point; choosing D simply makes the unknown lever arm easy to solve for.
Why is the distance from A given as 4.5 − 3.6 rather than 3.6 m directly?
Because dx was measured from point D, so the position from A is the total length AD (4.5 m) minus dx.

units.name: 7.1 Force–couple systems
units.ov: This module covers couples (two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces giving pure moment with no net force) and equivalent force-couple systems. It then reduces a coplanar 4-force system to a single resultant R, a force-couple system at a point, and the line of action of R. Everything rests on two checks, \(\sum F\) and \(\sum M\) about the same point, which are used to move forces, replace systems, and locate the resultant.
must: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action. Net force is zero and it gives pure rotation: \(\sum F=F-F=0\).
Moment of a couple \(M=Fd\), where d is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action (not the distance from a moment centre or between the points of application).
A couple's moment is the same about every point, so it is a free vector. Check: \(M_A=F(a+d)-Fa=Fd\), and a drops out.
Moving a force F to a new point requires adding a couple \(M=Fd\), with d the perpendicular distance moved. The result is the same F at the new point plus a couple M.
Two force systems are equivalent only if both the resultant force and the resultant moment about the same point match. Matching \(\sum F\) alone is not enough.
Resolve inclined forces first: \(R_x=\sum F_x=50+250\cos45^\circ=226.8\) N and \(R_y=\sum F_y=-100-250\sin45^\circ=-276.8\) N. Down and left are negative.
Resultant magnitude \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\approx358\) N. Direction \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\approx50.7^\circ\) below the +x axis (down-right). Check the quadrant from the signs.
Force-couple system at A: R acts at A, plus \(M_A=\sum M_A=-(250\cos45^\circ)(1)-(100)(3.5)\approx-527\) N·m (clockwise). State the sign convention and use perpendicular arms.
Line of action of R: equate the moment of R about A to \(M_A\). Only \(R_x\) has a moment about a point on the y-axis, so \(226.8\,d=526.8\), giving \(d\approx2.32\) m.

Rigid-bar equilibrium with a couple: the two bar forces must be equal and opposite, and \(\sum M_A=0\) gives \(F_2(4)-200=0\), so \(F_2=50\) N (units N, not N·m). The bar's force pair forms an anticlockwise couple balancing the applied clockwise 200 N·m.
conn: Moving a force to another point (force-couple) is the same operation used to reduce the 4-force system to R plus \(M_A\). The added couple is the moment of the force about the new point.
The resultant R and \(M_A\) combine to give the line of action. Divide \(M_A\) by the relevant force component to get the offset d, which turns the force-couple system back into a single force.
Couples in equilibrium problems: a bar with an applied couple needs an equal and opposite couple from two equal, opposite forces. Use \(\sum F=0\) to link the forces and \(\sum M=0\) to find them.
Component resolution feeds both the force sums (R, θ) and the moments (the 45° force's moment arm). A wrong component or sign propagates into R, θ, \(M_A\) and d.
exq: A rigid weightless bar has an applied clockwise couple of 200 N·m. Forces \(F_1\) at A and \(F_2\) 4 m from A hold it in equilibrium. Find \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), state their directions, and explain why the answer is independent of the moment centre.

A 4-force coplanar system contains 50 N horizontal, 100 N downward and 250 N at 45° forces, with moment arms of 1 m and 3.5 m about A. Find \(R_x\), \(R_y\), the magnitude R and the direction θ of the resultant, and say which quadrant it lies in.
For the same system, find the equivalent force-couple system at A, giving \(M_A\) with its sense. Then find where the line of action of R crosses the y-axis, showing \(d\approx2.32\) m.

A 50 N force acts at R. Replace it with an equivalent force-couple system at a point S a perpendicular distance d away. Give the force and the couple moment with its sense, and show that \(\sum F\) and \(\sum M_A\) match the original.
Two forces of 80 N, 0.6 m apart, form a couple. Show that the moment about two different points A and B is identical (\(M=Fd=48\) N·m). State why adding the two forces to get a resultant is wrong.

notes.t: Couples and the moment of a couple
pts: A couple is two equal and opposite forces not acting through the same point; it produces pure rotation with no net force.
For a couple, the sum of forces in any direction is zero, so there is no tendency to translate.
The moment of a couple is the same about any point, so its magnitude does not depend on where the reference point A is located.
The moment of a couple is found by taking the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the two forces.
defs: Couple
The moment produced by two equal and opposite forces that do not act through the same point.
eqs: Moment of a couple about point A
\(M_{A}\) = moment of the couple about A (N·m); F = magnitude of each force (N); a = distance from A to the first force (m); d = perpendicular distance between the two forces (m)
Sum of vertical forces for a couple
\sum \(F_{y}\) = net force in the y-direction (N); F = magnitude of each force (N)
tips: Do not use the distance a from A when finding the couple moment; the answer depends only on \( d \), so \( M_A = Fd \) regardless of where A is.
A couple produces pure rotation with no net force, so do not add the forces as if they reinforce each other; they cancel in the sum.
rq: Why does the moment of a couple not change when you choose a different reference point A?
Because the two equal and opposite forces have a net force of zero, so shifting the reference point changes the moments of the two forces by equal and opposite amounts, leaving only F·d.
What happens to the moment of a couple if the two forces are moved along their lines of action so they are still equal, opposite and separated by d?
The moment is unchanged, since it depends only on F and the perpendicular distance d between the forces, not their position.

notes.t: Couples
pts: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces; its moment is the same about every moment centre.
The couple's moment is the force magnitude times the perpendicular distance between the lines of action, so it is independent of where moments are taken.
Two forces forming a couple can be replaced by a single pure moment acting at any point on the body.
defs: Couple
A system of two parallel forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction whose lines of action are separated by a perpendicular distance; it produces a pure moment with no net force.
eqs: M = moment of the couple (N·m); F = magnitude of one force of the couple (N); d = perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance d between the lines of action, not the distance from the moment centre to a force.
A couple's moment is a free vector: it can be moved anywhere on the body without changing its effect, so don't add the forces' individual moments about a point unless you handle the signs correctly.
rq: Why does a couple's moment not depend on the chosen moment centre, unlike a single force's moment?
Because the two forces have zero net force, so the sum of their moments about any point equals F times the separation d, which is fixed.

notes.t: Equivalent force-couple systems
pts: A force acting at point R can be moved to another point S by adding an equal and opposite pair of forces at S, which creates a couple.
The couple formed by the pair of forces produces a moment equal to the force magnitude times the perpendicular distance between the lines of action.
The result is an equivalent force-couple system at point S: the same force F at S plus a couple moment M.
defs: Couple
A pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces whose net force is zero but which produces a pure moment.
Equivalent force-couple system
A force acting at a chosen point together with a couple moment that has the same external effect as the original force acting at a different point.
eqs: Magnitude of the couple moment produced when a force is moved to a new point
M = couple moment (N·m); F = force magnitude (N); d = perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces (m)
tips: The distance d in M = Fd is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces, not the distance between the points R and S.
Units: ensure d is in metres when F is in newtons, giving M in N·m.
rq: Why must the two added forces at S be equal in magnitude to F and opposite in direction, rather than just any pair of forces?
Because the added pair must sum to zero net force so the system is unchanged, and the added force at S must equal the original F so the translated force has the same effect.
What would happen to the couple moment if S were moved closer to the line of action of F through R?
The perpendicular distance d would decrease, so the couple moment M = Fd would decrease, becoming zero when S lies on the line of action of F.

notes.t: Four-force couple systems: equivalent couples on a rigid bar
pts: For a rigid weightless bar in equilibrium, the resultant force is zero so the two bar forces must be equal and opposite.
Taking moments about A eliminates F1, so the moment of F2 about A must balance the applied 200 Nm couple.
The forces F1 and F2 together form an anticlockwise couple of 200 Nm, equal and opposite to the applied couple.
A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces; its moment is the same about any point, so it can be moved freely on the body.
defs: Couple
A pair of equal, opposite and non-collinear forces whose net force is zero but whose net moment is non-zero.
eqs: \(F_1\) = force at A (N); \(F_2\) = force at 4 m from A (N)
tips: Watch the sign convention: the applied 200 Nm is clockwise, so the force-couple moment must be taken as anticlockwise to balance it.
Units: the lever arm must be in metres and the couple in N·m, so F2 = 200/4 gives 50 N, not 50 N·m.
rq: Why does taking moments about point A give the value of F2 directly without needing F1?
Because F1 acts at A, so its moment arm about A is zero and it contributes nothing to the moment equation.
What happens to the couple moment if the two forces are moved to different points along the bar?
Nothing changes: a couple's moment is the same about any point, so it can be relocated along the bar.

notes.t: Equivalent force-couple systems
pts: Two force systems are equivalent if they have the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any chosen point.
Moving a force from one point to another requires adding a couple equal to the force times the perpendicular distance moved.

System (1) is a single 50 N force at A with zero moment about A; systems (2) and (3) are the same 50 N force shifted with a couple, so their moment about A is not zero, yet the moment check shows each sums to zero about A.
Equivalence is checked by summing forces (∑\(F_{y}\)) and moments about a common point (∑\(M_{A}\)) for each system.
defs: Equivalent force systems
Force systems that produce the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about the same point, so they have identical external effect on a rigid body.
Couple
A pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces (or a pure moment) that produces rotation without net force.
eqs: Moment of a force about point A (equilibrium check of resultant moment)
\(F\) = force magnitude (N); \(d\) = perpendicular distance from A (m); \(M_c\) = couple moment (N·m)
tips: Always check both ∑F and ∑M about the same reference point; matching only the force is not enough.
Use consistent units: convert distances to metres so moments come out in N·m.
rq: Why does system (2) with a 25 N·m couple at the midpoint give the same moment about A as the 50 N force at A?
Moving the 50 N force 0.5 m to the midpoint adds a moment of 50 × 0.5 = 25 N·m that must be balanced by the couple; the check 50 × 0.5 − 25 = 0 shows the couple cancels this, so they are equivalent.
What would change if the couple in system (3) were 25 N·m instead of 50 N·m?
The moment about A would be 50 × 1 − 25 = 25 N·m ≠ 0, so the system would no longer be equivalent to a single 50 N force at A.

notes.t: Actions of a force system: translation, couple and rotation
pts: A force acting through the mass centre of a body tends only to translate it, with no rotation.
Two parallel forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction form a couple, which tends to rotate the body only, with no translation.
A force applied off the mass centre both translates and rotates the body, the offset distance d producing the turning effect.
defs: Couple
A pair of parallel forces of equal magnitude acting in opposite directions along different lines of action; it produces pure rotation with no net translation.
tips: A couple produces no net translation; do not add its two forces to get a resultant force — its effect is a moment equal to F × d.
Distinguish the mass centre (where a force causes only translation) from any other point, where an offset distance d gives rotation as well.
rq: Why does a single force applied through the mass centre produce no rotation?
Its line of action passes through the mass centre, so its moment about the mass centre is zero; it only translates the body.
What happens to the rotational effect of a force applied off the mass centre if the offset distance d is increased?
The turning effect (moment) increases in proportion to d, since moment = F × d for a fixed force F.

notes.t: Equivalent force-couple systems and resultant force of coplanar forces on a beam
pts: Any system of forces can be replaced at a chosen point by a single force plus a couple moment (force-couple system) without changing its external effect.
Moving a force to a new point requires adding a couple equal to the moment of that force about the new point.
An equivalent single resultant force R is found by summing the force components; its line of action is then located by moment equivalence about a convenient point.
The line of action of R is located where it crosses the y-axis, found by equating its moment about the origin to the total moment of the original forces.
defs: Force-couple system
An equivalent system consisting of a single force acting at a specified point together with a couple moment, producing the same external effect as the original forces.
Resultant force
The single force obtained by vector summation of all forces in a system, equivalent to the original system for translational effect.
eqs: Moment of forces about point A (force-couple moment)
\(M_A\) = couple moment at A (N·m); \(r\) = position vector from A (m); \(F\) = applied force (N)
tips: Watch the 45° force: resolve it into x and y components before summing forces and taking moments.
Keep sign conventions for moments consistent (counter-clockwise positive) and check units (N, m, N·m).
rq: Why must a couple be added when a force is moved to a new point?
Moving a force to a different point changes its moment about that point, so a couple equal to the original moment about the new point must be added to keep the external effect unchanged.
How does the line of action of R relate to the moments of the original forces?
R's moment about any point must equal the sum of the moments of the original forces about that point, so its position is found by moment equivalence.

notes.t: Statics: Resultant of a 4-Force Coplanar System
pts: Resolve each inclined force into x and y components before summing; the horizontal and vertical resultants are found separately.
The magnitude of the resultant comes from Pythagoras applied to the summed components.
The direction of the resultant is the inverse tangent of the vertical over horizontal resultant component.
Forces acting downward or to the left are taken as negative when summing components.
defs: Resultant force
A single force equivalent to the vector sum of all forces acting on a body, having the same effect on translation.
eqs: R = resultant magnitude (N); \(R_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); \(R_{y}\) = vertical component (N)
θ = angle of resultant to x-axis (°); \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\) = components (N)
tips: Watch signs: forces pointing down or left must be negative in the component sums.
Angle θ from tan⁻¹ gives the direction relative to the x-axis; check the quadrant (here \(R_{y}\) is negative, so the resultant points down-right).
rq: Why is the 250 N force split into cos 45° and sin 45° components rather than used directly?
Only components along perpendicular axes can be added algebraically; the inclined force's effect is split into its x and y parts.
What would change in R if the 50 N force acted in the negative x direction?
Rx would become −50 + 250 cos 45° = 126.8 N, so the magnitude and angle would both change.

notes.t: Equivalent Force-Couple System at a Point
pts: Replace the system of forces with a single resultant force R at A plus a couple moment \(M_{A}\) about A; the resultant is found by summing the force components.
The couple moment at A is the sum of the moments of all applied forces about A, taking the sense of rotation consistently (here clockwise taken as negative).
The magnitude of the resultant is found from its Cartesian components, and its direction is given by the angle the resultant makes with the x-axis.
Components of the resultant are obtained from the horizontal and vertical force sums: 226.8 N to the right and 276.8 N downward.
defs: Force-couple system
An equivalent system consisting of a single force acting at a chosen point together with a couple moment, which has the same external effect as the original forces.
eqs: R = resultant force (N); \(R_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); \(R_{y}\) = vertical component (N)
θ = angle of resultant from x-axis (°); \(R_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); \(R_{y}\) = vertical component (N)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); F = applied force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
tips: Keep a consistent sign convention for moments (here anticlockwise positive or negative throughout) and state it; mixing signs gives wrong couple values.
Ensure the moment arm is the perpendicular distance to the line of action, not the distance along the beam, and convert the 45° force into components before taking moments.
rq: Why does the 250 N force at 45° contribute to the moment only through its vertical component?

Its moment arm is taken from the vertical component 250 sin45° acting at A only via the horizontal-directed term; the horizontal component 250 cos45° acts along the line through A, and the moment in the solution uses 250 cos45° × 1 because the 1 m offset is the perpendicular distance to that component's line of action.
What would change if the couple were taken about point B instead of A?

The resultant force R would be unchanged, but the couple moment would change, since \(M_{B}\) = \(M_{A}\) + (moment of R about the shift from A to B); the force-couple pair is only equivalent at the chosen reference point.

notes.t: Equivalent force system: resultant force and line of action crossing an axis
pts: A system of forces can be replaced by a single resultant force R together with a moment about a chosen point.
The line of action of R is found by equating the moment of R about a point to the sum of moments of the original forces about that point.
Where the line of action crosses the y-axis, the moment arm is the perpendicular distance d from point A, so the moment is the horizontal component times d.
Taking moments about A gives the position d of the line of action, here found to be 2.32 m above A.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same net effect (force and moment) as a system of forces acting on a body.
Line of action
The straight line along which a force acts; it determines the moment arm of the force about any point.
eqs: Moment of R about point A, used to locate its line of action
\(M_{A}\) = moment about point A (N·m); d = perpendicular distance from A to the line of action (m)
tips: Keep consistent sign convention for moments (anticlockwise positive) when equating the resultant moment to the sum of the original moments.
Check units: force in N multiplied by distance in m gives N·m, and the answer d must be in metres.
rq: Why is the moment of R about A equal to the horizontal force times d, rather than the full force times d?
Only the component perpendicular to the moment arm produces moment; here the 226.8 N force is horizontal and acts at distance d vertically from A, so its moment arm is d.
What would happen to the crossing point on the y-axis if the resultant's moment about A were zero?
The line of action would pass through A, so d would be zero and the line would cross the y-axis at the origin, the point A.

units.name: 8.1 Static equilibrium basics
units.ov: This module introduces static equilibrium: a body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero, so it has no acceleration or rotation. It is the foundation for later statics work such as free-body diagrams, reactions, trusses and frames, where these two conditions are applied to solve for unknown forces.
must: Equilibrium means zero resultant force AND zero resultant moment: \(\sum \vec{F}=0\) and \(\sum M=0\)
Checking forces alone is a classic error: a pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action gives a couple, so the body still rotates
Static equilibrium includes constant velocity in a straight line without rotation, not only rest, because acceleration is zero
Force balance is a vector sum: resolve into components, so \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) (and \(\sum F_z=0\) in 3D)
Moment balance holds about ANY point, so choose the point to eliminate unknown forces (put it where unknown lines of action cross)
Moments are in N·m, with a consistent sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive); moment = force × perpendicular distance
Seesaw model: equilibrium about a pivot requires \(F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2\) when the forces are on opposite sides of the pivot
In 2D there are three independent equations (\(\sum F_x, \sum F_y, \sum M\)), so at most three unknowns can be found
State the conditions explicitly and show the method in written answers (draw the body, forces, chosen moment point, then solve)
conn: Free-body diagrams: you must isolate the body and include all forces and reactions before the equilibrium equations can be applied
Force resolution (trigonometry and vectors) combines with moment calculation: moments of inclined forces need perpendicular distance or components
Choosing the moment point cleverly links to solving simultaneous equations for support reactions, since it reduces the unknowns per equation
Equilibrium vs Newton's laws: zero net force and moment means zero linear and angular acceleration, including constant-velocity motion
exq: State the two conditions for static equilibrium and explain why zero resultant force alone does not guarantee equilibrium, using a sketch of two equal and opposite forces with offset lines of action.

A uniform seesaw of length 4 m pivots at its centre. A 300 N child sits 1.5 m from the pivot. Where must a 450 N child sit on the other side for equilibrium? What is the reaction at the pivot (neglect the seesaw weight)?
A beam is acted on by forces of 50 N, 80 N and an unknown force F at known positions. Determine F and its position so the beam is in equilibrium, showing \(\sum F=0\) and \(\sum M=0\).
A car travels at a constant 20 m/s on a straight level road. Is it in static equilibrium? Justify, and state the resultant force and moment.
Show that if a body is in equilibrium, the sum of moments is zero about any point, by taking moments about two different points for a given set of forces.

notes.t: Equilibrium in mechanics
pts: Engineering systems in mechanics are analysed using the principles of equilibrium.
The seesaw image illustrates a system balanced about a pivot, where forces and moments on either side are equal so nothing accelerates.
defs: Equilibrium
The state of a body or system in which the net force and net moment acting on it are zero, so it has no acceleration (remains at rest or moves at constant velocity).
tips: Equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net moment; checking only forces is a common mistake.
rq: Why does a seesaw balance when the two children have different masses?
Because the heavier child sits closer to the pivot, so the moments about the pivot (force × distance) on both sides are equal, giving zero net moment.

notes.t: Static equilibrium
pts: A body is in static equilibrium if it is stationary, or moves at constant velocity in a straight line without rotating.
Equilibrium requires the net force on the body to be zero.
Equilibrium also requires the net moment on the body to be zero; this holds about any chosen point.
defs: Static equilibrium
A state in which a body is either at rest or moving with constant velocity in a straight line without rotation, so that the resultant force and resultant moment acting on it are both zero.
eqs: Force equilibrium condition (resultant force is zero)
\(\sum \vec{F}\) = vector sum of all forces acting on the body (N)
Moment equilibrium condition (resultant moment is zero about any point)
\(\sum M\) = sum of all moments about any chosen point (N·m)
tips: Equilibrium needs both the resultant force AND the resultant moment to be zero; satisfying only force balance is not enough.
Constant velocity in a straight line still counts as equilibrium, so do not assume equilibrium only means 'at rest'.
rq: Why can you choose any point to take moments about in a statics problem?

Because for a body in static equilibrium the resultant moment is zero about any point, so the choice of point does not change the result; a well-chosen point (e.g. where unknown forces act) simplifies the algebra.
Can a body moving at constant velocity be in equilibrium even though it is not stationary? What must also be true?
Yes, provided it moves in a straight line at constant speed without rotation; then the net force and net moment are still zero.

units.name: 8.2 Free-body diagrams: concept and systems
units.ov: This module introduces the free-body diagram (FBD) as the essential first step in any statics or mechanics problem: isolate a chosen body or system, remove its supports and neighbours, and replace them with the forces and moments they exert. It extends this to multi-part systems such as engines, skeletons and lifts, where separate FBDs reveal internal joint forces. The FBD is the bridge between a physical situation and the equilibrium equations used to solve it.
must: Definition: an FBD is a sketch of a single isolated body showing all external forces and couples acting on it, and it is the basis for applying equilibrium equations.
Always begin by clearly defining the body or system and its boundary, because the choice of boundary decides which forces are external.
Isolate the body completely: remove supports, connections and contacting bodies, and draw none of them (leaving a support drawn in is a common error).
Replace every removed support or contact with the forces and moments it exerts, including reaction forces at supports and contact points as well as applied loads.
Fixed or built-in supports exert reaction moments as well as forces, so include both.
Forces from parts you have cut away must be drawn in as external forces on the body, never ignored.
For multi-part structures, split the system into separate FBDs whenever internal joint forces are needed. Treating it as one rigid body only gives the external reactions.
Forces at a joint between two parts act in equal and opposite pairs on the two separate FBDs (Newton's third law), so keep directions consistent.
Apply the equilibrium equations \(\sum \mathbf{F}=0\) and \(\sum \mathbf{M}=0\) only after the FBD is complete.
conn: FBD and equilibrium equations: a missing or wrong force in the diagram propagates directly into wrong \(\sum F\) and \(\sum M\) equations.
Choice of system boundary and internal forces: a whole-structure FBD gives support reactions, while splitting at joints exposes internal forces, and exam problems often need both in sequence.
Support types and reactions: identifying the support (pin, roller, fixed) determines which reaction forces and moments appear on the FBD.
Newton's third law and multi-body analysis: the equal-and-opposite joint forces link the FBDs of connected parts, giving simultaneous equations.
exq: Draw the FBD of a cantilever beam of length 2 m, built in at one end, carrying a 5 kN point load at the free end. State all reactions at the support, then calculate their values.

A two-member frame is pin-jointed at the middle and pinned to the ground at both ends. Draw an FBD of the whole frame and of each member separately, showing all joint forces with correct equal-and-opposite directions.
A ladder of mass 15 kg rests against a smooth wall and on rough ground. Draw its FBD, identify every force, and find the friction force needed for equilibrium at a given angle.
Explain why an FBD of a whole engine cannot be used to find the force in the connecting rod. Which FBDs are needed instead?
Identify the errors in a given FBD that still shows the support drawn in and omits a reaction moment at a built-in end, and correct it.

notes.t: Free-body diagrams
pts: Before studying the effect of forces, first define which body or mechanical system is to be analysed.
All forces acting on the chosen body must be represented in a free-body diagram.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch of an isolated body showing all external forces (and couples) acting on it, used as the basis for applying equilibrium equations.
tips: Define the boundary of the system clearly before drawing; forces from parts you have cut away must be drawn in, not ignored.
Include reaction forces at supports and contact points, not just applied loads.
rq: Why must every force acting on the body be shown, including ones you might consider unimportant?
Omitting any force makes the equilibrium equations incorrect, because the sum of forces and moments must account for all external actions on the isolated body.

notes.t: Free-body diagrams
pts: A free-body diagram starts by clearly defining the single body or mechanical system to be analysed.
The body must be isolated completely from all surrounding and contacting bodies before analysis.
Supports, connections and holding devices are removed and replaced by the forces and moments they exert on the body.
The free-body diagram is the essential first step in solving mechanics problems.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch of a single isolated body showing all external forces and moments acting on it, with supports and contacting bodies replaced by the forces and moments they exert.
tips: Do not forget to include reaction moments at fixed or built-in supports, not just reaction forces.
Show the body alone; leaving a support drawn in the diagram is a common error.
rq: Why must supports be replaced by forces and moments rather than simply ignored?
Supports and contacts exert reaction forces and moments on the body; ignoring them would leave the body unbalanced in the analysis and make equilibrium equations incorrect.
What would go wrong if you analysed a body while still including its neighbouring bodies?
Internal forces between bodies would be mixed with external forces, complicating the equations and making it hard to find the unknown reactions directly.

notes.t: Mechanical systems with many interacting parts
pts: Real mechanical systems such as the human skeleton, engines, lifts, telescope mirrors and ship hulls are made up of many interacting components.
Equilibrium analysis of such systems requires identifying each part and the forces transmitted between them.
tips: Do not treat a multi-part structure as a single rigid body when internal forces at joints are needed; split it into separate free-body diagrams.
rq: Why is it useful to treat a complex system such as a scissor lift as a set of interacting parts rather than one body?
Each part can be isolated with a free-body diagram, showing internal forces at connections, so equilibrium equations can be written for each part and solved.

units.name: 8.3 Smooth and rough surface contact forces
units.ov: This material covers how contact between bodies and supports is idealised so that free-body diagrams can be drawn correctly. Smooth contact gives a purely normal compressive reaction. Rough contact adds a tangential friction force that opposes sliding or the tendency to slide. Correct force directions feed directly into the equilibrium equations.
must: A smooth surface has no friction, so its reaction is purely normal: perpendicular to the common tangent at the contact point.
A rough surface gives two components: a normal force \(N\) and a tangential friction force \(F_f\).
Friction opposes the direction of sliding, or the tendency to slide, not the direction of the applied load.
The normal contact force is always compressive: it pushes into each body and never pulls.
On curved or inclined surfaces, the normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the contact point, not to the horizontal or the body's edge.
A roller or ball support transmits only a force perpendicular to the supporting surface and allows free movement along it.
A pin transmits a force in any direction in the plane, so two components, but no moment (\(M=0\)) because it allows rotation.
A rigid (fixed) support prevents translation and rotation, so it gives two force components plus a moment.
Draw the free-body diagram first: choose the idealisation (smooth or rough), show every reaction, then apply \(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0\).
conn: Support idealisation sets the number of unknown reactions (roller 1, pin 2, fixed 3), which must match the available equilibrium equations \(\sum F_x,\sum F_y,\sum M\).
Smooth versus rough contact decides whether \(F_f\) appears on the free-body diagram. The wording 'smooth' sets \(F_f=0\) and reduces the number of unknowns.
Inclined or curved contact needs the tangent direction to be found first, then the normal and friction directions to be resolved into x and y components in the equilibrium equations.
The friction direction depends on the sliding tendency, so the sign of \(F_f\) in the equilibrium equations links directly to checking which way the body would move.
exq: A ladder of weight W and length L rests against a smooth vertical wall and on rough ground at 60° to the horizontal. Draw the free-body diagram, state the direction of each reaction, and find the normal and friction forces at the base.

A uniform rod rests inside a smooth hemispherical bowl, touching the rim at one point and the bowl surface at another. Determine the direction of each contact force and use equilibrium to find their magnitudes.

A block of mass 20 kg is on a rough 30° incline, held by a horizontal force. Draw the free-body diagram, give the direction of friction for the case where the block tends to slide down, and calculate N and \(F_f\).
A beam is supported by a pin at A and a roller at B on a 45° incline. State the unknown reactions at each support, explain why the moment at A is zero, and find the reactions under a given load.
Explain, with sketches, the difference between a smooth and a rough contact. Give two common errors in drawing contact forces on a curved surface and how to avoid them.

notes.t: Modelling the action of forces
pts: Engineers must know which type of force acts between bodies in contact and at supports, since this determines how the body is modelled.
Contact between bodies can be idealised as smooth (frictionless, force normal to surface) or rough (friction can act tangentially).
Roller or ball supports transmit only a force perpendicular to the supporting surface, allowing free movement along it.
A pinned connection transmits forces in any direction in the plane but no moment, allowing free rotation.
A rigid fixing prevents translation and rotation, so it can transmit both forces and a moment.
tips: Do not assume a pin resists moment; a pinned connection allows rotation, so the moment at the pin is zero.
Smooth-surface contact gives no friction force; assuming friction when the surface is stated smooth is a common error.
rq: Why does a roller support give only one reaction component while a pinned connection gives two?

A roller allows free movement along the surface, so only a normal reaction acts; a pin prevents translation in both directions, so it has horizontal and vertical reactions, but still no moment because it allows rotation.
What would change in a model if a smooth surface were replaced by a rough one?
A tangential friction force would be added to the normal reaction, which can resist sliding and must be included in equilibrium equations.

notes.t: Smooth surfaces in equilibrium
pts: A perfectly smooth surface offers no resistance to sliding parallel to the surface, i.e. there is no friction.
Because friction is absent, the reaction exerted by a smooth surface has no tangential component and acts only normal to the surface.
At a point of contact, the reaction is perpendicular to the common tangent at that point.
defs: Smooth surface
An idealised surface offering no resistance to sliding parallel to it, so friction is assumed to be completely absent and the contact reaction is purely normal to the surface.
tips: Do not include a frictional (tangential) component in the reaction of a smooth surface; only the normal reaction is present.
For curved surfaces at a point of contact, the normal is perpendicular to the tangent, not to the horizontal or the body's edge.
rq: Why must the reaction from a smooth surface be normal to the surface rather than at some angle?
Any tangential component would be a frictional force resisting sliding; since a smooth surface has zero friction, the only possible reaction is normal to the surface.
How do you find the direction of the reaction at a point where a rod touches a smooth curved surface?
Draw the tangent to the curve at the contact point; the reaction acts along the normal, perpendicular to that tangent.

notes.t: Smooth contact forces
pts: A smooth (frictionless) contact surface can only exert a reaction force perpendicular to the surface.
The contact force is compressive, pushing the bodies apart rather than pulling them together.
The contact force acts normal to the common tangent at the point of contact, for curved or inclined surfaces too.
defs: Smooth contact
A contact surface with no friction, so the reaction force it exerts acts only perpendicular (normal) to the surface at the point of contact.
tips: Do not draw a smooth-contact reaction at an angle to the surface; it must be perpendicular to the tangent at the contact point.
Check the sign: the contact force on each body is compressive (directed into that body), not tensile.
rq: Why can a smooth surface not exert a force parallel to itself?
Parallel (tangential) force would be friction; a smooth surface has no friction, so the only possible reaction is normal to the surface.
How do you find the direction of the contact force on a sphere touching an inclined plane?
Draw the common tangent at the contact point and take the normal to it, which passes through the centre of the sphere; the force is compressive along that line.

notes.t: Rough surface and friction force
pts: A rough surface resists sliding between two bodies in contact.
Surface friction produces a force acting parallel (tangential) to the contact surface.
The friction force always acts opposite to the direction of sliding (motion).
Contact pressure produces a normal (perpendicular) component of the contact force, from the compressive contact force.
defs: Friction force
The tangential force developed at a contact surface that resists relative sliding between the surfaces and acts opposite to the direction of sliding.
Normal component
The component of the contact force acting perpendicular to the contact surface, arising from the compressive contact force.
tips: Friction always opposes the direction of sliding, not the direction of applied load; draw it on the free-body diagram opposite to the motion.
Do not confuse the tangential friction force with the normal component; both must be shown on the contact surface in equilibrium problems.
rq: Why does the friction force point opposite to the sliding direction rather than along it?
Friction is a resisting force; it opposes the relative sliding motion (or tendency to slide) between the two surfaces.
If a block is pushed to the right and slides, which way does the friction force act and why does the surface need a normal component?
Friction acts to the left, opposing sliding; the normal component is the compressive contact force pushing the surfaces together, which is what allows the tangential friction force to exist.

notes.t: Rough surface contact forces
pts: At a rough surface, the contact force has a normal component N that is compressive and a tangential component Fₓ that is friction.
The normal force N acts perpendicular to the contact surface, pushing the surfaces apart.
The friction force \(F_{f}\) acts tangentially to the surface, opposing the relative sliding or tendency to slide.
defs: Normal force (N)
The component of the contact force perpendicular to the contact surface; it is compressive.
Friction force (\(F_{f}\))
The component of the contact force tangential to the contact surface, resisting relative motion.
tips: Do not confuse the compressive normal force N (always perpendicular to the surface) with the friction force \(F_{f}\) (always tangential to it) when drawing free-body diagrams.
Friction acts along the contact surface, not perpendicular to it; the direction must oppose motion, so check the sign carefully in equilibrium equations.
rq: Why must the normal force and friction force be shown as separate components rather than one contact force?

Because the normal component is perpendicular to the surface and the friction component is tangential; each is resolved along its own direction, so they can be balanced independently in equilibrium equations.
In the diagrams, why does the friction force point opposite to the direction of potential motion?
Friction opposes the relative motion or tendency to slide between the surfaces, so it acts against the direction of impending or actual sliding.

units.name: 8.4 Support reactions: rollers, cables, pins, built-in supports
units.ov: This material classifies the common 2D supports (roller/ball, cable, pin, built-in) by the motions they prevent and therefore the reactions they supply. The rule is that a support provides a reaction for each motion it blocks: a force for blocked translation and a moment for blocked rotation. Drawing these correctly on a free body diagram is the first step in every equilibrium problem.
must: A support reaction exists for each motion it prevents: a force for blocked translation, a moment for blocked rotation.
Roller/ball (frictionless) support: one unknown, a compressive force normal to the contact surface, with no component along the surface.
The roller reaction must be perpendicular to the contact tangent, so on an inclined surface it is not vertical.
Cable/rope/chain: one unknown, tension \(T\) only. It pulls along the cable and away from the body, and it can never push.
Resolving cable tension at angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal: \(T_x = T\cos\theta,\ T_y = T\sin\theta\). Check which angle is given before using sin and cos.
Pin: two unknowns, \(R_x\) and \(R_y\), and no moment, so rotation is free. The resultant is \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\).
Built-in (fixed) support: three unknowns in 2D, \(R_x\), \(R_y\) and a reaction moment \(M\). Never omit \(M\).
Use a consistent sign convention (e.g. counter-clockwise positive) when summing moments including the support moment \(M\).
Count unknowns against the three 2D equilibrium equations \(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0\) to check the problem is solvable.

Draw the reaction directions carefully (compressive away from the surface into the body, tension away from the body). Reactions with assumed directions may come out negative, which just means they point the opposite way.
conn: Support type determines the number of unknowns in the free body diagram, which determines whether \(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0\) can solve the problem (statical determinacy).
Cable tension resolution (trigonometry) feeds into force and moment equilibrium, e.g. a beam held by a cable and a pin.
Pin versus fixed support: a fixed support adds a moment reaction, which changes the moment equation and the number of unknowns.
Roller on an inclined surface combines the normal-direction rule with resolving components, then force and moment balance.
exq: A uniform 5 m beam of weight 400 N is pinned at A and supported at B by a cable at 30° to the horizontal. Draw the free body diagram, then find the cable tension and the pin reaction components and resultant \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\).

A cantilever of length 3 m carries a 2 kN point load at its free end and a 1 kN/m uniformly distributed load. Find the reactions \(R_x\), \(R_y\) and the moment \(M\) at the built-in support, stating your sign convention.

A ladder rests on a frictionless floor (roller) and a smooth wall, held by a horizontal rope at the base. Draw the free body diagram, state the direction of each reaction, and determine the rope tension.
A bar rests on a roller on a 40° inclined surface at one end and is pinned at the other. Explain why the roller reaction is not vertical, and find the reactions given a 1.5 kN load at mid-span.
Explain, with sketches, why a pin cannot provide a moment reaction while a built-in support can, and state the number of unknown reactions for roller, cable, pin and fixed supports in 2D.

notes.t: Roller or ball connection (support reactions)
pts: A roller or ball support eliminates friction, so it cannot resist a force parallel to the surface (in the sliding direction).
The support transmits only a compressive force acting normal (perpendicular) to the tangent or surface at the point of contact, so it provides a single reaction component.
defs: Roller or ball connection
A frictionless support that allows free movement parallel to the contact surface and transmits only a compressive reaction force normal to that surface at the point of contact.
tips: Do not draw a horizontal reaction at a roller support; the reaction must act perpendicular to the contact surface.
The reaction is compressive, so it points away from the surface into the supported body (check the direction arrow carefully).
rq: Why can a roller support not provide a horizontal reaction on a beam?
Because it is frictionless, so it cannot develop a force along the sliding (tangential) direction; it only supplies a normal reaction.
What would change if the roller support were replaced by a pin support at the same location?
The pin could also resist a force parallel to the surface, adding a horizontal reaction component, since friction-free sliding is no longer permitted.

notes.t: Flexible cable (or chain or rope) forces
pts: A flexible cable always exerts a tension force on the body it is attached to.
The tension force points away from the body, along the direction of the cable.
The cable angle θ is measured from the horizontal, and the tension T resolves into horizontal and vertical components.
defs: Tension force
A pulling force transmitted along a flexible cable, chain or rope, directed away from the body to which the cable is attached and along the cable's line of action.
eqs: Horizontal and vertical components of cable tension at angle θ to the horizontal
T = cable tension (N); θ = angle of cable to horizontal (degrees or radians); \(T_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); \(T_{y}\) = vertical component (N)
tips: Do not draw a cable force pointing towards the body; a cable can only pull, so the arrow must point away from the body along the cable.
Make sure θ is measured from the horizontal (or as stated in the diagram) before resolving T into components with cos θ and sin θ.
rq: Why must the tension force always point away from the body rather than towards it?
A cable can only pull, not push, so the force it exerts on the body acts along the cable, away from the body toward the anchor point.
If the angle θ increases while T stays the same, what happens to the horizontal component of the tension?
The horizontal component T cos θ decreases, since cos θ falls as θ increases.

notes.t: Pinned connection (support reactions)
pts: A pin stops translation of the rigid body in any direction but allows it to rotate freely about the pin.
Because translation is blocked in every direction, the pin must provide a reaction force with both x and y components.
A pin cannot resist a moment, so the reaction has no couple component and rotation remains free.
defs: Pin (pinned connection)
A support or joint that restrains translation in all directions but permits rotation, transmitting an x and y reaction force and no moment.
eqs: Reaction force from a pin (resultant of components)
\(R_x\) = horizontal reaction component (N); \(R_y\) = vertical reaction component (N); \(R\) = resultant reaction force (N)
tips: Do not show a moment reaction at a pin; only \(R_x\) and \(R_y\) should appear on the free body diagram.
Do not confuse a pin (two reaction components) with a roller or smooth surface (one reaction component perpendicular to the surface).
rq: Why can a pin not carry a moment, even though it carries forces in two directions?
A pin is a single point connection that lets the body rotate about it freely; a moment would have to be resisted by a fixed (rotationally restrained) connection, which a pin does not provide.
If a rigid body is supported by a pin and a roller, how many unknown reactions are there and why does this matter?
Three unknowns (\(R_x\), \(R_y\) at the pin and one normal force at the roller), which matches the three equilibrium equations for a 2D rigid body, so it is statically determinate.

notes.t: Built-in (fixed) supports
pts: A built-in support resists both rotation and translation of the member it is attached to.
The support supplies a reaction force that prevents translation; it has horizontal and vertical components.
The support also supplies a reaction moment that prevents rotation, so it has three unknown reactions in 2D.
defs: Built-in (fixed) support
A support that prevents both translation and rotation of the connected member, producing two force reactions and one moment reaction in 2D.
tips: Do not omit the reaction moment \(M\) at a fixed support; students often draw only \(R_x\) and \(R_y\).
Choose a consistent sign convention for \(M\) (e.g. counter-clockwise positive) when summing moments.
rq: Why does a built-in support have three unknown reactions in 2D while a pin support has only two?
A pin resists translation in x and y only, giving \(R_x\) and \(R_y\); a built-in support also resists rotation, adding a reaction moment \(M\), giving three unknowns.
What would happen to the beam's equilibrium if the moment \(M\) at the wall were removed?
The beam could rotate freely about the wall, so it would no longer be in static equilibrium under a transverse load; the moment is needed to balance the moment of the applied loads.

units.name: 8.5 Drawing free-body diagrams with examples
units.ov: This material teaches how to draw a free-body diagram (FBD): choose a body or system, isolate it with its full external boundary, and show every external force crossing that boundary. It is applied to a man pulling a block on a rough surface (two separate FBDs linked by rope tension and friction) and to a pivoted cable hoist beam (weights, cable tension, pin reactions). A correct FBD is the necessary first step before writing any equilibrium equations.
must: An FBD isolates a chosen body or group of bodies, shows its complete external boundary, and shows all external forces as arrows.
Decide first which body or system to isolate; this choice determines which forces are external and which are internal.
Only external forces appear on the FBD; internal forces between parts of the chosen system are never drawn.
Check every force crossing the boundary (weight, supports, contacts, cables) before writing equilibrium equations.
Weight \( W = mg \) acts downward at the centre of mass G, not at the pivot or support.
Man-and-block problem: draw separate FBDs; the rope tension acts on each body in opposite directions and is equal for a light rope.
