Friction on the block opposes its motion or tendency to move; friction on the man acts forward (in the direction opposite his pull) to stop his feet slipping. This is a common sign error.
Vertical equilibrium gives \( N_{block}=m_b g \) and \( N_{man}=m_m g \) when the rope is horizontal; with an inclined rope the tension's vertical component must be included.
Static friction takes any value up to its maximum, \( F \le \mu_s N \); it equals the maximum only at impending slip.
Hoist beam: include the beam weight \( m_1 g \) at G, load weight \( m_2 g \) at end A, cable tension at B, and pin reaction components at O.
conn: FBDs lead to equilibrium equations \( \sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M_O=0 \); a missing or misplaced force gives wrong answers, especially in the moment equation.
Friction and normal reaction link through \( F\le\mu_s N \): the FBD gives N from vertical equilibrium, then the limiting friction determines whether slipping occurs.

Isolating different bodies or systems (man, block, or both together) changes which forces are internal or external. Tension is internal for the combined system, which is a useful check on the separate FBDs.
The hoist beam combines moments about O (weights at G and A, cable at B) with force balance to find the cable tension and the pin reaction components.
exq: A man of mass 80 kg pulls a block of mass 50 kg along rough ground with a horizontal rope. Draw separate FBDs and find the normal reactions, assuming \( g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \). If the block is about to slip with \( \mu_s=0.4 \), find the rope tension and the friction force required at the man's feet.
For the same man-and-block system, what minimum coefficient of static friction is needed between the man's shoes and the ground to avoid slipping when he pulls with the tension found above?

A hoist beam of mass \( m_1 \) pivoted at O carries a load \( m_2 \) at end A, supported by a cable at B. Draw the FBD of the beam, showing all forces and their points of application, and write the three equilibrium equations.
For the hoist beam with given dimensions (OG, OB, OA), \( m_1=100\ \mathrm{kg} \) and \( m_2=200\ \mathrm{kg} \), find the cable tension and the magnitude and direction of the pin reaction at O.
Explain why the rope tension does not appear on an FBD of the combined man-and-block system, and why it must appear on each separate FBD.

notes.t: Drawing a free-body diagram
pts: Begin by deciding clearly which body or combination of bodies to isolate.
Isolate the chosen body with a diagram showing its complete external boundary.
Represent every force acting on the isolated body on the diagram.
defs: Free-body diagram
A diagram that isolates a chosen body or group of bodies from its surroundings, showing its complete external boundary and all external forces acting on it.
eqs: Weight of the isolated body (gravitational force acting downward)
W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
tips: Only forces acting on the isolated body belong on its free-body diagram; internal forces between parts of the chosen system are not shown.
Check that every force crossing the boundary (weight, supports, contacts) is included before writing equilibrium equations.
rq: Why must the boundary of the free-body diagram be drawn completely around the chosen body?
So that every external force acting across the boundary is captured; missing a boundary crossing means missing a force and getting the equilibrium equations wrong.
In the apple example, why is the contact force from the stalk shown as acting upward while the weight acts downward?
The stalk supports the apple, so it pulls up on it (tension/contact force), while gravity pulls the apple's mass down toward the Earth.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a man pulling a block on a rough surface
pts: Each body is isolated and its free-body diagram drawn: forces on the block (weight, tension, friction, normal) and on the man (weight, tension, friction, normal).
Tension in the rope acts on the block and on the man in opposite directions, equal in magnitude for a light rope.
Friction on the block opposes its motion or tendency to move, while friction on the man acts forward to prevent his feet slipping.
Normal reactions from the ground act vertically upward and balance the weights of the block and the man.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch showing one body isolated from its surroundings, with all external forces acting on it drawn as arrows.
Static friction
The friction force between surfaces in contact that prevents relative sliding and can take any value up to its maximum.
eqs: Vertical equilibrium of the block (normal reaction balances weight)
\(N_{\text{on block}}\) = normal reaction on the block (N); \(m_{b}\) = mass of the block (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m \(s^{-2}\))
\(N_{\text{on man}}\) = normal reaction on the man (N); \(m_{m}\) = mass of the man (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m \(s^{-2}\))
tips: Draw the free-body diagram for each body separately; do not combine the block and man into one diagram with internal forces included.
Friction on the man opposes the pull, a common sign error; check that the direction of each friction force is consistent with equilibrium.
rq: Why must the friction on the man act in the direction of the pull rather than opposite to it?
Because the rope tension pulls the man toward the block, so friction at his feet must push him the other way, opposite the pull, to keep him in equilibrium and prevent slipping.
What would happen to the block's friction force if the man pulled harder but the block did not move?
Static friction on the block would increase to match the applied tension, since it adjusts up to its maximum value to maintain equilibrium.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a cable hoist beam: free-body diagram
pts: Draw a free-body diagram isolating the hoist beam, showing all external forces: cable tension, pin reactions at O, and weights of the beam and load.
The engineering system is a cable hoist consisting of a beam of mass m₁ pivoted at O, with a load of mass m₂ hanging from end A and a cable attached at B.
tips: Do not omit the beam's own weight \( m_1 g \) from the free-body diagram; it acts at G, not at the pivot O.
Make sure the load weight \( m_2 g \) is applied at end A, the point where the load hangs, not at the cable attachment B.
rq: Why must the pin reactions \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) be included in the free-body diagram even though they are not known in advance?
Because O is a support that exerts unknown reaction forces on the beam; these are external forces that must be represented so the equilibrium equations can be applied and solved for them.
Why is the weight m₁g drawn at G rather than at the pivot O?
The weight of a body acts through its centre of gravity G, and its moment about O depends on the distance from O to G, which is what produces the turning effect.

units.name: 8.6 First condition of equilibrium: force balance and concurrent forces
units.ov: The first condition of static equilibrium says the vector sum of all external forces on a body is zero, so it has no linear acceleration. In practice you draw a free-body diagram, resolve every force into components, and solve \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) for the unknowns. For concurrent forces, such as a knot with ropes, no moment arises, so this condition alone is enough. Otherwise the second condition (moments) is also needed.
must: First condition: \(\sum \vec{F}=0\), which splits for coplanar systems into \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\).
Draw a complete free-body diagram: isolate the body and show its weight and every contact or external force, checking each surface and support.
Resolve forces into components before summing. Never add magnitudes directly.
Weight is \(W=mg\) in newtons, so a 10 kg mass gives \(98\) N. Never put mass in kg into a force balance.
Concurrent forces have lines of action through one point, so there is no net moment and the first condition alone suffices.
\(\sum F=0\) is necessary but not sufficient for full equilibrium in general; the moment condition \(\sum M=0\) must also hold to prevent rotation.
Check the angle reference (horizontal vs vertical) before choosing sin or cos, and keep one sign convention (e.g. right and up positive).
Knot example (45° left rope, 30° right rope, 98 N load): \(-T_L\cos45^\circ+T_R\cos30^\circ=0\) and \(T_L\sin45^\circ+T_R\sin30^\circ-98=0\).
Solve the knot equations as simultaneous linear equations: \(T_L=1.225\,T_R\), so \(1.366\,T_R=98\), giving \(T_R=71.7\) N and \(T_L=87.8\) N.
Equilibrium includes constant-velocity motion, not just rest, because the condition is zero acceleration.
conn: Free-body diagrams link to component resolution: a missing force or a wrong sin/cos choice gives incorrect simultaneous equations.

Concurrent-force equilibrium links to the second condition (moments): the first condition alone is valid only if all lines of action meet at a point, and non-concurrent systems need \(\sum M=0\) as well.
Weight \(W=mg\) links to rope tension: the hanging mass fixes the vertical load that the angled tensions must balance, and steeper or shallower angles change how large the tensions become.
Sign conventions link to the algebra: a wrong sign in \(\sum F_x\) or \(\sum F_y\) changes the simultaneous solution and can give a wrong or negative tension.
exq: A 10 kg mass hangs from a knot supported by two ropes at 45° and 30° to the horizontal. Draw the free-body diagram, write \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\), and find both tensions (expect about 87.8 N and 71.7 N).
Redo the knot problem with a 20 kg mass, or with the rope angles changed to 60° and 30°. How do the tensions change, and what happens as a rope approaches horizontal?
Explain why \(\sum F=0\) is necessary but not sufficient for equilibrium. Give an example of a non-concurrent force system with zero net force that still rotates.
A body is acted on by three concurrent coplanar forces: 50 N at 0°, 80 N at 120°, and an unknown force. Find the magnitude and direction of the force that gives equilibrium.

State the common errors in setting up equilibrium equations (omitting weight, adding magnitudes, mixing mass and weight, wrong angle reference). Show how each would alter the result in a hanging-knot problem.

notes.t: First condition of static equilibrium
pts: For a body in static equilibrium, the vector sum of all forces acting on it must be zero, so there is no net force.
Because the net force is zero, an object in static equilibrium has no linear acceleration and does not translate.
defs: Static equilibrium
The state of a body at rest (or moving at constant velocity) in which the vector sum of all external forces acting on it is zero, so it has no linear acceleration.
eqs: First condition of static equilibrium (vector form)
\(\sum \vec{F}\) = vector sum of all external forces acting on the body (N)
First condition expanded as sum of individual forces
\(F_1, F_2, F_3, \ldots\) = individual forces acting on the body (N)
tips: Forces must be summed as vectors (with direction/components), not as magnitudes; forces in opposite directions cancel only if they are equal and collinear.
The condition \(\sum F = 0\) is necessary but not sufficient for full equilibrium; the second condition (sum of moments = 0) must also hold for rotation to be absent.
rq: Why does a zero net force imply that an object does not translate?
By Newton's second law, \(\sum F = ma\); if \(\sum F = 0\) then \(a = 0\), so the body's velocity does not change and it does not accelerate linearly.
Can an object in static equilibrium be moving?
Yes, if it moves at constant velocity; the condition is zero net force (zero acceleration), not necessarily zero velocity.

notes.t: Solving equilibrium problems
pts: Include every force acting on the body before writing equilibrium equations.
A free-body diagram must show the weight and all contact forces acting on the body.
Forces are vectors, so they must be resolved into components before summing.
The first condition of static equilibrium is that the net force on the body is zero.
For coplanar force systems the vector equation splits into two scalar equations, one per axis.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch of a single isolated body showing its weight and all contact and external forces acting on it, used to set up equilibrium equations.
First condition of static equilibrium
A body is in static equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero.
eqs: First condition of static equilibrium (vector form)
tips: Forgetting the weight or a contact force on the free-body diagram is a common error; check every surface and support.
Adding force magnitudes directly instead of their components ignores direction and gives wrong results.
rq: Why must forces be resolved into components before applying ΣF = 0 to a coplanar system?
Because forces are vectors with direction; components along perpendicular axes can be summed as scalars, giving two independent equations.
What would happen to the equilibrium equations if you forgot a contact force on the free-body diagram?
The sums would be incorrect, so the calculated unknown forces would be wrong and the body would appear unbalanced.

notes.t: First condition of static equilibrium (concurrent forces)
pts: For a body in equilibrium with concurrent forces, the net force in each direction must be zero, so the first condition can be applied alone.
A 10 kg mass hanging at rest has its weight balanced by the rope tension acting upward.
Weight is found as mass times gravitational acceleration, giving mg = 98 N for 10 kg.
defs: Static equilibrium
A state in which a body is at rest and the net force and net moment acting on it are both zero.
Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point, so no net moment arises and only the force balance is needed.
eqs: Force balance in the vertical direction (first condition) for the hanging mass
\(\Sigma F_y\) = sum of vertical forces (N); \(T\) = rope tension (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
tips: Do not confuse mass (kg) with weight (N): always compute \(W = mg\) before using it in a force balance.
Only apply the first condition alone when all forces are concurrent; otherwise also apply the moment (second) condition.
rq: Why can the first condition be used alone for this rope-and-mass system, without considering moments?
All forces (tension and weight) act along the same vertical line through a common point, so they are concurrent and produce no net moment.
Why is the tension equal to 98 N rather than 10 N?
Equilibrium requires T = mg, and weight is \(m g = 10 \times 9.81 \approx 98\) N, not the mass value in kg.

notes.t: First condition of static equilibrium: concurrent forces example
pts: For a body in static equilibrium the net force is zero, so the forces at a concurrent point must balance in both horizontal and vertical directions.
The 10 kg mass hanging from the junction gives a downward weight that must be balanced by the tensions in the other two ropes.
The two new ropes make angles of 45° and 30° with the horizontal, so their tensions must be resolved into components to find the unknown forces.
defs: Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point; for equilibrium their vector sum must be zero.
eqs: Weight of the suspended mass (vertical force down)
W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
First condition of equilibrium, horizontal and vertical components
\(F_x\) = horizontal force component (N); \(F_y\) = vertical force component (N)
tips: Use the weight \( W = mg \) (in N), not the mass in kg, when balancing forces.
Make sure angles are measured from the correct reference (horizontal or vertical) before applying sine and cosine to the tensions.
rq: Why must the horizontal and vertical force components be solved separately rather than the total force magnitude?
Because equilibrium requires the net force to be zero in each direction independently; the components of each rope's tension must sum to zero in x and in y.
What would happen to the required tensions if the 30° rope were made more horizontal?
Its horizontal component would be larger for the same tension, so the required tension in that rope would decrease, while the vertical support must still equal the weight.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a particle: resolving forces at a joined rope knot
pts: A knot at rest is in equilibrium, so the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero, which gives two scalar equations.
Resolve every force into x- and y-components before summing; angles are measured from the horizontal.
Set ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 separately, then solve the resulting pair of simultaneous linear equations for the unknown tensions.
defs: Equilibrium (particle)
A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero, so the net force in each perpendicular direction is zero.
Free body diagram
A sketch isolating the body of interest and showing all external forces acting on it, with their directions and angles.
eqs: Horizontal force balance at the knot
\(T_L\) = tension in left rope (N); \(T_R\) = tension in right rope (N)
Vertical force balance at the knot
\(T_L\) = tension in left rope (N); \(T_R\) = tension in right rope (N); 98 = weight/load acting downward (N)
tips: Keep consistent sign conventions (e.g. right and up positive) when writing ΣFx and ΣFy; a sign error flips the tension solution.
Angles in component resolution are measured from the horizontal (x-axis) here; using the wrong trig function (sin vs cos) for a component is a common error.
rq: Why must the x-equation be solved before substituting into the y-equation, and what does eliminating a variable achieve?
The two equations are coupled; the x-equation relates \(T_{L}\) to \(T_{R}\), so substituting it into the y-equation leaves a single equation in one unknown, which can then be solved directly.
What would change if the 45° rope were replaced by one at 60° to the horizontal?
The cos and sin coefficients change (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° = 0.866), so both component equations and the resulting numerical tensions must be recalculated.

units.name: 9.1 Equilibrium conditions and the moment condition
units.ov: This material covers the two conditions for static equilibrium: zero net force (no linear acceleration) and zero net moment (no angular acceleration). Moments are force times perpendicular distance about a chosen point, and both conditions must hold together. Solving problems means resolving forces into components, choosing a pivot, and applying a consistent sign convention.
must: Full equilibrium needs both \( \sum F = 0 \) and \( \sum M = 0 \); satisfying only one is not enough
Moment definition: \( M = F d_\perp \), where \( d_\perp \) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (units N·m)
Take all moments about the same point; the pivot is arbitrary, so choose one that eliminates unknown forces
Use a consistent sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive) for every moment in the sum
Resolve forces into components first: \( \sum F_x = 0 \) and \( \sum F_y = 0 \), as \( \sum F \) is a vector sum
In 2D this gives three independent equations (\( \sum F_x, \sum F_y, \sum M \)), so at most three unknowns can be found
Definition of static equilibrium: at rest, with no linear or angular acceleration
Only external forces enter the sums; draw a free-body diagram showing every external force and reaction
Check results by taking moments about a second point; the answer should still satisfy \( \sum M = 0 \)
conn: Free-body diagrams link to both conditions: the diagram supplies every force and its line of action for the force and moment sums
Choosing a clever pivot links the moment equation to the force equations: moments about a point where unknown reactions act eliminate them, leaving single-unknown equations
Resolving forces into components links trigonometry to the moment calculation, since the perpendicular distance or the perpendicular force component must be found for inclined forces
Beams, ladders and cantilevers combine weight, support reactions and friction, so \( \sum F \) and \( \sum M \) must be solved simultaneously
exq: A uniform beam of length 4 m and weight 200 N rests on supports at its ends and carries a 500 N load 1 m from the left end. Find the two support reactions using \( \sum F = 0 \) and \( \sum M = 0 \).
Explain why \( \sum F = 0 \) alone does not guarantee equilibrium, giving an example of a body with zero net force but non-zero net moment (e.g. a couple).
A uniform ladder of length 5 m and weight 300 N leans against a smooth wall at 60° to the horizontal. Find the wall reaction and the friction force needed at the ground to keep it in equilibrium.

A 2 m light rod is pivoted at one end and held horizontal by a cable at 30° to the rod, attached at the other end, with a 100 N load hung at its midpoint. Find the cable tension and the pivot reaction components.
Show that the choice of pivot does not affect the result: for a given loaded beam, solve by taking moments about two different points and compare.

notes.t: Second condition of static equilibrium
pts: For an object in static equilibrium, the net moment (torque) about any point must be zero, so it has no tendency to rotate.
This is the rotational condition; it complements the force condition (net force zero) for full static equilibrium.
Zero net moment means an object in equilibrium does not rotate.
defs: Static equilibrium
A state in which an object is at rest and has no linear acceleration or angular acceleration, so the net force and net moment acting on it are both zero.
Moment
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from that point.
eqs: Second condition of static equilibrium (sum of moments equals zero)
\( \sum M \) = sum of all moments acting on the object (N·m); \( M \) = individual moment (N·m)
tips: Moments must be taken about the same point for every force; the choice of pivot is arbitrary but must be consistent.
Use consistent sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive) and SI units of N·m for moments.
rq: Why must the net moment be zero for an object to remain in equilibrium rather than just the net force?
Zero net force stops straight-line acceleration, but a non-zero net moment would cause angular acceleration (rotation); both conditions are needed to prevent both translation and rotation.

notes.t: Equilibrium conditions
pts: For a body in equilibrium, the net force acting on it must be zero so it does not accelerate linearly.
For a body in equilibrium, the net moment acting on it must be zero so it does not accelerate rotationally.
Both conditions must hold together: zero net force and zero net moment together mean the body neither translates nor rotates.
defs: Equilibrium
A state in which a body has no translational or rotational acceleration, i.e. the net force and net moment acting on it are both zero.
eqs: \( \sum F \) = vector sum of all external forces acting on the body (N)
\( \sum M \) = sum of all moments about any chosen point acting on the body (N·m)
tips: Equilibrium requires both \( \sum F = 0 \) and \( \sum M = 0 \); satisfying only the force equation is not enough.
Moments must be taken about a consistent point, and forces should be resolved into components before summing.
rq: Why must both \( \sum F = 0 \) and \( \sum M = 0 \) be satisfied, rather than just one of them?
Zero net force alone prevents translation but not rotation (e.g. a couple), and zero net moment alone prevents rotation but not translation; both are needed for no translation and no rotation.
What would happen to a body if \( \sum F = 0 \) but \( \sum M \neq 0 \)?
It would not translate but would rotate with angular acceleration, so it is not in equilibrium.

units.name: 9.2 Equilibrium of non-concurrent co-planar force systems
units.ov: This module covers equilibrium of rigid bodies under non-concurrent co-planar forces, where lines of action do not meet at a point, so force balance and moment balance must both hold. The standard set is \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M=0\), and there are alternative equivalent sets using two or three moment equations. The skill is choosing moment centres and equation sets to isolate unknowns and avoid simultaneous equations.
must: Three independent equations for a planar rigid body: \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M=0\), so at most 3 unknowns can be solved by statics
Non-concurrent system: lines of action do not share a common point, so force balance alone is insufficient and moments must be enforced
Moments can be taken about ANY point; choose a point where unknown forces act so they drop out of the equation
Alternative set 1: \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum M_{@1}=0\), \(\sum M_{@2}=0\), valid only if the moment centres are suitably placed (the line joining 1 and 2 not perpendicular to x)
Alternative set 2: \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M_{@1}=0\), \(\sum M_{@2}=0\), valid only if the line joining 1 and 2 is not perpendicular to y
Alternative set 3: three moment equations about three points, which must NOT be collinear, otherwise the equations are dependent
Use the same moment centre for every force within one moment equation; never mix reference points
Adopt one sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive) and consistent units (N and N·m, or kN and kN·m)
Resolve forces into components first, and use moment = force × perpendicular distance, or the components method with their respective perpendicular distances
Check the answer by writing an extra equilibrium equation (e.g. a moment about a new point) that should also sum to zero
conn: Free-body diagrams feed directly into the equilibrium equations: a missing reaction or a wrongly drawn force direction ruins every equation
Choice of moment centre links to the alternative equation sets: well-placed centres give decoupled equations, but badly placed (collinear) ones give dependent equations
Distributed loads must be replaced by equivalent point loads at the centroid before moment equations are written
Support types (pin, roller, fixed) determine the number of unknown reactions, and hence whether the problem is statically determinate with 3 equations
exq: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a 10 kN point load 2 m from the left pin and a UDL of 4 kN/m over the right 3 m. Draw the FBD and find the reactions using moments about both supports, checking with \(\sum F_y=0\).
A uniform ladder of weight 200 N and length 5 m rests against a smooth wall at 60° to a rough floor. Find the wall and floor reactions and the minimum friction coefficient needed for equilibrium.

For a bracket loaded by three non-concurrent forces, show using set 3 (three moment equations) that the reactions can be found with no force resolution. State the condition on the chosen points and explain what happens if they are collinear.
A pin-jointed crane with a boom and a tie rod supports a 15 kN load. Select moment centres that let you find the tie tension directly, then find the pin reaction components.
Explain why the alternative set \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum M_{@1}=0\), \(\sum M_{@2}=0\) fails when points 1 and 2 are placed in particular positions, and give a numerical example.

notes.t: Equilibrium of non-concurrent co-planar force systems
pts: For a non-concurrent co-planar force system, equilibrium requires both the net force in each direction and the net moment to vanish.
Force components along the x and y axes must each sum to zero.
Moments about any chosen point must sum to zero; the choice of point is free and can be used to simplify the calculation.
defs: Non-concurrent force system
A set of forces whose lines of action do not all pass through a single common point, so both force balance and moment balance must be enforced.
eqs: \( F_x \) = force component along the x-axis (N)
\( F_y \) = force component along the y-axis (N)
\( M \) = moment of a force about the chosen point (N·m)
tips: Moments must be taken about the same point for all forces; mixing reference points gives wrong answers.
Keep consistent sign convention (e.g. counter-clockwise positive) and consistent SI units (N and N·m) throughout.
rq: Why must three independent equations be used for a non-concurrent co-planar system, rather than just the two force equations?
Because forces that do not share a common point can produce a net turning effect (moment) even when the net force is zero; the moment equation is an independent condition that prevents rotation.
Why can the moment equation be written about any point?
If the whole system is in equilibrium, the total moment is zero about every point, so choosing a point where unknown forces act (giving zero moment) simplifies the algebra.

notes.t: Equilibrium of non-concurrent force systems
pts: For non-concurrent forces, the standard three equations can be replaced by alternative moment-based sets of equilibrium equations.
Two alternative sets use two moment equations plus one force-resolution equation, provided the moment centres are chosen appropriately.
A third set uses three moment equations about three different points; the three points must not lie on a straight line.
eqs: Alternative equilibrium set 1 (two moments and one force resolution)
\(F_x\) = force component in x-direction (N); \(M_{@1}, M_{@2}\) = moments about points 1 and 2 (N·m)
Alternative equilibrium set 2 (two moments and one force resolution)
\(F_y\) = force component in y-direction (N); \(M_{@1}, M_{@2}\) = moments about points 1 and 2 (N·m)
\(M_{@1}, M_{@2}, M_{@3}\) = moments about three non-collinear points (N·m)
tips: Do not choose three moment centres that lie on one straight line; the equations become dependent and the solution is invalid.
Keep units consistent: force in N and moments in N·m (or kN and kN·m) when substituting into the equilibrium equations.
rq: Why must the three points in the all-moment equilibrium set not lie on a straight line?

If the points are collinear, the three moment equations are not independent: the moment equations cannot constrain the force component perpendicular to that line, so equilibrium is not fully enforced.
What if you chose the two moment centres in set 1 to be on a line parallel to the x-axis?

Choosing points that are aligned so the x-direction force resolution is redundant (or the system is degenerate) means the set would not uniquely determine the forces; the points should be placed to give independent equations.

units.name: 9.3 Example 1: hinged beam with a wire
units.ov: This material covers 2D static equilibrium of a weightless rigid beam pinned at A, supported by a vertical wire at C and carrying point loads. A free-body diagram turns the problem into three unknowns (\(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\), T) and three equilibrium equations. Taking moments about the hinge first gives T directly, and force balances then give the hinge reactions.
must: Three 2D equilibrium equations: \( \sum F_x=0 \), \( \sum F_y=0 \), \( \sum M=0 \) about any point.
Draw a correct free-body diagram: remove the supports, show all loads and reactions, and define axes and a sign convention.
A hinge (pin) gives two reaction components \(R_x, R_y\) and no moment.
A wire carries tension only, acting along the wire. Here it is vertical and pulls up at C.
Take moments about A to eliminate \(R_x\) and \(R_y\): \( T\times0.35-60\times0.2-20\times0.6=0 \).
Solve: \( T=24/0.35\approx 68.6\) N.
Substitute back into the vertical balance \( R_y+T-60-20=0 \) to get \( R_y\approx 11.4\) N.
\( \sum F_x=0 \) gives \( R_x=0 \) because there are no horizontal loads.
Convert mm to m before forming moments (0.2, 0.35 and 0.6 m from A). Otherwise moments are wrong by a factor of 1000.
Moment signs: the wire moment is opposite in sense to the load moments. Check the answer with a second moment equation about another point.
conn: Choice of moment point and solution order: moments about A isolate T, and T then feeds the force equations for \(R_y\).
Free-body diagram and equation count: three unknowns need three independent equations, which links to statical determinacy.
Sign convention and units: a wrong moment sign or an mm/m slip gives a wrong T, and every later reaction inherits the error.
Support type determines the unknowns: a hinge gives two forces, a wire gives one tension along its line, and this links to later truss and frame problems.
exq: A weightless rigid beam is hinged at A and held by a vertical wire at C, 350 mm from A. Loads of 60 N and 20 N act at 200 mm and 600 mm from A. Draw the free-body diagram and find the wire tension.
For the same beam, find the magnitude and direction of the hinge reaction at A, and verify your answer with moments about C.
If the wire can carry at most 50 N, find the maximum value of the 20 N load, or the maximum distance it can be placed from A, before the wire fails.
Explain why \(R_x=0\) here. How would the solution change if the wire were inclined at 30° to the vertical?
Explain why moments are taken about the hinge first. Show that moments about C give the same \(R_y\) without using the force balance.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a Rigid Beam with a Hinge and a Wire (Example 1)
pts: Treat the weightless rigid beam as a free body; the hinge at A gives unknown horizontal and vertical reactions, and the wire gives an unknown tension at C.
Take moments about the hinge A to eliminate the unknown hinge reactions and find the wire tension directly.
Resolve forces vertically and horizontally to find the components of the hinge reaction once the wire force is known.
defs: Hinge (pin support)
A support that prevents translation in both directions but allows rotation, so it can provide a reaction force with horizontal and vertical components but no moment.
eqs: Moment equilibrium about the hinge A (gives wire tension)
Vertical force equilibrium (gives vertical hinge reaction)
tips: Use consistent distances: 200 mm, 350 mm (200+150) and 600 mm (200+150+250) must be converted to metres before forming moments in N·m.
The wire is vertical, so its tension acts vertically upward at C; do not forget to include its direction in the force balance.
rq: Why is it convenient to take moments about the hinge A rather than about C or B?
The hinge reaction passes through A, so its moment about A is zero, leaving only the wire tension and the 60 N and 20 N loads, which allows the wire force to be found in one equation.
What would change if the beam had weight?
The weight would act at its centre of gravity and add a downward load and moment, so it must be included in both force and moment equilibrium.

notes.t: Free-body diagrams and equilibrium of a hinged beam with a wire
pts: Free-body diagram: replace the pinned/hinge support with its x and y reaction components.
Replace the wire with a tension force acting along the wire, then label all forces and define a coordinate system.
Unknowns \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\) and T give three unknowns, so three independent equilibrium equations are needed.
Two-dimensional equilibrium uses the sum of forces in x, the sum of forces in y and the sum of moments about a point.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch of a body isolated from its supports, showing all applied loads and the reaction forces that the supports exert on it, with a chosen coordinate system.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = force components in the x direction (N)
\(F_{y}\) = force components in the y direction (N)
M = moments of forces about the chosen point (N·mm)
tips: Keep all lengths consistent in mm when taking moments, and convert to metres if the required unit is SI.
Check the direction of the wire tension: it pulls the beam upward toward the ceiling, so it is shown as an upward force T.
rq: Why is the hinge replaced by two force components rather than one force?
A pin or hinge can resist forces in any direction in the plane, so its unknown reaction has two components, \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\), and it provides no moment.
Why does the wire become a tension force that acts along the wire?
A wire can only pull, not push, so its effect on the beam is a single tension T directed along the wire, away from the beam.

notes.t: Equations of static equilibrium – worked example
pts: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of forces in each direction and the sum of moments about any point must all be zero.
Taking moments about a support (point A) eliminates the unknown reactions at that point, so the unknown tension T can be found directly.
Once one unknown is found, substitute it into another equilibrium equation to find the remaining unknown reaction.
Horizontal reaction \(R_{x}\) is zero because there are no horizontal applied loads.
defs: Static equilibrium
A condition in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are zero, so the body does not accelerate or rotate.
eqs: \(R_y\) = vertical reaction at A (N); \(T\) = tension at C (N)
\(T\) = tension (N); distances in m from A (0.2 m to B-load, 0.35 m to C, 0.6 m to D)
tips: Check distances are converted to metres consistently (mm to m) before multiplying by forces in N, otherwise moments are wrong by a factor of 1000.
Use the correct sign convention for moments: a force on the opposite side of the pivot must give the opposite sign; ensure the T term and the load terms have opposite signs.
rq: Why does taking moments about point A let us find T without knowing \(R_{y}\)?
Because \(R_{y}\) acts at A, its moment arm about A is zero, so it drops out of the moment equation, leaving only T and the applied loads.
Why is \(R_{x}\) = 0 in this example?
There are no applied horizontal forces, so the only horizontal force sum is zero and \(R_{x}\) must balance nothing.

units.name: 9.4 Example 2: fixed support reactions on a loaded frame
units.ov: This material covers finding the reactions at a fixed (cantilever-type) support on a loaded frame by treating the whole frame as a rigid body in static equilibrium. A free-body diagram is drawn, then \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\) and \(\sum M_A=0\) give the three unknowns \(F_{Ax}\), \(F_{Ay}\) and \(M_A\). In Example 2 the loads of 400 N at the midpoint of BC and 200 N at C give \(F_{Ax}=0\), \(F_{Ay}=600\) N and \(M_A=800\) N m.
must: A fixed support supplies three reactions: horizontal force \(F_{Ax}\), vertical force \(F_{Ay}\) and a moment \(M_A\) (it prevents translation in two directions and rotation).
Planar equilibrium needs three independent equations: \(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M_A=0\).
Always start with a clear free-body diagram showing all applied loads and all reactions, including the moment reaction.
Horizontal equilibrium: no horizontal applied loads, so \(F_{Ax}=0\).
Vertical equilibrium: \(F_{Ay}-400-200=0\Rightarrow F_{Ay}=600\) N, which equals the total downward load.
Take moments about A so that \(F_{Ax}\) and \(F_{Ay}\) act through A and drop out of the moment equation.
Moment equilibrium: \(0=-(400\times1)-(200\times2)+M_A\Rightarrow M_A=800\) N m, anticlockwise to oppose the clockwise load moments.
Moment = force × perpendicular distance (the moment arm), not member length. Here the arms are 1 m (midpoint of BC) and 2 m (C), measured horizontally for vertical loads.
Use a consistent sign convention (e.g. clockwise negative) and consistent units (N, m), and check that the reaction moment's sense opposes the applied moments.
Read the geometry carefully: the 3 m and 2 m vertical dimensions are different and do not affect the moments of vertical loads, since only horizontal distances matter.
conn: Free-body diagram → equilibrium equations: the reaction components and directions you draw fix the signs in all three equations.
Choice of moment point → simplicity: taking moments about A eliminates two unknowns, so \(M_A\) can be found directly without the force equations.
Distributed or midpoint loads → point loads: the 400 N load acts at the midpoint of BC, so its arm is 1 m, which feeds directly into the moment sum.
Geometry → moment arms: vertical loads use horizontal distances, so vertical dimensions such as 3 m and 2 m matter only for horizontal loads or when checking the geometry.
exq: Draw the free-body diagram for the frame with 400 N at the midpoint of BC and 200 N at C (BC = 2 m). State the reaction components at the fixed support A and the number of independent equilibrium equations available.
Calculate \(F_{Ax}\), \(F_{Ay}\) and \(M_A\) for the frame in Example 2, and state the direction (sense) of \(M_A\).
If the 200 N load at C is moved to the midpoint of BC, recalculate \(M_A\) and \(F_{Ay}\). Explain which change and which stays the same.
A horizontal 100 N force is added at C, with C 3 m above A. Find the new \(F_{Ax}\) and \(M_A\), showing the sign convention you use.
Explain why taking moments about A removes \(F_{Ax}\) and \(F_{Ay}\), and verify the answer by taking moments about C.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a loaded frame: reactions at a fixed support
pts: A fixed support at A provides three reaction components: horizontal force, vertical force and moment, which must balance the applied loads.
Dimensions from the figure: BC spans 2 m horizontally (1 m + 1 m) and the vertical member from A to B is 3 m high, with B 2 m above the level of D's connection line.
The 400 N load acts vertically down at the midpoint of member BC, and the 200 N load acts vertically down at C.
Use the three equilibrium equations for the whole frame: sum of horizontal forces, sum of vertical forces and sum of moments about A all equal zero.
defs: Fixed support
A support that prevents translation in two directions and rotation, so it can supply a horizontal force, a vertical force and a moment reaction.
eqs: Equilibrium of forces in x and y, and moments about A
\(F_x\) = horizontal force (N); \(F_y\) = vertical force (N); \(M_A\) = moment about support A (N·m)
tips: Keep track of the 3 m and 2 m dimensions carefully: the 2 m is the height of BC-level measurement relative to D, not the full column height from A.
Check consistent units (N and m) and sign convention for moments before summing.
rq: Why must the moment equilibrium be taken about point A rather than an arbitrary point?

Taking moments about A eliminates the unknown reaction forces at the fixed support, so the moment equation contains only the applied loads and the unknown moment reaction (or reactions you choose to solve for).
How many unknown reactions does the fixed support at A introduce, and how many equations are available for the whole frame?
Three unknowns (horizontal, vertical and moment reactions) and three independent equilibrium equations, so the frame is statically determinate for reactions.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a rigid body: solving support reactions (Example 2)
pts: For a planar body in equilibrium, the sum of horizontal forces, vertical forces and moments about any point must each equal zero.
Moments are taken about support A, so the unknown reactions \(F_{\text{Ax}}\) and \(F_{\text{Ay}}\) produce no moment about A and drop out of the moment equation.
Clockwise moments are taken as negative and the reaction moment \(M_{A}\) is added to balance them, giving an anticlockwise reaction of 800 Nm.
The vertical reaction equals the sum of the downward applied loads, here 400 N + 200 N = 600 N.
defs: Free-body diagram
A sketch of a body isolated from its supports, showing all applied loads and reaction forces and moments acting on it, used to apply equilibrium equations.
Equilibrium
The condition in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are both zero, so the body does not accelerate or rotate.
eqs: \(F_{\text{Ay}}\) = vertical reaction at A (N); 400 N and 200 N = applied downward loads (N)
\(M_{A}\) = reaction moment at A (N m); distances 1 m and 2 m = moment arms (m)
tips: Keep a consistent sign convention for moments: a moment that is clockwise and one that is anticlockwise must have opposite signs in the sum.
Use the perpendicular distance (moment arm) in metres from the point of rotation, not the length of the member, when calculating moments in N m.
rq: Why does taking moments about point A let you find \(M_{A}\) without knowing \(F_{\text{Ax}}\) or \(F_{\text{Ay}}\)?
Both \(F_{\text{Ax}}\) and \(F_{\text{Ay}}\) act through point A, so their moment arms about A are zero and they contribute nothing to the moment sum.
What would happen to \(M_{A}\) if the 200 N load were moved from 2 m to 3 m from A?
The moment of the 200 N load would increase to 600 N m, so \(M_{A}\) would become 1000 N m (anticlockwise), since \(M_{A}\) = 400×1 + 200×3.

units.name: 9.5 Example 3: beam with pin support and cable
units.ov: This example analyses a rigid beam held by a pin support at the wall and an inclined cable, carrying its own weight (200 N) and a man (600 N). Static equilibrium (\(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M=0\)) is applied by taking moments about the pin to find the cable tension first, then using force balance to find the pin reaction components.
must: Static equilibrium needs \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\) and \(\sum M=0\) about any point.
Take moments about the pin first: the unknown reaction has zero moment arm and drops out, so T can be found directly.
Moment equation: \(T\sin53^\circ(8)-200(4)-600(2)=0\), so \(T=2000/(8\sin53^\circ)\approx313\) N.

Resolve the cable tension into \(T\cos53^\circ\) (horizontal) and \(T\sin53^\circ\) (vertical). Only the vertical component has a moment about the pin, because the horizontal component's line of action passes through it.
A pin support gives horizontal and vertical reactions \(R_x\), \(R_y\) but no moment, since it allows free rotation.
Force balance gives \(R_x=T\cos53^\circ\) and \(R_y=800-T\sin53^\circ\). Solve for T first, then substitute.
The weights act at the right points: beam weight 200 N at its centre (4 m), man 600 N at 2 m. Using 0 m or 8 m is a common error.
Sign convention must be consistent: moments from the cable oppose those from the weights. Use N and m throughout so moments are in N·m.
Check the answer: the resultant reaction should balance the cable force and the weights. Confirm \(R_y\) is physically sensible, e.g. by taking moments about a second point.
conn: Moment-first strategy links to free-body diagrams: choosing the moment point at the unknown reaction reduces simultaneous equations to a sequential solution.
Resolving forces by trigonometry feeds into both the moment equation (only the vertical component) and the force equations (both components).
The pin reaction found here (\(R_x\), \(R_y\), and its resultant) can feed into later pin shear or bearing stress calculations.
Changing the man's position turns this into a variable-load problem: T and the reactions vary linearly with position, and the cable's maximum tension limits how far he can walk.
exq: Using the given geometry (8 m beam, cable at 53°, 200 N beam, 600 N man at 2 m), calculate the cable tension by taking moments about the pin, showing why the wall reaction does not appear.
Find the horizontal and vertical pin reactions and the magnitude and direction of the resultant reaction.
The man walks to a distance x from the wall. Derive T as a function of x, and find x if the cable can carry at most 500 N.
Explain why a pin gives no reaction moment, and state what changes in the analysis if the pin were replaced by a fixed (built-in) support.
A student writes the moment equation using T instead of \(T\sin53^\circ\) with an 8 m arm. Identify the error, explain why it is wrong, and give the correct result.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a beam with a pin support and cable (Example 3)
pts: For a body in equilibrium, the net force and net moment about any point must both be zero.
Taking moments about the pin removes the unknown wall reaction, so the cable tension can be found directly.
The cable's tension has both horizontal and vertical components; only the vertical component provides a moment about the pin.
The wall force has unknown horizontal and vertical components, which are found from force balance once the tension is known.
The beam's weight acts at its centre (4 m from the wall), and the man's weight acts at 2 m from the wall.
defs: Pin connection
A support that resists translation in both directions (horizontal and vertical reaction forces) but allows free rotation, so it exerts no moment.
eqs: Moment balance about the pin (solves cable tension)
\(T\) = cable tension (N); \(W_{beam}=200\) N acting at 4 m; \(W_{man}=600\) N acting at 2 m
\sum F_x=0:\; R_x = T\cos(53^\circ),\quad \sum F_y=0:\; R_y = 800 - T\sin(53^\circ)
tips: Use the cable's angle correctly: the moment arm of the tension is the full 8 m only for the vertical component \(T\sin(53^\circ)\), not \(T\) itself.
Place the beam weight at its centre (4 m) and the man at 2 m; using 8 m or 0 m for either load is a common error.
rq: Why is moment balance taken about the pin rather than the cable end?
Because the pin's reaction forces have zero moment arm about the pin, so the unknown wall force drops out and the equation contains only the known loads and the tension T.
What if the man moved closer to the wall? How would the cable tension change?
Moving the man closer reduces his moment arm about the pin, so less tension is required; the tension decreases.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a rigid body: solving with moment equation first
pts: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of forces in x and y and the sum of moments about any point must all be zero.
Taking moments about a point where unknown forces act eliminates those forces from the moment equation, so the remaining unknown can be found directly.
Resolve the inclined tension T into components T cos 53° (horizontal) and T sin 53° (vertical) before writing the equilibrium equations.
Moments of the 600 N and 200 N loads about A are taken from their distances 2 m and 4 m, while the tension's vertical component acts at 8 m.
defs: Static equilibrium
A condition in which the net force and net moment acting on a body are both zero, so the body does not accelerate or rotate.
eqs: \(R_{x}\) = horizontal reaction at A (N); T = tension in cable (N)
\(R_{y}\) = vertical reaction at A (N); T = tension (N)
T = tension (N); distances in m; loads in N
tips: Make sure the angle is correct when resolving T: horizontal uses cos 53° and vertical uses sin 53°, and mixing them gives wrong answers.
Use consistent units (N for forces, m for distances) so that moment products are in N·m.
rq: Why is taking moments about A the best first step in this example?
Because \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) act at A and have zero moment arm about A, so the moment equation contains only T and the known loads, giving T = 313 N directly.
If the cable were attached at a different point, how would the moment equation change?
The moment arm of T sin 53° about A would change to the new horizontal distance from A, and the load distances would stay the same.

units.name: 9.6 Applications: tidal walkway and ladder
units.ov: This material applies 2D static equilibrium (\(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M=0\)) to a tidal walkway on rollers held by a horizontal wire, and to a uniform ladder supported at two points and held by a rope. In both, you draw a free-body diagram, choose a moment point that eliminates unknowns, then resolve forces to find the remaining reactions and tension. Success depends on correct geometry, moment arms, and consistent units (mass in kg gives weight \(W=mg\)).
must: Static equilibrium: \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M_P=0\) about any point P
Always convert mass to weight: \(W=300g\) N with \(g=9.81\) m/s² (about 2943 N), never 300 N
Roller support gives only a reaction perpendicular to the surface, so the walkway rollers give vertical reactions only
Walkway: the horizontal tension T has moment arm equal to the vertical height difference (4 m), not the sloped length
Walkway method: moments about A eliminate \(R_A\) and give T, then \(\sum F_y=0\) gives the other reaction
Uniform weight acts at the centre G (midpoint), so its horizontal moment arm is \(4\cos\theta\) for an 8 m ladder
Angle from geometry: \(\sin\theta=4/8\Rightarrow\theta=30^\circ\)
Moment arms are perpendicular distances: lengths along the ladder need \(\cos\theta\) (horizontal) or \(\sin\theta\) (vertical)
Ladder: moments about B give \(R_A\) from \(300g\cdot4\cos\theta=R_A\cdot8\cos\theta\), so \(R_A=150g\approx1472\) N
Then \(\sum F_y=0\) gives \(R_B\) and \(\sum F_x=0\) gives \(T=R_B\sin\theta\); choose the moment point to eliminate the most unknowns
conn: Roller supports (vertical reaction only) reduce unknowns, so the choice of moment point and the force resolutions combine to give a fully solvable system
Geometry (\(\sin\theta=4/8\)) feeds directly into moment arms and force components, so an angle error propagates through every equation
Moments give one reaction, vertical balance gives another, and horizontal balance gives the tension or friction, so the solution is a sequential chain where early errors carry through
Weight from mass (\(W=mg\)) links dynamics-style units to statics, so unit slips affect all numerical answers
exq: A 300 kg uniform walkway rests on rollers at A and B with a 4 m level difference and is held by a horizontal wire. Draw the free-body diagram, then take moments about A to find the wire tension T and find the vertical reactions at A and B.
A uniform 8 m ladder of mass 300 kg has its upper end 4 m above the lower end. Find the ladder angle and then the reaction at A using moments about B.
For the same ladder, use \(\sum F_y=0\) and \(\sum F_x=0\) to find \(R_B\) and the rope tension T, using g = 9.81 m/s².
Explain why the moment arm of the horizontal tension in the walkway problem is 4 m and not the walkway length, and why taking moments about A is the efficient choice.
Show how the answers change if the ladder is not uniform and G is at 3 m from the lower end along the ladder. Which equations change?

notes.t: Equilibrium of a tidal walkway: rollers, tension and reaction
pts: The walkway is free to move horizontally at its supports, so the rollers at A and B give vertical reactions only, which simplifies the equilibrium equations.
The walkway's self-weight acts vertically at its centre of mass G, so its moment about either support must be considered.
The wire tension T is horizontal, so its moment arm about A is the vertical rise between A and B, which is the 4 m level difference.
Take moments about A to eliminate the reaction at A and solve for T; then resolve vertically to find the reaction at A.
defs: Roller support
A support that exerts only a reaction perpendicular to the surface it rests on, allowing free movement parallel to that surface.
Centre of gravity G
The point through which the weight of a body acts; here the walkway's weight acts at its midpoint G.
eqs: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg) = 300; g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
tips: Ensure the moment arm of the horizontal tension T is the vertical height difference (4 m), not the sloped length of the walkway.
Keep units consistent: mass is 300 kg, so weight is \(W = 300g\) newtons; do not use 300 N directly.
rq: Why does a roller support at A produce only a vertical reaction, and why does that matter when taking moments?

A roller can move freely horizontally, so it cannot resist horizontal force; its reaction is perpendicular to the surface only. Taking moments about A then removes the unknown reaction at A, leaving T and W as the only unknowns in the moment equation.
What would happen to the tension T if the level difference between A and B increased?
T would change because its moment arm about A is the vertical height difference; for the same weight, a larger height difference gives a larger moment arm and therefore a different required tension.

notes.t: Equilibrium of a ladder: moments and force balance
pts: Take moments about a point where unknown reactions act to eliminate them and solve for the remaining reaction directly.
Resolve forces into x and y components; vertical balance gives one reaction, horizontal balance gives the tension or friction force.
The weight acts at the centre of gravity, so for a uniform ladder its moment arm is half the length measured along the ladder.
The angle is found from the geometry: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, here 4 m over 8 m gives θ = 30°.
defs: Static equilibrium
A body is in static equilibrium when the sum of all forces and the sum of all moments about any point are zero.
eqs: Moment equilibrium about B to find reaction at A
\(R_A\) = reaction at A (N); \(\theta\) = ladder angle (°); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
Vertical force equilibrium to find reaction at B
\(R_B\) = reaction at B (N); \(R_A\) = reaction at A (N); \(\theta\) = ladder angle (°)
Horizontal force equilibrium to find tension T
\(T\) = tension in the rope (N); \(R_B\) = reaction at B (N); \(\theta\) = ladder angle (°)
tips: Keep units consistent: g must be included (e.g. 300g N) and the final numeric values use g = 9.81 m/s².
Use the correct moment arms: horizontal distances from the pivot, which involve cos θ for lengths measured along the ladder.
rq: Why is moment taken about B rather than about the centre G?
Taking moments about B removes the unknown reaction \(R_{B}\) (its line of action passes through B), so \(R_{A}\) can be found from one equation.
What would happen to T if the ladder angle were made smaller?

Since T = \(R_{B}\) sin θ and \(R_{B}\) grows as the angle shrinks, the effect depends on the balance; checking via the equations shows the horizontal rope force must still balance the horizontal component of \(R_{B}\).
Why does the 300g weight contribute a moment of 300g × 4 cos θ?
The weight acts at the midpoint of the 8 m ladder, a horizontal lever arm of 4 cos θ from B.

units.name: 10.1 Friction basics: where it matters and what causes it
units.ov: This module introduces friction as a tangential force that opposes relative or attempted motion between real, rough surfaces, caused by interlocking asperities and dependent on both surface roughness and normal force. It distinguishes situations where friction should be minimised (gears, machines, forming processes) from those where it must be maximised (brakes, clutches, wedges, belt drives). These ideas lead into the limiting-friction condition \(F \le \mu_s N\), which governs whether slipping occurs.
must: Definition: friction is a tangential force opposing relative (or attempted) motion between contacting surfaces, arising from interlocking of surface irregularities
Direction: friction opposes the tendency of relative motion (impending or actual), not simply the direction of the applied force
Limiting condition: friction can only reach \(F_{max}=\mu_s N\); slipping occurs when the required friction exceeds this, so both \(\mu_s\) and \(N\) matter
Magnitude depends on both surface roughness (via the coefficient) and the normal force pressing surfaces together; roughness alone does not set it
Real surfaces are never ideal; do not assume frictionless contact unless the problem states it
Friction to minimise: gears, machines, forming processes; it causes energy loss, wear, higher required force and reduced tool life
Friction to maximise: brakes and clutches (slow or transmit motion), wedges (self-holding when friction is large enough), belt drives (power transmitted by belt-pulley friction)
Justify friction as helpful or harmful by context; avoid saying simply that it is 'bad' and state the effect on load, wear or tool life
A heavier body on the same surface gives greater friction because of the larger normal force
conn: Cause (asperity interlocking) links to magnitude: roughness enters through \(\mu\), weight enters through \(N\), combining in \(F\le\mu_s N\)
Direction of friction links to equilibrium problems: determine the tendency of motion first, then draw friction opposing it before applying \(\sum F=0\)
Wedges and belt drives combine the maximise-friction idea with the limiting condition: they work only if \(\mu_s N\) is enough to resist the load or transmit the torque
Minimise-versus-maximise contexts link to design trade-offs, such as lubricating gears and forming tools while keeping high friction at brake pads
exq: Explain, with reference to surface asperities, what causes friction, and state why a heavier block on the same surface is harder to move.

Give three engineering examples where friction should be minimised and three where it should be maximised, justifying each, including the effect of friction in forming processes on load and tool life.

A block of weight W rests on a rough surface with coefficient \(\mu_s\) and a horizontal force P is applied. Draw the free-body diagram, give the direction of friction, and find the P at which slipping begins.
A wedge holds a load in place. Explain how friction keeps it from slipping out and what condition involving \(\mu_s N\) must be satisfied.
Explain why a belt drive depends on friction and what happens when the required friction force exceeds \(\mu_s N\).

notes.t: Friction forces – basic characteristics
pts: Friction arises whenever two real (non-ideal) surfaces interact, so it is present in practically all engineering contacts.
Friction force always acts in the direction that opposes the tendency of motion between the surfaces.
tips: Friction direction is set by the tendency (impending or actual) of relative motion, not by the applied force direction alone.
Do not assume ideal frictionless surfaces in problems unless stated; real surfaces always produce friction.
rq: Why does friction act in the direction opposing the tendency of motion rather than the actual motion?
Friction is a reaction force: it resists the relative motion that would occur (or is occurring), so it is set up opposite to the impending or actual sliding direction.
If a block is at rest on an inclined surface, which way does friction act and why?
Up the slope, because gravity's component along the slope tends to make the block slide down, so friction opposes that tendency.

notes.t: Friction force: when to minimise it
pts: In some engineering situations friction is undesirable and its effect should be reduced, as it causes energy loss and wear.
Typical examples where friction must be minimised include gears, machines and forming processes.
tips: Do not assume friction is always harmful; state the context (e.g. needed for braking or grip) when justifying why it is minimised.
Friction in forming processes increases the required force, so mention the effect on load and tool life rather than just saying 'it is bad'.
rq: Why is friction desirable in some situations but undesirable in gears and machines?
In gears and machines friction causes energy losses (heat) and wear, reducing efficiency, so it is minimised; elsewhere (e.g. braking, grip) friction is needed to transmit force.
Why must friction be minimised in metal forming processes such as punch and die operations?
Friction opposes material flow, increasing the forming force and power required, causing tool wear and poorer surface finish of the workpiece.

notes.t: Friction force – when friction is wanted (maximised)
pts: In some engineering situations friction is beneficial and its effect should be maximised rather than minimised.
Brakes and clutches rely on large friction forces to slow or transmit motion between parts.
Wedges use friction to hold an object in place; the wedge will stay put when friction is large enough to resist the applied load.
Belt drives transmit power between pulleys through friction between the belt and the pulley surfaces.
tips: Do not assume friction is always a loss: in brakes, clutches, wedges and belt drives it is the useful force, so the design goal is the opposite of bearings or sliding parts.
When friction is maximised, check the limiting condition: friction force can only be as large as μ_s N, so the coefficient and normal force both determine whether slipping occurs.
rq: Why would an engineer deliberately design a wedge or belt drive to have high friction, while a bearing is designed to have low friction?
Wedges and belt drives need friction to hold position or transmit torque without slipping, whereas bearings need low friction to reduce energy loss, heat and wear while allowing motion.
What would happen to a brake if the friction coefficient between the pads and disc dropped sharply, for example when wet or overheated?
The friction force available to slow the disc would fall, so the braking torque and deceleration would reduce, increasing stopping distance.

notes.t: What causes friction
pts: Friction arises because two surfaces resist relative motion (or attempted motion) between them.
All real surfaces are irregular; contacting asperities interlock, and this interlocking produces the resisting force.
Rougher surfaces interlock more, so friction increases with roughness.
A heavier body pressing on the same surface experiences greater friction, so it is harder to move.
defs: Friction
A tangential force that opposes the relative (or attempted) motion between two contacting surfaces, arising from the interlocking of surface irregularities.
tips: Friction opposes the direction of motion or attempted motion, not necessarily the direction of the applied load.
Roughness alone does not determine friction magnitude; the normal force pressing the surfaces together also matters.
rq: Why would polishing two contacting surfaces reduce friction even though the crate's weight is unchanged?
Polishing smooths the asperities so they interlock less, reducing the resisting force between the surfaces.
Why does a heavier crate experience more friction on the same floor?
A heavier crate presses the surfaces together more strongly, causing larger interlocking of irregularities and hence greater friction.

units.name: 10.2 Dry friction: free-body diagram and static friction
units.ov: This module introduces dry (Coulomb) friction by first isolating a block in a free-body diagram (applied load P, weight mg, normal reaction N, friction \(F_{f}\)) and then applying equilibrium in x and y. Static friction is a self-adjusting reaction that equals the applied force until it reaches the limit \(\mu_s N\), at which point slipping is impending. The key skill is to find N from vertical equilibrium, then compare the friction required for equilibrium with the maximum available.
must: Draw a complete FBD: isolate the body and show P, mg, N (perpendicular to the surface) and \(F_f\) (parallel to the surface, opposing impending motion).
Apply \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) with consistent axes; resolve any inclined forces into components.
Find N from vertical equilibrium, e.g. \(N-mg=0\) for a horizontal surface with only horizontal P; N equals mg only when there are no other vertical forces.
Static friction is a reaction: for a body at rest, \(F_f\) is found from equilibrium (e.g. \(F_f=P\)), not from \(\mu_s N\).
General condition for no slip: \(F_f\le \mu_s N\); the body stays at rest while the friction required for equilibrium is within this limit.
At impending slip (limiting friction): \(F_f=P=\mu_s N\). Use this equality only at this point.
\(\mu_s\) is dimensionless and gives maximum static friction as a fraction of N; use N (not mg) in \(\mu_s N\).
Friction opposes the tendency of motion, so its direction is set by the direction P would cause motion.
Do not confuse N (normal) with \(F_f\) (tangential); check units: forces in N, m in kg, g in m/s\(^2\).
conn: FBD and equilibrium give N, which feeds directly into the friction limit \(\mu_s N\); errors in the FBD propagate into the slip criterion.
Inclined or angled applied forces change N (a vertical component of P adds to or reduces the normal reaction), thereby changing the maximum friction available.
Comparing the required friction (from equilibrium) with \(\mu_s N\) decides whether the body is in equilibrium, impending slip or sliding; this links to finding the minimum P to cause motion.
Tipping versus slipping: moment equilibrium combined with the friction limit determines which failure occurs first.
exq: A 20 kg block rests on a horizontal surface with \(\mu_s=0.4\). A horizontal force P is slowly increased. Draw the FBD, find N, and calculate the P at which slipping begins (take g = 9.81 m/s\(^2\)).
For the same 20 kg block, P = 60 N is applied horizontally. Determine the friction force acting and state whether the block is in equilibrium. Explain why \(F_f\neq\mu_s N\) here.
A 50 kg crate with \(\mu_s=0.3\) is pulled by a rope at 30° above the horizontal. Find the tension at impending slip, noting how N differs from mg.
A block is pushed down at an angle onto a horizontal surface. Show how N and the maximum friction change compared with a purely horizontal push, and find the P required to start sliding.

Explain, with an FBD, the difference between static friction in equilibrium, limiting friction, and the inequality \(F_f\le\mu_s N\), and state which equation applies to a block at rest under P below the limit.

notes.t: Dry Friction – free-body diagram of a block on a horizontal surface
pts: A free-body diagram isolates the block and shows all external forces: applied load P, friction \(F_{f}\) opposing motion, weight mg and normal reaction N.
The normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the contact surface and balances the weight in the vertical (y) direction.
Friction \(F_{f}\) acts parallel to the contact surface, opposing the tendency or direction of motion caused by P.
Equilibrium is applied in the x and y directions with the axes shown: sum of forces in x and sum of forces in y each set to zero.
defs: Dry friction
Resistive force that acts tangentially between two dry contacting surfaces, opposing relative motion or its tendency.
Free-body diagram
Sketch of a body isolated from its surroundings showing every external force and moment acting on it.
eqs: Vertical equilibrium of the block (normal reaction)
N = normal reaction (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
tips: Do not confuse the normal reaction N with the friction force \(F_{f}\); N is perpendicular to the surface while \(F_{f}\) is parallel to it.
Ensure the chosen x–y axes are used consistently when resolving P, mg and friction into components.
rq: Why does the normal force equal mg here, and what would change if P were pulled upward?
On a horizontal surface with no vertical applied load, vertical equilibrium gives N = mg. An upward component of P would reduce N to mg − \(P_{y}\), reducing the available friction.
Why is the friction force drawn opposing the direction of P?
Friction opposes the relative motion or tendency to move, so it acts in the direction opposite to the applied horizontal load.

notes.t: Static frictional forces
pts: When a body is at rest (no sliding), static friction equals the applied force and adjusts to balance it, up to a maximum.
Static friction has an upper limit; when the applied force reaches this limit the body is just about to slide.
The maximum static friction force is proportional to the normal reaction, with the constant of proportionality being the coefficient of static friction.
Static friction acts opposite to the direction of the impending motion and its magnitude is not fixed by the normal force alone.
defs: Coefficient of static friction (μ_s)
A dimensionless ratio giving the maximum static friction force between two surfaces as a fraction of the normal reaction force, just before sliding begins.
Normal reaction (N)
The contact force perpendicular to the surface, acting on the body from the surface, balancing the component of weight pressing into it.
eqs: Static friction (no sliding): friction equals applied force, below its limit
\(F_{f}\) = static friction force (N); P = applied horizontal force (N); μ_s = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
Limiting static friction (just about to slide)
\(F_{f}\) = limiting static friction force (N); P = applied force at impending slip (N); μ_s = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
\(F_{f}\) = static friction force (N); μ_s = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
tips: Do not use \(F_{f}\) = μ_s N for a body at rest unless it is just about to slide; otherwise use \(F_{f}\) = P from equilibrium.
Friction is always ≤ μ_s N, so the normal reaction N (not weight mg) must be used, and N may differ from mg if there are other vertical forces.
rq: Why does the static friction force change when P changes, even though the normal reaction stays the same?
Static friction is a reactive force that adjusts to match the applied force (\(F_{f}\) = P) to keep the body at rest, so it varies up to its maximum μ_sN.
What happens to the friction force once P exceeds μ_s N?
Friction cannot grow beyond μ_s N, so equilibrium fails and the body starts to slide; kinetic friction then applies.

units.name: 10.3 Coefficient of friction and kinetic friction
units.ov: This material introduces dry (Coulomb) friction: the dimensionless coefficient \( \mu \) relates friction force to the normal reaction, with static friction (\( \mu_s \)) governing the onset of slip and kinetic friction (\( \mu_k \)) governing sliding. Friction is combined with Newton's laws and equilibrium to find the normal force, decide whether a body slips, and calculate acceleration once it moves.
must: Kinetic friction while sliding: \( F_f = \mu_k N \), directed opposite to relative motion
Static friction is a variable force with \( F_f \le \mu_s N \); it equals \( \mu_s N \) only at impending slip (limiting equilibrium)
Always find N from equilibrium perpendicular to the surface; \( N \ne mg \) if there are vertical applied forces or an incline
Sliding block: \( \Sigma F = P - F_f = ma \), so \( a = (P - \mu_k N)/m \)
Typically \( \mu_s > \mu_k \): more force is needed to start motion than to maintain it, and friction drops to the kinetic value once slip begins
Friction depends on the normal load, not the contact area
\( \mu \) is dimensionless; never give it units
Decide the regime first: not sliding means use the static inequality (or equality at the limit), sliding means use \( \mu_k N \)
Slip-onset method: assume equilibrium, compute the required friction, and compare with \( \mu_s N \); the slope case gives impending slip when \( \tan\theta = \mu_s \)
conn: Free-body diagram and equilibrium give N, which feeds directly into \( F_f = \mu N \) (inclines, angled pulls, extra vertical loads)
Static friction check (\( F_f \le \mu_s N \)) decides whether to apply equilibrium or Newton's second law with \( \mu_k \)
Kinetic friction links to kinematics: the acceleration from \( P - \mu_k N = ma \) feeds into \( v = u + at \) and \( s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \)
The slope/cat-on-roof case links the friction angle to the coefficient: the slip condition \( \tan\theta = \mu_s \) arises from resolving weight parallel and perpendicular to the surface
exq: A 20 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with \( \mu_s = 0.5 \) and \( \mu_k = 0.4 \). A horizontal force P is increased gradually. Find the force at which it starts to slide, and the acceleration just after sliding starts at that same P.
A 10 kg block is pulled by a force of 50 N at 30° above the horizontal on a surface with \( \mu_k = 0.3 \). Draw the FBD, find N (not mg), the friction force and the acceleration.
A cat sits on a roof inclined at angle θ with \( \mu_s = 0.6 \). Determine the maximum angle before it slips, and the friction force at 25°. Explain why the mass does not matter.

A block of mass m is initially at rest and a horizontal force P below the slip threshold is applied. State and justify the friction force, then find the minimum P to move it and the distance travelled in 3 s once sliding with \( \mu_k \).
Explain why static friction is described by an inequality while kinetic friction is an equality, and why \( \mu_s > \mu_k \), referring to the force-versus-applied-load graph.

notes.t: Dry Friction – coefficient of friction (μ)
pts: The coefficient of friction μ characterises how much friction resists sliding between two dry surfaces, so it is the key quantity for whether a body slides.
The cat is shown on a sloped roof about to slide, so the question links the friction coefficient to the onset of slipping.
defs: Coefficient of friction (μ)
A dimensionless ratio of the friction force to the normal reaction between two dry contacting surfaces; a larger μ means more grip before sliding occurs.
tips: μ is dimensionless; do not give it units when reporting the coefficient of friction.
Distinguish static friction (impending slip, μ_s) from kinetic friction (μ_k) when answering onset-of-sliding questions.
rq: Why does the cat's answer involve μ rather than the cat's weight alone?
Because sliding depends on the ratio of friction to normal force, and μ is that ratio, so the weight only matters through the normal reaction.

notes.t: Kinetic frictional forces
pts: Once the block is sliding, friction opposes the relative motion and is modelled as proportional to the normal force, with the kinetic coefficient.
Net force in the horizontal direction is the applied force minus kinetic friction, and this net force equals mass times acceleration.
Kinetic friction acts opposite to the direction of motion (here to the left), so it reduces the net force from the pull P.
defs: Kinetic friction
The resisting force between two surfaces that are sliding relative to each other, acting opposite to the direction of relative motion.
Coefficient of kinetic friction
The dimensionless ratio \( \mu_k \) of the kinetic friction force to the normal force between two sliding surfaces.
eqs: Newton's second law for the sliding block (net horizontal force)
\( P \) = applied horizontal force (N); \( F_f \) = kinetic friction force (N); \( m \) = mass of block (kg); \( a \) = acceleration (m/s²)
\( F_f \) = kinetic friction force (N); \( \mu_k \) = coefficient of kinetic friction (dimensionless); \( N \) = normal force (N)
tips: Kinetic friction uses \( \mu_k \), not the static coefficient \( \mu_s \); use \( F_f = \mu_k N \) only while the block is actually sliding.
Friction acts opposite to motion and N is the normal force, not necessarily mg; check for vertical applied forces before writing N = mg.
rq: Why does the acceleration of the block stay constant while it slides at constant applied force P?
Because \( F_f = \mu_k N \) is constant when the normal force N (equal to mg on a level surface) is constant, so the net force \( P - F_f \) is constant and \( a = (P - F_f)/m \).
What would happen to the friction force if the block were pushed down harder from above, and why?
The normal force N would increase, so the kinetic friction \( F_f = \mu_k N \) would increase, reducing the net force and acceleration.

notes.t: Frictional forces: static and kinetic friction
pts: Static friction acts on a body at rest and adjusts up to a maximum value to prevent sliding.
Once the applied force exceeds the maximum static friction, the body slides and friction drops to the kinetic value, which stays roughly constant.
The coefficient of static friction is larger than the coefficient of kinetic friction, so starting motion takes more force than keeping it moving.
Friction force is proportional to the normal force N, which is why friction depends on the contact load rather than contact area.
defs: Static friction
The friction force between surfaces that are not sliding relative to each other; it has any value up to a maximum set by \( \mu_s N \).
Kinetic friction
The friction force opposing relative motion between sliding surfaces, equal to \( \mu_k N \).
Normal force (N)
The contact force perpendicular to the surfaces, balancing the component of weight pressing the bodies together.
