Dopants add extra electrons or holes, dramatically increasing carrier concentration, so resistivity falls over many orders of magnitude.

notes.t: Early semiconductor devices: crystal radio and first transistor
pts: Early crystal radios used a galena (PbS) crystal as a rectifying semiconductor detector.
The first transistor (1947) used metal point contacts pressed onto a germanium crystal.
Both devices show that semiconductor behaviour was exploited long before silicon electronics, with germanium as the first practical transistor material.
defs: Semiconductor
A material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators, and can be controlled by impurities, temperature or applied fields.
Galena
The mineral lead sulphide (PbS), a natural semiconductor used as a crystal detector in early radios.
tips: Do not confuse galena (PbS, a semiconductor) with the element lead; the chemical formula is needed for full marks.
Germanium is the material of the first transistor; silicon became dominant later, so do not assume silicon for the 1947 device.
rq: Why did early crystal radios need a 'cat's whisker' metal point pressed onto the crystal?
The point makes a small, localised metal–semiconductor contact that acts as a rectifier, allowing only one direction of current so the radio signal can be demodulated.
Why is germanium, rather than a metal, the active material in the 1947 transistor?
Germanium is a semiconductor whose conductivity can be modified by doping and by contacts, so it can amplify and switch signals, which metals cannot do.

notes.t: Semiconductor devices and Moore's Law
pts: Moore's Law predicts transistor density roughly doubles every two years, driving exponential growth in computing power.
Intel's transistor designs shrank from 90 nm (2003) to 14 nm (2014), with each generation introducing new materials or structures.
Strained silicon was used across most generations from 90 nm onward to boost carrier mobility.
High-k metal gate was introduced at 45 nm (2007) to reduce gate leakage in place of silicon dioxide.
FinFET three-dimensional gate structures were introduced at 22 nm (2011) to give better control of the channel.
defs: Moore's Law
The observation/prediction that the number of transistors per unit area on an integrated circuit doubles approximately every two years, leading to exponential growth in computing power.
tips: Moore's Law is an empirical trend, not a physical law; do not state it as a proven fundamental principle.
Check node labels (nm) and years carefully when comparing generations, as they are not always evenly spaced.
rq: Why does doubling transistor density every two years lead to exponential rather than linear growth in computing power?
Each doubling multiplies the previous total, so after n doublings the count grows as \(2^{n}\), which is exponential in time.
Why were new materials and structures like high-k metal gates and FinFETs needed as features shrank below 45 nm?
Very thin silicon dioxide gates leaked excessive current, and planar channels lost electrostatic control, so higher-k dielectrics and 3D fin gates were needed.

notes.t: Transistors: evolution of FinFET and nanowire device structures
pts: Early Intel 2011 transistors used fin-shaped silicon channels (FinFETs) with the gate wrapping around three sides of each fin, giving better electrostatic control than planar devices.
IBM's 2017 5 nm technology moved to stacked horizontal nanosheet/nanowire channels, increasing the gate-channel contact area per footprint.
IMEC 2017 devices use silicon nanowires (Si NW) surrounded by a work-function (WF) metal and a high-k gate dielectric (RMG-HK), i.e. gate-all-around structures.
The TEM image of Si(110) shows the atomic lattice: the lattice constant a = 5.43 Å gives the diamond-cubic spacing and projected columns appear as white spots on the TEM image.
defs: FinFET
A transistor in which the channel is a thin vertical silicon fin and the gate wraps around its sides, improving control of leakage current.
Gate-all-around (GAA)
A transistor architecture where the gate surrounds the channel on all sides, typically as nanowires or nanosheets, giving the best electrostatic control at small dimensions.
High-k dielectric (HK)
A gate insulator material with a high relative permittivity, allowing a thick physical layer with the same capacitance as thinner SiO₂.
Work-function (WF) metal
A gate metal chosen so its work function sets the threshold voltage of the transistor.
eqs: Projected lattice spacing for Si(110) viewing direction
tips: Do not confuse the lattice constant a with the projected spacing a/√2 seen in a (110) TEM view.
Dimensions such as 45 nm and 8 nm are nanometres; keep units consistent (1 nm = 10 Å) when comparing with lattice constants.
rq: Why does wrapping the gate around more sides of the channel reduce leakage current?
The gate field controls the channel from several directions, so it can switch the channel off more completely and reduce sub-threshold leakage.
Why do the TEM images show the atomic columns as white spots?
Electrons pass through the aligned atomic columns along the viewing direction, producing bright spots at the positions of the projected columns.

notes.t: Future transistor device architectures (TSMC vision)
pts: Transistor architecture has evolved from planar to FinFET, then nanosheet, with CFET (complementary FET) as the next stacked step to keep improving performance, power and area.
Beyond silicon, 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (e.g. WSe2, MoS2) offer scaling potential beyond Si and good electrostatic control of the channel.
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer high carrier mobility and potential for lower supply voltage \(V_{\text{DD}}\), reducing power consumption.
The chart plots PPA (performance, power, area) against year, showing the trend that device architecture gains are expected to flatten and new materials take over.
defs: FinFET
A transistor in which the channel is a raised fin of silicon with the gate wrapping around three sides, giving better electrostatic control than planar devices.
Nanosheet
A gate-all-around transistor whose channel consists of horizontal stacked thin sheets of silicon fully surrounded by the gate.
CFET
Complementary field-effect transistor: n-type and p-type devices stacked vertically to save area.
TMD
Transition metal dichalcogenide, a layered 2D semiconductor material such as WSe2 or MoS2.
CNT
Carbon nanotube, a rolled graphene cylinder with high carrier mobility used as a potential transistor channel.
tips: Do not confuse the architecture evolution (FinFET to nanosheet to CFET, still silicon) with the 'beyond Si' materials (2D TMDs, CNTs).
Remember PPA means performance, power and area, not pressure, pressure-area or similar.
rq: Why do 2D materials such as MoS2 offer better electrostatic control than bulk silicon at very small scales?
Their atomically thin layers allow the gate to control the whole channel, reducing leakage and short-channel effects.
Why would a lower \(V_{\text{DD}}\) be valuable for future transistors?
Dynamic power scales with \(V_{\text{DD}}\) squared, so lowering the supply voltage greatly reduces power consumption.

notes.t: Superconductors
pts: About half of the elements in the periodic table become superconducting when cooled to very low temperatures approaching absolute zero.
Superconductors carry electrical current with zero resistance, which allows very large currents without energy loss.
Superconductors can also produce high magnetic fields, which is why they are used in strong magnets.
Practical applications include MRI machines, levitating trains, power transmission, CERN particle accelerators, astronomy detectors and quantum computers.
defs: Superconductivity
A state in which a material's electrical resistance drops to exactly zero below a critical temperature, allowing current to flow without energy loss.
tips: Superconductivity only occurs below a critical temperature; do not state that these materials are superconducting at room temperature.
Zero resistance is the defining property; do not confuse superconductors with merely very good conductors such as copper.
rq: Why must superconductors be cooled to temperatures approaching absolute zero rather than just to room-temperature cooling?
Superconductivity only appears below a material-specific critical temperature; above it the material has normal, finite resistance.
Why is zero resistance important for an MRI magnet compared with a normal copper coil?
Zero resistance means the current does not decay and no continuous power is dissipated as heat, so a strong, stable field is maintained with little energy input.

units.name: 2.5 Composites and natural materials
units.ov: This module introduces composites as multi-phase materials whose distinct phases (reinforcement in a matrix) are engineered to give combined properties better than either constituent, with CFRP and the Boeing 787 as headline examples. It then turns to natural materials (wood, cork, leather, bone), which have low stiffness but good strength-to-weight and sometimes smart behaviour. The common thread is optimising properties, especially strength and stiffness per unit weight, through structure and constituent choice.
must: Definition: a composite has two or more phases that stay physically distinct (visible under a microscope), engineered so combined properties exceed those of the individual phases
Reinforcement (fibres or particles, e.g. glass, carbon) versus matrix (resin or polymer): know which is which and the role of each
Composite properties are not fixed: they depend on constituent materials, production method, and the amounts and shapes (fraction, geometry) of the components, plus the interface
Composite vs alloy: composite phases remain distinct, alloy phases are blended at the microscopic level
Thermoset polymer: cross-links irreversibly on curing and cannot be remelted; used as the matrix in dental composites (glass particles) and in resin composites
Applications: CFRP for high strength-to-weight (F1 monocoque tested to FIA loads; 787 fan case; fuselage made from joined rings with no rivets)
Boeing 787: about 50% composite by weight, so the volume share is higher; quote the basis correctly

Efficiency metric \(\frac{m_{TO}}{N_p\,d}\) in kg per passenger-km: DC3 about 817 vs 787 about 0.066, a roughly 12,000-fold difference (check kg vs tonnes; the notes' figures should be sanity-checked)
Natural materials (wood, cork, leather, bone): modulus generally below about 70 GPa, good strength-to-weight, variable properties (grain, hide quality)
Some natural materials are smart, responding usefully to their mechanical environment; do not confuse good strength with high stiffness, and keep GPa vs MPa straight
conn: Composite properties depend on constituents, geometry, and processing, so any estimate of stiffness or strength needs the fractions and shape of the reinforcement
Strength-to-weight links CFRP in aircraft and F1 to the reduction in take-off mass per passenger-km, which drives fuel efficiency
Natural materials such as wood and bone are effectively natural composites, with low modulus but good specific strength, and are comparable to engineered composites for lightweight design
Thermoset matrices link polymer chemistry (cross-linking) to composite processing and to whether the part can be recycled or reshaped
exq: Define a composite and explain how it differs from an alloy. Identify the reinforcement and matrix in (a) glass-fibre resin, (b) a dental composite, (c) CFRP.
The 787 is about 50% composite by weight. Explain why the volume fraction is larger, and give two reasons composites are chosen for the fuselage and fan case.

Calculate \(m_{TO}/(N_p d)\) for an aircraft with given take-off mass, passenger count and range, and compare with the DC3 value of 817 kg per passenger-km. Comment on the ratio and on the fairness of the comparison.
Why is a thermoset polymer suitable as a matrix for a dental restoration, and what limitation does it have regarding reprocessing?
Compare natural materials (wood, bone) with CFRP in modulus (below about 70 GPa for natural), strength-to-weight and variability. Which would you choose for a glider component, and why?

notes.t: Composites
pts: A composite is made from two or more distinct phases of material.
The separate phases are visible as distinct regions under a microscope.
Composites are generally used to optimise the properties of the individual phases, combining their strengths.
The example shown is glass fibres embedded in a resin matrix, where the fibres and resin remain separate phases.
defs: Composite
A material made from two or more phases that remain distinguishable (separate on a microscope), engineered so the combined properties are better than those of the individual phases.
tips: Do not confuse a composite with an alloy: in a composite the phases remain visibly separate, whereas alloy phases are usually blended at the microscopic level.
Remember the purpose is optimisation of combined properties, not simply mixing materials.
rq: Why is a composite designed with two phases rather than using one material with the best properties of both?
No single material may have all the required properties; combining phases lets each contribute its strength (e.g. stiffness from fibres, toughness/shaping from resin), optimising overall performance.
In the glass fibre/resin image, what would you expect to happen to the composite's stiffness if the fibres were removed?
Stiffness and strength would drop substantially, because the glass fibres carry most of the load and the resin alone is far weaker and less stiff.

notes.t: Composites
pts: A composite combines a reinforcing material (e.g. glass or carbon fibres) with a matrix (e.g. resin or polymer) to get properties neither has alone.
Carbon fibre reinforced polymers (CFRP) are used where high strength-to-weight is needed, such as F1 monocoques.
Dental composites use glass particles in a thermoset polymer matrix to give hard, durable restorations.
An F1 monocoque must withstand specified test loads set by the FIA, showing why high-performance composites are used structurally.
defs: Composite
A material made from two or more distinct constituents, a reinforcement (fibres or particles) embedded in a matrix, whose combined properties are superior to those of the individual components.
Thermoset polymer
A polymer that cross-links irreversibly when cured, so it cannot be remelted and reshaped by heating.
tips: Do not confuse the reinforcement with the matrix: the fibres/particles are the reinforcement, the resin/polymer is the matrix.
Remember that a composite's properties depend on both constituents and their interface, not on either alone.
rq: Why is carbon fibre reinforced polymer preferred over steel for an F1 monocoque?
CFRP has a very high strength-to-weight ratio, so it resists the required test loads while keeping the car light, improving performance and safety.
What role does the resin (matrix) play in fibreglass if the glass fibres carry most of the load?
The matrix binds the fibres together, transfers load between them, protects them from damage and environment, and keeps them aligned.

notes.t: Typical Properties of Composites
pts: Composite properties are not fixed; they depend on several factors
Component materials used strongly influence composite properties
The production method of the composite affects its final properties
The amounts and shapes of the components determine the composite's behaviour
tips: Do not state that composite properties are fixed for a given material pair; the page emphasises they depend on processing and geometry as well as constituents.
rq: Why can two composites made from the same two components have very different properties?
Because properties also depend on the production method and on the amounts and shapes (e.g. fibre vs particle) of the components, not only on the materials themselves.

notes.t: Composites in the Boeing 787 Dreamliner
pts: About half of the 787's structure by weight is composite, and by volume the share is even larger.
The fuselage is built from joined rings of composite, avoiding the rivets used in conventional metal fuselages.
The engine fan case is made from carbon fibre composite, combining high strength with low weight.
tips: Quote the basis correctly: 50% is by weight, so the volume fraction is higher, not 50%.
Do not confuse composites with metals; the lecture contrasts composite rings with metal bodies typically built with rivets.
rq: Why does a composite that is 50% by weight occupy more than 50% of the volume?
Composites are lighter than metals (lower density), so an equal mass of composite takes up a larger volume than the same mass of metal.
Why might joining composite fuselage rings without rivets be advantageous?
Rivet holes concentrate stress and can start cracks in composites, and drilling disrupts fibres; bonded or co-cured joints avoid these weaknesses and save weight.

notes.t: Aircraft comparison: material/fuel efficiency per passenger-km
pts: Modern aircraft carry far more mass per passenger-km, so lightweight, efficient designs drive a large reduction in kg per passenger-km over time.
The DC3 used about 817 kg of take-off weight per passenger-km, versus about 0.066 kg for the Boeing 787, roughly a 12,000-fold difference.
Comparing aircraft fairly requires normalising take-off weight by passengers and distance flown, not comparing raw weights.
eqs: \(m_{TO}\) = take-off mass (kg); \(N_{p}\) = number of passengers (-); d = distance per flight (km)
tips: Check units: the DC3 figure is 817 kg per passenger km and the 787 figure is 0.066 kg per passenger km; do not mix up kg and tonnes.
The metric is a mass per passenger-km, so state both the passenger count and the distance when comparing aircraft.
rq: Why does the 787's per-passenger figure look so much lower than the DC3's, even though its take-off weight is about 22 times larger?
Because it carries 290 passengers instead of 25 (about 11.6 times more) and flies 13000 km instead of 560 km (about 23 times further), so its mass is spread over far more passenger-km.
What would the metric be if you only compared take-off weight, and why is that misleading?
Take-off weight alone ignores capacity and range; a heavy aircraft carrying many passengers far may be more efficient than a light one carrying few short distances.

notes.t: Natural Materials
pts: Natural materials such as wood, cork, leather and bone are sourced directly from plants or animals rather than manufactured synthetically.
Examples listed on this slide are wood, cork, leather and bone, each illustrated with a practical product (cork stoppers and a leather boot).
tips: Do not assume natural materials have uniform properties; variability between samples (grain in wood, hide quality in leather) must be considered in design.
rq: Why is cork well suited to making wine bottle stoppers?
Cork is a lightweight, elastic, impermeable material with a cellular structure that compresses to seal a bottle and recovers its shape, while resisting liquid and gas penetration.
What distinguishes a natural material like leather from a synthetic material in terms of its structure and properties?

Leather is made from processed animal hide, so its properties (fibrous collagen network, breathability, variability between hides) come from biological structure rather than a controlled synthetic process.

notes.t: Properties of Natural Materials
pts: Natural materials generally have a lowish elastic modulus, below about 70 GPa.
Natural materials offer good strength relative to their weight, which suits lightweight structures such as gliders.
Some natural materials are smart: they respond to their mechanical environment.
defs: Smart material
A material that reacts to changes in its environment (here mechanical loading) in a useful, controllable way.
tips: Keep units consistent when comparing modulus values: GPa is \(10^{9}\) Pa, not MPa.
Do not confuse 'good strength' with 'high stiffness'; natural materials here are noted for low modulus.
rq: Why does a low modulus matter for a lightweight glider's wing?
A low modulus means the material deflects more under a given load, so stiffness must be checked against deflection limits even if strength is adequate.
Why is strength-to-weight ratio, rather than strength alone, the key figure of merit for a glider?
Because the glider must stay light to fly; a strong but heavy material would increase mass and reduce performance.

units.name: 2.6 Case studies: materials in hip joints, tyres, spark plugs and yachts
units.ov: This module is a set of case studies in materials selection: hip prostheses, aircraft tyres, spark plugs and yachts. In each, components are matched to materials by the property the function demands, such as wear resistance, biocompatibility, inertness, insulation, heat resistance, strength-to-weight ratio or tensile strength. The unifying skill is justifying each choice by function and not just listing materials.
must: Hip prosthesis: stem = Ti-6Al-4V, head = zirconia (ZrO\(_2\)) ceramic, cup liner = UHMWPE, cup backing = Ti-6Al-4V
Hip bearing pair: a hard, smooth ceramic head against a low-friction UHMWPE liner gives low wear; the ceramic is the hard part and the polymer is the sacrificial, low-friction part
Ti-6Al-4V = 6 wt% Al, 4 wt% V; high strength-to-weight ratio, biocompatible, bone integration
Do not confuse the cup (polymer liner) with the cup backing (metal shell); write UHMWPE in full as ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene
Aircraft tyre: rubber (elastomer) tread and walls, steel reinforcement, nitrogen inflation, aluminium alloy rim
Nitrogen is inert and non-flammable, so it reduces fire risk from hot brakes; the aluminium rim is light, so it reduces landing gear mass
Spark plug: ceramic body = electrical insulator that withstands heat and thermal shock; tungsten carbide electrodes resist erosion and heat; steel threads give strength and sealing
Yacht: steel hull, wooden mast and bowsprit, steel wire stays (high tensile strength), synthetic fabric sails (light, strong, rot- and UV-resistant)
Exam method: name the material, state the property, link it to the function; the same material class can play different roles (ceramics: hard in the hip head, insulating in the spark plug)
Avoid swaps: tyre rim is aluminium not steel; mast is wood and stays are steel wire; the spark plug ceramic insulates while the electrodes conduct
conn: Ceramics appear in the hip head (hardness and low wear) and the spark plug body (insulation and thermal shock resistance): the same material class is chosen for different properties
Steel is used in the tyre (reinforcement), the spark plug (threads) and the yacht (hull and stays), each time for strength or toughness, which links to stress, strength and tension
Lightweight choices (Ti alloy, aluminium rim, wooden spars, synthetic sails) link to strength-to-weight ratio, a common selection criterion
Wear and friction link the hip bearing pair and the spark plug electrodes, and both raise service-life and durability questions
exq: Name the four components of a hip joint replacement and the material for each. Explain why the head and cup are a ceramic/polymer pair.
Explain why aircraft tyres are filled with nitrogen rather than air, and why the rim is aluminium alloy rather than steel.
For a spark plug, identify the materials of the body, electrodes and threads and justify each by its required property.
A yacht uses steel for the hull and stays but wood for the mast. Discuss the property requirements of each and suggest an alternative material for the mast.
Define Ti-6Al-4V and UHMWPE and explain why each suits a biomedical implant.

notes.t: Joint Replacement (hip prosthesis materials)
pts: A hip joint replacement is built from several components, each with a material chosen for its role: stem, head, cup and cup backing.
The femoral stem is made from Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy, valued for good strength and biocompatibility and for bone integration.
The femoral head is zirconia (ceramic), giving very hard, smooth, low-wear articulation against the cup.
The cup (acetabular liner) is UHMWPE, a polymer with low friction and good wear resistance against the ceramic head.
The cup backing is Ti-6Al-4V alloy, providing structural support for the polymer liner.
defs: UHMWPE
Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene; a polymer with very long chains used as a low-friction, wear-resistant bearing surface in joint replacements.
Zirconia
Zirconium dioxide (ZrO₂) ceramic, very hard and smooth, used as a femoral head bearing surface to reduce wear.
Ti-6Al-4V
Titanium alloy containing 6 wt% aluminium and 4 wt% vanadium; high strength-to-weight ratio and good biocompatibility, widely used for implants.
tips: Do not confuse the cup (polymer liner) with the cup backing (metal shell); they are different materials.
State the full name (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene) rather than just 'plastic' when describing UHMWPE.
rq: Why is a hard ceramic head paired with a polymer cup rather than two metals?

A ceramic-on-polymer bearing has low friction and low wear; hard-on-hard or metal-on-metal pairings can generate wear debris and ion release, and the polymer cup absorbs load while reducing wear against the very hard head.
Why is a titanium alloy used for both the stem and the cup backing?
Ti-6Al-4V combines high strength, low density and excellent biocompatibility, so it can carry loads and integrate with bone without triggering rejection.

notes.t: Aircraft Tyre Construction and Materials
pts: An aircraft tyre is a composite-like assembly where each component uses a different material chosen for its function: flexible rubber for the tread and walls, steel for reinforcement, nitrogen for inflation, and aluminium alloy for the rim.
Steel is used to reinforce the tyre walls, providing strength to resist the high loads and deformation during landing and taxiing.
Nitrogen is used as the filling gas because it is inert and non-flammable, unlike air containing oxygen, reducing fire risk at high temperatures from braking.
The rim is made from an aluminium alloy, combining light weight with adequate strength to support the tyre and reduce landing gear mass.
The image shows a Boeing 737 NG main landing gear with the shock strut, gas charging valve and oil charging valve, which the tyre assembly is mounted on.
tips: Do not confuse the materials: tread/walls are rubber (elastomer), reinforcement is steel, and the rim is aluminium alloy, not steel.
Justify material choices by function (inertness, strength-to-weight ratio) rather than just listing them.
rq: Why is nitrogen preferred over compressed air for inflating aircraft tyres?
Nitrogen is inert and non-flammable, so it avoids oxidation and reduces fire risk from heat generated during braking, and it contains no moisture that could cause pressure variation with temperature.
Why is a lightweight aluminium alloy rim chosen rather than steel, even though steel is stronger per unit cross-section?
Aluminium alloys offer high strength-to-weight ratio, reducing landing gear mass, which is critical for aircraft performance and fuel efficiency.

notes.t: Spark plug materials
pts: A spark plug uses different materials for each function: a ceramic body for electrical insulation, tungsten carbide electrodes for wear and heat resistance, and steel screw threads for mechanical strength.
Ceramic insulates the electrodes electrically while withstanding high temperatures and thermal shock inside the combustion chamber.
Tungsten carbide electrodes resist erosion from repeated sparking and high temperatures, keeping the gap stable over long service life.
Steel threads provide the strength and toughness needed to screw into the engine head and seal under pressure.
tips: Match each component to the property it needs (insulation, wear/heat resistance, strength) rather than just listing materials.
Do not confuse the function of the ceramic body (insulator) with the conductive electrodes.
rq: Why can't the spark plug body be made of steel like the threads?
Steel is electrically conductive, so it would short-circuit the electrodes; a ceramic insulator is needed to keep the spark at the gap.
Why are tungsten carbide rather than plain steel used for the electrodes?
Tungsten carbide has very high hardness, melting point and erosion resistance, so it survives repeated sparking without wearing away quickly.

notes.t: Materials used in a yacht
pts: A yacht's hull is made of steel, chosen for strength and durability against sea loads.
The bow-sprit and mast are made of wood, a lightweight natural material suited to spars.
Stays, which support the mast, are made of steel wire, giving high tensile strength.
Sails are made from synthetic fabric, which is light, strong and resistant to rot and UV.
tips: Match each component to its material exactly as shown (e.g. mast = wood, stays = steel wire), not the other way round.
Remember that the bow-sprit is the spelling 'bowsprit'; the slide's 'bow-spit' is a typo.
rq: Why is steel wire rather than wood used for the stays, even though both are in the rigging?

Stays carry large tensile loads along their length; steel wire has far higher tensile strength and stiffness per unit cross-section than wood, which would be too weak and would fail in tension or fatigue.
Why would a designer choose a synthetic fabric for sails rather than natural cloth?
Synthetic fabrics such as polyester or nylon are stronger, lighter, resist rot and mildew, and keep their shape better when wet than natural cotton or linen.

units.name: 2.7 Stress, strain and Poisson's ratio
units.ov: This module defines stress (force per unit area) and strain (relative deformation) for normal and shear loading, then introduces Poisson's ratio to link axial extension to lateral contraction. It also covers engineering (nominal) strain and where it stops being valid. The ideas combine: a load gives stress, stress gives strain, and axial strain gives lateral strain and volume change via \( \nu \).
must: Normal stress: \( \sigma = F/A \), where A is the cross-section perpendicular to F, in m² to give Pa (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²; N/mm² = MPa)
Resolve oblique forces: normal component \( F_t \) gives \( \sigma = F_t/A \), parallel component \( F_s \) gives \( \tau = F_s/A \)
Engineering strain: \( \varepsilon = (l-l_0)/l_0 = \Delta L/L_0 \), dimensionless, using the original length (can be quoted as % or mm/mm)
Shear strain is a change in angle between originally perpendicular planes, not a change in length; normal strain is extension or shortening

Poisson's ratio: \( 
u = -\varepsilon_{lateral}/\varepsilon_{axial} \); the minus sign makes \( 
u \) positive because the strains have opposite signs, and \( 
u \) has no units
Lateral strain is \( \varepsilon_l = -\nu\varepsilon_{axial} \): tension thins the specimen and compression fattens it

Typical \( 0 < 
u < 0.5 \); \( 
u = 0.5 \) means constant volume (rubber, about 0.49); \( 
u \approx 0 \) for cork; auxetic foams have \( 
u < 0 \)
For \( \nu < 0.5 \), volume increases in tension and decreases in compression
Engineering strain is valid only for small deformations; use true (logarithmic) strain for large ones
Common errors: using deformed area or length, forgetting the negative sign in \( \nu \), mixing mm² with N, putting units on strain
conn: Stress and strain are linked by the material response: a force gives stress, which gives axial strain, and Poisson's ratio then gives the lateral strain and change in cross-section
Resolving an inclined force into normal and tangential components gives both \( \sigma \) and \( \tau \), which then lead to normal strain and shear strain
\( \nu \) links to volume change: axial and lateral strains together give \( \Delta V/V \), which is zero at \( \nu = 0.5 \)
Unit handling (mm² to m², Pa to MPa) is combined with strain calculations in numerical problems, e.g. stress then extension then new diameter
exq: A 12 mm diameter rod carries a 25 kN tensile load. Calculate the stress in MPa. If the 300 mm gauge length extends by 0.45 mm, find the engineering strain.
A bar of length 200 mm and diameter 10 mm is stretched by 0.5 mm and its diameter reduces by 0.003 mm. Calculate the axial strain, the lateral strain and Poisson's ratio.
A force of 10 kN acts at 30° to the normal of a 500 mm² cross-section. Resolve the force and find the tensile and shear stresses on the area.

Explain why \( 
u = 0.5 \) corresponds to constant volume. Compare rubber (\( 
u \approx 0.49 \)) and cork (\( 
u \approx 0 \)) under compression, and say why this matters for a cork bottle stopper.
Why is engineering strain \( (l-l_0)/l_0 \) inaccurate at large deformations, and what alternative measure would you use?

notes.t: Loading: stress and strain
pts: Applying a force produces deformation, and applying deformation results in a force, so the two are linked.
Stress is the internal force per unit area that a material experiences under load.
Strain measures the deformation of a material as the change in length relative to its original length.
defs: Stress
Force per unit area acting within a material; the intensity of internal force resisting an applied load.
Strain
The change in length of a material divided by its original length; a dimensionless measure of deformation.
eqs: \sigma = stress (Pa); F = applied force (N); A = cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
\varepsilon = strain (dimensionless); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{0}\) = original length (m)
tips: Stress is in pascals (N/\(m^{2}\)), while strain is dimensionless; do not give strain units.
Use the original (undeformed) area and length in the formulas, not the deformed values.
rq: Why is stress defined per unit area rather than as the raw force?
Dividing by area lets materials of different cross-sections be compared, since the same force on a thinner bar produces a higher internal intensity and greater deformation.
If a bar is stretched, does its strain depend on its original length?
Yes; for the same change in length, a longer bar has a smaller strain because strain is normalised by the original length.

notes.t: Unidirectional stress
pts: Stress is the applied force divided by the area perpendicular to that force.
A tensile force pulls the body apart, giving a tensile stress; the force acts normal to the cut face (area A).
defs: Unidirectional stress
Stress produced by a force acting along a single axis, normal to the cross-sectional area over which it is distributed.
eqs: \( \sigma \) = stress (Pa or N/m²); \( F \) = applied force (N); \( A \) = area perpendicular to the force (m²)
tips: Units trap: convert areas to m² (e.g. mm² × 10⁻⁶) so σ comes out in Pa; mixing mm² with N gives MPa only if handled consistently.
Use the cross-sectional area perpendicular to F, not the surface area of the whole specimen.
rq: Why must the area used in σ = F/A be the one perpendicular to the force rather than the total surface area of the body?
Stress is defined per unit area carrying the load; only the cross-section perpendicular to F transmits the force, so using other areas gives a wrong value.
What happens to the stress if the same force is applied over twice the cross-sectional area?
The stress halves, since σ = F/A and A doubles while F is unchanged.

notes.t: Multidirectional forces and stress components
pts: A general force system on a body can be combined into a mixture of tensile/compressive, shear and hydrostatic stresses.
To analyse a multidirectional force, resolve it into components normal to the area (tensile) and parallel to the area (shear), then calculate each stress separately.
defs: Tensile stress
Normal force per unit area acting perpendicular to the surface; the component of force pulling/pushing normal to the area A.
Shear stress
Force per unit area acting parallel to the surface, tending to cause sliding of one plane over another.
eqs: \sigma = tensile stress (Pa); \(F_{t}\) = force component normal to area (N); A = area (\(m^{2}\))
\tau = shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = force component parallel to area (N); A = area (\(m^{2}\))
tips: Use the component of force normal to the area (\(F_{t}\)) for tensile stress, not the total force F, unless the force is perpendicular to the area.
Stresses are in Pa (N/\(m^{2}\)); convert area units such as \(mm^{2}\) to \(m^{2}\) before substituting.
rq: Why must a multidirectional force be resolved into components before stresses are calculated?
Normal (tensile) and shear stresses act in different directions and cause different deformation; each must be computed from its own force component divided by the area.
What happens to the shear component if the force acts purely normal to the area?
The shear component is zero, so the stress is purely tensile/compressive: \( \tau = 0 \).

notes.t: Strain
pts: Applying force or stress to an object causes it to deform.
Strain is the normalised (relative) measure of deformation, so it is dimensionless.
Like stress, strain can be normal to the surface under consideration or perpendicular to that direction, giving tensile/compressive strain or shear strain.
defs: Strain
The normalised deformation of an object caused by an applied force or stress; a dimensionless measure of how much a body changes shape relative to its original dimensions.
Tensile/compressive strain
Normal strain acting in a direction perpendicular to the surface considered, producing extension (tensile) or shortening (compressive).
Shear strain
Strain produced by forces acting parallel to the surface, causing a change in angle between originally perpendicular planes rather than a change in length.
tips: Strain is dimensionless; do not assign it units such as m or Pa when quoting a strain value.
Do not confuse strain (deformation response) with stress (applied force per area).
rq: Why is strain described as 'normalised' deformation rather than just the change in length?
Normalising divides the deformation by the original dimension, so strain is dimensionless and comparable across specimens of different sizes.
How does a normal (tensile/compressive) strain differ from a shear strain in what it changes?
Normal strain changes the length of a line in the loading direction, while shear strain changes the angle between originally perpendicular lines.

notes.t: Tensile Strain
pts: Under tension a specimen extends along the load direction and contracts in the perpendicular directions.
Nominal tensile strain is the change in length u divided by the original length l, giving a dimensionless value.
Nominal lateral strain is the change in lateral dimension v divided by the original length l; it is also dimensionless and is negative for tension because the object contracts sideways.
defs: Nominal tensile strain
The extension of a specimen under tension divided by its original gauge length, \( \varepsilon_n = u/l \); a dimensionless quantity.
Nominal lateral strain
The change in a transverse dimension of a specimen under tension divided by the original length, \( \varepsilon_l = v/l \); a dimensionless quantity.
eqs: \( \varepsilon_n \) = nominal tensile strain (dimensionless); \( u \) = change in length (m); \( l \) = original length (m)
\( \varepsilon_l \) = nominal lateral strain (dimensionless); \( v \) = change in lateral dimension (m); \( l \) = original length (m)
tips: Do not confuse the nominal strains with the stress σ; strain is dimensionless and has no units such as Pa.
Use the original length l in the denominator, not the deformed length, when calculating nominal strain.
rq: Why does the lateral strain have the opposite sign to the tensile strain under tension?
Because the specimen extends along the load axis (positive strain) while it contracts in the perpendicular directions (negative lateral change), so the lateral strain is negative.
Why is strain a dimensionless quantity even though u and l are lengths?
Because it is a ratio of two lengths with the same units, so the units cancel.

notes.t: Poisson's ratio
pts: Tensile loading stretches a specimen along the load axis while it becomes thinner laterally.
Compressive loading shortens a specimen along the load axis while it becomes fatter laterally.
Poisson's ratio measures the ratio of lateral to axial strain, with a negative sign so that it is usually positive.
defs: Poisson's ratio
The negative ratio of lateral strain to axial (tensile) strain for a material under uniaxial loading; it describes how much a material contracts laterally when stretched axially.
eqs: Poisson's ratio from lateral and axial strain
\nu = Poisson's ratio (dimensionless); lateral strain = transverse strain (dimensionless); tensile strain = axial strain (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget the negative sign in the definition; lateral and tensile strains have opposite signs, so omitting it gives a negative ν.
Poisson's ratio is dimensionless, so do not attach units to it or to the strains when calculating.
rq: Why is there a minus sign in the Poisson's ratio equation, and what sign does ν normally have for common engineering materials?
Tensile strain is positive and lateral strain is negative (contraction) under tension, so the minus sign makes ν positive; typical values are positive, around 0.2–0.35 for most metals.

notes.t: Effect of Poisson's ratio
pts: Poisson's ratio is virtually always positive, with rare exceptions (some foams).
For typical materials Poisson's ratio lies between 0 and 0.5.
At ν = 0.5 the material's volume does not change under load (e.g. rubber, ν ≈ 0.49).
For ν < 0.5 volume increases in tension and decreases in compression.
Cork has ν ≈ 0.0, so it shows very little lateral expansion when compressed.
tips: Poisson's ratio is dimensionless; do not attach units to it.
The volume-change conclusions only hold for ν between 0 and 0.5 in normal materials; negative ν (auxetic foams) behaves differently.
rq: Why does a material with ν = 0.5 keep the same volume under load?
Lateral strain exactly offsets axial strain (volumetric strain = ε(1 − 2ν) = 0), so no net volume change occurs.
Why would a material with ν < 0.5 get bigger in volume when stretched?
Lateral contraction under tension is smaller than the axial elongation, so the net volumetric strain is positive.

notes.t: Engineering Strain
pts: Engineering strain is the change in length divided by the original length, a dimensionless measure of deformation.
The simple engineering strain definition applies at low strain levels, where the deformation is small.
defs: Engineering strain
The change in length of a specimen divided by its original length; a dimensionless quantity, often expressed as a percentage or in mm/mm.
eqs: Engineering strain (change in length over original length)
\varepsilon = engineering strain (dimensionless); l = final length (m); \(l_{0}\) = original length (m)
tips: Strain is dimensionless: do not attach units like m or mm to the final answer; express as a percentage only if asked.
The formula is only valid at low strain levels; for large deformations, true (logarithmic) strain should be used.
rq: Why is the change in length divided by the original length rather than the final length?

Strain is defined relative to the undeformed reference length \(l_{0}\), so the measure is consistent and comparable between specimens; dividing by l would give a different (true-strain-like) value and is not the engineering definition.

units.name: 2.8 Hooke's law and elastic moduli
units.ov: This module introduces Hooke's law: for small strains, stress is proportional to strain, and the constant of proportionality is an elastic modulus. There are three moduli, one for each loading type: Young's modulus E (tension/compression), shear modulus G (tangential loading) and bulk modulus K (uniform pressure). All three have the form stress/strain, so they share units of Pa, and strain is always dimensionless.
must: Hooke's law holds only for small strains (linear elastic region); the material returns to its original shape on unloading
Young's modulus: \( \sigma = E\varepsilon \), i.e. \( E=\dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L_i} \), for tensile or compressive loading
Shear modulus: \( \tau = G\gamma \), with \( \tau=F/A \) (F parallel to the face) and \( \gamma=\Delta x/h \)
Bulk modulus: \( p=-K\,\Delta V/V_0 \); the negative sign means a pressure increase gives a volume decrease
Match each modulus to its loading type: E to uniaxial, G to shear (shape change at constant volume), K to hydrostatic (volume change)
Shear stress acts parallel to the surface; normal stress acts perpendicular to it. Do not confuse them
Strain is dimensionless, so E, G, K and stress are all in Pa (N/m²). Watch GPa vs MPa, a factor of 1000
Typical E values: diamond ~1000 GPa, steel ~200 GPa, PMMA ~3.4 GPa, rubber 0.01–0.1 GPa, foams ~0.001 GPa; for a range such as GFRP's 7–45 GPa, the value depends on fibre fraction and orientation
Correct terminology: 'moduli' is the plural, and 'Young's modulus' needs the apostrophe; Young's modulus is also called the elastic modulus
conn: Stress = F/A appears in all three moduli, but the area and direction of F differ (normal area for E, parallel face for G, every face for K). Identifying this correctly is the first step in a calculation
Hooke's law links to the stress-strain curve: the modulus is the gradient of the linear region, and beyond the elastic limit the law no longer applies
Material property tables link stiffness to selection: a small E means a large deformation for a given load, so ΔL = FL/(AE) combines E with geometry
Shear strain Δx/h connects to geometry: for small angles γ ≈ θ in radians, so shear problems often need a trig or angle conversion
exq: A steel wire (E = 200 GPa) of length 2.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm carries a 150 N tensile load. Calculate the stress, strain and extension.
A rubber block 50 mm × 50 mm × 20 mm high (G = 0.5 MPa) has a tangential force of 40 N applied to its top face. Find the shear stress, shear strain and lateral displacement of the top face.
A solid is subjected to a hydrostatic pressure increase of 50 MPa and its volume falls by 0.05%. Calculate the bulk modulus and state which modulus applies and why.
Explain why Hooke's law is only an approximation, and why Young's modulus cannot be used for a shear problem. Give an example of each modulus's loading type.
Compare the stiffness of steel, PMMA and a foamed polymer using typical E values. Calculate the extension of identical bars under the same load, and explain why foams have such low moduli.

notes.t: Hooke's Law
pts: For small strains, strain is nearly proportional to stress.
Materials obeying this approximate proportionality over small strains are described as linearly elastic.
defs: Linearly elastic
A material behaviour in which, for small strains, strain is approximately proportional to stress, so the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
tips: Hooke's Law is only an approximation valid for small strains; do not assume strain is proportional to stress for large deformations.
rq: Why does Hooke's Law only apply to small strains?
At larger strains the stress-strain relationship departs from linearity (e.g. yielding or plastic deformation), so strain is no longer proportional to stress.

notes.t: Moduli (elastic moduli and stress-strain relationship)
pts: A modulus describes the stress-strain relationship of a material, i.e. its stiffness under a given type of loading.
There are three moduli, each corresponding to a different type of loading (tension/compression, shear, and bulk/volumetric).
The plural of modulus is moduli (Latin), not moduluses.
defs: Modulus (elastic modulus)
A material property giving the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region; a measure of stiffness describing the stress-strain relationship under a specific type of loading.
tips: Use the correct plural 'moduli' (not 'moduluses') in written answers.
Do not mix up the three moduli: each applies only to its specific loading type (e.g. do not use Young's modulus for shear).
rq: Why does a material need three different moduli rather than one?
Because materials respond differently to different loading types (axial tension/compression, shear, and hydrostatic pressure), so each loading mode has its own stress-strain ratio.

notes.t: Young's modulus (E)
pts: Young's modulus is the ratio of linear stress to linear strain within the elastic region.
Young's modulus is also called the elastic modulus, a measure of stiffness.
Named after Thomas Young, so the possessive form 'Young's modulus' is the correct spelling.
defs: Young's modulus (E)
The ratio of linear (tensile or compressive) stress to linear strain in the elastic region of a material; a measure of stiffness, also called the elastic modulus.
eqs: Hooke's law relating linear stress to linear strain via Young's modulus
\sigma = linear stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \varepsilon = linear strain (dimensionless)
tips: Write it as "Young's modulus" with an apostrophe, not "youngs modulus" or "young's modulus".
Strain is dimensionless, so the units of E are the same as stress (Pa or N/m²).
rq: Why is Young's modulus described as a measure of stiffness?
A material with a large E produces only a small strain for a given stress, so it resists elastic deformation more strongly.
If two materials have the same stress applied, which has the larger strain: the one with higher E or lower E?
The material with lower E has the larger strain, since \varepsilon = \sigma / E.

notes.t: Typical values of Young's modulus
pts: Young's modulus (stiffness) varies enormously across material classes, from ~1000 GPa for diamond down to ~0.001 GPa for foamed polymers.
Ceramics and diamond are the stiffest materials listed; metals such as steel, titanium, copper and aluminium lie in the tens to hundreds of GPa.
Polymers and elastomers are far less stiff: PMMA ~3.4 GPa, PE 0.2–1 GPa, rubber 0.01–0.1 GPa.
Composites and natural materials sit in between, and wood is stiffer along the grain than GFRP's lower range.
Foamed polymers are the least stiff, because their modulus depends largely on the air-filled structure rather than the solid material alone.
tips: Watch units: values are in GPa (\(10^{9}\) Pa); mixing with MPa differs by a factor of 1000.
Ranges such as GFRP 7–45 GPa depend on fibre fraction and orientation, so quote a range rather than a single value.
rq: Why is aluminium's modulus (~70 GPa) much lower than steel's (~210 GPa) even though both are metals?

Young's modulus depends on interatomic bonding stiffness and crystal structure; steel's stronger bonding and structure give a higher modulus, so modulus is largely set by bonding rather than by being a metal.
If a component must be stiff but light, which listed materials would you consider and why?
Stiffness per unit density matters: GFRP and wood (along grain) offer moderate modulus at low density, whereas diamond and alumina are very stiff but brittle and costly.

notes.t: Shear modulus (modulus of rigidity)
pts: Shear modulus G measures a material's resistance to shear deformation; it is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.
Shear stress τ is the tangential force F acting over area A parallel to the surface, so it is a force per unit area.
Within the elastic region, shear stress is directly proportional to shear strain, so the relationship is linear.
defs: Shear modulus (modulus of rigidity), G
The ratio of shear stress to shear strain in the elastic region of a material; a measure of its stiffness against shear deformation.
Shear stress, τ
Shear force divided by the area over which it acts, acting parallel to the surface.
eqs: Shear stress–shear strain relationship (Hooke's law in shear)
\tau = shear stress (Pa); G = shear modulus (Pa); \gamma = shear strain (dimensionless)
\tau = shear stress (Pa); F = applied tangential force (N); A = area over which the force acts (\(m^{2}\))
tips: Shear strain γ is dimensionless, so the units of G are the same as those of stress (Pa or N/\(m^{2}\)), not strain.
Do not confuse shear stress (force parallel to the surface, divided by area) with normal stress (force perpendicular to the surface).
rq: Why does a material with a higher shear modulus deform less under the same shear stress?
Since τ = Gγ, for a fixed τ a larger G gives a smaller shear strain γ, so the material is stiffer in shear.
If a force is doubled but the area over which it acts is also doubled, what happens to the shear stress?
Shear stress τ = F/A is unchanged, because the doubling of F and A cancels.

notes.t: Bulk modulus (K) – resistance to uniform compression
pts: Bulk modulus measures how strongly a material resists uniform (hydrostatic) compression, i.e. change in volume under equal pressure from all sides.
The hydrostatic pressure p is the force per unit area acting on each face of the cube, so it is a stress-type quantity.
Compression causes a fractional volume reduction; the negative sign in the relation means an increase in pressure produces a decrease in volume.
defs: Bulk modulus (K)
The ratio of hydrostatic pressure to the fractional volume change a material undergoes under uniform compression; a measure of resistance to uniform compression.
Hydrostatic pressure (p)
Uniform pressure applied equally from all directions, equal to force divided by area, F/A.
eqs: Bulk modulus relation: pressure versus fractional volume change under uniform compression
p = hydrostatic pressure (Pa); K = bulk modulus (Pa); \(\Delta V\) = change in volume (\(m^{3}\)); \(V_0\) = original volume (\(m^{3}\))
tips: Do not confuse hydrostatic pressure (uniform from all sides, bulk modulus) with uniaxial loading (Young's modulus); the bulk modulus applies only to uniform compression.
Keep units consistent: K and p are both in Pa, while \(\Delta V/V_0\) is dimensionless.
rq: Why does the equation include a negative sign, and what would the sign of ΔV be under compression?
Under compression the volume decreases, so \(\Delta V\) is negative; the minus sign makes the pressure p positive, and K is therefore a positive quantity.
Why is the bulk modulus a useful property for a material under water pressure, such as a submarine hull?
A high K means the material changes volume very little under uniform pressure, so it resists volume loss from all-round loading.

notes.t: Moduli - Summary
pts: Young's modulus is also called the elastic modulus and describes stiffness under tensile or compressive load.
Shear modulus describes resistance to shape change when a force acts tangentially across a fixed face.
Bulk modulus describes resistance to uniform volume change under pressure from all sides.
defs: Young's modulus
Ratio of tensile (or compressive) stress to tensile (or compressive) strain within the elastic region of a material.
Shear modulus
Ratio of shear stress to shear strain, where the force acts parallel to a surface and the shape of the body changes without volume change.
Bulk modulus
Ratio of hydrostatic (volumetric) stress to volumetric strain; a measure of a material's resistance to uniform compression.
eqs: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \sigma = normal stress (Pa); \varepsilon = normal strain (dimensionless); F = applied force (N); A = cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{i}\) = original length (m)

G = shear modulus (Pa); \tau = shear stress (Pa); \gamma = shear strain (dimensionless); F = tangential force (N); A = area of the face (\(m^{2}\)); \Delta x = lateral displacement (m); h = height (m)
B = bulk modulus (Pa); \Delta P = change in pressure (Pa); \Delta V = change in volume (\(m^{3}\)); \(V_{i}\) = initial volume (\(m^{3}\))
tips: Watch units: moduli are in Pa (N/\(m^{2}\)), not N/m or N, even though stress and strain combinations may look like force-based quantities.
Strain is dimensionless; do not add units such as m/m to it, and remember that shear strain is \Delta x/h, not an angle in degrees unless converted to radians for small angles.
rq: Why does the bulk modulus carry a negative sign in its definition?
An increase in pressure causes a decrease in volume, so \Delta P and \Delta V have opposite signs; the minus sign makes B positive.
What would happen to the shear modulus if a material could shear without any resistance?
G would be zero, meaning the material offers no resistance to shape change under tangential force.
Why can't a fluid have a finite shear modulus?
Fluids flow continuously under shear stress, so they cannot sustain a static shear strain and G is effectively zero.

units.name: 2.9 SI units and conclusion
units.ov: This short section covers SI units for stress, strain and modulus, then the seven SI base units and how they are defined by national metrology institutes. It closes the Materials I Lecture 2 survey of engineering materials and their physical properties, which the next lecture links to microscopic bonding. The key link is that stress is force per area, strain is dimensionless, and so modulus carries the units of stress.
must: Stress is force per unit area: \(\sigma = F/A\), with SI unit the pascal, \(1\,\text{Pa} = 1\,\text{N/m}^2\)
Because the pascal is tiny, stress is quoted in MPa (\(1\,\text{MPa}=10^6\,\text{Pa}=1\,\text{N/mm}^2\)); write MPa with a capital M and lowercase Pa, never Mpa
Strain is change in length divided by original length, \(\varepsilon=\Delta L/L_0\); it is dimensionless (a ratio of two lengths)
Strain is quoted as a percentage or in microstrain, where \(1\,\mu\varepsilon=10^{-6}\)
Modulus is \(E=\sigma/\varepsilon\); since \(\varepsilon\) is dimensionless, \(E\) has the units of stress (Pa, typically GPa for metals)
The seven SI base units are the second, metre, kilogram, kelvin, ampere, mole and candela; engineering mostly uses m, kg and s
Newton and pascal are derived units, not base units; e.g. \(\text{Pa}=\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\)

The base units are interdependent in their definitions: the second, kelvin and kilogram are defined independently of other base units, whereas the metre is defined via the speed of light and so depends on the second
Units are defined and maintained by National Metrology Institutes such as NPL (UK) and NIST (USA)
Lecture 2 surveyed the macroscopic properties of materials; the next lecture explains them through microscopic features such as chemical bond type
conn: Stress, strain and modulus: \(E=\sigma/\varepsilon\) requires consistent units (N, m, Pa) and conversion between MPa, GPa and microstrain, e.g. in an elongation calculation
Unit checking via dimensional analysis: breaking derived units (N, Pa) into base units (kg, m, s) to verify an equation
The metre depends on the second via the speed of light, which links the definition chain of base units to the role of NMIs in standards
Macroscopic modulus and strength (this lecture) link to bond type and microstructure (next lecture), so explanations of stiffness often combine both
exq: A steel rod of diameter 10 mm carries a tensile force of 20 kN. Calculate the stress in MPa, and the strain in microstrain if \(E=200\) GPa.
A strain gauge reads 850 \(\mu\varepsilon\) on an aluminium bar with \(E=70\) GPa. Calculate the stress in MPa, and the extension of a 2 m length of the bar.
Explain why strain is dimensionless and why Young's modulus has the same units as stress. Express the units of the pascal in SI base units.
List the seven SI base units with the quantity each measures, and explain which are defined independently and why the metre depends on the second.
Identify the errors in the following: 'The stress was 250 Mpa and the strain was 0.002 m/m, giving a modulus of 125000 N.'

notes.t: SI units for stress, strain and modulus
pts: Stress is force per unit area, measured in newtons per square metre, named the pascal.
The pascal is very small, so stress is usually quoted in megapascals (MPa), with capital M and lowercase Pa.
Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no units.
Strain is normally quoted as a percentage or in microstrain, where microstrain is \(10^{-6.}\)
Because modulus is stress divided by strain, and strain is dimensionless, modulus has the units of stress, Pa.
defs: Stress
Force per unit cross-sectional area, with SI units of N/m² (Pa).
Pascal (Pa)
The SI unit of stress, equal to 1 N/m².
Strain
Change in length divided by original length; a dimensionless quantity.
Microstrain (με)
A unit of strain equal to \(10^{-6}\) (one millionth) of a dimensionless strain.
eqs: Modulus (e.g. Young's modulus) from stress and strain
tips: Write MPa, not Mpa; mixing up the case of the prefix is a common unit error.
Strain has no units, so a modulus takes its units entirely from stress (Pa), not from strain.
rq: Why is strain dimensionless even though it is a length change?
Strain is a length divided by a length (m/m), so the metres cancel and no unit remains.
Why is it wrong to write 'Mpa' for megapascals?
The prefix M means mega (\(10^{6}\)) and must be capital; the unit Pa is a named unit with capital P, so the correct form is MPa.

notes.t: SI base units and their definitions
pts: Mostly we work with metres, kilograms and seconds (m, kg, s) in engineering.
The seven SI base units are kelvin, second, metre, kilogram, candela, mole and ampere; they are interdependent in their definitions.
The second, kelvin and kilogram are defined independently of any other base unit.
The metre is defined via the speed of light, so it depends on the definition of the second.
Units are defined by National Metrology Institutes such as NPL (UK) and NIST (USA).
defs: SI base unit

One of the seven fundamental units from which all other SI units are derived: second (time), metre (length), kilogram (mass), kelvin (temperature), ampere (electric current), mole (amount of substance) and candela (luminous intensity).
National Metrology Institute (NMI)
A national body (e.g. NPL in the UK, NIST in the USA) responsible for establishing and maintaining the standards that define units.
tips: Do not confuse base units with derived units such as newton or pascal; only seven are base units.
Remember the metre depends on the second, so the second is effectively more fundamental in the chain of definitions.
rq: Why does the definition of the metre depend on the second, while the kilogram does not depend on any other base unit?

The metre is defined via the speed of light, which is a distance per time, so it requires the second; the kilogram is defined by its own fixed reference (Planck constant), independent of other base units.
Why is it important that some base units are defined independently of others?
It means the system is self-consistent with no circular definitions, and each base quantity can be realised separately by its own measurement standard.

notes.t: Conclusion of Materials I Lecture 2
pts: The lecture gave a broad survey of the types of materials used in engineering.
The lecture outlined some of the physical properties of these materials.
The next lecture links these properties to microscopic features such as chemical bond type.
tips: Do not confuse the macroscopic properties surveyed in this lecture with the microscopic bonding explained in the next lecture.
rq: Why does the lecture argue that microscopic features such as bond type must be understood to explain material properties?
Because macroscopic properties such as strength, stiffness and conductivity arise from atomic-scale bonding and structure, so bond type determines how a material behaves.

units.name: 3.1 Why bonding matters: mechanical and electrical properties
units.ov: This lecture introduces why the way atoms are bonded and arranged controls a material's bulk behaviour. Interatomic bonds, which come from electron-nucleus interactions, together with atomic packing set stiffness, strength and density. In a solid, discrete atomic energy levels broaden into bands, and how electrons fill these bands decides whether the material is a metal, semiconductor or insulator.
must: Bonding type and atomic arrangement together determine a material's properties; composition alone does not
Interatomic bonds are attractive and repulsive forces between neighbouring atoms, and they set stiffness and strength
Atomic packing (the positions of atoms) is distinct from bonding (the forces between atoms), and both affect mechanical behaviour
Stiffness, strength and density all follow from how atoms are interconnected, so the strength-to-weight ratio depends on bond type
Compare strength and weight using density consistently, e.g. specific strength \(\sigma/\rho\); a stronger but much denser material may not be the better choice
Isolated atoms have discrete energy levels; in a solid, many interacting atoms broaden these into energy bands
Band filling by electrons decides whether a material is a metal, semiconductor or insulator
Do not classify a material as a conductor or insulator from its elements alone; the band structure and electron filling decide it
Exam answers should link bond type to observable properties rather than just listing bond types
conn: Bond type fixes both mechanical properties (stiffness, strength, density) and electrical properties (band structure), so one bonding model explains both
Atomic packing and bonding combine to set density, and density feeds into strength-to-weight ratio comparisons
Atomic energy levels lead to bands through the interaction of many atoms, which then leads to electrical classification by filling
Electron-nucleus interactions give rise to bonds, which give interatomic forces, which give stiffness and strength
exq: Explain how interatomic bonding determines stiffness and strength, distinguishing the role of bonding from that of atomic packing.

Two materials have strengths of 400 MPa and 250 MPa and densities of 7800 and 2700 kg/m³. Calculate the specific strength of each and state which is better for a lightweight component, justifying your answer.
Describe how discrete atomic energy levels become energy bands when atoms form a solid, and why isolated atoms do not have bands.
Explain how the filling of energy bands distinguishes a metal, a semiconductor and an insulator, and why composition alone cannot predict this.
Discuss why the type of atomic bonding governs the strength-to-weight ratio of a material, using examples of different material classes.

notes.t: Introduction to atomic bonding and energy bands in solids
pts: Types of bonding between atoms in a solid strongly influence its physical properties.
Electron–nucleus interactions within an atom give rise to the various types of bonds between atoms.
Discrete atomic energy levels spread into energy bands when atoms come together in a solid.
tips: Do not confuse the atomic energy levels of an isolated atom with the energy bands that form in a solid; bands arise only from many interacting atoms.
Remember that this page is introductory: exam answers should link bonding type to observable physical properties rather than just listing bond types.
rq: Why would the type of bonding in a solid affect properties such as melting point or electrical conductivity?

Bonding determines how strongly atoms are held together and how electrons are shared or localised, which governs cohesive energy (melting point) and the availability of mobile electrons (conductivity).
What happens to a single sharp atomic energy level when many atoms are brought together to form a solid?
It splits into many closely spaced levels that merge into a continuous energy band, due to interactions between neighbouring atoms.

notes.t: Mechanical properties: stiffness, strength and density
pts: Stiffness, strength and density of a material are governed by how its atoms are interconnected.
Mechanical properties arise from the forces acting between atoms, i.e. the interatomic bonds.
The arrangement (position) of atoms, i.e. atomic packing, also controls mechanical behaviour.
The key strength-to-weight ratio is determined by the type of atomic bonding.
defs: Interatomic bond
The attractive and repulsive force linking neighbouring atoms, which determines a material's stiffness and strength.
Atomic packing
The spatial arrangement of atoms in a material's structure, which affects its mechanical properties.
tips: Do not confuse atomic packing (arrangement of atoms) with interatomic bonding (forces between atoms); both influence properties but are different factors.
Strength-to-weight comparisons must use density consistently; a stronger material is not always the better choice if it is much denser.
rq: Why would two materials with identical atomic packing still have very different stiffness?
Because stiffness depends on the forces between atoms (the type of interatomic bonding), not only on their arrangement.
Why does the atomic bonding matter for strength-to-weight ratio rather than strength alone?
Because a light material with strong bonds can be strong yet low in density, so the ratio of strength to density is what makes it efficient.

notes.t: Electrical properties: metal, semiconductor or insulator
pts: Electrical behaviour depends on how atoms are interconnected, not just on the atoms themselves.
Atomic bonds merge to form bands, and how those bands are filled with electrons determines whether a material conducts, is a semiconductor, or is an insulator.
tips: Do not classify a material as a metal, semiconductor or insulator by its atomic composition alone; the band structure and electron filling decide it.
rq: Why would two materials made of the same atoms behave differently as a metal and as an insulator?
Because the way the atoms are interconnected and bonded affects how the bands form and how they are filled with electrons, which sets the electrical behaviour.
What determines whether a band-filled material conducts electricity?
Whether the electrons can move into empty states within a partly filled band (metal) or whether the band gap separating filled and empty bands is large (insulator) or small (semiconductor).

units.name: 3.2 Periodic table and atomic spectra
units.ov: This material covers how the periodic table organises elements by atomic number into groups (similar chemistry) and periods (same number of electron shells), and how atoms produce discrete line spectra. Both ideas rest on quantised electron energy levels: the electron configuration sets chemical behaviour, while transitions between levels set emitted and absorbed photon energies, as seen in hydrogen's Balmer series.
must: Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number; groups (columns) share chemical properties, periods (rows) share the number of electron shells
Photon energy: \(E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\), with \(h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\) J·s and \(c = 3.00\times10^{8}\) m/s
Gases emit and absorb only at specific wavelengths, giving line spectra; hot solids and liquids give continuous spectra
Emission: an electron falls to a lower level and releases a photon with energy equal to the level difference, \(\Delta E = E_{upper}-E_{lower}\)
Absorption: an electron is excited by a photon of exactly matching energy; absorption and emission lines occur at the same wavelengths
Emission spectrum = bright lines on a dark background; absorption spectrum = dark lines on a continuous coloured background
Balmer series: hydrogen transitions ending at \(n = 2\), which give the visible lines
Alkali metals (Group 1) have one valence electron and are highly reactive; noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells and are largely unreactive
Transition metals (groups 3–12) have partially filled d shells, giving coloured compounds and multiple oxidation states
Lanthanides and actinides are displayed separately beneath the table, not in the main body; do not mix up groups and periods
conn: Electron energy levels link the two halves: the outer-shell configuration determines a group's chemistry, and transitions between levels determine its spectral lines
Level difference \(\Delta E\) links to photon wavelength through \(E = hc/\lambda\), so a Balmer transition's energy gives its visible colour and vice versa

Emission and absorption are the reverse of one another, so a cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs the same wavelengths that the hot gas would emit (used to identify elements, e.g. in stars)
Valence electron count (one for alkali metals, full shell for noble gases) explains both reactivity trends and an element's position in the table
exq: Calculate the energy in joules and in eV of a photon of wavelength 656 nm (the red Balmer line), and state which transition produces it.
Explain, with sketches, the difference between the emission and absorption spectra of hydrogen, and state how their line positions compare.
An electron in hydrogen drops from \(n=3\) to \(n=2\), releasing a photon of energy \(3.03\times10^{-19}\) J. Find the photon's frequency and wavelength, and say whether it is visible.
Why do isolated gas atoms give line spectra while a hot solid gives a continuous spectrum? Relate your answer to quantised energy levels.
Distinguish between groups and periods, and explain why alkali metals are highly reactive while noble gases are inert, using their valence electrons.

notes.t: The Periodic Table
pts: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, with groups (columns) sharing similar chemical properties.
Elements are colour-coded by class: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, rare earths, radioactive rare earths, other metals, semimetals, non-metals, noble gases and hydrogen.
The lanthanide (rare earth) and actinide (radioactive rare earth) series are shown separately beneath the main table.
defs: Alkali metals
Group 1 metals (e.g. Li, Na, K) that are highly reactive, with one valence electron.
Transition metals
Elements in the central block (groups 3–12) with partially filled d-electron shells, typically forming coloured compounds and multiple oxidation states.
Noble gases
Group 18 elements (e.g. He, Ne, Ar) with full outer electron shells, making them largely chemically unreactive.
tips: Do not confuse the groups (columns, sharing chemical behaviour) with the periods (rows, sharing electron shell count).
Remember that the lanthanide and actinide series are displayed separately, not inserted into the main table body.
rq: Why do elements in the same group tend to behave chemically alike?
They have the same number of valence (outer-shell) electrons, which determines how they bond.
Why are the noble gases so unreactive compared with the alkali metals?
Noble gases have full outer electron shells and no tendency to gain or lose electrons, whereas alkali metals readily lose their single valence electron.

notes.t: Atomic spectra and the Balmer series in hydrogen
pts: Gases of elements emit and absorb light only at specific wavelengths, producing line spectra rather than continuous spectra.
Hydrogen's Balmer series is the classic example: transitions ending in the n = 2 level produce visible lines.
Emission spectra show bright coloured lines on a dark background, while absorption spectra show dark lines on a continuous coloured background; the lines occur at the same wavelengths.
Emission occurs when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, releasing a photon of energy equal to the level difference.
Absorption occurs when an electron is excited from a lower level (here n = 2) to a higher level by absorbing a photon of exactly the matching energy.
defs: Emission spectrum
The set of discrete wavelengths of light emitted by an excited gas as electrons drop to lower energy levels.
Absorption spectrum
The set of discrete wavelengths removed from a continuous light source when passed through a cool gas, as electrons are excited to higher levels.
Balmer series
The set of visible spectral lines of hydrogen produced by electron transitions to the n = 2 energy level.
eqs: Energy of a photon emitted or absorbed during an electron transition
E = photon energy (J); h = Planck's constant (J·s); \nu = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (m/s); \lambda = wavelength (m)
tips: Do not confuse the positions of emission and absorption lines: they coincide, but emission gives bright lines on dark while absorption gives dark lines on coloured background.
Remember that spectral lines are discrete; a continuous spectrum is produced by hot solids or liquids, not by isolated gas atoms.
rq: Why does a hot gas emit only certain colours, rather than a continuous rainbow like a hot solid?
Electrons in an isolated atom can occupy only discrete energy levels, so only photons matching the differences between those levels are emitted.
Why do the dark absorption lines appear at the same wavelengths as the bright emission lines?
The same energy level gaps govern both processes: an electron absorbs only photons matching a gap it can jump across, and emits photons matching the same gap when falling back.

units.name: 3.3 Bohr model, atomic number and isotopes
units.ov: This material introduces the Bohr model of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons carrying almost all the mass, with electrons in discrete orbits that absorb or emit photons when they jump. It then uses atomic number Z to define element identity and isotopes as same-Z, different-neutron-number variants (e.g. U-235 and U-238). The ideas connect through counting particles (protons, neutrons, electrons) and using the fundamental charge and mass constants.
must: Atomic number \(Z\) = number of protons; it alone defines the element
Mass number \(A = Z + N\) (protons + neutrons); neutron number \(N = A - Z\), e.g. U-235: \(N = 235 - 92 = 143\), U-238: \(N = 146\)
Isotopes: same \(Z\), different \(N\), so different mass number and atomic mass; changing protons changes the element
Neutral atom: electrons = protons; ions have unequal numbers (the exception)
Bohr model: nucleus of protons and neutrons, electrons in discrete orbits, held by electrostatic attraction
Electron jumps between orbits absorb or emit energy as a photon (optical photon)
Elementary charge \(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\): proton +, electron −, neutron 0
Masses: \(m_p \approx m_n = 1.67\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\), \(m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\) (protons are ~1800× heavier than electrons), so the nucleus holds almost all the mass
Use SI units (kg, C); Mg has \(Z = 12\), so 12 protons and 12 electrons when neutral
The Bohr model is a simplification: orbits are not exact physical trajectories; Bohr received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 (born 1885, died 1962)
conn: Atomic number and mass number: counting protons, neutrons and electrons for an isotope or ion, then using Z to identify the element
Particle counts with the charge and mass constants: net charge of an ion (\((N_p - N_e)e\)) and atomic mass from \(Z m_p + N m_n + Z m_e\)
Isotopes with the nuclear mass fraction: isotopes differ only in neutron mass, while electron mass is negligible, so mass changes are due to the nucleus
Electron orbit jumps with electrostatic attraction and photons: energy changes in the electron's orbit correspond to emitted or absorbed light
exq: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 both have Z = 92. Calculate the number of neutrons in each and explain why they are the same element but different isotopes.
Estimate the mass of a neutral magnesium atom (Z = 12, A = 24) using \(m_p\), \(m_n\) and \(m_e\), and calculate the fraction of this mass contributed by the electrons.
Calculate the total charge, in coulombs, of the protons in a magnesium nucleus and of the electrons in a neutral atom. What is the net charge? What would it be for an Mg\(^{2+}\) ion?
Describe the Bohr model of the atom, including what happens when an electron jumps between orbits, and state two limitations of the model.
