units.name: 5.2 Crystalline vs amorphous solids
units.ov: This material classifies solids by atomic arrangement: crystalline (long-range periodic order, e.g. metals and ceramics), amorphous (only short-range order, e.g. glasses and polymers) and semicrystalline (a mixture of both, e.g. high modulus polymers). The key idea is that structure, not chemistry, determines the type: the same SiO₂ can be crystalline sand or amorphous silica gel/glass, depending on atomic arrangement and cooling or complexity. These structural differences underlie differences in properties such as melting behaviour and deformation.
must: Crystalline solid: atoms in a periodic, repeating 3D array with long-range order (typically metals and ceramics)
Amorphous solid: no long-range periodic order, though short-range order remains (typically glasses and polymers)
Semicrystalline solid: crystalline regions interspersed with amorphous regions (typically high modulus polymers); it is not the same as amorphous
Same composition can be crystalline or amorphous: SiO₂ is crystalline in silica sand and amorphous in silica gel/glass, so the difference is structural, not chemical
Noncrystalline structures form when the structure is complex or cooling is rapid, which stops atoms arranging periodically
Amorphous does not mean liquid or structureless: amorphous solids are rigid and keep local bonding and short-range order, such as a fixed number of neighbours
Soda glass: a continuous random Si–O network with Na⁺ ions sitting in the gaps
Polymers: long chains of repeating units with strong covalent intramolecular bonds along the backbone but weak secondary bonds between chains
Amorphous and polymer solids have no regular unit cell, so they lack sharp melting points and simple slip-based deformation like crystalline metals
Glasses are amorphous even though they are ceramic-based; do not classify them as crystalline ceramics
conn: Processing and structure: rapid cooling or structural complexity gives amorphous solids, while slow cooling allows periodic packing. This links to why the same SiO₂ gives sand or glass, and to semicrystalline polymers.

Structure and bonding to properties: the absence of a unit cell means no simple slip planes and no sharp melting point, and weak inter-chain bonding in polymers explains their different mechanical and thermal behaviour compared with metals.

Classification by material class: metals and ceramics are crystalline, polymers and glasses are amorphous, and high modulus polymers are semicrystalline. Exceptions such as glass (a ceramic that is amorphous) are commonly tested.
exq: Define crystalline, amorphous and semicrystalline solids and give a typical material class for each.
Silica sand and silica gel both have composition SiO₂. Explain why they are different types of solid and sketch the atomic arrangement of each.
Describe the structure of soda glass, including the role of sodium ions, and explain why it is classified as amorphous rather than crystalline.
Explain how bonding in a polymer differs along a chain and between chains, and why polymers lack a regular unit cell and a sharp melting point compared with a metal.
Under what conditions do noncrystalline solids form, and why does a semicrystalline polymer have different properties from a fully amorphous one?

notes.t: Types of solids
pts: Crystalline solids have atoms packed in an organised, repeating structure; typically metals and ceramics.
Amorphous solids have atoms packed together randomly, with no long-range order; typically polymers and glasses.
Semicrystalline solids contain both crystalline regions and amorphous regions; typically high modulus polymers.
defs: Crystalline solid
A solid in which atoms are arranged in an organised, periodically repeating structure (long-range order).
Amorphous solid
A solid in which atoms are packed together randomly, with no long-range order.
Semicrystalline solid
A solid containing regions that are crystalline interspersed with regions that are amorphous.
tips: Do not confuse semicrystalline with amorphous: semicrystalline materials contain ordered crystalline regions as well as amorphous ones.
Glasses are amorphous even though they look solid; do not classify them as crystalline ceramics just because they are ceramic-based.
rq: Why are metals and ceramics typically crystalline, while polymers and glasses are typically amorphous?

Metals and ceramics bond in ways that favour ordered, close packing as atoms solidify, whereas polymer chains and glass network structures tend to freeze in a disordered state, and their long molecules or rapid cooling hinder ordering.
What might a semicrystalline polymer's properties look like compared with a fully amorphous one?
The crystalline regions add stiffness and a higher modulus, so semicrystalline polymers are generally stiffer and stronger than fully amorphous polymers of the same type.

notes.t: Types of solids: crystalline vs noncrystalline
pts: Crystalline materials have atoms packed in periodic, 3D arrays, typical of metals, many ceramics and some polymers.
Noncrystalline materials have atoms with no periodic packing; they form for complex structures or rapid cooling.
Noncrystalline materials occur for complex structures and under rapid cooling, which stops atoms arranging periodically.
Crystalline and noncrystalline SiO₂ share the same Si and O atoms but differ in long-range order: the crystalline form is periodic, the noncrystalline (glass) form is random.
defs: Crystalline material
A solid whose atoms are packed in a periodic, repeating three-dimensional array.
Noncrystalline (amorphous) material
A solid in which atoms have no periodic, long-range packing; also called amorphous.
tips: Do not confuse 'noncrystalline' with 'no atoms bonded': noncrystalline solids are still solids with local bonding, lacking only long-range periodic order.
Crystalline and noncrystalline forms of the same compound (e.g. SiO₂) have identical chemistry; the difference is structural, not compositional.
rq: Why does rapid cooling tend to produce a noncrystalline solid rather than a crystalline one?
Rapid cooling gives atoms too little time to diffuse and settle into periodic positions, so they freeze in a disordered arrangement.
Both crystalline and noncrystalline SiO₂ contain the same atoms, so what distinguishes them?
Their atomic arrangement: crystalline SiO₂ has a repeating 3D order, while noncrystalline SiO₂ has a random network with no long-range periodicity.

notes.t: Types of solids: crystalline vs noncrystalline (amorphous) SiO₂
pts: Silica sand is crystalline SiO₂, with Si and O atoms arranged in a regular, repeating long-range pattern.
Silica gel is noncrystalline (amorphous) SiO₂: the same Si–O building blocks form a disordered network with no long-range repeating order.
Both forms have the same chemical composition (SiO₂); the difference lies in atomic arrangement, not chemistry.
Crystalline solids show ordered, periodic atomic packing, whereas amorphous solids lack this long-range order despite being solid.
defs: Crystalline solid
A solid in which atoms are arranged in a regular, periodic, long-range repeating pattern.
Noncrystalline (amorphous) solid
A solid whose atoms lack long-range periodic order, though short-range order may exist between neighbouring atoms.
tips: Do not assume that different materials are needed for crystalline and amorphous forms; the same chemical composition can give both, depending on atomic arrangement.
Amorphous does not mean liquid or 'no structure': amorphous solids still have short-range order between neighbouring atoms.
rq: Why can silica sand and silica gel both be made of SiO₂ yet behave as different materials?

Because the atomic arrangement differs: sand is crystalline with ordered repeating structure, while silica gel is amorphous with a disordered network, changing properties such as packing and water adsorption.
What would happen to the regular order if the crystalline SiO₂ were melted and rapidly cooled?
The atoms would be frozen in a disordered arrangement, forming a noncrystalline (amorphous) solid such as glass, since there is insufficient time for periodic ordering.

notes.t: Types of solids: amorphous and polymer structures
pts: Amorphous solids such as soda glass have no long-range periodic arrangement of atoms; the silicon-oxygen network is randomly connected with sodium ions sitting in gaps.
In soda glass the silicon and oxygen atoms form a continuous random network, with sodium atoms held within the open spaces of the network.
A polymer molecule is a long chain of repeating carbon and hydrogen atoms, bonded covalently along the backbone, which gives strong intramolecular bonding but weaker bonding between chains.
Unlike crystalline metals, amorphous and polymer solids lack a regular repeating unit cell, so they do not show sharp melting points or simple slip-based deformation in the same way.
defs: Amorphous solid
A solid whose atoms lack long-range periodic order, having only short-range order such as a fixed number of neighbours around each atom.
Polymer
A large molecule built from many repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds, forming long chains.
tips: Do not confuse amorphous solids with crystalline solids: amorphous materials have no repeating unit cell, even though they are rigid.
Polymer chains are held together by strong covalent bonds along the chain but only weak secondary forces between chains; do not treat the whole polymer as a single strongly bonded network.
rq: Why can soda glass be solid yet still lack a crystal structure?
Its atoms are linked into a rigid, continuous three-dimensional network, so it is held together strongly, but the network has no repeating unit cell or long-range periodicity.
What would happen to the properties of soda glass if sodium oxide were removed from the network?
The network would be more tightly cross-linked, giving a higher melting/softening temperature and greater hardness, while sodium ions (which break Si–O–Si bonds) would no longer modify the structure.

units.name: 5.3 Carbon polymorphs: fullerenes, nanotubes, graphene
units.ov: This module surveys the polymorphs of carbon: diamond, graphite, amorphous carbon black, fullerenes (C60), carbon nanotubes and graphene. All share the same chemistry, and their very different properties come from how the atoms are arranged and bonded. Graphene (a single hexagonal sheet) is the building block that links graphite (stacked sheets), nanotubes (rolled sheets) and fullerenes (curved, closed sheets with pentagons).
must: Polymorphs have the same chemical composition but different atomic arrangements, and structure (not chemistry) determines properties.
Diamond is cubic, with each C atom tetrahedrally bonded to four neighbours, so it is very hard.
Graphite is stacked hexagonal-ring layers with weak (van der Waals) bonding between layers, so the layers slide easily.
Graphene is a single one-atom-thick honeycomb layer of graphite; it was isolated by Geim and Novoselov (Manchester, Nobel Prize in Physics 2010).
Fullerenes (e.g. C60, 'bucky balls') are discrete closed hollow cages of pentagons and hexagons, like a football. They are molecular solids, not extended networks.
Carbon nanotubes are rolled graphene sheets capped by half-buckyball hemispheres. They can be single-walled (SWNT, one layer) or multiwalled (MWNT, concentric layers).
Carbon black is amorphous, with no long-range crystalline order despite being pure carbon.
Name origin: fullerenes honour R. Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes use the same design principle. Spell it 'fullerene'.
Do not confuse graphene (single sheet) with graphite (many stacked sheets), or nanotubes (rolled sheet) with graphite (stacked layers).
conn: Graphene is the parent structure: stacked gives graphite, rolled gives a nanotube, and curved with pentagons gives a fullerene.
Bonding and structure explain properties: tetrahedral 3D bonding makes diamond hard, while weak interlayer bonding makes graphite slippery and soft.
Crystalline versus amorphous: diamond and graphite have long-range order, whereas carbon black lacks it, so composition alone cannot predict properties.
Molecular versus extended solids: C60 is a discrete molecule, whereas diamond and graphite are extended networks, which affects how each is described and used.
exq: Define a polymorph and explain, using diamond and graphite, why two materials of identical composition can have very different hardness.
Describe the structure of C60, stating the types of faces in the cage and the origin of the name 'bucky ball'.
Distinguish between single-walled and multiwalled carbon nanotubes, and explain how a nanotube is related to graphene and to fullerenes.
Compare graphene and graphite in terms of structure, thickness and interlayer bonding, and state who isolated graphene and when they were recognised.
Explain why carbon black is described as amorphous and how its structure differs from that of diamond.

notes.t: Carbon polymorphs
pts: Carbon exists in several polymorphic forms, each with different atomic arrangements and therefore different properties.
Diamond has a cubic crystal structure in which each carbon atom is bonded tetrahedrally to four neighbours, making it very hard.
Graphite consists of stacked layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings, with weak bonding between layers, so the layers slide over each other.
Fullerenes (bucky balls) and nanotubes are closed-cage or extended carbon structures, while graphene is a single layer of graphite.
Carbon black is an amorphous form of carbon, lacking long-range crystalline order.
defs: Polymorph
A material that can exist in more than one crystal structure (or atomic arrangement) while having the same chemical composition.
Fullerene
A closed-cage molecule of carbon atoms, such as C60, arranged in pentagons and hexagons (bucky ball).
Amorphous carbon
A form of carbon with no long-range crystalline order, such as carbon black.
tips: Do not confuse polymorphs (same composition, different structure) with allotropes-only terms; state clearly that the structure, not the chemistry, determines the properties.
Remember that carbon black is amorphous, so it has no regular crystal structure despite being made of carbon.
rq: Why can graphite be used as a lubricant and pencil lead, while diamond cannot?
In graphite, layers are bonded weakly to each other (van der Waals forces), so they slide easily; in diamond, every atom is strongly covalently bonded in 3D, so no easy slip plane exists.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. What explains their very different hardness?
The difference lies in the atomic arrangement and bonding: diamond's rigid tetrahedral 3D covalent network versus graphite's layered structure with weak interlayer bonding.

notes.t: Carbon: Fullerenes (Bucky Balls)
pts: Fullerene C60 is a carbon allotrope whose molecules form closed hollow cages.
The C60 cage is built from a mixture of pentagonal (5-sided) and hexagonal (6-sided) faces, like a football.
The name 'Bucky Balls' honours Richard Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes share the same design principle.
defs: Fullerene
A molecular form of carbon (e.g. C60) consisting of closed, hollow cages of carbon atoms arranged in pentagonal and hexagonal rings.
tips: Do not confuse fullerenes (discrete molecules, C60) with graphite or diamond (extended networks); fullerenes are molecular solids.
Remember the spelling and the name origin: 'fullerene' after R. Buckminster Fuller, not 'fullerine' in exam answers.
rq: Why must a closed carbon cage contain exactly 12 pentagons regardless of its size?
Euler's polyhedron theorem for a closed sphere of trivalent carbon atoms requires 12 pentagonal faces (with any number of hexagons) to close the surface; C60 has 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
What would happen to the cage if pentagons were replaced entirely by hexagons?
The surface would be flat (like graphene) and could not close into a sphere, so no hollow cage would form.

notes.t: Carbon nanotubes
pts: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical structures with half-buckyball caps at each end joined by tubular walls.
Carbon nanotubes can exist as a single wall or as multiple concentric walls.
defs: Carbon nanotube
A nanoscale cylinder of rolled-up graphene sheets capped at each end by half-buckyball (fullerene-like) hemispheres.
Single-walled nanotube
A carbon nanotube consisting of one cylindrical layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
Multiwalled nanotube
A carbon nanotube made of several concentric cylindrical layers of carbon atoms.
tips: Do not confuse carbon nanotubes (tubes with fullerene-type caps) with simple graphite; the structure is a rolled graphene sheet, not stacked layers.
rq: Why does a nanotube need hemispherical caps at its ends rather than simply open ends?
Open ends leave dangling bonds that are unstable; half-buckyball caps close the structure so every carbon atom is bonded to three neighbours, lowering energy.
How would the properties of a multiwalled nanotube differ from a single-walled one of the same diameter?

Multiwalled tubes have more layers, interlayer van der Waals interactions and typically larger overall diameter, usually making them less uniform and with different electrical behaviour than a single-walled tube.

notes.t: Carbon: graphene
pts: Graphene is a two-dimensional sheet of carbon atoms, essentially a single layer of graphite.
Graphene was isolated and studied experimentally by Geim and Novoselov at Manchester, recognised with the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
defs: Graphene
A two-dimensional sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice, one atom thick, forming the basic layer of graphite.
tips: Do not confuse graphene (single sheet) with graphite (many stacked sheets bonded by weak van der Waals forces).
Graphene is a single layer; quoting its thickness as a bulk-material value is a common error.
rq: Why is graphene described as two-dimensional even though it is made of carbon atoms that have three-dimensional bonding in diamond?

In graphene each carbon bonds in-plane to three neighbours (sp² bonding) and is only one atom thick, so the sheet has no thickness in the third dimension; diamond's sp³ tetrahedral network is three-dimensional.
What would happen to graphene's properties if you stacked many sheets together?
Stacking sheets gives bulk graphite, where weak van der Waals forces between layers allow them to slide, making graphite soft and lubricating.

units.name: 5.4 Crystal structure basics and assumptions
units.ov: This material introduces crystal structure as the way atoms pack in space, modelled with hard spheres joined by spring-like bonds and arranged to minimise energy. It builds from 2-D close packing to the three common metallic structures (BCC, FCC, HCP), and frames perfect lattices as a reference from which real defects and their effects on properties are later understood.
must: Crystal structure = arrangement of atoms in space; microstructure = grains and phase distribution. Do not confuse them.
Hard-sphere model: atoms are rigid spheres of fixed size, and only the bonds (spring-like) deform, at an energy cost.
Packing is driven by minimising the energy of the bonded atoms, not simply by maximising density. State this reasoning explicitly.
Packing depends on bond type and relative atomic size; structure can change with temperature (allotropy/polymorphism).
In 2-D, hexagonal packing leaves less empty space than square packing; close-packed layers stack to build 3-D structures.
There are 14 Bravais lattices, but most metals use only BCC, FCC or HCP.
BCC: atoms at 8 corners plus 1 at the centre, giving \(2\) atoms per unit cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+1\)).
FCC: atoms at 8 corners plus 6 face centres, giving \(4\) atoms per cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+6\times\tfrac12\)).
HCP is hexagonal (not cubic) with ABAB layer stacking and is close packed; FCC is also close packed (ABCABC stacking).
Real crystals always contain defects; the perfect lattice is only a reference model, and defects explain real properties.
conn: Energy minimisation and bond type determine the packing, which determines the structure (BCC/FCC/HCP) and so properties such as density and packing efficiency.
2-D close packing leads to 3-D stacking sequences: ABAB gives HCP, while ABC stacking gives FCC.
Unit-cell atom counting links to density calculations: \(\rho = nA/(V_c N_A)\), together with atomic radius and cell edge length \(a\).
Perfect lattice versus defects: the ideal structure is the baseline, and deviations (defects) explain deviations in mechanical behaviour.
exq: Calculate the number of atoms per unit cell for BCC and FCC, showing the corner and face contributions, and state which is more densely packed.
Explain why atoms adopt ordered crystal structures, referring to the hard-sphere and spring-bond assumptions and to energy minimisation.
Compare square and hexagonal 2-D packing and describe how close-packed layers are stacked to give HCP and FCC structures.
Distinguish between crystal structure and microstructure, and explain why a real crystal differs from the ideal lattice and why this matters.
Describe the unit cells of BCC, FCC and HCP, and explain why HCP is not classed as a cubic structure even though it is close packed.

notes.t: Crystal structure
pts: Crystal structure describes how atoms in a crystal are packed together in space.
The packing arrangement is governed by the type of interatomic bonds present.
The relative sizes of the atoms strongly influence the resulting packing arrangement.
Real crystals may be perfect or contain distortions from the ideal lattice.
A material can change between different crystal structures as temperature changes.
tips: Do not confuse crystal structure (arrangement of atoms) with microstructure (grain size and phase distribution).
Remember that real crystals are often imperfect, so ideal lattice descriptions are approximations.
rq: Why would two metals with similar bonding but very different atomic radii adopt different crystal structures?
Atomic size ratio changes how atoms can pack; different radii allow or prevent close packing in a given geometry, so the structure changes.
What might happen to a crystal structure when it is heated, and why?
It may transform to a different structure (polymorphism/allotropy) because the stable arrangement depends on temperature, as thermal energy changes the balance of packing and bonding.

notes.t: Crystal structure: assumptions for atomic packing
pts: Atoms are modelled as hard, spherical particles with fixed size.
Atoms themselves cannot change shape; only the bonds between them can deform.
Bonds act like springs: they deform easily but deforming them costs energy.
Crystal structures form because atoms arrange themselves to minimise the energy needed to hold them together.
tips: Do not confuse the assumptions: atoms are rigid, but the bonds between them are the deformable part that costs energy.
Packing is driven by minimising energy, not by maximising density alone; state this reasoning explicitly in exam answers.
rq: Why does treating atoms as non-deformable spheres still allow realistic crystal structures to be predicted?

Because the rigid-sphere packing sets the geometry, while the deformable bonds let the structure relax slightly; the energy-minimising arrangement is the one that packs spheres most efficiently with the least bond strain.
What would happen to packing if bonds were infinitely stiff?
Atoms could not adjust their separation to lower energy, so the structure would be fixed by the initial geometry and energy minimisation would have little effect on arrangement.

notes.t: Crystal structure: perfect structures, defects and their effects
pts: Study crystal structure in a logical sequence: first the ideal (perfect) lattice, then deviations from it, then how those deviations affect properties.
Real crystals always contain imperfections (defects), so the perfect structure is a reference model rather than an everyday reality.
Defects in the crystal structure change material behaviour, so their effects must be understood, not just their existence.
tips: Do not treat the perfect crystal as realistic; real materials always contain defects, which are essential to explaining their properties.
Remember that this slide is only an outline: the defects and their effects are developed in the following slides.
rq: Why do engineers begin with the perfect crystal structure before studying defects?
The perfect lattice provides a reference model; deviations from it (defects) can then be described and their effects on properties understood systematically.
If a metal's crystal contains no defects at all, what would you expect its strength to be compared with a real metal, and why?
Ideal, defect-free crystals are far stronger than real metals in theory, because defects such as dislocations are what allow plastic deformation at low stresses.

notes.t: Crystal structure: stacking atoms to minimize empty space
pts: In 2-D, atoms packed in a hexagonal arrangement leave less empty space than a square arrangement.
Close-packed 2-D layers can be stacked on top of each other to build 3-D crystal structures.
tips: Do not confuse the 2-D packing comparison with the full 3-D crystal: this slide only shows layers, not the stacking sequence of the 3-D structure.
Remember that the square arrangement is less dense; avoid claiming it is the most efficient packing.
rq: Why does the hexagonal arrangement of atoms leave less empty space than the square arrangement?

Each circle in the hexagonal layer touches six neighbours, so the circles nest into the gaps between one another, whereas in the square layer each circle touches only four neighbours, leaving larger gaps between them.
Why is stacking close-packed 2-D layers the natural next step toward a 3-D crystal?
Because the layers that already minimise empty space in 2-D can be repeated vertically, so the packing efficiency is preserved in three dimensions.

notes.t: Crystal structure: common packing arrangements
pts: There are 14 possible (Bravais) lattice arrangements for packing atoms in crystals.
Despite 14 possibilities, most common metallic structures are two cubic and one hexagonal.
The three common structures are BCC, FCC and HCP.
defs: Body Centred Cubic (BCC)
A cubic crystal structure with atoms at the 8 corners of the unit cell plus one atom at the cube centre.
Face Centred Cubic (FCC)
A cubic crystal structure with atoms at the 8 corners plus one atom at the centre of each of the 6 faces.
Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP)
A hexagonal crystal structure in which atoms are closely packed in layers with ABAB stacking, giving the highest packing efficiency of the common structures.
tips: Do not confuse BCC (2 atoms per cell) with FCC (4 atoms per cell) when counting atoms.
HCP is a hexagonal structure, not a cubic one, even though it is close packed.
rq: Why are only three of the 14 possible packing arrangements commonly found in metals?

Metals bond non-directionally (metallic bonding), so atoms pack to maximise density and coordination; BCC, FCC and HCP give high packing efficiency and are energetically favourable, unlike the other lattices.
What would change if the BCC structure were replaced by simple cubic packing?
Simple cubic has only 1 atom per cell and a packing fraction of about 0.52 versus 0.68 for BCC, so it is less dense and rarely occurs in metals.

units.name: 5.5 Close-packed structures: FCC vs HCP stacking
units.ov: This material covers close-packed crystal structures, in which atoms are modelled as hard spheres packed as densely as possible in layers. FCC (ABCABC stacking) and HCP (ABAB stacking) are built from identical close-packed layers and differ only in stacking sequence. Both have the same packing fraction (0.74), and which one a metal adopts is energy-driven but not examinable here.
must: FCC = Face Centred Cubic and HCP = Hexagonal Close Packed; give the full names when defining them
FCC stacking is \(ABCABC\), repeating every third layer, so layer 3 sits in a different position from layer 1
HCP stacking is \(ABAB\), repeating every second layer, so layers alternate between two positions
Both are close packed with the same packing fraction \(0.74\); HCP is not denser than FCC
The two structures differ only in stacking sequence, not in the close-packed layers themselves; identify the sequence before naming the structure
Atoms are modelled as hard spheres touching their nearest neighbours; this is a packing model, not real atomic overlap or bonding geometry
Each new layer sits in one of two hollow positions on the layer below; it cannot sit in any position and still be close packed
FCC unit cell has atoms at each corner and at the centre of each face; FCC is close packed but BCC is not
Examples: FCC metals are Al, Cu, Ni; HCP metals are Mg, Zn, Ti
Structure selection is energy-driven; the detailed reasons are not covered in this course
conn: The two-hollow-position rule produces both stacking sequences: ABAB if the third layer returns to the first position, ABCABC if it takes the other hollow
Same close-packed layers imply the same packing fraction (0.74), so stacking sequence alone cannot change density
Stacking sequence links to structure name and then to material examples (ABC gives FCC gives Al, Cu, Ni; AB gives HCP gives Mg, Zn, Ti)
The hard-sphere model links packing fraction to why FCC and HCP are contrasted with the non-close-packed BCC
exq: Define a close-packed structure and state the full names of FCC and HCP. (3 marks)
Sketch the stacking sequences of FCC and HCP, labelling the layer positions A, B and C, and state after how many layers each repeats.
A student claims HCP is more densely packed than FCC. Explain with reference to packing fraction (0.74) and stacking why this is wrong.
Explain why a new close-packed layer cannot sit in an arbitrary position on the layer below, and how the two hollow sites lead to FCC or HCP.
Classify aluminium, magnesium, copper and titanium as FCC or HCP, and state the stacking sequence of each.

notes.t: Close packed structures
pts: Atoms are modelled as hard spheres when describing crystal packing.
Atoms are packed in layers as closely as geometrically possible to minimise empty space.
Each new close-packed layer sits in one of two possible hollow positions on the layer below, so stacking sequences such as ABAB or ABCABC arise.
defs: Close packed structure
A crystal arrangement in which spherical atoms are packed as closely as possible, with each layer nestling into the hollows of the layer beneath it.
tips: Atoms are treated as hard spheres touching their nearest neighbours; do not confuse this model with real atomic overlap or bonding geometry.
Do not state that a close-packed layer can sit in any position; only the two hollow positions give close packing.
rq: Why does each new layer have only two possible positions rather than any position?

Each close-packed layer's atoms sit in the hollows formed by three neighbours in the layer below; of the two sets of hollows available (B and C relative to A), a new layer must occupy one of them to achieve close packing, giving two choices.
What would happen to packing efficiency if the spheres were stacked in a simple square array directly on top of each other?
Packing would be less efficient because the spheres would not nest into hollows, leaving more empty space, so the structure would not be close packed.

notes.t: Close packed structures
pts: Close packed structures are the two crystal structures in which atoms pack together as densely as possible.
There are two types of close packed structure: FCC and HCP.
FCC stands for Face Centred Cubic, a cubic close packed arrangement.
HCP stands for Hexagonal Close Packed, a hexagonal close packed arrangement.
defs: Close packed structure
A crystal structure in which atoms are arranged to fill space as efficiently as possible, giving the maximum packing density for equal-sized spheres.
FCC (Face Centred Cubic)
A close packed cubic crystal structure with atoms at each corner and at the centre of each face of the unit cell.
HCP (Hexagonal Close Packed)
A close packed hexagonal crystal structure with an ABAB stacking sequence of close packed layers.
tips: Do not confuse FCC with BCC; FCC is close packed, BCC is not.
Give the full names (Face Centred Cubic, Hexagonal Close Packed) rather than only the abbreviations when asked to define them.
rq: Why are FCC and HCP both called close packed, even though their unit cells have different shapes?

Both place atoms in layers that pack as densely as possible, giving the same maximum packing fraction (about 74%); they differ only in the stacking sequence of those layers (ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP).
What would you expect to change if the close packed layers were stacked in a different sequence?
The crystal structure would change, but the packing density would stay the same, since the close packed layers themselves are unchanged.

notes.t: FCC versus HCP crystal structures
pts: FCC and HCP are both close-packed structures built from stacked close-packed layers; they differ only in the stacking sequence of those layers.
In FCC, the layer stacking repeats in an ABCABC sequence, so the third layer sits in a different position from the first.
In HCP, the layer stacking repeats in an ABAB sequence, so the layers alternate between two positions.
The diagrams show close-packed layers of spheres sitting in the hollows of the layer below, with the layers shown as coloured rows of spheres.
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence with the crystal lattice: FCC and HCP both have the same close-packed layers, so identifying the stacking pattern (ABC versus AB) is what distinguishes them.
rq: Why do FCC and HCP have the same packing density even though their stacking sequences differ?

Both are close-packed arrangements: each layer of spheres sits in the hollows of the layer below, giving the maximum packing fraction of about 0.74, and the stacking variant does not change the local arrangement within each layer.

notes.t: FCC versus HCP stacking
pts: FCC and HCP are two close-packed structures that differ only in how successive layers of atoms are stacked.
FCC stacking repeats every third layer, giving the sequence ABCABC.
HCP stacking repeats every second layer, giving the sequence ABABAB.
Different metals adopt one stacking or the other depending on their atoms.
Common FCC metals include aluminium, copper and nickel; common HCP metals include magnesium, zinc and titanium.
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence with the crystal name: ABC gives FCC and AB gives HCP, so check the sequence before naming the structure.
FCC and HCP are both close-packed with the same packing fraction (0.74), so do not claim HCP is more densely packed than FCC.
rq: Why does the ABAB stacking give a hexagonal structure while ABCABC does not?

In ABAB stacking the B layer sits directly above the first A layer, so the layers repeat in a hexagonal pattern with a two-layer period; in ABCABC the third layer is offset from both previous layers, giving a cubic structure with a three-layer period.
If a metal's atoms are close-packed, what determines whether it forms FCC or HCP?
The stacking sequence the atoms adopt, which depends on the atoms involved, since both structures have the same packing density (74%).

notes.t: Crystallographic types
pts: Specific crystallographic types appear in particular materials, generally because of energy considerations.
The reasons for which crystal structure forms in a given material are not covered in this lecture course.
tips: This page only states that crystal type selection is energy-driven; do not assume the detailed energy arguments are examinable in this lecture course.
rq: Why would a material's crystal structure be expected to adopt the arrangement with the lowest energy?
Atoms settle into arrangements that minimise the system's total energy, so the stable crystal type is the one with the lowest energy for that material's bonding and atomic size.

units.name: 5.6 Unit cells and atom counting: FCC, HCP, BCC
units.ov: This material introduces the unit cell as the smallest repeating block that generates a whole crystal by translation. It shows how to count the effective atoms per cell for FCC, HCP and BCC by weighting each atom by the fraction of it lying inside the cell. The results are 4 for FCC, 6 for HCP and 2 for BCC, and these counts feed into later density and packing calculations.
must: Unit cell = smallest repeating entity; translating it in 3D builds the whole lattice
Atoms drawn in a cell are not atoms owned by the cell: weight each by its sharing fraction
Sharing fractions in cubic cells: corner \(1/8\), face centre \(1/2\), edge \(1/4\), interior \(1\)
FCC: \(N = \frac{8}{8} + \frac{6}{2} = 4\) atoms per cell (8 corners + 6 face centres, 14 drawn)
BCC: \(N = \frac{8}{8} + 1 = 2\) atoms per cell (8 corners + 1 body centre, 9 drawn)
HCP: \(N = \frac{12}{6} + \frac{2}{2} + 3 = 6\) atoms per cell (12 corners at \(1/6\), 2 basal face centres at \(1/2\), 3 interior atoms)
HCP corner atoms are shared by 6 cells, not 8, because the cell is hexagonal and not cubic
HCP is close-packed with hexagonal layers stacked ABAB; do not confuse it with FCC or BCC
Common errors: counting all drawn atoms as whole atoms, and mixing up 4 (FCC), 2 (BCC) and 6 (HCP)
The count \(N\) is dimensionless and must be an integer for a complete cell
conn: Atom counting \(N\) feeds into density: \(\rho = \frac{N A}{V_c N_A}\), where \(V_c\) comes from the cell geometry such as \(a^3\) for cubic cells
Counting atoms and cell geometry (relating \(a\) to atomic radius \(R\)) combine to give the atomic packing factor: \(\mathrm{APF} = \frac{N \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}{V_c}\)
The sharing-fraction method depends on cell shape: cubic cells use 1/8 at corners but hexagonal cells use 1/6, so the cell geometry determines the weighting
Close-packed structures (FCC and HCP) have higher packing and coordination than BCC, which links atom counts to material properties
exq: Define a unit cell. Show by calculation that an FCC unit cell contains 4 atoms and a BCC unit cell contains 2 atoms, stating the sharing fraction for each atom position.
An HCP unit cell has 12 corner atoms, 2 face-centre atoms and 3 interior atoms. Calculate the number of atoms per cell and explain why corner atoms contribute \(1/6\) rather than \(1/8\).
A student says an FCC cell has 14 atoms and a BCC cell has 9. Explain the error and give the correct effective counts.
Copper is FCC with lattice parameter \(a\) and atomic mass \(A\). Using the number of atoms per cell, derive an expression for its density and then evaluate it.
Compare FCC, BCC and HCP in terms of atoms per unit cell and stacking, and state which are close-packed.

notes.t: FCC unit cell
pts: FCC atoms form the corners of a cube, with further atoms at the centre of each face.
The FCC unit cell contains 14 atoms involved in it: 8 corner atoms and 6 face-centred atoms.
A unit cell is the small repeat entity from which the whole crystal structure can be built by translation.
Most unit cells are parallelepipeds or prisms in shape.
defs: Unit cell
The smallest repeating entity of a crystal structure; stacking copies of it in three dimensions generates the whole lattice.
tips: Do not count all 14 drawn atoms as belonging to one cell; corner and face atoms are shared, giving 4 effective atoms per FCC cell.
Remember the face-centre atoms are shared between two neighbouring cells, so each contributes only half.
rq: Why does the FCC unit cell contain 14 atoms when only 8 corner atoms are at the cube's vertices?

Corner atoms are shared by 8 cells (8 × 1/8 = 1) and face atoms are shared by 2 cells (6 × 1/2 = 3), so the cube holds 4 atoms in total; the 14 quoted counts all atoms touching the drawn cube, not atoms belonging to it.

notes.t: FCC unit cell: atoms per cell
pts: An FCC unit cell has 8 corner atoms, each shared by 8 cells, so each corner contributes 1/8 of an atom.
An FCC unit cell has 6 face-centred (side) atoms, each shared by 2 cells, so each face contributes 1/2 of an atom.
Adding the shared contributions gives 4 atoms per FCC unit cell.
eqs: Number of atoms per FCC unit cell (corner plus face contributions)

N = number of atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); 8 = number of corner atoms; 6 = number of face-centred atoms; 8 = number of cells sharing each corner atom; 2 = number of cells sharing each face atom
tips: Do not count all 8 corner and 6 face atoms as whole atoms; use the sharing fractions 1/8 and 1/2 to get 4 atoms per FCC cell.
Remember the sharing factors differ: corners are shared by 8 cells, faces by 2 cells.
rq: Why does a corner atom count as only 1/8 of an atom in the unit cell rather than a whole atom?
A corner atom is shared by 8 neighbouring unit cells meeting at that corner, so only one-eighth of it lies within any single cell.
What would the atom count be if you wrongly counted all 14 atoms as belonging entirely to one cell?
You would get 14, which overcounts; correct sharing gives 4 atoms per cell, showing why fractional contributions are needed.

notes.t: Corner atoms in unit cells
pts: A corner atom is shared by eight neighbouring unit cells, so only a fraction of it belongs to any one cell.
Because each corner atom is shared equally among 8 cells, each cell receives 1/8 of that atom.
Counting atoms per cell therefore requires weighting atoms by their position: corners count 1/8, so the cell's atom count is not simply the number of atoms drawn.
tips: Do not count a corner atom as a full atom in a single cell; always apply the 1/8 weighting when counting atoms per unit cell.
Remember this sharing rule applies to corners only; face- and edge-centred atoms are shared by different numbers of cells (2 and 4 respectively).
rq: Why does a corner atom contribute only 1/8 to a single unit cell rather than a full atom?
Because the atom sits at a corner shared by 8 cubes that meet there, and each cube receives an equal share, so 8 × 1/8 = 1 whole atom in total.
If a corner atom contributes 1/8 to each cell, how many atoms does a simple cubic unit cell (8 corner atoms) contain?
8 × 1/8 = 1 atom per unit cell.

notes.t: Hexagonal close packed (HCP) crystal structure
pts: HCP is a close-packed crystal structure with a hexagonal geometry.
The basic repeat unit consists of two layers, each containing seven atoms, with three atoms sitting between the layers.
A unit cell of HCP involves 17 atoms in total when atoms shared between neighbouring cells are counted.
defs: Hexagonal close packed (HCP)
A close-packed crystal structure in which atoms form hexagonal layers stacked in an ABAB sequence, with a basic repeat unit of two layers of seven atoms each plus three atoms between them.
tips: Do not confuse the 17 atoms counted in the repeat unit/unit cell with the number of atoms that actually belong to a single cell; shared atoms must be accounted for as fractions.
Remember HCP is hexagonal close packed, not body-centred or face-centred cubic; the close-packed layers follow an ABAB stacking sequence.
rq: Why does the HCP unit cell contain 17 atoms rather than the 6 or so you might count on a single cell's corners and faces?

Atoms on cell corners, faces and edges are shared with neighbouring cells, so only fractions of them belong to any one cell; the 17 atoms counted include the atoms in the full hexagonal prism arrangement and its shared contributions, reflecting the repeat unit of seven atoms per layer plus three between layers.
What would change in the stacking if the three atoms between the two layers were positioned directly above the atoms of the layers instead of in the hollows?
That arrangement would not be close packed; atoms must sit in the depressions of the adjacent layer to achieve the dense hexagonal packing characteristic of HCP.

notes.t: HCP unit cell atom count
pts: Atoms in a unit cell are shared with neighbouring cells, so only fractional shares of boundary atoms belong to each cell.
Each of the 12 corner atoms is shared by 6 cells, so it contributes 1/6 of an atom to one cell.
Each of the 2 central face atoms is shared by 2 cells, contributing 1/2 atom each.
The 3 central (interior) atoms belong entirely to one cell, contributing a full atom each.
Total atoms per HCP unit cell is 6.
eqs: Atoms per HCP unit cell (sum of shared contributions)
N = number of atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); 12 = corner atoms; 6 = cells sharing each corner atom; 2 = central face atoms; 2 = cells sharing each face atom; 3 = interior atoms
tips: Do not treat boundary atoms as belonging wholly to one cell; apply the sharing fraction (1/6 corner, 1/2 face, 1 interior).
Remember the total of 6 atoms per HCP cell; confusing it with FCC (4 atoms) or BCC (2 atoms) is a common error.
rq: Why is a corner atom counted as 1/6 of an atom rather than a full atom?
Each corner atom is shared among 6 neighbouring unit cells, so only one sixth of it lies within any single cell.
What would the count be if you wrongly treated all 12 corner atoms as belonging fully to one cell?
You would get 12 + 1 + 3 = 16 atoms, overcounting because corner atoms are shared; the correct total is 6.

notes.t: Body-centred cubic (BCC) crystal structure
pts: BCC has one atom at the centre of the cube, in addition to the corner atoms.
The unit cell of BCC contains nine atoms involved in the cell: eight corner atoms plus one central atom.
tips: Do not confuse the nine atoms drawn in the cell with the atoms effectively belonging to it: BCC has 2 atoms per unit cell once corner sharing is accounted for.
rq: Why does the BCC unit cell count nine atoms, but only two atoms actually belong to each cell in the lattice?

The nine atoms are those drawn in or touching the cell. Each of the eight corner atoms is shared by eight cells, contributing 1/8 each (total 1), and the central atom lies wholly inside, contributing 1, giving 2 atoms per cell.

notes.t: Atoms per unit cell in BCC structure
pts: A BCC unit cell has 8 corner atoms, each shared by 8 cells, so each corner contributes 1/8 atom to any one cell.
The single central body atom lies wholly inside one cell, so it contributes a full atom.
Total atoms per BCC unit cell = 8 × 1/8 + 1 = 2.
defs: Unit cell
The smallest repeating block of a crystal structure that, when stacked in three dimensions, generates the whole lattice.
eqs: Number of atoms per unit cell for BCC (corner atoms shared among cells plus body-centre atom)
N = total atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); 8 = number of corner atoms; 1/8 = fraction of each corner atom belonging to one cell; 1 = central atom wholly within the cell
tips: Do not count all 8 corner atoms as full atoms; each contributes only 1/8, giving 1 atom from corners plus the body-centre atom, total 2.
Remember the body-centre atom counts as 1 (it is not shared), so BCC is 2 atoms, not 9/8 or 8/8 alone.
rq: Why does a corner atom count as only 1/8 of an atom for a given cell?
A corner atom is shared by the 8 unit cells meeting at that corner, so each cell owns only 1/8 of it.
Why does the central atom count as a full atom while corner atoms do not?
The central atom lies entirely inside the one cell, so no other cell shares it.

units.name: 5.7 FCC layers, stacking and viewing directions
units.ov: This material links the FCC unit cell (atoms at the cube corners and face centres) to the close-packed layer picture. Close-packed {111} layers stack in an ABCABC… sequence along the cube body diagonal \(\langle111\rangle\), and what you see depends on the viewing direction. Stacking order (ABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP) is what separates FCC from HCP, even though both have 12 nearest neighbours.
must: FCC unit cell: atoms at the 8 corners and 6 face centres, giving \(8\times\tfrac18+6\times\tfrac12=4\) atoms per cell
Close-packed layers stack ABCABC… in FCC, so the pattern repeats every 3 layers; HCP stacks ABAB… and repeats every 2
The close-packed planes are {111}, perpendicular to the cube body diagonal \(\langle111\rangle\). They are not parallel to the cube faces
Each layer sits in the hollows of the layer below. A, B and C are the three distinct hollow/site positions, not different atom types
Viewed down \(\langle111\rangle\), the structure shows a hexagonal close-packed arrangement, with a central atom surrounded by 6 neighbours in the layer and B and C sites in the hollows
The appearance of the structure depends on viewing direction, so always state the direction when describing the stacking
Coordination number is 12 for both FCC and HCP, independent of how the layers are labelled
Geometry to be able to derive: close-packed atoms touch along the face diagonal, so \(a=2\sqrt{2}\,r\), and APF \(=\pi/(3\sqrt2)\approx0.74\)
Layer spacing along \(\langle111\rangle\) is \(d_{111}=a/\sqrt3\), and three layers make up one ABC repeat of length \(\sqrt3\,a\)
conn: Unit cell and layers: the same 4-atom cube can be described as ABC-stacked {111} planes, so questions ask you to move between the cube view and the layer view
Stacking and structure type: ABC versus ABAB determines FCC versus HCP. Both have the same coordination number (12) and packing fraction (0.74), so you need stacking to tell them apart
Geometry and density: \(a=2\sqrt2\,r\) combined with 4 atoms per cell gives the packing fraction and the theoretical density \(\rho=4M/(N_Aa^3)\)
Close-packed planes and directions: {111} planes and \(\langle110\rangle\) directions link to slip and ductility in later topics
exq: Sketch the FCC unit cell and show that it contains 4 atoms. Then use the face-diagonal relation \(a=2\sqrt2\,r\) to calculate the atomic packing factor.
Describe the ABCABC stacking of close-packed layers. Explain what A, B and C represent and how the FCC stacking differs from the ABAB stacking of HCP.
Copper is FCC with \(a=0.361\) nm. Calculate the atomic radius and the spacing between adjacent {111} planes, and state how many layers make up one stacking repeat.
Explain why the FCC structure looks different when viewed along a cube edge and along a body diagonal. Sketch each view and identify the hexagonal pattern.
State the coordination number of FCC and justify it. Explain why changing the stacking labels (A, B, C) does not change it.

notes.t: Relation of cells and layers in FCC structure
pts: FCC (face-centred cubic) is the crystal structure shown, with atoms at the cube corners and at the centre of each face.
Because FCC atoms pack in layers along a body diagonal, you must think in different directions to see the stacking pattern rather than just the unit cell faces.
The stacking sequence of close-packed layers is ABCABC, shown in the diagram as A, B, C, A repeating.
The triangular close-packed layers stack so that each layer sits in the hollows of the layer below, giving the pyramid-like arrangement of spheres shown.
defs: FCC (face-centred cubic)
A crystal structure with atoms at each cube corner and at the centre of each cube face, with close-packed layers stacked in an ABCABC sequence.
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence ABC (FCC) with ABAB (HCP); the sequence determines the structure type.
Remember that FCC is a cubic cell with atoms on corners and face centres; the layers lie on planes diagonal to the cube axes, not parallel to the cube faces.
rq: Why can't the FCC stacking be understood by looking only at the faces of a single cube?
Because the close-packed layers lie on planes that cut diagonally through the cell (e.g. the triangular planes shown), so the stacking sequence is only visible when viewed in different directions.
What would change if the stacking were ABABAB instead of ABCABC?
The structure would be hexagonal close-packed (HCP), not FCC, because layer C would be absent and layers would repeat every two layers.

notes.t: FCC crystal structure and viewing direction
pts: In an FCC structure the arrangement of atoms appears different depending on the direction from which it is viewed, so stacking sequence is seen in the close-packed planes.
Viewed along the close-packed stacking direction, the atom layers repeat in an ABCA sequence, showing three distinct layer positions before repeating.
The diagram labels atom positions A, B and C, which mark the three distinct stacking positions of close-packed layers in the FCC lattice.
Viewed down the cube body diagonal the structure shows a hexagonal pattern of atoms, with a central atom surrounded by layers of B and C positions.
defs: FCC (face-centred cubic)
A crystal structure with atoms at each corner and at the centre of each cube face, giving close-packed planes with an ABCABC stacking sequence.
tips: Do not assume the crystal looks the same in every view; always specify the viewing direction when describing FCC stacking.
Remember that the ABC sequence distinguishes FCC from HCP, which uses only ABAB stacking.
rq: Why does the same FCC crystal look different when viewed from different directions?

Because the atoms form close-packed layers stacked in a particular sequence; viewing along a cube edge shows a square arrangement, while viewing along the body diagonal reveals the hexagonal A, B, C stacking.
What would you expect to see if the layers were stacked as ABAB instead of ABCA?
That would describe a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, not FCC, since FCC requires the three-position ABC sequence.

notes.t: FCC stacking sequence and unit cell
pts: Close-packed layers stack in an ABCABC… sequence, with each new layer sitting in the hollows of the previous one.
The three possible close-packed site positions are labelled A, B and C; each layer occupies one of these sets of positions.
In the 2D projection, the A layer (green) forms the base, with B (blue) and C (orange) sites nestled in its hollows.
The FCC unit cell has atoms at the cube corners and face centres, which corresponds to the ABC layer stacking viewed in 3D.
defs: Stacking sequence
The repeating order in which close-packed atomic layers are placed on top of one another, labelled by the site positions they occupy (e.g. ABCABC… for FCC).
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence (ABC…) with the coordination number; FCC has 12 nearest neighbours regardless of how you label the layers.
Remember that A, B and C label site positions, not different atom types; all atoms in FCC are identical.
rq: Why can't two neighbouring close-packed layers both sit on A sites?
Atoms in adjacent close-packed layers must sit in the hollows of the layer below; placing a layer directly over the A sites would overlap atoms, so the next layer must use the B or C sites.
What would change in the stacking if the sequence were ABABAB… instead of ABCABC…?
It would give hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure rather than FCC, because the layer above the first A layer repeats the A positions after two layers.

units.name: 5.8 Simulations, packing summary and metal structures
units.ov: This material covers how metals pack their atoms into the crystal structures FCC, BCC and HCP, and how the VSME simulations help you visualise unit cells and atomic planes. The key idea is that packing efficiency separates close-packed FCC and HCP from the less dense BCC. Visualising planes such as (100), (110) and (111) underpins Miller index work, and tabulated atomic radii feed into geometric calculations.
must: FCC and HCP are the close-packed structures, giving the most efficient atomic packing
BCC (body centred cubic) is less close packed than FCC and HCP, but is still dense and not 'unpacked'
BCC unit cell: one atom at each of the 8 cube corners plus one at the body centre
Most common metals crystallise as FCC, BCC or HCP
Visualise the planes (100), (110) and (111) before attempting Miller index questions, rather than memorising diagrams
The VSME simulations show FCC and BCC planar atomic arrangements on (100), (110), (111), (112), (122) and (123); reduced-sphere display shows the arrangement more clearly than hard spheres
Metallic atomic radii are typically 0.12-0.18 nm, with lead the largest in the table; the values are supplied in exams, not memorised
Convert radii from nm to m or pm consistently before calculating
Tabulated radii apply to the structure listed, so do not assume the same radius in every crystal structure
conn: Packing efficiency links to structure type: close-packed FCC and HCP versus less dense BCC, which affects density calculations
Atomic radius combined with unit cell geometry (e.g. along a cube edge or face diagonal) gives lattice parameter and then density
Visualising planes in the simulation supports Miller index identification and planar atomic density comparisons for FCC versus BCC
Unit conversion of radii (nm, pm, m) feeds into every quantitative crystal-structure calculation
exq: Name the three common metallic crystal structures and state which are close packed and which is not. Explain why BCC is described as 'less close packed' rather than 'not packed'.
Describe the BCC unit cell, stating where the atoms sit, and sketch the atoms on the (110) plane of BCC.
Using a given atomic radius of 0.125 nm for an FCC metal, calculate the lattice parameter and express it in m and pm. State any assumption about which direction the atoms touch.
Sketch the (100), (110) and (111) planes in a cubic cell and give the Miller indices of a plane with stated intercepts.
A student uses the radius of a metal taken from a BCC table in an FCC calculation. Explain why this may be invalid.

notes.t: VSME interactive simulations for crystal structures
pts: The VSME interactive simulations accompany the Callister textbook and let you rotate 3-D atomic arrangements of crystal structures.
The module menu includes planar atomic arrangements for FCC and BCC, which can be viewed on the six crystallographic planes (100), (110), (111), (112), (122) and (123).
Atoms can be displayed as reduced spheres, showing the atomic arrangement more clearly than full hard spheres.
tips: Use the simulations to visualise planes such as (100), (110) and (111) before attempting Miller index questions, rather than relying on memory of the diagrams.
rq: Why is it useful to view a BCC structure rotated in 3-D rather than only as a flat 2-D diagram?
Rotating the 3-D model reveals how atoms are arranged along different crystallographic planes, which is hard to see from a single 2-D drawing.

notes.t: Packing of atoms in crystal structures
pts: FCC and HCP are the close-packed crystal structures, giving the most efficient packing of atoms.
BCC is less close packed than FCC and HCP, so its atoms occupy less of the available space.
BCC stands for Body Centred Cubic, meaning one atom sits at each cube corner plus one at the body centre.
defs: Close packed structure
A crystal structure in which atoms are arranged to fill space as efficiently as possible; FCC and HCP are the close-packed structures.
BCC (Body Centred Cubic)
A cubic crystal structure with an atom at each corner of the cube and one atom at the centre of the cube; less closely packed than FCC or HCP.
tips: Do not confuse 'less close packed' with 'not packed': BCC is still a dense metallic structure, just less dense than FCC or HCP.
Remember BCC is the less close packed structure; mixing up which structures are close packed is a common exam error.
rq: Why is BCC considered less close packed than FCC and HCP even though all three are common metallic structures?
BCC atoms occupy a smaller fraction of the available volume (about 68% packing factor) than FCC and HCP (about 74%), leaving more empty space between atoms.
What would you expect to happen to the packing efficiency if the central atom of a BCC cell were removed?
The atom count per cell would drop from two to one, reducing packing efficiency substantially, so the structure would no longer be BCC.

notes.t: Metals: crystal structures and atomic radii
pts: Common metals adopt one of three close-packed or near-close-packed crystal structures: FCC, BCC or HCP.
Atomic radii of common metals typically range from about 0.12 nm to 0.18 nm, with lead the largest in the table.
The table is reference data: students are not expected to memorise it, as textbooks and exam papers supply these values.
tips: Atomic radius values are given in nm, so convert to m or pm consistently before using them in any calculation.
Do not assume the radius of a metal is the same in every crystal structure; tabulated values are for the structure listed.
rq: Why might two metals with the same crystal structure (e.g. FCC aluminium and FCC lead) have very different atomic radii?

Atomic radius depends on the element's electron configuration and nuclear charge as well as crystal structure; lead's larger atoms (0.1750 nm) reflect its heavier, more electron-rich atoms compared with aluminium (0.1431 nm).
Why are the atomic radii of BCC iron (0.1241 nm) and FCC nickel (0.1246 nm) so similar even though their crystal structures differ?

Their structures differ only in packing arrangement; both contain atoms of similar size and electron structure, so the radii are close, though the coordination number and packing efficiency still differ.

units.name: 6.1 Lecture overview and resources
units.ov: The notes are only a title page and a resources page for 'Crystal Structure 2' (Lecture 6), which draws on Callister sections 3.4 to 3.5 and its companion website, with Tilley's Crystals & Crystal Structures as an alternative text. They contain no technical content, so the report below gives the standard Callister 3.4-3.5 syllabus (density from crystal structure, polymorphism, allotropy) as a revision framework. Check each point against your lecture slides and textbook.
must: Primary source: Callister sections 3.4-3.5, with the companion website for extra practice. Tilley is a secondary reference.
Unit-cell geometry for the cubic systems (SC, BCC, FCC): atoms per cell are 1, 2 and 4 respectively.
Relation between the cube edge \(a\) and atomic radius \(R\): SC \(a=2R\), BCC \(a=4R/\sqrt{3}\), FCC \(a=2R\sqrt{2}\).
Coordination number: SC 6, BCC 8, FCC 12.
Atomic packing factor \(APF=\frac{V_{atoms}}{V_{cell}}\): SC 0.52, BCC 0.68, FCC 0.74.
Theoretical density \(\rho=\frac{nA}{V_C N_A}\), with \(n\) atoms per cell, \(A\) atomic weight, \(V_C=a^3\) for cubic cells, and \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\).
Unit handling in density calculations: convert nm or Å to cm or m, and keep \(A\) in g/mol so \(\rho\) comes out in g/cm³.
HCP structure: 6 atoms per cell, CN 12, APF 0.74, ideal \(c/a=1.633\).

Polymorphism and allotropy: the same material can have different crystal structures, for example Fe is BCC→FCC→BCC on heating, and C exists as diamond and graphite. A structure change changes density and properties.
Ability to derive the \(a\)-\(R\) relations and the APF from the geometry of the close-packed direction, rather than just recalling them.
conn: Geometry links to density: the \(a\)-\(R\) relation gives \(V_C\), the structure gives \(n\), and together they give \(\rho\).
Packing factor and coordination number: FCC and HCP are close-packed (APF 0.74, CN 12), and this explains differences in density and in properties such as ductility.
Polymorphism links to density: a phase change such as BCC↔FCC in iron changes APF, so it changes volume and density. This is relevant to thermal expansion and heat treatment.
Experimental and theoretical density: comparing a calculated \(\rho\) with a measured value can indicate a structure or reveal defects such as vacancies.
exq: Copper is FCC with \(R=0.128\) nm and \(A=63.5\) g/mol. Calculate the unit cell edge length and the theoretical density.
Derive the atomic packing factor of BCC from first principles and compare it with FCC. Explain what the difference means for coordination number.
Iron changes from BCC (\(R=0.1241\) nm) to FCC (\(R=0.1292\) nm) at 912 °C. Calculate the percentage volume change on transformation and comment on the result.
A metal has \(A=95.9\) g/mol, \(\rho=10.22\) g/cm³ and \(R=0.136\) nm. Determine whether its structure is SC, BCC or FCC.
Define polymorphism and allotropy, with two examples, and explain why the properties of the polymorphs differ.
