units.name: 7.1 Course admin and tutorial sessions
units.ov: The notes are only title slides: a course admin and tutorial document that points to Materials 1 Lecture 7 (Crystal structure 3). They contain no worked content, so the report below draws on standard first-year crystal-structure material and should be checked against the actual lecture slides and tutorial sheets. The topics build on each other: unit cells and lattices lead to atomic packing, then to crystallographic directions and planes (Miller indices), and finally to density and defects.
must: Treat these notes as a placeholder: the real content is in Lecture 7 and the tutorial problem sheets, so work through those
Unit cell geometry for SC, BCC and FCC: atoms per cell are 1, 2 and 4, and coordination numbers are 6, 8 and 12
Relations between lattice parameter \(a\) and atomic radius \(R\): SC \(a=2R\), BCC \(a=4R/\sqrt{3}\), FCC \(a=2\sqrt{2}R\)
Atomic packing factor: \(APF = \frac{n V_{atom}}{V_{cell}}\), giving SC 0.52, BCC 0.68, FCC/HCP 0.74
Theoretical density: \(\rho = \frac{nA}{V_c N_A}\), with careful unit handling (g/cm³ or kg/m³)
Miller indices for directions \([uvw]\) and planes \((hkl)\): intercepts, reciprocals, clearing fractions, and negative indices written with a bar
Planar density and linear density, and how they identify close-packed planes and directions (slip systems)
HCP and FCC differ only in stacking sequence (ABAB vs ABCABC), and both have 12 nearest neighbours
Check tutorial feedback and administrative details such as assessment format and deadlines
conn: Geometry links to density: \(a\) from \(R\) gives \(V_c\), which gives both APF and \(\rho\) in a single question
Miller planes link to planar density, which links to slip and ductility (FCC is ductile because it has many close-packed slip systems)
Crystal structure links to properties: packing and coordination affect density, and structure affects deformation behaviour
Lattice parameter links to X-ray diffraction through Bragg's law \(n\lambda=2d\sin\theta\), where \(d\) depends on \(hkl\) and \(a\)
exq: Show that the APF of BCC is 0.68, stating the relationship between \(a\) and \(R\) and the number of atoms per cell.
Copper is FCC with \(R=0.128\) nm and \(A=63.5\) g/mol. Calculate its theoretical density.
Sketch the \((110)\) and \((111)\) planes and the \([1\bar{1}0]\) direction in a cubic cell, and give the Miller indices of a plane with intercepts \(a\), \(a/2\) and \(\infty\).
Calculate the planar density of the (100) and (111) planes in FCC with lattice parameter \(a\), and state which is close-packed.
Compare FCC and HCP structures in terms of stacking sequence, coordination number and APF, and explain why FCC metals are generally more ductile.

units.name: 7.2 Crystal structures of compounds: NaCl and UO₂
units.ov: This material extends crystal structure from single-element lattices (HCP, BCC, FCC) to ionic compounds, where the structure depends on the relative sizes of the ions. It works through NaCl (FCC Cl⁻ with Na⁺ in octahedral sites, coordination 6:6) and UO₂ (fluorite-type, FCC U with O in interstitial sites, coordination 8:4). Both examples are tied together by counting atoms per unit cell, using ionic radii for geometry, and calculating density.
must: Compound structures depend on the relative sizes of the ions, so HCP/BCC/FCC labels apply only to equal-sized atoms (or to the lattice of one ion type).
NaCl: FCC array of Cl⁻ with Na⁺ in the octahedral sites; ions alternate, and coordination number is 6 for both ions.
NaCl unit cell contains 4 Na⁺ and 4 Cl⁻, so n = 4 formula units per cell.
NaCl cell edge from touching ions along the edge: \( a = 2r_{Cl} + 2r_{Na} \approx 0.566\) nm (with \(r_{\text{Cl}}\) ≈ 0.181 nm, \(r_{\text{Na}}\) = 0.102 nm).
Density of a compound: \( \rho = \frac{n(A_{cation}+A_{anion})}{V_C N_A} \), summing the mass of every ion type in the cell; for NaCl use \( n(A_{Na}+A_{Cl}) \).
Unit conversions: nm to m (cubed gives 10⁻²⁷), g/mol to kg/mol; errors here give factors of 10²⁷ or 10³.
UO₂ is fluorite-type: U in an FCC array, 8 O ions inside the cell in the interstitial sites; coordination is U 8 : O 4.
Counting atoms per cell: corners ×1/8, faces ×1/2, internal ×1. Hence \( N_U = \frac{8}{8}+\frac{6}{2} = 4 \) and \( N_O = 8 \), giving the 1:2 ratio of UO₂.
Check stoichiometry from the atom count and coordination numbers (8:4 gives UO₂), not from the diagram alone.
Distinguish ionic from atomic radii, and NaCl's 6:6 coordination from CsCl's 8:8.
conn: Atom counting per unit cell feeds directly into the density formula: n is obtained from the sharing factors, and the stoichiometry check confirms it.
Ionic radii determine both the structure (which sites the smaller ion occupies) and the cell edge a, which gives \(V_{C}\) = a³ and hence the density.
Coordination number links geometry to stoichiometry: 8:4 in UO₂ gives 1:2, while 6:6 in NaCl gives 1:1.
The FCC lattice of single elements carries over to compounds as the framework of the larger ion (Cl⁻ or U), with the smaller ions in interstitial sites.
exq: Using \(r_{\text{Na}}\) = 0.102 nm and \(r_{\text{Cl}}\) = 0.181 nm, calculate the NaCl cell edge and its density (\(A_{\text{Na}}\) = 22.99 g/mol, \(A_{\text{Cl}}\) = 35.45 g/mol, n = 4). Give the answer in kg/m³.
Show by counting corner, face and internal atoms that the UO₂ fluorite unit cell contains 4 U and 8 O. State the coordination numbers and explain how they are consistent with the formula.
Explain why HCP, BCC and FCC cannot be applied directly to compounds such as NaCl, and describe how the relative ion size determines the structure.

Describe the NaCl structure: which ion forms the FCC array, which sites the other ion occupies, the coordination number and the number of ions per cell. Name two other compounds with the same structure.
A student calculates the NaCl density as 10²⁷ times too large or small. Identify the likely error and show the correct unit handling in the calculation.

notes.t: Crystal structure of compounds
pts: So far only single atom-type structures have been considered, such as HCP, BCC and FCC.
When all atoms are the same size, the packing gives an obvious, familiar crystal structure (HCP, BCC or FCC).
When atoms or ions differ in size, they pack differently from single-element structures, so the crystal structure changes.
The resulting crystal structure of a compound depends on the relative size of the atoms or ions present.
tips: Do not apply HCP, BCC or FCC directly to compounds; these only describe equal-sized atoms.
Always state that the structure of a compound depends on the relative size of its ions, not just their chemistry.
rq: Why can't the HCP, BCC or FCC structures simply be reused for a compound containing two different ions?
Those structures assume all atoms are the same size, so a mixture of differently sized atoms or ions packs into a different arrangement.
What is the main factor that decides the crystal structure of a compound?
The relative size of the atoms or ions in it.

notes.t: Sodium chloride (NaCl) crystal structure
pts: NaCl has a simple cubic arrangement in which Na+ and Cl- ions pack alternately, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge.
The Cl- ion (radius 0.180 nm) is much larger than the Na+ ion (radius 0.102 nm), so the anions form the framework and the smaller cations sit in the gaps between them.
The same structure is adopted by other ionic compounds such as KCl and MgO.
tips: Do not confuse the 'simple cubic' label with the unit cell of NaCl: the ions form a face-centred cubic lattice with a simple cubic-looking projection in this diagram, so state the ion arrangement carefully.
Keep radii in nm consistently when comparing ion sizes; mixing units (nm and pm) is a common error.
rq: Why does the smaller Na+ ion sit between the larger Cl- ions rather than the reverse arrangement?
Ionic packing is governed by the larger anions forming the framework, with cations occupying interstitial sites whose size fits the cation radius (0.102 nm vs 0.180 nm).
If the Na+ ion were as large as the Cl- ion, how would the structure change?
Equal-sized ions would no longer fit the interstitial sites; the packing ratio and coordination would change, so the NaCl structure would not be stable.

notes.t: Sodium chloride (NaCl) crystal structure
pts: NaCl has a face-centred cubic arrangement of Cl⁻ ions, with Na⁺ ions filling the octahedral sites between them, so the two ion types alternate.
Each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge, giving a coordination number of 6 for both Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
The cubic unit cell shows Cl⁻ at the corners and face centres, with Na⁺ at edge centres and the body centre.
defs: Alternating position of atoms
In NaCl, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions occupy neighbouring lattice sites in an alternating pattern, so each ion is bonded to ions of opposite charge.
tips: Do not confuse the coordination number of 6 in NaCl with the 8 found in CsCl-type structures.
Remember the ions are charged: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ must alternate so that opposite charges neighbour each other.
rq: Why does the alternating arrangement of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions give NaCl its stability?
Every ion sits next to ions of opposite charge, so electrostatic attraction is maximised while like-charge repulsion is minimised.
What would change if Na⁺ and Cl⁻ were the same size and charge pattern were not alternating?
The lattice would lose its ionic bonding balance and the coordination of six opposite-charge neighbours would no longer hold.

notes.t: Density of compounds
pts: For compounds, density uses the number and mass of each different atom type in the unit cell, not just one element.
Density is total mass of atoms in the unit cell divided by the unit cell volume.
The unit cell size may be taken from experimental data or calculated from crystal structure geometry.
defs: Unit cell
The smallest repeating volume of a crystal lattice that, when translated in three dimensions, generates the whole crystal structure.
eqs: Density of a compound from its unit cell

\rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); n = number of formula units (or atoms of each type) in the unit cell (dimensionless); A = atomic (or molar) mass (kg/mol or g/mol); \(V_{C}\) = volume of the unit cell (\(m^{3}\)); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (6.022\times10^{23} \(mol^{-1}\))
tips: Unit trap: convert atomic masses to kg/mol and unit cell edges to metres before calculating density in kg/\(m^{3.}\)
Remember to sum contributions from every element in the unit cell rather than using only one atom type.
rq: Why can't you use the density formula for an elemental metal directly on a compound?
A compound has several atom types with different masses and numbers per unit cell, so the total mass must sum n×A for each element before dividing by \(V_{C}\) \(N_{A}\).
If the unit cell volume is calculated from lattice parameters, what must you check about the units before computing density?
That the lattice parameters are converted to metres so \(V_{C}\) is in \(m^{3}\), and the molar mass is in kg/mol, giving density in kg/\(m^{3.}\)

notes.t: Density of Sodium Chloride (NaCl)
pts: NaCl has a simple cubic unit cell containing 4 Na⁺ and 4 Cl⁻ ions, so the formula units per cell is n = 4.
The cell edge a is set by touching ions along the cube edge: a = 2r_Cl + 2r_Na, giving a = 0.566 nm.
Density is found by summing the atomic masses of all ions in the cell and dividing by the cell volume times Avogadro's number.
Ionic radii differ markedly: the Cl⁻ ion (0.181 nm) is much larger than the Na⁺ ion (0.102 nm), and the mass of each ion is taken from its atomic weight.
defs: Unit cell
The smallest repeating volume of a crystal structure that, when translated in three dimensions, generates the whole lattice.
eqs: Density of an ionic crystal from its unit cell

\rho = density (kg/m³); n = number of formula units per cell (–); \(A_{Na}\), \(A_{Cl}\) = atomic masses of Na and Cl (kg/mol or g/mol); \(V_{c}\) = unit cell volume (m³); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (6.023×10²³ mol⁻¹)
a = cube edge length (m); \(r_{Cl}\), \(r_{Na}\) = ionic radii (m)
tips: Convert nm to m before computing volume: a³ must use 0.566 × 10⁻⁹ m, otherwise the density is wrong by a factor of 10²⁷.
Use atomic masses in consistent units (g/mol with \(N_{A}\) in mol⁻¹ gives g/cm³ or kg/m³ only after correct conversion).
rq: Why must the mass be summed over 4 Na⁺ and 4 Cl⁻ ions rather than using one ion of each?
The unit cell contains four formula units (NaCl pairs), so all eight ions contribute mass to the cell; using one pair would give density per formula unit, not per cell volume.
What would happen to the calculated density if the cell edge were taken as 0.566 × 10⁻⁹ m⁻¹ by mistake?
The unit is wrong: a must be in metres (0.566 × 10⁻⁹ m), and the volume is a³, so any slip in the exponent changes \(V_{c}\) by orders of magnitude and the density.
Why is the cell edge equal to 2r_Cl + 2r_Na rather than \(r_{\text{Cl}}\) + \(r_{\text{Na}}\)?
Along a cube edge the Cl⁻ and Na⁺ ions touch, and each edge spans one full ion diameter from each species, so the edge is the sum of two diameters, one Cl and one Na.

notes.t: Uranium oxide (UO₂) crystal structure
pts: Uranium ions form a face-centred cubic (FCC) array, with oxygen ions occupying the interstitial sites between them.
The ionic radii given (uranium much larger than oxygen) show why the oxygen ions fit into the gaps of the uranium lattice, giving a complex packing arrangement.
The structure is a fluorite-type arrangement: each uranium is surrounded by eight oxygen ions, and each oxygen by four uranium ions, so the stoichiometry must be 1:2.
defs: Face-centred cubic (FCC)
A crystal structure in which atoms sit at each corner and at the centre of each face of a cubic unit cell, giving four atoms per cell.
Interstitial site
A vacant space between the main lattice atoms into which smaller atoms (here oxygen) can fit.
tips: Do not confuse ionic radii with atomic radii; the values given are ionic radii used to check fit in the interstitial sites.
Always verify the stoichiometry from the coordination numbers (8:4 gives UO₂), not just from the picture.
rq: Why must the formula be UO₂ rather than UO, given the packing shown?
Each uranium is coordinated by eight oxygen ions and each oxygen by four uranium ions; this charge-balanced 1:2 ratio, with U⁴⁺ and O²⁻, gives UO₂ (the fluorite structure).
What would happen to the structure if the oxygen radius were larger than the interstitial gap allows?
The oxygen ions would not fit into the interstitial sites without distorting the lattice, so the packing would become unstable or the structure would change.

notes.t: Uranium Oxide (UO₂) unit cell composition
pts: In the fluorite-type UO₂ unit cell, uranium atoms are counted as 8 corner atoms each shared by 8 cells plus 6 face atoms each shared by 2 cells, giving 4 U atoms per cell.
All 8 oxygen atoms lie fully inside the cell, so they are not shared and each counts as one atom per cell.
The resulting ratio of uranium to oxygen atoms in the unit cell is 1:2, which matches the chemical formula UO₂.
defs: Unit cell
The smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice that, when translated in three dimensions, reproduces the whole crystal structure.
eqs: Number of uranium atoms per unit cell (sharing of corner and face atoms)
\(N_{U}\) = number of uranium atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); 8 corner atoms each shared by 8 cells; 6 face atoms each shared by 2 cells
Number of oxygen atoms per unit cell
\(N_{O}\) = number of oxygen atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); all oxygen atoms are internal to the cell
tips: Do not count corner or face atoms as whole atoms; forgetting the 1/8 and 1/2 sharing factors gives wrong atom counts.
Remember internal atoms belong entirely to the cell (factor 1), so the oxygen count is not divided by any sharing factor.
rq: Why does a corner atom count as only 1/8 of an atom when assigning atoms to a unit cell?
A corner atom is shared by 8 adjacent unit cells meeting at that corner, so each cell owns only 1/8 of it.
Why must the U:O ratio of the unit cell match the chemical formula UO₂ rather than being chosen freely?
Each unit cell is a repeating unit of the whole crystal, so its atom ratio must equal the bulk stoichiometry of the compound.

units.name: 7.3 Polymer chain packing and crystallinity
units.ov: This material explains how polymer chains pack, from the molecular structure of polyethylene to the coexistence of ordered crystalline and random amorphous regions. Chain regularity and side-group size determine how much crystallinity forms. Crystallinity in turn sets the overall density, which is calculated with a volume-fraction rule of mixtures.
must: Semi-crystalline density: \(\rho_{polymer}=\rho_{c}f_{c}+\rho_{a}f_{a}\), a volume-fraction-weighted average
Volume fractions sum to one: \(f_c+f_a=1\). Use volume fractions, never mass fractions, in this rule
Crystalline regions have ordered, aligned, densely packed chains; amorphous regions are randomly packed and less dense
Polymers are never fully crystalline: they always contain both crystalline and amorphous regions
Small, regular chains such as polyethylene crystallise readily
Bulky side groups (e.g. phenyl rings in polystyrene) hinder packing and limit crystallinity unless the chain has a regular repeat
Polyethylene density spans about 0.91–0.97 g/cm³, depending on organisation (close packing versus cross-linking)
Do not confuse ethylene (C=C monomer) with polyethylene (only single C–C bonds in the chain)
Keep units consistent: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so convert before using the density equation
conn: Chain structure (regularity, side-group size) controls crystallinity, which controls the volume fraction \(f_c\) and therefore the overall density
Measured density can be used inversely: rearrange the rule of mixtures with \(f_a=1-f_c\) to find the crystalline fraction
Polymerisation chemistry (C=C converted to C–C) links to chain flexibility and packing, and cross-linking disrupts ordered packing and changes density
exq: A polyethylene has \(\rho_c=1000\) kg/m³ and \(\rho_a=870\) kg/m³. Its measured density is 950 kg/m³. Calculate the volume fraction crystalline and amorphous.
Explain why polyethylene crystallises readily whereas polystyrene normally does not. State the condition under which a polymer with bulky side groups can still crystallise.
Define crystalline and amorphous regions in a polymer and explain why a polymer's density lies between the densities of the two regions.
A data sheet gives polyethylene density as 0.94 g/cm³. Convert it to kg/m³ and use it with given \(\rho_c\) and \(\rho_a\) to find \(f_c\). Explain why mass fractions cannot be used directly.
Describe how the structure of polyethylene differs from that of ethylene, and how chain packing or cross-linking explains the density range 0.91–0.97 g/cm³.

notes.t: Packing of Polymers
pts: How polymer chains pack depends on the polymer's molecular structure.
Polyethylene is formed by converting the C=C double bond of ethylene into single C–C bonds along a chain, with each carbon bonded to two hydrogens.
Polyethylene chains can either pack closely together or be cross-linked, which affects the material's organisation.
The density of polyethylene varies with its organisation, lying between 0.91 and 0.97 g/cm³.
tips: Do not confuse the monomer ethylene (C=C, a double bond) with the polymer polyethylene, which contains only single C–C bonds.
Density units are g/cm³; do not quote density in kg/m³ without converting (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³).
rq: Why does the density of polyethylene vary between 0.91 and 0.97 g/cm³ even though the chemical formula is the same?
Because the chains can pack more or less closely depending on their organisation (e.g. branching or crystallinity), so the same molecule gives different mass per unit volume.
How does cross-linking change the way polymer chains pack compared with chains that simply pack together?
Cross-linking creates covalent bonds between chains, locking them into a network that restricts their relative movement, unlike free chains that can slide and pack together.

notes.t: Packing of polymers: crystalline and amorphous regions
pts: Polymers contain organised crystalline regions where chains pack closely, giving higher density.
Amorphous regions have random chain packing, so they are less dense.
Overall polymer density is a volume-fraction-weighted average of the crystalline and amorphous densities.
The volume fractions of the two regions must sum to one.
defs: Crystalline region
An ordered region of a polymer in which chain segments pack regularly and densely.
Amorphous region
A randomly packed, less densely ordered region of a polymer.
eqs: Overall density of a semi-crystalline polymer (volume-fraction rule of mixtures)

\(\rho_{polymer}\) = overall density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); \(\rho_{crystalline}\) = density of crystalline regions (kg/\(m^{3}\)); \(\rho_{amorphous}\) = density of amorphous regions (kg/\(m^{3}\)); \(f_{crystalline}\) = volume fraction of crystalline regions (dimensionless); \(f_{amorphous}\) = volume fraction of amorphous regions (dimensionless)
\(f_{crystalline}\) = volume fraction crystalline (dimensionless); \(f_{amorphous}\) = volume fraction amorphous (dimensionless)
tips: Volume fractions must sum to 1; do not use mass fractions in the density rule of mixtures.
Use density values with consistent units (e.g. kg/\(m^{3}\)) when applying the overall density equation.
rq: Why does a higher crystalline volume fraction increase the overall density of a polymer?
Crystalline regions are more densely packed than amorphous regions, so a larger \( f_{crystalline} \) raises the weighted average density.
If a polymer had \( f_{crystalline} = 0.6 \), what must \( f_{amorphous} \) be, and why?
\( f_{amorphous} = 0.4 \), because the volume fractions must sum to 1.

notes.t: Packing and crystallinity of polymers
pts: Polymer chains pack together so that they become aligned, forming crystalline regions.
The spacing between groups of atoms depends on how large the side groups are and how easily the chains can be organised.
Simple polymers such as polyethylene (PE) readily form crystalline regions because the chains are regular and small.
Bulkier side groups, such as the phenyl rings in polystyrene, make regular packing less likely, so crystallinity is limited unless the chain structure is regular.
defs: Crystalline region (polymer)
A region of a polymer in which chains are packed in an ordered, aligned arrangement with a regular repeating unit cell.
tips: Crystallinity is never complete in polymers; they have crystalline and amorphous regions, so do not describe a polymer as fully crystalline.
Bulky side groups reduce crystallinity only if the chain is irregular; a regular repeat can still pack, so state the condition 'unless regular'.
rq: Why does polyethylene crystallise more readily than polystyrene?
PE has small, simple H side groups and a regular chain, so chains pack closely and aligned; polystyrene's bulky phenyl side groups hinder regular packing.
What would happen to the packing distance if the side groups were made larger?
The distance between groups of atoms would increase, because larger groups occupy more space, making the chains harder to pack tightly and organise.

units.name: 7.4 How solids form: nucleation and crystal growth
units.ov: This material introduces how solids form, mostly by solidification of a melt on cooling. It starts with the three phases of matter, distinguished by definite shape and volume. It then separates solidification into nucleation (first stable clusters), phase transition (disorder to ordered lattice) and crystal growth (atoms or ions adding at surface steps). The NaCl video illustrates these stages. Where each atom lands determines whether the lattice is perfect or contains defects.
must: Phase definitions: a solid has definite shape and volume; a liquid has definite volume but takes the shape of its container; a gas has neither
Most solids form by solidification from a melt (liquid phase) as it cools
Nucleation is the initial formation of a small, stable cluster of atoms or ions from the liquid or vapour
Nucleation and crystal growth are distinct stages: nucleation makes the first stable cluster, growth enlarges it
Phase transition: disordered material rearranges into an ordered crystal lattice
Crystal growth proceeds atom by atom (or ion by ion), with steps moving across the surface and adding one layer at a time
Atoms arriving at a correct lattice site extend the ordered crystal; atoms at incorrect sites create defects
Defects affect material properties, so the outcome depends on where each atom lands
Do not define a solid by hardness or rigidity; define it by definite shape and volume
NaCl video: ions come from a reservoir and form a nucleus, then an ordered (4,6) crystal appears; it is a 2D snapshot of a 3D process, so the image is not the full structure
conn: Melt cooling leads to nucleation, then phase transition to an ordered lattice, then growth. Questions often ask you to sequence these stages and say what happens at each
Atom-by-atom attachment links growth to defects: correct-site attachment gives an ordered crystal, wrong-site attachment gives defects that change properties
Phase definitions link to solidification: liquid (definite volume, no definite shape) becomes solid (definite shape and volume) as order develops
The NaCl example links the general model to a specific ionic crystal, so you may need to relate ion attachment at steps to the lattice, and recognise the limits of 2D images
exq: Define solid, liquid and gas in terms of shape and volume, and explain why a liquid is not described as having a definite shape.
Describe the stages by which a solid crystal forms from a melt, distinguishing nucleation, phase transition and crystal growth.
Explain how defects arise during crystal growth and why they matter for material properties.
Using the NaCl example, describe how a crystal grows by steps moving across the surface, and comment on the limitations of a 2D snapshot of the process.
A student says a nucleus and a growing crystal are the same thing. Explain why this is wrong, giving the role of each in solidification.

notes.t: How solids form: phases of matter
pts: Most solids are formed by solidifying from a melt (liquid phase) as they cool.
Matter exists in three common phases: gas, liquid and solid, distinguished by whether they have definite shape and volume.
A gas has neither definite shape nor definite volume.
A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
A solid has both definite shape and definite volume.
defs: Solid
A state of matter with definite shape and definite volume.
Liquid
A state of matter with definite volume but no definite shape, taking the shape of its container.
Gas
A state of matter with no definite shape or volume, expanding to fill its container.
Melt
The liquid phase of a material from which a solid is formed by solidification.
tips: Do not confuse a liquid's definite volume with a definite shape; liquids take the shape of their container.
Remember that a solid is defined by both definite shape and definite volume, not just by being hard or rigid.
rq: Why does a liquid take the shape of its container while still having a fixed volume?
Its atoms or molecules are close together so the volume is fixed, but they are not held in fixed positions, so they flow and adopt the container's shape.
What would you expect to happen to a gas placed in a sealed container that is halved in volume?
The gas expands to fill whatever container it is in, so it would be compressed to fill the smaller volume, with its pressure rising, since it has no definite volume of its own.

notes.t: How solids form: nucleation and atomic arrangement
pts: Solidification begins with small nuclei forming from the melt or vapour.
Each atom that reaches the growing surface settles into a position on the existing structure.
Atoms may attach in a correct lattice site (ordered crystal) or an incorrect site (defect), so the outcome depends on where each atom lands.
Growth proceeds atom by atom as the crystal lattice extends outward from each nucleus.
defs: Nucleus (in solidification)
A small cluster of atoms that forms first in a liquid or vapour and from which a solid crystal grows.
tips: Do not confuse nucleation (formation of the first small clusters) with growth (atoms adding to the existing nucleus).
Remember that atoms arriving at the wrong site create defects, which affect material properties.
rq: Why does the arrival of an atom at the wrong place produce a defect rather than a perfect crystal?
Because atoms that settle out of the regular lattice pattern break the periodic order, creating a defect in the crystal structure.
What would happen to the growth of a solid if nuclei did not form first?
Atoms would have no seed surface to attach to, so an ordered solid would not begin to grow and solidification could not proceed in a controlled way.

notes.t: How solids form: nucleation, phase transition and crystal growth of NaCl
pts: Solids form from a liquid or vapour by nucleation, where a small stable cluster of atoms or ions first appears.
Nucleation is followed by a phase transition, in which disordered material rearranges into an ordered crystal lattice.
The nucleus then grows by crystal growth, with atoms or ions adding at steps on the crystal surface.
In the NaCl video, the crystal forms from a hidden reservoir of ions at the nucleation stage before the ordered (4,6) crystal appears.
Growth proceeds as steps move across the crystal surface, adding ions one layer at a time.
defs: Nucleation
The initial formation of a small, stable cluster of atoms or ions from a parent phase, from which a crystal can grow.
Phase transition
The change of a material from one state of matter or structure to another, here from disordered material to an ordered crystal.
Crystal growth
The enlargement of a stable nucleus as atoms or ions attach to its surface, typically at steps, extending the ordered lattice.
tips: Do not confuse nucleation (formation of the first stable cluster) with crystal growth (enlargement of that cluster); they are distinct stages.
The video shows a 2D snapshot of a 3D process; avoid assuming the lattice seen in the image is the full crystal structure.
rq: Why does a crystal need a nucleus before it can grow?
A stable nucleus provides an ordered template onto which further atoms or ions can attach; without a stable cluster, the small clusters dissolve back into the parent phase.
What would you expect to happen to the time of nucleation if the solution were cooled more quickly?
Nucleation would typically occur sooner and at a higher density, since greater supersaturation or undercooling drives faster cluster formation.

units.name: 7.5 Point defects: vacancies and interstitials
units.ov: This material introduces crystal imperfections: point defects (vacancies, self-interstitials, substitutional and interstitial impurities) and line defects (dislocations). It quantifies how many vacancies exist at equilibrium (an Arrhenius/Boltzmann law) and how much space a cubic lattice offers an interstitial atom. It then links size mismatch to lattice distortion, internal stress and strengthening, as in carbon in iron.
must: Equilibrium vacancy count: \( N_v = N\exp(-Q_v/kT) \), rising exponentially with absolute temperature T (in K)
Unit consistency: \(Q_v\) in J/atom pairs with \(k=1.38\times10^{-23}\) J/K; \(Q_v\) in J/mol pairs with R (8.314 J/mol K)
Vacancy = missing atom, an interstitial = extra atom in a gap; both are point defects (0D), whereas a dislocation is a line defect (1D)
Even near melting only about 1 in \(10^4\) sites is vacant in most metals
Vacancies lower density because there are fewer atoms per unit volume (atomic mass is unchanged), and they strain nearby planes
Self-interstitial (host atom in a gap) vs interstitial impurity (small foreign atom in a gap) vs substitutional impurity (similar-size foreign atom on a lattice site)
Interstitial space in the cubic arrangement: centre-to-centre distance \( \sqrt{2}D \), so the available gap diameter is \( (\sqrt{2}-1)D \approx 0.414D \)
Any size mismatch (larger or smaller) distorts the lattice and creates internal (residual) stress
Carbon in γ-iron: \( r_C/r_{Fe} = 0.154/0.256 \approx 0.60 \), too large for a strain-free site, so the lattice is distorted
Interstitial alloying strengthens metals because the distorted lattice impedes dislocation motion
conn: Vacancy equation and thermal energy: a higher T increases \(N_v\) exponentially, which lowers density and increases lattice strain; this also underlies diffusion
Interstitial geometry and alloying: the \(0.414D\) gap limit compared with the C/Fe ratio of 0.60 explains the distortion, internal stress and solid-solution strengthening
Point defects and dislocations: the strain fields of vacancies and interstitials obstruct dislocation motion, linking defect type and dimensionality to mechanical strength
Defect classification and atom count: vacancy (fewer atoms), interstitial (extra atoms) and substitutional (same count) each change density and lattice distortion differently
exq: A metal has \(Q_v = 0.9\) eV/atom. Calculate the fraction of vacant sites at 300 K and at 1200 K (k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K), and comment on the ratio.

Derive the maximum diameter of an interstitial atom in a cubic arrangement of host atoms of diameter D, giving \((\sqrt{2}-1)D\). Does carbon (r = 0.154 nm) fit in iron (r = 0.256 nm) without distortion? Justify with the radius ratio.
Distinguish between a vacancy, a self-interstitial, a substitutional impurity and an interstitial impurity, stating the dimensionality of each defect and of a dislocation.
Explain why increasing temperature and increasing vacancy concentration reduce density, and why interstitial atoms raise internal stress and strength.
A material has \(N_v/N = 10^{-4}\) just below its melting point of 1300 K. Find \(Q_v\) in J/atom and in kJ/mol.

notes.t: Defects in crystal structures
pts: Real atomic structures contain imperfections; no crystal is perfect.
A missing atom from a lattice site is called a vacancy.
An extra atom squeezed into a non-lattice position is an interstitial defect.
A whole plane of atoms sitting in the wrong place is a dislocation.
defs: Vacancy
A point defect where an atom is missing from its normal lattice site.
Interstitial
A point defect where an extra atom occupies a space between regular lattice sites.
Dislocation
A line defect formed by a plane of atoms lying in the wrong place within the crystal.
tips: Do not confuse a vacancy (missing atom) with an interstitial (extra atom); both are point defects but have opposite atom counts.
Dislocations are line defects, not point defects; state their dimensionality correctly in exam answers.
rq: Why do imperfections like vacancies and dislocations matter for engineering materials even though they are tiny?
They control properties such as plastic deformation, strength and ductility, because dislocations move and allow metals to yield at stresses far below the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal.
How does a vacancy differ from an interstitial, and which would you expect to be more common in a metal and why?

A vacancy is a missing atom on a lattice site, whereas an interstitial is an extra atom in a gap between sites; vacancies are generally more common because they are energetically cheaper to form than squeezing an atom into an interstitial position.

notes.t: Vacancies in crystal structures
pts: A vacancy is a point defect where an atom is missing from its lattice position.
The equilibrium number of vacancies depends on temperature and rises as temperature increases.
Vacancies distort the surrounding crystal planes, creating local lattice strain.
More vacancies mean fewer atoms per unit volume, so the material's density decreases.
defs: Vacancy
A point defect in a crystal lattice in which an atom is missing from its normal lattice site.
tips: Do not confuse a vacancy (missing atom) with an interstitial (extra atom squeezed between lattice sites); both are point defects.
Remember that the density decrease from vacancies is a consequence of fewer atoms per unit volume, not a change in atomic mass.
rq: Why does density fall when the number of vacancies rises?
Each vacancy removes an atom from a fixed unit volume, so there are fewer atoms per unit volume and the mass per volume decreases.
What would you expect to happen to vacancy numbers if a metal is heated close to its melting point and then cooled quickly?
Many vacancies formed at high temperature are frozen in on rapid cooling, leaving more vacancies than the equilibrium value at room temperature.

notes.t: Vacancies in crystals
pts: Vacancies are missing atoms on lattice sites; their equilibrium number rises exponentially with temperature.
Forming a vacancy costs energy \(Q_{v}\), which must be supplied from thermal energy kT.
Even just below melting, only about 1 in \(10^{4}\) sites is vacant in most metals.
defs: Vacancy
A point defect in a crystal where an atom is missing from a normal lattice site.
Boltzmann's constant (k)
Constant relating thermal energy to temperature (k = 1.38×\(10^{-23}\) J/K); used with absolute temperature in exponential energy terms.
eqs: Equilibrium number of vacancies at temperature T

\(N_{v}\) = number of vacancies (dimensionless count); N = number of atomic sites (dimensionless count); \(Q_{v}\) = energy to form a vacancy (J); k = Boltzmann's constant (J/K); T = absolute temperature (K)
tips: Temperature must be in kelvin (absolute), not °C, when using exp(-\(Q_{v}\)/kT).
Use consistent units: if \(Q_{v}\) is in J/atom, k must be J/K; if \(Q_{v}\) is in J/mol, use the gas constant R instead of k.
rq: Why does the number of vacancies increase rapidly as temperature rises?
Higher T increases kT, making \(Q_{v}\)/kT smaller, so the exponential term (and \(N_{v}\)) grows.
What would happen to \(N_{v}\)/N if \(Q_{v}\) doubled while T stayed the same?
\(N_{v}\)/N would fall to its square, since exp(-2Q_v/kT) = [exp(-\(Q_{v}\)/kT)]^2, so far fewer vacancies form.

notes.t: Interstitial defects in crystal lattices
pts: A self-interstitial is an atom of the same type squeezed into an interstitial site, severely distorting the lattice.
A substitutional impurity is a different atom of similar size that replaces a host atom on a lattice site.
An interstitial impurity is a smaller foreign atom sitting in the gaps between host atoms, causing planes to distort.
defs: Self-interstitial
An atom of the same element as the host lattice that occupies an interstitial position between regular lattice sites, distorting the surrounding planes.
Substitutional impurity
A foreign atom of similar size that replaces a host atom on a regular lattice site.
Interstitial impurity atom
A small foreign atom that occupies a gap between host atoms in the lattice without displacing any host atom.
tips: Do not confuse a self-interstitial (same element as host) with an interstitial impurity (different, smaller element); the defect type depends on the atom identity and size.
Interstitial defects are distinct from substitutional ones: the interstitial atom occupies a gap, not a regular lattice site.
rq: Why does a small interstitial impurity distort the lattice less than a self-interstitial of the same size?

A smaller impurity fits into the gaps between host atoms, so it causes only local strain, whereas a self-interstitial is the same size as the host atoms and forces neighbouring planes apart much more severely.
What determines whether an impurity becomes substitutional or interstitial?
Its relative atomic size: similar-sized atoms substitute for host atoms on lattice sites, while much smaller atoms fit into interstitial gaps.

notes.t: Effect of interstitials on the lattice
pts: Interstitial atoms are normally not the same size as the host lattice atoms, so they distort the lattice structure.
The distortion of the lattice structure creates internal stress within the lattice.
tips: Do not assume interstitials only distort the lattice when they are larger; a size mismatch of either sign causes distortion and stress.
Stress from lattice distortion is internal (residual) stress within the lattice, not an externally applied stress.
rq: Why does an interstitial atom that is smaller than the host atoms still distort the lattice?

Any mismatch in size relative to the space available in the interstitial site pushes neighbouring atoms out of their ideal positions, so the lattice is distorted even if the interstitial is smaller than the host atoms.
How does lattice distortion from interstitials affect the mechanical behaviour of a metal?
The internal stress from distortion impedes dislocation motion, so the material becomes stronger and harder (solid-solution strengthening).

notes.t: Interstitial alloying atoms and available space in a cubic lattice
pts: Interstitial solute atoms must be much smaller than the host atoms, otherwise they distort the crystal structure.
In a cubic structure, the centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring major atoms along a face diagonal-based gap is \( \sqrt{2}D \), where D is the diameter of the major atoms.
The space available for an interstitial atom in the cubic arrangement is \( (\sqrt{2}-1)D \approx 0.414D \), so the interstitial radius limit is set by this gap.
defs: Interstitial alloying atom
A small solute atom that occupies a gap between the larger host (major) atoms of a crystal lattice rather than replacing a host atom.
eqs: Centre-to-centre distance between major atoms in a cubic structure
d = centre-to-centre distance (m); D = diameter of major atoms (m)
Maximum available interstitial space (diameter of largest interstitial atom)
D = diameter of major atoms (m); result is the available interstitial space (m)
tips: Do not confuse the centre-to-centre distance \( \sqrt{2}D \) with the available space \( (\sqrt{2}-1)D \); the space is the gap left after subtracting the radii of the two host atoms, which is \( (\sqrt{2}-1)D \) in diameter terms.
Remember the space is expressed in terms of D (the major atom diameter), so give the answer as a multiple of D or with consistent units.
rq: Why must interstitial atoms be much smaller than the host atoms?
Larger interstitials would not fit into the available gap, so they would push neighbouring host atoms apart and distort the crystal structure.
If the major atom diameter D were doubled, how would the available interstitial space change?
It would double, since the available space is proportional to D: \( (\sqrt{2}-1)(2D) = 0.828D \).

notes.t: Interstitial alloying atoms
pts: Small carbon atoms sit in the interstitial gaps between larger iron atoms in γ-iron, distorting the lattice.
The size mismatch is quantified by the radius ratio of carbon to iron, which is about 0.60; this is why interstitial sites are strained.
Interstitial alloying is a route to strengthening metals, because the distorted lattice impedes dislocation motion.
defs: Interstitial alloying atom
A small solute atom that occupies a gap between the host (solvent) atoms in the crystal lattice rather than replacing a host atom.
eqs: Atomic radius ratio used to judge interstitial size mismatch
\(r_{C}\) = radius of carbon atom (nm); \(r_{Fe}\) = radius of iron atom (nm)
tips: Radius ratio must use consistent units; the values are given in nm, so the ratio 0.154/0.256 is dimensionless and must not be confused with a percentage.
Do not confuse interstitial alloying (small solute in gaps) with substitutional alloying (solute replaces host atom at a lattice site).
rq: Why does a carbon atom in γ-iron distort the lattice even though it is much smaller than an iron atom?

Because the interstitial site is only a gap sized for a much smaller atom; a carbon atom of radius 0.154 nm still pushes neighbouring iron atoms apart, since the site is smaller than the carbon-plus-iron contact distance requires. The ratio of about 0.60 shows the site is strained.
What would you expect to happen to the lattice distortion if a solute atom with radius closer to that of iron were placed in the same site?
The distortion would be smaller, since a larger radius ratio means less mismatch with the host atoms and less strain around the solute.

units.name: 7.6 Dislocations: edge dislocation structure and motion
units.ov: This material introduces dislocations as line defects in crystals, focusing on the edge dislocation (an extra half-plane of atoms) and the Burgers vector that characterises it. It explains how an edge dislocation glides under shear stress by successive local bond breaking and reforming, which is why real metals deform plastically at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal.
must: A dislocation is a LINE defect (not a point defect like a vacancy or interstitial); the three types are edge, screw and mixed (mixed = edge + screw character).

An edge dislocation is an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the lattice; the dislocation line (symbol \(\perp\)) runs along the end of the half-plane and marks the boundary between slipped and unslipped crystal.
Strain field: with the extra half-plane above the slip plane, the lattice above the dislocation line is in compression and below it is in tension; the core is the most highly distorted region.
Burgers vector \(\mathbf{b}\): the magnitude and direction of the lattice displacement produced when the dislocation passes completely through the crystal. State both magnitude and direction.
For an edge dislocation \(\mathbf{b}\perp\) dislocation line (a screw dislocation has \(\mathbf{b}\parallel\) line); do not confuse \(\mathbf{b}\) with the line direction.
Under a shear stress \(\tau\), an edge dislocation glides in the slip direction (parallel to \(\tau\)) along the slip plane, moving one atomic spacing per step.

Mechanism of motion: bonds at the core break and reform with neighbouring atoms, one row at a time, so each atom shifts only a small fraction of an interatomic spacing and no atoms travel long distances.

Why dislocations matter: only local bonds break at once, so the stress needed for slip is far below the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal, explaining why real metals are weaker than ideal.
When a dislocation sweeps across a grain it produces a surface step of size \(|\mathbf{b}|\); plastic deformation is a shear process, not rigid sliding of whole planes.
Carpet analogy: moving a bump across a carpet needs far less force than dragging the whole carpet, just as moving a dislocation needs less force than shearing all bonds together.
conn: Dislocation glide links to theoretical vs actual shear strength: the perfect-crystal estimate requires breaking all bonds across a plane simultaneously, whereas dislocations break one row at a time, explaining low real yield stresses.

Burgers vector links to slip geometry: \(\mathbf{b}\) defines the slip direction and step height, and its relation to the line direction (perpendicular for edge, parallel for screw) distinguishes the dislocation types, with mixed having both.
Strain fields link to later strengthening ideas: compression above and tension below the core means dislocations interact with each other and with other defects, which affects how easily they move.
Applied shear stress \(\tau\) links macroscopic plastic deformation to atomic-scale motion: many dislocations gliding across grains produce surface steps and permanent shape change.
exq: Define an edge dislocation and sketch one, labelling the extra half-plane, the dislocation line (\(\perp\)), the core, and the regions of compressive and tensile strain.
Explain, using the idea of sequential bond breaking, why the stress needed to deform a crystal by dislocation motion is much lower than the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal.
Define the Burgers vector. For an edge dislocation, state its direction relative to the dislocation line and to the applied shear stress, and explain how it differs for a screw dislocation.
Describe step by step what happens when an edge dislocation glides across a grain under shear stress \(\tau\), including the final surface step and its size in terms of \(|\mathbf{b}|\).
Distinguish edge, screw and mixed dislocations, and explain why dislocations are line defects rather than point defects such as vacancies.

notes.t: Lattice imperfections: dislocations
pts: Lattice imperfections in crystals are called dislocations, which are line defects in the crystal structure.
There are three major types of dislocation: edge, screw and mixed.
defs: Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice around which atoms are displaced from their regular positions; a major type of lattice imperfection.
tips: Do not confuse dislocations (line defects) with point defects such as vacancies or interstitials.
Mixed dislocations contain both edge and screw character; they are not a separate fundamental defect type.
rq: Why do dislocations matter for the mechanical behaviour of metals?
They allow planes of atoms to slip past each other at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength, so they control plastic deformation, yield strength and ductility.
How does an edge dislocation differ from a screw dislocation?

An edge dislocation is an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the lattice, with the Burgers vector perpendicular to the line; a screw dislocation is a helical ramp of planes, with the Burgers vector parallel to the line.

notes.t: Edge Dislocation
pts: An edge dislocation is a line defect caused by an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal lattice.
Atoms just above the extra plane are compressed, so the lattice is under compressive strain there.
Atoms just below the extra plane are pulled apart, so the lattice is under tensile strain there.
The dislocation line is marked with the symbol ⊥, which represents the end of the extra half-plane.
The Burgers vector b shows the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by the dislocation.
defs: Edge dislocation
A line defect in a crystal where an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted into the lattice, distorting the surrounding planes.
Burgers vector
The vector b that describes the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion produced by a dislocation.
tips: Do not confuse compression and tension: squashed atoms are above the extra plane and stretched atoms are below it, which depends on the chosen orientation.
The Burgers vector is a vector with magnitude and direction; state both when describing a dislocation, not just its size.
rq: Why does plastic deformation occur more easily when dislocations are present than in a perfect crystal?
Dislocations allow planes of atoms to slip past each other one bond at a time, so the force needed is far lower than shearing an entire perfect plane at once.
What would happen to the strain above and below the extra plane if the inserted half-plane were removed?
The compression above and tension below would disappear, because the lattice would return to its perfect, undistorted arrangement.

notes.t: Edge Dislocation
pts: An edge dislocation is a line defect created by an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal structure.
Atomic bonds below the dislocation line are in tension (stretched), while bonds above it are in compression (squashed).
The core of the dislocation is the highly distorted region at the end of the extra half-plane, where the lattice is most strained.
The dislocation line runs along the end of the half-plane and marks the boundary between perfect and slipped crystal.
defs: Edge dislocation
A linear crystal defect in which an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted into the lattice, producing local compressive strain above and tensile strain below the dislocation line.
tips: Do not confuse the stretched region (below the dislocation line) with the squashed region (above it); the convention is that the extra half-plane sits above the slip plane.
Students often describe the dislocation as a point defect; it is a line defect extending along the core of the half-plane.
rq: Why does plastic deformation occur more easily in the presence of edge dislocations than in a perfect crystal?
Dislocations allow planes of atoms to slip one bond at a time at a much lower stress than shearing whole planes at once, because only the bonds at the core need to be broken and reformed.
What would happen to the stretched and squashed bonds if the extra half-plane were removed?
The strain fields would disappear and the lattice would return to its perfect, unstrained arrangement; the stretched bonds below and compressed bonds above would relax.

notes.t: Movement of edge dislocation
pts: Breaking all bonds at once in a perfect crystal is difficult, so plastic deformation would need very high stress.
Defects such as dislocations allow atoms to move relative to each other with much less force.
A dislocation moves by successively breaking stressed bonds and reforming them with neighbouring atoms, so only one row of bonds is disrupted at a time.
tips: Do not confuse the movement of a dislocation with the movement of whole atoms over large distances; each atom only shifts a small fraction of an interatomic spacing.
rq: Why does a dislocation allow a crystal to deform at a much lower stress than a perfect crystal would require?
Because only the bonds at the dislocation core are broken and reformed at any instant, so the dislocation moves through the lattice step by step rather than the whole plane shearing at once.

notes.t: Edge dislocation motion under shear stress
pts: Applying a shear stress τ causes an edge dislocation to move through the crystal, so plastic deformation occurs by dislocation glide rather than by all atomic planes sliding together.
As the dislocation moves, bonds at the dislocation core are broken and new bonds are re-formed with neighbouring atoms, one row at a time, so only a small local rearrangement is needed per step.

Because only local bond breaking is required, the stress needed to move a dislocation is far lower than the theoretical stress to shear a perfect crystal, which explains why real metals are weaker than ideal.
defs: Edge dislocation
A line defect in a crystal where an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted; the dislocation line marks the end of this extra half-plane and the lattice is distorted around it.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of dislocation motion with the direction of the shear stress τ; the slip direction is parallel to the applied shear stress.
Dislocation motion is not the same as the whole crystal planes sliding; only local bonds at the core break at once.
rq: Why does a dislocation move more easily than all the atoms in one plane sliding over another at once?
Only the bonds at the dislocation core break and re-form at any instant, so the required force is much smaller than breaking all bonds across the whole plane simultaneously.
What would happen to the stress needed for plastic deformation if a metal contained many more dislocations?
Dislocations interact and tangle, impeding each other's motion, so the stress needed to deform increases (work hardening).

notes.t: Edge dislocation
pts: An edge dislocation is a line defect where an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted into the crystal lattice.
The dislocation moves through the lattice by one atomic spacing at a time, so the extra half-plane steps through the crystal.
Lattice distortion is concentrated around the dislocation line, which is why dislocations allow plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength.
defs: Edge dislocation
A linear crystal defect in which an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted into the lattice; the line where the half-plane ends is the dislocation line.
tips: Do not confuse an edge dislocation (extra half-plane, perpendicular to slip) with a screw dislocation; the Burgers vector is perpendicular to the dislocation line for an edge dislocation.
The 'extra half-plane' is inserted above or below the slip plane; mixing up the sign convention is a common error.
rq: Why does a dislocation moving one atomic spacing at a time require far less stress than sliding one whole plane of atoms over another?
Only the bonds near the dislocation core are broken and re-formed at each step, so the local bond-breaking and required stress are much lower than for rigid slip of entire planes.
What would happen to a crystal's ductility if dislocations could not move?
Plastic deformation would require very high stresses approaching the theoretical strength, so the metal would be far stronger but brittle, with little ductility.

notes.t: Edge dislocation motion and slip across a grain
pts: An edge dislocation moves through the crystal one step at a time, so the lattice shifts gradually rather than all atoms moving at once.
Repeated glide of a single edge dislocation under shear stress τ eventually displaces one part of the crystal relative to the other across the whole grain, producing a step on the surface.
Shear stress τ applied in opposite directions to the top and bottom of the crystal drives the dislocation sweeping across the slip plane.
defs: Edge dislocation
A line defect in which an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted into the crystal lattice; its motion under shear stress causes plastic deformation by slip.
tips: Do not confuse the dislocation motion direction with the atomic displacement direction; the atoms move one step while the dislocation line travels across the grain.
Remember that the shear stress τ must act in the slip direction to cause dislocation glide.
rq: Why is it easier to move a dislocation across a grain than to shear the whole crystal plane at once?
Moving a dislocation breaks only a few atomic bonds at a time, so the stress needed is far lower than that required to shift entire planes of atoms simultaneously.
What would the surface of the grain look like after many dislocations have swept across it?
It would show a step, since each dislocation that exits the crystal displaces one part of the surface by one Burgers vector b.

notes.t: Edge dislocation and the Burgers vector
pts: An edge dislocation moves through the crystal by a sequence of small local bond-switching steps, not by moving all atoms at once.
The amount of lattice displacement produced by a dislocation's passage is a fixed vector called the Burgers vector, b.
The carpet analogy: a bump (the dislocation) travels across a heavy carpet, so the carpet is shifted one step at a time with far less force than dragging it whole.
defs: Burgers vector
The vector b giving the magnitude and direction of lattice displacement produced when a dislocation moves completely through a crystal; it characterises the dislocation.
tips: The Burgers vector is a vector: state both magnitude and direction, and do not confuse it with the dislocation line direction.
Dislocation motion is a shear process; it does not translate the whole crystal as a rigid block.
rq: Why does a dislocation move by many small steps rather than the whole crystal shifting at once?

Moving all atoms together requires breaking many bonds simultaneously and needs a very high stress; a dislocation only disturbs a few bonds at a time, so it moves at a much lower stress, like the carpet bump.

units.name: 7.7 Observing dislocations by TEM
units.ov: This material introduces dislocations as line defects that allow plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical strength, and shows that TEM can image them directly in electron-transparent foils (e.g. 100 nm stainless steel). It then links microstructure to properties: NbC nano-precipitates in steel are imaged at atomic resolution and strengthen the steel by impeding dislocation motion. The central idea is that strength is controlled by how easily dislocations move.
must: Definition: a dislocation is a 1D line defect across which atomic planes are displaced; its glide under shear stress produces plastic deformation
Dislocations explain why real metals yield at stresses far below the theoretical strength of a perfect lattice
Strengthening principle: anything that impedes dislocation motion (e.g. precipitates) raises strength
NbC precipitates are nano-crystals of a second phase in the Fe matrix, with a larger atomic spacing than Fe, deliberately added to slow dislocation propagation
TEM transmits electrons through a very thin specimen, so internal structure is resolved; bulk samples must be thinned to be electron-transparent (e.g. ~100 nm)
In TEM images dislocations appear as dark line segments, the traces of lattice distortion threading through the foil
At high resolution the dots are columns of atoms; TEM is the highest-resolution microscopy available
Distinguish defect dimensionality: dislocations (1D) vs point defects such as vacancies and interstitials (0D) vs planar defects such as grain boundaries (2D)
Image interpretation: false colour only highlights the precipitate and is not compositional data; use the scale bar (e.g. 5 nm) for true sizes
Application context: Nb-strengthened steel for car bodies; other high-strength steels for cutting tools
conn: Dislocation motion → plastic deformation → yield strength: obstacles such as precipitates (NbC) raise yield strength, so questions link the defect to mechanical properties
Lattice mismatch (NbC spacing larger than Fe) → local strain fields that interact with dislocations and hinder their glide
TEM sample requirement (thin foil) → what can be seen: the thin foil limits what is imaged, so the dark lines are projections of dislocation lines through the thickness
Defect classification (point, line, planar) → which feature is being imaged and how it affects properties
exq: Define a dislocation and explain how its movement leads to plastic deformation at stresses well below the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal.
Explain why a bulk steel sample cannot be imaged directly in TEM, and why a foil of about 100 nm thickness is used. What do dislocations look like in the resulting image?

A TEM image has a 5 nm scale bar that measures 25 mm on the printed page. A NbC precipitate measures 40 mm across. Calculate its true size and explain why the scale bar, not the image dimensions, must be used.
Describe how NbC nano-precipitates strengthen steel for car bodies. Why is a mismatch in atomic spacing relevant?
Compare dislocations, vacancies and grain boundaries in terms of dimensionality, and state which can be seen as lines in a TEM image of a thin foil.

notes.t: Dislocations observed by TEM
pts: Dislocations are line defects in the crystal lattice that allow plastic deformation to occur at stresses far below the theoretical strength.
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) can directly image dislocations in very thin specimens, here a 100 nm thick stainless steel sheet.
In the image, dislocations appear as dark line segments; they are the visible traces of the lattice distortion lines threading through the foil.
defs: Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice across which atomic planes are displaced; its movement under shear stress produces plastic deformation.
TEM (Transmission Electron Microscopy)
An imaging technique in which electrons pass through a very thin specimen, allowing internal microstructure such as dislocations to be resolved at atomic-scale resolution.
tips: Do not confuse dislocations (1D line defects) with point defects such as vacancies or interstitials, or with planar defects like grain boundaries.
TEM requires electron-transparent specimens; bulk samples cannot be imaged this way without thinning.
rq: Why must the specimen be only about 100 nm thick for TEM to show dislocations?
Electrons must be transmitted through the foil; thin samples let enough electrons pass to form an image, so the internal defects become visible.
Why do dislocations, rather than perfect crystals, explain the low yield strength of metals?
Dislocations let atomic planes slip one step at a time under small shear stresses, instead of shearing whole planes at once as the theoretical strength would require.

notes.t: TEM imaging of Niobium Carbide precipitates in steel
pts: TEM is the highest resolution microscopy available; the dots seen are actual columns of atoms.
NbC precipitate nano-crystals have a larger atomic spacing than the surrounding Fe atoms, visible in the lattice.
NbC nano-crystals are deliberately added to steel to strengthen it by slowing the propagation of dislocations.
The false colour is used only to highlight the NbC precipitate against the steel matrix; it is not part of the real data.
This Nb-strengthened steel is intended for car body applications, while other high-strength steels are used for cutting tools.
defs: Precipitate
A second-phase particle that forms within a metal matrix, here NbC nano-crystals, which strengthen the steel by impeding dislocation motion.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement produces plastic deformation; precipitates slow its propagation to increase strength.
tips: Do not confuse the false colour in the image with real compositional data; it is only a visual highlight.
The scale bar (5 nm) gives the only true length reference, so measure sizes from it rather than from the image dimensions.
rq: Why does a larger atomic spacing in the NbC precipitate, compared with the surrounding Fe lattice, help to strengthen the steel?
The lattice mismatch creates strain fields around the precipitate that act as obstacles, so dislocations need more stress to move past or cut through them.
Why must the false colour be ignored when reading the micrograph quantitatively?
False colour is added only to make the NbC particle stand out; the actual intensity and contrast details come from the imaging, not the colouring.
