units.name: 8.1 Course intro and student feedback
units.ov: The extracted notes are almost empty. They contain only a title slide for ENG 1033 Materials 1, Lecture 8 (Crystal Structure 4), and a heading 'Student Feedback'. The content below is therefore standard first-year crystal structure revision, not material taken from these pages, and it should be checked against the actual lecture slides.
must: Notes limitation: the pages give only the lecture title and 'Student Feedback', so check the real slides for the syllabus emphasis and any worked examples
The three common metallic structures are BCC, FCC and HCP, and you should be able to sketch each unit cell
Atoms per unit cell: simple cubic 1, BCC 2, FCC 4, HCP 6 (counted as the full hexagonal cell)
Coordination number and atomic packing factor: BCC 8 and 0.68, FCC 12 and 0.74, HCP 12 and 0.74
Relation between lattice parameter \(a\) and atomic radius \(R\): BCC \(a=4R/\sqrt{3}\), FCC \(a=2\sqrt{2}R\)
Theoretical density: \(\rho = \dfrac{nA}{V_c N_A}\), where \(n\) is atoms per cell, \(A\) the atomic mass, \(V_c\) the cell volume and \(N_A\) Avogadro's number
Miller indices for planes \((hkl)\) and directions \([uvw]\): use intercepts, take reciprocals and clear fractions, and know the negative-index notation
Close-packed planes and directions (FCC {111}, ⟨110⟩), which link to slip and ductility
Linear and planar atomic density, and the stacking sequences ABAB (HCP) and ABCABC (FCC)
conn: Packing factor, coordination number and density all follow from the same unit-cell geometry, so a density question usually starts by finding \(a\) from \(R\)
Miller indices connect to planar density and slip systems, which explain why FCC metals are ductile and HCP metals are less so
Stacking sequences link HCP and FCC, which have the same packing efficiency but different symmetry and slip behaviour
Crystal structure links to X-ray diffraction, where Bragg's law \(n\lambda=2d\sin\theta\) uses plane spacing derived from \(a\) and \((hkl)\)
exq: Copper is FCC with atomic radius 0.128 nm and atomic mass 63.5 g/mol. Calculate the lattice parameter and the theoretical density.
Show that the atomic packing factor of BCC is 0.68, stating the number of atoms per cell and the relation between \(a\) and \(R\).
Sketch the (110) plane and the [111] direction in a cubic cell, and determine the Miller indices of a plane with intercepts at \(a\), \(\infty\) and \(a/2\).
Calculate the planar atomic density of the (111) plane in FCC iron and compare it with the (100) plane. Which is close-packed?
Describe the ABAB and ABCABC stacking sequences, and explain how they relate to the HCP and FCC structures and to ductility.

units.name: 8.2 Dislocations: screw, edge and mixed
units.ov: This material covers line defects (dislocations) in crystals: screw, edge and mixed types, classified by the angle between the Burgers vector \(\mathbf{b}\) and the dislocation line direction \(\mathbf{t}\). Dislocations move by sequential bond breaking and re-forming, which lets crystals deform plastically at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength. The Burgers vector is the unifying quantity: it is found from a closed circuit around the line and stays constant along it, while the line direction, and therefore the edge/screw character, can change.
must: Dislocation = line defect (not a point or planar defect) that enables slip and plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal.
Classification by geometry: edge has \(\mathbf{b}\perp\) line; screw has \(\mathbf{b}\parallel\) line; mixed has \(\mathbf{b}\) at an intermediate angle, with both edge and screw components.
Burgers vector: the closure failure of a circuit drawn around the dislocation compared with the same circuit in a perfect crystal. It gives the magnitude and direction of the lattice distortion.
The Burgers vector is constant (same magnitude and direction) along the entire dislocation line, even when the line curves and its character changes from edge to screw.

Edge dislocation: caused by an extra half-plane of atoms. The line lies along the edge of that half-plane and separates slipped from unslipped crystal. The core is the highly distorted region around the line.

Screw dislocation: planes form a helical (spiral) ramp around the line, with no extra half-plane. It produces a surface step of one \(\mathbf{b}\), and the spiral step is a self-perpetuating growth site, so crystals can grow at low supersaturation.

Motion: bonds stretch, then break on one side and re-form on the other, so the line advances one atomic spacing per cycle. The plane does not slide rigidly. Net result is a displacement of \(\mathbf{b}\).

A screw dislocation moves perpendicular to its line, even though \(\mathbf{b}\) is parallel to the line. Its line direction is parallel to the slip direction, whereas the edge line is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}\).

Mixed dislocation: on one crystal face it looks like a screw, on the perpendicular face like an edge. The curved line has pure screw and pure edge orientations at its ends and mixed character between them.
Do not confuse dislocations (line defects) with vacancies and interstitials (point defects).
conn: Burgers vector and line direction: the angle between \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{t}\) fixes the character. Because \(\mathbf{b}\) is constant, a curved loop must change from screw to mixed to edge around its length.

Dislocation motion and plastic deformation: the bond-breaking mechanism explains why slip needs far lower stress than rigid sliding of a whole plane, linking to theoretical versus actual shear strength.

Line direction versus motion direction: the screw's \(\mathbf{b}\parallel\) line but it glides perpendicular to the line, and the edge's \(\mathbf{b}\perp\) line. Both produce the same net slip of \(\mathbf{b}\) at the surface.
Screw dislocation and crystal growth: the spiral ramp links defect geometry to growth steps and surface morphology.
exq: Define a dislocation and distinguish between edge, screw and mixed types in terms of the angle between the Burgers vector and the dislocation line. Sketch each.
Describe how a Burgers circuit is constructed around a dislocation and how \(\mathbf{b}\) is determined. Explain why \(\mathbf{b}\) is the same along a curved mixed dislocation.

Explain, step by step, how a screw dislocation moves through a crystal under shear stress, including bond stretching, breaking and re-forming. State the direction of motion relative to the line and to \(\mathbf{b}\), and the resulting surface step.
A dislocation loop has a single Burgers vector. Identify the points on the loop where it is pure screw, pure edge and mixed, and explain how it would appear on perpendicular crystal faces.
Explain why a screw dislocation allows crystal growth at low supersaturation, and why dislocations lower the stress needed for plastic deformation compared with a perfect crystal.

notes.t: Lattice imperfections: dislocations
pts: Lattice imperfections in crystals are called dislocations, which are line defects that allow plastic deformation.
There are three major types of dislocation: edge, screw and mixed.
defs: Dislocation
A linear lattice imperfection in a crystal across which atomic planes are displaced, enabling slip and plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength.
tips: Do not confuse dislocations (line defects) with point defects such as vacancies or interstitials.
Name all three types exactly as edge, screw and mixed; mixed dislocations contain both edge and screw character.
rq: Why do dislocations make metals far weaker than the theoretical shear strength predicts?
Dislocations let atomic planes slip one row at a time, so only a small local bond-breaking/shearing is needed instead of shearing the whole plane at once.
How does an edge dislocation differ from a screw dislocation in terms of the direction of the dislocation line relative to the Burgers vector?
In an edge dislocation the line is perpendicular to the Burgers vector; in a screw dislocation it is parallel to the Burgers vector; mixed dislocations have an intermediate angle.

notes.t: Lattice imperfections: dislocations
pts: Lattice imperfections of the crystal structure are called dislocations.
There are three major types of dislocation: edge, screw and mixed.
Edge dislocations were covered in Lecture 7, so this lecture extends to the remaining types.
defs: Dislocation
A linear lattice imperfection in a crystal, around which atoms are misaligned, that allows plastic deformation by slip at lower stress than in a perfect crystal.
tips: Do not confuse dislocations (line defects) with point defects such as vacancies or interstitials.
Edge dislocations are covered in Lecture 7; screw and mixed types are the new content here.
rq: Why do dislocations make metals easier to deform than a perfect crystal would be?
Dislocations allow planes of atoms to slip past one another one row at a time, so the stress needed is far lower than shearing a whole perfect plane at once.
How does a mixed dislocation differ from a pure edge or pure screw dislocation?
Its dislocation line is neither perpendicular nor parallel to the Burgers vector; it has both edge and screw components.

notes.t: Screw Dislocation
pts: A screw dislocation is a line defect where the crystal planes form a helical ramp around the dislocation line, so growth steps spiral outward from a centre.
The spiral step pattern seen in the image shows that the dislocation line runs perpendicular to the Burgers vector, which is parallel to the direction of the slip displacement.
Screw dislocations allow crystal growth at low supersaturation because the spiral step provides a continuous growth site that never runs out.
defs: Screw dislocation
A line defect in a crystal in which the lattice planes are displaced in a helical (spiral) manner about the dislocation line, with the Burgers vector parallel to the line direction.
tips: Do not confuse a screw dislocation (Burgers vector parallel to the line) with an edge dislocation (Burgers vector perpendicular to the line).
rq: Why does a screw dislocation produce a spiral growth pattern rather than closed concentric rings?
Because the atomic planes are continuously offset by one step around the dislocation line, so a single step winds continuously outward like a staircase, creating an unbroken spiral.
How does the Burgers vector of a screw dislocation differ from that of an edge dislocation?
For a screw dislocation the Burgers vector is parallel to the dislocation line, whereas for an edge dislocation it is perpendicular to the line.

notes.t: Screw dislocation
pts: A screw dislocation forms when a plane of atoms is displaced by one step, creating a helical ramp of atoms around the dislocation line.
The dislocation is a line defect: the distortion extends along a line rather than being localised at a single point.
The dislocation line is indicated by a curved arrow symbol (a loop-like arrow), and the Burgers vector b is perpendicular to the dislocation line... actually parallel to it for a screw dislocation.
defs: Screw dislocation
A linear crystal defect in which atomic planes are displaced by one step so that the lattice forms a helical ramp around the dislocation line; the Burgers vector is parallel to the dislocation line.
Burgers vector
The vector that describes the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by a dislocation, found by a closed circuit around the dislocation compared with a perfect crystal.
Dislocation line
The line along which the lattice distortion of a dislocation extends through the crystal.
tips: Do not confuse screw dislocations (Burgers vector parallel to the line) with edge dislocations (Burgers vector perpendicular to the line).
A dislocation is a line defect, not a point defect; the distortion extends along the whole line.
rq: Why does a screw dislocation's Burgers vector lie parallel to its line, unlike an edge dislocation?
In a screw dislocation the shear displacement is along the line direction, so b is parallel to the line; in an edge dislocation b is perpendicular to the line.
What would happen to plastic deformation if a screw dislocation could not move?
Slip would be hindered, so the metal would be harder and stronger, since dislocation motion is the mechanism of plastic deformation.

notes.t: Screw Dislocation
pts: A screw dislocation is a line defect where atomic planes spiral around the dislocation line, forming a helical ramp in the crystal.
In the top view, the dislocation appears where a plane of atoms ends partway through the crystal, so neighbouring atoms are displaced out of their correct lattice positions.
The Burgers vector b is parallel to the dislocation line, which distinguishes a screw dislocation from an edge dislocation where b is perpendicular to the line.
defs: Screw dislocation
A linear crystal defect in which atomic planes are displaced in a helical (spiral) arrangement around the dislocation line, with the Burgers vector parallel to that line.
tips: Do not confuse screw and edge dislocations: screw has b parallel to the line, edge has b perpendicular to it.
A screw dislocation is a line defect, not a point defect or planar defect; state this clearly when classifying imperfections.
rq: Why does a screw dislocation allow plastic deformation to occur at a lower stress than perfect shear of a crystal?

Because the atoms are displaced one at a time along the spiral step rather than all planes sliding at once, so only a small local displacement of the Burgers vector is needed to move the dislocation across the slip plane.
How would the atomic arrangement around the dislocation differ if the Burgers vector were perpendicular to the line instead?
It would be an edge dislocation, where an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted rather than a spiral ramp formed.

notes.t: Screw dislocation
pts: A screw dislocation moves through the crystal as bonds are broken and re-formed across the slip plane, rather than the whole plane sliding at once.

The screw dislocation line is the boundary between slipped and unslipped regions; atoms above and below the cut plane are displaced relative to each other in a helical (spiral) arrangement around the dislocation line.

Because the atomic arrangement forms a spiral ramp around the dislocation line, the dislocation has a line direction parallel to the slip direction, unlike an edge dislocation where the line is perpendicular to the Burgers vector.
defs: Screw dislocation

A line defect in a crystal where atomic planes are displaced in a helical (spiral) pattern around the dislocation line, with the Burgers vector parallel to the dislocation line; it moves by sequential bond breaking and re-forming.
tips: Do not confuse the screw dislocation's Burgers vector (parallel to the line) with the edge dislocation's (perpendicular to the line).
Describe the motion as bond breaking and re-forming, not as a whole plane sliding rigidly.
rq: Why does a dislocation allow a crystal to deform at a stress far lower than that needed to shear whole planes at once?
Only a narrow row of bonds is broken and re-formed at a time, so the dislocation sweeps through the crystal with much less force than moving a complete plane rigidly.
How does a screw dislocation's motion differ from an edge dislocation's in terms of the direction of slip relative to the dislocation line?
For a screw dislocation the slip direction is parallel to the dislocation line, so it moves perpendicular to its own line; for an edge dislocation the slip direction is perpendicular to the line.

notes.t: Screw dislocation motion through a crystal
pts: A screw dislocation moves through the crystal as bonds are successively broken and reformed, shifting one atom plane step by step.
Bond stretching occurs first as the atoms near the dislocation line are displaced, storing elastic strain before any bond breaks.
Bonds break on one side of the dislocation and re-form on the other side, so the dislocation line advances one atomic spacing per cycle.
The net result of repeated bond breaking and formation is a displacement of the crystal by one Burgers vector b, leaving a step on the surface.
defs: Screw dislocation

A line defect in which the atomic displacement is parallel to the dislocation line, producing a helical arrangement of planes around the line; it moves perpendicular to its line direction under shear stress.
Burgers vector (b)

The lattice vector describing the closure failure of a circuit around a dislocation; for a screw dislocation it is parallel to the dislocation line and gives the magnitude and direction of lattice displacement.
tips: Do not confuse screw and edge dislocations: for a screw, b is parallel to the line; for an edge, b is perpendicular to it.
Remember the motion direction is perpendicular to the dislocation line, even though the Burgers vector is parallel to it.
rq: Why does a screw dislocation move by bond breaking and re-forming rather than by all atoms moving at once?
Moving a whole plane at once would require far more energy; sequential bond breaking and re-formation lets the defect advance with a much lower stress, one bond row at a time.
What would happen to the crystal's shape if a screw dislocation travels fully across it?
The upper part of the crystal is displaced by one Burgers vector b relative to the lower part, creating a step of height b on the surface, which produces plastic deformation.

notes.t: Edge dislocation
pts: An edge dislocation is formed by an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal lattice, distorting the surrounding planes.
The dislocation line runs along the edge of the extra half-plane; the region of highest lattice distortion around this line is called the core.
The dislocation line is the boundary between the slipped and unslipped regions and is the linear defect that moves under shear stress to allow plastic deformation.
defs: Edge dislocation
A line defect in a crystal caused by an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the lattice, which distorts the surrounding planes and whose line is perpendicular to the Burgers vector.
Dislocation core
The region immediately around the dislocation line where lattice distortion is greatest and atoms are severely displaced from their ideal positions.
Dislocation line
The line along the edge of the extra half-plane of atoms, which marks the boundary between slipped and unslipped crystal and is the line along which the defect lies.
tips: Do not confuse the dislocation line with the core: the line is the defect's path, while the core is the highly distorted region around it.
Remember that an edge dislocation is a line defect, not a point defect or planar defect.
rq: Why does an edge dislocation allow metals to deform plastically at much lower stresses than would be needed to shear whole planes of atoms at once?
Because only the atoms at the core need to move at a time; the dislocation sweeps through the crystal one bond at a time, so the stress needed is far lower than shearing an entire plane rigidly.
What would happen to the lattice around the dislocation line if the extra half-plane were removed, and how does this relate to the compressed and stretched regions?
The lattice above the half-plane is compressed and below it is stretched; removing the half-plane would relieve this distortion, showing the strain field is caused by the inserted extra plane.

notes.t: Screw Dislocation
pts: A screw dislocation is a line defect where atoms are displaced in a spiral (helical) pattern around the dislocation line.
The Burgers vector is parallel to the dislocation line, which distinguishes a screw dislocation from an edge dislocation where the two are perpendicular.
defs: Screw dislocation
A line defect in a crystal in which atomic planes are displaced in a helical (spiral) fashion around the dislocation line, so the Burgers vector is parallel to the line.
tips: Do not confuse screw and edge dislocations: screw has Burgers vector parallel to the line, edge has it perpendicular.
Screw dislocations do not produce an extra half-plane of atoms, so they are not visible as an inserted plane in the lattice.
rq: Why does a screw dislocation's Burgers vector lie parallel to the line, and how does this differ from an edge dislocation?

The lattice is sheared in a helical path around the line, so the closure failure (Burgers circuit) is along the line direction; an edge dislocation has the Burgers vector perpendicular to the line because it arises from an extra half-plane of atoms.

notes.t: Mixed Dislocation
pts: A mixed dislocation has both edge and screw character along its line.
On one face of the crystal the dislocation looks like a screw dislocation.
On the perpendicular face the same dislocation looks like an edge dislocation.
defs: Mixed dislocation
A dislocation whose Burgers vector is neither parallel nor perpendicular to its line direction, so it has both edge and screw components along its length.
tips: Do not classify a mixed dislocation as purely edge or purely screw; it contains both components along the line.
The Burgers vector is constant along the dislocation line even though the edge and screw character vary.
rq: Why does the same dislocation appear as a screw on one face and an edge on another?

Its line direction is inclined to the Burgers vector; the component of the Burgers vector parallel to the line gives screw character and the perpendicular component gives edge character, so each face cuts the dislocation line differently.

notes.t: Mixed Dislocation
pts: A mixed dislocation has both edge and screw character along its length, so its defect line curves through the crystal.
The Burgers vector b is the same at every point along the curved dislocation line, even though the line direction changes.
The edge-character segment is where the extra half-plane of atoms ends, and the screw-character segment is where atomic planes form a helical ramp.
defs: Mixed dislocation
A dislocation whose line is neither purely parallel nor purely perpendicular to its Burgers vector; it has combined edge and screw components and forms a curved defect line through the crystal.
Burgers vector
The vector b that describes the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by a dislocation, found by a closed circuit around the defect compared with a perfect crystal.
tips: Do not assume a mixed dislocation is either purely edge or purely screw; state that its character varies along the line.
Remember the Burgers vector stays the same magnitude and direction along the whole dislocation, while the line direction changes.
rq: Why does a mixed dislocation curve through the crystal instead of running in a straight line?
Because its line direction changes along its length, transitioning between edge character (line perpendicular to b) and screw character (line parallel to b), so the defect line bends.
What would you expect to see at point A versus point B on the diagram?
Near A the dislocation line is mainly edge-like with the Burgers vector perpendicular to it, while toward B it becomes more screw-like with the Burgers vector parallel to the line.

units.name: 8.3 Crystal formation, grains and grain boundaries
units.ov: This module explains how polycrystalline solids form: crystals nucleate with random orientations, grow outward, and meet to form grains separated by grain boundaries. Boundaries are classified by misorientation (low angle as dislocation arrays, high angle, and twin boundaries). Because boundaries block dislocation glide, they control yield strength, which links microstructure to mechanical properties.
must: Formation sequence: nucleation first (small stable clusters with random orientation), then atom-by-atom growth, then impingement to form grains and boundaries
Grain = single crystal region with uniform lattice orientation; grain boundary = interface where atoms are not in perfect registry; grains are the same phase, not different materials
Nuclei (small initial clusters) are not grains (fully grown crystal regions)
Low-angle boundary: misorientation below about 10–15°, modelled as a regular array of dislocations; high-angle: large misorientation, poor atomic fit
Classification depends only on misorientation angle, not on grain size
Tilt boundary = wall of edge dislocations, rotation axis in the boundary plane; twist boundary = screw dislocation network, rotation axis normal to the boundary
Frank's relation \( D = b/\theta \) with \( \theta \) in radians: closer dislocation spacing means larger misorientation angle
Twin boundary = mirror-image lattice across the twin plane; formed by mechanical shear deformation or by heat treatment after mechanical work; distinct from an ordinary grain boundary
Dislocations glide within grains and pile up at grain boundaries; boundaries act as barriers, so they raise yield strength (dislocations are not created at boundaries)
Read grain size from the micrograph scale bar and check units (e.g. 2.4 µm bar)
conn: Nucleation with random orientation leads to differently oriented grains, which gives the boundaries that later block dislocations and set yield strength
Frank's relation links the dislocation model of low-angle boundaries to the misorientation angle, so a tilt boundary question combines edge dislocations, Burgers vector and radian conversion
Dislocation glide and pile-up connects plastic deformation to grain boundaries, so more boundaries (finer grains) means more barriers and higher yield strength
Mechanical deformation produces twins, and subsequent heat treatment can reorganise them, linking processing history to boundary type
exq: Describe the stages of crystal formation from nucleation to a polycrystalline structure, explaining why neighbouring grains have different orientations and how grain boundaries arise.

A tilt boundary in a metal has a Burgers vector of 0.25 nm and a misorientation of 2°. Calculate the dislocation spacing using \( D = b/\theta \). What happens to D if the angle doubles, and is the boundary low-angle?
Distinguish between tilt and twist boundaries, stating the dislocation type and the rotation axis relative to the boundary plane for each, with sketches.
Compare low-angle, high-angle and twin boundaries in terms of misorientation, atomic arrangement and how they form.
Explain, using dislocation motion, why grain boundaries increase the yield strength of a polycrystalline metal, and predict the effect of grain size on strength.

notes.t: How crystals form
pts: Crystals can form by deposition of atoms from a liquid or gas onto a surface.
Atoms arriving next to an existing atom release energy, so this site is energetically favourable and growth proceeds atom by atom.
tips: Do not confuse the formation route (deposition from liquid or gas) with the solidification of a melt; the page only describes deposition onto a surface.
rq: Why would an atom arriving on a surface prefer to settle next to an atom that is already bonded there rather than in an isolated spot?
Bonding to neighbouring atoms lowers the system's energy, so arriving beside an existing atom is more energy efficient, which drives ordered, crystalline growth.

notes.t: Crystal formation: nucleation and random orientation
pts: Crystallisation begins from small nuclei that form within the melt or solid.
Each nucleus starts with a random orientation, so grains grow with different lattice directions.
Growing grains meet and form grain boundaries where their orientations differ.
defs: Nucleus
A small stable cluster of atoms that forms in a melt and acts as the starting point for crystal growth.
tips: Do not confuse nuclei (initial small clusters) with grains (the fully grown crystal regions).
rq: Why does a polycrystalline solid contain grain boundaries rather than one continuous crystal?
Because many nuclei form independently with random orientations, and grains growing from them meet at boundaries where lattice orientation changes.
What would happen to the grain structure if all nuclei had the same orientation?
The grains would grow in a common orientation, giving a single crystal with no grain boundaries.

notes.t: Crystal formation
pts: As more atoms are deposited, they grow outward from the initial nuclei, forming crystal grains.
tips: Nucleation and growth are two distinct stages: nuclei form first, then atoms add to them; do not describe growth as occurring before nuclei exist.
rq: Why do the crystal grains in the image appear as separate blocks with different orientations rather than one continuous lattice?

Each nucleus forms independently at a different site and with a different crystallographic orientation, so when growing grains meet they cannot merge into one continuous lattice; the boundaries between them are grain boundaries.

notes.t: Crystal formation and grain structure
pts: During solidification, crystals grow from many separate nuclei, and where they meet they leave gaps or boundaries between them.
Each crystal (grain) forms from a different initial nucleus, so neighbouring grains have different crystallographic orientations.
defs: Grain
A single crystal region within a polycrystalline solid, with a uniform lattice orientation that differs from its neighbours.
Grain boundary
The interface between two grains of different orientation, where atoms are not in perfect lattice registry.
tips: Do not confuse grains (crystal regions) with grain boundaries (the interfaces between them); the boundary is the gap or disordered region.
Grains are not 'different materials' — they are the same crystal structure with different orientations.
rq: Why does a solid made of many grains have different properties in different directions only if the grains are aligned, and why is a random arrangement macroscopically isotropic?
Because randomly oriented grains average out their directional properties, so the bulk material behaves approximately isotropically, whereas aligned grains (texture) give anisotropic behaviour.
What would happen to the number of grain boundaries if solidification started from fewer nuclei?
Fewer nuclei give larger grains and fewer grain boundaries, since boundaries form where growing crystals from different nuclei meet.

notes.t: Crystal formation: grains and grain boundaries
pts: Crystallisation leads to the formation of grains, each a single crystal with its own orientation.
Adjacent grains meet at grain boundaries, where atomic arrangement is disrupted.
Micrographs (TEM and grain maps) show grains of different shading/orientation separated by boundary lines, with a 2.4 µm scale bar indicating grain size scale.
defs: Grain
A single crystal region within a polycrystalline solid, with a uniform lattice orientation, separated from neighbouring grains by grain boundaries.
Grain boundary
The interface between two adjacent grains of differing crystallographic orientation, where atoms are not in perfect lattice registry.
tips: Do not confuse grains (crystal regions) with grain boundaries (the interfaces between them); the boundary is not a grain.
Grain size in micrographs is read from the scale bar; check the units (µm) before quoting values.
rq: Why do grain boundaries form at all during solidification?
Nucleation occurs at many separate sites, so each growing crystal has a random orientation; when they impinge they meet at boundaries.
What would happen to the number of grain boundaries if solidification started from only one nucleus?
A single crystal would form with no grain boundaries, since all growth would share one lattice orientation.

notes.t: Grain boundaries and misalignment
pts: Grain boundaries are regions where atomic planes of neighbouring grains are misaligned.
The degree of misalignment is described by the angle between the orientations of adjacent grains, giving two classes.
Small (low) angle grain boundaries have a small misorientation and consist of regularly spaced dislocations.
High angle grain boundaries have large misorientation, so atoms are poorly matched across the boundary.
defs: Grain boundary
The interface between two grains (crystals) of the same phase with different crystallographic orientations, where atomic planes are misaligned.
Low (small) angle grain boundary
A grain boundary with a small misorientation angle between adjacent grains, typically below about 10–15°, described as an array of dislocations.
High angle grain boundary
A grain boundary with a large misorientation angle between adjacent grains, in which the atomic fit across the boundary is poor.
tips: Do not confuse the angle of misalignment with the grain size; the boundary classification depends only on the misorientation angle.
Low angle boundaries are generally taken as misorientations below about 15°, so state the threshold if asked to classify a boundary.
rq: Why are high angle grain boundaries more disruptive to atomic arrangement than low angle ones?
Large misorientation means atoms cannot fit neatly across the boundary, creating a wide region of disorder, whereas small misorientation can be accommodated by a regular array of dislocations.
What would you expect to happen to the number of grain boundaries if grain size is reduced?
More grain boundaries per unit volume form, increasing the total boundary area and the overall level of atomic misalignment in the material.

notes.t: Grain boundaries: small-angle boundaries as dislocation arrays
pts: Small-angle grain boundaries can be modelled as an array (row) of dislocations.
A tilt boundary is formed by a wall of edge dislocations, tilting the lattice about an axis lying in the boundary plane.
A twist boundary is formed by a network of screw dislocations, twisting one grain relative to its neighbour.
The misorientation angle θ grows with the spacing between dislocations, so closely spaced dislocations give a larger angle.
defs: Small-angle grain boundary
A low-angle boundary (typically misorientation below about 10–15°) between grains of nearly identical orientation, described as an array of dislocations.
Tilt boundary
A small-angle grain boundary consisting of a wall of parallel edge dislocations, producing a rotation about an axis lying in the boundary plane.
Twist boundary
A small-angle grain boundary formed from screw dislocations, in which the two grains are rotated about an axis perpendicular to the boundary plane.
eqs: Dislocation spacing in a tilt boundary (Frank's relation)
D = spacing between dislocations (m); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m); θ = misorientation angle (rad)
tips: Keep tilt (edge dislocations, rotation axis in the boundary plane) and twist (screw dislocations, rotation axis normal to the boundary) distinct; they are commonly swapped.
Angles in the dislocation spacing formula must be in radians, not degrees, when calculating D = b/θ.
rq: Why does a small-angle boundary look like a row of dislocations rather than a continuous wall of atoms?

At low misorientation the lattice mismatch is accommodated by isolated extra half-planes spaced periodically; between them the lattice is nearly perfect, so the boundary is a discrete array of dislocations.
What would happen to the boundary if the dislocations were packed closer together?
Spacing D = b/θ decreases, so the misorientation θ increases; the boundary becomes higher angle and the dislocation model breaks down as the cores overlap.

notes.t: Twin Boundary
pts: A twin boundary is an interface across which the lattice on one side is a mirror image of the lattice on the other side.
Twins form from mechanical deformation that produces shear stresses in the crystal.
Twins can also form when heat treatment is applied after mechanical work, which allows the twinned structure to develop or be reorganised.
defs: Twin boundary
A planar defect across which the crystal lattice is mirrored, so that the atomic arrangement on one side is the mirror image of that on the other side of the twin plane.
tips: Do not confuse a twin boundary (mirror-related lattices) with a simple grain boundary (differently oriented grains).
Remember that heat treatment is listed as a second route, typically applied after mechanical work, not as a replacement for it.
rq: Why does a shear stress, rather than a normal stress, tend to produce a twin boundary?

Shear stress displaces atomic planes parallel to the twin plane in a coordinated way, so that the lattice on one side is reflected across the plane rather than simply stretched or compressed, producing a mirror-related lattice.
How does a twin boundary differ from a grain boundary in terms of crystal orientation on either side?
A twin boundary has the two sides related by a mirror (symmetry) operation, whereas grains on either side of a grain boundary generally have different, unrelated orientations.

notes.t: Dislocations in grains and grain boundary control of yield
pts: Under applied load, dislocations glide through the crystal grains, producing plastic deformation.
Dislocations pile up (accumulate) against grain boundaries, which act as barriers to their motion.
Because of this blocking effect, grain boundaries control the yield strength and deformation behaviour of polycrystalline metals.
tips: Do not say dislocations are created at grain boundaries; they move through grains and accumulate at the boundaries.
Grain boundaries increase strength by impeding dislocation motion, not by themselves carrying the plastic flow.
rq: Why does a fine-grained metal typically have a higher yield strength than a coarse-grained one of the same composition?

Fine grains give more grain boundaries per unit volume, so dislocations pile up over shorter distances and are blocked more often, requiring higher stress to move them through the material (Hall-Petch effect).
What would happen to dislocation movement if grain boundaries were removed, e.g. in a single crystal?
Dislocations would not be stopped at boundaries and could glide over longer distances, so the material would generally yield at a lower stress.

units.name: 8.4 X-ray diffraction basics: EM waves and interference
units.ov: This material introduces X-ray diffraction as the standard way to measure crystal lattices. It builds on the electromagnetic spectrum and photon energy (\(E=h\nu=hc/\lambda\)), which show why X-rays with \(\lambda\sim0.1\) nm suit atomic spacings. It then covers wave superposition, constructive and destructive interference, which is the mechanism that gives diffraction peaks at specific angles.
must: X-ray diffraction works because X-ray wavelength (\(\sim10^{-10}\) m, about 0.1 nm) is comparable to atomic spacing; constructive interference at specific angles reveals plane spacing and lattice structure
Photon energy: \(E=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}\), proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength
Wave relation \(c=f\lambda\) holds for all EM waves in vacuum; higher frequency means shorter wavelength and more energy per photon
Typical values: visible light \(\sim10^{-6}\) m; X-rays \(\sim10^{-10}\) m with energy \(\sim4\times10^{3}\) eV
Constructive interference: waves in phase, same wavelength, amplitudes add (amplitude doubles for two equal waves); wavelength and frequency are unchanged
Destructive interference: equal amplitudes and opposite phase (half-wavelength shift) give zero resultant amplitude; unequal amplitudes give a reduced, non-zero result
Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so doubling amplitude gives 4× intensity; add amplitudes, not intensities
Scattering changes the direction and possibly the phase of a wave but keeps amplitude \(A\) and wavelength \(\lambda\)
Unit discipline: convert nm to m and eV to J before using \(E=hc/\lambda\)
conn: Photon energy and wavelength link to diffraction: calculating \(\lambda\) from \(E\) (in eV) shows whether the X-rays can resolve atomic spacings
Phase difference from scattering off different atoms (path difference) determines whether interference is constructive or destructive, which sets the diffraction angles
Amplitude superposition links to measured intensity: peak intensity is the amplitude squared, so in-phase scattering gives 4× the intensity of a single wave
Order-of-magnitude spectrum values link \(c=f\lambda\) and \(E=hf\), so frequency, wavelength and energy can be converted in multi-step problems
exq: Calculate the photon energy in J and eV of X-rays with \(\lambda=0.15\) nm, and compare it with visible light of \(\lambda=500\) nm.
Explain why X-rays, rather than visible light, are used to measure crystal lattices. Refer to wavelength and atomic spacing of about 0.1 nm.

Two waves of equal amplitude \(A\) and wavelength \(\lambda\) overlap. State the resultant amplitude and intensity relative to a single wave when they are (a) in phase and (b) exactly out of phase. What phase shift or path difference gives each case?
An X-ray photon has energy \(4\times10^{3}\) eV. Find its frequency and wavelength, and state whether the result is consistent with the typical X-ray wavelength.
Define constructive and destructive interference, and explain how scattering by atoms can produce each, and why this gives information about lattice structure.

notes.t: Measuring lattices with X-ray diffraction
pts: X-ray diffraction is the standard method used to measure crystal lattices.
X-rays are electromagnetic waves with a very short wavelength, short enough to probe atomic spacings.
X-rays can penetrate into the internal structure of a material and are deflected (diffracted) by its atoms, revealing the lattice arrangement.
defs: X-ray diffraction

A technique in which X-rays are scattered by the regularly spaced atoms of a crystal; constructive interference at specific angles gives information about the spacing of atomic planes and hence the lattice structure.
tips: Do not confuse X-rays with electrons or neutrons used in other diffraction methods; the question usually asks specifically for X-ray diffraction.
Remember that the diffraction effect depends on wavelength being comparable to atomic spacing (around 0.1 nm), not on the material being transparent.
rq: Why must the wavelength of the probe radiation be comparable to atomic spacings for diffraction to reveal lattice structure?

Diffraction only produces measurable interference effects when the wavelength is of the same order as the spacing between scattering centres (about 0.1 nm for atoms); longer wavelengths such as visible light would not resolve the lattice.
Why can X-rays probe the inside of a material rather than just its surface?
X-rays have high energy and short wavelength, so they penetrate far into the solid before being scattered by the atoms within it.

notes.t: Electromagnetic waves and quantised light energy
pts: Einstein proposed that light consists of quantised packets of electromagnetic energy (photons).
Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency: higher frequency means more energy.
Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength: shorter wavelength means more energy.
eqs: Energy of a photon from its frequency and from its wavelength
\(E\) = photon energy (J); \(h\) = Planck's constant (J·s); \(\nu\) = frequency (Hz); \(c\) = speed of light in vacuum (m/s); \(\lambda\) = wavelength (m)
tips: Energy is proportional to frequency but inversely proportional to wavelength; do not mix these up when wavelength is given in nm, so convert to metres before using \(E = hc/\lambda\).
Planck's constant is \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J·s; using eV without converting gives wrong magnitudes.
rq: Why does ultraviolet light cause sunburn while infrared light mainly causes heating?

UV has shorter wavelength and higher frequency, so each photon carries more energy (\(E = hc/\lambda\)), enough to damage molecular bonds in skin; infrared photons have lower energy and mainly increase molecular vibration (heat).
If the wavelength of light doubles, what happens to the energy of each photon, and why?
It halves, because \(E\) is inversely proportional to \(\lambda\) (\(E = hc/\lambda\)).

notes.t: Electromagnetic waves: energy, frequency and wavelength across the spectrum
pts: Electromagnetic waves span a huge range, from long-wavelength radio waves to very short-wavelength cosmic rays.
Photon energy increases as frequency increases; higher-frequency waves carry more energy per photon.
Wavelength decreases as frequency increases, so radio waves are long and gamma/cosmic rays are extremely short.
Visible light sits in a narrow band between infra-red and ultraviolet, with wavelength around \(10^{-6}\) m.
X-rays have a wavelength of about \(10^{-10}\) m and energy of about 4×\(10^{3}\) eV.
eqs: Relation between wave speed, frequency and wavelength (applies to all electromagnetic waves in vacuum)
c = speed of light (m \(s^{-1}\)); f = frequency (Hz); \lambda = wavelength (m)
E = photon energy (J, or eV on this table); h = Planck's constant (J s); f = frequency (Hz)
tips: Unit trap: energy is in eV on this table, while E = hf gives joules; convert with 1 eV = 1.6×\(10^{-19}\) J.
Note the table's frequencies and wavelengths are order-of-magnitude values, and the relation c = fλ holds only for vacuum/free-space speed.
rq: Why does the table show energy in eV rather than joules, and what does that imply for X-rays versus radio waves?
eV is a convenient unit at atomic scales; X-rays (~4×\(10^{3}\) eV) carry vastly more energy per photon than AM radio waves (~4×\(10^{-11}\) eV), which is why X-rays can ionise atoms.
If a wave's frequency doubles in vacuum, what happens to its wavelength?
It halves, since c = fλ is constant and λ is inversely proportional to f.

notes.t: Interaction of waves: constructive interference
pts: When two waves overlap in phase, their amplitudes add together, producing a wave of greater amplitude.
Constructive interference occurs when waves reinforce each other, so the resultant wave has double the amplitude of each individual wave when the two waves are in phase with the same wavelength.
A scattering event can alter the path of a wave, but the scattered wave (Wave 1' and Wave 2') keeps the same amplitude A and wavelength λ as the original wave.
defs: Constructive interference
The superposition of two or more waves in phase, where their displacements add to give a resultant wave of larger amplitude.
tips: Constructive interference only doubles the amplitude when the waves are exactly in phase; for other phase differences the resultant amplitude is smaller.
Interference changes amplitude but not wavelength or frequency of the resulting wave.
rq: Why does the resultant wave have the same wavelength λ as the individual waves?
Because the waves are in phase and superpose at every point, so the peaks and troughs coincide and the spacing between them is unchanged; only the amplitude changes.
What would happen to the resultant amplitude if the two waves were exactly out of phase instead?
They would cancel (destructive interference), giving a resultant amplitude of zero.

notes.t: Interaction of waves: destructive interference
pts: When two waves overlap, their amplitudes add together at each point in space.
When waves are out of phase and of equal amplitude, they cancel, producing a wave of zero amplitude; this is destructive interference.
Scattering events can shift the phase of a wave, so that a scattered wave may interfere destructively with the original wave.
defs: Destructive interference
The superposition of two waves of equal amplitude and opposite phase, so their amplitudes add to zero and the resultant wave has zero amplitude.
tips: Destructive interference requires equal amplitudes and opposite phase; unequal amplitudes give a reduced but non-zero resultant.
Do not confuse amplitude addition with intensity addition; intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude.
rq: Why does a scattered wave lead to zero amplitude only when it is out of phase with the original wave?
Amplitudes add algebraically; waves of equal amplitude and opposite sign (phase difference of 180°) sum to zero, whereas in-phase waves reinforce.
What would happen to the resultant amplitude if the two waves had equal amplitude but were in phase?
The amplitudes would add to 2A, giving constructive interference rather than zero amplitude.

units.name: 8.5 Bragg's Law: history, setup and derivation
units.ov: This material introduces Bragg's Law, the condition for constructive interference of X-rays scattered from parallel crystal planes, and shows how it is derived from the path difference between rays reflected from adjacent planes. It links the measurable diffraction angle \(\theta\) to the interplanar spacing \(d_{hkl}\), which is how X-ray diffraction is used to analyse crystal structure. It was developed by William and Lawrence Bragg, who shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics.
must: Bragg's Law: \( n\lambda = 2d_{hkl}\sin\theta \), the condition for constructive interference from a set of crystal planes
Meaning and units of each symbol: n is an integer order, \(\lambda\) is the X-ray wavelength, \(d_{hkl}\) is the interplanar spacing, \(\theta\) is the Bragg angle
\(\theta\) is the glancing angle between the beam and the planes, not the angle to the surface normal; using the normal gives \(\cos\theta\) and a wrong d
Derivation: path difference = SQ + QT = \(2d\sin\theta\), and setting this equal to \(n\lambda\) gives the law
Constructive interference requires a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths; the reflected waves are then in phase and give a strong diffracted beam
Incident and reflected rays make the same angle \(\theta\) with the planes
The X-rays must be coherent (constant phase relationship, same wavelength) for interference to occur
\(d_{hkl}\) is the perpendicular distance between adjacent parallel planes with Miller indices (hkl)
Keep \(\lambda\) and d in the same units (nm, Å or m) and check that the calculator is in degree mode when evaluating \(\sin\theta\)
Bragg's Law is credited to both William and Lawrence Bragg, who shared the 1915 Nobel Prize
conn: Miller indices and plane spacing: \(d_{hkl}\) is calculated from the lattice parameter, e.g. for cubic \(d=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}\). Combining this with Bragg's Law lets you find \(a\) or identify the structure from diffraction angles.

Geometry of the derivation and the sin/cos pitfall: the path difference \(2d\sin\theta\) comes from the glancing-angle geometry, so a question giving the angle to the normal needs converting first (\(\theta = 90^\circ - \text{angle to normal}\)).
Order of diffraction and angle: for fixed \(\lambda\) and d, higher n gives larger \(\theta\). Since \(\sin\theta \le 1\), only orders with \(n\lambda \le 2d\) are possible.
Crystal structure and diffraction (e.g. the Atomium activity): the atomic arrangement determines which planes exist and their spacings, and therefore the observed peak positions.
exq: Derive Bragg's Law \(n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta\) from a labelled diagram of two parallel planes, showing the path difference and stating the condition for constructive interference.
X-rays of wavelength 0.154 nm are diffracted from planes with \(d = 0.203\) nm. Calculate the Bragg angle for first-order diffraction, and state whether second-order diffraction is possible.
A first-order peak for the (111) planes of a cubic metal appears at \(\theta = 20^\circ\) with \(\lambda = 0.1542\) nm. Calculate \(d_{111}\) and the lattice parameter \(a\).
A question states the beam makes \(60^\circ\) with the surface normal. Explain which angle to use in Bragg's Law and calculate d for \(\lambda = 0.154\) nm and \(n = 1\).
Explain why the X-rays must be coherent and why diffraction is observed only at specific angles. Why does mixing nm and Å lead to errors?

notes.t: Bragg's Law – historical context
pts: Bragg's Law is named after William Bragg and his son Lawrence Bragg, who worked together on X-ray diffraction.
Sir William Bragg and Sir Lawrence Bragg jointly received the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1915 for their work on X-ray crystal analysis.
tips: Do not attribute Bragg's Law to only one Bragg; the 1915 Nobel was shared by father and son.
rq: Why does it matter that a father and son, rather than one scientist, are credited with this law?
It shows the work was a collaboration across generations; the law is named for both, so the attribution is to the joint team rather than a single discoverer.

notes.t: Interaction of X-rays with crystal planes (diffraction setup)
pts: An X-ray beam striking a crystalline specimen is partly scattered by atoms, and the scattered rays reinforce only in certain directions, producing a diffracted beam.
Incident and diffracted rays make the same angle θ with the atomic planes; the planes A, B are separated by the interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\).
Diffraction occurs when the extra path length between rays reflected from adjacent planes (S–Q–T) equals a whole number of wavelengths, so the reflected waves are in phase.
defs: Interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\)
The perpendicular distance between adjacent parallel crystal planes with Miller indices (hkl).
Diffraction
Constructive reinforcement of X-rays scattered by atoms in a crystal, occurring only in directions where path differences are whole wavelengths.
eqs: Bragg's law: condition for constructive interference of X-rays from planes
n = order of diffraction (integer); \lambda = X-ray wavelength (m); \(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing (m); \theta = Bragg angle between beam and planes (rad or °)
tips: Bragg's law uses the angle θ between the beam and the planes, not the angle to the surface normal; check which is given.
Keep units consistent: convert λ and \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) to the same unit (e.g. nm or Å) and check whether sinθ is evaluated with θ in degrees.
rq: Why does the diffracted beam appear only at certain angles rather than in all directions?
Scattered waves from successive planes interfere constructively only when the extra path (2d sinθ) is a whole number of wavelengths; otherwise they cancel out.
What would happen to the Bragg angle if the X-ray wavelength were doubled, with \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) fixed?
sinθ would double, so θ increases (the diffraction peak moves to a larger angle), provided 2d > nλ remains satisfied.

notes.t: Bragg's Law
pts: Coherent X-rays of the same wavelength reflecting from different atomic planes can interact, so their waves may add together.
The analysis assumes two planes of atoms separated by a spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\), with X-rays of wavelength λ striking at angle θ.
Constructive interference (strong diffracted beam) occurs only when the path difference between reflected waves is a whole number of wavelengths.
defs: Coherent X-rays
X-rays with a constant phase relationship and the same wavelength, so their waves can interfere constructively or destructively.
Angle of incidence θ
The angle between the incident X-ray beam and the crystal plane; the reflected beam leaves at the same angle θ.
eqs: Bragg's Law: condition for constructive interference of X-rays diffracted by a set of crystal planes
n = order of diffraction (integer, dimensionless); λ = X-ray wavelength (m); \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = spacing between planes (m); θ = angle of incidence/reflection (degrees or radians)
tips: Be careful that θ is the angle between the beam and the plane, not the angle between the beam and the surface normal; using the wrong angle gives wrong d values.
Keep units consistent: convert wavelength and plane spacing to the same unit (e.g. nm or Å) before applying nλ = 2d sinθ.
rq: Why must the X-rays be coherent and of the same wavelength for Bragg's Law to apply?
Only waves with the same wavelength and a fixed phase relationship produce a stable interference pattern; otherwise the phase differences vary randomly and no reliable constructive peak forms.
What would happen to the diffraction angle θ if you used X-rays of longer wavelength on the same crystal?
From nλ = 2d sinθ, a larger λ requires a larger sinθ, so the diffraction angle θ increases (provided sinθ stays ≤ 1).

notes.t: Bragg's Law
pts: Constructive interference of X-rays scattered from parallel crystal planes requires the path difference between the two reflected rays to be a whole number of wavelengths.
Path difference SQ + QT is found from geometry and equals twice the interplanar spacing times sin θ, giving the Bragg condition.
The relation nλ = 2d sin θ is known as Bragg's Law and links diffraction angle to interplanar spacing.
defs: Constructive interference
Reinforcement of waves scattered from different lattice planes when their path difference is an integer number of wavelengths, producing a diffracted beam.
eqs: Bragg's Law: condition for constructive diffraction from a set of crystal planes

n = order of diffraction (integer, dimensionless); \lambda = X-ray wavelength (m); \(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing of planes (hkl) (m); \theta = Bragg angle between incident beam and planes (rad or °)
tips: Use θ as the angle between the beam and the planes, not the angle between the beam and the surface normal; using the wrong angle gives wrong d values.
Keep λ and d in the same length units (e.g. nm or Å) before calculating; mixing units is a common error.
rq: Why must the path difference be an integer number of wavelengths rather than any value for a strong diffracted beam?
Only when the path difference is nλ are the scattered waves in phase, so they add constructively; other path differences cause partial or destructive cancellation.
Why does the path length term become 2d sin θ rather than d sin θ?
The incident and reflected rays each travel an extra d sin θ between adjacent planes, so the total extra path is the sum of both segments, 2d sin θ.

notes.t: Active Learning: Deriving Bragg's Law for X-ray Diffraction
pts: X-rays incident on parallel crystal planes separated by spacing d are reflected from each plane at the same angle θ as the incident beam.
Reflected rays from adjacent planes travel different path lengths; the extra distance (path difference) between path 1 and path 2 is what determines whether they interfere constructively.
Constructive interference occurs when the path difference XYZ equals a whole number of wavelengths, giving Bragg's law.
defs: Path difference
The extra distance travelled by a wave reflected from a lower crystal plane compared with one reflected from the plane above, measured along the rays (here XYZ).
eqs: Bragg's law: condition for constructive interference of X-rays diffracted by crystal planes
n = order of diffraction (integer, dimensionless); \lambda = X-ray wavelength (m); d = interplanar spacing (m); \theta = glancing angle between beam and planes (rad or °)
tips: Use θ as the angle between the beam and the planes, not the angle to the normal; using the wrong angle gives cos θ instead of sin θ.
Keep units consistent: wavelength and d-spacing must be in the same unit (e.g. nm or m) before calculating sin θ.
rq: Why does the path difference XYZ equal 2d sin θ rather than 2d cos θ?

The perpendicular distance between planes is d; the angle θ is measured between the rays and the planes, so the segments XY and YZ each equal d/sin θ, and the perpendicular projection gives the extra path 2d sin θ.
What happens to the diffracted beam if the path difference is half a wavelength?
The waves arrive out of phase and interfere destructively, so no diffraction peak is observed at that angle.

units.name: 8.6 Applying Bragg's Law: powder XRD and worked examples
units.ov: This material applies Bragg's law, \(n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta\), to powder XRD. Measured peak positions (2θ) give interplanar spacings \(d_{hkl}\). For cubic crystals these link through \(d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}\) to the lattice parameter \(a\) and the Miller indices of each peak. Worked examples (iron and tungsten, Cu Kα \(\lambda=0.1542\) nm) show how to index peaks, find \(a\) and state its uncertainty. The notes also contain inconsistencies in the iron examples that need care (see connections).
must: Bragg's law: \(n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta\), where θ is the glancing angle and n the order (usually n = 1 for these problems).
The powder-pattern x-axis is 2θ, so always halve it before using sinθ; this is the most common error.
Cubic spacing: \(d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}\). It is the square root of the sum of squares, not h+k+l, and it holds only for cubic systems.
Lattice parameter from a peak: \(a=\dfrac{n\lambda}{2\sin\theta}\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}\). Each peak gives an estimate of a, and the estimates should agree (about 0.287 nm for iron).
Miller indices are integers from the reciprocals of the axis intercepts. They label each peak, and (220) is the second-order reflection from the (110) family.
Indexing procedure: find θ, then d, then \(h^2+k^2+l^2\) (= \(a^2/d^2\), or ∝ \(\sin^2\theta\)). Compare the ratios of \(\sin^2\theta\) across peaks with the allowed sequences to assign (hkl).
Powder samples have crystals in all orientations, so every set of planes diffracts. Peak positions give structure and spacing; intensities reflect atomic arrangement.
Keep units consistent (nm vs m vs Å, degrees vs radians); λ = 0.1542 nm = 1.542×10⁻¹⁰ m.
Angles read from the plot are estimates, so quote a with an uncertainty and an appropriate number of significant figures; the error in θ propagates through sinθ.
BCC iron peaks are (110), (200), (211) with a ≈ 0.287 nm; the cubic spacings are \(d_{110}=a/\sqrt2\), \(d_{200}=a/2\), \(d_{211}=a/\sqrt6\).
conn: Crystal structure and selection rules: BCC allows only reflections with h+k+l even (110, 200, 211, 220, 310...). FCC allows only h, k, l all odd or all even (111, 200, 220...). The index sequence therefore identifies the lattice type. The notes label iron as 'FCC α-iron' while listing BCC peaks; α-iron is BCC, so be careful.
Bragg's law with the cubic d formula: combining them gives \(\sin^2\theta \propto h^2+k^2+l^2\). Ratios of \(\sin^2\theta\) between peaks reveal the indices without knowing a, and then a follows.
Lattice parameter and atomic geometry: a connects to atomic radius (BCC \(a=4R/\sqrt3\), FCC \(a=4R/\sqrt2\)) and to density calculations.
Measurement error and data handling: converting 2θ to θ, then to sinθ, then to a, with uncertainty ΔΘ propagated. Plotting a against peak or averaging gives a consistent value.
exq: Cu Kα X-rays (λ = 0.1542 nm) give a first-order (110) peak for BCC iron at 2θ = 44.7°. Calculate \(d_{110}\) and the lattice parameter a, and compare with 0.287 nm.

Powdered tungsten (BCC) gives peaks near 2θ = 40°, 58°, 73°, 87° and 100° with λ = 0.1542 nm. Calculate \(\sin^2\theta\) for each, find the ratios, index the peaks as (110), (200), (211), (220), (310), and determine a.
For a cubic crystal with a = 0.287 nm, calculate \(d_{110}\), \(d_{200}\) and \(d_{211}\), and the 2θ positions at which these first-order peaks occur for λ = 0.1542 nm.
A student reads θ = 22.0° ± 0.5° for the (110) peak of iron. Calculate a and its uncertainty, and state the result to a suitable number of significant figures.

Explain why a powder specimen produces diffraction peaks from all sets of planes. State which reflections are allowed for BCC and FCC, and explain why (100) is absent for BCC. Also explain why using 2θ directly in Bragg's law gives a wrong spacing.

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law: interplanar spacing and Miller indices
pts: Bragg's law relates diffraction angles to the spacing between planes of atoms, so measured angles can be used to find plane spacings.
Interplanar distances are identified by Miller indices h, k and l, which label each set of crystal planes.
For a cubic crystal, the spacing of a given (hkl) plane depends only on the lattice parameter a and the Miller indices.
Knowing the measured angles, the lattice parameter a and the indices h, k, l can be calculated.
defs: Miller indices (h k l)
Integers that describe the orientation of a set of crystal planes, defined by the reciprocals of the intercepts of the plane with the crystal axes.
eqs: Interplanar spacing for a cubic crystal
\(d_{hkl}\) = spacing between (hkl) planes (m or nm); a = lattice parameter of the cubic cell (m or nm); h, k, l = Miller indices (dimensionless integers)
tips: Do not confuse the lattice parameter a with the interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\); the formula only applies to cubic systems.
Keep units consistent (e.g. convert nm to m) when calculating a or \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) from Bragg's law.
rq: Why does a plane with larger Miller indices have a smaller interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\)?
Because the denominator √(h²+k²+l²) increases with larger indices, so \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = a/√(h²+k²+l²) decreases; such planes are more closely packed in the lattice.
If you measure a Bragg angle and know the wavelength, what must you determine before you can find a for a cubic crystal, and how?

First find \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) from Bragg's law nλ = 2d sinθ, then assume the indices (h, k, l) of the reflecting plane and rearrange \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = a/√(h²+k²+l²) to get a = \(d_{\text{hkl}}\)√(h²+k²+l²).

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law: powder X-ray diffraction
pts: A powdered sample contains crystals in all orientations, so scanning the X-ray angle reveals diffraction peaks from every set of planes.
The source and detector are moved together so the incident and reflected beams stay at the same angle θ, while the detector reads angle 2θ.
Each peak in the diffraction pattern corresponds to a family of crystal planes, labelled by Miller indices such as (111) and (200).
Peak positions identify the crystal structure and lattice spacing, while peak intensities reflect the atomic arrangement.
defs: Diffraction angle 2θ
The angle between the incident X-ray beam and the detector position; the x-axis of a powder diffraction pattern is plotted as 2θ.
Miller indices (hkl)
Integers in parentheses that label a set of parallel crystal planes, e.g. (111) or (200), and identify each diffraction peak.
eqs: Bragg's Law: relates X-ray wavelength and plane spacing to the diffraction angle at which constructive interference occurs

n = order of diffraction (integer, dimensionless); \lambda = X-ray wavelength (m); d = interplanar spacing of the crystal planes (m); \theta = Bragg angle, half the diffraction angle 2θ (degrees or radians)
tips: Do not confuse θ with 2θ: the x-axis of the diffraction pattern is 2θ, so divide by 2 before substituting into Bragg's law.
Keep angles in consistent units (degrees vs radians) and ensure λ and d use the same length unit when calculating.
rq: Why does a powder sample give peaks from many planes at once, while a single crystal gives only a few spots?
A powder has randomly oriented grains, so for any θ some grains have the planes oriented at the Bragg angle; a single crystal has one fixed orientation and only specific planes satisfy Bragg's law.
If the detector is at 2θ = 60°, what is the Bragg angle θ, and why is it not 60°?
θ = 30°; the detector measures 2θ, so the Bragg angle is half the measured diffraction angle.
What would happen to the peak positions if the X-ray wavelength were doubled?
By Bragg's law sinθ would double for the same d, so the peaks would shift to larger angles (or disappear if sinθ exceeds 1).

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law to BCC iron
pts: Interplanar spacing for a cubic lattice is found from the lattice parameter and Miller indices using 3D Pythagoras.
Miller indices (h k l) identify each set of crystal planes, e.g. the 111 plane has h=1, k=1, l=1.
Higher-order planes such as 220 are multiples of lower-order planes (here h=2, k=2, l=0).
The XRD pattern of BCC iron shows peaks labelled (110), (200) and (211), which are indexed to specific diffracting planes.
defs: Interplanar distance (\(d_{\text{hkl}}\))
The perpendicular spacing between adjacent parallel planes with Miller indices (hkl) in a crystal lattice; it is used in Bragg's law to relate diffraction angle to wavelength.
Miller indices (hkl)
Three integers describing the orientation of a set of crystal planes, reciprocal to the intercepts of the plane with the crystal axes.
eqs: Interplanar distance for a cubic crystal
\(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing (m); a = lattice parameter (m); h, k, l = Miller indices (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the 3D Pythagoras denominator with simply h+k+l; it is the square root of the sum of squares.
Index planes as multiples (220 = 2×110 for the same family) and remember the lattice parameter a must be in the same units as the desired d (e.g. convert pm or Å to m).
rq: Why does the 220 plane have a smaller interplanar distance than the 110 plane, even though both come from the same cubic lattice?

Because \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) is inversely proportional to √(h²+k²+l²); for 220, √(8)≈2.83 versus √2≈1.41 for 110, so \(d_{220}\) is half of \(d_{110}\) (it is the second-order reflection of the 110 planes).
What does the scaling of \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) with the lattice parameter a imply about the diffraction angle for a larger unit cell?
A larger a gives a larger \(d_{\text{hkl}}\), so by Bragg's law the peaks appear at smaller diffraction angles 2θ.

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law to α-iron (FCC)
pts: For FCC α-iron, the interplanar spacing of a (hkl) plane is found from the cubic lattice parameter a and the Miller indices.
The first-order peaks (n=1) are used to find the lattice parameter a from the measured diffraction angles 2θ, via λ = 0.1542 nm.
For each peak, a is calculated from \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) and Bragg's law, and the results are plotted on a graph to obtain a consistent value of a.
Peaks at 2θ = 44°, 65° and 82° correspond to the (110), (200) and (211) planes respectively.
defs: Interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\)
The perpendicular distance between adjacent parallel planes of the (hkl) family in a crystal lattice; for a cubic lattice it equals a/√(h²+k²+l²).
Bragg's law
Constructive interference of X-rays scattered by a crystal occurs when nλ = 2d sinθ, where n is the order of diffraction, λ the wavelength, d the interplanar spacing and θ the Bragg angle.
eqs: Interplanar spacing for a cubic lattice
\(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing (m or nm); a = lattice parameter (m or nm); h,k,l = Miller indices (dimensionless)
\(d_{110}\) = spacing of (110) planes (nm); a = lattice parameter (nm)
\(d_{200}\) = spacing of (200) planes (nm); a = lattice parameter (nm)
\(d_{211}\) = spacing of (211) planes (nm); a = lattice parameter (nm)
tips: Use θ (half of 2θ) in Bragg's law, not the full 2θ value measured on the diffractometer.
Keep units consistent: λ is given in nm, so a and d must also be in nm when calculating a.
rq: Why are the peaks at 2θ = 44°, 65° and 82° assigned to (110), (200) and (211) rather than other planes?
In FCC, only planes with all-even or all-odd Miller indices give diffraction peaks; (110), (200) and (211) are the first allowed reflections in order of increasing 2θ.
If the measured θ were doubled by mistake (using 2θ as θ), how would the calculated a change?
Since sinθ would be wrongly evaluated, d and hence a would be wrong; the calculated lattice parameter would be incorrect and inconsistent across the three peaks.

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law to lattice parameter calculation
pts: Bragg's law relates the interplanar spacing \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) to the diffraction angle θ and wavelength λ; for a cubic lattice \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = a/√(h²+k²+l²), so the lattice parameter a can be found from each measured peak.
Each diffraction peak gives its own estimate of a, and the results should agree (here ≈ 0.287 nm for two of the three peaks).
Angles read from a diffraction pattern are estimates, so uncertainty in θ propagates into the calculated lattice parameter and must be stated as error in the final result.
defs: Bragg's law

Condition for constructive interference of X-rays scattered by parallel crystal planes: nλ = 2d sinθ, where d is the interplanar spacing, θ the glancing angle, λ the wavelength and n the order of diffraction.
eqs: \(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing of planes (hkl) (nm); θ = Bragg angle (°); n = order of diffraction (dimensionless); λ = X-ray wavelength (nm)
Lattice parameter from first-order peak (110 planes, cubic)
a = cubic lattice parameter (nm); λ = wavelength = 0.1542 nm; θ = Bragg angle (°); h,k,l = Miller indices; n = order
Lattice parameter from d-spacing of cubic planes
\(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing (nm); a = lattice parameter (nm); h,k,l = Miller indices
tips: Use the Bragg angle θ (half the 2θ reading) in sinθ, not 2θ, when applying 2d sinθ = nλ.
Keep wavelength and lattice parameter in the same units (here nm, λ = 0.1542 nm) and quote final answers with the correct number of significant figures given the angle uncertainty.
rq: Why does the calculated lattice parameter differ between the three peaks, and which result would you trust most?

Small errors in measured angles (especially at low θ, where sinθ changes quickly) propagate into a; the consistent values near 0.287 nm from the higher-angle peaks are the most reliable, so the first peak (0.291 nm) is the most likely to contain angle-reading error.
Why must the order n be included, and what happens if you use n = 2 for a peak that is really first order?
n specifies which reflection (diffraction order) the peak corresponds to; using the wrong n changes the apparent d-spacing and gives a wrong a, so the correct n must be assigned to each peak.

notes.t: Application of Bragg's Law to powdered tungsten
pts: Bragg's law links the X-ray wavelength, lattice spacing and diffraction angle; each diffraction peak corresponds to a set of planes satisfying the law.
The task is to identify the Miller indices (hkl) of the first five peaks of powdered tungsten measured with X-rays of wavelength 0.1542 nm.
Peak positions are read from the diffraction angle 2θ axis of the intensity plot; the peaks occur near 40°, 58°, 73°, 87° and 100°.
defs: Diffraction angle 2θ
The angle between the incident X-ray beam and the diffracted beam; it is twice the Bragg angle θ and is the quantity plotted on the horizontal axis of an X-ray diffraction pattern.
Miller indices (hkl)
Three integers describing the orientation of a set of crystal planes, obtained as reciprocals of the plane intercepts on the crystal axes; they are used to label each diffraction peak.
eqs: Bragg's law relating diffraction angle to interplanar spacing
n = diffraction order (integer); \lambda = X-ray wavelength (m); \(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing of the (hkl) planes (m); \theta = Bragg angle, half the diffraction angle 2θ (degrees or radians)
Interplanar spacing for a cubic lattice (used with Bragg's law to find the indices)
\(d_{hkl}\) = interplanar spacing (m); a = lattice parameter of the cubic cell (m); h, k, l = Miller indices (integers)
tips: Bragg's law uses θ (half the angle), not 2θ; substituting the plotted 2θ directly gives a wrong d-spacing.
Keep the wavelength in consistent units: 0.1542 nm must be converted to metres (1.542 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) when calculating d in metres.
rq: Why must the peak positions be converted to d-spacings before the indices can be found?
Bragg's law gives \(d_{hkl}\) from λ and θ; since the indices are determined by the spacing through d = a/√(h²+k²+l²), the d-value is the link to the (hkl) planes.
If the first peak appears at a larger 2θ than the second, what does that imply about its d-spacing?
A larger θ means a smaller \(d_{hkl}\) for the same wavelength, because sinθ is inversely proportional to d in Bragg's law.

units.name: 4.1 Lecture introduction
units.ov: This introductory lecture frames the electrical and optical properties of materials and how they are measured experimentally. Band theory (energy bands, Fermi level, band-gap energy and thermal energy) is the unifying model that explains why conductors, semiconductors and insulators differ in both electrical conduction and optical response. The notes are only introductory, so the detail below goes beyond them using standard band-theory results; check it against your lecture slides.
must: Band theory explains why electrical and optical properties differ between materials: allowed electron energies form bands, separated by gaps with no allowed states.
Fermi energy level \(E_F\) is a reference energy (the highest occupied state at 0 K). It is NOT the band gap. Do not confuse the two.
Band-gap energy \(E_g\) is the energy range with no allowed electron states, between the valence band and the conduction band.
Thermal energy \(\sim k_BT\) (\(\approx 0.025\) eV at 300 K) compared with \(E_g\) determines how many electrons are excited into the conduction band.
Classification: metals have a partially filled band or overlapping bands (\(E_g\approx 0\)); semiconductors have small \(E_g\) (\(\sim 1\) eV); insulators have large \(E_g\) (\(>\sim 3\) eV).
Conductivity depends on the number of free carriers and their mobility, \(\sigma = n e \mu\) (plus a hole term in semiconductors). Resistivity is \(\rho = 1/\sigma\).
Optical response is linked to \(E_g\): a photon is absorbed if \(h\nu = hc/\lambda \ge E_g\), otherwise the material is transparent to it.
Electrical and optical properties are determined experimentally by measurement methods, for example resistance/resistivity measurements and optical transmission or absorption measurements.
conn: Band gap links electrical and optical behaviour: the same \(E_g\) sets the carrier density (via thermal excitation) and the photon absorption threshold \(\lambda_c = hc/E_g\).
Thermal energy and band gap together: raising T increases carrier excitation, so semiconductors' conductivity rises with T, while metals' conductivity falls because of increased scattering.
Fermi level position relative to the bands determines whether a material is metallic (inside a band) or semiconducting/insulating (inside the gap).
Measured quantities (resistivity, absorption edge) can be used to infer band-gap energy, linking the experimental methods to the theory.
exq: Explain, using band theory, why copper, silicon and diamond have very different electrical conductivities. Sketch the band diagram for each, marking the Fermi level and band gap.
Distinguish between the Fermi energy level and the band-gap energy. Where does the Fermi level lie in an intrinsic semiconductor?
Compare \(k_BT\) at 300 K with the band gaps of Si (1.1 eV) and diamond (about 5.5 eV). What does this imply about carrier excitation in each?
Calculate the longest wavelength of light absorbed by a semiconductor with \(E_g = 1.1\) eV. Is it transparent to visible light? Explain.
Describe how the electrical resistivity of a material can be measured experimentally, and how its variation with temperature distinguishes a metal from a semiconductor.

notes.t: Introduction to Electrical and Optical Properties of Materials
pts: This lecture covers the electrical and optical properties of materials.
Electrical and optical properties are determined experimentally by measurement methods, which are discussed in the lecture.
Band theory concepts (bands, Fermi energy level, band-gap energy and thermal energy) explain why electrical and optical properties differ between materials.
tips: Do not confuse the Fermi energy level with the band-gap energy: the Fermi level is a reference energy, while the band gap is the energy range with no allowed electron states.
rq: Why does the lecture use band-gap energy and thermal energy together to explain differences between materials?

Band-gap energy sets the energy needed to excite electrons across the gap into conduction, while thermal energy (\(k_{\text{BT}}\)) indicates how many electrons can be thermally excited; together they determine conductivity and optical absorption differences between materials.

units.name: 4.2 Ohm's law, resistivity and conductivity
units.ov: This module introduces Ohm's law (\(V = IR\)) and extends it to geometry-independent material properties: resistivity \(\rho\) and conductivity \(\sigma\).
