The net transport of atoms or molecules through a material driven by a concentration gradient, from regions of high to low concentration.
Carburization
A surface hardening process in which carbon diffuses into low-carbon steel, increasing surface carbon content and hardness.
Vitrification
Encapsulation of waste in a glass matrix to immobilise it and reduce diffusive release over long periods.
tips: Diffusion needs a driving force (concentration gradient); do not describe it as occurring only at high temperature without a gradient.
Name the specific diffusing species (e.g. carbon, Al, Cu) when giving application examples.
rq: Why does diffusion of Al or Cu into silicon matter for integrated circuits?
Unwanted metal atoms migrate into silicon, altering its electrical properties and shortening the circuit's operating life.
What makes a glove material unsafe against a chemical even if it looks intact?
Chemicals can diffuse through the polymer or rubber over time, reaching the skin without visibly damaging the glove.

notes.t: Self-diffusion and annealing
pts: Self-diffusion is atomic movement in a single-component material, where all exchanging atoms are the same type, so no chemical composition changes.
Self-diffusion matters during crystal growth, where atoms must migrate to correct positions in the lattice.
Annealing heats a material to increase diffusion, then cools it slowly, allowing atoms to rearrange and reduce defects.
The diagram shows atoms C, A, D and B swapping positions over a time interval, illustrating diffusion by vacancy/atom exchange within a lattice of identical atoms.
defs: Self-diffusion
Diffusion in a one-component material in which all atoms that exchange positions are of the same type, so the composition remains unchanged.
Annealing
A heat treatment in which a material is heated to increase atomic diffusion and then slowly cooled, reducing defects in the structure.
tips: Do not confuse self-diffusion (one component, same atom types) with interdiffusion (different atom types exchanging positions).
Annealing is a heat treatment that reduces defects; slow cooling is essential, rapid quenching does not achieve this.
rq: Why does heating a material speed up self-diffusion during annealing?
Higher temperature gives atoms more thermal energy, so more of them can jump into neighbouring lattice sites, increasing the diffusion rate and allowing defects to be eliminated.
If atoms A and B were different elements, would this still be self-diffusion?
No. Self-diffusion requires all exchanging atoms to be the same type; exchange between different species is interdiffusion.

units.name: 10.3 Atomic mechanisms: vacancy and interstitial diffusion
units.ov: This material covers the two main atomic mechanisms of solid-state diffusion: vacancy (substitutional) diffusion and interstitial diffusion. Both are thermally activated atomic jumps. Which mechanism operates, and how fast, depends on atom size, the availability of empty sites, and the activation energy for a jump.
must: Vacancy diffusion: an atom (host or substitutional) jumps into a neighbouring vacant lattice site, so the vacancy moves in the opposite direction.
Interstitial diffusion: a small atom moves between interstitial sites among the larger host atoms, without displacing them.
Interstitial diffusion is generally faster than vacancy diffusion because the atoms are smaller and more mobile, and many more empty interstitial sites are available than vacancies.
Vacancy diffusion rate depends on BOTH the vacancy concentration and the activation energy for the jump, not on the number of vacancies alone.
Vacancy concentration rises with temperature, so vacancy diffusion speeds up at elevated temperature. Typically \(N_v = N\exp(-Q_v/kT)\).
Self-diffusion (host atoms) and interdiffusion (impurity and host) both occur by the vacancy mechanism. Substitutional impurities diffuse this way too.
Interstitial diffusion is typical of small solutes (H, C, N, O). Substitutional atoms of similar size to the host do not diffuse interstitially.
A vacancy is a missing atom at a normal lattice site. A substitutional impurity is a foreign atom on a regular lattice site. Define both precisely.
The rate of a thermally activated jump scales as \(\exp(-Q/RT)\), so a lower activation energy or a higher temperature gives faster diffusion.
conn: Vacancy concentration and activation energy: the vacancy mechanism needs both a vacancy next to the atom and enough energy to make the jump. Both terms are temperature dependent, which links to the Arrhenius form of \(D\).

Atom size and mechanism: the size of the solute relative to the host decides whether it is substitutional (vacancy diffusion) or interstitial (fast diffusion). This links to alloy types such as C in Fe (interstitial) versus Ni in Cu (substitutional).

Mechanism and diffusion coefficient: interstitial diffusion has a lower activation energy and a larger \(D\) than vacancy diffusion at the same T. This feeds into Fick's laws and processes such as carburising.
Self-diffusion versus interdiffusion: both use the same vacancy mechanism, so the difference lies in whether a concentration gradient of a different species exists.
exq: Describe, with sketches, the vacancy and interstitial diffusion mechanisms. State which is faster and give two reasons.
Explain why the rate of vacancy diffusion increases with temperature, referring to both vacancy concentration and activation energy.
Carbon and nickel both diffuse in iron. Which would you expect to diffuse by an interstitial mechanism and which by a vacancy mechanism? Justify using atomic size.
Calculate the equilibrium vacancy fraction in a metal at 900 K, given \(Q_v = 1.0\) eV/atom, and compare it with the value at 300 K. Comment on the effect on diffusion rate.
Define self-diffusion and interdiffusion. Explain why both occur by the vacancy mechanism and what happens to a vacancy when an atom jumps into it.

notes.t: Vacancy diffusion in solids
pts: In vacancy diffusion, atoms move by exchanging position with neighbouring vacant lattice sites.
The same mechanism applies to substitutional impurity atoms, not just host atoms.
Diffusion rate rises with the number of vacancies, which can increase at elevated temperature.
Diffusion rate also depends on the activation energy needed for an atom to make the exchange.
Interdiffusion and self-diffusion both operate by the vacancy mechanism.
defs: Vacancy diffusion
Diffusion mechanism in which atoms (host or substitutional) jump into neighbouring vacant lattice sites, so the vacancy moves in the opposite direction.
Vacancy (defect)
A missing atom at a normal lattice site; vacancies provide the empty sites needed for atomic jumps.
Substitutional impurity
A foreign atom that replaces a host atom on a regular lattice site and can diffuse by the vacancy mechanism.
tips: Do not confuse vacancy diffusion (atoms jump into empty lattice sites) with interstitial diffusion (small atoms move between lattice sites).
Remember that diffusion rate depends on both vacancy concentration and activation energy, not vacancy number alone.
rq: Why does raising the temperature speed up vacancy diffusion?
Higher temperature increases the number of vacancies and gives atoms more thermal energy to overcome the activation energy for exchange.
Why can a substitutional atom diffuse by vacancies while an interstitial atom in this mechanism would not need one?
A substitutional atom sits on a lattice site and must swap with an adjacent vacancy; interstitial diffusion instead moves through the gaps between lattice atoms without needing vacancies.

notes.t: Interstitial diffusion mechanism
pts: In interstitial diffusion, a small atom moves from one interstitial site to an adjacent empty interstitial site between the larger host atoms.
Interstitial diffusion is faster than vacancy diffusion because interstitial atoms are smaller and more mobile.
Interstitial diffusion is faster than vacancy diffusion because there are many more empty interstitial positions available than vacancies.
defs: Interstitial diffusion
Diffusion mechanism in which small atoms migrate through the interstitial spaces between larger host atoms, without displacing them.
tips: Do not confuse interstitial diffusion (small atom moving between lattice sites) with vacancy diffusion (atoms exchanging with empty lattice sites); interstitial is generally faster.
Interstitial diffusion is typically associated with small solutes such as H, C, N, O, not with substitutional atoms of similar size.
rq: Why does interstitial diffusion occur more rapidly than vacancy diffusion, even though both involve atomic jumps?
Interstitial atoms are smaller and more mobile, and there are many more empty interstitial sites than vacancies, so jumps are more frequent and easier.
What would happen to the rate of interstitial diffusion if the interstitial atom were as large as the host atoms?
It would be much slower or hindered, since large atoms cannot fit easily between host atoms and would require lattice distortion or a vacancy mechanism instead.

units.name: 10.4 Industrial uses: carburising and semiconductor doping
units.ov: This material covers two industrial applications of solid-state diffusion: carburising (case hardening) of steel, where carbon is diffused into the surface to give a hard case and a tough core, and diffusion doping of silicon, where dopant atoms are diffused into the surface to form n-type and p-type regions in devices such as MOSFETs. Both rely on the same principle: a source of atoms at the surface, heat to drive thermal diffusion, and a limited penetration depth that localises the property change near the surface.
must: Carburising is a high-temperature treatment in which carbon diffuses from the atmosphere into the surface of steel, giving a hard surface and a tough core
Hardening mechanism: carbon forms carbide precipitates that pin dislocations, impede slip and raise hardness
Hardness vs toughness trade-off: more carbon means harder but less tough, so carbon is added only to the surface and the bulk composition stays largely unchanged
Benefits of the case: wear and fatigue resistance at the surface, with a ductile, tough bulk that resists fracture
Toughness is the ability to deform plastically without fracture; do not confuse it with hardness
Doping deliberately changes semiconductor conductivity by adding small, controlled amounts of impurity atoms
Phosphorus (Group 5) is a donor: its extra valence electron gives n-type silicon with electrons as majority carriers
Boron (Group 3) is an acceptor: electron deficiency creates holes, giving p-type silicon with holes as majority carriers
Diffusion doping process: deposit a dopant-rich layer on the surface, heat so the dopant diffuses in, and form doped regions such as MOSFET source, drain and channel
Diffusion only reaches a limited depth, so both the carburised case and the doped regions are shallow surface layers, not through-thickness
conn: Fick's laws and the diffusion depth scaling \( x \sim \sqrt{Dt} \), together with the Arrhenius temperature dependence \( D = D_0 e^{-Q/RT} \), determine case depth in carburising and junction depth in doping

Both processes use a high surface concentration as the source with diffusion into a lower-concentration bulk, so concentration-depth profiles and boundary conditions (constant surface concentration) apply to each

Microstructure links to properties: carbide precipitates pin dislocations in steel, while dopant atoms change carrier type in silicon; both are a diffusion-controlled change in surface composition giving a property gradient

Interstitial vs substitutional diffusion: carbon diffuses interstitially in iron and is fast, whereas dopants such as P and B in silicon are mainly substitutional and slower, so processing temperatures and times differ
exq: Explain why carburised steel is hard at the surface yet tough in the core. Describe the role of carbide precipitates and dislocations, and why the whole component is not simply made high-carbon.

Using the constant-surface-concentration solution of Fick's second law, calculate the time needed to reach a carbon concentration of 0.4 wt% at 0.5 mm depth in steel at 950 °C, given \( D_0 \), \( Q \), surface and bulk concentrations.
Distinguish between n-type and p-type silicon, naming a typical dopant for each and explaining how the dopant group determines the majority carriers.
Describe the diffusion doping process used to form the source and drain regions of a MOSFET, and explain why the doped regions are shallow.
By what factor does the diffusion depth change if the carburising temperature is raised from 900 °C to 1000 °C for the same time? State your assumptions and use \( D = D_0 e^{-Q/RT} \).

notes.t: Carburising (case hardening) of steel by carbon diffusion
pts: Carburising is a high-temperature heat treatment in which carbon diffuses into the surface of iron-based metal from the surrounding atmosphere.
Carbon forms carbide precipitates that pin dislocations, impeding slip and so increasing hardness.
Higher carbon content reduces toughness, so carbon is only diffused into the outer surface.
The result is a component hard at the surface (wear resistance, fatigue resistance) but tough in the bulk.
defs: Carburising (case hardening)
A high-temperature heat treatment that diffuses carbon into the surface of a steel so the surface becomes hard while the core remains tough.
Toughness
The ability of a material to plastically deform without fracture.
Carbide precipitate
Fine particles of a metal-carbon compound formed in steel that pin dislocations and hinder slip, increasing hardness.
tips: Do not confuse hardness with toughness: adding carbon increases hardness but reduces toughness, which is why only the surface is carburised.
Carburising hardens by diffusion of carbon into the surface; the bulk composition remains largely unchanged.
rq: Why does diffusing carbon into only the surface give a better component than making the whole part high-carbon?
Carbon raises hardness and wear/fatigue resistance but reduces toughness; a hard surface over a tough core combines both properties.
How do carbide precipitates make steel harder?
They pin dislocations, preventing dislocation movement (slip), so plastic deformation requires higher stress.

notes.t: Processing Using Diffusion: Doping Semiconductors
pts: Doping deliberately changes a semiconductor's conductivity by adding controlled impurity atoms.
In a MOSFET, the doped source, drain and channel regions at the surface are formed by diffusion.
Phosphorus (a Group 5 donor with extra valence electron) doped into silicon gives n-type material.
Boron doping produces p-type semiconductors (acceptor impurity, electron deficiency/holes).
Diffusion doping process: deposit dopant-rich layer on surface, heat, dopant diffuses into silicon to form doped regions.
defs: Doping
Intentional addition of small, controlled amounts of impurity atoms to a semiconductor to deliberately change its electrical conductivity.
n-type semiconductor
Semiconductor doped with donor impurities (e.g. phosphorus in silicon) that supply extra electrons as the majority charge carriers.
p-type semiconductor
Semiconductor doped with acceptor impurities (e.g. boron in silicon) that create holes as the majority charge carriers.
tips: Do not confuse donor (phosphorus, n-type) and acceptor (boron, p-type) dopants; the dopant group determines the carrier type.
Diffusion doping only reaches a limited depth from the surface, so doped regions are shallow, not through the whole wafer.
rq: Why must the doped regions be formed only at the surface in a MOSFET rather than through the whole wafer?

The MOSFET's source, drain and channel are surface device structures controlled by the gate above the SiO₂ layer; doping only the surface region defines these active regions while the bulk substrate keeps its original type.
What would happen to the n-type silicon regions if boron were used instead of phosphorus?
Boron is a Group 3 acceptor, so it would create p-type regions instead of n-type, reversing the carrier type in those regions.

units.name: 10.5 Diffusion flux and Fick's first law (steady state)
units.ov: This material defines diffusion flux \(J\) as mass (or moles) transferred per unit area per unit time, and shows how it is measured from the steady-state slope of a cumulative mass vs time plot. It then introduces Fick's first law, \(J=-D\,dC/dx\), for steady-state diffusion, and applies it to a thin barrier (a butyl rubber glove) with a linear concentration profile, so that the gradient becomes a finite difference across the thickness.
must: Definition of flux: \(J=\frac{M}{At}=\frac{1}{A}\frac{dM}{dt}\), in kg/(m²·s), mol/(m²·s) or atoms/(m²·s)
Fick's first law: \(J=-D\frac{dC}{dx}\), valid for steady state, where \(J\) is proportional to the concentration gradient
Meaning of the minus sign: diffusion runs from high to low concentration, so the gradient is negative and \(J\) is positive in the direction of diffusion
Steady state means the mass entering equals the mass leaving, so the flux does not change with time and the profile is time-independent
Linear-profile approximation: \(\frac{dC}{dx}\approx\frac{C_2-C_1}{x_2-x_1}\), so \(J=-D\frac{C_2-C_1}{\Delta x}\) for a thin plate or membrane
Units of \(D\) (m² s⁻¹ or cm² s⁻¹) and consistent unit use: convert cm/mm/min to the same basis before substituting, since \(J\) must come out in the matching units
Experimental measurement: use the linear steady-state slope of mass vs time, not the initial curved transient, then divide by area \(A\) to get \(J\)
Glove example: \(C_1\) is the outside face concentration and \(C_2\) the inside face, \(x\) is the thickness, and the result is \(J\approx1.16\times10^{-5}\) g/(cm²·s)
\(D\) is a material- and temperature-dependent property, and a thicker barrier or smaller \(\Delta C\) reduces the flux
conn: Measuring flux from the mass-time slope (\(J=\frac{1}{A}\frac{dM}{dt}\)) is combined with Fick's first law to extract \(D\) from membrane experiments
The steady-state and linear-profile assumptions together allow \(dC/dx\) to be replaced by \(\Delta C/\Delta x\), turning a calculus law into a simple algebraic one
Total transfer rate links flux to area and time: \(M=JAt\), so a flux calculation is often followed by finding mass permeated through a glove or membrane over a given time
Unit conversions (g, cm vs kg, m) and the sign convention interact: a wrong gradient direction or mixed units gives a wrong sign or magnitude of \(J\)
exq: State Fick's first law and explain the meaning of each term and the minus sign. Under what conditions does it apply?

A butyl rubber glove of thickness 0.04 cm has methylene chloride concentrations of 0.44 g/cm³ on the outer face and 0.02 g/cm³ on the inner face, with \(D=110\times10^{-8}\) cm²/s. Calculate the steady-state flux, and then the mass passing through a 100 cm² area in 1 hour.
A membrane of area 5 cm² passes 2 g of gas in 40 minutes at steady state. Calculate \(J\) in kg/(m²·s). If the concentration difference across its 1 mm thickness is 50 kg/m³, find \(D\).
Explain why the initial part of a mass-versus-time plot should not be used to determine flux, and describe how you would find \(J\) from the experimental curve.
For the glove example, show how the flux changes if the thickness is doubled or if the inner-face concentration rises, and discuss what this means for protective clothing design.

notes.t: Measuring diffusion flux
pts: Diffusion flux J is the mass (or moles) transferred per unit area per unit time, quantifying the rate of mass transfer.
Empirically, make a thin membrane of known area A, impose a concentration gradient, and measure how fast atoms or molecules pass through.
Flux is proportional to the slope of a plot of cumulative mass diffused against time, so the steady-state slope gives J.
defs: Diffusion flux (J)
The rate of mass (or moles) transported through a unit cross-sectional area per unit time.
eqs: Diffusion flux as mass transferred per area per time
\(J\) = diffusion flux (kg/(m²·s) or atoms/(m²·s)); \(M\) = mass or moles transferred (kg or mol); \(A\) = cross-sectional area (m²); \(t\) = time (s)
Flux as rate of change of mass per area (differential form)
\(dM/dt\) = rate of mass diffusing through the membrane (kg/s or mol/s); \(A\) = membrane area (m²)
tips: Check units: J in kg/(m²·s) or atoms/(m²·s); using cm² or minutes without conversion gives wrong values.
Use the linear (steady-state) part of the mass-time curve; the initial curved section is not the true flux.
rq: Why is the slope of the mass-versus-time graph used to find J rather than a single mass reading?
Because the slope gives the steady rate dM/dt; a single reading includes the initial transient and does not give a rate, so J = (1/A)(dM/dt) is measured from the linear portion.
If the membrane area doubles but the same mass diffuses in the same time, what happens to J?
J halves, since J = M/(At) is inversely proportional to area for fixed M and t.

notes.t: Steady-State Diffusion and Fick's First Law
pts: Steady-state diffusion occurs when the mass of species entering a solid equals the mass exiting, so the diffusion rate does not change with time.
Diffusion flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, with diffusion going down the gradient from high to low concentration.
For a linear concentration profile across a thin plate, the gradient can be approximated by a finite difference between the two faces.
defs: Steady-state diffusion
A diffusion condition in which the mass of diffusing species entering a solid equals the mass leaving it, so the rate of diffusion is independent of time.
Flux (J)
The amount of diffusing species passing through a unit area per unit time, in the direction of diffusion.
Concentration gradient
The rate of change of concentration with distance, dC/dx, which drives diffusion.
Diffusion coefficient (D)
A material- and temperature-dependent constant describing how quickly a species diffuses, with SI units of m²/s.
eqs: Fick's first law: diffusion flux through a solid under steady state
Finite-difference approximation of concentration gradient for a linear profile
\(C_1, C_2\) = concentrations at faces (mol/m³); \(x_1, x_2\) = positions of faces (m)
tips: Keep the sign convention: diffusion goes from high to low concentration, so the minus sign in J = −D dC/dx is essential; the gradient itself is negative.
Check units: D is in m²/s, concentration in mol/m³ and x in m, so J comes out in mol/m²·s; mixing mm and m gives errors.
rq: Why does the negative sign appear in Fick's first law, and what would happen to the sign of J if it were omitted?
Concentration decreases in the direction of diffusion, so dC/dx is negative; the minus sign makes J positive, meaning diffusion flows from high to low concentration.
Why is the steady-state condition important for using a linear gradient across a thin plate?
Under steady state the concentration profile is constant in time, so a linear profile between the two faces can be assumed and dC/dx approximated by (C₂ − C₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
If the diffusion coefficient D doubles at a higher temperature while the gradient stays the same, what happens to the flux?
The flux J doubles, since J is directly proportional to D for a fixed concentration gradient.

notes.t: Diffusive flux through a membrane: Chemical Protective Clothing example
pts: Steady-state diffusion through a thin barrier (glove wall) is driven by the concentration difference across it, so flux is found from Fick's first law.
Methylene chloride can be absorbed through skin, so the glove material must limit its transport.
The diffusion coefficient of the solute in butyl rubber sets how fast the chemical permeates the glove.
The relevant concentrations are the surface concentrations on the two faces of the glove, \(C_{1}\) on the outside and \(C_{2}\) on the inside.
defs: Diffusive flux (J)
The amount of substance crossing a unit area per unit time, measured in the direction of decreasing concentration.
eqs: Steady-state diffusive flux through a thin barrier (Fick's first law)
J = diffusive flux (g/(\(cm^{2}\)·s)); D = diffusion coefficient (\(cm^{2}\)/s); \(C_{1}\), \(C_{2}\) = surface concentrations on each face (g/\(cm^{3}\)); x = thickness of the glove (cm)
tips: Keep units consistent: D is given in \(cm^{2}\)/s and thickness in cm, so the flux comes out in g/(\(cm^{2}\)·s).
Do not confuse the outside concentration \(C_{1}\) with the inside concentration \(C_{2}\) when substituting into the gradient term.
rq: Why is the flux negative in the Fick's law form, and why do we take its magnitude when reporting the result?

Diffusion runs from high to low concentration, so with \(C_{2}\) < \(C_{1}\) the gradient is negative; the minus sign makes J positive in the direction of transport, and the magnitude gives the permeation rate.
What would happen to the flux if the glove were twice as thick, all else equal?
The flux would halve, because flux is inversely proportional to the thickness x for a fixed concentration difference and D.

notes.t: Steady-state diffusion flux with linear concentration gradient (glove permeation example)
pts: Under steady state with an assumed linear concentration gradient, the flux is approximated by the finite-difference form of Fick's first law.
Flux is driven by the concentration difference across the glove thickness; diffusion moves material from high to low concentration, hence the negative sign.
Substituting the given D, concentrations and thickness gives a flux of about 1.16 × 10⁻⁵ g/(cm²·s).
defs: Flux (J)
The amount of substance passing through a unit area per unit time, in the direction of diffusion.
Diffusion coefficient (D)
A material- and temperature-dependent constant describing how readily a species diffuses through a medium.
eqs: Fick's first law (flux with finite-difference approximation of gradient)
J = diffusion flux (g/(cm²·s)); D = diffusion coefficient (cm²/s); C = concentration (g/cm³); x = position (cm)
tips: Unit trap: D is given in cm²/s and thickness in cm, so convert consistently before computing flux; the answer is in g/(cm²·s).
The linear gradient result is an approximation valid only for steady state with a roughly linear concentration profile across the barrier.
rq: Why is the sign negative in Fick's first law, and what does a positive J mean?
Diffusion occurs down the concentration gradient (dC/dx < 0 in the direction of flow), so the minus sign makes J positive in the direction of transport.
Why must the concentration difference be divided by the thickness of the glove, not the total width of the materials?
The gradient is the change in concentration over the distance the species actually diffuses, which is the glove thickness x₂ − x₁ = 0.04 cm.

units.name: 10.6 Diffusion in polymers and membrane permeability
units.ov: This material covers how gases cross polymer walls such as PET bottles and polyethylene films, by sorption at the inner surface, diffusion through the wall and desorption at the outer surface. Fick's First Law is adapted so that flux is driven by pressure difference, with the permeability coefficient \(P_M\) combining solubility and diffusivity. Polymer structure (amorphous vs crystalline regions, density) and membrane thickness then control how fast gas is lost.
must: Membrane flux equation: \(J = -P_M \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta x}\), where the driving force is the pressure difference, not the concentration gradient
Units: \(J\) in cm³ STP/(cm²·s); \(P_M\) in (cm³ STP)(cm)/(cm²·s·Pa); \(\Delta P\) in Pa; \(\Delta x\) in cm. Never mix m and cm
The tabulated \(P_M\) values are given ×10⁻¹³, so multiply by 10⁻¹³ before calculating
Three-stage transport: sorption at the inside surface, diffusion through the wall, desorption at the outside surface. Sorption is not the same as diffusion
\(P_M\) combines solubility and diffusivity; a larger \(P_M\) means faster permeation
Flux is inversely proportional to thickness, \(J \propto 1/\Delta x\), so doubling the wall thickness halves the flux
Amorphous regions (random, loosely packed chains) allow faster sorption and diffusion than crystalline regions (ordered, tightly packed). A polymer does not behave uniformly
HDPE is a much better barrier than LDPE, with \(P_M\) about 7 to 25 times lower, because it has higher density and crystallinity
Water vapour permeates polyethylene much more readily than O₂, N₂ or CO₂ and has the largest \(P_M\) in the table
The negative sign only indicates that flux runs down the pressure gradient, so the magnitude is used in calculations
conn: Crystallinity and density link to \(P_M\): higher crystallinity (HDPE) means fewer amorphous pathways, lower solubility and diffusivity, lower \(P_M\), and so lower flux and better packaging

Fick's First Law links to the membrane equation: the form is the same (flux proportional to a gradient over a distance), but \(P_M\) and \(\Delta P\) replace \(D\) and \(\Delta C\), so concentration-based and pressure-based problems should be compared

Thickness and material choice trade off in design: a thinner wall of a low-\(P_M\) polymer can match a thicker wall of a high-\(P_M\) polymer, so questions often ask for the thickness needed to meet a leak-rate target
Flux per unit area becomes total gas loss when multiplied by area and time, which combines with unit conversion and STP volumes
exq: A PET or polyethylene bottle wall of thickness 0.5 mm has a CO₂ pressure difference of 2×10⁵ Pa across it. Given \(P_M\) (×10⁻¹³ in the table), calculate the flux \(J\), taking care to convert mm to cm and to apply the 10⁻¹³ factor. Then find the volume of CO₂ lost through 0.04 m² of wall in 24 hours.

Compare O₂ flux through LDPE and HDPE films of equal thickness and pressure difference, using the tabulated \(P_M\) values. Explain the ratio (roughly 7 to 25) in terms of amorphous and crystalline regions.
A film's thickness is doubled and the pressure difference is halved. By what factor does the flux change? Then calculate the thickness needed to reduce the flux to a specified target.
Describe the three stages by which gas passes through a polymer wall, and distinguish sorption from diffusion. Why does water vapour have a much larger \(P_M\) than N₂ in polyethylene?
Explain why the negative sign appears in \(J = -P_M \Delta P/\Delta x\) and state the units of each term. Show that the units of \(P_M\) are consistent with those of \(J\).

notes.t: Diffusion in Polymers
pts: Polymers used in packaging, e.g. PET drinks bottles, can let gas pass through them over time.
Polymers have amorphous and crystalline regions; gas is absorbed into the polymer and diffuses through it over time.
Gas transport through a polymer wall occurs in three stages: sorption at the inside surface, diffusion through the wall, and desorption at the outside surface.
defs: Amorphous region
Part of a polymer where chains are randomly arranged and loosely packed, allowing easier gas absorption and diffusion.
Crystalline region
Part of a polymer where chains are ordered and tightly packed, through which gas diffuses less readily.
tips: Do not confuse sorption (uptake of gas into the polymer surface) with diffusion (movement through the wall).
Amorphous regions allow faster gas diffusion than crystalline regions; do not assume the whole polymer behaves uniformly.
rq: Why does CO₂ slowly escape from a plastic drinks bottle even when the cap is sealed?
CO₂ is sorbed into the polymer wall, diffuses through the amorphous regions, and is desorbed to the outside air.
Why would a bottle made with a higher proportion of crystalline polymer keep fizz longer?
Crystalline regions are tightly packed and ordered, so gas diffuses through them more slowly than through amorphous regions.

notes.t: Diffusion through polymer membranes (permeability)
pts: Fick's First Law is modified for membranes: flux is driven by the pressure difference across the membrane rather than a concentration gradient.
Permeability coefficient \(P_{M}\) combines solubility and diffusivity; the larger \(P_{M}\), the faster gas passes through the polymer.
Flux is inversely proportional to membrane thickness: thicker membranes slow gas transport.
Higher density polyethylene (HDPE) is a far better gas barrier than LDPE, with permeability values roughly 7 to 25 times lower.
Water vapour permeates polyethylene much more readily than the gases O2, N2 or CO2, giving the largest \(P_{M}\) values in the table.
defs: Permeability coefficient (\(P_{M}\))
A material constant describing how easily a gas passes through a polymer membrane under a unit pressure difference and unit thickness, expressed in (cm³ STP)(cm)/(cm²·s·Pa).
Diffusion flux (J)
The volume of gas (cm³ at STP) passing through a unit membrane area per unit time.
eqs: Permeation flux through a polymer membrane (modified Fick's First Law)
J = diffusion flux (cm³ STP/(cm²·s)); \(P_{M}\) = permeability coefficient (cm³ STP·cm/(cm²·s·Pa)); ΔP = pressure difference across membrane (Pa); Δx = membrane thickness (cm)
tips: Watch units: \(P_{M}\) is given ×10⁻¹³, so multiply by 10⁻¹³ before calculating; the negative sign only indicates flux runs down the pressure gradient.
Use Δx in cm and ΔP in Pa consistently with \(P_{M}\)'s units; mixing metres and centimetres gives wrong answers.
rq: Why does the table list H2O with permeability values about 10 to 100 times larger than the gases?
Water vapour is much more soluble in polyethylene and/or diffuses more readily, so the product of solubility and diffusivity (\(P_{M}\)) is far greater than for the non-polar gases.
If a packaging film of LDPE is replaced by one twice as thick, what happens to the gas flux, all else equal?
The flux halves, since J is inversely proportional to Δx.

units.name: 10.7 Temperature dependence of diffusion (Arrhenius)
units.ov: This material covers how the diffusion coefficient D depends on absolute temperature through the Arrhenius relation \(D = D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT)\). It also covers how activation energy and diffusion mechanism (interstitial vs substitutional) and crystal structure set the size of D. These ideas are applied in the Cu-in-Si worked example, where D at one temperature is used to find D at another.
must: Arrhenius relation: \(D = D_0\exp\left(-\frac{Q_d}{RT}\right)\), where D is in m²/s, \(D_0\) is the pre-exponential factor in m²/s, \(Q_d\) is in J/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol·K and T is in K
Always convert °C to K (add 273) before substituting; a Celsius value in the exponent is the most common error
Keep energy units consistent: \(Q_d\) in J/mol with R = 8.314 J/mol·K (so convert kJ/mol to J/mol), or eV/atom with k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K
D rises exponentially with T, so a small temperature increase gives a large increase in D; a larger \(Q_d\) gives a smaller D and a stronger temperature sensitivity

Two-temperature method when \(D_0\) is unknown: \(\ln\frac{D_2}{D_1} = -\frac{Q_d}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right)\), or find \(D_0 = D_1\exp(Q_d/RT_1)\) and then substitute it to get \(D_2\)
Linearised form: \(\ln D = \ln D_0 - \frac{Q_d}{R}\frac{1}{T}\); a plot of ln D (or log D) against 1/T (or 1000/T) is a straight line with slope \(-Q_d/R\) and intercept \(\ln D_0\)
Worked example, Cu in Si: \(Q_d\) = 41.5 kJ/mol, T from 573 K to 623 K, giving \(D_2 \approx 15.7\times10^{-11}\) m²/s
Interstitial diffusion (e.g. C in Fe) is much faster than substitutional diffusion (e.g. Fe in Fe, Al in Al), because small atoms move through gaps in the lattice and the barrier is lower
Crystal structure affects D: on the plot, C diffuses at a different rate in α-Fe (BCC) than in γ-Fe (FCC), and Fe self-diffusion in γ-Fe is the slowest system shown
On log-scale plots, each major tick is a factor of 10 in D, not a linear step; read the axes carefully
conn: Arrhenius plot and activation energy: the slope of log D against 1/T gives \(Q_d\), and the intercept gives \(D_0\). Questions often ask you to extract both from two data points or from a graph.

Mechanism and activation energy: interstitial paths have a low \(Q_d\) and substitutional paths a high \(Q_d\), which explains the ordering of lines on the plot and why the lines have different slopes.
Temperature and unit conversion: the exponential amplifies any error in T or in the \(Q_d\)/R units, so a numerical question tests the conversions as well as the formula.

Diffusion coefficient and process design: D from the Arrhenius equation feeds into diffusion-time and penetration problems (e.g. heat treatment, doping, carburising), where a higher temperature shortens the time needed.
exq: Cu diffuses in Si with \(Q_d\) = 41.5 kJ/mol. Given D at 300 °C, calculate \(D_0\) and then D at 350 °C. Show the conversion to kelvin and state the factor by which D increases.
Two measurements give D = \(1\times10^{-14}\) m²/s at 800 K and D = \(1\times10^{-12}\) m²/s at 1000 K. Calculate \(Q_d\) in kJ/mol and eV/atom, and \(D_0\).
On an Arrhenius plot (log D against 1000/T), explain why the lines are straight, how to obtain \(Q_d\) from the slope, and why C in γ-Fe lies above Fe self-diffusion in γ-Fe.
By what factor does D change when T rises from 500 °C to 600 °C for \(Q_d\) = 80 kJ/mol, compared with \(Q_d\) = 200 kJ/mol? Comment on how \(Q_d\) affects temperature sensitivity.
Explain the difference between interstitial and substitutional diffusion, and say which has the larger \(Q_d\) and why. Give one example of each.

notes.t: Diffusion and Temperature
pts: Diffusion coefficient increases exponentially with absolute temperature, so diffusion speeds up rapidly as the material is heated.
The activation energy \(Q_{d}\) is the energy barrier atoms must overcome to jump between sites; a larger \(Q_{d}\) means a smaller D at a given temperature.
The gas constant R is Boltzmann's constant expressed per mole, so \(Q_{d}\) and R must use consistent energy units.
defs: Diffusion coefficient (D)
A measure of how quickly atoms or species diffuse through a material, in m²/s; it increases with temperature via an Arrhenius-type relationship.
Activation energy for diffusion (\(Q_{d}\))
The energy required to make an atom move from one site to another in the lattice; expressed in J/mol or eV/atom.
Pre-exponential factor (\(D_{o}\))
A temperature-independent constant with the units of D (m²/s) that scales the diffusion coefficient in the Arrhenius equation.
eqs: Temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient (Arrhenius relation)
\(D\) = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); \(D_o\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_d\) = activation energy (J/mol); \(R\) = gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K); \(T\) = absolute temperature (K)
tips: Unit trap: always convert temperature to kelvin (K = °C + 273) before substituting into the exponential.
Check energy units: if \(Q_{d}\) is in eV/atom, use Boltzmann's constant (8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K) rather than R = 8.314 J/mol·K, or convert consistently.
rq: Why must T be in kelvin rather than degrees Celsius in this equation?

The exponential term depends on the ratio \(Q_{d}\)/(RT); the Arrhenius form assumes an absolute zero of energy, so T must be absolute (K). Using °C gives wrong, even meaningless, values, including division by zero at 0 °C.
What happens to D if the activation energy \(Q_{d}\) is doubled while T stays the same?
Since D depends on exp(−\(Q_{d}\)/RT), doubling \(Q_{d}\) squares the exponential factor, so D decreases dramatically, making diffusion much slower.

notes.t: Diffusion and Temperature
pts: The diffusion coefficient D increases exponentially with absolute temperature T, so small temperature rises cause large increases in diffusion rate.
Interstitial diffusion (e.g. carbon in iron) is much faster than substitutional diffusion (e.g. Al in Al, Fe in Fe) because interstitial atoms are small and move through gaps in the lattice.
On an Arrhenius-style plot of log D against 1000 K/T, each diffusion system appears as a straight line, whose slope relates to the activation energy for diffusion.
Carbon diffuses more slowly in α-Fe (BCC) than in γ-Fe (FCC) at the same temperature region shown on the plot ordering, so the crystal structure affects D.
Self-diffusion of Fe in γ-Fe has the lowest D of the systems shown, reflecting slow substitutional diffusion at lower temperatures.
defs: Diffusion coefficient (D)
A measure of how quickly atoms diffuse through a material, in m²/s; it depends exponentially on temperature.
Interstitial diffusion
Diffusion in which small solute atoms (such as C in Fe) move between host lattice sites, generally much faster than substitutional diffusion.
Substitutional diffusion
Diffusion in which atoms move by exchanging places with vacancies or host atoms on lattice sites; generally slower than interstitial diffusion.
eqs: Temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient (Arrhenius form, implied by the plot)
D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); \(D_{0}\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy for diffusion (J/mol); R = gas constant (8.314 J/(mol·K)); T = absolute temperature (K)
tips: Use absolute temperature (K) in any exponential relationship; the axis labels in °C are not valid in the exponent.
Read the log scale carefully: each major tick is a factor of 10 change in D, not a linear step.
rq: Why does the plot use 1000 K/T on the horizontal axis rather than T directly?
Because D depends exponentially on 1/T, plotting log D against 1/T gives straight lines whose slope gives the activation energy.
Why is carbon diffusion in iron so much faster than iron self-diffusion at the same temperature?
Carbon is a small interstitial atom that fits into lattice gaps, whereas Fe moves substitutionally by exchanging with vacancies, which requires more energy.

notes.t: Temperature dependence of diffusion coefficient (Cu into Si example)
pts: The diffusion coefficient depends exponentially on absolute temperature through the Arrhenius form, so small temperature changes cause large changes in D.
D₀ (pre-exponential factor) is usually unknown, so it can be eliminated by writing the equation at two temperatures and taking the ratio or logs.
Temperatures must be converted to kelvin before use in the exponential term.
Worked example: given D at 300 °C and \(Q_{d}\) = 41.5 kJ/mol for Cu in Si, find D at 350 °C.
defs: Activation energy for diffusion
The energy per mole required for an atom to make a diffusive jump; it sets how strongly D changes with temperature.
eqs: Arrhenius temperature dependence of diffusion coefficient
D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); \(D_{0}\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy for diffusion (J/mol); R = gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K); T = absolute temperature (K)
Pre-exponential factor from a known D at \(T_{1}\)
\(D_{0}\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(D_{1}\) = known diffusion coefficient at \(T_{1}\) (m²/s)
tips: Convert 300 °C and 350 °C to kelvin (573 K and 623 K) before substituting into the exponential.
Keep units consistent: \(Q_{d}\) in J/mol with R = 8.314 J/mol·K, not kJ/mol.
rq: Why can D₀ be eliminated when comparing two temperatures, and what does the ratio D₂/D₁ depend on?
Taking the ratio cancels D₀, leaving D₂/D₁ = exp[−(\(Q_{d}\)/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)], which depends only on \(Q_{d}\) and the two absolute temperatures.
What happens to D if \(Q_{d}\) is larger, all else equal?
D changes more steeply with temperature, since the exponential term is more sensitive to 1/T when \(Q_{d}\) is large.

notes.t: Temperature dependence of diffusion coefficient: worked example Cu into Si
pts: Pre-exponential factor \(D_{0}\) is substituted from earlier calculation before solving for the diffusion coefficient at the new temperature.
The diffusion coefficient at temperature \(T_{2}\) is found by inserting \(D_{0}\), the activation energy \(Q_{d}\) and \(T_{2}\) into the Arrhenius-type expression.
Diffusion coefficient increases exponentially with temperature, so a small rise in T gives a large rise in D.
eqs: Temperature dependence of diffusion coefficient (Arrhenius form)

\(D_{2}\) = diffusion coefficient at \(T_{2}\) (m²/s); \(D_{0}\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy for diffusion (J/mol); R = gas constant (J/mol·K); \(T_{2}\) = absolute temperature (K)
Worked result for Cu into Si
\(D_{2}\) = diffusion coefficient of Cu in Si at \(T_{2}\) (m²/s)
tips: Always convert temperature to kelvin before substituting into the exponential term.
Check units: D is in m²/s, and \(Q_{d}\) and R must share energy units (J/mol with R = 8.314 J/mol·K).
rq: Why must T be in kelvin when using the exponential term?
The Arrhenius exponent depends on the ratio \(Q_{d}\)/(RT); using °C gives wrong, physically meaningless values because the zero point is arbitrary.
What happens to \(D_{2}\) if the activation energy \(Q_{d}\) is larger?
The exponent becomes more negative, so \(D_{2}\) is smaller; diffusion is more temperature-sensitive when \(Q_{d}\) is high.

units.name: 10.8 Non-steady state diffusion and Fick's second law
units.ov: This material covers non-steady state diffusion, where concentration varies with both position and time, C(x,t), and is governed by Fick's second law, \( \partial C/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 C/\partial x^2 \). For a semi-infinite solid with constant surface concentration \(C_s\) and uniform initial concentration \(C_0\), the solution is expressed with the error function. Solving problems means stating the boundary conditions, forming the dimensionless argument \( x/(2\sqrt{Dt}) \), and reading erf values from a table with interpolation.
must: Fick's second law: \( \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2} \); use it whenever C changes with time, and not Fick's first law (\( J=-D\,dC/dx \)), which is for steady state
Error-function solution for constant surface concentration: \( \frac{C(x,t)-C_0}{C_s-C_0}=1-\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right) \)
State the boundary conditions: \(t=0\): \(C=C_0\) for all \(x\ge0\); \(t>0\): \(C=C_s\) at \(x=0\) and \(C=C_0\) at \(x=\infty\)
Definition: \( \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^z e^{-y^2}dy \); erf(0)=0, erf(z)→1 for large z (about 2.8 on the table)
Distinguish \(C_s\) (fixed surface value) from \(C_0\) (initial bulk value); the normalised form works for any units (kg/m³ or wt%) as long as they are consistent
Units: D in m²/s, x in m, t in s, so \( x/(2\sqrt{Dt}) \) is dimensionless; convert hours to seconds and mm to m
Solving method: calculate the left side \((C-C_0)/(C_s-C_0)\), get erf(z)=1−that value, find z from the table by interpolation, then solve \(x\), \(t\) or \(D\) from \(z=x/(2\sqrt{Dt})\)
Fixed concentration at a given depth means fixed z, so \( x^2/(Dt)=\text{constant} \): \( x_1^2/(D_1t_1)=x_2^2/(D_2t_2) \); depth scales as \( \sqrt{Dt} \), so doubling the depth needs 4× the time
The profile penetrates deeper and flattens with time (\(t_0<t_1<t_2<t_3\)); D is temperature dependent through an Arrhenius law
Interpolate linearly between table entries rather than using the nearest value, and don't confuse the z column with the erf(z) column
conn: Fick's first law (flux, steady state) versus second law (time-dependent): the second law comes from combining the first law with conservation of mass, and the first law gives the flux at the surface once C(x,t) is known
The Arrhenius temperature dependence \( D=D_0\exp(-Q/RT) \) combines with the erf solution: find D at the process temperature, then calculate time or depth, e.g. carburising steel
Boundary conditions determine the solution: the same erf form applies to carburising, decarburising or doping by changing \(C_s\) and \(C_0\) (\(C_s<C_0\) for loss of species)
The scaling \( x\propto\sqrt{Dt} \) links to comparing two heat treatments, where equal z means equal concentration at the same depth so \(Dt\) must be equal
exq: A steel with 0.20 wt% C is carburised at 950 °C with a constant surface concentration of 1.0 wt% C. Given D = 1.6×10⁻¹¹ m²/s, calculate the time needed to reach 0.60 wt% C at a depth of 1.0 mm, using the erf table and interpolation.

State Fick's second law and write the initial and boundary conditions for copper diffusing into an aluminium bar with constant surface concentration \(C_s\) and initial concentration \(C_0\). Sketch C(x,t) for four increasing times.

A carburising treatment takes 10 h at 900 °C to reach a given carbon concentration at 0.5 mm depth. Find the time needed to reach the same concentration at 1.5 mm at the same temperature, and then at a temperature where D is doubled.
Explain why Fick's first law cannot be used for a time-dependent problem, and define the error function, giving its values at z=0 and for large z.

Using \( \frac{C-C_0}{C_s-C_0}=1-\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right) \) and measured concentrations at a known depth and time, determine D, and use it to predict the concentration at a different depth after a different time.

notes.t: Non-steady state diffusion and Fick's Second Law
pts: In non-steady state diffusion the concentration of the diffusing species depends on both position and time, so C is a function of x and t.
Non-steady state diffusion is described using Fick's Second Law rather than Fick's First Law.
Fick's Second Law is a second order partial differential equation; its solution involves the Gaussian error function.
defs: Non-steady state diffusion
Diffusion in which the concentration of the diffusing species changes with time at a given position, so C = C(x,t).
eqs: Fick's Second Law: rate of change of concentration with time due to diffusion
C = concentration of diffusing species (mol/\(m^{3}\) or kg/\(m^{3}\)); t = time (s); x = position (m); D = diffusion coefficient (\(m^{2}\)/s)
tips: Do not use Fick's First Law (J = -D dC/dx) for time-dependent problems; use the second law with \( \partial C/\partial t \).
Keep units consistent: D is in \(m^{2}\)/s, so x and \( \sqrt{Dt} \) must use metres and seconds.
rq: Why can Fick's First Law not describe a situation where the concentration changes with time?
Fick's First Law assumes steady state (the concentration gradient does not change with time), so it has no time derivative; Fick's Second Law adds the time dependence via \( \partial C/\partial t \).
Why does the solution of Fick's Second Law involve the Gaussian error function erf(z)?
Because the second-order PDE with time and position dependence, under typical boundary conditions, yields a similarity solution in the variable \( x/\sqrt{Dt} \), which leads to erf.

notes.t: Non-steady state diffusion: boundary conditions for copper into aluminum
pts: Non-steady state diffusion: concentration at a point changes with time, so Fick's second law is needed rather than the first law.
Copper atoms diffuse into an aluminum bar whose surface concentration is held constant at \(C_{S}\) while the bulk starts at pre-existing concentration \(C_{o}\).
Initially (t = 0) the whole bar has concentration \(C_{o}\) for all positions from the surface to infinite depth.
For t > 0 the surface is held at constant concentration \(C_{S}\) (x = 0), and deep inside the bar concentration remains \(C_{o}\) (x = ∞).
As time increases (\(t_{0}\) < \(t_{1}\) < \(t_{2}\) < \(t_{3}\)) the penetration depth of the diffusing species grows and the profile flattens.
defs: Non-steady state diffusion
Diffusion in which the concentration at any point in the material changes with time, so the flux and concentration gradient vary with time.
Surface concentration \(C_{S}\)
The constant concentration of the diffusing species maintained at the surface (x = 0) for t > 0.
Pre-existing concentration \(C_{o}\)
The uniform initial concentration of the diffusing species throughout the bulk of the material before diffusion begins.
tips: Do not apply the steady-state (Fick's first law) solution to a problem where concentration changes with time; use the non-steady state (Fick's second law) with the correct boundary conditions.
Check which boundary conditions apply: initial condition at t = 0 and the surface condition for t > 0 must both be stated before solving.
rq: Why does the concentration at x = ∞ remain \(C_{o}\) for all t > 0, even though copper is diffusing in?
The semi-infinite bar is so deep that diffusing atoms have not penetrated that far in finite time; the bulk stays at the pre-existing concentration \(C_{o}\).
What would happen to the profiles if the surface concentration \(C_{S}\) were increased?

The concentration gradient near the surface would increase, so the diffusion flux and the concentration at each depth would rise, though the penetration depth at a given time would be governed by time and D, not by \(C_{S}\) alone.

notes.t: Diffusion solution for constant surface concentration (error function)
pts: The concentration profile depends on distance x and time t, measured from the surface held at constant concentration Cs.
Concentration falls from Cs at the surface toward the bulk value C0 deeper into the material; the penetration depth grows with time.
The solution is written as a normalised concentration difference, so it is valid for any Cs and C0.
defs: Error function erf(z)
A special function defined as the integral from 0 to z of 2/√π times e^(-y²) dy; it is tabulated or available in software such as Matlab and Mathematica.
eqs: Concentration at depth x and time t for constant surface concentration diffusion

C(x,t) = concentration at depth x and time t (kg/m³ or wt%); \(C_{s}\) = surface concentration (kg/m³ or wt%); \(C_{0}\) = initial uniform concentration (kg/m³ or wt%); x = distance from surface (m); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); t = time (s)
z = argument (dimensionless); y = dummy integration variable (dimensionless)
tips: Check units: x must be in metres and Dt in m²/s-consistent units so the argument of erf is dimensionless.
Do not confuse \(C_{s}\) (surface concentration) with \(C_{0}\) (initial bulk concentration); the solution only applies when the surface concentration is constant.
rq: Why does the concentration at a fixed depth x rise over time, and what happens to the penetration depth as t increases?
Diffusion spreads solute deeper as time increases; since erf's argument x/(2√(Dt)) decreases with t, C(x,t) rises toward Cs, and the penetration depth scales with √(Dt).
What happens to the argument of erf if you double the diffusion coefficient D at fixed x and t?
The argument x/(2√(Dt)) decreases by a factor of √2, so the concentration at that depth increases, as diffusion is faster.

notes.t: Example Table of Error Function Values
pts: The error function erf(z) gives tabulated values for z from 0 to about 2.8, and erf(z) rises from 0 toward 1 as z increases.
Values of erf(z) are read from the table by matching the z value; intermediate values are needed for interpolation.
defs: Error function, erf(z)
A mathematical function of z, defined by an integral, that is used in diffusion solutions; it equals 0 at z = 0 and approaches 1 as z becomes large.
tips: Do not confuse the table's z column with erf(z); read the value in the adjacent column matching the given z.
Interpolate between tabulated z values rather than assuming the nearest entry is exact.
rq: Why does erf(z) approach 1 for large z, and what does this imply for diffusion depth?
erf(z) tends to 1 as z grows, so the concentration term approaches its limiting value; deep positions correspond to large z where the diffusion profile has almost fully changed.

units.name: 10.9 Case study: Cu interconnects and diffusion barriers in Si ICs
units.ov: This case study shows how materials selection for Si integrated circuit interconnects trades electrical conductivity against diffusion into silicon during heat treatment up to about 500 °C. Al was used for years because it diffuses least into Si. Cu, with higher conductivity and less heat dissipation, replaced it (1997 ITRS) once conductive ceramic diffusion barriers (TiN, TaN) were available. Throughout, the diffusion coefficient D(T) is the quantity used to judge both metals and barriers.
must: An interconnect is a thin, narrow conducting path linking components on an IC, so it needs high electrical conductivity \(\sigma\), in \((\Omega\,\mathrm{m})^{-1}\).
Ag has the highest conductivity in the table, so it is the best choice only if cost is discounted. State this condition explicitly, since cost would otherwise favour Al or Cu.
Post-metallisation heat treatments up to about 500 °C drive diffusion. Significant metal diffusion into Si can destroy the IC's electrical function.
The D vs \(1/T\) plot gives Cu, Au and Ag all diffusing faster in Si than Al. Al has the lowest D, which is why it was preferred for many years despite its lower conductivity.

The diffusion coefficient is Arrhenius: \(D=D_0\exp(-Q/RT)\). It rises strongly with temperature, so compare materials at the same T. A straight line on the \(\ln D\) vs \(1/T\) plot has slope \(-Q/R\).
Cu replaced Al (1997 ITRS) because of its higher conductivity. This means less heat dissipated, and it lets the industry keep pace with Moore's law (transistor count doubling about every 18 months).
Cu's fast diffusion in Si is the reason a barrier is needed, not a reason to reject Cu.
A diffusion barrier sits between Cu and Si. It must block diffusion in both directions (Cu into Si, and barrier atoms into Si) and itself be a good electrical conductor.
TiN and TaN (conductive ceramics) have diffusion properties for Cu comparable to Al's, so they work as barriers. TiZrN was also tested. Lower D of Cu in the barrier means a better barrier.
The design logic is a trade-off between two properties, high \(\sigma\) (favours Cu) and low D (favours Al). The barrier layer resolves it by decoupling them.
conn: Arrhenius diffusion and processing temperature: the 500 °C heat treatments set the D values used to judge metals and barriers, and a small T rise gives an exponential rise in D and in the depth of Cu penetration.

Materials selection trade-offs: conductivity vs diffusion vs cost (Ag vs Cu vs Al) leads to a composite solution (Cu plus barrier). This links to bonding and ceramic properties, where ceramics are normally insulators but TiN and TaN are conductive.
Conductivity and heat dissipation: higher \(\sigma\) means lower resistive (Joule) heating, so higher device density and Moore's law scaling are possible.
Reading the D vs \(1/T\) graph: comparing materials at fixed T and extracting activation energy from the slope links the case study to the diffusion calculations (Fick's laws, \(x\sim\sqrt{Dt}\)).
exq: Explain why Ag is not used for IC interconnects even though it has the highest conductivity in the table, and why Al was used for many years. State the assumption behind choosing Ag.

Using the D vs \(1/T\) plot for Cu, Au, Ag and Al in Si, rank the metals by how far they diffuse at 500 °C. Estimate the diffusion distance \(x\approx\sqrt{Dt}\) for a 1 h anneal and say whether it is acceptable for a device feature of about 100 nm.
Why did the 1997 ITRS roadmap choose to replace Al with Cu? Discuss conductivity, heat dissipation and Moore's law, and explain why Cu needed a barrier layer.
List the requirements of a diffusion barrier between Cu and Si. Explain why TiN and TaN are suitable and how you would use diffusion coefficient data to compare TiZrN, TiN and TaN.
Given \(D=D_0\exp(-Q/RT)\), show how Q and \(D_0\) are found from two points on a \(\ln D\) vs \(1/T\) plot. By what factor does D change for Cu in Si between 400 °C and 500 °C?

notes.t: Case study: diffusion of metals into Si for integrated circuits
pts: Interconnects are very thin, narrow conducting paths on an IC, so they need high electrical conductivity.
From the conductivity table, silver has the highest conductivity, making it the suggested interconnect material when cost is discounted.
The IC is subjected to further heat treatments up to about 500 °C after metallisation, which drives diffusion.
If metal diffuses significantly into the silicon, the electrical functionality of the IC may be destroyed.
defs: Interconnect
A very thin, narrow conducting path that connects components on an integrated circuit and must have high electrical conductivity.
tips: Conductivity is given in (Ω·m)⁻¹ (siemens/m); do not confuse it with resistivity in Ω·m when comparing the table values.
Choosing silver assumes cost is discounted; state this condition explicitly, as cost would otherwise favour aluminium or copper.
rq: Why is silver preferred over aluminium for interconnects even though aluminium is cheaper?

Silver has the highest electrical conductivity in the table (\( 6.8 \times 10^7 \) (Ω·m)⁻¹ vs \( 3.8 \times 10^7 \) (Ω·m)⁻¹ for Al), so it gives lower resistive loss in narrow tracks; cost is set aside in this comparison.
Why does the 500 °C heat treatment matter for the choice of interconnect metal, not just its conductivity?
Heat promotes diffusion of the metal into silicon; significant diffusion can short or degrade junctions and destroy IC functionality, so a metal must also be stable at these temperatures.

notes.t: Case study: replacing Al with Cu for Si integrated circuit interconnects
pts: Figure shows diffusion coefficients of Cu, Au, Ag and Al in Si versus reciprocal temperature; Al has the lowest diffusion coefficient, so it diffuses least into Si.
Al was preferred for many years despite its lower electrical conductivity than Cu, because of its low diffusion into Si.
Cu has higher electrical conductivity than Al, so the 1997 ITRS roadmap chose to replace Al with Cu.
Replacing Al with Cu lets the industry keep pace with Moore's law (MOSFET count on a chip doubling about every 18 months).
Cu interconnects dissipate less heat, a benefit of its better conductivity.
defs: Diffusion coefficient
A measure of how fast a species (e.g. a metal atom) diffuses through a host material; a lower value means slower diffusion into the host.
tips: Do not confuse low diffusion (good for Al) with high conductivity (good for Cu); the choice trades off these two properties.
Cu's diffusion into Si is the reason a barrier layer is needed, not a reason to avoid Cu.
rq: Cu has higher conductivity and Al has lower diffusion into Si. Why was Cu still adopted, and what did it require?
Higher conductivity lowers resistance and heat; Cu's higher diffusion into Si requires a barrier layer, so thin tantalum or tantalum nitride is deposited beneath Cu.

notes.t: Diffusion barriers for Cu interconnects
pts: A diffusion barrier is needed between Cu and Si so that Cu does not diffuse into Si and the barrier material does not diffuse into Si.
The barrier material must also be a good electrical conductor so that it does not impede current flow in the interconnect.
Diffusion coefficients of Cu into candidate barrier materials (TiZrN, TiN, TaN) were measured versus temperature; lower D means a better barrier.
TiN and TaN perform as well as Al in diffusion properties while being ceramics that are good conductors.
Because these barriers work, Cu can be used for interconnects in microprocessors, so less heat is dissipated in the interconnects.
defs: Diffusion barrier
A thin layer placed between two materials (here Cu and Si) that prevents atoms of each material from diffusing into the other while remaining electrically conductive.
tips: Do not confuse D with the diffusion rate: D is strongly temperature dependent (Arrhenius), so compare barriers at the same temperature on the graph.
Remember the barrier must satisfy two conditions: blocking diffusion in both directions AND being electrically conductive.
rq: Why does a low diffusion coefficient D at a given temperature indicate a better barrier material?
A low D means Cu atoms move very slowly through the barrier, so little Cu reaches the Si and degrades the device over time.
Why is a ceramic such as TiN useful as a barrier even though ceramics are usually poor conductors?
TiN and TaN are ceramics that are nonetheless good electrical conductors, so they block diffusion without adding significant resistance.

units.name: 10.10 Conclusions, resources and course logistics
units.ov: This material wraps up the diffusion topic and sets out logistics for ENG1033 Materials 1. Diffusion is a thermally driven random-walk process described by Fick's laws, with the diffusion coefficient D set by an Arrhenius temperature dependence. It underpins case hardening of steels and semiconductor doping. The logistics cover assessment: labs 20%, a 90-minute exam 80%.
must: Diffusion is a thermally driven random walk of atoms giving net transport from high to low concentration and mixing of materials
Arrhenius relation: \( D = D_0 \exp\left(-\frac{Q_d}{RT}\right) \), with D and \(D_0\) in m²/s
Use absolute temperature T in kelvin (T(K) = °C + 273) in the exponent, never °C
Keep units consistent: \(Q_d\) in J/mol with \(R = 8.314\) J/(mol·K)
Fick's First Law covers steady-state diffusion; Fick's Second Law covers non-steady-state diffusion; both define D
D is a material- and temperature-dependent constant relating flux to concentration gradient
Applications: case hardening of steels (metallurgy) and dopant introduction in semiconductors
Diffusion is characterised experimentally by measuring concentration gradients at interfaces between materials
Assessment: exam is 80% (in person, mid-December, 90 min, multiple choice plus 2 long questions); Labs 1 and 2 are 20% combined
Lab reports/worksheets are due 2 weeks after your own lab session, not after the scheduled week
conn: Arrhenius dependence of D links to Fick's laws: temperature changes D, which sets the flux in the first law and the rate of profile evolution in the second law
Two-temperature problems: take the ratio \(D_1/D_2\) or plot \(\ln D\) vs \(1/T\) to get \(Q_d\) (slope \(=-Q_d/R\)) and \(D_0\) (intercept), then use D in Fick's laws
Case hardening and doping design: choose temperature (via D) and time to reach a required concentration at a given depth, combining Arrhenius with the Fick's Second Law solution
Concentration-gradient measurement at interfaces connects to lab work and to extracting D experimentally
exq: State the Arrhenius relation for the diffusion coefficient, define each term with units, and explain why T must be in kelvin.
Carbon diffuses in a steel with \(D_0 = 2.3\times10^{-5}\) m²/s and \(Q_d = 148\) kJ/mol. Calculate D at 900 °C and at 1000 °C, and the factor by which the diffusion rate increases.
Measured D values are \(D_1\) at \(T_1\) and \(D_2\) at \(T_2\). Derive an expression for \(Q_d\) and describe how an Arrhenius plot of \(\ln D\) against \(1/T\) gives \(Q_d\) and \(D_0\).
Distinguish Fick's First and Second Laws, say when each applies, and explain how diffusion is exploited in case hardening of steel and doping of semiconductors.
Explain how a diffusion coefficient can be determined experimentally from concentration gradients at an interface between two materials, and why temperature control is critical.

notes.t: Diffusion: conclusions and the temperature dependence of D
pts: Diffusion is a thermally driven random walk that mixes materials and underpins important processing technologies.
Diffusion is used in metallurgy for case hardening of steels and in semiconductors to introduce dopants.
Diffusion is characterised by measuring concentration gradients at interfaces between materials.
Fick's First Law describes steady-state diffusion and Fick's Second Law describes non-steady-state diffusion, both defining the diffusion coefficient D.
The diffusion coefficient D depends strongly on temperature through an Arrhenius-type relation.
defs: Diffusion
Thermally driven random walk process by which atoms move through a material, leading to mixing and net transport from regions of high to low concentration.
Diffusion coefficient (D)
Material- and temperature-dependent proportionality constant relating the diffusion flux to the concentration gradient in Fick's laws.
eqs: Temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient (Arrhenius relation)

\(D\) = diffusion coefficient (\(m^{2}\)/s); \(D_0\) = pre-exponential factor (\(m^{2}\)/s); \(Q_d\) = activation energy for diffusion (J/mol); \(R\) = gas constant (8.314 J/(mol·K)); \(T\) = absolute temperature (K)
tips: Use absolute temperature (K) in the exponential term, not degrees Celsius.
Keep units consistent: \(Q_{d}\) in J/mol must match R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
rq: Why does increasing temperature increase D so strongly, and what does a larger \(Q_{d}\) imply?

Higher T increases the exponent term exp(-\(Q_{d}\)/RT) toward 1, giving exponentially larger D; a larger \(Q_{d}\) means D is more sensitive to temperature because atoms need more energy to jump between sites.
Why are Fick's First and Second Laws distinguished by the steady or non-steady state?
First Law applies when the concentration profile does not change with time (constant flux); Second Law is needed when concentration varies with both position and time.

notes.t: ENG1033 Materials 1: coming up (course logistics and assessment)
pts: Lectures run weeks 6-10 with Professor Daniel Mulvihill; tutorial 2 sessions start in week 6.
Lab 1 and Lab 2 are assessed and together make up 20% of the course mark; each report or worksheet is due 2 weeks after the lab session.
The final exam is in person in mid December (date/time TBC), worth 80% of the course mark, 90 minutes long.
The exam combines multiple choice questions with 2 long questions.
tips: Lab reports and worksheets are due 2 weeks after your own lab session, not after the scheduled week, so check your individual session date.
rq: Why does the course weight the final exam at 80% but the labs at only 20%, and what does this imply for revision priorities?

The exam tests the whole course's theory, so it dominates the mark; students should prioritise lecture content and exam practice while still meeting lab deadlines, since these are fixed, lower-weight, and easier to secure.

units.name: 11.1 Modulus and interatomic bonding
units.ov: This material introduces modulus as a material's resistance to elastic deformation, which comes from how easily atoms move relative to one another. In crystalline materials this is set by interatomic bond stiffness, so the primary/secondary bond classification from the Atomic Bonds lecture explains why modulus varies. In amorphous materials, such as polymers, it depends on chain entanglement. The notes are mostly conceptual and give no equations, so the marks are in clear definitions and linking mechanism to material class.
must: Modulus is resistance to deformation (stiffness), determined by how easily atoms move relative to each other.
Modulus is not strength: a stiff material (high \(E\)) can still fail at low stress.
Crystalline materials: modulus is controlled by the stiffness of the interatomic bonds.
Amorphous materials (polymers): modulus is controlled by how entangled the polymer chains are.
Primary (strong) bonds are ionic, covalent and metallic. They form by electron transfer or sharing.
Secondary (weak) bonds are van der Waals and hydrogen bonds. They arise from electrostatic attraction between dipoles.
Hydrogen bonds are secondary, though stronger than typical van der Waals forces. Do not misclassify them as primary.
Stiffer bonds mean a higher modulus, so materials with primary bonding are generally stiffer than those held mainly by secondary bonds. Lightly bonded or weakly entangled systems are more compliant.
Always state the mechanism that matches the material class: bond stiffness for crystals, chain entanglement for amorphous materials.
conn: Bond type (primary vs secondary) sets bond stiffness, which sets the modulus of crystalline materials. Questions often ask you to rank materials by modulus using their bonding.
Modulus versus strength: questions may ask you to separate stiffness (resistance to deformation) from failure stress, using a stiff but brittle material as the example.

Crystalline versus amorphous: the same word, modulus, has different atomic origins. Polymers can combine strong covalent bonds along chains with weak secondary bonds between chains, so the weak bonds and the entanglement govern the stiffness.
The force–separation curve of a bond links to modulus: a steeper curve at equilibrium separation means a stiffer bond and a higher \(E\).
exq: Define modulus and explain, at the atomic level, why it is a measure of resistance to deformation rather than of strength.
Compare the origin of modulus in a crystalline metal and in an amorphous polymer. What controls it in each case?
Classify ionic, covalent, metallic, van der Waals and hydrogen bonds as primary or secondary. Explain how bond type influences the modulus of a material.
A ceramic has a high modulus but fractures at a low applied stress. Explain how this is possible, and say what this shows about modulus versus strength.
Rank a covalently bonded ceramic, a metal and a polymer with secondary bonding between chains in order of expected modulus, and justify your ranking in terms of bonding.

notes.t: Modulus
pts: Modulus measures a material's resistance to deformation.
It arises from how easily atoms move relative to each other.
In crystalline materials modulus depends on the stiffness of interatomic bonds.
In amorphous materials modulus depends on how entangled the polymer chains are.
defs: Modulus
A material property describing resistance to deformation, determined by how easily atoms move relative to one another.
tips: Modulus describes resistance to deformation, not strength; a stiff material can still fail at low stress.
Remember the mechanism differs: bond stiffness for crystals, chain entanglement for amorphous materials.
rq: Why would a crystalline metal and an amorphous polymer have different moduli even if both are loaded elastically?
Crystalline materials resist deformation through stiff interatomic bonds, whereas amorphous polymers resist through entanglement of chains, which limits how easily chains slide past each other.
What would you expect to happen to modulus if interatomic bonds were weakened in a crystal?
Atoms would move more easily relative to each other, so the material would deform more readily and the modulus would fall.

notes.t: Types of Bonds
pts: Bonds are grouped into primary (strong) bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Secondary bonds are weaker than primary bonds and include van der Waals and hydrogen bonds.
This page is a reminder of material already covered in the Atomic Bonds lecture.
defs: Primary (strong) bond
A strong interatomic bond formed by electron transfer or sharing, comprising ionic, covalent and metallic types.
Secondary (weak) bond
A weaker bond between atoms or molecules arising from electrostatic attraction of dipoles, comprising van der Waals and hydrogen bonds.
tips: Do not confuse 'primary' with 'primary bond strength' ordering: primary bonds are the strong group, secondary bonds are the weak group.
Hydrogen bonds are a type of secondary bond even though they are stronger than typical van der Waals forces.
rq: Why are secondary bonds generally weaker than primary bonds, and what does this imply for melting point?
Secondary bonds rely on weak dipole or induced-dipole attractions rather than electron transfer or sharing, so less energy is needed to break them, giving lower melting points.
Why are hydrogen bonds grouped with van der Waals bonds despite being a distinct type?
Both are secondary bonds involving electrostatic attraction between dipoles, and both are much weaker than primary bonds.

units.name: 11.2 Theoretical modulus from bond stiffness and energy
units.ov: This material shows how a material's Young's modulus can be estimated from atomic bonding. Each interatomic bond is treated as a spring whose stiffness is the slope of the force–separation curve, or the curvature of the bond-energy curve, at r₀. Counting bonds per unit area (N = 1/r₀²) and linking bond stretch to strain gives E ≈ S₀/r₀. This is an idealised upper-bound estimate, and stiffer bonds give a higher E.
must: Theoretical Young's modulus: \( E = S_0/r_0 \), with S₀ in N/m and r₀ in m giving E in Pa.
Bond stiffness is the local gradient \( S = dF/dr \), evaluated at r₀ for the modulus, and not the ratio F/r.
Energy–force–stiffness chain: \( F = dU/dr \) and \( S_0 = dF/dr = d^2U/dr^2 \) at r₀. Be aware that the sign of F depends on convention, with the attractive force often written \( F=-dU/dr \).
Small-strain linear law: \( F = S_0(r-r_0) \). The force is zero at r = r₀, and S₀ is roughly constant only for small strains.
Derivation: \( \sigma = N S_0 (r-r_0) \), \( \varepsilon = (r-r_0)/r_0 \), and \( N = 1/r_0^2 \), so \( \sigma = (S_0/r_0)\varepsilon \). Be able to reproduce every step.
Strain is dimensionless, \( \varepsilon=(r-r_0)/r_0 \), and stress is the force per unit area carried by the bonds crossing that area.
Bond stiffness (slope at r₀) is not bond strength (depth of the energy well or peak force). A steeper F–r slope at r₀ gives a higher E.
Equilibrium spacing r₀ is where attractive and repulsive forces balance, so the net force is zero and U is at a minimum.
The theoretical E assumes all bonds are identical, stretch together and respond linearly. Real moduli are usually lower because of defects and microstructure, so the estimate is an upper bound.
Unit discipline: convert nm to m, because a slip gives an answer wrong by orders of magnitude. Example: \( S_0=50 \) N/m and \( r_0=0.25 \) nm give \( E=200 \) GPa.
conn: Energy curve to modulus: the U–r curve gives F by differentiating once and S₀ by differentiating twice at r₀, and S₀ then feeds into E = S₀/r₀.
Microscopic to macroscopic: the bond-level force law F = S₀(r−r₀), combined with bond density 1/r₀² and strain (r−r₀)/r₀, becomes the macroscopic Hooke's law σ = Eε.

Bond type and material properties: a deep, narrow energy well means a steep F–r slope and a high E. Questions often contrast stiffness with strength, and the theoretical E with measured values (defects, microstructure).
Local and average gradients: S = dF/dr at r₀ versus F/r, and small-strain linearity versus large-strain nonlinearity, are the usual pitfalls in calculation questions.
exq: Derive E = S₀/r₀ starting from a bond modelled as a spring. State the definitions of stress, strain and bond density, and explain each assumption.
A bond has stiffness S₀ = 40 N/m and equilibrium spacing r₀ = 0.28 nm. Calculate the theoretical Young's modulus in GPa, and the force on one bond at 1% strain.
The bond energy is given as \( U(r) = -A/r + B/r^n \). Find r₀ from dU/dr = 0, then find S₀ = d²U/dr² at r₀, and hence E.
Two materials have F–r curves with different slopes at r₀. Explain which has the higher modulus, and why a higher peak bond force does not necessarily mean a higher modulus.
Explain why the theoretical modulus is an upper bound. Why does the linear law F = S₀(r−r₀) fail at large strains, and why does using F/r instead of dF/dr give the wrong stiffness?

notes.t: Theoretical Modulus – bond stiffness
pts: Macroscopic deformation requires stretching of interatomic bonds, so bond behaviour sets the material's stiffness.
Each interatomic bond is modelled as a spring, which gives a simple way to estimate the stiffness of a material from atomic bonding.
Bond stiffness is the gradient of the force–separation curve, evaluated at the separation r, so it is largest where the force changes fastest with distance.
In the diagram, the equilibrium spacing r₀ is the rest length of the bond and r is the stretched length, so the displacement from equilibrium is r − r₀.
defs: Bond stiffness (S)
The rate of change of the force exerted by an interatomic bond with respect to the change in interatomic separation; it measures how resistant a bond is to being stretched or compressed.
Equilibrium distance (r₀)
