Failure favours the planes of greatest shear stress. In an isotropic material under uniaxial tension or compression these lie at \( \theta = 45^\circ \) to the load.
Planes of maximum shear (45° to the load) are different from planes of maximum normal stress (perpendicular to the load).
Isotropic means properties are the same in all directions. The 45° result may not hold for anisotropic materials such as single crystals.
Strain is dimensionless, so 0.005 equals 0.5%. State which form you use to avoid errors.
conn: Slip of atomic planes (microscopic mechanism) links to the 45° maximum shear plane (continuum stress analysis), which explains the angled shear bands seen in yielded tensile specimens.
The elastic limit and the strain at which bonds start to fail link to the start of plastic deformation on a stress-strain curve, and so to the definition of yield strength.
Isotropy underlies the 45° result, so questions may ask how anisotropy or crystal orientation changes the critical slip plane.
Uniaxial tension and compression give the same 45° plane, linking the loading mode to the shear that causes yield, which leads on to Mohr's circle and the Tresca criterion.
exq: Define elastic and plastic deformation at the atomic level. Using sketches of atomic planes under shear, explain what the lattice looks like after unloading in each case.

A metal rod is loaded in uniaxial tension. State the angle of the plane of maximum shear stress to the load axis and explain why yielding occurs on this plane rather than the plane of maximum normal stress.

A metal has an elastic strain limit of about 0.5%. A 200 mm specimen is stretched by 0.8 mm and unloaded. Is it permanently deformed? Justify your answer with the strain value and state any assumptions.
Explain why the statement 'elastic deformation involves no change in shape' is wrong. What actually distinguishes elastic from plastic deformation?
Under what conditions does the 45° maximum shear plane result apply? Discuss how it might differ for an anisotropic material.

notes.t: Elastic deformation
pts: Elastic deformation is reversible: atomic bonds stretch but stay intact, so the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
For metals, elastic behaviour typically holds only up to about 0.5% strain (0.005).
Beyond the elastic limit, plastic deformation begins: bonds fail and new ones form, so the deformation is permanent.
defs: Elastic deformation
Reversible deformation in which atomic bonds stretch without breaking, so the material returns to its original shape once the load is removed.
Plastic deformation
Permanent deformation that occurs after the elastic limit, in which atomic bonds fail and new bonds form, so the shape is not recovered on unloading.
tips: Do not confuse the elastic limit with the yield strength in general; the 0.5% figure is a typical value for metals, not a universal constant.
Strain is dimensionless: 0.005 and 0.5% are the same value, so state the form used clearly to avoid unit or percentage errors.
rq: Why does unloading a metal within its elastic range return it exactly to its original length, while unloading it beyond that range does not?

Within the elastic range the atomic bonds only stretch and remain intact, so the stored energy is recovered and the structure springs back. Beyond it, bonds fail and reform in new positions, so the displacement is permanent.
What would you expect to happen to the elastic limit of a metal if its strain were limited to 0.2% during loading?
The metal would remain entirely elastic, since 0.2% is below the typical elastic limit of about 0.5% for metals, so it would fully recover on unloading.

notes.t: Elastic and Plastic Deformation
pts: Elastic deformation is reversible: the material changes shape under load and fully recovers its original shape once the load is removed.
Plastic deformation is permanent: the material changes shape under load but does not return to its original shape after the load is removed.
Under shear loading, atomic planes slide relative to one another; in the elastic case the planes spring back when the load is removed, leaving the lattice unchanged.
In plastic deformation, the atomic planes are displaced permanently by slip, so the lattice is left in a new, shifted arrangement after unloading.
defs: Elastic deformation
A reversible change in shape that occurs when a load is applied and disappears completely when the load is removed, the material returning to its original shape.
Plastic deformation
An irreversible change in shape that persists after the load is removed; the material does not return to its original shape.
Shear
A loading mode in which forces act parallel to a surface, causing layers of atoms to slide relative to one another.
tips: Do not confuse elastic deformation with plastic deformation: the key discriminator is whether the shape is recovered after the load is removed, not whether shape changes under load (both change shape under load).
Elastic deformation is not 'no deformation': the shape does change under load; only the recovery distinguishes it from plastic deformation.
rq: Why does an elastically deformed metal spring back to its original shape, while a plastically deformed one does not?

In elastic deformation atomic bonds are stretched or displaced but not permanently broken or rearranged, so they restore the original configuration when unloaded. In plastic deformation planes of atoms slide past one another permanently (slip), so the new arrangement persists after unloading.
What would you expect to observe on a stress–strain curve if a material is loaded beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded?
The unloading curve is roughly parallel to the elastic slope but does not return to zero strain; a permanent (plastic) strain remains.

notes.t: Yield and maximum shear stress
pts: Yielding is driven by shear acting on planes of atoms within the material.
Failure favourably occurs along the planes where shear stress is greatest.
For isotropic materials in uniaxial tension or compression, the maximum shear plane is inclined at 45° to the load.
defs: Yield
Onset of permanent (plastic) deformation in a material, driven by shear stress acting on planes of atoms rather than by normal stress alone.
Isotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties are the same in all directions.
eqs: Maximum shear stress under uniaxial load (plane angle)
\theta = angle between maximum shear plane and applied load (degrees)
tips: Do not confuse the planes of maximum shear (45° to the load) with the planes of maximum normal stress (perpendicular to the load).
This 45° result applies to isotropic materials under uniaxial loading; anisotropic materials may have different critical planes.
rq: Why does yielding occur on 45° planes in a tensile test rather than on the plane perpendicular to the load?
On the plane perpendicular to the load the shear stress is zero; the shear stress is maximised at 45° to the load, so yielding by shear is favoured there.
What would happen to the orientation of the maximum shear planes in a brittle material that fails by normal stress?
Brittle materials fail by normal (tensile) stress on planes perpendicular to the load, so the 45° shear-plane argument does not govern their failure.

units.name: 12.2 Slip mechanisms and slip systems in FCC, BCC, HCP
units.ov: This material explains yield in crystalline metals as dislocation glide (slip) on specific crystallographic planes and in specific directions, which are set by the crystal structure. A slip system is a slip plane plus a slip direction within it. The number of slip systems in FCC, BCC and HCP then explains the differences in ductility between them.
must: Yield in crystalline metals is dislocation motion; slip needs far less stress than moving whole planes of atoms at once (theoretical shear strength)
Slip plane = the plane of highest atomic packing density (largest interplanar spacing, lowest resistance); slip direction = the close-packed direction within that plane
A slip system = one slip plane + one slip direction; the number of systems is planes × directions per plane, and you must give both
FCC: slip on {111} planes along ⟨110⟩ face diagonals (not cube edges), giving 12 slip systems (4 planes × 3 directions), so FCC is highly ductile
BCC: slip along ⟨111⟩ cube diagonals, with many systems (up to 48 in the notes), so it is generally ductile
HCP: slip is restricted to directions parallel to the basal plane, giving only 3 slip systems, so it is less ductile and tends towards brittleness
More slip systems means easier plastic deformation and greater ductility; this is not the same as higher or lower yield strength
Slip is driven by shear stress resolved onto the slip plane and direction; the applied tensile stress alone does not give the slip direction
Slip family = a group of symmetry-equivalent slip systems with the same plane and direction type
HCP ductility is a trend only: Ti and Zn can become ductile at elevated temperature as extra slip systems activate
conn: Packing density links to slip: the densest planes have the largest spacing and the lowest shear resistance, so they are the slip planes. The densest direction within them has the smallest Burgers displacement, so it is the slip direction.
Crystal structure sets the number of slip systems, and that number sets ductility (FCC/BCC ductile, HCP less so). Temperature can modify this by activating extra systems.

Dislocation motion links to resolved shear stress: yield occurs when the shear stress on a slip system reaches a critical value, so the orientation of the plane and direction relative to the load matters.

Unit-cell geometry links to the Miller indices of slip: face diagonals in FCC and body diagonals in BCC give the ⟨110⟩ and ⟨111⟩ directions, and confusing these with cube edges gives the wrong slip system.
exq: Define slip plane, slip direction and slip system. For an FCC crystal, state the slip plane family and slip direction family and show how the 12 slip systems arise (4 planes × 3 directions).
Explain why slip occurs on the most densely packed planes and along close-packed directions, referring to interplanar spacing, atomic spacing and Burgers displacement.

Compare the number of slip systems in FCC (12), BCC (up to 48) and HCP (3). Explain how this accounts for their relative ductility, and why HCP metals such as Ti or Zn can become more ductile at high temperature.

A single FCC crystal is loaded in tension. Explain why the tensile stress must be resolved onto the slip plane and slip direction, and state what the resolved shear stress must reach for yield to begin.
Sketch an FCC unit cell and mark one {111} slip plane and one ⟨110⟩ slip direction within it. Explain why cube edges are not slip directions in FCC.

notes.t: Mechanisms of Yield
pts: Yield in crystalline metals occurs when dislocations move through the material, allowing permanent (plastic) deformation.
Atoms move preferentially along specific slip planes and in specific slip directions, which requires far less energy than moving everything at once.
The available slip planes and directions are set by the crystal structure (e.g. FCC, BCC, HCP), so they differ between materials.

Slip generally occurs on the planes with the highest atomic packing density, since atoms there are spaced furthest apart and the interplanar spacing is largest, giving the lowest resistance to motion.
defs: Slip plane
A crystallographic plane, usually of highest atomic packing density, along which atoms preferentially glide during plastic deformation.
Slip direction
The close-packed crystallographic direction within a slip plane along which atoms move during slip.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement through the material carries plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength.
tips: Slip systems depend on the crystal structure, so do not assume every metal slips on the same planes.
Slip planes are the highest packing density planes; do not confuse them with the lowest density planes.
rq: Why is slip on the highest packing density planes easier than on sparsely packed planes?
Closely packed planes have larger interplanar spacing and fewer bonds to break per unit displacement, so the lattice resistance (Peierls stress) to dislocation motion is lower.
If a metal has few slip systems, what does this imply for its ductility?
Fewer independent slip systems limit the ability to accommodate arbitrary deformation, so the metal tends to be less ductile (e.g. HCP metals).

notes.t: Mechanisms of Yield: Slip in FCC Crystals
pts: In FCC metals, plastic deformation by slip occurs on the most densely packed planes, since these require the smallest shear force to move.
Slip proceeds along the close-packed direction, the line of highest linear atomic density, because the atomic spacing is smallest and the Burgers displacement is minimal.
In an FCC cell, the slip direction lies along the face diagonals (⟨110⟩-type directions) within the close-packed {111} planes.
tips: Do not confuse the slip plane (the most densely packed plane) with the slip direction (the close-packed line within it); both must be identified.
Slip in FCC is along face diagonals, not cube edges; using edge directions gives the wrong slip system.
rq: Why do slip planes and slip directions both favour the most densely packed arrangements?

Closely packed planes have the largest interplanar spacing and weakest bonding between them, so less shear stress is needed; the close-packed direction has the smallest slip displacement, minimising lattice distortion and energy.
What would happen to the number of slip systems if the crystal were not FCC but had only one close-packed plane family?
Fewer independent slip systems would be available, so the material would be less ductile, since plastic deformation requires enough systems to accommodate arbitrary shape change.

notes.t: FCC slip directions and slip systems
pts: Slip occurs when one plane of atoms (red) moves over the adjacent plane (blue) under shear stress.
During slip, atoms in the slipping plane shift to neighbouring equivalent lattice sites: a top corner atom moves to a mid back face position.
Slip proceeds along close-packed directions, so the atoms move between mid-face and corner positions that are the same type of site.
An FCC crystal has 12 slip systems, which makes FCC metals generally highly ductile.
defs: Slip plane
The crystallographic plane on which one part of a crystal slides over another under shear stress, producing plastic deformation.
Slip system
A combination of a slip plane and a slip direction within it; the number of slip systems determines how easily a metal deforms plastically.
Shear stress
A stress acting parallel to a plane, which causes layers of atoms to slide relative to each other and drives dislocation motion/slip.
tips: Slip occurs in close-packed planes and close-packed directions, not on arbitrary planes; do not count the 12 slip systems without including both plane and direction.
Shear stress must be resolved onto the slip plane and slip direction; the applied tensile stress alone does not indicate the slip direction.
rq: Why does FCC have more slip systems than BCC or HCP metals, and what does this mean for ductility?

FCC has 4 close-packed {111} planes each with 3 close-packed <110> directions, giving 12 slip systems; more systems allow slip to occur under many orientations of applied stress, so FCC metals are generally more ductile.
What would happen to slip if the shear stress acted in the opposite direction to the arrows shown?
Slip would occur in the opposite sense (the red plane would move the other way); the slip plane and slip direction are unchanged, only the sense of motion reverses.

notes.t: Slip directions in BCC and HCP crystal structures
pts: In BCC metals, slip occurs along the cube diagonal <111> directions, giving many available slip systems.
BCC structures have up to 48 slip systems, which makes them generally more ductile than HCP metals.
In HCP metals, slip directions lie only parallel to the basal plane, so slip is restricted.
HCP structures have only 3 slip systems, limiting plastic deformation and making them less ductile.
defs: Slip system
A combination of a slip plane and a slip direction along which dislocations move to produce plastic deformation.
tips: Do not confuse slip directions with slip planes; the count of slip systems depends on both.
Remember that the HCP restriction to the basal plane is why HCP metals are typically less ductile than BCC or FCC metals.
rq: Why does having fewer slip systems make HCP metals less ductile?
Fewer slip systems means fewer independent ways for dislocations to move, so the metal cannot easily accommodate arbitrary plastic strain without fracturing.
Why are BCC slip directions along cube diagonals rather than cube edges?
The cube diagonal <111> directions have the closest atomic packing and shortest Burgers vector in BCC, so they are the preferred slip directions.

notes.t: Slip systems
pts: Slip planes are the crystallographic planes on which dislocation glide (slip) can occur; the slip plane set gives the number of possible planes for slip.
Slip directions are the directions along which slip occurs within each slip plane.
A slip system is the combination of one slip plane with one slip direction; together they determine the possible options for slip to occur.
defs: Slip system
A combination of a slip plane and a slip direction on that plane along which dislocations glide, representing one possible way plastic deformation can occur in a crystal.
Slip plane
A crystallographic plane along which dislocation glide and plastic slip take place, usually the most densely packed planes.
Slip direction
The crystallographic direction, lying in a slip plane, along which slip (shear displacement) occurs.
Slip family
A group of equivalent slip systems related by crystal symmetry, sharing the same type of plane and direction.
tips: Do not count planes and directions separately; the number of slip systems comes from combining them (planes × directions per plane).
Slip systems are not just planes: a plane alone does not define slip, the direction must also be specified.
rq: Why does the number of slip systems in a crystal structure strongly influence its ductility?
More slip systems give more independent options for slip, so dislocations can glide under many stress orientations, allowing greater plastic deformation (higher ductility).
If a crystal has 4 slip planes and each plane has 3 slip directions, how many slip systems are there?
4 × 3 = 12 slip systems, since each slip system is one plane combined with one direction on that plane.

notes.t: Number of slip systems and ductility of crystal structures
pts: Slip systems are the combinations of slip planes and slip directions along which dislocations move; the more of them a material has, the more easily it can deform plastically.
Because BCC and FCC structures have many slip systems, they are generally ductile.
HCP structures have fewer available slip systems, so they tend to be more brittle.
tips: Do not confuse the number of slip systems with strength: more slip systems increase ductility by allowing easier deformation, not necessarily higher yield strength.
Ductility is a general trend; HCP metals such as titanium or zinc can show good ductility at elevated temperatures when additional slip systems activate.
rq: Why does having more slip systems make a metal more ductile rather than stronger?

More slip systems let dislocations glide on many planes and directions, so plastic deformation can occur at lower stress without fracturing; this allows large plastic strain before failure, i.e. ductility.
Why might an HCP metal fail by brittle fracture even though it can still slip?

Its few slip systems (often limited to basal slip at room temperature) may not be able to accommodate a general strain, so stress concentrates until cleavage or cracking occurs before significant plastic deformation.

units.name: 12.3 Resolved shear stress and slip in polycrystals
units.ov: This material links single-crystal yielding to real polycrystalline behaviour. Slip begins on a slip system when the resolved shear stress \(\tau_R\), which depends on loading and orientation, reaches the material constant \(\tau_{crss}\). In polycrystals, grains have different orientations, so slip starts in different grains at different applied stresses and in different directions, and this shows up as slip lines on a polished surface.
must: Yield on a slip system occurs when \(\tau_R = \tau_{crss}\)
\(\tau_R = F_s/A_s\): the shear force along the slip direction divided by the slip plane area
\(\tau_{crss}\) is a material property, independent of loading orientation and not recalculated per load; \(\tau_R\) depends on plane orientation and loading
Use the slip plane area \(A_s\), not the cross-sectional area \(A_0\), and resolve the force along the slip direction
Slip is dislocation motion on specific slip planes in specific slip directions, and it leaves a step on the surface
A slip system is a slip plane (normal \(n_s\)) plus a slip direction

In a uniaxial tension test on a zinc (HCP) single crystal, slip occurs on the plane with the maximum resolved shear stress, at about 45° to the load axis (the notes' value; the geometry is not derived)
In polycrystals each grain has its own orientation, so slip directions differ between grains and slip is not uniform across the sample
Slip lines are fine parallel surface steps within grains, seen on a pre-polished surface (e.g. copper). They are not cracks, grain boundaries or polishing scratches
conn: Orientation \(\rightarrow\) \(\tau_R\) \(\rightarrow\) yield: the same applied load gives different \(\tau_R\) in different grains, so the grains best oriented yield first and the others later
\(\tau_{crss}\) is the fixed threshold. Comparing it with \(\tau_R\), which varies with geometry, gives the applied stress at yield
Slip mechanism and observation: dislocation glide on slip systems produces surface steps, seen as slip lines, whose differing directions between grains reflect grain orientation
Single-crystal and polycrystal results: a single crystal shows one dominant slip plane (e.g. zinc at about 45°), while a polycrystal shows many slip systems active across grains
exq: A single crystal is loaded in tension with force \(F\). The slip plane has area \(A_s\) and the force component along the slip direction is \(F_s\). Calculate \(\tau_R\), and state the condition for yield if \(\tau_{crss}\) is given.
Explain the difference between resolved shear stress and critically resolved shear stress. Which one depends on loading orientation, and which is a material property? Justify your answer.
Why is the area of the slip plane \(A_s\) used rather than the cross-sectional area \(A_0\) when calculating \(\tau_R\)? Describe how the shear force is resolved.

A polished copper polycrystal is deformed and shows fine parallel lines that change direction between grains. Explain what the lines are, why their direction varies, and how you would distinguish them from grain boundaries or scratches.
For a zinc single crystal in uniaxial tension, on which plane does slip appear first, and why? If \(\tau_{crss}\) is known, how would you find the applied stress at yield?

notes.t: When yield occurs: resolved vs critically resolved shear stress
pts: Resolved shear stress on a slip plane depends on the chosen plane and the applied loading; it is the shear force divided by the slip plane area.
Critically resolved shear stress is a property of the material, not of the loading geometry.
Yield occurs on a plane once the resolved shear stress reaches the critical value.
In a loaded zinc single crystal (HCP) under uniaxial tension, slip appears on the plane of maximum resolved shear stress, at about 45°.
defs: Resolved shear stress (τR)
The shear stress acting along the slip direction on a chosen slip plane, equal to the shear component of the applied force divided by the slip plane area; depends on plane orientation and loading.
Critically resolved shear stress (τcrss)
The minimum resolved shear stress on a slip system required to initiate slip (yield); a material property independent of loading orientation.
Slip plane normal (ns)
The unit vector perpendicular to the slip plane, used with the slip direction to define the slip system.
eqs: Resolved shear stress on the slip plane
\(\tau_{R}\) = resolved shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = shear force along the slip direction (N); \(A_{s}\) = area of the slip plane (\(m^{2}\))
Yield condition on a slip plane
\(\tau_{R}\) = resolved shear stress (Pa); \(\tau_{crss}\) = critically resolved shear stress (Pa)
tips: Do not confuse τR (depends on loading and orientation) with τcrss (a material property); τcrss is not recalculated per load.
Use the area along the slip plane, As, not the cross-sectional area A0, when computing τR; the shear force must be resolved along the slip direction.
rq: Why does the same applied tensile stress cause yield in one grain orientation but not another?

Because the resolved shear stress τR depends on the slip plane and direction orientation relative to the load; if τR on the most favourably oriented system reaches τcrss, yield occurs, otherwise it does not.
Why is slip observed at 45° to the tensile axis in the single crystal?
Shear stress is maximum on planes at 45° to the load axis, so τR is largest there and reaches τcrss first.
What would happen to yield onset if τcrss were doubled, with the same loading?
Yield would require a load about twice as large, since τR must reach the doubled τcrss before slip starts.

notes.t: Real slip in polycrystalline metals
pts: Slip occurs in many grains, each with slip in a different crystallographic direction, because neighbouring grains have different orientations.
Slip steps appear on the polished surface after plastic deformation, revealing the slip planes as fine parallel lines within each grain.
The micrograph shows copper whose surface was carefully polished before deformation, so surface features are attributable to slip rather than to the original finish.
defs: Slip
Plastic deformation by movement of dislocations along specific crystallographic planes (slip planes) in specific directions (slip directions), producing a step on the surface of the material.
Grain
A single crystal region within a polycrystalline metal, with its own crystallographic orientation, separated from neighbouring grains by grain boundaries.
tips: Slip lines are visible surface steps, not cracks; do not confuse them with grain boundaries or scratches from polishing.
Each grain shows slip in a different direction because orientation varies between grains, so slip is not a single uniform direction across the whole sample.
rq: Why do slip lines appear in different directions in different grains of the same copper sample?
Each grain has a different crystallographic orientation, so the slip planes and directions favoured by the applied stress differ from grain to grain.
Why was the surface polished before deformation in this experiment?
A smooth, well-polished surface means that the lines seen after deformation are slip steps created by plastic deformation, not scratches or existing surface roughness.

units.name: 12.4 Dislocations and the mechanism of slip
units.ov: This material classifies crystal defects by dimensionality (point, line, planar and volume) and focuses on dislocations, both edge and screw. It then explains that metals yield by dislocation glide on slip planes under shear stress, which needs far less stress than rigid slip of whole planes. The link is that defect geometry (line, Burgers vector) determines how plastic deformation happens.
must: Defect dimensionality: point defects are 0D, dislocations 1D, grain and twin boundaries 2D, and voids or other volume defects 3D.
Point defects: vacancy (lattice gap), interstitial (extra atom), substitutional (foreign atom on a lattice site), plus defects in compound semiconductors.
Edge (step) dislocation: an extra half-plane of atoms ends at the dislocation line, and the Burgers vector \(\mathbf{b}\) is perpendicular to the line.

Screw dislocation: the planes form a helical ramp around the line, and \(\mathbf{b}\) is parallel to the line. Classify by the orientation of \(\mathbf{b}\) relative to the line, not by appearance in diagrams.
Slip is dislocation motion, not rigid sliding of whole planes. The dislocation advances one step at a time, breaking and re-forming only one row of bonds per step.

Applied shear stress drives the dislocation across the slip plane. Its passage leaves a single unit (one Burgers vector) step of slip at the surface, and large plastic strain needs many dislocations passing.
Slip plane: the crystallographic plane on which dislocations glide, and it is where the atomic layers are displaced.
Dislocations explain why real yield stress is far below the theoretical strength (\(\tau_{th}\sim G/10\) to \(G/30\)), because bonds break sequentially rather than all at once.
Each grain contains millions of dislocations, so plastic deformation of metals is relatively easy.
Grain boundary: an interface between crystals of different orientation. Twin boundary: the lattice is mirrored across the boundary plane.
conn: Dislocation type (edge or screw) and \(\mathbf{b}\) direction link defect geometry to the direction of slip and the resulting surface step.
Dislocation glide explains the gap between theoretical and measured shear strength, and so connects to yield stress and ductility.
Grain boundaries and other defects (point defects, other dislocations) are 'obstacles' to dislocation motion, which links defect classes to strengthening and to the ease of plastic deformation.
Shear stress on the slip plane (resolved shear stress) connects the applied load, slip systems and the onset of yield.
exq: Sketch an edge dislocation and a screw dislocation. Mark the dislocation line and the Burgers vector, and state their relative orientation in each case.
Explain, with a sequence of diagrams, how an edge dislocation moves under shear stress and produces a unit step of slip at the surface.

Why is the yield stress of a metal much lower than the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal? Estimate the ratio using \(\tau_{th}\approx G/10\) and discuss the role of breaking one bond at a time.
Classify the following by dimensionality and give a definition of each: vacancy, interstitial, screw dislocation, grain boundary, twin boundary, void.
Why is slip not described as rigid sliding of whole atomic planes, and how does the presence of millions of dislocations per grain make metals easy to deform plastically?

notes.t: Defects and dislocations in crystalline materials
pts: Point defects are zero-dimensional disorder, including lattice gaps (vacancies), interstitial extra particles, substitutional defects and defects in compound semiconductors.
Dislocations are one-dimensional disorder and come in two types: step (edge) dislocations and screw dislocations.
Two- and three-dimensional defects include surfaces such as grain and twin boundaries, and volume defects.
A step (edge) dislocation is an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the lattice, with the dislocation line at its end.
A screw dislocation forms a spiral ramp around the dislocation line, so growth steps wind around its core as shown by the spiral pattern.
defs: Point defect
A zero-dimensional imperfection in a crystal lattice at a single site, such as a vacancy (lattice gap), interstitial atom, or substitutional impurity.
Dislocation
A one-dimensional line defect in a crystal lattice across which atomic planes are displaced, allowing plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical strength.
Step (edge) dislocation
A line defect produced by an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal, terminating at the dislocation line.
Screw dislocation
A line defect in which atomic planes form a helical ramp around the dislocation line, with Burgers vector parallel to the line.
Grain boundary
A two-dimensional interface separating crystals (grains) of different orientation in a polycrystalline material.
Twin boundary
A two-dimensional interface across which the crystal lattice is mirrored, so the two sides are symmetric about the boundary plane.
tips: Do not confuse the dimensionality of defects: point defects are 0D, dislocations are 1D, and grain boundaries and twin boundaries are 2D.
Distinguish the two dislocation types by the orientation of the Burgers vector relative to the dislocation line, not just by their appearance in diagrams.
rq: Why do dislocations allow metals to deform plastically at much lower stresses than the theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal?

Because a dislocation moves through the lattice by breaking and reforming only a few bonds at a time, so only a small local shift is needed per step rather than the simultaneous shearing of entire planes.
What is the key geometric difference between an edge dislocation and a screw dislocation?
In an edge dislocation the Burgers vector is perpendicular to the dislocation line (extra half-plane), whereas in a screw dislocation it is parallel to the line (helical ramp).

notes.t: Mechanism of slip: dislocation movement
pts: Metals yield by dislocations moving through the crystal, not by whole atomic planes sliding at once.
A dislocation moves one step at a time, breaking and re-forming only one atomic bond per step, which needs far less energy than breaking every bond across the slip plane.
Shear stress applied to the crystal drives the edge dislocation line across the slip plane, producing a unit step of slip at the surface.
Each grain contains millions of dislocations, so permanent (plastic) deformation of metals is relatively easy.
defs: Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice (here an edge dislocation) whose movement under shear stress allows plastic deformation by slip.
Slip plane
The crystallographic plane along which dislocations glide and atomic layers are displaced relative to one another during plastic deformation.
tips: Do not describe slip as whole atomic planes sliding rigidly; the mechanism is dislocation motion, one bond at a time.
Remember that the step produced by one dislocation passing through is a single unit step of slip, not a large displacement.
rq: Why does moving a dislocation through a grain require less energy than shearing an entire plane of atoms at once?
Only one atomic bond is broken and re-formed at each step, rather than every bond across the whole slip plane being broken simultaneously.
What would happen to a metal's ability to deform permanently if dislocations were absent or locked in place?
Slip would require breaking all bonds on the plane together, so yield stress would be much higher and permanent deformation far harder.

units.name: 12.5 Tensile stages and yield behaviour (gradual, upper/lower yield)
units.ov: This material describes the four stages of a tensile test (elastic, work hardening, necking, failure) and how yielding occurs, either gradually (copper, 0.2% offset) or sharply with upper and lower yield points (low carbon steel). Both behaviours are explained by dislocation motion, solute pinning, work hardening and grain boundary obstruction, and the same mechanisms govern the strength seen on the stress-strain curve.
must: Four stages of the engineering curve: linear elastic, work hardening, necking, failure. TS is the peak at point M and fracture occurs at F.
Tensile strength is the maximum engineering stress (point M), not the fracture stress (point F). Necking begins at TS.
Engineering stress uses the original area, so the post-TS fall is an artefact of that definition. True stress uses instantaneous area and may still rise.
Yielding is plastic deformation by dislocation slip through the lattice. Work hardening is the rise in flow stress as dislocations multiply and obstruct each other.
Gradual yield (e.g. copper) has a smooth elastic-to-plastic transition. Yield strength is the 0.2% offset stress (\(\varepsilon=0.002\)), and the offset must always be stated.
Low carbon steel shows an upper yield point (a peak) followed by a lower yield plateau at near-constant stress. The lower yield stress is normally quoted as the design yield strength.

The upper yield point is the stress needed to unpin dislocations held by solute atoms (carbon). After unpinning, dislocations move easily, so the material is effectively perfectly plastic on the plateau, then work hardens.

The apparent stress drop is due to localised yielding, not true weakening. Yielding then moves to unhardened regions, giving discrete hinges (Lüders-type bands) in mild steel. Gradual yield spreads smoothly, giving a smooth bend.
Grain boundaries block dislocations, which pile up against them. The pile-up size is \(n=\dfrac{\alpha\tau d}{Gb}\), so larger grains give longer pile-ups and lower yield strength.
Check units in the pile-up equation: \(\tau\) (Pa), \(d\) and \(b\) (m, not mixed with mm), and \(d\) is the grain size, not the boundary thickness.
conn: Dislocation pinning by solutes explains the upper/lower yield point, while grain boundary pile-ups explain grain size strengthening. Both are the same idea of obstacles to dislocation motion, and both change the yield stress.

Work hardening links the yield plateau, the rising stress to TS, and hinge formation. Hardened regions stop yielding, so deformation moves elsewhere, and later necking occurs when hardening can no longer offset the loss of area.
Engineering versus true stress connects necking and TS. Explain why engineering stress falls after M while true stress rises, and why TS is not the fracture stress.
Choosing the yield definition depends on curve type: 0.2% offset for gradual yield and lower yield stress for steel with a plateau.
exq: Sketch an engineering stress-strain curve for a ductile metal and label the elastic region, yield, work hardening, TS (point M), necking and fracture (point F). Explain why the engineering stress falls between M and F even though the true stress rises.

Describe how you would determine the yield strength of copper from a stress-strain curve using the 0.2% offset method. Why must the offset be quoted, and why is this method not needed for low carbon steel?
Using dislocation theory, explain the upper and lower yield points in low carbon steel. Why does the stress appear to drop, and what causes the stress to rise again after the plateau?
Explain why a bent mild steel bar shows discrete hinges whereas a bent copper wire bends smoothly. Refer to work hardening and where yielding initiates.
Using \(n=\alpha\tau d/(Gb)\), calculate how the number of dislocations in a pile-up changes if the grain size is halved at constant \(\tau\). Explain the consequence for yield strength.

notes.t: Stages of tensile deformation: elastic, work hardening, necking, failure
pts: Under tensile loading, a metal passes through four regions: linear elastic, work hardening, necking and failure.
In the linear elastic region stress is proportional to strain and the specimen returns to its original length when unloaded.
Beyond yield the metal work hardens, so stress keeps rising with strain until it reaches the tensile strength TS at point M.
After TS, deformation localises into a narrowing neck, so the engineering stress falls even though the true stress may still rise.
The specimen finally fractures at point F, the end of the curve.
defs: Tensile strength (TS)
The maximum engineering stress a material can sustain in tension, corresponding to the peak of the stress–strain curve, after which necking begins.
Work hardening
Increase in flow stress with plastic strain as dislocations multiply and interact, making further deformation harder.
Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a ductile specimen under tension, starting at the tensile strength.
tips: Do not confuse tensile strength (maximum on the curve, point M) with fracture stress (point F); the curve drops after necking in engineering stress terms.
Engineering stress uses original area, so the post-necking decrease is an artefact of that definition; true stress uses instantaneous area.
rq: Why does the engineering stress fall after point M even though the metal is still being strengthened by work hardening?

Because the cross-sectional area drops rapidly within the neck; the load-bearing area shrinks faster than the work-hardening increase in flow stress, so the engineering (load/original area) stress decreases.
What would happen to the stress–strain curve if the specimen were unloaded in the work hardening region and reloaded?
It would unload elastically along a line parallel to the elastic slope and reload along that line, so the yield point is effectively raised to the previous maximum stress.

notes.t: Yield behaviour in metals
pts: Yielding requires slip, i.e. plastic deformation occurs by movement of dislocations through the crystal lattice.
Yield can be gradual, as in copper, where the stress-strain curve bends smoothly from elastic to plastic behaviour; yield strength is found using the 0.002 (0.2%) offset method.
Yield can be very sudden, as in low carbon steel, which shows an upper yield point followed by a lower yield point and a plateau of nearly constant stress.
defs: Yield strength (\(\sigma_y\))
The stress at which a material begins to deform plastically; for materials without a sharp yield point it is taken as the stress at 0.2% (0.002) offset strain.
Upper yield point
The peak stress reached at the onset of yielding in low carbon steel, after which the stress drops sharply.
Lower yield point
The approximately constant stress plateau that follows the upper yield point in low carbon steel, during which deformation proceeds at nearly constant load.
tips: Do not confuse the upper yield point (a peak) with the lower yield point (the plateau); the yield stress is normally quoted as the lower yield stress for steel.
For materials with gradual yielding, always state the offset (0.2%) when giving yield strength, otherwise the value is undefined.
rq: Why does copper show a smooth, gradual yield while low carbon steel shows a sharp upper and lower yield point?

Copper has no interstitial atoms pinning dislocations, so yielding is gradual as dislocations move and multiply. In low carbon steel, carbon/nitrogen interstitials lock dislocations (Cottrell atmospheres); a higher stress is needed to break them free (upper yield), then dislocations move easily at lower stress (lower yield plateau).
Why is a 0.2% offset used to define yield strength for copper instead of the elastic limit?

The elastic limit is hard to measure precisely because the transition from elastic to plastic is gradual; the 0.002 offset gives a reproducible, well-defined value of stress at which a small permanent strain has occurred.

notes.t: Yield behaviour: gradual yield
pts: With gradual yield, once yielding starts at one point, the stress does not visibly drop while strain continues.
Yielding is work hardened at the first point, so yield then spreads to neighbouring regions almost seamlessly.
Because deformation spreads gradually along the length, the resulting bend is smooth rather than a sharp kink, as the copper wire example shows.
tips: Gradual yield means there is no sharp upper and lower yield point, so the 0.2% proof stress is usually used to define yield strength.
rq: Why does a gradually yielding material like copper bend smoothly instead of forming a sharp kink?
Yielding at one point work hardens that region, so further deformation moves to adjacent material, spreading plastic strain over a wider length and giving a smooth bend.

notes.t: Upper and Lower Yield Points in Steels
pts: Upper yield point marks the onset of plastic deformation, the stress needed to unpin dislocations held by solute atoms such as carbon.
After the upper yield point, engineering stress apparently drops, then the material deforms at a near-constant stress called the lower yield point.
During the lower yield plateau, dislocations are unpinned and easy to move, so the material is effectively perfectly plastic.
Beyond the plateau, stress rises again with strain because dislocation motion is increasingly inhibited by work hardening.
The curve shows three regions: elastic (linear), perfectly plastic (lower yield plateau), and work hardening (rising stress).
defs: Upper yield point
The peak stress at which plastic deformation begins in low-carbon steels, required to break dislocations free from solute atom pinning.
Lower yield point
The near-constant stress at which steel continues to deform plastically after the upper yield point, as unpinned dislocations move easily.
Work (strain) hardening
Increase in flow stress with plastic strain as dislocation motion becomes increasingly obstructed.
tips: Do not confuse the upper yield point (peak, needed to start plastic flow) with the lower yield point (plateau stress used as the design yield strength value).
Upper and lower yield points are characteristic of low-carbon steels; materials without solute pinning show a smooth transition to plastic flow.
rq: Why does the stress drop from the upper yield point to the lower yield point?
Once dislocations are unpinned from solute atoms (e.g. carbon), they move easily, so less stress is needed to keep deforming the material.
Why does the lower yield plateau appear to be 'perfectly plastic'?
Stress stays nearly constant while strain increases, because unpinned dislocations move freely without further hardening.

notes.t: Yield behaviour (upper and lower yield, hinge formation)
pts: Once a material has yielded at one point, further deformation at that same point becomes easier, so the stress-strain curve shows an apparent drop in stress.
Continued straining eventually causes work hardening, making the material stronger and harder at the yielded region.
Deformation then initiates at a new location that has not yet work hardened, so yielding spreads along the member.
The repeated localised yielding appears as a series of discrete 'hinges' along the bar.
Mild steel is the example shown, displaying this behaviour clearly in a bent bar.
tips: Do not confuse the apparent stress drop in upper/lower yield behaviour with the material actually becoming weaker; the drop is due to localised yielding and the material later work hardens.
Hinges form because yielding moves to unhardened regions; a uniform bend would not produce a series of discrete hinges.
rq: Why does the stress drop after the upper yield point in mild steel, even though the material is still being strained?
Yielding at one point makes further deformation there easier, so the load needed to keep straining falls, giving an apparent decrease in stress on the stress-strain curve.
Why does deformation jump to a new location rather than continuing at the same point?
The already-yielded region has work hardened and is now stronger, so the next plastic deformation occurs at an unhardened part of the bar, forming another hinge.

notes.t: Yield and Dislocations
pts: During yielding, dislocations move through the crystal lattice of the material.
Grain boundaries act as barriers that stop dislocation movement, so dislocations pile up against them.
The number of dislocations that can pile up at a grain boundary depends on shear stress, grain size, and the material's energy per dislocation and Burgers vector.
defs: Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement allows plastic deformation (yielding) to occur at stresses far below the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal.
Grain boundary
The interface between two grains (crystals) of differing orientation in a polycrystalline material; it acts as an obstacle to dislocation motion.
Characteristic grain size (d)
The average diameter of grains in a polycrystalline microstructure, used as the length scale in dislocation pile-up models.
Burgers vector (b)
The vector describing the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by a dislocation.
eqs: Number of dislocations in a pile-up at a grain boundary

\(n\) = number of dislocations in the pile (dimensionless); \(\alpha\) = constant (dimensionless); \(\tau\) = shear stress (Pa); \(d\) = grain size (m); \(G\) = energy per dislocation / shear modulus term (J m⁻² or Pa, per the lecture's definition); \(b\) = Burgers vector magnitude (m)
tips: Check units: \(\tau\) (Pa) × \(d\) (m) / (\(G\) × \(b\)) must give a dimensionless \(n\); mixing mm and m for \(d\) and \(b\) gives wrong answers.
Remember \(d\) is the grain size, not the grain boundary thickness; larger grains give longer pile-ups and lower yield strength.
rq: Why does a smaller grain size increase the yield strength of a material?

Smaller grains mean more grain boundaries per unit volume, and the pile-up length \(n\) is proportional to \(d\); fewer dislocations can pile up, so a higher stress is needed to push dislocations across boundaries and start yielding.
What would happen to the number of dislocations in a pile if the shear stress were doubled, all else equal?
\(n\) is directly proportional to \(\tau\), so the pile-up would contain twice as many dislocations, increasing local stress at the grain boundary and promoting slip into neighbouring grains.

units.name: 12.6 Strengthening: strain hardening and Hall-Petch
units.ov: Plastic deformation in metals occurs by dislocation motion, so strengthening works by hindering that motion. Strain hardening raises dislocation density, so dislocation strain fields interact and the yield stress rises. Grain refinement adds grain-boundary barriers, and the Hall-Petch relation links yield stress quantitatively to grain size.
must: Plastic deformation in metals is by dislocation motion, so strengthening means making dislocation motion harder
Strain hardening: plastic deformation raises dislocation density, so yield stress \( \sigma_y \) and hardness increase
Mechanism of strain hardening: dislocation strain fields interact, repel and restrict one another, so a higher stress is needed to keep deforming
On unloading and reloading after plastic strain, the new yield point is raised; more plastic strain gives a larger rise
Strain hardening only occurs in the plastic regime. Elastic loading does not increase dislocation density, and the elastic modulus is unchanged by plastic deformation
Hall-Petch: \( \sigma_y = \sigma_i + \frac{k}{\sqrt{D}} \), where \( \sigma_i \) is the friction stress, \( k \) is a grain-boundary constant and \( D \) is the mean grain diameter
Smaller grains give more grain-boundary area and so more barriers to dislocation glide, giving higher yield strength
D enters as \( 1/\sqrt{D} \), not \( 1/D \). Use D in metres with k in Pa·\( m^{1/2} \) to get \( \sigma_y \) in Pa
Hall-Petch is empirical, not derived from first principles. \( \sigma_i \) and k are material-dependent constants
Definitions to quote: dislocation = line defect whose movement allows plastic deformation; strain hardening = strength increase from plastic deformation due to higher dislocation density
conn: Dislocation motion is the common basis: strain hardening adds dislocations that obstruct each other, while Hall-Petch adds grain boundaries that obstruct glide
Strain hardening and the stress-strain curve: the raised yield point on reloading links plastic strain, yield stress and unchanged elastic modulus
Hall-Petch can be used with two data points to find \( \sigma_i \) and k, then predict yield stress at a new grain size, with unit care (µm to m)
Both mechanisms raise strength, so questions may ask for the effect on yield stress, hardness and microstructure when they are combined
exq: Explain, in terms of dislocations, why a metal that has been cold worked has a higher yield stress on reloading. Why is the elastic modulus unchanged?
A steel has \( \sigma_y = 200 \) MPa at \( D = 100\ \mu m \) and 300 MPa at \( D = 25\ \mu m \). Use Hall-Petch to find \( \sigma_i \) and k, then predict \( \sigma_y \) for \( D = 10\ \mu m \).
Using \( \sigma_y = \sigma_i + k/\sqrt{D} \), by what factor must D be reduced to double the Hall-Petch contribution \( k/\sqrt{D} \)? Comment on why a linear \( 1/D \) dependence would be wrong.
Define strain hardening and dislocation. Describe how increasing dislocation density hinders further plastic deformation.
Compare strain hardening and grain-size strengthening: how does each restrict dislocation motion, and what does the Hall-Petch equation say about grain boundaries?

notes.t: Mechanisms of Strengthening in Metals: Strain Hardening
pts: Plastic deformation in metals occurs through the movement of dislocations, so strengthening mechanisms work by restricting or hindering this motion.
Most strengthening mechanisms rely on making dislocation motion more difficult.
Strain hardening: the material becomes stronger as plastic strain increases, because plastic deformation raises dislocation density.
Interacting dislocation strain fields repel and restrict one another, so the stress required to continue deforming increases.
Greater plastic deformation gives a larger increase in yield stress \( \sigma_y \); on unloading and reloading, the new yield point is raised.
defs: Strain hardening
An increase in a metal's strength and hardness resulting from plastic deformation, caused by a rise in dislocation density and mutual interference of dislocation strain fields.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement allows plastic deformation to occur.
tips: Strain hardening strengthens a metal only in the plastic regime; elastic loading does not increase dislocation density.
Do not confuse strain hardening with work softening or with the elastic modulus, which is not changed by plastic deformation.
rq: Why does plastic deformation make a metal harder to deform further?
Plastic deformation increases dislocation density; the dislocations' strain fields repel and restrict each other, so more stress is needed to move them.
What would happen to the yield stress if a strain-hardened metal is unloaded and then reloaded?
The new yield stress is higher (\( \sigma_{y1} \) rather than \( \sigma_{y0} \)), so the metal behaves elastically up to the previously reached stress level.

notes.t: Hall-Petch Law
pts: Yield strength of many metals rises as grain size falls, because grain boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Smaller grains give a greater total grain boundary area, so more barriers to dislocation glide.
The relationship between yield strength and grain size is empirical rather than derived from first principles.
eqs: Hall-Petch relation: yield stress as a function of average grain diameter

\(\sigma_y\) = yield stress (Pa); \(\sigma_i\) = friction stress opposing dislocation motion, material-dependent (Pa); \(k\) = material constant related to grain boundaries (Pa·\(m^{1/2}\)); \(D\) = average grain diameter (m)
tips: Grain diameter D enters as \(1/\sqrt{D}\), not as \(1/D\); do not substitute a linear dependence.
Ensure D is in metres (SI) when using k in Pa·\(m^{1/2}\), otherwise the units of σ_y will be wrong.
rq: Why does reducing grain size increase yield strength, rather than making the metal weaker?
Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion, so dislocations pile up and more stress is needed to make slip propagate across grains.
What would happen to the yield stress predicted by the law if the average grain diameter D became very large?
The \(k/\sqrt{D}\) term tends to zero, so \(\sigma_y\) approaches \(\sigma_i\), the intrinsic lattice friction stress.

units.name: 12.7 Necking, true vs engineering stress and strain
units.ov: This module covers the regions of a tensile stress-strain curve (elastic, yield, strain hardening, necking, fracture) and the difference between engineering and true measures of stress and strain. Engineering values use original dimensions and are convenient for design, while true values use instantaneous dimensions and show what the material actually experiences, especially after necking. The two sets of definitions explain why the engineering curve falls after the ultimate stress while the true curve keeps rising.
must: Engineering stress \( \sigma_{eng}=F/A_0 \) uses the original area; true stress \( \sigma_{true}=F/A_i \) uses the instantaneous area.

Engineering strain \( \varepsilon_{eng}=\Delta l/l_0 \); true strain \( \varepsilon_{true}=\ln(l_i/l_0) \). Note the notes' line '\( \varepsilon_{eng}=l_i/l_0 \)' is a slip: the correct form is \( (l_i-l_0)/l_0 \), so \( l_i/l_0 = 1+\varepsilon_{eng} \).
Curve sequence: linear elastic (O to proportional limit), yield, perfectly plastic flow, strain hardening (C to D), ultimate stress (D), necking, fracture (E).

After the ultimate stress the engineering stress falls because \( A_0 \) is used, while the true stress keeps rising because the actual area shrinks. The fall is a result of the definition, not material weakening.
Necking is localised area reduction at the weakest point (not necessarily the centre of the gauge length); deformation concentrates there and fracture occurs within the neck.
Ultimate stress is the maximum engineering stress and marks the onset of necking.
Strain hardening arises from dislocation build-up and entanglement, which raises the stress needed for further plastic deformation.
Proportional limit (Hooke's law ends) and yield stress (plastic deformation begins) are different definitions, though close on the curve.
Use consistent units (m² with Pa, or mm² with MPa); strains are dimensionless.
True quantities matter at large strains; at small strains the engineering and true values are nearly equal.
conn: Necking links to the stress definitions: the load falls, so \( F/A_0 \) falls, but \( A_i \) falls faster, so \( F/A_i \) rises.
Strain hardening links to necking: necking begins at the ultimate stress, where the hardening effect is overtaken by the loss of area.
Engineering and true strain agree at small strain, since \( \ln(1+\varepsilon)\approx\varepsilon \), but diverge at large strain; this is why the choice of definition matters in the plastic region.
Proportional limit, Hooke's law and Young's modulus link the elastic region to the yield and plastic behaviour that follows.
exq: A bar of \( A_0=100\ \text{mm}^2 \) carries a force of 30 kN after necking, when the neck area is 60 mm². Calculate the engineering and true stresses and explain why they differ.
A specimen of original length 50 mm is stretched to 60 mm. Calculate the engineering strain and the true strain, and comment on the difference.

Sketch an engineering and a true stress-strain curve on the same axes. Label the proportional limit, yield, strain hardening, ultimate stress, necking and fracture, and explain why the curves diverge after the ultimate stress.
Explain why necking begins at the ultimate stress and why it may occur away from the centre of the gauge length.
Distinguish between the proportional limit and the yield stress, and describe the microstructural cause of work hardening.

notes.t: Tensile loading regions
pts: Perfectly plastic region: yielding occurs throughout the sample; strain increases while stress stays at the yield stress.
Strain (work) hardening: crystal structure changes and dislocations build up and entangle, so the material's strength increases with strain.
Necking: after the ultimate stress the cross-sectional area reduces locally, so the engineering stress falls until fracture.
The curve shows a linear elastic region from O to the proportional limit, followed by yield, plastic flow, strain hardening, necking and fracture.
defs: Yield stress
The stress at which a material begins to deform plastically, i.e. permanent deformation begins when the load is removed.
Ultimate stress
The maximum engineering stress reached on the stress-strain curve, after which necking begins.
Proportional limit
The highest stress up to which stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke's law holds).
Work hardening
Increase in a metal's strength and hardness caused by plastic deformation, due to dislocation build-up and entanglement.
Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a tensile specimen after the ultimate stress, leading to fracture.
tips: Engineering stress is calculated using the original area; after necking the true stress is higher than the plotted curve suggests.
Do not confuse the proportional limit with the yield stress; they are close on this curve but are different definitions.
rq: Why does the stress stay constant in the perfectly plastic region even though strain keeps increasing?
Dislocations move freely with yielding spread through the sample, so plastic flow occurs at a constant (yield) stress.
Why does the engineering stress fall after the ultimate stress even though the material is still being strengthened by work hardening?
Reduction of cross-sectional area during necking lowers the load-bearing area, which outweighs the hardening effect when calculating stress from the original area.

notes.t: Necking in tensile testing
pts: Necking can initiate at the weakest point of the gauge section, even if that weakness is very small.
Once necking starts, the cross-sectional area continues to reduce locally, so deformation concentrates in the neck.
As necking proceeds the load falls: engineering stress (based on original area) decreases, while true stress (based on actual area) increases.
Fracture ultimately occurs within the region of necking.
defs: Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a ductile specimen under tension, occurring at its weakest point and leading to concentrated deformation before fracture.
tips: Do not confuse engineering and true stress: engineering stress uses the original area (decreases after necking), true stress uses the instantaneous area (increases).
Necking location is not necessarily the centre of the gauge section; it forms at the weakest point, which may be anywhere within it.
rq: Why does true stress keep increasing during necking even though the applied load is falling?
Because true stress is load divided by the actual, rapidly shrinking cross-sectional area, and the area reduces faster than the load falls, so the ratio rises.
Why does engineering stress fall during necking even though the material is strengthening locally?
Engineering stress uses the original area, which is constant, so only the falling load affects it; the decrease in load drives engineering stress down.

notes.t: True vs Engineering stress
pts: Engineering stress is the easiest to calculate, using the original cross-sectional area.
Engineering stress is most useful for engineers in design calculations.
True stress describes what happens to individual areas of material as it deforms, using the instantaneous area.
defs: Engineering stress
Force divided by the original (initial) cross-sectional area of a specimen; easy to calculate and widely used in design.
True stress
Force divided by the instantaneous cross-sectional area of the specimen at that moment of loading, accounting for changes in area during deformation.
eqs: \( \sigma_{eng} \) = engineering stress (Pa); \( F \) = force (N); \( A_0 \) = initial cross-sectional area (m²)
\( \sigma_{true} \) = true stress (Pa); \( F \) = force (N); \( A_i \) = instantaneous cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Do not mix the two: engineering stress always divides by the initial area \( A_0 \), true stress by the instantaneous area \( A_i \).
Check that the area is in m² (or mm² consistently) before dividing, so the stress comes out in Pa or MPa.
rq: Why would true stress be higher than engineering stress during tensile loading?
As the specimen necks and elongates, the instantaneous area \( A_i \) becomes smaller than \( A_0 \), so dividing the same force by a smaller area gives a larger stress.
Why might an engineer still prefer engineering stress even though true stress is more physically accurate?
Engineering stress is simpler to calculate because it only needs the original dimensions, which are known before loading, and it suits design within small deformations.

notes.t: True vs Engineering stress in a stress-strain curve
pts: Engineering stress uses the original cross-sectional area, so it is the solid curve that falls after the ultimate stress due to necking.
True stress uses the instantaneous area, so the dotted curve keeps rising past the ultimate stress and continues to E'.
The linear region O–A obeys Hooke's law; stress is proportional to strain up to the proportional limit.
Perfect plasticity (yielding) occurs between A/B and C, where stress stays roughly constant while strain increases.
Necking begins after the ultimate stress at D, localising deformation until fracture at E.
defs: Ultimate stress
The maximum engineering stress reached on the stress-strain curve, marking the onset of necking.
Yield stress
The stress at which a material begins to deform plastically, marked by the transition from elastic behaviour.
Proportional limit
The highest stress up to which stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke's law holds).
Strain hardening
Increase in stress required for further plastic deformation after yielding, between C and D.
tips: Do not compare engineering and true stress values beyond the ultimate stress; the engineering curve falls only because of the definition, not because the material weakens.
Remember that true stress is calculated with the instantaneous area, which must be used when strains are large.
rq: Why does the engineering stress curve fall after point D while the true stress curve keeps rising?
Engineering stress divides by the original area, which ignores the reduction in area from necking; true stress divides by the smaller instantaneous area, so it keeps increasing until fracture.
What would happen to the engineering stress curve if the specimen did not neck?
The engineering and true stress curves would nearly coincide, since the cross-sectional area would change little.

notes.t: True vs Engineering strain
pts: Engineering strain is the easiest strain to calculate, so it is the most useful for engineers.
Engineering strain is the change in length divided by the original length, \( l_0 \).
True strain compares the change in length with the length just a moment before, not the original length.
True strain works out as the natural logarithm of the ratio \( l_i / l_0 \).
defs: Engineering strain
Change in length divided by the original length of the specimen; a dimensionless measure of deformation based on the starting dimension.
True strain
Change in length divided by the instantaneous length at each moment, equal to the natural log of the ratio of instantaneous to original length.
eqs: \( \varepsilon_{eng} \) = engineering strain (dimensionless); \( \Delta l \) = change in length (m); \( l_0 \) = original length (m); \( l_i \) = instantaneous length (m)

\( \varepsilon_{true} \) = true strain (dimensionless); \( \Delta l \) = change in length (m); \( l \) = instantaneous length (m); \( l_i \) = instantaneous length (m); \( l_0 \) = original length (m)
tips: Do not mix up the two: true strain is \( \ln(l_i/l_0) \), not \( (l_i - l_0)/l_0 \); using the wrong formula gives different values at large strains.
Strains are dimensionless, so do not attach units such as mm or m to the final strain value.
rq: Why would a true strain of 0.5 and an engineering strain of 0.5 not describe the same deformation?

They are defined against different reference lengths: engineering strain uses the original length \( l_0 \), while true strain uses the instantaneous length, so they diverge as deformation grows large.
Why is true strain the natural log of \( l_i/l_0 \) rather than a simple ratio?
Summing incremental strains \( dl/l \) over the deformation integrates to \( \ln(l_i/l_0) \), so true strain is the cumulative sum of small changes relative to the current length.

units.name: 12.8 Ductility and temperature effects; further reading
units.ov: This material defines ductility as the plastic deformation a material sustains before fracture, quantified by percent elongation (%EL) and percent reduction in area (%RA). It then shows that ductility depends strongly on temperature: for iron, cooling raises yield and tensile strength but cuts strain to fracture, leading to brittle failure with little warning. Together these ideas show that strength and ductility trade off, and that a ductility value is only meaningful at a stated test temperature.
must: Ductility = plastic deformation sustained before fracture, measured by %EL or %RA
\(\%EL = \frac{l_f - l_0}{l_0}\times 100\), where \(l_f\) is the gauge length at fracture and \(l_0\) the original gauge length
\(\%RA = \frac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times 100\), where \(A_0\) is the original area and \(A_f\) the area at fracture
Both measures are relative to the ORIGINAL dimension (\(l_0\) or \(A_0\)), never the final one; this is a common error
Lowering temperature raises yield and tensile strength of iron but reduces ductility
Iron at -200°C: very stiff and brittle, fractures at strain below ~0.03 with a very steep curve
Iron at -100°C: intermediate; peak stress ~440 MPa, fracture strain ~0.4
Iron at 25°C: lowest strength (initial yield ~150 MPa, peak ~300 MPa) but greatest ductility (fracture strain ~0.45)
Higher strength at low temperature does not mean a better material: cold iron fails with little warning, so always check strain at fracture
Always state the test temperature when quoting ductility, and read the correct stress axis (left in MPa, right likely ksi)
conn: Stress-strain curve and ductility: fracture strain read from the curve gives ductility, and the plastic region's extent distinguishes brittle from ductile behaviour

Temperature and the strength-ductility trade-off: the same material has higher yield/UTS but lower fracture strain when cold, which matters in material selection and design for low-temperature service
%EL and %RA from tensile test data: the lab results (\(l_0\), \(l_f\), \(A_0\), \(A_f\)) feed both formulas, and the final length must be measured on the fractured specimen
Brittle versus ductile failure and safety: low ductility means little warning before fracture, linking material properties to failure mode and design margins
exq: A tensile specimen has \(l_0 = 50\) mm and \(A_0 = 80\) mm². After fracture \(l_f = 64\) mm and \(A_f = 52\) mm². Calculate %EL and %RA and comment on which indicates ductility more reliably.
Describe, with sketches of stress-strain curves, how the behaviour of iron changes at 25°C, -100°C and -200°C. Quote approximate yield/peak stresses and fracture strains.
A student calculates %EL as \((l_f - l_0)/l_f\times100\). Explain the error and find the percentage error in the result if \(l_0=40\) mm and \(l_f=50\) mm.
A steel component is to operate at -100°C instead of 25°C. Discuss using the iron data whether higher strength makes it a better choice, with reference to ductility and failure warning.
Why must the test temperature be stated when reporting ductility? Define ductility and explain how it is measured in a mechanical testing lab.

notes.t: Ductility
pts: Ductility is a measure of the deformation a material undergoes before failure.
Ductility can be quantified either by percentage elongation (change in length) or percentage reduction in area of the failed specimen.
Ductility is highly temperature dependent; brittle materials show little plastic strain before fracture, whereas ductile materials show extensive plastic deformation.
defs: Ductility
The extent of plastic deformation a material sustains before fracture, measured as percent elongation or percent reduction in area.
eqs: \(l_f\) = gauge length at fracture (m); \(l_0\) = original gauge length (m); %EL is dimensionless (%)
\(A_0\) = original cross-sectional area (m²); \(A_f\) = cross-sectional area at fracture (m²); %RA is dimensionless (%)
tips: Both %EL and %RA are percentages of the original value (\(l_0\) or \(A_0\)), not of the final value; using the final dimension in the denominator is a common error.
Ductility is a material property that depends on temperature; always state the test temperature when comparing ductility values.
rq: Why does the brittle curve in the stress-strain diagram end at a much smaller strain than the ductile curve, even if its peak stress is similar?

A brittle material fractures soon after yielding with little plastic deformation, so its failure strain (point C) is small; a ductile material undergoes extensive plastic deformation (to C') before fracture, giving a large %EL and %RA.
Why might two specimens of the same metal give different %EL values if tested at different temperatures?

Temperature changes atomic mobility and dislocation movement; at higher temperatures more slip occurs and the material is more ductile, while at low temperatures it can become brittle, so ductility is temperature dependent.

notes.t: Effect of temperature on the stress-strain behaviour of iron
pts: Lowering the temperature of iron increases its yield and tensile strength, but reduces its ductility.
At −200°C iron is very stiff and brittle: it fractures at very small strain (under about 0.03) with a very steep curve.
At −100°C iron has intermediate strength (peak stress around 440 MPa) and fractures at strain of roughly 0.4.
At 25°C iron yields at lower stress (about 150 MPa initially) and reaches a lower peak (about 300 MPa) but shows the greatest strain before fracture (about 0.45).
Ductility (strain to fracture) falls as temperature decreases, so cold iron fails with little warning.
tips: Read the stress axis carefully: the left axis is in MPa (0–800) while the right axis is a different scale (0–120, likely ksi), so do not mix them up.
Higher strength at low temperature does not mean a better material; always check strain at fracture, since ductility decreases.
rq: Why does iron become brittle at −200°C even though it is stronger there?

At low temperature thermal energy is insufficient to help dislocations move, so plastic deformation is suppressed and the metal fractures before much strain accumulates, reducing ductility despite higher strength.
Which temperature would you choose for a component that must absorb large deformation before failing, and why?
25°C (room temperature), because it shows the largest strain to fracture (about 0.45), i.e. the greatest ductility and energy absorption.

units.name: 13.1 Stresses on inclined planes
units.ov: This material shows how to find the normal and shear stresses on an oblique plane cut through a bar under axial tension. The method resolves the axial force F into components normal and tangential to the plane and divides by the inclined area A sec θ. The results explain why ductile materials fail by slip on planes at about 45° to the load axis.
must: Normal stress on an inclined plane: \( \sigma_n = \frac{F}{A}\cos^2\theta = \sigma_x\cos^2\theta \), maximum at θ = 0 and zero at θ = 90°
Shear stress on an inclined plane: \( |\tau_s| = \frac{F}{A}\sin\theta\cos\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_x\sin2\theta \), zero at 0° and 90°
Maximum shear stress is \( \tau_{max}=\sigma_x/2 \), acting at θ = 45° and 135° to the plane normal, where \( \sigma_n = \sigma_x/2 \) too
Inclined area is \( A' = A\sec\theta = A/\cos\theta \). Stresses are plane force divided by A', not by A
Force resolution from equilibrium: \( F_n = F\cos\theta \) and \( F_s = -F\sin\theta \) (minus sign is direction only)

Always define θ: here it is the angle between the plane normal and the load axis (the cut is at θ to the cross-section). Check this before choosing sin or cos, and set the calculator to degrees or radians
Draw a free body diagram and rotate the axes so that one axis is normal and the other tangential to the plane, then apply \( \sum \mathbf{F}=0 \)
If shear strength is below half the tensile strength, failure occurs by shear on 45° planes, as in ductile steel slip lines. This is not universal for all materials
The maximum normal stress plane (θ = 0, perpendicular to the load) is different from the maximum shear plane (45°)
conn: Stress transformation links to yield criteria: Tresca uses \( \tau_{max}=\sigma_x/2 \), so yield in a tensile test occurs when \( \sigma_y/2 \) equals the shear yield strength
Combining the \( \cos^2\theta \) and \( \sin2\theta \) results leads to Mohr's circle, where the two stresses on a plane lie on a circle of radius \( \sigma_x/2 \)
The same method links tensile test observations (45° slip lines, cup-and-cone fracture) to the shear strength versus tensile strength comparison
Axial stress \( \sigma=F/A \) from earlier lectures feeds directly in as \( \sigma_x \), so stress and strain calculations feed into inclined-plane checks
exq: A 20 mm diameter bar carries a tensile load of 50 kN. Calculate the normal and shear stress on a plane whose normal is at 30° to the axis, and state the inclined area.
Derive \( \sigma_n=\sigma_x\cos^2\theta \) and \( \tau=-\tfrac12\sigma_x\sin2\theta \) from a free body diagram of an inclined section, stating how θ is defined and why the area is A sec θ.
A steel bar has tensile yield strength 300 MPa and shear strength 140 MPa. Find the plane where shear is maximum, the stress values there, and whether shear failure on 45° planes is expected.
At what angle is the shear stress equal to the normal stress on an inclined plane under uniaxial tension, and what are their magnitudes in terms of \( \sigma_x \)?
Explain why a ductile tensile specimen shows slip lines at about 45° to the axis, and the condition under which this occurs.

notes.t: Stress transformations
pts: Earlier lectures covered stresses on planes perpendicular and parallel to the applied load only.
Observing stress on an inclined section of the same bulk material is a natural next question.
Equilibrium of the cut-off part requires a system of forces acting on the inclined plane, so the stress there is generally more complex than a simple normal stress.
Stress on an inclined plane therefore generally has both normal and shear components, which must be found by transforming the stresses from the original planes.
tips: Do not assume an inclined plane carries only normal stress; shear stress generally also acts on it.
Remember that stress transformation applies to the same material point, so the stresses on the inclined section are related to, not independent of, the applied load.
rq: Why must there be forces on an inclined internal plane even when the bar is simply loaded in tension?

Any imaginary cut through a body in equilibrium exposes internal forces; for the cut-off portion to remain in equilibrium, forces must act on the inclined plane, and these resolve into normal and shear components.
What if the stress is only a normal stress on the perpendicular plane: would the inclined plane carry only normal stress?
No. Resolving the load over an inclined plane generally produces both a normal stress and a shear stress, so the stress state is more complex than on the principal planes.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes under axial tensile load
pts: An axial tensile force F is applied to a bar; the normal cross-sectional area is \(A_{\text{cs}}\), so the normal stress on that plane is σ = F/\(A_{\text{cs}}\).
An arbitrary cut at angle θ to the normal creates the inclined plane AB; the area of this plane is larger than \(A_{\text{cs}}\).
Resolving the force F on the inclined plane gives both a normal component and a shear component, which depend on θ.
defs: Inclined (oblique) plane
A cross-section of a loaded body cut at an arbitrary angle θ to the plane normal to the load; the stresses on it are found by resolving the applied force onto that plane.
eqs: Normal stress on the cross-section normal to the load
