F = applied axial force (N); \(A_{cs}\) = cross-sectional area normal to the load (\(m^{2}\)); \(\sigma_{0}\) = normal stress (Pa)
tips: Do not use \(A_{\text{cs}}\) as the area of the inclined plane; the inclined area is \(A_{\text{cs}}\) divided by \( \cos\theta \).
Keep θ measured from the normal to the load direction (y-axis), not from the bar's axis, when resolving forces.
rq: Why is the area of the inclined plane AB larger than \(A_{\text{cs}}\), and what does this imply for the stress on that plane?
\(A_{inc}\) = \(A_{cs}\)/\cos\theta > \(A_{cs}\), so for the same force F the average stress on the inclined plane is smaller than \(\sigma_{0}\) = F/\(A_{cs}\).
Why does a tensile bar fail along a plane at an angle rather than only across its cross-section?
Resolving F on an inclined plane creates shear stress as well as normal stress; shear is maximum at θ = 45°, so ductile materials may yield along inclined planes.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes: equilibrium and rotated reference frame
pts: For a body in equilibrium, the vector sum of all forces must be zero, which allows the normal and tangential forces on an inclined plane to be found by resolving the applied force.
Redrawing the system as a free body diagram makes it easier to resolve the applied force F into components along the inclined plane.
The reference frame is rotated through the plane angle θ so that one axis lies normal to the AB plane and the other lies tangential to it.
The normal force \(F_{n}\) and tangential (shear) force \(F_{s}\) on plane AB are the components of F in the rotated frame, and dividing them by the plane area gives the normal and shear stresses.
defs: Normal force (\(F_{n}\))
The component of the applied force acting perpendicular to the inclined plane, producing normal stress on that plane.
Tangential (shear) force (\(F_{s}\))
The component of the applied force acting parallel to the inclined plane, producing shear stress on that plane.
eqs: Equilibrium condition for forces on the body
tips: Be careful that the angle θ is measured from the vertical in the original diagram but from the x-axis in the rotated frame; check which reference angle you are using before resolving F.
rq: Why is it useful to rotate the reference frame through θ rather than keep the original x–y axes when analysing plane AB?

Rotating the frame aligns one axis normal to AB and one tangential to it, so \(F_{n}\) and \(F_{s}\) are direct components of F and no further trigonometric resolution of stresses on the plane is needed.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes: normal force equilibrium
pts: A force F acting horizontally resolves into components along the inclined plane normal (\(F_{n}\)) and the plane (shear) direction; the normal component is F cos θ.
Equilibrium of forces along the normal to the inclined AB plane gives the normal force as F cos θ.
The shear component along the plane, \(F_{s}\), balances the F sin θ component, so the normal force is found by projecting F onto the plane normal.
defs: Inclined plane normal force
The component of an applied force acting perpendicular to an inclined plane, found by resolving the force along the plane normal at angle θ to the reference axis.
eqs: Normal force on inclined plane from equilibrium along \(F_{n}\)
F = applied force (N); θ = inclination angle of plane (rad or °); \(F_{n}\) = normal force on the inclined plane (N)
tips: Check that θ is measured from the correct reference axis (x-axis here); using sin instead of cos for the normal component is a common error.
Keep angles and units consistent (degrees vs radians) when evaluating F cos θ on a calculator.
rq: Why does the normal component of F equal F cos θ rather than F sin θ?
θ is measured from the x-axis to the plane's direction; the normal lies at θ from the x-axis, so the projection of F onto the normal is F cos θ, while F sin θ is the component along the plane.
What would happen to \(F_{n}\) if the plane were rotated so that θ = 90°?
\(F_{n}\) = F cos 90° = 0, so the force is entirely parallel to the plane and produces no normal force.

notes.t: Equilibrium along an inclined stress plane
pts: Resolve the applied force F into components normal and tangential to the inclined plane; the tangential component is F sin θ.
For equilibrium, the shear force \(F_{s}\) on the inclined AB plane must balance the tangential component of F, so \(F_{s}\) takes the opposite sign.
The normal force \(F_{n}\) on the inclined plane is associated with the component F cos θ, measured from the x-axis at angle θ.
defs: Inclined stress plane
A plane cut through a body at angle θ to the reference axes, on which the applied force resolves into a normal force \(F_{n}\) and a tangential (shear) force \(F_{s}\).
eqs: Equilibrium along the tangential (shear) direction of the inclined plane
F = applied force (N); θ = angle of inclined plane to x-axis (rad or °); \(F_{s}\) = tangential (shear) force on the plane (N)
Shear force on the inclined plane from equilibrium
F = applied force (N); θ = inclination angle (rad or °); \(F_{s}\) = shear force (N); the negative sign indicates direction opposite to the resolved component
tips: Check the angle θ is measured from the x-axis to the inclined plane; using cos θ for the shear component swaps normal and tangential forces.
The minus sign in \(F_{s}\) = −F sin θ indicates direction, not a negative magnitude; report the magnitude as F sin θ with direction stated.
rq: Why does the shear force \(F_{s}\) come out negative, and what does that tell you about its direction?

Because \(F_{s}\) is defined along the positive \(F_{s}\) axis while the resolved component F sin θ acts in the opposite sense; the minus sign means \(F_{s}\) points opposite to the chosen positive direction.
Why is the tangential component F sin θ rather than F cos θ for the equilibrium along \(F_{s}\)?
The \(F_{s}\) direction is tangential to the inclined plane, and the component of F along that direction is F sin θ, whereas F cos θ acts normal to the plane.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes: normal and shear stress on an oblique section
pts: On a plane inclined at θ, the normal stress is the axial force component divided by the inclined area A sec θ
Normal stress on the inclined plane reduces to F/A times cos²θ, so it is maximal when θ = 0
Shear stress on the inclined plane is −(F/A) sin θ cos θ, which is maximal at θ = 45°
The inclined cross-sectional area is larger than the normal area A by the factor sec θ
defs: Normal stress on an inclined plane
Stress acting perpendicular to the inclined plane, equal to the normal force on that plane divided by its area.
Shear stress on an inclined plane
Stress acting tangentially (parallel) to the inclined plane, equal to the shear force on that plane divided by its area.
eqs: Normal stress on the inclined AB plane
\(\sigma_{n}\) = normal stress (Pa); \(F_{n}\) = normal force on AB (N); F = applied axial force (N); A = cross-sectional area normal to F (m²); \theta = inclination angle of the plane (rad or °)
Shear stress on the inclined AB plane
\(\tau_{s}\) = shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = shear force on AB (N); F = applied axial force (N); A = cross-sectional area normal to F (m²); \theta = inclination angle (rad or °)
A' = inclined plane area (m²); A = cross-sectional area normal to F (m²); \theta = inclination angle (rad or °)
tips: Do not confuse A with A′: forces are resolved over the cross-section A, but stresses on the plane must be divided by the inclined area A′ = A sec θ.
Watch the sign of shear stress and check that θ is measured between the plane and the cross-section, in consistent units (degrees vs radians) on your calculator.
rq: Why does the inclined area become A sec θ rather than A cos θ?
The inclined plane is longer than its projection onto the cross-section; the projected width A equals A′ cos θ, so A′ = A / cos θ = A sec θ.
What happens to the normal and shear stress when θ = 45°?
σ_n = (F/A)cos²45° = F/(2A) and |τ_s| = (F/A)sin45°cos45° = F/(2A), so both are equal to half the axial stress, and shear is at its maximum.
Why is the shear stress negative in the sign convention shown?
The shear force \(F_{s}\) acts in the opposite sense to the chosen positive tangential direction of the AB plane, so the magnitude sinθ cosθ is given a minus sign.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes
pts: On a plane inclined at angle θ to the bar axis, the normal stress is the direct stress resolved onto that plane.
The normal stress falls from σx at θ = 0 to zero at θ = 90°, as the plane becomes parallel to the load.
The shear stress on the inclined plane is greatest at 45° and 135°, where it equals half the direct stress.
The shear stress is a sine-of-2θ function, so it is zero at 0° and 90°, where no shear acts on the plane.
eqs: Normal stress on an inclined plane under uniaxial direct stress
\(\sigma_n\) = normal stress on the inclined plane (Pa); \(\sigma_x\) = direct stress normal to the bar axis (Pa); \(\theta\) = angle of the plane to the bar axis (degrees or rad)
Shear stress on an inclined plane under uniaxial direct stress
\(\tau_s\) = shear stress on the inclined plane (Pa); \(\sigma_x\) = direct stress (Pa); \(\theta\) = angle of the plane to the bar axis (degrees or rad)
tips: Keep the sign convention for shear stress consistent (−τs is written here); mixing signs gives the wrong direction of shear on the plane.
Angles must be used consistently: sin 2θ requires θ and 2θ in the same units, so check the calculator is in degrees or radians.
rq: Why is the maximum shear stress at 45° and not at 90°, even though the normal stress is zero at 90°?

Shear is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_x\sin 2\theta\), which peaks when \(2\theta = 90°\), i.e. \(\theta = 45°\). At 90° the plane is parallel to the load, so there is no force component along it and hence no shear.
What happens to the normal and shear stresses if the bar is loaded in pure tension versus pure compression?

The stress equations hold for either sign of \(\sigma_x\); the normal stress changes sign with \(\sigma_x\), while the magnitude of the shear stress is the same, so the sign convention of \(\tau_s\) must be checked.
Why does a ductile bar tend to fail along a 45° plane in tension?
Shear stress is maximum at 45°, so yielding by shear occurs on these planes first, producing the characteristic slant fracture.

notes.t: Inclined stress planes
pts: When shear strength is less than half the tensile strength, tensile failure occurs along planes of maximum shear stress.
Maximum shear stress planes lie at 45° to the loading axis, so failure surfaces are inclined rather than perpendicular to the load.
The steel specimen in tension (isotropic) shows slip lines/failure planes at about 45° to the axis, illustrating the observed behaviour.
defs: Maximum shear stress plane
The plane inclined at 45° to the principal (loading) axis on which shear stress is largest; failure occurs along it when shear strength is low relative to tensile strength.
tips: Do not confuse the 45° shear planes with the plane of maximum normal stress, which is perpendicular to the axis.
The shear-strength-less-than-half-tensile-strength condition must be stated; the 45° failure is not universal for all materials.
rq: Why does a ductile specimen in uniaxial tension fail along a 45° plane rather than a plane perpendicular to the load?

Because the maximum shear stress acts on planes at 45° to the axis, and when shear strength is less than half the tensile strength, shear failure along those planes occurs before the normal-stress (perpendicular) fracture.
What would you expect to change if the shear strength were greater than half the tensile strength?
The 45° shear failure would be less likely to dominate; failure would tend to occur on the plane perpendicular to the load, driven by normal (tensile) stress.

units.name: 13.2 Stress notation and principal stresses
units.ov: This material sets up the language of stress at a point: direct and shear stresses, their subscripts and sign conventions, and principal stresses, which are the normal stresses on planes with zero shear. It then explains why principal stresses matter: under complex 3D loading a yield criterion is needed to predict yielding from the uniaxial yield strength alone, and it is expressed in terms of the principal stresses.
must: Principal stress: a normal stress on a plane where the shear stress is zero; the three, \( \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 \), act on mutually perpendicular directions
Direct stresses \( \sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z \) act normal to a face and are labelled by their axis; tension is positive and compression negative
Shear stress \( \tau_{ij} \): first subscript i is the face normal, second subscript j is the shear direction, so \( \tau_{xy} \ne \tau_{yx} \) as labels (they are different stresses)
Shear sign rule: positive when the face normal and the stress direction are both positive or both negative relative to the axes; otherwise negative
Angles of inclined planes are positive when measured anticlockwise
Number of non-zero principal stresses: uniaxial has one (two are zero), plane stress has two (one is zero), 3D stress has three (none are zero)
Principal stresses can be tensile or compressive, so keep signs consistent when substituting values
Principal stresses can describe any stress system, so they characterise the stress at a point in general
Yielding is not simply the largest normal stress reaching the uniaxial yield strength; under combined stresses a yield criterion must be applied
A yield criterion needs only simple tension or compression test data (the uniaxial yield strength) to predict yielding under complex stress, replacing uneconomical trial and error
conn: Sign conventions and principal stresses: wrongly signed tensile or compressive values (or shear signs) give wrong principal stresses and hence a wrong yield prediction
Loading state and principal stresses: identify whether the problem is uniaxial, plane stress or 3D to know which principal stresses are zero before applying a criterion
Principal stresses and yield criteria: criteria take \( \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 \) as inputs and compare the result to the uniaxial yield strength to get a safety factor
Shear subscripts and face orientation: correct identification of face normal and shear direction links the stress element sketch to the stress components used in calculations
exq: Define a principal stress. For a component under plane stress, state how many principal stresses are non-zero and the direction relationship between them.
A stress element shows a shear stress on the face with normal in +y acting in the −x direction. Write its subscript notation and determine its sign using the convention.
State the number of zero principal stresses for uniaxial, plane stress and 3D stress states, and give a practical loading example of each.
Explain why a material cannot be assumed to yield when the largest principal stress reaches the uniaxial yield strength, and describe what a yield criterion needs as material input.

Given principal stresses such as \( \sigma_1 = 100 \) MPa and \( \sigma_3 = -60 \) MPa, explain how the signs are handled and why a yield criterion is needed to check safety against a uniaxial yield strength.

notes.t: Stress symbols, subscripts and sign conventions
pts: Direct stresses act normal to a face and are labelled by their axis: σx, σy, σz.
Shear stresses carry two subscripts: the first gives the normal to the face, the second gives the direction of the shear stress.
Tensile stress is positive and compressive stress is negative.
A shear stress is positive when the stress direction and the plane normal are both positive or both negative relative to the axes; otherwise it is negative.
Angles between an inclined plane and a coordinate axis are positive when measured anticlockwise.
defs: Direct stress
Normal stress acting perpendicular to a face; tensile is positive, compressive is negative.
Shear stress τ_ij
Stress acting parallel to a face, where i is the normal direction of the face and j is the direction of the shear stress.
tips: Do not confuse the two subscripts: the first gives the face normal and the second gives the shear direction, so τ_xy and τ_yx are different stresses.
A shear stress sign depends on both the face normal and the stress direction; check that both are taken relative to the coordinate axes.
rq: Why does τ_xy act on the x-face but point in the y-direction?
The first subscript x identifies the face (normal to x); the second subscript y gives the direction in which the shear stress acts on that face.
If a shear stress acts on a face whose normal points in the negative x-direction, and the stress points in the negative y-direction, what is its sign?
Positive, because both the face normal and the stress direction are in the negative sense.

notes.t: Principal stresses
pts: A principal stress acts along a direction in which there is no shear stress.
Principal stresses can be either tensile or compressive.
The three principal stresses act along three mutually perpendicular directions.
The number of non-zero principal stresses depends on the loading state: one for uniaxial, two for plane stress, three for 3D stress.
Principal stresses can describe any stress system, so they are a general way to characterise stress at a point.
defs: Principal stress
A normal stress acting on a plane where the shear stress is zero; the three principal stresses \( \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 \) act along three mutually perpendicular directions.
tips: Principal stresses may be tensile or compressive; keep the sign convention consistent when substituting values.
Do not confuse the number of zero principal stresses: uniaxial has two zero, plane stress has one zero, and 3D stress has none.
rq: Why must principal stress directions be mutually perpendicular, and what does this imply about the shear stresses on the principal planes?
The principal directions are orthogonal eigenvectors of the symmetric stress tensor, so the shear stresses on the principal planes are all zero.
If a bar is in uniaxial tension, why are two of its principal stresses zero, and what is the value of the third?
No stress acts on the lateral faces, so \( \sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0 \), and the third principal stress equals the applied stress \( \sigma_1 \).

notes.t: Principal stresses and the need for a yield criterion
pts: Most real loads produce three-dimensional stress fields, which make designing against yielding hard.
Trial and error can find a safe design under complex stress but is uneconomical, so a theory is needed.
A theoretical yield criterion predicts yielding under complex stress states from measurable material behaviour.
Once a yield criterion exists, only the yield strength from simple tension or compression is needed for design.
tips: Do not assume yielding occurs when the single largest normal stress reaches the uniaxial yield strength; under combined stresses a yield criterion must be applied.
Remember that the yield criterion only needs simple tension or compression test data, so the uniaxial yield strength is the sole material input required.
rq: Why can't a designer simply use the tensile yield strength when a component is loaded in three dimensions?

Because multi-axial stresses interact, so yielding depends on the combination of stresses, not on one stress alone; a yield criterion is needed to combine them into an equivalent comparison with the simple-tension yield point.
What would you lose by relying only on trial and error for a complex loading case?
Testing every geometry and load case is costly and slow; a validated yield criterion lets the designer predict yielding analytically from the simple-tension yield point.

units.name: 13.3 Yield criteria and Tresca criterion
units.ov: This material introduces yield criteria for ductile materials, which yield by shear-driven slip, and develops the Tresca (maximum shear stress) criterion in detail. Tresca is calibrated against the uniaxial tensile test (\(\tau_Y=\sigma_Y/2\)), written in terms of principal stress differences, then drawn as a hexagonal yield locus in plane stress and as a hexagonal prism in 3D principal stress space. Von Mises (distortion energy) is introduced only as the alternative criterion.
must: Tresca: yielding begins when \(\tau_{max}\) equals the shear stress at yield in uniaxial tension, \(\tau_{max}=\tau_Y=\sigma_Y/2\).
Principal-stress form: \(\tau_{max}=\max\left(\frac{|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|}{2},\frac{|\sigma_1-\sigma_3|}{2},\frac{|\sigma_2-\sigma_3|}{2}\right)\), including \(\sigma_3=0\) in plane stress.

Equivalent difference form: yield when \(\max(|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|,|\sigma_1-\sigma_3|,|\sigma_2-\sigma_3|)=\sigma_Y\). Keep the factor of 2 consistent and do not mix the shear form (\(\sigma_Y/2\)) with the difference form (\(\sigma_Y\)).

Always use principal stresses with correct signs (tension positive, compression negative), ordered \(\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3\), not normal stresses on arbitrary planes. If a stress state is not principal, find the principal stresses first.
Plane stress locus: a hexagon in the \(\sigma_1\)–\(\sigma_2\) plane with vertices at \(\pm\sigma_Y\) on the axes. Inside it the material is elastic; on the boundary it yields.
Same-sign quadrants: \(\sigma_3=0\) is the min or max principal stress, so yield occurs when \(|\sigma_1|=\sigma_Y\) or \(|\sigma_2|=\sigma_Y\) (the square-cornered sides).
Opposite-sign quadrants: yield when \(|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|=\sigma_Y\) (the sloped sides).
3D yield surface: a hexagonal prism whose axis is the hydrostatic line \(\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma_3\), equally inclined to the three axes. The plane stress hexagon is the \(\sigma_3=0\) slice.
Tresca is pressure-independent: adding equal hydrostatic stress to all principal stresses does not change whether yield occurs, because the differences are unchanged.
Conceptual: yield is by slip, i.e. shear, so the criteria apply to ductile materials and not brittle ones. Tresca uses maximum shear stress, Von Mises uses shear-strain (distortion) energy.
conn: Mohr's circle / stress transformation gives the principal stresses, which are the input to Tresca. A typical question goes from applied loads to principal stresses to a yield check.
Uniaxial tensile test data (\(\sigma_Y\)) calibrates the criterion, so the factor of safety follows from comparing the Tresca equivalent stress \(\sigma_1-\sigma_3\) with \(\sigma_Y\).
Thin-walled pressure vessels (hoop \(\sigma_\theta=pr/t\), axial \(pr/2t\), radial approximately 0) combine with Tresca to find the yield pressure, and the choice of \(\sigma_3\) matters.
The 2D hexagon and the 3D prism are linked: the plane stress case is a slice, and the hydrostatic axis explains the pressure independence. Von Mises comparison questions use the same loci.
exq: A steel has \(\sigma_Y=250\) MPa. A point has principal stresses \(\sigma_1=150\), \(\sigma_2=-100\), \(\sigma_3=0\) MPa. Use Tresca to decide whether it yields and find the factor of safety.

For plane stress with \(\sigma_1=200\) MPa and \(\sigma_2=120\) MPa (same sign), find the Tresca \(\tau_{max}\) and state which quadrant condition applies. What \(\sigma_1\) causes yield if \(\sigma_Y=300\) MPa and \(\sigma_2=-100\) MPa?

Sketch the Tresca hexagon in the \(\sigma_1\)–\(\sigma_2\) plane, labelling the vertices in terms of \(\sigma_Y\), and explain why the sides are vertical/horizontal in some quadrants and sloped in others.
A thin-walled cylinder (radius 100 mm, wall 2 mm, \(\sigma_Y=300\) MPa) is under internal pressure. Using Tresca with the radial stress taken as zero, find the pressure at yield.

Explain why the 3D Tresca yield surface is a hexagonal prism along the hydrostatic axis and what this implies for the effect of hydrostatic pressure on yielding. Show that stresses (100, 100, 100) MPa never yield.

notes.t: Yield criterion
pts: Plastic deformation occurs when atoms slip within the crystal structure of a material.
Slip is caused by shearing action, so yield criteria for ductile materials are based on shear.
Two commonly used yield criteria for ductile materials are the Tresca and Von Mises criteria.
Tresca uses the maximum shear stress as the yield condition; Von Mises uses shear-strain energy.
defs: Slip
Shear-driven movement of atoms along crystal planes in the crystalline structure of a material, which produces plastic deformation.
Tresca criterion
Yield criterion stating that yielding begins when the maximum shear stress reaches a critical value (half the yield stress in uniaxial tension).
Von Mises criterion
Yield criterion stating that yielding begins when the shear-strain energy (distortion energy) reaches a critical value.
tips: Do not confuse the two criteria: Tresca is maximum shear stress, Von Mises is shear-strain energy.
Both criteria apply to ductile materials; brittle materials are not governed by these shear-based yield criteria.
rq: Why are yield criteria for ductile materials based on shear rather than on normal stress alone?
Plastic deformation is driven by slip of atoms, which depends on shearing action, so shear stress is the physically relevant quantity.
How do Tresca and Von Mises criteria differ in what they predict for the same loading?
Tresca uses the maximum shear stress and is more conservative; Von Mises uses shear-strain energy and typically predicts yield at a slightly higher stress.

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion
pts: A state of stress in 3D is fully described by three mutually orthogonal principal stresses.
Tresca proposed that yielding occurs when the maximum shear stress reaches a critical value.
For a general 3D stress system, the maximum shear stress is the largest of the three pairwise half-differences of principal stresses.
defs: Principal stresses
The normal stresses acting on a set of mutually orthogonal planes on which the shear stresses are zero; they fully define the stress state at a point.
Tresca criterion
A yield criterion stating that yielding begins when the maximum shear stress in a material reaches a critical value (based on the largest difference between principal stresses).
eqs: Maximum shear stress for a general 3D stress system (Tresca)
tips: Do not forget the division by 2 in the shear stress expression; using the full difference gives twice the correct τmax.
Check that principal stresses are ordered and taken with their signs (tension positive, compression negative) before computing differences.
rq: Why is the maximum shear stress found from differences between principal stresses rather than from the stresses themselves?
Shear stress is driven by the difference between normal stresses; a hydrostatic (equal) stress state produces no shear, so only differences matter.
If σ1 is the largest and σ3 the smallest principal stress, which term in the Tresca equation will govern τmax?
The term (σ1 − σ3)/2, since it is the largest difference.

notes.t: Tresca criterion
pts: Under uniaxial tension only, the only non-zero principal stress is σ1, so the maximum shear stress is half of σ1.
At yield, the maximum shear stress equals half the yield stress, so yield is governed by shear rather than tensile stress (Tresca's engineering theory).
defs: Uniaxial tension
A loading state in which only one principal stress (σ1) is non-zero, with σ2 = σ3 = 0.
eqs: Maximum shear stress under uniaxial tension
\(\tau_{max}\) = maximum shear stress (Pa); \(\sigma_1\) = largest principal stress (Pa)
\(\tau_Y\) = shear stress at yield (Pa); \(\sigma_Y\) = tensile yield stress (Pa)
tips: Check the loading condition: τ_max = σ1/2 is valid only for uniaxial tension where σ2 = σ3 = 0.
Do not confuse τ_Y = σ_Y/2 with σ_Y; yield is compared using shear stress, so keep the factor of 2 consistent.
rq: Why does the Tresca criterion predict yield from shear stress when the load is a simple tensile pull?
Because a uniaxial tensile stress produces maximum shear on planes at 45°, and yield is assumed to occur when this maximum shear reaches half the yield stress, τ_Y = σ_Y/2.
What would happen to τ_max if σ2 and σ3 were non-zero, not zero?
τ_max would no longer equal σ1/2 alone; it would be the largest of (σ1−σ2)/2, (σ2−σ3)/2 and (σ1−σ3)/2, so the simple uniaxial result no longer applies.

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion
pts: Yield is predicted when the maximum shear stress in the material reaches the maximum shear stress at yield in a simple uniaxial tensile test.
Tresca's criterion is expressed in terms of principal stress differences, so it depends on the largest difference between any two principal stresses.
In simple tension the maximum shear stress at yield is half the uniaxial yield stress, which sets the threshold for the shear-based form.
defs: Tresca criterion
A yield criterion stating that yielding occurs when the maximum shear stress in a material equals the maximum shear stress at yield in a simple uniaxial tensile test.
Uniaxial yield stress
The stress at which a material begins to yield in simple tension, denoted \( \sigma_Y \).
eqs: Maximum shear stress from principal stresses (Tresca yield condition)
\( \tau_{max} \) = maximum shear stress (Pa); \( \tau_Y \) = shear stress at yield (Pa); \( \sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 \) = principal stresses (Pa); \( \sigma_Y \) = uniaxial yield stress (Pa)
Tresca yield condition in terms of principal stress differences
tips: Use the principal stresses \( \sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 \), not the normal stresses on an arbitrary plane, when applying the criterion.
Don't confuse the shear form (\( \sigma_Y/2 \)) with the stress-difference form (\( \sigma_Y \)); mixing them doubles or halves the result.
rq: Why is the Tresca yield condition written with a factor of 2 on the left-hand side but not on the right-hand side of the principal stress difference form?

Because the maximum shear stress is half the maximum principal stress difference, \( \tau_{max} = (\sigma_1-\sigma_3)/2 \), so the equal-to-\( \sigma_Y \) form removes the 2 while the shear form keeps \( \sigma_Y/2 \).
What would happen to the yield prediction if the sign convention for principal stresses were ignored?

The differences must be taken as the maximum of the pairwise differences (largest minus smallest), so ignoring order could give a wrong or negative value; the criterion uses the maximum absolute principal stress difference.

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion for biaxial (plane) stress
pts: For plane stress (σ₃ = 0), the Tresca criterion can be drawn as a 2D yield locus in the σ₁–σ₂ plane.
Same-sign quadrants: σ₃ = 0 is the minimum principal stress, so the largest shear stress uses σ₃ and yield occurs when the non-zero stress reaches the yield strength.
Opposite-sign quadrants: σ₃ = 0 is no longer the minimum principal stress, so the largest shear stress is set by σ₁ and σ₂ directly, giving the sloped sides of the hexagon.
The yield locus is a hexagon in the σ₁–σ₂ plane with vertices at ±σY on each axis and points where σ₁ − σ₂ = ±σY.
Inside the hexagon there is no yield; on its boundary yield occurs.
defs: Plane stress
A stress state in which one principal stress (here σ₃) is zero, so the material is loaded biaxially in two principal directions.
Principal stresses
The normal stresses acting on planes where shear stress is zero, conventionally ordered σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ σ₃.
Maximum shear stress (τmax)
Half the difference between the largest and smallest principal stresses; in Tresca it is the quantity compared with the yield value.
eqs: Tresca yield condition in terms of maximum shear stress at yield
τ_max = maximum shear stress (Pa); σ_Y = uniaxial yield strength (Pa)
Same-sign quadrants: yield when a non-zero principal stress equals yield strength
σ₁, σ₂ = non-zero principal stresses (Pa); σ_Y = yield strength (Pa)
Opposite-sign quadrants: yield condition for the hexagon's sloped sides
σ₁, σ₂ = principal stresses (Pa); σ_Y = yield strength (Pa)
tips: Check the signs of σ₁ and σ₂ first: same-sign quadrants use σ₃ = 0 as the minimum, opposite-sign quadrants use σ₁ − σ₂ directly.
Keep the factor of 2 consistent: τmax = σ_Y/2 at yield, so σ_Y is the full stress difference, not the shear.
rq: Why does the sloped edge of the hexagon use σ₁ − σ₂ rather than σ₁ − 0 when σ₁ and σ₂ have opposite signs?
Because with σ₃ = 0 lying between σ₁ and σ₂ in value, σ₃ is no longer the minimum principal stress, so the maximum shear is (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 instead of involving σ₃.
What if σ₁ and σ₂ are both tensile and σ₁ > σ₂ > 0? Which stress is the minimum and what is τmax?
σ₃ = 0 is the minimum, so τmax = (σ₁ − 0)/2 = σ₁/2; yield occurs when σ₁ = σ_Y.
Why is the Tresca locus a hexagon rather than a circle?
Tresca uses the maximum shear stress, which is piecewise linear in the principal stresses depending on which principal stress is the maximum or minimum, creating straight edges and corners.

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion in 3D stress space
pts: In 3D, the Tresca yield surface is the 2D hexagon extruded along the hydrostatic axis (σ1=σ2=σ3), forming a prism.
The longitudinal axis is equally inclined to the three principal stress axes σ1, σ2 and σ3.
The hexagon shown is the cross-section for σ3 = 0, i.e. a plane stress slice of the prism.
Hydrostatic stress states (σ1=σ2=σ3) lie along the prism axis and never cause yielding, so the yield locus is independent of pressure.
defs: Yield locus
The surface in principal stress space that separates elastic states from yielded states; for Tresca it is a hexagonal prism whose axis is the hydrostatic line.
tips: Do not confuse the 3D Tresca prism with the 2D hexagon: the 2D hexagon is one slice (σ3 = 0) of the 3D surface.
Tresca yield is pressure-independent, so adding equal hydrostatic stress to all principal stresses does not change whether yielding occurs.
rq: Why does the Tresca yield surface extend along the line σ1=σ2=σ3 rather than being a closed shape around the origin?

Hydrostatic (equal, all-round) stress produces no shear stress, so it cannot cause yielding; the criterion depends only on differences between principal stresses, so the surface is a prism parallel to the hydrostatic axis.
What does the hexagon at σ3 = 0 represent?
A cross-section of the prism corresponding to plane stress, where one principal stress is zero and the yield condition is checked in the σ1–σ2 plane.

units.name: 13.4 Von Mises criterion
units.ov: This module covers the von Mises (distortion energy) yield criterion for ductile materials. Total elastic strain energy is split into a volumetric part and a shape-change part, and only the shape-change part drives yielding. This gives a single equivalent stress computed from the principal stresses and compared with the uniaxial yield strength. It is shown geometrically as an ellipse in 2D plane stress and a cylinder about the hydrostatic axis in 3D.
must: Huber's idea: elastic strain energy = volumetric (volume-change) part + distortion (shape-change) part, and yielding is governed by the distortion part only
Yield begins when the distortion energy per unit volume equals its value at yield in simple uniaxial tension
Yield condition: \((\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2+(\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2+(\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2=2\sigma_Y^2\)

Equivalent stress: \(\sigma_e=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2+(\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2+(\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2]^{1/2}\); yield when \(\sigma_e\ge\sigma_Y\). Compare \(\sigma_e\) with \(\sigma_Y\), not \(\sigma_e^2\)
Inputs must be principal stresses in consistent units (Pa or MPa); a general stress state must first be reduced to principal stresses
2D plane stress (\(\sigma_3=0\)): the locus is an ellipse in (\(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)) space crossing the axes at \(\pm\sigma_Y\); inside is elastic, on or outside is yield
3D: the yield surface is a cylinder whose axis is the hydrostatic line \(\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma_3\), which is equally inclined to the three axes. Hydrostatic stress alone never causes yield
The 2D ellipse is the \(\sigma_3=0\) section of the 3D cylinder, not the whole surface
Von Mises (distortion energy, ellipse) differs from Tresca (maximum shear stress, hexagon). They coincide at the uniaxial points on the axes but differ elsewhere
The criterion applies to ductile yielding under multiaxial stress, not brittle fracture. Originators: Huber, Maxwell, von Mises and Hencky
conn: Principal stresses (e.g. from Mohr's circle or stress transformation) feed the equivalent stress formula, so a question may give \(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau_{xy}\) and ask whether the material yields
Equivalent stress compared with \(\sigma_Y\) gives a factor of safety, \(\sigma_Y/\sigma_e\), which links to design loads in pressure vessels, shafts and beams

Algebraic criterion and geometric locus are the same thing: setting \(\sigma_3=0\) in the yield condition gives the ellipse, and testing a point inside or outside it is the same as checking \(\sigma_e<\sigma_Y\)
Comparing von Mises with Tresca: both give the same yield in uniaxial tension, but they differ under biaxial or shear loading, with Tresca more conservative (hexagon inside the ellipse)
exq: A component has principal stresses of 150, 60 and 0 MPa and \(\sigma_Y=200\) MPa. Calculate the von Mises equivalent stress, state whether it yields, and give the factor of safety.
Explain Huber's split of elastic strain energy into volumetric and distortion parts. Why does hydrostatic stress not cause yielding, and how is this shown by the yield cylinder?

Starting from the 3D von Mises condition, derive the plane-stress (\(\sigma_3=0\)) yield condition and show that the ellipse crosses the axes at \(\pm\sigma_Y\). Find the value of \(\sigma_1\) at yield when \(\sigma_2=-\sigma_1\) (pure shear).

Sketch the von Mises ellipse and the Tresca hexagon in (\(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)) space for the same \(\sigma_Y\). Mark where they coincide and identify a stress state that Tresca predicts to yield but von Mises predicts to be elastic.

A thin-walled pressure vessel has hoop stress \(\sigma_1=2\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\approx0\). Use the von Mises criterion to find the maximum internal pressure before yielding for given radius, wall thickness and \(\sigma_Y\).

notes.t: Von Mises criterion
pts: Huber (1904) split total elastic strain energy into a volumetric part and a shape-change (distortion) part.
Maxwell, von Mises and Hencky independently proposed that yield occurs when enough energy is input to distort the material.
Yielding is governed by the distortion energy, not the volume-change energy, which led to the von Mises criterion.
defs: Elastic strain energy
The energy stored in a material when it is elastically deformed, recoverable on unloading; Huber divided it into volumetric and shape-change components.
Von Mises criterion
A yield criterion stating that yielding begins when the distortion (shape-change) energy per unit volume reaches the value at yield in simple tension.
tips: Do not confuse the von Mises criterion (distortion energy) with the Tresca criterion (maximum shear stress); they give different yield predictions.
The criterion applies to ductile materials under multiaxial stress; it does not describe brittle fracture.
rq: Why would yielding depend only on shape-change energy rather than volume-change energy?
Plastic yielding is caused by distortion (shear) of the material; uniform volume change does not produce yielding in metals, so only the distortion energy is relevant.
What would happen to the predicted yield point if the volumetric energy were included in the criterion?
The prediction would be wrong for hydrostatic stress states, which do not cause yield in ductile metals, so the criterion would overpredict yielding under pressure.

notes.t: Von Mises yield criterion
pts: The von Mises criterion predicts when yielding begins under a general multiaxial stress state, using the three principal stresses.
Yield commences when the combined squared differences of principal stresses equal twice the square of the yield strength.
The von Mises equivalent stress reduces the multiaxial state to a single value that is compared with the yield strength in a uniaxial test.
The material is considered to have yielded when the equivalent stress exceeds the yield strength.
defs: Von Mises equivalent stress
A single scalar stress computed from the principal stresses, which is compared with the uniaxial yield strength to decide whether a material has yielded.
Yield
The onset of permanent (plastic) deformation in a material, occurring when the equivalent stress exceeds the yield strength.
eqs: Von Mises yield condition (onset of yield)
\(\sigma_e\) = von Mises equivalent stress (Pa); \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\) = principal stresses (Pa)
tips: The two forms are equivalent: the first is \(\sigma_e = \sigma_Y\) at yield, so compare \(\sigma_e\) with \(\sigma_Y\), not \(\sigma_e^2\) with \(\sigma_Y\).
Check that the stresses are principal stresses and that consistent units (Pa or MPa) are used throughout.
rq: Why does the criterion use differences between principal stresses rather than their absolute values?
Yielding is driven by shear (distortion) stresses, which depend on differences between principal stresses; adding the same hydrostatic stress to all three does not cause yield.
If σ1 = σ2 = σ3 (pure hydrostatic stress), what is σe and what does this imply?
All difference terms are zero, so σe = 0; the material does not yield under hydrostatic pressure.

notes.t: Von Mises criterion – graphical representation in 2D
pts: In 2D, the von Mises yield criterion plotted in principal stress space (σ₁, σ₂) gives an ellipse rather than a circle or hexagon.
The ellipse is the locus of stress states where the maximum shear strain energy equals that at yield in uniaxial tension; stress states inside it are elastic.
The ellipse crosses the axes at ±σ_Y, where σ_Y is the uniaxial yield strength, so uniaxial loading along σ₁ or σ₂ yields at the same magnitude.
defs: Von Mises criterion
A yield criterion stating that yielding occurs when the distortion (shear) strain energy per unit volume reaches the value at yield in simple uniaxial tension.
tips: Do not confuse the von Mises ellipse (distortion energy) with the Tresca hexagon (maximum shear stress); both coincide at the axes but differ elsewhere.
Points inside the ellipse are elastic; only stress states on or outside the curve cause yielding.
rq: Why does the von Mises yield locus appear as an ellipse rather than a hexagon in the σ₁–σ₂ plane?

Because the von Mises criterion is based on distortion energy, which is a quadratic function of the stresses, giving a smooth elliptical curve; the Tresca criterion (maximum shear stress) is linear and gives a hexagon.
What does the point where the ellipse crosses the σ₁ axis represent physically?
Uniaxial tensile yielding in the σ₁ direction, where σ₁ = σ_Y and σ₂ = 0.

notes.t: Von Mises criterion in 3D stress space
pts: In 3D, the yield surface is a cylinder whose axis is equally inclined to the principal stress axes σ1, σ2 and σ3.
The cylinder axis represents the hydrostatic stress line σ1 = σ2 = σ3, which does not cause yielding.
The cross-section of the cylinder perpendicular to its axis is an ellipse when one principal stress is zero (σ3 = 0), showing the 2D plane-stress yield locus.
The yield locus is the boundary of the elastic region; stress states inside it are elastic and states on it yield.
defs: Yield locus (von Mises)
The surface in principal stress space, a cylinder equally inclined to the σ1, σ2, σ3 axes, that separates elastic from plastic stress states.
tips: Do not confuse the hydrostatic axis σ1 = σ2 = σ3 with the yield surface itself; hydrostatic stress alone does not cause yielding.
The ellipse shown is the 2D plane-stress section (σ3 = 0), not the full 3D cylinder.
rq: Why does the cylinder's axis lie along σ1 = σ2 = σ3 rather than along one of the stress axes?

Because the von Mises criterion depends only on deviatoric stress; pure hydrostatic stress (equal principal stresses) produces no shear distortion and therefore cannot cause yielding, so the axis of symmetry is the hydrostatic line.
What shape does the yield locus take if you slice the cylinder with the plane σ3 = 0, and why?
An ellipse, because the cylinder is a circle in cross-section perpendicular to its axis and the plane σ3 = 0 cuts it obliquely, producing an elliptical outline in the σ1–σ2 plane.

units.name: 13.5 Comparing Tresca and von Mises
units.ov: This section compares the two main yield criteria for ductile materials under multi-axial stress, Tresca (maximum shear stress) and von Mises (distortion energy), by plotting them as yield envelopes in the principal-stress plane. Tresca gives a hexagon and von Mises an ellipse that passes through the hexagon's six vertices. The two agree in uniaxial loading and differ most in biaxial states, with Tresca being the more conservative. The choice between them comes down to conservatism, material type and ease of calculation.
must: Tresca: yield when \( \tau_{max}=\sigma_Y/2 \), i.e. \( \max(|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|,|\sigma_2-\sigma_3|,|\sigma_3-\sigma_1|)=\sigma_Y \). In plane stress include \( \sigma_3=0 \). The envelope is a hexagon with straight edges.

Von Mises: yield when distortion (shear-strain) energy per unit volume equals that at uniaxial yield. In plane stress \( \sigma_1^2-\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2^2=\sigma_Y^2 \). The envelope is an ellipse.
The Tresca hexagon lies inside the von Mises ellipse, so Tresca predicts yield earlier and is the more conservative criterion. The reason to choose it for design is safety, not accuracy.
The criteria agree in uniaxial tension and compression, so any difference only appears in multi-axial states.

The boundaries coincide at six points: the four axis intercepts (\( \sigma_1=0 \) or \( \sigma_2=0 \)) and the two equal-biaxial points \( \sigma_1=\sigma_2=\pm\sigma_Y \). The notes' phrase 'six points on the axes' is loose, because only four of these lie on the axes.

The gap is largest where \( \sigma_1=-\sigma_2 \) (pure shear). Tresca gives \( \tau_Y=0.5\sigma_Y \) and von Mises gives \( \tau_Y=\sigma_Y/\sqrt3\approx0.577\sigma_Y \), a ratio of about 15%. This is the maximum difference between the criteria.
Definition of the yield envelope: the closed locus in principal-stress space separating elastic states (inside) from yielding (on or outside).

Von Mises is the usual choice for polycrystalline materials, which cover most engineering metals. It is also the standard in FEA because it is a smooth function that is easy to compute. Tresca is associated with single crystals, a claim you should quote as in the notes.

Exam wording: say 'Tresca gives the higher equivalent stress, or lower allowable load, so it is safer'. Don't say von Mises is always higher or always lower, because the two are equal on the coincidence points.
conn: Mohr's circle gives \( \sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 \) and \( \tau_{max} \) from a stress state. These feed directly into the Tresca check, and into the von Mises equivalent stress, which is then compared with \( \sigma_Y \) to find the factor of safety.
Uniaxial tensile test data give \( \sigma_Y \), which calibrates both criteria. This is why they agree on the axes, and why \( \tau_Y \) for torsion is derived from \( \sigma_Y \).

Thin-walled pressure vessels (hoop \( \sigma_1=pr/t \), axial \( \sigma_2=pr/2t \)) and combined bending and torsion of shafts are classic biaxial cases where the two criteria give different factors of safety.
Plotting a load path on the yield envelope links geometry to design: a point inside the curve is safe, and the ratio of distances to the curve along the load line gives the factor of safety.
exq: Sketch the Tresca and von Mises yield envelopes in the \( \sigma_1\)-\( \sigma_2 \) plane for plane stress. Mark the points where they coincide, state which is more conservative, and explain why.

A plane-stress element has \( \sigma_1=100 \) MPa and \( \sigma_2=-100 \) MPa, with \( \sigma_Y=200 \) MPa. Does it yield under Tresca? Under von Mises? (Tresca: \( \sigma_1-\sigma_2=200 \), so yield is just reached. Von Mises: \( \sigma_{eq}\approx173 \) MPa, so it is safe.)

A material with \( \sigma_Y=250 \) MPa carries \( \sigma_1=150 \) MPa and \( \sigma_2=75 \) MPa. Find the factor of safety by each criterion and comment on the difference. (Tresca about 1.67, von Mises about 1.92.)
Show that for pure shear the von Mises yield shear stress is \( \sigma_Y/\sqrt3 \) and the Tresca value is \( \sigma_Y/2 \). Find the percentage difference between the two criteria.
Explain why von Mises is used in FEA and for polycrystalline metals, yet Tresca may still be chosen in design. Name the stress states where the two give identical results.

notes.t: Yield envelope: von Mises vs Tresca criteria
pts: The von Mises (shear-strain energy) boundary is an ellipse in the principal-stress plane that lies outside the Tresca hexagon, touching it at the same six points on the axes.
Both criteria give the same yield stress in uniaxial tension or compression, since the boundaries meet at \( \sigma_Y \) on each axis.
Tresca (maximum shear stress) predicts yield when the largest shear stress reaches half the yield stress, giving a hexagonal envelope with straight edges.
The two criteria differ most in biaxial stress states, where von Mises is less conservative, so the Tresca hexagon lies inside the ellipse and predicts yield earlier.
defs: Yield envelope (locus)
The closed curve in principal-stress space that separates elastic stress states from those that cause yielding.
Von Mises criterion
Yielding occurs when the distortion (shear-strain) energy per unit volume reaches that of yielding in uniaxial tension.
Tresca criterion
Yielding occurs when the maximum shear stress reaches half the uniaxial yield stress.
tips: Do not assume the two criteria differ in uniaxial tension; they agree there, so differences only appear for multi-axial stress states.
Remember the Tresca hexagon lies inside the von Mises ellipse, so Tresca is the more conservative criterion.
rq: Why does the Tresca hexagon touch the von Mises ellipse at the axis points but lie inside it elsewhere?
Both criteria reduce to the same uniaxial yield value along the axes, but in biaxial states the Tresca maximum-shear condition is more restrictive, so its boundary is inside the von Mises ellipse.
Which criterion would you choose for a conservative design under biaxial loading, and why?
Tresca, because its envelope lies inside the von Mises ellipse, so it predicts yield at lower stresses and gives a safer margin.

notes.t: Tresca or von Mises – which to use?
pts: Von Mises is the more common choice for polycrystalline materials, which make up most engineering materials.
Tresca is favoured for single crystal materials.
Von Mises predicts higher values before yield than Tresca, except in certain biaxial stress states where the two coincide.
Because Tresca gives the higher (more conservative) stress estimate in general, it is the safer criterion for design.
Von Mises is widely used in FEA programs because it is easier to calculate, and most materials are polycrystalline.
tips: Do not assume von Mises is always the higher stress: the two criteria coincide when \( \sigma_1 = 0 \), \( \sigma_2 = 0 \) or \( \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 \) in biaxial states.
Choosing Tresca is justified by conservatism in design, not by it being more accurate for polycrystalline materials; state the reason explicitly in exam answers.
rq: Why does von Mises predict higher pre-yield stress than Tresca in most biaxial states, yet the two agree when \( \sigma_1 = 0 \), \( \sigma_2 = 0 \) or \( \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 \)?

Von Mises is an ellipse-based criterion lying outside the Tresca hexagon, touching it at the vertices (where one principal stress is zero or the two principal stresses are equal); elsewhere the hexagon's edges lie closer to the origin, so Tresca gives a lower equivalent stress.
Why might a designer prefer Tresca even though von Mises is more accurate for most polycrystalline metals?
Tresca gives a higher equivalent stress in general, so designing to it is conservative and gives a safety margin against yielding.

units.name: 13.6 Worked example: yield of a torsion-loaded shaft
units.ov: This worked example finds the torque at which a solid 30 mm diameter steel shaft first yields in pure torsion, using both the Tresca and von Mises criteria. Torsion gives a pure-shear state with principal stresses \(\pm\tau\) and 0, where \(\tau=2T/\pi r^3\). Each criterion turns that stress state into a yield torque, and the two results are then compared. The numbers imply \(\sigma_Y\approx 800\) MPa, although the notes never state it.
must: Torsion of a solid shaft gives pure shear \(\tau=\frac{2T}{\pi r^3}\) at the surface, with principal stresses \(+\tau,\,0,\,-\tau\) (the zero is the radial or free-surface direction).
Tresca: yield when the largest principal stress difference equals \(\sigma_Y\), i.e. \(\tau_{max}=\sigma_Y/2\). Always compare all three differences and take the largest.
Tresca for this shaft: \(\sigma_1-\sigma_3=2\tau=\frac{4T}{\pi r^3}=\sigma_Y\Rightarrow T_{max}=\frac{\pi r^3\sigma_Y}{4}\approx 2120.58\) N·m.
von Mises: \((\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2+(\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2+(\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2=2\sigma_Y^2\). Keep the factor of 2 on the right.
von Mises in pure torsion: \(6\tau^2=2\sigma_Y^2\Rightarrow\tau=\sigma_Y/\sqrt3\Rightarrow T_{max}=\frac{\pi r^3\sigma_Y}{2\sqrt3}\approx 2448.63\) N·m.
Ratio \(T_{vM}/T_{Tresca}=2/\sqrt3\approx1.155\): von Mises allows about 15.5% more torque, so Tresca is the more conservative criterion.
Shear yield strength is \(\sigma_Y/2\) under Tresca and \(\sigma_Y/\sqrt3\approx0.577\sigma_Y\) under von Mises. Use the right one for the criterion in question.
Units: use \(r=0.015\) m (radius, not the 30 mm diameter) and \(\sigma_Y\) in Pa before cubing. A mistake in \(r\) is magnified by \(r^3\).
Design practice: apply a factor of safety to the (Tresca) yield torque and never design at it. The formulas hold only for elastic, solid circular sections in pure torsion.
conn: Torsion shear formula to principal stresses: finding \(\tau=Tr/J\) (\(=2T/\pi r^3\) at the surface) comes first, then Mohr's circle or the pure-shear state gives \(\pm\tau\), which feeds either yield criterion.
Tresca vs von Mises: both reduce to a shear-stress limit on \(\tau\) (\(\sigma_Y/2\) vs \(\sigma_Y/\sqrt3\)), so the \(2/\sqrt3\) ratio of torques follows directly from the two shear yield strengths.
Yield criteria and factor of safety: the yield torque becomes an allowable torque \(T_{max}/n\), which can be inverted to size the shaft radius, \(r=(4nT/\pi\sigma_Y)^{1/3}\) for Tresca.

Combined loading: if bending or axial load is added, the principal stresses are no longer \(\pm\tau\). The same Tresca and von Mises expressions apply, but the principal stresses must be recalculated and reordered first.
exq: A solid steel shaft of diameter 30 mm has \(\sigma_Y=800\) MPa. Calculate the maximum torque before yield using (a) Tresca and (b) von Mises, and state which is more conservative.

Derive from first principles the principal stresses at the surface of a solid circular shaft under torque \(T\). Hence show that the von Mises equivalent stress is \(\sqrt3\,\tau\) and the Tresca equivalent stress is \(2\tau\).
Show that \(T_{vM}/T_{Tresca}=2/\sqrt3\) for a solid shaft in pure torsion, and explain why the two criteria differ by about 15%.
A shaft must carry 1500 N·m with a factor of safety of 1.5 against Tresca yield (\(\sigma_Y=800\) MPa). Find the minimum shaft diameter, then the von Mises factor of safety for that diameter.

A student uses 30 mm as the radius in \(T=\pi r^3\sigma_Y/4\). By what factor is the answer wrong, and what other unit mistake could occur? Discuss, and explain why the criteria are limited to elastic, solid circular sections.

notes.t: Yield criteria for a torsion-loaded steel shaft (Tresca and von Mises)
pts: Under pure torsion the principal stresses are equal and opposite, so the shaft is in shear; yielding is checked with the maximum shear / equivalent stress criteria.
Tresca yields when the maximum shear stress reaches half the yield stress, i.e. the difference between the largest and smallest principal stresses reaches the yield stress.
von Mises uses an equivalent stress built from all three principal stresses; it is less conservative than Tresca and gives a higher allowable torque.
defs: Tresca yield criterion
Yielding occurs when the maximum shear stress, (σ_max − σ_min)/2, equals half the uniaxial yield stress σ_y/2.
von Mises yield criterion
Yielding occurs when the equivalent stress √(½[(σ_1−σ_2)²+(σ_2−σ_3)²+(σ_3−σ_1)²]) equals the uniaxial yield stress σ_y.
eqs: Principal stresses in torsion of a solid shaft
\(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\) = principal stresses (Pa); \(T\) = applied torque (N·m); \(r\) = shaft radius (m)
von Mises yield condition for this stress state
tips: Convert the 30 mm diameter to a radius of 0.015 m before using T = πr³σ/4; using 30 mm directly gives a result off by a factor of 8 in r³.
Check the stress state: Tresca uses σ1−σ2 (not σ1 alone), and von Mises uses the combined expression with all three principal stresses.
rq: Why does the Tresca criterion give a lower allowable torque than von Mises for this shaft?
Tresca depends only on the maximum shear stress (σ1−σ2 here), ignoring the intermediate stress, so it is more conservative; von Mises averages all differences and predicts yielding at a higher load.
Why is σ3 = 0 and what does it imply for the surface of the shaft?
The outer surface is free of normal stress in the radial direction, so the surface is in plane stress with only σ1 and σ2 acting.
What is the numerical value of the Tresca torque for d = 30 mm and σy = 800 MPa?

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion
pts: Tresca predicts yield when the maximum shear stress reaches half the uniaxial yield stress value
Yield depends on the maximum principal stress difference in a 3D stress state
Yield stress in simple tension sets the threshold for the 3D state
defs: Tresca yield criterion
Yield occurs when the maximum principal stress difference in a 3D stress state equals the uniaxial yield stress in simple tension.
Uniaxial yield stress
The stress at which a material yields under simple tension, denoted \( \sigma_Y \).
eqs: \( \tau_{max} \) = maximum shear stress (Pa); \( \tau_Y \) = shear stress at yield (Pa); \( \sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 \) = principal stresses (Pa); \( \sigma_Y \) = uniaxial yield stress (Pa)
Tresca yield condition in stress difference form
tips: Keep track of which form you use: the shear form has \( \sigma_Y/2 \) on the right, the stress-difference form has \( \sigma_Y \).
Always take the maximum of the three differences using the largest and smallest principal stresses; the order of \( \sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 \) must be consistent.
rq: Why is the Tresca criterion expressed using differences between principal stresses rather than the stresses themselves?
Shear stress is driven by stress differences; hydrostatic (equal all-round) stress causes no shear and so does not promote yielding.
Why does the shear form divide by 2 while the stress-difference form does not?
Maximum shear stress is half the maximum principal stress difference, so \( \tau_Y = \sigma_Y/2 \).

notes.t: Tresca criterion: maximum principal stress difference from 3D stress state
pts: Tresca yield criterion uses the largest difference between principal stresses; the candidate pairs are σ1−σ2, σ2−σ3 and σ1−σ3, and the largest is identified.
For this stress state σ1−σ2 = 4T/(πr³) is the largest difference, so it governs the Tresca check.
Principal stresses are ordered so that σ1 is the largest and σ3 the smallest, so differences are taken as larger minus smaller.
defs: Maximum shear stress (Tresca) criterion
Yielding occurs when the maximum difference between principal stresses reaches the yield stress in simple tension; the largest of |σ1−σ2|, |σ2−σ3|, |σ1−σ3| is compared with σ_y.
Principal stresses
Normal stresses acting on planes where shear stress is zero; for a 3D state they are labelled σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3.
eqs: Maximum principal stress difference (Tresca, from σ1−σ2)
σ1, σ2 = principal stresses (Pa); T = applied torque (N·m); r = shaft radius (m)
σ2, σ3 = principal stresses (Pa); T = torque (N·m); r = radius (m)
σ1, σ3 = principal stresses (Pa); T = torque (N·m); r = radius (m)
tips: Compare all three principal stress differences and take the largest in magnitude; do not assume σ1−σ3 is the largest just because it involves the extreme stresses.
Watch signs when subtracting a negative stress: σ1−σ2 = 2T/πr³ − (−2T/πr³) = 4T/πr³, not 0.
rq: Why is σ1−σ2 chosen rather than σ1−σ3, even though both involve σ1?
Because σ2 is negative (−2T/πr³) and σ3 is zero, so σ1−σ2 = 4T/πr³ is larger than σ1−σ3 = 2T/πr³ and it governs yielding.
What would happen to the maximum difference if the stress state were purely hydrostatic (σ1=σ2=σ3)?
All differences would be zero, so the Tresca criterion predicts no yielding, consistent with hydrostatic pressure not causing shear-driven yield.

notes.t: Tresca yield criterion applied to maximum torque in a circular shaft
pts: Tresca yield criterion: yield starts when the maximum principal stress difference equals the yield stress in simple tension.
For a solid circular shaft in torsion, the shear stress relation gives the yield condition in terms of applied torque T and radius r.
Rearranging the yield condition makes T the subject, giving the maximum torque that can be applied before yield.
defs: Tresca yield criterion
Yield initiates when the maximum principal stress difference equals the yield stress in simple tension.
eqs: Tresca yield condition for a solid circular shaft in torsion (yield point)
\(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa); T = applied torque (N·m); r = shaft radius (m)
T = maximum torque (N·m); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa); r = shaft radius (m)
tips: Use SI units: convert radius from mm to m before cubing, otherwise the torque is wrong by orders of magnitude.
The result T ≈ 2120.58 N·m applies only while the shaft is elastic; the formula assumes a solid circular section under pure torsion.
rq: Why must the radius be converted from mm to m before substituting into T = σ_Y π r³ / 4?
SI units are needed for consistency: r = 15 × 10⁻³ m, so r³ is in m³ and the result is in N·m; using mm would give a wrong torque by a factor of 10⁹.
What would happen to the maximum torque if the shaft radius doubled?
Since T is proportional to r³, doubling r multiplies the maximum torque by 8.

notes.t: Von Mises yield criterion applied to a torsion-loaded shaft
pts: The von Mises criterion compares the principal stress differences to twice the square of the yield stress; yielding begins when the combined squared differences reach that value.
For a shaft in pure torsion the principal stresses are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so the stress state is σ1 = τ, σ2 = 0, σ3 = −τ with τ = 2T/(πr³).
Substituting the principal stresses gives the common term 2T/(πr³) squared, which sums to 6 times that term squared on the left-hand side.
defs: Von Mises yield criterion
A failure criterion stating that yielding occurs when the distortion energy reaches the value for uniaxial yield, written as (σ1−σ2)² + (σ2−σ3)² + (σ3−σ1)² = 2σY².
eqs: Von Mises yield condition in principal stresses
Shear stress in a solid circular shaft under torque
\(\tau\) = shear stress (Pa); \(T\) = applied torque (N·m); \(r\) = shaft radius (m)
Reduced von Mises form for pure torsion
tips: Keep the factor of 2 in 2σY² on the right-hand side; forgetting it gives an incorrect yield torque.
Check that the shear stress uses the radius r cubed (r³) and that T is in N·m so stresses come out in Pa.
rq: Why do the principal stresses for pure torsion come out as +τ, 0, −τ rather than all positive?
Pure shear is equivalent to equal tension and compression on planes at 45°, so the principal stresses are equal and opposite, with the intermediate principal stress zero.
Why does the von Mises expression need squared differences rather than simple differences?
Squaring removes the sign of each difference so the criterion depends only on magnitude, making it independent of stress direction and giving a symmetric yield surface.

notes.t: Maximum torque from von Mises yield criterion (shaft)
pts: For a solid shaft in torsion, the von Mises criterion is met when the equivalent stress reaches the yield stress; the shear stress from torque T is \( \tau = \frac{2T}{\pi r^3} \), so \( \left(\frac{2T}{\pi r^3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{3}\sigma_Y^2 \) at yield.
Rearranging gives the maximum torque by solving for T, where the \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \) factor converts yield stress into a shear yield stress.
Substituting radius and yield stress values into the final expression gives the maximum allowable torque in newton-metres.
eqs: Shear stress in a solid circular shaft under torque (rearranged to torque at yield via von Mises)
\(T\) = maximum torque (N·m); \(r\) = shaft radius (m); \(\sigma_Y\) = yield stress (Pa)
von Mises yield condition for torsion of a solid shaft
tips: Keep units consistent: convert radius from mm to m (15 mm = 15 × 10⁻³ m) and stress from MPa to Pa before substituting, otherwise T is wrong by orders of magnitude.
Remember the von Mises shear factor \( 1/\sqrt{3} \) applies to torsion; do not use the plain tensile yield stress directly.
rq: Why does the von Mises criterion give a torque limit involving \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \) rather than the full yield stress?
In pure shear the von Mises equivalent stress is \( \sqrt{3}\tau \), so yield occurs when \( \tau = \sigma_Y/\sqrt{3} \), i.e. shear yield is about 0.577 of tensile yield.
What would happen to the maximum torque if the shaft radius doubled?
Torque scales with \( r^3 \), so it would increase by a factor of 8.

notes.t: Torsion of shafts: Tresca vs von Mises yield torque comparison
pts: Tresca yield criterion gives a lower maximum allowable torque (2120.58 Nm) than von Mises (2448.63 Nm) for the same shaft.
Von Mises permits roughly 15% higher torque before yield starts, so Tresca is the more conservative criterion.
If expected torques approach these levels, further analytical or experimental investigation is prudent.
Design should use a maximum shear stress that sits a factor of safety below the Tresca or von Mises limit.
eqs: Ratio of von Mises to Tresca yield torque, used to check the ~15% difference
\(T_{vM}\) = von Mises yield torque (N·m); \(T_{Tresca}\) = Tresca yield torque (N·m)
tips: Always design against the more conservative (Tresca) limit and apply a factor of safety; do not design right at the yield torque.
Keep torque units consistent (N·m) when comparing criteria, and remember the ~15% difference is relative to the Tresca value.
rq: Why does the Tresca criterion give a lower allowable torque than von Mises for the same shaft?
Tresca is based on the maximum shear stress (the largest principal stress difference), which reaches yield earlier than the von Mises distortion-energy criterion under pure torsion.
What would you change in the design if the expected torque were close to the Tresca limit?
Apply a factor of safety below the Tresca limit, and consider further analysis or experimental testing before accepting the design.
