units.name: 14.1 Fracture & failure: stress-strain curve properties
units.ov: This module introduces how the shape of a stress-strain curve describes a material's mechanical behaviour before fracture. Stiffness comes from the elastic slope, strength from the stress level reached, and ductility from the plastic strain before failure. Toughness and resilience are energy-per-volume measures taken from areas under the curve, so they combine strength and ductility (toughness) or strength and stiffness (resilience).
must: Stiffness = gradient of the initial linear elastic region, \(E=\sigma/\varepsilon\); steep means stiff, shallow means flexible
Strength = stress a material can sustain before failure (height of the curve); it is not the same as stiffness, so a material can be strong but flexible, or stiff but weak
Ductile = large plastic strain between yield and fracture; brittle = little or no plastic deformation, judged from the post-yield region and not the elastic slope
Toughness = total area under the stress-strain curve up to fracture, the energy absorbed per unit volume; strong and ductile means tough
Resilience = area under the elastic portion only, \(U_r=\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_y\varepsilon_y=\sigma_y^2/2E\); the energy recovered on unloading
Units of toughness and resilience are energy per unit volume, \(\mathrm{J/m^3}\) (equivalent to Pa), found as the area of stress × strain, not stress units used as a measure of strength
High resilience needs high yield strength and low stiffness (flexible but strong, e.g. springs), since \(U_r\propto\sigma_y^2/E\)
Compare curves systematically: slope (stiffness), peak stress (strength), strain at fracture (ductility), total area (toughness), elastic area (resilience)
A brittle material can be strong and stiff yet have low toughness because the area under its curve is small
conn: Toughness combines strength and ductility, so a strong but brittle material (ceramic) can be less tough than a moderately strong ductile metal
Resilience links stiffness and strength through \(\sigma_y^2/2E\): raising yield stress increases it, raising E reduces it
Ductile versus brittle behaviour determines the failure mode (necking and warning versus sudden fracture), which feeds into later fracture and design topics
Reading a curve connects graphical features to definitions: gradient gives E, height gives strength, areas give energies
exq: Three stress-strain curves A, B and C are sketched. Rank them by stiffness, strength, ductility, toughness and resilience, justifying each ranking from the graph.
A material has E = 200 GPa and yield stress 400 MPa. Calculate its resilience in \(\mathrm{MJ/m^3}\) and the volume of material needed to absorb 50 J elastically.
Explain why a material can be strong but not stiff, and give a sketch of two curves illustrating this.
Estimate the toughness of a ductile material from a simplified curve (linear elastic up to 300 MPa at strain 0.002, then plateau at 400 MPa to strain 0.25). State the units.
Define ductile and brittle and explain why elastic slope cannot be used to classify them. Which of the two is likely to be tougher, and why?

notes.t: Possible stress-strain curves: stiffness, ductility, strength, toughness, resilience
pts: Stiffness is the slope of the initial linear (elastic) part of the curve; a steep slope means a stiff material.
Ductile materials undergo large plastic strain (curve keeps rising/flattens gradually) before fracture, whereas brittle materials fail with little or no plastic deformation.
Strength is the stress level reached (height of the curve); a weak material fails at a low stress.
Toughness is the area under the whole stress-strain curve (energy absorbed to fracture), so a strong and ductile material is tough.
Resilience is the energy stored per unit volume up to the elastic limit (area under the initial linear portion); flexible materials with low stiffness and high strength are resilient.
defs: Stiff
A material with a steep initial elastic slope, i.e. large stress needed for a given small strain (high modulus of elasticity).
Flexible
A material with a shallow initial elastic slope, i.e. undergoes large elastic strain for a small stress (low modulus).
Ductile
Able to undergo significant plastic deformation before fracture.
Brittle
Fractures with little or no plastic deformation after the elastic region.
Toughness
Ability to absorb energy before fracture, equal to the total area under the stress-strain curve.
Resilience
Ability to absorb elastic strain energy without permanent deformation, equal to the area under the elastic portion of the curve.
tips: Do not confuse strength (peak stress) with stiffness (slope of elastic region); a curve can be strong but flexible.
Toughness and resilience are energies per unit volume, so their units are J/m³ (area under curve), not stress units like Pa.
rq: Why can a stiff, strong material still have low toughness?
If it is brittle, its stress-strain curve ends soon after the elastic region, so the area under the curve (energy absorbed) is small despite high strength.
Two materials have the same yield stress, but one is flexible and one is stiff. Which stores more elastic energy per unit volume before yielding, and why?
The flexible one, because resilience is the area under the elastic portion, and a lower modulus allows a larger strain at the same stress, giving more area.

notes.t: Possible stress-strain curves: stiffness, strength and ductility
pts: Stiffness is read from the gradient of the stress-strain curve in the elastic region; a steep gradient means stiff, a shallow one means flexible.
Strength is the stress a material can carry before it breaks, so strong materials sustain higher stress before fracture than weak ones.
Ductile materials undergo large plastic deformation between yield and fracture, whereas brittle materials show little or no yield behaviour before failing.
Ductility/brittleness is judged from post-yield behaviour, not from elastic stiffness or strength.
defs: Stiffness
The resistance of a material to elastic deformation, given by the gradient of the linear elastic part of the stress-strain curve.
Strength
The magnitude of stress a material can withstand before it fractures.
Ductile
A material that deforms plastically to a large extent between yield and fracture.
Brittle
A material that fractures with little or no yielding or plastic deformation.
tips: Do not confuse strength (stress at fracture) with stiffness (elastic gradient); a stiff material is not necessarily strong.
Ductile and brittle are classified by behaviour after yield, so judge them from the plastic region of the curve, not the elastic slope.
rq: Why can a material be stiff yet weak, and what would the stress-strain curve look like?

Stiffness depends on the elastic gradient while strength depends on the stress at fracture; a material can have a steep elastic slope but fracture at a low stress, so the curve rises steeply then ends early.
If two materials have identical elastic gradients, does it follow that they have the same ductility?
No. Ductility is determined by post-yield behaviour, so materials with the same stiffness can differ greatly in how much they deform between yield and fracture.

units.name: 14.2 Ductile vs brittle fracture and cup-and-cone surfaces
units.ov: This material contrasts ductile and brittle fracture in tension, using the amount of plastic deformation before failure, the presence of necking, and the appearance of the fracture surface as the main indicators. Ductile metals neck and then fail by cup-and-cone fracture, which combines central void coalescence with outer shear lips. Brittle materials fail suddenly, with a flat surface and often multiple fragments. The ideas connect through energy absorption: the more plastic work done, the more ductile the failure and the more warning it gives.
must: Ductility is the capacity for significant plastic deformation (elongation and necking) before fracture. The amount of plastic yielding before failure is the key indicator of ductile versus brittle behaviour.

Brittle fracture occurs with little or no plastic deformation and no visible necking. It is sudden, and the crack propagates rapidly after initiation. It gives little warning, so it is the more dangerous mode in design.
Necking is a localised reduction in cross-sectional area. It begins after the ultimate tensile stress (UTS) and precedes ductile fracture. It is not the onset of yield.
Cup-and-cone fracture is the characteristic ductile fracture morphology. It has mating cup-shaped and cone-shaped surfaces and is a visible signature of large plastic deformation.
Cup-and-cone sequence: necking, then internal voids nucleate, grow and coalesce at the neck centre. This forms a flat central region perpendicular to the load. The crack then spreads outward.
The outer lips of a cup-and-cone fracture fail in shear at about 45° to the loading axis. The centre fails perpendicular to the load.
Brittle fracture surfaces are flat and show little deformation. Identify the fracture mode from the surface appearance.

Ductile fracture usually gives a single fracture surface. One crack relieves stress elsewhere, and the energy goes into plastic deformation and crack propagation. Brittle fracture often gives multiple fragments.
Medium-ductility materials show some necking and a jagged or cup-like surface. Ductility is a spectrum, not a binary property.
Strength and ductility are independent. 'Brittle' does not mean 'weak', so consider them separately.
conn: Stress-strain curve and necking: necking starts after the UTS, so the engineering stress falls while local true stress rises. The elongation and reduction in area measured after fracture quantify ductility.

Energy absorption and fracture surface: large plastic work gives a single cup-and-cone surface. Little plastic work and rapid crack propagation give flat surfaces and multiple fragments. This links to toughness and impact testing.
Microscopic and macroscopic mechanisms: void nucleation, growth and coalescence in the centre, and 45° shear at the edges (maximum shear stress), explain the cup-and-cone geometry.
Design and safety: the failure mode determines whether there is warning before failure, which drives material selection and safety factors.
exq: Describe, with labelled sketches, the stages leading to cup-and-cone fracture in a ductile tensile specimen. State the mechanism in the central region and at the outer lips, and the angle of the lips to the load axis.

Compare ductile and brittle fracture in terms of plastic deformation, necking, fracture surface appearance, number of fragments, energy absorbed and warning before failure. Explain why brittle failure is more dangerous in design.
A tensile specimen fails with a flat surface perpendicular to the load and no visible necking. Identify the fracture mode and justify it. Does this tell you the material is weak? Explain.

A specimen of original diameter 10 mm has a neck diameter of 6 mm at fracture. Calculate the percentage reduction in area and comment on the ductility. Where on the stress-strain curve does necking begin?
Explain why the outer region of a cup-and-cone fracture fails at about 45° while the centre fails perpendicular to the load, and why ductile fracture typically yields a single fracture surface.

notes.t: Types of fracture
pts: Ductile materials neck down to a point before failing, showing large plastic deformation.
Medium ductility materials show some necking and a cup-like or jagged fracture surface before failure.
Brittle materials fracture with almost no plastic deformation and no visible necking, separating cleanly across the section.
The amount of plastic yielding before fracture is an important indicator of how ductile or brittle a material is.
defs: Ductility
The ability of a material to undergo significant plastic deformation (necking/elongation) before fracture under tensile loading.
Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a specimen under tension, occurring after the ultimate tensile stress, which precedes ductile fracture.
Brittle fracture
Fracture occurring with little or no plastic deformation, typically sudden and with the specimen separating without necking.
tips: Do not confuse necking with yielding: necking is a geometric localisation of deformation that occurs after the ultimate tensile stress, not the onset of yield.
Brittle fracture does not mean a material is weak; it refers to limited plastic deformation before failure, so strength and ductility must be considered separately.
rq: Why is a ductile fracture generally considered safer in engineering structures than a brittle one?
Ductile materials yield and deform visibly before failing, giving warning and allowing stress redistribution, whereas brittle materials fail suddenly without warning.
What observable features distinguish the three fracture types in a tensile test?
Highly ductile: strong necking to a point; medium ductility: partial necking with a jagged centre; brittle: flat, square-ended fracture with no necking.

notes.t: Fracture surfaces: cup and cone fractures in ductile materials
pts: Ductile materials typically fail by a cup and cone fracture: the fracture starts in the centre of the neck and propagates outward, producing a cup-shaped surface on one piece and a matching cone-shaped surface on the other.

The cup and cone shape is a visible signature of substantial plastic deformation before final failure, distinguishing ductile fracture from brittle fracture, which shows little deformation and a flat surface.
defs: Cup and cone fracture

A ductile fracture morphology in which the central region fails by internal void growth and coalescence, followed by shear fracture at roughly 45° to the load axis at the outer edge, giving mating cup-shaped and cone-shaped surfaces.
tips: Do not confuse the cup and cone fracture (ductile) with the flat fracture surface of brittle materials; identify the fracture mode from the surface appearance.
The outer cone region fails in shear at about 45° to the loading axis, not perpendicular to it; the centre fails perpendicular to the load.
rq: Why does a ductile specimen form a cup and cone shape rather than breaking cleanly flat across the section?

Necking concentrates plastic deformation; voids nucleate and grow in the highly stressed centre, which then coalesce and the final failure occurs by shear at about 45° at the outer surface, creating the cup and cone.
What would you expect the fracture surface to look like for a brittle material such as glass, and why?
A flat, smooth surface perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress, because brittle fracture propagates rapidly by cleavage with negligible plastic deformation.

notes.t: Fracture surfaces: cup and cone
pts: Cup and cone fracture forms after necking in a ductile metal, with the fracture surface showing both shear and void-based failure.
The fracture surface combines a shear direction with voids that nucleate, grow and join up to form the crack.
The central flat region is formed by void growth and coalescence, while the outer lips are shear failure at roughly 45° to the loading axis.
defs: Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a ductile specimen under tensile load, occurring after the ultimate tensile stress is reached, which precedes cup and cone fracture.
tips: Cup and cone is a feature of ductile fracture; do not confuse it with the flat, brittle fracture surface.
Remember the fracture pattern appears after necking, not before it.
rq: Why does a ductile metal fail with a cup and cone shape rather than a flat, brittle fracture?

Necking concentrates plastic deformation; voids nucleate in the necked centre and coalesce into a central crack, which then grows outward and finishes by shear at the edges, giving the cup and cone profile.
What would you expect the fracture surface to look like for a brittle material, and why is it different?
Flat and smooth, with little or no necking or plastic deformation, since brittle materials cleave along crystal planes without void growth or shear lips.

notes.t: Ductile vs Brittle fracture
pts: Ductile fracture generally produces a single fracture surface, because initiating one crack relieves stress elsewhere in the component.
Energy absorbed during ductile fracture is used up propagating the crack, so less energy remains available to nucleate additional cracks.
The image shows a ductile fracture in a tensile specimen: large plastic deformation and necking before the fracture surface forms.
defs: Ductile fracture
Fracture preceded by significant plastic deformation, typically producing a single fracture surface with energy absorbed in both deformation and crack propagation.
tips: Do not confuse ductile fracture (large plastic deformation, single surface) with brittle fracture (little deformation, multiple cracks); the distinction is the energy absorbed.
rq: Why does ductile fracture usually produce only one fracture surface rather than many cracks?
Once one crack initiates, it relieves the stress in the surrounding material, so stresses elsewhere drop below the level needed to nucleate other cracks.
What would happen to the number of fracture surfaces if the energy consumed by crack propagation were not absorbed by the material?
More energy would remain available to initiate additional cracks, so multiple fracture surfaces could form, as is more typical of brittle failure.

notes.t: Ductile vs Brittle Fracture
pts: Once a brittle crack is initiated, it propagates rapidly through the material with little plastic deformation.
Brittle fracture typically produces multiple fracture surfaces, as the component breaks into several separate pieces.
defs: Brittle fracture
Fracture of a material with little or no plastic deformation, occurring suddenly after crack initiation and propagating rapidly, often yielding multiple fragments.
tips: Do not confuse brittle fracture with ductile fracture: brittle failure shows little warning and little plastic deformation, so it is more dangerous in design.
rq: Why does a brittle material fracture into many separate pieces rather than stretching before failure?
Because once a crack starts it runs very quickly with little plastic deformation to absorb energy, so the material shatters along multiple fracture surfaces.

units.name: 14.3 Griffith's theory of fracture
units.ov: Griffith's theory treats brittle fracture as an energy balance. Elastic strain energy released from the material around a crack pays for the surface energy of the two new crack faces. Setting d\(U\)/d\(c\) = 0 gives a critical crack length, or equivalently a fracture stress \(\sigma \propto 1/\sqrt{c}\). The simple unstressed-cylinder model overestimates the stress by \(\sqrt{2}\), and a refined calculation corrects this.
must: Energy balance: crack growth is possible only when the strain energy released is at least the surface energy needed. The released elastic energy is not the same quantity as the surface energy consumed.
Elastic energy released (simple model, unstressed cylinder of radius \(c\)): \(U_E=-\frac{\pi c^2 t\sigma^2}{2E}\). It scales as \(c^2\) and \(\sigma^2\).
Surface energy: \(U_s=4ct\gamma_s\), from two faces × length \(2c\) × thickness \(t\) × \(\gamma_s\) in J/m². It scales linearly with \(c\).

Total energy \(U=U_E+U_s\), so \(\frac{dU}{dc}=-\frac{\pi c t\sigma^2}{E}+4t\gamma_s\). The crack grows spontaneously once \(dU/dc\) reaches zero and the total energy would fall with further extension. Note that the notes' '\(dU/dc\ge 0\)' wording is muddled. \(U\) is at a maximum at the critical length, so the equilibrium is unstable.
Critical crack length (simple model): \(2c=\frac{8\gamma_s E}{\pi\sigma^2}\). Cracks longer than this grow, and a higher \(\sigma\) gives a shorter critical crack.
Simple Griffith fracture stress: \(\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{4\gamma_s E}{\pi c}}\). Longer cracks fracture at lower stress, with \(\sigma\propto c^{-1/2}\).
Refined, accurate result (use this in calculations): \(\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma_s E}{\pi c}}\). The simple version is too high by \(\sqrt{2}\), about 41%.

Define \(c\) carefully: it is the half-length of an internal crack (full length \(2c\)) or the full length of a surface crack. Using the wrong one gives a \(\sqrt{2}\) error, or a factor of 2 in length.
Check units: \(\gamma_s\) in J/m², \(E\) and \(\sigma\) in Pa, and \(c\), \(t\) in m. Use \(\sigma\), not strain \(\varepsilon=\sigma/E\), in \(U_E\).
Derivation route: write \(U_E\) and \(U_s\), differentiate with respect to \(c\), set the result to zero, and rearrange for \(c\) or \(\sigma\).
conn: Hooke's law and strain energy density link to fracture. \(\sigma^2/2E\) per unit volume multiplied by the cylinder volume \(\pi c^2 t\) gives \(U_E\).
Energy minimisation and calculus link to fracture. Setting \(dU/dc=0\) gives the critical crack length, and the sign of \(dU/dc\) shows whether the crack grows or is stable.
Material properties set strength. A high \(E\gamma_s\) means high fracture stress, which explains why brittle ceramics and glass are weak in tension despite strong bonds, because flaws dominate.
Design and inspection link to fracture. The largest flaw an inspection can miss sets the allowable stress, and a given working stress sets the maximum tolerable flaw size.
exq: Derive Griffith's critical stress \(\sigma=\sqrt{4\gamma_s E/(\pi c)}\) from the elastic energy released \(U_E\) and the surface energy \(U_s\). State the energy criterion for crack growth and explain whether the critical point is a maximum or a minimum of \(U\).

A glass plate (\(E=70\) GPa, \(\gamma_s=1\) J/m²) has an internal crack of length 2c = 20 µm. Calculate the fracture stress using the refined Griffith formula and compare it with the simple formula. What is the percentage difference?

For a steel with \(E=200\) GPa and \(\gamma_s=2\) J/m² under an applied stress of 100 MPa, find the critical internal crack length using \(2c=8\gamma_s E/(\pi\sigma^2)\). How does it change if the stress doubles?

Explain why a surface crack of length c has the same Griffith fracture stress as an internal crack of length 2c. Then compare the stress needed to fracture a material with a 50 µm surface crack and one with a 50 µm internal crack.
Explain why the simple Griffith model, with its unstressed cylinder around the crack, overestimates the fracture stress. By what factor is it wrong, and how does the refined equation differ?

notes.t: Fracture: energy balance for creating fracture surfaces
pts: A fracture creates two new fracture surfaces, so it always involves forming new surface area.
Forming new surfaces costs energy, which must be supplied for crack growth to occur.
The energy needed for new surfaces is supplied by elastic strain energy released from the stressed material as the crack grows.
tips: Do not confuse the surface energy consumed in fracture with the elastic strain energy that is released; the balance is between the two.
rq: Why must elastic strain energy be released for a crack to grow, rather than simply being stored?
Crack growth creates new surface area, which requires energy; releasing stored elastic energy supplies this, and if enough is released the crack can propagate.

notes.t: Fracture - Griffith's theory
pts: Griffith's model considers a plate of thickness t containing a crack of length 2c under applied stress σ.
Around the crack there is an unloaded cylindrical region of diameter 2c and length t, where the stress is relieved.
The theory was originally described by Griffith in 1922 and forms the basis of brittle fracture analysis.
tips: Do not confuse the crack length 2c with the half-length c; the diagram labels the full crack as 2c and the half-length as c.
rq: Why does the unloaded cylindrical region around the crack matter for the energy balance in Griffith's theory?
Stress relief in that region releases elastic strain energy, which is available to create new crack surface; this energy release drives crack growth when it exceeds the surface energy cost.

notes.t: Fracture - Griffith's theory
pts: Releasing a crack in a stressed body frees elastic strain energy stored in the cylinder of material around it, which drives crack growth.
Creating new crack surfaces costs surface energy, proportional to crack length and thickness, so crack growth requires energy input.
For a crack to grow, the rate of change of energy with crack length must increase, i.e. the energy balance favours extension when the released elastic energy exceeds the surface energy cost.
defs: Surface energy (γ_s)
The energy per unit area required to create a new surface in a material, stored at the newly formed crack faces.
eqs: Elastic energy released by the crack (volume × area under force-extension curve)
\(U_E\) = elastic energy released (J); \(c\) = half crack length (m); \(t\) = specimen thickness (m); \(\sigma\) = applied stress (Pa); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa)
Surface energy required to create the crack surfaces
\(U_s\) = surface energy (J); \(c\) = half crack length (m); \(t\) = thickness (m); \(\gamma_s\) = surface energy per unit area (J/m²)
tips: Keep consistent units: \(\gamma_s\) is in J/m², so \(U_s = 4ct\gamma_s\) gives J only if \(c\) and \(t\) are in metres.
The stress in \(U_E\) is the applied stress σ; do not confuse it with the strain ε, which equals σ/E.
rq: Why does the elastic energy term carry a negative sign, and what does this imply for the energy balance of the cracked body?
The released elastic energy reduces the total stored energy of the body as the crack grows, so it is a loss from the system that provides the energy available to create the new surfaces.
If crack length c doubles at constant stress, how do \(U_{E}\) and \(U_{s}\) change, and which term grows faster?
\(U_{E}\) scales with c² (it quadruples), while \(U_{s}\) scales with c (it doubles), so the elastic energy term changes more rapidly with crack length.

notes.t: Fracture - Griffith's theory
pts: Griffith's energy balance: total energy change of a cracked plate is the elastic energy released (negative term) plus the surface energy created by the crack (positive term).
The crack grows only when the change in total energy with crack half-length is non-negative, i.e. dU/dc ≥ 0.
Setting dU/dc = 0 gives the critical crack length, below which the crack will not spontaneously propagate; a higher applied stress σ gives a shorter critical crack.
defs: Critical crack length
The crack length at which the total energy of the system stops decreasing with crack growth (dU/dc = 0); cracks longer than this grow spontaneously under the applied stress.
eqs: Derivative of total energy with respect to half-crack length (energy balance)

\(U\) = total potential energy (J); \(c\) = half crack length (m); \(t\) = plate thickness (m); \(\sigma\) = applied stress (Pa); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy per unit area (J/m²)
Critical crack length for crack growth
\(2c\) = critical crack length (m); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy (J/m²); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa); \(\sigma\) = applied stress (Pa)
tips: Be careful to distinguish half-crack length c from full crack length 2c; the critical crack length formula is quoted for 2c.
Keep units consistent: surface energy in J/m², E and σ in Pa, so 2c comes out in metres.
rq: Why does the elastic energy term carry a negative sign while the surface energy term is positive?

Creating a crack releases stored elastic strain energy (energy decreases, negative contribution, proportional to c²), whereas creating new crack surfaces requires energy input (positive contribution, proportional to c).
What happens to the critical crack length if the applied stress is doubled?
It falls by a factor of four, since 2c is inversely proportional to σ²; higher stress allows smaller flaws to grow.

notes.t: Fracture - Griffith's theory (surface cracks)
pts: Griffith's analysis can be applied equally to a surface crack of length c, so the same fracture criterion holds for surface flaws.
Fracture stress depends on crack length: longer cracks fracture at lower applied stress, since σ falls as c increases.
The stated result covers both an internal crack of length 2c and a surface crack of length c, so the same formula applies to either geometry when c is defined consistently.
eqs: Griffith fracture stress for a crack of length 2c (or surface crack of length c)
\sigma = fracture stress (Pa); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy per unit area (J/\(m^{2}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa); c = half-length of internal crack or length of surface crack (m)
tips: Keep track of whether c denotes the half-length of an internal crack or the full length of a surface crack; mixing them up changes the answer by a factor of √2.
Check units consistently: γs in J/m² and E in Pa give σ in Pa when c is in metres.
rq: Why does a surface crack of length c give the same fracture stress as an internal crack of length 2c?

Because a surface crack is effectively half of an internal crack of length 2c; the surface crack relieves stress on only one side, so its critical length is half and the formula is the same with c as the defining length.
What happens to the fracture stress if the crack length doubles?
It falls by a factor of √2, since σ is proportional to 1/√c.

notes.t: Fracture - Griffith's theory (refined)
pts: Griffith's simple energy-balance assumption of an unstressed zone around a crack is an oversimplification, so the basic result is only approximate.
A more accurate calculation gives a relationship between fracture stress, surface energy, Young's modulus and crack length.
The simplistic version of the Griffith result overestimates the fracture stress by a factor of √2 (about 41% too high).
defs: Surface energy (γ_s)
The energy required per unit area to create a new surface, which is the energy term balanced against elastic strain energy released in Griffith's crack theory.
eqs: Griffith fracture stress (refined, more accurate calculation)
\sigma = fracture stress (Pa); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy (J \(m^{-2}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa); c = half-length of an internal crack (m)
tips: Remember the simple Griffith result overestimates strength by √2; use the corrected form 2γ_sE/(πc) under the square root in exam calculations.
Keep units consistent: γ_s in J m⁻² and E in Pa give σ in Pa, and c is the half-length of an internal crack, not the full length.
rq: Why does the simplistic Griffith expression overestimate the fracture stress, and by how much?
Its assumption of a simple unstressed region around the crack is too crude; the accurate calculation shows the simple result is too high by a factor of √2 (≈41%).
If the crack length c doubles, what happens to the predicted fracture stress?
Since σ ∝ 1/√c, the fracture stress falls by a factor of √2, so larger flaws make materials weaker.

units.name: 14.4 Stress intensity factor and fracture toughness
units.ov: This material introduces the stress intensity factor K, which combines applied stress and crack length, and compares it with the material property fracture toughness \(K_{c}\) to predict brittle fracture. It also introduces toughness \(G_{c}\), the energy absorbed per unit crack area, as a second, energy-based measure of fracture resistance. Fracture occurs when K reaches \(K_{c}\), so the ideas link loading, flaw size and material choice.
must: Stress intensity factor for a crack of length a under stress σ: \( K = \sigma\sqrt{\pi a} \)
Fracture criterion: fracture occurs when \( K = K_c \); there is no fracture while \( K < K_c \)
Fracture toughness \( K_c \) is the critical stress intensity factor, the value of K at which a crack becomes unstable. It is a material property in MPa \( m^{1/2} \)
Toughness \( G_c \) is the critical strain energy release rate, the energy absorbed per unit area of crack created, in kJ \( m^{-2} \)
K has units MPa \( m^{1/2} \) (equivalently MN \( m^{-3/2} \)). Do not confuse it with stress in MPa
\( G_c \) and \( K_c \) are different measures and cannot be interchanged without a relation between them
K rises with both stress and the square root of crack length, so doubling a gives a factor of \( \sqrt{2} \) increase in K
Rearrange the criterion for design: critical stress \( \sigma_c = K_c/\sqrt{\pi a} \) and critical crack length \( a_c = K_c^2/(\pi\sigma^2) \)
Use consistent units: convert crack length to metres and stress to MPa so that K comes out in MPa \( m^{1/2} \)
conn: Stress and crack length combine in K, which is compared with \( K_c \). A question may give two of σ, a and \( K_c \) and ask for the third, for example the maximum safe stress or the largest tolerable flaw
Material selection links \( K_c \) to design: a higher \( K_c \) allows larger flaws or higher stresses before fracture, which ties to inspection limits on detectable crack size

\( G_c \) (energy) and \( K_c \) (stress-based) describe the same fracture event from two viewpoints. Questions may ask you to explain why they have different units and are not directly interchangeable
Fracture (K compared with \( K_c \)) competes with yield (σ compared with the yield stress). The lower of the two failure stresses governs
exq: A plate contains a crack of length 2 mm and carries a stress of 200 MPa. Calculate K using \( K=\sigma\sqrt{\pi a} \) and state whether fracture occurs if \( K_c = 30 \) MPa \( m^{1/2} \).
A component with \( K_c = 50 \) MPa \( m^{1/2} \) works at 250 MPa. Find the critical crack length \( a_c \), and the new \( a_c \) if the stress is increased by 20%.
Define toughness \( G_c \) and fracture toughness \( K_c \). State their units and explain why one cannot be substituted for the other.
Two materials have \( K_c \) of 25 and 60 MPa \( m^{1/2} \). For a given crack of 1 mm, compare the maximum stresses each can carry before fracture.
Explain why K is quoted in MPa \( m^{1/2} \) and not MPa, and show how the units arise from \( \sigma\sqrt{\pi a} \).

notes.t: Factors calculated: stress intensity factor and fracture toughness
pts: The stress intensity factor K is calculated from applied stress and crack length, with units MN \(m^{-3/2}\) or MPa \(m^{1/2}\).
Two measures describe a material's resistance to fracture: toughness \(G_{c}\) and fracture toughness \(K_{c}\).
Toughness \(G_{c}\) (critical strain energy release rate) is the energy absorbed per unit area of crack created, in kJ \(m^{-2}\).
Fracture toughness \(K_{c}\) (critical stress intensity factor) is the material property that controls fracture, in MPa \(m^{1/2}\).
Fracture occurs when the calculated stress intensity factor reaches the material's critical value.
defs: Toughness (\(G_{c}\))
Critical strain energy release rate: the energy absorbed in creating a unit area of crack, measured in kJ \(m^{-2}\).
Fracture toughness (\(K_{c}\))
Critical stress intensity factor: the value of K at which a crack becomes unstable and the material fractures, in MPa \(m^{1/2}\).
eqs: Stress intensity factor for a crack of length a under stress σ
K = stress intensity factor (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); σ = applied stress (MPa); a = crack length (m)
K = applied stress intensity factor (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); \(K_{c}\) = fracture toughness (MPa \(m^{1/2}\))
tips: Stress intensity factor units are MPa \(m^{1/2}\) (equivalently MN \(m^{-3/2}\)); do not confuse with stress in MPa.
Note that \(G_{c}\) (kJ \(m^{-2}\)) and \(K_{c}\) (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)) are different measures of toughness and are not interchangeable without a relation between them.
rq: Why does a longer crack cause fracture at a lower applied stress?
Because K = σ√(πa) grows with crack length a, so a larger crack reaches the critical \(K_{c}\) at a smaller σ.
Two materials have the same \(K_{c}\). Which will fracture first under the same stress if one has a larger crack?
The one with the larger crack, since K = σ√(πa) is larger for the longer crack and reaches \(K_{c}\) first.

units.name: 14.5 Fracture surfaces: ductile dimples and brittle origins
units.ov: This material covers how fracture surfaces record the failure mechanism. Ductile fracture proceeds by necking, void nucleation at inclusions, void growth and linkage, then shearing to the surface. It leaves dimpled surfaces whose shape shows the local loading mode. Brittle fracture involves little plastic deformation and leaves flat faces with chevron/river markings that point back to the origin. Both are read from the surface: dimples give the local stress state, and chevrons give the crack direction and starting point.
must: Ductile fracture sequence: necking → void nucleation → void growth and linkage → shearing at the surface → final fracture
Voids nucleate at non-metallic inclusions or second-phase particles, by particle cracking or decohesion from the matrix
Dimple shape shows the local loading mode: equiaxed (round) dimples mean pure tension; elongated (oval) dimples mean shear or tensile tearing
Elongated dimples align with the shear or tearing direction, so tearing and shear can look similar; use the surrounding geometry to tell them apart
Cup-and-cone surface: a central fibrous region of linked voids surrounded by a shear lip, with the final shear at roughly 45° to the load axis
Necking is a geometric instability that starts after the ultimate tensile stress; it is not fracture, which only occurs after void linkage and shearing
Brittle failure: little or no plastic deformation before rupture; sudden and catastrophic, starting from a pre-existing flaw or stress concentration; flat fracture faces
Brittle fracture origin: chevron/river markings radiate back towards the initiation site and show the direction of crack growth
Ductile surfaces are dimpled; brittle surfaces are flat with cleavage facets. Never describe a dimpled steel surface as brittle
Dimple shape indicates the local stress state, not the magnitude of the load
conn: Stress–strain curve and fracture: necking begins at the UTS, and the void stages that follow explain the cup-and-cone surface and its shear lip
Fractography as diagnosis: combine dimple shape (loading mode), the dimpled vs flat morphology (ductile vs brittle), and chevron direction (origin) to reconstruct the failure
Microstructure and toughness: inclusions and second-phase particles control void nucleation, so they affect ductility, while flaws and stress concentrations govern brittle initiation
Load direction and geometry: tension, shear and tearing give different dimple shapes, so the surrounding geometry is needed to infer the loading mode
exq: List and explain, in order, the stages of ductile fracture in a tensile specimen. Where do the voids nucleate and why does the final shear occur at about 45°?

A fracture surface shows elongated, oval dimples all pointing the same way. What loading modes could cause this? What extra evidence would distinguish shear from tensile tearing, and how do these dimples differ from those formed in pure tension?
Sketch a cup-and-cone fracture and label the fibrous central region and the shear lip. Describe the microscopic features seen in each region.

A failed component shows a flat fracture surface with chevron markings. Explain how you would find the fracture origin and crack direction, and state what this suggests about plastic deformation and the failure type compared with a ductile failure.
Explain why necking is not the same as fracture. At what point on the stress–strain curve does necking begin, and what happens inside the neck before final failure?

notes.t: Direction of load and dimple shape in ductile fracture
pts: The direction of the applied load determines the shape of dimples on the fracture surface.
Pure tension produces equiaxed (round) dimples, as the void grows equally in all directions.
Shear loading stretches voids into oval/elongated dimples aligned with the shear direction.
Crack opening (tensile tearing) also produces elongated dimples, with the elongation following the tearing direction.
defs: Dimple
A bowl-shaped microscopic cavity on a ductile fracture surface formed by void nucleation, growth and coalescence; its shape reveals the local loading mode.
Equiaxed dimple
A round dimple formed under uniaxial tension, where the void grows equally in all directions.
Elongated dimple
An oval dimple formed under shear or tensile tearing, where voids are stretched along the loading direction.
tips: Don't confuse crack opening (tensile tearing) with pure tension: both can give elongated dimples, so the dimple shape alone doesn't always separate them; consider the surrounding geometry.
Dimple shape indicates the local stress state, not the overall load magnitude.
rq: Why does shear loading produce oval dimples rather than round ones?
Shear stretches the void along the shear direction, so the void and resulting dimple elongate instead of growing equally in all directions.
If you see round dimples on a fracture surface, what can you infer about the loading?
The fracture was dominated by tensile (normal) stress, with the void growing equally in all directions.

notes.t: Ductile Fracture
pts: Ductile failure proceeds through a sequence: necking, void nucleation, void growth and linkage, shearing at the surface, then final fracture.
Non-metallic particles (inclusions/second-phase particles) act as sites where voids nucleate, typically by particle cracking or decohesion from the matrix.
Voids grow and link up in the necked region, forming an internal crack that is later sheared to the surface at roughly 45° to the load axis.
The fracture surface of a ductile metal shows a dimpled (cup-and-cone) morphology: a central fibrous region of linked voids surrounded by a shear lip.
defs: Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a ductile specimen under tension, occurring after the ultimate tensile stress is reached, which concentrates further deformation.
Void nucleation
The initial formation of microscopic cavities in a ductile metal, usually at inclusions or second-phase particles, under plastic straining.
Void growth and linkage
Expansion of nucleated voids under plastic deformation and their coalescence into a larger internal crack.
Shearing at surface
Final stage in which the internal crack is sheared through the outer surface of the specimen, forming shear lips.
tips: Do not confuse necking (geometric instability, a diffuse-to-localised deformation) with fracture; fracture occurs after void linkage and shearing.
Ductile fracture surfaces show dimples, not the flat cleavage facets seen in brittle fracture; don't describe steel's ductile surface as brittle.
rq: Why do non-metallic particles in steel promote ductile fracture rather than simply being harmless inclusions?
They act as stress concentrators and void nucleation sites; under plastic strain they crack or debond from the matrix, creating voids that grow and link, so the ductile failure starts earlier.
What would you expect the fracture surface to look like if the steel were much cleaner (fewer particles)?
Fewer nucleation sites mean fewer, larger dimples and a smoother, less dimpled surface, with the material needing more strain before voids form.

notes.t: Brittle Failure
pts: Brittle fracture surfaces show a fracture origin marked by arrows, from which the crack initiated and spread.
Chevron-like river markings on the fracture faces radiate back towards the initiation site, showing the direction of crack growth.
defs: Brittle failure
Fracture of a material with little or no plastic deformation prior to rupture, typically occurring suddenly and catastrophically from a pre-existing flaw or stress concentration.
tips: Do not confuse brittle failure (little plastic deformation, flat fracture faces) with ductile failure (necking and cup-and-cone fracture).
rq: Why does the fracture surface show markings radiating away from the arrowed point?
Because the crack starts at a single origin and propagates outward; the markings point back to the initiation site, so they reveal where failure began.

units.name: 14.6 Failure of particle composites
units.ov: This section explains how particulate composites fail: the filler is rarely the weak link, and failure instead starts in the matrix or at the filler-matrix interface. Stress concentrates at the particle poles (along the load direction), where debonding or matrix cracking begins. Chemical coupling of filler to matrix is the main route to reducing interfacial failure.
must: In particulate composites the filler rarely governs failure; identify the matrix or the interface as the critical site
The filler-matrix interface is a common failure point (debonding)
The matrix is a likely failure site, especially with excess filler
Stress concentrates at the particle poles, which lie along the loading direction, so failure initiates there
Two failure modes at the pole: debonding at the interface, or matrix cracking just above the pole; state both
Stress concentration: a local rise in stress around a discontinuity (particle, hole, notch) that can greatly exceed the average applied stress \( (\sigma_{local} = K_t\,\sigma_{avg}) \)
Interfacial failure is reduced by chemically coupling the filler to the matrix (coupling agents)
Increasing filler content does not fix interfacial failure; it tends to worsen matrix failure
Do not confuse the poles (highest stress) with the equatorial sides (lower stress)
Evidence: photoelastic fringes (Hull, 1992) show the stress pattern at the poles; SEM fracture surfaces (Zhang & Tanner, 2003) show debonded particles and matrix failure
conn: Stress concentration around particles links to notch and hole behaviour: a particle acts like a discontinuity that raises local stress above the average
Interface strength links to chemical coupling and to filler loading: better bonding delays debonding, but excess filler weakens the matrix
Load direction determines the pole locations, so the stress analysis, the failure location and the fracture surface appearance are all connected
Photoelastic stress patterns link to SEM fracture surfaces: predicted high-stress sites match observed debonding and matrix cracking
exq: Explain why the filler is rarely the critical component in failure of a particulate composite, and name the two more likely failure sites.
Sketch a spherical particle in a matrix under uniaxial tension. Mark where stress is highest and describe the two failure modes that can start there.
A particulate composite shows poor strength owing to particle debonding. Propose and justify a method to improve it, and explain why simply adding more filler would be ineffective.
Define stress concentration. If the local stress at a particle pole is 2.5 times the average applied stress of 40 MPa, what is the local stress, and how does this explain failure initiation?
Describe what photoelastic fringe patterns and SEM fracture surfaces each reveal about failure around particles.

notes.t: Failure of composites
pts: The matrix is a likely failure site, especially when there is excess filler.
The filler is rarely the critical component in failure of particulate composites.
The interface between filler and matrix is a common point of failure.
Interfacial failure can be reduced by chemically coupling the filler to the matrix.
tips: Do not assume the filler is the weak point; in particulate composites it rarely governs failure, so the matrix or interface should be identified instead.
Interfacial failure is reduced by chemical coupling, not by simply increasing filler content, which tends to worsen matrix failure.
rq: Why would adding excess filler make the matrix more likely to fail?
Excess filler leaves less matrix to bind particles and transfer load, so the matrix becomes the weak, continuous phase that cracks or deforms first.
Why does chemically coupling filler to matrix improve performance?
Coupling agents create strong bonds across the interface, so load transfers efficiently and debonding (interfacial failure) is suppressed.

notes.t: Failure around particles in composites
pts: Stress concentrates at the poles of a particle embedded in a matrix, so failure starts there.
Failure appears as debonding at the particle pole, or cracking in the matrix just above the pole where stress is highest.
Photoelastic fringes (Hull, 1992) show the stress pattern concentrated at the poles, while SEM fracture surfaces (Zhang & Tanner, 2003) show the resulting debonded particles and matrix failure.
defs: Stress concentration
Local increase in stress around a discontinuity such as a particle, hole or notch, which can greatly exceed the average applied stress and initiate failure.
Debonding
Separation of a particle from the surrounding matrix at the particle–matrix interface, typically at the poles where stress is highest.
tips: Do not confuse the poles (along the load direction, highest stress) with the equatorial sides of the particle, which carry lower stress.
Failure can be debonding at the interface or matrix cracking just above the pole; state both as possible modes.
rq: Why do the poles of a particle, rather than its sides, carry the highest stress when the composite is loaded?
Load transfer around a rigid particle causes the matrix stress to be amplified at the poles aligned with the loading direction, where the stress field is most concentrated.
What would you expect to happen to failure location if the particle–matrix bond were very strong?
Debonding would be suppressed, so failure would shift to cracking in the matrix just above the poles, where stress is highest.

units.name: 14.7 Failure of fibre-reinforced composites
units.ov: This material explains how fibre-reinforced composites fail as a result of fibre-matrix interaction, not the strength of either constituent alone. It links the stress profile in a short fibre (load transfer length, critical strength) to the failure modes under tension (resin cracking, fibre breakage, crack spreading across fibres) and then to fracture-surface appearance and toughness (flat fracture versus fibre pull-out). Matrix strength and stiffness and the interface bond decide which mode occurs.
must: Composite failure depends on fibre-matrix interaction; never assume fibres alone set the strength.
Stress in a short fibre is zero at the free ends and rises towards the middle; the centre carries the highest load.
A fibre fails when its stress reaches the critical strength \(\sigma_f^*\); the plateau at \(\sigma_f^*\) is reached only in the central region.
Load transfers over \(L_c/2\) at each end of a fibre, so the critical length is \(L_c\); keep \(L_c\) and \(L_c/2\) distinct.
Matrix strength and modulus determine the failure mode: resin fails first (single crack bridged by fibres, or multiple resin cracks) or fibres fail first (staggered breaks, matrix largely intact).
Fracture model: stress is initially uniform; fibres break at random places because flaws vary in strength, so failure is statistical, not at a fixed stress.
A broken fibre sheds its load to the matrix, and stress relaxes over a short length either side of the break; uniform stress does not hold locally.
A fibre break creates a stress concentration in neighbouring fibres, and the crack grows sideways, spreading progressively across the fibres perpendicular to the load.
Strong, well-bonded matrix gives a smooth fracture surface across fibres and resin; a weak matrix or interface gives debonding and fibre pull-out, which absorbs energy and toughens the composite.
A stronger matrix does not automatically mean a tougher composite; the interface bond decides between flat fracture and pull-out.
conn: Short-fibre stress profile and \(L_c\) connect to the fracture model: a fibre shorter than \(L_c\) never reaches \(\sigma_f^*\), so it pulls out rather than breaks.
Random fibre breaks and relaxation zones connect to stress concentrations: each break loads its neighbours and drives crack spread across fibres.
Matrix strength/modulus connects to the failure mode (resin cracking vs staggered fibre breakage), and interface strength connects to fracture surface and toughness (pull-out vs flat).
Strength and toughness trade off: a strong bond raises load transfer and strength but gives brittle flat fracture, while a weak interface gives pull-out energy absorption.
exq: Sketch the tensile stress distribution along a short fibre embedded in a matrix. Explain why the stress is zero at the ends, mark \(L_c/2\) and \(\sigma_f^*\), and state what happens if the fibre is shorter than \(L_c\).
Describe the four tensile failure behaviours of a long-fibre composite, noting which of the resin or the fibres breaks first in each. Which diagram is not a failure mode, and why?
Explain how a single fibre break leads to failure across the fibres, using the terms stress concentration, load transfer and stress relaxation, and say why the process is statistical.

Two composites use the same fibres: one has a strong, well-bonded matrix and the other a weak interface. Compare their fracture surfaces, energy absorption and toughness, and explain why the stronger matrix is not necessarily tougher.
A fibre has a critical length \(L_c = 4\) mm. Find the length over which load is transferred at each end, and say whether a 3 mm fibre could reach \(\sigma_f^*\).

notes.t: Failure of fibre reinforced composites
pts: Failure of a fibre reinforced composite depends on how the fibres and matrix interact, not on either constituent alone.
The strength and elastic modulus of the matrix determine which type of failure occurs in the composite.
tips: Do not assume the fibres alone set the composite strength; always consider the fibre-matrix interaction.
rq: Why would a weak or compliant matrix change the failure mode of a composite even if the fibres are strong?

A weak or low-modulus matrix cannot transfer load effectively between fibres or hold them in place, so failure tends to be governed by matrix or fibre-matrix interface failure (e.g. debonding, matrix cracking) rather than fibre fracture.

notes.t: Stress distribution around a short fibre
pts: Stress at the fibre ends is zero, rising towards the fibre middle.
Stress in the middle of a short fibre is higher than at its ends, so the fibre centre carries the greatest load.
If the central stress reaches the fibre's critical strength, the fibre fails.

For a short fibre, the stress plateau reaches the critical strength σ_f* only over the central region once the fibre is long enough, with load transfer occurring over a length \(L_{c}\)/2 at each end.
defs: Critical fibre strength
The maximum stress a fibre can carry (σ_f*) before it fractures; if the stress in the fibre exceeds this value, the fibre fails.
tips: Do not assume the stress is uniform along a short fibre; the stress is zero at the free ends and only reaches σ_f* in the central region.
Keep track of whether a length refers to the full critical length \(L_{c}\) or the half-length \(L_{c}\)/2 shown in the diagram.
rq: Why does the stress in a short fibre peak at its middle rather than its ends?
Because the matrix transfers load to the fibre through shear at the interface; the ends are free (zero stress), and load builds up along the fibre length toward the centre.
What happens to the fibre if the central stress is pushed above σ_f*?
The fibre fractures at its centre, the most highly stressed point.

notes.t: Failure modes around a long fibre in a composite
pts: Under tensile load, the fibre and surrounding resin deform together; failure then depends on which constituent breaks first.
If the resin fails before the fibres, a single crack forms across the resin and the fibres bridge it until they fail.
Multiple resin failures occur when several cracks form in the resin around the fibre before final fracture.
If the fibres fail before the resin, the fibre breaks in a staggered pattern while the matrix remains largely intact.
tips: Do not confuse the failure modes: in (b) a single resin crack forms and fibres bridge it, whereas in (c) many resin cracks form before fracture.
Diagram (a) shows the undamaged fibre under load, not a failure mode, so do not list it as one of the four failure types.
rq: Why does a stronger fibre-matrix interface tend to favour multiple resin cracking rather than a single resin crack?

A strong interface transfers load efficiently into the fibre, so the resin near the fibre breaks into many small cracks, each with a short load-transfer length, instead of one large crack that lets the fibres bridge it.
What would happen to the failure mode if the fibres were much weaker than the resin?
The fibres would fail first (case d), breaking at many points along their length while the resin stays intact, because the fibre strength is reached before the matrix fracture strain.

notes.t: Fracture model for fibre-reinforced composites
pts: The model assumes the stress in the material is uniform before any fibre breaks.
Fibres fail at random locations along their length, because of flaws of varying strength.
When a fibre breaks, the load it carried is transferred to the surrounding matrix, which causes stress relaxation near the break.
The diagram shows broken-fibre regions where stress relaxes over a short length on either side of each break, with the matrix carrying load across these zones.
tips: The model's assumption of uniform stress is a simplification; real stress is concentrated near breaks, so do not assume it holds locally.
Remember that breaks occur randomly, so fibre failure is a statistical process rather than occurring at a fixed stress.
rq: Why does a broken fibre create a region of stress relaxation rather than the whole composite failing at once?

Load is shed from the broken fibre into the matrix through shear transfer over a finite length, so stress returns to the fibre's full value only some distance from the break; the rest of the fibres are only locally affected.
What would happen to the model's predictions if the fibre strengths were all identical rather than randomly distributed?
Fibres would tend to fail together at a single stress level, so the sequential, random breakage pattern and gradual loss of load-bearing capacity would not be captured; failure would be sudden.

notes.t: Failure across fibres in fibre-reinforced composites
pts: A single fibre fracture raises the load on neighbouring intact fibres, creating a local stress concentration.
The stress concentration allows a crack to grow sideways from the broken fibre into adjacent fibres.
Failure therefore spreads progressively across the fibre bundle, shown as a crack running perpendicular to the loading direction between fibres.
defs: Stress concentration
A localised increase in stress around a discontinuity or broken element, such as a fractured fibre, that is higher than the average stress in the material.
tips: Do not confuse this failure mode with a single fibre breaking alone; the key point is that the crack spreads progressively across adjacent fibres.
Failure across fibres is a local, sequential mechanism, so avoid describing it as a uniform reduction in strength.
rq: Why does a single broken fibre not simply leave the composite with a slightly lower strength, but can cause the whole composite to fail?

The broken fibre's load is transferred to adjacent intact fibres, creating a stress concentration that can make them fail, and the crack then propagates across neighbouring fibres in a progressive, cascading failure.
What would you expect to change if the matrix between fibres were much stronger and tougher?
A stronger, tougher matrix would resist crack growth between fibres, limiting progressive failure and better distributing load, so the composite would fail more gradually.

notes.t: Fibre composite failure
pts: Failure mode of a fibre composite depends on the strength of the matrix relative to the fibre/interface.
A strong matrix bonded well to the fibres gives a relatively smooth fracture surface running across both fibres and resin.
A weak matrix or weak interface lets the matrix debond from the fibres, so the fibres pull out of the matrix, absorbing energy and toughening the composite.
defs: Fibre pull-out
Failure mechanism in which fibres debond from a weak matrix/interface and slide out before fracturing, dissipating energy and increasing toughness.
tips: Do not assume a stronger matrix always gives a tougher composite; the interface bond determines whether fibres pull out or fail flat across the fracture.
Identify the failure mode from the fracture surface: smooth across fibres = strong bond; fibres protruding and pulled out = debonding.
rq: Why does a weak fibre–matrix interface often make a composite tougher rather than weaker?
Debonding and fibre pull-out absorb energy through friction and extra fracture surface area, so cracks propagate more slowly and the fibres keep carrying load after the matrix cracks.
What does a smooth fracture surface crossing both fibres and resin tell you about the interface?
That the matrix is strong and the fibre–matrix bond is good, so the crack passes straight through the fibres rather than along the interface.

units.name: 14.8 Fracture modes (I, II, III)
units.ov: The module classifies how a crack can be loaded into three fracture modes: Mode I (opening), Mode II (in-plane shear or sliding) and Mode III (out-of-plane shear or tearing). The modes are distinguished by the direction of crack-face displacement relative to the crack plane and the crack front. Any real loading is a combination of these three, and fracture surface features such as dimples can support the identification. Note: the notes describe Mode III displacement as 'perpendicular to the fracture plane', which is wrong. Mode III displacement lies in the crack plane, parallel to the crack front (see the first connection).
must: Three fracture modes are defined by crack-face displacement relative to the crack plane and the crack front: I opening, II in-plane shear, III out-of-plane shear (tearing).
Mode I: tensile load perpendicular to the crack plane, so the faces pull directly apart. It is the most common and most critical mode in design.
Mode II: shear load that slides the faces in opposite directions, parallel to the crack plane and perpendicular to the crack front.
Mode III: shear load that displaces the faces in opposite directions, in the crack plane and parallel to the crack front, giving a tearing action (like tearing paper). The faces do not move apart.
Quick test: Mode I displacement is normal to the crack plane; Mode II is in the plane and normal to the front; Mode III is in the plane and parallel to the front.
Identify the mode from the direction of the applied load or displacement relative to the crack, not from how the fracture surface looks.

Shear (Mode II) fracture surfaces show oval dimples elongated in the shear direction, formed by void nucleation and coalescence, with a rough, sheared texture. The dimple shape indicates the local shear direction.
Mode I surfaces form matching halves that separate cleanly, as in a tensile block.
Use the standard numbering (I, II, III) in exam answers, even if a source names a mode without giving its number.
Draw a clear sketch for each mode, showing the crack plane, the crack front and the displacement arrows of the upper and lower faces.
conn: Modes II and III are both shear modes. They differ only in whether the sliding is perpendicular to the crack front (II) or parallel to it (III), so always refer to the crack front when distinguishing them.
Applied load direction links to mode: tension normal to the crack gives Mode I, while in-plane shear or torsion-type loading gives Mode II or III. Real components often see mixed-mode loading.
Fracture mode links to fracture surface evidence (dimples, texture) used in failure analysis to infer the loading direction and the failure mechanism (ductile void coalescence under shear).
Mode I links to later fracture mechanics, where stress intensity and toughness (e.g. \(K_{Ic}\)) are usually defined for opening-mode loading.
exq: Sketch and define Modes I, II and III, labelling the crack plane, the crack front and the direction of displacement of each crack face.

A plate with an edge crack is loaded in uniaxial tension perpendicular to the crack. A second identical plate has the load applied parallel to the crack front as a shear force on its faces. Identify the mode in each case and justify your answer.

A fracture surface shows oval dimples elongated in one direction with a rough, sheared texture. Which mode does this suggest, what mechanism formed the dimples, and what do their elongation direction tell you?
Explain why Mode II and Mode III are often confused and give a rule, based on the crack front, for distinguishing them. Give one real example of each type of loading.
A shaft with a circumferential crack is loaded in pure torsion. Which fracture mode does this mainly produce, and how would the mode change if an axial tensile load were also applied?

notes.t: Direction of failure: fracture load modes
pts: Three major load directions lead to fracture, known as fracture modes.
Mode 1 is opening (tensile) loading, where the crack faces are pulled apart perpendicular to the crack plane.
The upper and lower surfaces of a Mode 1 fracture separate, as shown in the Pascoe (1972) sketch.
Derby et al. (1992) show a Mode 1 crack in a block under tension, with the fracture surfaces forming matching halves.
defs: Mode 1 fracture
Crack opening under tensile loading applied perpendicular to the crack plane, so the crack faces move directly apart.
tips: Do not confuse Mode 1 (opening, tension) with tearing (Mode 3, out-of-plane shear); the page names tearing without numbering it, so use the standard mode numbering in exam answers.
Identify the mode from the direction of the applied load relative to the crack plane, not from the appearance of the fracture surface.
rq: Why is Mode 1 (opening) loading usually the most critical for brittle materials?
Tensile stress perpendicular to the crack plane drives crack opening most efficiently, so cracks propagate readily under it, and it is the dominant failure mode in most engineering design checks.

notes.t: Direction of failure: Mode 2 (shear) fracture
pts: Mode 2 fracture is caused by shear loading that slides the two crack faces parallel to the plane of the fracture, in opposite directions.
In Mode 2 the crack surfaces slide past each other, so the fracture surfaces show shear-type features such as oval dimples and rough, sheared texture.
The schematic shows opposing shear displacements of the upper and lower halves of the specimen, with the crack propagating in its own plane.
Mode 2 is one of the three basic crack-opening modes (Mode 1 opening, Mode 2 in-plane shear, Mode 3 out-of-plane tearing) used to classify fracture.
defs: Mode 2 (in-plane shear) fracture
A fracture mode in which the crack faces are displaced parallel to the crack plane and perpendicular to the crack front, so the crack is loaded in shear in the plane of the fracture.
Oval dimple
A dimple-shaped feature on a fracture surface, elongated in the direction of shear, formed by void nucleation and coalescence under shear loading; its shape indicates the local shear direction.
tips: Do not confuse Mode 2 (in-plane shear, sliding) with Mode 1 (opening under tension); the crack faces move parallel to each other in Mode 2.
Remember Mode 3 is out-of-plane shear (tearing), which is different from the in-plane shear of Mode 2.
rq: Why does shear loading in Mode 2 produce oval dimples rather than round ones?
Shear stretches the voids and dimples in the direction of shear, so they become elongated (oval) rather than equiaxed as in tensile (Mode 1) fracture.
How could you tell from a fracture surface whether a failure was Mode 1 or Mode 2?
Mode 1 gives mainly equiaxed dimples or flat cleavage facets normal to the load; Mode 2 gives elongated oval dimples and rubbing/sheared features lying in the fracture plane.

notes.t: Direction of failure – Mode 3 (shear out of plane)
pts: Mode 3 is out-of-plane shear (tearing): the crack faces slide relative to each other parallel to the crack front, perpendicular to the fracture plane.
Mode 3 is one of the three basic crack-opening modes (Mode 1 opening, Mode 2 in-plane sliding, Mode 3 tearing), which together describe how a crack surface is loaded.
defs: Mode 3 (tearing mode)
A fracture loading mode in which the crack surfaces are displaced in opposite directions parallel to the crack front and perpendicular to the crack plane, i.e. shear out of the plane of the fracture.
tips: Do not confuse Mode 2 (in-plane shear) with Mode 3 (out-of-plane shear); identify the direction of displacement relative to the crack front.
Mode 3 is the fracture mode named in the slide; the diagram is credited to Pascoe (1972).
rq: Why is Mode 3 shear described as 'out of plane' rather than 'in plane' like Mode 2?
In Mode 2 the crack faces slide within the crack plane, perpendicular to the crack front; in Mode 3 they slide out of that plane, parallel to the crack front (tearing).
Why might a component fail in Mode 3 under torsion more readily than in Mode 1?
Torsion produces shear stresses acting parallel to the crack front, which open the crack in tearing (Mode 3) rather than pulling its faces apart as in Mode 1.

Meanwhile, ask your lecturer or consult past papers for the typical question format on chapter 14 material.

units.name: 15.1 Ductile vs brittle fracture modes
units.ov: This module classifies fracture by how the crack propagates: brittle cracks are rapid and unstable with little plastic deformation, while ductile cracks are slow and stable with extensive plasticity. It links macroscopic appearance (cup-and-cone versus flat, bright, faceted surfaces) to microscopic mechanisms (void nucleation, growth and linkage versus transgranular cleavage or intergranular separation). The practical point is that ductile failure gives warning and absorbs energy, whereas brittle failure is sudden and fragmenting.
must: Fracture has three stages (crack formation, propagation, final failure); the mode is defined by the propagation stage, not initiation
Brittle fracture: rapid, unstable crack growth with little or no plastic deformation; it continues without any increase in stress and leaves a smooth, flat surface normal to the load
Ductile fracture: slow, stable crack growth with significant plastic deformation near the crack; more stress or strain is needed to extend the crack, so it gives warning
Ductile failure sequence: necking, void nucleation inside the neck, void growth and linkage into an internal crack, shear at the surface, final fracture
Cup-and-cone surface: central fibrous, dimpled region from void coalescence, surrounded by a shear lip at about \(45^\circ\) to the tensile axis (the plane of maximum shear stress)
Transgranular fracture runs through grains by cleavage on crystallographic planes, giving flat, bright facets; intergranular fracture runs along grain boundaries, leaving faceted, separated grains
Intergranular cracks follow grain boundaries because these are weak paths (segregation, precipitates, weak bonding); brittle does not imply transgranular
Ductility is the plastic deformation before fracture, not strength; do not confuse the two, and a brittle material can look strong yet fail without warning
Failure outcome: brittle failure gives many fragments with low energy absorption; ductile failure leaves one piece with high energy absorption
Voids nucleate at inclusions, second-phase particles or grain boundaries; necking (geometric instability) comes first, then void damage (microstructural)
conn: Necking, void nucleation and the 45° shear lip: the neck raises local stress, voids form inside it, and the final shear follows maximum shear stress planes, producing the cup-and-cone

Crack path versus fracture mode: transgranular and intergranular are both brittle paths, so classify by the amount of plasticity and the crack stability, then separately by the path through the microstructure

Stable versus unstable cracks links to energy absorption and warning: ductile cracks need continued energy input, while brittle cracks self-propagate, which explains the safety implications and the preference for ductile design

Microstructural weak points (inclusions, grain boundaries, precipitates) govern both ductile void nucleation and brittle intergranular cracking, so the same features can drive different modes depending on the conditions
exq: Define brittle and ductile fracture, referring to crack stability, plastic deformation, and the stress needed for propagation. Explain why 'slow' and 'stable' are not equivalent.
Describe, with labelled sketches, the five stages of ductile cup-and-cone failure in a tensile specimen. At what angle does the shear lip form, and why?

A fracture surface is flat, bright and faceted, perpendicular to the load. Identify the fracture mode and say how you would distinguish transgranular from intergranular cracking in the micrographs. Why must scale bars be used when comparing images of 160 mm and 3 mm width?
Compare the failure of a ductile steel bar and an alumina rod in terms of deformation, energy absorbed, number of fragments, and warning given. Why is ductile failure generally preferred in design?
Explain why intergranular brittle fracture can occur in 304 stainless steel and polypropylene. Which microstructural features weaken the grain boundaries?

notes.t: Fracture modes: ductile vs brittle
pts: Fracture proceeds in three steps: crack formation, crack propagation and final failure.
The fracture mode is determined by the mechanism by which the crack propagates.
Brittle fracture: cracks spread rapidly with little or no plastic deformation, and are unstable; once started they continue without increasing stress, giving a smoother fracture surface.
Ductile fracture: plastic deformation occurs near the crack, propagation is relatively slow, the crack is stable and there is appreciable deformation before fracture.
defs: Brittle fracture
Rapid, unstable crack propagation with little or no plastic deformation; once initiated it proceeds spontaneously without increasing stress and gives a smooth fracture surface.
Ductile fracture
Slow, stable crack propagation accompanied by significant plastic deformation in the vicinity of the crack and appreciable deformation before failure.
tips: Do not confuse 'stable' with 'slow' in isolation: the key distinction is that brittle cracks are unstable (self-propagating) while ductile cracks are stable (need increasing stress to grow).
Remember the three stages of fracture (formation, propagation, final failure); the mode is defined by the propagation stage, not by the initiation stage.
rq: Why does brittle fracture produce a smoother fracture surface than ductile fracture?

Brittle cracks propagate rapidly along a cleavage-like path with little plastic deformation to roughen the surface, whereas ductile cracks tear through plastically deforming material, producing a rougher surface.
What does it mean that a brittle crack is 'unstable' while a ductile crack is 'stable', and why does this matter for design?

An unstable crack accelerates and fails without further load increase, giving little warning; a stable crack grows only with increasing stress, so ductile failure is usually detectable before catastrophic fracture, which is why ductile behaviour is preferred.

notes.t: Types of fracture: ductile vs brittle
pts: Fracture behaviour is classified by how much plastic deformation (yield) occurs before the material breaks.
Highly ductile materials neck down to a point before separating, showing large plastic deformation.
Medium ductility materials show some necking and cup-and-cone style rough fracture surfaces before failing.
Brittle fracture occurs with little or no plastic deformation, so the component fails suddenly with no visible warning.
Ductile fracture is usually more desirable because deformation gives warning before failure.
defs: Ductile fracture
Fracture preceded by significant plastic deformation and necking, giving visible warning before the material separates.
Brittle fracture
Fracture occurring with little or no plastic deformation, happening suddenly without warning.
tips: Do not confuse ductility with strength: ductility is the amount of plastic deformation before fracture, not the stress at which failure occurs.
Brittle fracture gives no warning, so it is dangerous even when the material's strength appears adequate.
rq: Why is a ductile fracture preferred in engineering design even if the material is not stronger?
Large plastic deformation before failure gives visible warning (necking, sagging), allowing inspection or repair before catastrophic collapse.
Why can a brittle material fail at a stress well below its yield strength?
It has little plastic deformation to redistribute stress, so cracks propagate rapidly once they start, causing sudden failure.

notes.t: Brittle fracture surfaces – transgranular (intragranular) fracture
pts: In transgranular fracture the crack propagates through the grains themselves, cleaving across the crystal lattice.
The 316 stainless steel micrograph shows the crack path cutting straight through grains, with fracture surfaces that are flat and cleavage-like, indicating brittle behaviour.
In alumina (Al Oxide ceramic), the fracture surface shows step-like cleavage facets across grains, typical of brittle transgranular fracture in ceramics.
The two micrographs are shown at very different scales (160 mm and 3 mm field widths), so features must be compared with the scale bars, not by eye.
defs: Transgranular (intragranular) fracture
Crack propagation through the interior of grains, cutting across grain boundaries, usually by cleavage along crystallographic planes; a characteristic brittle fracture mode.
Brittle fracture
Fracture occurring with little or no macroscopic plastic deformation, rapid crack propagation and low energy absorption.
tips: Compare features only using the given scale bars: the steel image spans 160 mm and the alumina image spans 3 mm, so their feature sizes are not comparable directly.
Do not confuse transgranular (through grains) with intergranular (along grain boundaries) fracture.
rq: Why does a transgranular crack appear to cut straight through grains rather than follow the grain boundaries?
Because the energy needed to cleave along crystallographic planes inside the grain is lower than the energy needed to separate the grain boundaries, so the crack takes the intragranular path.
What in the ceramic micrograph tells you the fracture is brittle rather than ductile?
The fracture surface is faceted and flat with step-like cleavage features and no evidence of necking or dimpled microvoid coalescence.

notes.t: Brittle intergranular fracture surfaces
pts: Intergranular brittle fracture: the crack travels along grain boundaries rather than through the grains, so the fracture surface shows separated grain facets.
In 304 stainless steel the cracks follow grain boundaries, leaving the grains intact and outlining them as a network.
In polypropylene the fracture surface shows clearly faceted grain-like regions separated at boundaries, indicating the same brittle mechanism operates in polymers.
Grain boundaries are weaker paths than the grain interiors, often due to segregation, precipitates or weak bonding, so cracks preferentially propagate along them.
defs: Intergranular fracture
Fracture in which the crack propagates along grain boundaries, separating individual grains; typically a brittle mode, producing a faceted fracture surface.
tips: Do not confuse intergranular (along grain boundaries) with transgranular (through grains); check which path the crack follows.
Brittle does not always mean transgranular—intergranular brittle fracture is also brittle, with little plastic deformation.
