rq: Why does a brittle crack choose grain boundaries rather than cutting straight through the grains?
Grain boundaries are regions of atomic mismatch and often contain impurities or precipitates, so they have lower fracture energy and offer an easier path for crack propagation.
How can you tell from a fracture surface that failure was intergranular rather than transgranular?
Intergranular surfaces show flat, faceted grain outlines with smooth grain-boundary faces, whereas transgranular brittle fracture shows cleavage planes cutting across grains.

notes.t: Brittle failure
pts: Brittle failure fractures the material into many pieces.
Brittle failure occurs with little plastic deformation before fracture.
defs: Brittle failure
Fracture of a material with little or no plastic deformation prior to breaking, typically producing many fragments.
tips: Do not confuse brittle failure with ductile failure, which shows significant plastic deformation (necking) before fracture.
rq: Why is brittle failure dangerous in structural design even when the material's strength seems adequate?
Because it gives little visible warning (little deformation), so fracture occurs suddenly without the yielding that would normally signal overload.

notes.t: Evolution of a ductile failure
pts: Ductile failure proceeds in stages: necking, void nucleation, void growth and linkage, shearing at the surface, then final fracture.
Necking localises deformation so the cross-section reduces locally, raising the local stress and setting up internal voids.
Voids nucleate inside the necked region and grow and link together to form an internal crack.
The crack grows towards the surface and the final shear lip forms at roughly 45° to the load axis, giving a cup-and-cone fracture.
The fracture surface shows a central fibrous, dimpled region surrounded by a shear lip, with the outer ring at about 45° to the tensile axis.
defs: Necking
Localised reduction in cross-sectional area of a ductile specimen under tension, occurring after the ultimate tensile stress, which concentrates deformation in one region.
Void nucleation
The initial formation of microscopic voids, typically at inclusions, second-phase particles or grain boundaries, within the necked region during plastic deformation.
Void growth and linkage
Expansion of nucleated voids under continued plastic straining until neighbouring voids coalesce to form an internal crack.
Shear at surface
Final stage of ductile fracture in which the internal crack propagates outward along planes of maximum shear stress, around 45° to the tensile axis, forming shear lips.
tips: Do not confuse necking (geometric instability) with void nucleation (microstructural damage); necking occurs first and voids form inside the neck.
The 45° shear lip is a consequence of maximum shear stress planes; do not state it as perpendicular to the load.
rq: Why does the final ductile fracture surface form at about 45° to the load axis rather than perpendicular to it?
Maximum shear stress acts on planes at 45° to the tensile axis, so the final shear fracture at the outer edge follows these planes, producing shear lips.
What would happen to the failure sequence if the material contained very few inclusions or second-phase particles?
Void nucleation would be delayed or suppressed, so the material would tend to neck further before voids form, usually leading to a more ductile failure with a longer necking stage.

notes.t: Ductile failure
pts: Ductile failure leaves the component in one piece because the material deforms extensively before fracturing.
Ductile failure is accompanied by a large amount of plastic deformation, which absorbs energy during the deforming process.
defs: Ductile failure
Fracture preceded by significant plastic deformation, absorbing energy; the failed parts usually remain in one piece, giving warning before final separation.
tips: Do not confuse ductile failure (large deformation, one piece, energy absorbed) with brittle failure (little or no deformation, sudden fracture into pieces).
rq: Why is ductile failure generally preferred in engineering structures even though it is not 'stronger'?
Large plastic deformation gives visible warning before fracture and absorbs energy, so overloads are noticed and damage is less sudden and catastrophic.

notes.t: Ductile vs. brittle fracture surfaces
pts: A ductile metal necks and fractures in a cup-and-cone shape, showing plastic deformation before failure.
A brittle material fractures with little or no plastic deformation, leaving flat, grainy surfaces perpendicular to the load.
The cup-and-cone profile results from void nucleation and growth in the centre, then shear fracture at the outer edge at about 45°.
Brittle fracture surfaces appear bright and faceted because they reflect light from cleavage planes.
defs: Ductility
The ability of a material to undergo significant plastic deformation (necking, elongation) before fracture.
Brittle fracture
Sudden fracture with little or no plastic deformation, typically along cleavage planes, with flat surfaces normal to the applied tensile stress.
Cup-and-cone fracture
A ductile fracture mode in which the surface shows a central flat (cup) region and an outer shear lip (cone), formed by void coalescence in the centre and shear at the edge.
tips: Do not confuse fracture appearance with strength: ductile vs. brittle describes energy absorption and deformation before failure, not necessarily how strong the material is.
Remember that the cup-and-cone is a ductile fracture signature; seeing a flat, grainy surface perpendicular to the load indicates brittle behaviour.
rq: Why does the brittle specimen show almost no necking, even though both bars were loaded in tension?
Brittle materials cannot accommodate plastic flow, so cracks propagate rapidly along cleavage planes before any local reduction in cross-section can occur.
What would you expect to see on the fracture surface of a ductile specimen if you examined it closely in the cup region versus the cone region?
The cup (centre) shows a dimpled, fibrous texture from microvoid coalescence; the cone (edge) is smoother, formed by shear at about 45° to the load.

units.name: 15.2 Preventing fracture: crack initiation and growth
units.ov: This module explains fracture as a two-stage process: a crack must first initiate, typically at the surface or at stress concentrations, and then grow by creating new surface, which costs energy. Prevention therefore means either stopping initiation, for example by making the material tougher, or deflecting and arresting a crack once it exists. The ideas connect through loading, flaws and stress concentrations, then energy, then toughness and design.
must: Fracture needs both initiation and growth, so stopping either stage prevents failure; prevention must address the crack growth mechanisms
Ultimate strength (max stress before fracture) is not yield strength (onset of permanent deformation); the relevant strength (tensile, fatigue, compressive, shear) depends on the loading
Cracks almost always start at the surface or at internal stress concentrations, not in the middle of a sound bulk material
Stress concentration: a localised region where stress greatly exceeds nominal stress, typically at notches, geometric discontinuities and flaws
Crack origins fall into two separate categories: material flaws (manufacturing defects, fatigue or creep damage, corrosion) and surface damage (wear and tear, misuse, operating-environment stresses)
Crack growth needs energy because new crack surface is created; the energy scales with the new surface area, not with volume, so a longer crack needs more energy
Two strategies: prevent initiation, or control the crack once started by deflecting it from critical paths or arresting it; for a given crack these are alternatives
Toughness is resistance to crack propagation; it is not the same as strength, since a high-strength material can still be brittle
Making the material tougher is the first strategy for preventing failure
conn: Stress concentrations and flaws link to initiation: the geometry and surface condition set where and when cracks start, so design (avoid sharp notches) and surface finish matter
Energy for new surface links to toughness: a tougher material absorbs more energy per unit crack area, so cracks are harder to propagate
Strength versus toughness: questions often contrast a strong but brittle material with a tougher, weaker one under a given loading (tensile, fatigue, etc.)
Crack origins (corrosion, fatigue and creep damage, wear) link to service environment, so prevention includes inspection, coatings and maintenance as well as material choice
exq: Explain why fracture requires both crack initiation and crack growth, and describe the two broad strategies for preventing failure.
Distinguish between ultimate strength, yield strength and toughness. Give an example of a material that is strong but brittle, and explain why it can still crack easily.

List and classify the common origins of cracks in a component. Why do cracks usually start at the surface or at stress concentrations, and how would you redesign a component with a sharp internal corner to reduce this risk?

Explain why growing a crack requires energy, and why this energy depends on the area of new surface created rather than the volume of material. What happens to the energy requirement as the crack lengthens?
A component is loaded cyclically in a corrosive environment. Identify likely crack initiation sites and mechanisms, and propose measures both to prevent initiation and to deflect or arrest cracks.

notes.t: Preventing fracture
pts: Fracture happens when a material is loaded beyond its ultimate strength.
The relevant strength may be tensile, fatigue, compressive or shear strength, depending on the loading.
A fracture must first initiate (a crack forms) and then grow before failure occurs.
To prevent fracture leading to failure, the crack growth mechanisms must be stopped.
tips: Do not confuse ultimate strength (the maximum stress before fracture) with yield strength (onset of permanent deformation).
Fracture requires both initiation and growth; stopping only one stage does not guarantee prevention of failure.
rq: Why is it not enough just to prevent crack initiation to stop fracture failure?
A crack that has already initiated can still grow under load, so growth mechanisms must also be stopped to prevent failure.
Why does the type of loading (tensile, fatigue, compressive, shear) matter when assessing fracture?
Each loading mode has its own strength limit and failure mechanism, so the relevant strength must be identified for the loading applied.

notes.t: Initiation of a fracture
pts: Cracks almost always start at the surface or at a point of stress concentration inside a component.
Material flaws act as crack origins: manufacturing defects, fatigue or creep damage, and chemical attack such as corrosion.
Surface damage from wear and tear, misuse, or operating-environment stresses also initiates cracks.
defs: Stress concentration
A localised region where stress is significantly higher than the nominal stress, typically at geometric discontinuities, notches or flaws, where cracks tend to initiate.
tips: Do not assume cracks start in the middle of a component; state that initiation is almost always at the surface or at stress concentrations.
List the origins correctly: flaws (material) versus surface damage (wear, misuse, operating stresses) are two separate categories.
rq: Why are cracks so much more likely to start at the surface than in the interior of a component?

Surfaces are exposed to the environment (corrosion), machining/wear damage and the highest bending/surface stresses, and surfaces lack the constraint of surrounding material, so flaws there are most critical.
How could a manufacturing defect that is harmless under static load become a fracture origin in service?
Cyclic loading (fatigue) or long-term creep can grow the flaw gradually until it reaches a critical size, at which point fast fracture occurs.

notes.t: Crack growth
pts: Growing a crack requires energy because new crack surfaces must be created.
The longer the fracture, the greater the area of new surface produced, so more energy is needed.
tips: Remember that the energy term relates to the area of new surface created, not the change in volume of the material.
rq: Why does crack growth require energy even though no material is added or removed?
Extending a crack creates new surfaces, and creating surface area requires energy to break the atomic bonds across the crack plane.
What would happen to the energy needed for crack growth if a crack doubled in length?
The area of new surface roughly doubles, so the energy required to extend it also roughly doubles (for a constant crack-front width).

notes.t: Addressing crack growth
pts: Crack growth can be addressed either by preventing the crack from starting, or by controlling it once it has started.
Once a crack exists, design measures can deflect it away from critical paths or arrest it so it stops growing.
tips: The two strategies are alternatives (OR): initiation prevention or deflection/arrest, not both needed at once for the same crack.
rq: Why is preventing crack initiation generally preferable to arresting a crack that has already formed?
Once a crack has initiated, it can grow under cyclic or sustained loading and lead to sudden fracture, so stopping initiation avoids the risk entirely rather than relying on controlling growth.

notes.t: Stopping crack growth: making materials tougher
pts: The first strategy to prevent failure is to stop a crack from initiating by making the material tougher, i.e. more resistant to crack propagation.
The question posed is how to stop a crack from initiating, which frames crack prevention as the starting point before considering growth.
tips: Do not confuse toughness with strength: a high-strength material can still be brittle and crack easily.
rq: Why does the page frame the answer as making the material tougher rather than just stronger?

Toughness measures the ability to resist crack initiation and propagation (energy absorbed before fracture), whereas strength only measures the stress at which yielding or fracture occurs; a strong but brittle material can still fail suddenly from a small crack.

units.name: 15.3 Grain size reduction and Hall-Petch strengthening
units.ov: This module explains how grain boundaries strengthen metals by blocking dislocation motion, and how refining grain size raises yield strength according to the Hall-Petch relation. It links dislocation pile-ups at boundaries to the \( d^{-1/2} \) dependence, then shows how grain refinement is achieved in practice (rapid cooling, inoculants) for aerospace alloys.
must: Hall-Petch relation: \( \sigma_Y = \sigma_0 + k_y d^{-1/2} \), where \( \sigma_0 \) is the friction stress, \( k_y \) the strengthening coefficient and \( d \) the grain size
Strength is increased by smaller grains: yield strength is linear in \( d^{-1/2} \) (not \( d^{-1} \) or \( d^{1/2} \)), and a negative exponent means a finer grain gives higher strength
Grain boundaries block slip because neighbouring grains have different lattice orientations, so dislocations must change slip direction; a larger misorientation gives a stronger barrier

Dislocation pile-up at a boundary produces a back-stress that resists further slip and concentrates stress; pile-up size \( n = \frac{\alpha \tau d}{G b} \) scales with grain size \( d \) and shear stress \( \tau \)
Core principle: hindering dislocation motion makes a material stronger and harder but usually more brittle, while free dislocations give a softer, more ductile material
Grain refinement is an unusual strengthening mechanism: the notes state it raises strength, ductility, fracture toughness and fatigue life together
Units: convert \( d \) to metres for SI use, since the slide plot uses mm, and \( k_y \) has units of Pa·m\(^{1/2}\)
Methods of refining grains: rapid cooling during casting (more nuclei, less time for growth) and inoculants (e.g. Ti and B added to liquid Al) that provide nucleation sites
Aerospace metals have grain sizes of roughly 1 to several hundred µm; smaller grains mean more grains and more boundary area
Definitions to state precisely: dislocation, slip, grain boundary, misorientation, pile-up, Burgers vector \( b \), inoculant, ultimate strength
conn: Dislocation pile-up leads to Hall-Petch: more dislocations pile up in larger grains (\( n \propto d \)), so the stress concentration at the boundary is larger and slip transmits across it at lower applied stress, whereas small grains need higher applied stress, which gives the \( d^{-1/2} \) dependence
Strength-ductility trade-off versus grain refinement: other strengthening mechanisms reduce ductility, but grain refinement is the exception, so be able to contrast it with them
Solidification processing links to mechanical properties: cooling rate and inoculant additions control nucleation, which sets grain size, which sets yield strength through Hall-Petch

Misorientation angle and grain boundary area together determine the total barrier effect, and lattice structure (e.g. BCC grains in the stainless steel example) sets the slip systems that must be matched across a boundary
exq: A steel has \( \sigma_0 = 70 \) MPa and \( k_y = 0.74 \) MPa·m\(^{1/2}\). Calculate the yield strength for grain diameters of 100 µm and 10 µm, and comment on the effect of a tenfold reduction in grain size, taking care with units.
Two yield strengths are given for an alloy at two grain sizes (e.g. 150 MPa at 64 µm and 200 MPa at 16 µm). Determine \( \sigma_0 \) and \( k_y \), then predict the yield strength at 4 µm.
Explain, using dislocation pile-up and misorientation, why grain boundaries strengthen a metal and why yield strength is linear in \( d^{-1/2} \).
Using \( n = \alpha \tau d/(Gb) \), explain how the number of dislocations in a pile-up changes when grain size is halved, and relate this to yield strength.
Describe two industrial methods for producing fine-grained aerospace aluminium, explaining the mechanism of each, and state why grain refinement is preferable to many other strengthening methods.

notes.t: Toughening a material: dislocation motion and strengthening
pts: Fracture occurs when a material is loaded beyond its ultimate strength.
Strengthening mechanisms are based on the relationship between dislocation motion and mechanical behaviour.
Constraining dislocation motion makes a material stronger and harder but more brittle.
Less constrained dislocations give a weaker, softer and more ductile material.
Most strengthening techniques work by restricting or hindering dislocation motion.
defs: Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement allows plastic deformation of the material.
Ultimate strength
The maximum stress a material can withstand before fracture occurs.
tips: Do not confuse strength with toughness: increasing strength by hindering dislocations usually reduces ductility and toughness.
Remember the trade-off: constrained dislocations means harder and more brittle; free dislocations means softer and more ductile.
rq: Why does restricting dislocation motion increase hardness but reduce ductility?

Dislocations are the carriers of plastic deformation; hindering their movement requires higher stress to deform the material, so it is harder, but with little plastic deformation before fracture it becomes brittle.
Why is a strong material not automatically a tough one?
Strengthening restricts dislocation motion, which reduces the ability to absorb energy through plastic deformation, so toughness (energy absorbed before fracture) can fall even as strength rises.

notes.t: Grain size reduction and grain boundary strengthening
pts: The average grain diameter influences the mechanical properties of a metal.
Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion (slip), so they strengthen the material.
Barrier strength increases with the angle of misorientation between neighbouring grains, because dislocations pile up at the boundary.
Each grain is a region of the same crystal lattice with a different orientation (here BCC in the stainless steel shown), so the boundary separates two differently oriented lattices.
Refining the grain size increases the total grain boundary area, giving more barriers to slip and hence higher strength.
defs: Grain boundary
The interface between two adjacent grains of the same phase with different crystallographic orientations; it impedes dislocation motion.
Slip
Plastic deformation by the movement of dislocations along slip planes in a crystal.
Misorientation
The difference in crystallographic orientation between two neighbouring grains; larger misorientation gives a stronger barrier.
Dislocation pile-up
The accumulation of dislocations against an obstacle such as a grain boundary, producing a back-stress that resists further slip.
tips: Do not confuse grain diameter with grain boundary area: smaller diameter means more boundary area and greater strengthening.
Grain boundary strengthening is a Hall–Petch effect; the strength increase is with decreasing grain size, not increasing.
rq: Why does a finer grain structure give a stronger metal rather than just more grain boundaries?
Smaller grains mean more grain boundaries per unit volume, so dislocations are blocked more often and pile up over shorter distances, requiring higher stress to continue slip.
Why does a high-angle boundary block slip more effectively than a low-angle one?
A larger misorientation means the slip planes do not line up across the boundary, so dislocations cannot easily pass through and must pile up.

notes.t: Grain size reduction and strengthening (Hall-Petch)
pts: Smaller grains give more grain boundaries, which act as barriers to dislocation slip, so yield strength rises.
Grain refinement increases strength, ductility, fracture toughness and fatigue life together, not just strength.
Yield strength plotted against \( d^{-1/2} \) gives a straight line, so the Hall-Petch relation is linear in \( d^{-1/2} \).
Dislocations pile up against grain boundaries; the number in a pile-up scales with grain size and applied shear stress.
defs: Hall-Petch relation
Empirical relationship stating that yield strength increases with the inverse square root of grain size, \( \sigma_Y = \sigma_0 + k_y d^{-1/2} \).
Dislocation pile-up
A group of dislocations stacked against an obstacle such as a grain boundary, which concentrates stress and resists further slip.
Burgers vector (\( b \))
The vector describing the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by a dislocation.
eqs: Hall-Petch equation: yield strength vs grain size
\(\sigma_Y\) = yield strength (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_0\) = friction stress opposing dislocation motion (Pa or MPa); \(k_y\) = strengthening coefficient (Pa·\(m^{1/2}\)); \(d\) = grain size (m)
Number of dislocations in a pile-up

\(n\) = number of dislocations (dimensionless); \(\alpha\) = constant (dimensionless); \(\tau\) = shear stress (Pa); \(d\) = grain size (m); \(G\) = energy per dislocation (J/m)... as given on slide; \(b\) = Burgers vector magnitude (m)
tips: Use \(d^{-1/2}\) not \(d^{-1}\) or \(d^{1/2}\); the exponent is negative one half, and forgetting the sign reverses the trend.
Grain size must be in metres in SI when substituting into \(\sigma_Y = \sigma_0 + k_y d^{-1/2}\); the slide's plot uses mm, so unit conversion is a common trap.
rq: Why does halving the grain size not halve the yield strength increase?

Because the Hall-Petch dependence is on \( d^{-1/2} \), so strength gains are proportional to the inverse square root of grain size and diminish as grains get larger; each halving adds less strength than the last.
What happens to the number of dislocations in a pile-up if grain size doubles, all else equal?
\( n \) is proportional to \( d \), so it doubles, meaning larger grains hold longer pile-ups and concentrate more stress at boundaries, which is why they are weaker.

notes.t: Grain size reduction in aerospace metals
pts: Grain size of aerospace metals is refined to roughly 1 to several hundred micrometres.
Rapid cooling of molten metal during solidification casting produces finer grains because fewer atoms have time to organise into large crystals.
Grain-refining elements called inoculants are added to the melt to promote nucleation of many small grains.
Small additions of titanium and boron to liquid aluminium are a standard example of grain refinement by inoculation.
defs: Inoculant
A grain-refining element added in small amounts to a molten metal to increase the number of nucleation sites, producing a finer grain structure on solidification.
tips: Do not confuse grain size with grain count: finer grains means more grains per unit area, not larger ones.
Give the grain size range with units (micrometres, µm), not millimetres.
rq: Why does rapid cooling during solidification give a finer grain size?
Rapid cooling creates a high undercooling, so many nuclei form quickly and grow only briefly before meeting each other, leaving many small grains instead of a few large ones.
Why are only small amounts of Ti and B added to the aluminium melt?
They act as nucleation sites (e.g. TiB₂ particles) that promote many grains; large additions are unnecessary and can cause other defects or cost.

units.name: 15.4 Solid solution strengthening in alloys
units.ov: This module explains how dissolving solute atoms in a parent metal lattice strengthens it by hindering dislocation motion. It covers substitutional solutes (brass, bronze) and interstitial solutes (carbon in steel), the strain-field mechanism behind pinning, and how carbon content sets steel's strength-ductility balance. The central link is lattice distortion → strain fields → dislocation pinning → higher yield strength and hardness but lower ductility.
must: Solid solution strengthening: solute atoms dissolved in the host lattice distort it, and the resulting strain fields impede dislocation motion, raising yield strength and hardness
Substitutional alloy: solute of similar size randomly replaces host atoms on lattice sites (brass = Zn in Cu, bronze = Sn in Cu)
Interstitial alloy: much smaller solute sits in gaps between host atoms (steel = C in Fe)
Strengthening comes from size mismatch: an identical-sized impurity gives little strain and little strengthening, so both smaller and larger substituents strengthen

Small substitutional atoms produce a tensile strain field and migrate to the compressive region above an edge dislocation; large atoms produce a compressive field and migrate to the tensile region below it
Segregation of solute around the dislocation core pins it, so a larger shear stress is needed to move it; strength and hardness rise while ductility usually falls
Solid solution (single phase, mixed in one lattice) differs from a two-phase alloy (distinct phases that prefer self-contact)
Steel: interstitial Fe-C alloy with at most about 2% C by mass; above this it is cast iron (2-4% C), which is strong in compression but brittle and weak in tension
Steel grades by carbon: low/mild up to 0.25% (ductile, beams, sheet, wire); medium 0.25-0.6% (machine parts); high 0.6-2% (hard, brittle, cutting tools)
Brass is about 60Cu/40Zn (some as low as 5% Zn) and bronze about 88Cu/12Sn; both are stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure Cu; compositions are by weight
conn: Atomic size mismatch determines the type of solid solution (substitutional versus interstitial) and the sign of the strain field, which determines where solute segregates relative to the dislocation
Dislocation pinning links microstructure to mechanical properties: higher yield strength and hardness trade off against ductility, as seen in rising carbon content in steel
Interstitial mechanism (C in Fe) connects to the carbon-content classification of steels and to the application choice (ductile beams versus brittle tools versus cast iron engine blocks)
Solid solution versus two-phase alloy: single-phase mixing in one lattice versus phase separation, which ties to the alloying and phase-diagram discussion
exq: Explain, with sketches of the strain fields, why a smaller substitutional solute segregates above an edge dislocation while a larger one segregates below it, and how this pinning raises yield strength.

Distinguish substitutional and interstitial solid solutions, giving the atomic size criterion and one example of each (brass, bronze, steel), and state why identical-size impurities give almost no strengthening.
A steel contains 0.45% C by mass. Classify it, state its expected strength, hardness and ductility relative to a 0.15% C steel, and suggest two suitable applications.
Why is steel limited to about 2% carbon? Compare the properties and uses of high carbon steel and cast iron (2-4% C), including behaviour in tension versus compression.
Brass is 60% Cu and 40% Zn by weight. Describe how Zn strengthens copper, and explain why it matters whether the composition is quoted as weight or atomic percent when converting.

notes.t: Metal Alloys and Solid Solution Strengthening
pts: Alloying adds atoms of one or more elements to a parent metal to improve its properties.
Solid solution strengthening makes a metal stronger by dissolving solute atoms in the parent metal lattice.
Solute atoms in the lattice hinder dislocation movement, so the metal becomes stronger and harder.
Substitutional alloys replace parent atoms at lattice sites, as the solute and solvent atoms are similar in size and like each other equally.
Interstitial alloys have small solute atoms that squeeze into gaps between the larger parent atoms.
defs: Alloying
The addition of atoms from one or more elements to a parent metal to improve its properties.
Solid solution strengthening
Increasing a metal's strength by adding solute atoms into the parent metal lattice, which hinder dislocation movement.
Substitutional alloy
A solid solution in which solute atoms randomly replace parent atoms on lattice sites.
Interstitial alloy
A solid solution in which small solute atoms occupy gaps between the larger parent atoms in the lattice.
Two-phase alloy
An alloy in which the two components stay in distinct phases because they prefer contact with themselves rather than each other.
tips: Do not confuse a solid solution (single phase, atoms mixed in one lattice) with a two-phase alloy (distinct phases).
Interstitial solutes must be much smaller than the parent atoms; substitutional solutes are of similar size.
rq: Why does adding solute atoms make a metal harder, given that the atoms are just distributed randomly through the lattice?
Solute atoms distort the lattice around them, creating local strain fields that interact with and hinder dislocations, making them harder to move.
What determines whether a solute forms a substitutional or an interstitial solid solution?
Relative atomic size: similar-sized solute atoms replace parent atoms (substitutional), while very small solute atoms fit into interstitial gaps.

notes.t: Metal Alloys and Solid Solution Strengthening
pts: Impurity atoms distort the crystal lattice and generate local stress around them.
The distorted strain field around an impurity acts as an obstacle that resists dislocation movement, strengthening the alloy.
A smaller substitutional impurity creates local stresses (at A and B) that oppose dislocation motion, compressing/pulling the lattice in a way that resists the dislocation.
A larger substitutional impurity also creates opposing local stresses (at C and D), so both smaller and larger substitutional atoms can strengthen the metal by hindering dislocations.
defs: Substitutional impurity
An foreign atom that replaces a host atom on its lattice site; its size relative to the host atom determines the strain field it produces.
Solid solution strengthening
Increase in yield strength of a metal caused by solute atoms distorting the lattice, creating strain fields that impede dislocation motion.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement produces plastic deformation.
tips: Solid solution strengthening depends on lattice distortion: an impurity of identical size produces little strain and gives little strengthening.
Do not confuse substitutional impurities (replace host atoms on lattice sites) with interstitial impurities (sit between lattice sites).
rq: Why does a larger or smaller substitutional impurity both strengthen the metal, rather than only one size?

Either size distorts the lattice: a smaller atom creates a tensile strain field and a larger atom a compressive one. In both cases the local stress field opposes dislocation motion, so both act as barriers.
What would happen to dislocation motion if the impurity produced no lattice distortion?
Without a strain field there would be no local stress to oppose the dislocation, so no pinning or barrier effect and no solid solution strengthening.

notes.t: Smaller substitutional atoms and solid solution strengthening
pts: Small substitutional impurity atoms create a tensile strain field, which is attracted to the compressive strain field above an edge dislocation.
Small impurities segregate to the dislocation, pinning it so a larger shear stress is needed to move it, which strengthens the alloy.
Panel (a) shows a smaller solute atom compressing its neighbours, while panel (b) shows small solute atoms clustering around the edge dislocation core.
defs: Substitutional impurity
A solute atom that replaces a host atom on its lattice site; it strains the lattice according to its size relative to the host atom.
Tensile impurity
A solute atom smaller than the host atom, which pulls neighbouring atoms inward and produces a local tensile strain field.
Compressive strain field
The region of lattice compression located above an edge dislocation line, where atoms are squeezed together.
tips: Do not confuse tensile and compressive: a small solute creates tensile strain in the lattice, but it sits in the compressive region of the dislocation.
Strengthening arises from the attraction between solute and dislocation strain fields, not from the solute simply being harder than the host atom.
rq: Why does a small solute atom reduce the mobility of a dislocation rather than increase it?

The small atom's tensile field sits in the dislocation's compressive region, so the two strain fields interact favourably and the solute is attracted to the dislocation, anchoring it and requiring more shear stress to move it.
What would happen to the required shear stress if the impurity atom were larger than the host atom instead?

A larger impurity would create a compressive field, which would sit in the dislocation's tensile region above or below the line; the interaction would be less favourable, so the strengthening effect would be weaker, and the impurity would tend to sit below the line.

notes.t: Larger substitutional atoms and dislocation pinning
pts: Large (compressive) substitutional impurities sit in the lattice where the surrounding atoms are stretched apart, so they are drawn toward the tensile strain field below the dislocation line.
Accumulation of these solute atoms around the dislocation pins it, so the dislocation becomes harder to move and its mobility is reduced, which strengthens the metal (solid solution strengthening).
defs: Substitutional impurity
A solute atom that replaces a host atom on its lattice site; it causes local lattice strain because its size differs from the host atom.
tips: Large (compressive) impurities go to the tensile region, and small impurities go to the compressive region; do not swap these.
Pinning reduces dislocation mobility, which increases strength and hardness but usually reduces ductility.
rq: Why does a larger substitutional atom migrate to the region below the dislocation line rather than above it?
Below the edge dislocation line the lattice is in tension (atoms are spread apart), which has room to accommodate a larger atom, lowering the strain energy of the system.
What would happen to the strengthening effect if the solute atoms were smaller than the host atoms instead?

Smaller solute atoms would sit in the compressive region above the dislocation line, and would still pin dislocations, but the strengthening relies on the strain field interaction, so the effect would be from a different side of the dislocation.

notes.t: Substitutional alloys and solid solution strengthening (brass)
pts: Brass is a substitutional alloy of zinc dissolved in copper, with zinc atoms replacing copper atoms on lattice sites.
Zinc atoms are larger than copper atoms, so they distort the surrounding lattice and create a stress field.
The lattice stress field from solute atoms hinders dislocation movement, which strengthens and hardens the alloy.
As a result, brass is stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure copper.
Common brass is about 60% copper and 40% zinc, though some brasses contain as little as 5% zinc.
defs: Substitutional alloy
An alloy in which solute atoms replace host (solvent) atoms on regular lattice sites; it typically forms when the atoms are of similar size.
Solid solution strengthening
Increasing the strength of a metal by adding solute atoms that dissolve in the lattice, whose size mismatch creates local stress fields that impede dislocation motion.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement allows plastic deformation; obstacles to its motion increase yield strength.
tips: Do not confuse substitutional alloys (atoms replace host atoms) with interstitial alloys (small atoms fit between lattice sites); brass is substitutional.
Percentages in brass compositions are usually by weight, not atomic percent; state the basis if asked to convert.
rq: Why does a larger solute atom strengthen the lattice more than a solute atom of the same size as the host?
A size mismatch distorts the lattice and creates a local stress field; a same-size atom causes little distortion, so it provides little resistance to dislocation motion.
What would happen to the strength of brass if zinc content were increased well beyond 40%?
Strengthening is not unlimited; at higher zinc levels other phases can form, changing properties, so strength and ductility trends depend on the composition and phase structure.

notes.t: Substitutional alloys and solid solution strengthening (bronze)
pts: In a substitutional alloy, solute atoms replace host atoms on lattice sites; bronze is tin substituting for copper atoms.
Tin atoms are larger than copper atoms, so they distort the lattice and create local stress fields.
These stress fields interact with dislocations and hinder their movement, which strengthens and hardens the metal.
Compared with pure copper, bronze is stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant.
A typical modern bronze contains roughly 88% copper and 12% tin by composition.
defs: Substitutional alloy
An alloy in which solute atoms occupy lattice sites normally occupied by host (solvent) atoms, typically when atomic sizes are similar.
tips: Solute atoms in a substitutional alloy replace host atoms on lattice sites; do not confuse with interstitial alloys where small atoms sit between lattice sites.
Strengthening arises from size mismatch causing lattice strain, not from the alloy simply being a mixture; state the mechanism (hindered dislocation movement).
rq: Why does a larger solute atom strengthen a metal rather than just change its density?

The larger atom distorts the surrounding lattice and creates a local stress field; dislocations are attracted to or impeded by these fields, so more stress is needed to move them, increasing strength and hardness.
What would happen to the strengthening if tin atoms were about the same size as copper atoms?
The size mismatch, and hence the lattice strain, would be small, so the strengthening effect would be much weaker, since strengthening relies on the distortion of the lattice.

notes.t: Interstitial alloys and solid solution strengthening (steel)
pts: Steel is an interstitial alloy of iron with carbon solute atoms, where small carbon atoms occupy gaps between the larger iron atoms.
Interstitial carbon atoms distort the iron lattice and hinder the movement of dislocations, so the alloy is stronger and harder than wrought iron.
The carbon content of steel is limited to a maximum of about 2%.
defs: Interstitial alloy
An alloy in which small solute atoms occupy the interstitial (gap) sites between the larger host atoms of the solvent lattice.
Solid solution strengthening
Increase in strength and hardness of a metal caused by solute atoms dissolved in its crystal lattice, which impede dislocation motion.
tips: Do not confuse interstitial alloys (small solute in gaps, e.g. C in Fe) with substitutional alloys (solute replaces host atoms, e.g. Cu in Ni); state the atomic size criterion.
Remember steel's carbon limit is a maximum of about 2%; quoting a value above this describes cast iron, not steel.
rq: Why does a small carbon atom strengthen iron more effectively than a larger solute atom would in the same interstitial position?

Small carbon atoms fit into the gaps of the iron lattice causing localised lattice distortion (strain fields) that interact with and pin dislocations; large atoms would instead be substitutional or cause excessive strain, so the interstitial site is the one that suits carbon.
What would happen to the strength of steel if the carbon content were increased well beyond 2%?

Beyond about 2% carbon the material is no longer steel; it becomes cast iron, which is hard but brittle, because excess carbon forms cementite and graphite phases rather than remaining in solid solution.

notes.t: Steel types and properties by carbon content
pts: Steel properties are governed mainly by carbon content: more carbon gives higher strength and hardness but lower ductility.
Low carbon/mild steel (up to 0.25% C) is ductile and easy to form, so it suits beams, sheet and wire.
Medium carbon steel (0.25 to 0.6% C) balances strength and hardness for rotating or load-bearing machine parts.
High carbon steel (0.6 to 2% C) is very hard and strong but brittle, so it suits cutting tools and drill bits.
Cast iron (2 to 4% C) is strong in compression but brittle and weak in tension, so it suits engine blocks and brake discs.
defs: Ductility
The ability of a material to undergo significant plastic deformation (e.g. stretching into wire) before fracture.
tips: Carbon content ranges are percentages by mass; do not confuse 0.25% with 0.25 (a fraction) when quoting values.
Ductile and strong are not the same property; higher carbon increases strength but reduces ductility.
rq: Why can cast iron be used for engine blocks even though it is brittle?
Engine blocks are mainly subjected to compressive loads, where cast iron is strong, so its poor tensile performance is less critical.
What would happen to ductility if a mild steel component were heat-treated to contain 0.6% carbon?
Ductility would fall and strength and hardness would rise, moving it toward medium/high carbon steel behaviour.

units.name: 15.5 Precipitate strengthening and cast iron
units.ov: This module explains how fine, hard second-phase particles (precipitates) pin dislocations and raise yield strength, quantified by the Orowan bowing relation \(\tau_y = 2T/(bL)\). It applies the idea to iron carbide (cementite) in steel, then to graphite flakes in cast iron, which help in compression and wear but harm tensile strength, as the Tay Bridge failure showed. The common thread is that the type, size and spacing of the second phase control mechanical behaviour.
must: Orowan yield (critical shear) stress: \(\tau_Y = \frac{2T}{bL}\), so strength is inversely proportional to precipitate spacing \(L\).
Derivation: the critical configuration is a semicircular bowed dislocation, giving \(\tau b L = 2T\); resistive force per unit length \(f_0=\tau b = 2T/L\).
\(L\) is the spacing between precipitates, not the particle diameter; precipitates must be fine and well dispersed, and coarse particles strengthen much less.
Mechanism: hard precipitates pin dislocations, so a higher stress is needed to bow or cut through and yield occurs when the dislocation breaks free.
Variables and units: \(T\) is line tension (energy per unit length, N), \(b\) is the Burgers vector (m), \(L\) is in m, giving \(\tau\) in Pa; check that \(\tau b L\) has units of N.
Precipitate strengthening differs from solid solution strengthening: precipitates are distinct second-phase particles, whereas solute atoms are dissolved in the lattice.
Steel: ferrite (BCC, at most 0.022 wt% C) cannot hold excess carbon, which forms hard Fe\(_3\)C (cementite) precipitates that block dislocations, raising strength and hardness.
Cast iron: more than about 2% C gives graphite flakes; high compressive strength, hardness and wear resistance (graphite lubricates), but poor tensile strength.
Cast iron is weak in tension because cracks start at the matrix/flake interface (flakes act as stress concentrators), while compression is fine; steel is below about 2% C.
Tay Bridge (28 Dec 1879, about 75 deaths): cast iron's tensile weakness under off-axis wind bending was one contributing cause, alongside design and wind loading.
conn: Orowan bowing links to cementite in steel: carbon content sets the amount and spacing of Fe\(_3\)C, and so \(L\) and the yield stress via \(\tau_y = 2T/(bL)\).

Steel versus cast iron: the same 'precipitate' idea gives opposite outcomes. Fine, hard, rounded cementite blocks dislocations and strengthens, while brittle graphite flakes act as crack initiators and weaken tensile behaviour.
Line tension relates to shear modulus (\(T \sim Gb^2\)), so a stiffer lattice or smaller \(b\) and \(L\) changes \(\tau_y\); this combines dislocation theory with the quantitative formula.
Cast iron's tension/compression asymmetry connects to the Tay Bridge case and to application choices (engine blocks and brake discs in compression or wear versus structures in bending).
exq: Derive the critical shear stress for a dislocation bowing between precipitates, starting from the semicircular configuration \(\tau b L = 2T\), and state the assumptions.
An alloy has precipitate spacing \(L = 100\) nm, \(b = 0.286\) nm and line tension \(T = 4\times10^{-9}\) N. Calculate \(\tau_Y\). By what factor does it change if the spacing is halved?
Explain why fine, closely spaced precipitates give greater strengthening than coarse ones at the same volume fraction, and why \(L\) rather than particle diameter appears in the equation.
Describe how cementite strengthens steel, referring to the solubility limit of carbon in ferrite (0.022 wt%), and contrast this with solid solution strengthening.
Why does cast iron have high compressive strength and wear resistance but poor tensile strength? Discuss the role of graphite flakes and evaluate how far this explains the Tay Bridge collapse.

notes.t: Precipitate strengthening
pts: Precipitates are formed during alloying, e.g. iron carbide in steels and copper in aluminium (Duralumin).
Precipitates act as obstacles that pin dislocations, preventing their movement through the lattice.
Pinning dislocations stops them or slows them down, so the material requires higher stress to deform plastically, i.e. it is stronger.
defs: Precipitate strengthening
Strengthening of an alloy by fine second-phase particles that form from a supersaturated solid solution and impede dislocation motion.
tips: Do not confuse precipitate strengthening with solid solution strengthening: here the second phase is a distinct particle, not solute atoms dissolved in the lattice.
Precipitates must be fine and well dispersed; large, coarse particles give much weaker strengthening.
rq: Why does a fine, evenly distributed precipitate strengthen a metal more than a few large precipitates of the same volume fraction?

Fine, closely spaced precipitates present more obstacles per unit slip distance, so dislocations must bow or cut through them more often, raising the flow stress; widely spaced large particles let dislocations pass between them more easily.
What would happen to the strength of an aluminium–copper alloy if it were heated too long at high temperature before quenching and ageing?
The precipitates would coarsen (overageing), spacing between them would increase, and the strengthening effect would decrease.

notes.t: Precipitate strengthening (Orowan bowing)
pts: Hard precipitates block dislocation glide; the dislocation must bow between them to pass, which requires a critical shear stress.
At the critical configuration the bowed dislocation segment is a semicircle, so the line tension forces on either side balance the applied stress.
The resistive force per unit length exerted by the precipitates equals the applied stress times the Burgers vector, and it is inversely proportional to precipitate spacing.
Yield occurs when the dislocation breaks free from the precipitates, so the yield stress is inversely proportional to particle spacing: closer precipitates give higher strength.
Line tension T is the energy per unit length of dislocation, so the critical stress increases with stiffer dislocations (larger shear modulus) and smaller spacing L.
defs: Precipitate strengthening
Increasing yield strength by dispersing hard second-phase particles that obstruct dislocation motion, so dislocations must bow around or cut through them.
Line tension (T)
The energy per unit length of a dislocation line, which acts along the dislocation and resists its bending into a curved bulge.
Burgers vector (b)
The vector describing the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion caused by a dislocation; its magnitude sets the slip step size.
eqs: Critical configuration for dislocation bowing between precipitates
\tau = applied shear stress (Pa); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m); L = distance between precipitates (m); T = line tension (N)
Resistive force exerted by precipitates per unit length of dislocation
\(f_{0}\) = resistive force per unit length (N/m); \tau = applied shear stress (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m); T = line tension (N); L = precipitate spacing (m)
Yield (critical) shear stress for Orowan bowing
\(\tau_{Y}\) = yield shear stress (Pa); T = line tension (N); b = Burgers vector (m); L = precipitate spacing (m)
tips: Do not confuse L (distance between precipitates) with particle diameter; the formula uses spacing between obstacles.
Keep units consistent: T in N, b and L in metres, giving τ in Pa; check that \(\tau b L\) has units of N.
rq: Why does reducing the spacing L between precipitates increase the yield stress?
A smaller L means the dislocation is more tightly pinned, so the critical bowing radius is smaller and a larger applied stress is needed; from τ_Y = 2T/(bL), τ_Y is inversely proportional to L.
What would happen to the yield stress if the precipitates were replaced by a softer particle that dislocations could cut through?
The Orowan bowing mechanism would no longer apply; the strengthening would depend on a different mechanism (e.g. particle cutting), so the 2T/(bL) relation would not hold.

notes.t: Precipitate strengthening
pts: Closely spaced precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, so the closer they are packed, the higher the yield stress.
The critical resolved shear stress needed to move dislocations past precipitates scales inversely with the precipitate spacing L, so the curve falls steeply as L increases.
defs: Precipitate strengthening
Strengthening of an alloy by fine particles dispersed in the matrix that impede dislocation motion, raising the yield stress.
eqs: Yield (critical shear) stress from precipitate spacing, for dislocations bowing between precipitates
\(\tau_{y}\) = critical resolved shear (yield) stress (Pa); T = line tension of the dislocation (N); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m); L = spacing between precipitates (m)
tips: Yield stress is inversely proportional to spacing L, not to precipitate size; do not confuse the two when interpreting the curve.
Keep units consistent: T in N and b, L in metres give \(\tau_y\) in Pa.
rq: Why does the yield stress rise as the precipitate spacing L decreases?
Smaller spacing forces dislocations to bow more tightly (smaller radius of curvature), requiring a larger shear stress to push them past the precipitates, so \(\tau_y \propto 1/L\).
What would happen to \(\tau_y\) if the precipitates were coarsened so that L doubled?
\(\tau_y\) would halve, since \(\tau_y\) is inversely proportional to L, showing why over-aging weakens the alloy.

notes.t: Precipitate strengthening in steel (iron carbide / cementite)
pts: Excess carbon beyond the solubility limit in the Fe lattice forms separate iron carbide regions.
Hard Fe3C (cementite) particles act as rigid obstacles that impede dislocation movement, raising strength and hardness.
Ferrite is the BCC iron lattice holding only a small amount of solute carbon, so extra carbon must be accommodated as carbide.
defs: Cementite
Iron carbide, Fe3C, a hard intermetallic phase formed when carbon exceeds its solubility in the iron lattice; it strengthens steel by blocking dislocations.
Ferrite
The BCC iron phase (α) containing only a small amount of dissolved carbon, at most 0.022 wt%.
tips: Ferrite holds at most about {{0.022 wt%}} carbon; do not confuse ferrite's small carbon content with the total carbon in the steel.
Do not state that cementite dissolves in the lattice; it is a separate precipitated phase.
rq: Why does adding more carbon beyond a point not simply dissolve further in the iron lattice?
The BCC Fe lattice can only accommodate a limited amount of interstitial carbon (max 0.022 wt% in ferrite); beyond this solubility limit the excess carbon precipitates as Fe3C.
How does a hard particle increase strength, and what would happen if the particles were soft and deformable?

Rigid particles act as obstacles that dislocations must bypass, raising the stress needed to move them; soft deformable particles would let dislocations cut through or deform around them, giving little strengthening.

notes.t: Cast Iron: graphite flakes, strengths and weaknesses
pts: Cast iron forms when carbon content exceeds about 2%, so graphite precipitates as flakes within the iron matrix.
The graphite flakes give cast iron high compressive strength and good hardness and wear resistance, since graphite acts as a lubricant.
Cast iron has poor tensile strength because cracks start at the interface between the soft iron matrix and the hard, brittle graphite flakes and propagate under tension.
Typical applications exploit compressive loading and wear resistance: engine blocks, brake discs, gear housings and sliding components.
defs: Cast iron
An iron-carbon alloy with carbon content above about 2%, in which carbon precipitates as graphite flakes, giving high compressive strength and wear resistance but poor tensile strength.
Graphite flakes
Brittle, hard carbon precipitates in cast iron that act as internal stress concentrators and provide lubrication.
tips: Do not confuse cast iron (above about 2% carbon) with steel (below about 2% carbon); the 2% threshold is the key distinguishing condition.
Remember that graphite both lubricates (good for wear) and weakens tensile strength (cracks start at the graphite interface); state both effects when asked why cast iron behaves as it does.
rq: Why does cast iron fail in tension at much lower loads than in compression?

Cracks initiate at the sharp, brittle graphite flake/iron interfaces, which concentrate stress; under tension these cracks open and propagate, whereas compression tends to close them, so the material resists crushing well.
Why is graphite beneficial for sliding components even though it weakens the metal?
Graphite is a good solid lubricant, reducing friction and wear at sliding surfaces, which offsets its weakening effect where loads are mainly compressive.

notes.t: Tay Bridge Disaster and cast iron in tension
pts: Cast iron piers are strong in compression but weak in tension, so bending from off-axis storm loads is dangerous.
Graphite flakes in cast iron act as internal crack initiators, so cracks propagate under tensile stress.
Material weakness in tension was one contributing cause of the collapse, not the sole cause.
The collapse on 28 Dec 1879 killed around 75 people.
Mass-produced structural steel was not yet available at the time, which limited material choice.
defs: Cast iron
A brittle iron-carbon alloy (high carbon, typically above about 2 wt%) with graphite flakes; strong in compression but poor in tension.
Tensile stress
Stress that pulls a material apart, acting along the loading direction and tending to open and propagate cracks.
tips: Do not state that cast iron is weak in general; its weakness is specifically in tension, and its compressive strength is high.
The Tay Bridge failure had several causes (design, wind loading, material); cast iron's tensile weakness was only one contributing reason, so avoid attributing the collapse to material alone.
rq: Why would a column that safely carries its design vertical load still fail when a storm pushes sideways on it?

Off-axis (lateral) wind loading produces bending, which puts one face of the column in tension. Cast iron is weak in tension, so cracks initiate at graphite flakes and propagate, even though the same column is strong in compression.
If the Tay Bridge had been built with mass-produced steel, which property would most directly reduce the failure risk and why?
Steel's much higher tensile strength and ductility, plus the absence of graphite flakes, would resist tensile cracking and allow yielding before fracture.

units.name: 15.6 Work hardening
units.ov: Work hardening (strain hardening or cold working) is the increase in strength and hardness of a ductile metal as it is plastically deformed below its recrystallisation temperature. The mechanism is that plastic strain multiplies dislocations, which impede one another, so the flow stress rises while ductility falls. The degree of hardening is quantified by percent cold work, based on reduction in cross-sectional area.
must: Definition: work hardening = increase in strength and hardness of a ductile metal through plastic deformation below the recrystallisation temperature (synonyms: strain hardening, cold working).
Mechanism: plastic deformation raises dislocation density, so the mean dislocation spacing shrinks, interactions and blocking increase, and motion becomes harder.
Consequence: the flow stress needed to keep deforming the metal rises as deformation proceeds.
Percent cold work: \(\%CW = \frac{A_0 - A_d}{A_0}\times 100\), based on cross-sectional area reduction, not length change.
Trends with %CW: yield strength and tensile strength increase and ductility decreases; this is the strength-ductility trade-off.
Shape of the curves: yield strength rises rapidly at low %CW and levels off at high %CW, while tensile strength keeps rising in brass and steel over the range shown (1040 steel, brass, copper).
Applies only to plastic deformation of ductile metals; it does not occur in elastic loading and does not describe brittle materials.
Do not confuse with solid-solution or grain-size strengthening: work hardening comes from increased dislocation density, not from dislocations moving more easily.
Cold working occurs below the recrystallisation temperature; at higher temperatures recrystallisation removes the hardening effect.
conn: Dislocation theory and work hardening: plastic strain gives dislocation multiplication, higher dislocation density, greater resistance to slip, then higher yield and flow stress.

Work hardening and the tensile test: yielding marks the onset of hardening, so the rising stress-strain curve past yield, strength gain and ductility loss all link to \(\%CW\) calculations using area.
Cold working and recrystallisation or annealing: the temperature relative to recrystallisation decides whether strain hardening is retained or removed, so ductility can be restored.
Comparing strengthening mechanisms: work hardening vs solid-solution vs grain-size strengthening, each acting on dislocation motion differently.
exq: Define work hardening and explain, in terms of dislocation density and spacing, why a metal's flow stress increases during cold working.
A copper wire of diameter 10 mm is drawn to 8 mm diameter at room temperature. Calculate the percent cold work and estimate the yield strength and ductility change using the cold-work charts.

Explain why percent cold work is defined using cross-sectional area rather than length, and show how an incorrect length-ratio calculation would give a different value for a bar reduced from 20 mm to 15 mm diameter.
Sketch how yield strength, tensile strength and ductility vary with percent cold work for brass, and comment on why yield strength levels off while tensile strength continues to rise.
Why does work hardening not occur in elastic loading or in brittle materials, and how does it differ from solid-solution and grain-size strengthening?

notes.t: Work hardening
pts: Work hardening is the process by which a ductile metal becomes harder and stronger as it is plastically deformed.
Work hardening is also called strain hardening or cold working, since the deformation occurs at relatively low temperature.
The charts show that yield strength and tensile strength rise as percent cold work increases, for 1040 steel, brass and copper.
Strengthening is rapid at low cold work and levels off at high cold work for yield strength, whereas tensile strength keeps rising in brass and steel over the range shown.
Ductility decreases as the metal is work hardened, which is the trade-off for the gain in strength.
defs: Work hardening
The increase in hardness and strength of a ductile metal caused by plastic deformation at temperatures where recrystallisation does not occur.
Strain hardening
Another name for work hardening; strengthening produced by plastic strain (dislocation multiplication and interaction).
Cold working
Plastic deformation of a metal below its recrystallisation temperature, which causes work hardening.
Percent cold work
The percentage reduction in cross-sectional area of a metal produced by plastic deformation at room temperature.
eqs: \(\%CW\) = percent cold work (%); \(A_0\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_d\) = cross-sectional area after deformation (\(m^{2}\))
tips: Percent cold work is based on area reduction, not length change; using the wrong ratio gives incorrect values.
Work hardening only applies to plastic deformation of ductile metals; it does not describe elastic loading or brittle materials.
rq: Why does the yield strength of 1040 steel rise steeply at small amounts of cold work but flatten at large amounts?
Dislocation density increases rapidly at first, so dislocations impede each other more; at high density the additional obstruction per unit strain diminishes, so the curve levels off.
Why must a metal be ductile for work hardening to be useful in forming?
Ductility allows large plastic deformation without fracture; a brittle metal would crack before achieving meaningful strain hardening.
What would you expect to happen to the strength of a work-hardened copper component if it were heated above its recrystallisation temperature?
The strength would drop back toward its original value because new strain-free grains form and dislocation density falls (annealing).

notes.t: Work hardening
pts: Dislocations impede each other's motion, so increasing their number makes further plastic deformation harder.
Plastic deformation raises dislocation density, which is the mechanism behind work hardening.
As dislocations multiply, the mean spacing between them shrinks, increasing interaction and blocking.
Higher dislocation density raises the resistance to dislocation motion, strengthening the metal.
Consequently, the flow stress needed to keep deforming the metal rises as work hardening proceeds.
tips: Work hardening is caused by increasing dislocation density, not by the dislocations moving more easily; do not confuse it with solid-solution or grain-size strengthening.
Work hardening occurs during plastic deformation (above the yield point); it does not occur in purely elastic loading.
rq: Why does cold working a metal make it stronger but less ductile?

Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations; their mutual interference (tangling and blocking) raises the stress needed for further slip, so strength rises while the remaining capacity for slip, and hence ductility, falls.
What would happen to the flow stress if dislocation spacing were halved?
Dislocation density roughly quadruples for a given area, so interactions and resistance to motion increase, and the flow stress rises accordingly.

units.name: 15.7 Stopping cracks: fibres and rubber particles in composites
units.ov: This module covers how obstacles in a crack's path deflect or arrest it, using fibres in brittle matrices (e.g. SiC in glass) and rubber particles in polymers (e.g. RTPMMA). Both rely on absorbing energy so that less is available to create new fracture surfaces. Fibres do this by debonding, pull-out and bridging; rubber particles do it by stretching and tearing. Design trade-offs such as interface strength and transparency determine how well each works.
must: Deflection changes the crack path, whereas arrest stops growth completely. Do not use the terms interchangeably.
Fibre toughening in a brittle matrix works through three mechanisms: interfacial debonding, fibre pull-out, and crack-tip blunting that reduces the driving force until the crack arrests.
Debonding is driven by the crack-tip stress field separating fibre from matrix along the interface, and it consumes energy.
A fibre–matrix interface must be weak enough to debond. A too-strong bond removes the toughening mechanism.
In SiC/glass ceramic composites, toughening comes from fibre pull-out and crack bridging, not plastic deformation. Fracture surfaces show pulled-out fibres rather than clean breaks.
Stiffness of the glass/SiC composite: the fibres (\(E\approx 400\) GPa) are much stiffer than the glass (\(E\approx 76\) GPa), so they carry a large share of the load. Do not mix up the two moduli.

Rubber particles toughen a polymer by stretching and tearing when the crack reaches them, absorbing energy so less remains for new surface. Elastic particles also pull the crack faces together, resisting opening.
Rubber particles raise toughness, not stiffness or strength. Do not claim they make the polymer stronger.
RTPMMA needs small, narrowly distributed particles whose refractive index matches PMMA, to avoid light scattering and keep it clear. Strong particle–matrix adhesion is needed for stress transfer.
Be clear about structure: PMMA is the continuous matrix and the rubber is the dispersed phase. Do not confuse the fibre as crack stopper with the fibre as the load-bearing phase.
conn: Interface strength links the fibre and rubber cases: fibres need a relatively weak interface to debond, while rubber particles need strong adhesion to transfer stress. Be ready to explain why the two differ.
Stiffness versus toughness: fibres are stiff and load-bearing as well as crack stoppers, while rubber particles add toughness without adding stiffness or strength.
Energy-absorption arguments (debonding, pull-out, stretching) link to the energy balance for fracture: more energy absorbed means less available for new crack surface, so toughness rises.
Optical design constraints (particle size, refractive-index matching) compete with toughening in RTPMMA, so a glass-replacement question combines both.
exq: Describe step by step what happens when a crack in a brittle glass matrix meets a SiC fibre. Name the energy-absorbing mechanisms and explain how the crack is arrested rather than merely deflected.
Explain why a very strong fibre–matrix bond can reduce the toughness of a ceramic matrix composite. What interface property is desirable?
Using \(E_{glass}=76\) GPa and \(E_{SiC}=400\) GPa, estimate the composite modulus for a given fibre volume fraction, and comment on which phase carries more of the load.
Explain how rubber particles toughen a polymer, and why they do not increase its strength or stiffness.

Rubber-toughened PMMA is proposed to replace glass in a transparent shatter-resistant panel. State the requirements on particle size, size distribution, refractive index and adhesion, and justify each.

notes.t: Stopping crack growth
pts: Cracks can be deflected or arrested by placing an obstacle in their path
The guiding question is how to deflect or arrest a crack
tips: Deflection and arrest are different outcomes: deflection changes the crack path, while arrest stops growth completely; do not use the terms interchangeably.
rq: Why might placing a second phase or obstacle ahead of a crack make it harder for the crack to continue growing?
The obstacle can deflect the crack path, forcing it to change direction and consume more energy, or arrest it by blunting the tip and reducing the local stress intensity at the crack front.

notes.t: Fibres as crack stoppers in composites
pts: In a brittle matrix, a crack runs until it meets a fibre, where it is stopped or deflected.
The crack-tip stress field separates (debonds) the fibre from the matrix at the interface.
Energy is absorbed by debonding and by pulling the fibres out of the matrix, toughening the composite.
The crack tip is blunted and its driving force reduced until the crack is arrested.
defs: Crack stopper (fibre reinforcement)
A fibre that intercepts a propagating crack in a brittle matrix, causing interfacial debonding, fibre pull-out and crack-tip blunting that absorb energy and arrest the crack.
Debonding
Separation of the fibre from the surrounding matrix along the interface, caused by the crack-tip stress field, which consumes energy.
tips: Do not confuse the fibre acting as a crack stopper with the fibre being the load-bearing phase; here the emphasis is on energy absorption and crack arrest.
Toughening relies on a weak-enough fibre–matrix interface to allow debonding; a too-strong bond removes this mechanism.
rq: Why does debonding at the fibre–matrix interface increase the toughness of the composite rather than simply weakening it?
Creating the new debonded surfaces and frictionally pulling the fibre out consumes energy that would otherwise drive the crack forward, so more work is needed to propagate it.
What would happen to the crack-stopping ability if the fibre were strongly bonded to the matrix?
Strong bonding prevents debonding and pull-out, so the crack would pass through the fibre (or the interface would not absorb energy), losing the toughening mechanism.

notes.t: Fibers in ceramic matrix composites (glass reinforced with SiC fibers)
pts: SiC fibres are much stiffer than the glass matrix, so they carry a large share of the load in the composite.
The composite is formed by infiltrating/mixing the fibres with a glass slurry, then consolidating it.
The fracture surface shows fibres pulled out and bridging the crack rather than fracturing cleanly, which absorbs energy and toughens the ceramic.
defs: Ceramic matrix composite
A brittle ceramic (here glass) reinforced with stiff, strong fibres (here SiC) that improve toughness by bridging cracks and enabling fibre pull-out.
tips: Do not confuse the glass matrix modulus (76 GPa) with the SiC fibre modulus (400 GPa) when computing composite stiffness.
Ceramic composites are toughened by fibre pull-out and crack bridging, not by plastic deformation as in metals.
rq: Why does the much higher modulus of SiC (400 GPa) versus glass (76 GPa) matter for load sharing?
Under equal strain the stiffer SiC fibres carry a proportionally larger stress and load, so they bear most of the applied load and the composite stiffness is raised.
Why does fibre pull-out in the fracture surface make the composite tougher than monolithic glass?
Cracks are bridged by intact fibres and pulling them out requires frictional work, dissipating energy and preventing sudden brittle failure.

notes.t: Rubber particles in composites: toughening mechanism
pts: Rubber particles in a polymer matrix toughen it because they stretch when a crack reaches them.
Stretching the particles absorbs energy, so less energy remains to create new fracture surfaces.
Each rubbery particle requires more energy to tear before it breaks, raising the composite's toughness.
Elastic rubber particles also act to pull the crack faces back together, resisting crack opening.
defs: Toughening (by rubber particles)
Increasing a polymer's fracture resistance by dispersing rubbery particles that stretch and absorb energy as a crack passes, and bridge/close the crack faces.
tips: Rubber particles toughen the polymer by absorbing energy; they do not increase its stiffness or strength, so don't claim they make it stronger.
Remember that the energy is absorbed by stretching and tearing the particles, not by the crack simply stopping at them.
rq: Why does stretching a rubber particle make the polymer tougher rather than just weaker?
The energy spent stretching and tearing the particle is taken from the energy available for creating new fracture surfaces, so more total energy is needed for the crack to propagate.
What would happen to toughness if the rubber particles were bonded very weakly to the matrix?
They would debond rather than stretch and tear, absorbing less energy, so the toughening effect would be reduced.

notes.t: Applications of rubbery particles: rubber-toughened PMMA (RTPMMA)
pts: RTPMMA is a possible replacement for glass where high toughness and shatter resistance are needed.
Transparency must be preserved, so the dispersed rubber phase is carefully controlled rather than just added for toughness.
Small, narrowly distributed rubber particles avoid light scattering that would make the material cloudy.
The rubber particles' refractive index should match the PMMA matrix so light passes through without scattering.
Strong particle-matrix adhesion lets the rubber transfer stress and absorb energy, improving toughness.
defs: RTPMMA
Rubber-toughened polymethylmethacrylate: a transparent PMMA matrix containing dispersed rubber particles that increase toughness and shatter resistance while retaining optical clarity.
tips: Transparency and toughness are competing requirements: small, index-matched, narrowly distributed particles are needed to keep the material clear.
Do not confuse the rubber phase (dispersed particles) with the PMMA matrix (continuous phase) when describing the structure.
rq: Why would a mismatch in refractive index between rubber particles and the PMMA matrix make the material opaque even if the particles are small?
Light is scattered at each interface where the refractive index changes; a mismatch causes scattering that makes the material cloudy or translucent, so index matching is needed for transparency.
What would happen to toughness if the rubber particles did not adhere strongly to the matrix?
Stress could not be transferred to the particles, and debonding at the interface would occur, so the rubber would not effectively absorb energy and toughness would be poor.

units.name: 16.1 Time effects and viscoelasticity basics
units.ov: This material introduces time-dependent mechanical behaviour. Metals and ceramics are treated as essentially time-independent, while polymers, composites, powders and soils show significant time effects. Viscoelasticity combines recoverable elastic and fluid-like viscous responses, and the clearest way to tell elastic, viscous and viscoelastic materials apart is to compare their strain-time curves under a step stress.
must: Definition: viscoelastic materials combine elastic (recoverable, solid-like) and viscous (time-dependent, fluid-like) behaviour, so stress or strain changes with time under load
Which materials are viscoelastic: polymers, polymer composites, powders and soils show significant time effects; metals and ceramics show only very limited ones
Elastic response to a step stress: strain is instantaneous, constant while the stress is held, and fully recovered on unloading, \(\varepsilon=\sigma/E\)
Viscous response to a step stress: strain rises linearly with time, \(\varepsilon\propto t\) (constant strain rate), and is not recovered on unloading (permanent flow)
Viscoelastic response to a step stress: instantaneous elastic jump, then creep (strain increasing at a decreasing rate) under constant stress
Viscoelastic response on unloading: an instant elastic recovery, then gradual decay of strain (delayed elasticity). Recovery is partial or slow, and any remaining strain is permanent
Viscoelastic materials do not have a single constant modulus; the response depends on loading rate and duration, so always check whether loading rate matters
Reading strain-time graphs: flat strain under constant stress means elastic only; rising strain means viscous flow or creep; a gradual return after unloading means viscoelastic
Definitions: 'elastic' means spontaneously returning to the original bulk or shape after contraction, distortion or dilation; 'visco' means fluid-like and rate/time dependent
conn: Step-stress strain-time graphs link the three material types: elastic (instant, fully recovered), viscous (linear rise, no recovery) and viscoelastic (a mixture of both)
Material classes link to modelling choices: polymers and soils need time-dependent analysis, while metals and ceramics can usually be treated as time-independent elastic solids
Time-dependent strain under constant load (creep) links to the loss of a fixed modulus: apparent stiffness depends on loading duration and rate
Recovery behaviour links to permanent deformation: the viscous part is not recovered, so unloading curves show how much flow occurred
exq: Define viscoelasticity and state which classes of material (polymers, metals, ceramics, composites, soils) show significant time effects, and which do not.

Sketch strain-time curves for an elastic, a viscous and a viscoelastic material subjected to a step stress that is applied and later removed. Label the instantaneous jump, creep, delayed recovery and any permanent strain.

A material under constant stress shows strain increasing linearly with time and no recovery on unloading. Classify its behaviour and justify your answer. How would the curve differ for a viscoelastic material?
Explain why a single constant Young's modulus is inadequate for a polymer loaded at two different rates, and discuss how the measured response would change.
Explain the terms 'visco' and 'elastic' in viscoelasticity, and describe what happens to the strain of a viscoelastic material immediately after unloading and at long times afterwards.

notes.t: Time effects in materials
pts: Time and rate of loading are usually assumed to have little effect on material response in basic analysis.
In metals and ceramics, time effects exist but are very limited.
In polymers, polymer composites, powders and soils, time effects can be significant and must be considered.
Materials whose behaviour depends substantially on time are classed as viscoelastic.
defs: Viscoelastic
A class of materials in which the mechanical response depends substantially on time and rate of loading, combining elastic (recoverable) and viscous (time-dependent) behaviour.
tips: Do not assume time-independent (purely elastic) behaviour for polymers, composites, powders or soils; check whether loading rate matters.
Viscoelastic does not mean metals or ceramics: those show only very limited time effects.
rq: Why can the rate of loading be ignored for steel but not for a polymer?
