conn: Surface roughness and stress concentrations (geometry, notches) shorten the initiation stage, which links design and finishing choices to total fatigue life

Paris law links crack length growth to \(\Delta K\propto\Delta\sigma\sqrt{a}\), so growth accelerates until the critical length, which is tied to the maximum stress and remaining area (ultimate failure)
The four-stage sequence maps directly onto fracture surface zones: origin, (invisible Stage I), striated Stage II region, rough overload region
Slip mechanism (PSBs, 45° shear planes) explains why Stage I is shear-driven but Stage II turns to mode I perpendicular to the tensile stress
exq: Describe, with sketches, the four stages of fatigue failure in a metal and state the crack orientation and typical growth rate in each.
Explain how persistent slip bands, extrusions and intrusions initiate a fatigue crack even when the nominal stress is below yield.

A component obeys \(da/dN=(\Delta K)^m\) with \(\Delta K\sim\Delta\sigma\sqrt{a}\). If \(\Delta\sigma\) is doubled at fixed crack length and m = 3, by what factor does the growth rate change? What if the crack length doubles instead?
Sketch and annotate a fatigue fracture surface, identifying the crack origin, beach marks/striations and the final rupture zone, and explain what each tells you about the failure.
List four design or manufacturing measures to extend fatigue life and explain the mechanism by which each works (e.g. rounding a sharp corner, polishing, shot peening).

notes.t: Crack initiation and growth
pts: A crack begins at a single point (the crack origin) in the material.
From the origin the crack then propagates progressively through the material.
Fracture surface markings (beach/ratchet-type lines) radiate outward from the origin, showing the direction of crack growth.
The final rupture region is where the remaining cross-section fails suddenly once it can no longer carry the load.
defs: Crack origin
The point on a component's surface or interior where a crack first initiates; fracture surface features converge back to it.
tips: Do not confuse the crack origin (where failure starts) with the final rupture zone (where the last material fails).
rq: Why can fracture surfaces be used to locate where a failure started?
Growth markings on the fracture surface radiate outward from the initiation site, so tracing them back identifies the crack origin.
Why does the final rupture zone look different from the region around the origin?
Slow, progressive growth produces smooth, marked areas near the origin, while the remaining section fails rapidly and gives a rougher final rupture area.

notes.t: Micro-mechanism of fatigue failure in metals
pts: Cyclic (fluctuating) stress causes plastic deformation in localised regions even when the nominal stress is below yield, which nucleates cracks.
Crack initiation and growth occur even in a largely defect-free material, so fatigue failure does not require pre-existing flaws.
Fatigue failure occurs at a much lower stress than the ultimate tensile strength because damage accumulates over many cycles.
Fatigue failure progresses through four stages: crack initiation, stage (i) growth, stage (ii) growth, and ultimate failure.
Fatigue fracture surfaces show a smooth initiation zone, beach-like propagation rings, and a final catastrophic rupture zone.
defs: Fatigue failure
Fracture of a material under repeated or fluctuating stress at levels well below its ultimate tensile strength, caused by progressive crack initiation and growth.
Elastic deformation
Recoverable deformation in which the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
Plastic deformation
Permanent deformation that remains after the load is removed, occurring beyond the yield point.
Ultimate tensile strength (UTS)
The maximum engineering stress a material can withstand under monotonic tensile loading before necking and fracture.
Yield strength
The stress at which a material begins to deform plastically under monotonic loading.
tips: Do not assume fatigue requires pre-existing defects; the page stresses that cyclic deformation alone can initiate cracks in a largely defect-free material.
Do not confuse the yield strength σY with the UTS; fatigue failure can occur well below UTS, and the fluctuating stress lies in the elastic region in the diagram.
rq: Why can a fatigue crack start in a material that contains no obvious defects?
Cyclic loading causes localised plastic slip in grains (persistent slip bands) even when the average stress is elastic; this slip creates surface intrusions/extrusions that nucleate micro-cracks.
What would you expect to happen to fatigue life if the stress amplitude were increased?
Fatigue life would decrease, because larger cyclic plastic strain accelerates crack initiation and growth, so fewer cycles are needed to reach failure.
Why is the fatigue failure stress lower than the UTS, even though the same material is used?
Under monotonic load failure requires the single peak stress to reach UTS, whereas fatigue accumulates irreversible cyclic damage over many cycles, so failure occurs at a lower stress.

notes.t: Fatigue: first stage crack initiation
pts: Under cyclic loading, slip occurs repeatedly on persistent slip bands within grains, creating surface steps.
Extrusions (in tension-slip) and intrusions (in compression-slip) form at the surface and act as local stress concentrations where cracks start.
Higher surface roughness provides more stress concentrators, so crack initiation happens faster and fatigue life is reduced.
Stage I growth follows slip planes at roughly 45° to the stress axis, before the crack switches to a path perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress in Stage II.
defs: Persistent slip band (PSB)
A band of intense, localised cyclic slip within a grain that survives repeated load cycles and is the site where surface extrusions and intrusions develop.
Extrusion
A ridge of material pushed out of the surface by slip reversal in a persistent slip band, acting as a stress concentrator and crack nucleation site.
Intrusion
A notch-like depression formed on the surface by slip in a persistent slip band, which can nucleate a fatigue crack.
tips: Do not confuse extrusions (material pushed out, tension-side slip) with intrusions (material pushed in, compression-side slip).
Crack initiation is driven by localised slip, not the nominal applied stress, so calculating nominal stress alone will underestimate local damage.
rq: Why do extrusions and intrusions nucleate cracks even though the applied stress is well below the yield strength?

Slip is highly localised in persistent slip bands, so the local stress and strain at the surface step are much higher than the nominal stress, creating a stress concentration that exceeds the local fatigue strength.
What would happen to fatigue life if the component were polished to remove surface roughness?
Fewer intrusions and extrusions would form, so crack initiation would be delayed and total fatigue life would increase.

notes.t: Fatigue second stage: Stage (i) crack growth
pts: Stage (i) growth is a shear crack that propagates along persistent slip bands, crystallographic planes of maximum shear.
The crack lies at about 45° to the principal stress direction, where shear stress is maximum.
Growth is stable and slow, giving a smooth fracture surface, so it is not yet the catastrophic stage.
Growth is very slow, of order 1 nm per cycle, so this stage consumes a large share of fatigue life in the early phase.
Stage (i) growth is confined to roughly one grain size before the crack transitions to stage (ii).
defs: Stage (i) crack growth
Early fatigue crack growth in which a shear crack propagates along slip bands at about 45° to the principal stress, at very low rates (~1 nm/cycle), confined to about one grain size.
Persistent slip bands
Localised planar bands of intense slip formed during cyclic loading that provide the easy path for stage (i) crack growth.
tips: Do not confuse stage (i) (shear, smooth, slow, along slip bands) with stage (ii) (perpendicular to the principal stress, faster growth).
Remember the crack orientation is 45° to the principal stress, not parallel or perpendicular to it.
rq: Why does the stage (i) crack grow at about 45° to the principal stress rather than perpendicular to it?
Shear stress is maximum at 45° to the principal stress, so slip and shear cracking occur on those planes, whereas the normal (tensile) stress that drives opening is maximum perpendicular to it.
Why does a stage (i) crack stop growing after roughly one grain size?
Grain boundaries act as barriers that change the slip plane orientation, so the crack can no longer follow a single slip band and must transition to stage (ii) growth on a different plane.

notes.t: Fatigue Stage II: crack growth (propagation)
pts: In stage II the crack turns to grow perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress, becoming a mode 1 crack.
Each loading cycle advances the crack by a small increment Δa, so growth is cycle-by-cycle.
Crack opening/closing and the plastic zone at the crack tip extend the crack length in every cycle.
Fatigue striations (beach marks) on the fracture surface record each opening and closing cycle.
defs: Mode 1 crack
A crack loaded in opening (tensile) mode, where the crack faces open perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress direction.
Fatigue striations
Parallel ridges on a fatigue fracture surface, each produced by one load cycle advancing the crack front; also called beach markings.
tips: Do not confuse stage II (striation-producing, Δa per cycle) with stage I (shear-driven growth along slip bands).
Striations are not the same as the final overload fracture region; they appear only in the stable crack growth zone.
rq: Why do fatigue striations form a set of evenly spaced lines on the fracture surface?
Each loading cycle advances the crack by a small Δa, and each advance leaves one striation, so spacing reflects the crack growth per cycle.
Why does the crack change direction to become perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress in stage II?
Once it has left the shear-dominated stage I, the crack is driven by tensile opening, so it grows in mode 1 perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress.

notes.t: Fourth stage of fatigue failure: ultimate failure
pts: Once the crack reaches a critical length, it propagates spontaneously and the component fails almost instantaneously.
Failure occurs because the remaining uncracked cross-section can no longer carry the maximum applied stress.
Stage (i) crack growth occurs over a very small distance near the initiation site, so it is not visible on the fracture surface.
The fracture surface shows the initiation point, the stage (ii) propagation region with curved beach-type marks, and the final ultimate failure zone with a rough appearance.
defs: Ultimate failure
The final, rapid fracture of a component that occurs when the crack reaches a critical length and the remaining cross-section can no longer support the maximum applied stress.
Critical crack length
The crack length at which the remaining load-bearing material can no longer sustain the maximum applied stress, causing spontaneous unstable propagation.
tips: Do not confuse stage (i) and stage (ii): stage (i) is slow initiation near the origin and is usually invisible, while stage (ii) is the visible propagation region.
Ultimate failure is governed by the remaining cross-sectional area and the maximum applied stress, not by the initial crack location alone.
rq: Why does the fracture surface show a smooth, curved propagation region but a rough final zone?

The smooth curved marks record the slow, stable stage (ii) crack growth over many load cycles, while the rough zone is produced by rapid, unstable fracture when the remaining section fails in one overload.
What would happen to the critical crack length if the maximum applied stress were increased?
The critical crack length would decrease, since less remaining material can support the higher stress, so ultimate failure would occur at a shorter crack.

notes.t: Contributors to fatigue crack formation
pts: Sharp changes in geometry create stress concentrations where cracks tend to start.
Rough surfaces act as local stress raisers, initiating cracks under cyclic loading.
Surface tensile stresses open cracks, promoting their growth during each load cycle.
Internal defects and inclusions act as initiation sites for fatigue cracks within the material.
Plastic flow localised at a stress concentration produces a plastic zone from which the fatigue crack forms under the cyclic stress \( \Delta\sigma \).
defs: Stress concentration
A localised increase in stress caused by an abrupt change in geometry, such as a notch, hole, fillet or sharp corner.
Stress raiser
A surface feature such as roughness or a scratch that locally amplifies stress and serves as a site for crack initiation.
tips: Do not confuse nominal stress with local stress: fatigue cracks start where the local stress at a concentration or roughness peak is much higher than the nominal stress.
Surface tensile stresses open cracks; compressive surface stresses (e.g. shot peening) tend to inhibit crack formation.
rq: Why does a smooth-surfaced component typically resist fatigue better than a rough one of the same material?
Roughness creates local stress raisers, so the local stress at the surface exceeds the nominal stress, making crack initiation easier.
Why are surface tensile stresses especially harmful in fatigue compared with internal ones?
Surface tensile stresses open cracks at the free surface, where crack initiation is most likely and no surface constraint resists them.

notes.t: Crack initiation and stress concentrations
pts: Large components usually contain manufacturing defects, which can act as the starting points for cracks.
Small components are statistically more likely to be free of defects, so they are less prone to crack initiation.
Before a crack can grow, a first crack must initiate, which is often the hardest stage of failure.
Sharp geometric changes concentrate stress at corners and notches; rounding such features (the 'better' design) reduces the local stress and the chance of crack initiation.
tips: Do not confuse crack initiation with crack growth; this slide concerns initiation, which is driven by defects and local stress concentrations.
Stress concentrations are local peaks, so the nominal (average) stress can look safe while the local stress at a sharp corner is far higher.
rq: Why is a small component less likely to fail by crack initiation than a large one of the same material?
A small component is more likely to be defect free, and fewer manufacturing defects means fewer sites from which a first crack can initiate.
Why does the 'better' shoulder design resist cracking even though the load is the same?
Its smooth, larger-radius fillet reduces the stress concentration factor at the change in section, so the peak local stress is lower and a crack is less likely to initiate there.

notes.t: Crack initiation and growth
pts: Cracks grow incrementally in discrete steps rather than continuously.
Stepwise growth leaves beach marks showing alternating fast and slow growth regions on the fracture surface.
The rate of crack growth per load cycle is controlled by the stress intensity range ΔK.
Since ΔK scales with Δσ√a, crack growth rate increases as the crack lengthens under constant stress range.
The exponent m is material dependent and must be determined experimentally.
defs: Beach marks
Concentric ridge patterns on a fatigue fracture surface that show the successive positions of a crack front during stepwise growth, reflecting periods of faster and slower crack propagation.
Stress intensity range (ΔK)
The difference between maximum and minimum stress intensity factors in a loading cycle, which drives fatigue crack growth.
eqs: Paris law: fatigue crack growth rate as a power law of stress intensity range
\(da/dN\) = crack growth rate per cycle (m/cycle); \(\Delta K\) = stress intensity range (MPa√m); \(m\) = material constant (dimensionless)
Proportionality of stress intensity range to stress range and crack length
\(\Delta K\) = stress intensity range (MPa√m); \(\Delta\sigma\) = stress range (MPa); \(a\) = crack length (m)
tips: Do not treat m as a universal constant; it depends on the material and must be found experimentally.
Keep ΔK (range) distinct from K (maximum); the growth law uses the stress intensity range, not the peak value.
rq: Why does a fatigue crack's growth rate accelerate as it gets longer even if the applied load stays constant?
Because ΔK ∝ Δσ√a increases with crack length a, so the driving force ΔK grows and, through the power law with exponent m, da/dN increases.
How would you determine the value of m for a new material?
Experimentally, by testing crack growth under controlled cyclic loading, measuring da/dN against ΔK, and fitting a straight line on log-log axes whose slope gives m.

units.name: 17.3 Service fatigue loading: cabin pressure and thermal cycles
units.ov: This material covers how an aircraft structure accumulates fatigue damage in service from two sources: mechanical cycles (gust loads on top of the cabin pressurisation cycle) and thermal cycles (ground to cold cruise and back). Both are repeated, low-frequency load histories, so failure is governed by cycle amplitude and cycle count, not by a single peak load. The ideas connect through the flight as the basic unit of damage: each flight adds one pressurisation cycle, one thermal cycle and many small gust cycles.
must: Service loads are cyclic, so the failure mode is fatigue, not static overload; damage depends on stress amplitude and number of cycles \(N\).
Each flight is one load cycle: the ground-cruise-ground pressurisation cycle (a large, slow, low-frequency cycle) gives hoop and longitudinal stress in the fuselage skin.
Gust loads about level flight (level, level+gust, level−gust) give many small-amplitude cycles superimposed on the slower pressurisation cycle.
The load-time history is a superposition of a slow large cycle and fast small cycles, so the real loading is variable amplitude, not constant amplitude.
Damage accumulates every flight, so fatigue life is counted in flights or cycles, and the total is the sum over all cycle types.
Thermal fatigue is progressive cracking from repeated temperature changes where expansion and contraction are constrained, producing cyclic thermal stress.
Thermal stress for a fully constrained member is \(\sigma = E\alpha\Delta T\), so it depends on the temperature range \(\Delta T\) and cycle count, not on absolute temperature.
Cruise skin temperature is about \(-40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) while the cabin stays warm and pressurised, so thermal and pressure cycles occur together on every flight.
Do not confuse thermal fatigue (cyclic temperature change) with creep (sustained load at high temperature).
The diagrams are schematic: do not quote magnitudes from them, and do not treat gust or pressure loads as static.
conn: Pressurisation cycle + gust cycles: superposition gives a variable-amplitude spectrum, which leads to cycle counting and cumulative damage rules such as Miner's rule \(\sum n_i/N_i=1\).
Thermal cycle + pressurisation cycle: both occur once per flight, so their stresses combine, and the mean stress and range affect the S-N life.
Thermal stress \(E\alpha\Delta T\) links thermal expansion and constraint to fatigue: the stress amplitude from \(\Delta T\) can be compared with the mechanical stress amplitude.
Thin-walled pressure vessel stresses (\(\sigma_h = pr/t\)) link the cabin pressure differential to the fatigue stress range in the skin.
exq: Sketch the load-time history for one flight of a pressurised aircraft, showing the pressurisation cycle and gust cycles, and explain why this is a fatigue problem rather than a static overload problem.
A fuselage skin has radius \(r\), thickness \(t\) and cabin pressure differential \(\Delta p\). Calculate the hoop stress range per flight and estimate the fatigue life if the S-N curve is given.

An aluminium panel (\(E=70\) GPa, \(\alpha=23\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\)) is fully constrained and cycles from \(+20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) on the ground to \(-40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) at cruise. Calculate the thermal stress range and discuss its effect on fatigue life.
Define thermal fatigue and explain how it differs from creep. Why is the temperature range more important than the absolute temperature?
Explain how gust loads and pressurisation cycles are combined in a service load spectrum, and describe how Miner's rule could be used to estimate the number of flights to failure.

notes.t: Fatigue – cabin pressure and gust loading cycles
pts: The diagram shows a fatigue loading history: repeated gust-induced load cycles about level flight, combined with a cabin pressurisation cycle from ground to cruise and back.
Each flight produces cyclic stresses from gusts (level, level+gust, level−gust) superimposed on a slower pressurisation cycle, so fatigue damage accumulates with every flight.
The loading is a repeated (cyclic) load history, not a single peak load, so the relevant failure mode is fatigue rather than static overload.
tips: Do not treat gust and pressurisation loads as static; fatigue depends on the number and amplitude of stress cycles.
Remember the diagram is a schematic load-time history, so exact magnitudes are not given and should not be quoted as numbers.
rq: Why does the cabin pressure cycle matter for fatigue even though the gust loads are larger in number?

Each pressurisation cycle is one large, slow stress cycle per flight that adds damage to the structure (e.g. fuselage skin around openings), so it is a major contributor to the fatigue life alongside the many small gust cycles.
What would happen to the fatigue life if the number of gust cycles per flight doubled?
Accumulated damage per flight would roughly double (Miner's linear damage rule), so the number of flights to failure would roughly halve, assuming the same stress amplitudes.

notes.t: Thermal Fatigue in Aircraft Structures
pts: Aircraft structures experience repeated temperature cycles during a single flight, from ground temperature to very cold cruise altitude and back, which can cause thermal fatigue.
During cruise, the skin temperature falls to roughly -40 °C while cabin pressurisation is maintained, so the structure cycles between cold cruise and warm cabin/ground conditions.
Superimposed on the temperature cycle, level flight with gusts produces small repeated load fluctuations, so thermal and mechanical loading combine to drive fatigue.
The diagram (Pascoe, 1972) shows the temperature profile for a winter flight, indicating a rapid temperature drop at climb and a rise on descent.
defs: Thermal fatigue
Progressive damage and cracking of a material caused by repeated cycles of temperature change, where thermal expansion and contraction are constrained, producing cyclic stresses.
tips: Thermal fatigue depends on the temperature range (ΔT) and the number of cycles, not just the absolute temperature.
Do not confuse thermal fatigue with creep, which occurs under sustained load at high temperature.
rq: Why does a temperature cycle cause fatigue even if the peak stress is low?
Because restrained thermal expansion/contraction produces repeated stress reversals, and cumulative cycling nucleates and grows cracks even below the static strength.
What would happen to the thermal fatigue severity if the aircraft flew a short hop instead of a long winter flight to Florida?
The temperature range and number of full cycles per flight would be smaller, so cumulative thermal damage per flight would be reduced.

units.name: 17.4 Fatigue cycle parameters and stress ratio
units.ov: This module defines how a fatigue stress cycle is described: by \(\sigma_{max}\), \(\sigma_{min}\), and the derived quantities range, amplitude, mean stress and stress ratio \(R\). These parameters classify cycles (reversed, alternating, repeated, fluctuating) and let you compare tests. Mean stress matters because, for the same amplitude, a higher tensile mean reduces fatigue life.
must: Stress amplitude \(\sigma_a=\frac{\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}}{2}=\frac{\Delta\sigma}{2}\) is half the range, not the peak stress
Stress range \(\Delta\sigma=\sigma_r=\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min}=2\sigma_a\)
Mean stress \(\sigma_m=\frac{\sigma_{max}+\sigma_{min}}{2}\), signed, using tension positive and compression negative
Stress ratio \(R=\sigma_{min}/\sigma_{max}\) (standard convention). One slide gives \(\sigma_{max}/\sigma_{min}\), which is inverted, so check the exam's definition
Key R values: fully reversed \(R=-1\) (\(\sigma_m=0\)); zero-to-tension \(R=0\) (\(\sigma_{min}=0\)); nearly static \(R\to1\)

Slide p25 says zero-to-tension gives R→∞ and zero-to-compression gives R=0. This is only true with the inverted \(\sigma_{max}/\sigma_{min}\) definition. With \(R=\sigma_{min}/\sigma_{max}\), zero-to-tension gives \(R=0\) and zero-to-compression is undefined (\(\sigma_{max}=0\))
Reversed cycle: \(\sigma_m=0\), the most common lab test. Alternating: \(\sigma_{max}>0\) and \(\sigma_{min}<0\) with unequal magnitudes, so \(\sigma_m\neq0\)

Repeated cycle: \(\sigma_{min}=0\) or \(\sigma_{max}=0\), so the cycle lies on one side of zero. Fluctuating cycle: \(\sigma_{max}\), \(\sigma_{min}\) and \(\sigma_m\) all have the same sign, so it never crosses zero
Inverse relations: \(\sigma_{max}=\sigma_m+\sigma_a\) and \(\sigma_{min}=\sigma_m-\sigma_a\)
At fixed amplitude, a larger tensile mean stress shortens fatigue life, so the mean must be reported with the amplitude
conn: Given any two of \(\sigma_{max},\sigma_{min},\sigma_a,\sigma_m,R\), you can find the rest, e.g. \(\sigma_a\) and \(R\) give \(\sigma_{max}=2\sigma_a/(1-R)\)
Classifying a cycle (reversed, alternating, repeated, fluctuating) comes from the signs of \(\sigma_{max}\), \(\sigma_{min}\) and \(\sigma_m\), which links to the R value
Mean stress effect links these parameters to S–N curves and mean-stress corrections (Goodman, Gerber): the S–N data for \(R=-1\) must be adjusted when \(\sigma_m\neq0\)
Real irregular load histories must be broken into cycles (cycle counting), and each cycle is described by \(\sigma_a\) and \(\sigma_m\) for damage summation
exq: A component sees \(\sigma_{max}=300\) MPa and \(\sigma_{min}=-100\) MPa. Calculate the range, amplitude, mean stress and R, and classify the cycle.
A cycle has \(\sigma_{max}=200\) MPa and \(R=0.5\). Find \(\sigma_{min}\), \(\sigma_a\) and \(\sigma_m\), and say whether the cycle is fluctuating.
Sketch stress–time plots for reversed, alternating, repeated and fluctuating cycles, labelling \(\sigma_{max}\), \(\sigma_{min}\), \(\sigma_a\), \(\sigma_m\) and giving typical R values.

Explain why a stress of \(\sigma_a=150\) MPa with \(\sigma_m=100\) MPa is more damaging than \(\sigma_a=150\) MPa with \(\sigma_m=0\). Why does the R definition matter when quoting R for zero-to-tension loading?
A cycle runs from 0 to \(-250\) MPa. Find \(\sigma_a\) and \(\sigma_m\), and discuss why R is problematic for this cycle.

notes.t: Factors in fatigue: stress amplitude and mean stress
pts: Fatigue loading is described by a stress (or strain) amplitude, the alternating part of the cycle about its mean.
The mean stress is the steady level about which the cycle oscillates; it can be zero or non-zero.
Stress cycles can be fully reversed (zero mean) or offset (tensile or compressive mean), and the mean level shifts the whole waveform.
For the same amplitude, a larger mean stress generally reduces fatigue life, so the mean must be considered alongside the amplitude.
defs: Stress amplitude \( \sigma_a \)
Half the difference between the maximum and minimum stress in a fatigue cycle; the alternating component of the stress.
Mean stress \( \sigma_m \)
The average of the maximum and minimum stresses in a fatigue cycle, about which the stress oscillates.
eqs: Stress amplitude in a fatigue cycle
\( \sigma_a \) = stress amplitude (Pa); \( \sigma_{max} \) = maximum stress (Pa); \( \sigma_{min} \) = minimum stress (Pa)
Mean stress in a fatigue cycle
\( \sigma_m \) = mean stress (Pa); \( \sigma_{max} \) = maximum stress (Pa); \( \sigma_{min} \) = minimum stress (Pa)
tips: Do not confuse stress amplitude with peak stress: σa = (σmax − σmin)/2, not σmax.
Mean stress is the average of max and min, not the average of the amplitude and zero; sign matters since stresses can be negative.
rq: Why does a cycle with σm = σa fail sooner than one with σm = 0 at the same amplitude?
A tensile mean stress holds the crack open and raises the peak stress, so cracks grow faster and fatigue life is shorter.
What is the mean stress of a cycle that swings between −50 MPa and +150 MPa?
σm = (150 + (−50))/2 = 50 MPa, with amplitude σa = 100 MPa.

notes.t: Factors in fatigue: stress parameters
pts: Fatigue loading is described by the maximum and minimum stress in each cycle.
The stress range is the difference between maximum and minimum stress in a cycle.
Stress amplitude is half the stress range and is the alternating component of the cycle.
The stress ratio R describes the type of cyclic loading (e.g. R = -1 fully reversed).
defs: Stress range
The difference between the maximum and minimum stress in a fatigue cycle.
Stress amplitude
Half of the stress range; the alternating stress component about the mean stress.
Stress ratio
The ratio of minimum to maximum stress in a cycle (note: the slide defines it as max over min, which is the inverse of the usual convention).
eqs: \(\sigma_r\) = stress range (MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa)
\(R\) = stress ratio (dimensionless); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa)
tips: Stress ratio on this slide is defined as σmax/σmin, but the standard convention is R = σmin/σmax; check which definition your exam uses.
Stress range is a difference, so it can be negative-sign-sensitive: always subtract minimum from maximum, and keep the amplitude as half of the range, not the full range.
rq: Why is the stress amplitude, rather than the maximum stress alone, a useful measure of fatigue loading?
Fatigue damage is driven by the cyclic (alternating) component; amplitude captures how much stress swings each cycle, independent of the static mean stress.
If σmax = 200 MPa and σmin = -200 MPa, what are the stress range and amplitude?
Stress range = 400 MPa; amplitude = 200 MPa.

notes.t: Notation for a fatigue cycle
pts: Stress amplitude is half the difference between maximum and minimum stress in a cycle
Stress range is the full swing between peak and trough, equal to twice the amplitude
Mean stress is the midpoint between maximum and minimum stress; it sets the cycle's average load level
Stress ratio R describes cycle type: R = -1 is fully reversed, R = 0 is tension-zero, R approaching 1 is nearly static
Real-world loading is irregular, so cycles must be counted and characterised rather than assumed sinusoidal
defs: Stress amplitude (σa)
Half the difference between maximum and minimum stress in a cycle; the alternating component of the load.
Stress range (σr or Δσ)
The total variation in stress over one cycle, from minimum to maximum; equal to twice the stress amplitude.
Mean stress (σm)
The average of maximum and minimum stress in a cycle; the static (steady) component of loading.
Stress ratio (R)
The ratio of minimum to maximum stress in a cycle, R = σmin/σmax, used to classify the loading type.
eqs: \(\sigma_a\) = stress amplitude (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa or MPa)
\(\sigma_r\) or \(\Delta\sigma\) = stress range (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_a\) = stress amplitude (Pa or MPa)
\(\sigma_m\) = mean stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa or MPa)
\(R\) = stress ratio (dimensionless); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa or MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa or MPa)
tips: Do not confuse stress amplitude (σa, half the swing) with stress range (Δσ, full swing); using σa where Δσ is required doubles or halves your answer.
Stress ratio R is min over max, not max over min; check the sign of σmin, since a compressive minimum gives negative R.
rq: Why is the stress range twice the stress amplitude rather than equal to it?
Because the amplitude measures only the distance from the mean (or zero) to a peak, while the range spans from trough to peak, i.e. both sides of the cycle: Δσ = σmax − σmin = 2σa.
If a cycle has σmax = 120 MPa and σmin = −40 MPa, what is the mean stress and what does its sign tell you?
σm = (120 + (−40))/2 = 40 MPa, a positive (tensile) mean stress, meaning the cycle is biased toward tension.
What value of R corresponds to a fully reversed cycle, and why does it matter for fatigue?
R = −1 (σmax = −σmin, zero mean stress); it is the standard fatigue test condition, giving the purest alternating stress.

notes.t: Stress sign convention and stress ratio R
pts: Tensile stress is taken as positive and compressive stress as negative.
Fully reversed tension-compression cycles, with equal and opposite maximum and minimum stresses, have a stress ratio of R = -1.
A cycle that goes from zero stress up to a maximum tensile stress has R tending to infinity, because the minimum stress is zero.
A cycle that goes from zero stress down to a maximum compressive stress has R = 0, because the maximum stress is zero.
defs: Stress ratio R
The ratio of minimum to maximum stress in a fatigue cycle, R = \(\sigma_{min}/\sigma_{max}\), with compression negative and tension positive.
eqs: Stress ratio for a fatigue cycle
\(R\) = stress ratio (dimensionless); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa)
tips: Watch the sign: compression is negative, so \(\sigma_{min}\) in a compressive cycle is the more negative value, not the smaller magnitude.
For a zero-to-tension or zero-to-compression cycle, R is 0 or infinity; do not try to compute these as ordinary numbers in calculations.
rq: Why does a fully reversed cycle give R = -1 rather than R = 0?
Because the maximum tensile stress and maximum compressive stress are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, so \(\sigma_{min} = -\sigma_{max}\) and their ratio is -1.
What happens to R if the cycle is from zero to a tensile peak, and why is that a problem for the formula?

R tends to infinity because the denominator \(\sigma_{max}\) is not zero but the numerator \(\sigma_{min}\) is zero, making the formula's behaviour singular; the ratio is taken as \(\sigma_{max}/0\), which is undefined in the usual sense.

notes.t: Types of fatigue test based on position of the mean stress
pts: Reversed cycle fatigue has zero mean stress, so the stress alternates equally about zero; it is the most common type used in laboratory testing.
Alternating cycle fatigue has a positive maximum and a negative minimum of different magnitudes, so the mean stress may be positive or negative.
Repeated cycle fatigue has either the minimum or the maximum stress equal to zero, so the whole cycle lies on one side (tensile or compressive) of the axis.
Fluctuating cycle fatigue has maximum, minimum and mean stress all of the same sign, so the cycle never crosses zero.
defs: Reversed cycle fatigue
Fatigue loading in which the stress cycle is symmetric about zero, so the mean stress is zero (\( \sigma_m = 0 \)).
Repeated cycle fatigue
Fatigue loading in which either \( \sigma_{min} \) or \( \sigma_{max} \) is zero, so the cycle lies entirely in tension or entirely in compression.
Fluctuating cycle fatigue
Fatigue loading in which \( \sigma_{max} \), \( \sigma_{min} \) and \( \sigma_m \) are all positive or all negative.
tips: Do not confuse alternating cycle fatigue (maximum and minimum of opposite sign) with fluctuating cycle fatigue (all of one sign); check the sign of \( \sigma_{max} \) and \( \sigma_{min} \) first.
Mean stress is \( \sigma_m = (\sigma_{max}+\sigma_{min})/2 \); it can be positive or negative in alternating cycles, so do not assume it is zero unless the cycle is explicitly reversed.
rq: Why is reversed cycle fatigue (zero mean stress) the most common choice in laboratory testing?
Because it isolates the effect of the stress amplitude alone, with no mean-stress term, making results easier to compare and interpret.
If a cycle has \( \sigma_{max} = 0 \) and \( \sigma_{min} = -120 \) MPa, which fatigue type is it and why?
Repeated cycle fatigue, because one extreme is zero and the whole cycle lies on the compressive side of the axis.

units.name: 17.5 Fatigue testing: loading, stress vs strain control
units.ov: This material covers how fatigue tests are run in the laboratory: the machines and waveforms, the practical limits on test frequency, constant amplitude versus random loading, and the difference between stress-controlled and strain-controlled cyclic tests. The central idea is that the choice of test and control variable determines what is imposed and what is measured, and this in turn determines which material behaviour (ratcheting, softening, comparability of data) is revealed.
must: Stress control: the applied stress amplitude is fixed (input) and strain is the measured response; strain amplitude and mean can grow over time (ratcheting/creep-type behaviour).
Strain control: the strain amplitude is fixed (input) and stress is the measured response; stress amplitude falls over cycles, indicating cyclic softening or relaxation.
Always state which variable is held constant and which responds, and link this to the real loading condition being modelled.
Standard materials fatigue data come from constant amplitude tests because the results are directly comparable between materials.
Random loading represents service conditions better, but the varying load history makes comparing stress levels and fatigue lives between materials difficult.
Servo-hydraulic machines can apply virtually any waveform (sinusoidal, saw-tooth, square) and axial, multi-axial, bending, torsional or combined bending-torsion loading.
Practical maximum test frequency for metals is about 100 Hz, because higher frequencies cause localised heating; do not assume the same limit for other materials.
Fatigue tests are long (days, weeks or months), which motivates frequency choice and limits the number of tests.
In stress-controlled cyclic tests the strain envelope widens with cycles; compare hysteresis loops from early and late cycles to characterise the behaviour.
In viscoelastic materials under sinusoidal strain, the stress response lags the strain; check whether a question concerns amplitude or mean value.
conn: Test frequency and material: the 100 Hz limit for metals comes from heating, which connects test duration, cost and the validity of results, since heating alters the material's behaviour.

Control mode and cyclic response: stress control shows increasing strain (ratcheting), while strain control shows decreasing stress (softening); both describe the same material change viewed through a different controlled variable.
Realism versus comparability: random loading mimics service but standard constant amplitude tests are used for data, so design use of the data requires applying it to service loading.
Hysteresis loops link the two control modes: loop shape and its change between early and late cycles show strain accumulation under stress control and stress decay under strain control.
exq: Define stress control and strain control in cyclic testing. For each, state what is held constant, what is measured, and how the response changes with cycle number as the material degrades.

Explain why standard fatigue data are obtained from constant amplitude tests even though random loading is more representative of service. What are the drawbacks of random loading for comparing materials?

A metal specimen is to be tested for \(10^{7}\) cycles. Calculate the minimum test time at the practical maximum frequency of 100 Hz, and explain why this frequency limit exists. Does it necessarily apply to other materials?

Sketch the strain-time trace for a stress-controlled sinusoidal test in which the strain envelope widens, and the stress-time trace for a strain-controlled test showing cyclic softening. Describe what each shows about the material.
Which control mode would you choose to model a component under a fixed applied load, and which for a component whose deformation is constrained? Justify your answer.

notes.t: Fatigue testing in the laboratory
pts: Servo-hydraulic machines can apply virtually any loading waveform, such as sinusoidal, saw-tooth or square wave.
Axial, multi-axial, bending, torsional and combined bending-torsion fatigue tests are all possible.
Fatigue tests are long-duration, lasting days, weeks or even months.
For metals there is a practical maximum test frequency of about 100 Hz, because localised heating occurs at higher frequencies.
tips: The 100 Hz limit applies specifically to metals; the limit for other materials is not given on this page and should not be assumed the same.
rq: Why can't fatigue tests on metals simply be run faster to save time?
Above about 100 Hz, localised heating effects arise, which alter the material's behaviour and invalidate the test, so the frequency is practically limited to about 100 Hz for metals.

notes.t: Random loading cycles in fatigue testing
pts: Random loading better represents real service conditions than constant amplitude loading.
Random loading makes it hard to compare stress levels and fatigue lives between materials, because the load history varies.
For this reason, standard materials fatigue testing is normally carried out using constant amplitude tests, which give directly comparable results.
tips: Do not confuse the realism of random loading with its suitability for material comparison; standard materials data come from constant amplitude tests.
rq: Why would engineers use constant amplitude tests to rank materials even though random loading is more realistic?

Constant amplitude tests keep stress range and mean stress fixed, so fatigue lives and stress levels from different materials can be compared directly; random histories vary, making such comparison difficult.

notes.t: Stress vs Strain Control in Material Testing
pts: The choice between stress and strain control depends on what behaviour is being modelled.
Under stress control the applied stress is held constant, so strain grows as the material fails.
Under strain control the strain is held constant, so the stress falls as the material fails.
defs: Stress control
A loading mode in which the stress is kept constant during the test, so the resulting strain increases as the material fails (e.g. creep-type behaviour).
Strain control
A loading mode in which the strain is kept constant during the test, so the resulting stress decreases as the material fails (e.g. softening/post-peak behaviour).
tips: Do not confuse the two: in stress control it is the strain that increases, in strain control it is the stress that decreases.
Always state which variable is held constant and which one responds, linked to the real loading condition being modelled.
rq: Why would a strain-controlled test be needed to capture the post-peak softening of a brittle material?
Under stress control the specimen would fail suddenly once peak stress is reached; holding strain constant lets the stress fall gradually, so the softening branch can be measured.
If you want to model creep of a component under constant service load, which control mode should you use and why?
Stress control, because the load (stress) is constant in service, so the strain is allowed to increase over time.

notes.t: Stress Control in Cyclic (Fatigue) Testing
pts: Under stress control, a sinusoidal stress of fixed amplitude is applied cyclically to the specimen.
The strain response is measured; for a stress-controlled test, strain may increase with time (ratcheting/creep-type behaviour) rather than remaining constant.
The strain amplitude envelope widens over time, showing progressive increase in strain for constant stress amplitude.
Hysteresis loops and cycle-by-cycle strain changes can be compared between early and late cycles to characterise material behaviour.
defs: Stress control
A cyclic test mode in which the applied stress amplitude is held constant and the resulting strain is measured as a function of time or cycles.
tips: Do not confuse stress control with strain control: in stress control the strain amplitude is the response, not the input.
Check whether the question asks about amplitude (envelope) or mean value when interpreting the strain–time trace.
rq: Why does the strain envelope increase with time under constant stress amplitude?
Because the material accumulates permanent (plastic or creep) deformation each cycle, so the same stress produces progressively larger strain.
What would you expect to see in the strain trace if the material were purely elastic?
A strain waveform exactly in phase with the stress and of constant amplitude, with no envelope growth.

notes.t: Strain-controlled cyclic loading and stress response
pts: In strain control, a sinusoidal strain is imposed on the specimen over time, and the resulting stress is measured.
With a sinusoidal strain input, the stress response lags behind the strain in a viscoelastic material.
Under constant strain amplitude, the stress amplitude decreases over successive cycles, indicating stress relaxation or cyclic softening.
tips: Do not confuse strain control (strain imposed, stress measured) with stress control (stress imposed, strain measured).
rq: Why does the stress amplitude decrease over successive cycles under constant strain amplitude?
The material relaxes or softens cyclically (e.g. viscoelastic relaxation, microstructural change), so the same strain produces a smaller stress.

units.name: 17.6 S-N curves, fatigue limit and scatter
units.ov: This module covers how fatigue life is characterised: S-N (Wöhler) curves of stress amplitude against log cycles to failure, the distinction between a true fatigue limit (steels, titanium) and an endurance limit at a stated cycle count (Al, Cu, Mg), and the scatter in results handled by P-S-N curves and Weibull analysis. It also contrasts stress-controlled and strain-controlled testing, using bone cements as an example. The common thread is that fatigue life is a statistical, test-condition-dependent property, so any quoted value needs its conditions stated (mean stress, cycle count, probability, control mode).
must: S-N (Wöhler) curve: stress amplitude \(\sigma_a\) on the vertical axis against cycles to failure \(N_f\) on a log horizontal axis; read it either way (allowable stress for a required life, or life at a given stress)

Stress amplitude is the semi-range: \(\sigma_a=(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2\); S-N curves normally assume fully reversed cycling (zero mean stress), and a non-zero mean stress changes the allowable amplitude

Fatigue limit (steels, titanium alloys): the curve plateaus, and below this stress amplitude failure is not expected at any number of cycles; for most steels it is about \(0.5\,\sigma_{UTS}\) (mild steel ≈ 200 MN/m² in the notes)
Endurance limit (Al, Cu, Mg and their alloys, with no true plateau): the stress amplitude giving failure at a stated number of cycles, conventionally \(10^7\); always quote the cycle count
Never quote a fatigue limit for aluminium (e.g. 24S-T3), whose curve keeps falling with N
The log N axis means equal spacing is equal ratios of cycles, and a difference of 1 in log N is a factor of 10 in life; do not read it linearly
Fatigue results scatter even for nominally identical specimens, so a single S-N line is insufficient and a probabilistic treatment is needed

P-S-N curves: a family of S-N curves, each for a probability of failure P (e.g. 0.1, 0.5, 0.9); at a given stress a higher P means failure at fewer cycles, so the curve is lower in life; Weibull analysis is the statistical model behind this

Stress-controlled testing holds the stress amplitude constant, while strain-controlled testing holds the strain amplitude constant; material rankings can differ between the two (bone cements: Simplex lasts longest under stress control, Boneloc does best at low strain under strain control)
Always state which method you are using (S-N vs Weibull) and check the axes and units: stress in MPa or MN/m², strain dimensionless
conn: Fatigue limit versus endurance limit: identifying the material class (steel/Ti versus Al/Cu/Mg) decides whether you read a plateau stress or the stress at \(10^7\) cycles
Scatter leads to P-S-N: a design stress from a mean S-N curve (P = 0.5) gives a 50% failure chance, so safe design needs a low-P curve, linking to safety factors and Weibull analysis
Mean stress and stress amplitude: S-N data apply only to zero mean stress, so a loaded component with a non-zero mean needs the cycle converted to an amplitude and corrected before using the curve

Control mode and material ranking: comparing materials requires the same control mode, because stiffness and strain differ, so stress-controlled and strain-controlled curves can rank materials differently
exq: Sketch S-N curves for mild steel and for an aluminium alloy on axes of \(\sigma_a\) versus \(\log N_f\) from \(10^4\) to \(10^8\). Explain why one has a fatigue limit and the other needs an endurance limit, and state the conventional cycle count.

A steel has UTS = 600 MPa. Estimate its fatigue limit. A component sees a fully reversed stress of ±250 MPa. Is infinite life expected? Then give the stress amplitude for a cycle with \(\sigma_{max}=300\) MPa and \(\sigma_{min}=-100\) MPa, and comment on the mean stress.

Explain why fatigue data scatter and how a P-S-N diagram represents this. For P = 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 at a fixed stress amplitude, state which gives the shortest life and which curve you would use to design for a 10% failure risk.

On an S-N plot a specimen at 300 MPa fails at \(10^5\) cycles and another at 250 MPa fails at \(10^6\) cycles. Calculate the factor increase in life and explain why equal spacing on the log axis does not mean equal cycle increments.

Distinguish stress-controlled from strain-controlled fatigue testing using the bone cement data. Why might Simplex Vacuum Mix outperform Boneloc under stress control while Boneloc does best at low strain under strain control?

notes.t: Analysis of fatigue data
pts: Fatigue data can be analysed by testing at multiple stress levels and plotting an S-N curve of stress against cycles to failure.
The S-N curve is also known as the Wöhler curve.
Alternatively, fatigue data can be analysed in terms of probability of failure using Weibull analysis.
defs: S-N curve (Wöhler curve)
A plot of applied stress amplitude S against the number of cycles to failure N, used to characterise a material's fatigue behaviour.
Weibull analysis
A probability-of-failure based statistical analysis of fatigue data that models the distribution of failure stresses or lifetimes.
tips: Do not confuse the S-N (Wöhler) curve, which uses multiple stress levels, with Weibull analysis, which is probability based; state which one you are using.
Remember the S-N curve axes: stress on the vertical axis and number of cycles to failure N on the horizontal axis, often on a log scale.
rq: Why might an engineer choose Weibull analysis instead of an S-N curve for fatigue data?
Weibull analysis gives the probability of failure at a given stress or life, capturing scatter in fatigue results, whereas an S-N curve gives a single characteristic stress-life relationship.
What does each point on an S-N curve represent?
The number of cycles to failure obtained when a specimen is cycled at a particular stress amplitude.

notes.t: The S-N curve (fatigue life)
pts: An S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to fatigue fracture, and is used to predict fatigue life under cyclic loading.
Read from the curve in one direction, it gives the maximum stress amplitude that can be sustained for a required number of cycles.
Read in the other direction, it gives the number of cycles to failure for a given stress amplitude.
Mild steel shows a clear fatigue limit: its curve levels off at about 200 MN/m² so, at this stress, failure is not expected at very high cycle counts.
The aluminium alloy (24S-T3) has no distinct endurance limit; its stress amplitude keeps falling as cycles increase, so a fatigue strength at a stated cycle count (e.g. 10⁸) must be quoted.
defs: Stress amplitude (σₐ)
Half the range of cyclic stress, i.e. the semi-range of stress about the mean stress, in MN/m² (Pa).
Cycles to failure (\(N_{f}\))
The number of load cycles a component endures at a given stress amplitude before fatigue fracture occurs.
Fully reversed (zero mean stress) cycling
Cyclic loading in which the mean stress is zero, so the stress alternates equally between tension and compression.
tips: Ensure the curve applies to fully reversed (zero mean stress) cycling; with a non-zero mean stress the allowable amplitude changes.
Use the log scale for cycles: the axis runs 10⁴ to 10⁸, so do not read values as linear increments.
rq: Why does the mild steel curve flatten out while the aluminium curve keeps falling?

Mild steel has a fatigue (endurance) limit below which it can survive indefinitely, around 200 MN/m²; aluminium alloys lack a true limit, so failure eventually occurs at any stress amplitude given enough cycles.
What would happen to the cycles-to-failure for an aluminium component if the stress amplitude were reduced from 250 to 150 MN/m²?
\(N_{f}\) would increase greatly (from roughly 10⁵ towards 10⁷ cycles or more), since fatigue life rises steeply as stress amplitude falls.

notes.t: The S-N curve: fatigue limit vs endurance limit
pts: Steels and titanium alloys show a fatigue limit: stress amplitude stops decreasing with cycles to failure once a plateau is reached.
The fatigue limit is also called the fatigue strength; for most steels it is about 50% of the UTS.
Non-ferrous metals and alloys (Al, Cu, Mg) show no realistic lower limit, so an endurance limit must be specified for a chosen number of cycles.
The endurance limit is the stress amplitude that gives failure at a stated cycle count, here taken as \(10^{7}\) cycles.
On the S-N plot the stress amplitude σ_a falls as the number of cycles to failure \(N_{f}\) increases, with \(N_{f}\) on a log scale.
defs: Fatigue limit (fatigue strength)
The stress amplitude below which a material (typically steel or titanium) does not fail, regardless of the number of cycles applied.
Endurance limit
For materials with no true fatigue limit (e.g. Al, Cu, Mg), the stress amplitude at which failure occurs after a specified number of cycles, conventionally \(10^{7.}\)
tips: Do not quote a fatigue limit for aluminium, copper or magnesium; quote an endurance limit and state the cycle count (\(10^{7}\)) it applies to.
Remember that \(N_{f}\) is plotted on a logarithmic axis, so equal spacing corresponds to equal ratios of cycles, not equal numbers of cycles.
rq: Why can't aluminium alloys be given a fatigue limit in the same way as steel?

Their S-N curve keeps falling with increasing cycles with no flat plateau, so no realistic stress exists below which they never fail; hence an endurance limit at a stated cycle count (\(10^{7}\)) is specified.
If a steel component is designed to operate at 50% of its UTS, what should you expect for its fatigue life?
Roughly at or below its fatigue strength, so it should survive a very large (effectively infinite) number of cycles, since the rule of thumb puts the fatigue limit near 50% of UTS.

notes.t: Probabilistic fatigue data: the P-S-N curve
pts: Fatigue test results scatter, even between nominally identical samples, so a single S-N line is insufficient.
A probabilistic approach is therefore useful for fatigue design, giving the chance of failure at a given stress amplitude and life.
The P-S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure with one curve per probability of failure P (e.g. P = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9).
For a given stress amplitude, a higher probability of failure corresponds to a curve lying higher, i.e. failure at fewer cycles is more likely.
The diagram shown is for zero mean stress, with cycles to failure plotted on a logarithmic scale.
defs: P-S-N curve
A family of stress amplitude versus cycles-to-failure curves, each labelled with a probability of failure P, showing the statistical scatter of fatigue life.
Probability of failure (P)
The fraction of test specimens expected to fail at a given stress amplitude and number of cycles.
tips: Do not confuse P (probability of failure) with stress or life; P is a fraction or percentage labelling each curve.
Remember the x-axis is cycles to failure on a logarithmic scale, so curves appear straight-ish and spacing is not linear.
rq: Why does a 90% failure-probability curve lie above the 10% curve on a P-S-N plot?
At a given stress amplitude, a specimen is more likely to fail, so fewer cycles are needed; the curve for higher P sits at higher stress for the same life.
Why is a deterministic S-N curve alone risky for design?
It ignores scatter between samples, so it may not reflect the failure risk at chosen stress and life; a probabilistic curve quantifies that risk.

notes.t: Stress-controlled vs strain-controlled fatigue of bone cements
pts: Strain-controlled fatigue curves plot applied strain against log cycles to failure; higher strain gives fewer cycles to failure.
Stress-controlled fatigue curves plot applied stress (MPa) against log cycles to failure; the same material shows different ranking and scatter than under strain control.
Under stress control, Simplex Vacuum Mix lasts longest at each stress level, while Boneloc has the shortest fatigue life.
Under strain control, Boneloc achieves the most cycles at low strain, so the material ranking differs between control modes.
defs: Log cycles to failure
The base-10 logarithm of the number of load cycles a specimen sustains before fracturing at a given stress or strain amplitude.
Strain-controlled fatigue
Fatigue testing in which the strain amplitude is held constant and the number of cycles to failure is recorded.
Stress-controlled fatigue
Fatigue testing in which the stress amplitude is held constant and the number of cycles to failure is recorded.
tips: Check which axis is stress (MPa) and which is strain (dimensionless) before comparing curves; they are not interchangeable.
Log cycles to failure means the exponent, so a difference of 1 on the axis is a factor of 10 in cycles.
rq: Why can the material ranking differ between stress-controlled and strain-controlled fatigue tests?
Because the two tests fix different variables; a material that deforms less under a given stress may not deform less under a given strain, so the failure order can change.
What would you expect to happen to log cycles to failure if the applied stress amplitude is increased?
It decreases: higher stress amplitude causes failure after fewer cycles, giving a downward-sloping S-N type curve.

units.name: 17.7 High vs low cycle fatigue and application examples
units.ov: This material separates high cycle fatigue (elastic, stress-based, long life) from low cycle fatigue (plastic strain each cycle, strain-based, short life). It then applies the classification to real components (engine blades, steel bridges, suspension bolts, aircraft wings) by identifying mechanical, thermal and chemical sources of cyclic loading. The link is that the yield criterion decides the regime, the regime decides the test and analysis method, and the loading sources decide the stress cycle.
must: High cycle fatigue (HCF): peak stress below yield (\(\sigma_{max}<\sigma_y\)), elastic deformation, long life (more than about \(10^4\) to \(10^5\) cycles)
Low cycle fatigue (LCF): peak stress exceeds yield (\(\sigma_{max}>\sigma_y\) or \(|\sigma_{min}|>\sigma_y\)), plastic strain every cycle, short life (fewer than about \(10^4\) to \(10^5\) cycles)
The deciding criterion is stress relative to yield, not cycle count; the boundary is approximate and the notes quote both \(10^4\) and \(10^5\), so state which figure you use and say it is typical
LCF needs a strain-based life parameter and cyclic strain-controlled testing; HCF uses stress-based analysis and cyclic stress-controlled testing
Fatigue is progressive, localised damage from repeated fluctuating stress, and it can cause failure well below static yield or tensile strength
Only the varying (cyclic) component of stress drives fatigue; a steady mean load such as bridge dead weight sets the mean stress but is not itself the fatigue driver
Fatigue sources fall into three categories, mechanical, thermal and chemical, and they often act together
Engine blades: thermal cycling (ground vs cruise), centrifugal tensile stress that varies with each start-stop cycle, and bird strike impact
Bridges: traffic (main dynamic load) and wind are mechanical, weather cycles are thermal, de-icing chemicals are chemical; dead weight is the mean load

Suspension bolts and wings: bolt loads from vehicle weight, cornering and speed bumps plus road salt; wing loads from ground vs in-air weight, storms and turbulence plus de-icing fluid and temperature change
conn: Yield criterion, regime, method: \(\sigma_{max}\) vs \(\sigma_y\) decides HCF or LCF, which decides stress-based or strain-based analysis and stress-controlled or strain-controlled testing
Mean vs alternating stress: dead weight (mean) combined with traffic (cyclic) gives the stress cycle, linking the bridge example to the idea that only the fluctuating part drives fatigue
Environment and mechanics together: salt or de-icer accelerates crack initiation and growth under cyclic mechanical load, so thermal, chemical and mechanical sources must all be listed
Classification of an application: for a component like an engine blade, identify every cyclic source, then judge whether peak stress exceeds yield to assign HCF or LCF
exq: Define high and low cycle fatigue, giving the stress condition relative to yield and the typical cycle counts (\(10^4\) to \(10^5\)). Why is the cycle count only a guide?

A component has \(\sigma_y = 350\) MPa and sees a cyclic stress between +400 MPa and -400 MPa. Classify the fatigue regime, justify it, and state the appropriate test control and life-prediction parameter.
Explain why a strain-based approach is used for low cycle fatigue but a stress-based approach is adequate for high cycle fatigue.
List and classify (mechanical, thermal, chemical) the fatigue loading sources on an aircraft engine blade, and explain why centrifugal load is not purely static.
For a steel bridge, distinguish the mean load from the fatigue loads, identify the sources of each, and name the chemical and thermal contributions.

notes.t: High vs low cycle fatigue
pts: High cycle fatigue: applied stresses stay below yield, so no plastic deformation occurs in the cycles.
High cycle fatigue typically fails after more than about \(10^{4}\) cycles.
Low cycle fatigue: applied stresses exceed yield, so plastic deformation is included in each cycle.
Low cycle fatigue typically fails in fewer than about \(10^{4}\) cycles.
defs: High cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure under cyclic stresses below the yield strength, with no macroscopic plastic deformation, typically lasting more than \(10^4\) cycles.
Low cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure under cyclic stresses above the yield strength, where plastic deformation occurs in each cycle, typically failing in fewer than \(10^4\) cycles.
tips: Do not confuse the regimes: high cycle means below yield (elastic), low cycle means above yield (plastic); the \(10^{4}\) cycle figure is typical, not an exact cut-off.
State the cycle count with the power of ten (\(10^{4}\)) and the stress condition relative to yield in your answer.
rq: Why does the \(10^{4}\)-cycle boundary separate the two regimes rather than the stress magnitude alone?

The boundary reflects the stress level relative to yield: stresses below yield give long lives (>\(10^{4}\) cycles) with elastic-only behaviour, while stresses above yield cause plastic strain each cycle and failure within fewer cycles; the cycle count is a typical indicator of this behaviour.
What would happen to the fatigue regime of a component if its cyclic stress amplitude is raised from below yield to above yield?
It moves from high cycle to low cycle fatigue, because plastic deformation is introduced each cycle and the life drops below about \(10^{4}\) cycles.

notes.t: Distinction between high and low cycle fatigue
pts: Low cycle fatigue occurs at fewer than about \(10^{5}\) cycles, where peak stress exceeds yield so plastic strain occurs every cycle.
Because plastic strain occurs each cycle in low cycle fatigue, a strain-based parameter should be used for life prediction in metals.
High cycle fatigue occurs at more than about \(10^{5}\) cycles, where peak stress is generally below yield, i.e. in the elastic range.
For high cycle fatigue a stress-based analysis is adequate and a cyclic stress-controlled test is most appropriate.
Low cycle fatigue is tested with cyclic strain-controlled tests, while high cycle fatigue uses cyclic stress-controlled tests.
defs: Low cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure at fewer than about \(10^{5}\) cycles (\(N_{f}\) < \(10^{5}\)), where the maximum stress exceeds the yield strength so plastic strain occurs in every cycle.
High cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure at more than about \(10^{5}\) cycles (\(N_{f}\) > \(10^{5}\)), where the stress is generally below yield so deformation is elastic and stress-based analysis is adequate.
eqs: \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
\(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
tips: The \(10^{5}\) cycle boundary is approximate; the deciding condition is whether the maximum stress exceeds yield.
Check whether stress exceeds yield (plastic, strain-based) or stays below it (elastic, stress-based) rather than judging by cycle count alone.
rq: Why must a strain-based parameter rather than a stress-based one be used for low cycle fatigue in metals?
Because peak stress exceeds yield, so permanent plastic strain accumulates every cycle; strain describes this deformation and governs life better than stress.
What would happen to the appropriate analysis if a high cycle fatigue component were loaded so its maximum stress rose above yield?
Plastic strain would occur each cycle, so the regime would become low cycle fatigue and a strain-based approach and strain-controlled testing would be needed.

notes.t: Fatigue loading in aircraft engine blades
pts: Aircraft engine blades experience fatigue from both thermal cycling and mechanical loading.
Thermal fatigue arises from temperature swings between airport ground level and cruise altitude.
Centrifugal force from rotation imposes a steady and cyclic tensile stress on each blade.
Bird strike is a sudden mechanical impact that can initiate or grow fatigue cracks.
tips: Do not treat centrifugal load as purely static; it fluctuates with each start-stop cycle, so it contributes to fatigue.
Identify all sources of cyclic loading (thermal, centrifugal, impact) when classifying the fatigue type, not just the dominant one.
rq: Why is a blade's fatigue life affected by flights to 30,000 feet even if the blade is never loaded at full power on the ground?
Each flight cycle takes the blade through a large temperature change, so thermal stresses are repeatedly applied and removed, accumulating fatigue damage regardless of mechanical load.
Why does the centrifugal stress in a rotating blade count as fatigue loading rather than a static load?
The engine starts, runs, and stops on every flight, so the centrifugal stress rises and falls cyclically, producing repeated stress reversals/fluctuations that cause fatigue.

notes.t: Fatigue loading types in steel bridges
pts: Fatigue in a steel bridge can be driven by thermal, chemical and mechanical sources; weather cycles cause thermal fatigue.
De-icing chemicals act as a chemical source of degradation contributing to fatigue damage.
Dead weight of the bridge gives a steady mean load, which is not itself the fatigue-driving component.
Traffic weight produces dynamic, fluctuating loads that are the main source of mechanical fatigue loading.
Wind loads are a further mechanical source of cyclic stress.
defs: Fatigue
Progressive, localised structural damage caused by repeated fluctuating stresses, leading to crack initiation and failure at stresses well below the static strength.
Mean load (dead weight)
The steady, permanent load from the structure's own weight, which sets the mean stress about which cyclic stresses vary.
Dynamic (fatigue) loads
Time-varying loads from moving traffic that cause cyclic stress ranges responsible for fatigue damage.
tips: Do not confuse mean (dead) load with fatigue load: only the varying component of stress drives fatigue.
Remember that fatigue can be triggered by thermal, chemical and mechanical sources together, not just by traffic.
rq: Why does the dead weight of the bridge not by itself cause fatigue, even though it is a large load?
Because it is essentially constant, so it produces a mean stress with no cyclic stress range; fatigue requires fluctuating stress, supplied by traffic and wind.
Why might thermal weather cycles cause fatigue in a steel bridge even without any traffic?
Daily and seasonal temperature changes cause repeated expansion and contraction; if restrained, this produces cyclic thermal stresses.

notes.t: Fatigue types: service loading and environment
pts: Fatigue in a car suspension bolt is driven by cyclic stress from mechanical loads such as vehicle weight, cornering and speed bumps.
Thermal cycling from weather can also cause fatigue damage in components through repeated expansion and contraction.
A chemical environment, such as road salt, can accelerate crack initiation and growth under cyclic loading.
The stress σ shown on the bolted joint is a fluctuating (alternating) stress, which is the signature of fatigue loading.
defs: Fatigue
Progressive, localised cracking and failure of a material under repeated or fluctuating stresses, usually at levels well below the static yield or tensile strength.
tips: Classify each loading source correctly: mechanical (weight, cornering, speed bumps), thermal (weather) and chemical (salt) fatigue are distinct categories.
Do not confuse fatigue with simple overload: fatigue involves repeated loading, so the stress need not exceed the static strength to cause failure.
rq: Why can a bolt fail by fatigue even when the static load it carries is well below its yield strength?
Because repeated fluctuating stresses initiate and grow cracks progressively, so failure occurs at stress amplitudes far below the static strength.
Why would salt from roads matter for a suspension bolt that is loaded purely mechanically?
A corrosive environment combined with cyclic stress promotes crack initiation and growth (corrosion-fatigue), lowering the fatigue life compared with dry conditions.

notes.t: Fatigue types in aircraft wings
pts: Aircraft wings experience fatigue from several environmental and loading sources, not just one.
Thermal fatigue arises from temperature cycling due to weather and from the change between ground and flying height.
Chemical environment fatigue can be driven by de-icing fluids that come into contact with the wing structure.
Mechanical fatigue comes from cyclic loads such as the on-ground weight of the wings, in-air weight of the aircraft, storms and clear air turbulence.
tips: Do not treat fatigue as only mechanical; thermal and chemical environments also contribute and should be listed when asked for fatigue types.
Distinguish the on-ground weight of the wings from the in-air loading of the aircraft, since they produce different stress cycles.
rq: Why is clear air turbulence a fatigue concern even though it is not a severe single-event load?

Its repeated, fluctuating gust loads cause many stress cycles over the aircraft's life, and fatigue damage accumulates from repeated cycling even when each individual load is well below the static strength.
How could de-icer contribute to fatigue of a wing structure?
A chemical environment can cause corrosion or environmentally assisted crack growth, so combined chemical attack and cyclic stress accelerates fatigue cracking compared with cycling in air alone.

units.name: 17.8 Fatigue limit and factors affecting fatigue life
units.ov: This module covers the S–N curve and the fatigue limit, which exists for steels and titanium alloys but not for aluminium alloys. It then covers the factors that shift fatigue life: mean stress, loading frequency (important for polymers because of hysteretic heating), and surface compressive stress treatments. The unifying idea is that fatigue life depends on crack initiation and growth at the surface, so anything that raises the local tensile stress or the temperature shortens life, and anything that puts the surface in compression extends it.
must: S–N curve: stress amplitude (MPa) against cycles to failure N on a log scale; steel and titanium alloys flatten out at the fatigue limit, typically at about \(10^7\) cycles
Fatigue limit: the stress amplitude below which failure does not occur however many cycles are applied; aluminium alloys have none, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated N (e.g. \(10^8\))
Stress amplitude \(\sigma_a=(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2\) and mean stress \(\sigma_m=(\sigma_{max}+\sigma_{min})/2\) are different quantities; don't confuse them
Tensile mean stress lowers the S–N curve, so life at a given amplitude is shorter; zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest life, and static tensile strength is unaffected
Metals below yield: frequency has only a limited effect, because the response is purely elastic and the energy is returned each cycle with no hysteresis loss
Polymers are viscoelastic: energy in per cycle is not equal to energy out, and the hysteresis loop area \(W_d=\oint\sigma\,d\varepsilon\) is dissipated as heat
Self-heating in polymers shortens life at higher frequency; PMMA bone cement at ±30 MPa in air failed at \(\log_{10}N\approx3.3\) (5 Hz) against about 4.1 (2 Hz), and the 5 Hz specimens were warm
Read log axes correctly: \(\log_{10}N=4\) means \(10^4\) cycles, so the 5 Hz result is about \(2\times10^3\) cycles against about \(1.3\times10^4\) at 2 Hz, roughly a factor of 6 fewer
Surface compressive stress suppresses the growth of surface cracks, which are the usual fatigue initiation sites, and so extends life

Shot peening plastically deforms the surface layer so it is left in residual compression; carburizing diffuses carbon into the surface of low-carbon steel from a C-rich gas, and the compressive layer arises together with hardening, not from diffusion alone
conn: Mean stress and surface treatments: shot peening and carburizing impose residual compressive stress, which acts like a lower (compressive) mean stress and moves the S–N curve up
S–N curve shape and material choice: a steel with a fatigue limit can be designed for infinite life below that amplitude, whereas aluminium must be designed for a finite life at a stated N

Frequency, hysteresis and material class: metals below yield have no hysteresis and so are insensitive to frequency, while polymers have a hysteresis loop, heating and reduced life; yielding in metals brings frequency effects back
Units and log scales link all the S–N reading questions: stress in MPa (N/mm²) and N on a log axis, so reading values off the graph requires care
exq: Sketch S–N curves for a steel and an aluminium alloy. Mark the fatigue limit, state at roughly what N it is defined, and explain how you would specify an allowable stress for the aluminium.

A component sees stresses cycling between +200 MPa and −60 MPa. Calculate the stress amplitude and mean stress, then explain with a sketch how the S–N curve and fatigue life change if the mean stress is made more tensile.

PMMA bone cement tested at ±30 MPa in air gives \(\log_{10}N\approx4.1\) at 2 Hz and 3.3 at 5 Hz. Convert these to cycles, find the ratio, and explain the difference using hysteresis and heating. Why would a steel specimen below yield show little frequency dependence?
Explain how shot peening and carburizing improve the fatigue life of a steel shaft. Relate your answer to surface cracks and to mean stress.

Define the energy dissipated per cycle \(W_d=\oint\sigma\,d\varepsilon\). Sketch the hysteresis loops for a metal below yield and a polymer, and discuss how the loop area affects specimen temperature and fatigue life.

notes.t: Fatigue limit (endurance limit)
pts: Some materials (e.g. steel, titanium alloys) have a stress amplitude below which fatigue failure does not occur, however many cycles are applied.
The fatigue limit is typically defined at about \(10^{7}\) load cycles in testing; beyond this the S–N curve becomes flat.
Aluminium alloys show no clear endurance limit; their S–N curve keeps falling, so they will eventually fail at any stress level.
The vertical axis is the peak value of repeated tensile stress (MPa) and the horizontal axis is the number of cycles to failure on a log scale.
defs: Fatigue limit (endurance limit)
The stress amplitude below which a material can withstand an infinite (practically ~\(10^{7}\) or more) number of load cycles without fatigue failure.
S–N curve
A plot of stress amplitude against number of cycles to failure; for materials with an endurance limit it levels off horizontally, while for others it keeps decreasing.
tips: Do not assume every metal has a fatigue limit; aluminium alloys do not, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated number of cycles instead.
Check units: the stress axis is in MPa (N/mm²), and the cycle count is dimensionless but must be given on a log scale.
rq: Why can't aluminium alloys be designed using an endurance limit like steel?
Their S–N curve has no horizontal plateau, so failure eventually occurs at any stress level; a finite fatigue life must be specified instead (e.g. at \(10^{8}\) cycles).
Why is the horizontal axis plotted on a logarithmic scale?
Fatigue lives span many orders of magnitude (\(10^{4}\) to \(10^{8}\) cycles), so a log scale displays the whole range clearly and makes the knee and plateau visible.

notes.t: Effect of mean stress on fatigue life
pts: Increasing the mean (tensile) stress reduces the number of cycles to failure at a given stress amplitude.
Curves shift downward as mean stress becomes more tensile, so fatigue life is shorter for the same stress amplitude.
Near-zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest fatigue life for the same stress amplitude.
On an S–N (stress amplitude vs cycles to failure) plot, a horizontal line at fixed amplitude crosses each curve at a different N, showing the reduction in life.
defs: Mean stress (\( \sigma_m \))
The average of the maximum and minimum stresses in a fatigue cycle; tensile mean stress is harmful to fatigue life.
Stress amplitude (\( \sigma \))
Half the range of stress in a cyclic loading, plotted on the vertical axis of an S–N diagram.
Cycles to failure (\( N \))
The number of load cycles a material withstands before fatigue fracture at a given stress level.
