tips: Do not confuse stress amplitude with mean stress; the graph holds amplitude on the vertical axis and changes the mean stress as the curve parameter.
Remember that the effect applies to fatigue (cyclic) loading only; mean stress does not change the static tensile strength of the material.
rq: Why does a tensile mean stress shorten fatigue life even when the stress amplitude is unchanged?
A tensile mean stress raises the peak stress in each cycle, so crack initiation and growth occur more readily, reducing the cycles to failure.
If two components have the same stress amplitude but one has compressive mean stress, which will last longer and why?
The compressive-mean-stress component, because compressive mean stress tends to keep cracks closed and lowers the effective tensile stress at the crack tip.

notes.t: Effect of frequency on fatigue/cyclic loading
pts: In metals, loading frequency has only a limited effect on behaviour.
Below yield, metals respond purely elastically, so no hysteresis losses accumulate.
In metals each load cycle returns all the energy put in, so little energy is retained in the material.
In polymers, frequency can have a substantial effect because they are viscoelastic and dissipate energy.
tips: Do not assume frequency is irrelevant for all materials: the 'limited effect' statement applies to metals below yield, not to polymers.
Remember the metal result holds only for purely elastic loading; above yield, plastic work makes frequency relevant again.
rq: Why does loading frequency matter much more for polymers than for metals below yield?

Polymers are viscoelastic: part of the input energy is dissipated as heat each cycle (hysteresis), and the response depends on time/rate. Metals below yield are purely elastic, so energy in equals energy returned and little is retained.
What would happen to the heat generated in a polymer component if the loading frequency were increased?
More energy is dissipated per unit time, so the temperature rises faster, which can soften the polymer, change its stiffness and accelerate fatigue or creep damage.

notes.t: Effect of loading frequency on fatigue life of polymers (PMMA bone cement)
pts: Polymers rarely show purely elastic behaviour, so energy input per cycle is not fully recovered on unloading.
Energy put in per load cycle is not equal to energy got out, so some is absorbed (hysteresis) each cycle.
Absorbed energy that cannot escape is retained as heat, raising specimen temperature and accelerating failure.
At ±30 MPa in air, PMMA specimens tested at 5 Hz failed after far fewer cycles than at 2 Hz (about log10 N ≈ 3.3 vs ≈ 4.1).
5 Hz specimens were warm to the touch after testing, evidence of self-heating due to energy absorption.
defs: Hysteresis (in polymers)
Energy dissipated per load cycle as the stress–strain loading and unloading paths do not coincide, shown as an enclosed loop area; the dissipated energy typically appears as heat.
eqs: Energy dissipated per cycle (area of hysteresis loop)
\(W_{d}\) = energy dissipated per cycle (J/\(m^{3}\)); \sigma = stress (Pa); \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless)
tips: Plot is log10 of cycles to failure: a value of 4 means \(10^{4}\) cycles, not 4 cycles; don't confuse the logarithmic axis with linear.
Frequency alone is not a material property; results only apply to the stated stress amplitude, environment (in air) and material (PMMA), and heating effects depend on specimen size and heat loss.
rq: Why does a higher testing frequency reduce fatigue life of PMMA even though the stress amplitude is the same?
More cycles per second means more energy absorbed per unit time, causing more self-heating that cannot be released; the heat softens/degrades the polymer and reduces cycles to failure.
What would you expect to happen to the temperature of a PMMA specimen if the loading frequency were lowered to 0.5 Hz at the same stress amplitude?
Less heat generated per unit time, so the specimen would stay cooler and its fatigue life would be longer, since heat can be lost to surroundings between cycles.

notes.t: Improving Fatigue Life: Surface Compressive Stress
pts: Imposing a compressive surface stress suppresses the growth of surface cracks, which are the usual starting points of fatigue failure.
A near-zero or compressive mean stress gives the highest stress amplitude for a given number of cycles to failure, so fatigue life is longest; increasing tensile mean stress lowers the S–N curve.
Shot peening bombards the surface with small shot particles, plastically deforming the surface layer so it is left in compression.
Carburizing diffuses carbon into the surface from a C-rich gas, producing a surface layer that is put into compression on treatment, which suppresses crack growth.
defs: Mean stress (\(\sigma_m\))
The average of the maximum and minimum stresses in a fatigue cycle; tensile mean stress reduces fatigue life, while zero or compressive mean stress improves it.
Stress amplitude (S)
Half the range of cyclic stress in a fatigue test, plotted against cycles to failure on an S–N curve.
Shot peening
A surface treatment in which small hard particles are fired at a component to introduce residual compressive stress in the surface layer, improving fatigue resistance.
Carburizing
A surface hardening process in which carbon diffuses into low-carbon steel from a carbon-rich atmosphere, creating a hard, compressively stressed surface layer.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of the mean stress effect: tensile mean stress reduces fatigue life, so the curves shift down as \(\sigma_m\) increases.
Carburizing creates compression only after the treatment combined with hardening (quenching); carbon diffusion alone does not give the compressive layer.
rq: Why does a compressive surface stress improve fatigue life even when the applied load cycles are unchanged?

Fatigue cracks nucleate and grow at the surface; compressive residual stress offsets the applied tensile stress there, so the effective stress range driving crack growth is reduced and cracks are suppressed.
Two components have the same stress amplitude, but one is operated with a large tensile mean stress. Which will fail first and why?
The component with the large tensile mean stress fails first, because its S–N curve lies lower, so fewer cycles are needed to reach failure at the same amplitude.

units.name: 17.9 Miner's rule for cumulative damage
units.ov: Miner's rule is a linear cumulative damage model for fatigue under variable-amplitude loading. Each block of \(n_i\) cycles at one stress level uses up a fraction \(n_i/N_{f,i}\) of life, with \(N_{f,i}\) read from the S–N curve, and failure is predicted when the fractions sum to 1. Dividing 1 by the damage accumulated per load period (e.g. per week) gives the predicted life.
must: Miner's rule: failure when \(\sum_i n_i/N_{f,i}=1\), where \(n_i\) is the cycles applied at level \(i\) and \(N_{f,i}\) is the cycles to failure at that level
Damage fraction \(D_i=n_i/N_{f,i}\) is dimensionless, and it is the fractions that get summed, never the raw cycle counts \(n_i\)
\(N_{f,i}\) must come from the S–N curve at the same stress amplitude or range as \(n_i\); mixing stress levels in one ratio is a common error
Life from repeated loading: \(T=1/\sum_i (n_i/N_{f,i})_{\text{per week}}\), which gives weeks only because the damage is a per-week rate
Worked example: 0.001 (100 MPa) + 0.01 (300 MPa) = 0.011 per week, so \(T\approx 91\) weeks
The higher stress level usually dominates the damage; check which term is largest in a block
Assumptions: damage accumulates linearly and load sequence is ignored, so the rule is empirical, not exact, and can be non-conservative for some orderings
Stress levels below the endurance limit have \(N_f\to\infty\) and contribute roughly zero damage on the simple S–N reading
Partial-life problems: if one block uses \(D_1\) of life, the remaining life at another stress is \(n_2=(1-D_1)N_{f,2}\)
conn: S–N curve reading (log-scale \(N_f\) at a given \(\sigma_a\)) feeds directly into the Miner sum, so errors in reading a log axis carry through to the life prediction
Stress amplitude, mean stress and stress range from the cyclic loading definitions determine which S–N curve and \(N_f\) to use
Damage per period leads to life in periods, then conversion to years or hours using the cycle frequency or duty cycle
Endurance limit and safety factors link to Miner's rule: a stress below the limit gives no damage, while a design factor reduces the allowable \(D\) below 1
exq: A component sees \(10^{4}\) cycles per week at 100 MPa (\(N_f=10^7\)) and \(10^{3}\) cycles per week at 300 MPa (\(N_f=10^5\)). Compute the damage per week and the predicted life in weeks.
A part is loaded for 2×\(10^{5}\) cycles at a stress where \(N_f=10^6\). Using Miner's rule, how many further cycles can it endure at a second stress where \(N_f=5\times10^4\)?
Use a given S–N curve to read \(N_f\) at three stress amplitudes, then find the total damage for a specified loading spectrum and state whether failure is predicted.
Explain why Miner's rule can be non-conservative and give two limitations, such as load sequence effects and its empirical, linear nature.
A block history is repeated until failure and contains 5 stress levels. Find the number of blocks to failure and identify which level contributes most damage.

notes.t: Minor's Rule: cumulative fatigue damage under varying stress cycles
pts: Real components see varying stress waveforms, so life predictions must handle changing stress amplitudes rather than a single constant waveform.
Damage from each series of cycles at one stress level is the fraction of endured cycles to cycles to failure at that level.
Minor's Rule assumes damage accumulates linearly; total damage from all series of cycles must sum to 100% (failure).
defs: Minor's Rule
Linear cumulative damage rule stating that failure occurs when the sum of fractional damages \(n_{i}\)/\(N_{f}\),i over all stress levels equals one.
Cycles to failure \(N_{f}\),i
Number of cycles at stress amplitude σ_a,i needed to fail the component at that stress level, read from the S–N (failure) curve.
eqs: Minor's Rule: condition for fatigue failure under varying stress amplitudes
\(n_{i}\) = number of cycles endured at stress level i (dimensionless); \(N_{f,i}\) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless); m = number of stress levels (dimensionless)
tips: Do not sum raw cycle counts \(n_{i}\); each term must be divided by the cycles to failure \(N_{f}\),i at that specific stress amplitude before summing.
Minor's Rule assumes linear damage accumulation and ignores load sequence effects, so predictions can be non-conservative for some orderings of cycles.
rq: Why does Minor's Rule sum fractions of damage rather than simply counting total cycles endured?

Because cycles at high stress amplitude cause far more damage than cycles at low amplitude; each cycle is weighted by its share of the cycles to failure at that stress level, so the sum of fractional damages indicates how close the component is to failure.
If a component has \(n_{1}\)/\(N_{f}\),1 = 0.4 at one stress level, what must the rest of the load history contribute for failure to be predicted?
The remaining damage fractions must sum to 0.6, i.e. the other stress levels together must account for 60% of the damage.

notes.t: Adding sets of cycles (Miner's rule)
pts: Miner's rule is an empirical rule for cumulative fatigue damage from several loading regimes.
Each set of cycles consumes a fraction of the total fatigue life.
Failure is predicted when the summed fractional damage reaches one.
defs: Miner's rule
Empirical linear damage rule stating that fatigue failure occurs when the sum of cycle ratios applied to cycles-to-failure at each loading level equals one.
Cycles to failure (\(N_{\text{fi}}\))
The number of cycles at a given loading regime (stress range) that would cause fatigue failure if applied alone.
Cycles applied (\(N_{i}\))
The number of cycles actually applied at loading regime i.
eqs: Miner's cumulative damage criterion (failure when sum equals 1)
\(N_{i}\) = number of cycles applied at regime i (dimensionless count); \(N_{fi}\) = cycles to failure at regime i (dimensionless count); \(\sum_{i}\) = sum over all loading regimes
tips: Miner's rule is empirical and ignores load sequence effects; do not claim it is exact for variable-amplitude loading.
\(N_{i}\) and \(N_{\text{fi}}\) must be counts at the same stress range; mixing different stress ranges in one ratio is a common error.
rq: Why does Miner's rule assume damage adds linearly, and what does a sum less than 1 tell you about remaining life?

It is an empirical simplification that each cycle at a level uses a fixed fraction of life, independent of order. A sum below 1 means the component has not yet failed and remaining life is the unused fraction (1 minus the sum) of the total fatigue life.
What if the same number of cycles is applied at a high stress range versus a low stress range?
High stress range cycles have a much smaller \(N_{\text{fi}}\), so they consume a larger fraction of life (\(N_{i}\)/\(N_{\text{fi}}\) is larger), contributing more damage per cycle.

notes.t: Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage
pts: Each load level contributes a damage fraction equal to applied cycles divided by cycles to failure at that stress; damage fractions are summed.
Failure is predicted when the summed damage fraction reaches 1 (100% damage); the time to failure is the reciprocal of the damage accumulated per week.
Weekly damage here is 0.001 from the 100 MPa loading plus 0.01 from the 300 MPa loading, giving 0.011 per week.
defs: Damage fraction (Miner's rule)
The fraction of fatigue life consumed by a given number of cycles at a given stress amplitude, equal to \(n_i/N_i\); failure is expected when the sum of these fractions equals 1.
eqs: Miner's rule cumulative damage at failure
\(n_i\) = applied cycles at stress level i (dimensionless count); \(N_i\) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless count)
Predicted life in weeks from weekly damage
\(T\) = expected life (weeks); \(\sum n_i/N_i\) per week = damage fraction accumulated per week (dimensionless)
tips: Keep consistent units: damage fractions are dimensionless, so the life result in weeks comes only from the per-week damage rate, not from mixing cycles and weeks.
Use cycles to failure at each specific stress amplitude (\(N_i\)) rather than the cycles applied, and do not forget to sum all stress levels before taking the reciprocal.
rq: Why can the damage fractions from 100 MPa and 300 MPa simply be added together?
Miner's rule assumes linear damage accumulation, so each stress level's cycles consume a fixed share of life independent of the order of loading, and the total damage is their sum.
What would happen to the predicted life if the 300 MPa loading were doubled to 1000 cycles per week?
Its damage fraction doubles to 0.02, so weekly damage becomes 0.021 and life falls to about 1/0.021 ≈ 47.6 weeks.

units.name: 18.1 Material selection criteria and the materials cycle
units.ov: This module introduces the criteria used to choose engineering materials and places that choice within the materials cycle. Properties are split into intrinsic (bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical, surface) and attributive (price, availability, production, aesthetics) groups, and good selection weighs all of them together. The materials cycle shows that this choice affects the whole product life from extraction to disposal or recycling, which links selection to cost and sustainability.
must: Intrinsic properties are inherent to the material: bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical and surface properties.
Attributive properties are assigned by external factors: price and availability, production properties (ease of manufacture and fabrication) and aesthetics (appearance, texture).
Material selection must draw on all branches of the property diagram, not only bulk mechanical properties such as strength and stiffness.
Materials cycle order: raw materials → synthesis and processing → engineered materials → design, manufacture and assembly → products → use (construction, transport, energy, health) → waste.
At the waste stage, material is either recycled/reused or discarded to the environment, which closes the loop back to raw materials.
Recycle/reuse feeds back into synthesis and processing, not directly into product manufacture, so the cycle is a loop and not a straight line.
Raw materials (ores, minerals) are extracted from the Earth; engineered materials are the result of synthesis and processing to give specific properties. Do not mix these up.
Recycling reduces the demand for new raw materials, which is the main link between the cycle and sustainability.
Material choice affects the whole product life cycle (manufacture, use, end of life), not just performance in service.
conn: Attributive properties such as cost, availability and manufacturability constrain which materials with suitable intrinsic properties can actually be used, so selection is a trade-off between the two groups.
Material choice at the design stage determines how easily the product can be recycled or reused at end of life, which links selection to the sustainability loop.
Recycling and availability are linked: higher recycling rates reduce demand for raw material extraction, which affects price and supply security.
Production properties (ease of fabrication) connect the 'manufacture and assembly' stage of the cycle to the attributive branch of the property diagram.
exq: Define intrinsic and attributive properties. Classify each of these as intrinsic or attributive and justify your answers: yield strength, price per kg, thermal conductivity, surface hardness, surface finish appearance, ease of welding.
Sketch the materials cycle, labelling raw materials, engineered materials, products, use, waste, and the recycle/reuse path. Explain where recycled material re-enters the cycle and why.

A company is choosing a material for a consumer product. Discuss why bulk mechanical properties alone are not sufficient, and list the other property groups that must be considered with an example of each.
Explain the difference between raw materials and engineered materials, giving one example of each, and describe how recycling reduces the need for raw material extraction.
Discuss how the choice of material at the design stage can influence sustainability across the whole product life cycle, referring to the materials cycle.

notes.t: Choosing Materials: Properties Considered in Design
pts: Material properties split into intrinsic properties (inherent to the material itself) and attributive properties (depend on cost, supply and how the material is made or looks).
Intrinsic properties include bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical and surface properties.
Attributive properties include price and availability, production properties (ease of manufacture, fabrication) and aesthetic properties (appearance, texture).
Material selection for design draws on all these property groups together, not on mechanical properties alone.
defs: Intrinsic property
A property inherent to the material itself, such as bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical or surface properties, independent of how or where it is used.
Attributive property
A property attributed to a material by external factors such as price, availability, ease of production and aesthetics, rather than by its inherent physics.
tips: Do not confuse intrinsic properties (inherent to the material) with attributive properties (cost, production, appearance), which depend on external factors.
Design selection should consider all branches of the property diagram, not only bulk mechanical properties.
rq: Why might a material with excellent bulk mechanical properties still be rejected for a consumer product?
Because attributive properties such as price, availability, ease of manufacture or aesthetic appearance and texture can outweigh intrinsic performance in the design decision.
Which property group would determine whether a component's surface resists wear, and why is it classed as intrinsic?
Surface properties; they belong to the intrinsic group because they are a physical characteristic of the material's surface itself.

notes.t: The Materials Cycle
pts: Materials flow in a closed cycle: raw materials are synthesised and processed into engineered materials, which are designed, manufactured and assembled into products.
Products are used across many application areas such as construction, transportation, energy and health before they become waste.
Waste can be recycled or reused and fed back into synthesis and processing, reducing the need for new raw materials.
Materials that are not recycled are discarded as waste and ultimately returned to the environment, closing the loop back to raw materials extracted from the Earth.
The cycle links materials science to engineering design, manufacturing and sustainability, showing that material choice affects the whole product life cycle.
defs: Raw materials
Naturally occurring substances extracted from the Earth (e.g. ores, minerals) that are the starting point for engineered materials.
Engineered materials
Materials produced by synthesis and processing of raw materials to achieve specific properties for an intended application.
Recycle/reuse
Recovering used material from waste and returning it to synthesis and processing, either as the same material or a new one.
tips: Do not treat the cycle as a straight line: recycle/reuse feeds back into synthesis and processing, not directly into product manufacture.
Remember that 'raw materials' are extracted from the Earth, while 'engineered materials' have been synthesised or processed; mixing these up is a common error.
rq: Why does recycling reduce environmental impact compared with always extracting new raw materials?
It reduces demand for mining and extraction, lowering energy use, emissions and the depletion of finite natural resources, and it reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill.
What would happen to the cycle if no waste were recycled or reused?
Every product would need fresh raw materials, so the loop would become a linear 'extract–make–dispose' flow, increasing resource depletion and waste accumulation.

units.name: 18.2 Sources and abundance of raw materials
units.ov: This module covers where engineering materials come from (mining, synthesis from oil, growing, processing) and how abundant the elements are in the crust, oceans and atmosphere. The key link is that abundance by weight percent determines which elements are plentiful, and so which raw materials (metal ores, ceramics, polymers) are available. A side page on diamond carats provides a unit-conversion example that is not core materials content.
must: Around 15 billion tonnes of raw material are extracted worldwide each year
Metals come from mining ores; ceramics come from mined raw materials, either used directly or after processing (never say all ceramics are simply mined)
Polymers are artificial (from oil or other raw products) or natural (grown, e.g. rubber)
Composites are mixtures of other material classes, so their source depends on their constituents
Do not confuse natural materials (e.g. wood) with natural polymers: both are grown but belong to different material classes
Crust by weight: oxygen 47 wt%, silicon 27 wt%
Oceans: oxygen 85 wt%, hydrogen 10 wt% (water, H₂O). Atmosphere: nitrogen 79 wt%, oxygen 19 wt%, argon 2 wt%
Oxygen is the only element abundant in all three reservoirs; carbon is scarce in all (0.02 wt% crust, 0.002 wt% oceans, 0.04 wt% CO₂ in air)
Wt% is a mass fraction of the reservoir, not an atomic percentage; listed values do not sum to 100, and atmospheric CO₂ is a compound so it should not be compared directly with elemental carbon
Carat conversion: \(m_g = m_{ct}/5\) since 1 ct = 200 mg; e.g. 16.08 ct ≈ 3216 mg ≈ 3.2 g (carat is mass, not karat gold purity)
conn: Abundance and source: the dominance of oxygen and silicon in the crust explains why many mined raw materials are oxides and silicates, which relates to ceramics and to metal ores
Material class and source: classification (metal, polymer, ceramic, composite) determines the extraction route, and composites inherit the sources of their constituents

Wt% and compounds: the oceans' 85 wt% oxygen and 10 wt% hydrogen arise from water, and atmospheric carbon appears as CO₂, so interpreting a table requires distinguishing elements from compounds and mass from atomic fractions
Scarcity versus importance: carbon is rare in every reservoir yet underpins polymers (oil-based), so low abundance does not imply low engineering use
exq: State the two most abundant elements in the Earth's crust with their wt%, and explain why oxygen is the only element abundant in the crust, oceans and atmosphere.
Describe the sources of each of the four material classes. Why is it incorrect to say that all ceramics are simply mined, and how does wood differ from a natural polymer such as rubber?
Define weight percent. Explain why the wt% values in the abundance table do not sum to 100, and why 0.04 wt% CO₂ in air cannot be compared directly with 0.02 wt% carbon in the crust.
A 16.08 ct fancy vivid pink diamond sold for $28.5 million. Convert its mass to grams, then calculate the price per gram.
If 15 billion tonnes of raw material are extracted annually, estimate the mass of oxygen that would be present in a 15 billion tonne sample of crustal material at 47 wt%, and state any assumptions.

notes.t: Sources of materials
pts: Worldwide, around 15 billion tonnes of raw material are extracted per year.
Metals are obtained by mining ores from the earth.
Polymers are either artificial (made from oil or other raw products) or natural (grown, e.g. rubber).
Ceramics come from mined raw materials, either directly or after processing.
Composites are mixtures of the other material classes, so their source depends on the type.
tips: Do not confuse natural materials (grown, e.g. wood) with natural polymers; both are grown but belong to different material classes.
Ceramics may be mined directly or processed from mined raw materials, so do not state that all ceramics are simply mined.
rq: Why are polymers classed as either artificial or natural, and what does this imply about their source?
Artificial polymers are synthesised from oil or other raw chemical feedstocks, whereas natural polymers (such as rubber from rubber tapping) are grown by living organisms.
Why can a composite's source not be assigned to a single category?
Composites are mixtures of metals, polymers, ceramics and natural materials, so their raw sources combine those of each constituent.

notes.t: Abundance of elements in the crust, oceans and atmosphere
pts: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust (47 wt%), followed by silicon (27 wt%).
Oxygen dominates the oceans (85 wt%), with hydrogen second (10 wt%), reflecting water as H₂O.
The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen (79 wt%), with oxygen (19 wt%) and argon (2 wt%) making up nearly all of the rest.
Oxygen appears in all three reservoirs, so it is the only element that is abundant across crust, oceans and atmosphere.
Carbon is very scarce in all three reservoirs (0.02 wt% crust, 0.002 wt% oceans, 0.04 wt% as CO₂ in air).
defs: Weight percent (Wt%)
The mass of a given element as a percentage of the total mass of the reservoir (crust, oceans or atmosphere) in which it occurs.
tips: Wt% values are mass fractions and do not sum to 100 across a table, since only the major elements are listed; do not treat them as atomic percentages.
CO₂ in the atmosphere is listed as a compound (0.04 wt%), not as an element, so do not compare it directly with elemental carbon values.
rq: Why does oxygen appear at high percentage in the crust, oceans and atmosphere, while nitrogen does not appear in the crust or oceans table?

Oxygen is bound into silicate minerals in the crust and into water in the oceans, and free O₂ is present in air; nitrogen is largely unreactive and stays as N₂ gas in the atmosphere, so it is not listed as a major component of the crust or oceans.
Why might silicon be far more abundant in the crust (27 wt%) than in the oceans (not listed at all)?
Silicon combines with oxygen to form silicates and silica, which are the main rock-forming minerals, and these remain solid in the crust rather than dissolving into seawater.

notes.t: Diamond carat weight and auction value (not a materials lecture page)
pts: The carat is a unit of mass used for gemstones, with 1 carat equal to 200 milligrams.
A 16.08 ct fancy vivid pink diamond weighing 3.2 g sold for $28.5 million at Christie's Geneva in 2015, a world auction record for a fancy vivid pink diamond.
eqs: Converting carat weight to mass in grams
\(m_{g}\) = mass in grams (g); \(m_{ct}\) = mass in carats (ct)
tips: Do not confuse the metric carat (mass, 200 mg) with the karat (gold purity); the page's unit is carats.
Check the arithmetic: 16.08 ct × 200 mg = 3216 mg ≈ 3.2 g, consistent with the quoted mass.
rq: Why does the page list the carat-to-milligram conversion next to a gemstone rather than a steel sample?
Carats are the standard unit for gemstone mass, so the conversion lets you relate a diamond's carat weight to its physical mass in grams or milligrams.

units.name: 18.3 Material costs and price trends
units.ov: This module covers how material cost is defined and why it varies: price per tonne set by world commodity markets, processing cost per object, and environmental cost. It shows short-term volatility (gold, stainless steel 304 vs 316) against a long-term upward trend driven by ore depletion and energy costs, with recycling as the counter. It ends with UK import data showing that a few bulk materials dominate by cost.
must: Raw material prices fluctuate in the short term but tend to rise in the long term; always state both
Long-term rise is driven by depletion of rich ore deposits (lower-grade ores must be processed) and rising energy costs
Recycling cuts the energy needed to produce a material, lowering both cost and environmental impact, so it counters rising cost
Material cost is quoted per unit mass (e.g. £, € or $ per tonne), whereas processing cost is per manufactured object; do not mix the units directly
Processing cost depends on shaping and can outweigh raw material cost for complex shapes
Environmental cost includes extraction/production impact, resource availability and recyclability, not just price
Price per tonne is set by world supply and demand and commodity markets, and is shifted unpredictably by politics and weather, so quote the date or source of cost data
Stainless steel: 316 is consistently dearer than 304 over 2004–2010; both peaked around 2007–08 and fell sharply in 2008–09 (a commodity cycle); prices are US$ per tonne for cold rolled coil (CRC)
Distinguish actual transaction prices from MEPS forecasts (Aug 2009) when reading price charts, and read the axis units carefully
UK imports by cost (Ashby & Jones): iron & steel 27.0%, wood & timber 21.0%, copper 13.0%, together about 61%; silver & platinum 6.5%, tungsten 0.3%, mercury 0.2%; shares are by cost, not weight
conn: Ore depletion, energy cost and recycling combine into one argument: depletion and energy raise production cost, recycling reduces energy use and so cost and environmental impact
Cost per tonne versus processing cost per object: a cheap material may be a poor choice if its shape is costly to make, so unit consistency matters in material selection
Commodity price volatility (gold, 304/316 steel) versus the long-term rising trend: forecasts like MEPS can be wrong, so dated sources are needed
Import cost shares reflect both price and quantity: bulk materials dominate by cost, while high-priced metals such as silver and platinum punch above their volume
exq: Explain why raw material costs fluctuate in the short term yet tend to rise in the long term, and describe how recycling affects this.
Distinguish between material cost, processing cost and environmental cost. State the units for each and explain why a cheap material per tonne might not give the cheapest component.
A graph shows 304 and 316 stainless steel CRC prices (US$/tonne) for 2004–2010 with MEPS forecasts. Describe the trends, compare the two grades, and comment on how reliable the forecasts were.

Using the UK import data, calculate the combined cost share of iron & steel, wood & timber and copper. Explain why the percentages must not be read as tonnage, and why silver & platinum at 6.5% outweigh tungsten at 0.3%.
Discuss how world supply and demand, politics and weather affect the price per tonne of a material, and why cost data should be dated when used in material selection.

notes.t: Financial choices: raw material costs and recycling
pts: Raw material costs fluctuate in the short term but tend to rise over the long term.
Long-term cost rise is driven by depletion of rich ore deposits, so lower-grade ores must be processed.
Rising energy costs push up the cost of producing materials, since extraction and processing are energy-intensive.
Using recycled materials significantly reduces the energy needed to produce a material, lowering both cost and environmental impact.
tips: Do not confuse short-term price fluctuation with the long-term upward trend in raw material costs; state both when asked.
Explain the cost link: rising energy costs and depleted ores both increase production cost, and recycling counters this by cutting energy use.
rq: Why does recycling a metal usually cost less energy than producing it from ore?
Recycling skips the energy-intensive steps of mining, ore reduction (e.g. smelting/electrolysis) and refining, only needing to melt and reprocess existing material.
Why might a material's price fall in one year yet still show a rising long-term trend?
Short-term prices fluctuate with supply, demand and market conditions, whereas the long-term trend is set by structural factors such as ore depletion and rising energy costs.

notes.t: Cost of materials selection
pts: Material cost is commonly expressed as price per unit mass, such as £, € or $ per tonne.
Processing cost is judged per manufactured object, so it depends on how the material is shaped, not just its raw price.
Environmental cost considers the impact of extracting or producing the material, how available the resource is, and whether it can be recycled.
defs: Processing cost
The cost of manufacturing a component from a material, quoted per object made, which can outweigh raw material cost for complex shapes.
Recyclability
The ability of a material to be recovered and reprocessed at end of life, reducing environmental cost and resource demand.
tips: Keep units consistent: material cost is per mass (tonne⁻¹), whereas processing cost is per object, so don't mix them directly.
Environmental cost is not just price: include extraction/production impact, resource availability and recyclability when justifying a choice.
rq: Why might a cheap material per tonne still give an expensive component?
Because processing cost per object (machining, forming, joining, finishing) can dominate; a hard-to-shape material may cost far more to make into the part than its raw price suggests.
Why is comparing materials by price per tonne alone misleading?
Density and the amount of material needed differ, and processing cost per object and environmental factors are ignored, so the true cost of the finished part can be different.

notes.t: Costs per tonne of materials
pts: The cost per tonne of a material is not fixed; it varies with the material chosen.
Price is set by the balance between world supply and demand for the material.
Prices are driven by the current state of world commodity markets.
Political events and even weather can shift material costs unpredictably.
tips: Material cost per tonne is market-dependent and time-varying, so always state the date or source of cost data when comparing materials.
rq: Why might two materials with similar performance have very different costs per tonne?
Because each material's cost depends on its own world supply and demand and its commodity market conditions, not just its properties.
Why is a material cost estimate from last year potentially unreliable for a design decision today?
Commodity prices respond to changing supply, demand, politics and weather, so the cost per tonne can change over time.

notes.t: Stainless steel price trends (304 vs 316)
pts: 316 stainless steel consistently trades at a higher price than 304 across the whole 2004–2010 period.
Both grades peaked around 2007–2008 and then fell sharply in 2008–2009, reflecting a commodity price cycle.
The chart compares actual transaction prices with MEPS forecasts made in August 2009, which were used to predict future prices.
Prices are quoted as transaction prices in US dollars per tonne for cold rolled coil (CRC).
defs: Cold rolled coil (CRC)
Stainless steel sheet strip rolled at room temperature after hot rolling, giving a good surface finish and tight tolerances; priced per tonne in the market.
tips: Read the y-axis as US$ per tonne, not per kg or per ton, when quoting price values.
Distinguish actual transaction prices (solid lines) from MEPS forecasts (markers) when interpreting future trends.
rq: Why might 316 stainless steel be more expensive than 304 even though both are austenitic stainless steels?
316 contains molybdenum (about 2–3%), which improves corrosion resistance, especially against chlorides, and the added alloying element raises its cost.
What might cause the sharp price fall in late 2008 to early 2009 shown on the chart?
A global economic downturn reduced demand for steel, so market prices dropped sharply.

notes.t: UK imported materials by cost percentage
pts: Iron & steel is the largest single category of UK imported materials by cost, at 27.0%.
Wood & timber and copper together make up a large share of imports, at 21.0% and 13.0% respectively.
Imports are dominated by a few bulk materials: iron & steel, wood & timber and copper account for about 61% of cost.
Precious and specialist metals such as silver & platinum (6.5%) contribute far more by cost than tungsten (0.3%) or mercury (0.2%).
Data source is Ashby & Jones, so the chart reflects a published materials-flow analysis rather than raw customs figures.
tips: Percentages here are by cost, not by weight; do not interpret them as shares of tonnage.
The percentages sum to roughly 100%, so use them as proportions of total import value when comparing materials.
rq: Why might a material with a low tonnage (e.g. platinum) still have a high share of import cost?
Its cost per kilogram is very high, so a small mass of material can represent a large share of total import value.
What would you expect to change about this ranking if the data were expressed by mass rather than by cost?
Bulk, low-price materials such as wood and iron/steel would likely rise in rank, while high-value metals like silver, platinum and tungsten would fall.

units.name: 18.4 Relative costs of engineering materials
units.ov: This material introduces relative cost, a dimensionless measure of a material's price per kilogram normalised to rolled A36 plain carbon steel (= 100). It compares metals and non-metals on a logarithmic scale, from cheap bulk materials such as concrete and wood to expensive ones such as precious metals, diamond and carbon fibre. Cost is treated as a selection criterion alongside properties: a costly material is chosen only when its performance justifies the premium.
must: Definition: \( \bar{c} = \dfrac{(\$/\text{kg})}{(\$/\text{kg})_{\text{ref}}} \), where the reference is rolled A36 plain carbon steel with \( \bar{c}=100 \).
Relative cost is dimensionless and has no units. It is not a £ or $ value, and the reference must always be stated when quoting it.
Interpreting values: \( \bar{c}=1000 \) means ten times the cost per kg of steel, and \( \bar{c}=50 \) means half the cost.
Relative cost is used because it fluctuates less than absolute prices over time, currency and date.
The chart axis is logarithmic, so equal vertical distances mean multiplicative cost ratios, not additive differences.

Metals: structural metals (steels, Al alloys, Cu) cost a few to tens of times steel. Au and Pt are orders of magnitude more, so they are used only where performance justifies it. Ti alloys cost about 2× commercially pure Ti.

Non-metals: concrete (about 6) and wood (about 80–420) are very cheap; alumina is about 2× steel. Glasses and polymers span a wide range, and diamond and high-performance carbon fibre cost thousands of times more than steel.
Cost ranges reflect grade, processing and supply, so a single value is not always meaningful.
Cost per kg is not cost per component. Density and required volume matter, and the cost is weighed against property benefits in selection.
conn: Relative cost with the property selection charts: choose the material that meets the property requirement (strength, stiffness) at the lowest cost, so cost is a constraint or objective alongside the property indices.
Cost per kg with density: a material cheaper per kg but much denser may cost more for a given volume, which links cost to mass and component design.
Log-scale reading with ratio calculations: read the chart values, then convert them into multiples or fractions of the steel cost.
Alloying and processing with cost: Ti alloys cost about twice as much as pure Ti, and grade variation explains the cost ranges for ceramics, polymers and wood.
exq: Define relative cost, state the reference material and its assigned value, and explain why relative cost is preferred to absolute $/kg for comparing materials over time.
A material has \( \bar{c}=1500 \) and steel costs \$0.80/kg. Calculate the material's cost per kg and explain what the value means. Why is this calculation only valid if the reference is stated?

Using the relative cost values, compare concrete (about 6), alumina (about 200) and gold. By roughly how many times does each cost more or less than steel, and why is a log axis needed to show them on one chart?
Titanium alloys cost about twice as much as commercially pure titanium. Explain the reasons for the cost premium, and when it is justified by the selection criteria.
Explain why a material with a low \( \bar{c} \) is not necessarily cheapest for a component, and describe how density and required volume would change the comparison between materials.

notes.t: Financial cost: relative cost of materials
pts: Relative cost normalises each material's $/kg to a reference material, so it fluctuates less over time than actual cost.
The reference material is rolled A36 plain carbon steel, assigned a relative cost of 100.
On the log-scale chart, metals such as Pt and Au sit far above steel, while concrete and wood sit at the cheap end.
Polymers and commodity fibres such as E-glass cluster at low relative cost, while diamond and high-end ceramics lie at the top of the range.
defs: Relative cost (\(\bar{c}\))
The cost per kilogram of a material divided by the cost per kilogram of a reference material (rolled A36 plain carbon steel = 100); dimensionless and less volatile than absolute prices.
Reference material
The benchmark material against which all other materials' costs are normalised, here rolled A36 plain carbon steel.
eqs: \(\bar{c}\) = relative cost (dimensionless); \((\$/\text{kg})\) = cost per kilogram of the material (\$/kg); \((\$/\text{kg})_{\text{ref material}}\) = cost per kilogram of the reference material (\$/kg)
tips: Do not confuse relative cost (dimensionless, steel = 100) with absolute cost in $/kg; always state the reference when quoting a value.
The chart uses a logarithmic axis, so equal vertical distances represent multiplicative, not additive, differences in cost.
rq: Why is relative cost more useful than actual $/kg when comparing materials over decades?
Absolute prices move with market, supply and inflation effects; dividing by a reference material's price cancels much of this common movement, so the ratio changes less.
If steel's price doubles and a polymer's price also doubles, what happens to the polymer's relative cost?
It stays the same, because the ratio of the two prices is unchanged; this is why relative cost is more stable.

notes.t: Relative costs of metals
pts: Costs are expressed relative to rolled A36 plain carbon steel, which is set as the baseline of 100.
Common structural engineering metals such as steels, aluminium alloys and copper are only a few to tens of times the cost of plain carbon steel.
Precious metals such as gold and platinum are many orders of magnitude more expensive than plain carbon steel, so they are used only where performance justifies the cost.
Titanium alloys cost roughly twice as much as commercially pure titanium, reflecting the added alloying and processing cost.
Material cost is a key selection criterion alongside properties; a high-performance metal is chosen only when its benefits outweigh a large cost premium.
defs: Relative cost
Cost of a material expressed as a dimensionless ratio to a reference material (here rolled A36 plain carbon steel = 100), allowing comparison independent of market price fluctuations.
tips: Relative cost values are dimensionless ratios; do not quote them as £ or $ amounts without a stated reference price.
Remember the scale is relative to A36 steel = 100, so a value of 1,000 means ten times the cost of the steel baseline, not one thousand pounds.
rq: Why are costs quoted relative to a reference material rather than in £ per kg?
Absolute prices fluctuate with time and market, whereas a ratio to a fixed reference (steel = 100) remains roughly constant and allows direct comparison of materials.
Why would an engineer accept a stainless steel costing 400 times more than plain carbon steel but not a gold component of similar mass?

Stainless steel offers corrosion resistance and strength that justify its premium at a modest multiple of steel's cost, whereas gold's ~14,000-fold premium is only justified for very specialised functions such as electrical contacts or biomedical uses.

notes.t: Relative costs of non-metallic engineering materials
pts: Costs are given relative to rolled A36 plain carbon steel, which is set to 100 as the baseline.
Common structural and bulk materials such as concrete and wood are very cheap compared with steel, at about 6 and 80–420 respectively.
Engineering ceramics like alumina cost about twice as much as steel, while glasses and polymers span a wide range.
Gem-quality and synthetic diamond, and high-performance carbon fibre, are many thousands of times more expensive than steel.
Cost ranges reflect variation in grade, processing and supply, so a single value is not always meaningful.
defs: Relative cost
Cost of a material expressed as a dimensionless ratio to a reference material (here rolled A36 plain carbon steel = 100), allowing comparison independent of currency or date.
tips: Relative costs are dimensionless ratios; do not attach units such as £/kg to these values.
Do not compare values from different baselines; all figures here are referenced to rolled A36 steel = 100.
rq: Why might a material with a low cost per kilogram still be unsuitable for a high-performance component?

Cost is only one selection criterion; low-cost materials such as concrete or wood may lack the required strength, stiffness, toughness or temperature resistance, so performance requirements must be satisfied before cost is compared.
What would happen to the relative cost ranking if the baseline were changed from steel to concrete?

All values would be rescaled by the same factor (steel's value relative to concrete), so the ranking order stays the same but the numerical values change; concrete would become 100 and steel about 16.7.

units.name: 18.5 Energy and production costs
units.ov: This material covers why materials differ in cost: the energy and financial costs across a material's life cycle (extraction, refining, waste, transport twice, end-of-life), the embodied energy of common materials in GJ per tonne, and how ore concentration sets production cost and whether a deposit is worth mining. The ideas connect because embodied energy and ore grade both drive price, but total cost must be judged over the whole life cycle and not by raw-material price alone.
must: Life-cycle cost stages: extraction \(\rightarrow\) refining (purifying, distilling) \(\rightarrow\) waste handling \(\rightarrow\) transport \(\rightarrow\) end-of-life; a low raw-material price does not imply a low total cost
Transport is counted twice: to further manufacture, then to the final point of use; never omit either leg
DEF Embodied energy: total energy to extract, process, manufacture and deliver a material, quoted per unit mass (GJ per tonne)
Metals (aluminium, copper, zinc) need far more energy per tonne than most materials, and aluminium is the highest of those listed
Cement, brick and gravel have very low embodied energy compared with metals and plastics
Plastics and copper are given as ranges because production energy depends on process and source material (e.g. primary vs recycled)
Unit conversion: \(1\ \text{GJ/tonne} = 1\ \text{MJ/kg}\) (divide GJ per tonne by 1000 to get GJ/kg); convert before combining with density or component mass, e.g. \(E_{component}=m\times e\)
Production cost depends on ore concentration: lower concentration means higher refining cost (e.g. Welsh or Northern Irish gold vs South African gold)
Viability is relative to value: as a material's price rises, lower-grade deposits become economic to mine, so the same deposit can be unviable at one price and viable at a higher price

Concentration is not the same as quantity: a large but dilute deposit can still be expensive; high embodied energy does not automatically mean worse performance or higher cost, so consider service life and recycling too
conn: Embodied energy per unit mass \(\times\) density and component volume gives energy per component, so a high-energy-per-tonne material can win if the part is lighter or lasts longer
Ore concentration drives refining energy, which feeds into embodied energy and price, which in turn decides which deposits are viable
Transport (counted twice) and end-of-life legislation add to life-cycle cost, which can change the ranking made on production energy alone
Recycling lowers embodied energy (explaining the ranges for copper and plastics) and reduces waste disposal and end-of-life costs
exq: List and explain the stages that contribute to the energy (financial) cost of a material over its life cycle, and explain why transport must be counted twice.

Using embodied energy values in GJ/tonne, compare the energy to make a 2 kg component in aluminium with the same component in a plastic or in steel. State the unit conversions used and comment on the effect of density.
Explain why South African gold ore is cheaper to refine than Welsh or Northern Irish gold, and why a rise in the price of gold can make previously uneconomic deposits worth mining.

Why do plastics and copper have a range of embodied energy values rather than a single figure? Discuss how recycling and service life could change a choice between a high-energy metal and a low-energy material.
Define embodied energy and discuss why a material with a low raw-material price may still have a high total life-cycle cost.

notes.t: Energy (financial) costs of materials
pts: Energy cost starts with extracting the raw material from the ground or wherever it is found.
Refining steps such as purifying and distilling consume energy and add cost.
Waste products must be disposed of, or ideally used in other applications, which carries cost.
Transport is incurred twice: to the point of further manufacture and then to the final point of use.
End-of-life costs are growing in importance because of legislation.
tips: Count transport twice where a material is moved to further manufacture and then to final use; do not omit either leg.
Energy cost is a life-cycle concept: a low raw-material price alone does not mean a low total cost.
rq: Why might a material with a cheap extraction cost still have a high total energy cost?
Because purification, distillation, waste disposal, transport and end-of-life costs can add substantially to the total energy/financial cost over the life cycle.
Why are end-of-life costs becoming more significant for engineers choosing materials?
Legislation increasingly requires recycling or safe disposal, so end-of-life cost is now a real financial burden that must be included in material selection.

notes.t: Energy production costs of materials
pts: Metals such as aluminium, copper and zinc require far more energy per tonne to produce than most other materials, with aluminium the highest of those listed.
Construction materials like cement, brick and gravel have very low embodied energy compared with metals and plastics.
Energy to produce a material is quoted per unit mass, so comparing materials requires using a consistent basis (GJ per tonne).
Plastics and copper have ranges rather than single values because production energy depends on process and source of material.
defs: Embodied energy
The total energy required to extract, process, manufacture and deliver a material, usually expressed per unit mass (GJ per tonne).
tips: Keep units consistent: the table gives GJ per tonne, so convert to per kg (divide by 1000 → GJ/kg, or MJ/kg) before comparing with densities or per-component figures.
Do not assume higher energy means higher cost or worse performance; embodied energy must be considered together with service life and recycling potential.
rq: Why might a lightweight aluminium component be selected despite its high production energy per tonne?
Because its low density means less mass is needed, and energy saved in service (e.g. transport) can outweigh the high production energy over the component's life.
Why is gravel's production energy so low (0.2 GJ/tonne) compared with aluminium (280 GJ/tonne)?
Gravel is only crushed and sorted from naturally occurring rock, whereas aluminium requires mining bauxite, chemical refining and very energy-intensive electrolysis.

notes.t: Production costs of materials
pts: Production cost depends on how concentrated the material is at a given point in the Earth's crust.
Low concentration of a material raises refining costs, e.g. Welsh or Northern Irish gold versus South African gold.
As the value of a material increases, lower-grade (less concentrated) deposits become economically viable to mine.
tips: Do not confuse concentration with quantity: a large deposit can still be expensive if the material is dilute in the ore.
Remember that viability is relative to the material's value; the same deposit can be unviable at one price and viable at a higher price.
rq: Why would a mining company be willing to extract a low-concentration gold deposit when the gold price rises?
Higher value raises revenue per unit of ore, so the extra refining and processing cost of a low-grade deposit can be covered, making it viable.
Why is South African gold typically cheaper to produce than Welsh gold, even though both are gold?
South African deposits are more concentrated, so less ore must be processed to obtain the same amount of gold, reducing refining costs.

units.name: 18.6 Resource availability and material shortages
units.ov: This material covers how the availability of mineral resources is classified, from identified and unidentified ore through to economically mineable reserves, and how engineers respond when materials become scarce. Reserves depend on geological certainty, grade, price and technology, so they change over time. The responses to shortage (efficient design, substitution or technology change, and recycling or reuse) all act to reduce demand for newly mined material or to expand the usable supply.
must: Reserve = identified ore that can be mined economically at current prices and technology, i.e. grade \( \geq \) minimum mineable grade
Minimum mineable grade = the lowest grade at which extraction is economically viable; ore below it is not reserve
Identified ore has known location, quantity and grade with reasonable geological certainty; unidentified ore is only presumed or expected
McKelvey-style diagram: moving right means geological certainty decreases; moving down means economic feasibility decreases
Prospecting moves ore from unidentified towards identified, enlarging the potential resource base but not directly the reserve
Improved mining technology (or higher prices) lowers the effective minimum mineable grade, converting identified ore into reserve
Reserves are not total resources: large unidentified or sub-economic ore is not reserve, and reserves vary with economics and technology
Four responses to shortage: efficient design, direct substitution, change of technology to use abundant materials, recycling or reuse
Distinguish direct substitution (same function, different material) from technology change (different design using available materials)
Distinguish recycling (material reprocessed) from reuse (item or component kept in service without reprocessing)
conn: Technology and price link to reserves: better mining lowers the minimum mineable grade, so identified sub-economic ore becomes reserve, while prospecting increases identified ore only
Shortage responses act on different sides of the supply and demand balance: prospecting and technology expand supply, while efficient design, substitution and recycling reduce demand for new material
Geological certainty (horizontal axis) and economic feasibility (vertical axis) combine to define the reserve region, so a change in either shifts the boundary
Substitution and technology change affect material selection and design, so a shortage of one material can drive the choice of another and a change in product design
exq: Define reserve, identified ore and minimum mineable grade. Sketch the resource classification diagram, label the axes and shade the reserve region.
Explain, using the diagram, how (a) increased prospecting and (b) improved mining technology each change the reserve and the identified resource. Why is a reserve not a fixed quantity?

A copper ore body has an average grade below the current minimum mineable grade. State two ways it could become classed as reserve, and explain why unidentified ore of high grade still cannot be counted as reserve.
Compare direct substitution with changing the technology as responses to a material shortage, giving an engineering example of each.
Distinguish recycling from reuse, give an example of each, and discuss how each reduces demand for newly mined material.

notes.t: Availability of mineral resources: reserves and identified vs unidentified ore
pts: A reserve is ore that is identified and economically mineable, i.e. above the minimum mineable grade.
Ore below the minimum mineable grade is not economic and so is excluded from reserves.
Increasing prospecting moves ore from unidentified towards identified, enlarging the potential resource base.
Improved mining technology lowers the effective minimum mineable grade, converting identified ore into reserve.
Moving right on the diagram, geological certainty decreases, while moving down, economic feasibility decreases.
defs: Reserve
The portion of identified ore that can be mined economically at current prices and technology, i.e. with grade at or above the minimum mineable grade.
Minimum mineable grade
The lowest ore grade at which extraction is economically viable; ore below this grade is not classed as reserve.
Identified ore
Mineral deposits whose location, quantity and grade are known with a reasonable degree of geological certainty.
Unidentified ore
Mineral deposits that are presumed or expected but not yet located or confirmed by prospecting.
tips: Do not confuse reserves with total resources: unidentified ore is not a reserve even if it is large.
Remember that a reserve depends on economics and technology, so it can change over time.
rq: Why can a deposit that was once not a reserve become one without any new discovery?
Improved mining technology or higher metal prices can lower the minimum mineable grade, so previously uneconomic identified ore becomes economic reserve.
What happens to reserves if the minimum mineable grade rises?
Reserves shrink, because ore that was previously above the cutoff falls below it and becomes uneconomic.

notes.t: Response to material shortages
pts: Shortages can be addressed by designing more efficiently so current materials are used more effectively.
Replacement is one response: either directly substitute a scarce material, or change the technology so that more abundant materials can be used.
Recycling or reusing materials recovers existing material so it can be used again, reducing demand for new supply.
tips: Distinguish direct substitution (same function, different material) from changing the technology (different design that uses available materials).
Recycling is not the same as reuse: recycling reprocesses material, while reuse keeps the item or component in service without reprocessing.
rq: Why might changing the technology be better than direct substitution when a material becomes scarce?

Direct substitution swaps one material for another with similar properties, which may itself be scarce or costly; changing the technology lets the design exploit materials that are plentiful, even if they require a different design approach.
How does efficient design reduce pressure on a material's supply without changing the material at all?
It reduces the amount of material needed per product (lighter, thinner, better-optimised components), so the same supply serves more products.

units.name: 18.7 Replacing materials: historical examples
units.ov: This module uses five historical case studies (plumbing pipes, light filaments, milk containers, sutures, aircraft wings) to show how materials are replaced when new requirements appear. Each replacement balances processing, joining, mechanical properties, cost, energy use, health and recyclability. The common method is to compare materials against the function's requirements and to use specific properties where weight matters.
must: Material replacement is a trade-off: a new material fixes one drawback (toxicity, lifetime, energy, weight) while it may introduce another (joining, cost, Hg, recyclability)

Pipes: lead (low melting point, easy to process and join, but heavy metal toxicity) → copper (higher melting point, bendable, non-toxic pipe, still joined with lead solder) → polymer (light, easily processed, non-toxic, harder to bend, needs new joining technology)
Heavy metal toxicity is long-term harm from accumulation of metals such as lead; it drove the replacement of lead, whereas low melting point is a processing advantage, not the cause of replacement

Filaments: coated cotton (short life from oxidation) → tungsten (good light, expensive, wastes energy as heat) → fluorescent (lower energy, contains Hg, newer technology) → LED (lowest energy, avoids the Hg issue)

Milk containers: glass is reusable but brittle below 0°C; plastic bags work below 0°C but are non-reusable and non-recyclable; plastic bottles are single-material, so recyclable, and blow moulded; Tetrapak is multi-material, so hard to recycle
Blow moulding: a heated plastic tube (parison) is inflated inside a mould to form hollow items such as bottles

Sutures: catgut (sheep mucosa, must be sourced, provokes a biological response); silk and nylon (easily obtained, non-degradable, remain in the body); polyglycolic acid (degrades in vivo in about 3-10 days, minimal response)
Aircraft wings: fabric on wood (light, weak, not stiff) → steel (strong, stiff, dense) → aluminium (better strength and stiffness per weight) → fibre composites (low density, anisotropic)

Compare materials by specific properties (strength/density, stiffness/density), not absolute values; stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation, so higher stiffness means smaller strain for a given stress
Anisotropic means properties vary with direction; fibre composites are not isotropic, since fibre orientation controls the properties
conn: Specific stiffness and strength (property/density) link the wing case to the general materials selection method, and anisotropy of composites links to design of fibre direction
Processing and joining (melting point, bending, solder, blow moulding) link the pipe and milk container cases, since a material must be manufacturable as well as functional
Environmental and health factors (toxicity, Hg, recyclability, biodegradation) link lead pipes, fluorescent lamps, Tetrapak and sutures as non-mechanical selection criteria
Brittleness and temperature (glass below 0°C) link to ductile-brittle behaviour and service conditions in selection
exq: Describe the sequence of materials used for water pipes from lead to polymers. For each, state one advantage and one disadvantage in terms of processing, joining and health.
Compare tungsten, fluorescent and LED lighting in terms of energy use, hazardous materials and technology maturity. Why was coated cotton unsuitable as a filament?

A milk container must be usable at temperatures below 0°C and be recyclable. Evaluate glass, plastic bags, plastic bottles and Tetrapak against these criteria, and explain how blow moulding produces bottles.
Explain why polyglycolic acid is preferred to silk, nylon or catgut for internal sutures. Discuss degradation time (3-10 days) and biological response.
Explain why aluminium replaced steel and wood-fabric in aircraft wings. Use specific stiffness or strength (divided by density) in your argument and say why anisotropy matters for fibre composites.

notes.t: Replacing materials in plumbing: lead, copper, polymer pipes
pts: Romans used lead pipes because lead has a low melting point, is easily processed and joined, but causes long-term heavy metal toxicity.
Copper replaced lead: higher melting temperature, easy to bend, joined with lead solder, and non-toxic.
Polymeric pipes are light weight and easily processed but harder to bend and need new joining technology; they are non-toxic.
Material replacement is driven by health concerns (toxicity) balanced against processing, joining and mechanical properties.
defs: Heavy metal toxicity
Long-term harmful effects on the body caused by accumulation of heavy metals such as lead.
tips: Do not confuse melting point with toxicity: lead's low melting point makes it easy to process, while its toxicity is the reason it was replaced.
Remember copper pipes are still joined with lead solder in this context; the non-toxic claim applies to the pipe material.
rq: Why did copper replace lead for pipes even though lead was easier to join?
Lead is toxic over the long term; copper is non-toxic, has a higher melting temperature and is easy to bend, and copper pipes can still be joined using lead solder.
What trade-off comes with switching from copper to polymeric pipes?
Polymers are lighter and easy to process and non-toxic, but are harder to bend and require new joining technology instead of soldering.

notes.t: Replacing materials in light filaments
pts: Early light filaments were coated cotton, which had a short life because of oxidation.
Tungsten gives good light but is expensive and wastes much energy as heat.
Fluorescent lights consume less energy but use newer technology and contain small amounts of mercury (Hg).
LED lights have even lower energy consumption than fluorescent lights.
tips: Do not confuse the reasons for replacement: cotton failed on lifetime (oxidation), tungsten on cost and energy waste.
Remember that fluorescent lights reduce energy use but introduce a hazardous material (Hg), a trade-off that LEDs avoid.
rq: Why is tungsten, despite giving good light, being replaced as a filament material?
It is expensive and much of the electrical energy is wasted as heat rather than light, making it inefficient.
Why might fluorescent lights be considered a compromise compared with LEDs?
They save energy relative to tungsten but use newer technology and contain small amounts of mercury, a toxic material, whereas LEDs use even less energy.

notes.t: Replacing materials: milk containers
pts: Glass milk bottles are reusable but brittle at low temperature, fracturing if used below 0°C.
Plastic bags remain usable below 0°C but are non-reusable and non-recyclable.
Plastic bottles are made of a single material, so they can be recycled; they are blow moulded.
Tetrapak cartons combine multiple materials, so they cannot be recycled easily and are continuously manufactured.
defs: Blow moulding
A process in which heated plastic tube (parison) is inflated inside a mould to form hollow items such as bottles.
tips: Do not assume 'reusable' implies suitable at all temperatures; check the low-temperature condition (0°C) for brittle materials.
Tetrapak is hard to recycle because of multiple materials, not because it is a polymer of a single type.
rq: Why can plastic bottles be recycled while Tetrapak cartons generally cannot?
Plastic bottles are a single material that can be melted and reprocessed, whereas Tetrapak is a laminate of multiple materials that are difficult to separate.
Why would glass bottles be unsuitable for frozen milk even though they are reusable?
Glass is brittle at low temperature and fractures below 0°C, so a material that is tough at low temperature (plastic bag) is required.

notes.t: Replacing materials: sutures
pts: Catgut sutures are actually made from sheep mucosa; they must be obtained and can provoke some biological response.
Silk is easily obtained and can be sterilised, but it is non-degradable.
Nylon is easily obtained but is non-degradable, so it stays in the body.
Polyglycolic acid degrades in vivo in about 3-10 days with minimal response, making it a biodegradable suture option.
defs: Suture
A surgical thread used to hold tissue together while it heals, chosen by how easily it is obtained, how it degrades in the body, and how much biological response it provokes.
Non-degradable suture
A suture material (e.g. silk, nylon) that is not broken down by the body and remains in tissue after healing.
tips: Do not confuse 'cat gut' with cat tissue; it is sheep mucosa, and the term is historical.
Silk is easily sterilised and obtained, but its non-degradable nature is the key reason it is not chosen for absorbable closures.
rq: Why might a surgeon prefer polyglycolic acid over silk for internal tissue closure?
Polyglycolic acid degrades in vivo within about 3-10 days with minimal response, so no permanent foreign material remains, whereas silk is non-degradable and stays in the body.
What is the main drawback of catgut despite its natural origin?
It must be specially obtained from sheep mucosa and can cause some biological response in the patient.

notes.t: Replacing materials in airplane wings
pts: Early aircraft wings used fabric covering wooden frames, which are light but weak and not stiff.
Steel is dense but offers high strength and high stiffness, so it is heavy for aircraft use.
Aluminium gives better strength and stiffness relative to its weight, which made it a major advance for aircraft wings.
Fibre composites have lower density than metals and their properties depend on direction (anisotropic).
defs: Stiffness
Resistance of a material to elastic deformation under an applied load; the higher the stiffness, the smaller the strain for a given stress.
Anisotropic
Having material properties that vary with the direction of loading, as in fibre-reinforced composites whose fibres align in specific directions.
tips: Compare materials using specific properties (strength or stiffness divided by density), not absolute values; steel is stronger but heavier.
Do not describe fibre composites as isotropic; their properties depend on fibre direction.
rq: Why was aluminium preferred over steel for aircraft wings even though steel is stronger in absolute terms?
Aluminium has better strength and stiffness per unit weight (specific properties), and aircraft performance depends strongly on keeping mass low.
Why might a fibre composite wing be designed differently in different directions?
Because composites are anisotropic: fibres give high strength and stiffness along their direction, so layup is chosen to match the expected loads.

units.name: 18.8 Recycling materials and energy savings
units.ov: This material covers why and how engineering materials are recycled: environmental benefits, the economics of collection and transport, and the energy saved compared with producing virgin material (embodied energy in GJ per tonne). It then looks at material-specific recycling challenges for metals, glass and polymers, where recyclability depends on structure, corrosion, toxicity, sorting and degradation of properties.
must: Recycling benefits are reduced pollution emissions and reduced landfill volume (not just reduced material production); design for end-of-life recovery makes it easier
Economics limits recycling as much as technical feasibility: collection and transport costs decide viability
Embodied energy = total energy to extract, process and manufacture a material, per unit mass (GJ/tonne); bracketed table values are the energy when recycled feedstock is used

Aluminium has very high primary production energy, so recycling saves the most energy; Al, PET and copper show sharp cuts, while paper, glass and steel give smaller absolute savings; Al is the most commonly recycled metal

Metal recycling: reprocessing can use less energy and produce less waste and pollution than refining ore, but corrosion-prone metals are hard to recycle, and toxic metals (Cd, Hg) are hazardous waste, hard to reprocess and must not go to landfill
Glass: little economic incentive because raw materials are cheap and glass is dense, so transport is costly; it is not unrecyclable
Glass must be sorted by colour (clear, amber, green, brown), type (plate vs container) and composition (soda-lime, leaded, borosilicate), since melting behaviour and properties differ
Thermoplastics can be ground, melted and reshaped, but must be sorted by polymer type and their properties degrade with each cycle, so recycling is not infinitely repeatable
Thermosets are cross-linked and cannot be remelted; they are ground for filler or depolymerized to monomer

Recycled polymers are often downgraded and virgin grades are needed for food-contact and high-performance uses; know the polymer abbreviations and uses (PET bottles, HDPE milk containers, PP manhole covers, LDPE bags)
conn: Embodied energy and economics: high energy saving (Al) combined with manageable collection and transport cost makes recycling viable, whereas glass has low energy saving, cheap raw material and high transport cost, so it is weak economically
Polymer structure and recyclability: linking thermoplastic versus thermoset (cross-linking) to remelting, sorting, property degradation and the downgraded products
Corrosion and toxicity of metals link material properties to reprocessing difficulty and disposal route (hazardous waste, not landfill)
Design for disassembly links to recycling: products must be taken apart and materials separated, which affects sorting, cost and the purity of recycled material
exq: Explain why aluminium is the metal that saves the most energy when recycled, using embodied energy in GJ/tonne. For a product using X tonnes of Al, calculate the energy saved if virgin production is A GJ/t and recycled is B GJ/t.
Discuss why glass is recycled less than its scale suggests, covering economics, transport and the need to sort by colour, type and composition.
Compare the recyclability of thermoplastics and thermosets, describing the molecular reason and the routes available for thermosets (filler, depolymerization).
Give the environmental benefits of recycling and explain how collection and transport costs can make recycling unviable.

Why are corrosion-prone and toxic metals (Cd, Hg) difficult to recycle, and how should they be handled? Name one typical recycled use for each of PET, HDPE, PP and LDPE and explain why recycled polymers cannot always replace virgin material.

notes.t: Recycling materials
pts: Good product design makes recycling easier, so designers should plan for end-of-life recovery.
Recycling reduces the environmental burden by cutting pollution emissions and the volume of waste sent to landfill.
Recovering materials requires the product to be taken apart or broken up before materials can be separated.
Collection and transportation costs strongly influence whether recycling is economically viable.
tips: Do not forget that economics, not just technical feasibility, limits recycling: collection and transport costs can make recycling unviable.
Recycling benefits are about reduced pollution emissions and reduced landfill deposits, not reduced material production alone.
rq: Why does designing a product for disassembly improve the economics of recycling?
Easy disassembly lowers the labour and processing cost of separating materials, so less of the recovered value is consumed by recovery effort.
What might make a recycling scheme fail even though the material is technically recyclable?
High collection and transportation costs can outweigh the value of the recovered material, making the scheme uneconomic.

notes.t: Energy to produce materials and energy saved by recycling
pts: Producing aluminium from raw ore needs far more energy per tonne than most other common materials, so recycling it saves the most energy.
Figures in brackets show the energy needed when recycled material is used instead of virgin material; recycling cuts energy use sharply for Al, PET and copper.
Paper and glass have low production energies, so recycling gives smaller absolute energy savings per tonne.
Steel is cheap in energy per tonne to produce from ore, so its recycled value is listed without a large saving in this table.
defs: Embodied energy
The total energy required to extract, process and manufacture a material, expressed per unit mass (here GJ per tonne).
tips: Check units: the table is in GJ per tonne, so do not mix with kWh or MJ without conversion.
The bracketed values are energy when using recycled material, not extra energy added to the virgin figures.
rq: Why does recycling aluminium save far more energy than recycling steel, even though both are metals?
Aluminium is produced from ore by electrolysis, which is very energy-intensive (237 GJ/t vs 20 GJ/t for steel), so the energy avoided by reusing scrap is much larger.
If a tonne of recycled aluminium needs 17 GJ, how much energy is saved compared with virgin aluminium?
237 − 17 = 220 GJ per tonne, about a 93% saving.

notes.t: Recycling metals
pts: Aluminium is the most commonly recycled metal.
Reprocessing metals can be more energy efficient than refining raw ore.
Reprocessing metals can produce less waste and pollution than refining raw ore.
Metals susceptible to corrosion are difficult to recycle.
Toxic metals such as cadmium and mercury must be handled as hazardous waste, are difficult to reprocess, and should not go to landfill.
defs: Corrosion
Degradation of a metal through chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment, which makes recycling the metal difficult.
tips: Recycling is not always easy: metals prone to corrosion are hard to recycle, so do not assume all metals recycle equally well.
Toxic metals are difficult to reprocess and must not go to landfill; do not state that they can simply be discarded with ordinary waste.
rq: Why is reprocessing scrap metal usually more energy efficient than refining raw ore?
