Refining ore requires breaking down and chemically reducing the mineral compound, which is energy intensive; recycling starts from metal already in its elemental form, so it needs only melting and purification.
Why must cadmium and mercury never be sent to landfill, even though they are present in small amounts in scrap?
They are toxic and can leach into soil and water, so they must be handled as hazardous waste and kept out of general waste streams.

notes.t: Recycling of glass
pts: Glasses are the most common commercial ceramics, so recycling them matters at scale.
There is little economic incentive to recycle glass because raw materials are cheap.
Glass is relatively dense, so transporting it for recycling is expensive.
Recycled glass must be sorted by colour (clear, amber, green, brown) before remelting, because mixed colours degrade the product.
Glass must also be sorted by type (plate vs. container) and by composition (soda-lime, leaded, borosilicate), since these have different melting behaviour and properties.
defs: Commercial ceramic
An inorganic, non-metallic, usually crystalline or glassy solid produced by heating; glass is the most common commercial ceramic.
Soda-lime glass
The most common glass type (used for bottles and windows), made mainly from silica with soda (Na2O) and lime (CaO) additions.
Borosilicate glass
A glass containing boron oxide, giving low thermal expansion and high thermal shock resistance (e.g. laboratory glassware).
tips: Do not confuse the three composition families: soda-lime (common), leaded (high refractive index) and borosilicate (thermal shock resistant); sorting must respect these differences.
Explain the economic reason fully: cheap raw materials plus high transport cost, not that glass cannot be recycled.
rq: Why does the low value of raw materials make glass recycling less attractive, even though glass can be remelted indefinitely?
Because virgin raw materials (sand, soda ash, limestone) are so cheap that recycled cullet gives little cost saving, while collection, sorting and high-density transport still cost money.
What would happen to the quality of recycled glass if clear and green cullet were mixed together?
The product would be discoloured (e.g. greenish or brown), reducing its value and suitability for clear-glass applications, which is why colour sorting is needed.

notes.t: Recycling polymers: thermoplastics vs thermosets
pts: Thermoplastics are easily recycled by grinding, melting and reshaping into new products.
Thermoplastic waste must be sorted by polymer type before recycling.
Thermoplastic properties degrade with each reuse cycle.
Thermosetting polymers are more difficult to recycle because they cannot simply be remelted.
Thermosets can be ground up and used as filler, or depolymerized back to monomer.
defs: Thermoplastic polymer
A polymer that softens and can be melted and reshaped repeatedly on heating, and so is easily recycled.
Thermosetting polymer
A polymer that is cross-linked during curing and cannot be remelted; it degrades rather than softening on heating, making recycling difficult.
Depolymerization
Chemical breakdown of a polymer back into its constituent monomers, which can then be used to make new polymer.
tips: Do not say thermosets can be melted and reshaped; this is the defining property of thermoplastics only.
Remember that recycled thermoplastic properties degrade each cycle, so recycling is not infinitely repeatable.
rq: Why can thermoplastics be recycled by melting while thermosets cannot?

Thermoplastics have linear or branched chains held by weak secondary bonds that break on heating, allowing remelting; thermosets have a cross-linked network of strong covalent bonds that does not melt.
Why must thermoplastic waste be sorted by polymer type before recycling?
Different polymers melt at different temperatures and are often incompatible when mixed, so a blend would give poor, unpredictable properties.

notes.t: Recycling Polymers: virgin uses and recycled products
pts: Each common polymer has characteristic virgin applications (e.g. PET for drinks bottles, HDPE for milk and detergent containers).
Recycled PET is turned into a wide range of products, including bottles, surfboards, skis and egg cartons.
Recycled HDPE is commonly reused in durable outdoor and infrastructure items such as drain pipes, traffic cones and stadium seats.
Recycled PP is used for heavy-duty items such as manhole covers, lawn mower wheels and car battery parts, reflecting its toughness.
Recycled LDPE is typically downgraded into low-demand items such as rubbish bin liners and shopping bags.
tips: Do not assume recycled polymers can replace virgin material in all applications; food-contact and high-performance uses usually require virgin grades.
Polymer abbreviations (PET, HDPE, PVC, LDPE, PP, PS) are often confused; learn each with its typical virgin use.
rq: Why might recycled HDPE be suitable for traffic cones and drain pipes but not for food-contact packaging?

Recycled material is often mixed or contaminated, so it is generally not approved for food contact; recycled HDPE is instead used for durable, non-food applications where strength and weathering resistance matter.
Why do many recycled polymers end up in products of lower value than the original (downcycling)?
Repeated processing degrades polymer chains and introduces contamination, so recycled material often has poorer properties and is used in less demanding applications.

units.name: 19.1 Course intro and material selection framework
units.ov: This introductory lecture frames material selection as a systematic optimisation problem rather than a search for a single 'best' material. Candidate materials are judged on mechanical, electrical, magnetic and optical properties, plus processability, environmental resistance, cost and availability, with their relative weight set by the application. The method separates the objective (e.g. minimise weight or cost) from fixed design requirements and from free variables such as thickness, and is then applied through worked examples.
must: Material selection is a systematic optimisation problem: define the objective, constraints and free variables before comparing any materials.
There is no single best material; the answer always depends on the application, and stating this explicitly earns marks.
Property classes to consider: mechanical, electrical, magnetic and optical.
Non-property criteria must also appear in a complete answer: processability, resistance to environmental deterioration, cost and availability.
The objective is the quantity to minimise (typically weight or cost) and is distinct from the constraints.
Fixed design requirements (size/shape, strength target, crane arm length, door size, deflection limit) set the constraints and are not adjustable.
Free variables, such as thickness, depend on the material chosen and are tuned to just meet the constraints.
Workflow: state objective, list fixed requirements, identify free variables, then compare materials on that defined basis.
Common mark losses: listing only mechanical properties, naming a generic 'strongest' material, and confusing objective with constraint.
conn: Constraint to free variable to objective: a fixed deflection or strength requirement determines the required thickness for each material, which determines the weight or cost being minimised.
Application determines criteria weighting: the same material list gives different rankings if the objective changes (weight vs cost), or if environmental or processing demands dominate.
Technical properties versus practical criteria: a material that is optimal mechanically may be rejected on cost, availability, processability or corrosion, so exam answers should combine both.

Fixed shape and size link to the optimisation: because the geometry is specified, material properties alone (via the free thickness) drive the comparison, which leads into the worked-example performance indices.
exq: A component must be chosen for a crane arm of fixed length and a fixed maximum deflection. State the objective, the fixed requirements and the free variable, and explain why each is classified that way.
List the property classes and practical criteria you would consider when selecting a material for a door, and explain how the importance of each depends on the application.
Explain why 'which is the strongest material?' is not a valid selection question. Reframe it as a well-posed optimisation problem for minimum weight.

For a beam with fixed size/shape requirement and a specified deflection, identify which quantities are variable once the material is chosen, and describe how you would compare two candidate materials on a minimum-cost basis.
Give two examples where a material that is best on mechanical grounds would be rejected due to processability, environmental deterioration, cost or availability.

notes.t: Choosing Materials
pts: Material selection must weigh several property classes: mechanical, electrical, magnetic, optical.
Processability and resistance to deterioration in the environment also constrain the choice.
Cost and availability are practical criteria alongside technical properties.
The relative importance of each criterion depends on the intended application, so there is no single best material.
tips: Do not list only mechanical properties; a complete answer must include processability, environmental deterioration, cost and availability.
Stating the answer depends on application is required; a generic 'strongest material' answer loses marks.
rq: Why can't one material be declared 'best' without knowing the application?
Because each criterion (e.g. strength, conductivity, cost, environmental resistance) has different priority depending on the function, so the optimum trades these off differently for each use.
Why might a material with excellent mechanical properties still be rejected for a product?
Poor processability, rapid deterioration in the operating environment, high cost, or limited availability can each make it unsuitable despite good mechanical performance.

notes.t: Choosing materials: optimisation framework
pts: Material choice is an optimisation problem to be solved systematically.
The object usually has a size/shape that is already specified by the design.
Typically we seek to minimise a quantity such as weight or cost for the given object.
Before optimising, identify which design parameters are free (variable) and which are constrained (fixed).
tips: Don't confuse the objective (what you minimise, e.g. weight or cost) with the constraints (what is fixed, e.g. size/shape).
Make sure the objective and fixed quantities are stated before comparing materials, otherwise the comparison has no defined basis.
rq: Why must the fixed geometry (size/shape) be specified before choosing a material to minimise weight?

Because the mass depends on both material density and the geometry; with geometry fixed, only the material properties vary, so the comparison between materials is fair and the objective is well defined.
What would go wrong if you treated a variable as fixed in a material selection problem?
You would exclude or misrank candidates; the optimum found would be constrained artificially and may not be the true best solution.

notes.t: Choosing design variables in material selection
pts: Split the design problem into fixed requirements and adjustable variables.
Design requirements are fixed targets such as final strength, crane arm length, door size or arm deflection.
Variable factors depend on material choice and can be tuned, for example the thickness of the object.
The method is demonstrated by working through worked examples.
tips: Do not treat fixed design requirements (e.g. deflection limit) as variables to be adjusted; they set the constraints.
Identify the variable factors (e.g. thickness) only after the material choice is made, since they depend on it.
rq: Why must design requirements be fixed before choosing a material and thickness?
Requirements such as strength, deflection or size define the targets the design must meet; the material and dimensions are then selected to satisfy them.
Why would changing the material change the factors that can be varied?
Different materials have different properties (e.g. stiffness, strength), so the thickness or other dimensions needed to meet the requirements change accordingly.

units.name: 19.2 Car door design example
units.ov: This material is a short qualitative introduction to sizing a car door: height and width come from the opening the door must close, while thickness comes from the strength and weight of the chosen materials. Door styles such as gull-wing and scissor doors (Tesla Model X, McLaren F1) change the shape and motion but not these sizing principles. The notes give no formulae, so the main skill is explaining the design logic clearly.
must: Door height and width are set by the size of the opening it must close.
Door thickness is set by the strength and weight of the materials used, not by the opening.
Size (set by the opening) and thickness (set by material strength and weight) are determined by different factors; do not confuse them.
Door shape can vary (gull-wing, scissor) while the same sizing principles still hold.
Examples to cite: Tesla Model X (gull-wing/falcon-wing style) and McLaren F1 (scissor-style/dihedral door).
The page gives qualitative design rules only; do not invent a formula or numbers in exam answers.
Thickness involves a trade-off: stronger material allows a thinner door, while weight pushes towards lighter material or less material.
Good answers state the governing factor for each dimension explicitly and then justify it.
conn: Material selection links to thickness: a stronger or lighter material permits a different thickness, so strength-to-weight reasoning applies.
Opening size links to door size: the body-structure opening fixes the door's height and width, whatever the door style.
Door style (hinge and motion) is separate from sizing: unusual doors change how the door opens but not how it is sized.
Strength versus weight trade-off links to wider vehicle design goals such as mass and structural performance.
exq: State which factors determine a car door's height and width, and which determine its thickness. Explain why they differ.
Explain why a gull-wing door, such as the Tesla Model X's, still follows the same sizing principles as a conventional door.
A designer switches the door material to a stronger, lighter one. Discuss qualitatively how this affects thickness and why the opening size is unchanged.
Compare the door design considerations of a conventional door and a scissor-style door (e.g. McLaren F1), identifying what changes and what does not.
Critically discuss why a quantitative formula for door thickness cannot be taken from this material alone, and what information you would need to size the door.

notes.t: Car door design: size and thickness
pts: The door's height and width are set by the size of the opening it must close.
The door's thickness is governed by the strength and weight of the materials used.
Gull-wing and scissor-style doors (e.g. Tesla Model X, McLaren F1) show that door shape can be varied while the sizing principles still hold.
tips: Do not confuse door size (set by the opening) with door thickness (set by material strength and weight); the two are determined by different factors.
This page gives qualitative design rules only; no quantitative formula is provided, so avoid inventing one in exam answers.
rq: Why must a door's thickness be a materials-selection trade-off rather than simply made as thick as possible?

Thicker doors are stronger but heavier; the designer must balance strength (to resist impact and load) against weight (fuel economy, performance, handling), choosing materials with suitable strength-to-weight ratio.
What would happen to the required door size if the vehicle's body opening were made larger, and why does that not automatically make the door thicker?
The door must be made taller/wider to cover the larger space, but its thickness depends on the loads and materials, not on the opening's area, so thickness can stay the same.

units.name: 19.3 Crane beam problem and design constraints
units.ov: This material sets up a design case study: a crane support beam idealised as a square-section cantilever that must be long enough to clear the building and stiff enough to limit deflection under the furniture load. It classifies the quantities in the deflection equation as fixed (l, F), material-dependent (E) or free (t), which is the basis for minimising weight at a required stiffness.
must: Tip deflection of a square-section cantilever under end load: \( \delta = \frac{4 l^{3} F}{E t^{4}} \)
Scaling: \( \delta \propto l^3 \) and \( \delta \propto 1/t^4 \), so doubling \( t \) cuts deflection by 16 and doubling \( l \) raises it by 8
Variable classification: \( l \) and \( F \) are fixed by the problem, \( E \) is set by material choice, \( t \) is the free design variable
Stiffness (resistance to deflection, set by \( E \) and geometry) is different from strength (resistance to yielding or failure); this case is mainly about stiffness
The design objective is to minimise beam weight subject to a deflection limit \( \delta \le \delta_{max} \)
Length is a design requirement: the beam must reach far enough to keep the furniture clear of the building wall
The load to design for is the furniture at the point of lift, not just the crane self-weight
Young's modulus \( E \) is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in the elastic region
Use SI units throughout (m, N, Pa) and state the assumed material before substituting \( E \)
Rearranging for the required thickness gives \( t = \left(\frac{4 l^3 F}{E\,\delta_{max}}\right)^{1/4} \)
conn: Deflection equation and weight: the stiffness constraint fixes \( t \), and \( t^2 l\rho \) then gives mass, so the material choice affects both \( E \) and density \( \rho \)

Free vs fixed variables and material selection: once \( t \) is expressed in terms of \( E \), the choice of material enters through \( E \) and \( \rho \), which leads to a material performance index
Stiffness vs strength: a beam that meets the deflection limit must still be checked against yield, so questions often ask for both
Length vs deflection: the \( l^3 \) dependence conflicts with the need for reach, forcing a trade-off between clearance and required thickness
exq: A square-section cantilever of length 3 m carries an end load of 2 kN. Using \( \delta = 4 l^3 F/(E t^4) \) with steel (E = 210 GPa), find the minimum \( t \) for a tip deflection of at most 10 mm.
By what factor does tip deflection change if the length is increased by 20% and the thickness is increased by 10%, with all else constant? Show your working.
Classify \( l \), \( F \), \( E \) and \( t \) as fixed, material-dependent or free design variables for the crane beam, and justify each classification.
Explain the difference between strength and stiffness in the context of the crane beam, and say why a strength-only check would be incomplete.

Derive an expression for the beam mass in terms of \( \rho \), \( E \), \( l \), \( F \) and \( \delta_{max} \), and use it to compare an aluminium beam (E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2700 kg/m³) with a steel beam (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7850 kg/m³).

notes.t: Case Study 1: Design of a crane support beam
pts: The task is to design a support for an external crane used to lift furniture into a building.
The support is idealised as a rectangular beam whose length and stiffness must be specified in design.
The beam is loaded by the furniture being lifted into the building, so it must carry that load safely.
tips: Remember that the beam is designed for both length and stiffness; a strength-only check is incomplete.
Ensure the load considered is the furniture load at the point of lift, not just the self-weight of the crane.
rq: Why is a rectangular beam model a reasonable simplification for this crane support?
A rectangular cross-section gives simple, standard expressions for second moment of area and stiffness, allowing the required length and stiffness to be calculated easily.
Why does stiffness, not just strength, matter for a crane support beam?
Excessive deflection under the furniture load could make the lift unsafe or unstable, so the beam must be stiff enough as well as strong enough.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Length and stiffness concerns in a building beam
pts: The beam must be long enough to support the furniture so that it does not hit the outside of the building during lifting.
The beam must be stiff so that it does not deflect too much under the load of the furniture.
Both length and strength (stiffness) are design concerns for the lifting beam in this case study.
tips: Do not confuse strength (resistance to failure/yielding) with stiffness (resistance to deflection); this case is primarily about stiffness.
When sizing a beam for deflection, the design must consider length, since deflection grows rapidly with span.
rq: Why does a longer beam have a larger deflection under the same load, and why does this matter for the furniture?

Deflection increases with span length (roughly with the cube of length for a point load on a cantilever-type beam), so a longer beam sags more; excessive sag can bring the load into contact with the building or stop it reaching the target.
What would you change in the beam design if the beam had to be longer but still not deflect more?
Increase the second moment of area (stiffness) by using a deeper or stronger cross-section or a stiffer material, since stiffness, not just strength, controls deflection.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Minimising weight for given stiffness (square-section cantilever beam deflec
pts: The page introduces a design case: minimise the weight of a beam while meeting a required stiffness (limit on deflection).

For a cantilever of square cross-section with side t and length l under end load F, the tip deflection is given by Eqn 1, which shows deflection scales with l cubed and inversely with t to the fourth power.
eqs: Tip deflection of a square-section cantilever beam under end load F (Eqn 1)
\(\delta\) = tip deflection (m); \(l\) = beam length (m); \(F\) = end load (N); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa); \(t\) = side length of square cross-section (m)
tips: Deflection depends on t to the fourth power, not the second; mixing up the power when comparing designs is a common error.
Keep units consistent (SI: l in m, F in N, E in Pa) before substituting into Eqn 1.
rq: Why does halving the section side t increase the deflection by a factor of 16 rather than 2?
Because δ ∝ 1/t⁴, so halving t gives (1/2)⁻⁴ = 16 times the deflection.
If the beam must be lightened while keeping the same stiffness, which variables can be changed and how does that affect the design?
Stiffness depends on E, t and l; reducing mass while keeping δ fixed means choosing a material with higher E or a geometry with a suitable t, since mass scales with t² × l for a fixed square section.

notes.t: Case Study 1: defining variables in a design problem
pts: Length l and applied force F are fixed by the problem statement, so they cannot be chosen by the designer.
Young's modulus E is a material property, so it is selected through the choice of material.
Thickness t is a free design variable that the engineer can set, within practical limits.
defs: Young's modulus (E)
The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in the elastic region of a material; a measure of its stiffness.
tips: Do not treat thickness \( t \) as fixed by the problem; it is a free design variable and must be stated as a choice, within reasonable physical limits.
Young's modulus \( E \) changes with material, so always state the material assumed before substituting a value for \( E \), and keep units in GPa or Pa consistently.
rq: Why can the designer change t but not F or l when optimising a component?
F and l are specified by the problem (the load and the geometry required), whereas t is a design variable that the engineer may choose freely within reason, so it is the variable to optimise.
Why is E treated as a choice rather than a given quantity?
E depends only on the material selected, so choosing a different material changes E; it is therefore a design choice governed by material selection.

units.name: 19.4 Deriving the minimum-mass stiffness material index
units.ov: This material derives a minimum-mass material index for a beam that must meet a stiffness (deflection) constraint. The deflection equation fixes the thickness needed, \( t^4 = 4l^3F/(E\delta) \). The mass equation \( M = l t^2\rho \) then gives mass in terms of that thickness. Eliminating \( t \) gives \( M \) as a product of a specification bracket and a material bracket, and the material bracket is used to rank materials.
must: Deflection constraint (cantilever, square section): \( t^4 = \dfrac{4l^3F}{E\delta} \), so the required thickness is set by stiffness.
Mass of the beam: \( M = l t^2 \rho \), so \( t^2 = M/(l\rho) \).
Eliminate \( t \) by squaring the mass relation: \( t^4 = (M/l\rho)^2 = 4l^3F/(E\delta) \).

Result: \( M^2 = \dfrac{4l^5F\rho^2}{E\delta} \), so \( M = \left(\dfrac{4l^5F}{\delta}\right)^{1/2}\left(\dfrac{\rho^2}{E}\right)^{1/2} = \left(\dfrac{4l^5F}{\delta}\right)^{1/2}\dfrac{\rho}{E^{1/2}} \). Don't forget the square root.
Separate the variables. \( l, F, \delta \) are fixed by the specification (function and geometry). \( E, \rho \) are the material properties you choose.

Correction to the notes: \( M \) here is the beam MASS, and we want to MINIMISE it. So minimise \( \rho/E^{1/2} \) (equivalently \( \rho^2/E \)), i.e. MAXIMISE the material index \( E^{1/2}/\rho \). The note saying 'larger M is better' is wrong.
The specification bracket is identical for every candidate material, so only \( E^{1/2}/\rho \) ranks materials.
Units: \( E \) in Pa, lengths in m, \( F \) in N, \( \delta \) in m. \( 4l^3F/(E\delta) \) has units m⁴, not dimensionless, and \( M \) comes out in kg.
Take roots only at the end: \( t^4 \) from the deflection equation, \( t^2 \) from the mass equation. Don't mix them up.

The index's exponent on \( E \) depends on the loading and shape (here a beam of fixed section shape, with thickness free). A different constraint or geometry gives a different index, e.g. \( E/\rho \) for a tie.
conn: Beam deflection (\( \delta = Fl^3/3EI \), \( I = t^4/12 \)) gives the \( t^4 \) relation, which links to the mass equation through the shared variable \( t \).
Material index \( E^{1/2}/\rho \) leads to Ashby chart selection: a line of slope 2 on log E vs log ρ axes, with candidate materials ranked by their position relative to that line.
Fixed-specification and free-material variables lead to separating function, geometry and material, so the index can be applied to any beam problem.
Minimising mass leads to the trade-off between stiffness and density: a stiff but dense material may lose to a less stiff, much lighter one, e.g. CFRP or wood versus steel.
exq: Derive the minimum-mass index for a cantilever of square section \( t\times t \), length \( l \), with maximum deflection \( \delta \) under tip load \( F \). State which combination of \( E \) and \( \rho \) must be maximised.

Using \( M = (4l^5F/\delta)^{1/2}\,\rho/E^{1/2} \), find the mass of a beam with \( l = 0.5 \) m, \( F = 100 \) N, \( \delta = 2 \) mm for steel (\( E = 210 \) GPa, \( \rho = 7800 \) kg/m³) and for aluminium (\( E = 70 \) GPa, \( \rho = 2700 \) kg/m³). Which is lighter, and by what percentage?
Rank steel, aluminium and CFRP (\( E = 70 \) GPa, \( \rho = 1600 \) kg/m³) by \( E^{1/2}/\rho \). Explain why this ranking differs from ranking by \( E/\rho \).
A student claims that a larger \( M \) indicates a better material. Identify and correct the error, and explain what \( M \) represents and which direction is optimal.
Show that for a fixed-mass beam, doubling the allowable deflection \( \delta \) changes the required mass by a factor \( 1/\sqrt{2} \). What does this say about the thickness?

notes.t: Case Study 1: Beam mass and deflection rearrangement
pts: Beam mass depends on its length, thickness squared and material density, so mass is a function of t.
Deflection equation is rearranged to make thickness to the fourth power the subject, giving the thickness needed for a given allowable deflection.
Mass equation is rearranged to give thickness squared as mass divided by length and density, linking geometry to mass.
defs: Density (\( \rho \))
Mass per unit volume of the beam material, the quantity that links beam volume to mass.
eqs: \( t \) = beam thickness (m); \( l \) = beam length (m); \( F \) = applied force (N); \( E \) = Young's modulus (Pa); \( \delta \) = deflection (m)
\( M \) = mass (kg); \( l \) = beam length (m); \( t \) = beam thickness (m); \( \rho \) = density (kg/m³)
\( t \) = beam thickness (m); \( M \) = mass (kg); \( l \) = beam length (m); \( \rho \) = density (kg/m³)
tips: Keep units consistent: E in Pa (N/m²), lengths in metres and forces in newtons before substituting into t⁴ = 4l³F/(Eδ).
Do not confuse t² (from the mass equation) with t⁴ (from the deflection equation); take the fourth root or square root only at the final step.
rq: Why does the deflection equation depend on thickness to the fourth power rather than the second?
Second moment of area for a rectangular section scales with thickness cubed, and the stiffness/deflection relation adds one more power of t, giving t⁴ overall in the deflection formula.
If you double the beam thickness, by what factor does the deflection change for the same load and length?
Deflection falls by a factor of 16, because δ is proportional to 1/t⁴.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Eliminating beam thickness t
pts: Eliminating t (or \(t^{4}\)) between the two beam equations yields a relation free of thickness, so the result depends only on force, deflection and length.
Because thickness drops out, the result holds regardless of how thick the beam is.
Force, deflection and length are the key quantities governing the design relation.
eqs: Relation between beam thickness, load, deflection and length, after eliminating t (Eqn 3)
t = beam thickness (m); l = beam length (m); F = applied force (N); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \delta = deflection (m); M = mass (kg); \rho = density (kg \(m^{-3}\))
tips: Remember that \(t^{4}\) appears, not t; take the fourth root only if t itself is required.
Check units consistently: E in Pa and δ in m must be used so that the ratio 4l^3F/(Eδ) is dimensionless as required.
rq: Why is it useful to eliminate t rather than another variable when selecting a beam?

Because t is not a design requirement; eliminating it leaves a relation between F, δ and l that can be applied to any thickness, so the designer can choose material and length from the functional requirements.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Minimum-mass beam design
pts: Goal is the lightest possible beam, so the mass M is the quantity to calculate from the design relation.
Mass follows from a squared relation, so M is the square root of the expression involving length, load, density and modulus.
Next step is to sort the parameters into those the designer can vary and those fixed by the specification or material, then group them.
eqs: Mass of a beam designed for a given stiffness/strength (Eqn 4)
M^2 = \frac{4 l^5 F \rho^2}{E \delta} \Rightarrow M = \left(\frac{4 l^5 F \rho^2}{E \delta}\right)^{1/2}
M = beam mass (kg); l = beam length (m); F = applied load (N); \rho = material density (kg \(m^{-3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \delta = allowable deflection (m)
tips: Keep units consistent: E in Pa and \(\delta\) in m so that \(E\delta\) is consistent with \(\rho^2 l^5 F\) when taking the square root.
Don't forget the square root when moving from \(M^2\) to M; forgetting it gives the wrong power-law scaling.
rq: Why does the equation give M as a square root, and what does that imply for reducing mass by halving the beam length?
M is the square root of the product, so M scales with \(l^{5/2}\); halving length reduces mass by a factor of \(2^{5/2}\approx 5.7\).
Which parameters would a designer normally treat as fixed, and which as variable?
Load F and allowable deflection \(\delta\) are usually defined by the specification; length, material (\(\rho\), E) and cross-section are variable choices.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Material index for a beam under stiffness constraint
pts: Beam length l, applied force F and deflection δ are fixed by the problem specification, so they describe the beam's function and geometry requirements.
Young's modulus E and density ρ depend only on the material chosen, so they are the variables we optimise over when selecting a material.
The performance metric M combines beam properties (left bracket) with material properties (right bracket) and is separated so the material can be ranked independently of the design.
For a given beam, a larger value of M indicates a better material choice for minimising mass under this stiffness requirement, so materials are ranked by M.
defs: Young's modulus (E)
The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in the linear elastic region; a measure of material stiffness.
Density (ρ)
Mass per unit volume of the material.
eqs: Material performance index for a beam under a stiffness constraint (maximise M)
M = performance index (dimensionless in this grouping); l = beam length (m); F = applied force (N); δ = deflection (m); ρ = density (kg m⁻³); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
tips: Check units consistently: E in Pa (N m⁻²), ρ in kg m⁻³, δ in m, so the combined index must be dimensionally consistent before ranking materials.
Do not rank materials using the beam-geometry bracket; it is identical for all candidates, so only the material term \( \rho^{2}/E \) differentiates them.
rq: Why is the expression split into two brackets, and why does only the second bracket change when the material changes?

The first bracket depends only on geometry and loading (l, F, δ), which are fixed by the problem; the second bracket contains only material properties (ρ and E), so changing material changes only that term and allows materials to be ranked independently of the beam design.
If two materials have the same density, which one gives a higher M, and what does that imply for the beam?

The material with the higher E gives a lower value of ρ²/E, hence a lower M; for maximising M the stiffer material is worse in this grouping, so the criterion must be interpreted with care, i.e. the index should be maximised or minimised according to the stated objective.

units.name: 19.5 Ranking materials by ρ²/E and Ashby charts
units.ov: This material covers selecting materials for minimum-mass, stiffness-limited components (beams and ties) using the performance index \(M=\rho^2/E\), or equivalently \((\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\), ranked numerically and graphically on Ashby \(E\)–\(\rho\) charts. The ranking shows CFRP lightest and steel worst, and multiplying by relative price shows that the cost-weighted choice can differ sharply. The final selection must balance performance with practicality.
must: Stiffness-limited minimum-mass index: minimise \(M=\rho^2/E\); lower is lighter. Equivalently minimise \((\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\), which gives the same ranking.
Table values: CFRP 0.09 (best), wood 0.17, PU foam 0.41, steel 0.55 (worst). Ranking by \((\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\): CFRP, wood, GFRP, aluminium, concrete, PU foam, steel.
Do not rank by \(E\) alone or \(\rho\) alone. Steel is stiff but dense; PU foam is light but its very low modulus dominates the index.
Cost-weighted index \(C=(\rho^2/E)\,p^*\), with \(p^*\) the relative price per unit mass. Costs: CFRP 1,800, steel 55, wood 12. Cost-weighted rankings differ sharply from mass-only rankings.

Ashby diagram: log-log plot of \(E\) against \(\rho\). A selection line of constant \(\rho^2/E\) is drawn, and materials are chosen in the favoured direction (high \(E\) for a given \(\rho\), above and left of the line).

Gradient of the selection line: \(E=\rho^2/M\) gives \(\log E=2\log\rho-\log M\), a slope of 2 on log-log axes (slope 1/2 for \(E^{1/2}/\rho\) with axes swapped). Read the gradient from the log scales, not by eye on a linear plot.
Shortlisting and practical choice: screen with the index, then check cost, availability and processing. CFRP is best on performance but very expensive; GFRP is cheaper but less stiff.
Units: \(\rho\) in Mg m⁻³ and \(E\) in GPa give index values comparable only within the table. Use consistent SI units (kg/m³, Pa) when computing \((\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\) in absolute terms.
Definitions: CFRP is a carbon-fibre reinforced polymer composite with high stiffness-to-weight ratio at high cost; GFRP is a glass-fibre equivalent that is cheaper and less stiff.
conn: Index to chart: \(\rho^2/E=\text{const}\) becomes a straight line of slope 2 on the log-log \(E\)–\(\rho\) Ashby chart, so the numerical ranking and the graphical method give the same result.
Performance versus cost: the mass index \(\rho^2/E\) multiplied by \(p^*\) gives the cost index, so the best material on mass (CFRP) can be the worst on cost.
Screening then practicality: the index shortlists candidates, and then availability, processing and cost decide the final choice, e.g. wood or GFRP instead of CFRP.
Beam and tie objectives: the same minimum-mass, stiffness-limited framing underlies the index derivation, and the choice of objective and constraint fixes the line gradient.
exq: Using given \(\rho\) and \(E\) data for steel, aluminium, wood and CFRP, calculate \(\rho^2/E\) (and \((\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\)) for each, rank them for a minimum-mass stiffness-limited beam, and state which is lightest.

Given relative prices, compute the cost-weighted index \(C=(\rho^2/E)p^*\) for CFRP (1,800), steel (55) and wood (12). Compare this with the mass-only ranking and recommend a material, justifying your choice.

Show that a line of constant \(\rho^2/E\) has slope 2 on a log-log \(E\)–\(\rho\) Ashby chart. Sketch how you would position a selection line through steel to find materials that are lighter for the same stiffness.
Explain why steel and PU foam both score poorly on \(\rho^2/E\) despite being at opposite extremes of stiffness and density.
Discuss why the best material on the performance index may not be the best practical choice, using CFRP and GFRP as examples.

notes.t: Case Study 1a: material selection using the ρ²/E index for minimum-mass stiffness-limited
pts: The ρ²/E column ranks materials for minimum mass in a stiffness-limited beam or tie: a lower value means a lighter component for the same stiffness.
Among the listed materials, CFRP has the lowest ρ²/E (0.09), so it gives the lightest stiffness-limited design; wood (0.17) is next.
Steel has the highest ρ²/E (0.55) despite high stiffness, because its high density penalises mass; PU foam is high (0.41) because its very low modulus dominates.
The final column multiplies ρ²/E by relative price, so the cost-weighted ranking can differ sharply from the mass-only ranking (CFRP is 1,800, wood is 12, steel is 55).
defs: Stiffness-limited minimum-mass index
A material performance index M = ρ²/E to minimise for a light component that must meet a required bending or axial stiffness.
eqs: \(M\) = performance index (Mg² m⁻⁶ GPa⁻¹ in this table's units); \(\rho\) = density (Mg m⁻³); \(E\) = Young's modulus (GPa)
\(C\) = relative cost index; \(\rho^{2}/E\) = mass index above; \(p^{*}\) = relative price per unit mass (dimensionless, normalised)
tips: Do not rank by E alone or by density alone; the index ρ²/E must be minimised, so a high-modulus material is not automatically the lightest choice.
Check the units: the table uses GPa for E and Mg m⁻³ for ρ, so the values are only comparable within this table, not as absolute quantities.
rq: Why does a low E require a higher density to achieve the same stiffness, and why is ρ squared rather than ρ in the index?

For a beam of fixed stiffness \(EI\), the mass scales with \(\rho A L\) and the section size scales with \(E\); eliminating area gives \(m \propto \rho \sqrt{L^{4}/E}\), so the index is \(\rho^{2}/E\).
Why might CFRP be rejected in practice even though it ranks first on ρ²/E?
Its relative price (20,000) is far higher than the others, so the cost index is 1,800, the highest in the table.

notes.t: Case Study 1: ranking materials by the index (ρ²/E)^(1/2)
pts: Materials are ranked by the index (ρ²/E)^½; lowest value is best for a light, stiff design.
Ranking from lowest to highest index: CFRP, wood, GFRP, aluminium, concrete, PU foam, steel.
CFRP gives the best performance on this index but is very expensive, so cost must be weighed against performance.
defs: CFRP
Carbon fibre reinforced plastic: a polymer matrix composite reinforced with carbon fibres, offering high stiffness-to-weight ratio at high cost.
GFRP
Glass fibre reinforced polymer: a polymer matrix composite reinforced with glass fibres, cheaper than CFRP with lower stiffness.
eqs: Material performance index for a light, stiff tie/beam in tension (minimise mass for given stiffness)
tips: Lower (ρ²/E)^½ is better here; do not assume a higher index value means better performance.
Ranking alone ignores cost; always state that CFRP's performance advantage comes at a very high price.
rq: Why does a lower value of (ρ²/E)^½ indicate a better material for a light, stiff component?
The index is derived for minimising mass under a stiffness constraint; a lower value means less mass is needed to achieve the required stiffness.
If CFRP ranks best but is very expensive, how would you decide between CFRP and GFRP for a real product?
Add a cost constraint and compare cost-weighted performance indices, judging whether the mass saving justifies the higher price.

notes.t: Case Study 1: Choosing materials with Ashby diagrams (Method 2)
pts: Method 2 selects materials by plotting Young's modulus E against density ρ on a chart.
Lines of constant material-property expression (gradient) are drawn on the chart; materials lying furthest in the favoured direction are the 'best'.
For a stiffness-driven, mass-minimised design the best materials have the highest E for a given density, i.e. they sit highest on the chart.
Such material selection charts are known as Ashby diagrams.
defs: Ashby diagram
A material property chart plotting one property against another (here E against ρ) on log scales, used with performance-index lines to shortlist the best materials for a design objective.
tips: Students often pick the highest E overall; remember the design objective (stiffness per unit mass) fixes the gradient of the selection line.
Read the gradient of the performance line from the axes' scales; on log–log charts it is not the same as a simple slope on a linear plot.
rq: Why is the best material read as the one with the highest E at a given density rather than simply the highest E?
For a light, stiff component the mass matters as well as stiffness, so the performance index is E/ρ; the material that gives the most stiffness per unit mass is preferred.
What would a line of gradient 1 on a log E–ρ chart represent?
A constant value of E/ρ, i.e. the performance index for a stiff, light design; materials lying above the line for a given density outperform those below it.

notes.t: Case study 1: selecting best and most practical materials
pts: Materials are first screened to find those that best meet the stated criteria.
Engineering knowledge or other data can be used to identify candidate materials.
The final choice must balance performance with practicality, not performance alone.
tips: Do not stop at the top performance ranking; check practicality (cost, availability, processing) before concluding the selection.
rq: Why is a material that scores best on performance criteria not automatically the right choice?
Because practical factors such as cost, availability, manufacturability or environmental suitability may rule it out, so the final selection must consider practicality alongside performance.

units.name: 19.6 Minimising cost: relative cost and beam choice
units.ov: This material uses Ashby-style selection to find the cheapest material for a stiff cantilever beam. It starts with tip deflection \(\delta = 4l^3F/(Et^4)\), which sets the stiffness constraint. It then eliminates the free dimension \(t\) to get a cost index combining relative price, density and modulus, \(\bar{p}\,(\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\), which is minimised. Relative cost is normalised to rolled A36 steel = 100. Practical points (wood, concrete, steel I-beams) show that shape and construction matter as well as the index.
must: Cantilever tip deflection with end load on a square section: \(\delta = \frac{4 l^3 F}{E t^4}\)
Scaling: \(\delta \propto l^3\), \(\delta \propto 1/E\) and \(\delta \propto 1/t^4\), so section thickness is the strongest lever for stiffness
Relative cost: \(\bar{c} = (\$/\mathrm{kg})/(\$/\mathrm{kg})_{ref}\), dimensionless, with rolled A36 steel = 100 (not a price in $ or £)
Cost of a beam for a given stiffness: \(\text{Price} = \left(\frac{4 l^5 F}{\delta}\right)^{1/2}\bar{p}\left(\frac{\rho^2}{E}\right)^{1/2}\)
The cost index \(\bar{p}\,(\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\) is MINIMISED, equivalently maximising \(E^{1/2}/(\rho\,\bar{p})\)
Derivation: fix \(\delta\), solve for \(t=(4l^3F/(E\delta))^{1/4}\), mass \(m=\rho t^2 l\), cost \(=\bar{p}\,m\), giving the index with \(l^5\), \(F/\delta\) as the geometry/load factor
Use consistent SI units (N, m, Pa, kg/m³); mixing mm/GPa gives large errors in \(\delta\) and wrong rankings
Typical relative costs: concrete ~0.05, polymers (PP, PS, LDPE, HDPE) near or below 100, carbon fibre/CFRE prepreg well above 100, gold/platinum ~10,000-20,000
In practice wood and concrete are the best beam materials, and steel is used as I-beams because shape puts material where it is most useful
The formulas apply only to this load case, support and section; other cases change the constants and exponents
conn: Beam deflection formula to performance index: eliminating the free variable \(t\) by fixing \(\delta\) converts a geometry equation into a material-only index
Relative cost to the index: \(\bar{p}\) multiplies the mass-based term, so a cheap material with a modest \(E^{1/2}/\rho\) can beat a stiff, light but expensive one such as CFRP
Material index to shape: section shape (I-beam) improves bending stiffness per unit mass, so it can change which material wins in practice
Units and scaling: because \(\delta \propto t^{-4}\), a small error in \(t\) or in unit conversion gives a large error in stiffness
exq: Derive the cost of a square-section cantilever of length \(l\) that must deflect no more than \(\delta\) under end load \(F\), and state the material index to minimise.

A square cantilever with \(l = 0.5\) m, \(F = 100\) N and \(E = 200\) GPa has \(t = 20\) mm. Calculate the tip deflection, then find the new deflection if \(t\) is increased by 20% or if \(l\) is doubled.

Steel (\(\bar{p}=100\), \(\rho=7850\) kg/m³, \(E=210\) GPa) is compared with a material of \(\bar{p}=300\), \(\rho=1600\) kg/m³ and \(E=130\) GPa. Evaluate \(\bar{p}(\rho^2/E)^{1/2}\) for each and decide which gives the cheaper beam of equal stiffness.
Explain why relative cost is used instead of actual price, define it, and state what a relative cost of 0.05 for concrete means.
Explain why steel beams are made as I-sections and why wood and concrete are common beam materials, referring to the performance index and to shape.

notes.t: Case Study 1a: Minimising cost for stiffness (cantilever beam deflection)
pts: The page gives the tip deflection of a square-section cantilever beam under an end load; stiffness depends strongly on the section thickness.
Deflection scales with the cube of length and inversely with the fourth power of thickness, so thickness is the most powerful lever for stiffness.
This relation is the starting point for material/geometry selection: to minimise cost for a required stiffness, trade off material cost against E and section size.
defs: Young's modulus (E)
The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in the linear-elastic region; a measure of material stiffness.
eqs: Tip deflection of a square-section cantilever beam under end load F
\(\delta\) = tip deflection (m); \(l\) = beam length (m); \(F\) = applied force (N); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa); \(t\) = square section side thickness (m)
tips: Keep units consistent: F in N, l and t in m, E in Pa, giving δ in m; mixing mm and m changes the result by large factors.
The formula applies to a cantilever with an end load on a square section; a different support or load case or section shape changes the constant and exponents.
rq: Why does halving the thickness t increase the deflection by a factor of 16 rather than 2?
Deflection is proportional to 1/\(t^{4}\), so halving t multiplies δ by \(2^{4}\) = 16.
If you need a stiffer beam at the same cost, why might a material with higher E not be the best choice?
Cost-effective stiffness depends on E per unit cost and density/section geometry; a cheaper material with lower E can be used with a larger section to achieve the same stiffness at lower cost.

notes.t: Financial cost: relative cost of materials
pts: Relative cost normalises a material's price per kg against a reference material, so it fluctuates less over time than actual cost.
The reference material is rolled A36 plain carbon steel, which is assigned a relative cost of 100.
Relative cost ranges widely across classes: concrete sits near 0.05 while platinum and gold reach around 10,000 to 20,000, and diamond is also very high.
Polymers such as PP, PS, LDPE and HDPE are among the cheapest materials, close to or below the reference value.
Fibre-reinforced composites are generally more expensive than steel, with carbon fibre and CFRE prepreg well above 100 and wood/GFRE lower.
defs: Relative cost
The price per unit mass of a material divided by the price per unit mass of a reference material (rolled A36 plain carbon steel = 100); a dimensionless number.
eqs: \bar{c} = relative cost (dimensionless); \$/\mathrm{kg} = price of the material (\$ per kg); (\$/\mathrm{kg})_{\mathrm{ref\ material}} = price of reference material, rolled A36 plain carbon steel (\$ per kg)
tips: Relative cost is a ratio, so it has no units; do not quote it in $/kg.
Relative cost is not the same as actual price: a value of 10 means ten times the reference steel's price per kg, not £10 or $10.
rq: Why is relative cost preferred over actual cost when comparing materials in design?
Actual prices fluctuate with market conditions, whereas relative cost against a common reference changes less over time, so comparisons stay meaningful.
If a material has a relative cost of 2, how does its price per kg compare with plain carbon steel?
It costs twice as much per kg as the reference steel, since \(\bar{c}=\frac{\$/\mathrm{kg}}{(\$/\mathrm{kg})_{\mathrm{ref}}}\) = 2.

notes.t: Case Study 1a: Minimising cost per unit mass of a beam
pts: Adding cost per unit mass means the relative price per kg is included in the performance index, which must be minimised.
The relative price per kg, p̄, enters the index as a multiplier on the material term (ρ²/E)^(1/2), so cheaper materials with low density and high modulus give lower cost.
Material performance is described by two properties: density ρ and Young's modulus E, combined as √(ρ²/E) together with price.
defs: Relative price (p̄)
The cost of a material per kilogram, expressed relative to a reference material, used to compare materials on cost in a performance index.
eqs: Cost of a beam (price) to be minimised, combining geometry, load and material cost

\text{Price} = total cost of the component (currency); \(l\) = length (m); \(F\) = applied load (N); \(\delta\) = allowable deflection (m); \(\bar{p}\) = relative price per kg (dimensionless); \(\rho\) = density (kg/m³); \(E\) = Young's modulus (Pa)
tips: Price is minimised, so materials with the smallest value of the index are preferred, not the largest.
Density must be in kg/m³ and modulus in Pa consistently; mixing GPa with kg/m³ gives wrong rankings.
rq: Why must the price per kg be included as a separate factor rather than only using density and modulus?

Density and modulus measure how well a material performs mechanically, but two materials with identical performance can differ greatly in cost; p̄ captures that cost difference so the index reflects total price, not just mass.
What would happen to the optimal material choice if p̄ doubled for every material?
The Price index would double for all materials equally, so the ranking of materials would be unchanged; only the absolute cost changes, because p̄ is a common multiplier.

notes.t: Case Study 1a: Choosing materials for structural beams
pts: For structural beams, wood and concrete are the best two options and are used regularly in practice.
Steel is used in I-beam form because it can be manufactured so that material sits in the most useful place of the cross-section.
Material choice for a beam depends on how it is used and shaped, not just on the material alone.
tips: Do not assume the strongest material is always the best choice; cost, availability, and construction practicality matter.
Shape (e.g., I-section) affects bending stiffness and strength as much as the material's properties.
rq: Why is an I-beam shape efficient for bending loads, even though the material is the same steel throughout?

Bending stress is greatest at the top and bottom flanges and near zero at the neutral axis, so placing material in the flanges (far from the neutral axis) gives high second moment of area for little weight.
Why might wood and concrete be preferred over steel for some building beams despite steel's higher strength?
They are cheaper, readily available, easier to work with on site, and adequate for the loads and spans typical of buildings; steel is reserved where its high strength-to-weight is needed.
