formulas.name: Normal (tensile/compressive) stress
formulas.vars: \sigma = normal stress (Pa = N \(m^{-2}\)); F = applied force normal to the area (N); A = cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Bar under uniaxial tension or compression (take tension positive); also applies to each axis in biaxial loading.

formulas.name: Shear stress (pure shear / torsion)
formulas.vars: \tau = shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = shear force parallel to the area (N); A = area over which the shear force acts (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Force acts parallel to the surface, e.g. a piece under torsion or shear.

formulas.name: Hoop stress in a thin-walled cylinder
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{h}\) = hoop stress (Pa); p = pressure difference between inside and outside (Pa); r = cylinder radius (m); t = wall thickness (m)
formulas.use: Thin-walled cylinder (t \ll r) under internal pressure.

formulas.name: Hydrostatic pressure
formulas.vars: p = hydrostatic pressure (Pa); F = force normal to the face (N); A = area of the face (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Equal compressive stress on all faces; compression is taken as negative stress, so p is positive.

formulas.name: Resistance of a wire
formulas.vars: R = resistance (Ω); \rho = resistivity (Ω·m); L = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
formulas.use: Uniform wire or conductor with current along its length

formulas.name: Silicon lattice constant (diamond cubic)
formulas.vars: a = cubic lattice constant (Å)
formulas.use: Reference value for the Si unit cell

formulas.name: Projected lattice spacing, Si viewed along [110]
formulas.vars: a = lattice constant (Å)
formulas.use: Atomic spacing seen when viewing Si along the 110 direction

formulas.name: Mass-based efficiency per passenger-kilometre
formulas.vars: \(m_{TO}\) = take-off mass (kg); \(N_{p}\) = number of passengers (-); d = distance per flight (km)
formulas.use: Comparing vehicle or aircraft mass efficiency; lower is better

formulas.name: Normal (tensile) stress
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); F = force normal to area (N); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
formulas.use: Force applied perpendicular to the area

formulas.name: Engineering (nominal) tensile strain
formulas.vars: \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{0}\) = original length (m); l = final length (m)
formulas.use: Axial extension or compression

formulas.name: Poisson's ratio
formulas.vars: \nu = Poisson's ratio (-); \(\varepsilon_{lateral}\) = transverse strain (-); \(\varepsilon_{axial}\) = axial strain (-)
formulas.use: Relates lateral contraction to axial extension

formulas.name: Shear stress
formulas.vars: \tau = shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = force parallel to area (N); A = area (m²)
formulas.use: Force applied tangentially to a surface

formulas.name: Nominal lateral strain
formulas.vars: \(\varepsilon_{l}\) = lateral strain (-); v = change in lateral dimension (m); l = original length (m)
formulas.use: Definition of the transverse strain used in Poisson's ratio (as given in the notes)

formulas.name: Hooke's law (Young's modulus)
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \varepsilon = strain (-); F = force (N); A = area (m²); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{i}\) = original length (m)
formulas.use: Linear elastic tensile or compressive deformation

formulas.name: Shear modulus (Hooke's law in shear)
formulas.vars: \tau = shear stress (Pa); G = shear modulus (Pa); \gamma = shear strain (-); F = tangential force (N); A = face area (m²); \Delta x = lateral displacement (m); h = height (m)
formulas.use: Linear elastic shear deformation

formulas.name: Bulk modulus
formulas.vars: p, \Delta P = pressure (change) (Pa); K = bulk modulus (Pa); \Delta V = volume change (m³); \(V_{0}\), \(V_{i}\) = initial volume (m³)
formulas.use: Uniform hydrostatic compression; volume decreases as pressure rises

formulas.name: Photon energy for an electron transition
formulas.vars: E = photon energy (J); h = Planck's constant (J·s); \nu = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (m/s); \lambda = wavelength (m)
formulas.use: Energy emitted or absorbed when an electron changes level (E = energy difference between levels).

formulas.name: Elementary charge
formulas.vars: e = magnitude of proton/electron charge (C)
formulas.use: Charge of a proton (+e) or electron (−e); needed for ion charges and eV conversions.

formulas.name: Proton and neutron mass
formulas.vars: \(m_{p}\) = proton mass (kg); \(m_{n}\) = neutron mass (kg)
formulas.use: Estimating atomic mass from nucleon number.

formulas.name: Electron mass
formulas.vars: \(m_{e}\) = electron mass (kg)
formulas.use: Electron mass is negligible compared with nucleon mass.

formulas.name: Maximum electrons in a subshell
formulas.vars: \(N_{e}\) = maximum electrons (dimensionless); l = angular quantum number (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Filling subshells: s=2, p=6, d=10, f=14.

formulas.name: Number of orbitals in a subshell
formulas.vars: \(N_{orb}\) = number of orbitals (dimensionless); l = angular quantum number (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Each orbital holds 2 electrons; l = 0, 1, 2, 3 for s, p, d, f.

formulas.name: Potential energy of an ion pair
formulas.vars: U = ion pair potential energy (J); \(U_{i}\) = energy to create the ions (J); q = ionic charge (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of free space (F/m); r = interionic separation (m); B = repulsion constant (J·\(m^{n}\)); n = repulsion exponent (typically ~12)
formulas.use: Ionic energy curve; the minimum gives the equilibrium separation and bond energy.

formulas.name: Coulomb attraction energy between ions
formulas.vars: U = potential energy (J); q = ion charge magnitude (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of free space (F/m); r = inter-ion distance (m)
formulas.use: Attractive term for oppositely charged ions.

formulas.name: Repulsion energy between ions
formulas.vars: U = repulsive energy (J); B = constant (J·\(m^{n}\)); r = inter-ion distance (m); n = repulsion exponent (typically 6–12)
formulas.use: Short-range repulsion from overlapping electron clouds.

formulas.name: Coulomb force between two charges
formulas.vars: F = electrostatic force (N); q = charge on each particle (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of vacuum (F/m); r = separation (m)
formulas.use: Force between two point charges; for unequal charges replace q² by q₁q₂.

formulas.name: Potential energy from force
formulas.vars: U = potential energy (J); F = force (N); r = separation (m); q = charge (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of vacuum (F/m)
formulas.use: Relates force and energy; the sign gives attraction or repulsion.

formulas.name: Net interatomic potential energy of a covalent bond
formulas.vars: U = potential energy (J); r = interatomic separation (m); A = attractive constant (J·\(m^{m}\)); B = repulsive constant (J·\(m^{n}\)); m, n = exponents with m < n
formulas.use: Bond energy curve; the minimum gives bond length and bond energy.

formulas.name: Net potential energy between two ions
formulas.vars: \(E_{N}\) = net potential energy (J); \(E_{A}\) = attractive energy (J); \(E_{R}\) = repulsive energy (J); r = interatomic separation (m); A = attractive constant (J·m); B = repulsive constant (J·\(m^{n}\)); n = repulsion exponent (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Describes bonding between two ions or atoms. The equilibrium separation is at the minimum of \(E_{N}\), where \(dE_{N}\)/dr = 0.

formulas.name: Atoms per unit cell, general counting rule
formulas.vars: N = atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); \(N_{\text{corner}}\), \(N_{\text{face}}\), \(N_{\text{edge}}\), \(N_{\text{interior}}\) = atoms at corners, faces, edges and inside the cell. The 1/8, 1/2 and 1/4 fractions are the shares of each atom belonging to one cell. This applies to cubic cells; HCP corner atoms are shared by 6 cells, so use 1/6.
formulas.use: Counts atoms in any cubic unit cell by weighting each atom by the fraction of it lying inside the cell.

formulas.name: FCC atoms per unit cell
formulas.vars: 8 = corner atoms, each shared by 8 cells; 6 = face atoms, each shared by 2 cells; N = atoms per unit cell (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Face-centred cubic structure.

formulas.name: BCC atoms per unit cell
formulas.vars: 8 = corner atoms, each shared by 8 cells; 1 = body-centre atom wholly inside the cell; N = atoms per unit cell (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Body-centred cubic structure.

formulas.name: HCP atoms per unit cell
formulas.vars: 12 = corner atoms, each shared by 6 cells; 2 = central atoms on the top and bottom faces, each shared by 2 cells; 3 = interior atoms; N = atoms per unit cell (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Hexagonal close-packed structure.

formulas.name: FCC lattice parameter from atomic radius
formulas.vars: a = cube edge length (m); R = atomic radius (m)
formulas.use: FCC: atoms touch along the face diagonal, so \sqrt{2}a=4R (equivalently \(a^{2}\)+\(a^{2}\)=(4R)^2)

formulas.name: FCC unit cell volume
formulas.vars: \(V_{C}\) = cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); a = cell edge (m); R = atomic radius (m)
formulas.use: FCC density and packing calculations

formulas.name: BCC lattice parameter from atomic radius
formulas.vars: a = cube edge length (m); R = atomic radius (m)
formulas.use: BCC: atoms touch along the body diagonal, \(a^{2}\)+\(a^{2}\)+\(a^{2}\)=(4R)^2

formulas.name: BCC atomic radius from lattice parameter
formulas.vars: R = atomic radius (m); a = lattice parameter (m)
formulas.use: Rearrangement of the above for BCC

formulas.name: BCC unit cell volume
formulas.vars: \(V_{C}\) = cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); a = lattice parameter (m); R = atomic radius (m)
formulas.use: BCC density and packing calculations

formulas.name: HCP unit cell volume (a, c)
formulas.vars: \(V_{C}\) = cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); \(A_{\text{base}}\) = hexagonal base area (\(m^{2}\)); a = basal edge (m); c = cell height (m)
formulas.use: HCP; base is 6 equilateral triangles of side a, \(A_{\text{base}}\)=6(\sqrt{3}/4)\(a^{2}\)

formulas.name: HCP atomic radius–lattice parameter relation
formulas.vars: a = basal lattice parameter (m); r = atomic radius (m)
formulas.use: Atoms touch in the basal plane

formulas.name: HCP unit cell volume in terms of r
formulas.vars: \(V_{C}\) = cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); r = atomic radius (m); c = cell height (m)
formulas.use: Using a=2r; base area 6\sqrt{3}\(r^{2}\) (each triangle \sqrt{3}\(r^{2}\))

formulas.name: Theoretical density
formulas.vars: \rho = density (g \(cm^{-3}\) or kg \(m^{-3}\)); n = atoms per unit cell; A = atomic weight (g \(mol^{-1}\)); \(V_{C}\) = cell volume (\(cm^{3}\) or \(m^{3}\)); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (6.022\times10^{23} \(mol^{-1}\))
formulas.use: Keep units consistent; n = 4 (FCC), 2 (BCC), 6 (HCP)

formulas.name: Cubic cell volume
formulas.vars: \(V_{C}\) = cell volume; a = cell edge length
formulas.use: Cubic structures (SC, BCC, FCC)

formulas.name: Density definition
formulas.vars: \rho = density (kg \(m^{-3}\)); m = mass (kg); V = volume (\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: General definition

topics.topic: Unit cell density and atom counting

formulas.name: Density of a crystal from its unit cell
formulas.vars: \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); n = formula units (or atoms) per unit cell (–); A = molar mass of the formula unit (kg/mol, or g/mol with consistent units); \(V_{C}\) = unit cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (6.022\times10^{23} \(mol^{-1}\))
formulas.use: Any cubic or other crystal. For a compound, A is the sum of atomic masses in one formula unit, e.g. \(A_{Na}\)+\(A_{Cl}\) for NaCl.

formulas.name: Atoms per unit cell by sharing (FCC example: U in UO₂)
formulas.vars: N = atoms per cell (–); \(N_{int}\) = atoms wholly inside the cell; \(N_{face}\) = face atoms (each shared by 2 cells); \(N_{corner}\) = corner atoms (each shared by 8 cells)
formulas.use: Counting n before using the density formula. UO₂ (fluorite) has 4 U and 8 O (all internal), so n = 4 formula units.

formulas.name: Cell edge from ionic radii (NaCl, anions and cations touching along the cube edge)
formulas.vars: a = cube edge length (m); \(r_{Cl}\), \(r_{Na}\) = ionic radii (m)
formulas.use: Rock-salt structure, to get \(V_{C}\) = \(a^{3}\) for the density calculation.

formulas.name: Density of a semi-crystalline polymer (rule of mixtures)
formulas.vars: \(\rho_{polymer}\) = overall density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); \(\rho_{crystalline}\), \(\rho_{amorphous}\) = densities of the crystalline and amorphous regions (kg/\(m^{3}\)); f = volume fractions (–)
formulas.use: Finding the degree of crystallinity from measured densities; combine with \(f_{crystalline}\)+\(f_{amorphous}\)=1.

formulas.name: Volume fraction constraint
formulas.vars: \(f_{crystalline}\), \(f_{amorphous}\) = volume fractions (–)
formulas.use: Eliminates one unknown in the rule of mixtures.

formulas.name: Equilibrium vacancy concentration
formulas.vars: \(N_{v}\) = number of vacancies (–); N = number of atomic sites (–); \(Q_{v}\) = energy to form a vacancy (J per vacancy; use R and J/mol if \(Q_{v}\) is molar); k = Boltzmann's constant (1.38\times10^{-23} J/K); T = absolute temperature (K)
formulas.use: Vacancies rise exponentially with temperature; T must be in kelvin.

formulas.name: Centre-to-centre distance of major atoms (cubic structure)
formulas.vars: d = centre-to-centre distance (m); D = diameter of major atoms (m)
formulas.use: Used to find the interstitial space in the geometry considered in the notes.

formulas.name: Maximum interstitial atom diameter
formulas.vars: \(d_{int}\) = largest interstitial atom diameter that fits (m); D = diameter of major atoms (m)
formulas.use: Checking whether an interstitial atom fits without distortion.

formulas.name: Radius ratio for interstitial size mismatch (C in Fe)
formulas.vars: \(r_{C}\) = carbon atom radius (nm); \(r_{Fe}\) = iron atom radius (nm)
formulas.use: Compare with the allowed ratio of about 0.414 to see that C strains the Fe lattice.

formulas.name: Dislocation spacing in a tilt boundary (Frank's relation)
formulas.vars: D = dislocation spacing (m); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m); θ = misorientation angle (rad)
formulas.use: Low-angle tilt boundary (small θ), modelled as an array of edge dislocations.

formulas.name: Photon energy from frequency or wavelength
formulas.vars: E = photon energy (J); h = Planck's constant (J·s); ν = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (m/s); λ = wavelength (m)
formulas.use: Convert between X-ray wavelength and photon energy (divide by 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ to get eV).

formulas.name: Wave speed relation for EM waves
formulas.vars: c = speed of light in vacuum (m/s); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m)
formulas.use: Convert between frequency and wavelength of EM waves in vacuum.

formulas.name: Bragg's law
formulas.vars: n = order of diffraction (integer); λ = X-ray wavelength (m); \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = interplanar spacing (m); θ = Bragg angle between beam and planes, half the diffraction angle 2θ (rad or °)
formulas.use: Condition for constructive interference of X-rays from a set of crystal planes; used to find d, λ or θ from XRD peaks.

formulas.name: Interplanar spacing, cubic crystal
formulas.vars: \(d_{\text{hkl}}\) = spacing of (hkl) planes (m); a = cubic lattice parameter (m); h,k,l = Miller indices (integers)
formulas.use: Cubic lattices only; combine with Bragg's law to index peaks or find a.

formulas.name: Lattice parameter from a diffraction peak (cubic)
formulas.vars: a = cubic lattice parameter (m); n = order; λ = wavelength (m); θ = Bragg angle (°); h,k,l = Miller indices
formulas.use: Obtained by combining Bragg's law with the cubic d-spacing formula; n=1 for first-order peak.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.vars: V = voltage across element (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Relates voltage, current and resistance for an ohmic conductor; rearrange as I = V/R or R = V/I.

formulas.name: Resistance of a uniform conductor
formulas.vars: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); σ = conductivity (S/m); L = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
formulas.use: Uniform wire or bar with current flowing along its length.

formulas.name: Conductivity and resistivity
formulas.vars: σ = conductivity ((Ω·m)^{-1} = S/m); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m)
formulas.use: Convert between resistivity and conductivity.

formulas.name: Geometry-independent Ohm's law (field form)
formulas.vars: E = ΔV/L = electric field (V/m); J = I/A = current density (A/m²); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m)
formulas.use: Material property form of Ohm's law, independent of sample size.

formulas.name: Band-gap energy
formulas.vars: \(E_{g}\) = band gap (J or eV); \(E_{C}\) = conduction band minimum (J or eV); \(E_{V}\) = valence band maximum (J or eV)
formulas.use: Energy separation between valence and conduction bands.

formulas.name: Thermal energy per particle
formulas.vars: \(E_{\text{thermal}}\) = thermal energy (J); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K); T = absolute temperature (K)
formulas.use: Compare with \(E_{g}\) to judge thermal excitation of electrons across the gap.

formulas.name: Average particle velocity from thermal energy
formulas.vars: v = average velocity (m/s); m = particle mass (kg); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (J/K); T = temperature (K)
formulas.use: Obtained by setting \(E_{\text{thermal}}\) = ½mv².

formulas.name: Kinetic energy
formulas.vars: E = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s)
formulas.use: Equate to \(k_{B}\) T to estimate thermal speed.

formulas.name: Photon energy (Planck–Einstein)
formulas.vars: E = photon energy (J); h = Planck constant (6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s); ν = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (3.00×10⁸ m/s); λ = wavelength (m)
formulas.use: Photon energy from frequency or wavelength; divide by 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ to convert J to eV.

formulas.name: Wave speed relation for light
formulas.vars: c = speed of light (m/s); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m)
formulas.use: Convert between frequency and wavelength of EM radiation in vacuum.

formulas.name: Speed of light from vacuum constants
formulas.vars: c = speed of light in vacuum (m/s); ε₀ = permittivity of vacuum (F/m); μ₀ = permeability of vacuum (H/m)
formulas.use: Maxwell's result that light is an electromagnetic wave.

formulas.name: Absorption condition
formulas.vars: \(E_{\text{photon}}\) = photon energy (J); h = Planck constant (J·s); c = speed of light (m/s); λ = wavelength (m); \(E_{g}\) = band gap (J)
formulas.use: A semiconductor absorbs photons with energy at least the band gap; transparent otherwise. Cutoff λ = hc/\(E_{g}\).

formulas.name: Beer–Lambert transmission
formulas.vars: \(I_{\text{out}}\) = transmitted intensity (W/m²); \(I_{\text{in}}\) = incident intensity (W/m²); α = absorption coefficient (m⁻¹); L = thickness (m)
formulas.use: Intensity transmitted through a uniform slab of absorbing material.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.vars: V = voltage drop (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Relates voltage, current and resistance of a conductor.

formulas.name: Resistivity from resistance
formulas.vars: \rho = resistivity (Ω·m); R = resistance (Ω); A = cross-sectional area (m²); \ell = current path length (m)
formulas.use: Finding resistivity or resistance from sample geometry.

formulas.name: Conductivity
formulas.vars: \sigma = conductivity (S/m); \rho = resistivity (Ω·m)
formulas.use: Converting between resistivity and conductivity.

formulas.name: Ohm's law, current density form
formulas.vars: J = current density (A/m²); \sigma = conductivity (S/m); \mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m)
formulas.use: Microscopic form of Ohm's law; valid when electrons are scattered (ohmic conductor).

formulas.name: Current density
formulas.vars: J = current density (A/m²); I = current (A); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
formulas.use: Uniform current through cross-section.

formulas.name: Electric field in a uniform bar
formulas.vars: \mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m); V = applied voltage (V); L = bar length (m)
formulas.use: Uniform field along a conductor.

formulas.name: Drift velocity
formulas.vars: \(v_{D}\) = drift velocity (m/s); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (m²/V·s); \mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m)
formulas.use: Average electron velocity in a field with scattering.

formulas.name: Force on an electron
formulas.vars: F = force (N); e = electron charge (−1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C); \mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m)
formulas.use: Force from the applied field; combine with F = ma.

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.vars: F = force (N); m = electron mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²)
formulas.use: Without scattering the electron accelerates continuously, so no Ohm's law.

formulas.name: Mean free path
formulas.vars: l = mean free path (m); \(v_{F}\) = Fermi velocity (m/s); \tau = scattering time (s)
formulas.use: Distance travelled between scattering events.

formulas.name: Wiedemann-Franz law / Lorenz number
formulas.vars: L = Lorenz number (W·Ω/K²); \kappa = thermal conductivity (W/m·K); \sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); T = temperature (K); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (J/K); e = electron charge (C)
formulas.use: Relates thermal and electrical conductivity of metals; κ/σ ∝ T.

formulas.name: Electronic thermal conductivity
formulas.latex: \kappa_{el} = \frac{1}{3} C_e v_F l = \frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T \tau}{3m}
formulas.vars: \(\kappa_{el}\) = electronic thermal conductivity (W/m·K); \(C_{e}\) = electronic specific heat (J/m³·K); \(v_{F}\) = Fermi velocity (m/s); l = mean free path (m); n = electron density (m⁻³); \tau = scattering time (s); m = electron mass (kg)
formulas.use: Heat carried by free electrons in metals.

formulas.name: Conductivity of a metal
formulas.vars: \sigma = conductivity (S/m); n = electron concentration (m⁻³); |e| = electron charge magnitude (C); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (m²/V·s)
formulas.use: Metals: conduction by electrons only.

formulas.name: Conductivity of a semiconductor
formulas.vars: n, p = electron, hole concentration (m⁻³); |e| = electron charge magnitude (C); \(\mu_{e}\), \(\mu_{h}\) = electron, hole mobility (m²/V·s)
formulas.use: Intrinsic semiconductors (n = p) and general case.

formulas.name: n-type semiconductor
formulas.vars: n = electron concentration (m⁻³); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (m²/V·s)
formulas.use: Donor-doped, n ≫ p.

formulas.name: p-type semiconductor
formulas.vars: p = hole concentration (m⁻³); \(\mu_{h}\) = hole mobility (m²/V·s)
formulas.use: Acceptor-doped, p ≫ n.

formulas.name: Parallel-plate capacitance with dielectric
formulas.vars: C = capacitance (F); \(\varepsilon_{r}\) = relative permittivity; \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m; A = plate area (m²); L = plate separation (m)
formulas.use: Capacitor with a dielectric between plates.

formulas.name: Charge on a capacitor
formulas.vars: Q = charge (C); C = capacitance (F); V = voltage (V)
formulas.use: Charge stored at a given voltage.

formulas.name: Dipole moment
formulas.vars: \mu = dipole moment (C·m); q = charge magnitude (C); r = separation (m)
formulas.use: Polarisation of a charge pair.

formulas.name: Refractive index
formulas.vars: n = refractive index; c = speed of light in vacuum (m/s); v = speed of light in medium (m/s)
formulas.use: Light slows in a medium.

formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.vars: \(n_{1}\), \(n_{2}\) = indices of first and second media; \(\theta_{i}\) = incidence angle; \(\theta_{r}\) = refraction angle
formulas.use: Refraction at an interface; for glass to air \(n_{2}\) = 1, so sinθ_r = \(n_{1}\) sinθ_i.

topics.topic: Total internal reflection and optical fibres

formulas.name: Critical angle
formulas.vars: \(\theta_{c}\) = critical angle; \(n_{1}\) = denser medium index (core); \(n_{2}\) = less dense medium index (cladding)
formulas.use: Total internal reflection for incidence angle > θ_c, requires \(n_{1}\) > \(n_{2}\).

formulas.name: Fibre index contrast
formulas.vars: \(n_{1}\) = core index; \(n_{2}\) = cladding index
formulas.use: Typical small core-cladding index difference in optical fibres.

topics.topic: Diffusion flux and Fick's first law (steady state)

formulas.name: Fick's first law
formulas.vars: J = diffusion flux (mol/(m²·s) or kg/(m²·s)); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); C = concentration (mol/m³); x = position (m)
formulas.use: Steady-state diffusion, where the flux is constant in time. The minus sign means flow runs down the concentration gradient.

formulas.name: Steady-state flux across a thin barrier (linear profile)
formulas.vars: \(C_{1}\), \(C_{2}\) = concentrations at the two faces (mol/m³); \(x_{2}\) - \(x_{1}\) = barrier thickness (m); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s)
formulas.use: Steady state with a linear concentration profile, e.g. a membrane or glove. Replaces dC/dx by ΔC/Δx.

formulas.name: Definition of diffusion flux
formulas.vars: J = flux (kg/(m²·s) or atoms/(m²·s)); M = mass or moles transferred (kg or mol); A = cross-sectional area (m²); t = time (s)
formulas.use: Use to convert between flux and mass transferred, given area and time.

topics.topic: Diffusion in polymers and membrane permeability

formulas.name: Permeation flux through a polymer membrane
formulas.vars: J = flux (cm³ STP/(cm²·s)); \(P_{M}\) = permeability coefficient (cm³ STP·cm/(cm²·s·Pa)); ΔP = pressure difference across the membrane (Pa); Δx = membrane thickness (cm)
formulas.use: Gas permeation through a polymer membrane. It is Fick's first law with pressure in place of concentration.

formulas.name: Arrhenius equation for the diffusion coefficient
formulas.vars: D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); \(D_{0}\) = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy for diffusion (J/mol); R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T = absolute temperature (K)
formulas.use: Find D at a given temperature. T must be in kelvin. D rises sharply with T.

formulas.name: Pre-exponential factor from a known D
formulas.vars: \(D_{1}\) = known diffusion coefficient at \(T_{1}\) (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy (J/mol); R = gas constant (J/(mol·K)); \(T_{1}\) = temperature (K)
formulas.use: Find \(D_{0}\) from one measured D, then use it to find D at another temperature.

formulas.name: Ratio of D at two temperatures
formulas.vars: \(D_{1}\), \(D_{2}\) = diffusion coefficients at \(T_{1}\), \(T_{2}\) (m²/s); \(T_{1}\), \(T_{2}\) = absolute temperatures (K)
formulas.use: Find \(D_{2}\) or \(Q_{d}\) from two data points without needing \(D_{0}\). Follows from the Arrhenius equation, and the slope of ln D against 1/T is -\(Q_{d}\)/R.

topics.topic: Non-steady-state diffusion and Fick's second law

formulas.name: Solution for a semi-infinite solid with constant surface concentration
formulas.vars: C(x,t) = concentration at depth x and time t (kg/m³ or wt%); \(C_{s}\) = constant surface concentration; \(C_{0}\) = initial uniform concentration; x = distance from surface (m); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); t = time (s)
formulas.use: Non-steady-state diffusion into a semi-infinite solid, e.g. carburising. Look up erf values in a table.

formulas.name: Fick's second law
formulas.vars: C = concentration (mol/m³ or kg/m³); t = time (s); x = position (m); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s)
formulas.use: Non-steady-state diffusion, where the concentration changes with time. Assumes D is constant.

formulas.name: Error function definition
formulas.vars: z = argument (dimensionless); y = dummy integration variable
formulas.use: Defines erf used in the solution of Fick's second law. erf(0)=0 and erf(∞)=1.

formulas.name: Theoretical Young's modulus from bond stiffness
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium atomic separation (m)
formulas.use: Estimate the modulus from the stiffness of a single interatomic bond.

formulas.name: Bond stiffness at equilibrium from force or energy
formulas.vars: \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); F = interatomic force (N); U = bond energy (J); r = separation (m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium separation (m)
formulas.use: Find the stiffness from the slope of the F–r curve or the curvature of the U–r curve at \(r_{0}\).

formulas.name: Force from bond energy
formulas.vars: F = force (N); U = bond energy (J); r = separation (m)
formulas.use: Obtain the force from the energy curve (sign convention as in the lecture).

formulas.name: Linear bond force for small displacement
formulas.vars: F = force (N); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); r = separation (m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium separation (m)
formulas.use: Valid only for small displacements about \(r_{0}\).

formulas.name: Bond number density per unit area
formulas.vars: N = bonds per unit area (\(m^{-2}\)); \(r_{0}\) = bond spacing (m)
formulas.use: Used to derive E from the stress carried by N bonds.

formulas.name: Stress carried by N stretched bonds
formulas.latex: \sigma = N S_0 (r - r_0) = N S_0 r_0 \varepsilon = \frac{S_0}{r_0}\varepsilon
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); N = bonds per unit area (\(m^{-2}\)); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); \varepsilon = strain; \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium spacing (m)

formulas.name: Strain of a bond
formulas.vars: \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless); r = stretched bond length (m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium length (m)
formulas.use: Relates bond extension to strain.

formulas.name: Young's modulus
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \sigma = normal stress (Pa); \varepsilon = linear strain (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Slope of the linear elastic region of the stress–strain curve.

formulas.name: Engineering stress
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); F = applied force (N); \(A_{0}\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Tensile or compressive loading.

formulas.name: Engineering strain
formulas.vars: \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{0}\) = original length (m)
formulas.use: Tensile or compressive loading.

formulas.name: Shear modulus
formulas.vars: G = shear modulus (Pa); \tau = shear stress (Pa); \gamma = shear strain (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Elastic response to shear.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: Response to hydrostatic pressure; the minus sign makes K positive as volume decreases.

topics.topic: Poisson's ratio and relations between moduli

formulas.name: Poisson's ratio
formulas.vars: \nu = Poisson's ratio (dimensionless); \(\varepsilon_{x}\) = lateral strain; \(\varepsilon_{z}\) = axial strain
formulas.use: Lateral contraction under axial tension.

formulas.name: Shear modulus from E and \nu
formulas.vars: G = shear modulus (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus from E and \nu
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus from G and \nu
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); G = shear modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Axial and lateral strain definitions
formulas.vars: \Delta l = change in length (m); \(l_{0}\) = original length (m); \Delta w = change in width (m); \(w_{0}\) = original width (m)
formulas.use: Used to compute \nu from measurements.

formulas.name: Longitudinal composite modulus (upper bound, Voigt)
formulas.latex: E_{cl} = E_m V_m + E_f V_f = E_m(1-V_f) + E_f V_f
formulas.vars: \(E_{cl}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\), \(E_{f}\) = matrix and fibre moduli (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Loading parallel to the fibres (equal strain in both phases); upper bound on the modulus.

formulas.name: Composite stress rule of mixtures
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{c}\), \(\sigma_{m}\), \(\sigma_{f}\) = composite, matrix and fibre stresses (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Isostrain loading, from force balance.

formulas.name: Load balance
formulas.latex: F_c = F_m + F_f \;\Rightarrow\; \sigma_c A_c = \sigma_m A_m + \sigma_f A_f
formulas.vars: F = load (N); \sigma = stress (Pa); A = cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); subscripts c, m, f = composite, matrix, fibre
formulas.use: Starting point for isostrain derivations.

formulas.name: Volume fraction from area fraction
formulas.vars: V = volume fraction; A = cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Phases of equal length.

formulas.name: Transverse composite modulus (lower bound, Reuss)
formulas.vars: \(E_{ct}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\), \(E_{f}\) = matrix and fibre moduli (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Loading perpendicular to the layers or fibres (equal stress in both phases); lower bound on the modulus.

formulas.name: Composite strain rule of mixtures
formulas.vars: \(\varepsilon_{c}\), \(\varepsilon_{m}\), \(\varepsilon_{f}\) = composite, matrix and fibre strains; \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Isostress loading.

formulas.name: Stress and strain in each layer
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); F = force (N); A = area (\(m^{2}\)); E = layer modulus (Pa); \delta = layer deformation (m); t = layer thickness (m)
formulas.use: Layered series model where each layer carries the same stress.

formulas.name: Yield condition on a slip plane
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{R}\) = resolved shear stress (Pa); \(\tau_{crss}\) = critical resolved shear stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Slip starts, and the crystal yields, when the resolved shear stress on a slip system reaches \(\tau_{crss}\).

formulas.name: Resolved shear stress on the slip plane
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{R}\) = resolved shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = shear force along the slip direction (N); \(A_{s}\) = area of the slip plane (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Shear stress that drives slip. Under uniaxial load F on area A, \(F_{s}\) = F\cos\lambda and \(A_{s}\) = A/\cos\phi.

formulas.name: Plane of maximum shear stress
formulas.vars: \theta = angle between the maximum shear plane and the applied load (degrees)
formulas.use: Under uniaxial loading, shear stress is greatest on planes at 45° to the load axis.

formulas.name: Hall-Petch relation
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{i}\) = friction stress opposing dislocation motion (Pa); k = grain-boundary strengthening constant (Pa \(m^{1/2}\)); D = average grain diameter (m)
formulas.use: Smaller grains give a higher yield stress, because grain boundaries block dislocations.

formulas.name: Number of dislocations in a pile-up
formulas.vars: n = number of dislocations (dimensionless); \alpha = constant (dimensionless); \tau = shear stress (Pa); d = grain size (m); G = shear modulus term as defined in the lecture; b = Burgers vector magnitude (m)
formulas.use: Estimates the pile-up at a grain boundary. A larger grain gives a longer pile-up and a larger stress concentration, which explains Hall-Petch.

topics.topic: True and engineering stress and strain

formulas.name: Engineering stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{eng}\) = engineering stress (Pa); F = force (N); \(A_{0}\) = initial cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Standard tensile test stress, based on the original area.

formulas.name: True stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{true}\) = true stress (Pa); F = force (N); \(A_{i}\) = instantaneous cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Use when the area changes appreciably, e.g. during necking.

formulas.name: Engineering strain
formulas.vars: \(\varepsilon_{eng}\) = engineering strain (dimensionless); \Delta l = change in length (m); \(l_{0}\) = original length (m); \(l_{i}\) = instantaneous length (m)
formulas.use: Strain relative to the original length.

formulas.name: True strain
formulas.vars: \(\varepsilon_{true}\) = true strain (dimensionless); \(l_{i}\) = instantaneous length (m); \(l_{0}\) = original length (m)
formulas.use: Incremental strain summed over the deformation, d\varepsilon = dl/l. Use at large strains.

formulas.name: Percent elongation
formulas.vars: \(l_{f}\) = gauge length at fracture (m); \(l_{0}\) = original gauge length (m)
formulas.use: Measures ductility from the tensile test, based on the change in length.

formulas.name: Percent reduction in area
formulas.vars: \(A_{0}\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_{f}\) = cross-sectional area at fracture (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Measures ductility from the tensile test, based on the change in area.

formulas.name: Normal stress on an inclined plane (uniaxial loading)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{n}\) = normal stress on plane (Pa); F = axial force (N); A = cross-sectional area normal to F (\(m^{2}\)); \(\sigma_{x}\) = F/A = axial stress (Pa); \theta = angle between plane normal and load axis (rad or °)
formulas.use: Uniaxial tension or compression; resolve the stress onto a plane at angle θ

formulas.name: Shear stress on an inclined plane (uniaxial loading)
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{s}\) = shear stress on plane (Pa); \(\sigma_{x}\) = F/A (Pa); \theta = plane angle (rad or °)
formulas.use: Maximum magnitude σ_x/2 at θ=45°; sign shows direction only

formulas.name: Uniaxial stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{0}\) = normal stress (Pa); F = axial force (N); \(A_{cs}\) = cross-sectional area normal to load (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Stress on the section normal to the load

formulas.name: Inclined section area
formulas.vars: A' = inclined plane area (\(m^{2}\)); A = normal cross-section area (\(m^{2}\)); \theta = inclination angle
formulas.use: Converts forces on the inclined plane into stresses

formulas.name: Force components on inclined plane
formulas.vars: \(F_{n}\) = normal force (N); \(F_{s}\) = shear (tangential) force (N); F = applied force (N); \theta = inclination angle
formulas.use: From equilibrium \sum \mathbf{F}=0 of the cut body

formulas.name: Tresca yield condition
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\),\(\sigma_{3}\) = principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = uniaxial yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield occurs when the largest principal stress difference reaches σ_Y

formulas.name: Maximum shear stress and shear yield stress (Tresca)
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{max}\) = max shear stress (Pa); \(\tau_{Y}\) = shear stress at yield (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = tensile yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield when τ_max = τ_Y; uniaxial tension gives τ_max = σ_1/2

formulas.name: 2D Tresca hexagon sides
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\) = in-plane principal stresses (Pa), \(\sigma_{3}\)=0; \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Plane stress yield locus: same-sign quadrants vs opposite-sign quadrants

formulas.name: Von Mises yield condition
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\),\(\sigma_{3}\) = principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield strength (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield when equivalent stress reaches σ_Y; ductile metals

formulas.name: Von Mises equivalent stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{e}\) = equivalent stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{i}\) = principal stresses (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield when \(\sigma_{e}\)=\(\sigma_{Y}\)

formulas.name: Von Mises in plane stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\) = in-plane principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Case \(\sigma_{3}\)=0

formulas.name: Principal stresses in torsion of a solid shaft
formulas.vars: T = torque (N·m); r = shaft radius (m); \(\sigma_{i}\) = principal stresses (Pa)
formulas.use: Surface of a solid circular shaft in pure torsion; surface shear stress \tau=2T/(\pi \(r^{3}\))

formulas.name: Tresca yield torque, solid shaft
formulas.vars: \(T_{max}\) = yield torque (N·m); r = radius (m); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Torsional yield by Tresca

formulas.name: Von Mises yield torque, solid shaft
formulas.vars: \(T_{max}\) = yield torque (N·m); r = radius (m); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Torsional yield by von Mises

formulas.name: Ratio of von Mises to Tresca yield torque
formulas.vars: \(T_{vM}\), \(T_{Tresca}\) = yield torques (N·m)
formulas.use: Pure shear: von Mises predicts ~15% higher torque than Tresca

formulas.name: Griffith fracture stress (internal crack of length 2c)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{f}\) = fracture stress (Pa); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy per unit area (J/\(m^{2}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa); c = half-length of internal crack (m)
formulas.use: Refined Griffith result for brittle materials. The simpler energy balance below gives a factor 4 instead of 2 in the numerator (\sqrt{4\gamma_s E/\pi c}); quote the version your notes specify.

formulas.name: Energy balance for crack growth (condition for fracture)
formulas.vars: U = total energy (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); \sigma = applied stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy per unit area (J/\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Crack becomes unstable when the elastic energy released equals the surface energy needed (dU/dc = 0).

formulas.name: Critical crack length
formulas.vars: 2c = critical crack length (m); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy (J/\(m^{2}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \sigma = applied stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Crack length above which the crack grows at stress \sigma (from the simple energy balance).

formulas.name: Elastic energy released by crack
formulas.vars: \(U_{E}\) = elastic energy released (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); \sigma = stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Building block of the Griffith energy balance.

formulas.name: Surface energy of crack
formulas.vars: \(U_{s}\) = surface energy (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); \(\gamma_{s}\) = surface energy per unit area (J/\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Energy needed to create the two crack faces (area 2·2c·t).

topics.topic: Stress intensity factor and fracture toughness

formulas.name: Stress intensity factor
formulas.vars: K = stress intensity factor (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); \sigma = applied stress (MPa); a = crack length (m)
formulas.use: Gives the crack-tip loading for a crack of length a under applied stress.

formulas.name: Fracture criterion
formulas.vars: K = applied stress intensity factor (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); \(K_{c}\) = fracture toughness (MPa \(m^{1/2}\))
formulas.use: Fracture occurs when K reaches \(K_{c}\); so \(\sigma_{f}\)=\(K_{c}\)/\sqrt{\pi a}.

formulas.name: Hall-Petch equation (yield strength vs grain size)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield strength (Pa); \(\sigma_{0}\) = friction stress opposing dislocation motion (Pa); \(k_{y}\) = strengthening coefficient (Pa·\(m^{1/2}\)); d = grain size (m)
formulas.use: Yield strength increases as grain size decreases; plot \(\sigma_{Y}\) against \(d^{-1/2}\) to get a straight line.

formulas.name: Number of dislocations in a pile-up
formulas.vars: n = number of dislocations (dimensionless); \alpha = constant (dimensionless); \tau = shear stress (Pa); d = grain size (m); G = shear modulus (Pa) (slide labels it as energy per dislocation); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m)
formulas.use: Larger grains give longer pile-ups and larger stress concentration at the grain boundary. This is the basis of the Hall-Petch derivation.

formulas.name: Yield (critical) shear stress for dislocation bowing between precipitates
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{Y}\) = critical resolved shear (yield) stress (Pa); T = dislocation line tension (N); b = Burgers vector magnitude (m); L = precipitate spacing (m)
formulas.use: Dislocations bow between precipitates. Closer spacing gives higher strength.

formulas.name: Critical bowing force balance
formulas.vars: \tau = applied shear stress (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m); L = precipitate spacing (m); T = line tension (N)
formulas.use: Force balance at the critical configuration, where the bowed dislocation is a semicircle. Rearranging gives \(\tau_{Y}\).

formulas.name: Resistive force per unit dislocation length
formulas.vars: \(f_{0}\) = resistive force per unit length (N/m); \tau = applied shear stress (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m); T = line tension (N); L = precipitate spacing (m)
formulas.use: Force per unit length that the precipitates exert on the dislocation.

formulas.name: Percent cold work
formulas.vars: \%CW = percent cold work (%); \(A_{0}\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_{d}\) = cross-sectional area after deformation (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Measures the degree of plastic deformation. Higher %CW gives higher strength and lower ductility.

formulas.name: Homologous temperature
formulas.vars: \(T_{h}\) = homologous temperature (dimensionless); T = absolute operating temperature (K); \(T_{m}\) = absolute melting temperature (K)
formulas.use: Compare operating temperature to melting point, with both in kelvin, e.g. for aircraft engine blades.

formulas.name: Creep threshold condition
formulas.vars: T = absolute operating temperature (K); \(T_{m}\) = absolute melting temperature (K); \(T_{\text{creep}}\) = threshold temperature for significant creep (K)
formulas.use: Creep is significant above about 0.4 \(T_{m}\), so check this first. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

formulas.name: Celsius to kelvin conversion
formulas.vars: T = temperature (K or °C)
formulas.use: Convert before calculating homologous temperature.

formulas.name: Relaxation modulus
formulas.vars: \(E_{r}\)(t) = relaxation modulus (Pa); \sigma(t) = stress at time t (Pa); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = constant applied strain (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Stress relaxation test: strain held constant while the stress decays over time.

formulas.name: Stress ratio
formulas.vars: R = stress ratio (dimensionless); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Characterises a loading cycle. R = -1 is fully reversed tension-compression. (Take care: the notes' p.23 version with max/min is an error.)

formulas.name: Stress range
formulas.vars: \Delta\sigma = stress range (MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{a}\) = stress amplitude (MPa)
formulas.use: Use for the stress range in a cycle; it drives \Delta K in crack growth.

formulas.name: Stress amplitude
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{a}\) = stress amplitude (MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{r}\) = stress range (MPa)
formulas.use: Alternating stress about the mean; used for S-N data.

formulas.name: Mean stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{m}\) = mean stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Midpoint of the stress cycle.

formulas.name: Fully reversed cycle
formulas.vars: R = stress ratio (dimensionless); \(\sigma_{m}\) = mean stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Symmetric tension-compression cycle.

formulas.name: Paris law
formulas.vars: da/dN = crack growth per cycle (m/cycle); \Delta K = stress intensity range (MPa√m); A = material constant (the notes' form omits it); m = material exponent (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Stable (mid-range) fatigue crack growth. Integrate to get the number of cycles to failure.

formulas.name: Stress intensity range
formulas.vars: \Delta K = stress intensity range (MPa√m); \Delta\sigma = stress range (MPa); a = crack length (m)
formulas.use: Shows that growth accelerates as the crack lengthens. Include the geometry factor Y in full form: \Delta K = Y\Delta\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}.

formulas.name: Low cycle fatigue condition
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Plastic deformation occurs each cycle, giving short life.

formulas.name: High cycle fatigue condition
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (MPa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Stresses remain elastic, giving long life (many cycles).

formulas.name: Energy dissipated per cycle
formulas.vars: \(W_{d}\) = energy dissipated per cycle (J/\(m^{3}\)); \sigma = stress (Pa); \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Equals the area of the stress-strain hysteresis loop.

formulas.name: Miner's cumulative damage criterion
formulas.vars: \(n_{i}\) = cycles applied at stress level i (dimensionless); \(N_{f,i}\) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Failure under variable-amplitude loading when the sum reaches 1.

formulas.name: Predicted life from damage per block
formulas.vars: T = expected life (weeks); (\sum \(n_{i}\)/\(N_{f,i}\))_{per week} = damage fraction per week (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Life in repeated load blocks (here weeks) from the damage accumulated per block.

topics.topic: Sources and abundance of raw materials

formulas.name: Carat to gram conversion
formulas.vars: \(m_{g}\) = mass (g); \(m_{ct}\) = mass (carats, ct)
formulas.use: Converting gem mass from carats to grams (1 ct = 0.2 g).

formulas.name: Relative cost of a material
formulas.vars: \bar{c} = relative cost (dimensionless); (\$/kg) = cost per kilogram of the material (\$/kg); (\$/kg)_{ref material} = cost per kilogram of the reference material (\$/kg)
formulas.use: Comparing material costs against a reference material (commonly mild/reinforcing steel) on a per-mass basis.

formulas.name: Tip deflection of square-section cantilever under end load
formulas.vars: \delta = tip deflection (m); l = beam length (m); F = end load (N); E = Young's modulus (Pa); t = side of square cross-section (m)
formulas.use: Stiffness constraint for a cantilever with square section; rearrange to \(t^{4}\) = 4l^3F/(E\delta).

formulas.name: Mass of beam (objective function)
formulas.vars: M = mass (kg); l = length (m); t = side of square section (m); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: Quantity to minimise; eliminate free variable t using the stiffness constraint.

formulas.name: Minimum mass for a given stiffness (t eliminated)
formulas.vars: M = beam mass (kg); l = length (m); F = load (N); \delta = allowable deflection (m); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Shows the first bracket is geometry/load and the second is the material; minimise M by minimising \(\rho^{2}\)/E.

formulas.name: Elimination of t (combined constraint)
formulas.vars: t = side (m); l = length (m); F = load (N); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \delta = deflection (m); M = mass (kg); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: Intermediate step: equate \(t^{4}\) from stiffness with (\(t^{2}\))^2 from mass, \(t^{2}\) = M/(l\rho).

topics.topic: Material performance index and Ashby ranking

formulas.name: Stiffness-limited light beam index
formulas.vars: \rho = density (Mg/\(m^{3}\) or kg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (GPa or Pa)
formulas.use: Rank materials for the lightest stiff beam of given deflection; lower \(\rho^{2}\)/E is better. Used on Ashby charts.

formulas.name: Price of beam for given stiffness
formulas.vars: Price = cost of component; l = length (m); F = load (N); \delta = allowable deflection (m); \bar{p} = relative price per kg; \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Minimising cost rather than mass: M multiplied by price per kg.

formulas.name: Cost-weighted performance index
formulas.vars: C = relative cost index; \(\rho^{2}\)/E = mass index; \bar{p} = relative price per unit mass (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Rank materials for the cheapest stiff beam; lower C is better.

formulas.name: Relative cost of material
formulas.vars: \bar{p} = relative cost (dimensionless); \$/kg = price per kg; ref = rolled A36 plain carbon steel
formulas.use: Normalise material prices to the reference steel.
